Congenital Hepatic Disease: Portosystemic
Vascular Shunts, Microvascular Dysplasia,
and Glycogen Storage Disease
The most common congenital cause of hepatic‐induced
hypoglycemia is portosytemic vascular anomalies
(PSVA). PSVA is really an “umbrella term” which includes
dogs with extrahepatic shunting (PSVA‐E) or intrahe­
patic shunting (PSVA‐I). In addition, many small‐breed
dogs with PSVA have concurrent microvascular dyspla­
sia (MVD). The prevalence of hypoglycemia in dogs with
PSVA varies from 5% to 10%. The hypoglycemia associ­
ated with PSVA is presumably caused by chronic hepatic
hypoperfusion which leads to insufficient glycogen
stores and inadequate hepatocellular function to support
gluconeogenesis.
Signalment

There is no gender predilection while the average age at
presentation is 1.5 years for PSVA‐E and 1.0 year for
PSVA‐I, although dogs can be as young as 1 month or as
old as 12 years. Significant difference in body weight
between PSVA‐E and PSVA‐I correlates with the long‐
recognized propensity for PSVA‐E to occur in small‐
breed dogs and PSVA‐I to occur in large‐breed dogs.
Breed prevalence for PSVA‐E implicates high risk in the
Yorkshire terrier and several other small breeds includ­
ing shih tzu, Maltese, pug, miniature schnauzer, West
Highland white terriers, bichon frise, miniature and toy
poodles, Havanese, cairn terriers, silky terriers, and mix­
tures of these breeds. The most prevalent breed with
PSVA‐I is the Labrador retriever, followed by mixed‐
breed dogs and Siberian huskies.
History

Historical features of PSVA include pediatric hypoglyce­
mia, small body stature (runt of the litter), episodic inap­
petence, vomiting, salivation, polyuria and polydipsia,
and signs associated with ammonium biurate urolithiasis
(hematuria, stranguria, and pollakiuria). Neurobehavioral
signs of hepatic encephalopathy may be unapparent or
may include ataxia, obsessive circling, and head pressing.
Laboratory Findings

In a cohort of 610 dogs with PSVA at Cornell University,
no dog with a portosystemic shunt was undetected when

tested with paired serum bile acids. Therefore, the most
reliable tests for detection of a portosystemic shunt are
paired fasting and postprandial bile acid (100% detec­
tion), 80% demonstrate low protein C activity (this test
reflects the severity of shunting), >60% show microcyto­
sis, low total protein and cholesterol, and a urine specific
gravity <1.025, and biurate crystalluria occurs in approx­
imately 33% and 22% of PSVA‐E and PSVA‐I respec­
tively. It is important to remember that usually, biopsy
alone cannot differentiate PSVA and MVD and that
MVD alone is not associated with signs of illness (e.g.,
clinical hypoglycemia).
Other Diagnostics

Imaging studies are needed to differentiate PSVA‐E from
PSVA‐I and MVD and are important for surgical and
medical treatments. These include transsplenic micro­
bubble studies, transsplenic and colorectal technetium‐
99m scintigraphy. However, the gold standard of imaging
studies is contrast multisector CT imaging and three‐
dimensional image reconstruction, which provides
­optimal comprehensive information for diagnosis and
surgical planning for PSVA.
Treatment

It is inarguable that optimal therapy for symptomatic
PSVA is shunt attenuation. However, it is important to
remember that all symptomatic PSVA dogs will benefit
from medical management, yet all dogs do not require all
forms of therapy. For example, a wide spectrum of PSVA
patients at Cornell University have been managed medi­
cally with survival outcome and survival duration no dif­
ferent than for shunt ligation.
Glycogen Storage Diseases
Glycogen storage diseases (GSD) are rare congenital
hepatic disorders in which hypoglycemia results from
the inability to convert glycogen to glucose because of
the absolute or relative deficiency of the enzymes neces­
sary for the breakdown of glycogen stores in the liver.
Type III GSD (Cori disease), a deficiency of amylo‐1,6‐
glucosidase, was documented in puppies with massive
hepatomegaly caused by glycogen accumulation, failure
to thrive, and muscle weakness. Type I GSD (von Gierke
disease) has been documented in the Maltese breed.
This uncommon disorder is a deficiency of glucose‐6‐
phosphatase caused by a defect in the glucose‐6‐phos­
phatase gene. Affected puppies develop progressive
hepatomegaly characterized by diffuse hepatocellular
vacuolization, tremors, weakness, and neurologic signs
when hypoglycemic. Biochemical abnormalities include
fasting hypoglycemia, hypercholesterolemia, hypertri­
glyceridemia, and elevated uric acid levels. Confirmatory

105

VetBooks.ir

106

Section 2 Endocrine Disease

tests include histologic evaluation of liver biopsies and
specific enzyme assays that are rarely performed in vet­
erinary medicine. And lastly, GSD type IV has been doc­
umented in a family of Norwegian forest cats. It leads to
death as a result of perinatal hypoglycemic collapse or
late juvenile‐onset neuromuscular degeneration.
Idiopathic Causes of Liver‐Associated
Hypoglycemia in Young Animals: Neonatal
and Juvenile Hypoglycemia
Neonatal Hypoglycemia

The blood glucose concentration in the healthy neonate
falls during the first few hours after birth because of the
loss of continuous transplacental infusion of glucose.
Thereafter, the neonate is dependent on glycogenolysis
and gluconeogenesis to maintain euglycemia between
feedings. Limited glycogen stores, small muscle mass,
and lack of adipose tissue as alternative energy sources
place the neonate at risk for hypoglycemia. That said, the
ill neonate should always be evaluated for hypoglycemia,
especially if sepsis, toxic milk syndrome, or starvation is
suspected or hypothermia is noted. Orally administered
glucose or frequent bottle feeding can help correct or
prevent hypoglycemia.
Juvenile Hypoglycemia

Hypoglycemia of toy and miniature breed dogs younger
than 6 months of age is common. Deficiency of gluco­
neogenic precursors such as the amino acid alanine or an
age‐related transient malfunction or deficiency of
enzymes responsible for gluconeogenesis is implicated
in this syndrome. Insufficient food supply of any cause
such as starvation or gastrointestinal disturbances may
cause hypoglycemia within 24 hours of fasting. In addi­
tion, underlying conditions such as PSVA that cause ano­
rexia or impaired liver function may contribute to the
precipitation of this syndrome. Many of these puppies
have a history of being recently purchased along with a
recent change in environment and diet. Presenting signs
may include weakness, depression, vomiting and diar­
rhea with or without intestinal parasites, ataxia, stupor,
and seizures. Similar forms of juvenile hypoglycemia
have not been well documented in kittens.
Treatment and Prognosis

Intravenous administration of a 20% or 50% dextrose
solution (0.8 mL to 0.2 mL per 100 g body weight respec­
tively) is indicated if there are neurologic signs. If the pup
can take the glucose solution orally, this is administered
at regular intervals until appetite returns. The small
amounts of food are given at two‐hour intervals. If tube
feeding is needed, oral rehydration is guided by electro­
lyte measurements. Clinical improvement occurs rapidly

following glucose administration. The prognosis is good
if hypoglycemia is corrected before brain damage occurs.
The risk of developing hypoglycemia decreases with
increasing age and body weight.
Nonislet Cell Tumor‐Induced Hypoglycemia
Hypoglycemia can be a manifestation of neoplastic dis­
ease. Tumors related to the occurrence of hypoglycemia
can, as a general rule, be divided into three groups. First,
tumors can produce excess insulin such as pancre­
atic insulinomas or ectopic insulin‐producing tumors.
Second, hypoglycemia can be caused by tumor‐related
factors such as destruction of the liver by massive tumor
infiltration. And lastly, there is now convincing evidence
that secretion of insulin‐like growth factor (IGF)‐2 and
incompletely processed IGFs (e.g., pro‐IGF‐2 or “big”‐
IGF‐2) causes hypoglycemia in humans. This mecha­
nism has also been documented in a few cases of
hypoglycemia in dogs. Nonislet cell tumor‐induced
hypoglycemia (NICTH) can arise in virtually every
benign and malignant tumor. However, it mainly occurs
in patients with solid tumors of mesenchymal (e.g., leio­
myosarcoma, fibrosarcoma) and epithelial origin (e.g.,
hepatoma, hepatocellular carcinoma), but rarely in
patients with tumors of hematopoietic or neuroendo­
crine origin. The most frequent nonpancreatic tumors
associated with hypoglycemia are leiomyoma, leiomyo­
sarcoma, hepatoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, and
tumors with extensive hepatic metastasis.
Pathophysiology

Understanding the cause of hypoglycemia with NICTH
involves a brief review of the IGF system. The IGF sys­
tem is composed of two IGF ligands (IGF‐1 and IGF‐2)
and two IGF receptors: the IGF‐1 receptor (IGF1R)
and IGF‐2 receptor (IGF2R). Both IGF‐1 and IGF‐2 are
structurally and functionally related to insulin but the
glucose‐lowering effect of IGFs is 10 times lower than
that of insulin, although in healthy human subjects the
serum concentration of IGFs is about 1000 times
higher than insulin. The crucial event in the develop­
ment of NICTH seems to be overexpression of the
IGF‐2 gene by the tumor. NICTH is characterized by
recurrent fasting hypoglycemia and is associated with
the secretion of precursors of IGF‐2 (“big”‐IGF‐2) by
the tumor.
Diagnosis

Dogs with hypoglycemia caused by NICTH are usually
brought to the veterinarian with clinical signs of hypo­
glycemia, or hypoglycemia may be noted on a biochemi­
cal profile in an asymptomatic patient during a wellness
exam. The diagnosis of a nonislet cell tumor requires a

VetBooks.ir

13 Hypoglycemia in Patients without Diabetes Mellitus

thorough physical examination, thoracic and abdominal
radiographs, abdominal ultrasonography, and histo­
pathologic examination of the tumor, which is often
located in the abdominal cavity.
Treatment

The long‐term therapeutic strategies in NICTH involve
complete removal of the tumor or reduction of the
tumor mass. In order to treat hypoglycemia, a short‐
term beneficial effect is best achieved with (continu­
ous) parenteral administration of glucose and dietary
guidelines. Glucocorticoids, at least in humans, seem
to be the most effective form of medical therapy in
terms of long‐term relief from hypoglycemia by stimu­
lating glyconeogenesis and suppressing, although not
in all cases, the production of “big”‐IGF‐2. In addition,
moderate to high doses of glucocorticoids may cause
shrinkage of the tumor.
Hypoadrenocorticism
Incidence

Hypoadrenocorticism should always be on the rule‐out
list for hypoglycemia. Of 506 dogs diagnosed with
hypoadrenocorticism at UC Davis Veterinary Medical
Teaching Hospital, 116 (25%) were hypoglycemic at the
time of diagnosis. Interestingly, however, clinical signs
attributable to hypoglycemia appear to be uncommon.
In this cohort of cases, hypoglycemic seizures and other
clinical signs that may have been caused by hypoglyce­
mia, such as ataxia and disorientation, were observed in
only 30 dogs (6%).
Pathophysiology and Treatment

With glucocorticoid deficiency, glucose production by
the liver (i.e., gluconeogenesis) is decreased and the sen­
sitivity of insulin receptors in peripheral tissues is
increased. In tandem, these factors predispose the ani­
mal with adrenal insufficiency to hypoglycemia. That
said, the blood glucose concentration should always be
measured in a dog suspected or known to have hypoad­
renocorticism. A 2.5–5% dextrose infusion, usually
added to lactated Ringer’s or normal saline solution,
should be administered as soon as hypoglycemia is docu­
mented in addition to glucocorticoid replacement ther­
apy. If the pretreatment serum sodium and potassium
concentrations are normal, mineralocorticoid replace­
ment is not necessary over the short term, and may never
be indicated in some dogs with adrenal insufficiency
(atypical hypoadrenocorticism). These dogs, despite low
serum aldosterone concentrations, are able to maintain
normal serum sodium and potassium levels for reasons
that are unclear.

Critical Illness and Hypoglycemia: Renal
Failure, Acquired Liver Disease, Sepsis,
and Virulent Babesiosis
Renal Failure

Renal failure is associated with hypoglycemia in critically
ill diabetic and nondiabetic human patients, but the
impact of renal failure on the blood glucose concentra­
tion is unpredictable in dogs and cats. In most cases, the
blood glucose concentration is normal. However, hyper­
glycemia may develop as a result of uremic‐induced car­
bohydrate intolerance and insulin resistance in a dog or
cat with impaired insulin secretion; this phenomenon
has been referred to as “pseudodiabetes.” Alternatively,
renal failure may induce hypoglycemia.
Several mechanisms for the development of hypoglyce­
mia during renal insufficiency have been proposed. These
include reduced renal gluconeogenesis and decreased
caloric intake related to inappetence. Normally, renal glu­
coneogenesis may supply as much as 45% of new glucose
during prolonged starvation. Additional defects in glu­
cose homeostasis occur in renal insufficiency, including
an increased insulin half‐life related to decreased renal
degradation or excretion of insulin, impaired hepatic gly­
cogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, inadequate glucose
counterregulatory responses, or a combination of these
factors. It should be emphasized that hypoglycemia is
rarely the cause of death in the critically ill patient with
renal failure and is considered more a marker for multi­
system failure than a cause of mortality.
Acquired Hepatic Dysfunction

Hypoglycemia has been associated with a wide spectrum
of liver diseases in people. These disorders include eve­
rything from type 1 glycogen storage disease, cirrhosis,
viral hepatitis, procainamide‐induced hepatitis, chole­
cystitis, and metastatic infiltration to fulminant liver fail­
ure after cardiac arrest. In dogs and cats, hypoglycemia
often results from severe destruction of the liver from
bacterial infection, hepatotoxins, neoplasia, and chronic
fibrosis/cirrhosis with the development of acquired por­
tosystemic shunts. The underlying cause of hypoglyce­
mia results from inadequate amounts of functional liver
tissue for optimal gluconeogenesis and glycogen storage
to maintain normal blood glucose levels.
The diagnosis of acquired liver dysfunction is usually
quite straightforward. Common CBC, serum biochemi­
cal profile and urinalysis abnormalities may include
microcytosis, low serum albumin, BUN and cholesterol
concentrations, elevated serum bilirubin levels, elevated
paired serum bile acid concentrations, ammonium biu­
rate crystals in the urine, radiographic evidence of abnor­
mal liver size, and/or ultrasonographic changes consistent
with abnormal echotexture or liver size. A liver biopsy is

107

VetBooks.ir

108

Section 2 Endocrine Disease

necessary to determine the exact cause of the liver disor­
der and may help guide specific treatment options such as
the selective use of antibiotics, glucocorticoids, copper
chelation, ciclosporin, lactulose, and dietary therapy.
Sepsis‐Induced Hypoglycemia

Systemic illness caused by microbial (usually bacteria)
invasion of normally sterile parts of the body is referred
to as sepsis. Sepsis plus organ dysfunction or hypoperfu­
sion is termed severe sepsis. And severe sepsis accompa­
nied by hypotension is termed septic shock.
Impaired glucose homeostasis has been well docu­
mented in patients with sepsis. Hyperglycemia is the
most common blood glucose abnormality seen early in
the course of bacterial sepsis. In preterminal sepsis, pro­
found hypoglycemia may occur because of hyperinsu­
linemia, increased tissue uptake of glucose, and the
failure of hepatic glucose production. It is postulated
that sepsis‐related hypoglycemia is a manifestation of
nonspecific inflammatory responses mediated by high
levels of cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor and
interleukin‐6.
The signs and symptoms of sepsis are highly variable.
They are influenced by the virulence and “bioburden’ (the
amount) of the organism, the portal of entry (e.g., skin,
gut, urinary tract) and host susceptibility (the young and
very old and patients with weakened immune systems are
most at risk). Patients with sepsis can present with a fever
or hypothermia and CBC findings may show a leukocyto­
sis with a left shift or leukopenia. Common causes of sep­
sis‐induced hypoglycemia include parvovirus infection,
prostatic and liver abscesses, pyothorax, pyometra, hem­
orrhagic gastroenteritis, and gram‐negative bacteremia.
The diagnosis of sepsis‐induced hypoglycemia is often
one of suspicion or identification of an infection based on
history, physical examination and CBC findings, and
other diagnostics such as bacterial cultures, radiography
and ultrasonography, and resolution of hypoglycemia
after initiation of antibiotic therapy.
Virulent Babesiosis

Hypoglycemia has been identified as a life‐threatening
metabolic complication in almost 20% of severely ill dogs
suffering from babesiosis caused by Babesia canis rossi.
This highly virulent subspecies of Babesia canis is
endemic only to South Africa. Clinical signs include pale
mucous membranes, depression, tachycardia, tachyp­
nea, anorexia, weakness, splenomegaly, and fever. The
clinical signs are attributed to tissue hypoxia resulting
from anemia and a concomitant systemic inflammatory
response syndrome caused by marked cytokine release.
The severe form of the disease is characterized by hemo­
lytic anemia and severe acid–base derangements, with
secondary multiple organ failure and complications such

as acute renal failure, hepatopathy with marked icterus,
hypoglycemia, acute respiratory distress syndrome,
­cerebral pathology, and additional immune‐mediated
erythrocyte destruction. Mortality is around 12%. A fea­
ture of the disease is that, in contrast to babesiosis in
other domestic species, pups and immature dogs are also
severely affected. Only one case of Babesia canis rossi
has been reported in a dog in the United States and that
was a dog imported from South Africa.
Several contributing factors have been implicated as
causes of the hypoglycemia. These include increased
peripheral requirement for glucose during febrile and
critical illness, obligatory demands of the parasites that
use glucose as their major fuel, hyperinsulinemia, failure
of hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, and
increased glucose consumption by anaerobic glycolysis
because of tissue hypoxia.
Blood glucose concentration should ideally be meas­
ured in all dogs requiring inpatient treatment for babe­
siosis, but is mandatory in collapsed dogs, puppies and
dogs with severe anemia, vomiting, or icterus. Many
dogs have probably been misdiagnosed with cerebral
babesiosis in the past, and hypoglycemia should be sus­
pected in any dog with coma or other neurologic signs.
Response to treatment with selected antibabesial com­
pounds such as imidocarb dipropionate, atovaquone,
azithromycin, clindamycin, and doxycycline is variable,
and intravenous dextrose does not reliably improve gly­
cemic status or survival.
Persistent Hyperinsulinemic Hypoglycemic
Syndrome
In humans, persistent hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia of
infancy (PHHI) represents the most common cause of
hyperinsulinism in neonates and children; currently,
many authors prefer the term congenital hyperinsulin­
ism (CHI). Severe recurrent hypoglycemia associated
with an inappropriate elevation of serum insulin defines
CHI. This disturbance of the normal relationship
between glucose concentration and insulin secretion is
caused by a variety of genetic mutations. If left untreated,
CHI can lead to brain damage or death secondary to
severe hypoglycemia. Although it was initially thought to
affect only infants and children, numerous cases have
been reported in adults of all ages but at a much lower
incidence. CHI is often poorly responsive or unrespon­
sive to medical management, necessitating 95% or near‐
total pancreatectomy.
Recently, a persistent hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemic
syndrome, not associated with sepsis or insulinoma, was
diagnosed in two dogs. Both dogs were less than 12
months of age. The clinical signs in these dogs were
­similar; hypoglycemic‐induced seizures unresponsive to

VetBooks.ir

intravenous glucose administration and anticonvulsant
therapy. The owners of these dogs chose euthanasia
because of poor response to therapy and poor prognosis.
Blood was cultured from one dog using a special enrich­
ment PCR media to rule in or rule out an infection
caused by a fastidious bacteria; Bartonella hensalae
was amplified and sequenced from this dog’s blood. In
the other dog, Bartonella kohlerae was amplified and
sequenced retrospectively from paraffin‐embedded
­tissue. Despite isolating Bartonella spp. from both dogs,
it is unclear whether B. hensalae and B. kohlerae contrib­
uted to the pathogenesis of this unusual and rare
­hypoglycemic syndrome. That said, persistent hyperin­
sulinemic hypoglycemic syndrome should be suspected
in any young dog with hypoglycemia refractory to intra­
venous glucose. Moreover, until more is known about
the cause of this syndrome, testing and treating
for Bartonella should be a diagnostic and therapeutic
consideration.
Xylitol Toxicity
Xylitol exposure, even in small amounts, can cause hypo­
glycemia and severe liver damage in dogs. Xylitol is a 5‐
carbon sugar alcohol that is used primarily as an artificial
sweetener that has less than two‐thirds of the calories of
most sugars. The two major sources of xylitol exposure
are food and dental or medical products. Initially, expo­
sure to xylitol in dogs was from “sugar‐free” chewing
gums. However, with demands from human diabetic
patients, particularly because of the popularity of Atkins‐
like “low‐carb” diets, many foods now contain xylitol. A
large number of low‐carbohydrate foods, including
breads, candies, gums, and deserts, have xylitol as the
sweetener of choice. Xylitol has a wide margin of safety
in mammals with the exception of dogs. Oral exposures
as low as 0.1 mg/kg have induced hypoglycemia in the
dog, and levels of 0.5 mg/kg have resulted in hepatotoxic­
ity in some dogs. For example, one piece of Trident gum
contains 0.22 g of xylitol and the popular breath mint Ice
Breakers contains 1 g of xylitol per piece and therefore,
nine pieces of Trident or two Ice Breaker pieces could
potentially cause xylitol toxicity in a 20 kg dog. The lit­
erature reports no cases of xylitol toxicity in cats.

has been steadily rising over the last few years, with a
resultant surge in xylitol cases reported to the APCC.
Clinical Signs and Laboratory Abnormalities

In laboratory experiments, xylitol directly stimulates
insulin synthesis and secretion within 30 minutes after
ingestion. However, in clinical cases, the onset of clinical
signs varies based on the form of xylitol used in the prod­
uct ingested. The powder used in candies and mints is
absorbed quickly and signs can be seen in 30 minutes.
Gum must be chewed to release the xylitol. If the gum is
swallowed whole it leaches into the stomach, and the
onset of clinical signs can be delayed 8–18 hours.
Vomiting is often the first symptom. Clinical signs can
include ataxia, depression, dilated pupils, and seizures
(related to hypoglycemia), and lethargy, inappetence,
vomiting, and diarrhea (related to liver failure).
Laboratory abnormalities initially include hyperinsuline­
mia, hypoglycemia, hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia,
and increased AST and ALT concentrations. Dogs that
do not exhibit hypoglycemia immediately after ingestion
of xylitol may still develop acute liver failure. These dogs
may develop severe signs 24–72 hours later.
Diagnosis

The diagnosis of xylitol toxicity is made by history of
exposure, clinical signs, and serum biochemical abnor­
malities consistent with xylitol poisoning. Because the
serum half‐life of xylitol is about two minutes and there
is rapid progression of the toxic effect, testing for xylitol
in the blood is not realistic.
Treatment and Monitoring

Blood glucose levels should be determined initially and
monitored at least every four hours for 24 hours or
longer, as indicated. Liver enzyme levels and prothrom­
bin time/partial thromboplastin time (PT/PTT) should
be monitored every 24 hours for 48–72 hours. It is not
uncommon to have a transient elevation in ALT (300–
800) very quickly after ingestion. Electrolyte status and
packed cell volume (PCV) should also be monitored
regularly.
There is no antidote for xylitol toxicity.
Induce emesis if the xylitol ingestion is recent.
●● Use of activated charcoal is of limited efficacy with
xylitol because it is not effective at binding xylitol.
●● IV fluid support: important to restore or maintain
hydration, treat hypoglycemia, and prevent or treat
disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Patients
with normal blood glucose levels should receive a 2.5%
dextrose solution.
●● Hypoglycemia caused by xylitol toxicity is usually
responsive to IV dextrose solutions. Refractory cases

Prevalence

Recently, there has been a rapid increase in the number
of products containing xylitol. According to the ASPCA
Animal Poison Control Center (APCC), the number of
reported xylitol exposures in dogs has been increasing
steadily and exponentially over the past few years. In
2007, theAPCC began to log xylitol cases. That year, the
center received 1764 calls about xylitol. In 2012, the fig­
ure was 3184. The number of products containing xylitol

Duration of Treatment and Prognosis

The length of treatment depends on the severity of clini­
cal signs. Treatment for cases without liver involvement
may last 1–3 days. Treatment should continue until glu­
cose levels are normal. Treatment of cases with liver
involvement may last weeks. The prognosis for patients
that only develop hypoglycemia is good. Prognosis for
patients who develop liver failure is guarded and depends
on the severity of the disease. Typically, there are no lin­
gering medical issues once liver problems have been suc­
cessfully resolved.

­Diagnostic Approach to Disorders
Associated with Hypoglycemia
After confirming the finding of hypoglycemia, the
­history (including exposure to insulin, sulfonylureas,
or xylitol), signalment, physical exam findings, and a
careful review of available laboratory data guide the
evaluation. This information will either provide clues
to the cause of hypoglycemia or exclude hypoglycemia
caused by acknowledged drugs or toxins, critical ill­
nesses, hormone deficiencies, or a nonislet cell tumor.
A test of adrenocortical function is reasonable although

hypoadrenocorticism is not commonly found as a cause
of hypoglycemia in dogs in the absence of other clinical
clues. Nonislet cell tumor hypoglycemia is often associ­
ated with a large, clinically apparent mesenchymal
tumor (e.g., leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma) as well as
epithelial tumors that are associated with the liver (e.g.,
hepatoma or hepatocellular carcinoma).
As part of the signalment, age of the animal can be
quite useful in narrowing down the long list of rule‐outs
for hypoglycemia. For example, hypoglycemia in a puppy
or kitten is often idiopathic in origin or related to starva­
tion, PSVA, or sepsis. In young adult dogs, hypoglycemia is
usually caused by hepatic insufficiency, hypoadrenocor­
ticism, or sepsis. And in older dogs, hepatic insufficiency,
insulinoma (see Chapter XX), nonislet cell tumor‐induced
hypoglycemia, hypoadrenocorticism, and sepsis are the
most common causes of hypoglycemia.
The results of routine and specialized tests can also be
quite helpful diagnostically. For example, dogs with adre­
nal insufficiency without the classic electrolyte changes
of hyperkalemia and hyponatremia often have hypoal­
buminemia, hypocholesterolemia and a resting cortisol
<2 μg/dL, although an ACTH response test is required
for a definitive diagnosis. Paired fasting and postprandial
serum bile acids are diagnostic for virtually all dogs with
a portosystemic shunt, and CBC findings which include
a neutrophilic leukocytosis with a left shift in a hypogly­
cemic febrile dog or cat are highly suggestive of sepsis.
When the cause of the hypoglycemic disorder is not
evident in a seemingly well adult dog, serum glucose and
insulin concentrations should be measured during an
episode of spontaneous hypoglycemia to rule out an
insulinoma. The key pathophysiologic feature of endog­
enous hyperinsulinism (e.g., an insulinoma) is the failure
of insulin secretion to fall to very low rates as blood
­glucose concentrations fall to hypoglycemic levels.

Canine Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndromes
Deborah Greco, DVM, PhD, DACVIM (SAIM)
Desert Veterinary Specialists, Palm Desert, CA, USA

Many endocrine disorders, such as lymphocytic thyroid­
itis, hypoadrenocorticism, and type 1 diabetes mellitus,
have an autoimmune basis. When endocrine immune
disorders occur in the same individual, they are known
as autoimmune polyglandular syndromes (APS). These
syndromes (APS) can be further divided into APS type 1
(diabetes ­mellitus, ectodermal mucositis, etc.), APS type
2 (hypoadrenocorticism, hypothyroidism, etc.), and APS
type 3 (liver cirrhosis plus endocrinopathies). The com­
bination of hypoadrenocorticism and hypothyroidism is
called Schmidt syndrome after the pathologist who
described concurrence of these two diseases in human
beings. Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2 is
the only one that has been described in dogs.

­Etiology and Pathophysiology
Polyendocrine gland failure or autoimmune polyglan­
dular syndrome, the most common form of which is APS
type 2, has been well documented in humans. Autoimmune
polyglandular syndrome type 2 is defined as the occur­
rence of two or more of the following disorders in the
same individual: adrenal insufficiency, primary hypothy­
roidism, type 1 diabetes mellitus (DM), primary hypog­
onadism (premature ovarian failure, immune‐mediated
orchitis), myasthenia gravis, megaesophagus, immune‐
mediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA), immune‐mediated
thrombocytopenia (ITP), hypoparathyroidism, hypopitu­
itarism, and celiac disease.
Circulating organ‐specific autoantibodies are com­
monly present in APS type 2. Environmental factors
­combined with an HLA‐associated genetic predisposi­
tion are thought to trigger the process. Cell‐mediated
immune abnormalities in the type 2 syndrome include
defects and alterations of cell surface markers, but the
most consistent abnormality is a functional defect leading

to a decrease in suppressor T cell activity. Approximately
45% of all human patients with idiopathic (autoimmune)
adrenal insufficiency will develop one or more additional
endocrinopathies (usually hypothyroidism).
The genetics of APS has been studied extensively in
human beings. APS 2 is inherited as an autosomal domi­
nant trait in humans associated with the presence of
human leukocyte antigens (HLA). In families where this
syndrome has been documented in several individuals,
the inheritance of major histocompatibility loci haplo­
type correlates most strongly with the disease. Many
individuals with this haplotype have circulating organ‐
specific autoantibodies directed against cytochrome
P450 without clinical signs of disease. Recently, one study
found that a higher proportion of dogs with hypoadreno­
corticism were P450scc autoantibody p
­ositive when
compared to hospital controls (24% vs 1%). Lymphocytic
and plasmacytic destruction of the affected endocrine
glands may be documented histologically.
Hypoadrenocorticism is the most common initial endo­
crinopathy observed in polyendocrine gland failure in
dogs and is usually followed by the development of hypo­
thyroidism. However, type 1 diabetes combined with
immune‐mediated thyroid disease (Hashimoto t­ hyroiditis)
is also a common combination of immune endocrinopa­
thies in humans and has been described in dogs. Studies
show that 45–50% of humans with adrenal insufficiency
associated with polyendocrine gland failure (onset 20–30
years) develop a second endocrinopathy. The most com­
mon ­second endocrinopathy, primary hypothyroidism,
develops 10–20 years after the first endocrinopathy.
In a retrospective of 225 cases of canine hypoad­
renocorticism, 4% of the dogs (n = 9) also suffered from
hypothyroidism, two dogs had concurrent IDDM and
hypoadrenocorticism, and one had concurrent hypoad­
renocorticism, hypothyroidism, IDDM, and hypopar­
athyroidism. Another retrospective of 45 dogs with

In cases of combined DM and hypothyroidism, diabetes

­History and Clinical Signs

In two studies, dogs with concurrent diabetes and hypo­
thyroidism showed significantly lower serum sodium
concentration and had significantly higher fasting serum
cholesterol compared with nonhypothyroid diabetic
dogs; similarly, dogs with hypoadrenocorticism com­
bined with hypothyroidism exhibited significantly lower
sodium and higher serum cholesterol than dogs with
hypoadrenocorticism alone. These two chemistry abnor­
malities are highly suggestive of hypothyroidism in a dog
with otherwise well‐regulated hypoadrenocorticism or
in a poorly regulated diabetic dog. Severe hyponatremia
(<120 meq/L) is a sign of Schmidt syndrome in humans.
Thyroid testing should be performed in diabetics dogs
that exhibit poor glucose regulation, persistent hypona­
tremia and hypercholesterolemia, obesity or weight gain,
lethargy, dermatologic disease, and regurgitation.
Resting serum cortisol concentration is often subnormal
(<2 μg/dL) in dogs that suffer from APS 2 that manifests as
hypoadrenocorticism and all will show inadequate
response to adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimu­
lation. Endogenous ACTH levels should be increased due
to primary adrenal insufficiency and loss of negative feed­
back to the pituitary gland. One reported case of Schmidt
syndrome (APS 2) had evidence of lymphocytic adenohy­
pophysitis in addition to adrenalitis and thyroid gland
atrophy; immune‐mediated pituitary disorders have been
reported in humans as well. Mean basal thyroxine (T4)
and free T4 levels are usually low to low normal and
endogenous thyroid‐stimulating hormone (TSH) is usu­
ally elevated in dogs with multiple endocrinopathies
resulting from APS.

Most of the dogs in reported studies were diagnosed with
hypoadrenocorticism initially and the mean age of onset
of the disease was in young adulthood. Dogs are usually
diagnosed with a second endocrinopathy approximately
one year after the first endocrinopathy.
A familial tendency was observed in one study where
two dogs were mother and daughter and one dog had a
sibling with hypoadrenocorticism. Hypoadrenocorticism
is inherited in several breeds, including standard ­poodles,
West Highland white terriers, Nova Scotia duck tolling
retrievers, Portuguese water dogs, and Leonbergers; how­
ever, there may be different DLA haplotypes depending
on breed. There is a distinct breed predisposition for
primary hypothyroidism with golden retrievers,
­
Doberman pinschers, Irish setters, miniature schnauzers,
dachshunds, cocker spaniels, and beagles. Diabetes
­mellitus (type 1a), which has an autoimmune basis, is seen
with increased frequency in Samoyeds, Tibetan ­terriers,
Australian terriers, keeshonds and several other breeds. In
fact, one study showed that the DLA‐DRB1*009/DQA1*/
DQB1*008 haplotype was associated with DM in certain
breeds (Samoyed, Tibetan, and cairn terriers) and that the
DLA‐DQA1*001 allele is also associated with hypothy­
roidism in dogs, suggesting a common susceptibility allele
for canine immune‐mediated endocrinopathies.
A decreasing insulin requirement is often the earliest
sign of adrenal insufficiency in a patient with type 1
­diabetes mellitus secondary to APS in human beings.
In contrast, dogs with concurrent hypothyroidism
and IDDM often have increasing insulin requirements;
hypothyroidism may cause insulin resistance resulting
from lipid abnormalities or other factors.
The most common presenting complaints for hypoad­
renocorticism as the initial diagnosis include lethargy,
collapse, vomiting, weight loss, weakness, ataxia, a­ norexia,
bradycardia, megaesophagus, and diarrhea. Clinico­
pathologic features include hyponatremia, hypercholes­
terolemia, hyperkalemia, hypochloremia, azotemia,
hypocalcemia, and hypercalcemia.
In dogs diagnosed with hypoadrenocorticism as
the initial endocrinopathy, thyroid evaluation is often

­Diagnosis and Prognosis

­Therapy
Treatment of multiple endocrinopathies consists of
­specific hormone replacement. For dogs with hypoad­
renocorticism, treatment with fludrocortisone (0.018 mg/
kg PO q24h) or deoxycorticosterone pivalate (DOCP)
(1 mg/kg IM monthly) should be initiated first, followed
by levothyroxine therapy (22 μg/kg once or twice daily
PO). One should be aware that aggressive levothyroxine
therapy might precipitate a life‐threatening adrenal c­ risis

VetBooks.ir

14 Canine Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndromes

in a patient with APS so starting once daily would be sug­
gested. When the hypothyroid and hypoadrenal states
occur concurrently, the rate of clearance of cortisol and
cholesterol is reduced due to low serum t­hyroxine con­
centrations. When thyroid supplementation is initiated,
cortisol clearance increases suddenly without a compen­
satory increase in cortisol synthesis because of destruc­
tion of adrenal tissue. As a result, ­thyroid therapy may
precipitate an adrenal crisis. Hence, one should assess
adrenal function prior to initiation of levothyroxine ther­
apy in animals with suspected m
­ ultiple endocrinopa­
thies. In dogs with diabetes mellitus and hypothyroidism,
one must balance the insulin dose with the levothyroxine
therapy. A reduction of 25% of the insulin dose is recom­
mended when starting levothyroxine at 22 μg/kg BID. In
dogs with hypoadrenocorticism and diabetes mellitus,
the insulin dose will need to be gradually increased as
supplementation with glucocorticoids (0.22 mg/kg PO
q24h) and DOCP will cause insulin resistance.

­Conclusion
In summary, multiple endocrine deficiencies occur with a
low incidence in dogs with hypoadrenocorticism, hypo­
thyroidism, IDDM, and perhaps hypoparathyroidism.
This syndrome appears to be similar to APS 2 of human
beings. Veterinarians should be aware of some of the fea­
tures, such as persistent hyponatremia and hypercholes­
terolemia, which may indicate the presence of multiple
endocrinopathies in the same individual. Dogs with
hypoadrenocorticism that exhibit inadequate response to
therapy, persistent hypercholesterolemia and hypona­
tremia despite normalization of serum potassium, derma­
tologic disease, and/or bradycardia should be evaluated
for thyroid function. Diabetic dogs that exhibit inadequate
glycemic control associated with persistent hyponatremia,
hypercholesterolemia (>500 mg/dL), obesity and derma­
tologic disease should also be tested for hypothyroidism.

Approach to the Patient with Suspected Cardiovascular Disease
Ingrid Ljungvall, DVM, PhD, DECVIM-CA (Cardiology) and Jens Häggström, DVM, PhD, DECVIM-CA (Cardiology)
Department of Clinical Sciences, Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, Uppsala, Sweden

Suspicion of cardiac disease in dogs and cats may arise
due to information obtained from owner complaints
and/or physical findings. Unfortunately, most of the
common clinical signs of heart disease are not specific
for heart disease. Likewise, heart disease may occur concurrently with other disease, making it unclear whether
the clinical signs are due to cardiac disease or something
else. The approach to the patient with suspected cardiovascular disease is therefore to obtain as much information as possible in order to make a correct diagnosis.

­Signalment
Signalment information is the first step in the clinical w
­ ork‐
up of a patient with suspected heart disease as some diseases are more commonly seen in specific types of animals.
However, this type of data is only supportive in nature, and
does not provide sufficient evidence for a definite diagnosis.
The signalment data should include information concerning age, species, breed, sex, and geographic location.
Age
Age can provide valuable information in a patient with
suspected cardiac disease; congenital heart disease,
which is defined as a heart defect present at birth, is more
likely in young pets. However, congenital heart disease
may remain undiscovered in middle‐aged or old dogs and
cats not previously examined by a veterinarian. Acquired
heart disease, defined as a heart condition developing
after birth, is most frequently found in middle‐aged and
old dogs and cats, although its presence in a younger
individual cannot be excluded. For both dogs and cats,
presence of cardiac neoplasia is more common in older
individuals. Extracardiac disease may affect the heart by
causing myocyte damage in dogs and cats of any age.

Species and Breed
Some specific heart diseases, both congenital and
acquired, are more commonly identified in individuals of
certain breeds compared to others (see separate disease
chapters), which supports a genetic background for these
disorders.
Sex
Very little is known concerning the effect of sex on the
prevalence of congenital heart disease in dogs and cats.
In most studies, no sex predilection has been reported.
However, sex appears to affect the prevalence of the
most common forms of acquired heart disease in dogs
(myxomatous mitral valve disease [MMVD] and dilated
cardiomyopathy [DCM]) and cats (cardiomyopathy).
Males appear affected at an earlier age in both cats and
dogs, which leads to a slightly higher proportion of
affected individuals at a given age and a higher cause‐
specific mortality. The reason for this influence of sex is
unknown.
Geographic Location
Information concerning the geographic origin of the pet
is important because the prevalence of certain congenital and acquired heart diseases differs between continents, countries, and even within countries. Again, this
likely reflects different gene pools within breeds, but it
underlines the importance of interpreting results of disease prevalence with caution. It is also important to
obtain information about where the animal has lived
geographically because some diseases, for example parasitic diseases (e.g., dirofilarosis), are prevalent in certain
areas but nonexistent in others.

Section 3 Cardiovascular Disease

­Case History and Owner Complaints
A thorough medical history provides important information and is an integral part of the cardiovascular
examination. The questions may vary depending on the
nature of the animal’s health problem. Information
obtained from the owner interview and findings at the
physical examination are used to formulate a problem
list, which can be used in the decision to pursue further
clinical testing.
Dogs and cats with heart disease can present with clinical signs related to the heart condition but also, the pet
can be completely free of signs of disease and the only reason for the cardiac examination is an incidental finding of
a heart murmur or arrhythmia. Common owner complaints for a pet with heart disease include increased respiratory rate (tachypnea), difficulty of breathing and
changed respiratory pattern (dyspnea), coughing (unusual
in cats), abdominal distension (ascites), fainting (syncope),
tongue and mucous membrane cyanosis, weight loss, and
weakness and exercise intolerance. These signs of heart
disease can be grouped into four main categories:
respiratory abnormalities caused by left‐sided congestive heart failure (CHF)
●● exercise intolerance, weakness, wasting, and syncope
caused by low cardiac output
●● abdominal distension caused by right‐sided CHF
●● cyanosis caused by reduced oxygenation of peripheral
blood.
●●

Unfortunately, none of these signs is specific for heart disease, and may be caused by a wide variety of disorders.
Dyspnea, Tachypnea, and Cough
The most common sequela of heart disease in dogs and
cats is left‐sided CHF. The increased pulmonary venous
pressure leads to pulmonary congestion and edema formation, causing respiratory signs such as dyspnea,
tachypnea, and cough (unusual in cats). Dyspnea may
appear in many different forms in pets with heart disease. In working dogs, an experienced owner might note
a changed respiratory character during and/or after work
at an earlier stage of disease. However, many dogs and
cats do not exercise in this intense manner, which means
that owners do not observe changed respiration until it is
apparent at rest (at a comparably advanced stage).
In general, the respiratory rate gradually increases followed by a worsening of dyspnea, but the respiratory
signs may develop at different rates in different diseases
and individuals. Accordingly, it is useful to have the
owner monitoring the respiratory rate at home in an animal at risk for developing CHF. Dogs and cats without
decompensated CHF have in general a sleeping/resting

respiratory rate of <30/min. As a general rule, long‐
standing (weeks or months) respiratory signs that have
not worsened over time speak against CHF. Respiratory
signs, with or without cough, while lying down or asleep,
a phenomenon called nocturnal dyspnea/coughing, are
common early signs of left‐sided CHF. The severity of
dyspnea can range from mild, with only minimal changes
in breathing pattern and respiratory rate, to severe life‐
threatening dyspnea, when the pet is unwilling to lie
down (orthopnea), usually with respiratory rates >50/
min. The owner often describes changed breathing
sounds in animals with severe pulmonary edema. Cats
with left‐sided CHF frequently develop pleural effusion
alone or in addition to pulmonary edema, and these cats
can exhibit a paradoxical breathing pattern.
Dogs presenting with left‐sided decompensated CHF
may present with cough. Cough is not commonly associated with CHF in cats, and owner complaints of coughing in cats should raise the suspicion of other respiratory
disease. In dogs, there is also a problem distinguishing
cough caused by other diseases, such as small bronchial
disease and tracheal collapse, from cough associated
with pronounced cardiomegaly with or without CHF.
There is no definitive way of distinguishing cardiac from
noncardiac cough in dogs. A noncardiac cough is more
frequently nonproductive, loud and “honky,” whereas
cough caused by left‐sided CHF can be softer and may
have a more productive “wet” character, in particular
in large dogs with DCM where co‐existing respiratory
disease is less common.
Exercise Intolerance, Weakness, Wasting,
and Syncope
Variable degrees of weakness and exercise intolerance
often develop in dogs and cats with heart disease.
However, exercise intolerance can be difficult to assess in
cats. Weakness and exercise intolerance can occur as a
consequence of a reduced cardiac output resulting in
reduced peripheral perfusion with reduced oxygen and
nutrient delivery to skeletal muscles.
Weakness, exercise intolerance, and syncopal events
can develop due to pulmonary hypertension or cardiac
arrhythmia, intermittent or sustained, in dogs and cats
with heart disease. Pets with sustained bradycardia or
tachycardia are often weak even at rest and exhibit significant exercise intolerance. In cases of intermittent
arrhythmia, the owner often describes a rapid change in
the dog’s behavior, consciousness, or postural tone.
Defecation and urination can accompany these events.
Even though syncope can occur in dogs and cats with
heart disease, it is not specific for heart disease or heart
failure, which underlines the importance of obtaining an
accurate and detailed case history.

VetBooks.ir

15 Approach to the Patient with Suspected Cardiovascular Disease ﻿

In dogs with CHF and a chronic reduction of peripheral
perfusion, a loss of body weight may be apparent.
Sequential measurements of body weight over time can be
useful to identify subtle weight loss. However, identification of weight loss may be problematic if loss of muscle
mass is masked by concurrent fluid retention.
Abdominal Distension
Abdominal distension can be caused by a wide variety of
diseases, both cardiac and noncardiac in origin. In heart
disease, abdominal distension is the result of right‐sided
CHF leading to congestion of abdominal organs (such as
the liver) and transudation of fluid into the abdominal
cavity. This usually occurs slowly, and remains unnoticed by the owner until quite advanced stages. In other
conditions, such as pericardial effusion, the ascites may
develop more rapidly.
Cyanosis
Cyanosis is defined as a blue to blue‐gray discoloration of the mucous membranes as the result of
increased ­concentration of deoxygenated hemoglobin.
It can be evident on physical examination and also
described by the owner. Discoloration of the tongue
and mucous membranes is a common complaint of
owners suspecting heart disease in their pet, but can
be difficult to identify or replicate at the clinic.
Additionally, cyanosis can be difficult to identify
because of pigmentation of the skin and mucous membranes. Cyanosis in veterinary patients is usually associated with severe left‐sided CHF or congenital heart
disease. In case of severe left‐sided CHF, other significant signs of disease always accompany the cyanosis.
In some cases of congenital heart disease leading to
right‐to‐left shunting of blood, some animals can
have reduced exercise capacity, pelvic limb weakness
and frequently have to sit down during play or exercise. Depending on the degree of shunting, some of
these a­ nimals can be cyanotic at rest but the cyanosis
becomes more apparent with physical exercise.

­Physical Examination
A thorough physical examination is the foundation for
the clinical work‐up in dogs and cats with suspected heart
disease. The examination includes general inspection and
observation (e.g., attitude, body condition, mobility,
degree of anxiety, and respiratory pattern), and a thorough physical examination to identify abnormalities in
other organ systems. The cardiovascular examination
includes evaluation of the peripheral circulation (mucous

membranes), systemic veins (jugular veins), peripheral
arterial pulses, the precordium (left and right chest wall
over the heart), palpation of abdomen to identify ascites,
and auscultation of heart and lungs.
Mucous Membranes
The mucous membrane color and capillary refill time
are used to evaluate peripheral perfusion. The mucous
membranes of the oral cavity are usually used for this
purpose, but also ocular and caudal (vaginal or preputial) membranes can be examined. Preferably findings of caudal membranes should be compared with
findings in the oral cavity. Findings of bluish discoloration are suggestive of cyanosis (see earlier), darkish red is suggestive of erythrocytosis, and pale
membranes are suggestive of anemia and/or decreased
perfusion. Capillary refill time (CRT) is conducted to
evaluate peripheral perfusion. While commonly performed, CRT is a comparably insensitive method to
detect abnormal perfusion.
Systemic Veins
The jugular veins should be inspected in cases with suspected heart disease, and clipping or wetting of the fur
may be required to visualize these vessels. Distension or
pulsations of the jugular veins, while the animal is sitting
with the neck moderately extended, are indicative of
increased systemic venous pressure (right‐sided CHF) or
occlusion (most commonly neoplasia or thrombosis) of
the vessel at the level between the right heart and the jugular vein. Because there is no valve between the right atrium
and the systemic veins, changes in pressure in the right
atrium are transmitted within the systemic veins, and can
be caused by right atrial contractions at high systemic
venous pressure or tricuspid regurgitation. Sometimes,
the carotid arterial pulse is transmitted through the soft
tissues, mimicking a venous pulsation (so‐called false
venous pulsations). Differentiation between true and false
venous pulsations can be obtained by applying pressure to
the jugular vein at a level slightly below the area of the
pulsation. If the pulsation disappears, it is a sign of true
venous pulsation; if it continues, it is a sign of false venous
pulsation.
Peripheral Arterial Pulsations
The strength and quality of the femoral arterial pulses
are subjectively assessed by simultaneous palpation of
both femoral arteries in a standing animal. Sufficient
pressure should be placed on the vessels to occlude them,
so that pulsation is no longer palpable. The pressure is
then slowly released until maximal pulsation is evident.

Evaluation of Fluid Accumulation

This subjective evaluation provides information on the
pulse pressure (i.e. the difference between systemic arterial peak systolic and diastolic pressures) and potential
presence of various heart diseases.
The quality of pulses in the two limbs should be compared, particularly in cats. Absent femoral arterial pulse in
one or both limbs may be indicative of arterial thromboembolism. The femoral artery should be palpated simultaneously with cardiac auscultation to detect heartbeats that
do not produce pulses. Arrhythmias can cause the heart to
contract before it is properly filled with blood, producing
variable pulses or pulse deficits.

Right‐sided CHF leads to accumulation of fluid in body
cavities, most commonly in the abdomen. The abdomen
should therefore be palpated for ballottement and the
presence of fluid accumulation (ascites). Mild ascites is
difficult to detect, whereas moderate to severe ascites is
comparably easy to detect. Pleural effusion is more difficult to detect and thoracic radiography or centesis is
often required to obtain a definite diagnosis. The limbs
should also be inspected for the presence of peripheral
edema, although this is an extremely unusual finding in
dogs and cats with heart disease.

Palpation of the Precordium

Auscultation

The precordium is evaluated by placing palms and fingers on each side of the thorax over the cardiac ostia
(Figure 15.1). Normally, the cardiac contraction (precordial impulse) is best felt on the left side of the thorax over
the apical area. Changes in cardiac size and shape, or
space‐occupying thoracic masses can cause a shift of the
location of the precordial impulse. A weak impulse can
be caused by obesity, hypovolemia, thoracic masses,
pleural or pericardial effusion, or pneumothorax.
Increased precordial impulse can be caused by hyperkinetic conditions such as stress or anemia or conditions
characterized by cardiac volume overload and cardiomegaly, such as severe MMVD or DCM. Severe valvular
regurgitation or stenosis can cause palpable “buzzing”
vibrations called a precordial thrill. The intensity of the
auscultated heart murmur is always greatest over the
area of the thrill.

(a)

Cardiac auscultation is an important component of the
physical examination in dogs and cats with suspected cardiac disease. An exact diagnosis can seldom be established
based solely on cardiac auscultation, but optimal auscultation technique can substantially narrow down the list of
differential diagnoses. Auscultation allows assessment of
heart rate, rhythm, and presence of abnormal sounds, such
as murmur, click, and additional heart sounds.
Auscultation should be performed in a quiet environment, and background noise should be minimized. The
animal should preferably be standing on all four limbs
during cardiac auscultation as abnormal sounds, which
can easily be mistaken for heart murmurs, can arise in a
recumbent animal due to rubbing of the heart against the
chest wall. Furthermore, localization of the area of origin
of different cardiac sounds is more easily achieved in a

(b)

standing animal. The entire cardiac area should be
­auscultated thoroughly. The areas of auscultation of the
heart are shown in Figure 15.1.
The areas of the ventral thorax adjacent to the sternum
should always be auscultated in cats, as murmurs and gallop rhythms often are heard best at this location. If
needed, the animal’s mouth should be manually gently
closed for brief periods of time as panting can generate
referred sounds, which can be mistaken for murmurs.
Evaluation of heart sounds and murmurs is often difficult
in purring cats. The purring can be stopped by quickly
occluding a nostril, by placing the cat in the proximity of
a running tap, by holding cotton wool soaked in alcohol
near the cat’s nose, or by blowing short bursts of air into
the face of the cat. Breathing sounds, especially in cats,
can be mistaken for sounds originating from the heart,
and differentiating heart sounds from breath sounds can
be facilitated by watching the cat’s breathing pattern
while simultaneously ausculting the heart.
Heart Rate and Rhythm

Dogs in CHF are likely to be tachycardic, although the
degree of tachycardia may be modest. Tachycardia in
CHF patients results from parasympathetic withdrawal
and increased sympathetic tone. Cats in decompensated
CHF may present with normal, increased or decreased
heart rate. Healthy dogs have either a regular heart
rhythm or a respiratory sinus arrhythmia where the heart
rate increases during inspiration and decreases during
expiration due to changes in vagal tone. This phenomenon can be exaggerated, particularly in the presence of
respiratory disease. Dogs presenting with respiratory
sinus arrhythmia are unlikely to be in decompensated
CHF with pulmonary edema. Healthy cats normally have
a regular heart rhythm, and the finding of respiratory
sinus arrhythmia in cats warrants further examination of
potential respiratory disease. Other arrhythmias in dogs
and cats, such as the detection of premature beats or long
periods of asystole, can indicate presence of heart disease,
and further diagnostic tests such as an electrocardiogram
are then indicated.
Heart Sounds and Murmurs

Two heart sounds are normally audible in healthy dogs
and cats. The first heart sound (S1), which is heard
loudest at the heart apex, occurs concurrently with closure of the atrioventricular valves, whereas the second
heart sound (S2), which is heard loudest at the heart
base, occurs concurrently with closure of the semilunar
valves. The intensity of heart sounds is influenced by
many factors, such as auscultation technique, body
condition, and presence of cardiac disease. Heart sound
intensity can be decreased in animals affected by obesity, pericardial or pleural effusions, space‐occupying

lesions (such as thoracic masses), diaphragmatic
­hernias, shock, bradycardias, or severely affected myocardial function. The intensity of S2 is commonly
dampened in dogs with severe MMVD. Heart sound
intensity can be increased in animals with increased
sympathetic tone, cardiac enlargement, or in those with
narrow chest conformation. Intensity of heart sounds
often varies from beat to beat in animals affected
by cardiac arrhythmias, such as atrial fibrillation and
ventricular tachycardia.
In dogs and cats, the presence of S3 and/or S4 signifies a gallop heart sound (tripling or quadrupling of the
heart sounds, resembling the canter of a horse), and is
generally an indication of myocardial disease in dogs
and cats. The S3 (ventricular gallop) occurs early in
diastole, and is associated with rapid ventricular filling
during early diastole into a ventricle with decreased
compliance, and is typically heard in dogs with conditions characterized by ventricular volume overload,
such as DCM, MMVD or patent ductus arteriosus
(PDA). The S4 (atrial gallop) occurs later in diastole,
and is associated with vigorous atrial contractions in
animals with conditions characterized by increased
resistance to ventricular emptying or impaired ventricular compliance. This typically occurs in disorders with
ventricular concentric hypertrophy, such as in cats with
hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) or systemic
hypertension. The S4 can also be present in dogs with
third‐degree atrioventricular (AV) block, dogs with
ruptured chordae tendineae, or even in healthy cats due
to decreasing ventricular compliance with age. The S3
and S4 can be superimposed in animals with tachycardia (most commonly in cats), resulting in one additional
diastolic sound called a summation gallop.
Systolic clicks are transient, mid to late systolic
sounds, which are higher in frequency than gallop
sounds and are mainly heard in dogs with abnormal AV
valve leaflet movement, such as mitral valve prolapse in
dogs affected by mild MMVD. Clicks occurring in early
systole can be associated with abnormal valve leaflet
movement or great vessel dilation in dogs with aortic or
pulmonic stenosis.
Murmurs are auditory vibrations caused by high‐
velocity and turbulent blood flow through the heart and
vessels. Murmurs can be characterized by timing within
the cardiac cycle, anatomic location, radiation area,
intensity (loudness), frequency (pitch), and shape of
vibration pattern (which is visualized by phonocardiography). Most cardiovascular diseases in dogs and cats
result in systolic murmurs, which most commonly start
immediately after the S1, but they can also start later in
systole. Systolic murmurs can last for only a portion of
the systole (early, mid or late systolic murmurs), throughout systole from the end of S1 to the beginning of S2

123

VetBooks.ir

124

Section 3 Cardiovascular Disease

(holosystolic murmur), or, rarely, throughout systole from
the beginning of S1 to the end of S2 (pansystolic murmur). Diastolic turbulent blood flow is rare in dogs and
cats, and can be relatively difficult to detect. Diastolic
murmurs most commonly start immediately after the S2.
Continuous murmurs last throughout systole and diastole. The most common heart disease associated with a
continuous murmur is PDA where the murmur commonly peaks in intensity at the time of the S2.
Point of maximum intensity (PMI) of a murmur is
commonly the location over the thorax where the murmur is loudest, and can serve as a guide to the origin of
the murmur. The PMI is associated with a particular
valve region (i.e., pulmonic, aortic, mitral, tricuspid).
The small size of the feline heart makes it difficult to distinguish the different valve areas on the thorax.
Accordingly, localization of murmurs in cats is often
described as sternal versus parasternal, base versus apex,
and left versus right. The areas of auscultation of the
heart in dogs are shown in Figure 15.1. The area of murmur radiation refers to how widely the murmur can be
heard from the PMI, and generally increases with
increasing turbulence.

Murmurs are traditionally graded on a scale of 1–6.
However, evidence exists that a four‐grade scale can be
used for some heart diseases without losing clinically
important information (Table 15.1).
For some cardiac diseases, such as MMVD and aortic/
pulmonic stenosis, grading of murmurs serves as a rough
estimate of disease severity. However, a lack of agreement
exists between severity of cardiac disease and murmur
grade for other conditions, such as for ventricular septal
defects, dilated or restrictive cardiomyopathy (DCM/
RCM), and feline cardiomyopathies. Although the majority of dogs with heart disease have an audible murmur, it is
important to remember that some cardiac diseases (such
as pericardial diseases, cardiac neoplasia, DCM, atrial septal defects [ASD], right‐to‐left shunting PDA, and primary
myocardial diseases in cats) do not necessarily produce
blood flow turbulence and an audible murmur (Table 15.2).
Presence of a heart murmur does not always signal structural cardiac disease as murmurs in cats and dogs can also
arise due to other physiologic processes. Physiologic murmurs tend to be fairly quiet (grade 1/6–3/6), and may vary in
intensity with changes in heart rate. Mild dynamic right ventricular outflow tract obstruction is a common cause of murmurs in healthy cats in stressful situations such as examination
at a veterinary hospital. Puppies and kittens may have “innocent” physiologic murmurs assumed to arise due to large
stroke volumes relative to the size of their great vessels and/
or due to physiologic anemia. These murmurs usually disappear before approximately 5 months of age. Murmurs may
also be created in an anemic animal due to the combination
of decreased blood viscosity and increased stroke volume.
High‐output diseases, such as chronic renal disease and
hyperthyroidism, can also give rise to a systolic murmur due
to increased velocity of the ejected blood. Finally, murmurs
are common in fit dogs with athletic hearts, where the murmurs are caused by mild mitral/tricuspid valve insufficiency
and/or a large stroke volume into the aorta.
Respiratory Auscultation
Normal respiratory sounds differ in frequency (pitch),
intensity (loudness), and timing along different parts of
the animal’s upper and lower respiratory tract. Normal
lung sounds are comparably soft sounds heard louder on
inspiration than expiration, whereas normal sounds auscultated over the trachea are much louder and higher
pitched and heard well on both inspiration and expiration. Based on location and sound characteristics, normal lung sounds are commonly termed vesicular,
bronchial, or bronchovesicular, even though the term
“vesicular” incorrectly implies that sounds are made in
the vesicles (alveoli) of the lung.
Auscultation of the lungs of a cardiovascular patient
may reveal abnormal sounds superimposed on normal

lung sounds. Auscultation of dogs and cats presenting
with pulmonary edema often reveals harsh lung sounds,

Crackles are interrupted, nonmusical, crepitant sounds,
which in general are associated with conditions in which
some airways are closed. Crackles should not be considered pathognomic for pulmonary edema as primary respiratory disease can also produce crackles. Wheezes,
which are high‐frequency musical sounds of longer
duration associated with narrowing of an airway, can
also be heard in animals with pulmonary edema. Animals

can present with interstitial pulmonary edema without
any abnormal auscultatory sounds other than increased
bronchovesicular sounds due to hyperpnea.
Attenuated or absent bronchovesicular sounds can be
due to pleural effusion or shallow breathing. Animals
with pleural space disease, such as pleural effusion in
cats in decompensated CHF, often present with a paradoxical respiratory pattern with prominent abdominal
wall movements. Thoracic auscultation in these animals
may reveal dull lung sounds, muffled heart sounds, or an
auscultable fluid line.

Imaging in Cardiovascular Disease
Valérie Chetboul, DVM, PhD, DECVIM-CA (Cardiology)
National Veterinary School at Alfort, Maisons‐Alfort, France

The diagnosis of canine and feline heart diseases as well as
that of heart failure is predominantly based on thoracic
radiography associated with standard transthoracic echocardiography, also called conventional echocardiography.
In the late 1980s, the miniaturization of tran­sesophageal
probes led to the use of transesophageal echocardiography
especially for analyzing specific abnormalities or for monitoring surgical and interventional techniques. During the
last decade, newer imaging modalities such as tissue
Doppler imaging, strain and strain rate imaging, and
speckle tracking echocardiography have been introduced
in veterinary cardiology, allowing an accurate assessment
of myocardial performance, deformation, and synchrony.
The following chapter provides an overview of these imaging techniques and their application in clinical settings,
with particular emphasis on the two most commonly
used in practice: thoracic radiography and conventional
echocardiography.

­Cardiac Radiography
Although most radiographic findings are not specific and
therefore do not lead to an accurate definitive diagnosis
of a given heart disease, thoracic radiography remains a
key complementary examination to detect heart enlargement, assess the presence or absence of congestive heart
failure, and distinguish between respiratory and cardiovascular diseases.
Normal Thoracic Radiography
Heart and thoracic vessels should be systematically
evaluated on at least two good‐quality views taken
during inspiration – the dorsoventral view and a lateral
view. Ventrodorsal views may also be used, but dorsoventral views usually provide a better definition of

caudal pulmonary vessels and of the hilar area than the
ventrodorsal view, and therefore allow a better assessment of cardiogenic pulmonary edema, particularly in
the canine species. Additionally, dorsoventral views
are often better tolerated than ventrodorsal views in
the case of dyspnea. Ventrodorsal views, which are
most often associated with a more central position of
the heart within the thorax, may sometimes be used to
complement the dorsoventral view to detect small volumes of pleural effusion and to better assess specific
lung lesions.
In both canine and feline species, the heart shape is
most often relatively ovoid with a pointed ventral apex.
Nevertheless, several noncardiac factors (Table 16.1) can
influence heart size and shape, including respiratory
phase, pericardial fat accumulation (Figure 16.1), age and,
most of all, breed (see details below and Figure 16.2). All
these are important to take into consideration, as they
may be a source of misinterpretation of cardiomegaly.
Lateral Views

Either right or left lateral views may be performed.
Nevertheless, as some variations may exist according to
positioning of the patient, the same lateral projection
should be used to ensure a reliable comparison of radiographic findings over time in sequential radiographs.
On lateral views, the heart, which is located between
the third and sixth intercostal spaces, tends to “lie”
more on the sternum in cats than in dogs, and in older
cats (>7 years old) more than in younger cats (Figure
16.3). The maximum heart width (or maximum cranial–caudal diameter) is usually around two intercostal
spaces in the cat and between 2.5 and 3.5 intercostal
spaces in the dog, with breed variations (Figures 16.2
and 16.3). For example, the heart in “barrel‐chested”
dogs tends to be more globular, with a greater sternal

The vertebral heart score (VHS) may be used to objectively assess heart size, and to confirm and determine
the severity of cardiomegaly in both cats and dogs
(Figure 16.5). The mean ± SD canine VHS is 9.7 ± 0.5
vertebrae (range: 8.5–10.6). Nevertheless, VHS values
are influenced by breed‐dependent heart shape and size,
thoracic conformation (long versus short thorax), and
thoracic vertebrae abnormalities such as hemivertebrae.
For example, abnormal thoracic vertebrae have recently
been shown to be associated with a significant increase
of VHS in the bulldog and Boston terrier. Such breed‐
dependent variations of VHS (Table 16.2) represent a
limitation of the vertebral heart‐size method in the dog.
Nevertheless, the VHS system is easy to use and may be
helpful to objectively compare heart size in sequential
radiographs.
Feline VHS seems to be less subject to variations
than canine VHS, with normal values of 7.5 ± 0.3
vertebrae.

Common Abnormal Cardiac Radiographic
Patterns
Congenital and acquired heart diseases can be responsible
for generalized or localized cardiac enlargement associated with changes in the intrathoracic blood vessels. The
main cardiac causes responsible for left, right and global
heart enlargement are presented in Table 16.3 and in
Figures 16.7–16.12.
Left Heart Diseases (Figures 16.7–16.10)
Left Atrial Enlargement

On lateral views, left atrial enlargement is characterized by:
straightening of the dorsocaudal part of the cardiac
silhouette
●● dorsal elevation of the caudal portion of the trachea
and tracheal bifurcation (carina)
●● separation of the normally superimposed caudal main
bronchi owing to a disproportionate dorsal elevation
of the latter (with a more dorsal position of the left
bronchus as compared to the right).
●●

Figure 16.5 Calculation of the vertebral heart score (VHS) from a
thoracic lateral radiograph in a normal mixed‐breed dog. The
cardiac long‐axis dimension (L) represents the combined size of
the left atrium and the left ventricle, and is measured from the
cardiac apex to the base where it intersects the tracheal
bifurcation. The cardiac short‐axis dimension (S) is perpendicular
to L, and is measured at the point of maximum cardiac width,
which usually corresponds to the point at which the cardiac
silhouette intersects the ventral border of the caudal vena cava
(as shown here). S therefore includes left and right cardiac
chambers in the region of the coronary groove. L and S cardiac
dimensions are then transposed on the vertebral column and
recorded as the corresponding number of vertebrae (v), as
measured caudally from the cranial edge of the fourth thoracic
vertebra (T4). These values are summed to calculate the VHS. As
in the present case, L is equal to 5 v and S to 3.9 v, the VHS value
is 8.9 v, which is within normal ranges (8.5–10.6 v according to
Buchanan et al., J Am Vet Med Assoc 1995; 206: 194–9). Source:
Medical Imaging Unit, ENVA.

A clock face analogy can be used to approximately
localize the normal cardiovascular structures responsible
for the cardiac silhouette (Figure 16.6). This clock face
analogy can help in identifying the origin of bulges and
deformations of the cardiac silhouette associated with
heart diseases.
The VHS can also be calculated on the dorsoventral
view as follows: sum of cardiac long‐axis (distance
from cardiac apex to base) and short‐axis dimensions
(perpendicular to the long‐axis measurement at the
maximum cardiac width) assessed in vertebrae beginning with the cranial edge of the fourth vertebra on
the lateral radiograph. The feline VHS on the dorsoventral view is 8.1 ± 0.45 vertebrae. Also in the cat,
the maximum short‐axis cardiac dimension on the
dorsoventral view, ­compared with the thoracic spine
beginning at the cranial edge of the fourth vertebra on
the lateral chest radiograph, is usually less than four
vertebrae.

enlargement of the left auricular appendage (dog and
cat) and the left atrium (cat)
●● the presence of a round soft tissue opacity covering the

left atrial dilation in the dog (Figures 16.7b and 16.8c).
●●

Similar abnormal patterns are detected on the ventrodorsal view.

Left‐Sided Congestive Heart Failure

In the case of left‐sided congestive heart failure, prominent pulmonary veins owing to venous congestion are
seen, particularly in the hilar area (as they enter the left
atrium) on lateral views. The pulmonary vein diameter
appears greater than that of the corresponding arteries.
This asymmetry is easiest to detect for cranial vessels on

lateral views (where the pulmonary veins are ventral to
the accompanying arteries), and for caudal vessels on the

increased sternal contact, with widening and increased

●● a shift to the left of the cardiac apex in the case of

●●

Similar abnormal patterns are detected on the ventrodorsal view.
Right‐Sided Congestive Heart Failure

Thoracic radiographic signs of right‐sided congestive
heart failure include visualization of right heart
enlargement associated with widening of the caudal
vena cava (whose normal diameter is usually approximately that of the descending thoracic aorta) and interlobar pleural fissures secondary to pleural effusion
(with lung collapse and rounded pulmonary borders in
severe cases).
Extrathoracic radiographic signs include hepatomegaly (extension of the liver caudally to the last rib with
abnormally round margins and caudal displacement of
the stomach) and ascites, which is characterized by
abdominal distension and increased fluid opacity with
loss of intraabdominal details.

Diseases

heart diseases are presented in Table 16.3 and in

­Conventional Echocardiography
Over the last 30 years, standard transthoracic echocardiography has become a major imaging tool for the diagnosis, management, and follow‐up of canine and feline
heart diseases, allowing noninvasive assessment of heart
morphology (ventricles, atria, cardiac valves, auricular
appendages) and function, as well as examination of the
anatomy of the proximal great vessels.
General Principles and Technique
Conventional echocardiography combines 2D and M‐
mode imaging. M‐mode echocardiography provides
one‐dimensional views of the heart, while 2D echocardiography displays cross‐sectional or 2D cardiac images
(in transverse and longitudinal planes) moving in real

time. M‐mode echocardiograms display motion over
time of the various tissue interfaces crossed by the linear M‐mode ultrasound beam. Currently, the 2D mode
is always used to guide accurate placement of the
M‐mode cursor, which appears as a vertical line on
2D echocardiograms. M‐mode echocardiography has a
much higher spatial and temporal resolution than 2D
echocardiography, and therefore allows recording of
the motion of subtle cardiac structures.
Transthoracic 2D and M‐mode echocardiography
can be performed on animals in lateral recumbency or
in standing position, as the measurements obtained in
both positions show similar variability. Some animals
may not tolerate a recumbent position because of discomfort or dyspnea, making the standing position easier and more suitable. Placing the patient in lateral
recumbency decreases lung interference but, on the
other hand, may increase stress in nervous animals.

When patients are echoed in a recumbent position, a
special scanning table with a cutout is needed, and
images are obtained from beneath the table through the
table hole. The standing position does not require a
specific scanning table, as the animal is gently restrained
against an assistant to keep its position stable. For both
animal positions, the transducer is placed on the thoracic wall in an intercostal space over the precordial
impulse area, close to the ­sternum, to obtain parasternal views. However, subcostal (or subxiphoid) views
may sometimes be used for Doppler assessment of the
aortic outflow (as they may provide a better Doppler
beam alignment than parasternal views).
In most cases where manual restraint is sufficient,
sedation is avoided as it can alter systolic function and
may affect cardiac dimensions.

Most animals do not require clipping of hair over the
area of contact on the thoracic wall (more than 90% of
the patients at our unit are not clipped for conventional
echocardiographic examinations or for advanced ultrasound techniques, such as tissue Doppler imaging).
Acoustic gel helps to provide an optimal air‐free contact
between the probe and the thoracic wall.
High‐frequency transducers are characterized by low
penetrating power but high resolution. Conversely, low‐
frequency transducers are characterized by high penetrating power but low resolution. In canine and feline
cardiology, transducer frequencies are usually between
2.5 and 12 MHz. Transducer frequencies are commonly
adjusted during a single echocardiographic examination, depending on the location and size of the cardiovascular structures tested. As most commercially
