The previously beneficial augmentation of preload and
afterload now only serves to promote development of
congestion or amplify contractility‐afterload mismatch.
This cycle of disease progression continues as venous
pressures continue to rise, cardiac output declines, congestion develops, and clinical signs of heart failure begin
to emerge.
Myocyte Loss

A reduction in the number of viable myocytes or dysfunction of the viable myocytes may account for a component of reduced myocardial contractile function.
Cardiomyocyte death appears to occur via necrosis,
apoptosis, and autophagy although it is uncertain if all
three are distinctive events or a continuum of overlapping processes. Exposure of norepinephrine to cultured
mammalian cardiomyocytes produces a concentration‐
dependent decrease in viability and pathophysiologic
levels of AT II also promote myocytolysis. Therefore, it
seems that myocyte loss can occur via mechanisms
beyond ischemia and many of these mechanisms, including catecholamines, AT II, reactive oxygen species, nitric
oxide, inflammatory cytokines and mechanical strain,
are increased in the failing myocardium.
Reexpression of Fetal and Neonatal Genes and Altered
Contractile Proteins

Heart failure seems to alter both quantitative and qualitative protein expression, which may impair cardiac contractility. Isoforms of contractile proteins that are present
during fetal and neonatal life, when protein synthesis is
rapid, have been identified in some animal models of hypertrophy and myocardial failure. Pressure overload hypertrophy in rats produces a shift from the rapid myosin heavy
chain (MHC) isoform (V1) to the slow MHC isoform (V3),
enabling normal tension generation but at a lower energy
cost by reaching the tension more slowly. However, in species with a predominant V3 ventricular MHC isoform,
including dogs, cats, and humans, this change seems less
critical to development of heart failure. Fetal phenotypic
expression of other contractile proteins, including myosin
light chain, troponin‐I and troponin‐C, has been identified
in the myocardium of humans with heart failure and may
contribute to a decrease in cardiac contractile function.
Altered Excitation‐Contraction Coupling

Calcium is a critical ion in regulating myocardial contraction and relaxation. Alterations in calcium conductance
across the sarcolemma, release from the sarcoplasmic

181

VetBooks.ir

182

Section 3 Cardiovascular Disease

reticulum, or its resequestration into the sarcoplasmic
reticulum may exert profoundly negative consequences
on cardiac performance. Myocytes from humans with
heart failure exhibit a prolonged action potential with a
blunted rise in intracellular Ca2+ during depolarization
and a slowed rate of decline during repolarization. Slower
Ca2+ delivery to the contractile proteins during systole and
excessive cytosolic Ca2+ during diastole may contribute to
both systolic and diastolic dysfunction. The failing myocardium also displays a negative force–frequency relationship. Rather than progressive increases in ventricular
contractility with increasing heart rate, humans with heart
failure have little or no increase in contractility with
increased frequency of stimulation. This alteration is presumably related to impaired Ca2+ cycling between the sarcoplasmic reticulum and the cytosol.
Calcium conductance, release, and resequestration are
critical components of normal cardiac function and
numerous pumps and channels are responsible for coordinating events. Studies in failing human myocardium
have found that mRNA and protein levels of SERCA,
voltage‐dependent Ca2+ channels, and the calcium
release channel on the sarcoplasmic reticulum are
reduced. Alterations in proteins responsible for Ca2+
cycling in dogs have also been identified. Therefore,
altered expression or function of these proteins may negatively impact systolic and diastolic function.
Changes within the Extracellular Matrix

Ventricular remodeling is a key feature of heart failure
regardless of the underlying cardiac disease or underlying phenotype (e.g., volume overload, pressure overload,
primary cardiomyopathy). Changes within the ventricular geometry and function must be viewed as a summation of events occurring at the level of the cardiomyocyte,
the vascular compartment, and within the extracellular
matrix (ECM). Although once only viewed as scaffolding, there is now growing recognition that the ECM
mediates mechanical and biological signals that contribute to the progression of heart failure.
Regulation and turnover of the ECM is a complex process dictated by mechanical stress, neurohormonal activation, inflammation, and oxidative stress. Accelerated
growth of both the myocyte and ECM produced by pressure overload yield left ventricular concentric hypertrophy.
Left ventricular thickening negatively impacts both of
the fundamental processes that dictate diastolic function – active relaxation and passive stiffness. Shifting
­isoforms and phosphorylation sites of cytoskeletal proteins
(e.g., titin) can impair myocyte relaxation and hamper
active relaxation/early cardiac filling. Accumulation of
­collagen within the ECM increases ventricular stiffness,
thus reducing myocardial compliance and impairing
­passive ventricular filling. Volume overload triggers left

ventricular eccentric hypertrophy/remodeling with
increased ECM turnover via an increase in the matrix
metalloproteinases (MMPs)/tissue inhibitors of matrix
metalloproteinases (TIMPs) ratio. The MMPs degrade
collagen and other matrix components while the TIMPs
either inhibit or prevent MMP activation. Isoform shifts
from type I to type III collagen further contribute to a net
degradation of collagen with resultant chamber dilation
and progressive wall thinning.
During the compensated phase, the remodeling
­contributes to increased ventricular compliance with preserved systolic function. Ultimately, the progression to
decompensated failure is complex and includes a combination of ECM degradation and profibrotic ­
synthesis
mediated concomitantly at different subcellular locations
and within different regions of the ventricle.
Alterations in Cardiac Metabolism

The heart requires a high rate of adenosine triphosphate
(ATP) hydrolysis because of its continuous mechanical
work and therefore requires a constant supply of oxygen
and fuel. Oxidation of fatty acids (FA) accounts for
approximately 70–90% of ATP production in the fasted
state while glucose utilization increases in the fed state.
Because of the fundamental roles metabolism and ATP
generation have in maintenance of cardiac structure and
function, it is reasonable to hypothesize that alterations
in cardiac metabolism have a role in the pathophysiology
of heart failure. Studies in animal models and humans
with advanced heart failure and systolic dysfunction
have reported a decrease in the phosphocreatine/ATP
ratio, ATP content, and ATP movement through creatine
kinase. It is uncertain whether these alterations serve as
a primary contributor to the progressive nature of heart
failure or are simply an adaptation to decreased ventricular function, but significant mitochondrial changes are
present in various models of cardiac hypertrophy and
failure.
Decreased cardiac energy production may be secondary to impaired substrate use or altered mitochondrial
function. Studies of heart failure with systolic dysfunction have identified reduced mRNA and protein expression of FA transporters with reduced cardiac FA
utilization and ATP production. Studies of glucose oxidation are variable with reports of decreased, unchanged
or increased glucose uptake. Varying results likely
depend on the stage and type of disease, but these results
may also be influenced via the channeling of pyruvate
into anaplerotic pathways. Flux of pyruvate through anaplerotic pathways appears to be a hallmark of metabolic
remodeling and reduces its availability for oxidation and
energy production by pyruvate dehydrogenase.
Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH)
is also consumed by induction of anaplerotic pathways

VetBooks.ir

18 Pathophysiology of Heart Failure

which may lead to dysregulation of cellular oxidative
stress, thereby contributing to the progressive nature of
heart failure. Mitochondrial reactive oxygen species may
produce mitochondrial damage, activation of mitogen‐
activated protein kinases, cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis, again suggesting that alterations in organelles of
metabolism may contribute to ventricular remodeling.
The reactive oxygen species and mitochondrial damage
are also strong mediators of autophagy in certain settings
and may serve as an additional mechanism for remodeling and progression to heart failure.
Hemodynamics of Heart Failure
and Development of Pulmonary Edema
Progressive disturbances of systolic and diastolic
­function may ultimately lead to development of systemic
or pulmonary venous congestion as a consequence of
elevated venous pressure. Increased plasma volume (via
sodium and water retention) and reduced venous capacitance (via venoconstriction) no longer augment systolic
function in the failing heart and instead merely precipitate clinical signs associated with congestion.
Pulmonary capillary wedge pressures exceeding
25 mmHg are likely to precipitate signs of left‐sided heart
failure, including cough and increased respiratory rate and
effort. Pulmonary edema develops when the movement of
fluid from the blood to the interstitial space, and in some
instances to the alveoli, exceeds the return of fluid from the
interstitial space to the blood and its drainage through the
lymphatics. There is normally a continuous exchange of
fluid, colloid, and solutes from the vasculature into the
interstitial space so a pathologic state exists only when
there is an increase in the net flux of fluid, colloid, and solutes from the vasculature into the interstitial space. The
total microvascular filtration rate can change as a result of
changes in filtration surface area, membrane permeability
to water, hydrostatic and colloidal osmotic pressures, and
membrane permeability to protein. Lymphatic flow will
similarly be dictated by the hydrostatic pressure of the
interstitium, the pumping pressure within the lymphatics,
the systemic venous pressure, and the resistance to flow.
During stage 1 of pulmonary edema development, the
interstitial volume remains normal due to the compensatory
increase in lymphatic flow. In most tissues, the increase in
the hydrostatic interstitial pressure with the development of
interstitial edema would serve to inhibit microvascular filtration and enhance lymph flow. However, the interstitial
pressure rarely reaches high enough values to use this protective mechanism because (a) the increase in the interstitial
compliance allows large volume increases with small pressure increases and (b) alveolar flooding occurs at relatively
low interstitial pressures (2–3 mmHg). The more protective
mechanism in the lung is the decreased resistance to

­lymphatic flow as microvascular filtration increases. The
proposed mechanism is believed to be subsequent to
­“tethering” of the initial lymphatics to surrounding structures which pull the lymph vessels open as the interstitial
volume increases, thus increasing the radius and filtration of
the lymphatics.
Stage 2 occurs when the lymphatics’ capacity to
remove the interstitial fluid is overwhelmed. During
this stage, fluid and colloid accumulate in the interstitial areas around bronchioles, arterioles, and venules.
Fluid ­accumulation occurs within the peribronchial
and perivascular interstitial space (versus adjacent to
the alveolar capillary membrane) because of its more
negative pressure and more compliant properties. The
enlarged lymphatics and free fluid form cuffs around
the bronchioles and pulmonary blood vessels and may
subsequently compress the small airways and blood
vessels. Gas exchange may be relatively unaffected in
the early stages of edema if there is no increase in the
alveolar‐capillary membrane thickness along the thin
side of the interstitial space. But as capillary filtrate
continues to accumulate, the less compliant interstitium around the alveolar‐capillary septa also fills, the
interstitial pressure rises, and alveolar flooding begins
(stage 3). Arterial oxygenation decreases and in severe
cases death may ensue.

­Therapeutic Implications
Understanding of the pathophysiologic mechanisms
of heart failure enables development of therapeutic
strategies to provide symptomatic benefit and slow
the natural history of disease progression. With the
long‐standing recognition that fluid retention and
poor pump function contribute to pulmonary and
systemic venous congestion and low cardiac output,
the initial therapeutic strategies were to reduce
preload and afterload while augmenting contractility.
We continue to use these strategies today via the
administration of diuretics and inodilators to combat
many forms of heart failure. With further advances in
the understanding of cardiac remodeling, agents
capable of blocking critical neurohormonal pathways,
including ACE inhibitors, beta‐blockers, and aldosterone antagonists, were developed to prolong survival without imposing significant alterations in
cardiac loading conditions. And with further advances
in the understanding of myocyte loss, altered gene
expression, dysregulation of excitation‐contraction
coupling, degradation of the extracellular matrix and
deranged cardiac metabolism, new therapeutic agents
will continue to be identified in an effort to one day
halt the inevitable cycle that leads to heart failure.

Management of Heart Failure
Steven Rosenthal, DVM, DACVIM (Cardiology)1, and Mark A. Oyama, DVM, MSCE, DACVIM (Cardiology)2
1
2

CVCA Cardiac Care for Pets, Towson, MD, USA
Department of Clinical Sciences and Advanced Medicine, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA

Successful management of both acute and chronic heart
failure typically involves alleviation of congestion,
improvement in cardiac output and organ perfusion, and
maintenance of normal blood pressure and cardiac
rhythm. Patients with heart failure can be categorized
into those with subtle symptoms such as mild exercise
intolerance or respiratory signs versus patients with
debilitating and life‐threatening clinical signs such as
severe respiratory distress, collapse, syncope, or cardiogenic shock. Congestive heart failure (CHF) specifically
refers to patients with evidence of congestion in the form
of pleural or abdominal effusion, pulmonary edema or,
much less commonly, peripheral edema.
A variety of cardiac medications are used to restore and
maintain adequate cardiac function, along with diet
changes, nutritional supplements, and body cavity centesis.
During therapy of both acute and chronic heart failure,
patient hydration status, electrolytes, renal function, blood
pressure, urine output, respiratory rate and effort, and body
weight are monitored. During this time, patient quality of
life can remain very high in the absence of significant
amounts of congestion or adverse medication side‐effects.
As heart disease progresses, doses and number of cardiac
drugs are increased along with increasing risk of adverse
effects. In this chapter, the therapy of chronic, acute, and
refractory heart failure will be presented.

­Management of Chronic Heart Failure
The major goals of treatment of CHF are to alleviate and
prevent mild clinical signs, reduce likelihood of recurrent episodes of acute life‐threatening heart failure, and
increase longevity.
Management begins with a thorough medical history
and physical examination. Subtle changes in the resting

respiratory rate and/or exercise capacity can be useful
gauges that help clinicians formulate or modify treatment plans. In this capacity, owner education and home
monitoring are essential components of successful therapy. Rarely do canine or feline patient with early CHF
cough nor do they exhibit dramatic changes in activity or
exercise. Thus, daily monitoring of their resting home
respiratory rate is often the most effective monitoring
tool to detect CHF symptoms in their early stages.
Common oral medications for treatment of chronic heart
failure can be divided into the following five main groups:
diuretics, vasodilators, modulators of neurohormonal systems, antiarrhythmic agents, and positive inotropes. Some
medications will have effects in more than one group. In
addition to these conventional therapies, nutritional supplements and dietary modification are often beneficial. In
order to limit adverse reactions to medications, close monitoring of electrolytes, biochemical parameters, hydration
status, and blood pressure along with serial cardiac‐specific
tests (i.e., chest radiographs, electrocardiograms, echocardiograms) aid the practitioner in achieving effective treatment. Each patient responds to medications differently and
therapy is individualized to each cardiac patient.
Treatment of chronic heart failure depends almost
entirely on medical therapy. Exceptions would include
CHF due to bradycardia that is treated with artificial pacing, or CHF due to congenital heart defects such as patent
ductus arteriosus that are treated using surgery or minimally invasive catheter‐based techniques. Advancements
in the surgical management of degenerative valve disease
have been made over the past few years but due to cost
and limited surgical centers that perform the surgery, surgical valve repair or replacement is not a widely available
option for most pet owners. Due to the lack of controlled
clinical trial data, some of the therapy for both chronic
and acute heart failure is based on expert opinion.

Drugs for Treatment of Chronic Heart Failure
(Table 19.1)
Diuretics

Diuretics increase production of urine through affecting the kidney’s physiologic handling of water and
electrolytes. Diuretics result in an increased loss of
sodium (natriuresis) that is followed by water and
other electrolytes. Diuretics are the first‐line therapy
in patients with chronic CHF, but despite their efficacy
in resolving and preventing congestion, they are not
typically used as monotherapy due to their activation
of the renin‐angiotensin‐aldosterone system (RAAS).
One instance when diuretics are contraindicated for
the treatment of CHF is in patients with pericardial
effusion and cardiac tamponade. In this group, cardiac
output is markedly dependent on preload, and aggressive diuresis will worsen cardiac output, potentially
leading to cardiogenic shock.
Furosemide

Furosemide is first‐line therapy in the management of
chronic CHF. The goal of therapy is to prescribe the lowest diuretic dose required to control the clinical symptoms of congestion and edema. Compared to treatment
of pulmonary edema, relatively higher diuretic dosages
are often required to help resolve body cavity effusions,
such as pleural or abdominal effusion. In these instances,
routine thoracocentesis or abdominocentesis can aid in
minimizing the dose of furosemide needed.
There is a wide range of doses reported in the veterinary literature. In the authors’ experience, furosemide
doses of 1–4 mg/kg orally every 8–24 hours are utilized
in treating chronic CHF in the dog. The typical starting
dose of oral furosemide for a dog with first‐time CHF is
2–3 mg/kg/day. Cats are particularly sensitive to the
dehydrating effects of furosemide and dosages of 1–2 mg/
kg every 12–48 hours are preferred, with most cats
receiving a total of 1–2 mg/kg/day for first‐time CHF.
Lower doses spread over shorter dosage intervals may
result in less diuretic resistance as high doses can lead to
rebound effects and resistance due to greater stimulation
of the RAAS. Pet owners who become adept at monitoring respiratory rates and effort can often make small
adjustments in furosemide dosing at home to prevent
recurrent CHF symptoms.
Adverse effects of diuretics include electrolyte imbalances such as hypokalemia (often mitigated with the
concurrent use of angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEI) or spironolactone), hyponatremia, azotemia,
dehydration, and urinary ­incontinence. Renal function
and serum electrolytes should be routinely monitored.
The frequency of monitoring is based on furosemide
dosage, concurrent medications, previous bloodwork

results, and presence of concomitant conditions such as
renal insufficiency. The authors recommend checking
serum blood profiles within the first 10 days after starting
or changing an existing dose of furosemide, after which
routine rechecks every 3–6 months are performed.
Doses of furosemide might also be adjusted after adding
concomitant agents that can affect renal perfusion (i.e.,
vasodilators, positive inotropes, other diuretics, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory agents, etc.).
Spironolactone

Spironolactone is a diuretic as well as a neurohormonal
blocking agent due to its inhibition of aldosterone. In
chronic CHF, benefits of spironolactone involve modest
diuresis and antiremodeling effects on the myocardium,
kidneys, and vasculature through its blockade of aldosterone receptors. In humans and experimental animal
models, spironolactone reduces pathologic tissue hypertrophy and fibrosis. In both human and veterinary
patients, spironolactone improves survival times in
patients with chronic CHF. Based on anecdotal experience, one author (SR) recommends considering spironolactone therapy in patients with progressive heart
enlargement that have not yet experienced CHF, as well
as those patients with chronic heart failure. In dogs with
abdominal or pleural effusion, spironolactone is often
co‐administered with furosemide to help slow the recurrence of the effusion. Typical spironolactone dose in
dogs is 2 mg/kg/day. Monitoring of renal function and
electrolytes is recommended in a fashion similar to furosemide. The benefit of spironolactone in cats with CHF
is unknown. Previous study in cats suggests that 1.7–
3.3 mg/kg/day was well tolerated.
In dogs, adverse reactions include anorexia and hypersalivation that may be mitigated by administration with
food or in a gelatin capsule, azotemia, and electrolyte
imbalances. Reformulated and flavored preparations of
spironolactone are difficult to administer due to their
still unpleasant taste. Due to its potassium‐sparing
effects, spironolactone can also predispose to hyperkalemia. This is most common when spironolactone is
used in combination with an ACEI.
Vasodilators

In the late 1980s and early 1990s, the use of vasodilators
became part of the standard CHF treatment in both
human and veterinary medicine. The benefits for the
hemodynamic and, in the case of ACEI, neurohormonal
aspects of heart failure contributed to widespread use
across many different species and many types of heart
disease. ACEI, nitrates, amlodipine, hydralazine, and
sildenafil are the most common agents utilized in veterinary patients. The majority of clinical data in veterinary
medicine involves ACEI for the treatment of chronic

CHF and ACEI are considered the first‐line choice for
vasodilator therapy in dogs and cats with CHF. In humans,
angiotensin receptor blockers can be used if ACEI are not
tolerated (intractable cough is a common side‐effect), but
relatively little is known about the use of angiotensin
receptor blockers in veterinary patients with chronic CHF.
ACE Inhibitors

ACE inhibitors are commonly used, including benazepril
(0.25–0.5 mg/kg PO q12–24h in dogs and cats), enalapril
(0.5 mg/kg PO S‐BID in dogs and cats), lisinopril (0.25–
0.5 mg/kg PO SID in dogs), ramipril (0.25 mg/kg PO SID
in dogs), and imidipril (0.25–0.5 mg/kg PO SID in dogs).
There is no obvious clinical benefit of one ACEI over the
other and their differences lie in their absorption, metabolism, and excretion. Benazepril is activated in the liver to
benazeprilat and, in dogs, is equally excreted by the biliary and renal routes while in cats, benazepril is primarily
excreted by the biliary route. Enalapril is activated in the
liver to its active metabolite, enalaprilat, and excreted by
the kidneys. Lisinopril is absorbed in its active form and
excreted by the kidney while ramipril may have more
effect on tissue‐specific RAAS and is partially excreted in
the urine and feces.
The authors typically use enalapril as the first choice
due to long‐standing clinical experience with this agent
as well as the convenient sizes of commercially available
tablets in the US (2.5, 5, 10, and 20 mg). In instances of

known renal dysfunction, benazepril is often the ACEI of
choice due to its nonrenal excretion, especially in feline
patients. Lisinopril is absorbed in its active form and does
not require hepatic metabolism to be active. Lisinopril is
excreted in the urine, and this drug could be chosen for
patients with concurrent cardiac and hepatic disease.
In general, ACEI are well tolerated. The most common
adverse events are azotemia and hypotension. In the
authors’ experience, initiating full dosing of an ACEI
during concomitant aggressive diuretic treatment of
acute CHF can occasionally lead to hypotension and
severe azotemia. ACEI do not appear essential for the
successful resolution of acute CHF, and the authors usually initiate ACEI therapy only once patients are stable
with only mild or no remaining CHF (see Treatment of
Acute Heart Failure later) and when hydration status and
blood pressure are adequate. ACEI are not particularly
potent arterial vasodilators and their benefits are most
likely due to the long‐term suppression of the RAAS.
The authors recommend checking a baseline renal and
electrolyte profile and within the first 10 days after starting the medication. Owners should be instructed to
monitor for poor appetite, lethargy, vomiting, or changes
in water consumption or urine output.
In instances where underlying renal insufficiency or
volume depletion is present, the authors occasionally
start enalapril at either 0.5 mg/kg q24h or 0.25 mg/kg
BID for the first 3–5 days of treatment and titrating to a

VetBooks.ir

19 Management of Heart Failure

higher dose over the first 7–10 days of treatment. Blood
pressure, renal function, and electrolyte monitoring is
performed every 3–6 months thereafter. In humans, idiosyncratic nocturnal cough is an important adverse
effect, but this has not been reported in dogs, and any
coughing is usually due to concurrent chronic airway
disease.
Other Vasodilators

Other vasodilators used for treatment of chronic CHF
include hydralazine, amlodipine, and nitrates. These
agents are discussed in the section regarding treatment
of refractory heart failure.
Positive Inotropes

Use of positive inotropes for the treatment of heart failure has been a subject of controversy due to a potential
increase in the risk of sudden death due to arrhythmias.
Conventional positive inotropes such as digoxin, dobutamine, and dopamine act by increasing cytosolic calcium that improves cardiac contractility but might also
precipitate cardiac arrhythmias. The objective of positive inotropic therapy is to increase myocardial contractility and improve cardiac output and organ perfusion.
Digoxin and pimobendan are the two most commonly
used agents for the treatment of chronic CHF in the veterinary patient.
Digoxin

Digoxin is one of the oldest cardiac medications known
and has positive inotropic and negative chronotropic
(slowing conduction through the atrioventricular [AV]
node) effects, as well as beneficial effects on the baroreceptors and neurohormonal axis such as the RAAS.
Even though it has been used for over 200 years, its benefits for survival have not been proven. In dogs,
pimobendan has largely supplanted digoxin as the positive inotrope of choice. Digoxin is associated with a high
incidence of adverse reactions including gastrointestinal
upset and cardiac arrhythmias. The recommended
canine dose is 0.005–0.0075 mg/kg q12h. In cats, digoxin
is not commonly used, in part due to the drug’s long half‐
life. The feline dose is ¼ of a 0.125 mg tablet (0.03125 mg)
every other day for smaller cats and once a day for larger
cats. The dosage in patients with renal disease is reduced
since digoxin is excreted by the kidneys. Dosage should
be based on lean body mass and reduced in obese pets or
those with significant ascites. Oral absorption of digoxin
can be altered by the formulation, concurrent medications, or food. The elixir (0.05 mg/mL) is better absorbed
than the tablet formulation although is not palatable to
most cats. As such, slightly lower doses are often prescribed when using the elixir over tablets. Antacid agents
like sucralfate will reduce the absorption of digoxin, as

will diets high in fiber. Certain antibiotics like tetracyclines will alter the bacterial flora and may increase
serum digoxin levels.
The primary indication for digoxin in dogs (and to a
much lesser extent in cats) with heart disease is to slow
AV nodal conduction and ventricular response rate in
patients with atrial fibrillation. Digoxin is indicated for
the treatment of atrial fibrillation, persistent atrial and
sinus tachycardias, and progressive myocardial dysfunction. It may also help reduce syncope in patients with
severe mitral regurgitation due to its pharmacologic
effects, including its effects on baroreceptors.
Contraindications for use include complex ventricular
arrhythmias, renal disease, atrioventricular block, certain types of ventricular preexcitation, and sinus node
dysfunction.
Due to the risk of toxicity, serum digoxin levels are
typically monitored 10–14 days after initiation or any
dose changes. Blood should be drawn 6–8 hours post pill
to assess “trough” concentrations. Traditionally, serum
digoxin levels between 0.8 and 2.0 ng/dL have been considered to be therapeutic. Based on recent data in
humans, the authors commonly target a lower serum
level of 0.6–1.2 ng/dL as lower levels remain beneficial
but with a lower incidence of adverse reactions. In the
authors’ experience, gastrointestinal upset and anorexia
can occur at levels as low as 1.5 ng/dL. Anecdotally, miniature schnauzers and Doberman pinschers are more
sensitive to digoxin and lower starting doses are recommended for these breeds (no greater than 0.125 mg q12h
as a starting dose in Dobermans regardless of their body
weight). Pet owners are recommended to administer the
digoxin along a consistent interval and regimen. Since
certain foods and medications can alter absorption, the
owner should continue the same feeding and dosing regimen once therapeutic serum levels are achieved.
Changes in renal function will affect digoxin excretion,
and digoxin and electrolyte levels are routinely evaluated
every six months or when changes are made in concurrent medications.
Pimobendan

Pimobendan is widely used for the treatment of canine
heart failure secondary to dilated cardiomyopathy
(DCM) and myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD).
Recently, studies have shown the benefits of this agent in
the preclinical stage of MMVD once a moderate degree
of radiographic and echocardiographic cardiac enlargement has developed.
Pimobendan is a calcium sensitizer and phosphodiesterase inhibitor and its benefits are a result of the combination of positive inotropic properties along with effects
as a vasodilator. Its dual action is often indicated by the
term “inodilator.” Pimobendan is used as the first‐line

189

VetBooks.ir

190

Section 3 Cardiovascular Disease

positive inotrope and forms part of standard “quadruple
therapy” for CHF in dogs along with ACEI, furosemide,
and spironolactone. The recommended dose in dogs is
0.5 mg/kg/day divided into two doses given 12 hours
apart. Pimobendan has also been shown to prolong time
to CHF and death in asymptomatic Doberman pinschers
with echocardiographic evidence of reduced systolic
function and ventricular enlargement consistent with
preclinical DCM. In humans, positive inotropes exacerbate cardiac arrhythmias that can lead to increased risk
of sudden death, and use of pimobendan in Doberman
pinschers with preclinical DCM and severe ventricular
arrhythmias has not been specifically evaluated.
In general, pimobendan is well tolerated. The most
common adverse reaction is anorexia and diarrhea that
often resolves at lessened dosage. Pimobendan should be
used with caution in disorders with a ventricular outflow
tract obstruction such as congenital subvalvular aortic
stenosis or hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.
Pimobendan does not have an approved use in cats
with CHF, but has been occasionally used in cats with
heart failure. Pimobendan is not recommended in the
preclinical stages of feline cardiomyopathy or in cats
with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction.
Pimobendan is most often used in cats with systolic
myocardial dysfunction that is associated with dilated
cardiomyopathy as well as end‐stage hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), restrictive cardiomyopathy
(RCM), and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy cases. Most reports of pimobendan use in cats
utilize the same dosing protocol that is used in dogs
(0.25 mg/kg BID). The overall safety and efficacy of
pimobendan in cats requires further study.
Beta‐Adrenergic Blockers

Beta‐adrenergic blockers (BB) are part of standard care
in humans with systolic dysfunction. Chronic administration of BB such as carvedilol or metoprolol results in
improved contractility, myocardial protection from circulating catecholamines, and improved survival.
Whether or not BB benefit veterinary patients with heart
disease or failure is unknown as there are relatively limited data compared to ACEI and pimobendan. The three
most common clinical situations for which BB are typically considered are rate control of atrial fibrillation
wherein BB are co‐administered with digoxin, in the preclinical or stable heart failure phase of DCM in dogs, and
in cats with HCM or RCM, with special consideration
for cats with dynamic left ventricular outflow tract
obstruction.
Beta‐adrenergic blockers are often used in conjunction with digoxin to treat persistent supraventricular
arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation (see Chapter 21).
The BB dose can be gradually up titrated to achieve

target heart rate. Overly aggressive combinations of
­
digoxin, BB, and calcium channel blockers can produce
bradycardia. Some cardiologists recommend BB during
the preclinical phase of DCM in dogs. Successful institution and titration of BB is regarded as easier in the
­preclinical phase as opposed to starting BB after deve­
lopment of CHF. Sudden withdrawal of BB can result
in reflex tachycardia so that dosing should continue
even if CHF eventually occurs. However, the dosage may
require adjustment based on clinical symptoms, blood
pressure, and heart rate. Limited studies in dogs indicate
that titration of BB is relatively well tolerated by patients,
but the long‐term effect on cardiac function and survival is unknown.
In general, BB should only be introduced in patients
free of active CHF as their negative inotropic properties
can acutely reduce cardiac function and exacerbate clinical signs. When used in dogs with DCM, BB are typically
titrated upward over 4–8 weeks. The initial prescribed
dosage of BB is as little as 1/10th of the target dose and
titrated upward based on heart rate and blood pressure.
The authors will often temporarily increase the dose of
concurrent furosemide while introducing BB in patients
with advanced disease. Gradual reduction in the dosage
over several weeks is recommended if a decision is made
to cease treatment with chronic BB. Systemic hypotension can be seen when BB are used concomitantly with
vasodilatory drugs such as ACEI or pimobendan. BB use
in the preclinical phase of MMVD is not recommended.
BB are commonly used to slow heart rate in cats with
HCM or RCM, especially if left ventricular outflow tract
obstruction due to systolic anterior motion of the mitral
valve is present (see Chapter 27). BB are usually not prescribed to cats with active CHF; rather, they are used in
the preclinical or stable heart failure phases. Typically,
BB are titrated to achieve in‐hospital heart rate less than
160 bpm in cats. Monitoring of heart rate, systolic blood
pressure, and severity of left ventricular outflow tract
obstruction is recommended in cats with HCM.
The various BB are classified according to their selectivity for different beta‐receptors. Additionally, there are
differences involving lipophilicity, metabolism, antiarrhythmic effects, and vasodilatory properties amongst
the various BB. The most common BB used in veterinary
cardiology include atenolol, carvedilol, metoprolol, and
sotalol.
Atenolol is a beta‐1‐specific antagonist dosed at
0.25–1 mg/kg BID in dogs and 6.25–12.5 mg/cat q12–
24h in feline patients. Atenolol is commonly used in the
treatment of HCM in cats and congenital subvalvular
aortic stenosis in dogs. Carvedilol is a nonspecific BB,
acting on both beta‐1 and beta‐2 receptors, and has
adjunctive alpha‐1‐adrenergic blocking effects leading to
vasodilation. Carvedilol is metabolized in the liver and

VetBooks.ir

19 Management of Heart Failure

there are rare reports of hepatotoxicity. Initial dosage of
carvedilol is 0.05–0.1 mg/kg BID and is slowly titrated
upward over 4–8 weeks to a final target dose of 0.5–
1.0 mg/kg BID. Metoprolol is a beta‐1‐specific antagonist that is metabolized by the liver. Target dose is
0.2–0.4 mg/kg BID and 0.4–1 mg/kg q24h for the sustained‐release preparation. In humans, studies suggest a
benefit of sustained‐release formulations due to more
stable blood levels. Sotalol is a nonselective BB with
potassium channel‐blocking antiarrhythmic properties.
It is primarily used as an antiarrhythmic agent in dogs
with DCM or arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy and is dosed at 1–3 mg/kg BID in dogs and
2 mg/kg BID in cats (see Chapter 20).
Calcium Channel Blockers

Diltiazem, amlodipine, and rarely verapamil are calcium
channel blockers (CCB) used in the management of
chronic heart failure. Differences in the three agents
center around their propensity for cardiac effects on heart
rate and myocardial contractility versus peripheral effects
of smooth muscle relaxation and peripheral vasodilation.
Among the most commonly used CCB, amlodipine has
the greatest vasodilatory properties, followed by diltiazem
and then verapamil. Conversely, verapamil is a potent
negative cardiac chronotrope and negative inotrope, followed by diltiazem and then amlodipine, the latter of
which has very little effect on cardiac myocardial tissue.
In dogs, the most common indication for diltiazem is
for ventricular rate control in atrial fibrillation and is
dosed at 0.5–1.5 mg/kg q8h (See Chapter 21) Sustained‐
release preparations (Cardizem® CD and Dilacor®) are
dosed at 3 mg/kg BID in dogs. Diltiazem is often prescribed in cats with HCM with or without atrial fibrillation and including cats with left ventricular outflow tract
obstruction. The authors use either diltiazem or atenolol
in cats with severe HCM and echocardiographic evidence of diastolic dysfunction. Diltiazem is typically
added to the treatment regimen once the cat is receiving
furosemide, ACEI, and antithrombotic agents. In cases
of active CHF, the authors often delay initiation of CCB
or BB until after the patient is stable on the aforementioned cardiac drugs to try to reduce the incidence of
adverse reactions, such as bradycardia or hypotension.
In cats, diltiazem is dosed at 7.5 mg/cat q8h. Sustained‐
release diltiazem preparations are available (Cardizem
CD, 10 mg/kg q24h; Dilacor XR 30 mg/cat q12 h).
Canine patients generally tolerate diltiazem while cats
have a higher incidence of gastrointestinal upset, loss of
appetite, and hypersalivation. The authors recommend
administering diltiazem with food or encapsulating the
tablet in a gelatin capsule to hide the adverse taste from
the cat. Diltiazem has some negative inotropic effects
that can exacerbate signs of CHF, although this is less

common than with BB. Diltiazem also has mild vasodilatory properties and monitoring blood pressure and heart
rate is recommended.
Verapamil is rarely used in veterinary patients although
it is commonly used in humans with HCM. One author
(SR) has seen benefit in feline HCM patients with severe
left ventricular hypertrophy and dynamic left ventricular
outflow tract obstruction. Verapamil provides heart rate
control in addition to supposed effects on diastolic function. Gastrointestinal side effects are common when
using verapamil and can be minimized by administering
with food. In cats, verapamil has a starting dose of 1 mg/
kg BID with upward titration based on clinical signs,
heart rate, and blood pressure over 2–3 weeks to a maximal dose of 5 mg/kg BID, with a target heart rate between
120 and 160 bpm. Amlodipine will be discussed under
the refractory treatment of congestive heart failure.
Antithrombotic Therapy
Thromboembolism is a common risk factor in human
patients with chronic heart failure, especially in the presence of atrial fibrillation. In dogs, clinical systemic arterial thrombosis is uncommon while in cats, arterial
thromboembolism is a devastating clinical complication
of cardiomyopathy. The exact mechanism behind arterial thrombosis is complex and the most effective strategy to prevent and treat is unknown.
Chronic oral agents commonly administered to reduce
the risk of thrombosis are aspirin and clopidrogrel. Less
commonly, warfarin or injectable unfractionated or low
molecular weight heparin are used. More recently, the use
of factor Xa inhibitors like rivaroxaban and apixaban has
been recommended for patients with recurrent emboli or
poor tolerance to other antithrombotic agents. In one
study, clopidogrel was more effective than aspirin in preventing reoccurrence of thromboembolism in cats with a
previous history of thrombus. Antithrombotic agents are
also empirically administered in cases with a perceived
increased risk thromboembolism. These risk factors
include the presence of an intracardiac thrombus, spontaneous echocardiographic contrast (“smoke”), severe left
atrial dilation, protein‐losing nephropathies, hypoproteinemia, pulmonary hypertension, immune‐mediated
hemolytic anemia or heartworm disease. For aspirin therapy, the authors utilize 20–81 mg/cat q72h in cats and
1–5 mg/kg q24h in dogs. Clopidrogrel is dosed at ¼ of a
75 mg tablet (18.75 mg) q24h in cats and 3–5 mg/kg q24h
in dogs. Cats, in particular, often do not like the taste of
clopidrogel, which can lead to vomiting, hypersalivation,
anorexia, and difficulties in pill administration.
Antithrombotics agents can lead to adverse reactions
when used with corticosteroids or nonsteroidal antiinflammatory agents and might reduce the efficacy of

191

VetBooks.ir

192

Section 3 Cardiovascular Disease

some cardiac therapies such as diuretics or spironolactone. During administration, renal function is monitored and pet owners are instructed about possible
gastrointestinal side‐effects. Chronic monitoring of
coagulation profiles is not required with aspirin and
clopidrogel and thus they are more commonly used in
veterinary patients than anticoagulant agents such as
warfarin or heparin.
Dietary Modifications
Maintenance of caloric intake is essential in the management of chronic heart failure. Traditionally, restriction of
sodium was regarded as beneficial for the management
of heart disease despite concern that very low sodium
diets may further activate the RAAS. Diets that are mildly
(80–100 mg Na/100 kcal) or moderately (50–80 mg
Na/100 kcal) restricted in sodium should be considered
for patients with chronic CHF. Severely sodium‐restricted
diets (<50 mg Na/100 kcal) are reserved for patients with
advanced heart failure, severe hypertension, or cardiogenic body cavity effusions. Monitoring of blood electrolytes, in particular sodium and potassium, is important if
severely sodium‐restricted diets are fed.
Chronic heart failure is a catabolic state and results in
a progressive loss of body condition and muscle tone.
This “cardiac cachexia” requires adequate caloric and
protein intake. In patients with concurrent renal disease,
protein intake needs to be balanced between these competing conditions. The catabolic state is partly a result of
inflammatory mediators and some evidence suggests the
benefit of fish‐based omega 3 fatty acids to help slow
weight loss. Supplementation with the omega 3 fatty
acids is typically considered in patients with weight loss
and muscle wasting as well as in patients with ventricular
arrhythmias (see Chapter 26). Care should be taken to
avoid the fish oils that are combined with other sources
such as flax seed oil or cod liver oil due to the potential
for vitamin D toxicosis. Fish oil is dosed based on the
amount of beneficial omega 3 fatty acids provided. In
dogs, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic
acid (DHA) are dosed at 40 mg/kg and 25 mg/kg per day,
respectively.
Taurine deficiency is a known cause of dilated cardiomyopathy in cats, but due to universal supplementation
in commercial cat food, this form of cardiomyopathy is
rarely detected. In rare cases of feline taurine deficiency,
patients are supplemented with taurine at 250 mg PO
BID. Taurine deficiency has also been reported in various breeds of dogs, including Newfoundlands, American
cocker spaniels, and golden retrievers. In these dogs,
taurine‐deficient DCM is treated with 35 mg/kg taurine
BID. A complete diet history and whole blood or plasma
taurine assay are recommended by the authors in any

dog with apparent DCM diagnosed in a breed other than
the “typical” breeds (i.e., Doberman pinscher, Great
Dane, boxer, mastiff, or Irish wolfhound) known for this
disease. L‐carnitine (50 mg/kg PO TID) and coenzyme
Q10 (30–90 mg PO BID) are two additional supplements.
L‐carnitine is most commonly considered in American
cocker spaniels that are taurine deficient. Unlike taurine
deficiency, diagnosis of L‐carnitine deficiency requires
myocardial biopsy, which is rarely performed. In a small
unpublished evaluation of Dalmatians with dilated cardiomyopathy, one of the authors (SR) found improved
survival times when taurine, carnitine, and coenzyme
Q10 were administered along with conventional cardiac
therapy.

­Therapy for Refractory Chronic
Heart Failure
As previously described, conventional treatment of
chronic CHF in dogs consists of “quadruple” therapy
with furosemide, ACEI, pimobendan, and spironolactone. In patients with refractory CHF despite conventional therapy, additional treatments are provided in
order to combat recurrent symptoms of heart failure.
Additional Diuretics
Recurrent CHF necessitates gradual increases in the
doses of diuretics such as furosemide and spironolactone. A common clinical observance is the apparent
reduction of diuretic efficacy as furosemide doses
approach 6–12 mg/kg/day in dogs and 3–4 mg/kg/day in
cats. The reasons for diuretic resistance are varied and
complex. One cause is the reduction of oral bioavailability and resultant decrease in plasma concentration. This,
coupled with poor organ perfusion due to low cardiac
output, reduces the delivery of furosemide to the
nephron. In cases of advanced CHF, and particularly in
cases of recurrent abdominal or pleural effusion, the
authors often consider replacing one or more oral
administrations of furosemide with a daily subcutaneous injection of furosemide. Anecdotal experience indicates that restoration of diuresis can often be achieved
using this strategy. As with insulin injections, owners
can quickly learn to how administer SC injections at
home. Injectable furosemide is light sensitive and owners are instructed to keep the drug out of direct light.
Injectable furosemide is relatively alkaline and may
cause reactions at the injection site that include local
scabbing or plaque formation. In the authors’ experience, these appear less common when using the Salix®
brand of furosemide.

VetBooks.ir

19 Management of Heart Failure

A common strategy in patients with refractory CHF is
to layer additional diuretics onto the existing furosemide
therapy. This strategy of “sequential nephron blockade”
involves adding diuretics that act at sites other than the
loop of Henle. Addition of hydrochlorthiazide (0.5 mg/kg
SID or 1 mg/kg q48 h) or, if not already being administered, spironolactone (2 mg/kg/day) can be considered.
Adverse reactions to high‐dose or multiple diuretics
include severe azotemia, anorexia, dehydration, and
electrolyte abnormalities. This is particularly important
in patients are partially anorexic or eating diets severely
restricted in sodium.
Another option to improve diuresis is to replace furosemide with another diuretic such as torsemide (alternative spelling, torasemide). Torsemide, like furosemide, is
a loop diuretic. In humans, torsemide is characterized by
more reliable gastrointestinal absorption, a longer half‐
life, and adjunctive antialdosterone effects. In dogs, torsemide has a longer half‐life and is well suited for both
resolution and long‐term control of CHF. Torsemide is
markedly more potent than furosemide and the recommended dose range for treatment of CHF in dogs is 0.1–
0.6 mg/kg SID. Dogs with mild CHF typically require
0.1–0.3 mg/kg SID and any increases in dose in response
to reoccurrence of clinical signs are done in 0.1 mg/kg/
day increments. In dogs with CHF refractory to existing
doses of furosemide (typically >6 mg/kg/day), replacement of furosemide involves replacing the total daily
dose of furosemide with 1/10th to 1/20th the dosage of
torsemide. For example, if the existing furosemide dose
was 25 mg BID, the equivalent torsemide dose would be
1/10th to 1/20th of 50 mg or 2.5–5 mg per day. There are
limited reports of use of torsemide in cats. The dose
range in cats is likely similar to that in dogs. Torsemide,
like all diuretics, requires close monitoring of renal function, electrolytes, blood pressure, hydration status, and
body weight.
Clinicians might wish to consult with a specialist to
discuss individualized treatment and monitoring plans
in patients with refractory CHF. In general, the need for
diuretics in addition to or in place of furosemide in
patients with refractory signs of CHF is considered a
poor prognostic sign.
Volume depletion is caused by high dose and potent
diuretics and affects renal excretion of other cardiac
drugs, such as digoxin, and close monitoring of such
drugs is needed.
Thus, the risk for digoxin toxicity increases with worsening hypovolemia. In late stages of CHF, free water
retention by arginine vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone)
can result in severe hyponatremia and hypochloremia.
These electrolyte derangements can be difficult to treat.
Occasionally, cautious addition of sodium chloride or
potassium chloride to the diet, warm sodium chloride

enemas, diuretic reduction, or cautious restriction of
water intake can be performed. Hyponatremia is considered a poor prognostic sign in dogs with chronic CHF.
Additional Vasodilators
Patients with refractory CHF might benefit from vasodilator therapy in addition to standard administration of
ACEI. In these instances, use of arterial vasodilators
such as hydralazine or amlodipine is occasionally considered. Due to the perceived relationship between afterload (which is approximated by the aortic systolic blood
pressure) and degree of mitral regurgitation, arterial
vasodilators are often considered in dogs with refractory
CHF due to MMVD, but their efficacy in reducing the
degree of regurgitation is unknown. The limiting factor
in the administration of additional vasodilators is systemic hypotension, and vasodilators are not prescribed
if the baseline systemic systolic blood pressure is
<100 mmHg. Amlodipine (0.–0.4 mg/kg PO BID in dogs
and cats) is a calcium channel blocker with potent antihypertensive properties. A starting dosage of 0.1 mg/kg
BID and uptitrating over two weeks to the higher dosage
of 0.3–0.4 mg/kg BID is typically well tolerated. Prior to
the widespread use of amlodipine as an antihypertensive
agent in both dogs and cats, hydralazine was often used
in dogs and continues to be an option in refractory cases
of canine MMVD. Hydralazine (0.5–2 mg/kg PO BID) is
a direct‐acting vasodilator with a shorter half‐life and
more rapid onset of action than amlodipine. Thus, acute
hypotension and reflex tachycardia are more common
than with amlodipine. In emergency situations where
acute arterial vasodilation is needed (i.e., acute life‐
threatening CHF or systemic hypertension), hydralazine
is considered. Common adverse effects of hydralazine
include hypotension and gastrointestinal signs.
Oral nitrate compounds such as sustained‐release
isosorbide dinitrate or mononitrate (0.5–2.0 mg/kg PO
BID in dogs and cats) are infrequently used as a venous
vasodilator. Administration is usually performed when
signs of congestion persist despite diuretic usage or further increases in diuretic usage are hindered by concomitant azotemia or arterial hypotension. Due to rapid
development of tolerance, oral nitrates are typically
administered in two doses eight hours apart with a 16‐
hour drug‐free interval. In humans who are intolerant of
ACEI, hydralazine or amlodipine along with an oral
nitrate is administered, albeit with less clinical benefit
than ACEI.
Pulmonary hypertension (PHT) (see Chapter 23) is a
common complication in patients with advanced heart
failure, especially those with MMVD. Signs of PHT
include right‐sided heart failure, syncope, and persistent
tachypnea in the absence of pulmonary edema.

Echocardiography can help confirm the diagnosis.
Phosphodiesterase V inhibitors, such as sildenafil
(1–3 mg/kg PO TID) or tadalafil (1 mg/kg PO SID) are
variably effective. In the authors’ experience, sildenafil
seems to be more effective than tadalafil. Both drugs can
be very expensive, especially in large‐breed dogs. Both
agents are well tolerated in dogs. Rarely, inguinal flushing
and gastrointestinal upset are noted. Systemic hypotension is rare. Monitoring of the clinical symptoms as well
as pulmonary and systemic pressures is recommended.
Positive Inotropes
In cases of refractory heart failure due to DCM or
MMVD, off‐label dosages of pimobendan are often utilized. The authors will increase frequency of dosing from
0.25 mg/kg BID to TID followed by a slow titration to
0.5 mg/kg TID as needed. Additional pimobendan can
also be effective in cases of biventricular heart failure as
well as in patients with PHT. Cats with DCM or other
forms of systolic dysfunction also appear to tolerate
doses of pimobendan greater than 0.25 mg/kg BID. On
rare occasions, three days of dobutamine infusion in the
hospital at 2.5–10 μg/kg/min can be considered as there
might be some residual positive inotropic benefit for
some time after the hospitalization. Oral digoxin can be
added to the existing treatment regimen, especially if
tachyarrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation are present.
Care should be taken to monitor serum digoxin levels to
avoid toxicity.
Cough Suppression
Many canine patients with chronic heart failure develop a
cough secondary to bronchial compression as a result of
bronchomalacia and severe atrial dilation. In the absence
of CHF, a variable amount of cough suppression is
achieved with hydrocodone (0.22–0.44 mg/kg PO B‐QID)
or butorphanol (0.55 mg/kg PO B‐QID). Bronchodilators,
such as aminophylline or theophylline, are typically
ineffective.

­Therapy of Acute Life‐Threatening
Heart Failure
Therapy for acute‐life threatening heart failure is based
on many of the same principles that guide therapy for
chronic heart failure, namely diuresis to alleviate congestion, vasodilators to reduce preload and afterload, and
positive inotropes to improve myocardial contractility
(Table 19.2). In acute heart failure, hemodynamic abnormalities such as congestion and low cardiac output predominate and therapy is targeted towards resolution of

congestion, such as pulmonary edema, pleural effusion,
or ascites, and improvement of forward cardiac output
and tissue perfusion. In general, more attention is given
to stabilization of hemodynamics versus interruption of
neurohormonal systems, such as the RAAS or sympathetic nervous systems that are so critical to treatment of
chronic heart failure.
Diuretics
Diuretics are a mainstay of treatment of acute CHF.
Treatment induces potent and rapid diuresis. Parameters
commonly monitored during diuresis include respiratory rate and effort, body weight, urine production, electrolytes, renal function, and blood pressure. Furosemide
is the most commonly used diuretic for the treatment of
acute CHF. When given by IV, IM, or SC routes, diuresis
begins within 5–10 minutes and reaches a peak at 30–60
minutes with duration of action between two and three
hours. A typical initial dose is 2–4 mg/kg IV/IM/SC in
dogs and 1–2 mg/kg IV/IM/SC in cats. Because of its
relatively short duration of action, repeated bolus injections of furosemide are needed if respiratory rate and
other clinical signs are not improved within 2–4 hours
after initial dose. During administration, patients should
produce large quantities of dilute urine, and failure to
induce diuresis should alert clinicians to the possibility
of underlying renal dysfunction, poor forward cardiac
output, and/or reduced renal perfusion. In patients with
left‐sided CHF such as pulmonary edema, the simplest
way to monitor response to diuretics is to monitor
­respiratory rate and effort. Most patients with severe
pulmonary edema will exhibit respiratory rates at presentation >45 breaths/min with increased abdominal
effort and orthopnea. As diuretics resolve pulmonary
edema, the respiratory rate and effort should begin to
decrease, signaling an ability to reduce frequency of diuretic injections to q6–8h. Continued improvement in
respiratory rate and effort over the subsequent 12–24
hours leads to replacement of parenteral furosemide
with oral furosemide.
Diuretic therapy for treatment of acute CHF should be
personalized for individual patients depending on the
severity of clinical signs, current or previous therapy
with oral diuretics, co‐administration of other heart failure medications, hydration status, renal function, and
blood pressure. In general, patients with extreme respiratory distress or those already receiving oral diuretics
will require higher initial starting doses and more frequent repeated boluses, while those with preexisting
renal dysfunction, dehydration, or low blood pressure
will require more conservative dosing. Renal and electrolyte bloodwork as well as blood pressure measurement are typically performed as soon as practicable after

these signs, temporary cessation of diuretic administration along with replacement fluids administered either

respiratory compromise and prescribed dose of diuretics. There is no “one size fits all” formula for diuretic
administration and clinicians should constantly reassess
their therapy during the first 18–24 hours. The authors
discourage the routine use of IV fluid administration at
the same time diuretics are being administered. Rather,
they recommend offering water ad libitum during treatment of acute CHF to allow patients to semi‐self‐regulate their hydration status. Given the potency of the loop
diuretics, patients will be unable to consume enough
water to replace the fluids being lost. In cases of dire
CHF or instances where patients obsessively drink
repeated quantities of water when offered, water restriction might be needed.
While diuretics are generally considered a highly effective means of relieving congestion, inadequate response
to diuretics or the inability to administer sufficient doses
due to renal disease necessitates additional strategies to
improve renal perfusion and decrease intravascular pressure though positive inotropes and vasodilators.
Positive Inotropes
Acute heart failure is accompanied by decreased cardiac
output. Decreased tissue perfusion, particularly to the
kidneys, activates sodium‐ and water‐retaining mechanisms, such as the RAAS and SNS, leading to signs of
congestion. Poor perfusion of the proximal convoluted
tubule can decrease response to furosemide as active
secretion of furosemide into the nephron’s intraluminal
space is required for its diuretic effect. Positive inotropes
increase myocardial contractility and cardiac output and
are particularly indicated in instances of low‐output (forward) heart failure wherein signs of cardiac shock, such
as weakness, pallor, hypotension, and hypothermia, are
evident. Positive inotropes are often used in dogs with
DCM, and less commonly in dogs with MMVD. Because
most forms of feline cardiomyopathy are diastolic in
nature, positive inotropes are rarely used in cats with
heart failure. Positive inotropes act via increased binding
of calcium ions to the myocardial actin‐myosin‐troponin
complex, either by increasing intracellular calcium concentration or by increasing the sensitivity of the actin‐
myosin‐troponin complex to calcium binding.
Commonly administered positive inotropes include
sympathomimetic agents such as dopamine or dobutamine, calcium sensitizers such as pimobendan, and
intracellular calcium agents such as digoxin. Dopamine
is a precursor of norepinephrine while dobutamine is a
synthetic catecholamine, and both agents bind to myocyte beta‐adrenergic receptors in order to increase myocardial contractility and heart rate. At high doses, both
agents also act on peripheral alpha‐1 receptors to cause
unwanted arterial vasoconstriction. In dogs, dopamine

(1–10 μg/kg/min) or dobutamine (2.5–10 μg/kg/min) are
administered via constant rate infusion (CRI) and titrated
upwards to effect. Both agents are diluted in small volumes of 5% dextrose to limit the total volume of fluids
administered to dogs with acute CHF. During administration, blood pressure, mentation, muscle tone, urine
output, and other indices of improved tissue perfusion
such as body temperature or blood lactate guide dose
titration. For both dopamine and dobutamine, the rate‐
limiting factor during administration is tachycardia,
tachyarrhythmias, or excessive vasoconstriction. Efficacy
likely is best within the first 48 hours of administration,
after which the effects wane as beta‐receptors are saturated or downregulated.
Pimobendan is a calcium sensitizer and phosphodieterase inhibitor. Its positive inotropic action is due to its
ability to increase the binding of calcium ions to the
actin‐­
myosin‐troponin complex without a substantial
increase in intracellular calcium concentration. This
mechanism provides improved cardiac contractility
without substantial concomitant increases in myocardial
oxygen or energy demands. Pimobendan (0.25 mg/kg PO
BID or 0.15 mg/kg IV once in dogs followed by start of
oral dosing 12 hours after injection) can used in place of
either dopamine or dobutamine when constant rate infusion is not practical. Pimobendan is well tolerated in dogs
with acute CHF and oral dosing continues into the chronic
phase of CHF once the acute episode of CHF is resolved.
Digoxin is a digitalis glycoside with modest positive
inotropic effect as well as ability to reduce or slow conduction through the AV node. Its use in acute heart failure is limited by its variable oral bioavailability, long
half‐life, and narrow therapeutic window. Use of digoxin
for acute heart failure has been largely replaced by
pimobendan except in instances of atrial fibrillation or
supraventricular tachycardia wherein oral digoxin
(0.005–0.0075 mg/kg PO BID) is used to help slow the
ventricular heart rate. The long‐half life of digoxin precludes rapid achievement of therapeutic serum levels,
and digoxin therapy is usually combined with other antiarrhythmic agents such as diltiazem (see Chapter 21).
Toxicity includes arrhythmias and gastrointestinal signs
such as vomiting, anorexia, and diarrhea. The authors
discourage the use of IV digoxin administration due to a
high incidence of toxicity.
Vasodilators
Venous and arterial vasodilators reduce preload and
afterload, respectively. In cases of acute CHF, venous
vasodilation is often used in conjunction with diuretics
to help rapidly relieve congestion. Arterial vasodilation
reduces peripheral vascular resistance/afterload and
encourages improved cardiac output.

VetBooks.ir

19 Management of Heart Failure

Nitroprusside is a potent mixed vasodilator capable of
both venous and arterial vasodilation. It acts by releasing
nitric oxide, which induces vascular smooth muscle
relaxation. Nitroprusside is metabolized very rapidly and
is administered via CRI (1–10 μg/kg/min in dogs). Its
rate‐limiting factor is systemic arterial hypotension, and
blood pressure monitoring is highly recommended during use. Typically, the dosage is adjusted to achieve a systolic arterial blood pressure no lower than 90 mmHg.
The short half‐life of nitroprusside allows clinicians to
effectively make changes in infusion rates in response to
blood pressure. Nitroprusside, while highly effective, is
only occasionally used due to its need for CRI and sensitivity to light that requires the administration set to be
covered in light‐protective wrapping. Similar to dopamine or dobutamine, nitroprusside infusions are given
short term, typically not longer than 48 hours. At very
high doses or for extended periods of administration,
accumulation of nitroprusside metabolites such as
cyanogen can result in toxicity. Nitroprusside is rarely
used in cats. At the time of writing, supply shortages of
nitroprusside have severely curtailed its use and alternative nitric oxide donors such as IV nitroglycerin (1–10 μg/
kg/min) have been used.
ACE Inhibitors
ACE inhibitors form a cornerstone of therapy of chronic
CHF. Their utility in acute life‐threatening CHF is less
evident. Compared to hydralazine or nitroprusside, the
arterial dilating effects of ACEI are modest. ACEI’s ability to decrease AT II and aldosterone production appears
more beneficial over longer periods of time as opposed

to rapidly acting short‐term effects in acute CHF. The
rate‐limiting factors affecting ACEI use include azotemia
and systemic arterial hypotension. The authors occasionally delay initiation of ACEI until acute CHF is stabilized with diuretics, positive inotropes, and other
vasodilators, and are especially cautious in patients
already suffering from systemic hypotension or in those
that required very high doses of diuretics to alleviate
congestion and are significantly dehydrated. In these
cases, ACEI administration might be delayed until the
patient’s hydration status and renal bloodwork are
reevaluated. They are then prescribed as part of the
chronic CHF therapy with close monitoring of renal
bloodwork and systemic blood pressure.
Additional Therapies for Acute CHF
Oxygen supplementation is provided in cases of respiratory compromise and hypoxemia. Inspired O2 concentration is typically increased to 40% through the use
of oxygen cages or, in the case of large dogs, nasal insufflation. Manual removal of pleural, pericardial, or
abdominal fluid should be performed if these effusions
are a cause of respiratory compromise. In patients that
are extremely anxious, mild sedation with morphine
(0.1–1.0 mg/kg SC/IM in dogs), acepromazine (0.1–
0.2 mg/kg SC/IM in dogs) or butorphanol (0.1–0.3 mg/
kg IM/IV in dogs or cats) can be considered. Care must
be taken to avoid oversedation as further compromise
of respiratory function can result. Bronchodilators
such as aminophylline or theophylline or cough suppressants such as hydrocodone are rarely needed in
cases of acute CHF.

Ventricular Arrhythmias
Amara H. Estrada, DVM, DACVIM (Cardiology)1 and Romain Pariaut, DVM, DACVIM (Cardiology),
DECVIM-CA (Cardiology)2
1
2

Department of Small Animal Clinical Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA
Department of Clinical Sciences, College of Veterinary Medicine, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Ventricular arrhythmias (VA) such as single ventricular
premature depolarizations (contractions) (VPCs) can be
seen in normal animals in low numbers (less than 50 per
24‐hour period on a Holter monitor). They are very commonly seen in association with noncardiac disease, possibly due to myocardial ischemia, electrolyte abnormalities
or other factors surrounding the underlying disease. For
example, VPCs can be seen following vehicular trauma
(traumatic myocarditis), surgery, gastric dilation and volvulus, splenic disease, immune‐mediated hemolytic anemia and/or polycythemia, hypoxia, the use of anesthetic
agents (especially thiobarbiturates), pancreatitis, prostatitis, and neurologic disease. Thus, ventricular arrhythmias are relatively common to any number of different
systemic diseases. They may also be associated with
­primary underlying myocardial diseases such as dilated
cardiomyopathy in Doberman pinschers and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy in boxers. They
can also be idiopathic in origin, meaning that no underlying systemic or cardiac disorder can be identified.
The most important clinical considerations with VPCs
are whether there is an underlying systemic or cardiac
cause of the VPCs and whether there is the need to treat
the VA. Decisions to treat VA should be based on hemodynamic consequences and the risk of degeneration of the VA
into an unstable rhythm such as ventricular fibrillation.
Single VPCs do not cause clinical signs as they are transient
and hemodynamically not significant. What is more
important is attempting to identify malignant characteristics of VPCs or patient groups that might be more susceptible to the development of an unstable rhythm that can
lead to sudden death. However, our ability to predict the
likelihood of sudden death associated with VPCs is poor. It

appears that in dogs and cats with VPCs and no underlying
heart disease, the number of VPCs is not predictive of the
risk of sudden death, which in this setting is typically low.
When there is underlying myocardial disease, the presence
of VPCs may indicate an increased risk of sudden death or
simply be a marker for the severity of the disease (for example, Doberman pinschers with dilated cardiomyopathy or
cats with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy). The presence of
VPCs in boxers with familial ventricular arrhythmias may
indicate an increased risk of sudden death.

­Signalment
Certain breeds with specific underlying cardiac diseases are
predisposed to malignant VA. Doberman pinschers with
dilated cardiomyopathy, boxers with arrhythmogenic right
ventricular cardiomyopathy, dogs with severe subaortic stenosis, young German shepherds with i­nherited ventricular
arrhythmias, dogs and cats with myocarditis and cats with
hypertrophic cardiomyopathy represent situations where a
VA may signal increased risk for clinical signs or sudden
death. Other than the specific patient groups and underlying type of cardiac diseases mentioned above, there is no
other specific age, breed or sex predilection

­History and Clinical Signs
Dogs with VA secondary to systemic disease often do not
need the VA to be treated as the arrhythmia tends to be
self‐limiting if the underlying disease is addressed. For
example, a patient with VPCs and gastric dilation‐volvulus does not necessarily require antiarrhythmic therapy
for the VPCs, and instead needs relief of the dilation and
volvulus. This will in turn lead to resolution of the

arrhythmias, usually within 72 hours. Dogs with single
VPCs and underlying myocardial disease may or may not

need to further investigate the arrhythmia (e.g., with

An example would be a Doberman pinscher with
dilated cardiomyopathy, who is already receiving therapy
but is found to have a newly discovered ventricular
arrhythmia. Immediate introduction of antiarrhythmic
therapy in this case may or may not be appropriate and
further evaluation with Holter monitoring would be recommended. Patients with VPCs do not show clinical
signs associated with only single premature beats. Even
with ventricular tachycardia, if the rate of the ventricular
is below 200–220 bpm, no clinical signs may be present.
The rate at which a ventricular tachycardia will cause
clinical signs will depend on many underlying factors
such as rate, underlying myocardial function, species,
and/or breed. Typically, however, when the rate of the
ventricular tachycardia is rapid (greater than 250 bpm),
signs of poor cardiac output will be present and syncope
may occur. Clinical signs will also be influenced by the
degree of underlying heart disease. Thus, the patient
with systolic dysfunction and ventricular arrhythmias
may exhibit clinical signs at a slower ventricular rate than
a patient without underlying myocardial disease and
ventricular tachycardia. Patients with more serious ventricular arrhythmias (ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation) and compromised/diminished myocardial
function may have a history of exercise intolerance,
shortness of breath, syncope or near syncope.

­Diagnosis
Two basic ECG characteristics of VPCs are that they
are premature in their timing (earlier than the sinus
beat) and they are wide and bizarre in morphology
compared to the sinus beat (Figures 20.2 and 20.3).
They appear wide and bizarre because VPCs originate
below the bundle of His and therefore cannot take
advantage of the specialized conduction system. They
therefore must depolarize the ventricles muscle cell to
muscle cell. This is relatively slow and produces a wide
and bizarre complex. QRS complexes can be positive or
negative in lead II, depending on the site of origin of the
VPC, and they have no relationship to the P‐waves.
Because depolarization occurs in an abnormal fashion,
repolarization is also abnormal and there is typically a
large and bizarre T‐wave which is opposite in polarity
to the VPC.

Ventricular premature depolarizations can occur in
patterns such as ventricular bigeminy (every other beat is
a VPC) and ventricular trigeminy (every third beat is a
VPC). This type of pattern, however, does not correlate
with severity or potential malignancy of a ventricular
rhythm. More important characteristics of potentially
dangerous ventricular arrhythmias include the rate of
firing of a VPC and the morphology of a ventricular
rhythm. If a VPC fires rapidly and occurs close to the
peak of the preceding T‐wave (so‐called R‐on‐T phenomenon), depolarization during this time may predispose to ventricular fibrillation (Figure 20.4).
Ventricular rhythms can be monomorphic (one
morphology) or polymorphic (several different mor­
phologies), with the polymorphism generally considered
to imply multiple origins or pathways for the arrhythmia,
thus increasing the potential for degeneration into a
malignant arrhythmia (Figure 20.5).
A ventricular couplet is two consecutive VPCs, a
­ventricular triplet is three consecutive VPCs, and ventricular tachycardia is >3 consecutive VPCs occurring at
a rate of >170–180 bpm. Ventricular tachycardia is
­considered sustained if it lasts >30 seconds and nonsustained if it lasts <30 seconds. A ventricular rhythm that is
less than approximately 140–170 bpm is not truly a
­tachycardia and is therefore best termed an accelerated
idioventricular rhythm (sometimes referred to as slow
ventricular tachycardia) (Figure 20.6).
Accelerated idioventricular rhythms are seen commonly in hospitalized patients in association with noncardiac diseases as mentioned in the beginning of the chapter.
These are often benign, the rate is too slow to cause ­clinical
signs and they often do not require therapy.

­Therapy
Prior to discussing specific therapeutic interventions, it is
important to review the main objectives of treating a ventricular arrhythmia: (1) to improve hemodynamics in order
to alleviate clinical signs and (2) to prevent sudden death.
When making the decision to treat or not, it is important to attempt to determine whether the arrhythmia is
causing hemodynamic compromise. A healthy heart can
tolerate many types of VA whereas a diseased heart
­cannot. Therefore, the presence or absence of underlying
cardiac disease is an important factor in this decision.
Evaluation of the peripheral pulse quality, mucous membrane color, attitude of the patient, and arterial blood
pressure can be helpful in determining whether hemodynamics are being affected. Sustained ventricular tachycardia at a high rate is more likely to cause hemodynamic
compromise than an idioventricular rhythm or a ventricular tachycardia firing at slower rates.

The second important consideration for decisions
regarding the initiation of antiarrhythmic or other
­therapeutic intervention for a ventricular arrhythmia is
whether the arrhythmia is likely to degenerate into

­ventricular fibrillation, which will cause sudden death.
Again, the presence or absence of underlying cardiac disease is important since a healthy heart can tolerate more
than a diseased heart. It is believed that the faster the

ventricular tachycardia, the more likely a beat will fall

Acute Therapy of Ventricular Tachycardia
Initial therapy for dogs or cats with ventricular tachycardia that is thought to be malignant and directly related to
the current clinical signs is an IV bolus of lidocaine
(see Table 20.1 for doses).
Lidocaine should be used with caution in cats, as they
are very sensitive to its CNS effects. In both cats and
dogs, it is important to determine plasma or serum
potassium concentration as lidocaine will be less effective when hypokalemia is present. Thus, if lidocaine fails
to convert a ventricular rhythm, assessment of a patient’s
electrolyte values, specifically potassium, is required.
Additionally, hyperkalemia can also be a cause of sinoventricular rhythms which can mimic the appearance of
ventricular tachycardia in a cat.
Fortunately, most ventricular arrhythmias are responsive to therapy with lidocaine. However, some severe
ventricular arrhythmias may not terminate following
lidocaine injection, and in this situation, IV procainamide would be the next antiarrhythmic to administer.

Intravenous procainamide may result in hypotension and
should therefore be administered slowly. With refractory
ventricular arrhythmias, magnesium sulfate supplementation can also be considered. Magnesium has primary
antiarrhythmic properties similar to Class III agents, so
supplementation works well in combination with lidocaine or other Class I agents. Early administration may

VetBooks.ir
