Ventricular Septal Defects

Ventricular septal defects are the most common form of
CHD in cats, and are also seen in ~9% of dogs with
CHD. The pathophysiology of VSD is such that small
defects (restrictive) may be well tolerated and not result
in overt signs of cardiac dysfunction. Larger defects,
however, result in the shunting of large volumes of blood
from the left ventricle to the pulmonary circulation. The
result of this increased pulmonary flow is damage to the
lung vasculature and volume overload as the blood
returns to the left heart. VSDs can occur in several different areas along the interventricular septum and
numerous classification schemes have been developed

to characterize the location of the defect. Exact confirmation of the size of the defect and secondary cardiac
changes (e.g., aortic insufficiency or left ventricular
enlargement) carry prognostic information for the
­clients. Additionally, some defects may be in a location
amenable to catheter‐based closure.
Atrial Septal Defects

As with a VSD, an atrial septal defect is a hole in the
intracardiac septum separating the left and right heart.
ASD is a rare defect in small animals, accounting for
2–6% of cases. In addition, it is often seen in association
with other defects.

VetBooks.ir

24 Congenital Heart Disease

The degree of shunting depends on the size of the
defect and the relative resistance of the pulmonary versus the systemic circulation. Typically, flow is driven
from the left atrium across the ASD to the right,
thereby increasing blood flow through the lungs. In
contrast to left‐to‐right shunts such as PDA and VSD
that result in left heart enlargement, atrial‐level shunts
cause right heart enlargement as the increased pulmonary venous return is shunted to the right atrium. With
profound shunting, pulmonary hypertension and shunt
reversal (Eisenmenger’s physiology) may occur. Flow
across the atrial septum may also develop if right atrial
pressure becomes elevated, even in the presence of a
normally formed atrial septum. This develops because
the atrial septum is composed of two membranes that
are closed during the first week of life as left atrial
pressure exceeds right atrial pressure. If the animal has
right‐sided heart disease that elevates right atrial pressure (pulmonary stenosis, tricuspid dysplasia, tetralogy of Fallot), then the membranes may remain
separate and allow flow across the atrial septum
from right to left, referred to as a patent foramen
ovale (PFO).
In the setting of a large ASD or concurrent defects,
presenting signs will be an asymptomatic heart murmur,
pulmonary overcirculation, or weakness, lethargy, or
cyanosis associated with pulmonary hypertension and
shunt reversal.
Atrioventricular Septal Defects

Defects of the atrioventricular septum (AVSD) may be
considered separate from ASD or VSD. The atrioventricular septum is composed of centrally located tissue
derived from the endocardial cushions. With an AVSD,
defects may occur in the interatrial septum above the
atrioventricular valves (a primum defect) or the interventricular septum just below the atrioventricular
valves (inlet VSD), and may cause concurrent malformations of the ­atrioventricular valves. These defects
were formerly referred to as endocardial cushion
defects or defects in the atrioventricular canal. Signs
vary depending on the relative size of each defect,
but both congestive heart failure and cyanosis are
common. AVSDs are relatively uncommon in dogs,
but are seen in roughly 10% of cats with CHD.
The diagnosis is made by demonstration of the atrioventricular valves in the same imaging plane and variably sized defects in the ventral interatrial septum,
inlet interventricular septum, and septal leaflets of the
atrioventricular valves. There are also partial forms of
AVSD recognized, depending on the presence/absence
of atrial and ventricular septal defects as well as
the degree of development of distinct mitral and tricuspid annuli.

Stenotic Valve Lesions
Subaortic Stenosis

Aortic stenosis occurs almost exclusively in the dog and
is very rare in the cat. In almost all cases, obstruction is
the result of subaortic tissue that narrows the left ventricular outflow tract. The tissue may be a discrete
fibrous ridge or a tunnel‐like narrowing. Rarely, valvar
aortic stenosis is seen with fusion and/or thickening of
the valve leaflets. In order to maintain forward stroke
volume, such that the same volume of blood is pumped
out of the left ventricle with each heartbeat, the blood
must accelerate through the narrowing at a higher velocity. This requires that a greater left ventricular pressure
be generated. The elevated left ventricular pressure leads
to increased left ventricular wall stress and the development of concentric left ventricular hypertrophy.
The natural history of SAS includes a near normal
lifespan for patients with mild disease; those with
moderate to severe disease may experience exercise
­
intolerance, syncope, left‐sided congestive heart failure,
or sudden cardiac death. All patients with SAS are
believed to be at higher risk for development of bacterial
endocarditis due to damage of aortic valve integrity from
the turbulent, high‐velocity jet. As such, antibiotic
prophylaxis is advised for surgical or dental procedures,
or in cases of potential bacteremia (e.g., skin laceration).
Screening young dogs for SAS bears some mention.
First, SAS may progress as the dog grows because the
subvalvar ridge does not change in size while the heart
and stroke volume increase with the patient’s development. Therefore, the final assessment of severity can
only be made when the patient is full grown or nearly so.
Second, screening breeding dogs for mild disease is a
very real clinical problem as some breeds (boxer, greyhound, etc.) have aortic flow velocities that, with excitement, may be considered mild stenosis. This creates a
gray zone between normal and mildly affected that can
make breeding recommendations challenging.
Pulmonary Valve Stenosis

Pulmonary valve stenosis (PS) is principally a disease of
the valve leaflets and/or annulus, rather than the subvalvar region as in SAS. PS comes in varying forms – fusion
of the valve leaflets resulting in a narrowed orifice and
doming valves, valvular thickening and dysplasia resulting in thick immobile valves that do not open normally,
and annular hypoplasia where the valve annulus is abnormally small. The same hemodynamic derangements
described above for SAS apply to the right ventricle in
patients with PS. Right ventricular concentric hypertrophy is common and at times can be so severe as to create
a dynamic and muscular subvalvar obstruction. In these
instances, the right ventricle (RV) hypertrophies to such

233

VetBooks.ir

234

Section 3 Cardiovascular Disease

an extent that it obstructs blood flow from getting out of
the right heart during contraction.
The natural history of PS is more benign than for SAS,
although patients may similarly suffer exercise intolerance, syncope, sudden cardiac death, and right‐sided
congestive heart failure if the disease is severe. Dogs with
PS do not appear to be at an increased risk for endocarditis. Elevated right atrial pressure in the presence of a
PFO may allow shunting of blood across the atrial septum from right to left and the development of cyanosis
and secondary erythrocytosis. PFO is seen in ~30% of
dogs with PS as the atrial septum does not close normally
at birth due to elevated right atrial pressure. If flow from
the right atrium to left atrium is substantial across a PFO,
the animal may have significant mixing of poorly
­oxygenated blood from the right atrium to the left and
clinical cyanosis.
Mitral and Tricuspid Valve Stenosis

Mitral valve dysplasia (MVD) and TVD may result in stenosis of these valves. Atrioventricular valve stenosis is
rare in small animals, but both mitral stenosis and tricuspid stenosis are occasionally encountered in dogs and
cats. These lesions lead to progressive atrial enlargement, atrial arrhythmias, and congestive heart failure if
left untreated.
Regurgitant Valve Lesions
Mitral and Tricuspid Valve Dysplasia

Congenital malformations of the atrioventricular valves
are considered rare in dogs, but account for a greater
proportion of congenital heart disease in cats. Mitral
valve dysplasia or TVD is a developmental abnormality
of valve formation, resulting in abnormal leaflet shape,
attachment, and/or function. Animals with MVD or
TVD have pathology that typically results in regurgitation of the affected valve; however, a combination of stenosis and regurgitation may be encountered. Chronic
mitral valve regurgitation leads to left ventricular and
left atrial volume overload and dilation in the setting of
MVD, which may lead to left‐sided congestive heart failure. Similar progression may be seen in the right heart
for TVD. Postmortem findings of dysplastic atrioventricular valves display fused and malformed leaflets with
shortened chordae tendineae. Direct attachment from
the papillary muscle to the valve is common.
Aortic and Pulmonary Valve Dysplasia

Congenital defects of the semilunar valves typically
result in stenosis, as described above. In both SAS and
PS, regurgitation, or insufficiency, of the affected valve is
commonly observed by color Doppler imaging.
Pulmonary valve insufficiency can even be seen in the

majority of otherwise apparently healthy dogs when
screened by Doppler echocardiography. However, aortic
or pulmonary insufficiency is typically well tolerated and
seldom of clinical significance. Rarely, cases of aortic or
pulmonary valve dysplasia resulting in a predominantly
regurgitant valve with severe insufficiency are detected,
which may progress to cardiac decompensation.
Malformations of the Great Vessels
Vascular Ring Anomalies

Several malformations of the arterial system have been
described in animals; the most common clinical presentation is a pediatric animal with dysphagia. The basic
pathophysiology of these malformations is an embryologic defect resulting from abnormal persistence or
regression of fetal vascular structures (aortic arches),
ultimately leading to an abnormal spatial arrangement of
the major intrathoracic arteries relative to the trachea
and esophagus. Clinical signs are the direct result of
extraluminal compression of the esophagus (resulting in
megaesophagus, regurgitation, or aspiration pneumonia) and/or trachea (resulting in inspiratory stridor,
coughing, or dyspnea). Persistence of the right aortic
arch is the most common vascular ring observed in small
animals. Therapy is directed at surgical decompression
and transection of the offending structure, though
esophageal dysfunction may persist if not corrected at a
young age.
Cyanotic Heart Disease
Tetralogy of Fallot

Cyanotic heart disease is not common in small animals,
but tetralogy of Fallot (ToF) is recognized in 2–6% of
cases of CHD. ToF is the most common cyanotic CHD
of humans and the four components of the tetralogy are
right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, right ventricular hypertrophy, VSD, and dextroposition of the
aorta. The underlying pathophysiology of this defect is
believed to result from incomplete rotation and faulty
partitioning of the developmental outflow tracts
(­comprising the distal portions of the left and right
­ventricles and the proximal portion of the great vessels). In simple terms, the aorta receives more of the
embryologic tissue and aortic development occurs at
the expense of the pulmonary trunk. Therefore, the
­ventricular septum cannot close because the aorta is
enlarged and deviated to the right. The result of right
ventricular outflow obstruction with a VSD is that
deoxygenated blood is diverted to the systemic circulation, causing cyanosis, weakness, and collapse. Long‐
standing sequelae include erythrocytosis and blood
hyperviscosity due to increased erythropoiesis.

VetBooks.ir

24 Congenital Heart Disease

­Epidemiology
The prevalence of CHD in the dog and cat is difficult to
quantify due to a lack of routine perinatal care, occurrence
of conditions that are not apparent on routine physical
examination, and hospital biases in published reports.
The work of Detweiler and Patterson in the Philadelphia
area suggested a CHD prevalence rate of 0.56% among
5000 dogs surveyed in the mid‐twentieth century, while
Buchanan found a rate of 0.67% for all dogs presented to
the University of Pennsylvania between 1987 and 1989.
While the true prevalence of CHD in dogs and cats is
unknown, there are data available evaluating the relative
incidence of specific malformations in each species. The
author compiled data from several studies in an attempt
to summarize the relative prevalence of CHD in small
animals. Ten applicable studies of CHD prevalence in
dogs were found in the veterinary literature, comprising a
sum of 4694 defects. When totaled, PDA (26%), SAS
(24%), and PS (22%) were the most common and of nearly
equal incidence. As such, these three diseases should be
highest on a practitioner’s differential list when listening
to a puppy with a loud heart murmur; other congenital
malformations of the heart are less common.
There are fewer data available about CHD prevalence
in the cat. When evaluating several studies of CHD prevalence in cats, five studies covering 435 defects can be
found. Ventricular septal defect appears to be the most
common defect in the cat, comprising over 18% of cases.
PDA is not generally considered a common disease in
the cat, compared to the dog, but was noted in over 11%
of defects. Dysplasia of the atrioventricular valves (mitral
or tricuspid) each accounted for an additional 10% of
defects. Feline CHD, therefore, should be considered
­distinct from and with a different incidence of common
defects than canine CHD. Semilunar valve disease
(PS and SAS) is exceedingly rare in cats.

­Signalment
Age
Most animals with CHD present at a young age. However,
adult animals with undiagnosed CHD may present later
in life and often as a result of complications (heart failure, syncope, or cyanosis) from their cardiovascular disorder if it was not detected at an earlier age.
Sex
Both sexes are commonly afflicted with CHD, though
sex predilections for some specific conditions have
been identified. PDA has been reported to occur more

commonly in female dogs, with a 3:1 female predominance. Pulmonary valve stenosis has not been recognized as having gender predominance except in the
English bulldog, where males are more commonly
afflicted than females. A male predominance for TVD
has also been reported in the veterinary literature. In the
cat, a male predominance has been suggested for atrioventricular valve malformation, aortic stenosis, and
­tricuspid valve dysplasia.
Breed
Numerous breed predilections have been reported for
animals with CHD, particularly dogs. Table 24.1 shows a
listing of common defects and the breeds known or suspected to have an increased prevalence of each defect.
This table should not be considered authoritative or
exhaustive, as spontaneous defects can occur in any breed
at any time. Additionally, the incidence of CHD will likely
change as breed populations continue to evolve. In the
cat, few breed predilections are recognized other than
endocardial fibroelastosis, which is reported to have a
higher prevalence in Burmese and Siamese breeds.

­History and Clinical Signs
Animals with complex defects or severe CHD may present within the first days to weeks of life due to failure to
thrive, dyspnea, cyanosis, or syncope. It is likely that
most puppies and kittens with severe cardiac malformations die early in life and prior to veterinary examination.
The common history for dogs and cats with CHD is that
of an asymptomatic pet with an appointment for a wellness exam, deworming, and vaccination. Auscultation
during the physical examination of these patients is often
the first and earliest clue that CHD may be present – as
such, careful and thorough examination of all young animals is advised.

­Diagnosis
Auscultation
Screening for congenital cardiac disease typically begins
with a thorough physical examination performed at the
first general health examination. Auscultation is imperative for screening of CHD as the most common forms of
CHD typically present with a systolic (SAS, PS, VSD,
TVD) or continuous (PDA) murmur. Auscultation in
puppies and kittens should be performed in a quiet room
with appropriate restraint and sufficient time devoted to
a thorough examination.

24 Congenital Heart Disease

For dogs, all valve areas should be evaluated, including
the mitral valve area on the left thoracic wall where the apical impulse is felt most strongly, the semilunar valve area
(aortic and pulmonary valves) at the left heart base (the
ventral 2nd–4th intercostal spaces), the area of the great
vessels just dorsal to the left heart base, and the tricuspid
valve area on the right thoracic wall. In the cat, localization
of individual valve areas is more problematic and auscultation is usually directed along the left and right sternal border, moving from caudal to cranial on either side.
Murmur location and intensity are useful in differentiating between types of CHD as well as for distinguishing
a physiologic or innocent murmur from that caused by
CHD. Left and right apical systolic murmurs are commonly due to atrioventricular valve regurgitation and, in
a young animal, if an apical systolic murmur is heard,
defects of MVD and TVD should be considered most
strongly. The murmur of a typical membranous VSD is
harsh and systolic at the right sternal boarder. Left basilar systolic murmurs can be more problematic as they
can indicate either an innocent murmur or CHD such as
SAS, PS, or ASD. High‐intensity murmurs (grade IV–VI
or louder) usually indicate the presence of significant
CHD regardless of location and are an indication for
more advanced diagnostics. However, less intense murmurs (grade III–VI or less) may originate either from
CHD or an innocent cause.
Evaluating left basilar systolic murmurs with a rubric
of the 6 Ss (Table 24.2) can be useful to try and guide the
need for additional diagnostic testing. In general, a soft
left basilar systolic murmur heard in a young puppy or
kitten that decreases in intensity over the first months of
life and/or disappears by 6 months of age is likely to be
innocent. If the murmur is loud or harsh, continuous or

diastolic in duration, or associated with concurrent
­cardiac signs (arrhythmia, cough, syncope), then CHD
should be considered more likely and further testing
should be advised.
Other aspects of a cardiac physical examination
include evaluation of the mucous membranes, jugular
veins, and pulse quality. Mucous membranes should be
evaluated for evidence of cyanosis, which may be indicative of a right‐to‐left intracardiac shunt. Very poor
peripheral perfusion can be suggested by pale mucous
membranes and/or a prolonged capillary refill time even
in the absence of an obvious heart murmur. Hypokinetic
femoral pulses are commonly detected in moderate to
severe SAS, while a hyperkinetic pulse quality is suggestive of a wide pulse pressure from PDA or severe aortic
insufficiency. Jugular pulsation with or without distension can suggest tricuspid regurgitation or elevated
right‐sided pressures due to tricuspid valve dysplasia,
PS, or pulmonary hypertension from severe left‐to‐right
shunting defects.
Additional Diagnostic Tests
While the physical examination is an important aspect of
screening for the presence of CHD, it is difficult to make
a definitive diagnosis from signalment and physical
examination alone. Ancillary diagnostic tests, like thoracic radiography and electrocardiography (ECG), may
be useful in narrowing the differential diagnostic list and
determining disease severity, but can also add cost to the
initial evaluation without providing definitive diagnostic
information. In current veterinary practice, echocardiography with Doppler is considered the gold standard
diagnostic test for confirmation of CHD.

Electrocardiography

Thoracic Radiography

Electrocardiography may be beneficial in detecting cardiac changes related to CHD, though is most useful for
characterizing dysrhythmias heard on auscultation.
CHDs that cause ventricular enlargement, such as PS
and SAS, may provide a substrate for ventricular
arrhythmias secondary to myocardial ischemia.
However, ECG is a more specific rather than sensitive
test as animals with CHD may have a normal ECG.
Figure 24.2 shows examples of rhythm disturbances that
may be seen in the setting of CHD. Again, it should be
noted that such findings are supportive of a diagnosis,
but not definitive.

Similar to ECG, thoracic radiographs provide useful supplementary information in the evaluation of a patient with
suspected CHD. However, thoracic radiography is most
useful when the veterinarian suspects an animal’s heart
disease has decompensated and resulted in pulmonary
edema or pleural effusion. If signs of r­ espiratory compromise or cough are apparent on examination, thoracic radiographs are strongly advised. In the asymptomatic animal
with a murmur, however, they are less specific than echocardiography in confirming a diagnosis. Figure 24.3 provides examples of radiographic ­evidence of decompensated

Cardiac Biomarkers: Troponin and NT‐proBNP

In recent years, the use of cardiac biomarkers to screen
­animals for the presence of acquired cardiovascular ­disease
has gained in popularity. The biomarkers receiving the

most attention in veterinary cardiology include cardiac
troponin I (cTnI) and the amino terminus of the prohormone B‐type natriuretic peptide (NT‐proBNP). There
have been no comprehensive studies looking at the utility

Section 3 Cardiovascular Disease

of these tests in animals with CHD, though evidence in
human cardiology suggests that these markers are often
elevated in children with severe CHD. At this time, no
guidance can be given for or against the utility of cardiac
biomarkers in screening animals for CHD.
Echocardiography

History, physical examination, thoracic radiography, and
ECG are all useful diagnostic tests for determining the
presence of CHD, but are less capable of making a definitive diagnosis, assessing disease severity, or ruling out
the presence of multiple or complex congenital lesions.
In veterinary medicine, echocardiography with Doppler
is the noninvasive gold standard for definitive diagnosis
of CHD. All animals with a high suspicion of CHD should
ideally have a detailed echocardiogram performed by a
veterinarian trained in the diagnosis of CHD.
Echocardiography allows for the detection of specific
types of CHD, the presence of concomitant defects, and
assessment of disease severity, risk for complications,
direction of cardiac shunting, estimate of intracardiac
pressures, and likelihood of congestive heart failure.
Echocardiography is also necessary in assessing the need
for therapy as well as for planning interventional or surgical options. Figure 24.4 provides representative two‐
dimensional images of common CHD seen in the dog
and cat by echocardiography.
Angiography

Nonselective or selective angiography with fluoroscopic
visualization of cardiac structures was historically the
definitive test for CHD prior to the advent of echocardiography. For some defects, angiography is still utilized, particularly for lesions of the great vessels that are not easily
appreciated by ultrasound. Figure 24.5 shows a nonselective, digitally subtracted angiogram of a right‐to‐left
shunting PDA in a cat, while Figure 24.6 shows a right ventriculogram from a dog with PS. In practice, angiography
is used most commonly at the time of interventional therapy to confirm the diagnosis, visualize the defect to be
addressed, and guide intervention with balloon or device,
as discussed in the interventional therapy section.
Cross‐Sectional Imaging

Cardiac computed tomography and magnetic resonance
imaging allow three‐dimensional reconstructions of the
heart and great vessels. Such imaging modalities are
commonly employed in human medicine to evaluate
children with CHD and case reports of their use in veterinary medicine are present in the literature. Figure 24.7
shows a three‐dimensional reconstruction of a computed tomographic angiogram in a dog with PS. The
benefit of cross‐sectional imaging is likely greatest in
instances of complex CHD where the cardiac anatomy
can be viewed from multiple perspectives in situ.

­Therapy
Medical Therapy
Asymptomatic Disease

Treatment of asymptomatic CHD depends on the
­specific underlying disease and its severity, so definitive
diagnosis is essential. In general, diseases of moderate to
severe outflow tract obstruction causing concentric
hypertrophy (e.g., SAS and PS) are treated by the author
with beta‐blockers such as atenolol. Atenolol is typically
uptitrated in dose over 4–8 weeks, starting at 0.2–0.5 mg/
kg (0.1–0.2 mg/lb) q12h PO and increasing to a target
dose of 1–1.5 mg/kg (0.4–0.7 mg/lb) q12h PO. The
rationale for such therapy is that beta‐blockers help to
reduce the force of myocardial contraction, thereby
reducing myocardial oxygen demand and protecting the
diseased/hypertrophied myocardium. The antiarrhythmic properties of atenolol are also believed to be of
­benefit as these patients are at risk for life‐threatening
arrhythmias. Atenolol is often chosen given its low cost,
appropriate size tablets, and ease of administration.
Therapy for asymptomatic diseases of volume overload such as moderate to severe mitral or tricuspid
regurgitation and left‐to‐right shunting defects like PDA,
prior to development of CHF, is controversial. However,
the addition of angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE)
inhibitors such as enalapril at 0.5 mg/kg (0.2 mg/lb) q12h
PO is common if there is severe ventricular dilation,
impaired cardiac output, and atrial enlargement suggesting high risk for development of CHF.
Symptomatic Disease

Medical therapy of symptomatic CHD depends on the
type of lesion and developing clinical signs. Diseases
of outflow tract obstruction (SAS, PS) commonly cause
exercise intolerance and syncope related to reduced
­cardiac output, inappropriate baroreceptor activation,
and/or ventricular arrhythmias. Life‐threatening or
symptomatic ventricular arrhythmias are treated with
antiarrhythmic agents. Sotalol at a dose of 1–2 mg/kg
(0.4–0.9 mg/lb) q12h PO is typically the first‐line antiarrhythmic of choice so long as ventricular function is not
severely depressed. Syncope that occurs without ventricular arrhythmias (presumed to be reflex‐mediated
­syncope whereby the cardiac hypertrophy stimulates an
exaggerated baroreceptor response) is typically treated
with beta‐blockade. Modification of exercise level with
avoidance of high‐level intense or burst activity will also
commonly reduce this clinical sign.
Diseases of left‐sided volume overload will commonly cause symptoms of cough in the dog prior to the
onset of CHF due to severe left atrial enlargement and
resultant left bronchial compression. Bronchial compression in the absence of CHF may be treated with

with coughing, tachypnea, and respiratory distress
secondary to pulmonary edema, whereas right‐sided
­
CHF presents with signs of jugular distension, hepatomegaly, ascites, and/or pleural effusion. CHF, regardless
of cause, is treated with diuretics and ACE inhibitors.

In the author’s experience, right‐sided CHF will commonly need higher doses of oral furosemide or an alternative diuretic such as torsemide due to the potential for
intestinal edema causing decreased gastrointestinal
absorption. ACE inhibitors should always be used in the
treatment of chronic CHF to decrease RAAS activation
associated with advanced heart failure and diuretic
administration.
Pimobendan has become standard of care in the treatment of CHF secondary to acquired cardiac diseases,
such as dilated cardiomyopathy and chronic degenerative valve disease. While no definitive data are available
on the use of pimobendan in congenital cardiac disease,
most cardiologists advocate its use with CHF due to
­diseases of volume overload such as PDA or mitral valve
dysplasia. The administration of pimobendan as a treatment for CHF secondary to diseases of pressure overload
like SAS and PS is becoming more commonplace.
However, extralabel use of pimobendan should be done
cautiously in the setting of outflow tract obstruction due
to potential for increase in pressure gradient, wall stress,
and myocardial oxygen consumption. Consultation with
a veterinary cardiologist is advised prior to pimobendan
use in cases of SAS and PS with CHF.
Surgical and Interventional Therapy
Congenital heart disease can be palliated medically, as
noted above, but also may be treated by minimally invasive (interventional) or traditional surgical techniques
whenever possible. An accurate diagnosis of CHD is
­critical to appropriately guide therapy as some animals
can go on to live a normal life if treated early.
(a)

(b)

The decision to operate or pursue transcatheter therapy
relates to the expertise of the veterinarian performing
the procedure, anatomy of the defect, and client preference. Prospective comparison studies are lacking in veterinary medicine, though retrospective data on PDA
closure suggest comparable to improved outcomes from
a transcatheter approach compared to surgery. Novel
devices, such as the Amplatz™ canine ductal occluder,
have greatly improved the ease with which PDA occlusion can be performed from a transarterial approach
(Figure 24.8). Gordon et al. showed complete PDA occlusion in 40 of 41 dogs treated by a transarterial canine‐
specific device with no perioperative mortality compared
to a reported perioperative mortality of 2–8% in the surgical literature during open PDA ligation [1].
The CHD conditions which currently have a well‐
established surgical or interventional treatment option
include PDA, persistent right aortic arch (PRAA), and
PS. Dogs with VSD or ASD have been successfully
treated by both surgical and interventional techniques
and, though costly, open surgical repair and newer transcatheter devices for closure of these defects may be
­considered for the motivated client. Cyanotic ToF dogs
can be palliated by surgical construction of a systemic‐
to‐pulmonary anastamosis, typically a modified Blalock–
Taussig shunt, which improves pulmonary blood flow
and lessens central cyanosis. Open‐heart repair of ToF
has also been described in the dog. Atrioventricular
valve dysplasia is seldom treated by surgical or interventional techniques but if a stenotic component is present,
balloon valvuloplasty of the tricuspid or mitral valve may
be considered. Open surgical repair of a dysplastic valve
may also be considered for the motivated client.

­Prognosis
The prognosis for the animal with CHD is heavily
dependent on the underlying condition and the severity
of the defect. Mild stenosis of the semilunar valves (PS,
SAS) rarely causes morbidity or altered survival.
Conversely, dogs with severe SAS have been reported to
have median survival of only 1.5–4 years. For left‐to‐
right shunting lesions, prognosis is highly dependent on
the volume of shunt flow. Small shunts (e.g., restrictive
VSDs) are often well tolerated and can be associated with
a normal lifespan. Large PDAs, however, are known to

result in mortality of 60% or more within a year of diagnosis if they are not closed by surgery or intervention.
For most CHD, there is a paucity of literature on prognosis and survival. Experienced cardiologists have seen animals with severe disease live a near‐normal lifespan, while
other animals with moderate disease die from the defect
prematurely. At the present time, predicting the precise
prognosis for an individual animal with CHD is very difficult. Serial evaluations to detect asymptomatic cardiac
dysfunction or dysrhythmias, as well as the development of
clinical signs (cough, lethargy, collapse, etc.), are currently
the methods used to monitor these animals.

Valvular Heart Disease
Michele Borgarelli, DVM, PhD, DECVIM (Cardiology)
Department of Small Animal Clinical Sciences, Virginia‐Maryland Regional College of Veterinary Medicine, Blacksburg, VA, USA

­Canine Degenerative Myxomatous
Mitral Valve Disease
Etiology and Pathophysiology
Canine chronic myxomatous mitral valve disease
(MMVD) is the result of a progressive myxomatous
degeneration of mitral valve leaflets and chordae tendinae. Pathologic changes include excessive deposition of
mucopolysaccharide, fragmentation of elastin, and disorganization and disruption of collagen.
The exact etiology of the disease has not been established. Because the disease has a high prevalence in some
breeds, such as Cavalier King Charles spaniel (CKCS), a
genetic predisposition has been hypothesized. Swenson
and co‐workers provided the first evidence of a genetic
predisposition in 1996. These authors reported that
CKCS dogs with a more severe disease status produced
more offspring with murmurs and with murmurs of
higher intensity than dogs with a low‐intensity status.
They concluded that MMVD is inherited as a polygenic
trait. The same etiology has been reported for other
breeds. It has also been reported that the threshold for
the expression of the disease is lower in males than in
females. This would explain why males present with the
disease at a younger age.
Recently, using a genome‐wide association study,
two specific loci associated with development of
MMVD in CKCS have been identified. It is likely that
other factors might contribute to the development of
the disease, including the anatomy of the mitral valve,
obesity, and exercise. Recently, serotonin has been
hypothesized as playing a role in the pathogenesis of
MMVD. However, despite similarities in the myxomatous pathology of serotoninergic and degenerative
mitral valves, a direct cause–effect relationship between
serotonin and the pathogenesis of MMVD has not
been established.

Activation of valvular interstitial cells (VICs) is likely
to play an important role in the pathogenesis of the disease. VICs represent the most common cell type in the
cardiac valves and are responsible for extracellular
matrix synthesis, valvular repair, and remodeling. VICs
are commonly present in a quiescent state but can be
activated by endothelial damage or valvular stress.
Activated VICs are able to synthesize collagen, fibronectin, elastin, and growth factors and are responsible for
extracellular matrix remodeling through production of
matrix metalloproteinases and their inhibitors (tissue
inhibitors of metalloproteinases [TIMPs]). Eventually,
this process leads to decreases in collagen content and
deposition of proteoglycan, typical of the myxomatous
degenerative process. In summary, it can be hypothesized that in dogs with a genetic predisposition for the
disease, mechanic stimuli can activate VICs with valvular remodeling and myxomatous degeneration. This
hypothesis would support the theory that myxomatous
degeneration is the end‐result of a continuous process of
damage and repair as a result of mitral valve stress.
The myxomatous degeneration of the valve leaflets
eventually leads to prolapse and valvular insufficiency.
Accordingly, mitral valve prolapse usually precedes
mitral valve insufficiency. Mild mitral valve insufficiency
is generally well tolerated by dogs and is not associated
with any compensatory response because it is not associated with decreased cardiac output. However, if the disease progresses and regurgitation through the mitral
valve into the left atrial becomes more severe, cardiac
output decreases and activation of compensatory mechanisms occurs. These mechanisms include activation of
the renin‐angiotensin‐aldosterone system (RAAS) and
sympathetic nervous system, and increased release of
endothelin, vasopressin, and natriuretic hormones. Due
to the chronic nature of the disease, these mechanisms
are not necessarily activated in the early stages of
MMVD. This consideration has important therapeutic

implications. In particular, when the RAAS becomes
activated in dogs with natural occurring MMVD has
been the source of much controversy. Some studies suggest that the RAAS might be activated relatively early in
the history of the disease, whereas other studies suggest
otherwise. Further complicating the picture is the observation that in dogs, alternative pathways for angiotensin
II production, such as the chymase pathway, may be particularly active. Moreover, it is possible that release of
natriuretic hormones from the dilated left atrium
and ventricle might balance RAAS and sympathetic
activation.
Moderate to severe mitral valve regurgitation leads to
left ventricular volume overload, left atrial and left ventricular enlargement. Mitral valve insufficiency due to
MMVD represents a unique hemodynamic condition
with increased preload and decreased afterload. This is
because a significant volume of left ventricular preload is
ejected into the left atrium at the beginning of systole.
Because the left atrium is a low‐pressure chamber, there
is no increase in cardiac work. This is likely the reason
why many dogs with severe mitral valve regurgitation
can tolerate this situation for a long time without presenting clinical signs.
Left ventricular eccentric hypertrophy, decreased
afterload, and increased sympathetic activation produce
hyperkinetic left ventricular function. Therefore, the
recognition of normal values for fractional shortening or
ejection fraction during an echocardiographic exam in
dogs with left ventricular enlargement suggests the presence of a systolic dysfunction. Systolic dysfunction has
been recognized to play an important role in disease progression and it is independent of clinical status. It has
been hypothesized that systolic dysfunction in dogs with
MMVD is the consequence of inadequate hypertrophy.
Wall stress imposed by pure volume overload might not
be a very potent stimulus for cardiac hypertrophy, and
experimental canine models of MMVD systolic dysfunction were associated with inadequate left ventricular
hypertrophy. Systolic dysfunction is more apparent in
large‐breed dogs affected by MMVD.
Left atrial function also plays an important role in the
pathophysiology of the disease. Slowly progressing mitral
valve regurgitation is associated with a progressive dilation of the left atrium. If left atrial compliance is maintained, filling pressure is also maintained close to normal
limits. Accordingly, patients with severe mitral regurgitation do not develop pulmonary edema. However,
chronic dilation of the left atrium is associated with left
atrial hypertrophy and remodeling that, with time,
decreases compliance and leads to development of pulmonary edema. In dogs with rupture of a major chorda
tendinea, there is an acute worsening of mitral regurgitation. In this condition, the left atrium has no time to

enlarge and there is a sudden increase of left atrial pressure with development of acute pulmonary edema.
Epidemiology
Myxomatous mitral valve disease is the most common
heart disease in dogs and the most frequent cause of congestive heart failure in this species. MMVD in dogs
­represents 75% of all cardiovascular disease in this species. The prevalence of the disease varies with age and
whether the study is based on necropsy, echocardiographic or clinical findings. The prevalence of MMVD
has also been correlated with breed. In some breeds,
such as the CKCS, the prevalence of the disease in animals older than 10 years is greater than 90%. Males are
also reported to develop the disease at a younger age
than females. Although the disease is more commonly
diagnosed in small‐breed dogs, it can occur in large‐
breed dogs.
History and Clinical Signs
Myxomatous mitral valve disease is a chronic disease in
which the clinical presentation is variable. Some patients
remain asymptomatic for all their lives, whereas others
develop life‐threating pulmonary edema and chronic
congestive heart failure (CHF). Most dogs with mild to
moderate MMVD are generally free of clinical signs.
The presence of clinical signs is generally related to the
severity of the disease. Dogs with pulmonary edema have
tachypnea and dyspnea. It has been reported that the
normal respiratory rate at rest for dogs should be less
than 30 breaths per minute. Accordingly, an increased
respiratory rate at rest might represent the first clinical
sign of worsening of the disease. Dogs with pulmonary
edema are often anxious and have difficulties sleeping.
They often cannot lie in lateral recumbency and prefer a
sternal position (orthopnea). Weight loss is common in
dogs with advanced stages of MMVD and CHF. Patients
that develop right‐sided heart failure have abdominal
distension due to ascites. Syncope is occasionally
reported in dogs with MMVD. Arrhythmias, pulmonary
hypertension, vasovagal syncope, and coughing can
cause syncope in these patients.
Cough represents the most common complaint for
dogs affected by MMVD, especially in small breeds. It
should be stressed that cough is a general clinical sign of
respiratory disease and its presence in a dog with a murmur is not an indicator for starting treatment for CHF.
Old small‐breed dogs are commonly affected by tracheobronchial disease and by MMVD. In these patients, the
cough is often the result of their primary respiratory disease and not heart disease. A recent study has shown
that cough was not associated with the presence of active

VetBooks.ir

25 Valvular Heart Disease

CHF in 206 dogs with MMVD at different stages. In this
study, cough was associated with left atrial enlargement
and the presence of an abnormal radiographic airway
pattern. Left atrial enlargement compressing the mainstem bronchus is believed to induce cough in patients
with primary bronchomalacia.
Diagnosis
The American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine
Specialty of Cardiology consensus panel has published
guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of canine
chronic valvular heart disease. The guidelines propose a
modification of a staging system for MMVD that is currently used to classify human patients with heart failure
(Table 25.1). This classification introduces the concept of
patients at risk for developing MMVD but that currently
do not have heart disease (stage A). The reason for introducing this stage is to encourage veterinarians to develop
appropriate screening programs and inform owners
regarding the risk of an animal developing the disease.
Diagnosis of MMVD is generally suspected following a
careful auscultation. In early stages of MMVD a midsystolic click may represent the only auscultatory finding.
The click is often intermittent and can be better appreciated at higher heart rates. It is believed the midsystolic
click is caused by vibration of the prolapsing mitral valve
leaflets and by the tensing of redundant chordae
tendineae. In dogs with mild MMVD and mild mitral

regurgitation, a low‐intensity, early systolic murmur
localized on the left apex can be heard. The murmur can
be intermittent and intensity can vary with heart rate
and phase of respiration. When moderate to severe
mitral regurgitation is present, the murmur becomes
holosystolic or pansystolic, more intense, and harsher. In
more severe cases, the murmur radiates to the base of
the left thorax and to the right side of the thorax. It
should be emphasized that the intensity of the murmur
does not always correlate with the severity of MMVD;
that is, loud murmurs do not automatically indicate
severe disease.
The auscultatory findings can be influenced by several
factors such as observer experience, obesity, panting,
presence of arrhythmias, and breeds. In a study on preclinical MMVD dogs, 26% of dogs with a confirmed
echocardiographic diagnosis of MMVD did not have a
murmur and large‐breed dogs with MMVD have less
intense murmurs compared with small‐breed dogs.
Thus, diagnosis of MMVD should not rely only on
­auscultatory findings. Indeed, the ACVIM consensus
recommends that although the presence of midsystolic
click or left apical murmur in a typical breed is strongly
suggestive of MMVD, echocardiographic confirmation
of the diagnosis is required. Echocardiography can evaluate the morphology of the valve leaflets and quantify
the degree of cardiac enlargement. The echocardiographic characteristics of MMVD include prolapse or
thickening of one or both mitral valve leaflets
(Figure 25.1).
Mitral valve prolapse is defined as an abnormal systolic displacement or bowing of the mitral valve leaflets
from the left ventricle toward the left atrium. In dogs,
some studies suggest that the right parasternal four‐
chamber, long‐axis view is the gold standard used to
identify the presence of mitral valve prolapse. Because

leaflets appear thickened and prolapse in the left atrium.

echocardiographic diagnosis of mitral valve prolapse is
dependent on the morphology of the valve, and because
the normal mitral valve and mitral valve annulus present
a wide range of normality, we recommend that the
­diagnosis of mitral valve prolapse should be confirmed
in at least two echocardiographic views. Indeed, we have
recently reported that in dogs, mitral valve morphology
is saddle shaped, similar to what has been reported in
people. Therefore, using the right parasternal long‐axis
view may lead to an overestimation of the mitral valve
prolapse.
The ACVIM consensus statement recommends
­thoracic radiography for all dogs with MMVD to assess
the hemodynamic significance of the murmur through
evaluation of heart size and pulmonary vasculature and
to obtain a baseline when the patient is asymptomatic.
Careful evaluation of thoracic radiographs may help in
diagnosing concomitant primary respiratory diseases
that may be the cause for clinical signs, such as cough or
dyspnea. Thoracic radiographs, together with physical
examination, are also essential for monitoring dogs with
MMVD. A change in radiographic cardiac dimensions
observed between two different time points has been
suggested as a powerful predictor of outcome in dogs
with MMVD.
Prognosis
Myxomatous mitral valve disease is characterized by a
long preclinical period and many affectws dogs die for
reasons other than CHF. A study including a population

of 558 dogs affected by MMVD at different stages has
shown that more than 70% dogs were alive at the end of
the follow‐up period of 6.6 years (Figure 25.2).
In another study of 256 dogs affected with preclinical
MMVD, the overall mortality was 27%, with cardiac
death accounting for 11% during the 833‐day observation period. The same study showed that 30/83 dogs that
were available for reexamination progressed to a more
advanced stage of MMVD. Reported risk factors associated with progression of the disease or death included
age, gender, intensity of heart murmur, degree of valve
prolapse, severity of valve lesions, the degree of mitral
valve regurgitation, degree of left atrial enlargement,
severity of eccentric hypertrophy, rupture of chordae
tendinae, and increased concentration of natriuretic
peptides. Left atrial enlargement, assessed by echocardiography, seems to represent one of the most reliable
independent predictors of death. The risk of death from
cardiac disease for dogs with a left atrium/aortic root
ratio exceeding 1.7 was 2.1 times that of dogs with
smaller atria.
Another study reported that plasma N‐terminal pro‐
brain natriuretic peptide (NT‐proBNP) concentration
and indexed left ventricular end‐diastolic diameter were
independent risk factors for development of first‐onset
CHF. The presence of pulmonary hypertension due to
MMVD was recently reported to be associated with
higher risk of death.
Therapy
The Asymptomatic Dog (Stage B: ACVIM
Consensus)

Treatment of dogs with asymptomatic MMVD has been
a subject of controversy over the past years. This stage
includes dogs with the disease who have never developed
CHF. This group represents the majority of dogs diagnosed with MMVD. The ACVIM consensus suggests
that asymptomatic dogs could be further subdivided into
those with no radiographic or echocardiographic evidence of cardiac enlargement (stage B1) and those with
evidence of cardiac remodeling suggested by the presence of left atrial and ventricular enlargement (stage B2).
This subclassification emphasizes the fact that asymptomatic dogs are a heterogeneous group, including patients
with very mild disease as well as those with more
advanced disease that are more likely to develop clinical
signs of CHF.
The ACVIM consensus group unanimously recommended not treating dogs with MMVD in stage B1 of the
disease. In contrast, no consensus was reached for dogs
in stage B2. Two multicenter double‐blinded studies
evaluating the efficacy of enalapril on delaying the onset
of CHF in stage 1B dogs with MMVD have shown no

VetBooks.ir

25 Valvular Heart Disease

significant effect of angiotensin converting enzyme
inhibitor (ACEI) therapy on the primary outcome variable, which was time from inclusion in the study to the
onset of signs of CHF. Based on these results and the
observation that only a relatively small percentage of
dogs with asymptomatic disease progress to CHF or die
as a consequence of the disease, the author does not
­support treatment with an ACEI.
A recent multicenter clinical trial reported that
pimobendan delays onset of congestive heart failure in a
subpopulation of dogs with stage B2. It should be highlighted that enrolled dogs had significant cardiomegaly
identified by specific echocardiographic criteria. It is
possible, although not proven, that dogs in advanced
stage B2 may benefit from other medical treatments
such as spironolactone. This emphasizes the importance
of developing biomarkers able to identify patients at
higher risk for developing CHF. A study conducted on
72 asymptomatic dogs with MMVD showed that NT‐
proBNP at a cut‐off of 466 pmol/L had 80% sensitivity
and 76% specificity in predicting 12‐month progression
to cardiac death or CHF. Although these data appear
very promising, further studies are needed to confirm
the value of NT‐proBNP in distinguishing those patients
that will progress to CHF. Accordingly, assessment of
stage B dogs should include evaluation of multiple
parameters including clinical, radiographic, and echocardiographic findings.
The Symptomatic Dog (Stage C: ACVIM Consensus)

According to the ACVIM consensus, stage C includes
animals with MMVD and current or previous clinical
signs of CHF. Management of these patients is based on
administration of a combination of several medications,
including diuretics, ACEIs, and pimobendan. Although
no study has proven the efficacy of furosemide in dogs
with MMVD, there is a general consensus that diuretics
are essential for patients with CHF. The majority of dogs
enrolled in the multicenter studies evaluating the ­efficacy
of the ACEI and pimobendan in symptomatic dogs with
MMVD were on concomitant treatment with furosemide. The diagnosis of CHF should be reevaluated if
­diuretics do not improve clinical signs in dogs with suspected CHF. The dosage of furosemide should be
adjusted in order to keep the patients free from clinical
signs. Although the suggested mean dosage for these
patients is 2 mg/kg PO q12h, it could range from 0.5 mg/
kg PO q12h to 4–6 mg/kg PO q8h.
In human patients with CHF, teaching patients to
adjust their furosemide dosage on the basis of monitoring their weight and their clinical signs significantly
reduces the number of hospitalizations and may be associated with prolonged survival. A similar approach with
dogs in CHF is desirable but difficult. The use of an ACEI

together with furosemide in stage C dogs is based on evidence provided by several multicenter double‐blind
studies which provide evidence that an ACEI added to
therapy including furosemide improved the quality of
life and survival time.
Two recent studies have shown that pimobendan
improved survival and quality of life in stage C dogs
compared to standard treatment with an ACEI and
furosemide. The first study was conducted as a blinded,
randomized, positive‐controlled, multicenter study and
included 76 dogs. The study had a mandatory 56‐day
treatment period that was followed by an optional long‐
term treatment phase. In this study, pimobendan significantly improved a clinical measure of disease severity
and survival. The results of this study led to a larger
study in 260 dogs with stage C MMVD. This was a prospective multicenter randomized single‐blinded study
and the primary endpoint was a composite of cardiac
death, euthanasia for heart failure, or treatment failure.
Dogs were randomized to therapy with either ACEI or
pimobendan. Pimobendan was associated with significant improvement in the endpoint variables and this
benefit persisted after adjusting for all baseline variables. All dogs enrolled in this study were on concomitant furosemide treatment. It should be stressed that
none of these studies answer the question of whether
triple therapy involving furosemide, ACEI, and
pimobendan would be superior to double therapy with
pimobendan plus furosemide. The ACVIM consensus
recommended that chronic management of stage C
dogs includes a combination of ACEI, pimobendan, and
furosemide.
Spironolactone has been recently approved in Europe
for treatment of dogs with MMVD. In one study, spironolactone when added to furosemide and ACEI +/− digoxin
decreased risk of cardiac‐related death or euthanasia for
cardiac reasons by 69% in dogs with moderate to severe
MMVD. The dosage of spironolactone used in the clinical trial was 2 mg/kg q24h. One criticism of this study is
that a relatively low number of cases reached the endpoint compared to other studies evaluating stage C dogs.
One possible mechanism of action for spironolactone
would be related to its antifibrotic effects. Geriatric dogs
affected by MMVD have intramyocardial arterial
changes associated with areas of replacement fibrosis.
The exact role of vascular or myocardial fibrosis in the
pathogenesis of MMVD is still to be clarified. Positive
effects of aldosterone blockers such as spironolactone
could also be related to the mechanism of aldosterone
escape. Aldosterone concentrations can be elevated in
dogs with MMVD despite receiving an ACEI. This phenomenon is dependent on the dose of concomitant furosemide and has been attributed to incomplete inhibition
of ACE activity.

Section 3 Cardiovascular Disease

Digoxin is commonly used to treat dogs with concomitant atrial fibrillation in order to control the heart rate.
There are no controlled studies in veterinary medicine
evaluating digoxin, but it is believed that its administration could improve clinical signs of heart failure in dogs.
In the author’s experience, most dogs can be managed
using a combination of furosemide, ACEI, pimobendan,
and spironolactone. Treatment should be individualized
for each patient and the goal is to keep the animal free of
clinical signs of CHF for as long as possible.
The Dog with Refractory Heart Failure (Stage D:
ACVIM Consensus)

Stage D includes dogs refractory to treatments for stage
C. Many of these dogs also have right‐sided heart failure,
which leads to congestion of the gastrointestinal tract
that can decrease absorption of oral medications.
Providing furosemide by subcutaneous injection may
help to restabilize the patient. Chronic use of furosemide
can also lead to furosemide resistance and it is likely that
many stage D patients develop this condition. In these
dogs the use of an alternative loop diuretic, such as
­torsemide, may represent a valid alternative. Adding a
diuretic with a different mechanism of action such as a
thiazide represents another alternative. The goal in these
cases is to induce “sequential nephron blockade” and
improve diuresis. Patients on high doses or combinations of diuretics should have their electrolytes and renal
function monitored closely.
Amlodipine at the dosage of 0.05–0.1 mg/kg q12h is
listed in the ACVIM consensus statement as a possible
treatment for dogs with stage D CHF in order to obtain a
more effective reduction in afterload and improve cardiac output. Arteriolar vasodilation associated with the
use of this drug can lead to severe hypotension. It is,
therefore, recommended to uptitrate the dosage of
amlodipine and monitor the blood pressure in order to
avoid hypotension. In the author’s experience, intravenous vasodilators, such as sodium nitroprusside, can
also help resolve an acute episode of pulmonary edema.

­Valvular Infectious Endocarditis
Etiology and Pathophysiology
Valvular infectious endocarditis (IE) is a severe acquired
valvular disease of dogs and cats that is frequently caused
by bacterial infections. The most common pathogens
associated with IE in the dog and the cat are Staphylococcus
and Streptoccoccus sp. Recently, Bartonella sp. has been
associated with IE, and has been considered responsible
for up to 28% of IE in the dog. Less commonly, IE has
been associated with fungi and Rickettsia spp. IE starts

with damage of the endothelium that triggers the coagulation process. IE requires ­bacteremia. The most common sources of bacteremia are discospondylitis,
prostatis, pneumonia, urinary tract infection, pyoderma,
and intravenous catheters. Circulating bacteria can bind
to the coagulum and induce inflammation that leads to
expression of integrins that further facilitate bacterial
adhesion to the damaged ­tissue. Some bacteria, such as
Staphylococcus sp., might increase their ability to bind to
the coagulum through increased expression of microbial
surface adhesive molecules. Vegetative lesions containing bacteria provide a protective barrier and obstacle to
antibiotic penetration. Moreover, bacteria can produce
enzymes that lead to further tissue damage.
The only cardiovascular disease associated with an
increased risk of IE is subaortic stenosis. Historically,
periodontal diseases have been thought to increase the
risk of bacterial endocarditis, but an association has
never been demonstrated.
Epidemiology
Infectious endocarditis is a rare condition in dogs and
cats. According to published data, prevalence of the
­disease varies from 0.005% to 0.09% in the dog. The
prevalence in cats has not been reported but IE is less
frequently noted in this species. A recent retrospective
study has suggested that IE is becoming more common.
This might be attributed to the increased recognition of
the disease due to the availability of echocardiography.
Large‐breed dogs are more commonly affected. A review
of published data shows that the mitral valve is most
commonly affected (60%) followed by the aortic valve
(29%). Both the aortic and mitral valves are affected in
5% of the dogs, whereas the pulmonic and tricuspid
valves are rarely affected in dogs (4%).
History and Clinical Signs
Clinical signs in patients with IE are various and nonspecific. Many patients show clinical signs related to the
underlying systemic disease that produced the bacteremia. Analysis of published case series including 183 dogs
with IE showed that the most common clinical sign is
lameness (67%), followed by anorexia (55%), lethargy
(55%), acute onset of respiratory distress (52%), and
­syncope/weakness (15%). Fever is reported in 48% of
cases. Presence of a murmur is reported in only 55% of
cases with a definitive diagnosis of IE. The reason for the
relatively low prevalence of murmurs may be similar to
what has been previously described for murmurs in
patients with MMVD. Moreover, when only the aortic
valve is affected, the murmur can be diastolic and
­difficult to recognize. The recognition of a new systolic

VetBooks.ir

25 Valvular Heart Disease

or diastolic murmur in a patient with a predisposing
condition should be considered suspicious for IE.
­
Patients with aortic IE and severe aortic insufficiency
may present bounding femoral pulses. Thirty‐seven
­percent of dogs with IE present with clinical signs of
CHF at the time of the diagnosis.
Diagnosis
Diagnosis of IE is challenging. Antemortem diagnosis
involves blood cultures, preferably performed before antibiotic treatment is started. Three to four blood samples
should be collected aseptically from different venous sites
at least one hour apart and submitted for aerobic and
anaerobic culture. Blood samples should also be collected
and cultured for Bartonella spp. Recently, polymerase
chain reaction (PCR) has been proposed as an alternative
method for the diagnosis of Bartonella i­nfection. A complete blood count (CBC) and serum biochemistry profile
should be performed in all patients with suspected IE in
order to assess multiorgan involvement. Leukocytosis,
thrombocytopenia, anemia, hypoalbuminemia, increased
liver enzymes, and azotemia are the most commonly
reported laboratory findings in dogs with IE.
Echocardiography allows the identification of vegetative
valvular lesions and assessment of the severity of the valvular insufficiency and is complementary to blood cultures in
establishing the diagnosis of IE in the dog and cat. Typical
lesions are represented by an hyperchoic, mobile, irregular‐
shaped mass adherent to the valve (Figure 25.3).
Valvular insufficiency is a common finding. Patients
with chronic valvular IE and severe valvular regurgitation
may present with left ventricular eccentric hypertrophy.
Although the presence of typical valvular lesions strongly
supports the diagnosis of IE, small lesions on the mitral
valve can be difficult to differentiate from lesions due to
myxomatous degeneration.
The diagnostic criteria for IE in dogs and cats is modified from the human “Duke criteria”. Major criteria for
diagnosis are a positive echocardiogram, new valvular
insufficiency, and a positive blood culture (≥2 positive
cultures or ≥3 positive cultures with common skin contaminants). Minor diagnostic criteria are fever, medium
to large dog (>15 kg), subaortic stenosis, thromboembolic disease, immune‐mediated disease, positive blood
cultures not meeting major criteria, and Bartonella
serology ≥1:1024. A definitive diagnosis of IE involves

Figure 25.3 Echocardiographic long axis image of the aortic
valve. A hyperchoic, mobile, irregular‐shaped mass is present
adherent to the valve leaflet.

the presence of two major criteria or one major and two
minor criteria. The presence of one major and one minor
criteria or three minor criteria is suspicious for IE.
Treatment
Long‐term bactericidal antibiotics are the main therapy
for patients affected by IE. Broad‐spectrum combinations of antibiotics such as enrofloxacin and ampicillin
should be administered empirically if blood culture is
not available or pending. Treatment of Bartonella spp.
involves doxycycline, fluoroquinolones, or azithromycin.
In dogs requiring hospitalization, intravenous aminoglycosides such as amikacin have been recommended.
Ideally, antibiotic therapy is guided by results of culture
and sensitivity testing. Oral antibiotics are often continued for 6–8 weeks. Serial echocardiograms or blood
­cultures are used to monitor response to therapy. Patients
with heart failure secondary to IE should be treated with
standard CHF treatment.
Prognosis
Generally, patients with IE have a relatively poor prognosis. Outcome is related to the degree of valvular
regurgitation and nature of the underlying predisposing
cause. Dogs with aortic IE fare worse than dogs with
mitral IE (three days versus 476 days median survival
time).

Canine Myocardial Disease
M. Lynne O’Sullivan, DVM, DVSc, DACVIM (Cardiology)
Department of Companion Animals, Atlantic Veterinary College, University of Prince Edward Island, Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, Canada

Canine myocardial diseases are those that affect the heart
muscle, as opposed to valvular, endocardial, or pericardial diseases. Cardiomyopathies are the most common
myocardial diseases in dogs, and are a “heterogenous
group of diseases of the myocardium associated with
mechanical and/or electrical dysfunction” according to
the American Heart Association. They may be classified
clinically according to structural and functional phenotype: dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive, and arrhythmogenic right ventricular. Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM)
is by far the most common cardiomyopathy in dogs.
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy
(ARVC) is seen most commonly in the boxer, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is reported in dogs but is
rare. Restrictive cardiomyopathy is not recognized in
dogs. Other forms of canine myocardial disease include
myocarditis (infectious, inflammatory, toxic, traumatic),
infiltrative disease (neoplastic, storage diseases), ischemic
disease, myocardial disease secondary to systemic hypertension, and muscular dystrophies affecting the heart.
The focus of this chapter is the cardiomyopathies.

­Dilated Cardiomyopathy
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Dilated cardiomyopathy is a primary myocardial disease
characterized by dilation and systolic dysfunction of the
left or both ventricles, in the absence of valvular, pericardial, congenital, coronary artery, or hypertensive heart
disease. The DCM phenotype may be the result of various myocardial insults, which are often not identified,
rendering many cases idiopathic. In dogs, those “insults”
are in many cases genetic mutations leading to altered
cardiac protein structure and function, particularly in
the pure breeds predisposed to DCM. In humans,

30–50% of cases of DCM are familial or inherited, and
mutations involving over 50 cardiac genes have been
described to date. Mutations in two genes (PDK4 and
titin) have been associated with DCM in Doberman pinschers in North America, but do not account for all
cases. The PDK4 mutation was not significantly associated with DCM in a group of European Dobermans in
which DCM was linked to a different chromosome
­(candidate genes yet unidentified). This highlights the
complex nature of the role that genetics play in this disease and that multiple genetic factors are involved, even
within one breed. Juvenile DCM in the Portuguese water
dog has been linked to chromosome 8 and candidate
gene identification is ongoing.
Additional well‐recognized etiologies in dogs include
nutritional deficiencies (taurine, carnitine) and tachycardia induced (secondary to sustained tachyarrhythmia).
Infectious and toxic causes of myocarditis, characterized
by myocardial inflammation and necrosis, can produce a
DCM‐like phenotype (ventricular dilation, systolic dysfunction, arrhythmias) in the chronic phase, and may be
worth considering as the underlying “insult” in certain
clinical presentations or geographic areas. Examples
include bacterial (e.g. Borrelia burgdorferi, Bartonella),
viral (e.g., parvovirus, West Nile virus), protozoal (e.g.,
Trypanosoma cruzi [Chagas disease], Toxoplasma gondii), fungal (e.g., Aspergillus, Blastomyces, Coccidioides),
and toxic (e.g., anthracyclines) agents. The above‐­
mentioned nonfamilial, nonidiopathic causes make up a
very small percentage of the total DCM caseload, as
­idiopathic or familial cases are most common.
On a whole‐heart level, the primary abnormality is a
reduction in contractility. This results in a reduction in
stroke volume (the volume ejected) and an increase
in end‐systolic volume (the volume remaining in the
heart after ejection), in turn resulting in progressive
increases in end‐diastolic volume. A reduction in

Clinical Small Animal Internal Medicine Volume I, First Edition. Edited by David S. Bruyette.
© 2020 John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Published 2020 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc.
Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/bruyette/clinical

VetBooks.ir

254

Section 3 Cardiovascular Disease

blood pressure and tissue perfusion activates a number
of ­neuroendocrine and cytokine systems intended to
maintain stroke volume and blood pressure, primarily
through sodium and water retention and vasoconstriction. Stretch receptors and remodeling pathways are
triggered, leading to lengthening of individual myocytes
(eccentric hypertrophy) and chamber dilation, maladaptive extracellular matrix remodeling, and cell death.
Consequences of these alterations in cardiac structure
and function ­eventually include congestive heart failure
(CHF) and arrhythmias (see Chapter 18).
Epidemiology
The prevalence of DCM among canine referral populations has been reported to be 0.3–1% (equivalent to 1–3
cases per 300 patients examined). Underreporting of sudden death (SD) cases might result in underestimation of
any figure, thus the true prevalence in the general dog
population is unknown. Any prevalence data will be
heavily influenced by the distribution of breeds and ages
(prevalence increases with age) of the population under
study. The prevalence is high in certain breeds based on
retrospective studies and prospective screening studies.
One European study of Irish wolfhounds (IW) found a
prevalence of 24%. In the Great Dane, prevalence has
ranged from 12% to 36% in different geographic areas.
Prevalence in Dobermans has ranged from 45% to 60% in
various studies. Some studies report overrepresentation
of males, while in Dobermans there are gender differences in how the disease manifests and at what age, with
females having a higher incidence of ventricular arrhythmias as the sole abnormality and males manifesting echocardiographic abnormalities and CHF at an e­ arlier age.
The mode of inheritance is known for specific breed
groups. In the Doberman and the Newfoundland, DCM
is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with incomplete penetrance. Both X‐linked and autosomal dominant
patterns of inheritance have been suggested in the Great
Dane, whereas inheritance is autosomal recessive with
sex‐specific alleles in the IW. The juvenile form described
in the Portuguese water dog is autosomal recessive.
The natural history of the disease is such that dogs
experience a preclinical or occult phase during which
echocardiographic or electrocardiographic evidence of
the disease is present (see Diagnosis) but clinical signs
are absent (ACVIM stage B). The length of this phase is
variable and likely extends over months to years, depending on the breed. In the Doberman, previous retrospective work suggested a median preclinical phase of just
over a year whereas new prospective clinical trial data
suggest a median of two years with the use of pimobendan.
The preclinical phase can be quite prolonged in the IW,
averaging 48 months in one trial.

The overt phase follows, characterized by the onset of
clinical signs including syncope, SD, or those typical of
CHF (ACVIM stage C). In the Doberman, 25–30% experience SD before CHF. Survival time following the onset
of CHF or syncope is again breed and etiology dependent, with Dobermans and Great Danes experiencing the
shortest survival times among breeds (see Prognosis).
Risk factors for the development of DCM apart from
breed may include taurine deficiency (in cocker spaniels,
Labrador and golden retrievers, or nontraditional DCM
breeds), sustained tachyarrhythmias, myocarditis, or
chemotherapy (anthracyclines).
Signalment
Dilated cardiomyopathy occurs predominantly in middle‐aged to older, medium‐ to large‐breed dogs. The
most commonly reported breeds in North America and
Europe include the Doberman pinscher, IW, Great Dane,
Newfoundland, boxer, Labrador and golden retrievers,
cocker spaniel, Scottish deerhound, Afghan hound, St
Bernard, German shepherd, Old English sheepdog,
Airedale terrier, standard poodle, Rottweiler, and ­mastiff.
Small‐breed dogs are uncommonly affected but sporadic
cases can be found.
Age at diagnosis is typically between 4 and 8 years,
depending on breed. Much younger and much older
dogs may certainly be affected, regardless of breed.
Specific juvenile forms of DCM are described in the
Portuguese water dog, Doberman, and toy Manchester
terrier, resulting in rapidly progressive CHF or SD at
weeks to months of age. Sporadic cases in very young
dogs of other breeds may occur, and should prompt
­consideration of viral myocarditis or primary tachyarrhythmia as an underlying cause.
Many studies report a gender bias in males. While this
is not corroborated in all studies of individual breeds, it
is the case for the majority of studies involving multiple
breeds. Male Dobermans and IWs may be affected at an
earlier age than females.
History and Clinical Signs
History may be unremarkable and preclinical cases identified by an incidental abnormality on physical exam
(such as a heart murmur, gallop, or arrhythmia) or by
prospective screening in high‐risk breeds. Some of these
dogs in the preclinical stage may have surprisingly profound cardiac dysfunction in the absence of clinical signs.
More often, dogs are presented because of clinical signs
of a fairly acute nature. Respiratory signs are the most
common, including coughing and/or increased respiratory rate or effort due to pulmonary edema from left‐
sided CHF. With severe pulmonary edema, expectoration

VetBooks.ir

26 Canine Myocardial Disease

of pink‐tinged fluid may be noted. Pleural effusion from
right‐sided CHF can also produce increased respiratory
rate and effort. Other signs include exercise intolerance,
weakness, syncope, abdominal distension due to ascites,
weight loss, and reduced appetite or anorexia (see
Chapter 15). Sometimes SD is the first clinical sign noted.
The typical clinical signs exhibited may vary by breed.
For example, Dobermans tend to have a higher incidence
of syncope and SD and their pulmonary edema and
resultant respiratory signs are often quite severe, whereas
IWs and Newfoundlands frequently present with evidence of right‐sided CHF (ascites and pleural effusion).
The most common abnormalities detected on physical
examination are a soft systolic murmur over the mitral or
tricuspid area (often grade 1–3/6) and weak peripheral
pulses. However, various studies have reported murmurs
in as few as 33% and as many as 76%, so the absence of a
murmur does not rule DCM out, and physical examination may be normal in the early preclinical phase.
Additional findings may include a diastolic gallop (low‐
frequency third heart sound), an arrhythmia (ventricular
premature contractions and atrial fibrillation most
­common), pulse deficits (if an arrhythmia is present),
and jugular venous distension or pulsation. For dogs in
CHF, additional findings may include pale or cyanotic
mucous membranes, increased lung sounds or pulmonary crackles, tachycardia, tachypnea, dyspnea, hypothermia, and hepatomegaly (hepatic congestion) or a
fluid wave (ascites) on abdominal palpation.
Diagnosis
The diagnosis of DCM involves a minimum of an
echocardiogram and electrocardiogram (ECG). Holter

recording (24‐hour ambulatory ECG) is the most appropriate form of ECG in breeds where ventricular arrhythmias are common or an early finding such as Dobermans,
for longer term heart rate (HR) assessment in atrial
fibrillation, or if a cause for syncope is sought. In cases
where echocardiography is not immediately available,
thoracic radiographs may be useful for detecting cardiomegaly, and plasma N‐terminal pro‐B‐type natriuretic
peptide (NT‐proBNP) level can be useful in Dobermans
for assessing likelihood of preclinical disease. For dogs
with suspected CHF, thoracic radiographs and serum
biochemistry should be performed. The role for blood‐
based tests including biomarkers, taurine levels, and
genetic tests is also discussed below. Screening should be
performed yearly in high‐risk breeds.
Electrocardiography

While arrhythmias are frequently reported on ECG
(89% of cases in one large retrospective study), they can
be very intermittent. Ventricular arrhythmias (VA)
­(ventricular premature contractions [VPCs] or ventricular tachycardia [VT]) and atrial fibrillation (AF) are most
common, but are not specific for DCM on their own
(Figures 26.1 and 26.2).
There are differences between breeds in arrhythmia
manifestation. VA are very common in Dobermans, boxers, and Great Danes, so their presence should always
raise suspicion of DCM in these breeds. In one study in
Dobermans, one or more VPCs on a 5‐min ECG was
almost 97% specific for detecting a level of VA on Holter
recording that would be suggestive of DCM. However,
the presence of VPCs on a 5‐min ECG alone is fairly
insensitive for detecting DCM. Studies report 44–64% of
affected Dobermans and 54% of affected Great Danes

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is more common in IWs and

(found in 75% of occult DCM cases, >90% of overt DCM

more advanced or overt disease. Importantly, giant‐
breed dogs can also have “lone” AF unassociated with
gross cardiac pathology, in which case the HR is often
normal. However, in the IW, it is hypothesized that AF
may be a precursor to DCM in many cases.
Additional ECG findings can include tall and wide
QRS complexes (lead II R‐wave >3.0 mV, QRS duration
>0.06 ms) associated with left ventricular (LV) enlargement, notched R‐waves associated with microscopic
ischemia, wide P‐waves (lead II P duration >0.04 ms)
associated with left atrial enlargement, and sinus tachycardia (particularly in CHF cases). Note that these ECG
findings are neither sensitive nor specific for DCM.

(a)

Holter Recording

Given that arrhythmias apart from AF are typically intermittent and in‐house ECGs are relatively insensitive,
Holter recordings can be very useful for diagnosing and
quantifying arrhythmias, for seeking cause of collapse by
coupling clinical signs with rhythm analysis, and for
assessing therapeutic response to antiarrhythmics. In
Dobermans, the presence of >300 VPCs/24h, or two subsequent recordings within a year with 50–300 VPCs/24h,
may be suggestive of DCM. Coupling a Holter recording
with a NT‐proBNP level can increase sensitivity for initial screening (see Circulating Biomarkers). Whether
these Holter criteria are appropriate for breeds other
than Dobermans is not known, but in one study, 70% of
affected Great Danes had a similar degree of arrhythmia.
Holter monitoring is also useful for monitoring HR in
cases of AF as it yields a more accurate assessment of rate
control. Care should be taken to utilize Holter analyses
that have been manually edited and verified by qualified
personnel as purely automated analyses are notoriously
inaccurate.

(b)

Thoracic Radiography

Thoracic radiographs are relatively insensitive to detect
the mild cardiac enlargement typical of occult cases. In
instances of more severe disease, they can reveal varying
degrees of cardiomegaly (left‐sided or generalized).
Thoracic radiographs are always indicated if CHF is suspected. In addition to LV enlargement, findings in CHF
include left atrial and possibly right‐sided enlargement,
pulmonary venous distension and varying degrees of
pulmonary edema (interstitial changes in mild to moderate cases and alveolar opacities with air bronchograms in
