Echocardiography

Echocardiography is necessary for identification and
quantification of the characteristic structural abnormalities, including LV chamber dilation and systolic dysfunction, and equally important for ruling out other cardiac
causes apart from DCM for these findings (e.g., valvular
disease, congenital shunt) (Figure 26.4).
Increased LV end‐systolic dimension (LVESD) and/or
volume (LVESV) is noted, along with increased LV end‐
diastolic dimension (LVEDD) and/or volume (LVEDV).

Linear dimensions (diameters) are generated from an M‐
mode of the LV in a short‐ or long‐axis view immediately
below the mitral valve, and volumes are preferentially
generated by tracing the LV endocardium in a right parasternal long‐axis or left apical four‐chamber view and
using automated software for Simpson’s method of discs.
These parameters are often indexed to body weight (BW)
or body surface area (BSA) to normalize for differences in
body size and conformation. In Dobermans, volume
indices have been shown to be more sensitive in detection of LV dilation than diameters. Normal parameters
and breed‐specific criteria suggesting the diagnosis of
DCM from various studies are presented in Table 26.1.
The reader is referred to the Further Reading list for more
detailed information on the methods and views used.
Left ventricle wall motion is globally and symmetrically reduced in most cases, but some dogs may have
increased septal motion compared to the free wall owing

is diagnostic of DCM and little emphasis should be
placed on this number alone. Having said that, in DCM
dogs with CHF, FS is often <15%.

atrial dilation with more advanced disease, reduced
mitral valve excursion, increased mitral valve E‐point to
septal separation, decreased LV sphericity index, and

right ventricular and atrial dilation with biventricular
disease.
Doppler findings can include secondary mitral regurgitation due to annulus dilation and papillary muscle
dysfunction, evidence of diastolic dysfunction (abnormal
transmitral flow patterns including impaired relaxation,
pseudonormal, and restrictive), reduced aortic velocities, and reduced myocardial tissue velocities.
Circulating Biomarkers

Cardiac biomarkers include hormones released by cardiac myocytes in response to stretch and other stimuli

VetBooks.ir

26 Canine Myocardial Disease

(NT‐proBNP), or substances released from myocardial
tissue in response to injury (cardiac troponin‐I [cTnI]).
Note that biomarker testing is never intended to be used
in isolation and should not replace gold standard testing
(e.g., echocardiography, thoracic radiography for CHF);
rather, it may be a tool to complement, and in some
instances justify, other indicated diagnostics. Diagnoses
and therapeutic recommendations cannot be made on
biomarker results alone.
The utility of NT‐proBNP in identifying likelihood of
occult disease has been examined in the Doberman. NT‐
proBNP >550 pmol/L had a sensitivity of 78.6% and
specificity of 90.4% for detecting echocardiographic
­
abnormalities in one study. It is more sensitive in the
detection of structural disease than arrhythmic disease.
Another study in Dobermans suggests that the combined
use of Holter monitoring and NT‐proBNP >457 pmol/L
(either being abnormal) yields increased sensitivity (94.5%)
and specificity (87.8%). A cTnI >0.22 ng/mL (Immulite®,
Troponin I, Diagnostics Products Corporation, Los
Angeles) yielded 79.5% sensitivity and 84.4% specificity for
detection of DCM in another study. Dobermans with
NT‐proBNP or cTnI greater than these values should be
evaluated with echocardiography.
For the differentiation of CHF from primary respiratory disease in dogs presenting with respiratory signs,
plasma NT‐proBNP >2447 pmol/L (using second‐­
generation assay) was 81.1% sensitive and 73.1% specific
in a study including 8% DCM cases in a variety of breeds.
This may have utility when physical exam and thoracic
radiography are ambiguous and echocardiography is not
available, but otherwise may not provide added value.
Plasma Taurine

Whole‐blood or plasma taurine should be measured
(using heparinized samples) in cocker spaniels, retrievers,
Dalmatians, any atypical DCM breed, or any case with a
history of lamb‐based diet, vegetarian diet, low‐protein
diet, grain‐free diet (currently being investigated), or any
unbalanced home‐made diet. Whole‐blood concentration
<150 nmol/mL or plasma concentration <40 nmol/mL
indicates significant taurine deficiency. Note that taurine
deficiency is not necessarily related to amounts of taurine
consumed, but may be due to abnormal absorption or
excretion of taurine or its precursor amino acids (methionine and cysteine), abnormal t­ aurine synthesis, or reduced
protein digestibility limiting availability of precursors.
Genetic Tests

Tests are available for two genetic markers associated with
DCM in Dobermans in North America (PDK4 and titin
mutations) through the Veterinary Genetics laboratory at
North Carolina State University (https://cvm.ncsu.edu/
nc-state-vet-hospital/small-animal/genetics/). Note that

these two mutations do not account for all DCM cases in
Dobermans, a negative test does not assure a dog will not
develop DCM, nor does a positive test assure the dog will
develop clinical disease. With this in mind, genetic testing
cannot replace standard clinical screening. Appropriate
sample types include EDTA whole‐blood or buccal swabs.
Results may be:
negative – individual does not carry that particular
mutation (but there may be other mutations so not
guaranteed to never develop DCM)
●● positive heterozygote – individual carries one copy of
the mutated gene and may or may not develop clinical
disease
●● positive homozygote – individual carries two copies of
the mutated gene and may or may not develop clinical
disease but if so, may be more severe.
●●

The greatest utility of genetic testing is determining suitability for breeding. It is recommended that homozygous
dogs not be bred, and heterozygous dogs should be bred
only to negative dogs and only so long as they do not
express the phenotype.
Therapy
Preclinical DCM (ACVIM Stage B)

Goals of therapy in preclinical cases include slowing systolic dysfunction, preventing ventricular remodeling and
disease progression, and delaying CHF or SD. Two drugs
for which there is evidence of these benefits are
pimobendan and angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEI). See Table 26.2 for all drug doses.
Pimobendan, a calcium sensitizer with positive inotropic and vasodilatory effects, delayed the progression
of preclinical disease in Dobermans in a multicenter,
placebo‐controlled, double‐blinded clinical trial. The
­
PROTECT trial enrolled 76 Dobermans with preclinical
DCM. The pimobendan group had a significantly longer
time to the composite endpoint of onset of CHF or SD
compared with the placebo group (63% increase in time
to endpoint, nine months longer). Additionally, the
pimobendan group had significantly longer overall survival time compared with the placebo group. There was
no increase in VA noted on one‐month recheck Holter
monitoring and no increase in SD in the pimobendan
group. It is important to note that all dogs in this study
had presence of echocardiographic systolic dysfunction,
so these results are not necessarily applicable to
Dobermans presenting with VA alone. Pimobendan was
also shown to prolong the time to CHF or SD in IWs with
preclinical DCM, AF, or both. The similarity in pathology and pathophysiology among different breeds would
suggest potential benefit in breeds other than Dobermans
and IWs, but specific studies are required.

ACEI, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor; CRI, constant rate

The role of the renin‐angiotensin‐aldosterone system
(RAAS) in maladaptive cardiac remodeling and progression of systolic dysfunction is well known. In addition to
their mixed vasodilatory and natriuretic properties, ACEI

exert benefit by antimyocardial remodeling effects. A retrospective study in Dobermans found that time to CHF
or SD was significantly prolonged with benazepril treatment, with a 55–64% reduction of risk of those outcomes
compared to no treatment. While the strength of evidence is not as strong as that for pimobendan, the author
advocates the use of ACEI in preclinical DCM based on
the collective evidence in the human and ­veterinary literature, unless there is a specific contraindication to this
class of drug. Evaluation of renal function one week after
initiation and periodically thereafter is recommended.
While there is good evidence in the human literature
that beta‐blocker therapy reverses LV remodeling,
improves LV systolic function and patient symptoms,
and prolongs life in chronic heart failure, clinical data are
lacking on the use and efficacy of beta‐blockers in canine
DCM. Concerns with beta‐blocker use typically include
hypotension or CHF due to bradycardia and negative
inotropy when first administering; therefore, they must
be used with caution and uptitrated slowly.
Taurine supplementation should be initiated in any
case suspected or documented to be due to taurine deficiency. L‐carnitine can be simultaneously added or initiated after three months if there is inadequate response
with taurine alone.
The patient with clinically significant VA is worthy of
separate consideration. In humans, the risk of SD increases
with declining systolic function or a history of syncope,
yet there is no clear evidence that any antiarrhythmic
(AA) drug is effective in preventing SD. In Dobermans,
increasing LVEDV, presence of VT, and VPCs yielding
instantaneous HR ≥260 bpm are associated with increased
risk of SD. There are no studies addressing the efficacy of
AA therapy in canine DCM. AA therapy may be considered in any DCM patient with frequent VPCs (>1 per
minute) or VA with higher ­complexity or rate (couplets,
triplets, or VT with instantaneous HR >180 bpm). Typical
choices for AA therapy include sotalol, a AA with both
beta‐blockade and K+ channel blockade properties (initiating low doses and titrating upwards is often advised due
to the beta‐blockade), mexiletine, a Na+ channel blocker,
or a combination of the two.
Monitoring the preclinical patient should include
physical examination, echocardiography, and ECG or
ideally Holter recording every 4–6 months. If AA therapy is initiated, it is best to monitor therapeutic efficacy
with Holter monitoring within 1–2 weeks of initiating
therapy. Due to a high degree of daily variability, an in‐
house ECG is an inadequate alternative.
Overt DCM (ACVIM Stage C, CHF): Outpatient
Therapy

Therapeutic goals in the CHF patient include resolution of clinical signs and improvement in quality of life

VetBooks.ir

26 Canine Myocardial Disease

in addition to delay in disease progression and prolongation of survival. Strategies include intravascular volume reduction to resolve pulmonary edema or decrease
cavitary effusions, improvement in hemodynamic
performance through decreased systemic vascular
­
resistance and improved contractility, neurohumoral
modulation, arrhythmia management, and nutritional
management.
The mainstay of treatment of edema and effusions
remains diuretics, with furosemide the most commonly
used agent. It may be administered orally or intravenously depending on the severity of CHF and whether
the patient is being treated as an inpatient or outpatient.
Following edema resolution, the dose may be lowered to
the effective dose that maintains the patient free of
­respiratory signs and edema. Given its relatively short
duration of action, dosing more than twice daily may be
more effective. Substantive pleural effusion or ascites
should be relieved with thoraco‐ and abdominocentesis,
respectively.
Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor is indicated
for RAAS blockade and vasodilatory effects, particularly
in the setting of furosemide use which heightens RAAS
stimulation. The results of veterinary clinical trials using
enalapril and benazepril report improved quality of life,
and although the improvements in survival did not reach
statistical significance for DCM dogs, there is clear
­evidence of mortality reduction in human patients and
ACEI use is considered standard therapy in dogs with
DCM and CHF.
Three placebo‐controlled trials have found significantly longer time to treatment failure or longer survival
time in DCM dogs treated with pimobendan in addition
to diuretics and ACEI, so pimobendan is considered part
of standard therapy for CHF due to DCM.
The aldosterone antagonist spironolactone significantly reduces morbidity and mortality in humans with
CHF and LV systolic dysfunction. While similar evidence
is lacking in dogs with DCM, a study in Dobermans with
CHF suggested a reduced risk of AF with spironolactone
therapy. Spironolactone is often used in the patient that
is still symptomatic despite use of triple therapy with
furosemide, ACEI, and pimobendan, whereas some,
including the author, advocate using it initially as part of
standard therapy. Spironolactone is licensed for use in
dogs with CHF in Europe.
Management of the overt DCM patient with VA
includes optimal management of congestion and hemodynamics to reduce sympathetic nervous system stimulation and improve perfusion. Specific AA therapy may
also be indicated. Patients with VA may be managed as
outlined above for the preclinical stage. DCM patients
with AF and in‐hospital HR >150 bpm are candidates for
rate control with AA therapy. While cardioversion to

sinus rhythm may be physiologically ideal, rate control is
much more feasible. Evidence suggests that the combination of diltiazem with digoxin is more efficacious for rate
control than either drug alone. A target mean HR
<125 bpm on Holter recording is ideal, and given higher
HR in hospital, target mean HR on in‐hospital ECG
should be <140–150 bpm. Alternative therapy choices
include a beta‐blocker or sotalol, though beta‐blockers
should not be initiated in the setting of acute or poorly
managed heart failure.
Cardiac cachexia is identified commonly in DCM CHF
patients and nutritional support is an important part of
therapy. Due to anorexia, increased energy requirements, and production of inflammatory cytokines, lean
muscle mass is lost in the chronic heart failure patient.
Management involves providing adequate calories and
protein, and there is evidence that supplementation with
omega‐3 fatty acids is beneficial. While diets restricted
in sodium are commonly advocated, the effects on quality of life or survival have not been assessed in dogs.
Overt DCM – Severe Life‐Threatening CHF

Parenteral means of decreasing intravascular volume,
increasing contractility, decreasing vascular resistance,
and treating arrhythmias may be necessary in cases of
severe CHF. Administration of oxygen by nasal prongs,
cannula or cage is indicated in the case of hypoxia.
Administration of intravenous (IV) furosemide by bolus
or constant rate infusion (CRI) is the single most important and effective strategy to initiate promptly. Multiple
boluses may be administered 30–60 minutes apart until
the respiratory rate drops 50% from initial presentation
or effort improves. If there is inadequate response after
three doses, CRI should be initiated. Alternatively, one
bolus followed immediately by CRI is preferred if the
patient has preexisting azotemia or is particularly severe.
Careful monitoring of volume status, renal function, and
electrolytes is required. Thoracocentesis is indicated if
substantive pleural effusion is contributing to dyspnea.
If rapid AF is present, initiation of IV diltiazem is indicated to reduce HR below 140–150 bpm. In cases of VA
in the setting of CHF, treatment may be warranted if VT
is present, signs of weakness or collapse are present, or
the patient is a breed with a high incidence of SD such as
Dobermans and boxers. IV lidocaine is typically the first
treatment of choice.
In the absence of arrhythmias, IV furosemide may be
enough to stabilize some patients whereas others will
require the addition of a parenteral positive inotrope +/−
vasodilator. Dobutamine CRI is the IV positive inotrope
of choice for treatment of severe edema and hypotension. Side‐effects include nausea/vomiting and exacerbation of VA, in which case the dose should be decreased.
It is important to note that if AF is present, IV diltiazem

261

VetBooks.ir

262

Section 3 Cardiovascular Disease

should be initiated for rate control before dobutamine to
avoid life‐threatening tachycardia. Dobutamine is typically administered for <72 hours due to the development
of receptor refractoriness. If dobutamine is not available
or feasible, then oral pimobendan should be started as
soon as possible.
Sodium nitroprusside is a potent mixed vasodilator
that may be added as a CRI for the treatment of severe
life‐threatening edema. Blood pressure must be monitored very frequently, preferably invasively and continuously. Side‐effects include hypotension (which can be
quickly resolved by stopping or decreasing the dose due
to its very short duration of action), and rarely cyanide
toxicity with high dose and prolonged use (>72 hours).
With the initiation of all of these infusions, careful attention must be paid to the volumes of fluids being administered, and solutions should be concentrated as much as
possible to reduce the total volume being administered.
Following stabilization, weaning of IV medications and
transition to the oral medications discussed above (as for
outpatient) is carried out.
For the refractory CHF patient (those with advanced
CHF that continue to have clinical signs despite standard
therapy – ACVIM stage D), management strategies
include confirming owner compliance with current
medications, identifying complicating concurrent conditions (poorly controlled or new arrhythmias, systemic
diseases such as hyperadrenocorticism, neoplasia, infectious or inflammatory conditions), and changing medication strategies. The latter can include an increase in
the frequency or change in route of furosemide administration (IV bolus or CRI for short periods), addition of
diuretics such as spironolactone or hydrochlorothiazide
(the latter should be accompanied by a reduction in furosemide dose), stricter sodium restriction, increase in
inodilator and/or ACEI dose, or short‐term parenteral
positive inotrope (dobutamine) or vasodilator (nitroprusside) administration as described above.
Follow‐up/Monitoring of Overt DCM

The focus of follow‐up is respiratory status (respiratory
rate and effort, degree of pulmonary edema or pleural
effusion on thoracic radiography), renal status and electrolyte balance (renal chemistry and electrolytes), body
condition and hydration (body weight, body condition
score [BCS]), HR and rhythm (auscultation, ECG or
Holter), and perfusion (body temperature, blood pressure, renal chemistry, electrolytes). These assessments
may be made as frequently as weekly at the initiation of
therapy to every 1–2 months once patients are stable.
While ACEI and pimobendan doses are often optimized
at the onset, diuretic doses are adjusted to balance pulmonary and renal/hydration needs. Following initiation
of or change in dose of AAs, recheck ECG or ideally

Holter is advised within 1–2 weeks to assess VA control
or rate control in the case of AF, and medications adjusted
accordingly. One cannot expect to eliminate VA but
rather a reduction of the frequency, complexity, and HR
is a reasonable goal (preferably reduction of >80%). In
the case of AF, HR targets must be individualized to what
appears to be optimal for the patient based on the assessments above, but a general guideline is a target mean HR
<125 bpm on Holter or <140–150 bpm in hospital.
Prognosis
Dogs with preclinical disease may go several years without clinical signs, so the diagnosis does not imply immediate risk of morbidity or mortality. Data on the length of
this phase are lacking for most breeds except the
Doberman and IW. Based on the PROTECT trial, the
median time to CHF or SD following diagnosis of occult
disease in Dobermans was 718 days in the pimobendan‐
treated group and 441 in the placebo group. IW may
have a very prolonged preclinical phase, with an average
of 48 months in a recent clinical trial.
Unless a reversible underlying cause is identified (e.g.,
taurine deficiency, primary tachyarrhythmia), the prognosis for DCM is often poor once overt clinical disease
(CHF) develops, with most survival times being in
months. The median survival time in a large retrospective study with mostly overt dogs was 19 weeks, with
one‐year and two‐year survival rates of 28% and 14%,
respectively. Fifty percent of dogs were euthanized for
their heart disease in this study, while 40% died from
their heart disease, and 3% died for other reasons,
emphasizing the almost inevitably terminal nature of
this disease. In the Doberman, one‐year survival rates of
10% or less have been reported, and treatment with triple therapy (ACEI, furosemide, pimobendan) yielded a
median survival time of 130 days. IW may have a better
prognosis once in CHF, with median survival time
of five months in those dying of their disease but
14 months in those still alive at the time of writing of
one study.
Factors associated with shorter time to CHF or SD in
the PROTECT trial included an increase in LVESD
index, increased baseline HR, and ≥4 VPCs on a 3‐min
ECG. Factors associated with negative prognosis in overt
DCM have included increased LVESV index, decreased
EF, presence of pulmonary edema on radiographs, presence of ascites, presence of VPCs on ECG, increased
serum creatinine, decreased plasma protein, Great Dane
breed, and restrictive transmitral flow pattern on
Doppler echocardiography. Factors associated with
increased risk of SD in Dobermans include larger LVEDV,
presence of VT, VPCs with instanteous HR ≥260 bpm,
and higher cTnI.

­Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular
Cardiomyopathy
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy is a
progressive myocardial disorder characterized by partial
to complete replacement of the right ventricular (RV)
myocardium with fatty or fibro‐fatty tissue, presence of
ventricular arrhythmias, and risk of SD. The distribution
of pathologic changes is greater in the subepicardium, and
the left ventricle is not spared despite being a predominantly RV disorder. In humans, a majority of cases are
familial or inherited and genetic mutations in at least 20
genes encoding mostly proteins of the desmosome (region
of intercalated discs between myocardial cells involved in
mechanical and electrical coupling) have been implicated.
A few nondesmosomal genes, including the cardiac ryanodine receptor (RyR2, calcium release channel of the sarcoplasmic reticulum), have also been involved.
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy is
likewise a familial (inherited) disorder in the boxer. The
disease, once referred to as “boxer cardiomyopathy,” has
been reclassified as ARVC due to its similarities with
the human disease. To date, none of the mutations
described in people have been found in the boxer.

Rather, an 8‐base pair deletion in the striatin gene has
been linked to ARVC in some American boxers, though
its causal role has been challenged. Striatin is an intercalated disc ­protein that co‐localizes with three of the desmosomal proteins implicated in ARVC in people. There
is also some suggestion that the RyR2 is involved as
affected boxers have a deficiency of calstabin2, a RyR2
protein.
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy in
dogs manifests as ventricular tachyarrhythmias predominantly of RV origin (left bundle branch block [LBBB]
configuration) and patients are at risk of SD from
­ventricular fibrillation (Figure 26.5).
Supraventricular tachyarrhythmias may also occasionally be noted. In boxers, the hearts are most often structurally normal on gross examination, unlike in humans
where RV dilation, systolic dysfunction, and aneurysms
are common. A small percent of boxers experience s­ ystolic
dysfunction and heart failure, whereas this may be more
common in English bulldogs, another affected breed.
Epidemiology
The true prevalence of ARVC in the boxer is unknown,
but anecdotally it would appear to be quite common.
The prevalence in other breeds is very low.

Figure 26.5 Nine‐lead ECG, 25 mm/s, 5 mm/mV. Right ventricular VPCs (left bundle branch block configuration) in a boxer with ARVC.
There are periods of ventricular bigeminy (alternating VPCs and sinus beats) and several VPC couplets.

The mode of inheritance in the boxer is autosomal
dominant with incomplete and age‐related penetrance
and variable expression. Dogs homozygous for the striatin mutation exhibit a more severe form of disease and
there may be association with myocardial failure.
The natural history of the disease in the boxer can be
quite variable. Frequently, dogs may present with
­incidental VA and remain asymptomatic for years. The
percentage of boxers that develop syncope has varied
from 33% to 68% in different studies. The percentage
that experienced SD in one prospective longitudinal
study was 31%. Less than 10% of boxers develop myocardial failure and CHF. In contrast, in a case series of 31
English bulldogs with ARVC, 52% had CHF (38% left‐
sided, 33% right‐sided, and 19% biventricular failure).
Risk factors for the development of ARVC apart from
breed are unknown. Risk of SD in boxers appears to be
higher with a previous history of syncope, more frequent
VPCs, more complex VA (couplets, triplets, runs of VT),
and more runs of VT. In humans, being a competitive
athlete has been linked with increased risk of SD,
suggesting the cardiac strain associated with intense
­
exercise can exacerbate VA.
Signalment
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy is
most common in the boxer breed. Males tend to be overrepresented. The average age at diagnosis is 5–7 years
but younger and older dogs may be affected. Multiple
cases are now also reported in the English bulldog.
Isolated cases of a similar RV cardiomyopathy have been
reported in a dachshund, bullmastiff, Labrador retriever,
Siberian husky, Shetland sheepdog, Dalmatian, and
Weimaraner.
History and Clinical Signs
Many boxers present without any clinical signs and are
detected incidentally through identification of an
arrhythmia on physical exam or through active screening programs. Roughly one‐third to two‐thirds may have
a history of syncope, and roughly one‐quarter experience exercise intolerance. Few present with respiratory
signs typical of CHF, whereas this appears to be more
common in English bulldogs. It is important to note that
there are other causes of syncope in the boxer apart from
ARVC.
Physical examination may be normal since the VA are
intermittent. Alternatively, intermittent premature beats
may be heard on auscultation, or rather the “pause” after
a premature beat may be more apparent than the premature beat itself. Bursts of tachycardia may also be noted
in more severely affected dogs. Dogs with arrhythmias

may have pulse deficits. Soft left base murmurs are
common in boxers and not specifically indicative of
­
myocardial disease.
Diagnosis
There is no gold standard for antemortem diagnosis of
ARVC in dogs. However, Holter recording is the most
valuable diagnostic tool, and should be performed in any
boxer with an auscultable arrhythmia, with a history of
exercise intolerance or syncope, for active screening in
any asymptomatic adult boxer especially with a family
history of ARVC or positive genotype (starting at >3
years of age), or for those in breeding programs.
Diagnostic criteria have yet to be clearly defined. Greater
than 100 VPCs per 24 hours of RV origin (LBBB configuration, “upright” orientation in lead II) is suspicious for
ARVC in the absence of another identifiable cause,
­particularly if there is increased complexity like couplets,
triplets, or VT, and >300 VPCs/24h is a more suggestive
threshold.
One study proposed three diagnostic criteria (>100
VPCs/24h, presence of couplets, and presence of R‐
on‐T phenomenon) with the presence of two out of
three possibly being a more robust way to identify the
disease. However, these or any other cut‐offs have yet to
be validated prospectively, and to rely solely on the total
VPC count may be erroneous. The complexity of the
arrhythmia and the complete clinical presentation
should be considered when making the diagnosis.
Holter recordings can have a high degree of day‐to‐day
variability (as much as 80%) and therefore may need to
be repeated in dogs with high suspicion yet equivocal
results.
Myocardial biopsy is not typically used for diagnosis
owing to anesthetic requirements and invasiveness, as
lesions may be missed given the epicardial and patchy
distribution of pathology, and the risk of adverse effects
including provocation of arrhythmias or cardiac
puncture.
Unlike in humans, imaging modalities including echocardiography have low diagnostic yield as they are often
normal. In few boxers will RV or LV dilation and systolic
dysfunction be appreciable whereas in a case series of
English bulldogs, 59% had subjective RV dilation. Cardiac
MRI may have utility in detecting the fatty infiltration
that characterizes the disease, but this remains to be
investigated thoroughly in dogs.
Circulating biomarkers including cTnI and NT‐
proBNP are not useful for detection of ARVC, based on
studies in boxers. While cTnI levels did correlate with
degree of arrhythmia, the degree of overlap with presumably normal boxers renders it an unsatisfactory
screening tool.

A genetic test for the striatin mutation in boxers is
available through the Veterinary Genetics laboratory at
North Carolina State University (https://cvm.ncsu.edu/
nc- st ate- ve t-ho spit al/small-animal/gene tic s/).
Interpretation and breeding recommendations are as for
the DCM genetic tests outlined above, and genetic
screening cannot replace clinical screening.
Therapy
While AAs have been shown to reduce VA frequency and
syncope, it is uncertain whether they decrease risk of SD
because studies are lacking. Nevertheless, AA therapy
remains the mainstay of ARVC treatment. A consensus
on arrhythmia threshold necessitating treatment is lacking, and each patient must be approached on a case‐by‐
case basis. Even asymptomatic dogs may be at risk of SD,
but this must be balanced with proarrhythmic risk of AA
drugs and owner factors including commitment to long‐
term therapy. Suggested candidates for AA therapy
include dogs with a history of syncope, those with VT
regardless of total VPC number, those with >300 VPC/24h
and increased complexity including couplets, triplets, or
R‐on‐T (rapid VPCs), or those with >1000 VPC/24h.
For immediate treatment of VT or VA causing weakness or collapse, intravenous lidocaine is recommended.
The most common and effective oral AAs are sotalol,
mexiletine, or a combination of the two in more refractory cases (see Table 26.2). Note that therapy may be
indicated prior to Holter recording, as in instances where
there is a history of syncope and VT is identified on ECG.
Therapy should be monitored by Holter examination
within 1–2 weeks of AA initiation, and periodically
thereafter (every six months). Therapeutic efficacy is
supported by a >80% reduction in arrhythmia number
and complexity. An increase in syncope post treatment
may suggest a proarrhythmic effect and should be evaluated with Holter promptly.
There is some evidence that oral supplementation with
omega‐3 fatty acids may also be beneficial (see Table 26.2).
For the minority that experience CHF (left, right, or
biventricular), therapy with ACEI, pimobendan, and
­diuretics is indicated as described above for DCM, in
addition to AA therapy. L‐carnitine may also be added
given positive response in a small family of boxers.
Prognosis
While all dogs with ARVC are at risk of SD, many
remain symptom free for years. In one prospective

study of boxers, the median survival time after identification of >300 VPC/24h was just over four years, and in
fact overall survival of the affected group was not significantly different from the control boxer group (survival to 10–11 years of age), whereas a retrospective
study of boxers with more advanced disease suggested a
median survival time of 365 days (range 7–1971 days).
The probability of death within a year was almost five
times greater with a history of syncope, just over five
times greater with >10 000 VPCs/24h, and 20 times
greater with >200 runs VT/24h. In a case series of
English bulldogs, a median survival time of 8.3 months
was reported, but whether the prognosis is truly worse
in that breed is not known, as it is likely that these dogs
had more advanced disease at the time of diagnosis than
other boxer studies.

­Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a primary myocardial
disease characterized by symmetric or asymmetric concentric hypertrophy (thickening) of the LV in the
absence of a stimulus for hypertrophy (e.g., stenosis or
hypertension), leading to diastolic dysfunction and
arrhythmias that may result in CHF or SD. In humans,
50% or more of cases are related to familial genetic
mutations. While common in the cat, HCM is very rare
in dogs. Like in the cat, dynamic LV outflow tract
obstruction (LVOTO) caused by systolic anterior
motion of the mitral valve (SAM) is described in some
cases.
Many cases of canine HCM appear to be in young
dogs, with males overrepresented. This has raised the
question as to whether the disease may be congenital
and furthermore, whether LVOTO may represent a form
of mitral valve dysplasia predisposing to SAM and secondary hypertrophy. Many affected breeds have been
reported and include the pointer, golden retriever,
Rottweiler, German shepherd, and shih tzu, amongst
others. Cases are frequently evaluated for the presence
of an incidental murmur which may be dynamic.
Echocardiography is necessary for diagnosis. Treatment
is targeted at reducing dynamic LVOTO with beta‐­
blockade (atenolol), and treating CHF or arrhythmias in
severe cases. A number of cases in young dogs have been
noted to resolve with maturity, while others have
­persisted and resulted in CHF or SD. It is difficult to
­estimate prognosis based on the sparse reports of this
disease in dogs.

Feline Myocardial Disease
Virginia Luis Fuentes, MA, VetMB, PhD, CertVR, DVC, MRCVS, DACVIM (Cardiology), DECVIM (Cardiology)
Department of Clinical Sciences and Services, Royal Veterinary College, University of London, Hatfield, Herts, UK

Myocardial disease is extremely common in cats and will
be encountered regularly by any feline clinician, but can
be hard to recognize. Feline myocardial disease is very
heterogeneous in presentation, clinical findings, and
prognosis. Without skilled echocardiography, identifying the different subclassifications of cardiomyopathy is
usually difficult. Fortunately, this is not usually necessary, as the main priorities for the clinician are to identify
those cats with a specific treatable cause of myocardial
disease, and to identify cats at high risk of congestive
heart failure (CHF) or aortic thromboembolism (ATE).

­Etiology
The term “myocardial disease” includes a range of conditions with varied etiologies. Cardiomyopathies are
­usually classified according to a phenotype based on
­cardiac structure and function (Figure 27.1).
The myocardium can be affected by systemic conditions such as hyperthyroidism, systemic hypertension,
and anemia, where disturbances in hemodynamic loading conditions may alter cardiac structure and function.
The myocardium has a limited range of responses to
injury or insult, so that different underlying causes can
result in the same phenotype. For example, dietary
­taurine deficiency, an uncontrolled tachyarrhythmia or
doxorubicin toxicity can all result in an identical “dilated
cardiomyopathy phenotype” characterized by systolic
dysfunction and ventricular dilation. In other cats, no
obvious underlying cause is identified, although a genetic
predisposition is suspected in some.
Traditionally, feline cardiomyopathies have been classified according to contemporary human classifications, but
controversy currently exists over whether human myocardial disease should be classified according to etiology or
phenotype. The most commonly recognized phenotype is
hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), characterized by

thickened left ventricular (LV) walls. Other phenotypes
include restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM), defined as
relatively normal LV walls but with atrial enlargement and
increased atrial pressures; dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM),
recognized by atrial and ventricular dilation with global
LV hypocontractility; and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC), which is typically manifested by fibrofatty replacement of predominantly the
right heart. There is considerable overlap between phenotypes, so an additional category of “unclassified cardiomyopathy” or “non-specific phenotype” is sometimes
used to describe patients with a phenotype that does not
correspond with any of the above criteria.
Unless a causative systemic disease or myocardial
insult can be identified, the etiology is unknown for most
cats with myocardial disease, although familial HCM is
recognized. A genetic cause has been established for
HCM in Maine Coon and ragdoll cats, where two different genetic mutations have been identified in the myosin‐binding protein C gene. In contrast, an HCM
phenotype has been associated with over 1400 different
mutations in humans, although a genetic cause is not
identified in all human HCM patients.

­Pathophysiology
The functional disturbance and consequent pathophysiology vary according to type of cardiomyopathy and
severity of disease. With mild myocardial abnormalities,
affected cats may not experience any obvious adverse
consequences. With severe or advanced myocardial
­disease, congestive heart failure is the most commonly
recognized sign. Sudden death is also a potential sequela,
but the prevalence is unknown and probably underestimated. Systemic or arterial thromboembolism is recognized in many advanced cases of cardiomyopathy with
left heart involvement.

Figure 27.1 Myocardial disease phenotypes. There is overlap in the cardiac characteristics between the different “classic” forms of
cardiomyopathy, and it can be difficult to differentiate cardiomyopathies with a genetic or unknown etiology from cardiomyopathies
caused by systemic disease on the basis of cardiac characteristics alone. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is defined as left ventricular (LV)
hypertrophy in the absence of an obvious cause, but hypertension, acromegaly, “transient myocardial thickening,” and hyperthyroidism
can all result in a phenotype that is identical to classic HCM. A minority of cats with severe (primary) HCM develop systolic dysfunction,
and are described as “end‐stage HCM,” overlapping with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM). A DCM phenotype can be produced by taurine
deficiency or a tachycardia‐mediated cardiomyopathy though no underlying cause is found in most cats with dilation of all four cardiac
chambers and global systolic dysfunction. The classic form of restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM) is defined as normal LV dimensions with
biatrial enlargement, but there is overlap with the above phenotypes. Not all cats fit into one of the categories listed above. Those with
predominantly right heart enlargement without an obvious cause are usually presumed to be arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy
(ARVC), but others do not fit any category and are sometimes called “unclassified cardiomyopathy” or “non-specific phenotype”.

HCM
Key pathologic features of HCM include increased LV
mass associated with myocyte disarray, interstitial myocardial fibrosis, and narrowing of small coronary arteries. Myocardial hypertrophy may result in delayed LV
relaxation, but this is usually well tolerated under normal
circumstances and is not likely to result in clinical signs.
Many cats with HCM will remain clinically stable provided they are not subjected to a sudden change in
hemodynamic load. Examples of such triggers include
the stress of a visit to the veterinarian, which increases
myocardial oxygen demand; general anesthesia, which
can reduce cardiac output; or intravenous fluid therapy,
which can result in volume loading. Any of these short‐
term hemodynamic stressors can cause a sudden increase

in left atrial (LA) pressures and acute pulmonary edema.
The cats with subclinical HCM that are most vulnerable
to these stressors are likely to be those with LA enlargement. Cats with massive LV hypertrophy may also be at
increased risk, but the relationship between LV wall
thickness and risk is not linear, and LA enlargement is a
better global indicator of advanced disease.
Many cats with well‐compensated HCM exhibit
dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction, which can be
either persistent or only induced by excitement/exertion.
Outflow tract obstruction is usually caused by systolic
anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve, where movement of the anterior mitral leaflet towards the interventricular septum during mid to late systole causes
obstruction to ejection of blood flow, as well as mitral

VetBooks.ir

27 Feline Myocardial Disease

regurgitation. Outflow tract obstruction can be severe
enough to result in a pressure gradient across the LV outflow tract of over 100 mmHg for much of systole. In
human HCM patients, the additional myocardial oxygen
consumption associated with outflow tract obstruction
can cause myocardial ischemia, which is further exacerbated by the concurrent narrowing of small coronary
arteries that is a feature of HCM in both humans and
cats. Clinical signs of outflow tract obstruction in human
HCM patients include exertional dyspnea and chest pain.
The exact clinical effect in cats is difficult to determine,
as chest pain could easily pass unnoticed by owners, and
the majority of affected cats appear to be subclinical.
Some owners report open‐mouth breathing during play,
despite an absence of documentable pulmonary edema.
With progression of HCM, diastolic filling of the LV
may be further impaired as interstitial fibrosis worsens,
and the LV myocardium becomes stiffer. Ischemic episodes can result in focal areas of myocardial damage,
resulting in replacement fibrosis. Neurohormonal activation adds to the problem by causing plasma volume
expansion through sodium and water retention, and
signs of chronic congestive heart failure become more
likely. Signs include pulmonary edema, pleural effusion
or both. Cats at this stage are also at risk of arterial
thromboembolism, as LA contractile function deteriorates with chronic LA enlargement. A minority of cats
will develop generalized LV systolic dysfunction, or large
areas of ventricular “scarring” with regional wall thinning and replacement fibrosis. Cats with increased wall
thickness but systolic dysfunction are sometimes
described as “end‐stage HCM” (ES‐HCM). Although
these cats may start with a nondilated hypertrophied LV,
over time the LV wall thickness may decrease and LV
diameter increases, so that ultimately they may bear little
resemblance to the classic HCM phenotype.
Occasionally, cats with HCM will present with acute
signs of cardiogenic shock, including hypotension, hypothermia, and, often, bradycardia. These low‐output signs
may or may not be accompanied by congestive signs.
RCM
Two forms of RCM have been reported: an endomyocardial form characterized by LV bridging scar (eRCM); and
a myocardial form where the LV appears structurally
normal but is poorly compliant (mRCM). Varying
degrees and distribution of myocardial fibrosis are common to both forms. Biatrial enlargement and increased
atrial pressures are also common to both. Cats diagnosed
with RCM usually demonstrate clinical signs, which can
include congestive heart failure, arrhythmias, arterial
thromboembolism, or low‐output signs. It is difficult to
differentiate RCM from the more advanced forms of

HCM with myocyte loss or ES‐HCM, and they may in
fact be part of the same wide spectrum of HCM.
DCM
This form of cardiomyopathy is now very uncommon in
cats, despite being the most common phenotype in dogs.
A DCM phenotype is characterized by systolic dysfunction with normal or reduced LV wall thickness and is
associated with an increase in diastolic and systolic ventricular dimensions. An association was identified in the
late 1980s between DCM in cats and dietary taurine bioavailability, and since that time, a change in pet food
manufacturing processes has resolved this problem.
Accordingly, most cats with a DCM phenotype are found
to have normal plasma taurine concentrations.
Congestive heart failure, arterial thromboembolism, and
low‐output signs are all common presentations for DCM.
Arterial Thromboembolism
All of the above forms of cardiomyopathy may lead to
intracardiac thrombus formation if disease is sufficiently
advanced (i.e., with left atrial enlargement and dysfunction). Arterial embolization of thrombus (ATE) into the
systemic circulation causes vascular occlusion and acute
ischemia of downstream tissues, resulting in severe pain,
electrolyte disturbances, acute renal injury, and for those
surviving the initial embolic episode, a high long‐term
risk of ATE recurrence or CHF. Nevertheless, a minority
of cats can survive for periods in excess of a year if they
recover from the acute crisis.
ARVC
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy also
occurs in humans and dogs, and is characterized by
fibrofatty replacement of myocytes. The extent and distribution of myocyte replacement are variable, and may
result in tachyarrhythmias and/or right atrial and right
ventricular dilation. Affected cats may be presented with
signs of syncope associated with tachyarrhythmias, but
can also develop right‐sided congestive signs with ascites.

­Epidemiology
The prevalence of HCM in cats is high; approximately
15% of apparently healthy cats are affected, with a prevalence increasing to nearly 30% of cats over 9 years of age.
The prevalence of RCM, DCM, and ARVC is harder to
gauge, but is likely considerably lower. HCM is the most
common type of feline cardiomyopathy, regardless of age,
breed or presenting signs. In the absence of longitudinal
epidemiologic studies, it is impossible to determine

269

VetBooks.ir

270

Section 3 Cardiovascular Disease

whether RCM is a separate form of cardiomyopathy or an
advanced stage variant of HCM.

­Signalment
There is a male predominance in cats with HCM. Most
cats with HCM are domestic nonpedigree cats, but a number of pedigree breeds are said to be predisposed, including
the Maine Coon, ragdoll, Persian, British shorthair, sphynx,
Cornish rex, and Norwegian forest cat. Siamese and
Oriental cats may be predisposed towards eRCM. Age at
diagnosis varies widely, as any age of cat can be affected
with HCM, including kittens and geriatric cats, but the
prevalence of LV hypertrophy increases with age.

­History and Clinical Signs
Cats with advanced myocardial disease are often perceived
by their owner to be healthy until shortly before the onset
of CHF, ATE, syncope or sudden death. Typical presenting
signs for CHF include respiratory distress and tachypnea,
whereas acute limb paralysis/paresis is the most common
presentation with ATE. Some cats may develop open‐
mouth breathing only with stress or exertion, and may be
found to have dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction.
Physical examination findings are varied. Murmurs are
common in cats with HCM but also in healthy cats with
normal hearts, so a murmur should not always be
assumed to indicate heart disease. Murmurs are less
common in the more severe forms of cardiomyopathy
than in well‐compensated HCM. A minority of cats with
cardiomyopathy have an audible gallop or arrhythmia,
and these auscultation findings are more likely to indicate advanced disease, though can also be detected in
some geriatric cats with only mild abnormalities.
A prominent apical impulse may be apparent in cats with
cardiomegaly or a hyperdynamic LV.
Physical exam findings in cats with congestive heart
failure will include tachypnea with increased respiratory
effort, crackles on pulmonary auscultation with severe
pulmonary edema, or absent breath sounds ventrally
with a pleural effusion. The presence of a gallop sound in
a cat with tachypnea and respiratory distress should
prompt treatment for congestive heart failure until further confirmatory tests are possible.

­Diagnosis
From the above descriptions, it is clear that establishing
a diagnosis of a particular type of cardiomyopathy in an
individual cat is challenging. To differentiate end‐stage

HCM, RCM, and UCM requires a high level of echocardiographic skill and experience. A precise diagnosis can
be challenging even for experienced cardiologists unless
a cat has a classic HCM or ARVC phenotype, due to poor
consensus on the definitions of each cardiomyopathy
type. Moreover, the labels “end‐stage HCM,” “RCM,” and
“UCM” might not actually reflect distinct disease entities
but rather different stages of a single condition. Instead,
diagnostic tests should be focused on confirming the
presence of heart disease; identifying any underlying
­systemic cause of cardiomyopathy that should be treated;
and identifying cats at high risk of CHF and ATE.
Is Heart Disease Present?
In practical terms, the clinician’s first priority when presented with a cat with clinical findings suggestive of heart
disease is to establish whether or not cardiac disease is
present. The approach will be different for cats with
­respiratory distress versus those that are asymptomatic.
Tachypneic Cats

Heart disease should always be considered in cats with
tachypnea, and the presence of a murmur, gallop or
arrhythmia should increase this suspicion (Figure 27.2).
Differentiation of congestive heart failure from other
causes of respiratory distress may require diagnostic
imaging, but the potential value of radiography or echocardiography must be weighed against the possible risk
of subjecting the patient to further stress that could
prove fatal. Ultrasound is generally better tolerated than
radiography, and has the advantage that patient positioning is less critical. Thoracic ultrasound can demonstrate pleural effusion and can even be used to indicate
pulmonary parenchymal changes as with pulmonary
edema (B‐line artifacts). If sufficient expertise is available, the most useful way to increase confidence of a cardiac cause of respiratory distress is to demonstrate LA
enlargement with echocardiography. Thoracic radiography can be used to identify pleural effusion, pulmonary
infiltrates, and assess cardiac size, but must be obtained
with great care to avoid compromising patient safety. A
point‐of‐care test is available to measure plasma NT‐
proBNP, providing a simple way to help differentiate
cats with respiratory distress due to heart failure versus
noncardiac causes.
Asymptomatic Cats

Myocardial disease should be considered in an otherwise
healthy cat when a murmur is detected, and should be
strongly suspected when a gallop or arrhythmia is auscultated (Figure 27.3). A very loud murmur (i.e., with a
precordial thrill) is usually associated with congenital
heart disease.

Is There an Underlying Systemic Cause
of Myocardial Disease?

Heart Disease Present; High Risk or Low Risk?

It is helpful to view feline myocardial disease in terms
of those with and without a specific systemic cause, as
treatment of any underlying cause is essential. It is
vital to identify hypertension, hyperthyroidism or
anemia, as specific treatment requirements will differ
for each. Blood pressure should be measured in all
cats with suspected heart disease, and T4 concentrations measured in older cats. Hematocrit should be
checked if there is any concern that anemia may be

One of the most useful prognostic indicators for cats
with cardiomyopathy is LA size. Cats with HCM and

Which Cardiomyopathy is This?
Echocardiography is a difficult technique in cats, and it
takes an experienced echocardiographer to differentiate
many of the more advanced cardiomyopathy phenotypes. Severe forms of ARVC may be easy to differentiate
from other cardiomyopathies, but hard to differentiate
from tricuspid dysplasia or conditions associated with
severe pulmonary hypertension. Milder or atypical forms
of any of the cardiomyopathies can be difficult to classify
on echocardiography, and can sometimes be challenging
even for cardiologists. At the other end of the spectrum,
it can be challenging to differentiate cats with mild HCM
from those with physiologic murmurs.
There are few clinical consequences in the short term
for incorrectly distinguishing normal cats from those
with mild HCM (apart from when screening prebreeding

pedigree cats for cardiomyopathy), providing these “low‐
risk” cats continue to be monitored over subsequent
years. The rate of progression from normal to mild
HCM, or mild HCM to “high‐risk” HCM is variable, so
such cats should be reevaluated at least annually.
Biomarkers can be helpful in this context, as low NT‐
proBNP concentrations should provide some reassurance that a cat continues to be low risk.

­Therapy
Cats with CHF
For cats with life‐threatening signs, therapy is focused
on relieving critical hypoxemia using a combination of
­parenteral furosemide, oxygen, and sedation as needed

VetBooks.ir

27 Feline Myocardial Disease

(butorphanol 0.3 mg/kg, IM or SC) for cats in distress.
Initially, furosemide should be given IV at 2 mg/kg, but
may be given IM until IV access can be secured.
Repeated doses are given every 30–60 minutes, to
effect. Response is assessed by monitoring respiratory
rate and effort, with the goal of returning respiratory
rates to normal (or at least <40 breaths/min). Renal
function and electrolytes should also be monitored, as
hypokalemia and elevations in BUN are common.
Although the effect of therapy on renal function and
electrolytes should be considered, the principal goal
should be the elimination of congestive signs.
Intravenous fluids should be avoided in the presence of
congestive heart failure, even in hypotensive cats (systolic blood pressure <100 mmHg). For hypothermic,
hypotensive cats without a heart murmur, pimobendan
(1.25 mg PO per cat) can be considered.
Hospitalized cats are often stressed, and once respiratory distress is controlled they may benefit from being
returned to their home environment.
Cats with “transient myocardial thickening” (TMT)
warrant a specific mention, as they have a better than
expected prognosis. The cause of TMT is unknown, but
affected cats are often young and have a history of a
recent stressful event. They usually present with CHF
associated with thickened LV walls, but if treated appropriately for their heart failure can make a full recovery,
with return to a normal cardiac phenotype.
For outpatient management, parenteral furosemide
can be replaced with oral furosemide. The goal of
long‐term management is to maintain control of congestive signs and to prevent ATE. Evidence‐based
selection of therapeutic agents for CHF management
in cats suffers from the absence of clinical trial data.
Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEI),
spironolactone, and pimobendan are all currently
used off‐label in the treatment of CHF in cats. ACEIs
have not been associated with any adverse effects in
­isease and in theory should
cats with cardiac d
counteract furosemide‐mediated activation of the
­
renin‐angiotensin‐aldosterone
system
(RAAS).
Spironolactone should also act on the RAAS and has
been reported to have favorable effects in experimental models of HCM, but its use was reported to result
in skin lesions in a small minority of cats. Pimobendan
is considered contraindicated in cats with HCM and
outflow tract obstruction, but is a logical choice for
treatment of cats with systolic dysfunction. Diltiazem
is rarely used, and beta‐adrenergic antagonists such as
atenolol are generally considered contraindicated in
the presence of congestive heart failure.
Cats with recurrent or persistent CHF despite appropriate doses of diuretics are generally managed by
increasing diuretic doses and adding medications

such as an ACEI and spironolactone. Cats that have
experienced an episode of CHF are likely to be at risk of
ATE, so should also receive antiplatelet treatment.
Clopidogrel is the first‐choice treatment for prevention
of ATE (18.75 mg per cat q24h PO), as aspirin (at either
5 mg/kg or 75 mg q72h) does not appear to be as effective, though is well tolerated.
Administering multiple medications is a problem with
many cats, so combining tablets in a single gelatine
­capsule can be helpful.
Asymptomatic Cats
Low‐Risk Cats

Many asymptomatic cats will have normal survival
times whether or not they receive treatment. It is debatable whether extending survival is possible in low‐risk
cats, although improving quality of life might be a
worthwhile aim. In human HCM patients, LV outflow
tract obstruction can be associated with chest pain and
exertional dyspnea, which can be relieved with atenolol
in some patients. Although atenolol does not seem to
confer an obvious survival benefit in cats with HCM
and LV outflow tract obstruction, there are anecdotal
reports that atenolol might improve activity levels in
some cats.
High‐Risk Cats

There are currently no therapies that are known to
reduce the risk of developing CHF in cats with myocardial disease, apart from treating hyperthyroidism, hypertension, and anemia when present. As high‐risk cats
are at risk of ATE, they should receive antiplatelet
treatment.

­Prognosis
Feline myocardial disease has a very varied prognosis,
ranging from a benign condition with minimal influence
on morbidity and mortality in many cats, to a disabling
and potentially fatal condition associated with respiratory distress, sudden death, and pain and paralysis.
Factors such as gallop sounds, arrhythmias, LA enlargement, and systolic dysfunction are indicators of a poor
prognosis and high risk of cardiac complications, and
absence of these factors is likely to indicate a more benign
outcome. Of these factors, LA enlargement is the most
important predictor and the ability to assess LA size with
echocardiography is extremely useful. By focusing on
potential risk, the complex issues of cardiomyopathy
classification are avoided and therapy can be directed at
cats that are in most need.

Pericardial Disease
Ashley B. Saunders, DVM, DACVIM (Cardiology) and Sonya G. Gordon, DVM, DVSc, DACVIM (Cardiology)
Department of Small Animal Clinical Sciences, College of Veterinary Medicine & Biomedical Sciences, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA

The pericardium is a multilayered structure surrounding
the heart that isolates the heart from the remainder of the
thorax. It creates a potential space that can be filled by
fluid, tissue, or air/gas. While pericardial disease is relatively uncommon, it can lead to life‐threatening conditions
when intrapericardial pressure rises and cardiac output is
compromised. A combination of restricted filling, reduced
diastolic function, partial obstruction to inflow into the
atria, and reduced cardiac output can manifest clinically as
weakness, collapse, tachycardia, jugular venous distension,
and ascites. Pericardiocentesis is recommended to alleviate
clinical signs of pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade. Congenital and acquired pericardial diseases in cats
and dogs will be discussed in detail.

Signalment

­Congenital

Intrapericardial Cysts

Etiology/Pathophysiology
Peritoneopericardial diaphragmatic hernia (PPDH)
occurs during development in dogs and cats when the
septum transversum does not form or fuse normally,
resulting in a communication that allows abdominal
contents to displace into the pericardial space. The tissues and organs herniated most often are omentum,
liver, gallbladder, and small intestine. Concurrent congenital abnormalities including portosystemic shunt are
often present in animals with PPDH.
Intrapericardial cysts have been rarely reported in dogs
and cats and in some cases were associated with PPDH.

Although these are congenital abnormalities, they can be
detected incidentally in adults so the age at presentation
can vary greatly.
History and Clinical Signs
PPDH

Clinical signs with PPDH depend on which abdominal
organs herniate. Up to 69% of animals have clinical signs
including tachypnea/dyspnea, cough, vomiting, anorexia,
and exercise intolerance. Common physical examination
abnormalities include muffled heart and lung sounds, borborygmus auscultated in the thorax, and heart murmur.
Symptomatic animals have presenting signs similar to
those with pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade
(see Pericardial Effusion section).
Diagnosis
Thoracic radiograph findings include enlarged or globoid cardiac silhouette and, in the case of PPDH, a loss of
distinction between the cardiac silhouette and diaphragm or abnormal densities (gas or fat) within the cardiac silhouette (Figure 28.1a,b). Ultrasound confirms the
presence of effusion and which organs have herniated.
The diagnosis of PPDH can be an incidental finding during diagnostic imaging for another reason.

Epidemiology

Therapy

The overall prevalence of PPDH at two veterinary institutions was 0.025%, with a greater prevalence in cats
than dogs.

Surgical repair of PPDH is recommended more often
for young animals (median age 1.1 years) and those
with clinical signs. Successful surgical management of

Prognosis
The majority of animals with clinical signs will improve
following surgical correction. The mortality rate following surgery for PPDH varies between 5.1% and 14%. The
mortality rate following surgical repair of PPDH is higher
if reexpansion pulmonary edema or hemorrhage occurs,
although improvements in anesthesia and postoperative
management have most likely improved the prognosis.

­Pericardial Effusion
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Accumulation of fluid within the pericardial space can
cause hemodynamic abnormalities depending on the
volume and rate of fluid accumulation as well as intracardiac filling pressures and compliance. The resulting
hemodynamic changes and decrease in cardiac output
create a clinical syndrome called cardiac tamponade,
where increased intrapericardial pressure equals or
exceeds intracardiac pressure, with the right side of the
heart most susceptible to compromise.
The most common causes of pericardial effusion in
dogs are neoplastic and idiopathic with rare cases of
infectious pericarditis (bacterial, fungal), coagulopathy,
left atrial tear, heart failure, foreign body, and uremia.
The most common causes of pericardial effusion in cats
are heart failure, neoplastic and infectious (viral) with rare
cases of coagulopathy, foreign body, and uremia.
Dogs
Neoplastic

Primary or metastatic neoplasia is the most commonly
reported cause of pericardial effusion in dogs. The incidence of hemangiosarcoma and aortic body tumors
(chemodectoma) is higher than mesothelioma with infrequent reports of thyroid carcinoma, myxoma, and others.
Hemangiosarcoma has a 10‐fold greater incidence
than aortic body tumors in dogs. They are typically
located in the right atrium/auricle and are highly malignant. The mean age at presentation is 9.8 years and mean
weight is 32 kg. Golden retrievers are overrepresented.
Survival times with combinations of pericardiocentesis,
pericardiectomy, tumor resection, and/or chemotherapy
are short.
Heart base tumors, most often chemodectoma or thyroid carcinoma, are located near the aorta and main
pulmonary artery. Chemoreceptor cells are found in
­
groups at the ventrolateral surface of the aorta and the

bifurcation of the carotid artery near the base of the heart.
The chemoreceptor system responds to changes in pH
and the partial pressure of arterial oxygen and carbon
dioxide in the blood. These tumors tend to be slow growing and locally invasive, causing compression or infiltration of adjacent structures. Chemodectomas can occur in
any breed but brachycephalic breeds appear predisposed
(boxer, bulldog, Boston terrier). Mean age at presentation
is 10 years. Heart base tumors are intimately associated
with vascular structures, making c­ omplete surgical excision and radiation therapy problematic. In dogs with
heart base tumors assumed to be chemodectomas and
clinically significant pericardial effusion, palliation with
pericardiectomy significantly extends survival. In the
absence of significant pericardial effusion, these tumors
can be an incidental finding in dogs undergoing an
echocardiogram for another indication.
Mesothelioma is a neoplasm of the pericardium and
serosal surfaces. It is relatively uncommon and is not
characterized by an easily identifiable discrete mass,
making it difficult to diagnose. Diagnosis of mesothelioma requires histopathology of the pericardium and is
therefore difficult to distinguish from idiopathic disease.
Mesothelioma can develop secondary to chronic effusions. The mean age at diagnosis is 9.5 years.
Idiopathic

A cause for pericardial effusion cannot be identified in
up to 23% of cases. Therefore, idiopathic is a diagnosis of
exclusion. Affected dogs are typically medium to large
breed and middle aged. The reported mean age is slightly
less than that reported for dogs with a neoplastic etiology. Of note, reports have identified small tumors on
necropsy and confirmed mesothelioma on histopathology of pericardial tissue in dogs initially diagnosed with
idiopathic effusions.
Infectious

Rare reports of systemic fungal disease (Coccidioides
immitis, Aspergillus niger), bacterial pericarditis (various
bacteria including botryomycosis) and protozoal infection with Leishmania chagasi have been associated with
pericardial effusion. In some cases, long‐term survival
can be achieved with a combination of surgical management and long‐term antibiotic or fungal therapy.
Other

A left atrial tear can occur in dogs with degenerative
mitral valve disease, most often resulting in acute clinical
decompensation. An echocardiogram performed at the
time may document evidence of a thrombus in the pericardial space. Pericardial effusion secondary to heart
failure is uncommon in dogs with heart disease and if it
does occur, the effusion is typically scant and does not

277

result in tamponade. Additional rarely reported causes
of pericardial effusion in dogs include renal failure/­
uremia, coagulopathy, and migrating foreign bodies
including grass awns, porcupine quills, and gun pellets.
Cats
Heart Failure

The most common cause of pericardial effusion in cats,
it can develop with any significant underlying heart
disease including hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The
­
volume of effusion is typically small with heart failure
and resolves with heart failure management. Cats with
heart failure‐associated pericardial effusion have a
shorter survival time than cats with pericardial effusion
not caused by heart disease.
Neoplastic

This is a rare cause of pericardial effusion in the cat. The
most common tumors reported in cats with pericardial
effusion are lymphoma, thymoma, mesothelioma, and
adenocarcinoma. The clinical effects of cardiac tumors
are related principally to compression or obstruction of
adjacent cardiac structures, infiltration of the myocardium, and development of pericardial effusion.
Infectious

In the past, infection was considered the most common
cause of pericardial effusion in the cat related to the
historical prevalence of feline infectious peritonitis
­
(­coronavirus). The prevalence of pericardial effusion in
cats with feline infectious peritonitis (coronavirus) is
9.6–12.8%.
Other

Additional rarely reported causes of pericardial effusion in cats include renal failure/uremia, trauma, and
coagulopathy.
Signalment
Dogs

In general, dogs are middle aged to older and large breed
(golden retriever, German shepherd). Golden retrievers
are the most overrepresented breed presenting with pericardial effusion. They are also the most commonly
reported breed with hemangiosarcoma. Brachycephalic
breeds are predisposed to heart base tumors (chemodectoma). A young adult dog of any breed would be more
likely to have an infectious or idiopathic cause.
Cats

Irrespective of cause, the most reported breed is domestic shorthair although pure breeds can be affected.
Median age at presentation is 6.0 years.

History and Clinical Signs
Patients can be affected to various degrees, ranging from
no overt clinical signs to severe compromise. Clinical signs,
when present, are often nonspecific and can include lethargy, anorexia, collapse, cough, and vomiting. Respiratory
signs (tachypnea, dyspnea, cough) are common complaints
in cats. Abnormal physical examination findings that are
suggestive of pericardial effusion can include muffled or
distant heart sounds, weak pulses or variation in pulse
quality with respiration, and tachycardia. Signs of overt
right heart failure (abdominal ­distension from ascites) and
evidence of increased right heart pressures, including jugular venous distension, can also be present.
Diagnosis
A complete diagnostic work‐up is recommended to
assess clinical status and create a treatment plan.
Evaluation includes but may not be limited to a complete
blood count, biochemistries, coagulation testing, urinalysis, blood pressure, thoracic radiographs, electrocardiography, and echocardiography. In addition, point‐of‐care
ultrasound in the emergency setting is helpful for rapidly
detecting pericardial effusion. Infectious disease testing
may be indicated in endemic areas or if one is suspected.
Additional tests may be indicated depending on clinical
status or presenting signs.
Thoracic Radiographs

An enlarged, globoid cardiac silhouette suggests the
presence of pericardial effusion (Figure 28.1c,d). Small‐
volume pericardial effusions may not cause a rounded
appearance. Additional findings include dorsal deviation
of the trachea, caudal vena cava distension, and hepatomegaly. Some specific abnormalities indicative of the
underlying diagnosis include abnormal bulges at the
heart base suggestive of a mass, left atrial enlargement in
degenerative mitral valve disease (Figure 28.1e,f ), and
pulmonary metastasis. When present, pleural effusion
often impedes assessment of the cardiac silhouette.
Pulmonary edema is uncommon in dogs with pericardial
effusion but can be present in cats with heart failure.
Echocardiography

Echocardiography (cardiac ultrasound) provides a noninvasive means of imaging the heart and surrounding
structures, and is superior to conventional radiography
for identifying pericardial effusion, which appears as a
hypoechoic space surrounding the heart (Figure 28.2).
Additionally, echocardiography can identify the etiology
of pericardial effusion, such as neoplastic or underlying
heart disease. Pericardial effusion provides a source of
ultrasonic contrast that is helpful when attempting to

visualize cardiac tumors, but therapeutic pericardiocentesis should not be delayed for an echocardiographic
examination in an unstable patient. Tumors are most
often located in the right atrial or auricular wall in the
case of hemangiosarcoma or at the heart base associated
with the aorta or main pulmonary artery (Figure 28.3).
They can also be found, more rarely, within the right
ventricular myocardium and right ventricular outflow
tract. Hemangiosarcomas frequently appear cavitary.
Both the right and left imaging windows are recommended for identification and localization. In addition to
identifying pericardial effusion, echocardiography can
provide evidence of cardiac tamponade by documenting
diastolic collapse of the right atrium and ventricle when
intrapericardial pressures exceed right atrial or ventricular end‐diastolic pressures (Figure 28.4). Left ventricular
internal dimensions will measure small when pericardial
effusion inhibits preload of the heart.
Pericardial Fluid Analysis

Pericardial fluid is typically hemorrhagic in appearance,
although opaque fluid can be seen with chylous effusions and exudates. Most cardiac tumors do not exfoliate well, and for this reason pericardial fluid analysis
and cytology often are unrewarding for the identification of cardiac tumors. Careful cytologic evaluation is
required so that reactive mesothelial cells are not
­mistaken for neoplastic cells. Occasionally, lymphoma
or an infectious cause can be documented. Culture and
sensitivity are indicated for the identification of effusions secondary to infectious etiologies.
Electrocardiography

The most common finding is sinus tachycardia
(Figure 28.5a), which is a physiologic compensatory

mechanism to improve cardiac output. Low‐voltage
QRS complexes can be indicative of pericardial effusion in dogs (Figure 28.5b). It is important to recognize
that QRS complexes are typically small in cats, making
this an insensitive indicator of effusion. Electrical
alternans, identified as a beat‐to‐beat variation in the
QRS complexes, is highly suggestive of pericardial
effusion, although it is only identified in a small number of dogs (Figure 28.5c). Lastly, a change (depression
or elevation) in the ST segment associated with myocardial hypoxia (Figure 28.5d) may be documented.
Ventricular arrhythmias are not uncommon and
supraventricular arrhythmias can also occur. Most
ECG abnormalities will resolve shortly after the
removal of pericardial effusion.
Laboratory Work

Comprehensive laboratory evaluation including complete blood count, biochemical analysis, coagulation
panel, and urinalysis can provide information regarding underlying etiology and the patient’s clinical status. Abnormalities are not uncommon but are often
nonspecific. Cardiac troponin I concentrations can be
increased in dogs with hemangiosarcoma (>0.25 ng/
mL) when compared to other causes of pericardial
effusion.
Neoplastic Evaluation

Cardiac tumors are located adjacent to important vascular structures, making the diagnosis challenging.
Definitive diagnosis is often made during surgery or at
necropsy. Surgical excisional biopsy has been described
for the diagnosis of hemangiosarcoma of the right auricle
and for chemodectoma but is often not performed as a
consequence of the overall risk to benefit ratio.

(a)

Advanced Imaging
Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging can provide additional information including
tumor location and the presence of metastatic
disease.
Therapy
The urgency of pericardiocentesis depends on the clinical status of the patient at the time of evaluation.
Acute Therapy

(b)

Critically ill animals require immediate stabilization
with intravenous fluid therapy to help restore cardiac
output, and pericardiocentesis to resolve tamponade.
Dyspneic patients may benefit from a combination of
oxygen supplementation and removal of pleural effusion
and/or ascites if the volume(s) are significant enough to
contribute to respiratory difficulty. Diuretic therapy with
furosemide is generally contraindicated because diuretics do not consistently remove free fluid from the pericardium and can contribute to further hemodynamic
compromise. One exception is the judicious use of
­furosemide in cats and dogs with pericardial effusion
secondary to congestive heart failure.
Pericardiocentesis

(c)

Pericardiocentesis is performed primarily in dogs and is
recommended when pericardial effusion is large volume
and/or contributing to hemodynamic compromise (tamponade). The majority of cats have small volume
­effusions secondary to heart failure that resolve with
heart failure management.
Several techniques for pericardiocentesis have been
described and the technique selected depends on the
clinical status of the patient, veterinarian comfort level
with the procedure, equipment availability, and technical
support. The objective of the procedure is to remove as
much pericardial fluid as possible. Complications can
occur during pericardiocentesis if the catheter contacts
the heart, resulting in arrhythmias, or lacerates lung or
other cardiac structures. Pericardial fluid removal typically provides an immediate clinical benefit noted by a
reduction in heart rate to a more normal range and an
improvement in pulse quality and blood pressure.
Equipment and Supplies

3.25 inch).

Preparation

Prior to performing the procedure, gather the supplies
appropriate for the patient’s size, demeanor, and clinical
status. Putting together a prestocked kit that contains
the necessary supplies for pericardiocentesis is very useful, especially for immediate access in an emergency situation. Light sedation may be required to facilitate the
procedure in some cases. The local anesthetic block can
be drawn into a syringe, and the right side of the thorax
can be shaved in preparation for the procedure.
Procedure (Figure 28.6)

Pericardiocentesis is routinely performed on the right
side of the thorax to utilize an approach through the cardiac notch between lung lobes and to avoid damage to
the lung and coronary arteries.

1) For the procedure, the patient is positioned in sternal
or lateral recumbency with continuous ECG attached.
2) Identify the ideal position for introducing the catheter into the thorax, which is often around the fifth or
sixth intercostal space, mid‐thorax at the costochondral junction. It can be found by flexing the right front
limb and swinging the leg across the thorax and using
the intercostal space where the point of the elbow
crosses the costochondral junction (Figure 28.6a) or
with ultrasound guidance (Figure 28.6b). A permanent marker can be used to identify the spot for catheter entry or to mark multiple spots on the perimeter
of the shaved area to triangulate the position.
3) Following sterile preparation of the pericardiocentesis site, inject a local anesthetic block to the skin,
intercostal muscles, and pleura (Figure 28.6c). The
discomfort associated with the local block can limit
its value in some dogs that would otherwise benefit
from sedation. After approximately five minutes, use
a scalpel blade to make a small stab incision in the
skin to facilitate catheter insertion and advancement.
4) Attach the catheter to the extension set tubing with a
three‐way stopcock placed between the extension set
tubing and a syringe. At the predetermined ideal pericardiocentesis site, advance the catheter through the
skin, followed by the intercostal muscles, avoiding the
caudal aspect of the rib where the intercostal vessels
are located, and into the pleural space (Figure 28.6d).
An assistant applying gentle negative pressure on the
syringe may encounter pleural effusion that is typically straw colored in patients with right heart failure.
Continue advancing the catheter until a scratching
sensation is detected when the needle comes into
contact with the pericardium. Continue to advance
