Monitoring and Follow‐Up

Pericardiocentesis often results in immediate clinical
improvement. Careful monitoring of the patient for further hemodynamic collapse or clinical improvement is
recommended following the procedure. Ideally, dogs
should not be sent home immediately after pericardiocentesis and are monitored in the hospital for 12–24 hours.
Rapid (minutes to hours) reaccumulation of pericardial
fluid and significant arrhythmias are possible following
pericardiocentesis. If pericardiectomy is not scheduled
(see Surgical Management for recommendations), recheck
within 2–4 weeks and consider pericardiectomy if the
pericardial effusion has reaccumulated.
Cancer Therapy
Palliative or definitive cancer therapy rarely is successful
with cardiac neoplasia. Complete surgical excision can
rarely be achieved because of tumor proximity to vital
structures. There are reports of a positive response to
chemotherapy for lymphoma and hemangiosarcoma.
Consultation with an oncologist is recommended for the
most current therapeutic strategies.
Surgical Management
Despite fluid removal and immediate clinical improvement, pericardial effusion is likely to recur in most
instances. Surgical pericardiectomy (partial or subtotal)
allows improved visualization for the surgeon to identify the underlying etiology and/or biopsy a tumor.
Echocardiography is very specific for identifying a tumor
but not 100% sensitive, particularly for small tumors that
may be readily identified by a surgeon. A small pericardial window provides palliation but can potentially lead
to constrictive pericarditis of the remaining pericardium
or allow herniation of a portion of the heart through the
pericardial opening. Pericardiectomy can be curative for
idiopathic and infectious etiologies and extend survival
for dogs with chemodectomas. Thoracoscopic pericardiectomy has the benefit of offering lower patient morbidity but requires a skilled operator to achieve optimum

results. Balloon pericardiotomy has been described as a
palliative procedure for neoplastic effusions.
Prognosis
Prognosis depends on the underlying cause of the effusion. Pericardiectomy can result in clinical improvement
or cure in idiopathic cases and in infectious cases when
combined with appropriate antibiotic or antifungal therapy. Pericardiectomy extends survival time in dogs with
heart base tumors and is associated with minimal
improvement with hemangiosarcoma and mesothelioma. In cats, prognosis with effusion secondary to heart
disease and heart failure is guarded to poor due to the
presence of severe underlying heart disease.

­Constrictive Pericarditis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Constrictive pericarditis is characterized by a stiff,
fibrous pericardium that impairs ventricular diastolic
filling even if no fluid is present. Although considered
uncommon, the diagnosis is difficult to make and can
be overlooked. It is characterized by an absence of pericardial effusion though combined constrictive‐effusive
disease does occur. Chronic pericardial and pleural
effusion including chylous effusion and infectious pericarditis secondary to fungal organisms can result in
constrictive pericarditis.
Signalment
Similar to pericardial effusion.
History and Clinical Signs
Similar to pericardial effusion with a high incidence of
signs of elevated right heart pressures.
Diagnosis
Echocardiography

Pericardial effusion is often absent or small volume.
Tamponade may be documented with only a small volume of effusion. The pericardium can appear thickened.
Advanced Doppler studies show respiratory changes in
the peak velocities of mitral and tricuspid valve inflow
profiles highly suggestive of constrictive physiology.
Cardiac Catheterization

Characteristic patterns in atrial and ventricular pressure
profiles are indicative of constrictive physiology although
administering a fluid bolus may be required to generate

VetBooks.ir

28 Pericardial Disease

the pattern. Right atrial pressure traces are characterized
by a prominent Y descent. Right ventricular pressure
traces have a characteristic dip and plateau (square root
sign) with elevated end‐diastolic pressure.
Therapy
Surgical management with subtotal pericardiectomy to
remove the fibrotic pericardium is generally required to

resolve clinical signs. If the epicardium is involved, epicardial stripping is more difficult and associated with
important complications.
Prognosis
Prognosis is poor without surgical management and
associated with an increased rate of complications with
epicardial involvement.

A Respiratory Pattern‐Based Approach to Dyspnea
Christopher G. Byers, DVM, DACVECC, DACVIM (SAIM), CVJ
CriticalCareDVM.com, Omaha, NE, USA

The initial approach to a patient with respiratory distress
is of the utmost importance as it can determine whether
these critical patients live or die. Classic clinical signs of
respiratory distress include tachypnea, head and neck
extension, open‐mouth breathing, anxiety, cyanosis,
nares flaring, abducted elbows, orthopnea, and paradoxical movement of the chest and/or abdomen. Overt signs
of respiratory distress are more commonly seen in dogs
than cats. Unfortunately, cats readily mask disease severity, and commonly the only evidence of respiratory dysfunction may be tachypnea and prominent respiratory
motions in sternal recumbency.
The first step in examining a patient with a respiratory
emergency is to perform a primary survey, efficiently
evaluating airway, breathing, and circulation (ABCs).
If the airway is not patent, it must be cleared of obstruction and immediate orotracheal intubation performed. If
an upper airway obstruction prevents orotracheal intubation, an emergency tracheostomy must be performed.
If there are no airway patency issues, a clinician should
evaluate the patient’s breathing pattern and work of
breathing. Particular attention should be given to the
phase of breathing affected, and effort should be made to
determine if the breathing pattern is obstructive or
restrictive.
Anatomical localization of the cause of respiratory distress is assessed through a “look, listen and feel” approach,
and may be a very powerful tool for assessing underlying
structural changes. Increased inspiratory effort is commonly associated with extrathoracic disorders while
increased expiratory effort is most often due to intrathoracic diseases. An obstructive breathing pattern indicates inappropriate movement of air into and/or out of
the lungs and is frequently associated with a slower respiratory rate and deeper breaths than normal. A restrictive breathing pattern is characterized by inadequate
expansion of the chest wall and/or lungs, resulting in

shallow tachypnea. The initial evaluation of a patient
should ideally begin from afar, as the breathing pattern
may change with manipulation. Making an accurate
assessment after handling can be far more challenging.

­Upper Airway
The upper respiratory tract, that includes the nares,
nasal cavity, pharynx, and larynx, is simply a conduit
from the nares to the glottis. Diseases of the upper respiratory tract are relatively common in both dogs and
cats (Table 29.1). Upon presentation, the owner may
report that a patient snores and/or has exercise intolerance, dysphagia, regurgitation, and/or posttussive retching. They may also report that these clinical signs
are associated with and/or exacerbated by excitement,
humidity, and/or elevated ambient temperatures.
Physical examination may identify referred upper airway
sounds, orthopnea, bilateral elbow abduction, restlessness, dysynchronous breathing, and cyanosis. Affected
patients commonly have abnormal respiratory sounds
and pattern of breathing; the classic upper airway breathing pattern is characterized by increased inspiratory
time and effort compared to expiration. Increased nasal
noise (stertor) and/or laryngeal noise (stridor) may also
be present, depending on the site of airflow turbulence.
Occasionally, pulmonary crackles that form due to
­noncardiogenic pulmonary edema may be auscultated.
Diseases of the upper airway commonly cause at least
partial airway obstruction that markedly reduces proper
airflow. The resultant turbulent airflow promotes the
formation of edema and inflammation that subsequently
increases the work of breathing and further narrows the
affected airway, creating a vicious cycle. Combined with
a reduced ability to effectively eliminate heat from the
body via evaporation, affected patients may readily

develop severe secondary hyperthermia. Patients
affected by upper airway disorders should always be handled with minimal restraint, as they may experience respiratory arrest with minimal manipulation.
Patients with upper airway diseases with partial obstruction should be given appropriate sedation and supplemental oxygenation as soon as possible in an effort to reduce
the work of breathing and anxiety. The least stressful
method of supplemental oxygen provision should be
employed, and viable options include flow‐by, facemask,
oxygen cage, nasal cannulation, modified Elizabethan collar (i.e., Crowe collar), and transtracheal catheterization.
A commonly used sedative protocol for cardiovascularly
unstable patients is the combination of a pure mu opioid
(i.e., fentanyl 2–4 μg/kg IV; oxymorphone 0.05–0.1 mg/kg
IV/IM; methadone 0.2–0.5 mg/kg IV; hydromorphone
0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV) with a benzodiazepine (i.e., diazepam
0.1–0.5 mg/kg IV; midazolam 0.2–0.4 mg/kg IV).
Acetylpromazine (0.02–0.1 mg/kg IV/IM) and butorphanol (0.1-0.2 mg/kg IV/SQ) may be appropriate for cardiovascularly stable patients.
While provision of sedation and supplemental oxygen is
sufficient to relieve clinical signs for many patients with
upper airway diseases, some will not meaningfully
respond. These patients must have their airways c­ aptured
via orotracheal intubation immediately, and the astute clinician must be prepared to perform an emergency tracheostomy for those patients with complete oropharyngeal
and/or laryngeal obstruction. Passive and active cooling
measures should be employed for patients with body temperatures greater than 40.5 °C (105 °F), but should be discontinued with body temperatures reach 39.4 °C (103 °F).
Once stable, a thorough physical examination should
be performed in an effort to determine the underlying
cause of the upper airways signs (if not obvious).
Diagnosis of specific airway abnormalities in an individual patient requires thorough evaluation of the nares,
oral and nasal pharynx, and larynx. Diagnostic investigation may include a sedated orolaryngeal examination,
aural and otoscopic examination, thoracic and cervical
radiography, tracheal fluoroscopy, and nasal computed

tomography with rhinoscopy. Arterial blood gas analysis
commonly identifies hypoxemia with hypercapnia.

­Lower Airway
The lower airway is composed of the intrathoracic
trachea, primary and lobar bronchi, and bronchiolar
­
arborization. Dogs may be affected most commonly by
intrathoracic tracheomalacia, bronchomalacia, and
chronic bronchitis, while feline patients are most commonly diagnosed with asthma. Foreign body obstruction
must be considered. While neoplasia may affect the
lower airway, they rarely induce acute dyspnea due to
their chronic, insidious nature. Owners may report a
chronic and/or progressive history of coughing that is
frequently productive although the sputum is most often
swallowed. Affected patients commonly have a respiratory pattern characterized by prolonged expiration
despite normal inspiratory time and effort; additionally,
a clinician may observe abdominal effort during expiration (abdominal push) and/or auscultate expiratory
wheezes. Patients may display orthopnea, and feline
patients may breathe with an opened mouth. A murmur
is not expected unless lower airway disease has contributed to the development of cor pulmonale. Tracheal
sensitivity may be noted in dogs with tracheobron­
chomalacia and chronic bronchitis.
Feline bronchial asthma is a common respiratory
­condition caused by altered immunosensitivity of the
respiratory tract to inhaled allergens. This hyperresponsiveness causes various structural and chemical changes
in the tracheobronchial tree, including adrenergic–­
cholinergic imbalance and abnormal mucus production.
No pathognomonic clinical signs and/or laboratory
assays have been identified, and definitive diagnosis is
based on history, physical examination findings, and
exclusion of other disease entities from the list of differential diagnoses.
The cause of canine chronic bronchitis is not definitively known, and is typically considered idiopathic in
nature. Establishment of a clear link between this disease
and environmental pollutants, hypersensitivity reactions,
and/or poor dental health has been challenging.
Accordingly, a definitive diagnosis is currently made with
documentation of lower airway inflammation and elimination of other potential causes. Tracheobronchomalacia
is characterized by progressive flaccidity of the tracheal
cartilages that results in collapse of the tracheal and/or
bronchial lumina. The definitive cause of this disease has
not yet been identified, and possible contributing factors
include airway allergies inducing chronic inflammation,
genetic predisposition, and cartilage matrix degeneration. During exhalation, the intrathoracic trachea and/or

VetBooks.ir

29 A Respiratory Pattern‐Based Approach to Dyspnea

bronchi collapse, contributing to common clinical signs,
most notably coughing. Definitive diagnosis is made via
imaging that may include thoracic and cervical radiography, fluoroscopy, and/or tracheobronchoscopy.
Clinicians should follow a standard and consistent
protocol for assessing and hopefully stabilizing a patient
suspected of having lower airway disease, focusing initially on performing an efficient primary survey. Patients
should be given appropriate sedation and supplemental
oxygenation as soon as possible in an effort to reduce the
work of breathing and anxiety. Minimal handling is
advocated, as the stress of manipulation may be lethal.
The least stressful method of supplemental oxygen provision should be employed, and viable options include
flow‐by, facemask, oxygen cage, nasal cannulation,
­modified Elizabethan collar (i.e., Crowe collar), and transtracheal catheterization.
A commonly used sedative protocol for cardiovascularly unstable patients is the combination of a pure mu
opioid (i.e., fentanyl 2–4 μg/kg IV; oxymorphone 0.05–
0.1 mg/kg IV/IM; methadone 0.2–0.5 mg/kg IV; hydromorphone 0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV) with a benzodiazepine (i.e.,
diazepam 0.1–0.5 mg/kg IV; midazolam 0.2–0.4 mg/kg
IV). Acetylpromazine (0.02–0.1 mg/kg IV/IM) and
butorphanol (0.1-0.2 mg/kg IV/SQ) may be appropriate
for cardiovascularly stable patients. Inhaled albuterol
(90–180 μg), a rapidly acting beta‐2 agonist, should be
administered; terbutaline (0.01 mg/kg SC) is a reasonable
alternative if a metered‐dose inhaler is not available.
Corticosteroids are commonly used for chronic management of feline asthma and canine chronic bronchitis, but
their use is not necessarily warranted in the initial management of these diseases; a brief (i.e., 7–10 days) tapering regime of antiinflammatory corticosteroid may be
beneficial in the acute management of tracheobronchomalacia to help break the cycle of coughing commonly present in affected patients.
Once stable, a thorough physical examination should
be performed in an effort to determine the underlying
cause of the lower airways signs. High‐quality, three‐
view thoracic radiographs are an essential part of the
diagnostic investigative process. Indirect visualization
via fluoroscopy and/or direct visualization of the lower
airways via tracheobronchoscopy may be invaluable, and
lower airway cytology and culture should be pursued to
rule out infectious diseases.

­Pleural Space
The pleural cavity is the potential space between the
parietal pleura associated with the body wall and visceral
pleura associated with lungs. When this potential space
is occupied by air, fluid, masses and/or viscera, the lungs

are unable to expand normally. As a result, intrapleural
pressure increases and ultimately exceeds the intrapulmonary pressure, effectively reducing tidal volume.
Accordingly, a patient must breathe rapidly to maintain
adequate minute ventilation. Classically, affected patients
manifest a restrictive breathing pattern characterized by
shallow tachypnea. With reduced tidal volume, alveoli
progressively collapse to cause hypoventilation and
hypoxemia due to ventilation–perfusion mismatch.
Thoracic auscultation varies depending on the nature
of the pleural disease. Pneumothorax may develop secondary to blunt or penetrating thoracic trauma, but may
also occur spontaneously due to primary pulmonary
parenchymal disease. A patient with pneumothorax has
lung sounds that are most audible ventrally. Pleural effusion may occur secondary to accumulation of blood
(hemothorax), infectious exudate (pyothorax), neoplasia,
chyle (chylothorax), and heart failure; hypervolemia and
hypovolemia are rare causes of pleural effusion. A patient
with pleural effusion commonly has dull ventral lung
sounds with audible and possible increased lungs sounds
dorsally. Borborygmi may be heard in those patients with
a congenital or traumatic pleuroperitoneal diaphragmatic
hernia. A cardiac murmur and/or dysrhythmia may be
auscultated in those living with heart disease.
Patients with pleural disease should be provided supplemental oxygenation as soon as possible via the least
stressful method. Sedation should also be administered,
ideally prior to thoracocentesis; this is not always feasible
if imminent respiratory arrest is anticipated. A commonly used sedative protocol for cardiovascularly unstable patients is the combination of a pure mu opioid
(i.e., fentanyl 2–4 μg/kg IV; oxymorphone 0.05–0.1 mg/
kg IV/IM; methadone 0.2–0.5 mg/kg IV; hydromorphone
0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV) with a benzodiazepine (i.e., diazepam
0.1–0.5 mg/kg IV; midazolam 0.2–0.4 mg/kg IV).
Diuretic therapy is not indicated for the emergency management of pleural space disease.
Thoracocentesis should generally be performed prior
to thoracic radiography if pleural space disease is suspected. A thoracocentesis is typically performed at the
seventh to ninth intercostal space. If a pneumothorax is
suspected, the site of pleural puncture is perpendicular
to the body wall just ventral to the thoracic hypaxial
musculature; the level of the costochondral junction is
the site of pleural puncture for those patients with suspected or confirmed pleural effusion. If available, thoracic focused assessment with sonography for trauma,
triage and tracking (tFAST3) may be used to confirm
pneumothorax and pleural ­effusion, help determine site
of pleural puncture, and may be performed in lateral or
sternal recumbency. Thoracocentesis has been uncommonly associated with hemorrhage, pulmonary parenchymal injury, and iatrogenic infectious disease

291

transmission. Rapid and fatal reexpansion pulmonary
edema may rarely occur in patients with chronic pleural
effusion. Ideally, pleural fluid and/or air should be
removed until negative p
­ ressure is achieved, but this is
not always possible. If negative pressure cannot be

Once stable, a thorough physical examination should
be performed in an effort to determine the underlying
cause. Traumatic pneumothorax commonly resolves
without surgical intervention, but injuries may require
several days to heal. The presence of pneumothorax without a history of trauma should always prompt a search for
pulmonary parenchymal disease. Pleural e­ ffusion should
be immediately evaluated in‐house for obvious sepsis
and/or neoplastic cells, and one should submit samples
(i.e., pleural fluid sample in EDTA‐containing tube,
unstained slide, fluid sample on appropriate culture
media) to a veterinary reference laboratory for evaluation
by a board‐certified veterinary clinical pathologist.
Echocardiography and cardiac biomarker (i.e., NT‐
proBNP) measurement may be helpful in those patients
suspected of living with cardiac disease, and diaphragmatic hernias should be surgically repaired as soon as the
patient is cardiovascularly and metabolically stable.

­Pulmonary Parenchyma
The pulmonary parenchyma may be affected by a number of diseases, and a thorough history will help the
astute clinician develop an appropriate diagnostic investigation and therapeutic interventions. Dogs frequently
have a history of a cough that may or may not be productive, but cats rarely manifest this clinical sign. A history
of laryngeal paralysis or recent vomiting should raise
concern for aspiration pneumonitis, and patients with
trauma may develop pulmonary contusions and/or noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. Recent generalized
seizure activity, electrocution, traumatic brain injury,
­
and/or strangulation should also raise concern for noncardiogenic pulmonary edema that develops secondary
to endothelial injury and vascular leakage into alveoli.
Conversely, patients with primary cardiac disease are at
risk for developing cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
Performing a complete physical examination is invaluable for patients with suspected pulmonary parenchymal
disease. Affected patients do not have a specific respiratory pattern, and frequently manifest respirations that
are rapid and deep. They may be presented with cyanosis
and dyspnea, and increased abdominal effort is relatively
common. Auscultation commonly reveals end‐inspira-

tory crackles, adventitious lung sounds that represent
the sudden opening of fluid‐filled alveoli. Alveolar fluid
may be blood, purulent exudate or transudate. Alveolar
hemorrhage may occur secondary to trauma and/or
coagulopathy. A patient with cardiogenic pulmonary
edema secondary to left‐sided heart disease may have a
systolic murmur and hypothermia while a patient with
pneumonia or aspiration pneumonitis may have pyrexia.
Patients should be efficiently examined for evidence of
ecchymoses, obvious soft tissue and/or orthopedic injury
and thermal injury (i.e., lingual or oral commissure).
Patients should be given appropriate sedation and supplemental oxygenation as soon as possible in an effort to
reduce the work of breathing and anxiety. The least
stressful method of supplemental oxygen provision
should be employed. A commonly used sedative protocol
for cardiovascularly unstable patients is the combination
of a pure mu opioid (i.e., fentanyl 2–4 μg/kg IV; oxymorphone 0.05–0.1 mg/kg IV/IM; methadone 0.2–0.5 mg/kg
IV; hydromorphone 0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV) with a benzodiazepine (i.e., diazepam 0.1–0.5 mg/kg IV; midazolam 0.2–
0.4 mg/kg IV). A single dose of furosemide (dogs: 2 mg/kg
IV/IM; cats: 1 mg/kg IV/IM) may be provided to those in
which primary heart disease is suspected to be contributing to clinical signs until a definitive diagnosis is made.
While provision of sedation and oxygen is sufficient to
relieve clinical signs, some will not meaningfully respond;
these patients must have their airways captured via orotracheal intubation immediately and mechanical ventilation should be initiated. Provision of positive end‐expiratory
pressure (PEEP) at a level of 3–5 cmH2O may promote
recruitment of collapsed alveoli.
Diagnostic imaging should be performed once the
patient has been appropriately stabilized. Commonly
employed thoracic imaging modalities include tFAST3,
veterinary bedside lung ultrasound examination
(VetBLUE), and thoracic radiography. A tFAST3 evaluation may be used to detect chest wall, lung, pleural and/
or pericardial pathology, and may be performed in lateral
or sternal recumbency. Five points are evaluated, and fur
is not shaved but rather is simply parted with alcohol or
sonographic gel (Table 29.2). Patients with pulmonary
parenchymal disease may have B‐lines (aka: comet tail
artifacts, lung rockets) that suggest interstitial disease or
interlobar edema is present; thus a clinician should be
suspicious of pulmonary edema (cardiogenic and noncardiogenic) and pneumonia/pneumonitis. A VetBLUE
scan is similar to a tFAST3, as it is performed rapidly in
sternal recumbency, measures the presence of B‐lines
and does not require hair coat shaving; in contrast, eight
locations (four per hemithorax) are evaluated during the
scan (see Table 29.2). The absence of B‐lines in all evaluated lung fields rules out pulmonary edema and suggests
a nonrespiratory cause of distress.

One must understand that VetBLUE and tFAST3 scans
do not replace the diagnostic utility of thoracic radiography
when evaluating patients with pulmonary parenchymal disease. Indeed, evaluation of soft tissue parenchymal patterns
may be uniquely helpful in determining the underlying disease process (Table 29.3). Interstitial, interstitial‐to‐alveolar,
and alveolar patterns are most commonly reported in
patients with pulmonary parenchymal diseases.
Animals with primary left‐sided cardiac disease may
have cardiomegaly, left atrial enlargement, and pulmonary
venous dilation. While a perihilar radiographic distribution is highly suggestive of cardiogenic pulmonary edema
in dogs, cats do not have classic radiographic patterns for
most parenchymal diseases. The choice of additional diagnostic investigation should be based on patient history
and physical examination. Tracheal washing or bronchoalveolar lavage for airway cytology and culture (bacterial & fungal) may be appropriate for patients with
suspected infectious pneumonia or aspiration pneumonia/pneumonitis. Metastatic screening via abdominal
radiography and/or ultrasonography may be indicated for
those patients suspected of living with neoplasia, and fungal urine antigen and serology should be performed in
those with suspected pulmonary mycoses. Definitive
treatment is based on a patient’s ultimate diagnosis.

­Pulmonary Thromboembolism
Pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE) occurs when
venous thrombi formed in large, deep veins travel

through the right side of the heart and lodge in the
­pulmonary arterial bed. The caudal lung lobes are more
likely to be involved as they receive most of the right
­ventricular output. Consequences of PTE include hypoxemia, bronchoconstriction, ventilation–perfusion (V–Q)
mismatch, and hyperventilation. With time, further
complications arise, including atelectasis, pulmonary
edema, and pleural effusion. Hemodynamic complications from PTE depend on the extent to which the
­pulmonary vasculature is occluded and the amount of
preexisting cardiac and pulmonary compromise. If pulmonary vasculature reserve capacity is exceeded, pulmonary vascular resistance increases to augment right
ventricular afterload and ventricular oxygen demand.
If the oxygen supply is exceeded, ischemia, ­dysrhythmias,
and/or right ventricular failure may occur. Decreased
cardiac output is caused by reduced pulmonary venous
return induced by pulmonary blood flow obstruction.
Diagnosing PTE is difficult. Clinical signs commonly
include tachypnea, dyspnea, and hypoxemia, none of
which is pathognomonic for PTE. Initial assessment
should include thoracic radiography, abdominal ultrasonography, arterial blood gas analysis, a complete blood
count, biochemical profile, urinalysis and heartworm
testing. Reported radiographic abnormalities associated
with PTE are pleural effusion, regional oligemia, alveolar
infiltrates, cardiomegaly, hyperlucent lung regions, and
enlargement of the main pulmonary artery. While the
majority of patients with PTE will have radiographic
abnormalities, radiographs may also be normal in 9–27%
of dogs and 7% of cats with PTE. Arterial blood gas
(ABG) analysis is frequently a very useful diagnostic tool.
In one canine PTE study, hypoxemia was documented in
80% of affected patients and increased alveolar‐arterial
(A‐a) gradients on room air in all dogs. Basic blood and
urine testing is performed in an effort to identify predisposing conditions, including hyperadrenocorticism, protein‐losing nephropathy, protein‐losing enteropathy,
hypothyroidism, and/or diabetes mellitus.
If these tests fail to identify an underlying disease process, echocardiography and measurement of prothrombin and partial thromboblastin times may be helpful.

Echocardiography may show a right‐sided thrombus or a
thrombus in the main pulmonary artery, or may also
demonstrate changes suggestive of pulmonary hypertension. A normal echocardiogram does not rule out PTE.
Measurement of D‐dimers may have diagnostic utility in
patients with PTE. A 2003 study determined that D‐
dimer concentrations >500 ng/mL were 100% sensitive
for predicting thromboembolic disease but specificity
was 70%; conversely, D‐dimer concentrations greater
than 1000 ng/mL had 80% sensitivity and 94% specificity.
The sensitivity of D‐dimer in the diagnosis of PTE is
more important than specificity, as false negatives may
have fatal consequences. Tests for hypercoagulability,
such as antithrombin, fibrinogen, and thromboelastography, should also be considered. Advanced imaging
such as V–Q scans, spiral computed tomography, and/or
pulmonary angiography might ultimately be required for
definitive diagnosis of PTE.
Pulmonary thromboemboli dissolution may begin
without treatment within hours of formation and completely dissolve within days. Nevertheless, a prothrombotic tendency persists to promote continued formation
of pulmonary thromboemboli. Goals of treatment are
reversal of the prothrombotic state and correction of
hemodynamic and pulmonary changes responsible for
morbidity and mortality. Treatment usually consists of
supportive care, oxygen supplementation, and anticoagulant therapy; systemic or locally delivered thrombolytic
agents may be used, but the benefits must be weighed
against potential serious risks. Oxygen administration
aims to correct hypoxemia caused by V–Q mismatch,
alveolar hypoventilation, and/or diffusion impairment.
However, the response to oxygen depends on the degree
of vascular obstruction; pulmonary shunt occurs when
more than 50% of the circulatory bed surface area is
occluded, yielding venous admixture and decreased oxygen responsiveness. Resolution of the underlying disease
process should always be the primary goal.

­Chest Wall
The chest wall is composed of bone and soft tissue structures, including skeletal muscles, external fascia, costal
parietal pleural nerves and vasculature; all play structural and functional roles in respiration. The craniodorsal external intercostals and parasternal intercostals
promote inspiration by pulling ribs in a cranial direction.
The interosseous portion of the internal intercostals and
the caudalmost external intercostals contribute to
­expiration by pulling the ribs caudally. Given the normal
negative pressure within the pleural space, it is potential
in nature with the parietal pleura held in constant contact with the visceral pleura in the absence of disease.

As thoracic cavity dimensions are increased in response
to respiratory muscle action, the lungs expand because
of the constant negative intrapleural pressure.
Common thoracic wall injuries include blunt trauma,
penetrating trauma, and flail chest. Blunt trauma may
cause crush and shear injuries to both soft tissues and
skeletal structures; advantageously, the skeletal structures of the chest wall are relatively resistant to blunt
force trauma. However, muscle is uniquely sensitive to
crushing injury, and when damaged in low‐velocity accidents may become edematous and inelastic, and may
lose the ability to efficiently and effectively contract.
Accordingly, thoracic wall compliance decreases and
work of breathing subsequently increases. This may
manifest as tachypnea but breaths may be shallow or
deep; subsequent hypoxemia and/or hypoventilation are
relatively common. High‐velocity accidents are also
associated with shearing injury. While soft tissue damage to the thoracic wall rarely contributes to patient
morbidity, energy may be readily transmitted to intrathoracic organs to induce both crush and shearing injuries
at these sites. Additionally, a blunt force applied laterally
to the thoracic wall may cause rib fractures. However,
pressure applied dorsoventrally to the thoracic cage
infrequently results in rib and/or sternebrae fractures
but such injuries may contribute to reduced thoracic
compliance.
Penetrating injuries to the thoracic wall are relatively
common in domestic dogs and cats, and common examples include bite injuries and missile (i.e., bullet, arrow)
trauma. These wounds readily induce stretching and
crushing of tissues in the direct path of penetration.
While the actual chest wall penetration is frequently a
minor issue in affected patients, one must be acutely
aware of the potential underlying pleural and intrathoracic injuries caused by the penetrating trauma. The type
and severity of injury directly influence how a patient is
presented, and the medical team must be prepared to
­triage a patient in profound respiratory distress that is in
need of immediate orotracheal intubation and intrathoracic stabilization.
Flail chest results from the segmental fracture and/or
dislocation of two or more adjacent ribs. This type of
injury is uncommon in dogs and cats because of the
inherent compliance and anatomic shape of the thoracic
cage. Blunt trauma and bite injuries are the most common causes of flail chest, and concurrent pulmonary
damage, most notably pulmonary contusions and direct
injury from costal fractures, is a major contributor to
morbidity associated with this condition; these contusions may lead to decreased pulmonary compliance,
hypoventilation, and shunting, all of which cause
­hypoxemia. The pathognomonic respiratory pattern is
paradoxical movement of the unstable ribs (flail
­

VetBooks.ir

29 A Respiratory Pattern‐Based Approach to Dyspnea

segment) during respiration. Splinting due to pain
­
­associated with respiration leads to a decreased cough
reflex, hypoventilation, hypoxemia, and atelectasis.
Several techniques for stabilization of flail chest have
been reported, but the primary focus should be on oxygen supplementation, underlying intrathoracic injuries,
and multimodal analgesia.

­Diaphragm
As a major respiratory muscle responsible for the creation of subatmospheric intrathoracic pressure, the diaphragm is essential for adequate oxygen and ventilation.
Many conditions may induce partial or complete
­diaphragmatic paralysis, including pleuroperitoneal hernias, botulism, and phrenic nerve damage or degeneration. The classic respiratory pattern of a patient with a
dysfunctional or ruptured diaphragm is tachypnea with
marked inspiratory excursion of the cranial half of the
thorax. Paradoxical abdominal movement is also common, and may be due to either thoracic displacement of
abdominal viscera during vigorous inspiration or an inability to maintain abdominal girth during inspiration.

­Nonrespiratory Causes
There are multiple causes of tachypnea and dyspnea that
do not directly arise from the respiratory tract. Perhaps
the most common example is nonpyogenic hyperthermia which may be the sole cause of respiratory signs or
be secondary to a concurrent medical condition.
Accordingly, measurement of body temperature is essen-

tial in patients presented with respiratory signs, and
appropriate cooling measures should be implemented
when hyperthermia is documented.
Intracranial diseases may directly stimulate the respiratory center located in the medulla. Patients with traumatic brain injury, intracranial neoplasia, and/or
inflammatory/infectious central nervous system diseases
may have abnormal respiratory patterns. Neurological
examination typically identifies other deficits that may
aid in determining a definitive diagnosis. Pain and acid–
base disorders may also induce tachypnea without
hypoxia in patients. Distension of the abdominal cavity is
another common cause of tachypnea and dyspnea in
dogs and cats, chiefly through elevation of intraabdominal hypertension and development of abdominal
compartment syndrome; specifically, intraabdominal
­
hypertension impairs diaphragmatic contraction,
thereby impeding the ability to generate subatmospheric
intrathoracic pressure. Additionally, pulmonary parenchyma may be compressed, leading to decreased oxygen
transport across the pulmonary capillary membrane,
increased alveolar dead space, and alveolar atelectasis.
Common examples of intraabdominal pathology that
may cause and/or contribute to respiratory compromise
include severe paralytic ileus, marked abdominal discomfort inducing splinting of abdominal musculature,
large‐volume peritoneal effusion, intraabdominal neoplasia, and gastric dilation‐volvulus. Whenever possible,
abdominal decompression should be performed, and
possible decompression methods include peritoneocentesis, therapy for ileus and capillary leak, adequate analgesia to allow for abdominal muscle relaxation, and
surgical decompression.

Feline Bronchial Asthma
Christine M. Serafin, DVM, DACVIM (SAIM)
The Animal Surgical Center of Michigan, Flint, Michigan, USA

Feline bronchial asthma is one of the most commonly
recognized diseases of the lower respiratory tract of cats
and is estimated to affect up to 5% of the cat population.
The broad range of clinical manifestations that characterizes this condition, its similarities to the human form
of the disease, the challenges inherent to its diagnosis,
and the necessity for life‐long treatment warrant significant consideration of feline bronchial asthma in both
human and veterinary respiratory medicine.

­Etiology and Pathophysiology
Feline bronchial disease is a general term that has been
applied to inflammatory disease of the lower airways
that does not have an apparent etiology. Feline asthma is
considered to be a specific form of bronchial disease
that is distinguished from other inflammatory airways
diseases by reversible airflow limitation. This airflow
obstruction is caused by smooth muscle hyperreactivity
and hypertrophy, increased mucus production, inflammation, and permanent airway remodeling. Airflow
restriction reverses either spontaneously or in response
to pharmacological intervention. Intermittent bronchoconstriction, predominantly eosinophilic lower airway
inflammation, and an allergic immunopathogenesis
differentiate feline asthma from chronic bronchitis,
­
which is typified by neutrophilic airway inflammation in
response to a previous insult. Accordingly, asthma is
recognized by its three hallmark features: airway
­
eosinophilic inflammation, hyperresponsiveness, and
­
permanent remodeling.
Although the exact etiopathogenesis has not been
determined, type I hypersensitivity response is widely
accepted to be the basis for the development of feline
bronchial asthma. This response begins with dendritic
cells within the airways that process inhaled allergen.
These cells migrate to the regional lymph nodes and

­present the antigen, bound to major histocompatibility
complex class II receptors, to naïve CD4+ T helper cells,
triggering these cells to differentiate into T helper 2 cells.
T helper 2 cells, in turn, produce interleukins (IL) 4, 5,
and 13. IL‐4 in particular induces B cells to switch from
production of immunoglobulin (Ig) G to antigen‐specific
IgE that then binds to Fc receptors on the surface of mast
cells. Allergen particles that are subsequently inhaled
cross‐link IgE molecules on the surface of mast cells,
­initiating an intracellular cascade of events that culminates in mast cell degranulation. Histamines and leukotrienes released from degranulating mast cells promote
increased vascular permeability, smooth muscle contraction, and mucus production, generating the clinical
manifestations associated with asthma. IL‐4, IL‐5, and
IL‐13 that are also released by mast cells recruit eosinophils to the airways. Major basic protein, eosinophil
­peroxidase, and cationic proteins released by degranulating eosinophils induce the tissue damage that characterizes asthma.

­Epidemiology
Cats of any age can develop asthma but young to
middle‐aged cats are most often affected. A predilection
for the Siamese breed has been proposed.

­History and Clinical Signs
A wide spectrum of clinical signs characterizes feline
asthma. Acute manifestations arise from bronchoconstriction and can include severe dyspnea, orthopnea,
tachypnea, cyanosis, open‐mouth breathing, and wheezing. Episodes of dyspnea may occur on a daily basis or as
infrequently as once or twice yearly. Chronic manifestations are typified by paroxysmal episodes of coughing.

The cough is usually described as harsh and “gagging”
and results from activation of bronchial cough receptors
by inflammatory debris, mucus, and smooth muscle
spasm. Inhalation of mechanical or chemical irritants
can trigger cough, leading to the sporadic nature of the
clinical signs. Further, acute exacerbations may be
observed in patients with chronic signs, which can result
in periodic wheezing or dyspnea in patients with a long‐
standing history of occasional cough. Clinical signs referable to the upper airways, including sneezing, nasal
discharge, and stertor, have been anecdotally reported in
asthmatic cats. In fact, histopathologic inflammatory
changes have been documented in the nasal passages of
cats with experimentally induced asthma. Inspiratory
stridor and dyspnea associated with dynamic upper airway obstruction have also been described in an asthmatic cat. Signs of systemic illness, including inappetence,
lethargy, and depression, are not typically reported.
Physical examination findings in asthmatic cats are
likewise variable. Due to the intermittent nature of the
clinical signs, physical examination may yield no abnormalities. Alternatively, observation of the respiratory
pattern may reveal an end‐expiratory “push” as air
trapped within the lungs following inspiration is
forcefully expelled through narrowed airways during
­
expiration. In severely affected patients, air trapping can
lead to lung hyperinflation, resulting in decreased
­compliance of the thoracic wall and, subsequently, a
“barrel‐shaped” appearance to the thorax. Tachypnea
with prolongation of the expiratory phase may be
observed at rest. Resistance to airflow caused by reduced
intraluminal airway diameter results in turbulence,
which is exhibited clinically as wheezing that may be
audible with or without a stethoscope. Inspiratory crackles, increased bronchial sounds, and/or rhonchi may also
be identified on thoracic auscultation, or no abnormal
sounds may be appreciated. In some patients, palpation
of the trachea elicits cough. Stress associated with
restraint can greatly exacerbate the clinical signs.

­Diagnosis
In human patients, asthma is definitively diagnosed on
the basis of pulmonary function testing such as spirometry that requires a voluntary expiratory maneuver. Since
such maneuvers are not feasible in feline patients, there
remains at present no gold standard diagnostic test by
which feline asthma is diagnosed.
Currently, clinical diagnosis relies on compatible clinical signs, pathology noted on thoracic radiography,
­airway cytology abnormalities, and exclusion of other
causes of similar findings. In an acute setting, conditions such as congestive heart failure and pleural space

disease can lead to respiratory distress that resembles
signs of severe asthma on initial evaluation. Plasma
­levels of N‐terminal pro‐brain natriuretic peptide (NT‐
proBNP) can be used to differentiate between congestive heart failure and primary respiratory disease in cats
with acute dyspnea when specific cut‐off values are
used. Parasitic bronchitis caused by Aelurostrongylus
abstrusus, Capillaria aerophila, Paragonimus kellicotti,
or pulmonary migration of Toxocara cati is characterized by eosinophilic lower airway inflammation and can
be associated with clinical signs that mimic chronic
manifestations of asthma. Heartworm‐associated respiratory disease complex should also be considered a
differential diagnosis for feline bronchial asthma.
Specific testing (i.e., Baermann fecal examination, fecal
flotation, heartworm antibody testing) should be performed to exclude these conditions before a diagnosis of
feline asthma is reached.
Laboratory abnormalities seen with feline asthma are
nonspecific but can include a peripheral eosinophilia,
occurring in 20–57% of patients. A peripheral neutrophilia can also be noted in moderately to severely affected
cats. Hyperproteinemia due to hyperglobulinemia may
develop consequent to chronic inflammation. Results of
serum biochemistry analysis are typically unremarkable.
Thoracic radiography is standardly employed in the
diagnostic evaluation of suspected asthmatics. However,
thoracic radiography should not be solely relied upon for
diagnosis, as findings can be variable and nonspecific.
A bronchial pattern is most commonly seen, consistent
with airway inflammatory infiltrates. Interstitial, alveolar,
and mixed patterns have also been documented in asthmatic patients. Consolidation of the right middle lung
lobe may be observed and results from obstruction of the
bronchus by mucus plugging that preferentially occurs in
this lung segment due to its perpendicular orientation to
the mainstem bronchus. Hyperinflation of the lungs,
identified by flattening of the diaphragm, is also consistent with asthma. Importantly, no pulmonary abnormalities may be detected in as many as 25% of cases.
Bronchoscopy provides additional information that
can be used to support a diagnosis of feline asthma. The
most common bronchoscopic finding identified in cats
with lower airways disease is airway obstruction by
mucus. Nodular irregularities of the epithelium, airway
hyperemia, static or dynamic airway collapse, and
­bronchial stenosis are also frequently seen. As with radiography, these findings are not specific for feline asthma.
Complications ranging from hemoglobin desaturation to
pneumothorax have been documented in up to 24% of
cats undergoing bronchoscopy. Pretreatment with terbutaline has been associated with a lower incidence of
these complications. When the necessary precautions
are taken, bronchoscopy can be performed safely in

VetBooks.ir

30 Feline Bronchial Asthma

­asthmatic cats and can provide evidence that is crucial
in reaching a diagnosis.
Airway cytology remains the most definitive means of
diagnosing feline bronchial asthma after other conditions
are excluded. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) can be
accomplished with bronchoscopic guidance to collect
samples from specific segments of the lower airways for
cytologic analysis. Alternatively, BAL can be performed
using an unguided technique in patients with diffuse distribution of disease when bronchoscopy is not available
or feasible. The procedure is performed under general
anesthesia that is induced and maintained with short‐­
acting injectable anesthetic agents such as propofol. Prior
to inducing anesthesia, the patient is preoxygenated for
5–10 minutes with flow‐by or mask oxygenation methods. The procedure is performed with the patient in sternal or lateral recumbency with the most diseased side
positioned ventrally. While avoiding oropharyngeal contamination as much as possible, the patient is intubated
with a sterile endotracheal tube. A sterile red rubber or
polypropylene catheter is then inserted through the
lumen of the endotracheal tube and advanced until resistance is met, indicating that the catheter is wedged within
a distal airway. Using a syringe, a 5 mL/kg bolus of
warmed, sterile 0.9% saline or phosphate buffered saline
is instilled through the catheter followed by a 5 mL bolus
of air. The empty syringe is then used to aspirate the fluid
from the airways. This may be repeated twice to obtain an
adequate sample. Retrieval of 46–68% of the total infusate
has been reported. The caudal half of the patient may be
elevated during aspiration to facilitate retrieval of fluid.
Supplemental oxygen is administered postprocedurally
for 5–10 minutes. Samples reserved for cytologic analysis
should be kept on ice and processed within one hour of
collection to avoid deterioration of cells. Hypoxemia is a
significant complication associated with BAL but can
usually be reversed with oxygen supplementation.
Bronchospasm may also occur as a consequence of BAL
and can be managed with bronchodilators.
Increased numbers of eosinophils are classically noted
in cytologic samples collected from the airways of
asthmatic cats. However, a significant neutrophilic
­
­component has also been reported in cats with both naturally occurring and experimentally induced asthma.
Discrepancy exists regarding the percentage of eosinophils considered abnormal within feline airway cytology
samples. Eosinophil proportions ranging from 16% to
28% have been documented in airway samples collected
from healthy cats. As such, cytologic findings must be
interpreted in light of other diagnostic results in order
for a diagnosis of asthma to be verified.
Bacterial culture of airway lavage samples collected
from cats with lower airways disease produces variable
results. Bacterial growth has been found in airway

­samples collected from healthy cats, though growth of
Mycoplasma spp. has not been documented. Therefore,
a diagnosis of secondary bacterial infection in an asthmatic patient must be based on growth of a large number
of colonies of a single organism or intracellular bacteria
seen cytologically. Organisms that have been detected on
airway samples collected from cats with bronchopulmonary disease include Pasteurella multocida, Streptococcus
spp., Staphylococcus spp., Mycoplasma spp., Moraxella
spp., and Bordetella spp.
Due to the degree of invasiveness, lung biopsies are not
routinely performed in the diagnostic evaluation of cats
with lower airways disease. Histopathology of postmortem lung samples from cats with experimentally induced
asthma revealed epithelial hypertrophy and hyperplasia,
marked smooth muscle hypertrophy of the terminal and
respiratory bronchioles, and mucous cell metaplasia.
Pulmonary function testing, though not employed
standardly in clinical settings, has been investigated as a
means of assessing asthmatic cats. Specifically, barometric whole‐body plethysmography (BWBP) has been
employed to assess airway responsiveness in cats with
experimentally induced asthma. This noninvasive technique measures pressure changes generated by an
awake, spontaneously breathing cat in a transparent,
ventilated chamber. Pause and enhanced pause are
­variables used to estimate lung resistance. These values
have been shown to increase significantly following
bronchoprovocation in healthy cats and cats with artificially induced asthma. Tidal breathing flow‐volume
loops have also been utilized to assess lung resistance in
cats with bronchial disease. These loops are generated
in awake cats using a facemask attached to a pneumotachograph to assess airflow. Cats with bronchial disease
have reduced expiratory flows and tidal breathing expiratory volumes and prolonged expiratory time compared
to healthy cats. Additionally, ventilator‐acquired
mechanics have been used to measure airway resistance,
positive end‐expiratory occlusion pressure, and end‐
expiratory breath hold pressure following bronchoprovocation in anesthetized cats with experimentally
induced asthma.
Advances in the diagnostic approach to feline asthma
have included the development of minimally invasive
methods that may have utility in a future clinical setting.
In particular, exhaled breath condensate (EBC) can be
collected from nonanesthetized cats briefly housed
within an acrylic chamber and analyzed for hydrogen
peroxide, a marker of oxidative stress. The concentration
of hydrogen peroxide in the EBC of artificially sensitized
cats has been shown to correlate with the degree of
eosinophilic lower airway inflammation, suggesting that
analysis of EBC may prove to be a useful screening tool
for suspected asthmatics.

Identifying the allergens responsible for inciting the
asthmatic response in individual cats is a critical step in
devising targeted therapies. Methods have been developed to detect IgE that is specific for the allergens used
in sensitization in the serum of cats with experimentally
induced asthma. Moreover, intradermal skin testing, a
practice most often used in the diagnosis of atopic
­dermatitis, has been shown to be a sensitive means of
detecting aeroallergen sensitization in experimental
models of asthma. Other minimally invasive immunodiagnostic methods that have been investigated in asthmatic patients include the use of flow cytometry to
detect ­proliferation of allergen‐specific T lymphocytes in
the peripheral blood.

­Treatment
Supplemental oxygen, stress reduction, and bronchodilation are the tenets of therapy for the asthmatic
cat in acute crisis. For the patient presenting with
dyspnea and cyanosis, supplemental oxygen should be
provided immediately at a FiO2 of 40%. This can be
effectively accomplished by placing the patient in an
oxygen cage, which also minimizes restraint and handling that can exacerbate dyspnea, with fatal outcomes
in some instances.
Beta‐2‐adrenergic agonists such as terbutaline are
most commonly used to induce bronchodilation in an
acute setting. Bronchodilation results from airway
smooth muscle relaxation triggered by stimulation of
beta‐2‐adrenergic receptors. Activation of these receptors triggers adenylyl cyclase to increase production of
cAMP, which sequesters intracellular calcium, thereby
reducing smooth muscle contraction. Other potentially
beneficial effects of these agents include inhibition of
mast cell mediator release and airway microvascular
leakage, increased mucociliary clearance, decreased
neutrophil activation and endothelial adhesion, and
induction of neutrophil apoptosis. Adverse effects associated with beta‐2‐adrenergic agonist therapy include
tachycardia, CNS stimulation, hypokalemia, and tremors. For this reason, these agents should be used with
caution in patients with co‐morbid cardiac disease,
hypertension, hyperthyroidism, seizure disorders, and
diabetes mellitus. Beta‐2‐adrenergic agonists can interact with tricyclic antidepressants such as amitriptyline
and clomipramine and should be used with caution in
patients receiving these medications. Terbutaline sulfate can be administered IM or SC at an initial dose
of 0.1 mg/kg to induce bronchodilation in an acute
­setting. Decreased respiratory rate is expected within
15–30 minutes of dosing, and repeated doses can be
administered as needed.

Albuterol sulfate is a beta‐2‐adrenergic agonist that
may be administered in inhalant form to cats presenting
with severe, acute dyspnea. A metered dose inhaler is
used to deliver the medication into a chamber device
attached to a facemask (Aerokat® Feline Aerosol
Chamber, Trudell Medical International). This apparatus facilitates inhalation of the aerosolized particles into
the lower airways. An initial dose of one 90 μg puff can
be administered to dyspneic patients that will tolerate
having the facemask held over the nose and mouth for
the 7–10 seconds necessary for the complete dose to be
inhaled. This dose may be repeated every 30 minutes for
up to four hours. Albuterol can also be dispensed for
at‐home administration as a “rescue inhaler” for management of acute exacerbations in established asthmatics until veterinary care can be provided. However,
chronic use of racemic albuterol should be avoided as
the S‐enantiomer in this mixture has been shown to
cause airway inflammation in healthy and experimentally asthmatic cats.
Status asthmaticus is defined in human medicine as
severe, acute asthma that is refractory to repeated doses
of beta‐agonists. Severely dyspneic feline asthmatics that
do not respond to bronchodilators and supplemental
oxygen may stabilize only after initiating antiinflammatory therapy with a rapidly acting glucocorticoid such as
dexamethasone sodium phosphate. An initial dose of
0.25–2 mg/kg can be administered IM or IV to quickly
reduce airway inflammation if necessary.
Lifelong glucocorticoid therapy is the key to chronic
management of feline asthma. Because the aeroallergen
that provokes the asthmatic response usually cannot be
identified or completely removed, avoidance of the
offending allergen is often impossible in feline patients.
Thus, it is postulated that lower airway inflammation is
continually present in asthmatic cats, even in the absence
of clinical signs. Lower airway inflammation has been
shown to persist in feline asthmatics treated with high‐
dose glucocorticoid therapy despite resolution of clinical
signs. To minimize the permanent airway remodeling
that ensues from long‐standing inflammation, continuous antiinflammatory therapy is necessary.
Glucocorticoids are the most effective antiinflammatory agents used in the management of feline asthma.
They exert their antiinflammatory effects by binding to a
cytosolic receptor, then translocating to the nucleus
where the glucocorticoid–receptor complex binds to a
glucocorticoid response element on the genes that regulate production of inflammatory cytokines such as IL‐3
and IL‐5. Glucocorticoids also increase vasoconstriction
to reduce airway edema; decrease airway hyperresponsiveness over time; decrease mucus secretion; inhibit
macrophages, T cells, eosinophils, and mast cells;
increase the synthesis of secretory leukocyte protease

VetBooks.ir

30 Feline Bronchial Asthma

inhibitor to reduce airway remodeling; and prevent the
downregulation of beta‐adrenergic receptors.
Orally administered glucocorticoids are used in the
initial management of stable asthmatics. Prednisolone is
preferred over prednisone in cats because of impaired
hepatic bioconversion of prednisone. No standardized
dosing regimen and tapering schedule exists for the use
of glucocorticoids in the management of feline bronchial asthma. Patients are typically started on therapy at
doses near or at the immunosuppressive range (1–2 mg/
kg PO q12h). Long‐term therapy with systemic glucocorticoids can be associated with numerous undesirable
effects such as polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, weight
gain, alopecia, thinning of the skin, increased susceptibility to infections, and the development of diabetes
mellitus. Systemic steroids can also exacerbate underlying cardiac disease. To minimize these complications,
the initial prednisolone dose is tapered by 25–50% once
clinical signs have resolved and after at least seven days
of therapy.
Inhaled glucocorticoids are associated with negligible
adverse effects compared to those seen with systemic
therapy and are a very effective means of managing
feline asthma long term. Inhaled steroids are minimally
absorbed into the systemic circulation and undergo
extensive first‐pass metabolism. Fluticasone propionate
is the most commonly prescribed inhaled glucocorticoid in veterinary medicine. It has the longest receptor
residency time and greatest lipophilicity of the inhaled
glucocorticoids as well as a high therapeutic index.
Treatment with inhaled fluticasone has been shown to
reduce airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness
in cats with naturally occurring lower airways disease
and in cats with experimentally induced asthma.
Suppression of the hypothalamic‐pituitary‐adrenocortical axis has been demonstrated in healthy cats following
treatment with inhaled glucocorticoids, but significant
suppression of the systemic immune response was not
noted. Fluticasone doses of 44 μg, 110 μg, and 220 μg
q12h were shown to reduce airway inflammation in
experimental models of feline asthma with similar efficacy. Fluticasone is available in a metered dose inhaler
formulation and can be administered to cats using a
chamber and facemask as with inhaled albuterol.
Systemic steroid therapy should be continued during
the first 14 days of treatment with fluticasone to allow
the inhaled glucocorticoid to reach full effect. The oral
glucocorticoid dose can then be gradually tapered and
eventually discontinued while inhalant therapy is continued long term. Inhaled budesonide (400 μg q12h) has
also been evaluated in asthmatic cats and has been
shown to reduce airway responsiveness while causing
suppression of the hypothalamic‐pituitary‐adrenal axis
in a subset of treated cats.

Methylxanthine bronchodilators can be used in
­conjunction with antiinflammatory therapy for chronic
management of refractory disease. Theophylline is the
methylxanthine derivative that has been studied most
extensively in cats. The mechanism by which methylxanthines induce bronchodilation is postulated to be
related to inhibition of phosphodiesterase, which leads
to increased intracellular cAMP and, subsequently,
smooth muscle relaxation. However, theophylline does
not inhibit phosphodiesterase at therapeutic concentrations. Inhibition of adenosine or interference with
intracellular calcium levels may instead explain the
­
bronchodilatory effects of these agents. Theophylline
also prevents mast cell degranulation, reduces microvascular leakage, and increases respiratory muscle
strength. When administered in the evening, sustained‐
release theophylline achieves higher peak plasma concentrations compared to morning administration. The
recommended dose of slow‐release preparations is
20–50 mg/kg PO q24h. Adverse effects associated with
methylxanthine derivatives include central nervous
­system stimulation, tachyarrhythmias, increased gastric
acid secretion, and diuresis. Because of this, methylxanthines should be used cautiously in patients with preexisting cardiac disease, seizure disorders, hyperthyroidism,
and gastric ulcers. Long‐acting bronchodilators such as
theophylline should be used adjunctively with steroid
therapy to achieve improved control of clinical signs in
patients that do not completely respond to glucocorticoid therapy alone.
Ciclosporin has been promoted for management of
feline asthma that is refractory to glucocorticoid and
bronchodilator therapy. A calcineurin inhibitor, ciclosporin inhibits T cell activation and proliferation by interfering with the transcription of genes related to cytokine
production, particularly IL‐2. In an experimental model
of feline asthma, treatment with ciclosporin prior to and
during chronic antigen challenge decreased the amount
of IL‐2 secreted from peripheral blood l­ymphocytes,
prevented an increase in airway hyperresponsiveness
­
after chronic antigen stimulation, and resulted in reduced
airway smooth muscle thickness and mucosal eosinophil
infiltration histologically compared to untreated cats.
Following acute antigen challenge in the same model,
pretreatment with ciclosporin did not prevent mast cell
degranulation or an increase in lung resistance. Despite
this, tracheal smooth muscle harvested from these artificially sensitized cats did not contract in response to antigen exposure when incubated with ciclosporin in vitro.
Given these differential findings, ciclosporin should be
reserved for patients with a poor response to standard
asthma therapies. An initial dose of 10 mg/kg PO q12h is
recommended with the goal of achieving blood trough
levels of 500–1000 ng/mL. Adverse effects associated

301

VetBooks.ir

302

Section 4 Respiratory Disease

with ciclosporin use in cats include anorexia and gastrointestinal upset. Nephrotoxicity and hepatotoxicity may
develop at high blood levels.
Antiserotonergics, antileukotrienes, and antihistamines have been investigated for use in feline asthma to
reduce airway inflammation while circumventing the
adverse effects associated with systemic glucocorticoid
therapy. Serotonin released during mast cell degranulation mediates airway smooth muscle contraction in cats.
Cyproheptadine, a serotonin receptor antagonist, has
been shown to attenuate constriction of airway smooth
muscle from antigen‐sensitized cats in vitro. In live cats
experimentally sensitized to aeroallergen, cyproheptadine did not uniformly diminish airway responsiveness,
degree of airway eosinophilic inflammation, plasma or
BAL fluid serotonin concentrations, or serum content of
allergen‐specific IgE following allergen challenge.
Similarly, cysteinyl leukotrienes are produced by mast
cells as well as eosinophils and contribute to many of the
pathophysiologic processes underlying asthma, including bronchoconstriction, smooth muscle proliferation,
mucus production, and inflammatory cell influx. The
leukotriene receptor antagonist zafirlukast was evaluated in an experimental model of feline asthma and was
demonstrated to have no effect on airway eosinophilia,
airway reactivity, or serum levels of allergen‐specific IgE
compared to placebo. In another study, urine concentrations of cysteinyl leukotrienes in allergen‐sensitized cats
did not increase after allergen challenge. These results
suggest that leukotrienes may not be a critical factor
in the generation of the feline asthmatic response.
Histamine plays a crucial role in inducing bronchoconstriction in human asthmatics, though its importance in
mediating the feline asthmatic response remains questionable. Cetirizine is a second‐generation histamine 1
receptor antagonist that has been evaluated in cats with
experimentally induced asthma and was shown to have
no effect on eosinophilic airway inflammation or plasma
histamine concentrations. Until additional studies are
conducted, pharmaceutical agents that inhibit serotonin,
leukotrienes, and histamine are not recommended as
monotherapy in the management of feline asthma.
Allergen‐specific immunotherapy holds promise as
the only potentially curative therapy for feline asthma.
This form of therapy, which is most commonly employed
in veterinary medicine in the management of atopic dermatitis, is proposed to alter the immune response so as
to reestablish tolerance to a specific allergen. In particular, rush immunotherapy (RIT) is a modified version of
allergen‐specific immunotherapy that involves subcutaneous administration of gradually increasing doses of a
specific antigen over an accelerated period of time, generally a couple of days or less. The immunomodulatory
effects of RIT are hypothesized to be related to production

of IgE‐blocking antibodies, induction of T cell
­unres­ponsiveness, shift from a T helper 2 to a T helper
1 cell response, elaboration of immunosuppressive
cytokines such as IL‐10 from T regulatory cells, and
decreased lymphocyte proliferation in response to allergen. In cats experimentally sensitized to Bermuda grass
allergen (BGA), RIT significantly decreased eosinophilic
airways inflammation, induced lymphocyte hyporesponsiveness to BGA, increased mRNA transcription of IL‐10
in BAL fluid, and decreased mRNA transcription of IL‐5
in BAL fluid. Adverse effects associated with RIT in this
model included localized swelling around the injection
site, increased heart and respiratory rate, hyperthermia,
vomiting, agitation, and systemic anaphylaxis noted in
one cat. These adverse effects were less severe when RIT
was adjuvanted with CpG oligodeoxynucleotides, immunostimulatory DNA sequences that induce a polarized
Th1 response. Intranasal administration of RIT has also
been evaluated in an experimental model of feline
asthma and was shown to be equally effective in reducing the degree of eosinophilic airway inflammation as
subcutaneously administered RIT, although subcutaneous RIT more consistently abolished the clinical signs
induced by aeroallergen challenge. Both antiinflammatory and immunomodulatory therapy may be necessary
in severely affected cats. When administered concurrently with RIT, oral glucocorticoid therapy has been
shown to dampen the long‐term effectiveness of RIT,
which may limit the benefits of RIT as monotherapy in
patients with severe disease.
The challenge in applying RIT to cats with naturally
occurring asthma lies in elucidating which antigen is
triggering the asthmatic response. Intradermal skin testing has been employed to identify the inciting antigens in
veterinary patients with atopic dermatitis. This method
has been shown to be highly sensitive in detecting a
known inciting antigen in cats artificially sensitized to a
specific allergen. Concurrently, detection of allergen‐
specific IgE in the serum of experimentally sensitized
cats was shown to be highly specific in identifying the
antigen used for sensitization. When evaluated in cats
with naturally occurring small airway disease, significantly more positive allergen reactions on serum IgE
testing and intradermal skin testing were noted compared to cats without airways disease, though the clinical
relevance of these allergens could not be determined.
Even though isolating the specific inciting antigen is the
ideal means of guiding immunotherapy, RIT using antigens that did not completely match those used to induce
the asthmatic phenotype in experimental feline models
was shown to reduce eosinophilic airways inflammation.
Immunotherapy is likely to play a prominent role in the
management of feline asthma in the future, but additional studies in patients with naturally occurring disease

VetBooks.ir

30 Feline Bronchial Asthma

are necessary before allergen‐specific immunotherapy
can be employed standardly in clinical practice.
Several novel therapies have been investigated using
cats with experimentally induced asthma and may be
applicable to the management of patients with naturally
occurring disease. Specifically, the antiinflammatory
effects of omega‐3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (ω3
PUFAs) extracted from New Zealand green‐lipped mussel have been evaluated in artificially sensitized cats.
Airway responsiveness but not eosinophilic inflammation decreased following treatment, suggesting that ω3
PUFAs may have some benefit as adjunctive therapy in
the management of feline asthma. Masitinib, a tyrosine
kinase inhibitor, has been demonstrated to reduce eosinophilic airway inflammation and improve respiratory
compliance in cats with experimental asthma and may
emerge as an effective treatment strategy for patients
with glucocorticoid intolerance or refractory disease.
Stem cell therapy has also been investigated as a means of
reducing airway remodeling, one of the hallmarks of
feline asthma. Administration of allogenic mesenchymal
stem cells to cats experimentally sensitized to a common
aeroallergen resulted in attenuation of changes consistent
with chronic lung remodeling based on computed tomography. Nebulized lidocaine has been evaluated in cats
with experimentally induced asthma and was shown to
reduce airway hyperresponsiveness without adverse
effects, indicating that it may be effective as palliative
therapy when used in combination with glucocorticoids.
Monitoring
Response to therapy is most effectively evaluated by
assessing clinical signs. Due to the intermittent nature of
clinical signs in some patients, overall improvement in
clinical condition should be judged after at least a few
weeks of therapy. Decreased frequency of episodes of
coughing and/or dyspnea is the expected outcome of successful treatment. A more objective assessment of clinical

improvement involves “cough counts” performed by
owners at home prior to and after starting therapy. Due to
permanent airway remodeling, radiographic manifestations of asthma may not change significantly with treatment, limiting the use of repeated thoracic radiography to
monitor response to therapy. The exception is radiographic evidence of atelectasis of the right middle lung
lobe, which is expected to resolve with antiinflammatory
and mucolytic therapy. The limited availability of pulmonary function testing prohibits its practical application as
a means of assessing response to treatment, but it may
prove useful for this purpose in the future.

­Prognosis
Most asthmatic patients that receive appropriate treatment demonstrate a favorable response with a good
long‐term prognosis. However, continuing antiinflammatory therapy for life is crucial to prevent further permanent airway remodeling unless the inciting allergen
can be identified and exposure prevented. Severe, refractory forms of feline asthma do exist and can present
management challenges. Moreover, even patients with
apparently well‐controlled asthma are at risk for potentially life‐threatening episodes of severe, acute bronchoconstriction. The adverse effects associated with
systemic glucocorticoid therapy can complicate prognosis and lead to the development of life‐limiting complications, including congestive heart failure and diabetes
mellitus. Long‐term treatment can be further impaired
by patients that will not tolerate oral administration of
medications or placement of the facemask required for
administration of inhalant therapy. In addition, the
expense associated with inhaled medications may prevent their use in some patients. Despite these challenges,
feline asthma is a readily manageable condition, and successful treatment can prevent acute death and significantly improve quality of life in the majority of patients.

Canine Chronic Bronchitis
Kevin Kumrow, DVM, DACVIM (SAIM)
Orchard Park Veterinary Medical Center, Orchard, Park, NY, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology

­History and Clinical Signs

Canine chronic bronchitis (CCB) is the most common
cause of a chronic cough. It is characterized by a cough
that is present for at least two months, inflammation in
the airways, and a lack of an identified underlying disease that may cause a cough. There is some evidence that
environmental pollutants, second‐hand smoke or other
inhaled noxious chemicals may be contributors to the
etiology. A specific role of bacteria in CCB has not been
established. The diagnosis of CCB is largely through
exclusion, and treatment is based on a patient’s clinical
history, diagnostic results and response to therapy.
Canine chronic bronchitis airway inflammation is neutrophilic, and there is an increase in the production of
mucus. The inflammatory response perpetuates the
coughing cycle, which in turn stimulates continued
inflammation. This positive feedback sets up a vicious
cycle that ultimately leads to permanent changes in the
airways, including hyperplasia of mucous glands and goblet cells, hypertrophy of smooth muscle, and fibrosis of the
lamina propria. These changes are often accompanied by
obstruction of small airways and airway collapse. Some
cases of chronic bronchitis can progress to permanent
dilation of the bronchi and destruction of the structural
integrity of the bronchial walls. This condition is known
as bronchiectasis. Cocker spaniels have an increased risk
of bronchiectasis. Left unidentified and untreated, the
aforementioned changes to the airway can contribute to
a progressive decline in lung function. Box 31.1 gives a list
of many of the common differentials for CCB.

The history and clinical signs of patients with CCB are
similar to those presenting for collapsing trachea and
mitral valve insufficiency. Patients with collapsing trachea
have a chronic cough associated with narrowing of the airway combined with chronic tracheal inflammation, and a
perpetual dry honking cough. Mitral valve insufficiency
can lead to enlargement of the left atrium and subsequent
compression of the mainstem bronchi that stimulates a
chronic coughing reflex. CCB is less commonly diagnosed
in large‐breed dogs. Exhaustive consideration of alternative causes of a chronic cough in these patients should
occur. For example, a Doberman with a history of cough
should be thoroughly evaluated for dilated cardiomyopathy, and heart failure should be suspected until proven
otherwise. A 12‐year‐old Labrador with a history of cough
should be evaluated for laryngeal paralysis with intermittent aspiration pneumonia or pulmonary metastatic
­disease. It is imperative that the clinician be astute in differentiating between the potential causes of chronic cough
as a misdiagnosis could result in inappropriate treatment
and a worsening of the patient’s condition.
A thorough history can assist in the differentiation of
CCB from other causes of chronic cough. Patients that
have had exposure to other dogs in any setting for any
period of time should be suspect for canine infectious
respiratory disease (CIRD). Commonly, exposure occurs
at a groomer, boarding facility, doggie day‐care, or dog
park, or via a visiting family pet or a new puppy in the
household; however, any known interaction, even limited, should raise suspicion. These patients can be any
age or breed, and can have clinical signs that range from
a mild dry‐hacking cough to systemic illness. Pets with
evidence of systemic disease that have a history of cough
are unlikely to have CCB as their primary ailment, and

­Epidemiology
The most common signalment for CCB is middle‐aged
to older, small‐breed dogs.

lethargy, and other behavior changes could lead to the
detection of a systemic illness. A clinical history should
also include questions that discuss potential exposure to
passive (second‐hand) smoke, the presence of excessive
environmental odors/perfumes, and prior prescriptions
or home remedies and their clinical effect on the cough.
Physical examination of most patients with CCB is relatively unremarkable. Patients tend to be systemically well,
with the only major clinical sign being coughing. Patients
are often seen due to an acute exacerbation in their coughing secondary to exposure to environmental irritants or
allergens, secondary development of a bacterial infection,
or the unveiling of an unrelated concurrent disease. Some
dogs will present with tachypnea or increased expiratory
effort (labored breathing). Physical examination should
focus on the cardiopulmonary system and signs of systemic illness (weight loss or gain, anorexia, lethargy, etc.).
Careful auscultation of the lungs can provide clues to lower
airway disease, and the presence or absence of a murmur
should be noted. Although heart disease and CCB can co‐
exist, the presence of a sinus arrhythmia supports the airway/pulmonary system as the primary cause of coughing.
Sometimes a cough can be elicited with palpation of
the trachea due to nonspecific inflammation of the airways. This may assist with characterization of the cough
by the clinician and exclude other conditions such as
