Arterial Blood Gas Analysis
Arterial blood gas analysis is paramount in patients with
pulmonary dysfunction, as it will provide rapid identification of hypoxemia, hypoventilation, and respiratory
failure. When arterial access is unobtainable, central
venous (ScvO2) or mixed venous (SvO2) oxygen saturation as well as venous CO2 (PvCO2) can be extrapolated
to evaluate respiratory function. Normally, ScvO2 is
10–15% higher than SvO2 but in states of circulatory
shock or failure, these two measurements closely parallel
one another. The normal arterial‐venous gradient for
PCO2 is 4–6 mmHg, but it may approach 10 mmHg in
some patients. This allows for serial ventilatory monitoring via venous blood sampling.

­Postoperative Management
Intense postoperative management following thoracic
surgery comprises adequate analgesia, appropriate
thoracostomy tube care, intravenous fluid therapy, and
intensive nursing care. Supplemental oxygen therapy is
often implemented in the immediate postoperative
period and occasionally continued mechanical ventilation is required.
Analgesia
Optimal analgesic protocols are critical for the postthoracotomy patient to prevent secondary hypoxemia,
hypoventilation, and cardiac arrhythmias. Multimodal
analgesia is preferred to avoid noxious effects of single‐
agent protocols. Combination therapy of systemic analgesics allows for synergistic analgesia and lower dosing
of each chosen drug. Local analgesia including intercostal nerve blocks, incisional diffusion catheters, and
intrapleural infusion of local anesthetics via the thoracostomy tube provides effective adjunctive analgesia.
Intercostal nerve blocks can provide very effective analgesia when utilized for lateral thoracotomy. It is recommended to perform the procedure at the intercostal
space of the incision, one space cranial and one space
caudal to the incision. As discussed later, much of the
postoperative pain seems to be associated with large‐
bore thoracostomy tubes.
Thoracostomy Tube Management and Pleural
Drainage
Thoracostomy tubes generally remain in place
for 12–24 hours post thoracotomy in patients
without ongoing pleural space disease, but certain
­

­circumstances may necessitate maintenance beyond
this ­
timeframe due to continual effusion, residual
pneumothorax, and for therapeutic lavage or delivery
of chemotherapeutics. Pleural drainage may be passive
or active, but active drainage is more commonly implemented in veterinary patients. The normal transpulmonary pressure is 4–8 mmHg, which is equivocal to
5–10 mL of suction in a syringe. Intrapleural infusion,
via the thoracostomy tube, of lidocaine and bupivacaine (1.0 mg/kg each) provides local analgesia following intermittent suction and may be performed
every 4–6 hours. The rationale behind using both lidocaine and bupivacaine is that the lidocaine provides
immediate relief and allows for a more comfortable
infusion of the longer‐acting bupivacaine. This method
of analgesia delivery has been investigated and deemed
safe in patients following pericardectomy.
Intermittent active suction is applied often postoperatively, but continuous active suction may be necessary
for larger volumes of air or effusion which compromise
ventilation. The pleural space in small animals can
accommodate approximately 100–140 mL/kg of fluid or
air. Beyond this volume, continuous pneumothorax or
hydrothorax (usually hemothorax) should be suspected.
Obstruction of the thoracostomy tube may rarely occur,
depending on tube diameter and viscosity of the thoracic
effusion. The Mac technique consists of turning the
thoracostomy tube 180° in each direction and observing
whether the tube returns to the prior position. This
method can be used to evaluate kinking of the tube when
persistent negative pressure is observed despite evidence
of significant pleural effusion or pneumothorax. If the
tube consistently spins back into the initial position, tube
kinking should be suspected.
The thoracostomy tube itself will induce approximately 2.0 mL/kg/day of pleural effusion. Once the volume of pleural effusion drops below this value, removal
of the thoracostomy tube may be considered. Ideally,
consistent negative pressure should be observed for 24
hours following pneumothorax prior to thoracostomy
tube removal.
Fluid Therapy
Fluid therapy is a mainstay of postthoracotomy therapy.
Most postoperative patients will require, at minimum,
maintenance fluid therapy, as they may be unwilling to
drink following surgery. Of further importance, continual
fluid losses via the thoracostomy tube should be
accounted for, and at least a percentage of this loss should
be replaced with IV fluids to avoid hypovolemia due to
third spacing. Postthoracotomy patients may experience
significant protein loss with pleural effusion. The ideal

VetBooks.ir

33 Surgical Approaches to Thoracic Disease

therapy for protein replacement in critically ill patients is
to provide enteral nutrition in order for the patient to
synthesize albumin.
Oxygen Therapy
Oxygen therapy may be provided intermittently via facemask or continuously by nasopharyngeal insufflation,
nasal prongs, oxygen cage, or intubation and mechanical
ventilation. Provision of intermittent supplemental oxygen at an FiO2 of 50–60% can be achieved via facemask
with oxygen flow rates of 8.0–12.0 L/min. Nasopharyngeal
insufflation or nasal prongs may be utilized with oxygen
flow rates of 50–150 mL/kg/min to achieve an FiO2 of
30–70%. More commonly, postoperative thoracotomy
patients are maintained in an oxygen cage with flow rates
of 0.5–1.0 L/min to maintain a FiO2 of 40–60%. Patients
requiring an FiO2 above 60% to maintain normoxemia
will likely require intubation and mechanical ventilation.
Caution must be exercised to avoid oxygen toxicity when
supplemental oxygen levels are maintained above 60%
for more than 24 hours.
When mechanical ventilation is utilized, PEEP ventilation can be beneficial to prevent atelectasis and
augment work of breathing. In contrast to the spontaneously breathing patient, permissive hypercapnia is
tolerated in mechanically ventilated postthoracotomy
patients. Arterial PCO2 may rise to 50 mmHg before
intervention is necessary, as long as normoxemia is
maintained. Proper humidification is an important
component of oxygen therapy for preservation of
proper mucociliary function and clearance of respiratory secretions.
Dyspnea
Dyspnea is the perceived feeling of breathlessness. The
pathophysiology of dyspnea is multifactorial and is
described elsewhere. Multiple therapeutic targets have
been investigated to decrease the perception of dyspnea
in human patients. In human studies, nebulized or aerosolized furosemide has been found to prevent bronchoconstriction and inhibit the cough reflex in addition to
reducing pulmonary vascular hydrostatic pressure and
edema when absorbed systemically. Furosemide has
been shown experimentally and clinically in people to
reduce bronchial slow‐acting receptors (SARs), thereby
reducing the sensation of dyspnea. Furosemide exerts a
diuretic effect when administered by the enteral or parenteral route via inhibition of the Na:K:2Cl co‐transporter within the thick ascending loop of Henle. A
similar mechanism is postulated for the antidyspneic
effect of nebulized furosemide causing a local increase in

sodium ion concentration within the airways, increasing
pulmonary stretch receptor activity.
Hypothermia
Hypothermia is an inevitable occurrence during and
immediately following thoracic surgery. Warming IV
fluids prior to administration can help diminish
large reductions in intraoperative body temperature.
Postoperative temperature monitoring, either intermittent or continuous, is recommended to ensure euthermia and active warming using warming blankets or
heat lamps should be performed until the patient’s temperature has reached 99.5 °F.
Arrhythmias
For hemodynamically significant, multifocal, sustained, or R‐on‐T phenomena ventricular arrhythmias,
lidocaine remains the mainstay therapy. Lidocaine may
also be useful to slow the heart rate, allowing differentiation of ventricular tachycardia from sinus tachycardia with bundle branch block. The waveform of the
latter often will not change following lidocaine bolus
(2.0 mg/kg IV), but P‐waves may be appreciable once
the heart rate has decelerated. For lidocaine‐responsive arrhythmias, a constant rate infusion of 60–80 μg/
kg/min may be implemented postoperatively. A beta‐
blocker may also be ­considered for patients that do not
have known underlying cardiac disease with compromised contractility. Anecdotally, sotalol 2.0 mg/kg PO
BID has favorable postoperative antiarrhythmic
­properties for patients with supraventricular and ventricular tachyarrhythmias.
Nursing Care
Nursing care is a critical yet often underemphasized
aspect of postthoracotomy care. Patients undergoing
median sternotomy often prefer lateral recumbency in
the immediate postoperative period due to incisional
pain. Turning or rotating the patient every 4–6 hours
prevents atelectasis and V–Q mismatching secondary to
gravitational forces in lateral recumbency. Turning the
patient also promotes patient comfort and hygiene.
Optimal analgesia aids in patient well‐being and may
promote tolerance of sternal recumbency and therefore
improved oxygenation and ventilation.
Complications
Complications post thoracotomy may include edema
formation, hypoproteinemia, continual pleural effusion,

329

VetBooks.ir

330

Section 4 Respiratory Disease

secondary infection, hemorrhage, residual or continuous
pneumothorax, seroma formation, sternal osteomyelitis,
pyrexia, iatrogenic chylothorax, fibrosing pleuritis, surgical dehiscence, and ipsilateral thoracic limb lameness
(lateral thoracotomy). Crystalloid fluid therapy, anorexia, vasculitis, and postoperative inflammation can
contribute to peripheral edema formation.
The most common complication involving the thoracostomy tube is improper placement. Insufficient subcutaneous tunnel formation with large‐bore thoracostomy
tubes can lead to continuous air leakage and pneumothorax. The thoracostomy tube percutaneous insertion
site should be inspected carefully when continuous
pneumothorax is observed. Continual pleural effusion
may be primary or secondary in origin, depending on the
etiology requiring thoracotomy. Pyothorax, chylothorax,
and neoplastic effusion represent sources of continual
pleural effusion during the postoperative period. Pleural
drainage is important to maintain proper ventilatory
function as well as oxygenation. However, excessive
pleural effusion can lead to significant systemic protein
and fluid loss with subsequent intravascular volume
depletion. Vasculitis and surgical inflammation are contributors to this protein‐losing pleuropathy and third
spacing, which may encourage perpetual effusion.
Resolution of the underlying disease process will likely
terminate the cause of effusion.
Infection is an undesirable complication in any postoperative patient. Preoperative infection may be present
in some patients, such as pyothoraces, in which septic
effusion necessitated surgical intervention. Continual
monitoring of thoracic fluid cytology and cell counts aids
in determining resolution of pyothorax. Responsible
antimicrobial administration is of paramount importance in the care of critically ill patients. A full discussion
on this topic can be found elsewhere. Generally speaking, clinicians should be familiar with antibiotic sensitivity patterns of common bacterial isolates from their
hospitals and deescalate coverage to single‐agent therapy
as soon as possible. Infection may be introduced intrathoracically via the thoracostomy tube or surgical incision.
This may be due to bacterial contamination associated
with prolonged surgical exposure, improper handling of
the thoracostomy tube, or bacterial invasion of the thoracostomy tube insertion site and/or surgical incision.
Appropriate samples should be obtained for bacterial
culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing when
­
infection is suspected. ­
Proper intraoperative hemostasis ensures minimal
postoperative hemorrhage, therefore significant
hemorrhagic pleural effusion is not expected in the
­

­postthoracotomy patient. Serosanguinous pleural effusion (PCV <25% of peripheral PCV) is a common and
expected occurrence with an indwelling thoracostomy
tube(s). However, hemothorax is diagnosed when the
pleural PCV exceeds peripheral PCV by 25% and warrants immediate investigation. When the volume of thoracic hemorrhage exceeds 10 mL/kg, autotransfusion
should be considered.
Proper postoperative incisional care can reduce
patient discomfort and surgical inflammation while
minimizing risk of infection. During the initial postoperative period, the thoracotomy incision as well as
thoracostomy tube insertion site(s) should be covered
with an impermeate adhesive dressing. This provides a
seal preventing air leakage with resultant pneumothorax while protecting against environmental contamination. Cold and warm compresses following surgery can
reduce incisional pain, swelling, and inflammation.
Cold compresses are usually applied during the immediate postthoracotomy period for 24–48 hours, with
warm compresses used thereafter.
An elevation in body temperature above normal in any
postoperative patient warrants immediate concern and
investigation. Hyperthermia may be secondary to
decreased heat dissipation (inability to pant due to pain,
excessive cage bedding), pharmacologic (mu opioid use
in cats), or pain induced. Postthoracotomy pyrexia may
be observed with infection, inflammation, or neoplasia.
Indwelling catheter sites should be inspected for
hyperemia, warmth or discomfort upon palpation.
Thoracostomy tube insertion sites should also be interrogated in a similar fashion. Complete blood count and
thoracic radiographs may also be considered when an
obvious etiology of pyrexia cannot be determined from
physical examination.
Surgical reexploration is rarely necessary following
thoracotomy, but is required for continuous pneumothoraces or hemothoraces that do not respond to medical management. Pneumothoraces, which fail to seal
despite continuous active suction, are an indication for
prompt reexploration to evaluate the pulmonary parenchyma (bullae or pneumatocele rupture) and previous
surgical sites (complete or partial lobectomy). Chronic
pleural effusion, despite prior thoracotomy, may also
necessitate a second surgery due to fibrosing pleuritis
or restrictive fibrin plaque formation on the surface of
the visceral pleura of the lung. Decortication may be
necessary if ­significant inelastic fibrin plaque formation has occurred restricting lung expansion. For perpetual pleural effusion, pleurodesis may also be
considered.

34
Pleural Effusion
Ashley Allen, DVM, DACVECC and Gareth Buckley, MA, VetMB, MRCVS, DACVECC
College of Veterinary Medicine, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA

Pleural effusion is the pathologic collection of fluid within
the pleural space resulting from one of three primary
mechanisms: disruption of pleural pressure homeostasis,
diminished lymphatic drainage, or increased mesothelial
and capillary endothelial permeability. Given the dynamic
state of the pleural space, overlap can occur between the
mechanisms of effusion, depending on the underlying
disease. Dogs and cats with pleural effusion present with
various clinical signs including lethargy, hyporexia,
tachypnea, dyspnea, and a paradoxical breathing pattern,
regardless of precipitating cause. History and physical
examination may help to formulate a differential diagnosis for pleural effusion, but ultimately collecting a sample
of the effusion for cytologic analysis and additional tests
provides the most important information to obtain an
accurate diagnosis. Treatment options and prognosis are
dependent on the underlying cause of pleural effusion.

­Anatomy and Physiology
The pleura lines the thoracic cavity and is a thin, serous
membrane with five layers: an outer fibroelastic layer, an
extensively vascularized subpleural loose connective tissue layer, an elastic superficial tissue layer, a loose connective submesothelial tissue layer, and a mesothelial
layer. The visceral pleura line the lungs, whereas the parietal pleura line the thoracic wall with the potential space
between the two known as the pleural space. The visceral
pleura functions to provide mechanical lung support,
limit lung expansion, and contribute to elastic recoil and
deflation of the lung. The parietal pleura is subdivided
into the costal, mediastinal, and diaphragmatic parietal
pleura and contains numerous lymphatic vessels that
form stomas between mesothelial cells for lymphatic
drainage. Lacunae are dilated lymphatic vessels in the
submesothelial parietal pleura where stomas form and

transport fluid back through the lymphatic system.
Compared to other species, dogs and cats have a thin
pleural surface, approximately 15 μm thick. The mediastinum divides the pleural space into a right and left
pleural cavity, although in dogs and cats the mediastinum
may not be complete, allowing for bilateral disease from
a unilateral origin. The highly metabolically and immunologically active multipotent mesothelial cells line the
entire pleural cavity and play an active role in pleural
fluid production and reabsorption. Sialomucins are negatively charged glycoconjugates which coat the free mesothelial surface, functioning to repel opposing membranes
as well as organisms, abnormal cells, and particles.
In healthy animals, a small volume of fluid is present in
the pleural space which facilitates smooth gliding of the
lung over the thoracic wall and transmission of forces
during normal respirations. Normal pleural fluid is low in
protein (<1.5 g/dL) and cellular content (1500–2500
cells/μL), consisting of mesothelial cells (9–30%), monocytes (61–77%), lymphocytes (7–11%), and neutrophils
(<2%). Healthy dogs and cats produce approximately
0.01–0.02 mL/kg/h of pleural fluid via microvascular filtration from pleural capillaries. Fluid crosses the pleural
capillary endothelium followed by the interstitium.
Pleural capillary endothelium imparts most of the resistance to flow; however, the resistive properties of the
endothelium and interstitium are additive, which
becomes significant during some disease processes that
interfere with the resistive properties of these layers. The
production and reabsorption of pleural fluid are multifactorial, dependent on Starling forces, solute flux, hydraulic
conductivity (the resistive properties of the two pleural
surfaces), total surface area, the solute reflection coefficient (ability of the surface to restrict larger molecules),
membrane diffusive permeability, pleural lymphatic
drainage via stomata in the parietal pleura, and cellular
mechanisms of transport by mesothelial cells (Table 34.1).

Normal pleural pressure is approximately –3 to
–5 cmH2O at functional residual capacity, becomes
greater (more negative) with deeper breaths, and is more
negative in the dorsal space compared to the ventral
space, decreasing by 0.5–0.7 cmH2O/cm in dogs. This
subatmospheric pleural pressure results from elastic
recoil forces of the lung exerting a force inward with the
propensity of the chest wall to expand outward and
serves to maintain lung inflation while decreasing the
work of breathing. Although reported as a single number, pleural pressure is a result of the dynamic nature of
the pleural space and represents a summation of the
pressure exerted by pleural fluid, regional pleural surface
deformation, and weight of the lung in dependent areas
of the thoracic cavity.

­Pathophysiology of Pleural Fluid
Accumulation
Pleural fluid volume depends on Starling forces, mesothelial cell activity, and lymphatic drainage; however, the
exact contribution of each of these mechanisms remains
somewhat elusive and varies during disease processes.
Starling forces which favor the formation of pleural
fluid include increased capillary hydrostatic pressure,
decreased capillary oncotic pressure, and increased capillary permeability. Mesothelial cells have apical microvilli that increase the surface area for exchange and
vesicles that allow for transcytosis of proteins from the
pleural space to the pleural interstitium. In addition,
indirect evidence suggests mesothelial cells are involved
in solute‐coupled liquid transport across the pleural surface. Lymphatics communicate directly with the pleural
cavity through openings between the mesothelial layer in
the parietal pleura, called stomas, and allow cells, ­protein,

and larger particles to be absorbed into the lymphatic
system through channels called lacunae. The maximal
reabsorption rate through pleural lymphatics is estimated to be 0.2–0.3 mL/kg/h, which is considerably
more than the normal daily rate of fluid accumulation.
Therefore, the accumulation of pleural fluid occurs when
the disease process overwhelms fluid reabsorption
capacity, reduces the ability of lymphatics to reabsorb
fluid, or increases production of fluid while simultaneously decreasing lymphatic clearance.
Pathologic fluid effusions are classified in two broad
categories: transudates and exudates. Transudative effusions typically accumulate secondary to an increase in
hydrostatic pressure or a reduction in plasma oncotic
pressure while the pleura remains normal, whereas exudative effusions typically accumulate secondary to various pleural pathologic conditions leading to increased
vascular permeability and/or diminished lymphatic fluid
reabsorption. Mesothelial cells play a pivotal role in the
development of exudative effusions by synthesizing
inflammatory cytokines, growth factors, and extracellular proteins. A classic example of increased systemic
venous hydrostatic pressure leading to a transudative
effusion is congestive heart failure. In addition, pulmonary thromboembolism, cardiac tamponade, heartworm
disease, and neoplasia can all lead to increased venous
hydrostatic pressure and therefore transudative pleural
effusion. In comparison, a classic example of an exudative effusion is pyothorax with an influx of inflammatory
cells, which can increase vascular permeability and
decreased lymphatic drainage (Table 34.2).
Regional changes in pleural pressure occur with the
accumulation of pleural effusion and the mechanism of
pressure change is controversial. Proposed theories to
explain the pressure difference center around the hydrostatic pressure contribution of a column of fluid in the
thorax and the changes in deformation forces as the lung
and thoracic wall become separated by fluid. The hydrostatic theory divides the pleural space into three distinct
pressure zones: the upper (dorsal) zone, middle zone,
and lower (ventral) zone. In the upper (dorsal) zone, the
pleural liquid thickness is normal and the pleural liquid
pressure is less than the pleural surface pressure. In the
middle zone, the pleural liquid thickness increases and
pleural liquid pressure equalizes with pleural surface
pressure at zero. In the lower (ventral) zone, the pleural
fluid thickness increases substantially and the pressure
becomes positive, displacing the lung from the thoracic
wall. In the other predominant theory, the pleural liquid
pressure is always equal to pleural surface pressure such
that pressure gradients caused by gravity and regional
differences in pleural surface pressure drive a small
­viscous flow of fluid in the normal pleural space and
surfaces are never in contact. As pleural effusion

Measuring pleural liquid pressure and pleural surface
can be challenging because the space is small and the
insertion of any device will cause an artifact by deforming
the surface. In the diseased thorax with an appreciable
amount of pleural effusion, these challenges become less
significant and pleural pressure measured is an accurate
representation of hydrostatic pressure at the level of the
catheter or transducer. During thoracocentesis or if an
indwelling thoracostomy tube is in place, pleural ­pressure
can be monitored in veterinary patients with a minimal
amount of equipment using a water manometer or pressure transducer. If using a pressure transducer, measurements are recorded in mmHg and should be converted to
be interpreted appropriately (1 mmHg = 1.36 cmH2O).
Pleural pressure monitoring may be beneficial with
chronic effusions when draining the effusion does not
necessarily equate to return to normal pleural physiology
because the pleural surface remains diseased. If the lungs
cannot expand appropriately after thoracocentesis, creating a situation of entrapped lung, the s­upraphysiologic
negative pressure created in the pleural cavity by removing the fluid may increase the risk of pneumothorax.

­Clinical Signs and Physical
Examination
Rapid intervention with minimal patient stress is paramount in patients with respiratory distress so it is important to be familiar with clinical signs and physical
examination findings indicative of certain disease processes. Time of onset, volume of fluid accumulation, and
inciting cause of pleural effusion all contribute to the
patient’s history and clinical signs.
Pleural effusion is a consequence of an underlying disease and vague historical clinical signs are often reported
including lethargy, exercise intolerance, weight loss, and
hyporexia or anorexia. In a retrospective study, tachypnea and dyspnea were the most commonly reported
complaints by owners, present in 95% of dogs with pleural effusion. Additional complaints, which may or may
not be an indication of the underlying disease, include
cough, polydipsia, vomiting, fever, collapse, diarrhea,
restlessness, reluctance to lie down, cervical extension,
hemoptysis, abdominal distension, melena, hematemesis, and halitosis. Severe pleural effusion may present as
open mouth breathing and cyanosis, especially if onset
is acute.
On physical examination, a restrictive breathing
­pattern seen as rapid and shallow breathing has historically been reported but recent literature suggests an
asynchronous (paradoxical) or inverse breathing
­pattern and decreased lung sounds on auscultation are
more common clinical findings in dogs and cats.
Paradoxical breathing refers to increased inspiratory
effort strong enough to pull the abdominal contents
toward the thorax, leading to a sunken flank appearance during inspiration and a bulging flank appearance
on expiration. Additional physical examination findings include muffled heart sounds, decreased ventral
lung sounds, shallow breathing, and inspiratory dyspnea. Patients with cardiac disease, such as heart failure,
pericardial effusion, or caval syndrome, may have a
murmur or crackles on thoracic auscultation, jugular
pulses, a positive hepatojugular reflex, and/or pulse
deficits. Patients with a coagulopathy causing pleural
effusion, such as anticoagulant rodenticide toxicity,
may have bruising, pale mucous membranes, weak
pulses, or tachycardia on physical examination. Masses
found on abdominal palpation, oral or dermatologic
examination may indicate a neoplastic cause for pleural
effusion. Mediastinal neoplasia should be suspected
with an incompressible cranial thorax in cats or Horner
syndrome in cats or dogs. Pain in the right cranial
abdominal quadrant with gastrointestinal signs may be
suggestive of pancreatitis as an underlying cause of
pleural effusion (Table 34.3).

­Diagnostics
Patient presentation, stability, and available resources
will often guide the diagnostic approach in patients with
pleural effusion. The cyanotic cat with open mouth
breathing will have a different initial diagnostic and
treatment plan from a dog presenting for vomiting or
diarrhea with scant pleural effusion found during routine testing for underlying gastrointestinal disease.
Regardless of the underlying pathology, the goal should
be patient stabilization first followed by a thorough
investigation into the inciting cause of pleural effusion
using imaging techniques, pleural fluid tests, and, if necessary, histopathology.
Imaging
Ultrasonography, radiography, and computed tomography (CT) are currently available imaging techniques in
dogs and cats with pleural effusion. In general, the
patient requiring emergent treatment for respiratory distress due to pleural effusion is likely to have an ultrasound in the emergency department initially followed by
thoracocentesis prior to the pursuit of additional imaging techniques whereas a stable patient will likely have
thoracic radiographs with or without a thoracic ultrasound followed by advanced imaging if necessary.
Although the name implies a single subset of patients,
which benefit from the test, the thoracic focused assessment with sonography for trauma (TFAST) is the most
common initial test in an emergency situation due to
pleural space disease because it allows for rapid assessment of the thoracic cavity with a therapeutic goal.
TFAST is performed with the patient in sternal or right
lateral recumbency and assessing five areas of the thoracic cavity: the right and left chest tube site (dorsolateral 7th–9th intercostal spaces), right and left pericardial
site (ventrolateral 5th–6th intercostal space), and the
diaphragmatico‐hepatic (subxiphoid) site. Pleural
­effusion is recognized as anechoic or echogenic fluid in
the pleural space and its presence may allow better
­visualization of some mediastinal masses. In people, the

diaphragmatico‐hepatic site is the most sensitive and
specific area to diagnose pleural effusion because it has
less air interface than the pericardial sites; however, with
breed conformation and size variation of veterinary
patients, this has yet to be prospectively evaluated.
Thoracic ultrasound is useful for the detection, characterization, and subjective quantification (by depth) of
pleural fluid, in addition to guiding therapeutic intervention. Abdominal ultrasound and echocardiogram may
also help determine the cause of pleural effusion.
Thoracic radiographs are useful to evaluate for the
presence of pleural effusion and survey the thoracic cavity for an underlying etiology. Radiographic signs of
pleural effusion include retraction of the lung margins
from the thoracic wall and sternum with increased
­opacity in the pleural space, widened interlobar fissures,
rounding of lung margins, pleural thickening, and
obscuring of the diaphragm and cardiac silhouette by
radiopaque fluid. Pleural fluid will often obscure structures in the thoracic cavity, including the heart, mediastinum, and diaphragm; therefore, in patients with
significant pleural effusion it is advantageous to perform
thoracocentesis, ideally ultrasound guided, prior to radiographs to allow better evaluation of intrathoracic structures. Since the pleura cannot normally be seen on
radiographs, if pleural lines are seen, horizontal beam
radiographs, in addition to the standard three‐view
series, may help differentiate pleural thickening from
pleural effusion because vertical beam projections are
limited by superimposition of fluid and soft tissue structures. In addition, more pleural effusion is present than
predicted based on vertical beam (standard‐view) radiographs because large fluid pockets are not struck head‐
on by the X‐ray beam; however, a horizontal beam allows
fluid to collect ventrally such that the X‐ray beam strikes
the fluid–lung interface tangentially. However, ultrasound remains the most sensitive test for detection of
small amounts of fluid.
Thoracic CT has become increasingly available in
­veterinary practice; CT allows better lesion delineation
and characterization than conventional radiography
for many thoracic disorders. Prior to thoracic CT,

VetBooks.ir

34 Pleural Effusion

­thoracocentesis should be performed to remove as much
fluid as possible to enhance visualization of intrathoracic
and extrathoracic structures. Patients are maintained in
dorsal or ventral recumbency, manually hyperventilated
immediately preceding the helical scan to decrease respiratory drive during a forced breath hold, and the entire
thorax is acquired using a slice collimation of 3–7 mm,
depending on patient size. During a single inspiratory
hold not exceeding one minute, the entire thorax is
scanned which determines the slice thickness of the
images, reserving the ability to make thinner slices of
areas of pathologic importance if needed. Both ultrasound and conventional radiographs are poorly sensitive
to determine vascular invasion, displacement of normal
anatomic structures, or invasion of adjacent structures
by mediastinal masses; however, CT enhances the ability
to determine the aggressiveness of the tumor prior to
surgical exploration. Regarding chylothorax, CT may be
superior to traditional radiographic lymphangiography
to show contrast enhancement of the thoracic duct.
Thoracic CT may also be indicated in dogs and cats with
pyothorax not responding to conventional management
or if a pleural or pulmonary foreign body or abscess is
suspected because this imaging technique eliminates
superimposition and silhouetting of intrathoracic structures. Pleural abscesses on CT often appear as ring‐
enhancing cystic structures with a fluid‐attenuating
core. Additional benefits of thoracic CT include identifying pleural thickness, small‐volume pneumothorax,
parenchymal lung masses, and peripheral bronchopleural fistulae.
Pleural Fluid Evaluation
Thoracocentesis is therapeutic and has the potential to
be diagnostic in any dog or cat with pleural effusion. In
the emergent respiratory patient, thoracocentesis should
be the first step after pleural effusion has been confirmed
by TFAST with a goal to remove as much fluid as possible, the exception being the coagulopathic patient. There
are no absolute contraindications to perform thoracocentesis but in coagulopathic patients, extreme caution
should be used if thoracocentesis is necessary and should
be reserved for patients in moderate to severe respiratory distress. In the absence of ultrasound availability,
thoracocentesis can be carefully performed in a dyspneic
patient prior to radiographs. The small risk associated
with thoracocentesis is outweighed by the major risk of
prolonged restraint for radiographs of a patient in severe
respiratory distress. Unilateral or bilateral thoracocentesis may be needed and is ideally performed with ultrasound guidance.
Gross appearance of aseptically collected pleural fluid
should be recorded, as well as protein content and

­cytologic characteristics. Samples should also be saved
in ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA, lavender
top), serum (red top) tubes, sterile tubes for culture, and/
or other tubes for effusion‐specific tests such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Information gained from
protein content and cellularity may help guide future
diagnostics or treatment. Gram stain should be performed if pyothorax is suspected on preliminary diagnostics to guide antimicrobial therapy while cultures are
pending. Sterile samples can be stored for bacterial,
f­ ungal, and/or Mycoplasma culture followed by antimicrobial susceptibility. Fluids are typically divided into
three categories based on protein content and nucleated
cell count: transudate, modified transudate, and exudate.
Subcategories of exudative effusions include hemorrhage, bile, chyle, septic and aseptic (Table 34.4).
Pure transudates are low in protein (<2.5 g/dL) and
total nucleated cell count (<1500 cells/μL) with a clear,
colorless, or straw‐colored appearance. Cytologic examination shows predominantly mononuclear cells such as
lymphocytes, macrophages, and mesothelial cells with
low to absent numbers of nondegenerate neutrophils.
Transudative pleural effusion is a consequence of either
increased hydrostatic or decreased oncotic pressure.
Liver disease, protein‐losing enteropathies and nephropathies, malnutrition, maldigestion, and malabsorption can
cause profound hypoalbuminemia with or without hypoglobulinemia, leading to decreased oncotic pressure. In
addition, chronic blood loss, intestinal parasitism, and

intestinal neoplasia can also cause significant hypoproteinemia. In general, albumin concentrations less than
1.0 g/dL cause oncotic pressure to be low enough for a
transudate to develop; however, if increased hydrostatic
pressure is also present, a pure transudate can be seen
with a higher albumin concentration.
Modified transudates are variable in protein content
(2.5–7.5 g/dL) and cell count (1000–7000 cells/μL).
Grossly, they can be tan and slightly turbid, to pink, or
opaque and white in appearance depending on the
underlying etiology. Most of the nucleated cells are mononuclear (macrophages, lymphocytes, or a combination
of both) with a lower number of mesothelial cells and
nondegenerate neutrophils. Modified transudates result
from increased vascular or lymphatic permeability with
or without increased hydrostatic pressure. They are
modified by the addition of proteins, cells, or chyle, and
classifying a fluid as a modified transudate implies the
disease process causing fluid to accumulate is noninflammatory. Most modified transudates are a consequence of obstructed venous or lymphatic drainage
secondary to numerous underlying diseases, with right‐
sided heart failure being most common. Some modified
transudates may become exudative effusions, especially
with chronicity because fluid in the pleural space is
inflammatory. Chylous effusion has been classified as
both a modified transudate and an exudate for this reason. Initially, chylous effusions contain a predominant
population of mononuclear cells (lymphocytes) and fluid
accumulates due to lymphatic obstruction from noninflamed vessels. In cats, chylous effusion can result from
congestive heart failure or heartworm disease. Additional
causes in veterinary species include lung atelectasis,
neoplasia, diaphragmatic or peritoneal‐pericardial hernias, lung lobe torsion, lymphangiectasia, cranial vena
cava thrombosis, trauma, restrictive pericarditis, pericardial disease, and mediastinal disease. Often, an underlying disease for chylous effusion is not identified and is
therefore idiopathic.
Exudates have a high protein concentration (>3.0 g/dL)
and nucleated cell count (>3000 cells/μL). Exudates vary
in gross appearance from white to amber to pink depending on etiology and are typically turbid. The predominant
cell type is the neutrophil, which may be nondegenerate
(aseptic) or degenerate (septic), with macrophages, lymphocytes, eosinophils, and mesothelial cells in lesser
quantities. Exudative effusions usually result from an
inflammatory process in the pleural cavity causing
release of cytokines and other vasoactive mediators,
leading to increased capillary permeability (filtration
coefficient). The initial inflammatory process can be due
to endogenous (chyle, neoplastic cells) or exogenous
(bacteria, fungi) mediators. Eosinophilic effusions
determined cytologically with >10% eosinophils are
­

infrequently reported in veterinary medicine; however, if
present, cancer is the most common underlying etiology,
followed by thoracic wall trauma, pneumothorax, congestive heart failure, and allergic hypersensitivity conditions. Pyogranulomatous inflammation may indicate
fungal or foreign body reaction. Cytologic slides should
be closely evaluated for the presence of intracellular bacteria and aerobic and anaerobic cultures with antimicrobial susceptibilities should always be submitted when
degenerate neutrophils are present. Nondegenerate
­neutrophils typically indicate a nonseptic process and
may be secondary to neoplasia, chronic diaphragmatic
hernia, lymphatic obstruction or leakage, and infectious
processes. If the patient has a history of recent cholecystectomy or trauma and yellow, nonseptic exudate is
­collected, bilothorax should be a differential and further
diagnostics performed.
Specific Pleural Fluid Tests

When chylothorax is suspected, triglyceride concentration should be analyzed in the pleural effusion and
patient’s serum. Diagnosis of chylothorax is confirmed if
the triglyceride concentration in the pleural fluid is
higher than the triglyceride concentration in the patient’s
serum. Decreased glucose (<60 mg/dL) in pleural fluid is
due to decreased transport of glucose to the pleural fluid
or increased utilization of glucose by mononuclear cells,
neutrophils, bacteria, or malignant cells. If the effusion
appears hemorrhagic, the packed cell volume (PCV) of
the pleural effusion should be compared to the PCV of
the patient, with hemothorax present if the pleural fluid
PCV is at least 25% of the patient’s PCV. Bilirubin should
be quantified in the pleural fluid and blood if bilothorax
is suspected, such as those patients with recent biliary
surgery or known/suspected trauma. If bilirubin in the
pleural fluid is higher than in the patient’s blood, bilothorax is diagnosed.
Pleural Pressure Monitoring

Normal pleural pressure in a dog or cat is negative with
respect to the atmosphere and functions to facilitate
lung inflation and reduce the work of breathing. Negative
intrapleural pressure is generated by the lymphatic system as it drains the normal, physiologic small volume of
pleural fluid present. As pleural effusions accumulate,
lung parenchyma collapses and intrathoracic pressure
increases. Dyspnea and tachypnea result due to collapsed parenchymal lung tissue and pleural pressure
becomes less negative, or positive to the atmosphere.
When the fluid is removed by thoracocentesis, the
expectation is that intrapleural pressure returns to its
normal negative pressure and the lungs can reexpand but
this is not always the case, especially with chronic
effusions. The pleural surface can become fibrinous,
­

VetBooks.ir

34 Pleural Effusion

thickened, and inflamed by chronic effusions, thus inhibiting reexpansion of the lungs once the effusion is
removed. In humans, this is termed lung entrapment as
the intrapleural pressure has become negative, but the
lungs cannot expand due to the formation of a visceral
pleural peel and persistent pleural effusion. This imparts
a large negative pressure on the diseased visceral pleural
surface, which may cause pain or increase risk of spontaneous pneumothorax.
Intrapleural pressure can be measured during thoracocentesis with several techniques, including a U‐shaped
water manometer, an “overdamped” water manometer,
or electronic pressure transducer systems such as those
used for invasive blood pressure monitoring. The role of
intrapleuaral pressure monitoring in veterinary medicine is an expanding area of interest and research.

­Pyothorax
Pyothorax is the accumulation of purulent exudative
effusion in the pleural space caused by infection. Young
(3–6 years) male dogs are more likely to be diagnosed
with pyothorax, with performance breeds being overrepresented. Dyspnea, tachypnea, pyrexia, lethargy, and
anorexia are the most common clinical signs in dogs. In
cats, pyothorax is more common in young (2–4 years)
domestic shorthairs, with no sex predilection, and the
most common initial clinical signs include hyporexia or

Thoracoscopy
Thoracoscopy is a minimally invasive technique which is
becoming more widespread in veterinary medicine and
can be used as both a diagnostic and therapeutic technique in veterinary patients with pleural effusion.
Advantages of thoracoscopy include obtaining pleural
biopsies, visualization of intrathoracic pathology, and
minimally invasive approach (Figure 34.1).
Properly collected thoracoscopic pleural biopsies are
adequate in quality and quantity to obtain a definitive
histopathologic diagnosis (Figure 34.2). Disadvantages
include general anesthesia, risk of pneumothorax, hemorrhage, infection, and potential need for thoracotomy if
unable to achieve definitive treatment (depending on
underlying disease) with thorascoscopy alone.
(a)

anorexia, lethargy, and/or dyspnea. Although more
­common in young animals, pyothorax can occur at any
age, with rare reports in neonatal dogs and cats.
Additional clinical signs include weight loss, nasal or
ocular discharge, hypersalivation, coughing, and exercise
intolerance. Clinical signs can be acute or chronic.
Physical examination findings often include tachypnea,
dyspnea, decreased ventral lung sounds, muffled heart
sounds, and restrictive respiratory pattern. Severe sepsis
and associated signs could occur in either species, with
pyothorax being the most common cause in a retrospective paper on cats with severe sepsis.
In dogs, causes include bite wounds, penetrating
­thoracic injury, foreign body inhalation, lung abscess,
parasitic migration, hematogenous spread, esophageal or
tracheal perforation, diskospondylitis, neoplasia with
lung abscessation, previous thoracic surgery, and thoracocentesis. In cats, causes include extension from a lung
parenchymal infection, foreign body migration, esophageal rupture, and penetrating thoracic wounds. Cats with
pyothorax are 3.8 times more likely to live in multiple cat
households, Pasteurella spp. are the most ­common bacterial isolate, and 14.5–40% of cases have a history of bite
wounds, thus adding support to the theory that bite
wounds are a common route of infection. Migrating
grass awns can be a common cause of ­pyothorax in dogs
and cats, depending on geographic location, but in many
cases the cause of infection is not identified.
Diagnosis is based on presence of an exudate, cytologic
slide evaluation, and positive bacterial cultures of aseptically collected pleural fluid. Intracellular bacteria identified on cytologic review confirms the diagnosis but if
intracellular bacteria are not seen and degenerate neutrophils are present, then bacterial cultures (aerobic and
anaerobic) should be performed (Figure 34.3). If the
patient has already been on antibiotics prior to collection

Figure 34.3 Pyothorax cytology. Pyothorax in a dog with a
predominance of mature, mildly karyolytic neutrophils that
sometimes contain bacilli or coccobacilli forms (Wright‐Giemsa
stain, 100× objective). Source: Photo courtesy of Sarah S.K. Beatty,
DVM, University of Florida.

of pleural effusion, diagnostic test results may not be
reflective of disease and a nonseptic exudate may be seen.
Many feline pyothorax infections are due to multiple
organisms and common bacterial isolates in feline
­pyothorax include Pasteurella spp., Clostridium spp.,
Fusobacterium spp., Bacteroides spp., Peptostreptococcus
anaerobius, Porphyromonas spp., Prevotella spp., and
Actinomyces spp. In dogs, enteric organisms are more
common than in cats and common bacterial isolates include Escherichia coli, Enterobacter cloacae,
Pasteurella spp., Actinomyces spp., Streptococcus canis,
Peptostreptococcus anaerobius, Bacteroides spp.,
Fusobacterium spp., and Porphyromonas spp. Additional
clinicopathologic findings seen in patients with pyothorax
include elevated liver enzymes, electrolyte disturbances,
hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia, hypoalbuminemia, mild
anemia, and leukocytosis due to neutrophilia.
Imaging techniques include thoracic ultrasound, radiographs, and CT. In clinical practice, thoracic ultrasound
is typically utilized initially because it is noninvasive,
does not require sedation, and can be used rapidly in
patients with respiratory disease for diagnosis and to
localize an area for therapeutic thoracocentesis. With
pyothorax, pleural fluid is often echogenic and wispy,
fibrinous strands can be seen along pleural margins.
Radiographs may be helpful once fluid has been removed
to determine if an underlying cause can be identified,
such as a lung mass lesion, focal pulmonary opacity, or
foreign body; however, as previously mentioned, an
underlying cause is rarely found. The use of CT is becoming more widespread in veterinary medicine but the role
of CT in canine pyothorax is controversial. A retrospective study in dogs with spontaneous pyothorax showed
that common CT findings include bilateral pleural fluid,
pleural gas (due to preimaging thoracocentesis or thoracostomy tube placement), pleural thickening, pulmonary
parenchymal abnormalities, and mediastinal involvement. Of the surgically managed dogs in this study, CT
correctly predicted the extent of disease in only 62.5%
and correctly identified the underlying cause in only
50%; therefore, surgical exploration remains the gold
standard to identify underlying pathology.
Treatment includes administration of appropriate
antimicrobials, intermittent or continuous thoracic
drainage, thoracic lavage, and surgery. Intravenous
broad‐spectrum antimicrobials with adequate anaerobic
coverage should be started once culture samples have
been collected and adjusted accordingly based on ­culture
and susceptibility results. Potentiated beta‐lactams are
reasonable first‐line therapy because they have efficacy
against Actinomyces spp., anaerobes, and some gram‐
negative organisms. Enrofloxacin is often added to
improve gram‐negative coverage while awaiting culture
results. Deescalation of antimicrobial therapy should be

VetBooks.ir

34 Pleural Effusion

considered once susceptibility data are available. Medical
management involves thoracocentesis alone (repeated as
needed) or placement of unilateral or bilateral indwelling
thoracostomy tubes with intermittent or continuous
suction and thoracic lavage along with appropriate antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. In general, large‐
bore trocar or surgically placed thoracostomy tubes are
preferred in larger patients; however, smaller thoracostomy tubes placed using a modified Seldinger technique
have been reported for management of pyothorax in
dogs. Surgical management involves exploratory thoracotomy, usually by median sternotomy, to lavage and
debride the pleural space, and break down any adhesions
causing pocketing of fluid, then insertion of thoracostomy tubes for postoperative care, in addition to appropriate antimicrobial therapy and supportive care.
Appropriate treatment of pyothorax is controversial
and there is no consensus on ideal therapy for all cases.
Failure of medical therapy or presence of a focal lesion
(abscess, tumor, or granuloma), foreign body, or evidence
of esophageal rupture found on imaging are indications
for surgical management in dogs or cats. In dogs, some
advocate for early surgical treatment regardless of
whether an underlying cause is identified, with the premise being that any other infectious disease such as peritonitis, septic arthritis, or abscess is best treated by
aggressive debridement and drainage. In a retrospective
paper on medical versus surgical treatment canine
­pyothorax, medical management was 5.4 times more
likely to fail compared to surgical treatment and more
dogs were free of disease at one year if treated surgically.
In contrast, other studies have not shown a survival benefit of surgery versus medical management and reported
success of medical management has ranged from 29% to
100%. If Actinomyces spp. are suspected on cytology or
cultured from dogs with pyothorax, surgical management is warranted because medical treatment has a high
rate of failure and a grass awn foreign body is a likely
underlying cause. In cats, medical management with
indwelling thoracostomy tubes is reported to have a survival rate of 73–95%, whereas surgical management has
been reported to have a 100% survival rate. Successful
management of chronic pyothorax in cats with unilateral
pneumonectomy has been reported.
With medical management alone or during the postoperative period, thoracic lavage is often recommended
to facilitate drainage of exudative fluid; however, there
are no large‐scale canine or feline studies to evaluate outcome with this method. Theoretical advantages of lavage
include minimizing bacteria and inflammatory mediators in the pleural space and dilution of exudative fluid,
which could clog the thoracostomy tube. Potential
­disadvantages include electrolyte disturbances such as
hypokalemia, which has been reported in a cat undergoing

thoracic lavage, and nosocomial infection if aseptic technique is not followed. Pleural lavage is performed by
slowly infusing 10–20 mL/kg of warmed, 0.9% saline into
the pleural space, waiting 10–15 minutes, and then withdrawing the fluid. If bilateral thoracostomy tubes are in
place, some advocate for using one side as an infusion
port and the opposite side as a withdrawal port.
Thoracostomy tubes are generally removed when fluid
production decreases to 3–5 mL/kg/day, in addition to
clinical improvement of the patient and cytologic confirmation of absence of infectious organisms. Time to resolution of disease is generally 5–8 days and patients should
be rechecked frequently as recurrence is possible.

­Chylothorax
Chylothorax is a syndrome characterized by the accumulation of chyle, the milky fluid consisting of lymph
and emulsified fat formed in the small intestines during
digestion, in the pleural space and is often idiopathic in
nature. Additional reported causes include traumatic or
surgical thoracic duct rupture, cranial vena cava thrombosis, lymphatic obstruction by cancer or fungal granuloma, cardiomyopathy, congenital defect, diaphragmatic
hernia, peritoneopericardial diaphragmatic hernia, lung
lobe torsion, pericardial effusion, tetralogy of Fallot, tricuspid dysplasia, cor triatriatum dexter, constrictive pericarditis, and heartworm disease. Although trauma has
been a reported cause of chylothorax in the literature, it
could not be experimentally reproduced in dogs by laceration or transection of the thoracic duct as the effusion
resolved within 10 days. Reported neoplasms associated
with lymphatic obstruction causing chylothorax include
thymoma, lymphosarcoma, lymphangiosarcoma, and
aortic body tumors. The rate of chyle production and
drainage in normal dogs is approximately 2–4 mL/kg/h.
Most of the body except the right forelimb and right
side of the head and neck drain into the thoracic duct in
dogs and cats. Intestinal lymphatics drain chyle into the
mesenteric lymph nodes, which then form larger ducts
that continue on to form the cisterna chyli, which is a
lymphatic reservoir located ventral to the first four lumbar vertebrae. The cisterna chyli continues cranially to
become the thoracic duct and eventually empty into the
brachiocephalic trunk. In dogs, the cisterna chyli and
caudal thoracic duct are located on the right side of the
mediastinum; however, the duct crosses from right to
left in the mid‐mediastinum to empty into the brachiocephalic trunk. In cats, the thoracic duct is typically only
located to the left side of the mediastinum. Thoracic
duct anatomy can vary within the same species.
Obstruction of the thoracic duct or cranial vena cava
causes lymphatic flow stasis and dilation. It is thought

341

VetBooks.ir

that increased pressure causes chyle to leak out of dilated
lymphatics, as would occur in other parts of the body
with lymphedema. With cardiac disease, chylous ­effusion
can develop due to impaired lymph drainage to the
venous circulatory system. In addition, hepatic congestion occurs with heart failure, which significantly
increases hepatic lymph production and therefore
thoracic duct flow. Pathophysiologic mechanisms for
­
idiopathic chylous effusion are not well elucidated.
Chylothorax can occur in any breed or age of dog or
cat, with Afghan hounds being overrepresented because
of the association between lung lobe torsion and chylothorax. Clinical signs are those typical of pleural effusions, including lethargy, hyporexia or anorexia, weight
loss, tachypnea, cough, and paradoxical or restrictive
breathing pattern. Diligent cardiothoracic auscultation
should be performed because of the association between
cardiac disease and chylothorax. Additional physical
examination findings include muffled heart sounds,
decreased ventral lung sounds, and increased dorsal lung
sounds. There are no consistent laboratory findings for
dogs or cats with chylothorax.
Diagnosis of chylothorax is based on examination of
pleural fluid, which grossly appears milky white to
opaque pink‐white, but can vary depending on nutritional status of the patient. Pleural fluid from thoracocentesis should be saved in EDTA for cytologic
examination and a serum separator tube for triglyceride
concentration analysis. The fluid is most often classified
as an exudate, but may be classified as a modified transudate depending on the protein and cell count. Cytologic
examination shows predominantly lymphocytes, small
numbers of macrophages, and nondegenerate neutrophils, which increase in numbers with chronicity of
­pleural effusion (Figure 34.4).
Definitive diagnosis is made by demonstrating higher
triglycerides in pleural fluid than in serum samples,
­collected at the same time. If the effusion triglyceride
concentration is >100 mg/dL, chylomicrons are seen
­
microscopically on a wet‐mount preparation, pleural cholesterol concentration is less than serum cholesterol concentration, or Sudan stain verifies lipid in the sample, then
it is also classified as chylous. Once the diagnosis of chylothorax has been made, additional diagnostics, including
complete blood count, chemistry profile, heartworm test,
thoracic radiographs, thoracic ultrasound, echocardiogram, thoracic CT, +/− abdominal imaging, should be
considered to determine if an underlying disease can be
found. Cats should also be tested for retroviral diseases.
Treatment of chylothorax should be directed at the
underlying disease but as the disease is often idiopathic,
targeted treatment is rarely possible. Resolution of respiratory distress by removing the pleural effusion should
be initial treatment, regardless of etiology. Chylous
­effusion is rich in lymphocytes, protein, lipid, and elec-

Figure 34.4 Chylothorax cytology. Chylothorax in a cat consisting

trolytes and removal of large quantities of chylous
­effusion can cause hypovolemia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoproteinemia, lymphopenia, weight loss,
and immunosuppression. Conservative medical treatment involves pleural evacuation and nutritional
­management. Surgical treatment for idiopathic chylous
effusion involves ligation of the thoracic duct with or
without various adjunctive procedures including subtotal pericardectomy, cisterna chyli ablation, and thoracic
omentalization.
Diets low in fat have been recommended for medical
management of chylothorax in dogs and cats to decrease
the volume of chyle production and therefore flow
through the thoracic duct; however, this has not been
experimentally validated in dogs or cats. Rutin is a commercially available benzopyrone nutritional supplement
used in humans for treating lymphedema and commonly
recommended for medical management of idiopathic
chylothorax, although no proven beneficial effects have
been demonstrated in dogs and cats. Theoretical beneficial actions of rutin include edema uptake by lymphatic
vessels, reduction of blood vessel permeability, and
enhancement of tissue macrophage number and function
to promote phagocytosis of protein in chylous fluid.
Octreotide, a somatostatin analogue, inhibits biliary, pancreatic, and gastric secretions, and is recommended in
humans with chylothorax to decrease thoracic duct flow;
however, use in dogs and cats requires further research.
Prior to surgical treatment, some form of thoracic
duct imaging is typically recommended to allow for
­surgical planning given the anatomic variation within
and between species. Mesenteric lymphangiography, or
the use of aqueous contrast material injected into a

VetBooks.ir

34 Pleural Effusion

­mesenteric lymph node to highlight the thoracic duct,
has been utilized for over 30 years in veterinary medicine to guide surgical planning and assess postoperative
success. Mesenteric lymphangiography is an invasive
procedure as it requires an exploratory laparotomy and
injection of contrast medium into a mesenteric lymphatic vessel or lymph node, followed by radiographs or
CT under general anesthesia; therefore less invasive procedures have since been developed for thoracic duct
imaging. More recent minimally invasive imaging
modalities include percutaneous mesenteric lymphadenography, laparoscopic mesenteric lymphadenography,
percutaneous popliteal lymphangiography, and subcutaneous or submucosal lymphography, and CT has largely
replaced conventional radiography as the ideal imaging
technique.
Surgical treatment is recommended if chylothorax is
persistent despite medical therapy because chyle is
inflammatory and can cause severe fibrosing pleuritis
or pericarditis. Thoracic duct ligation at the entry
point of the duct into the thorax is the most commonly ­p erformed surgical technique for dogs and cats
with idiopathic c­ hylothorax. The premise behind thoracic duct ligation is to create a stimulus for new lymphaticovenous connections to the caudal vena cava or
azygous vein outside the pleural space, thereby bypassing the thoracic duct and preventing intrathoracic
flow of chyle. Surgical approach to the thoracic duct
can be through a caudal intercostal thoracotomy, paracostal or ventral midline celiotomy with transdiaphragmatic extension, median sternotomy, or using
thoracoscopy.
Several adjunctive surgical procedures have been
combined with thoracic duct ligation in an effort to
increase success rate of treatment. Cisterna chyli ablation was developed because hypertension within the
cisterna chyli is thought to cause collateral lympathic
vessels to form around the thoracic duct ligation site.
Adjunctive subtotal pericardectomy is rationalized
because chronic chylous effusions can cause pericarditis, which in turn can increase right‐sided venous pressure and possibly impede chyle drainage from new
lymphaticovenous anastomoses. Other adjunctive or
alternative procedures are thoracic omentalization to
provide lymphatic drainage, pleurodesis to abolish the
pleural space, and cisterna chyli and thoracic duct
embolization, with the latter being a salvage procedure
if previous surgical attempts have failed. Surgical (conventional or thoracoscopic) success rates vary between
50% and 100% in dogs and 14.3% and 80% in cats.
Persistence of chylous or nonchylous pleural effusion is
the most common surgical complication. If surgical
treatment fails, then implantation of an active pleuroperitoneal shunt or PleuralPort device should be considered to manage long‐term effusion.

­Hemothorax
Hemothorax is defined as an exudative effusion in the pleural space with a PCV that is at least 25% of peripheral blood.
Iatrogenic hemorrhage during thoracocentesis should be
suspected if the sample contains platelets and lacks erythrophagocytosis on cytology. In general, causes of hemothorax can be divided into coagulopathic and noncoagulopathic.
Anticoagulant rodenticide toxicity is the most common
cause of coagulopathic hemothorax in veterinary patients
but disorders of primary hemostasis could also result in
hemothorax. Reported noncoagulopathic etiologies include
neoplasia, thoracic trauma, lung lobe torsion, pancreatitis,
pulmonary parasitic disease (Spirocerca lupi, Dirofiliaria
immitis, or Angiostrongylus vasorum), esophageal foreign
body, and pulmonary infarction. Therapeutic thoracocentesis should only be performed in patients with hemothorax
if respiratory distress is present on physical examination
because most of the blood will be reabsorbed once the
underlying cause is treated. Coagulation tests should be
performed prior to thoracocentesis and blood products
should be readily available. Fresh frozen plasma should be
administered to coagulopathic patients with hemothorax,
prior to or during therapeutic thoracocentesis, if this is
deemed necessary on patient evaluation. Thoracic ultrasound, echocardiography, and CT may be utilized to determine the underlying cause along with standard blood tests,
heartworm test, and fecal examination. Treatment is
directed at the underlying cause and emergency surgical
treatment may be necessary in some dogs or cats that are
nonresponsive to conservative management.

­Bilothorax
Bilothorax is the accumulation of a nonseptic, exudative
effusion high in bilirubin within the pleural space and is rare
in both veterinary and human medicine. It has only been
reported in a few veterinary patients, all of which had recent
hepatobiliary trauma (gunshot wound or penetrating
trauma) or biliary surgery. In one cat, the penetrating
trauma was iatrogenic; pleurobiliary fistulae occurred secondary to thoracotomy tube placement. The theorized
mechanism of bilothorax formation is from pleurobiliary
formation, with a presumptive ­diaphragmatic incongruity;
however, bile can also be carried across an intact diaphragm
by way of the ­lymphatic system. Diagnosis is confirmed if
the ratio of bilirubin in pleural fluid to serum is greater than
1:1. Given the rarity of bilothorax, optimal treatment is controversial. Medical management by placing thoracostomy
tubes with ­frequent pleural fluid drainage is recommended
to minimize bile pleuritis. If medical management fails, surgical exploration is recommended. Bilothorax in dogs and
cats appears to have a good prognosis, with a combined
100% survival rate of currently reported cases.

Section 4 Respiratory Disease

­Conclusion
Pleural effusion is a common consequence of several
underlying pathophysiologic processes in dogs and cats.
Historical findings can be acute or chronic and clinical

signs are variable, with many dogs and cats presenting with
a primary complaint related to lethargy, hyporexia, and/or
respiratory distress. A thorough diagnostic approach is
often needed to determine the underlying disease and subsequently guide treatment options and overall prognosis.

Approach to the Patient in the Critical Care Setting
Sarah Allen, DVM, DACVECC
Massachusetts Veterinary Referral Hospital, Woburn, MA, USA

Patients presenting to a veterinary emergency room represent a diverse array of illness and injury, ranging from
mild to life threatening. The use of a triage system allows
these patients to be systematically evaluated and prioritized based on presenting signs, history, and initial vital
parameters. While no triage system is perfect, success is
enhanced when staff are well trained. Every facility and
emergency team should have a standard triage system,
appropriately trained staff to perform triage, and a reliably equipped area to allow for efficient and prompt care
of these patients’ needs.
A clinician’s relationship with a critical patient often
begins upon presentation to the hospital or, in the case of
a referral center, upon admission to the intensive care
unit (ICU). As the direct definition of the word “critical”
states, a critical patient is one that is at a stage of disease
when an abrupt change for better or worse may be
expected, or that has an illness or condition involving
danger of death. Due to this unstable position, these
patients require intense and continuous assessment and
care and may benefit from consultation with a critical
care specialist.

­Physical Exam
A thorough initial physical exam, as well as frequent
sequential exams, should be performed with the goal of
promptly identifying current and evolving problems.
Advanced diagnostics may become necessary in order to
fully illuminate clinical findings but should never be used
in place of a physical exam. While each clinician should
have a routine by which they approach an exam, it may
be required that the order of the exam be varied in critically ill patients, based on each patient’s current condition and stability. Care must be taken to ensure that all
systems are assessed due to possible variation in exam

sequence. The exam may need to be performed in multiple phases to allow for patient comfort and safety.
Due to the critical condition of these patients, initial
exam time should be spent on evaluating critical systems, particularly airway and breathing, heart and circulation, and neurologic status. For patients in respiratory
distress, brief attempts at an exam may need to be interspersed between periods of rest in an oxygen chamber.
Observation of the patient’s respirations with attention
to chest wall and abdominal movement may also provide
information as to the cause of distress. Emphasis should
be placed on thoracic auscultation to help discern the
cause of distress, noting stridor, air movement or
increased/decreased lung sounds. If the patient is not
breathing or is ineffectively moving air, intubation and
manual ventilation is required.
The heart should be ausculted while peripheral pulses
are palpated. If heartbeat and pulses are absent, CPR
must be instituted immediately (see Chapter 37). If the
heart is beating and pulses are absent or irregular, further investigation and intervention are required to
restore effective circulation. During heart auscultation,
the heart rate and rhythm should be noted and heart
sounds should be evaluated for presence of murmurs or
muffled nature.
The patient’s neurologic status should be evaluated
and continuously monitored for alterations or deterioration. Particularly with trauma, signs of spinal cord injury
should be sought and appropriate stabilization initiated
prior to further manipulation of the patient. If traumatic
brain injury is suspected, efforts to increase cerebral perfusion and decrease intracranial pressure (ICP) should
be instituted, including blood pressure support, head
elevation, and minimal jugular vein occlusion. Judicious
IV fluid therapy is recommended to restore blood pressure to a minimum of a systolic of 90 mmHg or a mean of
60 mmHg.

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

Occasionally, emergency interventions are necessary
at the time of examination to stabilize the patient so that
further examination and diagnostics can be performed
and an overall treatment plan composed. If it is possible
to complete a comprehensive exam at the time of initial
evaluation, it should done.

­History
A complete history is required for appropriate care of a
critical patient. During triage and emergency presentation, the need for speed and efficiency often prevents the
gathering of a thorough history. Once the patient’s condition allows, further history to be discovered includes
past medical problems, past and recent surgical interventions, origin and travel history, and general wellness
and preventive care (vaccines, flea/tick/parasite prevention) schedule. Medications administered by the owner
should be determined, with specific questioning about
vitamins, supplements, and over‐the‐counter medications. Efforts should be made to obtain copies of medical
records from other veterinary facilities where the patient
has been treated recently and in the past. These records
should be carefully reviewed to identify areas in the
patient’s history that the owner may have forgotten or
misunderstood.

­Assessment
After the history and physical exam have been completed, time should be taken to document the information and to form an active problems list. The initial list
may consist of an identified problem without an underlying cause. Initial therapeutic interventions directed at
the current problem(s) should be initiated and the problem list and eventual diagnosis list updated as indicated
by response to therapy or results of additional diagnostics. While a written problem list is commonly used by
beginning clinicians and then discarded as clinicians
gain experience, with complicated cases it remains
essential to ensure best patient care.

­Record Keeping
Not only are formal medical records required by law,
they help the clinician keep the case documented and
organized and assist in transfer between clinicians and
facilities. Medical records also provide information for
follow‐up care after discharge and in the future. The
medical record should consist of the presenting history

and physical exam, a problem list, a diagnosis list, and
results of laboratory and imaging procedures. For the
duration of hospitalization, a minimum of one physical
exam should be documented daily as well as an updated
problem/diagnosis list and an updated treatment and
diagnostic plan. The ideal medical record will also document communications between the treating veterinarian
and owner and any consulting veterinarians that have
been involved.

­Client Communication
The assessment and medical management of a critical
patient are complicated and challenging enough. Adding
to the difficulty is the need for the clinician to communicate effectively and compassionately with the owner. As
the case evolves, the client needs to be informed of the
working diagnosis, financial costs, and short‐ and long‐
term prognosis for the current condition. Apprising the
owner of the risks and benefits of each proposed treatment or therapy is necessary in order for them to make
an informed decision. As many of these patients are
unstable, a CPR resuscitation code is a required topic of
conversation to ensure that the owner’s wishes are followed in the event of an arrest. Detailed written client
communications should be kept as part of the formal
medical record. These notes help all clinicians involved
with a case to know what has been discussed and when.
They are also invaluable should a case go to litigation.

­Referral
When treating a critically ill patient, a large consideration is whether the current facility can offer the patient
and client the level of care that they need and want.
While many facilities may be able to meet the minimum
standard of care, it is always best to inform the owner of
the option of referral, making sure to communicate the
pros and cons of transfer as well as the expected financial cost of treatment at another facility. While some
owners may opt to not pursue referral, many will elect
to transfer to a hospital that has 24‐hour doctor care or
other advanced capabilities. For many general practitioners, referral to a 24‐hour facility for any patient
requiring overnight IV fluids or observation is common. Cases may also need referral for advanced diagnostics including imaging (ultrasound, computed
tomography, magnetic resonance imaging), advanced
surgical procedures (soft tissue and orthopedic), or for
advanced therapeutics (long‐term ventilation, transfusion, dialysis).

VetBooks.ir

35 Approach to the Patient in the Critical Care Setting

Prior to referral of critically ill patients, the treating clinician should call the intended receiving facility and
speak to the specialist who will be taking control of the
case to ensure the transfer is made as safe and efficient as
possible. All available medical records should be copied
and should accompany the pet in a hard copy format.

­The “Rule of 20”
In addition to serial physical exams and frequent reevaluation of the active problem list, there are a multitude of
critical parameters that need to be evaluated at least
daily in the critical patient. Developed by Rebecca Kirby,
a founding Diplomate of the American College of
Veterinary Emergency and Critical Care, the “Rule of 20”
provides a comprehensive tool to guide the continuous
evaluation and integration of a patient’s organ systems,
laboratory findings and treatment and many critical care
specialists find it useful to refer to the “Rule of 20” on a
daily basis with critically ill patients. Each element will
be discussed below, many of which will be covered in
detail in other chapters.
Fluid Balance
Fluid therapy is a common treatment in critical patients
with a goal to reestablish and maintain hydration and to
ensure circulating volume is maintained. Often dehydration and hypovolemia require rapid fluid replacement in
the form of boluses. After initial volume expansion and
rehydration, each patient’s “maintenance” fluid needs
will differ due to underlying conditions, ongoing losses,
and variations in metabolism. Each patient will also have
a unique ability to tolerate administered fluids. The consequences of overhydration or inappropriate fluid redistribution include pulmonary edema, peripheral edema,
and third spacing of fluids within body cavities.
Assessment of response to administered fluids requires
monitoring of many parameters, including mucous
membrane color and moistness, skin turgor, heart rate,
and body weight. Each of these parameters should be
assessed several times per day. Monitoring of blood
­pressure and urine output can provide additional information on a patient’s needs. Monitoring of central
venous pressures and changes in blood gas variables
­(lactate, base deficit) are used for advanced monitoring
of fluid therapy.
Blood Pressure and Perfusion
There are many methods to monitor blood pressure,
including direct (via an arterial catheter and pressure

transducer) and indirect (Doppler and sphygmomanometer or oscilllometric measurements) options. A
good general goal is to maintain a mean arterial blood
pressure >60 mmHg and a systolic blood pressure
>90 mmHg for optimal organ and tissue perfusion.
Hypotension that is nonresponsive to fluid therapy
may indicate the presence of an underlying acid–base
or electrolyte disorder or the need to begin therapy
with a vasoactive agent. Central venous pressure and
lactate monitoring can provide additional information
on the need for vasopressor therapy. While less commonly encountered clinically, monitoring for and
treatment of hypertension are useful to prevent complications including retinal detachment, neurologic
impairment, and end‐organ injury.
Cardiac Function
Heart function should be evaluated not only by heart rate
and rhythm but also ability to effectively pump blood
forward through evaluation of peripheral limb temperatures and capillary refill time. Electrocardiographically
confirmed arrhythmias should be treated if perfusion is
compromised. Echocardiography is helpful in identifying
underlying structural heart disease as well as visualizing
cardiac filling and contractility. Additional treatments
directed at optimizing cardiac function, including IV
­fluids, inotropic support or afterload reduction, should
be introduced as indicated.
Albumin
Albumin is a blood protein produced by the liver that
plays an essential role in a multitude of physiologic
processes, including fluid balance, drug transport, tissue healing, and coagulation. Synthetic colloids can be
used to maintain fluid in the intravascular space but
they do not substitute for albumin’s other roles in the
body and may be associated with acute kidney injury.
Albumin levels <2 g/dL have been associated with a
poor prognosis in critically ill patients and may indicate the need for replacement with plasma (frozen or
fresh ­frozen) or canine albumin transfusions.
Oncotic Pull
Adequate oncotic pressure is required to maintain
appropriate intravascular volume and prevent interstitial fluid loss that can propagate hypovolemia and
edema formation. Oncotic pressure changes in direct
correlation with albumin concentration and can therefore be augmented with administration of natural
colloids.

VetBooks.ir
