Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

potentially lead to respiratory muscle fatigue and exhaustion. Such patients may be able to maintain acceptable
blood gas values for a period of time, but uncertainty lies
in how long this effort can be sustained. Determination
of excessive respiratory effort is largely subjective and
based on clinical judgment. Intermittent positive pressure ventilation (IPPV) is indicated in these patients to
avoid abrupt exhaustion, asphyxiation, and subsequent
arrest. Asphyxiation in experimental canine studies is
accompanied by an abrupt drop in heart rate of about
50 beats per minute. Any comparable drop in pulse rate
in a dog laboring to breath should prompt immediate
patient evaluation and careful consideration of intubation and mechanical ventilation. In these aforementioned
canine studies, failure to prevent complete asphyxiation
often leads to cardiac arrest in the form of pulseless
electrical activity; this is a particularly challenging form
of cardiac arrest to reverse and is often refractory to
therapy.
Patients with excessive respiratory effort usually have
an excessive mechanical or chemical load imposed upon
their respiratory system (see also Chapter 39).

­Ventilator Settings
Positive pressure ventilators achieve gas flow into the
lungs by generating positive airway pressure in a manner similar to that achieved by squeezing the rebreathing bag on an anesthetic machine. Modern therapeutic
ventilators have an array of settings that can be altered
to change the characteristics of the delivered breath.
Despite the complexity of many therapeutic ventilators,
there are only a few key settings that are essential to
understand in order to provide effective ventilation in
most cases. When choosing ventilator settings, the clinician must first select a mode of ventilation and then
input initial ventilator settings based on general guidelines (described below) and their own understanding of
the nature of the patient’s respiratory compromise.
Following initiation of mechanical ventilation, the ventilator settings are then adjusted as required to achieve
the blood gas, cardiopulmonary performance, and/or
oxygen delivery goals desired.
Ventilator Breath Types
There are three main ventilator volume delivery (breath)
patterns commonly used in veterinary medicine: assist/
control (A/C) ventilation, synchronized intermittent
mandatory ventilation (SIMV), and continuous spontaneous ventilation (CSV). Some ventilators only have
one breath pattern option, such as a compact volume‐
control ventilator designed for use in the operating

room. Modern therapeutic ventilators typically offer all
three formats.
In A/C ventilation, all breaths are completely machine
generated. These are termed mandatory breaths. In this
mode of ventilation, the clinician sets a minimum respiratory rate. If the trigger sensitivity (i.e., pressure or
flow alteration required to trigger delivery of a breath
that was not prescheduled to be delivered) is set appropriately then the patient can increase the respiratory
rate above this minimum value, but all breaths delivered
will be full ventilator‐delivered (mandatory) breaths.
The tidal volume of these ventilator breaths will depend
on the machine settings (and any patient–ventilator
dyssynchrony if present). Ventilator breaths can either
be pressure (PC) or volume controlled (VC). When VC
is employed, the clinician presets the desired tidal volume; the resultant peak airway pressure will be dependent on the size of the tidal volume chosen and the
compliance of the respiratory system. More compliant
lungs will accept a given volume at a lower peak pressure than less compliant lungs. In PC ventilation, the
clinician presets the peak airway pressure; in this setting, the tidal volume generated will depend on the level
of peak airway pressure chosen and the compliance of
the respiratory system. Assist/control ventilation provides maximum support of the respiratory system and is
used in patients with severe respiratory disease or those
with healthy lungs but reduced respiratory drive or ventilatory capacity.
In SIMV, the operator also sets the number of full
ventilator (mandatory) breaths to be delivered.
However, between these breaths the patient can
breathe spontaneously, depending on their needs. The
machine will try to synchronize the ventilator breaths
with the patient’s own respiratory efforts. This is
accomplished by partitioning the periods between
mandatory breaths into two periods. The first period
immediately follows a mandatory breath. During this
period, the patient may breathe spontaneously without triggering a machine‐delivered breath. The second
period is immediately prior to the next scheduled
mandatory breath. Patient effort during this period
will trigger early delivery of the next mandatory
breath. This latter period is the “synchronized” portion and is what distinguishes SIMV from intermittent
mandatory ventilation. As this mode combines full
ventilator breaths with spontaneous patient breaths, it
is often used for animals that need less than 100%
assistance from the ventilator or during the weaning
period. Neurologically impaired animals with highly
labile respiratory drive or patients with resolving lung
dysfunction may not need as much support as A/C
provides and SIMV can prove a useful option in these
conditions.

VetBooks.ir

40 Mechanical Ventilation

There are two widely available options for provision of
continuous spontaneous ventilation: continuous positive
airway pressure (CPAP) and pressure support ventilation
(PSV). In CPAP, the ventilator does not deliver breaths;
rather, all breaths are spontaneous breaths and are completely patient generated. The respiratory rate, inspiratory time, and tidal volume are all determined by the
patient. CPAP provides a constant level of positive airway pressure (the amount is preset by the operator)
throughout the respiratory cycle. Airway pressure is thus
maintained at supraatmospheric pressures throughout
the respiratory cycle. CPAP has the potential benefits of
decreasing respiratory system resistance and increasing
pulmonary compliance. These effects as well as the
increase in mean airway pressure may serve to improve
gas exchange and oxygenation relative to what the patient
could achieve without this support. Increased pulmonary compliance effects of CPAP can best be explained
by considering the shape of a typical lung pressure–volume relationship (aka compliance curve). Pulmonary
compliance curves are typically nonlinear with a flat
slope at volumes just above functional residual capacity
(FRC). This relatively flat slope indicates that changes in
pressure generated by early inspiratory effort are accompanied by only slight changes in lung volume (low compliance). CPAP can reduce the work of breathing by
shifting the starting point of breath initiation to a portion of the curve with a steeper slope (higher compliance). Further, maintaining the lung at a higher volume
increases mean airway diameter of noncartilaginous airways and reduces airway resistance. With modern ventilator models, the machine will alarm if the animal does
not generate adequate breaths or develops apnea. This
makes it a useful “monitoring” mode for weaning patients
or monitoring intubated patients.
As with CPAP, all PSV breaths are spontaneous breaths;
the ventilator does not trigger, deliver, or initiate any
breaths. In PSV, the tidal volume is generated by the
patient, but also augmented by the machine. The amount
of pressure support provided during the inspiratory period
depends on what level of PSV support the clinician has
prescribed. This mode reduces the effort required to
maintain adequate alveolar ventilation and gas exchange
in patients with adequate respiratory drive but reduced
ventilatory capacity. Pressure support ventilation can be
used independently, in conjunction with CPAP, or to augment the spontaneous breaths during SIMV.
Tidal Volume Settings
The normal tidal volume reported for dogs and cats is
generally in the range of 10–15 mL/kg although many
reports cite a tidal volume for healthy sedated cats of
approximately 20 mL/kg. Lower tidal volumes (6–8 mL/

kg) may be targeted in animals with severe lung disease
to avoid overdistension of the less severely diseased lung
tissue. When using volume control ventilation, the clinician presets the desired tidal volume. As overdistension
of the lung can lead to significant alveolar injury, it is recommended to start with no more than 10 mL/kg initially.
The tidal volume can subsequently be increased if it is
determined to be inadequate once an initial steady state
is achieved (typically 15 minutes after initiating IPPV or
following a settings adjustment). If pressure control ventilation is used then the operator presets a desired peak
airway pressure and once the animal is connected to the
ventilator, the tidal volume achieved with the preset
pressure is evaluated and peak inspiratory pressure
adjusted as needed. A tidal volume of around 10 mL/kg
would be an acceptable result in most cases.
The clinician must bear in mind that whole‐body carbon dioxide stores are enormous relative to the relatively
minimal whole‐body oxygen stores (excluding pinniped
mammals). Step changes in ventilation will result in
abrupt, modest changes in PaCO2, but a new steady‐state
value can take quite a long time to be reached. Only the
CO2 in large, well‐perfused organs can truly be considered rapidly exchangeable and this represents a small
fraction of whole‐body stores. Allowing 15 minutes to
pass prior to reassessing steady‐state PaCO2 values is a
clinically reasonable approach.
Airway Pressure Settings
Patients with healthy lungs such as hypoventilating anesthetized patients, patients with reduced respiratory
drive, or those with reduced ventilatory capacity typically only require peak airway pressures in the range of
8–15 cmH2O. Avoiding peak inspiratory pressures above
20 cmH2O is preferable whenever feasible. Animals with
significant lung disease often have relatively stiff lungs
and typically require higher airway pressures to achieve
adequate tidal volumes. Peak airway pressures as high as
30–35 cm H2O may be required in such animals. When
using pressure control ventilation, the peak airway pressure target is set by the clinician. Once the animal is connected to the ventilator, the tidal volume achieved with
that airway pressure should be determined. Alternatively,
in volume control, the tidal volume is preset and the
associated airway pressure needs to be monitored.
Initially, airway pressures of 10–15 cmH2O should be
targeted; higher airway pressures can be utilized if indicated by unacceptable blood gas values.
Trigger Settings
Most modern ventilators will allow the patient to trigger machine breaths, which allows breath delivery to be

395

VetBooks.ir

396

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

better matched to the patient’s intrinsic efforts. The
“trigger” or “sensitivity” setting determines what the
ventilator will acknowledge as a genuine inspiratory
effort by the patient. Appropriate trigger sensitivity is
essential to ensure the ventilator recognizes actual
respiratory efforts made by the patient while not
­
­delivering breaths as a result of minor fluctuations in
circuit pressure or flow. Appropriate trigger sensitivity
increases patient comfort, reduces dyssynchrony
between patient effort and machine delivery, and allows
the patient to increase the respiratory rate as required
by their needs. The trigger variable can be too sensitive
such that nonrespiratory efforts such as patient handling and cardiac contractions may initiate breaths.
This situation should be avoided as it leads to patient
discomfort, excessive mean airway pressures, breath
stacking, auto‐PEEP, and greater dyssynchrony. An airway pressure drop of –2 cmH2O or a gas flow change of
2 L/min are reasonable trigger sensitivity settings to
start with. These settings can then be altered as
required. Some ventilators (e.g., AutoTrak on the
Phillips Esprit line) have proprietary forms of trigger
sensing that combine the flow and pressure signals into
an integrated variable. Evidence of superiority of this
means of sensing patient inspiratory effort is currently
lacking in the veterinary literature.
Positive End‐Expiratory Pressure Settings
Positive end‐expiratory pressure (PEEP) maintains
pressure in the breathing circuit above atmospheric
pressure during exhalation so that the patient cannot
exhale all the way down to functional residual capacity
(FRC). This increased expiratory pressure maintains
the lung at a higher volume, with less small airway collapse, and improves oxygenating efficiency. PEEP may
also help to recruit alveoli collapsed due to atelectasis
or increased surface tension forces. Evidence suggests
that it may reduce ventilator‐induced lung injury by
altering cyclic stresses and strains on the alveoli and
peripheral airways. Typically, a small amount of PEEP
(~2 cmH2O) is applied in all ventilator modes to reduce
atelectasis and to account for the increased work of
breathing required simply due to the physical nature of
the ventilator circuit (e.g., valves, circuit resistance). In
patients with significant lung disease, much higher levels of PEEP may be required to improve oxygenating
ability. In continuous spontaneous ventilation, CPAP is
functionally equivalent to PEEP although they are
often generated by different means (i.e., closure of the
expiratory valve at supraatmospheric pressures versus
continuous inflow to maintain a given circuit pressure
during the expiratory phase).

Inspiratory:Expiratory (I:E) Ratio and Respiratory
Rate Settings
An operator‐set respiratory rate is available on nearly all
ventilators. A respiratory rate of 15–20 breaths per minute with an inspiratory time of approximately one second reflects typical initial ventilator settings in the
authors’ practice. These settings can then be adjusted as
needed to meet the patient’s needs. The ratio of the duration of the inspiratory phase relative to the expiratory
phase (I:E ratio) may be preset by the clinician or may be
a setting that is determined automatically based on rate
and inspiratory time settings. Commonly, an I:E ratio of
at least 1:2 is utilized to increase the likelihood that
patients are able to fully exhale prior to the delivery of
the next breath. As respiratory rates are increased, the
expiratory time will be reduced in order to accommodate
the increased number of breaths. High respiratory rates
can lead to a situation known as auto‐PEEP or intrinsic
PEEP if the patient is not able to fully exhale before the
start of the next inspiration. Such an occurrence can easily be detected by inspecting the flow scalar graphic if
waveform displays are available. Failure of expiratory
flow to return to zero before the next breath is delivered
is indicative of the presence of auto‐PEEP. To avoid this
problem, it is recommended to keep an I:E ratio of 1:1 or
higher whenever possible. If a higher respiratory rate is
required, a shorter inspiratory time will allow maintenance of an acceptable I:E ratio and is often better tolerated by the patient.
General Guidelines for Initial Ventilator Settings
As discussed above, the optimal ventilator settings for a
given patient cannot be predicted reliably. It is likely that
animals with hypoxemic respiratory failure will require
more aggressive settings than those with hypercapneic
respiratory failure. One must choose some initial settings prior to connecting the patient to the ventilator.
First the mode of ventilation must be selected; A/C,
SIMV or continuous spontaneous ventilation. If A/C or
SIMV are selected then it may be necessary to next
decide between volume control (VC) or pressure control
(PC) ventilation. The more modern and advanced the
ventilator, the more options one is likely to have.
Ventilator manufacturers are creating new proprietary
ventilation modes faster than clinicans can evaluate
them. Even the most renowned respiratory therapists in
the world admit that they cannot keep up with every
mode becoming available. This situation is unlikely to
change as equipment manufacturers are often less than
forthright about how these novel modes are designed.
The settings that need to be selected will vary with the

VetBooks.ir

40 Mechanical Ventilation

mode of ventilation chosen. In VC the tidal volume is
preset by the operator, once the patient is connected to
the machine the operator should note the peak inspiratory pressure associated with this tidal volume and
determine whether it is acceptable for this patient. In PC
ventilation, the clinician presets the peak airway pressure. Once the patient is connected to the ventilator the
operator will need to note the tidal volume and mean airway pressure and determine whether they are acceptable
for this patient.
These settings can then be altered as needed once the
patient is connected to the ventilator. Whenever possible, it is best to have the ventilator already running and
confirmed to be working properly before the patient is
connected. When this is not possible, for example initiating mechanical ventilation for patients already on an
anesthetic machine, then it is best to start with quite
conservative settings and titrate them upwards as
required to avoid inadvertent over‐distension of the
lung. It is imperative to always have a method for performing manual ventilation (e.g. Ambu‐bag, Bain’s circuit) close at hand during IPPV in case of equipment
malfunction, power failure, or operator error.

­Mechanical Ventilation for Hypoxemic
Respiratory Failure
Patients suffering from hypoxemic respiratory failure
often require inspiratory pressure settings that are substantially greater than normal. Pulmonary parenchymal
disease often reduces lung compliance and increases airway resistance. The result is that higher pressures will be
needed to achieve the same tidal volume. It is now recognized that excessive distension of the lung (or volutrauma) is a major cause of ventilator‐induced lung
injury. For this reason, it is recommended to deliver
smaller tidal volumes when ventilating patients with significant pulmonary parenchymal disease. In very severe
lung disease such as ARDS, it may be necessary to deliver
tidal volumes as low as 6 mL/kg.
Anesthesia
Unless the patient has significant neuromuscular or
intracranial disease, anesthesia will be necessary to allow
positive pressure ventilation and maintenance of an airway. Balanced anesthesia incorporating 2–3 drugs is
advised to reduce the dose required (and adverse effects)
of any single agent. Propofol or alfaxalone infusions are
commonly used anesthetic agents in conjunction with a
benzodiazepine and/or an opioid and/or a dexmedetomidine infusion. The aim is to keep the patient anesthetized

sufficiently such that it will tolerate the endotracheal
tube and PPV but to avoid excessive depth of anesthesia
in an effort to minimize the adverse effects of the anesthetic drugs. This requires some experience in anesthetic
monitoring and constant tinkering with the anesthetic
drug infusion rates as drug requirements will change
with time.
Typical intravenous anesthetic doses used to maintain
patients on mechanical ventilators at the authors’ practice include the following.
Midazolam: loading dose 0.2–0.4 mg/kg IV; constant
rate infusion (CRI) 0.1–0.5 mg/kg/h IV.
●● Propofol: loading dose 0.5–2.0 mg/kg IV; CRI 0.05–
0.4 mg/kg/min IV.
●● Fentanyl: loading dose 2–5 μg/kg IV; CRI 1–7 μg/kg/h IV.
●●

The vast majority of patients receiving long‐term
mechanical ventilatory support in our practice are
anesthetized with some combination of these three
agents. The occasional patient will also receive a dexmedetomidine infusion (0.1–3.0 μg/kg/h) either as a
replacement for one of those three agents or in addition
to them. Etomidate is rarely if ever given and has
resulted in marked suppression of adrenal function
when it was employed. Diazepam may be substituted
for midazolam as required. Pentobarbital, once a mainstay in our practice, is rarely used now due to relative
expense, reduced availability due to shortages, and prolonged recovery times.
Anesthetic depth should be formally assessed every
hour and recorded on the patient’s flow sheet/medical
record, but caregivers should be continuously assessing
anesthetic depth as they work on the patient. It is important to have drug dose charts that correctly convert the
mg/kg/h drug doses to mL/h for the drug concentration
you are using. In addition, it is recommended to have precalculated some “rescue doses” of drugs in case animals
suddenly become light and try to extubate themselves.
Initial Stabilization on the Ventilator
When patients are first connected to the ventilator circuit, an inspired oxygen fraction (FiO2) of 100% is advised
as a safety measure. The FiO2 can be reduced later once
stabilization of the patient has been achieved. When
ventilating patients with hypoxemic respiratory failure, it
can be beneficial to keep them in sternal recumbency
during the initial stabilization period. These animals frequently oxygenate better in sternal recumbency than in
other body positions. After connection, the patient’s thoracic wall is observed for appropriate movement. When
insufficient or excessive thoracic wall motion is observed,
the ventilator settings should be adjusted appropriately.

397

VetBooks.ir

398

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

The thorax is next auscultated bilaterally to ensure breath
sounds are audible. Next, other monitoring parameters
are evaluated (e.g., blood pressure, ECG, pulse oximeter,
ETCO2, etc.). Once the patient appears stable, serial arterial blood gas analysis is ideal for accurate titration of ventilator settings. If an arterial blood sample is not available,
a venous blood gas can be used to assess PCO2 if cardiac
output is not excessively low. The evaluation of oxygenation by pulse oximetry is the standard of care in some settings (e.g., human neonatology) and may serve as both a
noninvasive alternative and a means of reducing iatrogenic blood loss.
Goals of Mechanical Ventilation
The goal of IPPV therapy is to maintain acceptable
blood gas values with the lowest level of ventilator support possible. The optimal ventilator settings for each
individual patient cannot be predicted and are determined through a careful process of trial and error. The
patient should be fully evaluated after every change in
ventilator settings, including blood gas analysis whenever possible. It is advisable to make only one change in
ventilator settings at a time in order to accurately evaluate what effect each change alone has on gas exchange.
Whenever feasible, it is advised to allow 15 minutes to
pass before reevaluating PaCO2. Whole‐body stores of
carbon dioxide are quite large and a quarter of an hour
or more may be required for a new steady state to be
reached. Common blood gas goals of mechanical ventilation include a PaO2 of 80–120 mmHg (or SpO2 >95%)
and a PaCO2 of 35–55 mmHg (35–40 mmHg in patients
with intracranial hypertension).
In some settings, permissive hypercapnia may be
employed. In this approach, PaCO2 is allowed to climb
higher to 60–70 mmHg as long as the resultant acidemia
does not become too severe (pH <7.1). This approach is
often taken when the clinician fears that maintaining
carbon dioxide tensions within the normal target range
will require injurious ventilator settings. Permissive
hypoxemia approaches may also be employed at times.
With this approach, the clinician focuses on maintaining
central venous hemoglobin saturations (SCVO2) above
65–68%. Hypoxemia (PaO2 <80 mmHg) is tolerated as
long as tissue oxygen delivery appears adequate based on
SCVO2 readings. This approach reflects a school of
thought in which it is felt that clinicians should focus
more on maintaining adequate global oxygen delivery
rather than arterial blood gas values.
Adjustments to Improve PaO2
If the PaO2 is higher than the desired range (>120–
150 mmHg), the first priority should be to decrease the

FiO2 until it is <60%. Once FiO2 is less than 60%,
emphasis shifts to reducing PEEP and peak airway
pressure. If the PaO2 is lower than desired (<80 mmHg),
the first option is to increase the FiO2. If there is an
acute and severe drop in PaO2, placing the animal on
100% oxygen is appropriate until the issue can be
resolved and more definitive therapy can be provided.
Ultimately, it is hoped that manipulation of ventilator
settings will increase the oxygenating efficiency of the
lung and allow lowering of the FiO2 once again. All
increases in oxygenation are obtained by raising FiO2,
mean airway pressure, or both. Mean airway pressure
may be increased by increasing peak pressure, respiratory rate, PEEP, inspiratory time, or the format of flow
delivery (e.g., block versus sine versus descending
ramp flow patterns). Acute hypoxemic episodes are
life‐threatening complications that require immediate
intervention.
Adjustments to Improve PaCO2
The PaCO2 is dependent on alveolar minute ventilation, which is the product of the effective tidal volume
(excluding dead space volume) and the respiratory rate.
If the PaCO2 is higher than the desired range then the
respiratory rate, tidal volume, or both should be
increased. If the PaCO2 is too low, the respiratory rate
and/or tidal volume should be decreased. Excessive
gas trapping may lead to carbon dioxide retention.
Increasing expiratory time or reducing I:E ratio may
increase alveolar ventilation in this circumstance. In
patients with lower airway or parenchymal disease,
inspiratory times that are too short may lead to minimal ventilation of alveoli with high time constants
(product of resistance and compliance). In this instance,
prolongation of the inspiratory time may enhance alveolar ventilation.
An abrupt increase in PaCO2 in the ventilator patient
may indicate a life‐threatening complication. Similarly,
an abrupt drop in end‐tidal carbon dioxide may reflect a
sudden increase in physiologic dead space (e.g., pulmonary thromboembolism) or an abrupt reduction in cardiac output.

­Nursing Care for Ventilator Patients
Nursing care of the ventilator patient is one of the most
labor‐intensive and important aspects of ventilator
patient management. Each ventilator patient usually
requires a dedicated caregiver and two or more people
are needed for many of the patient care procedures.
Nursing care includes airway management, oral and eye
care, catheter care, and recumbent patient care.

VetBooks.ir

40 Mechanical Ventilation

Humidification
Anesthetized patients are not able to cough or clear
airway secretions effectively and this can contribute
to development of ventilator‐associated pneumonia
(VAP) and tube occlusion. Airway management is essential in an effort to try to reduce these complications.
Gas flow bypasses the nasal passages during mechanical
ventilation and is therefore not humidified or filtered.
This can lead to a loss of heat and moisture, which can
damage the respiratory epithelium. Humidification is
also critical in making secretions less viscous and easier
to remove.
The breathing circuit should be humidified appropriately without excessive accumulation of liquid in the circuit. There are two basic options for airway humidification:
active heated water humidifiers or passive heat moisture
exchangers. The heated water humidifiers are very effective, are ideal in patients with substantial airway secretions, and help prevent hypothermia, which can be an
issue in small patients. They are expensive and unless
they are used in conjunction with heated wire circuits,
they are associated with substantial “rain out” in the
circuit. This refers to water accumulating in the limbs
of the breathing circuit, which in large volumes can
interfere with ventilator function. More concerning,
it greatly increases the risk of VAP. Heat moisture
exchangers (HME) are inexpensive devices that fit on
the end of the endotracheal tube and passively take heat
and moisture from the exhaled gas and return it to the
inhaled gas. They have been found to be equally effective at humidifying the airways as the active humidifiers
and may reduce the incidence of VAP by reducing
moisture in the circuit. They can occlude and this has
the potential to be a life‐threatening event. For this
reason, the authors advise that they be avoided in
patients with excessive airway secretions.
Suctioning
Airway suctioning is another critical aspect of airway
management. There are risks associated with this procedure, and proper technique must be followed. The
inhaled oxygen concentration should be increased to
100% prior to and during suctioning. The suction catheters should be sterile, soft, and flexible with more than
one distal opening and a proximal thumbhole to control
the level of suction. Sterile gloves should be worn and
sterile technique observed throughout the procedure.
Closed suction systems are also available which are helpful in maintaining sterility and preventing issues with
disconnection. Suction should be applied while withdrawing the catheter from the airway for no more than
five seconds at a time. This procedure can be repeated

two or three times as long as the patient’s oxygenation
remains adequate and the patient does not seem distressed. If suctioning is productive, it can be performed
as frequently as every 2–4 hours.
The risks of suction include hypoxemia, patient discomfort, damage to the tracheal mucosa, collapse of
small airways and alveoli, and contamination of the
lower airways.
If the secretions are too dry to suction well or adequate humidification is not being provided, small
­aliquots of sterile saline (0.2 mL/kg) may be instilled
into the airway prior to suctioning. This practice has
been challenged because of the lack of evidence of
beneficial effects coupled with the risk of introducing
infection.
Tracheal Tube Management
Ventilator patients require an artificial airway, which is
most commonly accomplished via endotracheal (ET)
intubation and general anesthesia. It is important that
ET tubes are sterile and ideally have high‐volume/low‐
pressure cuffs. Tracheal mucosal blood flow can be
occluded by pressures over 25–35 mmHg. Ideally, cuff
pressure should be maintained between 20 and 25 mmHg
and measured regularly with a pressure gauge system.
Higher pressures impede mucosal blood flow and may
lead to tracheal necrosis. Lower cuff pressures are associated with an increased risk of aspiration. Although frequently used, the pilot balloons do not correlate well
with cuff pressure and should not be used as an indicator
of appropriate inflation.
Tracheal injury can also be minimized by deflating
the cuff and repositioning the ET tube slightly to
change the pressure point and then reinflating the cuff
every four hours. The mouth and pharynx should be
flushed and suctioned prior to deflating the cuff.
Endotracheal tubes should be securely tied with IV
tubing or another nonporous material, which is less
likely than gauze to become saturated with oral secretions and bacteria. The ties should be moved and
secured in a different position every four hours to minimize lip trauma.
The endotracheal tube may need to be changed every
24–48 hours, depending on the amount and character of
the secretions. It is important to preoxygenate with 100%
oxygen prior to changing the tube and to be prepared for
a difficult intubation. Tracheostomy tubes should ideally
have an inner cannula, which should be cleaned every
four hours. If there is no cannula, the tube should be suctioned regularly and changed every 24 hours. The tracheostomy tube should also have a cuff to protect the
airway from the migration of oral secretions and to allow
PEEP to be used.

Oral Care
Care of the oral cavity is of the utmost importance in
these patients. Oral ulceration is a common problem
and with poor oral care may occur in 90% or more of
patients. Oral ulceration is a primary source of bacterial
proliferation and has been reported as a major cause of
VAP in human PPV patients. Prevention of oral ulceration with careful positioning of mouth gags, keeping
the tongue and mucous membranes moist, and frequent repositioning of the tongue and ET tube are
essential. The mouth and oropharynx should be carefully rinsed and suctioned every four hours. A chlorhexidine rinse of the mouth should be performed
every eight hours.

hours. Other indwelling catheters such as chest tubes
should be cared for as appropriate.

­Complications of Mechanical Ventilation
Hemodynamic Compromise

Ventilator patients are under anesthesia and require eye
care to prevent the development of corneal drying and
ulceration. Artificial tear ointment should be applied at
least every two hours. If an ulcer is suspected, fluorescein
staining should be performed and the patient should be
started on an antibiotic ophthalmic ointment. Temporary
tarsorrhaphy may be necessary in some cases.

Positive pressure ventilation can lead to reductions in
cardiac output in some patients. The associated increase
in intrathoracic pressure can reduce systemic venous
return which in the steady state is equal to cardiac
output. Although animals with higher mean airway
­
­pressures are at greater risk for developing impaired cardiovascular performance, those with significant pulmonary disease tend to have such poorly compliant lungs
that very little of the increased airway pressure is transferred to the cardiovascular system. Hemodynamic compromise secondary to PPV is more of a problem for
animals with concurrent hypovolemia or other causes of
reduced cardiac filling pressures. Continuous heart rate
and blood pressure monitoring is advised for all ventilator patients. Fluid and drug therapy should be given as
appropriate if hypovolemia or volume‐unresponsive
hypotension develops.

Recumbent Patient Care

Ventilator‐Associated Pneumonia

Prolonged recumbency can lead to muscle atrophy,
pressure sores, peripheral edema, and nerve damage.
Patients should be repositioned at least every four
hours and should have passive range of motion exercises performed. Ventilator patients should be kept on
sufficient padding that is changed immediately if soiled.
Frequent changes in body position also help prevent
the pooling of secretions in one region of the airways
and atelectasis of the dependent lung lobes. Turning
may be associated with desaturation in animals with
substantial pulmonary pathology; some patients will
not tolerate lateral recumbency in which case they may
require sternal recumbency with only their hips turned
regularly. Oxygenation should be monitored carefully
after changes in position. Sternal positioning is generally
associated with the best lung function and may be beneficial in hypoxemic patients.

In human medicine, VAP occurs in 10–48% of patients
and leads to an increase in mortality. Endotracheal intubation compromises the normal upper airway defenses
and bacteria from the oral cavity have greater access to
the lower airways. This problem can be compounded by
intermittent aspiration of oral secretions or gastroesophageal contents.
Ventilator‐associated pneumonia is typically diagnosed when new radiographic evidence of pulmonary
infiltrates is detected 48 hours or longer after beginning
IPPV. Decreases in oxygenation, a change in the character of airway secretions, new rhonchi or crackles, changes
in white blood cell count, and new fevers are also common clinical signs associated with VAP. Prevention of
VAP includes maintaining careful oral hygiene standards, including chlorhexidine rinses and the use of sterile
technique when handling the circuit or endotracheal or
tracheostomy tube. Minimizing circuit disconnections is
advised. It is now recommended in some guidelines that
ventilator circuits only be replaced every five days (earlier if gross contamination is evident). Many VAP infections have been found to come from the hands of
caregivers, so wearing gloves and frequent hand washing
are strongly recommended for all those dealing with ventilator patients. Wearing gloves should be considered
mandatory when dealing with the oral cavity.

Eye Care

Catheter Care
All indwelling catheters should receive diligent catheter
care as ventilator patients are at high risk for secondary
infections and catheters provide possible entry sites for
microorganisms. Urinary catheters require appropriate
cleaning and care every eight hours. Intravascular catheters should be unwrapped and cleaned every 24–48

Ventilator‐Induced Lung Injury
Ventilator‐induced lung injury (VILI) describes pulmonary damage that occurs as a result of stresses and strains
placed on lung tissues during PPV. In addition to increasing pulmonary pathology, in human medicine VILI has
been found to increase the incidence of multiple organ
dysfunction and patient mortality. It is believed that pulmonary inflammation resulting from VILI leads to the
elaboration of inflammatory mediators, which amplify
the systemic inflammatory response and subsequent
organ damage. Indeed, some have suggested that the
improved outcomes observed with lung‐protective ventilator strategies are not due to improvements in pulmonary performance but rather to reductions in distant
organ damage.
There are several mechanisms by which VILI can
occur. The two major proposed mechanisms are overdistension of the lung by excessive tidal volumes and repetitive alveolar and peripheral airway collapse. Titration of
ventilator settings should always be focused on providing the lowest possible level of ventilator support that
still allows the targeted goals to be achieved. When the
blood gas value goals cannot be achieved despite the use
of high airway pressures and PEEP, a valid alternative
approach is to change the blood gas goals for this particular patient. Permissive hypercapnia or permissive
hypoxemia‐based strategies may be employed in these
instances as described previously.
Oxygen Toxicity
Pulmonary oxygen toxicity is discussed elsewhere in this
text and the interested reader is referred to the appropriate sections (see also Chapter 39).
Pneumothorax
A pneumothorax can occur in the ventilator patient
when alveolar or airway rupture leads to air escaping
from the respiratory tract and accumulating in the pleural space. Although pneumothorax is a major concern
when high airway pressures are present, studies in
human patients have not been able to demonstrate a significant association between airway pressure and the
occurrence of pneumothorax. Rather, the incidence of
pneumothorax seems to vary with the nature of the lung
pathology present. Overdistension of the lung is thought
to be the major cause of pneumothorax. Thus, maintaining low tidal volumes, especially in patients with significant lung disease, is currently recommended.
Pneumothorax can be rapidly progressive in patients
receiving IPPV and it is imperative that it be recognized
early to avoid adverse outcomes. The acute onset of an

elevated PaCO2 and a decreased PaO2 is a common
early warning sign. Airway pressure would be expected
to be increasing if a pneumothorax occurs in a patient
being ventilated with volume control, while tidal volume would decrease if pressure control ventilation is
employed. Auscultation may reveal decreased lung
sounds, but this finding may be difficult to appreciate in
the mechanically ventilated patient. Thoracic radiographs will provide a definitive diagnosis, but are often
impractical. Thoracic ultrasound can also be helpful in
identifying a pneumothorax if the operator is suitably
trained and experienced.
Ultimately, a pneumothorax can be rapidly fatal in the
ventilator patient. If there is any doubt that one is present, a diagnostic thoracocentesis should be performed
immediately. If a pneumothorax is detected, unilateral or
bilateral chest tubes are likely to be required.
Weaning from Mechanical Ventilation
Weaning (or liberation) from the ventilator is generally
an ongoing process of gradual reduction in the ventilator
settings. Often, as the patient improves, the mode of ventilation may be changed to one that requires the animal
to perform an ever‐increasing proportion of the work of
breathing. SIMV and pressure support modes are often
employed for this purpose. If animals have been anesthetized for prolonged periods of time, it may take some
time (hours to days) for them to recover adequate ventilatory capacity. Some anesthetic protocols (e.g., barbiturates) employed for IPPV may have very prolonged
withdrawal periods. It is important to consider reducing
or changing the anesthetic drugs administered when
patients begin to improve and weaning becomes a realistic possibility.
Prior to discontinuance of IPPV, the patient should first
obtain certain physiologic goals, including the following:
the original disease process is stable or improving
a stable and appropriate level of respiratory drive has
been demonstrated
●● the patient no longer requires significant ventilator
support to achieve adequate gas exchange
●● adequate gas exchange efficiency has been restored
(i.e., PaO2:FiO2 ratio consistently above 200; greater
than 300 is preferred).
●●
●●

Reasons to suspect that a patient is not ready to be
weaned include cardiovascular instability, requirement
of high FiO2 (greater than 60%), high peak inspired airway pressures (>25 cmH2O), and/or high PEEP levels
(>5 cmH2O).
When a patient has improved sufficiently to consider
removing them from the ventilator, it is advised to first
determine if they can maintain spontaneous breathing

401

VetBooks.ir

402

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

while still intubated. During such a “spontaneous breathing trial,” the patient requires frequent, intensive monitoring. CPAP is often an ideal mode to use during a
spontaneous breathing trial as the tidal volume, respiratory rate, and end‐tidal carbon dioxide can all still be
closely monitored. The development of hypoxemia,
hypercapnia, hyperthermia, tachycardia, hypotension,
and/or tachypnea are all indications that the trial has
failed. Hypertension and the development of a rapid,
shallow breathing pattern are common markers used in
the authors’ practice to identify weaning failure. Positive
pressure ventilation should be reinstituted once weaning
failure has been identified.
In human medicine, it is frequently recommended to
perform spontaneous breathing trials daily once the
patient qualifies according to the criteria listed above.
When the patient can maintain adequate blood gases

without anxiety or fatigue, anesthesia can be discontinued and extubation performed.

­Nursing Care
No chapter on mechanical ventilation would be complete
without acknowledging the absolute requirement for
skilled, highly trained technicians. Patients receiving IPPV
require continuous monitoring and care. In the authors’
practice, the patient:nurse ratio for ventilator patients is
always 1:1. Additional nursing staff needs to be available
as required for turning, airway and oral hygiene, circuit
changes, and many other nursing procedures. Large numbers of highly skilled veterinary technicians are required
to provide mechanical ventilator support and may be the
single largest determinant of outcomes in many cases.

Approach to the Patient with Shock
James W. Barr, DVM, DACVECC
Blue Pearl Veterinary Partners, Tampa, FL, USA

Shock is a clinical entity that veterinarians come into con­
tact with regularly and is defined as inadequate delivery or
usage of oxygen at the cellular and subcellular level. The
result of cellular and tissue hypoxia is the central driver of
the pathology of shock. Subsequently, resolving this
hypoxia must be the clinician’s primary focus to effectively
treat a patient in shock. Cellular hypoxia results in the fail­
ure of energy‐dependent mechanisms. When cells lack
the necessary energy, dysfunction of the organelles occurs
which ultimately results in the death of the cell. When
cells die, organs become dysfunctional and compensatory
mechanisms meant to be protective instead exacerbate
injury and lead to the death of the organism.
Classically, shock has been defined as lack of organ
perfusion resulting from the impaired ability of the car­
diovascular system to deliver oxygen to the tissues of the
body. This can result from many diseases, but the global
effects are similar regardless of cause. There are clinical
situations in which the delivery of oxygen to the tissues is
normal or increased whilst the tissues are unable to use
the oxygen presented to them that can lead to shock.
This, fortunately, is not recognized often in veterinary
medicine so this chapter will focus on the failure of oxy­
gen delivery rather than failure of oxygen utilization.
It is often helpful to classify shock states according to
their underlying etiology. This enables formation of a
general treatment plan. In general, shock can be classified
as hypovolemic, cardiogenic, distributive, or obstructive.
Hypovolemic shock occurs when intravascular volume is
reduced, resulting in decreased cardiac output. This can
include whole‐blood loss (hemorrhagic shock) or loss of
plasma volume. Cardiogenic shock is a result of poor car­
diac function that reduces cardiac output. Distributive
shock develops from inappropriate vasodilation and
decreased resistance to blood flow lowering blood pres­
sure despite normal or even increased cardiac output.
Obstructive shock is a result of physical impedance of

diastolic filling of the heart and subsequent decrease in
cardiac output. It is possible for patients to fit more than
one category and limiting classification to a single cate­
gory can lead the clinician astray. For instance, patients
that are septic may have shock that has characteristics of
hypovolemic, cardiogenic, and distributive etiologies.
In addition to categorizing etiology, shock can be char­
acterized by severity as either compensated or decom­
pensated. The sympathetic nervous system attempts to
compensate for perceived decreases in intravascular vol­
ume and/or blood pressure, generating some of the clini­
cal signs associated with shock. While the etiologies
vary, there are commonalities in the clinical signs of
shock. The recognition of shock centers on identifying
the compensatory mechanisms the patient displays in
response to decreased oxygen delivery. If a patient is in
the compensated phase of shock, the sympathetic nerv­
ous system has been activated and the subsequent
increases in chronotropy, inotropy, and systemic vascu­
lar resistance (SVR) will all converge to increase oxygen
delivery. Patients in compensated shock will often have a
normal blood pressure and mentation on presentation,
but will likely have other clinical signs suggestive of
shock such as tachycardia and tachypnea. If the initiating
cause of shock has been removed then patients in com­
pensated shock may not progress further.
If the underlying etiology of shock is severe or persis­
tent, compensatory mechanisms will be unable to restore
oxygen delivery and the patient will progress to decom­
pensated shock. These animals will have profound clini­
cal signs including depressed mentation, cold extremities,
thready pulses, and hypotension. If left untreated,
patients in decompensated shock will generally progress
to an irreversible shock state in which compensatory
mechanisms cease to function. This is termed autoregulatory escape and results from global vasodilation as oxy­
gen‐starved tissues finally demand blood flow. Clinical

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

signs of autoregulatory escape include venous pooling,
bradycardia, and hypotension unresponsive to fluids or
vasopressors and eventual death.
There are some specific treatments for each type of
shock, but key similarities exist between all categories.
The ultimate goal in the treatment of shock is to restore
homeostasis by ensuring adequate oxygen delivery to the
tissues. For the most part, these treatments do not
address the underlying cause of shock; rather, they are
nonspecific augmentations of oxygen delivery. The ideal
treatment of shock would prevent death, allow the
patient time to heal from the initiating insult, and limit
ongoing injury as much as possible.

Chemoreceptors are sensory organs responsible for
monitoring the blood for appropriate concentrations of
key chemicals, primarily oxygen and carbon dioxide. The
carotid bodies, which are located near the carotid bifur­
cation, sense oxygen tension and the partial pressure of
carbon dioxide (CO2) in arterial blood. The aortic body,
located in the aortic root, senses pressure in addition to
oxygen and carbon dioxide tension and pH of arterial
blood. These chemoreceptors send signals to the medulla
oblongata to regulate breathing and blood pressure and
are a potent mechanism by which respiratory rate and
heart rate are controlled.
Compensatory Mechanisms

­Pathophysiology of Shock and Effect
on Organ Systems
Cellular Effects of Hypoxia
Shock occurs due to failure of oxygen delivery to the tis­
sues which results in cellular and mitochondrial hypoxia.
The resulting anaerobic metabolism leads to a significant
decrease in production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP)
with generation of lactate as a byproduct causing acido­
sis at both local and systemic levels.
The ATP deficiency that occurs during shock has numer­
ous detrimental effects on the cell. ATP‐dependent trans­
port proteins cease to function and membrane gradients of
electrolytes are lost. This results in cellular swelling, cellu­
lar death, and ultimately organ dysfunction if enough cel­
lular death occurs. Cell death resulting from hypoxia is
usually necrotic and not apoptotic, and can therefore
induce an inflammatory response. This organ failure, if not
corrected in time, results in the death of the organism.
Sensors of Cardiovascular Homeostasis
In order to maintain homeostasis, volume, pressure
(baroreceptors), and chemical status (chemoreceptors) of
the blood must be monitored at all times. This is the job
of afferent sensors in various parts of the body capable of
sensing a change in one or more of these variables. These
sensors send signals primarily to the autonomic nervous
system and if an abnormality is detected, cause physio­
logic responses intended to reestablish homeostasis.
Baroreceptors are mechanoreceptors located within
the walls of vessels that are excited with stretch of the
vessel wall (pressure) and are important for the beat‐
to‐beat regulation of blood pressure. The information
collected by baroreceptors is used to regulate the func­
tion of the heart, vascular smooth muscle tone, and
endocrine responses aimed at managing intravascular
volume.

During shock, hypoxia is sensed centrally which prompts
the firing of the respiratory center efferent nerves,
increasing the respiratory rate in an effort to raise the
amount of fresh gas presented to the alveoli to ensure
oxygen extraction from the atmosphere is maximized.
Control of cardiac output is regulated by the autonomic
nervous system. The sympathetic branch of the auto­
nomic nervous system acts on the areas of the heart that
have pacemaking capability (i.e., sinoatrial node, atria,
atrioventricular node ventricles). Sympathetic stimula­
tion results in an increase in sinoatrial node rate of firing,
decrease in atrioventricular node delay, and increase in
speed of the spread of an action potential through the
specialized myocardial conduction system. Sympathetic
stimulation directly increases the strength of contractility
through the action of epinephrine stimulating beta‐1‐
adrenergic receptors. Indirectly, sympathetic stimulation
increases inotropy by increasing vascular tone through
arteriolar vasoconstriction, increasing resistance to blood
flow (systemic vascular resistance) and blood pressure.
Preferential vasoconstriction shunts blood flow away
from peripheral sites and to the brain and heart, increas­
ing preload and causing a reflex increase in inotropy.
The parasympathetic branch of the autonomic nerv­
ous system regulates chronotropy (heart rate). Para­
sympathetic stimulation slows the heartbeat with little
effect on the strength of ventricular contractions. In
shock, parasympathetic tone is reduced to increase the
heart rate. The net result of the increase in sympathetic
tone and decrease in parasympathetic tone is increased
inotropy and chronotropy. As a consequence, most
patients in shock exhibit tachycardia. Patients with
hyperkalemia or in the decompensatory phase of shock
may demonstrate bradycardia, however.
Other less immediate compensatory mechanisms are
also activated during shock. The renin‐angiotensin‐
aldosterone system (RAAS) is activated and a nonos­
motic release of antidiuretic hormone in response to
hypotension occurs. Both of these responses attempt to

VetBooks.ir

41 Approach to the Patient with Shock

expand intravascular volume by inducing retention of
water. This process takes hours to days to occur and is
therefore of little use in the immediate compensatory
attempt to return homeostasis.
Macro‐ and Microcirculation
Clinicians often consider shock to be a macrocircula­
tory phenomenon (i.e., an absolute decrease in blood
flow and perfusion in large arteries). It must be remem­
bered, however, that the purpose of the entire circula­
tory system is to deliver blood through the capillaries
(microcirculation) to exchange oxygen and nutrients
and remove waste products from individual tissue beds.
While arteriolar constriction will increase global pres­
sures and improve macrocirculatory parameters, it can
reduce blood flow to the capillary or downstream side of
the arterioles.
Under normal conditions, arteriolar tone changes
from minute to minute depending on the metabolic
demand of the particular tissue bed in which it is located.
If a tissue demands more or less oxygen, concentrations
of metabolites including adenosine, oxygen, and carbon
dioxide will cause vasoconstriction or vasodilation. This
is termed chemical autoregulation and is key in coupling
blood flow to the metabolic needs of the tissue. In shock
states, however, sympathetic stimulation causes vaso­
constriction and overrides local tissue autoregulatory
mechanisms. This often reduces perfusion of the tissues
supplied by the constricted arterioles and, if oxygen con­
sumption is higher than oxygen delivery, will result in the
onset of anaerobic metabolism.
It is possible, if not common, for a patient in shock to
have normal or even increased cardiac output and blood
flow to the level of the arterioles yet have poor flow
through the capillaries. This alteration in microcircula­
tion is especially significant in septic shock and ischemia/
reperfusion injury.

­Diagnosis
A key feature of shock is that all organ systems are
affected due to a global decrease in oxygen delivery, dif­
ferentiating shock from local perfusion derangements.
Due to the systemic nature of shock, the compensatory
mechanisms in place are meant to preferentially perfuse
the organ systems most important for immediate sur­
vival. This means that the brain and heart are perfused at
the expense of the abdominal viscera such as the kidneys,
gastrointestinal (GI) tract, and liver. Therefore, the clini­
cal signs of shock represent the compensatory changes
that occur in response to, rather than directly from, the

cause of shock, meaning the underlying etiology of shock
may not be evident on initial physical exam since similar
clinical signs are present in all types of shock.
Tachycardia is one of the most consistent clinical signs
of shock and although it is a frequent finding, the etiol­
ogy is often multifactorial. The origin of tachycardia
typically belongs in one of three categories: related to
pain or anxiety, related to an appropriate physiologic
compensatory mechanism, or due to primary cardiac
disease. As usual, cats provide a notable exception to this
generalization and frequently present bradycardic, as do
dogs in the decompensatory or terminal stage of shock.
In general, bradycardia in the context of shock should be
considered a negative clinical sign and if recognized,
should elicit a rapid and diligent search for the underly­
ing reason for shock.
Pale mucous membranes can represent either anemia
or vasoconstriction and mucous membrane evaluation
provides a very crude assessment of hemoglobin
­concentration and microcirculation. While it is possi­
ble that a patient in shock is anemic, more commonly
mucous membrane pallor is due to vasoconstriction.
Capillary refill time (CRT) reflects the amount of time
it takes for blood to fill the capillaries after they have
been forcibly evacuated and provides an estimate of
the efficiency of microcirculation. Normal CRT ranges
from one to two seconds and prolongation of the CRT
would reflect microcirculatory disturbance. Patients
with pallor typically have a slow or difficult to evaluate
CRT due to anemia preventing appreciable blanching
of the mucous membranes. Occasionally, patients will
have bright red mucous membranes and faster than
normal CRT. This finding suggests the patient has vaso­
dilation in conjunction with normal or high cardiac
output and this occurs most frequently in septic shock
or in shock associated with heat stroke. It does not
imply that these patients have better than normal per­
fusion. Similarly, patients can have dark or dusky
mucous membranes and a prolonged CRT indicating
the presence of vasodilation and decreased cardiac
output, as is seen in cardiogenic shock. Patients with
these findings can have significant perfusion deficien­
cies and the clinician should seek to treat these patients
aggressively.
Weak pulses are inconsistently present in shock. If the
animal is in the compensated stage of shock, there is
likely sufficient blood pressure to generate a detectable
pulse. Some clinicians use the presence of a pulse in dif­
ferent areas of the vascular tree to give an estimate of
blood pressure and argue that detection of pulses in the
dorsal pedal artery and in the femoral artery represent
systolic pressures of 80 mmHg and 60 mmHg respec­
tively. There is limited evidence to support this finding
in veterinary medicine and quantitative measurement of

405

VetBooks.ir

406

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

blood pressure should always be used when available.
A systolic blood pressure of less than 90 mmHg or a
mean arterial pressure (MAP) of less than 60 mmHg
should be aggressively pursued.
Numerous factors can confound the interpretation of
pulses in clinical cases. Since the pulse that is palpated is
the difference between the systolic and diastolic pres­
sures, a small difference will cause the pulse to be weak or
thready and a large difference will cause the pulse to be
strong or bounding. None of these descriptions reflect
the actual pressure within the vessel, and all of these pulse
qualities can represent a patient in shock. An obstruction
to blood flow can also inhibit the detection of pulses, as is
the case in aortic thromboembolism by causing an abso­
lute reduction in blood flow through the artery.
Patients in shock also frequently demonstrate tachyp­
nea as the body attempts to maximize oxygen delivery to
the alveoli and subsequently to the arterial blood.
Respiratory rates in excess of 40 breaths per minute for a
dog and 60 breaths per minute for a cat are consistent
with shock. In this instance, tachypnea must be differen­
tiated from true dyspnea or respiratory distress, the
presence of which may indicate an underlying etiology
but does not lead to a diagnosis of shock. Tachypnea is
also a common response to pain, which may confound
the use of respiratory rates for evaluation of possible
shock. Often, evaluating the respiratory rate after admin­
istration of analgesia provides a better representation of
the patient’s ventilatory status.
Altered mentation is seen in patients in decompen­
sated shock as blood flow and oxygen delivery to the
brain are reduced. Since the brain has high demands for
energy and little reserve for energy production, cerebral
function and consciousness are affected early after
decompensation begins. The typical patient in compen­
sated shock will appear bright and alert while the patient
in early decompensated shock will be mildly to moder­
ately obtunded. As shock progresses so will mentation
change and patients that find themselves in late decom­
pensated shock will appear severely obtunded to stupor­
ous. Pain can also affect a patient’s response to its
environment and care should be taken to ensure that
changes in behavior are in fact due to altered mentation
rather than pain. Evaluation of mentation is especially
relevant in cases with head trauma when the level of con­
sciousness can be used as a prognostic sign or metric of
the severity of injury. In these cases, shock and pain
should be addressed before those assessments are made
or at the very least, they should be interpreted with these
facts in mind.
The GI tract is affected in almost all cases of shock as
evidenced by the ubiquity of the term “shock gut.” Recall
that the GI tract is one of the organ systems that is sacri­
ficed in order to divert the scarce blood flow toward the

heart and brain. This decrease in splanchnic blood flow
has a significant impact on the mucosal integrity of the
GI tract, leading to the vomiting and hemorrhagic diar­
rhea often seen in shock. As with most of the exam find­
ings associated with shock, GI signs are usually mild to
absent in animals in the compensatory stages of shock
and can be moderate to severe in animals that have pro­
gressed to the later stages of decompensated shock.
The use of biomarkers for detection of shock and co‐
morbidities has become widely accepted as standard of
care in human medicine. These measurements (i.e., elec­
trolytes, blood glucose, creatinine) can provide impor­
tant information regarding the underlying cause of shock
in addition to aiding in its recognition and diagnosis.
Biochemical abnormalities can be prognostic or diag­
nostic and can direct the clinician to appropriate thera­
peutic interventions. All patients in shock should have a
blood gas profile with lactate as a part of the initial and
ongoing evaluation of the patient whenever possible.
Lactate is an important marker of tissue perfusion and
has been the most widely used biomarker of shock in vet­
erinary patients. Lactate is easily measured in clinical
practice with a range of options from bench‐top blood
gas analyzers to handheld monitors that have been vali­
dated in veterinary patients. Blood lactate concentra­
tions greater than 2.5 mmol/L are indicative of significant
anaerobic metabolism and, in a patient with other signs
consistent with shock, should be considered to be diag­
nostic for failure of oxygen delivery.
The availability and use of ultrasound in veterinary
medicine has become very common. While not particu­
larly useful for the diagnosis of shock itself, ultrasound
has become especially useful because it allows identifica­
tion of the etiology faster. The use of focused assessment
with sonography for trauma (FAST) protocols for the
abdomen (AFAST) and thorax (TFAST) have been very
well described in veterinary medicine. These techniques
can be performed with minimal training and are quite
effective at the identification of fluid in cavities as well as
the presence of a poorly contracting heart or pneumo­
thorax. If available, and as long as positioning and
restraint will not be detrimental to the patient, ultra­
sound should be used to evaluate patients in shock to
attempt to determine the underlying cause. A descrip­
tion of the FAST procedures is provided in Chapter 46.

­Classification of Shock
The following provides a guide to the classification of
shock. The categorization of shock can be beneficial for
formulating a diagnostic and therapeutic approach to a
patient. While clinically useful, it should be reiterated
that a patient in shock might often have disease processes

VetBooks.ir

41 Approach to the Patient with Shock

occurring that overlap categories, and it is possible that
categorization may change as the underlying pathology
progresses. Therefore, a singular approach to each spe­
cific shock category is not possible.
Hypovolemic Shock
Hypovolemic shock occurs when there is an absolute or
perceived decrease in the intravascular volume. This is
the classic example of shock and is arguably the most
common cause of shock in veterinary patients.
Hypovolemic shock can result from a loss of whole blood,
loss of sodium‐rich fluid (plasma) or in severe cases lack
of adequate water intake. Chronic endocrine diseases can
occasionally present as a unique subset of hypovolemic
shock. As an example, a patient in a hypoadrenicortical
(Addisonian) crisis may be hypovolemic but may not
exhibit the typical clinical signs of shock.
Hemorrhagic shock is the classic example of hypov­
olemic shock. A distinguishing characteristic that sets
hemorrhagic shock apart from other causes of hypov­
olemic shock is the absolute loss of whole blood, which
can occur as overt blood loss from the laceration of a ves­
sel or covert blood loss resulting from cavitary bleeding.
A complicating component of hemorrhagic shock is the
necessary loss of red blood cell mass concurrent with the
loss of intravascular fluid. Patients suffering from hem­
orrhagic shock may only have shock completely amelio­
rated by the administration of both IV fluids and
hemoglobin‐containing products.
Cardiogenic Shock
Cardiogenic shock results from an inability of the heart
to move blood into the pulmonary or systemic circula­
tion. This is classically imagined to be a result of “for­
ward failure” of the heart due to the heart being unable to
maintain forward blood flow. As in the case of congestive
heart failure, this may occur in the face of normal or
increased preload. Due to the unique etiology and treat­
ment approach to cardiogenic shock, a closer examina­
tion will be made in Chapter 42.
Distributive Shock
Distributive shock describes shock that occurs primarily
due to loss of systemic vascular resistance (i.e., blood
pressure). This is most often a result of inappropriate
vasodilation resulting in decreased venous flow and thus
decreased preload. Recall that in the absence of signifi­
cant heart disease, preload is positively correlated with
cardiac output. Besides the decrease in cardiac output
that occurs in distributive shock, regional perfusion is
disrupted with loss of blood pressure.

The classic example of distributive or vasodilatory
shock is anaphylaxis whereby massive vasodilation low­
ers blood pressure to such a degree that capillary blood
flow decreases. This reduction in capillary blood flow
limits oxygen delivery to the tissues and results in tissue
oxygen debt. In addition to vasodilation, an increase in
the permeability of the capillaries results in a higher than
normal net movement of water from the intravascular
space to the interstitial space, further decreasing intra­
vascular volume and worsening hypotension.
Neurogenic shock is an uncommon manifestation of
CNS injury specifically in the brain, cervical or thoracic
spinal cord and results from a decrease in sympathetic
tone leading to significant loss of systemic vascular
resistance. The presumed mechanism behind this rapid
vasodilation is disruption of the autonomic paths in the
spinal cord and is different from “spinal shock,” which
refers to the temporary loss of function of the spinal cord
after spinal cord trauma.
Obstructive Shock
Obstructive shock results from impairment of blood
return to the heart. It is typically associated with intraab­
dominal disease that sequesters blood within the abdo­
men and decreases preload (e.g., gastric dilation and
volvulus [GDV]). Some argue that pericardial effusion
with cardiac tamponade is a form of obstructive shock.
Similar to GDV, during pericardial tamponade the intra­
pericardial pressure is higher than the venous pressure
and results in decreased preload of the right atrium.
Septic Shock
Septic shock can be considered a form of distributive
shock but has enough unique characteristics that it is
often classified as a separate entity. As a result of infec­
tion and systemic inflammation, fluid is lost to the
interstitium, water intake is decreased, systemic vascu­
lar resistance decreases, and myocardial performance is
impaired. The therapy for septic shock must address
each of these in turn as well as the underlying cause of
sepsis. Septic shock will be investigated in detail in
Chapter 43.

­Oxygen Delivery
At its most basic, there are two primary components of
oxygen delivery: cardiac output (CO) and arterial oxygen
content (CaO2). Therefore, a useful way to approach the
treatment of shock is to separate the components of the
cardiovascular system into the individual determinants

407

VetBooks.ir

408

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

of oxygen delivery (DO2). In fact, only seven parameters
can be manipulated to augment oxygen delivery: those
associated with cardiac output (heart rate, preload [end‐
diastolic volume], afterload [MAP], systemic vascular
resistance, and ejection fraction), and those associated
with arterial oxygen content (hemoglobin concentration
and partial pressure of inspired oxygen).
Cardiac Output
Cardiac output is determined by the amount of the blood
ejected from the heart with each beat (stroke volume)
and the rate at which the heart is beating (heart rate).
Stroke volume, in turn, is determined by the amount of
blood that returns to the heart (preload), the force that
must be overcome to eject blood out of the heart (after­
load/systemic vascular resistance), and the physical force
that the heart must generate to move blood (contractility
or inotropy). Cardiac output is arguably the easiest com­
ponent of DO2 to manipulate. Accordingly, increasing
preload is the most common initial treatment of shock
and is accomplished with the administration of IV fluids
and vasoactive medications to augment preload by
increasing venous pressure and consequently right ven­
tricular volume.
The heart has the ability to increase or decrease the
force of contraction (inotropy) exerted during systole.
Intrinsically, the heart pumps more powerfully when
there is a larger amount of blood present in the ventricle
at the end of diastole (Starling law of the heart).
Sympathetic stimulation can also increase the force of
contraction and is in fact the primary mechanism by
which inotropy can be altered by the clinician through
administration of beta‐1‐adrenergic agonists.
The impediment of flow that must be overcome to
eject blood out of the heart is the systemic vascular
resistance (afterload). This is the force that the cardiac
wall is placed under when it contracts in systole and is
usually considered as the mean arterial blood pressure
(MAP). Although convenient, this is not always accurate.
As an example, MAP and afterload are uncoupled when
an anatomic obstruction to flow exists, such as subaortic
stenosis. Manipulation of afterload (SVR and MAP) is
possible through the administration of agents acting on
specific vasoactive receptors (alpha, dopamine, and vas­
opressin). Most frequently, the goal is to increase both
SVR and MAP. Afterload reduction is infrequently a con­
cern in veterinary patients although it is common in
humans due to that species’ propensity for developing
primary hypertension.
Heart rate changes are important for the second‐to‐
second adjustment of cardiac output. During shock,
increases in heart rate typically parallel increases in inot­
ropy. Clinically, heart rate measurement is a useful tool

for diagnosing a patient in shock. Heart rate can be
manipulated pharmacologically with beta‐2‐adrenergic
agonists and anticholinergic drugs. However, the ability
of changes in heat rate to improve cardiac output is lim­
ited. Diastolic filling time is essential for preload and
tachycardia shortens the amount of time spent in dias­
tole during the cardiac cycle. At very high heart rates,
this shortened diastolic time can significantly decrease
preload and cardiac output. Patients in the decompensa­
tory stage of shock can become absolutely or relatively
bradycardic as the heart begins to fail due to poor oxygen
delivery to the heart itself.
Arterial Oxygen Content
Oxygen content of the blood is the sum of the oxygen
dissolved in the blood (PaO2) and the amount of oxygen
that is bound to hemoglobin. The amount of oxygen
bound to hemoglobin is a much more important con­
tributor to total blood oxygen content while PaO2 is a
more important indicator of the lungs’ ability to oxygen­
ate the blood.
Interventions directed at improving arterial oxygen
content include provision of supplemental oxygen
(increasing PaO2) and transfusion of hemoglobin in
the form of red blood cells or hemoglobin‐based oxy­
gen carriers (increasing oxygen‐carrying capacity).
The importance of hemoglobin concentration in oxy­
gen delivery cannot be overstated. Hemoglobin makes
the transport of oxygen in the blood and subsequent
offloading at the tissue bed much more efficient.
Consequently, raising hemoglobin is the best way to
improve arterial oxygen content if lung function and
ventilation are normal. Supplementation of oxygen to
those patients who are normoxic (have a normal PaO2)
will do little to increase the amount of oxygen pre­
sented to the tissues (assuming the supplementation is
at normal atmospheric pressure) when compared
to supplementation of hemoglobin. Consider a dog
breathing room air; assuming a hemoglobin concen­
tration of 6 g/dL (HCT 18%), PaO2 of 90 mmHg, and
arterial hemoglobin saturation (SaO2) of 95%, the cal­
culated CaO2 would be 8.0 mL O2/dL. By increasing
the fraction of inspired oxygen to 40%, the resultant
CaO2 would increase to 8.55 mL O2/dL for an 8%
increase. Now assume raising the hemoglobin with no
oxygen supplementation. By increasing the hemo­
globin concentration to 9 g/dL (HCT 28%), a CaO2 of
12 mL O2/dL can be achieved for a 54% increase. In
order to extract the most benefit from an increase in
hemoglobin concentration, it must be maximally satu­
rated with oxygen so oxygen supplementation is always
warranted during shock to ensure the highest possible
PaO2 is achieved.
