­Treatment
If possible, the treatment of shock should be directed at
the underlying cause and should be aggressive and com­
prehensive. Most patients in shock can be initially resus­
citated in a similar or identical manner with a few notable
exceptions. If the patient has an obvious cause of shock
with tachycardia without significant heart disease pre­
sent or suspected, then fluid therapy is almost always
beneficial. In cases of hypovolemic, distributive, or
obstructive shock, increasing intravascular volume often
results in significant improvement. The exception to
fluid administration for shock is cardiogenic etiology.
The type and dose of fluid administered for shock are
among the most controversial topics in medicine. In
most circumstances, isotonic crystalloids are as effective
or better, as safe or safer, and less expensive than any of
the other choices for the initial resuscitation of shock.
There are subtle nuances, with different resuscitative
fluid strategies for specific disease states, but in general
replacement crystalloid fluids are suitable choices.
The traditional dose of fluids for patients in shock for
dogs and cats respectively is 90 mL/kg and 60 mL/kg of
crystalloid fluids. This represents approximately one
blood volume that is intended to be administered over a
short period of time. Many patients do not require an
entire shock dose of fluids to be effectively resuscitated
so the most utilized clinical approach is to divide the
dose into four equal parts and administer the aliquots
until endpoints of resuscitation are reached. Although
effective at restoring circulating volume, the duration of
effect of replacement crystalloids is short due to rapid
redistribution of bolus fluids into the interstitial space.
For this reason, it may be necessary to administer subse­
quent boluses to maintain the desired volume expansion.
Unfortunately, overaggressive resuscitation can lead to
interstitial edema formation and dilutional coagulopa­
thy. Because of this risk, it is necessary to keep track of
the total volume of replacement crystalloid administered
to a patient and to consider alternative methods of resus­
citation if initial crystalloid boluses do not result in last­
ing resolution of shock.
Alternatives to replacement crystalloid fluids include
hypertonic saline, blood products (i.e., fresh frozen
plasma, fresh whole blood or packed red blood cells),
synthetic colloid solutions (i.e., hydroxyethyl starches),
albumin‐based colloid solutions (human serum albumin
or lyophilized canine albumin), hemoglobin‐based oxy­
gen carriers (HBOC), or combination of any of the above.
Of these, hypertonic saline and synthetic colloids are
used the most frequently.
Hypertonic saline has the advantage of being rela­
tively inexpensive and having a long shelf‐life. Doses of
4–6 mL/kg of 7.5% NaCl can be used in nondehydrated

traumatized or hemorrhaging patients and may be par­
ticularly useful for resuscitation of animals with head
trauma. Hypertonic saline recruits fluid from the intra­
cellular space to rapidly increase the intravascular vol­
ume, ­providing much needed volume expansion while
minimizing the risk of overresuscitation and edema for­
mation. Boluses of hypertonic saline can be administered
over a shorter period of time than boluses of isotonic
crystalloid fluids due to the smaller volume required.
Unfortunately, hypertonic saline behaves in a similar
manner to replacement crystalloids, with rapid redistri­
bution of fluid into the interstitial space, and because of
the high osmolarity of hypertonic saline and the absolute
solute load, repeated dosing is not recommended due
to the risk of hypernatremia. Relative or absolute con­
traindications to hypertonic saline include preexisting
­dehydration, hypernatremia or hyperosmolar conditions
(ex. hyperosmolar‐hyperglycemic diabetes mellitus). To
maintain the volume expansion derived from adminis­
tration of hypertonic saline, it is often combined with a
synthetic colloid such as hetastarch (10–20 mL/kg) and
administered together.
Colloids have been used successfully in the resuscita­
tion of patients in shock for years. However, controlled
studies have not consistently shown that colloidal solu­
tions are more effective at achieving resuscitation than
isotonic crystalloids. Theoretically, the use of a colloid
for resuscitation in patients with low serum protein or
those with edematous diseases may be preferred.
Incremental doses of 5 mL/kg of hydroxyethyl starch is
a reasonable starting point, with a total shock dose
equaling 10 mL/kg and 20 mL/kg for cats and dogs
respectively. Clinically, the primary utility of synthetic
colloids for resuscitation is to maintain the duration of
volume expansion achieved with isotonic crystalloids.
Synthetic colloids are almost never used alone for
resuscitation of a patient. Rather, they are co‐adminis­
tered with either isotonic or hypertonic crystalloids. An
effective resuscitation plan would include alternating
administration of isotonic crystalloid and colloid solu­
tions (1/4 volume aliquots of each) until resuscitation
has been achieved. Significant debate exists regarding
the impact of synthetic colloids on coagulation and
platelet function. There is little debate that synthetic
colloids can impair platelet function in vitro, but the
clinical implications are less clear. Perhaps of more clin­
ical import is the potential for synthetic colloids to
induce dilutional coagulopathy. For these reasons, syn­
thetic colloids should be used thoughtfully in patients
with thrombocytopenia/thrombocytopathia or docu­
mented coagulopathy. Ultimately, the clinician should
attempt resuscitation with the method they are most
comfortable with rather than attempting to use a resus­
citation strategy that is unfamiliar.

The use of blood products in shock resuscitation is not
routine since most patients have adequate oxygen‐carry­
ing capacity. If a patient has been administered an ade­
quate volume of fluid for resuscitation, has persistent
clinical signs of shock and requires oxygen‐carrying
capacity, then the administration of blood is indicated.
This can be in the form of packed red blood cells, whole
blood or hemoglobin‐based oxygen carriers. No agreed‐
upon transfusion trigger exists and the decision to
administer blood depends on the chronicity of the ane­
mia and the patient’s clinical signs. For patients with an
acute drop of 30–50% in packed cell volume (PCV), the
administration of blood should be strongly considered.
In these cases, a reasonable goal is to raise the PCV by
15–20% with a minimum PCV target of 20%. Typical
doses of 10 mL/kg of packed red blood cells or 20 mL/kg
of whole blood should be effective.
The actual rate of administration of blood products for
resuscitation will depend on the patient’s condition.
Under ideal circumstances, blood products are adminis­
tered slowly with careful monitoring for transfusion
reactions. Patients in shock, however, do not often have
the benefit of time and bolus administration may be
needed. In this case, care has to be taken as techniques
that apply pressure to the red blood cells or increase
shear stress, such as administration with an infusion bag
through a small‐bore catheter, can result in significant
lysis of transfused cells. When bolusing blood products,
it is best to allow blood to flow by gravity as quickly as
possible. Administration of blood should be through a
dedicated IV catheter, meaning that other resuscitative
fluids should be held during transfusion unless provided
through a different catheter or lumen (in the case of mul­
tilumen catheters). It is safe to administer normal saline
with blood products and co‐administration may improve
the fluid dynamics of the blood product and speed the
delivery rate.
The treatment of pain may be needed in many patients
with shock, and is mandatory if they have been trauma­
tized. In unstable painful patients, pain control should be
achieved with short‐acting pure mu opioid agonists (ex.
fentanyl, hydromorphone, oxymorphone or morphine)
administered via the intravenous or intramuscular route.
The dose should be adequate to effectively treat pain but
not depress respiration. This will help the clinician eval­
uate the patient, as it will mitigate the contribution of
pain to tachycardia. With pain controlled, the presence
of tachycardia likely indicates shock or hypoxia in the
traumatized patient. Typical doses of common analge­
sics are provided in Table 41.1.
Vasopressors and positive inotropes are rarely used
during the initial resuscitation of shock but can be
invaluable for the treatment or management of vasodi­
latory or septic shock that is refractory to resuscitation.

Administration of vasopressors or positive inotropes
should not be performed prior to adequate volume
expansion, with the possible exception of treating car­
diogenic shock due to systolic failure with a positive
inotrope. Clinically, the most frequently used vasopres­
sor during shock is epinephrine administered for the
acute treatment of anaphylaxis. A more detailed discus­
sion of vasopressors can be found in Chapter 43.
Some patients in shock will not be stabilized until the
underlying disease process has been corrected, as is
often the case with obstructive shock. Patients with sig­
nificant amounts of pericardial effusion causing cardiac
tamponade improve dramatically when even a small
amount of fluid is removed, as do patients with GDV fol­
lowing decompression of the abdomen. Patients in
obstructive shock often do not have an absolute volume
deficiency, but increasing preload can transiently
improve the diastolic filling of the heart while prepara­
tions for definitive treatment are under way.

­Reevaluation and Endpoints
of Resuscitation
The importance of reevaluating the patient during and
after resuscitation cannot be overstated. When evaluat­
ing the efficacy of treatment, the clinician expects physi­
ologic signs of shock to resolve. If resolution is not
achieved, further resuscitation is needed or reconsider­
ation of the diagnosis is necessary. As with all medical
treatments, it is necessary to have predetermined end­
points in mind to decide when treatment is no longer
needed. The optimal endpoints of resuscitation have
been debated for a number of years and although rec­
ommendations and general agreement exist, no consen­
sus has been reached. The ultimate endpoints of
resuscitation should tell the clinician when the patient
is out of shock, meaning adequate oxygen delivery to
all tissues has been reestablished. Possible endpoints

include physical exam findings or biochemical variables
(Box 41.1). These should be evaluated before, during,
and after therapy has been instituted.
Normalization of heart rate, respiratory rate, and
CRT as well as improvement of pulse quality have been
traditionally used by clinicians to judge if resuscitation
is complete. These endpoints are intuitive because
they coincide with the findings that are initially used to
determine if a patient is in shock. It follows that when
those findings normalize, resolution of shock has been
achieved. The reality is more complex as physical exam
endpoints can normalize while inadequate oxygen
delivery is ongoing at the cellular and subcellular level.
Therefore, the use of endpoints that include evaluation
of cellular oxygen usage such as lactate, base excess,
and hemoglobin saturation should be incorporated
into all shock treatment plans. In practice, resuscita­
tion should continue until there is resolution of the
physical exam endpoints, at which time analysis of the
biochemical endpoints should be performed. If those
endpoints have been reached then resuscitation is
complete; if biochemical derangements persist then
resuscitation efforts should continue until resolution is
achieved.
Blood Pressure
Blood pressure can be measured in a variety of ways but
is most commonly performed using a Doppler with
sphygmomanometer or a digital monitor with oscilllo­
metric capability. Unfortunately, blood pressure is an
unreliable predictor of perfusion as it is influenced by the
compensatory mechanisms previously discussed. In fact,
a patient can have significant microcirculatory hypoper­
fusion while maintaining normal blood pressure.
However, hypotension does occur as shock progresses
and when present should be aggressively treated with a
target of returning the systolic blood pressure to at least
90 mmHg and MAP to 60 mmHg.

Lactate
Because lactate is a byproduct of anaerobic metabolism,
has a relatively short half‐life and can be measured read­
ily, it is a very useful biomarker for shock. Lactate meas­
urement is an inexpensive adjunct to traditional physical
exam endpoints and its use has become standard of care
in human medicine.
In most cases, elevations in lactate occur secondary to
anaerobic metabolism, so by measuring the concentra­
tion of lactate in a blood sample, the clinician can form
an idea of whether or not anaerobic metabolism is occur­
ring. Occasionally, neoplastic or endocrine diseases can
cause the production of lactate to be higher than the
body’s ability to metabolize it, leading to elevation of
blood lactate concentration. Similarly, significant liver
disease or liver failure can reduce lactate clearance and
lead to hyperlactatemia. When lactate is elevated due to
causes other than anaerobic metabolism, it is termed
type B hyperlactatemia. Occasionally, strenuous exercise
can cause hyperlactatemia. This appears clinically in
patients with prolonged seizures or patients that require
aggressive restraint during examination or blood collec­
tion. These possibilities should be considered when a
patient has a high blood lactate concentration but no
other clinical signs that would indicate the presence of
shock. This is an uncommon occurrence in veterinary
medicine and an animal presented in shock with blood
lactate elevation should be assumed to have inadequate
oxygen delivery until proven otherwise.
The finding of elevated lactate alone does not neces­
sarily mean that global oxygen delivery is inadequate as
local perfusion abnormalities can have significant impact
on lactate concentration. Although absolute lactate con­
centration can be correlated with patient outcomes, lac­
tate clearance following resuscitative efforts is probably a
better prognostic indicator and patients with persistently
elevated lactate concentrations despite aggressive treat­
ment should be considered to have a worse prognosis. As
with all resuscitation endpoints, the results of lactate
measurement must be interpreted in light of the patient’s
clinical condition.
Mixed Venous or Central Venous Oxygen Saturation
Measurement of venous hemoglobin saturation can pro­
vide meaningful insight into the consumption of oxygen
within the body. The hemoglobin saturation of venous
blood is expected to be lower than that of arterial blood.
If this difference is greater than expected, it may indicate
that oxygen‐starved tissues are removing more oxygen
than usual from each hemoglobin molecule. This is best
explained by the oxygen extraction ratio (OER), which is
simply the mathematical ratio of the amount of oxygen

411

VetBooks.ir

412

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

that is delivered to the capillaries via the arteries and the
amount found in the venous blood draining the capillar­
ies. This ratio indicates the proportion of oxygen that
the mitochondria are using versus the amount supplied.
If venous blood has high hemoglobin saturation, then the
mitochondria did not consume as much oxygen as
expected. This may indicate low metabolic rate or mito­
chondrial dysfunction, as seen in sepsis. However, if
venous oxygen saturation is low, it suggests that the
mitochondria are extracting more oxygen than expected
and that an oxygen debt may be present.
Importantly, venous hemoglobin saturation only reflects
the oxygen consumption that is occurring in the tissue bed
that the blood is draining. As an example, if you were to
draw blood from a cephalic vein, you will only be gaining
knowledge about oxygen usage in the distal limb. Blood
drawn from the jugular vein will provide information
about oxygen consumption in the head, including the
brain. Under most circumstances, samples drawn from
the jugular vein are approximately reflective of oxygen
consumption throughout the body, but a better represen­
tation of the global oxygen usage would be venous blood
that has been mixed from all parts of the body. This ideal
sample is retrieved from the pulmonary artery and is
termed the mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2). The
pulmonary artery is not routinely catheterized in people
and even less frequently in veterinary patients, but there is
a strong correlation between mixed venous samples and
central venous samples (ScvO2) obtained from the cranial
vena cava or right atrium. Obtaining an ScvO2 sample is
much more feasible in clinical practice and can prove very
useful for guiding resuscitation efforts.

The most significant advantage of venous hemo­
globin saturation monitoring is that increases in OER
(i.e., lower than expected venous hemoglobin satura­
tion) may be evident before the onset of anaerobic
metabolism, giving the clinician an essential head start
in the treatment of shock. An ScvO2 of <70% indicates
that a patient is experiencing tissue oxygen debt. When
performing resuscitation, therefore, the goal is to main­
tain an ScvO2 of >70%. If this is not possible with the
administration of vascular expansion and vasopressor
support alone then treatment with red blood cells may
be indicated. Venous hemoglobin saturation may be
low for several reasons, including slow capillary transit
time (poor microperfusion), increased tissue demand
for oxygen, low arterial hemoglobin saturation or ane­
mia. Once again, venous hemoglobin saturation should
be interpreted with the patient’s overall condition in
mind.

­Conclusion
A simplified and systematic approach to the patient
in shock is necessary for successful management. It is
easy to become overwhelmed with the totality of clini­
cal implications and lose sight of the ultimate goal.
Approaching shock from the standpoint of oxygen
delivery makes the interventions that need to be
­considered finite and easier to implement. Frequent
reevaluation of the patient through the endpoints of
resuscitation will allow determination of the efficacy
of therapy.

Cardiogenic Shock
Nathan Peterson, DVM, DACVECC1 and James W. Barr DVM, DACVECC 2
1
2

VCA West Los Angeles Animal Hospital, Los Angeles, CA, USA
BluePearl Veterinary Partners, Tampa, FL, USA

­Pathophysiology
Cardiogenic shock occurs when oxygen delivery is insufficient to maintain normal aerobic cellular metabolism
as a result of cardiac dysfunction in the presence of adequate intravascular volume. In other words, cardiogenic
shock occurs when cardiac output is decreased despite
adequate blood volume. Importantly, cardiogenic shock
does not imply congestive heart failure (CHF) although
CHF can be present in cardiogenic shock patients.
Cardiogenic shock occurs in two settings. Forward
failure results from the heart’s inability to adequately
pump blood forward from either the left or right ventricle into either the aorta or main pulmonary artery
respectively. Backward failure, on the other hand, results
from inadequate ventricular filling of the heart during
diastole with a subsequent reduction in stroke volume
and cardiac output. Common conditions resulting in
forward failure of the heart include rupture of one or
more chordae tendinae or acute‐onset severe pulmonary
hypertension. Causes of backward failure include paroxysmal ventricular tachycardia or pericardial tamponade.
Cardiogenic shock is somewhat different from other
forms of shock due to the greater potential impact on the
myocardium. When cardiac dysfunction underlies the
development of shock, coronary perfusion is often
impaired as a result of increased right‐sided pressures or
decreased aortic root pressure. Because of the potential
for decreased coronary perfusion and subsequent
ischemic myocardial injury, it is imperative that cardiogenic shock is recognized early and treated aggressively.
When ventricular function or efficiency is acutely
diminished, cardiac output declines rapidly. If ventricular dysfunction is a result of systolic myocardial failure
(as seen with dilated cardiomyopathy), the force of
­ventricular contractions (inotropy) is not sufficient to
eject a normal volume of blood from the ventricles.

Since stroke volume is one of two determinants of
­cardiac output (cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume), a decrease in inotropy will reduce cardiac output
in a direct fashion unless compensation occurs by
increasing heart rate. Perceived ventricular dysfunction
also occurs when there is a sudden change in valvular
integrity resulting in an acute increase in regurgitant
fraction and decrease in cardiac output. If this occurs, a
large portion of the ventricular load is directed backwards through the atrioventricular valve rather than the
semilunar valves of the aorta or main pulmonary artery.
Although this occurrence is uncommon in the general
population, animals that have existing degenerative valvular disease are at an increased risk of suffering rupture
of one or more of the chordae tendinae.
Bradycardia is an uncommon cause of forward failure
and cardiogenic shock but can occur with third‐degree
atrioventricular block. This condition results in diminished cardiac output as a result of drastic reduction in
heart rate (the other main determinant of cardiac output). Regardless of the inciting cause of forward failure,
the end‐result is an increase in the end‐diastolic ventricular volume with subsequent increases in atrial volumes
and pressures. Cardiogenic shock from forward failure
states is often exacerbated by development of pulmonary
edema and hypoxemia.
Backward failure results from diseases that cause
decreased ventricular volume at end‐diastole. Since the
volume of blood pumped out of the heart is dependent
on the volume of blood present at the beginning of the
cardiac cycle, it follows that any decrease in this volume
will result in diminished cardiac output. The Frank
Starling law of the heart states that the greater the volume of the ventricle at end‐diastole, the more forceful
the corresponding contraction has to be to meet the
demand for greater output, effectively tying preload
(end‐diastolic volume) to cardiac output.

While it is convenient to consider the heart as consisting of two separate pumps (the left and right), it must be
remembered that the two operate in a dependent manner. The right heart is obligated to pump the same volume of blood that is returned to it from the venous
circulation in the same fashion that the left heart is obligated to pump the volume of blood that is returned from
the pulmonary circulation. This interdependence means
that dysfunction of either the left or right heart results in
a decrease in total cardiac output. Therefore, sudden
failure of one side of the heart will result in dysfunction
of the entire heart and can lead to cardiogenic shock.
Once global oxygen delivery is insufficient to maintain aerobic metabolism, the pathophysiology of shock
at the cellular level is identical regardless of the underlying etiology.

­Epidemiology
Many of the conditions that cause cardiogenic shock in
dogs are chronic, progressive diseases that have an acute
worsening. Myxomatous mitral valve disease can predispose dogs to rupturing one or more chordae tendinae,
leading to cardiogenic shock. Unfortunately, the severity
of valvular lesions is not predictive of risk of chordae
tendinae rupture in dogs so little can be done to predict
which patients will suffer from this condition. When
rupture of a first‐order chorda occurs, patients will often
exhibit acute, severe clinical signs. Rupture of second or
third‐order chordae may result in minimal to no clinical
signs and may only be detected during routine echocardiography or necropsy.
Pericardial effusion is arguably the most common
cause of cardiogenic shock in dogs and can occur more
or less acutely. Chronic pericardial effusion is less likely
to result in cardiogenic shock while acute pericardial
effusion almost uniformly causes tamponade and subsequent cardiogenic shock. Acute pericardial effusion can
occur secondary to a rapid bleeding event from a neoplastic lesion associated with the heart (hemangiosarcoma of the right atrium), or from rupture of one of the
vascular structures within the pericardial sac (atrial rupture in dogs or cats with severe left atrial enlargement
secondary to chronic cardiac disease). Idiopathic pericarditis is an uncommon cause of acute pericardial effusion but is a frequent cause of cardiac tamponade in
dogs. Pericardial effusion in cats is rare and infrequently
results in tamponade.
Canine heartworm disease can occur anywhere in the
continental United States, but the incidence reaches 45%
along the Atlantic and Gulf Coast regions and the
Mississippi River region. Caval syndrome can manifest
as cardiogenic shock when dogs have large heartworm

burdens that mature rapidly. The severity of disease is
directly related to worm burden and patient size and
caval syndrome occurs most often when worm burdens
approach 60–100 although it has been reported with
worm burdens as small as 12.
Tachyarrhythmias can result from primary conductional abnormalities such as arrythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) or may be secondary
to structural changes within the heart, as is the case
with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM). In fact, sudden
death due to ventricular tachycardia occurs in up
to 50% of Doberman pinschers affected with DCM.
A rare but severe form of ventricular tachycardia
called Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome can be seen
in dogs or cats with ventricular preexcitation. These
patients are at risk for development of paroxysmal
­ventricular tachycardia due to the establishment of a
reentry circuit that allows for the establishment of a
reciprocating tachycardia and are at increased risk of
developing cardiogenic shock.
Third‐degree atrioventricular (AV) block can result
from progression of a chronic infiltrative cardiac disease,
infectious disease (e.g., Chagas disease), myocarditis or
ingestion of cardiotoxins, including prescription medications (e.g., beta blockers, calcium channel blockers) or
plant alkaloids (e.g., digitalis glycosides). If acute in onset
(not preceded by second‐degree AV block), third‐degree
AV block can result in development of cardiogenic shock
although this is uncommon and usually coincident with
significant structural cardiac disease. Sick sinus syndrome is a disease that occurs primarily in miniature
schnauzers and infrequently in other breeds. It is characterized by periods of severe bradycardia or sinus arrest
with occasional paroxysmal tachycardia resulting in
potentially significant perfusion abnormalities.
Myocarditis is an extremely rare cause of cardiogenic
shock that can be caused by infectious organisms, trauma,
immune‐mediated diseases, and toxins. Infectious causes
of myocarditis include viral (parvo, distemper), bacterial
(various), rickettsial (Bartonella), and protozoal organisms
(Trypanosoma, Toxoplasma), among others. Myocarditis
can induce myocardial failure through a cycle of inflammation, myofiber dropout and fibrosis, the cumulative effect
of which is a clinical syndrome that mimics dilated cardiomyopathy. In general, myocarditis results in a subacute to
chronically progressive form of cardiac dysfunction, but
patients with undiagnosed myocarditis can present with
end‐stage disease in cardiogenic shock.
Rarely, intracardiac neoplasia can result in development of cardiogenic shock by directly affecting blood
flow within the heart itself. Neoplasia associated with
the atrioventricular valves, semilunar valves, right ventricular outflow tract, and right and left atria has been
described. Tumor types that have been reported include

VetBooks.ir

42 Cardiogenic Shock

ectopic thyroid carcinoma, hemangiosarcoma, and osteosarcoma, among others.
Cardiogenic shock in cats occurs infrequently. When it
does occur, it is usually due to cardiomyopathy (dilated
[DCM], restrictive [RCM) or hypertrophic [HCM] with
or without left ventricular outflow tract obstruction
[LVOT]). The clinical importance of LVOT obstruction
in cats with HCM is not fully understood but in cats with
severe LVOT secondary to HCM, the dynamic obstruction of the left ventricular outflow tract can result in significant decreases in cardiac output. A more common
cause of cardiogenic shock in cats is a form of “low‐output” heart failure, usually characterized by hypothermia,
bradycardia, and severe hypotension. This form of heart
failure appears to be more common in cats with RCM
and may be the result of ischemic heart injury.

­Signalment
Cardiogenic shock can occur in a patient of any age or
breed, making it difficult to describe a typical signalment, but because myocardial failure or neoplasia is
often the inciting cause of cardiac dysfunction, these
patients tend to be older middle‐aged to geriatric animals. Pericardial effusion occurs most commonly in
large‐ and giant‐breed dogs, although endocardial ruptures resulting in acute pericardial effusion appear to be
more common in older male small‐breed dogs, with
dachshunds and cocker spaniels being overrepresented.
Young dogs and cats with congenital cardiac abnormalities can develop cardiogenic shock. These patients
are often identified as having a cardiac abnormality during an early veterinary visit and have frequently exhausted
most if not all management options by the time cardiogenic shock develops. Therefore, when it occurs in these
patients, it is usually a terminal, irreversible event.
Canine heartworm disease occurs in middle‐aged dogs
of both sexes. Smaller dogs appear to be at greater risk of
developing caval syndrome and subsequently would be
at greater risk for development of cardiogenic shock,
likely due to the smaller worm burdens required to cause
significant clinical disease in these smaller patients.
Certain breed predispositions for cardiac disease exist
and by extension, these breeds may be at increased
risk for development of cardiogenic shock. Boxer dogs
are much more likely than other breeds to develop
arrythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy while
Doberman Pinschers are considered most at risk for
development of dilated cardiomyopathy. Both of these
conditions can lead to ventricular tachycardia with
­cardiogenic shock. Besides the potential for tachyarrhythmias, dogs with DCM are at risk for systolic failure. Large‐ to giant‐breed dogs are at increased risk for

development of atrial fibrillation. Cats are rarely able to
propagate atrial fibrillation due to their relatively small
atrial mass but cats with severe atrial enlargement due
to cardiomyopathy (Maine Coon, Himalayans) should
be considered to be at risk.

­History and Clinical Signs
A common historical complaint for animals presenting
with cardiogenic shock is collapse or syncope. Owners
commonly describe “seizures” rather than syncope so a
careful history must be taken to determine if intracranial
disease or seizures are in fact a contributing factor. A
thorough history includes the patient’s activity and
behavior immediately preceding and following the event,
state of consciousness during the event, and frequency of
events. Syncope can result from many different cardiac
conditions but brady‐ or tachyarrhythmias and pulmonary hypertension are the most common. Often syncope
in these animals is exercise induced and the occurrence
of syncope at rest should be considered evidence of
advanced disease. If a patient presenting in shock has a
history of syncope or collapse or if the owner describes
exercise‐induced “seizures,” the clinician should be alert
to the potential for a cardiogenic cause of shock. Most, if
not all, patients in cardiogenic shock will present with
acute exercise intolerance or weakness.
Regardless of the underlying cause of cardiogenic
shock, all of these patients will present with perceptible
derangements in perfusion parameters. The mucous
membranes may be pale (evidence of poor perfusion) or
cyanotic (evidence of hypoxemia). Delayed capillary
refill time is an indicator of poor peripheral perfusion. In
cases of severe shock, the mucous membranes may fail to
blanch altogether. Often, the distal extremities will be
cooler to the touch than the trunk. As shock progresses
from compensated to the early, then late decompensatory stages, the mental status will change and the patient
will become obtunded. Patients presenting obtunded to
stuporous are in the late stages of shock and without
timely intervention are likely to die.
As a general rule, patients in cardiogenic shock will
have one or more abnormal findings during cardiac auscultation. Animals with pericardial disease will often
have decreased heart sounds. Auscultation of animals
with myocardial dysfunction may reveal either brady‐ or
tachyarrhythmias. When present, arrhythmias can either
be regular (e.g., sustained ventricular tachycardia) or
irregular (e.g., atrial fibrillation). Cats often have gallop
rhythms although extra heart sounds can be present in
the dog also and usually indicate structural cardiac disease. Increases in adventitial lung sounds (crackles) may
be present in cases with forward failure that results in the

415

VetBooks.ir

416

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

development of pulmonary edema. Occasionally, acute
worsening of a previously detected murmur with or
without development of a precordial thrill is present
and may be indicative of rupture of a first‐order chorda
tendina.
In some instances, as in the case of cardiac tamponade,
the history may be one of subacute progression. Physical
exam findings suggestive of pericardial effusion include
muffled heart sounds, decreased precordial impulse,
detection of pulsus paradoxus (although weak pulses are
also common), and presence of jugular pulses. The finding of ascites and a positive hepatojugular reflex is more
likely to occur in cases of chronic pericardial effusion
and may be absent in the patient presenting with cardiogenic shock.
Respiratory distress may or may not occur as a result of
cardiogenic shock but respiratory failure is rare.
Tachypnea is likely to be present as a result of normal
compensatory mechanisms to improve oxygen delivery.
Significant hypoxia or hypoxemia can occur in situations
such as pulmonary hypertension or pulmonary edema
due to chordae tendinae rupture. For a more in‐depth
discussion on respiratory failure, the reader is referred to
Chapter 39.

­Diagnosis
Unique clinical characteristics of cardiogenic shock
include concurrent hypotension (systolic blood pressure
<90 mmHg or mean arterial pressure <60 mmHg),
decreased cardiac output, and elevated central venous or
left atrial pressures. There is no single diagnostic test
that will confirm the presence of cardiogenic shock.
Rather, the clinician will be forced to reconcile available
diagnostic results (limited by patient stability, availability
within the clinic, and finances) with the patient’s historical findings, presenting complaint, and physical exam
findings to achieve a diagnosis.
When presented with a patient in cardiogenic shock,
the clinician will be faced with the decision about
whether or not the restraint required to perform a diagnostic test is going to be tolerated by the patient.
Unfortunately, it may be necessary to delay or forego
some diagnostic tests that require restraint due to the
tenuous nature of the patient’s condition and every effort
should be made to limit stress to the patient. Staging of
testing can be helpful, focusing efforts on performing
tests in the order most likely to yield meaningful results.
As an example, it would be best to delay collection of
blood in order to obtain even a single thoracic radiograph or an electrocardiograph (ECG). Occasionally, it is
necessary to accept less than ideal results for testing
such as obtaining a single radiographic view rather than

orthogonal views or performing a limited echocardiogram or thoracic ultrasound rather than a complete
exam to preserve patient safety. In fact, thoracic ultrasound can often be performed in the ER with minimal
restrain and can produce repeatable results with a small
amount of training. It is extremely disappointing when
patients die during diagnostic procedures so the patient’s
condition, stability, and the value of the potential information obtained should be taken into consideration
prior to ordering or performing a test.
The use of ECG provides real‐time evaluation of the
electrical conductance of the heart and enables the clinician to determine the source of cardiac depolarization
and if a conduction abnormality exists. When evaluating
a patient with suspected cardiogenic shock, an ECG
should always be obtained. Patients are usually tolerant
of ECG leads placed with either alligator clips or pads.
The goal of ECG evaluation in this setting is to determine which cardiac cells are acting as pacemaker cells
and if electrical conduction is occurring in an organized
fashion. Therefore, patients can often be allowed to
remain in sternal recumbency with minimal restraint.
Evaluation of a lead II ECG should enable the clinician to
answer pertinent urgent questions. A more thorough
six‐lead ECG can be performed if the patient’s condition
is considered stable enough to allow for restraint in lateral recumbency. While the presence of sinus tachycardia will not enable diagnosis of cardiogenic shock (sinus
tachycardia is expected to occur in most shock states
regardless of etiology), the presence of paroxysmal ventricular tachycardia supports the diagnosis. Additionally,
the finding of multiform ventricular ectopy or electrical
alternans may increase the clinician’s suspicion of a cardiac origin of shock.
Radiography is a useful diagnostic tool and is readily
available in most veterinary facilities. When using radiography in the emergency setting, it is important to keep
patient safety in mind, realizing that the quality and
completeness of the study may have to be compromised
to ensure patient safety. Diagnostic radiographs can
often be obtained with minimal restraint. In fact, patients
can often be allowed to remain in sternal recumbency
while a dorsoventral (DV) projection is obtained. A single lateral or DV projection may provide clues regarding
the cause of shock (e.g., a globoid cardiac silhouette) but
orthogonal views are always preferred if possible.
Animals with rupture of a first‐order chorda may manifest fulminant pulmonary edema characterized by the
presence of an alveolar lung pattern while animals with
cardiogenic shock secondary to ventricular tachycardia
may have no radiographic abnormalities.
Echocardiography can be used to diagnose many of the
causes of cardiogenic shock. The minimally experienced
ultrasonographer will be able to recognize the presence of

VetBooks.ir

42 Cardiogenic Shock

pericardial effusion and will likely correctly identify tamponade if present. Additionally, with a small amount of
focused training, the emergency clinician can recognize
acute systolic failure (e.g., dilated cardiomyopathy).
Evaluation of ventricular function and filling pressures in
patients with chronic valvular disease requires more training and is complicated by the fact that ventricular systolic
and diastolic function changes with age and ­disease severity in dogs. The recognition of chordae tendinae rupture,
mild to moderate valvular insufficiency, caval syndrome
or pulmonary hypertension will likely require evaluation
by a veterinary cardiologist. Echocardiography can also
be used to identify rare causes of cardiogenic shock such
as intracardiac tumors.
The use of biomarkers in veterinary medicine is an
area of active investigation. While many biomarkers have
been studied and show promise for distinguishing cardiac disease from respiratory disease or for stratifying
severity of cardiac disease (NT‐proBNP, troponin‐I),
most are not available as point‐of‐care (POC) tests, limiting the clinical usefulness of these assays for evaluation
of the patient in cardiogenic shock. The exception to this
is troponin‐I, which is available as a POC test (iStat by
IDEXX) and has been shown in several veterinary studies to correlate with myocardial injury. A high troponin‐I
level in a patient presenting for shock should prompt the
clinician to further explore the possibility of an underlying cardiac cause. It should be noted, however, that troponin‐I levels have been shown to increase in dogs with
gastric dilation and volvulus and may be elevated in any
patient that has cardiovascular instability. The degree of
troponin‐I elevation is likely greater in dogs with myocardial injury than in those with shock of noncardiac origin. Therefore, the true utility of troponin‐I may be in its
ability to rule out myocardial injury in the acute setting.
Determination of cardiac output would provide strong
support for a diagnosis of cardiogenic shock, especially in
the absence of other possible causes of shock. While cardiac output monitoring technology exists in veterinary
medicine, its clinical use remains limited at this time.

­Therapy
Cardiogenic shock is a unique form of shock that is not
generally responsive to traditional treatments for other
types of shock, (i.e., volume expansion and vasopressor support). In fact, intravascular volume expansion
and vasopressor therapy can be detrimental or even
fatal when administered to a patient with cardiogenic
shock. Rather, cardiogenic shock must be treated primarily by improving cardiac performance and secondarily by altering vasomotor tone (usually reduction of
vasomotor tone).

As with all forms of shock, oxygen administration
should be started immediately upon recognition of the
shock state in an effort to maximize arterial oxygen content as far as possible. Oxygen can be provided by a variety of methods. The use of flow‐by oxygen with a mask
is easy to perform but requires constant restraint of the
patient. This method of oxygen supplementation is relatively inefficient unless a tight‐fitting mask is used.
Unfortunately, animals in shock are often intolerant of
having a mask held over their muzzles and they may
struggle or resist. Holding a tube attached to an oxygen
source in front of an animal’s face is an extremely inefficient method of providing oxygen but, recalling that
perfect is the enemy of good, is probably better than not
providing any supplemental oxygen. Occasionally, animals will tolerate placement of nasal prongs similar to
those used in human medicine. Due to the large size
of the prongs, this is most feasible in large‐breed,
no‐brachycephalic dogs.
A less labor‐intensive way of providing oxygen is
through the use of an oxygen chamber or cage. Purpose‐
built oxygen cages are available but require a significant
financial investment and utilize large amounts of oxygen.
A less expensive alternative is a plexiglass door with a
gasket attached to a standard cage that allows introduction of oxygen through a port. While this method is less
expensive than installing purpose‐made cages, the clinician has little control of the oxygen content and limited
ability to reduce carbon dioxide accumulation within the
cage. The amount of oxygen used in these cages is usually higher than in purpose‐made oxygen cages due to
leakage through imperfect seals.
When providing supplemental oxygen in the acute setting, the highest achievable FiO2 should be used. Once
the patient begins to stabilize, the FiO2 can be reduced to
below 60% to decrease the likelihood of oxygen toxicity
developing.
Animals with confirmed or suspected pulmonary
edema and cardiogenic shock should be given loop diuretics upon presentation. Loop diuretics are rapidly acting, effective diuretics that can quickly improve the
clinical condition of patients with pulmonary edema.
Furosemide (2 mg/kg) should be administered intramuscularly and repeated every 30–60 minutes as needed
until clinical signs improve. Attempts at IV catheter
placement or IV administration of diuretics can be considered but patient safety must always be kept in mind.
Sometimes it becomes apparent that without more
aggressive intervention (i.e., IV administration of medications), the patient’s condition will continue to deteriorate.
If, in the clinician’s mind, the patient is progressing irreversibly toward cardiopulmonary arrest unless such intervention is undertaken, all attempts should be made to
minimize the stress and duration of restraint by carefully

417

VetBooks.ir

418

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

choreographing the steps to be taken. The use of mild
sedatives can facilitate catheter placement in this situation. Administration of butorphanol (0.1–0.3 mg/kg) is
generally safe and is unlikely to have an untoward effect
on cardiac performance. The use of diuretics is not
expected to improve clinical signs in animals with pulmonary hypertension, tamponade, or tachycardia‐induced
cardiogenic shock but is also not likely to result in acute
decompensation.
Medications that increase cardiac contractility (positive inotropes) should be considered in animals that have
documented systolic dysfunction. It must be remembered that positive inotropes not only increase cardiac
contractility but also increase myocardial oxygen consumption. Dobutamine, an injectable beta‐adrenergic
agonist, can be administered as a constant rate infusion
to treat systolic failure. For dogs with strongly suspected
or confirmed systolic dysfunction, dobutamine can be
started at a rate of 2.5 μg/kg/min. The dose is uptitrated
every five minutes until systolic function improves or to
a maximum rate of 20 μg/kg/min. In certain clinical situations, systolic dysfunction cannot be confirmed due to
the patient’s condition or unavailability of echocardiography. In this situation, the clinician will rely on signalment and results of other diagnostic tests to determine if
systolic dysfunction is likely.
Systolic dysfunction in cats can be difficult to confirm
due to their rather tenuous condition when in cardiogenic shock, therefore inotropic support should be
considered in any cat presenting with heart failure and
bradycardia. The dose of dobutamine for cats ranges
from 1 to 5 μg/kg/min and should again be uptitrated
to effect. In some instances, it may be possible to
use pimobendan to improve cardiac contractility.
Pimobendan is a phosphodiesterase III inhibitor and a
calcium sensitizer that increases inotropy while reducing
vascular tone, making it an attractive treatment option
for many causes of cardiogenic shock. Unfortunately,
pimobendan is only available as an oral medication in the
United States, limiting its use in emergency situations.
Administering oral medications to patients in shock
should be avoided due to the stress associated with pilling
and concerns about absorption of the drug from the
underperfused gastrointestinal tract. An injectable form
of pimobendan has recently been approved for use in
Europe with a labeled dose of 0.15 mg/kg.
As mentioned earlier, the use of vasoactive medications
in cardiogenic shock is rare. Almost never,will a patient
with cardiogenic shock benefit from an increase in vascular tone alone. The same cannot be said for decreasing
vascular tone, however. Patients that are likely to benefit
from afterload reduction include those with rupture of a
first‐order chorda tendina or dilated cardiomyopathy – in
other words, patients with forward heart failure.

The most effective medication to achieve consistent,
rapid vasodilation is nitroprusside, which acts by increasing nitric oxide (a powerful arterial dilator) primarily at
the level of the arterioles. Due to the potential for profound hypotension, the use of nitroprusside should be
reserved for patients with confirmed congestive heart
failure and systolic or valvular dysfunction. When used,
nitroprusside is most effective as a constant rate infusion
(CRI) with doses starting at 1 μg/kg/min. As with dobutamine, nitroprusside dose should be uptitrated until the
desired effect is achieved or a maximum dose of 10 μg/
kg/min is reached. Patients being treated with nitroprusside should have their blood pressure monitored very
closely. Ideally, blood pressure is checked every 10–15
minutes until the target pressure (mean arterial pressure
[MAP] 70 mmHg, systemic arterial pressure [SAP]
90 mmHg) is achieved. Mean arterial pressures less than
60 mmHg or systolic pressures less than 90 mmHg should
be avoided due to the potential for additional organ
injury. An early sign of hypotension in patients on nitroprusside is vomiting and if this occurs the patient should
have blood pressure checked immediately and the CRI
rate adjusted accordingly. Fortunately, nitroprusside has
a very short half‐life so discontinuation of a CRI should
result in rapid recovery of blood pressure. Inadvertent,
abrupt cessation of nitroprusside should be avoided due
to the risk of rebound hypertension.
The use of nitroglycerine paste has been advocated in
the past. There is not good evidence to support its routine use and dosing of transdermal medications can be
notoriously difficult, especially in low cardiac output
states where absorption and perfusion are likely to be
impaired.
Sildenafil citrate is a phosphodiesterase V inhibitor that
has been shown to be useful for the treatment of pulmonary hypertension in dogs. While the use of sildenafil is
well documented for management of chronic pulmonary
hypertension, the benefits in the acute setting are less
clear. Sildenafil has a rapid onset of action so administration in a crisis would be expected to result in at least some
improvement in pulmonary pressure. Clinically, this
appears to be the case. As with pimobendan, however,
sildenafil is currently most widely available as an oral
medication and its administration needs to be carefully
considered prior to dosing. An injectable form of sildenafil is approved for use in human patients with pulmonary
hypertension but there are no descriptions of clinical use
in veterinary medicine. When given, the recommended
dose of sildenafil for management of pulmonary hypertension is 1–2 mg/kg PO TID.
Treatment of acute pericardial tamponade involves
immediate pericardiocentesis. Although the possibility
of continued, uncontrolled hemorrhage exists, the morbidity and possible mortality associated with tamponade

VetBooks.ir

42 Cardiogenic Shock

cannot be tolerated. If complete drainage is not achieved,
serial attempts can be made but may not be necessary.
Because the pericardial sac is essentially an enclosed
sphere, the removal of even a small amount of fluid will
exponentially decrease the pressure within the sac.
Observation of the pericardial space with ultrasound (if
available) following every attempt at pericardiocentesis
should be made. Often, the pericardium is lacerated during the attempt and although only a small amount of
fluid is retrieved, tamponade has been relieved and pericardial fluid has been drained into the thoracic cavity
where it is better tolerated. In cases where hemorrhage
cannot be controlled or multiple attempts at percutaneous pericardiocentesis are unsuccessful, emergency
thoracotomy may be required although this should only
be attempted as a last resort when death is believed to be
imminent or cardiac arrest has already occurred.
Treatment of tachyarrhythmias can be achieved
through one of two mechanisms: conversion of the
rhythm to a normal sinus rhythm or control of the rate of
ventricular contractions. Administration of antiarrhythmic medications can be used in an emergency setting to
treat patients with cardiogenic shock from tachyarrhythmias in an attempt to achieve either of these endpoints.
Due to the urgency inherent in this condition, injectable
antiarrhythmics are always preferred to oral formulations. Lidocaine or procainamide are considered first‐
line therapies for the treatment of ventricular tachycardia.
Control of ventricular tachycardia begins with a 2 mg/kg
slow bolus of lidocaine. If no response is seen, a second
dose of lidocaine can be administered. Occasionally,
rhythms that are refractory to lidocaine will respond to
procainamide so if the rhythm has not improved with
lidocaine, a dose of procainamide 5–15 mg/kg slow IV
can be attempted.
Amiodarone has recently been incorporated into the
human CPR guidelines developed by the American
Heart Association for use during cardiopulmonary arrest
as a treatment for pulseless ventricular tachycardia and
ventricular fibrillation refractory to electrical defibrillation. Amiodarone has been used as an oral medication in
veterinary medicine to treat many different arrhythmias,
including atrial fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia.
The use of injectable amiodarone is reported in veterinary patients but has been associated with development
of anaphylactic or anaphylactoid reactions. Due to these
potential adverse effects, it should be considered as a
second‐choice option for management of acute, life‐
threatening tachyarrhythmias. If amiodarone is going to
be used, the recommended starting dose is 5–10 mg/kg
as a slow IV bolus to effect and the amiodarone should
be diluted prior to administration.
Occasionally, dogs will present with supraventricular
tachycardia (SVT) or sinus tachycardia causing cardiogenic

shock as a result of toxin ingestion. For dogs with ECG‐
confirmed sinus tachycardia (with a rate >180 bpm), the
administration of beta‐blockers should be considered
once other causes of shock have been ruled out and the
absence of congestive heart failure has been confirmed.
Due to the need to urgently address cardiogenic shock,
injectable, ultra‐short‐acting beta‐blockers should be
used as first‐line treatment with oral formulations
reserved for patients that have stabilized. Esmolol administered as a bolus of 0.2–0.5 mg/kg followed by a CRI of
50–200 μg/kg/min is preferred. If bradycardia develops,
the CRI rate should be slowed or discontinued. Diltiazem
(5–20 μg/kg/min) can also be used and may be more
effective at managing nonsinus SVT. Because of their
negative inotropic effects, the use of beta‐blockers and
calcium channel blockers should be avoided in patients
with congestive heart failure.
Some cardiac rhythms are amenable to electrical cardioversion using a debrillator (atrial fibrillation, paroxysmal ventricular tachycardia). When used to perform
cardioversion, the energy delivered is generally much
lower (0.5–1 J/kg) than for defibrillation and the timing
of energy delivery must be synchronized with the R‐
wave of the ECG. The synchronization function on the
defibrillator should be activated and the energy dosage
should be selected. Once the synchronization function
has correctly identified the R‐waves, defibrillation can
be performed as usual. If the defibrillator is not equipped
with a synchronization feature then electrical cardioversion should not be attempted as inappropriately timed
delivery of the shock can result in ventricular fibrillation. Heavy opioid sedation or anesthesia should be
used if electrical cardioversion is going to be attempted
on a conscious patient to minimize discomfort associated with the procedure (see description for transcutaneous pacing).
Treatment of cardiogenic shock due to complete (third
degree) AV block consists of temporary or permanent
placement of a pacemaker. Temporary transcutaneous
pacing can be used in emergency situations and requires
little advanced training to be effective. Most modern
defibrillators are capable of performing temporary transcutaneous pacing while temporary transvenous pacing
may require the use of a pacemaker programmer or purpose‐made generator. Transcutaneous pacing is an
uncomfortable experience at best and requires general
anesthesia. To perform transcutaneous pacing, the
patient is prepared while awake. The fur is clipped over
the heart on both sides of the chest at the level of the
costochondral junction. The temporary pacing pads are
placed and plugged into the defibrillator base unit. Once
the patient is instrumented, a rapid‐sequence anesthetic
induction (IV bolus premed followed immediately by IV
bolus of induction agent) is performed and temporary

419

VetBooks.ir

420

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

pacing is begun. Once pacing has begun, the voltage of
the pacing leads is gradually increased until they are
“captured” by the heart. Evaluation of ECG, pulse oximetry or digital palpation of the pulses can be used to verify
capture. Transcutaneous pacing is always a stopgap
measure to allow time for the placement of either a temporary transvenous pacing mechanism or a permanent
pacemaker and should not be considered if these options
are not available.
Management of caval syndrome secondary to heartworm infection often requires direct removal of the
worms from the right heart. The use of a transvenous
approach has been well described and, provided the dog
survives the perioperative period, appears to be very
effective for management of acute caval syndrome.
Surgical management is also the best treatment for well‐
defined intracardiac tumors. Unfortunately, open‐heart
surgery requires total venous inflow occlusion or cardiac

bypass, significantly limiting its availability in veterinary
medicine at this time.

­Prognosis
Published mortality rates for cardiogenic shock in veterinary patients are lacking, but many human studies report
mortality rates of 50–80%. In most instances, the development of cardiogenic shock is a sequela to a severe
underlying structural or progressive conductive disease.
Therefore, both the short‐ and long‐term prognosis
should be considered guarded to poor. Patients that
recover from cardiogenic shock are usually left with residual cardiac dysfunction that is irreversible in nature. The
exception to this may be dogs that are treated for caval
syndrome secondary to canine heartworm disease and
animals receiving a pacemaker for bradyarrhythmias.

Septic Shock
James W. Barr, DVM, DACVECC
BluePearl Veterinary Partners, Tampa, FL, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
The ability of an organism to mount an inflammatory
response is necessary for the survival of nearly all life
forms. Through the simple interaction of the body with
its internal and external environments, a constant bombardment with infectious agents and minor injuries
occurs that is prevented from progressing to systemic
disease by the innate immune system. This process is
performed successfully on a continuous basis without
any conscious effort on the part of the organism or need
for prior exposure to offending antigens.
Unfortunately, these same mechanisms, which are
protective when functioning normally, can become
unregulated or overactive, resulting in added pathology,
perhaps even worse than the original insult would have
caused. This idea is reinforced by the fact that patients
often die of sequelae to infections or systemic inflammation rather than directly from the primary insult.
The systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS)
is the systemic manifestation of a response to an insult
and may result from anything creating inflammation.
Importantly, this can be the result of a systemic condition (e.g., heat stroke) or a severe local insult (e.g., pancreatitis). While systemic inflammation may be necessary
to combat the initial insult, when left unregulated it can
lead to severe consequences. The presence of certain
clinical findings is used to define SIRS and sepsis in both
veterinary and human medicine. Definitions for SIRS
have been proposed and are currently being used clinically (Table 43.1).
Since there is little difference between the clinical
appearance of SIRS and uncomplicated sepsis, the two
terms are often used interchangeably. When SIRS
occurs due to an infectious cause, the term used to
describe it is sepsis. As a result of these definitions,
it means that sepsis always occurs in conjunction

with SIRS while SIRS can exist without the presence of
sepsis. As is the case with most aspects of veterinary
medicine, sepsis/SIRS is not an all‐or‐nothing condition but rather occurs along a spectrum, the least severe
form of which is a hemodynamically stable patient that
fulfills the clinical criteria. Severe sepsis is defined as
sepsis with acute dysfunction of one or more organs.
Common examples of secondary organ dysfunction
include the development of a coagulopathy or acute
kidney injury. The worst permutation of the septic
spectrum is septic shock in which a patient not only fulfills criteria for severe sepsis but also has hypotension
and signs of shock that are not reversed with fluid therapy and is consequently vasopressor dependent.
Response to Infection or Injury
Innate Immunity

The immune system has evolved into two complementary systems that work together to fight infection and
mitigate the damage that occurs in the host: the innate
immune system and the adaptive immune system. For
convenience, they are often discussed separately, but it
should be remembered that neither branch works in isolation from the other and that cross‐talk and feedback
are constantly occurring between the two branches.
The innate immune system is the portion of the
immune system that is nonspecific and responds to any
insult that may be present without need for preexposure
while the adaptive arm of immunity is a more specialized
system that requires preexposure to an organism or antigen. The adaptive response can have infinite, very specific targets but unfortunately, the delay necessary to
recognize an antigen and synthesize antibodies in order
to mount a response makes adaptive immunity unsuitable as a primary means of defending the host from an
acute injury or novel infection.
