and urinalysis. The urinalysis is often incorrectly omitted
in clinical practice. Failure to perform a urinalysis may
prevent the clinician from uncovering evidence of renal
injury (casturia, crystalluria, etc.) prior to the onset of
azotemia. Once azotemia develops, the window of
opportunity for successful therapeutic intervention may
have closed for some patients. More specific diagnostic
testing may be recommended on a case‐by‐case basis,
depending on the specific toxin suspected. For instance,
blood ethylene glycol testing and determination of anion
gap and measurement of blood osmolality (if possible)
are recommended if ethylene glycol ingestion is suspected. Coagulation testing, such as prothrombin time
(PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT),
is recommended for suspected cases of rodenticide
ingestion.
The use of urine testing kits for illicit drug intoxication in veterinary patients has been described. One study
comparing urine test screen results with the gold standard
of urine toxin detection (gas chromatography/mass
spectrometry) found that an on‐site urine toxin screen
(QuickScreen Pro Multi‐Drug Screening Test) accurately
detected the presence of amphetamines, barbiturates,
benzodiazepines, and opiates in canine urine but did not
reliably detect THC (the main psychoactive substance in
marijuana) or methadone.
Certain Exposure to a Known Toxin
When a patient is known to have ingested a specific
substance, the clinician has a unique opportunity to
intervene. Contacting an animal poison control service
(such as the Animal Poison Control Center Hotline
[888‐426‐4435] or Pet Poison Helpline [855‐764‐7661])
provides access to a database containing all known
pharmacokinetics of the toxin, including toxic dose,
routes of metabolism, and excretion. Expected symptoms and recommended therapies to offset the toxicity
are also provided by these hotlines. A one‐time fee is
charged by the providers of these services.
If contacting a poison control center is not an
option, an internet‐based search utilizing a veterinary‐
specific network (such as the Veterinary Information
Network [VIN.com]) often provides much of the same
information. Even a search of free, nonveterinary
websites such as www.pubmed.gov can help locate
useful information or publications regarding treatment of a known toxin. If the toxin is a manufactured
product (i.e., not a naturally occurring toxin such as a
plant), the manufacturer of the product can be contacted. The manufacturer will have information
regarding the toxic potential of the substance and
may be able to provide treatment recommendations
based on the type of exposure.

When considering the approach to a patient known
to have ingested a toxin, many factors must be considered. If a patient is asymptomatic, the clinician must
consider the likelihood of toxic symptoms developing.
Although the exact dosage of toxin exposure is not
always known, treatment should proceed according to
the maximum possible dose. Let us consider, for example, an 80‐pound Labrador retriever with exposure to a
bottle of 200 mg ibuprofen tablets. The bottle initially
contained 100 tablets, but it had been opened prior to
this exposure. Twenty tablets were counted following
the ingestion but the owner is unsure how many tablets
are missing. In this scenario, the clinician should
approach the treatment of the dog as if 80 of the tablets
were ingested, constituting a toxic exposure dose of
220 mg/kg, even though the actual exposure was likely
less than this amount. Ibuprofen dosages above 125 mg/kg
have been reported to cause acute kidney injury in
dogs, so the clinician in this case should warn the client
of this risk and treat accordingly.
Every attempt should be made to establish a likely
timeline of exposure. When the development of significant symptomatic toxicity is a possibility, decontamination should be considered. Ingestion is the most common
route of toxin exposure so GI decontamination is often
needed. GI decontamination is no longer recommended
for every case of ingestion of a known toxin, but decontamination should be considered if there is a likelihood
of toxic symptoms developing (see “GI decontamination”
later in this chapter).
When the specific toxin and dosage are known and
symptoms are expected or present, available antidotes
should be administered as soon as possible. Timely
administration of an antidote following toxin exposure
is of utmost importance. Examples of common toxins for
which antidotes exist include ethylene glycol, anticoagulant
rodenticides, organophosphates, acetaminophen, and
opioids.
Two Common Examples: Timing is Everything

An in‐depth discussion of all known toxins is beyond
the scope of this chapter, but vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant rodenticides and ethylene glycol are two of
the most common toxins encountered in small animal
practice. The importance of establishing a timeline of
exposure whenever possible is highlighted by these two
poisons, because a successful outcome following intoxication depends on timely diagnosis and intervention.
Vitamin K1 antagonists inhibit activation of the vitamin K‐dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX, X, protein C
and S. These toxins typically take up to 48 hours to cause
prolongation in clotting times; clinical symptoms of
bleeding may take 4–5 days or longer to develop. Factor
VII has a significantly shorter half‐life than factors II, IX,

VetBooks.ir

45 Acute Poisoning

and X, so factor VII depletion results in the initial clotting
test abnormalities detected in animals with anticoagulant rodenticide ingestion. However, significant hemorrhage does not begin until factor II depletion occurs
3–4 days after toxin ingestion. Diagnosing anticoagulant rodenticide toxicity in the initial 3–4 days following
exposure allows for successful treatment prior to major
bleeding.
Many patients present for veterinary care very shortly
(e.g., one hour) after ingestion of anticoagulant rodenticide.
Unless a concurrent disorder of hemostasis is suspected
or clinical bleeding is present, coagulation testing is
unnecessary in these patients as long as the client is
absolutely certain that exposure occurred recently (e.g.,
within the past few hours). If exposure has occurred
more than 24 hours prior to presentation, or if timing of
exposure is unknown, diagnostic testing is indicated.
Common testing recommended for anticoagulant rodenticide toxicity includes packed cell volume (PCV), total
solids (TS), and clotting times (PT and aPTT). Activated
clotting time (ACT) can be tested if PT and aPTT are
unavailable. PT prolongation, which usually occurs
48 hours after ingestion, occurs prior to aPTT prolongation due to the short half‐life of factor VII (6.2 hours)
compared with factor II, IX, and X. aPTT prolongation
is typically seen after depletion of factor IX, whose half‐
life is 13.9 hours. Prolongation of both PT and aPTT is
expected prior to significant clinical bleeding following
anticoagulant rodenticide exposure. These different test
results at various time points after ingestion of anticoagulant rodenticide highlight the critical importance of
establishing a timeline of exposure whenever possible.
The “proteins induced by vitamin K antagonism” (PIVKA)
test and specific blood tests for anticoagulant rodenticide
levels are typically not useful in the acute diagnosis and
treatment of the routine small animal patient with anticoagulant rodenticide ingestion because plasma samples
must be sent to a diagnostic lab and there is delay in test
results. These tests may be indicated when anticoagulant
rodenticide toxicity is suspected but the patient has no
known exposure; however, samples must be collected
prior to treatment, and the clinician must proceed with
treatment before test results are available.
Treatment for a patient exposed to anticoagulant
rodenticide invariably involves enteral or parenteral
vitamin K1 therapy, but the timeline of exposure and
symptoms dictates the specific therapeutic plan for each
patient. Vitamin K1 (2.5–5 mg/kg/day IM, SC, or PO for
up to six weeks) can be started orally in the asymptomatic patient with recent exposure (<48 hours ago).
If more than 48 hours have passed since exposure and
coagulation tests are prolonged, but clinical bleeding is
not observed, a single dose of parenteral vitamin K1
can be given prior to starting oral vitamin K1 therapy.

Patients experiencing clinical bleeding secondary to
vitamin K antagonists should be treated with fresh
­frozen plasma (FFP) transfusion in addition to parenteral vitamin K1 administration.
Patients who may have ingested ethylene glycol (EG)
present a unique clinical challenge due to the extremely
time‐sensitive and dangerous nature of this toxicity. Cats
exposed to EG less than three hours prior to presentation (and dogs exposed less than eight hours prior to
presentation) must be aggressively tested and/or treated.
The presence of EG can be proven by blood tests, but
available tests are imperfect. Bedside tests include the
Kacey Ethylene Glycol Test Strips (Kacey Inc., Asheville,
NC) and the Catachem VetSpec Ethylene Glycol
Qualitative Test Kit (Catachem Inc., Oxford, CT). These
tests are subjective and based on visual determination of
color change, and the presence of other substances such
as proplylene glycol or ethanol may cause false‐positive
test results. The results of two small studies led to some
concern regarding the sensitivity and specificity of these
tests. One study evaluating the Kacey Ethylene Glycol
Test Strips published in 2008 reported a sensitivity of
only 56–67% for detection of 20 mg/dL EG (a potentially
lethal dose for cats) in blood. This study also reported a
specificity of 25–50% for detection of 80 mg/dL EG in
blood. The authors of the study concluded that the test
should not be used as a sole determinant of intoxication
due to the risk of both false‐positive and false‐negative
results.
The results of a second study were published in 2014 in
the Journal of Veterinary Emergency and Critical Care.
This study compared the Kacey Ethylene Glycol Test to
the Catachem VetSpec Etylene Glycol Qualitative Test
Kit. EG was added to canine blood at concentrations
ranging from 0 to 100 mg/dL, and 30 samples were evaluated separately by two individuals. The tests were
assigned a score of less than 20 mg/dL, 20–50 mg/dL, or
greater than 50 mg/dL. Sensitivity and specificity were
100% for the Kacey test, with good agreement between
two readers. In this study the VetSpec test performed
less well. Sensitivity and specificity were only 65%
and 70% respectively for one reader and 95% and 40% for
the other.
A separate publication evaluated an EG test kit
designed for use on a chemistry analyzer found in major
clinical pathology laboratories (the Hitachi P‐modular
800 chemistry analyzer). This test was found to accurately measure blood EG, and results were not significantly altered by the presence of propylene glycol.
Although the development and assessment of new
tests continue, most veterinary hospitals do not, at this
time, have a reliably sensitive and specific way to measure blood EG levels. Woods’ lamp evaluation of the oral
cavity, face, vomitus, and urine can provide evidence of

439

VetBooks.ir

440

exposure to EG since many formulations contain a fluorescent dye. Unfortunately, since some formulations do
not contain added dye, Woods’ lamp evaluation cannot
be used as a sole diagnostic test. Diagnosis of EG toxicity
must therefore be made based on clinical suspicion and
the presence of certain findings on any of the following
tests: osmole gap, anion gap, urinalysis (calcium oxalate
crystalluria), blood chemistry, or abdominal ultrasonography. Ethylene glycol is an effective osmole, and
the presence of significant ethylene glycol levels in the
blood can result in neurologic symptoms (e.g., ataxia
and stupor) due to hyperosmolality.
The presence of significant amounts of EG in the
blood leads to an increase in the “osmole gap,” which is
the difference between measured blood osmolality and
calculated blood osmolality (equation 1).

The normal whole‐blood osmole gap has been reported

a patient who may have been exposed to EG or who is
showing symptoms should raise clinical suspicion for EG
poisoning.
Fatalities due to EG toxicity are caused by acute renal
failure as EG metabolism leads to accumulation of
­metabolic acids such as glycolic and oxalic acid. This accumulation leads to a metabolic acidosis and an ­elevated
anion gap (AG) seen at approximately three hours after
ingestion, peaking at six hours, and lasting up to 48 hours.
AG can be determined using equation 3.

Normal AG is 12–24 mEq/L in dogs and 13–27 mEq/L
in cats. An elevated AG indicates accumulation of
unmeasured anions. An elevated AG is not specific to
EG intoxication, but an elevated AG 3–6 hours or more
after possible exposure to EG may be considered a sign
of EG exposure. The oxalic acid formed during metabolism of EG binds calcium, resulting in calcium oxalate
monohydrate crystalluria as early as three hours after
ingestion in cats (six hours in dogs).
In some cases, EG toxicity may not be diagnosed
prior to the development of oligoanuric renal failure.
Progressive azotemia may help establish a diagnosis of
EG poisoning, but this finding almost always indicates a
grave prognosis. Diagnosis of EG toxicity must be made
prior to the development of azotemia to allow the best
chance at survival. The different clinicopathologic find-

ings at different time points following EG ingestion again
demonstrate how important it is to establish a timeline
of possible exposure.
The treatment of EG toxicity is similarly dependent on
timing of exposure. Definitive treatment of EG ingestion
revolves around preventing accumulation of toxic metabolites. Metabolism of EG to glycolic acid by the enzyme
alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) is the most important step
in the development of EG toxicity. Veterinary patients
have traditionally been treated with IV ethanol administration. Ethanol is metabolized by ADH, and ADH has a
higher affinity for ethanol than EG. Administration of
ethanol, therefore, can limit glycolic acid accumulation.
At the same time, high rates of IV fluids can be given to
drive urinary excretion of unmetabolized EG molecules.
Ethanol administration can be an effective treatment for
EG ingestion, but long courses of treatment are needed
and side‐effects (including hyperosmolality, CNS signs
such as sedation, and GI signs such as vomiting) are frequently observed. ADH inhibitors such as 4‐methylpyrazole (4‐MP, also known as fomepazole) prevent
metabolism of EG to toxic metabolites while offering less
risk of side‐effects than ethanol. The primary drawbacks
to 4‐MP are limited availability and relatively high cost
compared with ethanol. Cats require very high doses of
4‐MP compared with dogs, making cats more likely to
develop side‐effects such as CNS depression and ataxia
following treatment with 4‐MP. Treatment of cats with
ADH inhibition using ethanol or 4‐MP is typically ineffective if not begun within three hours of ingestion,
whereas treatment of dogs is typically successfully if
started within eight hours of ingestion.
Hemodialysis is a very effective treatment for removal
of EG and glycolic acid; 90–95% of circulating EG can be
removed in a single hemodialysis session. Intermittent
hemodialysis may also effectively treat azotemia and
hyperkalemia in patients with acute kidney injury from
EG toxicity, allowing time to determine if recovery of
kidney function occurs over the span of several weeks.
Regardless of the mode of treatment, prompt intervention is of utmost importance due to the time‐dependent
nature of this lethal toxin.
Uncertain Exposure to a Known Toxin
When treating a patient who may or may not have been
exposed to a known toxic substance, the clinician must
formulate a diagnostic testing and treatment plan based
on the presence or absence of clinical symptoms, the
likelihood of clinical symptoms developing if toxic
exposure did in fact occur, and the danger of the toxin
involved. The clinician should consider contacting an
animal poison control center to obtain the most extensive
and up‐to‐date information regarding the probability of
toxicity from any possible exposure to the substance in

VetBooks.ir

45 Acute Poisoning

question. Patients exhibiting symptoms consistent with
toxicity from the substance should be treated as if they
have been poisoned, even if exposure cannot be completely confirmed. If symptoms of toxicity are not present and the possible toxicity is not life‐threatening, then
a “wait and see” approach of close monitoring may be all
that is needed. If signs of toxicity are not present, but the
toxin to which the patient was possibly exposed carries
some risk of significant morbidity, then decontamination
(see “Decontamination” later in this chapter) should be
considered if appropriate, and close monitoring should
be recommended. If the possible exposure involves a
toxin conferring serious risk of organ failure and/or
death, then aggressive testing to confirm or rule out
exposure is recommended. Decontamination and treatment should also be instituted, even if toxic exposure
cannot be definitively confirmed.
Certain Exposure to an Unknown Substance
Frequently, small animal veterinarians are presented with
a patient who was observed to lick, ingest or otherwise
contact an unknown substance. This situation typically
involves ingestion of a plant while outdoors. A good
familiarity with the local flora will prove useful to the
clinician in this instance. Even if the client has obtained a
sample of the ingested plant, it may be difficult or impossible for the clinician to identify whether or not the plant
is dangerous. If clinical symptoms are present and consistent with a poison known to be present in the local
environment, then treatment should proceed as if the
poisonous compound in question caused the symptoms.
One commonly encountered situation utilizing this
approach is the young, otherwise healthy dog presented
for muscle tremors after being exposed to rotten food or
compost. In this situation, the clinician cannot be completely certain that there has been toxin ingestion, and
even if ingestion is strongly suspected, the exact toxic
compound is unclear. The patient in this scenario is typically assumed to have ingested a tremorgenic mycotoxin.
Diagnostic testing of the patient should aim to rule out
other causes of muscle tremors (hypocalcemia, hypoglycemia, etc.). Once these other common causes have been
ruled out, treatment of this patient should involve centrally acting muscle relaxants such as methocarbamol
and supportive measures such as IV fluids to prevent
dehydration resulting from increased muscle activity in a
patient who is unable to drink properly. The client should
be informed that tremorgenic mycotoxin toxicity is
suspected but cannot be confirmed. If initial diagnostic
testing reveals no obvious cause of the symptoms, and if
symptoms do not improve over 24–48 hours despite
appropriate treatment for tremorgenic mycotoxin toxicity,
then further diagnostic testing is recommended to search
for a separate cause of the muscle tremors.

­Decontamination
Topical Decontamination
Topical exposure to a toxin most often involves parasiticides such as permethrins or pyrethrins. Patients with
topical poison exposure should be bathed thoroughly
in a mild soap (such as Dawn® liquid dishsoap) as soon
as safely possible. Minimum protective equipment for
veterinary personnel should include rubber gloves. Eye
protection and a rubber apron may be needed, depending
on the nature of the toxin involved.
Ocular Decontamination
Eye injury may occur when ocular surfaces contact a
caustic irritant. The resultant corneal damage can be
minor (only resulting in discomfort) or severe enough to
cause melting corneal ulceration. The pH of the ocular
irritant strongly influences the severity of corneal injury.
Acid compounds injure the corneal epithelium, but alkaline compounds are associated with more severe damage
and a higher likelihood of anterior chamber changes and
permanent vision impairment. The pH of an ocular
irritant can be checked by applying litmus paper to the
conjunctival fornix. This may help the clinician prepare
the client for the likelihood of severe damage.
Regardless of the specific chemical toxin, the degree of
damage is also related to the duration of exposure, so the
eye must be flushed as soon as possible. Continuous
flushing of the cornea should continue for at least
15 minutes following ocular surface exposure to a toxin;
many resources recommend a full 20–30 minutes of
flushing. The eye can be flushed using a balanced fluid
such as 0.9% NaCl or lactated Ringer’s solution (LRS). Tap
water is an acceptable flushing solution, but the hypoosmolality of tap water may contribute to corneal edema
formation following toxic injury. Bottles of eye wash solution are typically too small (i.e., contain too little volume)
to effectively flush the surface of the eye for 15 minutes
or longer. The damage caused by severe chemical burns
of the cornea can be reduced by using buffered eye wash
solutions such as Diphoterine®, but these solutions are
not available in most veterinary hospitals.
Gastrointestinal Decontamination
Emesis

Induction of emesis may be indicated whenever a toxin
has been ingested and may still be in the stomach. If
ingestion has occurred within the previous 4–6 hours, it
is reasonable to consider inducing emesis. While usually
a safe procedure, there are potential risks associated
with inducing emesis, including aspiration pneumonia
and esophageal or oropharyngeal injury. In general,

441

VetBooks.ir

442

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

only asymptomatic patients should be made to vomit, as
the risk for aspiration pneumonia is greatly increased by
CNS dysfunction or neuromuscular weakness. The risk
of esophageal or oropharyngeal injury is increased if
large or sharp objects have been ingested along with the
toxin. Though uncommon, these possible complications
must be considered and discussed with the client when
deciding whether or not to induce emesis in a patient
that has ingested a toxin. Patients that have ingested
caustic substances (e.g., bleach) or hydrocarbons (e.g.,
gasoline) should never be made to vomit. Ingestion of
zinc phosphide rodenticide leads to liberation of phosphine
gas in the acidic environment of the stomach; induction
of emesis following zinc phosphide rodenticide must be
done carefully in a well‐ventilated area (ideally, outdoors)
to reduce the risk of dangerous phosphine gas inhalation
by veterinary staff.
Hydrogen peroxide and apomorphine are the two
most common agents used to induce emesis in dogs.
Due to an increased risk of side‐effects, the use of syrup
of ipecac, sodium chloride salt, dishwashing liquid or
mustard powder is not recommended. Inducing emesis
is typically easy in canine patients. Hydrogen peroxide
(3%) can be given PO at a dose of 2.2 mL/kg (up to
a maximum of 45 mL) and repeated if vomiting has
not occurred within 10–15 minutes of administration.
Hydrogen peroxide causes vomiting by acting as a
local irritant in the oropharynx and stomach. Rarely,
protracted vomiting can occur after administration.
­
Occasionally, mild side‐effects such as lethargy and diarrhea can occur. Very rare instances of symptomatic gastric
ulceration or even gastric dilation and volvulus (GDV)
have been anecdotally reported following administration
of hydrogen peroxide. A prospective observational study
reported a relatively low incidence of mild side‐effects
(14%) in 70 clinical canine patients following induction
of emesis using hydrogen peroxide; no serious or life‐
threatening side‐effects were reported in this study.
Apomorphine is a centrally acting emetic agent that
reliably induces emesis in dogs by stimulation of the
chemoreceptor trigger zone. It can be given as a 0.03–
0.04 mg/kg intramuscular (IM) or IV injection. Vomiting
typically occurs soon after apomorphine injection.
If vomiting does not occur, dosing can be repeated once
or twice more, but the drug may depress the vomiting
center in the medulla, so repeat administration may be
unlikely to induce vomiting if the first dose was unsuccessful. Conjunctival application of apomorphine is also
a very effective way of inducing emesis in dogs. The conjunctiva should be thoroughly flushed after emesis to
limit further absorption of apomorphine and decrease
the risk of CNS depression or protracted vomiting. PO
administration of apomorphine to induce emesis is not
recommended due to slow absorption and high first‐pass

clearance by the liver. If prolonged vomiting occurs after
apomorphine treatment, administration of an injectable
antiemetic (e.g. maropitant, metoclopramide, or ondansetron) is indicated. Rarely, significant sedation will
occur after apomorphine administration. The sedative
effects of apomorphine can be reversed using naloxone.
Induction of emesis in cats is more challenging than in
dogs. Injectable administration of an alpha‐2‐adrenergic
agonist is currently the method of choice. Xylazine
is commonly given at a dose of 0.44 mg/kg IM for
this ­
purpose; as much as 1.1 mg/kg can be given.
Dexmedetomidine (20–40 μg/kg IM) can also be used.
One major drawback to the use of alpha‐2‐adrenergic
agonists for this purpose is that profound sedation
may occur. Reversal of the alpha‐2‐adrenergic agonist
using yohimbine (0.1 mg/kg IM or IV) or atipamezole
(50 μg/kg IM) is recommended following emesis to prevent sedation from interfering with interpretation of
symptoms of poisoning.
Gastric Lavage

When induction of emesis is unsuccessful or contraindicated and an ingested toxicant is likely to cause significant morbidity or mortality, gastric lavage may be
considered. Gastric lavage should always be done under
general anesthesia (unless the patient is already unconscious), and a cuffed endotracheal tube should always be
placed to guard the airway against aspiration of gastric
contents. Lavage is performed using warm (body temperature) water given through a large orogastric tube, keeping
the head below the level of the chest throughout the procedure to discourage aspiration of gastric contents (which
can occur even in the presence of a cuffed endotracheal
tube). Initial lavage volumes are typically 5–10 ml/kg, and
lavage is repeated until the fluid obtained from the stomach is completely clear. If indicated, a dose of activated
charcoal can then be given through the orogastric tube
prior to its removal. The tube should be kinked in more
than one place during removal from the stomach to prevent fluid within the tube from spilling into the airway.
Gastric lavage carries risks, including anesthesia and
aspiration pneumonia; careful consideration of the
­
risk:benefit ratio must ­precede this intervention.
GI Adsorption

Activated charcoal (AC) has been, and will likely continue to be, one of the most common treatments administered to veterinary patients who have ingested a toxin.
The use of AC in human medicine has recently been
critically reevaluated, and routine use has been discouraged due to a lack of evidence that its administration
affects outcome. There have been no published veterinary studies comparing conventional therapy with AC
versus conventional therapy alone. Inherent differences

VetBooks.ir

45 Acute Poisoning

between veterinary small animal patients and human
patients make the veterinary application of human
guidelines questionable. Veterinary patients may be
more likely than human patients to ingest large quantities of toxins, and paradoxically veterinary patients may
present for medical care sooner after ingestion than
human patients due to the intentional nature of many
human intoxications. Furthermore, advanced treatments
such as hemofiltration for toxin removal or prolonged,
aggressive hospital‐based care for treatment of organ
dysfunction are more readily available and more often
pursued in human medicine than in veterinary patients,
making it that much more important to limit toxin
adsorption in veterinary patients as much as possible
prior to signs of intoxication.
Products containing AC are administered at a dose of
1–5 g/kg body weight PO or via orogastric intubation to
bind any remaining toxin within the GI tract and prevent
further absorption of the toxin. AC administration is
indicated when the ingested poison binds to AC, is likely
to cause significant toxicity, and has been recently
ingested (within the past 4–6 hours) and/or undergoes
enterohepatic recirculation. Repeated dosing (every
4–6 hours for four total doses) is recommended for
dangerous toxins for which enterohepatic recirculation
is known to occur and no antidote is available. The use
of AC‐containing products may lead to vomiting, and
aspiration of gastric contents or charcoal creates a risk
of pneumonia. Injection of an antiemetic prior to AC
administration may help decrease the incidence of emesis.
AC may bind water within the GI tract, and repeated
doses have been associated with dehydration and
hypernatremia in rare cases. When repeated doses of AC
are needed, many sources recommend the repeat doses
be given at a lower dose (for instance, half the initial
administered dose), and IV fluid administration is recommended to help prevent significant dehydration. It is
also important that veterinarians and clients know which
patients have received AC so that the resultant black
stools are not misinterpreted as melena.
Activated charcoal binds to most but not all toxins; it
does not bind alcohols, heavy metals, or small organic
molecules. Use of AC is therefore not indicated for toxic
ingestions of xylitol, ethylene glycol, zinc, nitrates, or
sodium chlorate, among others. It is important to confirm that the suspected toxin binds to AC prior to
administration of AC. If the binding affinity of a poison
to AC is unknown by the clinician, a poison control
hotline should be contacted prior to administration.
Studies have shown that the timing of AC administration
in relation to toxin ingestion directly influences the
percentage of ingested toxin that is bound within the GI
tract. If AC use is indicated, it is important that the treatment be administered as soon as possible.

Few dogs (and almost no cats) willingly ingest AC
solutions. One commonly utilized clinical method of
administration involves combining the charcoal with a
small amount of highly palatable food. While the food
binds to the charcoal and reduces binding capacity, a
published veterinary study suggests the reduction in
toxin‐binding capacity is clinically insignificant.
Cathartics

Cathartics are given to speed GI transit times in an effort
to decrease the time a toxin is available for absorption
within the GI tract. The two types of cathartics used in
veterinary medicine are saccharides (e.g., sorbitol) and
saline (e.g., magnesium sulfate); sorbitol is the most
commonly used cathartic, and it is most commonly
stocked in veterinary hospitals as an AC‐sorbitol combination product. Because cathartics such as sorbitol act
by drawing water into the GI lumen, significant risk of
dehydration and hypernatremia exists with repeated use
of these products. When a cathartic is used, it is typically
only administered as a one‐time dose. The most common clinical practice is to give only the first dose of AC
with sorbitol, utilizing AC products without a cathartic
for repeated doses.
Decontamination of Blood
Extracorporeal Therapies

One of the most effective methods to treat certain
­poisonings is removal using extracorporeal therapies
such as hemodialysis and hemoperfusion. Hemodialysis
involves circulating blood through an extracorporeal circuit and allowing for transfer of solutes and water across
a semipermeable membrane. Toxins are good candidates
for removal via hemodialysis if they are relatively small
(<1500 daltons), poorly protein bound and with a low
volume of distribution. Ethylene glycol and aspirin are
examples of compounds that are readily cleared by hemodialysis. Hemoperfusion refers to the direct exposure of
blood in an extracorporeal circuit to an adsorbent column of charcoal or (less commonly) a different adsorbent
specially designed to bind a specific toxin. Hemoperfusion
greatly increases the number of poisons that can be
removed using extracorporeal therapy. Hemodialysis and
hemoperfusion require specialized, often expensive,
equipment and highly trained personnel. The availability
of hemoperfusion is currently limited in veterinary medicine, but the number of facilities offering this potentially
life‐saving intervention will likely increase in the future.
Intravenous Lipid Therapy

Administration of intravenous lipid emulsions (IVLE) is
a common therapy for the treatment of poisoning with
lipophilic toxins. IVLE therapy was first used to treat

443

VetBooks.ir

444

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

cardiotoxicity secondary to local anesthetic administration in humans. The proposed mechanism of action
involved overriding the local anesthetic‐induced inhibition of myocardial carnitine acylcarnitine translocase,
potentially by mass effect or competitive inhibition,
allowing fatty acids to reach the mitochondria and be
used for energy production.
Since its initial introduction into the arsenal of available
medical treatments, IVLE therapy has proven beneficial in
the treatment of lipophilic toxins other than local anesthetics. Many of these lipophilic toxins cause dysfunction
to organs other than the heart, yet their effects may still be
reversed by IVLE administration, suggesting that IVLE
treatment has a different or additional mechanism of
action beyond improved free fatty acid availability or
intracellular calcium accumulation. The most widely
proposed mechanism of action for the beneficial effects of
IVLE treatment of patients poisoned by liphophilic substances is the “lipid sink” theory. This theory states that
increasing the plasma lipid content “sequesters” lipophilic
toxins within the plasma, decreasing movement out of the
bloodstream and into target organs such as the brain.
Anecdotal and published reports describe successful
IVLE use in the treatment of a wide variety of toxins
ranging from local anesthetics (bupivacaine) and vasoactive drugs (amlodipine, propranolol) to antiparasitic
drugs (ivermectin, moxidectin) and antidepressant medications (bupropion, etc.). IV lipid emulsions are available
as 20% formulations. The optimal dose is unclear at this
time, but recommendations have been extrapolated from
available human literature, animal research, and veterinary case reports. Current guidelines suggest 1.5–4 mL/
kg IV bolus be given over one minute and followed by a
constant rate infusion (CRI) of 0.25 mL/kg/min over
30–60 minutes. Patients who fail to respond to this protocol may require additional boluses of 1.5 mL/kg every
4–6 hours for 24 hours. Continued CRI doses of up to

0.05 mL/kg/h for up to 24 hours can be considered for
patients who remain severely symptomatic. Utilizing a
“lowest effective dose” approach is recommended due to
the general lack of information regarding adverse effects
of IVLE therapy in veterinary patients.
Reported side‐effects in human medicine include
infection due to contamination of the lipid product,
anaphylactoid reactions, and allergic reaction to the egg
or soybean component of the IVLE. A syndrome known
as “fat overload syndrome” (FOS) has been observed in
humans. FOS is associated with fat embolism, liver
dysfunction, or coagulation system dysfunction (thrombocytopenia and prolonged clotting times). These side‐
effects have not yet been reported in clinical veterinary
patients, but the use of IVLE as a treatment for lipophilic
toxins is still somewhat new in veterinary medicine.
When considering IVLE administration, the clinician
must carefully weigh the severity and duration of toxic
symptoms against the cost and potential complications
associated with this intervention.

­Conclusion
Small animal veterinarians commonly encounter acute
poisoning. A sound, comprehensive approach to patient
care (building on the fundamentals of a good history,
physical exam, and diagnostic work‐up) is important for
diagnosing toxic exposure. A solid understanding of
common toxins and appropriate utilization of available
resources such as poison control hotlines help the
­clinician to establish the treatment plan most likely to
result in a successful outcome. Exciting new therapies
such as hemoperfusion and IVLE administration continue to evolve, making it important for the practicing
small animal clinician to remain up to date on the most
current available treatments.

Medical Management of Trauma and Burns
Nathan Peterson, DVM, DACVECC
VCA West Los Angeles Animal Hospital, Los Angeles, CA, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
The pathophysiology of trauma and burns is complex
and explains why trauma and burn wounds are capable
of affecting organs distant from the original insult and
why the clinical course of disease can be so variable. Our
current understanding of the pathophysiology of trauma
is based on the theory that both primary and secondary
insults contribute to morbidity and mortality. This is
termed the two‐hit theory. Primary insults (first hits)
result in direct tissue injury from the trauma or burn
(fractures, soft tissue destruction, organ rupture or
­vascular disruption). These factors are not under the
control of the veterinarian. Secondary insults can be
­further divided into endogenous or exogenous causes.
Typical endogenous second hits include shock, hypoxia,
ischemia/reperfusion injuries, and infection. Exogenous
(interventional) second hits include surgical trauma,
anesthetic complications, and transfusion of blood
products.
Systemic Inflammatory Response
The magnitude of the primary and secondary insults
determines the systemic inflammatory response of the
host. Immediately following a trauma load, the patient
begins mounting a systemic response composed of both
pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory components
intended to limit entry of microorganisms, on the one
hand, and limit secondary tissue damage, on the other.
The balance, or lack thereof, determines if the patient will
mount an appropriate response, or whether a pro-inflammatory or anti-inflammatory state will predominate.
Plasma levels of primary pro-inflammatory cytokines
rise within 1–2 hours following trauma. Secondary
­pro-inflammatory cytokines begin to rise several hours

following trauma and contribute to the systemic inflammation and activation of immune cells associated with
severe trauma. The culmination of this activation is an
increased number of circulating polymorphic nucleic
cells (PMNs) and additional tissue injury.
Concurrent with the systemic inflammatory response
(SIRS), an anti-inflammatory response called the
­compensatory anti-inflammatory response syndrome
(CARS) is taking place. The purpose of this response is
to minimize the tissue damage induced by the proinflammatory response and is achieved through release
of anti-inflammatory mediators that reduce the synthesis of pro-inflammatory cytokines by their action on
transcription factors necessary for their production.
Coagulation and Inflammation
Activation of the inflammatory system is closely tied to
activation of the coagulation and complement cascades.
Complement activation occurs through both the contact phase pathway and the classic pathway and results
in recruitment and activation of phagocytic cells, induction of the hepatic acute phase response, and degranulation of mast cells. Mast cell degranulation releases
vasoactive mediators including histamine, leading to
leukocyte adhesion and increased vascular permeability
(edema). Activation of the complement system also
results in activation of the coagulation ­cascade although
the most important inciting cause of activation of the
coagulation cascade in the context of trauma is through
the tissue factor pathway. Direct and secondary tissue
injury exposes tissue factor (TF) on the endothelial cell
surface which then complexes with factor VII (FVII) and
activates the coagulation cascade. In severely traumatized patients, activation of the coagulation cascade can
result in development of disseminated intravascular
coagulation (DIC).

Acute Phase Response
The release of pro-inflammatory cytokines tumor necrosis
factor (TNF)‐alpha, interleukin (IL)‐1‐beta, and IL‐6 following trauma induces the acute phase response in the
liver which results in up-regulation of positive acute
phase proteins, including fibrinogen and prothrombin.
At the same time positive acute phase proteins are being
up-regulated, the production of negative acute phase
proteins albumin, protein‐C, protein‐S, and antithrombin (AT) is reduced. The net effect of the acute phase
response is generally in the direction of enhanced coagulation through the increased production of prothrombin,
fibrinogen and the decreased production of endogenous
anticoagulants protein‐C, protein‐S, and AT. The resultant hypercoagulable state can contribute to the development of DIC in patients following severe trauma or
burns.
Ischemia and Reperfusion
Systemic ischemia can occur following trauma and is
attributed to hypoxemia and hypotension immediately
following trauma and during the early resuscitative
period (<24 hrs). Local ischemia can occur due to blunt
trauma, disruption of local blood supply or compartment
syndrome. During periods of ischemia, several important intracellular changes occur. As energy stores are
depleted, adenosine triphosphate (ATP) levels decrease
and ATP is degraded to adenosine diphosphate (ADP)
and hypoxanthine. As ischemia continues, intracellular
pH decreases and lactate, hypoxanthine and sodium and
calcium ion concentrations increase, leading to cellular
swelling. Upon reperfusion, oxygen interacts with
hypoxanthine, resulting in the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). This occurs within seconds of reintroduction of oxygen to ischemic tissues. Reactive
oxygen species are capable of causing lipid peroxidation
and cell death. The release of ROS into the systemic circulation and their subsequent delivery to the lungs following reperfusion may form the basis for the
development of acute lung injury associated with trauma.
The liver and gut may be particularly sensitive to ischemia/
reperfusion injury. In fact, ischemia and reperfusion of
the gut following shock and subsequent resuscitation
result in the gut becoming a source of proinflammatory
mediators capable of inducing SIRS.
Traumatic Brain Injury/Spinal Cord Injury
The response of the brain and spinal cord to trauma is
unique. Similar to general trauma, brain injury consists
of primary (direct result of trauma) and secondary injury
(subsequent to primary injury). Secondary brain and

spinal cord injury is composed of hemorrhage, edema,
vasospasm or enzymatically induced neurotoxicity. As
an organ, the brain is particularly sensitive to injury by
ROS due to high levels of unsaturated fatty acids and
low antioxidant capacity. Periods of hypoxia and hypotension lead to the accumulation of the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate in the interstitial compartment.
High extracellular levels of glutamate in addition to
intracellular depletion of ATP lead to accumulation of
calcium and sodium ions within the neuronal cell and
culminate in cellular dysfunction and death. Because of
this, several autoregulatory countermeasures have been
developed, including the brain’s ability to regulate blood
flow across a wide range of blood pressures. However, if
hypoxia or shock is severe enough in magnitude or duration, these defense mechanisms are overcome and secondary neuronal injury occurs.
It is important to remember that primary brain injury
can impair the autoregulatory functions of the brain,
making it susceptible to secondary injury that would
otherwise not occur. For this reason, initial resuscitative
measures should be focused on improving oxygen delivery
to the vital organs, especially the brain.
Burns
Local burns covering less than 30% of total body surface
area (TBSA) rarely cause severe systemic effects while
severe burns (those covering more than 30% of TBSA)
are capable of inducing a syndrome called “burn shock”
that is characterized by decreased intravascular volume,
reduced cardiac output (CO), and increased systemic
vascular resistance.
The physiologic response to burns is generally divided
into two distinct phases. The resuscitation phase begins
immediately following burn injury and is characterized
by depleted circulating volume with increased vascular
permeability and protein‐rich fluid loss into the interstitial space, resulting in edema formation of both burned
and unburned tissue. This phase coincides with a systemic response similar to that observed in severe
trauma patients as described above. Hypoproteinemia in
burn patients occurs secondary to protein loss in the
form of edema fluid and fluid loss from the affected skin
surface and can develop during the resuscitative phase of
burn management.
Following the resuscitation phase of burn injury
(3–5 days), a hyperdynamic/hypermetabolic phase, primarily mediated by counter-regulatory hormones
including cortisol, glucagon, and catecholamines, begins.
During the hyperdynamic phase, cardiac output is
increased and vascular permeability begins to return to
normal. In addition to the circulatory changes, an
increase in metabolic rate occurs that results in negative

VetBooks.ir

46 Medical Management of Trauma and Burns

energy balance with protein catabolism, gluconeogenesis,
glycogenolysis, hepatic insulin resistance, lipolysis,
decreased lean body mass, and fever. Ultimately, energy
requirements during this period can be increased threefold above basal metabolic rate.
Patients that suffered burn injuries in an enclosed structure fire are also at risk for developing inhalation injury.
The inhalation of hot gas and particulate debris results in
direct thermal injury to the airway mucosa and chemical
irritation. Patients are at risk for developing upper airway
obstruction, bronchospasm, small airway occlusion, pulmonary infection, and respiratory failure. The effect of
direct thermal injury and chemical irritation is development of an inflammatory response resulting in interstitial
edema formation. The damaged mucosal surface generates large amounts of cellular and necrotic debris, leading
to further inflammation and distal migration within the
bronchial tree with resultant lower airway plugging. This
typically occurs 3–5 days post inhalation injury and, in
conjunction with mucociliary dysfunction, can lead to
development of bronchopneumonia.

­Epidemiology
The incidence of trauma in veterinary medicine is relatively unknown with one large retrospective study finding that trauma accounted for 13% of admissions to an
urban referral hospital. When it does occur, trauma in
veterinary patients appears to be more likely to affect
dogs than cats, with dogs comprising approximately
80–90% of trauma patients. In dogs, the mechanism of
trauma is most likely to be blunt trauma associated with
vehicular injury followed by sharp trauma and animal
attacks. In the feline population, the mechanism of
trauma is often unknown. In cases where the mechanism
behind the trauma is known, cats are essentially equally
as likely to suffer from blunt vehicular trauma, falls from
height, crush injury or weapon‐related trauma. The prehospital mortality rate of veterinary patients suffering
trauma is unknown; in hospital, mortality ranges from
approximately 10% to 20%.
Blunt trauma in the canine patient is more thoroughly
described. The thorax and extremities are the most likely
sites of injury from blunt trauma in dogs, with pelvic
fracture, head trauma, and abdominal trauma occurring
less frequently. The most common thoracic injuries
incurred are pulmonary contusions, pneumothorax, and
chest wall trauma/rib fractures. In blunt abdominal
trauma, the most commonly encountered injuries are
hemoperitoneum (25%), body wall hernia (5%), and rupture of the urinary system (3%). The two most commonly
encountered orthopedic injuries are pelvic fractures
and long bone fractures. Axial orthopedic injuries are

relatively uncommon. Head trauma is more likely to be
encountered in animals with a higher total trauma load
and is associated with a worse outcome
Little is known about the incidence of penetrating
ballistic injuries in dogs and cats although a recent study
of military working dogs sheds some light on the topic.
Obviously, military and law enforcement working dogs
are at a higher risk than the general pet population of
ballistic trauma and that trauma is more likely to be due
to high‐velocity/high‐energy projectiles (rifle bullets). A
higher incidence of penetrating ballistic injury is also
likely in young, male dogs of the working breeds with
lower velocity/energy ballistics (shotgun pellets) more
likely.

­Signalment
Young (1–3 years) large‐breed dogs of both sexes are
more likely to suffer blunt trauma (hit by car) than small‐
breed dogs. Conversely, small‐breed dogs are more likely
than large‐breed dogs to be victims of animal attacks,
with males being more commonly affected than females.
Male cats are more likely to suffer trauma associated
with vehicles or animal interaction than female cats
while female cats appear more likely to fall from heights.
Burn injuries most often occur in the veterinary hospital
setting (heating pads) or structure fires; there is no
species, breed or sex predilection.

­History and Clinical Signs
The diagnosis of trauma is generally made based on
history and physical exam findings rather than diagnostic test results. Often, the medical history is incomplete
and it is not uncommon for the animal to be presented
by a Good Samaritan rather than the owner. Cats frequently present with no history but with physical exam
findings that are consistent with trauma.
Clinical signs associated with trauma will be dependent
on the mechanism behind the trauma and the location
on the body at which that trauma was inflicted. Typical
injuries following trauma include fractures, contusions
and abrasions, bruising or bleeding. Any animal presenting
with one or more of these findings should be considered
to have suffered trauma until proven otherwise. Blunt
trauma patients are frequently presented with few outward signs of trauma but often have difficulty breathing,
reluctance or inability to ambulate or decreased mentation.
Initially, clinical signs may be mild and the animal may
appear stable due to the catecholamine surge associated
with the fight or flight response. Animals suspected of

447

VetBooks.ir

448

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

suffering blunt trauma should be reevaluated frequently for new clinical signs or progression of existing
clinical signs.
Penetrating trauma is much less difficult to diagnose,
as these patients will have visible external wounds
­consistent with sharp or ballistic injuries. Very often in
penetrating trauma, the amount of apparent external
blood loss is small and animals with thick coats should
be closely inspected for small penetrating wounds.

­Diagnosis
Trauma is not often a diagnostic challenge. However,
elucidating the extent of injuries can be. In all cases of
suspected trauma, a complete medical history and a
detailed description of the traumatic event, if possible,
are essential. Owners should be asked about the patient’s
behavior immediately following the traumatic event.
Specifically, the owner should be questioned about loss
of consciousness, ambulation status, and whether the pet
has urinated since the event. The owner should be asked
to estimate the speed of the vehicle, height of the fall, and
size of attacking animal, as applicable. Additionally,
the owner should be asked to describe where on the pet
they believe most of the trauma occurred. If a car hit the
pet, the owner should be asked if the pet was seen traveling under the car or tire. If the pet was attacked by an
animal, it should be determined if the pet was bitten and
released or clenched and shaken. Finally, if a patient fell
from height, the type of substrate upon which they
landed should be ascertained.
A complete physical examination should be performed,
with special attention paid to the neurologic system and
thoracic and abdominal cavities. When evaluating the
neurologic system in a trauma patient, a stepwise
approach targeting life‐threatening injuries first is utilized.
The patient’s mentation and level of consciousness
(LOC) should be evaluated and their motor activity
should be noted. Decerebrate rigidity (extension of all
four limbs and opisthotonus) is associated with brainstem
compression and altered LOC. Decerebellate rigidity
(extension of forelimbs with hindlimb flexion) indicates
cerebellar herniation and may be associated with normal
or altered LOC. Motor function should be noted, taking
care to discriminate between spinal reflexes and voluntary movement. Finally, brainstem reflexes are assessed.
Pupil size, symmetry, and responsiveness are evaluated.
Attempts should be made to elicit an occulocephalic
reflex, taking care to avoid exacerbating possible cervical
injuries.
Following evaluation of the neurologic system, the
thorax should be evaluated for evidence of trauma.
A visual inspection of the thorax should be performed

and any lacerations, puncture wounds, abrasions or
bruising should be noted. The patient should be observed
while breathing prior to auscultation. Careful attention
should be paid to the rate, depth, and pattern of breathing. Paradoxical movement of the thoracic wall inward
during inspiration (flail chest) is indicative of segmental
fracture of contiguous ribs. Thoracic auscultation should
be performed in a quiet environment. The presence of
breath sounds should be evaluated. Decreased breath
sounds ventrally may indicate the presence of pleural
fluid whereas decreased or absent breath sounds dorsally
may indicate the presence of pneumothorax. In addition
to ventral and dorsal differences, the breath sounds in
each hemithorax should be compared to determine if
unilateral pleural space disease (e.g., tension pneumothorax) is present.
Once the presence of breath sounds is confirmed, the
quality of the sounds should be evaluated. Increases
in bronchovesicular sounds or the presence of focal or
diffuse crackles may indicate pulmonary contusion or
hemorrhage. Detection of borborygmi within the thoracic cavity indicates herniation of abdominal contents
through the diaphragm. Auscultation of the trachea
should also be performed. Tracheal injury may result in
loud guttural sounds while laryngeal injury may result in
higher pitched wheezes (stridor).
The oral mucous membranes should be evaluated for
color and capillary refill time (CRT). Pale mucous membranes can be present from anemia or peripheral vasoconstriction and decreased cardiac output, as seen with
shock. Cyanosis may be observed if severe pulmonary or
pleural space disease is present. Normal CRT is 1–2 seconds. Prolongation of CRT is consistent with decreased
cardiac output and early to late decompensated shock.
Patients in compensated shock may have a brisker than
normal CRT and mucous membrane color may be bright
pink to red.
The presence of cardiac sounds should be confirmed
and the rate and regularity of the rhythm should be noted.
Tachycardia can occur secondary to shock, pain or anxiety. Bradycardia may occur during shock in cats, but its
presence in dogs is a harbinger of circulatory collapse and
cardiopulmonary arrest. The absence of heart sounds
may indicate pleural space disease (hemothorax), pericardial effusion or cardiac arrest. Pulses should be palpated
during cardiac auscultation and should be evaluated for
strength and synchrony with the heart. Heart sounds that
do not generate a palpable pulse or pulses of varying
strength are abnormal and electrocardiography should be
considered. Severe peripheral vasoconstriction as seen in
shock states results in the distal limbs being cooler to the
touch than the trunk. A rectal temperature below normal
is consistent with decompensated shock and should be
considered a negative prognostic indicator.

VetBooks.ir

46 Medical Management of Trauma and Burns

Evaluation of the abdomen consists of visual inspection and palpation. Small puncture wounds over the
abdomen, especially puncture wounds associated with
animal bites, may belie severe trauma to the abdominal
wall or abdominal viscera. Abdominal distension with or
without a palpable fluid wave may occur with traumatic
hemoabdomen. Palpation of the urinary bladder should
be attempted although the presence of a palpable urinary
bladder does not exclude the possibility of uroabdomen.
A rectal exam should be performed in any animal that
suffered blunt trauma to the caudal half of the body.
Palpation of the pelvic ring for fractures and evaluation
of anal tone are important components of a complete
physical exam.
Assessment of the abdomen with ultrasound is becoming commonplace and has been shown to be a more sensitive indicator of free abdominal fluid than blind
four‐quadrant abdominocentesis or diagnostic peritoneal lavage. To perform an abdominal focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) exam, the
patient is placed in either left or right lateral recumbency.
The ultrasound probe is placed at the first location on
midline just caudal to the xyphoid process (diaphragmatico‐hepatic position). The probe is then rotated cranially, caudally, and laterally in both directions. If no free
fluid is observed then the probe is moved to the second
site. The process is repeated, targeting the four points of
investigation: diaphragmatico‐hepatic, spleno‐renal (left
body wall over the left kidney), cysto‐colic (midline over
the urinary bladder), and hepato‐renal (right body wall
over the right kidney). If free fluid is found, the test is
considered positive and an attempt should be made to
obtain a sample for evaluation.
In most cases, orthopedic and cutaneous wounds are
not immediately life threatening and their evaluation
should complete the physical examination when the
patient is deemed stable. The patient should be fully
evaluated for the presence of lacerations, puncture
wounds, abrasions or bruising. Gross deformity of
limbs is assessed followed by a detailed orthopedic
exam targeting long bones and joints of the appendicular skeleton. If not already done, the animal should be
observed ambulating, if able. Radiographs of any areas
of pain or instability should be obtained to determine
the extent of the injuries. Wounds should be gently
clipped to facilitate assessment.
Burn‐Specific Considerations
When evaluating patients that have been burned, it is
important to assess both the depth of the burn and the
TBSA affected. Burn depth is classified as follows: superficial burns, superficial partial thickness, deep partial
thickness, and full thickness. This terminology has

supplanted the older classification scheme of grading
burns by degree and provides a better description of
burn severity. It is important to remember that the depth
of the burn may vary across the affected area. Superficial
wounds are erythematous and may have a dry, flaky
appearance. Superficial partial‐thickness burns are
erythematous and moist. They blanch and blisters may
be present. Deep partial‐thickness burns are characterized by an absence of blisters and they appear waxy with
reduced pain sensation. Full‐thickness burns are white
and may have eschar formation. Hair is easily plucked
from the burn site.
Special attention should be paid to the airways of
patients that have suffered burns in fires. The oropharynx should be evaluated for the presence of soot and the
thorax should be carefully auscultated for evidence of
airway or pulmonary parenchymal injury. If the animal
smells of smoke then there is a high likelihood that
some degree of inhalation injury is present. Notation of
respiratory rate and effort should be made immediately
and respiratory patterns and oxygenation status should
be reevaluated regularly.

­Therapy
The treatment of trauma patients can be divided into two
distinct phases. The primary or acute phase of trauma
management is focused on restoration of systemic and
local oxygen delivery to preinjury levels to minimize secondary ischemic injury. The second phase of trauma
management lasts until the patient is discharged and
centers on maintaining oxygen delivery, definitive treatment of wounds or fractures, provision of nutritional
support, and pain management.
Primary Phase
Successful resuscitation begins with recognition of its
need. Resuscitation should be directed at reexpansion
of effective circulating volume and re-establishment of
systemic and local blood flow. The exact method of
resuscitation is less important than the goals that are
targeted. Classic resuscitation endpoints have focused
on macrocirculatory findings such as heart rate, pulse
quality, and blood pressure. Recent developments in
shock treatment have identified microcirculatory markers that may be better for determining when resuscitation is complete (i.e., adequate oxygen delivery and
usage has been restored).
Beyond the traditional resuscitation endpoints, the
evaluation of biochemical markers such as base deficit,
lactate, and central venous oxygen saturation has been
advocated for use in veterinary medicine. The rationale

449

VetBooks.ir

450

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

for using biochemical markers depends on the fact that
cellular hypoxia may continue despite normalization
of traditional resuscitation endpoints and the selected
markers can detect this ongoing oxygen debt. If undetected, occult shock can be prolonged and can lead to
further secondary injury. The best approach for determining when resuscitation is complete is one that incorporates both traditional and goal‐directed endpoints.
Volume expansion should be achieved using replacement crystalloid fluids, hypertonic crystalloid fluids,
synthetic colloids or blood products (packed red blood
cells, fresh frozen plasma, fresh whole blood) as needed,
although low‐volume resuscitation (hypertonic saline
and synthetic colloid) should be considered as the best
choice for patients suffering head trauma or pulmonary
contusions to minimize the likelihood of overresuscitation and exacerbation of vascular leak. There is no evidence that achieving supraphysiologic values for any of
the macrocirculatory variables confers a benefit; on the
contrary, overresuscitation may lead to increased morbidity (wound edema, fluid overload, dilutional coagulopathy) and should be avoided. Once normalization of
macrocirculatory variables occurs then biochemical
analysis should be performed to determine if oxygen
debt is ongoing.
The provision of supplemental oxygen should be considered in any patient that has suffered trauma to the
thorax or head, any patient in shock, or any patient that
may have suffered inhalation injury. The ideal method to
provide supplemental oxygen would allow the animal to
move freely without restraint and would not contribute
to stress. Oxygen cages or chambers approach this ideal.
Flow‐by oxygen or oxygen provided by facemask may
prove useful during the initial evaluation period when
it is imperative that the animal be handled. Nasal cannulation using purposemade nasal oxygen prongs is
well tolerated by some patients and may allow for provision of supplemental oxygen without significant restraint.
In rare circumstances, it may be necessary to secure
an airway via orotracheal intubation or tracheostomy.
In these cases, 100% oxygen is provided via an anesthetic
circuit or self‐inflating rescue bag.
Early analgesic management is an important part of
the resuscitation phase of trauma management. Once it
is determined that the patient’s life is not in immediate
danger, analgesia should be administered. In general,
veterinary patients are less sensitive to the respiratory
depressant effects of opioid medications and due to the
minimal impact on cardiac indices and their reversibility,
pure opioid agonists (morphine, hydromorphone, oxymorphone or fentanyl) should be considered the analgesic of choice in the acute setting. Head trauma patients
should be treated for pain once it is determined that their
neurologic status is stable. Completely withholding

­analgesia from head trauma patients is no longer advocated. Adequate analgesia improves patient comfort,
facilitates examination, and improves healing.
Primary Wound Management

The goal of wound management during the primary
phase of treatment is to prevent further contamination
of the wounds and prevent additional tissue injury
from occurring. Wounds should be clipped, cleaned
with an antiseptic solution (chlorhexidine or betadine)
and lavaged with saline. Following lavage, the wounds
should be gently probed for depth and extent and then
covered with a nonadherent sterile dressing until the
patient has been stabilized and definitive treatment is
possible. Very recent thermal burn wounds should be
lavaged with cool saline to arrest ongoing thermal
injury and should then be covered with silver sulfadiazine and a nonadherent bandage. Most chemical burns
can be immediately lavaged with tap water for 30 minutes although some alkaline agents may take longer to
remove. Elemental metals, including solid sodium, can
ignite when they come in contact with water and
should instead be covered with mineral oil. Wounds
should never be allowed to go unaddressed for longer
than 2–4 hours.
Any gross deformities suggesting luxation or fracture
should be identified. If fractures are present distal to the
stifle or elbow, the limb should be immobilized with a
soft bandage, ensuring that the joints above and below
the affected area are incorporated. Attempts to reduce
fractures are not necessary in the acute phase of management. Fractures of the humerus, femur, pelvis or scapula
are not bandaged due to muscular coverage and inability
to achieve adequate immobilization. Patients with suspected cervical or spinal fracture or luxation should
be sedated, treated for pain, and immobilized using a
backboard to prevent further injury to the spinal cord. If
sedation or analgesia is inadequate, these patients
often struggle and can exacerbate their injuries.
Luxations are treated in a similar fashion to fractures
and attempts at reduction should be delayed until the
patient’s condition has stabilized.
Secondary Phase
The secondary phase of treatment begins when the
endpoints of resuscitation have been met and the patient
is either admitted to the hospital or moved to surgery.
As stated previously, the focus of the secondary treatment phase is ensuring adequate oxygen delivery is
maintained and establishing definitive treatment for surgical wounds. Additionally, at this stage supportive care
including nutritional support, analgesia, and preventive
nursing care is considered.
