46 Medical Management of Trauma and Burns

Fluid Therapy

Arguably the most important part of medical management of trauma patients is fluid therapy. Trauma and
burn patients have unique fluid needs that require
special consideration. Judicious use of crystalloid fluids
in patients that suffer thoracic trauma and, in particular,
those that develop pulmonary contusions is needed. It
should be remembered that endothelial cell dysfunction
and perturbations in vascular integrity might contribute
to fluid loss from the intravascular space. Excessively
high volumes of crystalloid fluid may exacerbate pulmonary contusions due to their rapid redistribution into the
interstitial space following administration. Patients
with head trauma should be treated in a similar fashion.
If brain edema develops secondary to exuberant fluid
resuscitation, cerebral blood flow may be impaired. This
concern must be balanced by the need to maintain
adequate blood pressure for brain perfusion.
Hypoproteinemia is common in trauma patients,
especially following burn injury, animal bites, or crush
injury. The routine use of synthetic colloids in veterinary
medicine is somewhat controversial due to concerns associated with development of coagulopathy and possibly
renal failure. However, no clinical veterinary trials to
date have demonstrated a negative association and their
use should be considered to maintain colloid osmotic
pressure and reduce edema formation in nonaffected
tissue. In addition to its importance for maintaining colloid osmotic pressure (COP), albumin is an important
carrier molecule and facilitates healing. Therefore,
canine patients may benefit from receiving human serum
albumin or canine‐specific lyophilized albumin rather
than synthetic starches for colloidal support.
Pain Management

The importance of effective pain management goes
beyond the ethical consideration of ameliorating pain.
The presence of pain causes increases in sympathetic
tone and catecholamine secretion, leading to increased
cardiac output, peripheral vascular resistance, and myocardial oxygen consumption. While important for the
fight or flight response, these changes, if chronic, further impair oxygen delivery to tissues. In addition to the
cardiovascular effects of pain, a neuroendocrine
response occurs, resulting in elevated levels of catabolic
hormones including cortisol while a concurrent decrease
in the anabolic hormones insulin and testosterone is
present. The net result of the neuroendocrine response
is the development of a catabolic state characterized
by hyperglycemia, type B hyperlactatemia, and keto­
genesis. Treatment of pain reduces or eliminates these
responses, facilitates patient evaluation, improves
patient quality of life, and leads to more rapid healing
and reduced morbidity.

Patients that suffer severe trauma or burns should be
considered to be very painful and analgesia should be
provided liberally. The best method of pain management in traumatized or burned patients utilizes a multimodal approach. Pure opioid agonists are the mainstay
of pain management and should be provided early in the
course of treatment. Opioid medications have no ceiling
effect, meaning that there is no maximum dose at which
­further administration would not be expected to affect a
result. In most cases, administration should be continued throughout the duration of hospitalization. While
opioids are capable of depressing respiratory drive in
veterinary patients, this is rarely clinically relevant.
If there is concern over a patient’s ventilatory drive then
the dose of opioid can be reduced or broken into ­aliquots
and administered to effect.
The dissociative agent ketamine has some analgesic
properties, particularly for superficial pain. More importantly, perhaps, are the n‐methyl D‐aspartate (NMDA)
antagonistic properties of ketamine that may alter spinal
modulation and prevent or ameliorate central sensitization (wind‐up). In order to derive the full benefit of ketamine with regard to sensitization prevention, it should
be administered for at least 24 hours as a constant rate
infusion (CRI) (5–15 μg/kg/min). The use of ketamine
alone is not effective for deep or visceral pain and can
result in behavioral changes, therefore ketamine should
almost always be administered in conjunction with an
opioid. When discontinuing ketamine for patients that
have been on a CRI for longer than 24 hours, a gradual
reduction of the infusion rate over several hours is used
to prevent behavioral changes associated with abrupt
discontinuation.
Clinically, the alpha‐2‐agonists are most commonly
used for sedation although their use for pain management
is becoming more common. Their short half‐lives and
reversibility make them theoretically attractive options in
many trauma patients but careful consideration should be
taken prior to their use since clinically relevant cardiovascular side‐effects are possible. Animals in shock or with
significant heart disease (especially diseases causing
decreased systolic function) should not be administered
alpha‐2‐agonists. A CRI is often employed to most effectively use this class of drugs as a component of the pain
management protocol. When used at rates of 0.5–2 μg/
kg/h, dexmedetomidine can result in anxiolysis and analgesia without significant cardiovascular side‐effects.
Regional or local anesthesia should be considered as
an adjunct to traditional, systemic analgesic methods.
The use of regional or local anesthesia often requires
coordination with the surgical team since these interventions often require general anesthesia or sedation to be
performed. Placement of diffusion catheters for repeated
administration of local anesthetic medication should be

451

VetBooks.ir

452

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

considered at the time of surgery, if applicable; their use in
contaminated wounds (bite wounds) should be avoided,
however. Epidural administration or placement of an epidural catheter can provide excellent pain management
for animals with pelvic limb or pelvic ring trauma. If sacral
fracture or sacroiliac luxation is present or the landmarks
used for epidural administration are disrupted then
epidural administration should not be performed. Local
anesthetic drugs can also be used systemically, with IV
infusion of lidocaine being useful as both an analgesic
adjunct and a promotility agent for management of ileus.
Both blunt trauma and burn injury are capable of
inducing a very pronounced inflammatory state. The use
of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can
be very beneficial in these patients. However, animals
that are severely traumatized or are in shock should not
be administered NSAIDs until all tissue perfusion has
normalized and is not anticipated to change abruptly.
Patients with severe soft tissue injury or crush injury are
at risk for development of myoglobinuria and renal
failure. Any animal that has pigmenturia or evidence of
renal insufficiency should not receive NSAIDs. The decision to use NSAID medications should be deliberate and
if case selection is appropriate then NSAIDs may prove
to be a very useful analgesic adjunct. Due to the risk of
systemic side‐effects, including further impairment of
the already compromised immune system in these
patients, animals that have suffered severe trauma or
burn injury should not receive corticosteroid medications unless specifically indicated.
Many animals that suffer severe soft tissue injury
require repeated sedation events on concurrent days or
even multiple sedation events within the same 24‐hour
period. Patients that are going to require repeated sedation should be identified early in the course of hospitalization and measures should be taken to coordinate
their care. Following repeated sedation with the same
anesthetic medications it is common to see recovery
times become more prolonged and patients require
larger doses of drugs to achieve the same level of sedation due to the development of tolerance. It is good
practice to alter the sedation protocol every few days to
prevent development of tolerance or toxicity with
repeated dosing such as reported with propofol administration in cats. Additionally, animals that are sedated
serially are at risk for nutritional deficiency due to
repeated fasting. Efforts should be made to sedate the
animal at the same time every day to allow for the most
opportunities to provide nutrition.
Nutrition

The benefits of enteral nutrition (EN) for critically ill
patients are well documented and include stimulating
production of local antibody, prevention of villous

atrophy and prevention of gut‐derived inflammatory
complications. There are many ways of providing EN,
including voluntary ingestion, force feeding or syringe
feeding, nasogastric, nasoesophageal or nasojejunal
tube feeding or surgically placed feeding tube (esophagostomy tube, percutaneous gastrostomy tube, surgically
placed gastrostomy tube, jejunostomy tube or gastrojejunostomy tube). The best way to provide EN will likely
vary on an individual case basis and consideration should
be given to several factors when deciding the best
method for each patient.
Nasoesophageal or nasogastric feeding tubes are useful
for animals that are not stable enough for an anesthetic
event or for those that need a temporary bridge to
voluntary eating or placement of a longer term feeding
tube option. Nasogastric tubes can be useful for gastric
decompression in animals with severe ileus and delayed
gastric emptying. One major limitation to the use of
nasoenteral feeding tubes is the limited number of diets
that can be administered through the small diameter of
the tube. Although generally well tolerated in the hospital
setting, these tubes are not particularly useful to send
home with patients. Nasoenteral feeding tubes can be
used in most veterinary patients but some small dogs
and cats may not be able to accommodate the tubes
comfortably within the nasal cavity.
Animals that require a definitive surgical treatment
may benefit from placement of a longer term feeding
tube option at the time of surgery. Esophagostomy tubes
or PEG tubes can be placed quickly in patients under
general anesthesia. Esophagostomy tubes can be used for
provision of nutritional support immediately following
placement but are often limited in the types of food that
they can accommodate. Tube clogging is a common
problem and may necessitate altering the food formula
to a more watery consistency. Percutaneously placed
gastrostomy tubes cannot be used for nutritional support for the first 24 hours to prevent leakage of gastric
contents until a fibrous adhesion forms at the stoma.
Surgically placed gastrostomy or gastrojejunostomy
tubes can be utilized immediately.
The optimal timing of implementing nutritional support is not known but evidence suggests that earlier is
better. The clinician should strive to provide nutritional
support within the first 24–48 hours following severe
trauma or burns. Patients that are hemodynamically
compromised should not have nutritional support begun
until they are fully resuscitated and stable.
When starting nutritional support, it is important to
have a plan in place for meeting nutritional requirements. There is no evidence that provision of calories in
excess of basal energy requirement (BER) is beneficial; in
fact, it may be detrimental. Many formulas are available
for calculating caloric requirements but the basal energy

VetBooks.ir

46 Medical Management of Trauma and Burns

formula 30(BW in kg) +70 = kcal/day is both easy to use
and remember. When instituting a feeding plan, begin by
feeding a fraction (1/3 to 1/2) of the calculated resting
energy requirement (RER) for the first 24 hours with
the goal of achieving full RER over the next 48–72 hours.
It is common for the actual delivered kcal to be less
than the calculated requirement due to the fact that animals may be intolerant of the volume or rate required to
meet the RER, the need to water food down (reducing
the caloric density) to prevent tube clogging, or the
necessity to fast animals for sedation or anesthetic events.
Selection of a calorically dense formula (≥1 kcal/mL) is
best in most settings to ensure that the caloric target is
being reached. If available, the use of immune‐modulating formulas enriched with omega‐3 fatty acids and antioxidants may be a good choice.
Parenteral nutrition (PN) has been associated with a
variety of complications such as hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia, electrolyte disturbance (hypophosphatemia,
hypokalemia), and septiciemia. Although enteral nutrition is always preferable to parenteral nutrition, sometimes it is not feasible due to intolerance of EN or
nonfunctional GI tract (severe ileus, preexisting disease).
For patients that were healthy prior to trauma, PN is not
considered necessary for the first 5–7 days of hospitalization while the patient’s progress is monitored.
If anorexia persists or GI dysfunction becomes evident then PN should be instituted.
Trauma patients are at high risk for development of
ileus due to voluntary or involuntary immobilization,
opioid administration, pain, and general anesthesia.
Aggressive management of ileus should be attempted
with metoclopramide, cisapride, lidocaine, erythromycin
or ranitidine. Consideration should be given prior to routine treatment with H2 blockers due to the potential for
bacterial overgrowth in the proximal GI tract and subsequent complications. Ideally, the use of gastric alkalinizing medications would be based on evidence of gastric
ulceration or esophagitis or the probability of either of
these complications developing.
Transfusion

Severely traumatized patients may require red blood cell
or plasma component therapy due to hemorrhage or
development of complications such as DIC. Red blood
cell transfusion increases the oxygen‐carrying capacity
of the blood and helps to reestablish the oxygen reserve
normally present in health. Determining a transfusion
trigger is clinician dependent and no clear guidelines
have been established. The decision is made on a case‐
by‐case basis, carefully weighing the pros and cons of
each transfusion. As a general rule, the more acute the
drop in hemoglobin, the higher the transfusion trigger
since the necessary time to adapt to the decrease in blood

oxygen content has not passed. If a patient is exhibiting
clinical signs associated with anemia, is in hemorrhagic
shock refractory to crystalloid or colloid resuscitation, or
is undergoing a planned surgical procedure with anti­
cipated blood loss then transfusion of red blood cells
should be considered. The target packed red blood cell
volume (PCV) for blood transfusion is also unknown but
achieving a PCV of 25–30% is reasonable, with little evidence that higher values are beneficial. Improving blood
oxygen content can subsequently improve wound healing
and prevent or ameliorate secondary injury associated
with ischemia or inadequate oxygen delivery.
Since blood transfusion is becoming more common in
veterinary medicine, it is important to obtain a full
transfusion history from the owner prior to administration of any blood product. Pretransfusion testing will
vary by case according to how urgently the product is
needed. If time allows then complete pretransfusion
testing, including blood typing and major cross‐match,
should be performed. Blood typing of cats is mandatory
in all cases regardless of time sensitivity due to the
potential for fatal reactions to first‐time transfusions.
Cross‐matching of cats should be considered in all
transfusions if time permits due to the prevalence of
preformed antibodies in this species. It is not necessary
to cross‐match dogs receiving their first blood transfusion, as the existence of preformed antibodies is very
uncommon, and in the emergency setting a universal
donor or DEA 1.1‐negative donor unit can be given with
little to no pretransfusion testing. Animals that require
multiple transfusions during a hospitalization should
have a major cross‐match performed for all transfusions
occurring 72 hours after the first due to the risk of severe
hemolytic transfusion reaction.
The rate at which blood is administered is determined
by the patient’s volume status and cardiovascular stability.
In patients that are in hypovolemic shock secondary to
massive hemorrhage, blood can be administered as fast
as it will flow into the patient. Under more controlled
circumstances, most blood transfusions are started at
reduced rates that are gradually increased with the goal
of completing the transfusion over several hours. Close
attention should be paid to vital signs in an effort to
detect transfusion reactions early.
Fluid overload is an uncommon complication in dogs
receiving packed red blood cells but may be a concern in
cats (especially if underlying heart disease is present).
In addition to volume concerns, each red blood cell
transfusion will expose the patient to foreign antigen and
will stimulate an immune response to a greater or lesser
degree. In patients that are already experiencing systemic inflammation, this second hit may precipitate further injury, as in the case of transfusion‐related acute
lung injury.

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

Sepsis Prevention

While animals with penetrating injuries or with grossly
contaminated wounds should be started on antibiotics,
the use of prophylactic antibiotics in animals that have
suffered blunt trauma without disruption of the integument is controversial. When necessary, first‐generation
cephalosporins are generally adequate for wounds not
related to animal bites. Patients that suffer animal bites
should be treated with potentiated penicillins or fluoroquinolones to cover common oral pathogens. Available
evidence suggests that burn patients should not routinely
be administered prophylactic antibiotics. If signs of
infection develop, such as redness, new or worsening
pain, or malodorous or purulent discharge, then antibiotic therapy should be instituted at that time. As always,
antibiotic therapy guided by culture results is the best
practice and when possible, cultures should be obtained
prior to administration of antibiotics.
Strict adherence to catheter hygiene should always be
followed (gloves worn, IV lines kept off the floor), and IV
catheters should be monitored daily for signs of phlebitis
or infection and should be replaced or removed if present. Any patient that develops a fever while in hospital
should have all catheter and tube sites inspected for signs
of infection. In addition to daily visual inspection, catheter wraps should be changed daily. Urinary catheters
should be connected to a closed collection system upon
placement and the collection system should be changed
daily. IV fluid lines should be changed on a routine basis
and disconnections of the IV fluid line from the patient
should be avoided as much as possible. Any gross contamination of the IV line should be immediately cleaned
and the line should be changed.
Severely traumatized or burned patients should always
be handled with gloves to prevent colonization with
bacteria from caregivers. Colonization with methicillin‐
resistant Staphylococcus species is common in healthcare
professionals and can put patients at risk if normal barrier prophylaxis and hand hygiene are not followed.
Monitoring

Critically ill trauma and burn patients are at risk for
decompensating acutely due to myriad causes including
multiorgan failure, acute lung injury or acute respiratory
distress syndrome (ARDS), pulmonary thromboembolism, pneumonia, DIC or sepsis. Diligent monitoring of
these patients will allow the clinician to identify possible
complications early and increase the likelihood of successful intervention.
Severe trauma patients, especially those that have suffered traumatic brain injury or thoracic trauma, should
be placed on a respiratory watch and have both respiratory rate and effort evaluated at least hourly. Continuous
electrocardiographic monitoring should be strongly

­considered in all trauma patients, especially those with
­thoracic trauma. If continuous ECG monitoring is not
feasible then heart rate and pulse synchrony should be
checked frequently. Blood pressure monitoring should
be performed regularly. Monitoring mentation, central
venous pressure, direct arterial pressure, pulse oximetry,
urine output, and body weight can provide invaluable
information on progression of the patient’s condition.
Laboratory monitoring should include serial blood gas
analysis (venous or arterial), blood lactate and blood glucose measurement. Serum biochemistry analysis, complete blood count, and urinalysis should be performed at
admission and then every 2–3 days as the patient’s condition dictates. Coagulation assays should be considered
if DIC is suspected or if the patient has had substantial
blood loss or blood component therapy. Serial radiographs are useful for monitoring progression of pulmonary injury and serial ultrasound can aid in monitoring
progression of abdominal disease.
The nursing staff is often the first to be aware of a
patient’s changing condition and the longer they work
with a patient, the more attuned they become to subtle
changes in status. Therefore, a good working relationship with the nurses providing treatments is imperative
for successful monitoring of severely injured patients.
Preventive Nursing Care

It is important to prevent trauma patients from remaining
recumbent for long periods of time. Nonambulatory
patients should be repositioned several times a day to prevent pressure sores from developing. Mobility facilitates
mucus clearance from the lower airways and supervised
walks should be encouraged as soon as possible. If walks are
not possible, patients should have passive range of motion
performed several times a day. In addition to encouraging
mobility, recumbent patients should be provided with soft
bedding to distribute weight over pressure points and further decrease the likelihood of pressure ulcer formation.
A concerted effort should be made to keep the patient
clean and free from fecal or urine contamination. Prompt
removal of waste and bathing when necessary will aid in
prevention of fecal or urinary scalding that can lead to
compromise of the integumentary barrier. If urine or
fecal scalding is present then the fur from the area should
be clipped, the area should be cleaned with dilute antiseptic solution and a barrier ointment such as zinc oxide
should be applied several times a day. Many of these
patients may require urinary management such as
intermittent bladder catheterization, indwelling urinary
catheter placement or intermittent urinary bladder
expression. The presence of an indwelling urinary catheter is a risk factor for development of urinary tract
infection and can be an important contributor to
patient morbidity. If a urinary catheter is present then

VetBooks.ir

46 Medical Management of Trauma and Burns

the collection system should be maintained closed to
reduce the chances of ascending contamination and urinary tract infection.
Patients with bandages covering wounds should have
the bandages changed immediately if strikethrough is
present or if the bandage becomes contaminated with
feces or urine to prevent bacterial contamination of the
wound bed. Regardless of contamination, bandages
should be changed at least daily initially.
Burn‐Specific Therapy

In the early postresuscitation phase of burn management
(2–24 hours), patient fluid needs are likely to be much
greater than would normally be expected. With this in
mind, care should be taken to avoid excessive fluid
administration and the goals of fluid administration
should focus on maintaining blood pressure and urine
production within normal limits.
Due to decreased local perfusion, burn wounds should
be treated with topical antimicrobial agents and covered
with nonadherent dressings after initial decontamination to prevent bacterial colonization rather than relying
on systemic antimicrobial therapy. The topical antimicrobial of choice is silver sulfadiazine (SSD), which has a
broad antimicrobial spectrum and few side‐effects.
Manuka honey can be used as an alternative to SSD.
Rehabilitation

Comprehensive management of trauma and burn patients
does not end with hospital discharge. These patients
often require weeks to months of physical rehabilitation,
which should begin in hospital, to regain lost mobility
and to complete the healing process. Often patients are
discharged earlier than planned due to financial limitations of the owner. In these instances, it is imperative that
in‐depth discharge instructions be provided to the owner
on how to perform nursing care, including passive range
of motion, tube feedings, bladder expression, medication
administration, etc. Consideration should be given to
referring the client to a certified veterinary rehabilitation
specialist, especially if spinal trauma, long bone fractures
or severe soft tissue injuries were present. Burn patients
are at risk for development of contracture as burns heal
and physical therapy can help to prevent severe contracture deformity and maintain functional mobility.

­Prognosis
Euthanasia is always a confounding factor when determining prognostic factors in veterinary patients.
However, factors that appear to be correlated with an
increased mortality include higher injury severity score,
presence of head trauma, requirement of mechanical

ventilation, hemoperitoneum, and vertebral fractures.
Many scoring systems have been recommended for both
human and veterinary patients to help predict patient
outcomes. While care should be taken when using scoring systems to predict likely outcomes for individual
patients, they may be useful to assess risk of death.
The Animal Trauma Triage (ATT) Score (Box 46.1)
was developed to estimate risk of death following trauma.
The ATT is easy to use and has been validated in several
patient populations. The score uses a numerical value
from 0 to 3 in six categories with a total possible score of
18. For every one‐point increase in ATT, the patient’s
risk of death increases by 2.3–2.6 times. While the ATT
has proven useful in trauma patients, it fails to take into
account the presence of preexisting disease or nontarget
organ system evaluation.
The use of a Modified Glasgow Coma Score (MGCS)
for prognostication following head trauma has been
reported in the veterinary literature (Box 46.2). The
MGCS assigns a conglomerate score from 3 to 18 based
on scores ranging from 1 to 6 in three categories: motor
activity, brainstem reflexes, and level of consciousness.
The lower the score, the worse the patient’s performance
is within each category, and a total score of less than 8
correlates with 50% survival at 48 hours. While the utility
of a one‐time MCGS performed at presentation is open
for debate, serial evaluation can be used and may help
the clinician to make a more objective assessment of
the progression of traumatic brain injury. A worsening
MGCS during the first 24–48 hours should be considered a negative prognostic indicator. The short‐term
prognosis for dogs with traumatic brain injury is similar
to mortality rates for blunt trauma in general (12–15%).
The long‐term neurologic outcome of dogs surviving
after head trauma is generally considered to be good to
excellent. However, it is reported that 7% of dogs suffering head trauma develop a seizure disorder.
The prognosis for animals suffering blunt trauma is generally good with aggressive supportive care. Animals that
suffer blunt trauma secondary to vehicular injury have a
reported mortality rate of approximately 15–25%.
Negative prognostic indicators include cranium fractures,
recumbency at admission, development of DIC, multiple
organ dysfunction syndrome, the need for ventilation or
vasopressor therapy and cardiopulmonary arrest.
Animals that suffer bite wounds from larger animals
should be considered critically ill until proven otherwise.
The amount of trauma to the underlying tissue is disproportionate to the amount of external injury visible
during examination and all of these wounds should be
considered contaminated with bacteria. Small dogs and
cats that have been bitten by larger canids also are likely
to have a component of crush injury associated with the
wound. For these reasons, animals with severe bite injury

Venomous Snake Bites
Nathan Peterson, DVM, DACVECC
VCA West Los Angeles Animal Hospital, Los Angeles, CA, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
The degree of pathology related to snakebites is determined by
two main factors: the composition of the venom and the
amount of venom injected into the victim. In veterinary
medicine, there are two families of venomous snakes that
are responsible for the vast majority of envenomations: the
Viperidae and Elapidae. In general, vipers are capable of
injecting venom through hollow fangs and once they
(vipers) are mature, they have the ability to control the volume of venom injected with each bite. The Elapidae do not
have such an advanced venom delivery system and rely on
introduction of venom secreted from a venom gland
through a wound created by biting. These snakes use their
teeth and underdeveloped fangs in a chewing motion to
create the wound. Therefore, elapid envenomation usually
requires a snake to “adhere” or “chew” on a victim for some
amount of time to allow adequate envenomation and consequently, these snakes strike and hold to allow for venom
introduction whereas vipers strike and retreat, allowing the
venom injected during the bite to immobilize the patient.
The composition of snake venom is extremely complex and it varies between species and within species
based on geographic range. Venom composition also
varies with age of the snake and the time of year. There
are many potential effects of snake envenomation
including flaccid paralysis, systemic myolysis, coagulopathy and hemorrhage, renal damage/failure, cardiotoxicity, and local tissue injury at the bite site. While the
traditional view of venomous snakes was that vipers
caused local and hemorrhagic effects (hemotoxic
venom) and elapids caused systemic and nonhemorrhagic effects (neurotoxic venom), the reality is that any
species of snake is capable of producing venom that
can affect one or more of the body systems. Some Asian
and African cobras (vipers) produce profound tissue
injury while some South and Central American

­rattlesnakes (also vipers) produce primarily paralytic
or neurotoxic venoms.
The venom of the North American pit vipers (Crotalidae)
is typically classified as necrogenic/hemorrhagic and is
capable of causing massive tissue damage and inducing
life‐threatening inflammation or hemorrhage. The venom
is primarily composed of water, with proteins and peptides making up approximately 10% of the total volume. It
is this portion of the venom that is responsible for most of
the direct tissue injury and hemostatic perturbation seen
with envenomation. It is also this portion that is responsible for inducing endothelial cell damage leading to endothelial dysfunction, cell lysis, and ultimately circulatory
collapse. So far, over 60 purified polypeptides and approximately 50 enzymatic fractions have been identified with
at least 10 enzymes and 3–12 nonenzymatic proteins and
peptides present in any individual snake’s venom.
Hyaluronidase and collagenase act to break down
­connective tissue, facilitating the spread of venom and
beginning the digestive process. Together, these enzymes
are capable of causing massive tissue damage and necrosis and are responsible for many of the outward sings of
envenomation. The impact of envenomation on hemostasis is profound and can be considered in light of the
areas of hemostasis that are affected.
Venom proteins acting directly on coagulation factors
include procoagulant proteins such as factor V (FV) activators, FX activators, prothrombin activators, and
thrombin‐like enzymes. Anticoagulant venom factors
also exist and include FIX/X binding proteins, protein C
activators, thrombin inhibitors, and phospholipase A2.
Finally, factors acting on fibrinolysis include fibrinolytic
enzymes (metalloproteinases and serine proteases) and
plasminogen activator.
Many of the components of snake venom exert an effect
on platelet function. The C‐type lectins, disintegrins,
and proteinases inhibit platelets by a variety of

© 2020 John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Published 2020 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc.
Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/bruyette/clinical

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

­mechanisms, including interactions with von Willebrand
factor (vWF) receptors and fibrinogen receptors. Platelet
activation occurs through a thrombin‐like effect of proteinases and phospholipase A2, among other mediators.
Besides the effect of venom on primary and secondary
hemostasis, proteins in the venom can affect the endothelium. Metalloproteinases, disintegrins, and C‐type lectins degrade the blood vessel extracellular matrix, induce
endothelial cell apoptosis, and inhibit platelet binding
through interference with vWF. The net result of this
combined action is consumption of fibrin and development of bleeding diathesis that is not generally characterized by thrombosis or intravascular coagulation.
Neurotoxins contained in snake venom exhibit a
­predilection for peripheral nervous tissue and relatively
few are capable of crossing the blood–brain barrier.
Venoms that exert a primarily neurotoxic effect act as
either presynaptic (beta‐neurotoxins) or postsynaptic
(alpha‐neurotoxins) neuromuscular blocking agents;
most neurotoxic venoms contain toxins that affect both
the pre‐ and postsynaptic neuron. Presynaptic or beta‐
neurotoxins have been isolated from members of the
Elapidae and Viperidae (including Crotalidae) families.
Most of these toxins inhibit neurotransmitter (acetylcholine) release although a small number have been
identified that actually enhance neurotransmitter
release. Postsynaptic or alpha‐neurotoxins result in a
curare‐like syndrome by binding acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane or interfering with
acetylcholine interaction with its postsynaptic receptors. The degree of inhibition is related to the number
of receptors occupied by toxin molecules. Most of these
toxins bind irreversibly to the acetylcholine (ACh)
receptor although treatment with antivenin seems to
accelerate toxin–receptor dissociation.
A unique syndrome resulting in myokymia (spontaneous undulating fine contractions of multiple individual motor units) has been identified with venom from
timber rattlesnakes (Crotalus horridus). Primarily neurotoxic snake bites result in much less local tissue inflammation and pain than their necrogenic counterparts.
Large necrosing wounds are uncommon in these cases.

­Epidemiology
Of the approximately 2300 species of snakes worldwide,
about 420 are venomous. Venomous species can be
found on every continent except Antarctica, with members of the Viperidae family found throughout the world.
In North, Central, and South America, the Viperidae
family is represented primarily by the pit vipers
(Crotalidae) and is responsible for the majority of veterinary envenomations. The true incidence of veterinary

patients bitten by snakes every year is unknown but it is
estimated to be between 150 000 and 300 000. Animals
that are most at risk are those that live in a rural or semirural environment although dogs that are taken on walks
in wilderness areas are also at high risk, especially if
allowed off leash. There is a strong seasonal influence on
the incidence of snake bites, with the majority of bites
occurring in the spring and summer months.
The severity of a bite depends on several variables,
including the time that has elapsed since the snake’s last
meal (it takes approximately 20 days for pit vipers to
replenish venom stores), the motivation of the snake
(defensive or offensive), and its age. Bites from immature
snakes in the spring months are often more severe than
bites that occur later in the season since juvenile pit vipers
have not developed the ability to control the amount of
venom that is injected with each strike but rather deliver an
“all or nothing” bite. Therefore, somewhat counterintuitively, it is arguably better for an animal to be bitten by a
large adult pit viper than a juvenile. The metabolic demands
required to synthesize venom are quite high so adult snakes
will often deliver an initial “dry bite” (a bite containing no
venom) as an attempt to deter a pet from further harassing
them. Subsequent defensive strikes, however, are often
very severe as the snake continues to feel threatened and is
committed to finally deterring its assailant.
The most common location of bite wounds is the head
(79%) followed by extremities (16%) while bites to the
torso account for less than 2% of confirmed snake bites.
Additionally, single bites are much more common than
multiple bites, with multiple bites occurring approximately 15–30% of the time. The small puncture wounds
typical of snake bites are often difficult to locate and can
be easily overlooked, especially if no surrounding local
tissue reaction is present. Only 20–25% of known rattlesnake bites are actually envenomating.
Cats appear to be inherently more resistant to pit viper
venom than dogs. However, when cats do present for
veterinary care, their clinical condition is generally more
advanced. This may be due to cats’ habit of hiding and
avoiding human contact following a snake bite compared
to dogs who are more likely to seek human interaction.
Cats’ smaller body size and inclination to “toy” with
possible prey may also be contributing factors to explain
these findings.
The species of snake is known in less than 50% of cases
although this can often be inferred based on the known
ranges of different species. Owners should be discouraged from attempting to identify the snake due to the
danger that is posed with handling a live or very recently
dead snake. Envenomating bites can occur from recently
dead or decapitated snakes. These agonal bites typically
inject the entire volume of the venom gland, making
them very severe.

VetBooks.ir

47 Venomous Snake Bites

Coral snake envenomations are relatively uncommon
in the United States and are most likely to occur in the
southeastern US and Gulf Coast region. The infrequency
of bites is due to the reclusive nature and physical limitations of the snake. North American coral snakes are
small in size and have small fixed fangs that are incapable
of penetrating thick undercoats. Coral snakes depend on
venom being introduced through a chewing motion
rather than being injected. This requires the snake to be
attached to the victim for some time to allow sufficient
venom delivery. Dogs may even present to a veterinarian
with the snake still maintaining its grip on the victim.
Due to the rural location in which bites often occur
and the relative proximity or distance to veterinary care,
the time from bite to veterinary care is highly variable
but is usually within the first 2–3 hours.

­Signalment
Young dogs of both sexes are equally at risk of being
bitten by a snake. Although a clear breed predilection
has not been identified, the sporting and working breeds
appear to be overrepresented. Any dog or cat that spends
time outdoors, especially if off leash or unsupervised in a
rural or semirural environment, is at risk for being bitten
by a snake.

­History and Clinical Signs
Pets that have been bitten by snakes will have a very
short pertinent history that may include known exposure to snakes. Owners will often report the presence of
a swelling on the face or limbs that seems to be getting
worse rapidly. The pet will be exhibiting signs of pain and
may be either seeking or eschewing attention. Snakes are
reclusive animals and owners frequently do not see them
interact with their pet, making observation of a strike
uncommon. When presented with a patient that has
clinical signs consistent with snake bite, the veterinarian
should question the owner about observed snake activity
and possible exposure. Signs of snake envenomation
almost always occur within the first four hours but may
be delayed up to 24 hours, making the possibility of
determining when snake bite could have occurred relatively easy.
Patients with necrogenic snakebites will exhibit swelling or erythema around the puncture wounds. Localized
swelling is present in approximately 90–95% of cases at
the time of initial examination. If the patient is presented
very early following the bite then outward clinical signs
can be initially very mild and may easily be overlooked
but signs reliably appear within 30 minutes from the

time of bite. When evaluated early, these patients can be
mistaken as having a hypersensitivity reaction as is
commonly seen with Hymenoptera stings. If the owner
cannot provide a history that supports a diagnosis of
snake bite, these patients may initially be incorrectly
treated for hypersensitivity reactions. A distinguishing
feature of snake bite is significant pain associated with
the swelling whereas severe pain is generally absent in
hypersensitivity reactions. Petechiae may be seen at
presentation about 20% of the time.

­Diagnosis
The diagnosis of snake bite is usually suspected based on
a history of snake interaction observed or suspected by
the owner. Confirmation of the diagnosis is achieved
through examination of the patient with the presence of
characteristic puncture wounds and local, progressive
lymphedema.
Initial biochemical laboratory evaluation is usually
normal although creatine kinase (CK) and aspartate
aminotransferase(AST) may be elevated secondary to
muscular injury. Complete blood count may reveal
thrombocytopenia. When present, thrombocytopenia is
generally moderate (135 000–160 000 platelets/μL). Mild
to moderate leukocytosis may also be present during
the initial evaluation. Pit viper envenomation has been
shown to cause echinocytosis and a blood film revealing
significant echinocytosis is supportive of a diagnosis of
envenomation. Coagulation assays performed at the
time of hospitalization may reveal prolongation of
prothrombin time (PT), partial thromboplastin time
(PTT) or activated clotting time (ACT). When present,
the prototypical venom‐induced coagulopathy is defined
by low fibrinogen and platelet counts, increased fibrin
split products (FSP), normal D‐dimer concentration, and
prolonged PT and PTT. This characteristic coagulation
profile is due to the defibrination of plasma without
overt coagulation resulting in failure of D‐dimer concentration to become elevated. Clinically, D‐dimer levels are
often mildly elevated, most likely reflecting systemic
inflammation and clot formation at the site of the bite
wound. Recently, thromboelastography has been used to
evaluate dogs with snake bite and may prove a useful
adjunct for both diagnosis and prognosis.
Although uncommon, snake venom is capable of causing
cardiac arrhythmias. Routine monitoring of electrocardiographs (ECGs) is probably not necessary but any
animal that has tachycardia and/or an audible irregularity should have an ECG performed to evaluate for the
presence of potentially malignant arrhythmias. While
not specific, the presence of an arrhythmia in a patient
exhibiting signs of snake bite may support the diagnosis.

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

Diagnosing coral snake envenomation is complicated
by the lack of local tissue reaction and the fact that signs
may not develop for up to 12 hours following envenomation. Any patient exhibiting signs of a rapidly progressive
ascending paralysis in coral snake endemic areas should
be considered at risk and be treated appropriately.
Owners may not be as aware of coral snake exposure due
to the smaller size of the snakes and the lack of a warning
system such as a rattle.

­Therapy
First Aid
Appropriate veterinary care should not be delayed to
allow first aid measures to be performed. First aid for
snake bites has a long and storied past, including lancing
and suctioning the wound, placing tourniquets, ice packing, warm packing, and administering electroshock,
among other techniques. To date, none of these measures has demonstrated any improvement in outcome; in
fact, some can significantly worsen the clinical course of
disease. Placement of tourniquets may exacerbate the
amount of tissue injury by preventing dilution of the
venom as it is distributed throughout the body and prolonging the duration of time that venom is present in
the affected tissue bed. Envenomation that would not
otherwise induce tissue necrosis might therefore result
in massive tissue loss if a tourniquet is placed inappropriately in the field. Cold packing can induce local vasoconstriction and exacerbate tissue injury through a similar
mechanism. Incision and suction should never be performed. It is not likely to result in any improvement in
outcome and may put the care provider at risk. The best
first aid measure available is to immobilize the affected
area if possible and to transport the patient to the nearest
veterinary facility capable of treating snake bite. Due to
the preponderance of snake bites being located on the
head and muzzle of dogs and cats, immobilization is not
often feasible and rapid transport is the best option.
While first aid measures in necrogenic snake bites do
not include application of a tourniquet or compression
bandage, coral snake envenomations do benefit from
constriction. There is very little local tissue injury associated with coral snake envenomations, meaning the application of a tight compression bandage on the affected
area should be performed if possible.
Antivenin Therapy
Regardless of the primary effect of the venom, the mainstay of treatment for snake bite is the administration of
venom antibodies (antivenin) specific to the envenoming

species if possible. Because the effectiveness of antivenin
is dependent on binding circulating venom molecules, a
molar dosing regimen is followed, meaning that the
dose of antivenin is dependent on the volume of venom
injected rather than the patient’s body size. In fact,
smaller animals often require higher doses of antivenin
due to differences in the volume of distribution of venom
in a small versus large dog. Antivenin therapy is most
effective when instituted early in the disease course
although it is effective as long as circulating venom is
present and should be considered even many hours
after an envenomation if clinical signs are severe or progressive or if a coagulopathy develops.
Unfortunately, the cost of antivenin therapy can be
quite high and often results in patients receiving less
antivenin than ideal circumstances would dictate. When
faced with the predicament of whether or not to administer a dose of antivenin with the belief that it will not be
a completely effective dose, the clinician should err on
the side of treatment since binding even a portion of the
free venom may improve the clinical course.
There are currently two major types of antivenin commercially available. Polyvalent whole molecule antivenin
is derived from the serum of horses sensitized to several
North, Central, and South American pit viper species
and contains the entire IgG antibody and may contain
equine albumin, depending on manufacturer. The second type of antivenin is composed of the Fab portion only
of an ovine‐ or equine‐derived antibody rather than the
complete immunoglobulin molecule. Whole immunoglobulin antivenin is generally less expensive and more
readily available than Fab‐based antivenins but due to the
presence of the entire IgG molecule and possibly additional foreign proteins (equine or ovine albumin), the
possibility of hypersensitivity reaction is increased.
Antivenins containing the smaller Fab portion of the
immunoglobulin molecule are less immunogenic and
may be better able to diffuse into damaged tissue due to
their smaller size. However, this smaller size results in a
shorter elimination half‐life than the larger complete molecule antivenins. This can lead to a situation in which the
antivenin is eliminated more rapidly than it is capable of
binding circulating venom molecules, resulting in recurrence of clinical signs. If using an Fab‐based antivenin, the
clinician should be aware of this possibility and recognize the fact that repeated dosing may be needed every six
hours to most effectively treat the patient.
While the Fab‐based antivenins are less immunogenic
than the whole molecule formulations, both types of
antivenin are capable of causing immediate and delayed
immune reactions, with a reported incidence of 5–13%.
Anaphylactic (type I) or anaphylactoid hypersensitivity
reactions occur immediately upon administration of
antivenin, are dose related and are due to either an

VetBooks.ir

47 Venomous Snake Bites

IgE‐mediated response (type I) or direct activation of the
complement cascade (anaphylactoid). Signs of anaphylactoid reactions are identical to signs of true anaphylaxis and can range from mild facial edema and pruritus
to complete circulatory collapse. Premedication with
antihistamines has been reported but has not been
proven to be beneficial in reducing the incidence of reactions. Delayed (type III) hypersensitivity reactions have
been reported up to several weeks after administration
and are the result of immune complex formation and
complement activation. Clinical signs associated with
delayed type III hypersensitivity reactions include fever,
lethargy, vasculitis, peripheral edema, and glomerulonephritis. Type III hypersensitivity reactions are generally
self‐limiting but can rarely be life threatening. The risk of
hypersensitivity reactions, including acute anaphylactic
reactions, increases in animals that have been previously
treated with antivenin products.
When edema formation is severe or when the location of
the bite wound is likely to result in life‐threatening complications (airway obstruction), early and aggressive antivenin
therapy should be instituted. Antivenin should be administered to effect until the progression of the signs abates (i.e.,
there is no further evidence of new edema formation,
bruising has stopped spreading, and coagulopathy is controlled). Median doses of antivenin for dogs have been
reported as one vial (range 1–10), and beginning with one
vial given over 30 minutes is reasonable. Additional doses
can be administered every 30–60 minutes as needed. It
should be remembered that ­antivenin products have colloidal properties that can significantly expand the vascular
space. Volume overload is a concern in small patients,
especially those that require higher doses of antivenin.
Serial measurement of muzzle or limb circumference
can help the clinician decide whether progression has in
fact stopped. It is important to remember that as edema
matures, it becomes gravity dependent. Recognition of
edema migration rather than progression is difficult and
is best achieved through good‐quality serial evaluations.
Cage‐side rounds provide an opportunity for all staff to
observe the site, decreasing interobserver variation in
assessment. Similarly, maturation of bruising should
not be confused with ongoing bruising. Clipping the fur
from affected areas and marking the leading edge of
bruising can help the clinician differentiate the two. The
use of digital photography may aid the clinician in monitoring progression and can facilitate communication
between team members if questions arise.
It should be emphasized that snake bite‐induced
coagulopathy is not identical to other types of consumptive coagulopathy, so treatments used for common
coagulopathies are often ineffective if applied to snake
bite coagulopathy. Because the coagulopathy observed in
snake envenomation is the result of defibrination rather

than disseminated coagulation, the treatment of choice
is not factor replacement, at least not initially. The
underlying cause of defibrination is the presence or persistence of venom components in the blood. As long as
venom components are circulating, fibrin and fibrinogen
will continue to be degraded and treatment with factor
replacement therapy in the form of fresh frozen or frozen
plasma is not expected to be beneficial. In fact, administration of plasma products in the presence of circulating
venom may exacerbate coagulopathy by providing more
substrate for degradation, leading to higher levels of FSP,
which further inhibit coagulation. Consequently, the
most vital treatment is inactivation of circulating venom
components by administration of antivenin.
Even with early and aggressive antivenin therapy, bite
wounds to the head can result in severe, progressive edema
and swelling and may pose a threat to airways. Often, early
placement of a temporary tracheostomy is beneficial. Once
edema has stopped forming, it will become gravity dependent and can result in severe swelling of the ventral muzzle
and neck. If the decision to perform a tracheostomy is
made too late, the dissection through edematous tissue is
significantly more difficult.
If open wounds develop, they should be treated like
any other contaminated, large, soft tissue wound. Any
areas of necrosis should be surgically debrided; the
wound should be cleaned daily and protected with a
sterile bandage. Consultation with a surgeon should be
considered for large wounds or wounds involving the
joints. Primary closure of these wounds is rarely feasible
due to the large amount of tissue loss that occurs. When
wounds are present on limbs, the affected limb should be
immobilized in a functional position to reduce the likelihood of wound contracture resulting in decreased range
of motion. Most snake bites result in venom deposition
within subcutaneous tissue rather than muscle bellies, so
fasciotomy is rarely needed in dogs and cats.
Antibiotic therapy for snake bite is controversial in both
human and veterinary medicine. There is little evidence
that prophylactic antibiotic therapy improves the clinical
course or prevents wound infection. The rationale for
antibiotic use is grounded in the fact that bacterial cultures of snakes’ mouths document heavy pathogenic bacterial loads; however, the actual incidence of documented
infection is small. Therefore, the routine use of prophylactic antibiotics is likely not necessary and the decision to
treat with antibiotics is clinician dependent. If used,
broad‐spectrum antibiotics should be selected. Antibiotic
therapy is less controversial once a necrotic wound is present. As always, antibiotic therapy should be guided by
culture and sensitivity results when possible to allow for
deescalation and more responsible antibiotic usage.
Analgesia is an important component of snake bite treatment and should be considered early in the treatment

463

VetBooks.ir

464

Section 5 Critical Care Medicine

course. Administration of antivenin can reduce the acute
pain associated with the snake bite although antivenin
alone is insufficient to provide adequate analgesia. The use of
opioid analgesics has been discouraged due to the possible
respiratory depressant effects of this class of drugs. However,
clinically significant respiratory depression in veterinary
patients is uncommon with opioid medications and should
not be considered a reason for withholding their administration. Administration of bolus opioids may be insufficient
to manage the severe pain associated with snake bite.
Constant rate infusion (CRI) of fentanyl (3–5 μg/kg/h) or
morphine (0.1–0.3 mg/kg/h) should be considered in cases
of severe envenomation. As always, a multimodal approach
to pain management may be more effective than reliance on
a single analgesic protocol. Ketamine has good somatic
analgesic properties and a CRI (5–15 μg/kg/min) can be a
nice addition to the analgesic protocol for snake bite victims. Lidocaine (50 μg/kg/min) and dexmedetomidine CRI
(0.7–1.5 μg/kg/h) have both been demonstrated to provide
analgesia, especially when used in conjunction with opioids. The ultimate pain management strategy implemented
should take patient factors such as age, conformation, location and severity of envenomation, and cardiovascular status into consideration.
Edema formation of the face can impair the pet’s ability to
prehend food and move the lips and tongue. Accumulation
of mucus in the buccal pouch can lead to bacterial overgrowth and development of oral ulcerations. Good oral
care, including rinses with water and/or antiseptic solution,
should be instituted if muzzle swelling is severe.
Some components of snake venom have been demonstrated to result in mast cell degranulation. While
theoretical benefits of antihistamine administration
exist, the routine use of H1 and H2 blocking drugs is not
currently recommended for human snake bite victims and
their use in veterinary patients is up for debate.
As is often the case with corticosteroids, their use is controversial. There is little conclusive veterinary or human
literature to either support or refute their use for snake bite.
Due to the lack of evidence of a clear advantage to patients
receiving corticosteroids and their well‐documented side‐
effects, the routine use of corticosteroids in snake bite
cannot be advocated. Administration of corticosteroids
may be indicated if a patient develops signs of an acute or
delayed hypersensitivity reaction to antivenin administration. Similarly, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs
(NSAIDs) should not be administered to snake bite victims
until any venom‐induced coagulopathy has been effectively
managed due to the potential for NSAID‐induced thrombocytopathia. Following appropriate management of
coagulopathy and hemodynamic stabilization, NSAIDs
may prove useful in the analgesic management of snake bite
victims. Nonsteroidal antiinflammatory medications
should not be administered if myoglobinuria is present.

A rattlesnake vaccine (Red Rock Biologics, Woodland,
CA) is commercially available in the United States for
use against western diamondback rattlesnakes (C. atrox).
There are currently no peer‐reviewed studies evaluating
the clinical efficacy of vaccination in mitigating signs and
none are likely to be performed due to the high incidence
of dry bites and variability in venom dose between
patients. In fact, owners who have had their pets vaccinated may have a false sense of security when it comes to
snake bite and may be slower to seek veterinary care. For
this reason, it is not recommended to vaccinate for snake
bite. Aversion training is available but is also considered
unreliable as this too may result in a false sense of security when in snake habitats.

­Prognosis
Fatality associated with snake bite injury is generally
uncommon although these patients experience significant morbidity. Reported mortality rates range from 4%
to 20% and are correlated with antivenin treatment.
Despite the overall favorable prognosis for survival
from snake bite, many pets are euthanized due to the
financial burden associated with hospitalization and
antivenin therapy, which can easily reach several thousand dollars.
The prognosis is directly dependent on the severity of
the envenomation and the treatment received. Progression
of envenomation is subjective and can be difficult to
assess. One tool that can be utilized is the assignment of a
snake bite severity score (SSS) at the time of admission
and then every 4–6 hours for the first 24 hours (Box 47.1).
The SSS assigns a numerical value ranging from 0 to 4 in
six categories, with a total possible score ranging from 0
to 20, with more severe bites having higher scores. While
the SSS has not been validated in dogs and cannot be
used to assess a particular patient’s risk for death, it aids
the clinician in evaluating progression by assigning value
to objective findings.
The prognosis for patients exhibiting signs of neurotoxicity secondary to envenomation is less clear. The
severity of signs depends on the volume of venom introduced through the bite. Because of the limited local
­tissue reaction associated with coral snake bites, the
severity of envenomation may not be readily apparent at
the time of presentation. If patients develop severe clinical signs then the prognosis is guarded to poor if
mechanical ventilation is not available. Commercially
available coral snake antivenin is difficult to obtain but
has proven useful for treatment of elapid envenomation
in the US. Fortunately the majority of coral snake bites
are nonenvenomating (a consequence of the snake’s
primitive venom delivery system).

Gastrointestinal Imaging
Susanne M. Stieger‐Vanegas, DVM, PhD, DECVDI
Carlson College of Veterinary Medicine, Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, USA

­General Imaging Principles
Medical imaging is an important element of the clinical
work‐up of a patient with gastrointestinal disease. Plain
radiography is commonly used to evaluate patients with
suspected gastrointestinal disease, but plain radiography
can often be unremarkable and abdominal ultrasonogra­
phy or cross‐sectional imaging techniques such as con­
trast‐enhanced abdominal computed tomography might
be required to further evaluate the etiology of the disease.
Plain Radiography
Plain radiography is a widely available imaging technique
and in many cases, it is the principal method used to eval­
uate the abdomen. Numerous studies have evaluated the
usefulness of this technique in cats and dogs with sus­
pected lesions of the oral cavity, esophagus, and gastroin­
testinal tract, in patients with acute abdominal signs,
gastrointestinal foreign bodies, and small intestinal
obstructive disease. However, in the past decade, abdom­
inal ultrasound and more recently contrast‐enhanced
computed tomography have become major imaging
modalities in patients with acute or chronic gastrointesti­
nal signs. When abdominal radiographs are obtained,
they often are used as a screening test. Abdominal radio­
graphs have demonstrated the greatest value in patients
in whom intestinal obstruction and/or perforation and
urinary calculi are suspected. Therefore, the major
value of abdominal radiographs is to exclude intestinal
obstruction or free air in the peritoneal cavity secondary
to perforation of a hollow organ such as the gastrointesti­
nal tract. Despite advances in other imaging modalities,
plain radiography remains the first modality of choice in
patients with suspected gastrointestinal perforation.

Additionally, abdominal radiographs are often used to
evaluate tube or drain placement.
The most commonly used views are ventrodorsal (VD)
and right and/or left lateral recumbent views. The VD
view is usually preferred over the dorsoventral (DV)
view as it is easier to position the abdomen close to
and aligned with the cassette than in a DV view. There
differences in the radiographic appearance
are slight ­
between right and left lateral recumbent views, which
mainly include the change of position of mobile viscera
and of the gas and fluid in the gastrointestinal tract due
to the effect of ­gravity. Additional views, dependent on
the clinical q
­ uestion asked, may include DV for evalua­
tion of gas, contrast agent or foreign material in the
stomach. Lateral or VD views with a horizontal beam are
occasionally used to evaluate for the presence of gas/air
in the peritoneal cavity.
Imaging Contrast Agents and Pharmacoradiology
Contrast radiography or computed tomography are both
valuable imaging techniques, often providing additional
information in the management of patients with gastro­
intestinal signs. Typically, the greatest value is in patients
where radiographic and clinical signs suggesting gastro­
intestinal obstruction are equivocal. Contrast imaging
may help to identify the extent and cause of gastrointes­
tinal obstruction. Contrast agents currently used for gas­
trointestinal imaging can be classified into three groups:
(1) intraluminal contrast agents for gastrointestinal tract
studies; (2) intravascular contrast agents for computed
tomography (CT) and angiography; (3) contrast agents
for magnetic resonance tomography (MRI). These vari­
ous types of contrast agents are discussed separately in
the following sections.

Intraluminal Contrast Agents
Barium Sulfate

Barium sulfate suspension is the most commonly used
contrast agent for gastrointestinal radiographic studies
in veterinary medicine. Barium sulfate is a white crystal­
line powder, which is inert and does not support bacte­
rial growth. Coating of the mucosa of the gastrointestinal
tract or opacification of the lumen of the gastrointesti­
nal tract can require different barium formulations.
Throughout the gastrointestinal tract, the pH, type, and
amount of mucus and type of mucosa vary and therefore
optimal coating in one segment does not necessarily
result in optimal coating in another segment.
Aspiration of small amounts of barium formulations is
of very little clinical significance. Barium within the tra­
chea and main bronchi is usually cleared within 30 min­
utes. If barium aspiration is more extensive, it is retained
within the interstitium of the lungs and a very slow
decrease of barium in the lungs might be noted over sev­
eral months to years (Figure 48.1). If diffuse extensive
alveolar infiltration of barium occurs throughout the
lungs, though, this can lead to death of the patient.
Therefore, if major concerns for aspiration exist before
the study, nonionic iodinated contrast agents should be
considered.
Hypersensitivity reactions to barium have not been
reported in veterinary medicine, but have been reported
rarely in human medicine.
Barium leakage into the peritoneal cavity can occur
due to a preexisting perforation of the gastrointestinal
tract or secondary to a procedure such as a barium
enema. In veterinary medicine, it is commonly accepted
that the suspicion of gastrointestinal perforation is a
contraindication for barium studies in patients. Most of
(a)

our knowledge regarding barium peritonitis is from
human medicine but the small number of reported reac­
tions in small animals seem to be similar. If large amounts
of barium are spilled into the peritoneal cavity, profound
hypovolemia can develop secondary to exudation of
large quantities of fluid associated with the chemical
peritonitis. Furthermore, bacterial contamination may
lead to sepsis and shock within hours. If a barium leakage
occurs, immediate treatment should be started, includ­
ing intravenous fluid therapy and antibiotic adminis­
tration due to the commonly associated bacterial
contamination. Once the patient is stabilized, abdominal
surgery is commonly performed. However, barium can
be difficult to remove surgically as new barium formula­
tions can adhere strongly to the peritoneum.
Negative Contrast Agents

Air is one of the cheapest contrast agents for gastrointes­
tinal studies. In veterinary patients, it is most commonly
used to outline the colon, especially in patients where a
small intestinal foreign body is suspected. Another appli­
cation is in double contrast studies of the gastrointestinal
tract; the most common application of this technique is
in evaluating the stomach for the presence of a foreign
body or to identify the location of the colon and differen­
tiate the colon from small intestine in cases of intestinal
obstruction.
Iodinated Contrast Agents

Water‐soluble, iodine‐containing contrast agents are
most commonly used for gastrointestinal imaging when
esophageal or gastrointestinal perforations are sus­
pected. However, the role of water‐soluble iodinated
contrast agents and the merit of these compounds for

(b)

48 Gastrointestinal Imaging

general imaging of the gastrointestinal tract are areas of
controversy. Water‐soluble iodinated contrast agents do
not coat the gastrointestinal mucosa. The most com­
monly used iodinated contrast agents formulated for the
gastrointestinal tract are hypertonic and therefore pull
fluids into the intestinal tract, resulting in distension of
the intestinal lumen and better definition of the intesti­
nal walls. The hypertonicity and fluid pull into the gas­
trointestinal tract can result in diarrhea and dehydration.
If the contrast agent is aspirated or enters the lungs
through a fistulous tract from the esophagus, severe pul­
monary edema can result. If a perforation into the pleura
or lungs is suspected, nonionic iodinated contrast agents
can be used and are reported to be safer than ionic iodi­
nated contrast agents.
Intravascular Contrast Agents

All currently used contrast agents used for vascular
enhancement (except agents used for MRI) utilize
iodine for X‐ray absorption. Currently, the dominant
areas for use of intravascular contrast agents are CT
and MRI. No routine techniques have been described
for evaluation of the gastrointestinal tract using radiog­
raphy and intravascular contrast agents. Significant
improvements in the composition of intravascular con­
trast agents have been made in the past decades, mak­
ing them safer to use and better tolerated. As sodium
iodide is toxic, it must be delivered in a molecule struc­
ture that is safe to use. The closer the osmolarity of the
contrast agent is to water, the lower the toxicity of the
contrast agent. When iodinated contrast agents are
used, the patient should always be well hydrated as
iodinated contrast agents can cause renal toxicity.
Adverse reactions to intravenous iodinated contrast
agents are rare in veterinary patients, but can range
from anaphylactic shock to local reactions.
Ultrasonography
Ultrasonographic examination is one of the most useful
techniques for evaluating the gastrointestinal tract in
most veterinary patients. Ultrasound of the gastrointes­
tinal tract is not only used to make an initial diagnosis,
but also to monitor response to treatment or disease pro­
gression. Ultrasound can be used to evaluate superficial
aspects of the esophagus in the cervical area and in the
abdomen to evaluate the stomach to descending colon.
Superficial structures are better evaluated with a high­
frequency ultrasound probe, whereas deeper structures
may require the use of low‐frequency probes. Higher‐
frequency ultrasound probes have less tissue penetration
but provide a better resolution of intestinal structures,
including wall layering, compared to low‐frequency
ultrasound probes.

Ultrasound of the gastrointestinal tract provides infor­
mation about the gastrointestinal wall and peristalsis of
the gastrointestinal tract, which is information currently
not provided by any other diagnostic technique, includ­
ing radiography (plain and using oral or gastric contrast
agents), CT, and endoscopy. One of the biggest limita­
tions of the use of ultrasound when evaluating the
­gastrointestinal tract is its inability to penetrate air‐filled
structures, which can include air in the peritoneal cavity
secondary to a perforation or recent surgical procedure
or luminal air in the gastrointestinal tract. However,
this limitation can often be overcome by repositioning
the patient or ultrasound probe relative to the air‐filled
viscera or peritoneal air.
The ultrasound examination of the abdomen in the
dog and cat is commonly performed in lateral or dorsal
recumbency. Usually, the ultrasound exam is started cra­
nial in the abdomen for evaluation of the gastrointestinal
tract or other abdominal disease and then progresses
caudally, usually in the anatomic order of the gastroin­
testinal tract.
Computed Tomography of the
Gastrointestinal Tract
In small animals and humans, CT is used extensively to
evaluate the abdomen, but veterinary reports of its use to
evaluate the intestines, especially the intestinal wall, are
rare. Gastrointestinal CT has been used in veterinary
patients to diagnose intraluminal gastrointestinal foreign
bodies. However, no significant improvement in sensi­
tivity and specificity was reported in comparison to plain
film radiography. Future veterinary applications using
gastrointestinal CT are likely to develop, particularly
with the advent of new multidetector row helical CT
(MDCT) scanners. Faster scan times and greater spatial
resolution are achievable with these new scanners, allow­
ing for high‐resolution multiphasic and multiplanar
evaluation of the gastrointestinal tract, gastrointestinal
wall, and lumen.
In human medicine, CT enterography and enterocly­
sis, in which oral contrast is used to distend and illumi­
nate the gastrointestinal wall, are extensively used to
evaluate the gastrointestinal tract as they allow evalua­
tion of extraluminal pathology in addition to luminal dis­
ease. They are regularly used in the diagnosis and
treatment of inflammatory bowel disease, to assess the
severity and extent of disease, as well as inflammatory
activity. CT without luminal contrast has successfully
been used in dogs and cats to evaluate the anatomy of the
gastrointestinal tract, to assess segments of the gastroin­
testinal tract for the presence of intraluminal or wall
lesions, and to measure the intestinal width. The use of
gastrointestinal CT examination to evaluate for foreign

bodies and obstructive intestinal disease in small ani­
mals has not been shown to have statistically significant
increased sensitivity or specificity compared to plain
radiography. In gastrointestinal CT without the use of
intraluminal contrast agents, the lack of distension of the
small intestine hinders evaluation of the intestinal wall
throughout the entire gastrointestinal tract.
In human medicine, it has been well demonstrated
that a critical technical requirement for CT of the bowel
is full distension of a clear lumen with complete separa­
tion of the intestinal walls. In CT enterography, combi­
nations of positive and neutral attenuation oral contrast
agents are used, which allow distension of the intestinal
tract and outlining of the wall. Conventional positive
attenuation oral contrast media such as barium‐ or
iodine‐based agents are used for evaluation of the gas­
trointestinal tract similarly to their use in radiography or
fluoroscopy (Figure 48.2). Conventional positive attenu­
ation oral contrast agents allow visualization of the
mucosal detail and assessment of mucosal enhancement.
Neutral oral contrast agents, which are more commonly
used in human medicine, have an attenuation close to
water and are mainly used to distend the small intesti­
nal tract and therefore better outline the intestinal
walls, allowing for better evaluation for mural lesions.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
of the Gastrointestinal Tract
Magnetic resonance imaging is rarely used for evaluation
of the gastrointestinal tract in human and veterinary
patients. In human patients, new MRI applications for
imaging of the colon are being developed. The most
common use of MRI related to digestive disease in vet­
erinary patients involves imaging of the oral cavity or
cranial neck in patients where abscesses secondary to
perforating injuries or foreign bodies are suspected.
Gastrointestinal Scintigraphy
Ultrasound and contrast radiography continue to be the
most common imaging techniques used for the gastroin­
testinal tract. However, contrast radiography, similarly to
contrast‐enhanced CT, provides only very limited or no
information about esophageal or gastrointestinal motil­
ity. It has been suggested that esophageal scintigraphy
might provide valuable information in gastroesophageal

reflux patients. Scintigraphy is considered to be the gold
standard for noninvasive evaluation of gastric emptying
and intestinal transit times. Gastric emptying is evalu­

of the patient at defined intervals and in various posi­
