transit times in dogs is very high, however, which limits
the application of scintigraphy for clinical use.
Scintigraphy may have a use in clinical patients, if
serial studies are done so that progression or response to
treatment can be followed. However, in addition to the
high variability of the gastrointestinal transit times, the
lack of access to scintigraphy equipment and the need for
the use of radiopharmaceuticals, which requires radia­
tion safety precautions, limit the use of this technique in
the daily clinical work‐up of gastrointestinal disease.

­The Pharynx
Normal Anatomy and Examination Technique
The pharynx is at a three‐way crossroads of respiration,
swallowing, and vocalization. The pharynx is located
caudal to the oral and nasal cavities and cranial to the
esophagus; this region allows transport of food from the
mouth to the esophagus. During respiration, the phar­
ynx allows the passage of air from the nasopharynx to
the larynx. During vocalization, the pharynx functions
as a resonating chamber and can alter sounds. Disorders
of the pharynx may therefore result in dysfunction of
swallowing, respiration or vocalization. Patients may
therefore present with signs of dysphagia, choking, gag­
ging and retching, or voice changes and the generation of
unusual sounds.
Structural abnormalities of the pharynx are rare. The
most commonly reported congenital abnormality of the
pharynx is an elongated soft palate. Rarely, unilateral or
bilateral hypoplasia or aplasia of the soft palate or mid­
line clefts have been reported. Even less commonly,
nasopharyngeal or intrapharyngeal stenosis has been
described.
Head and neck survey radiographs are often a first step
to evaluate for problems in the oropharyngeal phase of
digestion. The most common radiographic views include
a lateral and DV or VD view of the head and neck. In the
VD and DV view, the pharyngeal and cricopharyngeal
structures can be difficult to evaluate due to the com­
plexity of the anatomy and the summation with adjacent
skeletal and soft tissue structures. Survey radiographs
are evaluated for the presence of anatomic abnormalities,
including clefts, fractures of the adjacent osseous struc­
tures including the hyoid apparatus and abnormalities or

fractures of the temporomandibular joints. With a cleft
palate, an abnormal connection between the oral and
nasal cavity exists, allowing food to enter the nasal cavity
from the oral cavity. Radiographically, lack of air filling
of the nasal cavity and abnormal content within the nasal
cavity may be noted. Neuropathies are less commonly
encountered reasons for oropharyngeal dysphagia.
Survey radiographs mainly provide morphometric infor­
mation in neuropathy patients, as there is often no ana­
tomic abnormality present. Although survey radiographs
followed by contrast radiographs with barium adminis­
tration can provide valuable information, fluoroscopy is
often needed to identify functional abnormalities.
Commonly, contrast imaging for pharyngeal motility
studies is performed by administering liquid barium sul­
fate contrast agent; this should always be followed by
administration of a mixture of solid food coated with
barium sulfate. Patients may exhibit more signs when
swallowing liquid or solid material and therefore both
aspects should be evaluated. Additionally, thoracic radi­
ographs should be considered, as secondary lung disease
might be present.
Ultrasound Examination of the Pharynx
Ultrasound is infrequently used to evaluate the pharyn­
geal area as the summation with surrounding air‐filled
and osseous structures limits the evaluation of this region.
Ultrasound has shown value if perforating injuries by
plant material are present and can help to identify pene­
trating foreign bodies and assist in surgical interventions.
Assessment of Pharyngeal Function
Dysphagia is a nonspecific term and mainly describes
abnormal swallowing. Common clinical signs include
regurgitation, recurrent respiratory disease or weight
loss. Dysphagia can result from functional or anatomic
lesions, which can be intrinsic to the alimentary tract or
extrinsic from adjacent structures causing compression
of the alimentary tract. Dysphagia can involve any or all
of the structures involved in swallowing, including the
tongue, hyoid apparatus, soft palate, pharyngeal muscle,
cranial esophageal sphincter, esophagus, and caudal
esophageal sphincter. Various classifications of dyspha­
gia have been made. Typically, dysphagia will be classi­
fied based on the location of the swallowing impairment
as oropharyngeal, esophageal, or gastroesophageal.
Oropharyngeal dysphagia can occur in any of three
different phases of swallowing: oral, pharyngeal, or cri­
copharyngeal. Dogs with disturbances in the oral phase
of swallowing usually have difficulty with prehension of
food and moving the bolus to the caudal aspect of the
tongue. The main indications for radiography in cases of

473

VetBooks.ir

474

Section 6 Gastrointestinal Disease

suspected oropharyngeal dysfunction include screening
for anatomic, mechanically obstructive lesions, particu­
larly if there is a history of trauma or concern for a neo­
plastic lesion. In the early stages of the disease, oral
neoplasms rarely cause swallowing disorders. When
swallowing disorders are noted secondary to neoplasia,
the disease process is typically very advanced.
In routine barium swallow studies, contrast medium
may be noted in the dependent buccal fold, oral cavity,
and valleculae. No contrast should be noted in the phar­
ynx, cranial esophageal sphincter, and esophagus.
Pharyngeal phase dysphagia is associated with inade­
quate peristalsis, leading to retention of the contrast
agent bolus in the oral cavity and reflux into the naso­
pharynx, oral cavity, and potentially the larynx.
With cricopharyngeal dysphagia, discoordination of the
motor activity of the pharynx, cricopharyngeus muscle,
and upper esophageal sphincter occurs. Cricopharyngeal
achalasia refers to a lack of opening of the cricopharyngeal
sphincter; radiographically, the passage of contrast agent
is impeded and contrast agent can reflux into the naso­
pharynx, larynx, oropharynx, and piriform recesses.
Cricopharyngeal chalasia is a failure to close the cri­
copharyngeal sphincter. Radiographically, this is seen
as a persistent passage of contrast agent between the
pharynx and cranial esophageal sphincter. Additional
reflux of contrast agent is typically noted, including
into the piriform recesses. Pharyngeal and cricopharyn­
geal dysphagia show similar patterns of retention of
contrast agent. If pharyngeal dysfunction is suspected,
it is important to evaluate the swallowing of liquid and
solid material.
Esophageal dysphagia causes a problem in transport of
food through the body of the esophagus. Gastroesophageal
dysphagia occurs secondary to a functional abnormality,
which includes a motility disturbance or an obstructive
process.

­The Esophagus
The esophagus is a muscular tube that extends from the
cricopharyngeus muscle at the level of the cricoid carti­
lage to the stomach. The largest aspect of the esophagus
is located within the middle mediastinum. The normal
esophagus is usually not visualized radiographically;
occasionally a normal esophagus can be visualized due to
small quantities of air present in the esophageal lumen
secondary to swallowing of air. A normal esophagus
might also be visualized if air is present in the mediasti­
num (pneumomediastinum). The normal esophagus may
also be dilated during or immediately following general
anesthesia; repeat radiographs can be necessary, with the
patient awake, to exclude esophageal disease. The normal

esophageal wall consists of four layers: mucosa, submu­
cosa, muscularis, and serosa. In the dog, the entire mus­
culature of the esophagus is striated. In the cat, the caudal
third of the esophagus, caudal to the heart base, is smooth
muscle. This causes obliquely directed folding of the
overlying mucosa of the esophagus, resulting in a charac­
teristic herringbone pattern noted during contrast imag­
ing studies of the esophagus in cats.
The most common indications for radiography of the
esophagus include a history of regurgitation and dyspha­
gia, recurrent unexplained respiratory illness, ptyalism,
gagging, change in attitude often associated with feed­
ing, or cervical pain and swelling. The most common
reasons for further imaging of the esophagus after survey
radiographs include generalized dilation (megaesopha­
gus), localized dilation, suspected esophagitis, esopha­
geal foreign body or masses, and esophageal perforation.
It is important to remember that failure to visualize the
esophagus on plain radiographs does not exclude the
presence of esophageal disease. An early sign of esopha­
geal disease might include the retention of air in the
esophagus noted on survey radiographs. This might war­
rant further evaluation of the esophagus, which can
include an upper gastrointestinal tract radiography or
endoscopy.
Upper Gastrointestinal Tract Radiography
(Esophagram)
An exhaustive examination of the esophagus includes
contrast radiographic examination as well as fluoro­
scopic evaluation of the motility of the esophagus.
Contrast radiography of the esophagus requires no spe­
cial preparation; however, plain radiographs should
always be obtained prior to administration of contrast
agent to outline abnormalities of the esophagus. It is
important to include the entire esophagus in the study,
from the pharyngeal area to the stomach.
The normal esophagus is collapsed after a primary
peristaltic wave and contrast studies should therefore be
performed with a reasonable amount of oral contrast
agent to ensure adequate coating and distension of the
esophagus for evaluation. Barium sulfate suspensions or
paste are usually administered at a dosage of 2–6 mL/kg
bodyweight. It is important to give a large enough bolus
(usually 5–20 mL of contrast agent) to ensure complete
swallowing. Smaller sized boluses may not stimulate a
strong primary esophageal peristalsis sufficient to clear
the contrast agent from the esophagus. Therefore, at
least medium‐sized fluid or solid boluses are recom­
mended for evaluation of swallowing and the esophagus.
The high‐density, low‐viscosity barium formulations
designed for the stomach and small intestinal tract also
coat the esophagus well. If, however, inadequate coating

VetBooks.ir

48 Gastrointestinal Imaging

of the esophagus results, barium paste should be used to
enhance coating of the mucosa.
Double contrast esophagus studies are commonly per­
formed in human patients but are rarely used in veteri­
nary medicine. In some patients, where air is present
in the dilated esophagus, it functions as an endogenous
negative contrast agent and no additional contrast
medium may be needed. If barium sulfate suspension is
used for the esophagram, no contrast should be remain­
ing in the esophagus in approximately 5 minutes; if bar­
ium paste is used, all contrast agent should be cleared
from the esophagus by approximately 30 minutes. In
general, in the normal esophagus, no contrast agent
should be stored or remain after a contrast agent study
has been performed.
In patients with suspected esophageal perforation,
water‐soluble contrast solutions should be used for eval­
uation of potential leakage from the esophagus. However,
water‐soluble iodine solution contrast agents should be
used with great care for an esophagram, as ionic iodi­
nated contrast agents are hypertonic and, when aspi­
rated, will most likely cause severe pulmonary edema. If
a bronchoesophageal fistula is suspected, nonionic iodi­
nated contrast solutions should be used to reduce the
risk of iatrogenic pulmonary edema. Water‐soluble con­
trast agents for outlining the esophagus are usually
administered at a dosage of 2–3 mL/kg bodyweight to
achieve approximately 700 mg iodine per kg bodyweight
and adequate distension of the esophagus. However, if
no contrast leakage is identified, a repeat study with a
higher density barium suspension can be performed to
allow visualization of a smaller sized lesion that was
potentially missed using a water‐soluble contrast agent.

It has been noted in studies in humans as well as experi­

identified post barium leakage through a very small
esophageal defect, nor was a significant interference
with subsequent radiographic evaluations noted. It has
been recommended to warm up the barium solution to
40 °C when a perforation is suspected, as this decreases
the viscosity of the barium sulfate solution without
decreasing the radiopacity and increases the sensitivity
of detecting smaller sites of leakage in the esophagus.
Generalized Esophageal Dilation (Megaesophagus)
Megaesophagus is a disorder caused by diminished
esophageal tone and hypomotility, causing generalized
dilation of the esophagus. Congenital and acquired forms
of megaesophagus are recognized in the dog and cat. The
underlying cause of congenital megaesophagus remains
unknown, but inadequate development of the esopha­
geal innervation or altered biochemical properties of the
esophagus have been discussed.
Survey radiographs are often diagnostic for a dilated
esophagus, when the esophagus contains food, water or
air (Figure 48.3).
On lateral radiographs, the dilated esophagus is usually
well demarcated dorsally by the longus colli muscle or
summating within the thoracic vertebrae and ventrally
summating with the dorsal aspect of the trachea, leaving
the impression of a dorsally thickened trachea wall (the
tracheal stripe sign; Figure 48.4). It is important not to
confuse the tracheal stripe sign with pneumomediasti­
num, where the esophagus is circumferentially sur­
rounded by air. In severe esophageal dilation, a ventral

esophagus is usually located on or to the right of midline.
A fluid‐ or gas‐filled, dilated esophagus typically shows a
V‐shape narrowing from cranially to caudally on a VD or

esophageal hiatus at the diaphragm. A contrast esopha­

between generalized and focal esophageal dilation.
Vascular Ring Anomalies
Vascular ring anomalies are the most common reason
for focal dilation of the esophagus in the cranial medi­
astinum. Other, less common causes for focal esophageal
dilation include bronchoesophageal fistulae, neoplasia
or strictures secondary to trauma of the esophagus. In
addition to regurgitation, patients with vascular ring
anomalies are often smaller than their littermates, have
an overall low body condition and can have a history of
regurgitation of solid food when weaning.
Vascular ring anomalies are developmental abnormali­
ties of the primordial aortic arches resulting in a com­
plete or partial circle of tissue around the trachea and the
esophagus, causing compression of the encircled struc­
tures. Most commonly, a focal dilation of the esophagus
cranial to the base of the heart is noted on imaging stud­
ies. Additionally, a marked focal leftward shift of the
­trachea is noted on DV or VD radiographs. A ventral
deviation of the esophagus can be noted on lateral radio­
graphs (Figure 48.5). In the dog, the persistent right aor­
tic arch is the most commonly encountered vascular

anomaly. In patients with persistent right aortic arch, the
aorta is formed by the right instead of the left fourth aor­
tic arch. The left ligamentum arteriosum, connecting
between the abnormally positioned aorta and the pul­
monary artery, creates a vascular ring anomaly around
the trachea and esophagus. Approximately one‐third of
these dogs also have an aberrant left subclavian artery,
which, in combination with the persistent right aortic
arch, can contribute to an additional partial ring forma­
tion, resulting in focal dilation of the esophagus.
In the cat, vascular ring anomalies occur less frequently
than in the dog and reported vascular anomalies include
a persistent right aortic arch with right or left ligamentum
arteriosum, double aortic arch or aortic coarctation. If, in
addition to the aforementioned imaging changes, a tra­
cheal stenosis and/or malformation of the tracheal rings
is present, a double aortic arch should be considered.
Contrast‐enhanced CT angiography will help to more
accurately define and outline the vascular anomaly
responsible for the focal dilation of the esophagus and
can therefore help to improve surgical planning.
Esophageal Foreign Bodies
Esophageal foreign bodies occur commonly in dogs, but
are less commonly noted in cats. Esophageal foreign bod­
ies are most commonly found in the caudal esophagus and
are often located between the heart base and the dia­
phragm. However, esophageal foreign bodies in the mid‐
mediastinum dorsal to the heart, in the cranial mediastinum
cranial to the heart as well as just caudal of the pharynx
have also been reported. Esophageal obstruction second­
ary to foreign bodies can lead to perforation (Figure 48.6).

Esophagitis, Gastroesophageal Reflux
Common causes for esophagitis include gastroesopha­
geal reflux, structural abnormalities of the hiatus of the
esophagus (hiatal hernia), neoplasia, trauma, medica­
tion, and chronic vomiting. Esophagitis is difficult to
diagnose on survey radiographs. On an esophagram, a
caudally thickened and irregular esophagus might be
noted. Radiographically, reflux esophagitis can be con­
firmed by filling the stomach with barium and pressing
on the stomach. If reflux esophagitis is present, reflux of
contrast agent into the esophagus is likely to be noted.
Esophageal Strictures
Esophageal strictures can occur secondary to severe ero­
sive esophagitis, and are often associated with perianes­
thetic esophageal reflux or secondary to foreign body
impaction, trauma or a surgery, where the esophagus
was displaced and/or manipulated, such as during ven­
tral cervical slot surgery. Plain contrast esophagram is
usually diagnostic, revealing a segment of esophagus that
persistently fails to dilate.
Esophageal Fistula
An esophageal fistula is an abnormal connection between
the esophagus and trachea, bronchus, lung parenchyma
or skin. Veterinary reports of esophageal fistulae are
rare. Esophageal fistulae are very rarely reported in dogs

and cats. The disease is occasionally reported in humans,
especially children. The most commonly reported clini­
cal signs include spontaneous coughing, coughing after
drinking water, and recurrent chronic respiratory disease.
The most commonly reported fistulae are congenital,
but acquired fistulae secondary to injury of the esopha­
gus, such as secondary to a foreign body, have been
observed. The most commonly reported acquired fistulae
are esophagobronchial, with less common reports of
esopha­gotracheal and rarely esophagoaortic fistulae. As
the clinical presentation of esophageal fistulae is similar
to patients with aspiration pneumonia, it is crucially
important to differentiate between the two conditions.
It is possible that the fistula opening can be identified
during bronchoscopy or endoscopy of the esophagus;
however, contrast agent swallowing studies using fluor­
oscopy are often more reliable for identification of the
connection between the trachea, bronchus or lung and
the esophagus. All images should be carefully evaluated
for leakage of contrast agent outside the esophagus. If a
fistula is suspected and not noted on an initial esopha­
gram, it might be necessary to dilute the barium contrast
medium (1:1) as dilution of the barium sulfate suspen­
sion decreases the viscosity and therefore allows visuali­
zation of smaller defects in the esophageal wall.
Additional imaging techniques, such as contrast‐
enhanced CT, might help to further define the precise
location and size of a fistula. In humans, the use of air as
a negative contrast agent to outline the esophagus has
further helped to demonstrate the presence of the
fistula.
Tumors of the Esophagus
Tumors of the esophagus are rare, likely accounting for
less than 0.5% of the tumors reported in cancers in dogs.
Similar epidemiologic studies in cats are currently lacking.
Clinical signs of esophagus disease such as regurgitation
are often only observed when the tumor has grown to
such a size that it is causing obstruction of the esophagus.
In the dog, leiomyomas or leiomyosarcomas affecting
the lower esophageal sphincter have been described
(Figure 48.8). Aggressive neoplasms of the esophagus are
extremely rare in dogs in areas not endemic for Spirocerca
lupi. Extremely rarely, squamous cell carcinomas, neu­
roendocrine carcinoma or adenocarcinomas of the
esophagus have been reported in the dog and cat.
Endoscopy of the esophagus may allow identification
of esophageal masses. Similarly, contrast radiography
will allow outlining of smaller masses. If the mass is large,
it is likely to be noted on survey radiographs (see
Figure 48.8). Additionally, tumors in the caudal esopha­
gus might also be noted during an abdominal ultrasound
exam, when the cardia of the stomach is evaluated.

Abnormalities of the Gastroesophageal Junction
Gastroesophageal Intussusception

Gastroesophageal intussusception is rare, and is caused
by invagination of the stomach without or with other
abdominal organs into the esophagus. This intussus­
ception is only possible if a predisposing condition such
as a megaesophagus, dilation of the esophageal sphincter
or chronic vomiting is present.
Radiographically, a well‐defined soft tissue mass is
present in the caudal esophagus. Rugal folds might be
seen within the soft tissue mass. Dilation of the more
orad esophagus might be noted. The stomach or part
of it might be absent on abdominal radiographs.
Sonographically, no stomach or only part of the stom­
ach might be identified in the abdomen. The cardia of
the stomach might be severely dilated.

(b)

peritoneopericardial hernias. Hiatal hernias may occur
as transient or persistent hernias. Transient or sliding
hernia is the most common form of hernia diagnosed in
dogs and cats, where it is most frequently diagnosed in
young animals. Occasionally, it is also noted in adult
animals, in whom it is more likely to be an acquired form.
The acquired form can occur secondary to trauma or
severe upper respiratory disease. Commonly represented
dog breeds include the English bulldog and SharPei.
In cats, domestic shorthairs are more commonly affected.
Animals with hiatal hernias may present with signs of
regurgitation, hypersalivation, vomiting, and delayed
growth. Sliding hernia may be difficult to diagnose due
to its intermittent nature.
Radiographically, a dilated esophagus and abnormally
cranial position of the stomach may be noted. In parae­
sophageal hernias, the gastroesophageal sphincter/junc­
tion remains in the correct position, but the fundus is
displaced through the hiatus into the caudal esophagus.

Hiatal Hernia

Diaphragmatic hernias are relatively common abnor­
malities. These hernias can involve the esophagus
in hiatal hernias (Figure 48.9) and paraesophageal
hernia, or the entry of stomach and abdominal viscera in

The stomach is the most distensible organ of the diges­
tive system, and plays an important role in the second
phase of digestion. The stomach is positioned caudal of
the liver and is fixed in position at the diaphragm and

479

VetBooks.ir

480

Section 6 Gastrointestinal Disease

duodenum. The stomach consists of four major anatomic
divisions: the cardia, fundus, body, and pylorus. There
are two sphincters, one each at the orad and aborad
aspects of the stomach. The caudal esophageal sphincter
extends into the cardia, while the pylorus is located at
the junction between the stomach and duodenum. The
pylorus is divided into the pyloric antrum and canal. The
pylorus has an important gatekeeper function, only
allowing smaller sized particles to exit the stomach into
the small intestinal tract.
Radiographic Examination of the Stomach
In a survey radiographic study, the stomach is located
predominantly to the left of midline with the cardia
located slightly to the left of midline, ventral to the 11th
and 12th thoracic vertebrae. The fundus is positioned
to the left of midline and just caudal to the liver and
­diaphragm. The fundus is the only aspect of the stom­
ach which can be in direct contact with the diaphragm.
The antrum is usually not distinctly outlined and is
located between the fundus and pyloroduodenal junc­
tion. The pylorus is located on or to the left of midline in
the cat and on midline or to the right of midline in the
dog. The gastric axis in the dog is usually perpendicular
to the spine or parallel with the ribs. In the cat, it is usu­
ally more perpendicular to the spine. In a lateral radio­
graph, the pylorus is located approximately at the ventral
aspect of the ninth rib.
Radiographic attenuation of the stomach is dependent
on its content. The stomach usually contains both gas
and fluid, but if the stomach is empty or only a small
amount of fluid is present in the stomach, it may be
difficult to visualize as it summates with the liver. The
stomach has rugal folds, which are usually best seen on a
contrast study or ultrasound evaluation. Rugal folds
within the fundus of the stomach often create a mosaic
pattern. In the body of the stomach, the rugal folds are
more parallel and in the pylorus the number of rugal
folds is reduced. Subjectively, rugal folds in the cat are
less prominent than in the dog.
Obtaining multiple projections in various positions of
the patient is important when evaluating the stomach
radiographically. Changing the position of the stomach
affects the position of the gas and fluid in the stomach.
In dorsal recumbency (VD view), gas is located in the
gastric body and pyloric antrum and can be noted as a
gas opacity structure summating with the stomach at the
right and left side of midline. In ventral recumbency (DV
view), the gas is present in the fundus of the stomach,
which is then the most dorsal aspect of the stomach. In a
DV view, a gas opacity structure is noted summating
with the left cranial aspect of the stomach in the location
of the fundus. In a right lateral recumbency view, the gas

is located in the fundus region and the fluid is located in
the gastric body/antrum. The fluid in the gastric body/
antrum creates a round, circular, soft tissue attenuating
area in the cranial abdomen, which is occasionally mis­
taken for a foreign body in the pylorus or a mass in the
cranial abdomen. In the left lateral recumbent view, gas
is present in the pyloric region, appearing as a gas opac­
ity oval or triangle‐shaped structure in the cranioventral
aspect of the abdomen (Figure 48.10).
Ultrasound Examination of the Stomach
An ultrasound examination of the stomach helps evalu­
ate the gastric mucosa and gastric content. If possible,
patients should be fasted for 12 hours before an ultra­
sound examination is performed as food in the stomach
might create artifacts. The stomach is positioned caudal
to the liver, predominantly central to left of midline, and
adjacent to the spleen. The cardia is located to the left of
midline and can usually be seen as a thick bulge with a
smooth mucosal outline at the border of the thoracic
esophagus to fundus. The pylorus is located to the right
or on midline in the dog and is usually on or slightly to
the left of midline in the cat. The stomach wall thickness
ranges from 3 to 5 mm in normal dogs and cats. The
pyloric wall thickness in the cat is 3.8–5 mm, which is
similar to established gastric wall thickness measure­
ments of 3–5 mm. Under optimal conditions, five layers
of the stomach and small intestine are visualized
(Figure 48.11). The innermost hyperechoic layer corre­
sponds to the luminal surface of the mucosa. The next
hypoechoic layer is the mucosa, which is followed by
another hyperechoic thin layer, the submucosa. The
outer hypoechoic layer is the muscularis, which is adja­
cent to the outermost hyperechoic layer, the subserosa/
serosal layer.
Gastrography
Indications for contrast studies of the stomach (gastrog­
raphy) include vomiting, regurgitation, a history of
foreign body consumption, chronic weight loss, bloat­
ing, and anorexia. Contraindications for performing gas­
trography include suspected gastric rupture, large
amounts of ingesta or large amounts of fluid in the stom­
ach. A potential contraindication could be a rigid stom­
ach as overfilling of the stomach might cause vomiting,
resulting in aspiration. Before a gastrography is per­
formed, survey radiographs of the abdomen should be
obtained. For all gastrography studies, 12 hours of fast­
ing of the patient is recommended to reduce the risk of
artifacts caused by food or other material in the stomach.
Most of the study can be performed without sedation of
the patient; however, if the patient is not sufficiently

recommended barium sulfate suspension volume can

pouch using a syringe, but if the patient struggles the
procedure should be stopped and orogastric tube place­

The diameter of the pylorus is usually approximately
half that of the body of the stomach; if it is larger than
that, disease of the pyloric canal may be present. The
peristaltic wave normally runs from the fundus to
the pylorus. During peristalsis, symmetric narrowing of
the gastric fundus to pylorus wall may be noted.
Expected times for gastric emptying of contrast are
quite variable. After administration of liquid barium
sulfate suspension, emptying of the stomach should
occur within the first 5–10 minutes, latest by 30 min­
utes. The stomach should be completely empty by a
maximum of 2.5–3.5 hours in the dog and 15–60 min­
utes in the cat, if the barium was not mixed with food.
Food material empties more slowly from the stomach
and it can take up to 12 hours to observe a completely
empty stomach. Emptying of the contrast agent from
the stomach can also occur very rapidly if the stomach
was empty and the dog fasted when the contrast study
was started. Delayed gastric emptying can be noted in
normal animals secondary to sedation, anesthesia, and
anxiety. Delayed gastric emptying is frequently observed
in anxious cats. Delayed gastric emptying can be noted
in a wide range of diseases including gastritis, pancrea­
titis, neoplasia of the gastric or duodenum wall, and
foreign bodies, to name a few.
Double contrast studies of the stomach are usually per­
formed if a mucosal lesion (e.g., ulcer, gastritis, n
­ eoplasia)
or presence of a foreign body is suspected. As this proce­
dure can take more time than a simple gastrogram, sedation
should be considered. Placement of an orogastric tube
reduces the risk of aspiration of contrast agent and
allows administration of air into the stomach. For a
­double contrast gastrography study, 1.5–3 mL/kg body­
weight barium 30% volume to weight suspension is given

before 20 mL/kg air is added. Four radiographic views of
the abdomen should be obtained. It is often helpful to
gently roll the patient to achieve an even coating of the
gastric wall before the four views are obtained.

Gastric Dilation
In gastric dilation, the stomach is distended without
change in shape and position. This can be acute, secondary
to aerophagia, gastritis, outflow obstruction, medical
treatment, or chronic, secondary to a chronic obstruc­
tive process of the pylorus or proximal duodenum.
On a survey radiograph, a hugely dilated stomach with
fluid and gas is noted (Figure 48.12). If the stomach is
mainly fluid dilated, the radiographic diagnosis of gastric
dilation may be more difficult as the stomach may appear
as a soft tissue attenuating mass and can therefore not
easily be distinguished from the liver. In these cases, caudal
displacement of the colon and the location and shape of
the soft tissue opacity might help to establish that the
stomach is dilated. It is important to remember that not
all patients with a gastric dilation have a mechanical
obstruction. Additionally, gastric dilation may occur
secondary to a mechanical obstruction of the duode­
num, or secondary to pancreatitis.
The key to differentiation of gastric dilation from gas­
tric dilation volvulus is the position of the pylorus. This is
best determined by evaluating the right and left lateral
recumbent views of the abdomen. In gastric dilation, the
pylorus and duodenum in a right lateral recumbent view
should be predominantly fluid filled, and in a left lateral
recumbent view usually contain variable amounts of gas.
Gastric Dilation Volvulus
Gastric dilation volvulus is a frequently encountered,
acute life‐threatening disease in dogs. Gastric dilation
volvulus rarely occurs in cats.

Figure 48.12 Gastric dilation. Ventrodorsal (a), left lateral (b), and right lateral (c) radiographs of the abdomen of a dog. Gas and fluid
dilation of the stomach is noted. The stomach is in correct position. No compartmentalization is noted.

In gastric dilation volvulus, the stomach is usually
abnormally distended, containing food, fluid and gas, and
has an unusual shape and position (Figure 48.13). Often a
rapid decision needs to be made on whether the stomach
is rotated and dilated or only dilated. On abdominal radio­
graphs, compartmentalization of the stomach is noted
(“Smurf’s head,” “Popeye’s arm”); if this happens, the stom­
ach can appear to consist of two cavities, resulting from
the dorsal and leftwards displacement of the gas‐filled
pylorus. The fundus tends to be ventrally and rightwards
positioned, if a 360° rotation is not present. The right lat­
eral radiographic view is often considered the most help­
ful view as it shows both abnormal gas filling and
displacement of the pylorus and cranial duodenum (see
Figure 48.13). In a normal right lateral view, the pylorus is
typically fluid filled. In gastric dilation volvulus, however,
gas is located in the pylorus and proximal duodenum.
(a)

(b)

The lack of gas distension of the stomach does not
preclude the presence of gastric volvulus. If a previous
gastric decompression has been performed, gastric
volvulus might be present for days to weeks or might be
seen at initial presentation. The radiographic principles
mentioned before remain, with the exception of a lack of
marked distension of the stomach.
The presence of gas in the gastric wall (pneumatosis)
or peritoneal cavity (pneumoperitoneum) is a very strong
indicator for gastric wall necrosis (Figure 48.14) if no
prior treatment, such as gastric decompression, has been
performed. However, it is important to remember that
radiographs are not very sensitive for evaluation of
gastric wall necrosis. Gas in the gastric wall might also
be noted during an ultrasound exam and if gas is present,
additional abdominal radiographs should be obtained, to
evaluate the position of the stomach.

If gastric dilation volvulus is present, no further imaging
is necessary and emergency procedures should be per­

Chronic Gastric Outlet/Pyloric Obstruction
Chronic gastric outlet (pyloric) obstruction occurs rela­
tively frequently secondary to either congenital or acquired
pyloric stenosis or abnormal function of the pylorus.
Pyloric obstruction is more frequently encountered in
dogs than in cats. Radiographic recognition of gastric out­
let obstruction often depends on the degree of distension
and content of the stomach, and duration of the disease.
Furthermore, positioning of the patient during radiogra­
phy and frequency of vomiting affect the radiographic
appearance of pyloric obstruction. Most frequently, the
stomach is distended with gas and fluid, which can easily be
noted on radiographs (Figure 48.15). It is important to
remember that not all patients with a gastric dilation have
a mechanical obstruction of the pylorus.
Gastric dilation may also occur secondary to mechan­
ical obstruction of the duodenum or with concurrent
pancreatitis. Left recumbent lateral views can help to
decide if a duodenal obstructive lesion is present, as gas
in the duodenum may be able to outline the cause of the
obstruction. Additionally, in chronic obstructive gas­
tropathy a “gravel sign” indicating retention of small
mineral attenuating material particles in the stomach
can sometimes be seen.
Contrast studies of the stomach or an ultrasound
examination are often needed to establish the cause and
site of outflow obstruction of the stomach. Contrast radiog­
raphy of the stomach in cases of chronic obstructive
Figure 48.15 Ventrodorsal and left lateral
radiographs of the abdomen of a
vomiting dog. Moderate dilation of the
stomach with fluid and gas is noted
(arrows). The gastric wall appears
subjectively thickened. An abdominal
ultrasound exam revealed moderate
thickening of the pylorus wall (arrowhead)
with loss of wall layering.

gastropathy may reveal delayed gastric emptying, focal
­
intraluminal contrast sparing areas in the pyloric antrum
with incomplete filling and blunting of the pyloric canal. If
contrast medium remains in the stomach 3–4 hours after
administration, this usually indicates pyloric obstructive
disease. Intraluminal filling defects in the pyloric antrum
are often caused by thickened mucosal fold(s) extending
into the lumen. The shape and radiographic appearance of
the contrast agent filling of the pylorus have been described
with various signs including the “beak,” “tit,” and “string”
signs. Lack of filling or only partial filling of the pyloric
canal has been described as the “beak” sign, where only a
small amount of contrast agent extends in the form of a
beak into the pyloric canal. The “tit” sign has been used
when a small outpouching remains at the lesser curvature
secondary to peristaltic waves. The “string” sign has been
used when contrast agent extends through the pyloric
canal but is concentrically narrowed secondary to circum­
ferential thickening of the pylorus wall.
On an ultrasound exam, mucosal or muscular thicken­
ing of the pylorus wall may be noted and may help to
differentiate between various etiologies of chronic outlet
obstruction. In dogs with chronic pyloric hypertrophy,
the hypertrophic muscularis may appear as a thick,
hypoechoic layer (Figures 48.15 and 48.16). Sonogra­
phically, the measured thickness of the muscularis may
help to categorize disease severity. The muscularis thick­
ness in the pylorus is greater than 3 mm in mild to
moderate hypertrophy and greater than 8 mm in severe
chronic pyloric stenosis in dogs. Forceful, but ineffective,
peristaltic contractions that fail to propel contents into
the duodenum may be seen in some patients with gastric
outflow obstruction.

Foreign Bodies
Gastrointestinal foreign bodies are a common diagnosis
in dogs and cats presenting for emergency veterinary
care (Figure 48.17). It can often be a challenge to diag­
nose gastrointestinal foreign bodies and decide if imme­
diate surgery is indicated. Preferably, before an imaging
study of the stomach is performed, the animal should be
fasted for 12 hours. Accumulation of a small amount of
fluid or gas in the stomach is normal even after fasting
for 12 hours. Mineral or metal attenuating material in
the stomach is easily recognized on survey radiographs.
Mineral attenuating material in the stomach could be
secondary to medical treatment of the patient, for
instance with medications containing bismuth or kaolin,
or this material could indicate delayed gastric emptying
secondary to a chronic obstructive process involving the
pylorus (“gravel sign”). Metal attenuating material in the
(a)

(b)

stomach might not always cause obstructive signs, but
might be toxic due to containing, for example, heavy
metals such as zinc. Therefore, in patients with intravas­
cular hemolysis, abdominal radiographs may be indi­
cated to evaluate for the presence of metallic foreign
objects. It is important to remember that aluminum is
relatively radiolucent, unlike a lot of other metals, and is
therefore difficult to detect on a survey radiograph.
Foreign bodies that are not mineral or metal attenu­
ating can be challenging to detect. If foreign body
ingestion is suspected, multiple views of the abdomen
should be obtained. The gravity dependence of the fluid
and gas in the stomach may help to outline a foreign
body. If no foreign body is identified, contrast
radiography, ultrasound or CT might provide more
­
information. On a contrast radiographic study, foreign
bodies are noted as a filling defect and this defect can
be mobile within the stomach. However, if the object is
large and/or the stomach is very empty, this object
might not move much when changing the position of
the stomach and might appear lodged in the stomach.
Additionally, porous foreign bodies, such as cloth mate­
rial or foam, may retain contrast agent and might be
seen at the end of a contrast study, when most of the
contrast agent has left the stomach.
On ultrasound, gastric foreign bodies are often hyper­
echoic with complete distal acoustic shadowing. If they
contain gas, areas of incomplete distal acoustic shadow­
ing can be noted. Additionally, they also may be
­recognized by their shape. Similar to radiography, foreign
bodies usually move when repositioning the patient, but
when the foreign body is large, it may show only minimal
mobility within the stomach.
Gastrointestinal perforation is less frequently seen
with foreign body ingestion, but has been reported when
sharp objects such as wood sticks, skewers, needles
(Figure 48.18) or multiple magnets are swallowed.

and Duodenum
Imaging Features of Gastritis

Figure 48.18 Longitudinal ultrasound image of a thin,
hyperechoic, linear foreign body perforating from the pylorus area

Gastrointestinal perforation is suspected when perito­
neal gas, with or without peritoneal fluid, is present
either radio‐ or sonographically. Additionally, on ultra­
sound an increased echogenicity of the mesenteric fat
can be noted. Occasionally gastrointestinal perforation
secondary to a foreign body may not occur acutely or
cause acute symptoms. Sometimes these foreign bodies
lead to distant chronic inflammatory processes, which
result in the occurrence of abscesses at unusual sites or
radiolucencies or mass effects on a radiograph months to
years later.
It should be remembered that more than one object
could have been ingested and the search for foreign
bodies should not be stopped at the stomach, but contin­
ued through the entire gastrointestinal tract.
Gastric Ulcers
Gastric ulcers might be seen on a contrast study of the
stomach or ultrasound examination. In a gastrographic
study, an outpouching of the gastric wall or defect with
adjacent increased thickness of the gastric wall might be
noted (“crater sign”). Additionally, the wall of the stom­
ach adjacent to the ulcer might be rigid, which is best
seen using fluoroscopy.
On an ultrasound exam, similar imaging features can
be noted, including focal thickening of the gastric wall
with a central area of decreased wall thickening (“crater”),
loss of normal wall layering, decreased motility of the
gastric wall, and retention of fluid in the stomach.
Additionally, small focal areas of hyperechogenicity with
reverberation artifacts suggesting microbubbles may be
present in the central aspect of the ulcer.

On survey radiographs, large rugae may be noted; this
may be most noticeable at the greater curvature of the
stomach. On a contrast radiographic study, large rugae
extending luminally and resulting in contrast‐sparing
areas are often present.
Sonographically, focal or circumferential wall thick­
ening, loss of wall layering and, especially in chronic
disease, a mass effect can be noted. Regional lymph
node involvement may be present. Inflammatory
­disease of the stomach may appear similar to neoplastic
or immune‐mediated disease or uremic gastropathy on
ultrasound (Figure 48.19).
Tumors of the Stomach
Primary gastric tumors are rare in the dog and cat and
account in the dog for less than 1% of all malignancies.
Benign (e.g., polyps, adenomas) and malignant (e.g.,
adenocarcinoma, lymphosarcoma, fibrosarcoma, leio­
myosarcoma, gastrointestinal stromal tumor) neoplasias
have been described. In the dog adenocarcinoma and in
the cat lymphoma are the most frequently diagnosed
gastric tumors. Most of the gastric tumors are epithelial
in origin and most frequently affect the distal two‐thirds
of the stomach. Benign masses such as polyps are more
commonly seen in the pyloric antrum and are often
unnoticed until an imaging exam or endoscopy is per­
formed. Gastric tumors can cause a pyloric outflow
obstruction or affect normal gastric motility. Gastric
adenocarcinomas in dogs can also present with ulcera­
tion of the gastric wall.
Radiographic Features of Gastric Tumors

Survey radiographs are often not sufficient to diagnose
gastric wall tumors, even when all four views of the
abdomen are obtained. On survey radiography, focal
areas of gastric wall thickening, loss of normal rugal
folds, and masses protruding into the lumen might be
noted. Pyloric outflow obstruction might be noted,
which can be characterized by a fluid‐distended stomach
and/or mass effect in the pyloric area. Usually survey
radiographs need to be followed by contrast radiography,
ultrasound or, when available, CT to further evaluate the
stomach and stage the disease.
On a contrast radiographic study, intraluminal masses
typically cause signs such as a filling defect in the con­
trast medium, abnormal appearance of the rugae, focal
unusual distension of the gastric wall, a lack of peristalsis
or delayed gastric emptying.

Ultrasound Features of Gastric Tumors

An ultrasound examination of the stomach can be useful in
diagnostic assessment for gastric neoplasia. However,
ultrasound examination of the stomach may be limited by
the presence of gas. Repositioning of the patient and thus
moving the gas will improve evaluation of the gastric wall.
The sensitivity of detection of gastric wall masses using
ultrasound has been reported to range between approxi­
mately 50% and 80% and is dependent on the experience of
the operator. The presence of fluid in the stomach, which
also can be administered prior to the ultrasound examina­
tion, may reduce the presence of air artifacts and therefore
enhance the visualization of gastric wall pathology.
Ultrasound examinations of gastric wall tumors often
demonstrate a variety of features, including loss of ­gastric
wall layering, masses arising from certain wall layers, pres­
ence of cavitations, asymmetric or symmetric thickening of
the wall, and the presence of peritoneal fluid (Figure 48.20).
Extension of the mass through the serosal surface may be
noted, most commonly seen with carcinoma. Additionally,
the involvement of regional lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and
intestine can be evaluated for staging the disease. Ultrasound
has been used to attempt to differentiate between various
gastric neoplasms, but poor correlation with histology was
noted. Ultrasound‐guided fine needle aspirates may be
helpful to accurately diagnose a gastric neoplasm.

Figure 48.20 Longitudinal ultrasound image of the stomach of a
cat. A large, eccentric gastric wall thickening with loss of normal
wall architecture and distortion of the wall is noted. Peritoneal
fluid is present. This was most concerning for neoplasia. Fine
needle aspirates confirmed a gastric carcinoma.

Computed Tomographic Features of Gastric Tumors

Computed tomography and magnetic resonance tomogra­
phy are commonly used in human patients to stage gas­
tric tumors, but currently no similar studies are ­available
in veterinary patients. Computed tomography can be

VetBooks.ir

48 Gastrointestinal Imaging

helpful to evaluate the extent of the gastric lesion and
stage disease. On CT images, a thickened gastric wall,
loss of wall layering, and contrast enhancement of the
wall might be seen. Additionally, enlargement and con­
trast enhancement of regional lymph nodes can be noted.
However, the CT criteria for gastric neoplasia might also
be seen in other benign disease such as gastritis.
Gastrointestinal Bleeding
A variety of diseases can result in gastrointestinal bleeding.
If the bleeding is caused by an ulceration or mass, con­
trast radiography and ultrasound may identify the site
of the bleeding. However, if minimal wall alteration is
present, contrast radiography and ultrasound might not
identify the cause of bleeding.

­Small Intestine
The small intestine consists of three segments: the
duodenum, jejunum, and ileum. The segments of the
small intestine in the dog and cat do not have charac­
teristic mucosal folds. The long mesentery of the small
intestines provides only a limited fixation of the small
intestine.
Radiographic Examination of the Small Intestine
The descending duodenum shows the most consistent
positioning of the small intestinal segments and is
located in the right craniolateral abdomen, running
parallel to the abdominal wall from just ventral to the
right kidney to the level of the 4th–5th lumbar vertebrae,
where it turns medially. The ascending duodenum runs
from the caudal duodenal flexure cranially and towards
midline. The jejunum is the largest portion of the small
intestine and is relatively evenly distributed throughout
the abdomen, from caudal to the stomach to cranial to
the urinary bladder. If the dog is very deep chested and
the gastrointestinal tract very empty, loops of small
intestine might be noted adjacent to the dorsal aspect of
the diaphragm. In obese animals, the small intestine is
often located more centrally in the abdomen due to dis­
placement by peritoneal fat.
In the cat, a large falciform fat pad may lead to caudal
displacement of the small intestine. The aborad portion
of the ileum might be visualized at the ileocecocolic
junction, which lies in a VD view right of midline at the
level of the second lumbar vertebra and in a lateral view
ventral of the approximately fourth lumbar vertebra. The
jejunum and ileum are otherwise indistinguishable radi­
ographically. The duodenum can be minimally wider
than the jejunum and ileum.

Usually the small intestinal segments are of very
­similar width and little variation in diameter is present.
The normal small intestinal diameter in the dog is usu­
ally less than 1.4 times the height of the midportion of
the fifth lumbar vertebral body or less than twice the
width of the 12th rib. In the cat, the normal small intes­
tinal diameter should be less than 12 mm. In the cat, the
small intestinal tract might have a more “string of pearls”
appearance, when compared to the dog. It is critical to
differentiate the small intestine from the large intestine
when decisions about an increased small intestinal
diameter are made.
If an animal has not eaten, the small intestines contain
a mixture of fluid and gas. In the dog, typically up to two‐
thirds of the small intestinal loops are gas filled and in
the cat usually very little gas is present in the small intes­
tine. Gas usually redistributes through the intestinal
tract relative to the position of the animal. In the left lat­
eral view, gas is often present in the duodenum as it is
located dorsally and on the right. However, positional
radiographs are less valuable for the redistribution of
gas in the small intestine compared to the stomach. The
small intestine can also contain small mineral or metal
attenuation structures depending on the diet, or if an
animal is an indiscriminate eater or is receiving medi­
cation. The visualization of medications in the intestinal
tract is dependent on their size and attenuation. Some
medications contain mineral to metal opaque material;
examples include calcium carbonate, iodinated com­
pounds, iron‐containing preparations, potassium, and
aluminum.
Gentle compression techniques using a wooden spatula
or spoon while obtaining abdominal radiographs can be
helpful to further evaluate segments of small intestine,
by reducing the summation from other abdominal
structures.
Ultrasound Examination of the Small Intestine
Similar to radiography, the descending duodenum is
the most consistently positioned section of the small
intestine and can therefore easily be followed using
ultrasound. The duodenum can typically be visual­
ized extending from the pylorus along the medial
aspect of the right abdominal wall caudally. After the
caudal duodenal flexure, the ascending duodenum
can be followed medially, but its aborad aspect can­
not be differentiated from the jejunum. The jejunum
is usually relatively evenly distributed throughout the
abdomen.
Throughout the duodenum and jejunum, the mucosa
is normally the thickest layer (Figure 48.21). The other
layers of the small intestinal wall are similar in thickness
and thinner than the mucosa.

Figure 48.21 Longitudinal ultrasound image of the descending

The total wall thickness is thinner in smaller dogs than
in large‐sized dogs, ranging from 2.9–4.7 mm in small
dogs, 3.0–5.5 mm in medium‐sized dogs to 3.1–5.7 mm
in large‐sized dogs, respectively. In cats, the small intes­
tinal wall usually ranges between 2 and 3 mm. Similar to
contrast radiography, care must be taken that, in the
descending duodenum, Peyer’s patches (see Figure 48.21)
are not misinterpreted as duodenal ulcers.
The mean number of peristaltic contractions noted in
the stomach and proximal duodenum is 4–5 contrac­
tions per minute. In the midabdominal small intestinal
tract, 1–3 contractions per minute are expected.
Contrast Radiography of the Small Intestine
Ultrasound has often replaced the need for contrast radi­
ographic studies as these studies of the small intestinal
tract are often laborious and time‐consuming. However,
if ultrasound is not available, contrast radiography is
helpful to evaluate luminal diameter, wall thickness,
mucosal surface, luminal content, and position of the
intestinal tract. This is especially helpful in patients in
which the abdominal serosal detail is decreased, due
to their young age, emaciation, or a disease process.
Furthermore, contrast radiography can provide addi­
tional information for evaluating intestinal transit times.
Before an upper gastrointestinal contrast study is per­
formed, orthogonal survey radiographs of the abdomen
should be done. If dilation of the intestine is present, sug­
gesting ileus, a contrast study might be contraindicated.
If the ileus is functional, the contrast agent will usually
move very slowly through the intestinal tract and if a
mechanical ileus (due to an obstructing foreign body, for

instance) is present, the time required to complete a
thorough contrast radiographic study may inappropri­
ately delay surgery. If, based on radiographs, an intestinal
perforation is suspected, the patient should be referred
to surgery. However, if an intestinal perforation is sus­
pected and on survey radiographs no signs of perforation
such as peritoneal gas are noted, a contrast radiographic
study may provide useful additional information. Usually
intestinal contrast studies are performed using barium
sulfate suspension; however, if a perforation is suspected,
an iodinated contrast agent may be preferred.
It is preferable that the patient is fasted before an
intestinal contrast imaging study is performed. Sedation
can affect the transit time of the contrast agent, and if
necessary the effect of sedation must be considered. In
dogs, acepromazine has shown minimal effects on
intestinal motility, while providing a reasonable level of
sedation. In cats, a combination of diazepam and keta­
mine shows a similarly low effect on intestinal motility
while providing an acceptable level of sedation, and is
preferable to acepromazine.
To perform a contrast study, the barium sulfate suspen­
sion or iodinated contrast agent is administered either
through an orogastric tube or orally using a syringe.
Orogastric tubing is preferred as it reduces the risk of aspi­
ration. It is important to remember that if an ionic iodi­
nated contrast agent is used, aspiration can lead to fatal
pulmonary edema and therefore great care should be taken
if these agents are used, especially in patients with a known
history of swallowing problems or being prone to aspira­
tion. The recommended volume of barium sulfate suspen­
sion is 8–12 mL/kg bodyweight for small or medium‐sized
dogs, 5–7 mL/kg for large‐sized dogs, and 12–20 mL/kg for
cats. Radiographs should be obtained at regular intervals.
As mentioned earlier, for the stomach all four views of the
abdomen should be obtained. However, for the small intes­
tinal tract, orthogonal views are often sufficient. Usually
radiographs at 0, 15, and 30 minutes and one, two, and
three hours post contrast agent administration are
obtained, until the contrast agent has reached the colon.
Barium sulfate contrast agent can usually be seen in the
duodenum within 15 minutes and in the jejunum within 30
minutes. After 90–120 minutes, it is common to see con­
trast at the level of the ileocecocolic junction. After 3–5
hours, it is common to see the contrast agent within the
ileum and colon. Usually, in the dog using barium, the tran­
sit time for the small intestine ranges from two to four
hours and emptying of the small intestine is typically noted
around five hours post administration. In the cat, the tran­
sit of barium is faster and ranges from one to two hours.
If an iodinated contrast agent is used, it is usually given
in a dose of 2–3 mL/kg bodyweight or approximately
700 mg iodine/kg bodyweight. Iodinated contrast agents
can be diluted 1:1. They have a faster transit time through

VetBooks.ir

48 Gastrointestinal Imaging

the intestinal tract, and reach the colon in approximately
half the time when compared with barium sulfate con­
trast agents. As the iodinated contrast agents transit
more rapidly through the gastrointestinal tract, radio­
graphic views should be obtained more frequently, usu­
ally every 10–30 minutes. As mentioned earlier, barium
sulfate is inert and not metabolized by the gastrointesti­
nal tract; however, iodinated contrast agents are absorbed
by the mucosa of the intestinal tract and therefore the
luminal contrast rapidly declines over time, making diag­
nosis of an intestinal lesion more difficult.
In the normal duodenum of the dog, small indenta­
tions of the contrast agent (“pseudoulceration”) might be
seen in the antimesenteric border of the wall. This is
normal, and results from the presence of Peyer’s patches.
In the cat, a strong beading of the small intestine (“string
of pearls” appearance) might be noted (Figure 48.22).
Barium‐impregnated polyethylene spheres (BIPS) have
been used in the past, but are now rarely used. Their
main indications are in the evaluation of transit time of
the gastrointestinal tract; however, their transit times
were variable and as no coating of the intestinal wall is
achieved, the indications for the use of BIPS are limited.

Figure 48.22 Upper gastrointestinal contrast radiographic study
of a cat. Strong beading of the small intestine is noted (“string of
pearls” appearance; white arrow). This is normal in the cat.

Inflammatory Disorders of the Small Intestine
Inflammatory bowel disease is a broad term encom­
passing all disease resulting in an inflammatory process
of the intestinal wall. On survey radiographs, usually no
abnormality is noted. It is important to remember that
on survey radiographs, an increase in thickness of the
small intestinal wall is difficult to impossible to assess
as the presence of fluid and mucus within the intestinal
tract can mimic intestinal wall thickening in loops of
intestine with normal wall thickness. On contrast radi­
ographic studies, a rapid transit of barium contrast
agent might be noted. Additionally, the mucosal surface
might be irregular and there might be a loss of normal
fimbriation of the mucosa. Enteritis may be generalized
or only involve segments of the small intestinal tract.
Usually no ileus is present.
Ultrasound Features of Inflammatory Disease
of the Small Intestine

The most common ultrasound finding noted in inflam­
matory disease is an increase in wall thickness with per­
sistently preserved normal wall architecture. It is
important to note that this is a nonspecific finding.
Additionally, in enteritis the intestinal wall can be
­normal. It is reported that in dogs, duodenum wall meas­
urements up to 6 mm and jejunum wall thickness meas­
urements up to 7 mm may be normal.
In inflammatory disease, thickening of the intestinal
wall can be local or generalized and as this is similarly
noted in patients with intestinal neoplasia, it can be
challenging to differentiate patients with neoplastic
from patients with inflammatory disease using imaging
alone. As an example, in feline patients with gastrointes­
tinal eosinophilic sclerosing fibroplasia, focal, mixed
echogenic masses with central hyperechoic areas and
loss of wall layering have been described. These central
hyperechoic areas within the masses were suspected to
correspond to the areas of fibrosis noted on histopathol­
ogy. These masses distort the normal intestinal wall
architecture, which is frequently described with neo­
plastic intestinal disease. Another inflammatory exam­
ple that can feature focal nonsymmetric thickening of
the intestinal wall with altered or loss of normal wall
layering is mast cell disease. In most animals with
inflammatory intestinal disease, when increased wall
thickness of the intestines is noted, the wall layering
remains preserved and the thickening tends to be sym­
metric and circumferential.

Small Intestinal Obstruction (Mechanical Ileus)
Radiographic findings in small intestinal obstruction
are dependent on the extent (incomplete or complete),
location, and duration of obstruction. Small intestinal
obstruction can occur secondary to foreign material,
intestinal neoplasia or a mass causing compression of the
intestinal lumen. Mineral or metal attenuating foreign
bodies are radiographically easily detected but non­
mineralized and nonmetallic foreign bodies within the
intestinal lumen or masses of the small intestinal tract
can be challenging to detect. Care should also be taken
that mineralizations in the mesenteric fat (mesenteric fat
necrosis, “Bates bodies”) summating with loops of intes­
tine are not confused with an intestinal foreign body
(Figure 48.23). Bates bodies are usually an incidental
finding and are more frequently seen in cats than in dogs.
Radiographic findings with mechanical intestinal
obstruction include intestinal distension, visible foreign
material, and stacking of small intestinal loops.
Ambiguous radiographs may require additional imaging
or repeat radiographs for optimum assessment. The most
common sign utilized to diagnose mechanical obstruc­
tion is the presence of variations in the appearance of seg­
ments of small intestine (Figure 48.24). Typically, more
orad loops are dilated and aborad to the obstruction there
is a normal‐sized population of small intestinal loops.
Various methods to assess the small intestinal diame­
ter have been suggested, including comparison of the
largest small intestinal diameter with the shortest height
of the fifth lumbar vertebral body. A ratio of less than
1.6 is considered the upper limit of normal small intesti­
nal diameter in dogs. If the values are below 1.6 an
obstructive process is very unlikely. The higher the ratio,

Another evaluation technique compares the largest small
intestinal diameter with the width of the 12th rib, with
two times the width of the 12th rib considered the upper
normal limit. In the cat, the small intestinal diameter
should not be greater than 1.2 cm. Another measure­
ment technique described in cats calculates a ratio of the
maximum width of a loop of small intestine, measured
from outer to outer wall, divided by the dorsoventral
height of the cranial endplate of the second lumbar
vertebra with both measured on a lateral radiograph of
the abdomen. Ratios lower than 2.0 were more likely
associated with a nonobstructive intestinal process and
with ratios larger than 3.0, the increased small intestinal
diameter was more than 70% likely to be associated with
an obstructive intestinal process (Table 48.2).
Single measurements should not be used as the sole
criterion for diagnosis of mechanical obstruction; other
radiographic findings and the history of the patient
should be evaluated when considering the differential
diagnoses. If the radiographic findings are equivocal
and repeat radiographs are obtained, the presence of
radiopaque foreign material in a similar location over a
24–48‐hour period should increase the suspicion of
mechanical ileus.

Small Intestinal Foreign Body

Radiographically, radiopaque foreign bodies are the easi­
est to identify. Foreign bodies containing air, especially
when creating a characteristic pattern such as in peach
pits, walnuts, or corncobs, can easily be identified radio­
graphically. If the foreign body leads to a complete
obstruction of the small intestine, an orad dilation of the
small intestine with normal intestinal diameter distal to
the obstruction is typically noted. However, if the
obstruction is incomplete or long‐standing, minimal or
no small intestinal dilation might be present.

In an ultrasound examination of the small intestine,
foreign material in the intestinal tract often appears
hyperechoic with strong distal complete acoustic shad­
owing. These shadowing structures often do not move
with peristalsis and fluid distension of the small intestine
orad to the lesion is often observed. Foreign bodies may
have a distinct shape and surface, which allows differen­
tiation of them from food material.
Linear Foreign Body

Linear foreign bodies cause plication of the small intes­
tine and are usually the result of swallowing a linear
object and fixation of part of the foreign material orally
or in the stomach. In the cat, linear foreign bodies are
often fixated around the caudal aspect of the tongue.
In the dog, most linear foreign bodies are restrained by
material in the stomach.
Classic radiographic features of linear foreign body
obstruction include plication or “bunching” of the small

intestine and the presence of intestinal intraluminal gas with
an abnormal angular or tear drop shape (Figure 48.25).
Perforation of the small intestine can occur, and in addition
to bunching of the small intestines, a reduced serosal detail
and free peritoneal gas may be seen (Figure 48.26).
Sonographically, an abnormal tortuous path of the
small intestine, often the duodenum, with a central hyper­
echoic, linear structure might be noted. Additionally, an
object with strong distal shadowing might be seen in the
pylorus of the stomach.
Intussusception

Intestinal intussusception can be gastroduondenal,
jejunojejunal (Figure 48.27), ileocolic, cecocolic, and
colonocolic.
Radiographically, severely dilated loops of intestine
might be noted. Sometimes a soft tissue attenuation
mass with orad gas in a convex shape is seen.

wall at the site of the intussusception.
Tumors of the Small Intestine

Intestinal tumors account for approximately 3–10% of
the tumors in cats and dogs. Approximately 75% of feline
intestinal tumors are caused by lymphoma, compared
to approximately 30% of intestinal tumors in the dog.
In dogs, adenocarcinoma, lymphoma, and tumors of
smooth muscle origin are most frequently seen.
If the intestinal neoplasm is small in size and does not
cause obstructive disease, abdominal radiographs are
often normal. If the intestinal mass is large or causes
obstructive disease, radiographic signs consistent with
mechanical ileus are noted. On contrast radiographic

studies, circumferential narrowing of the lumen of the
small intestine might be present.
Ultrasonographic findings in intestinal tumors vary
widely and include focal or diffuse intestinal wall thick­
ening, loss of normal wall layering, increased thickness
of the wall layers, altered echogenicity (Figure 48.28),
and loss of peristalsis. However, minimal sonographic or
no sonographic changes of the intestinal wall have also
been noted in lymphoma. Involvement of regional lymph
nodes may be present, characterized by increased size,
altered shape, and echogenicity. These observations may
increase the suspicion for intestinal neoplasia, and help
stage disease.
Intestinal Adhesions

There is limited information about the imaging of adhe­
sions in veterinary patients. If intestinal adhesions lead
to mechanical ileus, dilated loops of small intestine may
be noted. Radiographically, stacking of loops of small
intestine, which do not change position with repositioning

Intestinal Herniation

Intestinal herniation can occur through a defect in the
mesentery, abdominal or body wall, perineum or

­diaphragm. The position of the small intestine is usually
easily assessed using orthogonal radiographs. If there is a
loss of serosal detail such as in young or emaciated
patients or when peritoneal fluid is present, contrast
radiography or ultrasound may be required to evaluate
the position of the small intestine.
Small Intestinal Volvulus and/or Torsion

Small intestinal volvulus and/or torsion are rare in dogs
and have seldom been described in cats. In cases of
intestinal volvulus, the intestines rotate around the
­mesenteric axis, causing vascular compromise. Rotation
along the long axis of the intestine is termed torsion.

VetBooks.ir

48 Gastrointestinal Imaging

Both intestinal volvulus and torsion can occur concur­
rently. The most commonly involved segment of small
intestine in an intestinal volvulus of the dog is the jeju­
num. Radiographic findings in the early phases of this
disease are vague and nonspecific. It is not uncommon
that radiographs are normal. In the later phases of dis­
ease, generalized dilation of the intestines (paralytic
ileus) may be noted; sometimes a circular position of
the intestines might be present.
Paralytic (Functional) Ileus
Paralytic or functional ileus is a dysfunction of the
musculature of the gastrointestinal tract resulting in dys­
motility due to a variety of causes (neurologic, meta­
bolic, vascular impairment, toxic).
Establishing a radiographic diagnosis of functional
intestinal ileus can be challenging. The most common
radiographic finding is a diffusely dilated small intestinal
tract. Focal dilation of the small intestinal tract is more
commonly noted with mechanical obstruction but there
is likely a commonality between these two diseases.
A barium contrast radiographic study can be per­
formed and a diffuse dilation of the intestinal tract may
be noted; however, the lack of motility might result in
incomplete transport of the barium through the intesti­
nal tract and therefore in an incomplete evaluation of the
intestinal tract, or leave the false impression of obstruc­
tion. Ultrasound might provide more information as it
allows evaluation for the presence of intestinal peristalsis
in addition to identifying intraluminal or intramural
lesions. Sonographically amotile and stiff intestinal walls
may be noted.
Intestinal Ulceration/Perforation
Survey radiographs can be normal in intestinal ulceration
and perforation. However, in perforation, frequently
either peritoneal free gas and/or fluid can be seen.
Ulcerative disease of the intestinal tract is most com­
monly seen in the duodenum. As the normal Peyer’s
patches present in the duodenum can appear as focal
areas of thickening (“pseudoulcers”) on ultrasono­
graphic and contrast radiographic studies, care must be
taken to not confuse this normal finding with disease. In
a contrast radiographic study in ulcerative disease, focal
thickening of the intestinal wall with variable outpouch­
ings can be noted. If perforation has occurred, contrast
leakage into the peritoneal cavity may be present.
On ultrasound examination of patients with ulceration,
regional thickening of the intestinal wall with small
hyperechoic speckles representing gas in the intestinal
wall may be present. If perforation of the intestinal wall is
present, these hyerechoic speckles can be traced through

the intestinal wall into the surrounding mesenteric fat
and peritoneal cavity. Additional ultrasonographic
­findings noted with intestinal perforation can include
adjacent hyperechoic (bright) mesenteric fat, peritoneal
fluid, reduced gastrointestinal motility, corrugation of the
intestinal tract, and regional lymphadenopathy.
Postoperative Appearance of the Stomach
and Small Intestine
The most common reasons for obtaining postoperative
radiographs include the evaluation of feeding tube
placement (gastric, gastrojejunal, etc.) or if the patient is
not improving as expected post surgery. Postoperative
imaging studies are also used to determine a baseline
appearance, which may result in easier detection of post­
operative complications. The evaluation of postopera­
tive imaging studies can be challenging and it is crucially
important to be familiar with the anatomic and physio­
logic changes that occur during as well as postoperatively
and be familiar with the surgical technique used.
Radiography is often used as a first technique to eval­
uate for the extent of peritoneal gas and fluid, position of
the stomach and intestines as well as the presence and
position of surgical devices including drains and tubes.
As noted previously, functional ileus of the stomach and
intestines occurs commonly post surgery and can result
in vomiting, diarrhea or constipation. Radiography,
ultrasound, and CT can all be used to evaluate for the
presence of free peritoneal gas. Radiography is currently
the most commonly used technique, but a small volume
of free abdominal gas can be difficult to recognize on
conventional radiographs made with a vertically directed
X‐ray beam because the gas bubbles are small and irreg­
ular in shape and may be misinterpreted as bowel gas
unless they are located in a region where gastrointestinal
structures are normally not located. Radiographs can be
obtained with a horizontal X‐ray beam, with the patient
either in dorsal recumbency, so that the gas accumulates
beneath the abdominal wall, or in lateral recumbency, so
that the gas rises to the highest aspect of the abdomen
and can usually be found under the abdominal wall in the
craniodorsal abdomen. Most of the peritoneal gas is
absorbed in 3–7 days, but it has been reported that
peritoneal gas might be noted on radiographs for up to
25 days post surgery. Ultrasound is a highly sensitive
technique to evaluate for the presence of peritoneal gas,
but in studies in human patients, it has been noted that
the ability to detect gas is highly operator dependent.
Peritoneal fluid can be noted on radiographs for up to
1–2 weeks, especially if the fluid is proteinaceous such
as serum, blood, and lymph, which are absorbed more
slowly. Solutions containing water and electrolytes are
absorbed more rapidly by the peritoneal membrane and

497

VetBooks.ir
