might not be visualized after 24 hours on abdominal
radiographs.
Depending on the surgical intervention, radiographic
changes may or may not be present. Usually no changes
are noted if a partial gastrectomy or gastric biopsies
have been performed. Additionally, no displacement of
the stomach would be expected with these procedures.
If a gastropexy was performed to reduce the risk of a gas­
tric dilation volvulus in the future, or to inhibit ­cranial
movement of the stomach, it is expected that the pylorus
will be near the right lateroventral abdominal wall.
Commonly, the pyloric antrum will be displaced cau­
doventrally and will be noted caudal to the last rib. If an
enterotomy or intestinal biopsy has been performed,
usually no radiographic changes are expected.
Radiographic changes are only expected if the surgery
has led to adhesions or if an extensive intestinal resec­
tion has been performed.
Ultrasound can aid in visualizing the gastropexy or
enterotomy site to evaluate healing of the suture site and
for the presence of adhesions. The most common ultra­
sound features noted are alterations or loss of wall layer­
ing. An increase in wall thickness is commonly noted at
the site of the gastropexy or enterotomy. An increased
echogenicity of the mesenteric fat adjacent to the surgical
site and variable amounts of peritoneal fluid containing
hyperechoic particles may be noted. It is expected that
the increased echogenicity of the mesenteric fat and the
peritoneal fluid resolves in the majority of cases within
approximately 10 days post surgery.

Radiographic Examination of the Large Intestine
The cecum is located to the right of midline on ventro­
dorsal and centrally in the abdomen on lateral radio­
graphic views. In the dog, usually a characteristic gas
pattern of the cecum is noted (corkscrew‐ or C‐ or
S‐shaped appearance). In the cat, the cecum is not com­
monly seen. The colon is usually localized by its content.
The ascending colon can be identified when filled with
gas or fecal matter in the right cranial abdomen. The
transverse colon can be noted caudal to the stomach and
can be displaced caudally with enlargement of the stom­
ach or pancreas. The descending colon is usually located
left of midline, but if filled with a large amount of fecal
matter and the patient has been held in a right lateral
position, the descending colon may also be seen to the
right of midline in normal patients. The rectum is the
most caudal extension of the descending colon, starting
at the pelvic canal and ending at the anus.
Radiographic evaluation of the colon includes evalua­
tion of the content as well as the size of the colon. Most
of the feces should be seen in the colon with only a small
quantity present in the rectum. The normal diameter of
the colon can be quite variable and depends on defeca­
tion habits and time since last defecation. However, radi­
ographically, the normal colon diameter should be less
than the length of the fifth or seventh lumbar vertebral
body. The seventh lumbar vertebra is often more variable
in length than the fifth and therefore using the fifth lum­
bar vertebra might be a more reliable tool in the deci­
sion‐making process. Additionally, the colon diameter
should be less than three times the diameter of the small
intestine.

­Large Intestine
The large intestine consists of the cecum, colon, and
rectum. The cecum is a S‐shaped blind‐ending tube
located usually in the right cranial abdomen at the junc­
tion of the ileum and colon. The colon is divided into
three distinct anatomic areas: the ascending, trans­
verse, and descending colon. The colon is attached by a
short mesentery, which gives the colon a semifixed
position in the abdomen. The ascending colon contin­
ues from the ileum at the ileocecocolic junction and
runs in a cranial direction. The ascending colon is usu­
ally positioned caudal to the stomach and is frequently
noted to the right of midline; the ascending colon con­
tinues into the transverse colon. The transverse colon is
located caudal of the stomach and runs from right to
left in the abdomen. The descending colon continues
from the transverse colon and runs caudally along the
left lateral aspect of the abdomen. Once the descending
colon enters the pelvic canal, it is called the rectum,
which continues to the anus.

Ultrasound Examination of the Large Intestine
The ileocecocolic junction is usually noted in the right
cranial abdomen, but it can be quite mobile. Orad to the
ileocecocolic junction, the terminal portion of the ileum
can be noted, which can easily be followed orad. The
ileum has a distinct appearance, characterized by a
prominent submucosal layer and often folded appear­
ance of the luminal mucosa (see Figure 48.11). Adjacent
to the ileum, the cecum can be seen, which is a blind‐
ending sac on one side and can be followed to the ileoce­
cocolic junction on the other side. The cecum is often
difficult to examine using ultrasound, especially in the
dog, where the presence of gas in its lumen may limit its
evaluation. In the cat, the cecum usually does not con­
tain gas and therefore it is easier to evaluate. The cecal
wall tends to be more hypoechoic than the colon wall
and has an irregular luminal mucosal surface. From the
ileocecocolic junction, the ascending colon can be fol­
lowed cranially into the transverse colon, which then can

VetBooks.ir

48 Gastrointestinal Imaging

be followed caudally into the descending colon. The
descending colon can also be seen caudally in the abdo­
men, dorsal to the urinary bladder. Ultrasonographic
assessment of the rectum is limited due to its location
within the pelvic canal and therefore it is not accessible
with ultrasound. The cranial aspect of the rectum may be
visualized by tilting the ultrasound probe caudally from
cranioventral to the pelvic floor. Positioning the ultra­
sound probe from caudal in the anus area and tilting it
cranially can visualize the caudal aspect of the rectum.
Due to the typically hyperechoic content (fecal
material and gas) in the colon, the colon wall close to the
ultrasound probe may be the only aspect of the wall
that is easily seen. The colon wall has a characteristic
ultrasound appearance and is usually hyperechoic rela­
tive to the small intestine. All five layers of the colon wall
are of equal thickness and are thinner than in the small
intestine (see Figure 48.11). The colon wall in the dog
and cat is usually very thin and only measures 1–2 mm
in thickness, rarely exceeding 3 mm in normal dogs. If
the colon is very empty, luminal folding of the colon
wall can be noted and the wall might subjectively appear
thickened. It is a common finding that no peristalsis is
noted in the colon.
Barium Examination of the Large Intestine
Indications for performing a contrast study of the colon
include evaluation of the position and appearance of the
colon, the presence of strictures, suspected intussus­
ception, masses associated with the colon, congenital
abnormalities, or colitis. Patient preparation should
include fasting for 24 hours if no preexisting clinical con­
traindication is present. If only positional information of
the colon is needed, a pneumocolonography might pro­
vide sufficient information. It is important to remember
that an upper gastrointestinal contrast radiographic
study is often insufficient for evaluation of the colon
as the colon is incompletely distended with contrast
material and as fecal material often creates intraluminal
contrast filling defects, which can be misinterpreted as
mural or intraluminal lesions. Therefore, if a contrast
study is performed to evaluate the colon wall, a more
extensive preparation of the patient is required to ensure
that the colon is empty.
Patient preparation should include a laxative 24 hours
prior to cleansing enemas of the colon. For the contrast
radiographic procedure, sedation or anesthesia is pre­
ferred as it limits straining by the patient. Barium ene­
mas are best performed by placing a soft‐tipped catheter
with an inflatable cuff within the anal sphincter. The cuff
should be gently expanded to avoid overextension of the
rectum or anal sphincter. In unsedated patients, expan­
sion of the cuff or placement of a catheter into the ­rectum

might not be tolerated. Barium sulfate suspension
(5%) at 7–14 mL/kg bodyweight should be slowly infused
(over 5–7 min) to allow contrast to extend to the ile­
ocolic junction. If available, fluoroscopy can be used to
monitor the advancement of the contrast agent within
the colon and especially to ensure that contrast is not
infused beyond the ileocolic junction. Once the con­
trast agent is infused, the catheter should be closed off
and the patient should be gently rolled to allow for uni­
form coating of the colon. Ventrodorsal and right lateral
radiographic views should be obtained and additional
views should be added as needed to fully evaluate the
colon.
Double contrast radiography of the colon (double
contrast colonogram) can be performed by slowly and
carefully insufflating air into the colon after a barium
enema has been performed. Double contrast colonogra­
phy can improve evaluation of colon wall lesions, help
identify strictures, and improve evaluation of the ileoce­
cocolic junction.
The mucosal surface of the colon should be smooth,
continuous, and well defined when the colon is filled
with barium contrast agent. In the colon of the dog,
small lymph follicles can be found and this might present
radiographically as small focal areas of thickening of the
colon wall or spicules similar to very small ulcers. These
areas should become less apparent once the large intes­
tine is distended. In the cat, the largest aggregate of
lymph follicles can be noted in the ileal area and apex of
the cecum; however, this is usually not discernible on
radiographs.
Pneumocolonography
The most common reason pneumocolonography is per­
formed is to gain positional information about the colon,
allowing differentiation between small and large intes­
tines. Pneumocolonography provides a quick, safe, and
easy way to outline the entire colon but provides only
limited information about involvement of the mucosa,
wall thickness and areas of the colon which cannot
be distended. In cases where a wall lesion is suspected,
a barium enema should be performed. Pneumoco­
lonography is most easily performed by using either a
soft‐tipped catheter or catheter‐tipped syringe placed
within the anal sphincter. In general, 1–3 mL of air/kg
bodyweight should result in sufficient filling of the colon.
It is important to ensure that the entire colon, including
the cecum, is filled and distended with air. It is important
to close off the catheter or syringe once the colon is
insufflated to ensure that the air does not escape.
Ventrodorsal and right lateral radiographic views should
be obtained and additional views should be added as
needed to fully evaluate the colon.

VetBooks.ir

Computed Tomography of the Large Intestine
Computed tomography can be an excellent technique for
evaluating the large intestine. Similarly to radiography,
contrast is often needed to distend the colon and evalu­
ate all aspects of the intestinal wall. When the colon is
empty and the intestinal walls are collapsed, intestinal
wall lesions are very difficult or impossible to identify.
Additionally, if large amounts of fecal matter are present
in the colon, artifacts created by this might limit visuali­
zation of the colon wall. Therefore, similar to radiogra­
phy, optimal patient preparation, including cleansing
enemas, should be performed before a contrast CT study
of the abdomen is performed to evaluate the colon. The
normal anatomy of the colon and regional lymph nodes
is easily evaluated using CT and the ability to perform
dorsal and sagittal reconstructions of the CT images
helps to gain a better three‐dimensional understanding
of normal anatomy or pathologies. The colon wall is thin
and measures 1–2 mm in thickness.
Virtual endoscopy using CT images can be performed.
However, currently its use and clinical value are limited
as CT does not allow assessment of the color of the colon
wall or to obtain biopsies at the same time and evalua­
tion of the wall is limited (Figure 48.30).
Inflammatory Disorders of the Large Intestine
In the acute phase of colitis there may be no abnormality
present on survey or contrast radiographic studies.
Infrequently, in cases of mild colitis, contrast radio­
graphic studies show a mild thickening of the intestinal
wall. Small areas of focal thickening, consistent with
ulceration, may be noted. In more severe forms of colitis,
more extensive thickening of the colon wall with larger
areas of ulceration may be noted on contrast radiographic
studies. With increasing disease severity, spasm of the
colon might be present. With chronic colitis, decreased
width, shortening and enlargement of the colon have all
been described.

Figure 48.30 Virtual colonoscopy. Three‐dimensional
reconstruction virtual colonoscopy image of a normal colon.
Several colonic folds are visible.

On ultrasound examination, increased thickness of
the colon wall with loss of wall layering and decrease of
echogenicity of the colon wall may be noted. Mild
regional lymph node enlargement may be present.
Typhlitis can be challenging to diagnose clinically as
well as via imaging techniques. In mild to moderate
typhlitis, no radiographic changes are often noted; in
severe typhlitis on contrast radiographic studies, similar
changes as seen in colitis can be noted. On ultrasound,
thickening of the cecum wall with a decrease of echo­
genicity of the wall layers might be noted (Figure 48.31).
Tumors of the Large Intestine
Tumors of the large intestine account in dogs for more
than 60% of the gastrointestinal tumors diagnosed; how­
ever, it is important to remember that the prevalence of
gastrointestinal neoplasms in dogs is still only 3–10% of
all tumors diagnosed. Some benign tumors, especially
when polypoid, might not require extensive imaging.
Survey radiographs are often negative and do not pro­
vide additional information. Contrast radiography using
a barium enema or double contrast colonography may
allow localization of the colon wall thickening. However,
colonography only allows limited evaluation of regional
lymph nodes and other abdominal organs, such as the
liver. Therefore, if a malignant lesion is suspected,
­contrast‐enhanced CT or ultrasound (Figure 48.32) are
preferred. These techniques allow not only visualization
of the colon wall mass, but also staging of regional lymph
nodes, the peritoneum, and parenchymatous organs.
If a colon wall mass is suspected, CT may be preferred
over ultrasound, as lesions within the pelvic canal show
only limited accessibility using ultrasound due to the
lack of penetration of the ultrasound wave through the
osseous structures of the pelvic canal.
Megacolon
Megacolon is a broad descriptive term indicating
enlargement of the colon, which can be due to lack of
innervation or abnormal innervation of the colon wall,
mechanical obstruction (e.g. malunited pelvic fractures,
neoplasia, rectal stricture) or dietary or psychogenic
causes. Idiopathic megacolon is the most common rea­
son reported in the cat for enlargement of the colon.
Patients with megacolon often have a history of consti­
pation, painful or difficult defecation or tenesmus.
Classic radiographic findings in dogs and cats include
a marked increase in the diameter of the colon
(Figure 48.33). If the colon measures more than 1.5 times
the length of the fifth or seventh lumbar vertebra, or
more than three times the diameter of the small intes­
tine, this is suggestive of a megacolon.

Cecal or Colonic Intussusception
The most common intussusceptions seen in the colon
are ileocolic, cecocolic, and colonocolic. The intussus­
ception might be seen as a soft tissue attenuating
mass with round borders within the colon on survey
radiographs, especially when the colon is gas filled
(Figure 48.38).
In ileocolic intussusception, the cecum and ascending
colon are not filled with gas, whereas in normal dogs
some degree of gas filling is normally seen in the cecum.
In cecocolic intussusception, the cecum can be seen as a
radiolucent filling defect in the colon on a barium
enema. The ileocolic junction and ileum are persistently
normally seen (Figure 48.39).
Colonic Torsion and Volvulus
Colonic torsion and volvulus is a rare disease that has
a high mortality, similar to gastric and small intestinal
torsion and volvulus. A moderately to severely dis­
tended colon can be noted and the colon can be
abnormally positioned. Frequently the colon is dis­
placed cranially (Figure 48.40). However, radiographic
findings in colonic torsion or volvulus may also be
nonspecific and early exploration might be necessary
to correctly diagnose and correct a colonic torsion
or volvulus.

Figure 48.39 Cecocolic intussusception (cecal inversion) in a dog.
Ventrodorsal radiograph post barium enema demonstrating an
irregular‐shaped radiolucent filling defect in the ascending colon,
which is representing the cecum intussuscepted into the colon.
The ileum and ileocolic junction are normal and contrast filled.
No normal positioned cecum is identified.

Congenital Abnormalities of the Colon
A variety of congenital abnormalities have been described
for the colon in the dog and cat including a short colon,
atresia ani or rectum, double colon, diverticula, and fistula.

In patients with a short colon, the ileocecocolic junction
is often positioned left lateral of midline at the cranial
aspect of the descending colon. The clinical importance of
this finding is unclear. Most congenital colon abnormali­
ties require a contrast‐enhanced study, either using radiog­
raphy or CT, to fully evaluate the extent of the lesion.
Especially when fistulae are present, a combination of an
iodine enema and the use of intravenous iodinated con­
trast agents using CT might provide the best anatomic
information. In diverticulae, a herniation of the mucosal
layer through the muscular wall occurs. If a diverticulum is
present in the rectum, it might be confused with ­sacculation
on physical examination. Rarely, a diverticulum can rup­
ture, which can lead to a significant retroperitonitis and
peritonitis, which can be ­recognized radiographically by
free peritoneal and retroperitoneal gas.

Displacement of the Colon
The most common displacement of the colon and/or
rectum is into the perianal area, which occurs sec­
ondary to weakening or rupture of the pelvic dia­
phragm (perineal hernia). In addition to the
displacement of the colon and/or rectum, retroflex­
ion of the urinary bladder can occur, which causes
obstruction of the urethra. On radiographs, usually a
soft tissue attenuating mass can be seen in the peria­
nal area usually ventral and lateral to the tail. This is
often best seen on lateral radiographs. On ventrodor­
sal radiographs, lateral or caudal deviation of fecal
matter in the colon and rectum may be noted.
Sometimes a sigmoid shape of the colon and rectum
can be seen.

Gastrointestinal Endoscopy
Craig Ruaux, BVSc (Hons), PhD, MACVSc, DACVIM (SAIM)
School of Veterinary Science, Massey University, Palmerston North, New Zealand

Gastrointestinal endoscopy is an attractive diagnostic
tool for many gastrointestinal disease cases presenting to
companion animal practitioners. This technique can
allow direct visualization of the gastrointestinal mucosa
in the esophagus, stomach, upper part of the small intestine, colon, and distal ileum. While some of these procedures are straightforward, entry into the upper part of
the small intestine and the distal ileum can be quite challenging in some patients.
Endoscopy is often viewed as a much less invasive
method of obtaining gastrointestinal mucosal biopsy
samples than can be achieved with either exploratory
laparotomy/celiotomy or laparoscopy‐assisted full‐
thickness biopsies. While endoscopic biopsy has an
advantage of lower risk and less perioperative morbidity,
the quality of endoscopic biopsy samples is often found
wanting. This is particularly the case with the use of
smaller endoscopes with very narrow biopsy channels
that limit the size of the biopsy instruments that can be
passed.
With refurbished flexible endoscopy systems becoming more readily available on the market, and at reasonable prices, there is increasing utilization of these
instruments and procedures in generalist practices.
Competence in flexible gastrointestinal endoscopy
requires meaningful amounts of hands‐on practice, and
guidance from an experienced operator in a hands-on
training environment is the best way to achieve competence in a short period of time. The purpose of this chapter is to provide an overview of flexible endoscopic
equipment types, correct handling and manipulation of
the endoscope, methods for obtaining biopsies, a general
overview of the steps for several endoscopic procedures,
and the use of flexible endoscopy for some minimally
invasive therapeutic procedures such as feeding tube
placement and foreign body retrieval.

­Endoscopy Equipment Options
All visual light endoscopes operate by channeling light
from an external source, via fiberoptic light guides, to the
area of interest. This light then illuminates the area being
examined, and an image is formed. The actual mechanism leading to image formation is typically from one of
two options: either the use of additional fiberoptic elements to return the light via an objective lens at the operating end of the scope (these are commonly called
fiberscopes), or via direct capture of a digital image using
an imaging chip at the distal, patient end of the instrument (videoendoscopes) (Figure 49.1). Fiberscopes represent an older technology, and are usually cheaper than
equivalent‐sized videoendoscopes, but they do have significant shortcomings. Fiberscopes are more affected by
fiber breakage, as the image depends on light successfully
traveling in both directions. The image is often quite dim,
as there are more light losses involved with transit along
the length of the scope and back. The generation of medical records with these endoscopes is also more difficult,
requiring an accessory camera attached to the eyepiece,
representing another potential point of failure. While fiberscopes were long the mainstay of flexible endoscopy in
veterinary medicine, videoendoscopes are preferable due
to superior image quality, greater ease of use, and greater
ease of generation for permanent medical records.
Endoscopes used for gastrointestinal procedures
should feature four‐way tip deflection, allowing the deviation of the tip left or right of center and up or down. Tip
deviation is defined relative to the midline of the control
handle, with the control cluster in the operating hand.
Some smaller scopes, designed for airway examination
rather than gastrointestinal endoscopy, have only up and
down deflection controls while left to right turns are
made by turning the entire endoscope.

practices. This length may be limiting, however, for full
upper gastrointestinal examinations or colonoscopy in
very large‐breed dogs.
Bronchoscopes are not recommended for gastrointestinal endoscopy, as simultaneous up/down and left/right
tip deflections are important for successful navigation of
the upper gastrointestinal tract; it is almost impossible to
achieve this when the endoscope has already made several turns to reach the gastric antrum and pylorus.
Most operators hold the control cluster in the left hand
while holding and advancing the body of the endoscope
with the right hand. Operators with large hands may be
able to manipulate the control wheels using the fingers
and thumb of the left hand, while operators with small
hands will need to operate the control wheels with the
right hand while supporting the control cluster with the
left hand. The tension control levers (Figure 49.2) are
very useful for operators who must alternate between
right hand control manipulations and endoscope
advancement. With very long endoscopes, longer than
those typically used in companion animal practice, two
operators may be necessary to control endoscope
advancement and tip deflection separately.

­Record Keeping for Endoscopy
Procedures

Figure 49.1 A typical flexible videoendoscopy “tower” as used for
most gastrointestinal endoscopic procedures in companion
animal medicine. In this particular system, the light generator and
image processor are in the same unit, with separate vacuum
pump and image printer. In other systems the light source and
image‐processing functions may be separate components. Note
the large monitor and scope rack at the top of the tower. While
the scope rack is a safe place to rest the scope during the
procedure, it is not recommended to transport the scope
(particularly longer and heavier colonoscopes) on this rack when
moving the tower.

Flexible endoscopes are available in a variety of sizes,
with variations in both diameter and length. Greater
diameter endoscopes will typically have larger working
channels, allowing the use of larger biopsy instruments,
snares or foreign body retrieval devices. Larger diameter
endoscopes also have greater intrinsic stiffness, which
can be both beneficial (passing through restrictions such
as the antrum and pylorus is easier with a stiffer endoscope) and a complicating factor (it is difficult to make
very tight turns in very small animals). Generally, a flexible endoscope of around 7–9 mm diameter overall, and
working length of 120–150 cm, will be adequate for gastrointestinal procedures in most companion animal

Endoscopic examination findings are a critical part of the
medical record in patients undergoing these procedures.
Generation of a report will typically involve image capture from the endoscope and a written report detailing
findings and observations. Image captures should contain sufficient information to identify the patient, along
with the date of examination.
The actual content of the written component of the
report will obviously vary depending upon the area being
examined. The World Small Animal Veterinary
Association (WSAVA) has produced template documents encapsulating the essentials for endoscopy reports
for upper and lower gastrointestinal tract endoscopy
procedures; these files are available to download from
www.wsava.org/guidelines/gastrointestinal‐guidelines.
These forms include a section for recording the other
documentation modalities used, but the guidelines do
not make any particular recommendations regarding the
best choice of image capture modality.
Image capture systems are very variable, and all have
strengths and weaknesses. For quite some time, the use
of video printers, which capture images from the processing unit and print to photographic paper, was the
standard method. While some systems and practices
continue to use these printers, the specific printer
technology used (dye sublimation) is rarely used in

At the opposite extreme from the traditional dye sublimation printer, some modern endoscopy systems are
able to record digital video or digital still image captures
from the endoscope in real time, and then export the
resulting files to either a hospital‐wide DICOM system
or directly into a hospital electronic record system.
These capabilities are very useful for streamlining record
management in busy practices, and also provide the ability to show captures to clients and generate multiple copies that can be saved to removable media or transferred
digitally via email. The specific hospital management
systems and DICOM products that endoscopy systems
can interface with vary by manufacturer, and should be
considered if a practice is planning to purchase a newer
system. Aftermarket image capture and DICOM export
hardware are also available from some vendors, again

these systems can require significant configuration and
software support, which should be clarified during the
purchasing process.
A final option that is commonly used with refurbished
but older endoscopy systems is to attach some form of
recording device (commonly a CD or DVD recorder) to a
video output from the endoscope processor. In some
cases, it is possible to configure these systems to trigger
capture using either a foot pedal or the capture button on
the endoscope, but again as technology progresses and
changes, this is becoming increasingly difficult. The simplest, but most risky, option is to simply collect and
record all video from the video output and record it as a
continuous stream. If doing this, it is important to consider the length and size of the recording, as many upper
and lower gastrointestinal tract endoscopy procedures
will last for 1.5 hours or more. Use of CD/DVD recorder
systems also requires the endoscope operator or assisting technical staff to remember to start and stop recording, and finalize the recording to allow burning the final
disk. The disks themselves have variable, and often short,

useful lives after burning, and may not survive for the
duration necessary to meet legal requirements for record
keeping in some localities.
Given the combination of workflow advantages,
archivability, and integration with other hospital systems, systems that can achieve digital capture and archiving are generally the best option currently available, and
will have the greatest future proofing.

­Endoscope Handling
General Manipulations
The endoscope is a fragile instrument and needs to be
handled carefully and appropriately to avoid damage
to the scope and minimize risk to the patient.
Gastrointestinal endoscopy requires an adequate plane
of anesthesia. Mouth blocks or gags should be used to
keep the mouth open while carrying out upper gastrointestinal tract endoscopy. These both make entry of the
endoscope into the upper gastrointestinal tract easier,
and provide a degree of protection against the endoscope
body being bitten if patient anesthesia is inadequate.
Operation of the endoscope relies on fine control wires
that extend from the control cluster to the tip of the
scope, while light transmission and image formation rely
on the fine fiberoptic strands within the scope body.
Both of these components can be damaged if placed
under excess stress. To minimize stress on the endoscope
components, it is best to make fine adjustments of the
operating tip that allow general visualization of a target
area, while larger deviations and turns are made by turning the whole endoscope body rather than applying significant strain to the endoscope tip. A fine adjustment is
made using the control wheels, the scope is advanced
and turned using the entire scope body, then additional
adjustments are made to gradually bring the endoscope
into the desired position.
Visualization of some areas of the gastrointestinal
tract, particularly the gastric cardia and aboral surface of
the esophageal sphincter, requires more stressful maneuvers. Visualization of the cardia and lower oesophageal
sphincter usually requires a “J‐maneuver” where the tip
of the endoscope is placed into maximal upwards deflection (Figure 49.3). This position is particularly stressful
on the mechanical components of the endoscope, and
should only be used for as long as needed to adequately
visualize the anatomy in this region.
Passage of the endoscope through the pylorus into the
proximal duodenum is mildly stressful on the endoscope,
as in many dogs it requires a simultaneous downwards
and right tip deflection while pushing against some
resistance. Once the pylorus has been traversed,

Figure 49.3 Maximal upwards flexion of a flexible
videoendoscope, necessary for visualization of the gastric cardia,
aboral surface of the lower esophageal sphincter, and distal rectal
lumen. This position is highly stressful on the endoscope control
structures and fiberoptic elements, and should be held for as
short a period as possible. Do not introduce the endoscope into a
lumen (for instance, in an attempt to visualize the distal palate or
rectum) while holding the endoscope in this position, as the
additional compression on the distal end of the endoscope can
cause severe damage.

however, there is little to no stress applied to the endoscope as it is advanced along the duodenum.
The endoscope tip and body should be lubricated with
a water‐based lubricant before introduction into the gastrointestinal tract. In the initial stages of the upper gastrointestinal examination, particularly with smaller dogs
and cats, there is a risk that the endoscope may slip out
of the esophagus and, if not being held by the operator,
the tip may fall and hit the floor or other hard surfaces,
risking damage to the imaging system or the fiberoptics.
This can be particularly problematic for operators with
smaller hands who need to take their right hand off the
endoscope body to make tip deflections. Having an assistant hold and advance the endoscope body independently from the main operator can minimize the risk of
scope dislodgment and damage.
Biopsy Instruments and Working Channel Use
The biopsy and vacuum channel of the endoscope are
lined with a thin, rubberized material to allow adequate
flexibility while keeping the fiberoptics, control wires,
and imaging electronics sealed against water ingress.
Damage to the inner lining of the biopsy/vacuum channel can result in scope flooding and costly repairs, as the
entire endoscope must be disassembled to repair and
replace these parts.

VetBooks.ir

49 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy

It is imperative that biopsy instruments and retrieval
snares/baskets are held closed or within their protective
outer sheath when passing through the endoscope. Open
biopsy jaws or exteriorized retrieval instruments can
puncture or otherwise damage the internal lining of the
endoscope.
Occasionally, it is necessary to biopsy lesions that
require significant tip deflection for adequate visualization. A mass on the aboral surface of the esophageal
sphincter, for instance, will require a J‐maneuver for adequate visualization (see earlier). Attempting to pass a
biopsy instrument through the endoscope while it is in
this position is risky as the instrument is directly pushing
against the channel lining. It is less risky to retract the
endoscope slightly to allow the tip to relax, pass the
instrument until it is visualized leaving the endoscope
and within the gastric lumen, then return to the maximally flexed position to obtain the biopsy. Obtaining an
adequate biopsy from masses in this region can be quite
difficult, as the severe turns of the endoscope restrict the
ability of the biopsy instrument to move within the
channel.
After a biopsy is obtained, the biopsy instrument
should be kept completely closed until it has been
entirely removed from the biopsy channel. Foreign bodies are retracted with the retrieval instrument until they
are close to the operating end of the endoscope, then
removed by retracting the entire endoscope.

water‐moistened wet gauze or toweling to remove
grossly contaminating material.
Complete cleaning of the endoscope requires several
steps and use of different cleaning products to achieve
both physical cleaning and sterilization.
The first step of cleaning is typically achieved with an
enzymatic detergent solution. The endoscope is soaked
in this solution, then the outer surfaces gently wiped
down. The detergent solution is also pumped through
the biopsy and air/water channels using a manifold
(Figure 49.4) that attaches in place of the removable buttons. If manually cleaning the endoscope, these channels
are then further cleaned by passing specific cleaning
brushes.
After lower level cleaning with the enzymatic/detergent solution, higher level sterilization can be achieved
using specific sterilization fluids. These fluids are often
corrosive and toxic, and can produce toxic fumes. The
operator cleaning and sterilizing the endoscope must
wear adequate personal protective equipment, including
facemask and eye protection. After exposure to the sterilization solution is complete, the endoscope is thoroughly rinsed with sterile water, both externally and
through the internal channels. The sterilization solutions

Endoscope Cleaning and Maintenance
Care and maintenance of endoscopes require attention
to detail, care with handling of the instrument, and the
use of appropriate cleaning products and equipment.
These are expensive and fragile pieces of equipment, and
repair costs are high. Generally speaking, it will be best
for only one or two specific individuals (practitioner or
technician) to be tasked with cleaning and maintenance
of flexible endoscopes to ensure consistency of handling
and adequate knowledge of the necessary steps. While
some general observations are given here, manufacturer’s guidelines should be followed. This is particularly
important with respect to cleaning fluid selection, as different manufacturers use differing materials in their
endoscopes that may be damaged by inappropriate
cleaning solution use.
Endoscopes must be thoroughly and effectively
cleaned, on both external surfaces and within the biopsy/
vacuum and air/water channels, after use and before
storage. On completion of an examination, it is good
practice to suction plain or distilled water (not saline)
through the endoscope to clear material that may have
lodged within the working channel. The exterior body
of the endoscope should be wiped down with

are irritating to mucosal tissue, so it is important to
ensure that residues of the cleaning solution have been
removed before use on a patient.
Endoscopes should be stored dry, following effective
cleaning (Figure 49.5). If space is available, they can be
stored in specially constructed rack systems in a dedicated cabinet. Other items unrelated to endoscopy
should not be stored in the same cabinet to minimize the
risk of endoscope damage. If a dedicated cabinet is not
used, the cleaned and dried endoscope should be stored
in the original shipping/packing case to provide adequate
protection. Obviously, if transporting endoscopes in the
field or between hospital sites, they are best carried in
their specific transport case.
Effective complete cleaning and sterilization of an
endoscope can be quite time‐consuming. In practices
that carry out several procedures in a day, investment in
an automated scope cleaning and reprocessing system
can be cost‐effective, freeing up technician resources for
other tasks. These systems can automatically carry out
both the low‐and high‐level cleaning steps, final rinsing
of the endoscope and pressure testing without further

manual input, typically in less than one hour. These systems may also generate a record for each endoscope of
cleaning solution exposure times and pressure test
results, and monitor the age and use of the cleaning solutions. An additional advantage is that the operator is protected from the cleaning and sterilization fluids during
endoscope reprocessing.

­Endoscopic Terminology
Endoscopic evaluation of the gastrointestinal tract provides an opportunity to assess the gross appearance of
the gastrointestinal mucosa. Findings with gastrointestinal endoscopy therefore are usually descriptions of the
mucosa and attempt to define the ways, if any, in which
the mucosa differs from normal. Standardization of the
language used to describe endoscopy findings is useful to
maintain consistency in interpretations and comparison
across patients. The terms recommended for the description of the mucosa, most of which are also incorporated
into the WSAVA recommended reporting forms for gastrointestinal endoscopy procedures, are summarized in
Table 49.1 and discussed in greater detail below.
Friability
Friability refers to the susceptibility of the mucosa to
superficial damage and hemorrhage on contact with
either the endoscope tip/body or biopsy instruments.

The natural friability of the mucosa varies with the anatomy of the gastrointestinal tract, and this must be considered in the context of the examination findings. The
esophageal and gastric mucosae, for instance, are robust
and the normal mucosa should show little to no change
or damage from contact with the endoscope. This is particularly true of the esophagus, antral mucosa, and
pylorus. Compared to the stomach, the small intestinal
mucosa is more fragile, and even normal patients will
show some degree of superficial mucosal damage following contact with the endoscope, but there should not be
grossly visible “stripping” of the mucosa from the submucosa, and any bleeding following contact should be
minor (Figure 49.6). The large intestinal mucosa is more
robust than the small intestine, but is not as resistant to
impact damage as the gastric mucosa, thus contact with
a colonoscope will usually produce some visible change
in the mucosa, but this is less pronounced than in the
small intestine.

infiltration or lymphatic drainage disorders can lead to
an increase in granularity and a perceptible “piling” of
mucosa into more prominent folds that do not dissipate
with insufflation (Figure 49.7).

Granularity
Granularity refers to the visual texture of the mucosa.
Again, the normal texture of the mucosa varies across
the gastrointestinal tract. In the small intestine, both
increased and decreased granularity may be observed,
while villus blunting due to infiltration or mucosal denudation may result in an abnormally smooth appearance
of the small intestinal wall, or a “cobble stone” appearance caused by a patchy distribution of blunted villi.
Mucosal thickening and swelling secondary to cellular

Erosion(s)
Erosion(s) are preexisting, generally superficial, linear to
irregularly shaped mucosal defects, often marked by
mild intra‐ or submucosal hemorrhage. These must be
distinguished from lesions due to abnormalities in friability. Erosions represent an area of change in the gastrointestinal mucosa, but there should still be mucosa
present (Figure 49.8). Visible loss of the mucosa with crater formation and visible submucosa is more consistent
with ulceration than erosion. Erosions likely progress to
ulceration in some individuals; animals with nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drug (NSAID)‐induced gastritis,
for instance, commonly show numerous erosions. Many
erosions are linear or elongated oval shapes, oriented
along the longitudinal axis of the intestinal tract, likely
due to damage resulting from the passage of ingesta over
the diseased mucosa.
Lymphatic Dilation
Lymphatic vessels are usually only visible in the small
intestinal mucosa, and become more prominent in
deeper parts of the small intestine, such as the jejunum.
Lymphatic visibility is greater in the small intestine due
to the role of the intestinal lymphatics in fat absorption,

Abnormal lymphatic drainage is associated with
­“blebbing” and diffuse spread of lymph into the villi
and the submucosa. There may be solitary punctate
lesions spread diffusely throughout the small intestine,
or larger areas of contiguous leakage may be perceived
(Figure 49.9).
Mass Effects
Abnormal tissue entering the lumen of the gastrointestinal tract may arise from the mucosa or the submucosal
layers. Mucosal masses are usually readily identified due
to the obviously dysplastic appearance of the epithelium
(Figure 49.10). In some cases, the mucosa will be eroded

VetBooks.ir

49 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy

and ulcerated, and will bleed easily (i.e., highly friable) on
contact with the endoscope. Submucosal masses are recognized in areas where the lumen shows obvious architectural distortion that does not resolve with insufflation.
Submucosal masses are relatively easy to recognize
endoscopically, but the diagnostic yield from endoscopic
biopsy of these lesions is poor. Full‐thickness biopsy is
usually required for accurate diagnostic assessment of
submucosal or mural masses.
Hyperemia
The color of the intestinal mucosa can be assessed, and
perceptible alterations from normal (again, bearing in
mind that the mucosal coloration varies along the gastrointestinal tract) may be noticeable during an examination. While superficially attractive as a readily perceivable
abnormality, hyperemia is actually a poor indicator of
abnormalities within the mucosa. Many variables influence mucosal redness, including the hemodynamic state
of the patient, circulating red blood cell mass, local
changes in perfusion, and the overall color balance of the
imaging system being used. Some, but by no means all,
endoscopy imaging systems can have their color balance
(white balance) calibrated against a white background
material, which will improve the ability of the operator to
define changes in redness on that specific system, but not
all systems are readily calibrated, and calibration must be
carried out regularly. Due to these shortcomings, diffuse
hyperemia and other changes in mucosal coloration are
not usually considered useful diagnostic findings during
gastrointestinal endoscopy.

­Upper Gastrointestinal Endoscopy
Procedures
Esophagoscopy
Indications

Common indications for esophagoscopy in companion
animals include assessment of patients with dysphagia,
regurgitation, poor appetite, and hematemesis.
Esophagoscopy is also frequently useful in the diagnosis
and management of esophageal foreign bodies, strictures, and diverticulae. The esophagus is also, obviously,
traversed in the process of all other upper gastrointestinal examinations and should be thoroughly examined
during these procedures.
Patient Positioning

As esophagoscopy is commonly performed during
other upper gastrointestinal tract procedures, the
patient is typically placed in left lateral recumbence (the

positioning of choice for gastroduodenoscopy). If the
planned procedure is only involving the esophagus (foreign body removal or stricture ballooning, for example),
sternal or right lateral positioning can be used, but there
are no specific advantages of these positions over left lateral recumbence.
Equipment Choice

Both flexible and rigid endoscopes may have some utility
in examination of the esophagus, but in most patients
there is insufficient working length with rigid endoscopes to examine the entire esophagus. Flexible endoscopes with four‐way tip deflection and a working
channel are preferable, particularly if removal of a foreign body using flexible retrieval instruments is anticipated. Four‐way tip deflection gives the operator a
greater ability to manipulate the positions of grasping
forceps or basket snares. Air and water insufflation is
important, particularly for adequate examination of the
cranial esophagus.
General Technique and Landmarks

The neck is extended dorsally, and the endoscope passed
dorsally over the endotracheal tube to the retropharynx.
Gentle pressure against the retropharynx will result in
the passage of the endoscope through the upper esophageal sphincter and into the cervical esophagus.
The cervical esophagus is usually flacid and collapsed.
After passage through the upper esophageal sphincter,
air is insufflated to visualize the esophageal lumen. Once
fully insufflated, passage of the endoscope is usually
straightforward. Landmarks during the examination are
the thoracic inlet (where the esophagus changes direction slightly), heart base (where there is a slight narrowing of the esophageal lumen; usually the wall will show
motion due to cardiac movement), and the lower esophageal sphincter. The three landmark locations also represent areas of esophageal narrowing, and are the most
common sites to encounter obstructing foreign bodies.
Ideally, as much of the esophageal lumen as possible
should be visualized before advancing the endoscope
over large distances. In regurgitating patients, look
closely for wall defects or outpouchings that may represent esophageal diverticula, or areas of esophageal
lumen that do not insufflate fully (indicating possible
strictures).
Normal Findings

The cervical esophagus is normally flacid and collapsed
on entry. Insufflation reveals longitudinal mucosal folds,
which are flattened by air insufflation. Within the thoracic cavity, the esophagus is usually flaccid and shows a
patent lumen without need for further insufflation. The
normal esophagus will drape over the large vessels in a

515

VetBooks.ir

516

Section 6 Gastrointestinal Disease

normal animal; visualization of a strong pulsatile motion
from these vessels is not necessarily suggestive of a
megaesophagus.
The esophageal wall in dogs is usually smooth, or very
slightly corrugated, on full insufflation. The cat has a
series of mucosal folds in the distal third of the esophagus that give the normal esophageal lumen a “herring
bone” appearance in this species.
The lower esophageal sphincter is readily visualized in
most animals, assuming that there are no impeding foreign bodies. The lower esophageal sphincter is usually
closed on examination, but a relaxed and open sphincter
is not necessarily abnormal. Often, a small amount of
stable white foam (aerated saliva) is adherent on the distal esophageal mucosa, which is also normal.
Potential Abnormalities Observed
in Esophagoscopy Procedures
Esophagitis

Esophageal inflammation is a common finding in dogs
with gastrointestinal disease, particularly if there is gastroesophageal reflux or chronic vomiting. Changes in
the esophageal mucosa with esophagitis are highly variable, and often do not correlate closely with the perceived clinical severity of signs. The most common
changes seen with esophagitis are increased granularity
of the esophageal mucosa, hyperemia or erythema, and
mucosal erosions. Often, these changes are most pronounced in the distal esophagus, particularly if they are
secondary to gastroesophageal reflux (Figure 49.11).

In humans, chronic gastroesophageal reflux can lead
to squamous differentiation of the distal esophageal
mucosa, which is considered a preneoplastic change.
Similar changes are occasionally seen in dogs with
chronic gastroesophageal reflux, but the potential for
neoplastic transformation is unknown.
While a relaxed, partially dilated lower esophageal
sphincter is not necessarily an abnormal finding in dogs
and cats, the prolapse of gastric mucosa into the esophageal lumen is abnormal. This may occur as a result of
severe, chronic reflux esophagitis, hiatal hernias, or be
due to the presence of mass lesions on or just below the
lower esophageal sphincter (see Gastric Tumors, later).
Esophageal Foreign Bodies

Esophageal foreign bodies are a significant medical
emergency, and delays in detection and definitive treatment should be avoided as much as possible. Large
obstructing foreign bodies, such as bones, swallowed
chew toys, etc., are readily visualized. Common locations
for foreign body entrapment are at the thoracic inlet, cranial to the heart base, and cranial to the lower esophageal
sphincter, with the lower esophageal location being the
most common. Sharp, more linear objects such as needles, fish hooks, etc. may lodge at any point in the esophageal lumen, but again are most commonly encountered
at the thoracic inlet and cranial to the lower esophageal
sphincter. Sharp linear foreign bodies often accumulate
additional material such as hair, grass, and food fragments that can complicate assessment and removal.
Before endoscopy to assess and possibly attempt
removal of an esophageal foreign body, it is important to
have recent (ideally same day) thoracic radiographs with
at least two orthogonal views. These should be carefully
assessed for evidence of preexisting esophageal perforation (pneumomediastinum, mediastinitis, pneumo‐ or
pyothorax), as these indicate a need for earlier surgical
intervention. In addition, it is important to document
that the foreign body is still present, and apparently
within the lumen, before proceeding to esophagoscopy.
Strategies for foreign body removal are discussed
­further later.
Esophageal Diverticulae

Figure 49.11 Esophagitis, likely due to recurrent
gastroesophageal reflux, in a canine patient. There is increased
granularity and hyperemia of the distal esophageal mucosa, and
the lower esophageal sphincter is dilated. Some mild erosions are
also visible in the more proximal aspect of the esophageal
mucosa, particularly to the left of the image.

Esophageal diverticulae are outpouchings of the esophageal mucosa through defects in the mural musculature.
On endoscopic examination, these lesions may appear as
obvious outpouchings of the mucosa, they may look like
an additional lumen, or they may appear to be large
accumulations of hair and/or fermenting food material
entrapped within the diverticulum. Large diverticulae
are usually detected on plain radiographic examination
of the thorax as part of the work‐up for esophageal
disease.

VetBooks.ir

49 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy

Esophageal Neoplasia

Primary esophageal neoplasia is uncommon to rare in
both dogs and cats, with cats most frequently diagnosed.
Squamous cell carcinoma is occasionally diagnosed
within the thoracic esophagus, visualized as an eroded,
proliferative mass in the distal esophagus. This diagnosis
is most commonly made in elderly cats, and carries a
poor to grave prognosis. Preendoscopy work‐up including plain and contrast‐enhanced esophograms will often
reveal the soft tissue mass, which may initially be mistaken for a foreign body.
Gastroscopy
Indications

Common indications for gastroscopy include assessment
of recurrent vomiting, poor appetite, weight loss (assuming other significant co‐morbidities have been ruled
out), hematemesis (particularly if “coffee ground” vomiting is present), and attempts at removal of gastric foreign
bodies. Gastroscopic technique is also used for some
minimally invasive feeding tube placements (percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy [PEG] and percutaneous
endoscopic gastrostomy‐jejunostomy [PEG‐J]; see later).
The stomach must be traversed as part of the approach
to the small intestine for duodenoscopy, and should be
assessed thoroughly, including the collection of biopsies
from each area of the stomach, in any patient being
worked up for possible inflammatory disease of the gastrointestinal tract.
Patient Positioning

For most procedures involving gastroscopy, the patient
should be placed in left lateral recumbence. As the
pylorus is in the right side of the abdominal cavity in
both dogs and cats, left lateral recumbence will position
the antrum and pylorus dorsally, thus allowing gas to fill
these parts of the stomach. This is important for clear
visualization of a number of significant landmarks, and
greatly simplifies the process of transiting the antrum,
through the pylorus to the small intestine. Left lateral
recumbence will also typically cause foreign bodies that
are obstructing the pylorus to fall into the gastric body
under the influence of gravity. There is much greater
room to maneuver and less complex scope deviations
necessary to retrieve foreign bodies from the gastric
body than from within the antrum
One exception from the typical left lateral placement
for gastroscopy is made when the patient is having a
minimally invasive feeding assistance device placed, such
as a PEG or PEG‐J tube. These devices are placed through
the greater curvature of the stomach, exiting at the left
paranephric fossa, and thus placing the patient in right
lateral recumbence is necessary to improve visualization

of this region of the gastric wall. If the sole reason for the
gastroscopic procedure is PEG/PEG‐J tube placement,
the entire process is carried out in right lateral recumbence. If the feeding device is to be placed at the end of a
diagnostic upper gastrointestinal examination, it is best
to start in left lateral recumbence and then reposition the
patient after completion of the examination.
Equipment Choice

Gastroscopy requires the use of a flexible endoscope
with four‐way tip deflection. If the primary reason for
the procedure is foreign body retrieval from the stomach, a relatively large endoscope (7–9 mm diameter) can
be useful even in cats and very small dogs. For full visualization of all areas of the stomach and potential entry
into the duodenum via the pylorus, a smaller endoscope
might be advantageous with very small patients (for
instance, a 5–6 mm pediatric gastroscope), but with care
even a 7–9 mm endoscope can be advanced through the
pylorus of many smaller dogs and larger cats.
General Technique and Landmarks

Landmarks for visualization during gastroscopy include
the greater and lesser curvatures of the stomach, the cardia and aboral surface of the lower esophageal sphincter,
the incisura angularis, antrum, and pyloric sphincter. All
these areas and structures are readily accessible to examination in the majority of veterinary patients, assuming
careful and thorough technique is applied.
The stomach is entered via the lower esophageal
sphincter, which is straightforward with gentle application of pressure in the vast majority of veterinary
patients. One notable exception to this would be dogs
with severe megaesophagus, for any reason, where the
dilated and flaccid esophagus drapes into the thoracic
cavity, resulting in outpouchings that tend to capture the
endoscope, and significant elevation changes are necessary to reach the lower esophageal sphincter.
After entering the stomach via the lower esophageal
sphincter, a reduction in resistance to passage is felt. At
this point, with the working end of the endoscope just
entering into the cardia of the stomach, air insufflation is
started to moderately inflate the gastric lumen. During
insufflation, the gastric rugae should be closely observed
for areas that are not flattening out or show marked
apparent changes in rugal fold directions, as these can
indicate areas of wall infiltration and pathology. Directly
ahead of the endoscope from this position will be the
greater curvature of the stomach and the gastric body.
From this position, left and right deviations of the endoscope can be used to get a general overview of the gastric
lumen.
Rightwards deviation of the endoscope tip will provide
a view of the greater curvature descending to the antral

517

VetBooks.ir

518

Section 6 Gastrointestinal Disease

wall. Usually, the pyloric sphincter and inner antral
lumen are not visible from the lower esophageal sphincter, but the incisura angularis is easily identified and is an
important landmark for further manipulations.
Leftwards deviation of the endoscope tip from the lower
esophageal sphincter reveals the oral aspect of the fundus and greater curvature, but the cardia is not visible
from this position.
The endoscope tip is advanced into the gastric lumen
following insufflation, and the endoscope placed into a J
shape by maximal upwards deviation using the control
wheels. This will typically provide a view back towards
the face of the incisura and into the antrum, and should
allow visualization of the pyloric area. Applying rotational
torque to the endoscope will provide a view of the cardia
and the lower esophageal sphincter. The visualization of
the endoscope body entering via the lower esophageal
sphincter provides obvious confirmation that the cardia
and lower esophageal sphincter are being visualized.
Relaxing the strain on the upwards deviation control
and gently pushing the endoscope forwards will typically
result in the body of the endoscope contacting the greater
curvature of the stomach, and minor torqueing of the
endoscope towards the right (relative to the control cluster) will usually result in a view along the greater curvature into the antral lumen towards the pylorus. Gentle
forwards pressure is then applied to enter the antrum
and approach the pyloric sphincter.
Entry into the antrum and visualization of the pyloric
sphincter can become very difficult if the gastric body is
aggressively insufflated. Introducing more and more air is
tempting as it allows a larger field of view, but the resulting compression of the antrum, and greater distance of
greater curvature wall that must be traversed, make entry
to the antrum much more challenging. This is particularly true with very large dogs, where the entire 120–
150 cm working length of the endoscopes commonly
used in veterinary practice will be taken up by transit of
the esophagus and around the greater curvature.
After visualization of all areas of the stomach, the endoscope may then be advanced to and through the pylorus
to enter the duodenum if duodenoscopy is planned. This
technique is discussed in greater depth later.
Normal Findings

The mucosa of the gastric body is generally light pink to
red, and prominent rugal folds are apparent on first entry
to the stomach and early in the insufflation process. The
majority of the rugae run longitudinally around the
greater curvature of the stomach, which can be a useful
guide for orientation. Rugae should disappear as the
stomach becomes distended during insufflation, but
prolonged periods of aggressive insufflation should be
avoided due to the risk of respiratory and circulatory

compromise, and the greater difficulty of continued
examination. The mucosa should be smooth in appearance. The mucosa within the antrum is a lighter color
than in the main gastric body, and rugae are either absent
or greatly reduced. Patchy erythematous regions, particularly on the greater curvature, are normal. The
pylorus is usually not directly visible on first entry to the
antrum, but instead is surrounded by a number of
mucosal folds in the distal antrum. Careful observation
will usually allow visualization of small amounts of bile
reflux or transient opening of the pylorus.
Fluid, residual food particles, and foreign bodies will
tend to pool in the left fundus when the patient is in left
lateral recumbence. In normal animals, there will be
scant fluid or mucus present, while those with gastrointestinal disease can exhibit large pools of fluid, mucus,
and food particles. Excessive fluid will obscure visualization of the gastric mucosa in this region, and may camouflage foreign bodies. Ideally, as much fluid as possible
should be suctioned from the fundus during the examination. This will improve visualization, and also
decreases the risk of vomiting or regurgitation and aspiration on recovery.
Potential Abnormalities Observed
in Gastroscopy Procedures
Gastritis

Gastritis is commonly encountered during gastroscopy.
Gross changes that may be visible include marked reddening of the mucosa, thickening of the mucosa,
increased prominence and extent of mucosal erythema,
and thickening of the rugae resulting in slower and less
complete flattening of the rugae during insufflation.
While any or all of these changes should increase suspicion for the presence of gastritis, it is important to
remember that some patients may show histologic evidence of gastric inflammation with relatively mild to
nonexistent grossly visible changes. Biopsy collection is
crucial to allow accurate assessment. In many animals
with gastritis, the gastric mucosa is perceptibly “easier”
to biopsy, requiring less avulsion force to remove tissue.
Biopsy sites from animals with gastritis will often bleed
more freely. As greater volumes of bleeding can be seen
in animals with gastric inflammation, it is wise to biopsy
the stomach at the end of the gastroduodenoscopy procedure otherwise bleeding can result in obstruction of
the view.
Gastric Ulceration

Common causes of gastric ulceration include inappropriate or prolonged NSAID use and local neoplastic processes (particularly gastric carcinoma). Ulceration can
also be seen due to paraneoplastic effects from mast cell

49 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy

VetBooks.ir

regional prevalence of fungal or oomycete‐induced disease, these infections may also result in intraluminal
granuloma formation. Leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma
are rare in the gastrointestinal tract but when seen, are
most commonly associated with the lower esophageal
sphincter, and are most frequently identified in older,
female dogs.
As mural mass lesions may primarily affect the deeper
layers of the gastric wall, endoscopic biopsy samples are
often nondiagnostic. Obtaining multiple biopsy “bites”
from the same site, to allow sampling of the submucosa
and muscularis layers, increases the utility of endoscopic
biopsy samples for mural masses.
Gastric Parasites
Figure 49.12 Severe ulceration on the wall of the gastric lesser
curvature in a canine patient presenting with severe recurrent
vomiting. In the lower left quadrant of the image, close to the
endoscope, the upper edge of the incisura angularis is visible and
is also dramatically abnormal. This patient was diagnosed with
mucinous gastric carcinoma via endoscopic biopsy.

neoplasms and gastrinomas. Paraneoplastic ulceration
secondary to severe and persistent gastric hyperacidity is
often profound and severe.
Ulceration is usually seen in the secretory compartment of the stomach. The incisura angularis is also very
commonly affected, and is a particularly common site to
encounter NSAID‐induced ulcers. Large ulcers are typically visible as dark, depressed areas of necrotic tissue,
surrounded by an elevated rim of markedly reddened
and thickened mucosa (Figure 49.12). Biopsy of the
center of an ulcerated lesion is usually of little diagnostic
value as the tissues are necrotic; this is also associated
with risk for perforation of the ulcer. Biopsies for assessment should be taken from the rim at the periphery of
the ulcer, as well as several biopsies from nearby apparently normal tissue to screen for infiltrative processes.
Gastric ulceration due to NSAIDs cannot be differentiated from ulceration due to neoplasia, and as both
NSAID and neoplastic processes are more common in
older dogs, biopsy to rule out neoplasia is mandatory
even in patients receiving NSAIDs.
Mural Masses

Mass lesions affecting the gastric wall may be visualized
in any part of the stomach. Some potential causes
of gastric mural lesions include chronic inflammatory
change (polyps), lymphosarcoma, granulomatous
lesions due to foreign body penetration, and tumors
arising from smooth muscle (leiomyoma, leiomyosarcoma) or mesenchymal cells (gastrointestinal stromal
tumor [GIST], fibrosarcomas). In areas with high

Occasionally, gastric parasites, such as Physaloptera
spp., are observed during gastroscopy, typically in
patients being assessed for chronic vomiting. These
are small parasites, being around 3–4 cm long and very
slender. If the clinician does not suspect that they may be
present, it is easy to overlook them. As these worms are
susceptible to both pyrantel pamoate and most of the
macrocylic lactone parasiticides (ivermectin, selamectin,
etc.), this has become an uncommon diagnosis in client‐
owned animals.
Gastric Foreign Bodies

Gastric foreign body removal is a common indication
for gastroscopy in companion animals. Foreign bodies
may lodge in the antrum/pylorus or remain freely
mobile within the gastric lumen. Freely mobile foreign
bodies will usually be found in the left gastric body
when the patient is in left lateral recumbence, due to the
effect of gravity. Often, foreign bodies are associated
with or surrounded by large aggregations of hair, grass,
and other consumed materials, which can complicate
assessment and accurate deployment of foreign body
snares.
Foreign bodies lodged within the antrum/pylorus will
be visualized during the approach along the greater curvature. Patients with foreign bodies in this location, particularly if they are thought to be fabric based (carpet,
bedding material, wool, etc.), should be carefully assessed
for evidence of linear foreign body entrapment in the
small intestine before proceeding to gastroscopy, as
patients with linear entrapment within the small intestine are best assessed at exploratory surgery.
Assuming successful removal of a foreign body from
the stomach via endoscopy, it is strongly recommended
to obtain biopsies of the gastric (and, if possible, small
intestinal) mucosa before recovering the patient from
anesthesia. Particularly in middle‐aged to older animals,
pica may be the only sign of significant inflammatory
disease of the gastrointestinal tract.

Section 6 Gastrointestinal Disease

Duodenoscopy
Indications

Duodenoscopy is commonly indicated for the assessment of small intestinal disease in companion animals.
Mucosal assessment and biopsy are of value in cases with
unexplained weight loss, poor appetite, vomiting, and
diarrhea. Duodenoscopy may also yield useful information in patients with hematemesis or hematochezia, but
this is less commonly the case and these clinical signs are
not a primary indication for duodenoscopy. It is important to consider that the actual area of small intestine
accessible via endoscopy is limited in most patients. It is
unusual to be able to reach the jejunum in most veterinary patients, and thus large areas of the small intestine
are inaccessible for routine endoscopy. Consequently,
endoscopy is a poor choice for attempted assessment of
small intestinal diseases that are discrete in nature, such
as solitary ulcerative lesions or mural mass lesions.
Patient Positioning

Duodenoscopy procedures are almost invariably conducted with the patient in left lateral recumbence, as this
places the pyloric sphincter and gastric wall in the optimum position for passage into the duodenum.
Equipment Choice

Standard 7–9 mm diameter, 125–150 cm flexible endoscopes with four‐way tip deflection, air and water insufflation and an adequate working channel are useful in the
vast majority of veterinary patients. Remanufactured/
refurbished pediatric gastroscopes work well for cats
and smaller dogs. In larger dogs (30 kg+), 9–11 mm
160 cm+ colonoscopes tend to have better reach into the
duodenum.
General Technique and Landmarks

Navigation of the antrum and pylorus to enter the duodenum is one of the more challenging procedures in
companion animal gastroduodenoscopy. Traversal of the
stomach to the greater curvature, around to the entry to
the antrum and the approach to the pylorus will often
consume a large proportion of the working length of the
endoscope, and multiple turns can result in the endoscope tip moving in directions that are counterintuitive
relative to the control cluster and the operator’s hands.
Excessive insufflation of the stomach tends to increase
the difficulty of this procedure, as it changes the anatomy
of the antral opening, increases the distance of gastric
wall that will be traversed, and tends to increase pyloric
sphincter tone. If difficulty is experienced with this procedure, particularly if the endoscope is unable to pass the
incisura angularis, gas should be removed from the
stomach via suctioning.

The typical approach to the pylorus occurs by directing the endoscope towards the greater curvature, then
deflecting the endoscope tip using a J‐maneuver and
torquing the endoscope to allow visualization of the
incisura angularis. The endoscope is then advanced
slightly (sliding along the greater curvature) and the
upwards deflection is relaxed, allowing the end of the
endoscope to relax onto the antral wall. Once the tip of
the endoscope has entered the antrum, gentle forwards
pressure on the body of the endoscope will usually result
in forward motion of the working end of the endoscope
into the antral lumen towards the pylorus. If the endoscope is repeatedly “flipping” out of the antrum, or shows
paradoxical motion (the pylorus moving away as forwards pressure is applied), it is likely that there is excessive length of endoscope body within the gastric lumen
due to excess insufflation. The endoscope is retracted
into the gastric body, air is removed until the stomach is
perceptibly deflating (rugae should be readily visible, at a
minimum), and then the approach to the antrum can be
repeated.
The pylorus is identified by careful examination of the
center of the distal antral wall. In most animals, the circumferential muscle structure of the sphincter is easy to
appreciate, in others there may be mucosal folds or more
complex sphincter anatomy present, but most animals
will show at least one fold or sulcus of the mucosa that is
obviously deeper and more motile; this is the most likely
point to find the pyloric sphincter. Entry to the sphincter
typically involves incremental advancement of the endoscope body, while using progressive subtle tip deflections
with the control wheels to maintain the pyloric sphincter
within the center of view. As the endoscope tip impacts
the mucosa, it is normal to have a complete loss of vision;
gentle pressure is continually applied and the tip of the
endoscope deviated slightly to the right and downwards.
The endoscope operator should feel a forward motion
and the mucosa “glides by” the end of the scope, the
operator watches for a change in color of the mucosa
from a light red (antral mucosa) to a darker red to yellow
tinged color (duodenal mucosa and bile). When the
mucosal color changes, the endoscope is advanced for
several centimeters, then air is insufflated and the tip of
the scope gently diverted in several directions to obtain a
view of the lumen. Once the lumen is visible, the endoscope can be slowly retracted to allow examination of the
very cranial aspect of the duodenum.
If the endoscope is carefully positioned in the very cranial duodenum, it is usually possible to identify the duodenal papillae. There are two papillae in dogs; the more
cranial, larger papilla is the major duodenal papilla and
drains both biliary and pancreatic secretions, while the
smaller minor papilla drains only pancreatic secretions.
In the cat, only one papilla is visualized, and drains both

biliary and pancreatic secretions. The papilla(e) are a
useful landmark indicating that the working tip of the

(Figure 49.13).
As the endoscope is advanced along the duodenum, a
clear lumen is readily appreciated; this is the descending
duodenum. As the end of this lumen is approached, the
mucosa can be seen deviating to the left (assuming routine patient and endoscope orientation); this is the caudal duodenal flexure. If the endoscope can be coaxed
around this corner (which depends heavily on the working length available and the size of the patient), it is possible to enter the transverse duodenum, and after a short
distance another turn marks the beginning of the jejunum. It is relatively uncommon that this depth is reached
in veterinary patients.
The leftward deviating mucosa at the caudal duodenal
flexure is typically an easy site to biopsy. Biopsies are
obtained from this wall, and then the endoscope is slowly
withdrawn, 1–2 cm at a time, to allow biopsy of the
descending duodenal mucosa. Biopsy samples are collected progressively as the endoscope retracts, until the
working end falls back through the pylorus into the gastric antrum. At this point, the biopsy sample container
should be changed and a new container used for gastric
biopsy samples.
Normal Findings

As indicated above, observation of the duodenal
papilla(e) is a normal finding, particularly in dogs. The
duodenal mucosa should be pink to red, and show a fine
granular to almost velvety appearance (representing the
tips of the villi). Small amounts of bile and bile‐stained

lighter than the surrounding mucosa, and are slightly
depressed relative to the local mucosa. These represent
aggregations of lymphoid tissue and are not abnormal.
Potential Abnormalities Observed
in Duodenoscopy Procedures

Most of the abnormalities noted in endoscopic examinations of the duodenum relate to changes in the appearance or character of the mucosal surface. These changes
are not specific to any particular disease process, but
generally reflect changes in the cellularity and cellular
makeup of the mucosa.
The characters most commonly assessed for evidence
of abnormalities in the duodenum are granularity,
friability, presence of erosions, and abnormalities in
­
l­ ymphatic drainage.

Increasing granularity results in a “heaped” appearance of the mucosa; with severe change, there may be
apparent folds in the duodenal mucosa that do not
­dissipate with insufflation, while more subtle changes
lead to a “cobble stone” appearance of the mucosa (see
Figure 49.7).
Increasing friability is noted when impact with the
endoscope leads to excessive mucosal stripping and
bleeding from contact points. The mucosa is inherently
somewhat friable, but contact of the endoscope with a
normal mucosa should result in very minor to no loss of
mucosal surface (see Figure 49.8).
Erosions are preexisting areas of loss or compromise of
the mucosal surface. As some degree of mucosal contact
is inevitable as the endoscope proceeds along the duodenal lumen, it is important to assess for the presence of
erosions as the endoscope is advanced, not on withdrawal. Dramatic mucosal damage visible on withdrawal
of the endoscope is more compatible with a change in
friability than a diagnosis of erosions, as it represents
greater iatrogenic damage rather than preexisting
mucosal pathology.
Lymphatic drainage of the villi occurs via the lacteals,
which normally contain milky white lymph due to the
presence of fat micelles. This makes visualization of lacteals remarkably easy in many patients. Simply observing
lacteals within the villi, even in animals that have had an
overnight fast, is not evidence of a lymph drainage abnormality. Mucosal blebbing, representing rupture of the
lacteals and infiltration of lymph into the interstitium, is
an important finding. In patients with lymphangiectasia,

may occupy >80% of the volume of the villi. This degree

or due to the presence of a primary lymphatic vessel
