None of the mucosal changes described above can be
reliably detected in all cases of small intestinal disease,
and the agreement between observation of these abnormalities and the presence of histologically important
mucosal changes is poor at best. Small intestinal mucosal
biopsy samples should always be obtained during duodenoscopy procedures.

­Large Intestinal and Distal Small
Intestinal Procedures
Patient Preparation
Adequate patient preparation is critical before colonoscopy and ileoscopy procedures. The esophagus, stomach, and upper small intestine will usually be emptied of
ingesta with a 12–18‐hour fast. The large intestine, however, normally contains a large amount of fecal material,
mucus, and fluid that is not removed or resolved with
fasting alone. Other procedures, including oral preparation solutions and enema treatments in concert with
fasting, are necessary to allow adequate preparation for
this procedure.
Failure to remove fecal material adequately is a major
cause of incomplete or diagnostically misleading colonoscopy procedures. Visualization of the mucosa is often
severely hampered (potentially resulting in failure to
observe discrete lesions), and the time taken to complete
the examination is markedly extended.
A number of different approaches to colonoscopy
preparation have been described. Some practitioners use
only warm water enemas (along with 24–48 hours of
preprocedure fasting), or warm soapy water enemas.
Care must be taken with enema solutions that they are
not irritating (as can be the case with some solutions
marketed mainly for relief of constipation in humans)
and do not cause severe fluid or electrolyte shifts (phosphate‐based enemas are notorious for this effect in cats).
The author’s preferred approach is to use a combination of fasting with polyethylene glycol‐based oral preparation solutions (GoLYTELY® or similar) combined with
periprocedural enemas. The oral preparation solutions
produce dramatic osmotic diarrhea, so it is often beneficial to hospitalize the patient for easier maintenance and
cleaning. The solution is administered at a dose of
approximately 20–25 mL/kg via orogastric intubation,

VetBooks.ir

49 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy

starting the evening before the procedure is planned.
The solution is dosed three times (each at 20–25 mL/kg)
at 2–3‐hour intervals, starting approximately 18 hours
before the procedure is planned (early afternoon the day
before a planned morning procedure). The solution is
administered via either intermittent orogastric intubation or by mixing it with plain vanilla ice‐cream (one part
ice‐cream to two parts solution) and allowing the patient
to drink it. Many dogs will readily consume the resulting
solution. If oral intubation is used, the author considers
nasogastric intubation and trickle infusion to be strongly
contraindicated, as this is associated with increased risk
of aspiration pneumonia, which can be severe and life
threatening.
As the last of the evening doses of oral preparation
solution is given, a warm water enema (also 20–30 mL/
kg) is administered. The warm water enema is repeated
early in the morning on the day of the planned procedure
(around 7am for a 9am procedure), which should result
in passage of clear fluid with little to no fecal material or
mucus. If the morning enema continues to produce solid
fecal material, ideally the procedure will be delayed by
1–2 hours to allow a second morning enema, followed by
at least an hour of resting time to allow fluid absorption
and resolution of transient irritation of the colonic
mucosa.
An adequately prepared colon will allow easy and relatively unimpeded observation of the colonic mucosa
over the length of the large intestine. Minor adherent
material and mucus can usually be lavaged and flushed
from the colon using endoscope suction. Specific colonoscope irrigation and washing pump systems are available and routinely used in human patients, and may be
worth consideration in veterinary practices that carry
out a large number of large intestinal procedures. While
these pumps and washing systems can assist with final
cleaning and visualization of the colonic mucosa, they
are not a replacement for adequate preprocedural
preparation.
Proctoscopy
Indications

Proctoscopy is a useful technique for the assessment of
patients with predominantly or exclusively large intestinal symptoms, such as tenesmus, excess fecal mucus,
fecal urge incontinence, hematochezia, dyschezia, and
visible or palpable anorectal masses. As many of the
mucosal diseases affecting the large intestine tend to be
diffuse throughout the large intestinal lumen, and anorectal diseases are by definition limited to the distal large
intestine and anal canal, proctoscopy may be all that is
necessary to establish a useful working diagnosis in a
large intestinal disease case.

Patient Positioning

Typically, the patient is placed in right lateral recumbence for isolated proctoscopy procedures without
assessment of the transverse or descending colon and
ileocolic junction. Right lateral recumbence causes any
residual fluid from patient preparation to pool into the
transverse colon (which is oriented vertically when the
animal is in lateral recumbence), aiding in mucosal
visualization.
Equipment Choice

Proctoscopy can be achieved with either flexible or rigid
endoscopes. Refurbished human flexible colonoscopes,
up to 11 mm diameter, can be effectively used in most
dogs and cats, although some endoscope manipulations
such a J‐maneuvers (necessary for effective visualization
of some very distal rectoanal lesions) can be challenging
or impossible with this size endoscope in smaller dogs
and most cats.
Rigid proctoscopes can be very valuable for these procedures, as they usually feature large endoscope lumens
that allow passage of larger instruments, biopsy and cautery snares, and rigid forceps.
General Technique and Landmarks

The rigid proctoscope is lubricated well and introduced
through the anal sphincter gently, while an obturator is
in place. When resistance to passage of the proctoscope
reduces, marking entry of the proctoscope into the rectum, the obturator device is removed and the lighting
and visualization system (typically a rigid fiberoptic telescope and accessory camera) are attached. The proctoscope is then gently introduced into the colon lumen,
while the operator closely observes the mucosa. Air
insufflation is used as necessary to inflate and maintain
the colonic lumen. Rigid proctoscopes should not be
advanced if the lumen is not visible, as this increases the
risk of colon wall perforation, which is a major and
potentially life‐threatening complication.
With the larger lumen of the proctoscope, there is the
potential to use larger, rigid biopsy forceps and instruments to collect more substantial pieces of tissue than
with typical biopsy instruments used in flexible endoscopes. Some rigid biopsy instruments feature angled
biopsy cups, which make the process of sampling the
mucosa through the rigid lumen somewhat easier. Rigid
instruments with straight biopsy cups are still useful, but
may require removal of a small amount of insufflated air
to allow the mucosa to “drape” over the front of the endoscope lumen.
Normal Findings and Potential Abnormalities

Normal findings and potential abnormalities encountered during proctoscopy are identical to those seen

during flexible colonoscopy procedures, and are
described in the flexible colonoscopy section below.
Colonoscopy
Indications

Colonoscopy is commonly indicated for the assessment
of patients with predominantly or exclusively large intestinal symptoms, such as tenesmus, excess fecal mucus,
fecal urge incontinence, hematochezia, dyschezia, and
visible or palpable masses. Colonoscopy is also increasingly viewed as an important part of the overall approach
to any chronic gastrointestinal disease case, a means of
both assessing large intestinal involvement and collecting distal small intestinal biopsy samples via ileoscopy.
Patient Positioning

For most colonoscopy procedures, the patient should be
placed in left lateral recumbence. As well as being convenient for combination upper and lower gastrointestinal tract procedures performed sequentially under the
one anesthetic procedure, left lateral recumbence results
in residual fluid pooling in the descending colon; this
fluid is more readily suctioned from this position than if
in the transverse or ascending arms of the colon.
Colonoscopy procedures can also be carried out in sternal recumbence, which has the advantage that the anatomy of the colon is oriented in a “normal” position
relative to the endoscope operator. However, scrupulous
preparation is necessary to obtain optimum visualization
if this position is used.
Equipment Choice

Navigation of the entire large intestine to the ileocolic
junction requires the use of a flexible endoscope with
four‐way tip deflection, water and air insufflation, and a
good sized working channel. Refurbished human colonoscopes with working lengths of 150–175 cm and
9–11 mm diameter are appropriate for many small animal patients and usually feature 2.8 mm working channels, allowing the use of larger biopsy instruments. In
very small dogs and some cats, the use of these endoscopes may be more difficult, primarily due to the minimum turning radius of the endoscope tip rather than the
endoscope diameter. In these smaller patients, a pediatric gastroscope may be a better choice.
General Technique and Landmarks

The lubricated endoscope tip is gently introduced via the
anal sphincter. When a reduction in insertion pressure is
noted, indicating that the tip of the endoscope has traversed the anal sphincter and is sitting within the distal
rectum, the endoscopist should stop and insufflate while
moving the tip controls gently in order to visualize a

lumen. Unlike in the small intestine, where mucosal “fly
by” procedures are common, in the large intestine it is
generally best only to proceed forwards when there is a
visible lumen. As air insufflation proceeds, the pressure
of the accumulating gas may lead to leakage around the
endoscope at the anal sphincter. This can be overcome
by having an assistant apply gentle circumferential pressure around the anus; the same assistant can also advance
the main endoscope body while the main operator utilizes the tip deflection controls and air/water insufflation
to maintain visualization.
The distal rectum is assessed as soon as the lumen is
insufflated, examining for preexisting erosions and the
presence of mucosal masses. To obtain complete visualization of the distal rectum and the oral surface of the
anal sphincter requires a maximally flexed J‐maneuver,
which may not be feasible in smaller patients.
As the endoscope is advanced, the descending colon
wall is examined for changes in mucosal friability, granularity, and the presence of masses. If the patient is in left
lateral recumbence, some fluid pooling is to be expected
along the lumen of the descending colon; this fluid
should be aspirated as much as possible to optimize
mucosal visibility.
At the end of the descending colon, the lumen will
make a marked deviation into the transverse colon.
Ideally, this turn should be made with a target lumen visible, although this is not always feasible. Carefully assess
what mucosa is visible from the descending colon before
proceeding into the transverse colon; if severe ulceration
or erosions are present, it may be more prudent to limit
the examination to reduce the risk of perforation.
The transverse colon crosses the abdomen to reveal
the short ascending colon and the ileocolic junction.
This region is readily identified by the presence of a
proud, intraluminal button of mucosa surrounding the
ileocolic sphincter, while the nearby cecum is usually visible as a blind pouch close to the ileocolic sphincter. The
cecal mucosa is usually arrayed in longitudinal folds similar to the rugae of the stomach. Lymphatic follicles can
be quite prominent within the cecal mucosa.
Normal Findings

The normal colonic mucosa is smooth, a light pink in
color and readily distensible with air insufflation. The
ileocolic junction can be quite variable in appearance
(Figure 49.16). Depending upon the trajectory of the
endoscope approaching this region, the ileocolic sphincter may be visualized to the left or right, and the opening
of the cecum is also quite variable, in some cases showing a prominent “ridge” of tissue around the opening,
while in others the cecal opening is hard to distinguish
from the colon lumen and is appreciated only as a blind
sac near to the ileocolic sphincter.

49 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy

VetBooks.ir

mucosal defects are best assessed by collecting biopsies
from the adjacent, more normal‐appearing mucosa
rather than the center of the mass, as biopsies from this
region are usually of poor diagnostic quality due to tissue
necrosis, and the risk of perforation is increased
substantially.
Ileoscopy
Indications

Figure 49.16 Colonic view of the normal ileocolic junction in a
dog. The ileocolic sphincter, visible as a mushroom‐like protrusion

Above the ileocolic sphincter, the entry to the cecum is visible,
surrounded by a “ridge” of normal colonic mucosa. The anatomy of

Ileoscopy, while technically more challenging than many
other gastrointestinal endoscopy procedures, is strongly
recommended when endoscopic examination is being
conducted as part of the approach to patients with gastrointestinal disease, regardless of whether the primary
complaint is predominantly arising from upper or lower
gastrointestinal tract signs. It is not unusual to document
substantial histological disagreement between duodenal
and ileal mucosal biopsy specimens, with the ileal
mucosa often presenting with more severe changes. This
holds true with both dogs and cats.
Patient Positioning and Preparation

After careful assessment of the mucosa for consistency

biopsy samples should be obtained from areas of interest
and several areas that are apparently normal as the endoscope is withdrawn. Mass lesions may also be biopsied
but care must be taken to minimize the risk of colonic
wall perforation. Mass lesions or ulcerative lesions with
severe mucosal distortions (Figure 49.17) or deep

As ileoscopy requires a transcolonic approach, ideally
the patient will be placed in left lateral recumbence. This
is consistent with the positioning for upper gastrointestinal procedures. Ideally, the patient will receive preprocedural preparation for colonoscopy. If there is no plan to
fully assess the colonic mucosa and the sole reason for
the procedure is to attempt to biopsy the ileal mucosa, a
more abbreviated preparation protocol can be used,
essentially several warm water enemas administered the

provide sufficient space and visualization to allow traversal of the colon to the ileocolic junction, but there is a
greater risk that the lower intensity preparation will
result in inadequate visualization and failure of the
procedure.
Equipment Choice

Ileoscopy requires a flexible colonoscope with four‐way
tip deflection, air/water insufflation and a large working
channel, as used for colonoscopy procedures. Extra
length will be necessary to allow navigation into and
along the ileum, which may become limiting with larger
canine patients.
General Technique and Landmarks

The ileocolic junction is approached at the end of the
routine colonoscopy procedure, as described earlier. The
endoscope tip is brought into contact with the center of
the ileocolic sphincter, similarly to the antral approach to
the pylorus. As with the pyloric approach, excessive air

insufflation can compromise attempts to traverse the
sphincter. As there is little in the way of colonic wall close
to the sphincter, due to the disparity in ileal versus
colonic lumen diameters, full insufflation deprives the
endoscopist of support from the colon walls.
If the endoscope can be successfully maneuvered into
contact with the sphincter, gentle forwards pressure will
usually result in entry to the ileum. If the ileum cannot be
entered in this manner due to ileocolic anatomy, a flexible biopsy instrument can be threaded through the
working channel and ileocolic sphincter to act as a guide
wire. The instrument is advanced, cups closed, until it
has penetrated the ileal lumen for 2–3 cm. The biopsy
instrument is then held in place and the endoscope
advanced over it. It is not recommended to simply follow
the biopsy instrument with the endoscope, as this may
result in significant trauma to the ileal mucosa (which
has not been visualized).
Normal Findings

The normal ileal mucosa is grossly similar in appearance
to the duodenal and jejunal mucosa. The normal villus
structure results in a “velvet” appearance. The mucosa is
more friable than the duodenum, even in normal individuals. Villus lymphatics are not readily appreciated.
Potential Abnormalities Observed during
Ileoscopy Procedures

The ileal mucosa is assessed for changes in granularity,
friability, the existence of preexisting erosions or ulcerative lesions and mass effects, and these changes documented if seen. Mucosal biopsy specimens should always
be obtained from the ileum. If the endoscopist is unable
to traverse the ileocolic sphincter, it is possible to obtain
mucosal biopsy samples blindly by advancing a biopsy
instrument through the sphincter, although this should
be approached with caution as the risk of perforation is
higher without the ability to visualize preexisting lesions.

­Endoscopic Biopsy Technique
Endoscopic biopsies are an attractive option for more
complete diagnostic assessment of the gastrointestinal
tract, but are not without significant potential pitfalls.
Correct biopsy technique, careful sample handling, and
the collection of adequate sample numbers are all
­important to obtain the best diagnostic yield from these
samples.
Flexible endoscopic biopsy instruments are available
in several different types, including serrated or smooth
jaws, and with or without central needles. Theoretically
the central needle types are easier to lodge in the mucosa
but in practice there seems to be little advantage to these

types, and removal of the sample from the central needle
can be difficult. The biopsies are inherently fragile and
repeated “scraping” to remove the sample from the central needle can result in severe crush artifact distortion.
Endoscopic biopsy samples obtained using flexible
instruments are unavoidably small. Even the largest of
the flexible biopsy instruments that will fit in the endoscopes used most commonly in companion animal practice will typically only yield a 2.5–3 mm3 tissue sample
under most conditions. Most samples obtained endoscopically will have relatively little submucosal tissue
present, and in many cases small intestinal biopsies may
only yield villus tips. Correct technique is necessary to
avoid excessive crush artifacts or villus degloving.
Because of the extreme wide‐angle view and deep
depth of focus of the endoscope lens, and lack of depth
cues due to monocular vision, the distance between the
end of the endoscope, the biopsy instrument, and the
lesion to be biopsied can be difficult to judge. Once a site
for biopsy is identified, the biopsy instrument is carefully
deployed through the working channel until it is visible
to the operator. Fine tip adjustments can then be made to
align the instrument with the area to be biopsied, and
then the instrument is advanced to make contact with
the tissue. The flexible shaft of the biopsy instrument will
start to bend slightly as the instrument is pushed up
against the tissue. This bending is a good indicator that
an appropriate amount of pressure is being applied to the
tissue to provide the best chance of an adequate biopsy.
The biopsy instrument emerges from the distal face of
the endoscope (Figure 49.18), which will usually result in
the instrument running parallel to the gastrointestinal
lumen. If the endoscope is maneuvered close to a naturally occurring fold or corner in the lumen, it is possible
to directly sample tissue perpendicular to the distal
scope face. For biopsies from the wall in an area that does
not have a naturally occurring fold or local corner (such
as in the descending duodenum), a number of strategies
are available. Gently suctioning some of the insufflating
gas may result in formation of rugal folds. After minor
suction is applied, the endoscope tip is diverted towards
the mural surface using the tip deflection controls, then
the biopsy instrument is advanced out until just in view
and close to, but not touching, the mucosa. The biopsy
jaws should be open at this point. Full suction is then
applied, which will cause the lumen to collapse and the
mucosa to “drape” over the end of the scope. The biopsy
instrument is advanced very slightly and then the jaws
are closed. The biopsy is then collected.
The necessary action to collect an endoscopic biopsy is
with a sharp “snapping” pull on the instrument at the
control end of the scope. The aim is to avulse the mucosal
sample by breaking the submucosal tissue. If the tissue is
collected with a slower “drag” motion, it is not

VetBooks.ir

49 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy

Figure 49.18 A hemispherical jaw biopsy instrument exits the
distal end of a videoendoscope perpendicular to the imaging
components and parallel to the long axis of the gastrointestinal

uncommon to yield only mucus, or to deglove the villi
and retrieve only mucosal fragments. These samples are
usually not of diagnostic quality, as the loss of architectural context limits the ability of the pathologist to accurately assess the mucosa.
After collection, the biopsy instrument is removed
while leaving the endoscope in place. The instrument
should be kept closed until the instrument has been fully
removed from the endoscope and an assistant has
restrained the end of the instrument. The instrument is
then opened, and the tissue sample retrieved from within
the biopsy cups. Often, the tissue will be adherent to the
biopsy cups, and the tissue may need to be removed by
gentle manipulation with a fine hypodermic needle (typically 25 ga). “Stickiness” of the biopsy to the instrument
is more pronounced with smaller biopsy instruments
and in samples from the small intestinal mucosa.

Given that each individual sample is very small, and
may not be representative of the total of the pathologic
changes present in the patient, it is important to obtain
multiple biopsy samples from each organ sampled.
Assuming adequate biopsy technique and handling, at
least seven samples per site (i.e., seven each from upper
and lower small intestine, stomach) in dogs and 10 in
cats are necessary to achieve acceptable correlation with
full‐thickness biopsy results. If inadequate technique is
used, particularly in cats, there is a very real chance that
samples will have no diagnostic utility.
Biopsy of the gastric mucosa is somewhat more
straightforward than in the small intestine as the stomach is more readily distensible and the greater space
within the organ allows easier manipulation of the endoscope to a position perpendicular to the mucosa. The
gastric mucosa is more robust than the small intestinal
mucosa, and good‐quality biopsies are easier to obtain
from most areas of the stomach.
The esophageal mucosa is predominantly squamous
epithelium, and difficult to adequately biopsy unless
severe pathology is present.
Tissues from different sources (small intestine vs large
intestine vs stomach) should be handled and submitted
separately.
Postbiopsy handling of the tissues is also important
for maximum diagnostic utility. Different pathology services may have differing requirements for sample submission but generally speaking, it is best to organize
biopsy samples in a manner that will maintain consistent orientation as the samples are paraffin embedded
and sectioned. If feasible, samples can be directly placed
into sample handling cassettes, oriented with the
mucosa perpendicular to the base of the cassette. It is
important to use cassettes that are compatible with the
sample handling systems of the pathology laboratory.
The whole cassette can then be submerged in buffered
formalin for histologic assessment. This will result in
samples that are as close to parallel to the microtome
blade as possible, yielding a greater proportion of longitudinal sections of the villi. This is important to allow
the pathologist to assess characters such as villus blunting and the presence of inflammatory infiltrates within
the crypts.

­Endoscopic Interventions
PEG Tube Placement
Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tubes are useful
for providing long‐term nutritional support to veterinary
patients with severe esophageal or oral pathology, and
also for those with poor appetite due other co‐morbid

527

VetBooks.ir

528

Section 6 Gastrointestinal Disease

conditions. Placement of these devices is relatively
­simple, but care must be taken to minimize the risk of
complications.
Indications and Patient Choice

Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube placement
should be considered in patients with significant dysphagia, anorexia, esophageal or oral pathology with an anticipated need for nutritional support beyond 3–5 days.
PEG tubes may be placed in both canine and feline
patients, but are of particular use in dogs (particularly
larger breeds) where the placement of esophagostomy
tubes is more difficult due to the anatomy of the neck
and cervical esophagus. PEG tubes have the advantage of
larger lumens than are typically used in nasoesophageal
or esophageal feeding, and are generally well tolerated
such that they can be maintained for weeks to months.
After formation of a stable adhesion of the gastric wall to
the peritoneum and abdominal wall (generally after
10–14 days), it is feasible to convert PEG tubes to lower
profile gastrostomy tubes that are somewhat easier for
clients to maintain and do not feature extraabdominal
tubing that must be restrained and maintained.
Placement of PEG tubes is straightforward in most
patients. Difficulty can be encountered in patients with
megaesophagus, due primarily to negotiating the lower
esophageal sphincter in these patients. Large, deep‐
chested dogs can also be more difficult as the normal
gastric position in these patients is high under the thoracic cage, these patients can require substantial insufflation of the stomach to allow access, and the resulting
ostium and adhesions are under tension after the stomach is deflated. Larger breed, debilitated dogs have a
greater risk of tube failure and peritonitis so in these
patients it may be more prudent to place gastrostomy
tubes surgically.
While the procedure is relatively easy to describe, and
manufactured kits designed to make tube insertion simple are available, it is still prudent to have at least some
guidance from an experienced endoscopist when first
learning to place these tubes.
General Procedure

Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tubes are placed
exiting the flank on the left side, so the patient should be
placed in right lateral recumbence. The left paracostal
region is clipped and surgically prepared. The endoscope
is passed into the stomach, and air insufflated to distend
the stomach against the abdominal wall. While the endoscope operator is visualizing the gastric wall, an assistant
wearing sterile gloves palpates and presses on the region
of maximum distension, to allow the endoscopist to
establish where the tube will eventually be placed. The
endoscope is then manipulated to the point of

compression and the gastric wall transilluminated to
ensure that there are no major structures (particularly the
spleen) present between the gastric and abdominal walls.
The description given below assumes that a manufactured PEG tube kit is being used, which are provided
with the tube mechanically bonded to a loop of wire at
the proximal end, and a guide wire that features a loop at
the distal end. Techniques for the assembly of PEG tubes
using sterile pipette tips and standard suture materials
have been described, but with the ready availability of
commercial PEG kits in the veterinary market, the manufacture of tubes from a miscellany of materials is no
longer recommended.
Once the point of insertion is established, the sterile‐
gloved assistant passes a large hypodermic needle (typically 18–16 ga, 2+ inches) through the skin and gastric
wall, typically placed just ventral and slightly caudal to
rib 13. The endoscope operator monitors the hypodermic needle entry. Once the hypodermic needle is placed,
a guide wire with a terminal loop is threaded through the
lumen of the needle by the assistant, and captured by the
endoscopist using either flexible alligator or cup biopsy
forceps. Once the guide wire loop is captured, it is carefully pulled through the stomach, esophagus, and oral
cavity by withdrawing the endoscope. The assistant
should feed the guide wire via the needle, while monitoring closely to ensure that the full length of the guide wire
is not pulled into the stomach lumen.
After the loop of guide wire is withdrawn via the
mouth, it is attached to the proximal end of the tube by
passing the tube mushroom tip through the guide wire
loop, then through the tube’s own bonded wire loop,
resulting in the tube proximal end being attached to the
guide wire via linked loops.
The guide wire and linked tube, bonded tip first, are
withdrawn into the oral cavity, through the esophagus
and into the stomach lumen by the sterile‐gloved assistant. As the guide wire and linked proximal tube end
encounter the gastric wall, the wall is pulled up against
the flank. The bonded sharp tip of the tube is drawn
through the abdominal wall by continuous gentle traction. A small stab incision will usually be necessary at the
point of tube exit.
As the tube is withdrawn through the abdominal wall,
the endoscopist replaces the endoscope into the gastric
lumen and monitors the positioning of the distal mushroom tip against the gastric wall. The mushroom tip
should be placed with sufficient tension to hold the gastric wall against the abdominal wall, but excessive tension should be avoided as this may lead to gastric wall
necrosis below the mushroom tip and failure of the gastrostomy site. The mushroom tip should gently flatten
the gastric mucosa, but blanching of the mucosa should
not be visible on examination. If the mucosa is blanched,

VetBooks.ir

49 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy

the distracting tension on the tube must be loosened to
reduce the risk of gastric wall compromise.
When the operator is satisfied that the tube is correctly
positioned, the bonded sharp end is removed with heavy
bandage scissors and the tube retained against the external flank using a retaining anchor system. The gastrostomy site is bandaged and the tube trimmed to length
before assembly of a catheter tip closure to allow administration of food. The remaining tube should be loosely
restrained against the body using stockinet tubing and/or
an old t‐shirt, and an Elizabethan collar applied for at least
the first 4–5 days while a stable adhesion is being formed.
Assuming no complications in placement of the PEG
tube, administration of fluids (water initially) and then
liquid or blenderized diets can commence approximately
eight hours after the patient recovers from anesthesia.
PEG‐J Tube Placement
Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy‐jejunostomy
tubes are a refinement and addition to the PEG tube systems described above, with additional placement of a
tube into the jejunum. A PEG tube is placed as described
above, then a narrow feeding tube with a loop of suture
material at the distal end is threaded into the gastric
lumen via the gastrostomy tube. This second tube is captured at the loop of suture material, then the tube is carried through the pylorus and into the duodenum by the
endoscope. The second tube is carried as far as possible
distally by the endoscope, then gently threaded further to
reach the jejunum. The PEG and J‐tubes are then trimmed
and retained as previously described. The addition of the
J‐tube allows the delivery of liquid diets into the jejunum,
completely bypassing the duodenum. While nutrition is
being delivered to the jejunum, gastric secretions and
fluid can be suctioned via the PEG tube, which may help
to control vomiting in patients with severe gastric or pancreatic inflammation. As the patient recovers and the
stomach is more amenable to diet input, the J‐tube can be
removed and use of the PEG tube instituted.
While there are some theoretical benefits to the use of
PEG‐J tubes in animals with very severe pancreatic disease, the author rarely uses these tubes in these patients.
Instead, a multimodal antiemetic protocol is used along
with gastric tube or esophagostomy tube feeding. There is
no evidence to support the contention that “pancreatic
rest” is important for patients with pancreatitis, which is
the main imperative behind J‐tube feeding in most patients.
Foreign Body Removal
The use of endoscopy, either rigid (within the esophagus) or flexible (esophagus and stomach), is an attractive
first‐line option for management of this problem. The

potential for removal without surgery allows more rapid
recovery of the patient and reduces the risk of gastrointestinal perforation and/or wound dehiscence. This
potential must be tempered by the reality that often the
endoscopic removal of foreign bodies, particularly “slippery” gastric foreign bodies that can be quite fragile, can
take long periods of time and may not be feasible. It is
good practice to define an upper time limit for the endoscopic procedure before transitioning to surgical
management.
A variety of retrieval devices is available, with varying
strengths and indications (Figure 49.19). For esophageal
foreign bodies, it is often possible to use long, rigid forceps to grasp the foreign body. This is particularly helpful if using a rigid endoscope for the esophagoscopy, but
can also be carried out with flexible endoscopy equipment by carefully introducing the retrieval instrument
beside or above the endoscope that is viewing the foreign
body. Other retrieval instrument options include flexible
alligator forceps, deployable wire cages, three‐pronged
graspers, Foley catheters, wire loops and snares, and old
endoscopy biopsy forceps. The use of biopsy forceps for
foreign body retrieval will usually result in dulling of the
edges and loss of effective biopsy function so older forceps should be used.
There is no one technique or device that reliably succeeds in grasping and removal of all foreign bodies of any
specific type. While some general observations can be
made, such as alligator forceps have no utility with
rounded, smooth‐surfaced objects, most foreign body
retrievals will require the use of several different types of
instrument. For instance, flexible alligator or old biopsy
forceps may be used to reposition an object within the
gastric lumen, allowing application of a wire basket for
the actual retrieval process. Some foreign bodies will
require reorientation several times to allow a graspable
surface to be visualized. As wide a selection of retrieval
instruments as possible should be available to the
endoscopist. Foley catheters can be used to manipulate
and reposition some objects by threading them past the
obstruction, then inflating the balloon before applying
gentle distracting pressure.
It is particularly attractive to attempt esophageal foreign body removal endoscopically wherever possible,
as removal of foreign bodies from the thoracic esophagus via thoracotomy and esophagotomy is technically
difficult and has a high risk of wound dehiscence and
subsequent development of pneumomediastinum, pneumothorax, and pyothorax. As a general observation,
endoscopic removal of esophageal foreign bodies
becomes increasingly difficult as the time since obstruction increases. Esophageal mucosal swelling and erosion/ulceration can occur rapidly, and these changes
result in the foreign body becoming more and more

firmly wedged. If the foreign body can be solidly grasped,
a number of attempts to remove it via the oral cavity can
be made, but if the object is not mobilized by moderate
traction and the esophageal mucosa is showing increasing evidence of trauma/hemorrhage, a new strategy
should be followed. If the foreign body can be pushed
aborally into the stomach, this is often a preferable
option. Many bone foreign bodies or impacted dog
chews will dissipate once within the gastric lumen, while
indigestible foreign bodies can be removed via celiotomy
and gastrotomy with much lower risk of complications
than arise from a transthoracic route.
When attempting to retrieve foreign bodies, great
care should be taken that the gastrointestinal tract
wall is not compromised, either by excessive force
application or inadvertent perforation by sharp objects
(bone fragments, needles, etc.) as they are withdrawn.
It is also critical to assess the site of impaction after
withdrawal for evidence of mucosal ulceration and
abrasion. Within the gastric lumen, it is usually possible
to visualize the site of impaction after initial grasping of
the object, but with esophageal foreign bodies it will be
necessary to reintroduce the endoscope to assess the
mucosa. Severe circumferential mucosal damage, particularly if there is exposure of the submucosa, leaves
the patient with a high risk for esophageal stricture formation. It is also recommended to obtain thoracic
­radiographs following removal of esophageal foreign

bodies to assess for early signs of esophageal perforation such as pneumomediastinum or pneumothorax.
If the patient has evidence of severe esophagitis
and mucosal ulceration/abrasion, placement of a PEG
tube for postoperative nutritional support is strongly
recommended.
Esophageal Stricture Management
Esophageal stricture recognition and management via
either bougienage or balloon dilation are discussed in
detail in Chapter 52.

­Future Directions of Gastrointestinal
Endoscopy
After the unavoidably small size of biopsies achievable
using flexible endoscopy, probably the greatest
limitation of endoscopy in the gastrointestinal tract
­
of veterinary patients is the lack of ability to assess the
entire gastrointestinal tract. While many diseases
that affect the gastrointestinal tract are diffuse, and
thus duodenoscopy and distal ileoscopy will commonly
result in meaningful diagnostic findings, solitary lesions
in the deeper jejunum and proximal ileum are not
unknown.

A number of newer systems and strategies have been
described that have the potential to allow direct visualization of much larger proportions of the gastrointestinal
tract. The two most promising are double balloon push
and pull enteroscopy and the use of capsule endoscopy
systems.

Double Balloon Enteroscopy
Double balloon push and pull enteroscopy is carried out
using an endoscope with an inflatable balloon, similar to
a Foley catheter balloon, incorporated into the distal
endoscope tip, and an additional balloon on a mobile

531

VetBooks.ir

532

Section 6 Gastrointestinal Disease

cuff that surrounds the distal endoscope. These balloons
are sequentially inflated and deflated, and the endoscope
advanced, as the small intestinal loops fold up behind the
outer cuff. This technique has been described in a limited number of canine patients at the time of writing, and
has some limitations due to the overall diameter of the
specific endoscope/cuff combination (13.2 mm) and the
increased stiffness and turning radius of the endoscope.
The full exploration of the gastrointestinal tract using
this endoscope is also a longer procedure than is typical
for upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. An advantage of
this approach is that biopsy samples can be obtained
from a greater proportion of the gastrointestinal tract,
and discrete lesions within the jejunum may be able to be
sampled.
Capsule Endoscopy
Complete assessment of the entire gastrointestinal tract
of dogs can be obtained in a minimally invasive manner
through use of self‐contained capsule endoscopes. These
devices include cameras with 360° field of view, light
sources, and digital storage space within a plastic

enclosure that is similar in size and shape to a large capsule (Figure 49.20). The capsule is administered to the
patient orally, and after transit through the entire gastrointestinal tract is recovered to allow downloading of digital image files. These systems have advantages in avoiding
the need for anesthesia and postprocedural recovery, and
arguably allow assessment of the gastrointestinal tract in
a more natural state as the vascular changes induced by
patient preparation and anesthesia are avoided.
An obvious limitation of the capsule endoscopy systems is that they are unable to retrieve biopsies, and the
actual location where a lesion is observed cannot be
determined with great accuracy as the images are typically not accessible until after complete transit through
the gastrointestinal tract. This approach is very useful,
however, for a complete assessment of the gastrointestinal tract for focal lesions, bleeding ulcers, discrete
mucosal pathology changes, etc. (Figure 49.21).
Anatomic landmarks, such as the pylorus, major duodenal flexure, and ileocolic junction, are usually easily
identified, allowing some degree of certainty of the
­specific section of the gastrointestinal tract that can be
observed.

Diseases of the Oral Cavity and Salivary Glands

A history of ptyalism or drooling saliva, perioral +/− ocu­
lonasal discharge, anorexia, weight loss, unkempt hair
coat, vocalizing when eating, pawing at the mouth,
­rubbing the face on the furniture or carpeting, bruxism,
chattering, and/or hesitation to have the head or face
touched should prompt the clinician to perform a thor­
ough intraoral and extraoral examination. Oral and sali­
vary gland diseases can have various presentations, and
often the duration of clinical signs along with the distri­
bution of the lesions can aid in determining the etiology
of the condition (Table 50.1). Histologically, oral lesions
can range in appearance from areas of ulceration to vesi­
cles to even proliferation of tissues, whether it is through
hyperplasia, neoplasia or granulation tissue formation,
to areas of necrosis. Salivary gland enlargement follows a
spectrum, with the noninflamed form, known as
sialadenosis, followed by sialadenitis and finally necrotiz­
ing sialometaplasia. Neoplasia can also occur in the
­salivary glands. It is important to keep in mind that some
systemic diseases can manifest with oral lesions.
Additionally, some systemic diseases that lead to immu­
nosuppression can predispose patients to oral disease.

­Healthy Oral Tissues
and Salivary Glands
The masticatory and lining mucosa are the primary tis­
sues affected by oral inflammation. The epithelium of
the masticatory mucosa is moderately thick and fre­
quently ortho‐keratinized. It is inextensible and well
adapted to withstanding abrasion. The epithelium of the
lining mucosa is thicker than that of masticatory mucosa
and is nonkeratinized. The surface is flexible and the
submucosa is elastic, allowing it to stretch. Taste buds,
gingival crevicular fluid, and normal bacterial flora play
a role in protecting the oral cavity from insults. Taste

buds reject potentially toxic materials. The gingival cre­
vicular fluid is believed to cleanse the gingival sulcus,
improve adhesion of the epithelium to the tooth via
plasma proteins, possess antimicrobial properties, and
exert antibody activity to protect the gingiva. The nor­
mal bacterial flora of the oral cavity plays a role in the
innate resistance by preventing colonization and growth
of foreign microbes.
There are four major pairs of salivary glands: mandib­
ular, sublingual, parotid, and zygomatic. Minor salivary
glands can be found on the palate, alveolar, labial and
buccal mucosa, tongue, and along some of the ducts of
the major salivary glands. Cats have an additional pair of
mixed salivary glands found on the lingual aspect of the
mandibular first molar tooth, known as the linguomolar
gland. Secretory cells can be predominantly serous, pre­
dominantly mucous, or mixed. The secretory cells of the
salivary glands form acini, surrounding a central drain­
ing space that empties into the intercalated, striated, and
excretory ducts, successively. These ducts play a major
role in determining the composition of saliva. Saliva
cleanses the mouth, maintains tooth integrity, dilutes
noxious materials, contains antibodies and antimicrobi­
als, maintains the pH in the oral cavity, and plays a role in
the formation of the bolus of food and initial digestion,
depending on the species. The ducts and acini are
­surrounded by connective tissue carrying blood vessels
and nerves.

­Gingivitis and Periodontitis
Periodontal disease is commonly seen in dogs and cats
characterized by inflammation of the supporting struc­
tures of the tooth. Ninety‐six percent of 109 adult cats,
with a mean age of 6.2 +/− 5.2 years, showed evidence
of gingival inflammation in one study. A recent study

looking at the prevalence of disorders recorded in dogs
in attending primary care veterinary practices in England
revealed periodontal disease to be the second most fre­
quently identified disorder. Gingivitis is inflammation of
the gingiva, which may remain stable throughout the life
of the animal. However, with the aid of additional factors
and in a cyclical fashion, it may progress to periodontitis.
Periodontitis is inflammation of the periodontal liga­
ment, cementum and alveolar bone, resulting in pocket
formation, gingival recession, and alveolar bone loss
(Figure 50.1).
Histologically, the pulp tissue of teeth with advanced
periodontitis may undergo changes including acute and
chronic pulpitis, vascular congestion, and pulp necrosis.
These changes may be the result of occlusion of the vas­
cular channel by secondary or tertiary dentinal deposi­
tion, increased mobility of teeth with severe attachment
loss, or, less likely, the centripetal spread of infection or
inflammation into the pulp.
Up to 13% of cats suffering from periodontal disease
may have evidence of aggressive periodontitis. There is
also a strong association between periodontal disease

and type I tooth resorption. In one study, up to 72% of
teeth with type I resorption showed periodontitis, as
opposed to approximately 16% of teeth with type II
resorption. Tooth resorption has also been reported in
dogs but not necessarily in association to periodontitis.
It can occur in association to endodontic disease or with
oral neoplasia at tumor sites and at sites distant from
tumors.
A strong suspicion for a genetic predisposition towards
dental disease exists in cats and dogs. Pure‐bred cats are
said to develop dental calculus more commonly than
domestic shorthair cats. Additionally, rapidly progres­
sive and refractory periodontitis has been reported to
occur more commonly in young Somali and Abyssinian
cats exhibiting stomatitis or feline immunodeficiency
virus (FIV) involvement. A condition known as juvenile
hyperplastic gingivitis has been described in cats younger
than 2 years of age (Figure 50.2).
In dogs, a familial predisposition to gingival hyperpla­
sia has been found in the boxer. Smaller breeds and
brachycephalic pets can have crowding of their teeth and
malocclusion that can predispose them to periodontal

pressive states. Hypoplasia of root cementum has also
been implicated as a cause specifically in human cases of

juvenile periodontitis. Single amino acid variations
because of mutation in interleukin (IL)‐6, IL‐10, and
lactoferrin genes may result in a change in their func­
tionality which could play a role in the development of
disease. However, this has yet to be confirmed in pets.
Periodontal disease treatment has the goal of cleaning
and eliminating deep pockets with closed or open

­techniques, restoring a normal gingival contour via care­
ful gingivectomy and gingivoplasty, extracting teeth with
severe attachment loss, and instituting rigorous home
oral hygiene until elimination of potential causes of the
disease.
Medical management with antibiotic treatment may
occasionally be considered as an adjunct to definitive
treatment, in preparation for the procedure or in
patients where anesthesia is not an option. Amoxicillin‐
clavulanic acid (Clavamox®, Pfizer) has the highest in
vitro susceptibility against all isolates and all anaerobes
isolated from the subgingival spaces of cats. Additionally,
enrofloxacin (Baytril®, Bayer) shows high in vitro sus­

amoxicillin‐clavulanic acid has the highest in vitro sus­

susceptibility for gram‐­
negative aerobes. Anaerobic
bacteria oral bacteria in dogs appear to be susceptible to
amoxicillin‐clavulanic acid, doxycycline, and erythro­

to sulfa‐trimethoprim.
Despite the slight differences in susceptibility, no
major differences are found between the subgingival flo­
ras of dogs and cats with gingivitis. Evaluation of the
effects of systemic doxycycline use in dogs has shown a
significant improvement in gingival attachment and
bleeding with oral subantimicrobial doses of 2 mg/kg per
day. A short‐term (42 days) study evaluating the efficacy
of control of gingivitis with use of cefovecin sodium
(Convenia®, Pfizer) after a professional dental cleaning
showed no significant difference when compared to oral
administration of clindamycin.
In feline cases where professional dental cleaning and
extraction of severely affected teeth do not resolve peri­
odontal inflammation, patients should be tested
for feline immunodeficiency virus ( FIV)/feline leukemia
virus (FeLV) seropositivity. A greater prevalence and
increased severity of oral inflammation were noted in
cats infected with FIV. The disease was worse in those
with co‐infection of FIV with feline calicivirus (FCV), or
with FCV and FeLV.
When evaluating the systemic effects of periodontal
disease in dogs, a strong association has been found
between increasing severity of attachment loss with
changes in systemic inflammatory variables and renal
indices. Additionally, in dogs with advanced periodontal
disease, increases in systemic nitric oxide levels two
weeks after periodontal treatment have been reported,
but the response is idiosyncratic. In cats, the severity of
periodontitis has been associated with increases in glob­
ulins, alanine aminotransferase, and IgG blood l­evels,
suggesting that periodontal disease is not simply a local­
ized disease but may also affect patients systemically.

­Stomatitis
Stomatitis is a complex, chronic, and destructive inflam­
matory process affecting the epithelium and lamina
­propria, with frequent extension into the submucosal tis­
sues. This more widespread inflammation of the oral
mucosa is estimated to affect 0.7% of cats presented to
veterinary practices.
The etiology of stomatitis is not fully understood, but
it is suspected to be multifactorial and a response to
chronic stimulation by a still unidentified antigen. This
contrasts with the contact stomatitis or contact mucosal
ulceration that results from mucosal contact with an irri­
tant, allergen or antigen most often in areas of heavy
plaque burden. This condition is known as canine
chronic ulcerative stomatitis and chronic ulcerative
paradental stomatitis. However, the lesions are com­
monly referred to as “kissing ulcers” or “contact ulcers.”
Two cases of concurrent osteomyelitis and paradental
stomatitis have been reported. Epitheliotropic T cell
lymphoma and erythema multiforme have also been
reported as causes of an ulcerative stomatitis with minor
to no significant abnormalities in complete blood counts
and blood biochemical profiles of affected dogs. Whereas
cats are likely affected by the idiopathic form of this dis­
ease, in dogs the oral inflammation is often associated
with a systemic disease. Vesiculobullous autoimmune
disease, although sometimes confined to dermal tissues,
can present as oral lesions in up to 90% of patients with
pemphigus vulgaris and 50% of those with bullous
pemphigoid.
A similar type of lesion, called pyogenic granuloma,
that is proliferative rather than ulcerative in nature devel­
ops in the alveolar or buccal mucosa distobuccal to the
mandibular first molar tooth in cats (Figure 50.3). The
lesions may result from continued trauma secondary to a
tight caudal occlusion between the maxillary fourth pre­
molar and the mandibular first molar, or due to contin­
ued trauma from the maxillary fourth premolar on an
area of inflammation on the distobuccal aspect of the
mandibular first molar. Surgical excision of the mass and
blunting or extraction of the involved tooth or teeth have
been reported to be 100% effective.
Some of the common bacterial isolates in cats with sto­
matitis include Pasteurella pneumotropica, Pasteurella
multocida, and Capnocytophaga canimorsus. Prior expo­
sure to viral diseases such as FCV, feline herpesvirus
(FHV), FeLV, and FIV is thought to be a risk factor for
developing stomatitis. This is likely due to the progres­
sive decline in immune functions caused by infection
with FIV and FeLV. On the other hand, FCV does seem
to play a more direct role as shown by persistent s­ hedding
of this virus in all cats with chronic ulceroproliferative
stomatitis compared to only about 20% in normal cats.

VetBooks.ir

Figure 50.3 Photograph of a pyogenic granuloma in a 5‐year‐old
domestic shorthair. Copyright 2015 Alexander M. Reiter.

Ulcers on the tongue, philtrum, and palate can be seen in
cases of FHV, but they are infrequent compared to FCV
infection. Infection with FIV, FeLV, and FCV may also
influence disease severity. The role of infection with
Bartonella remains controversial. Infection with feline
panleukopenia virus, feline syncytium‐forming virus,
feline infectious peritonitis, and Candida albicans have
also been implicated as causes of stomatitis.
In cats with stomatitis, immunohistochemistry (IHC)
has shown that the number of CD79a+ cells, L1+ cells
and CD3+ T cells and the level of MHC class II expres­
sion tend to correlate with disease severity. Additionally,
CD8+ T cells are more numerous than CD4+ T cells, and
most of the plasma cells are of the IgG isotype. The num­
ber of cells labeled for CD3, CD4, CD8, CD79a, IgG, IgA
or L1 and the number of mast cells within the lamina
propria and submucosa are significantly increased in
affected patients. The epithelial compartment also has
more CD3+ T cells compared to healthy cats. Mast cell
density is also significantly increased in gingival tissues
adjacent to areas affected by stomatitis. IHC has proven
value in reaching a definitive diagnosis in dogs with
­stomatitis due to erythema multiforme and epithelio­
trophic T cell lymphoma. Immunohistochemistry, clon­
ality ­testing, repeated biopsies, and close follow‐up are
recommended in such difficult cases.
Animals affected by stomatitis will often show signs of
oral discomfort when eating, grooming, or when manip­
ulating their mouths. In addition to the often symmetric,
bright, ulcerated or proliferative lesions of the area lat­
eral to the palatoglossal folds, multiple areas can be
affected by inflammation including the gingiva, alveolar

mucosa, labial and buccal mucosa, the lateral margins of
the tongue and the areas of the hard palate that are in
contact with the teeth (Figure 50.4).
Physical examination findings may include a poor hair
coat and decreased body condition. Of cats with stoma­
titis, 49–61% show radiographic evidence of resorption
of multiple teeth. Periodontal disease is seen in all cases,
and retained tooth roots can be found in 56% of cases.
Differentiation into squamous cell carcinoma has been
reported in some cats.
Acutely, treatment for cats consists of controlling the
inflammation via immunosuppression or immune modu­
lation along with symptomatic control. In dogs, treat­
ment of the underlying cause is extremely important.
Glucocorticoids such as prednisone or prednisolone are
typically used at a dose of 0.5–1 mg/kg by mouth once
daily and can be effective in 73–86% of cases. Antibiotics
may also be used. However, only 30% of cases respond,
and the response is only transient. Amoxicillin‐clavulanic
acid (13.75 mg/kg q12h, PO) or clindamycin (5–11 mg/kg
q12h, PO) are most commonly used. Nutritional support
is sometimes necessary, especially in chronic cases with
severe weight loss and evidence of dehydration.
Otherwise, the patient should only be offered soft food. If
symptoms resolve or the patient improves significantly,
plaque control measures, namely daily tooth brushing,
should be instituted. However, many pets are too painful
to allow this. Pain control with sublingual buprenorphine
(0.01 mg/kg q8–12h, PO) or a transdermal fentanyl patch
should also be considered.
Chronically, treatment with glucocorticoids is not rec­
ommended due to the undesirable long‐term side‐effects
that may develop, including diabetes mellitus, polyuria,
and polydipsia. Full‐mouth extraction is recommended
in cats which has achieved a nearly 80% success rate with
either a complete cure in 60% of cases or a clinical cure in
20% of cases. In severe cases, transient treatment with
glucocorticoids (0.5–1 mg/kg q24h, PO) immediately
after full‐mouth extraction may be necessary. A recent
study comparing full‐mouth versus partial‐mouth
extraction in cats showed the extent of extractions not to
be associated with the overall response of treatment.
Additionally, the 68.8% of symptomatically or clinically
cured cats required extended medical management for a
finite period to achieve a positive outcome. In dogs, a
staged approach by removing severely diseased teeth is
recommended, and extraction of teeth directly in con­
tact with the areas of inflammation can be considered. A
professional dental cleaning should also be performed
until the underlying disease process is controlled.
When cases are refractory, treatment with interferon
omega may be considered. Daily use of this medication
(0.1 mU q24h, PO) in cats has resulted in significant
improvement of pain scores at 60 and 90 days post

Stomatitis can be a frustrating condition for the pet,
the owner, and the veterinarian. Retroviral status should
be assessed prior to therapy, as this may affect prognosis.
In dogs, prognosis is largely dependent on the underly­
ing systemic disease process.

­Odontogenic Tumors and Cysts
Odontogenic tumors are more common in dogs than
cats. Acanthomatous ameloblastomas are more com­
monly seen, followed closely by peripheral odontogenic
fibromas and focal fibrous hyperplasia. Acanthomatous
ameloblastoma commonly arises in the rostral lower jaw
whereas peripheral odontogenic fibromas and focal
fibrous hyperplasia tend to be more commonly seen in
the rostral upper jaw. A breed predisposition for devel­
opment of acanthomatous ameloblastoma has been
suggested, with golden retrievers, Akitas, Shetland
­
sheepdogs, and cocker spaniels being more commonly
reported. Peripheral odontogenic fibromas may also
have a predilection for castrated male dogs.
Azithromycin in systemic and toothpaste forms has
been used in the management of gingival hyperplasia
secondary to ciclosporin treatment in dogs. In this
report, there was a significant decrease in gingival sulcus
depth for the capsule group at week 8 and for the tooth­
paste group at weeks 2, 4, and 8. Gastrointestinal adverse
events occurred in all groups, but more frequently in the
patients treated systemically. Gingival recontouring to

VetBooks.ir

50 Diseases of the Oral Cavity and Salivary Glands

reduce the pseudopockets created by hyperplastic
­gingiva along with periodontal treatment can also be
recommended.
Extent of resection required to prevent tumor recur­
rence depends on the tumor type. A study describing the
clinical behavior of acanthomatous ameloblastoma
revealed 0% of patients had incomplete histopathologic
margins when 2 cm intended surgical margins were uti­
lized compared to 33% when 1 cm intended surgical
margins were utilized. However, it was found that regard­
less of postsurgical neoplasia‐free margin, no gross local
recurrence was noted in the oral cavity for a minimum
follow‐up of 12 months after surgery.
Odontogenic cysts are also commonly seen, with more
than half arising from unerupted teeth, mainly the man­
dibular first premolar teeth. This type of cyst is known as
a dentigerous (or tooth‐containing) cyst, and brachyce­
phalic dogs appear to have a predisposition to develop­
ment of these lesions. Dentigerous cysts are thought to
arise from the proliferation of basal cells in the lining
epithelium or the epithelium of the tooth crown but may
also arise from cell rests of Malassez. If the tooth fails to
erupt, the follicle remains and produces the sac lined by
stratified mucus or cutaneous epithelium. Cysts can be
very expansile, causing weakening of the bone involved
and root resorption of neighboring teeth. A potential for
pathologic fractures and tooth loss arises if these cysts
are not treated. Even though radiographic findings are
virtually pathognomonic, biopsy is always recommended
to confirm the clinical diagnosis and rule out any malig­
nancies that have been reported to arise in long‐standing
cases. In a survey of epithelial odontogenic tumors and
cysts in dogs and cats, six cystic lesions gave rise to basi‐
squamous cell carcinoma. This is thought to be associ­
ated with the deregulation of cell death in the lining
epithelium derived from odontogenic origin as shown by
immunoreaction for amelogenin and ssDNA.
Four other types of cysts have been described includ­
ing the lateral periodontal, radicular, gingival inclusion,
and odontogenic keratocyst. Thorough removal of the
cyst lining, extraction of the unerupted tooth, and extrac­
tion of teeth affected by cyst expansion should be
­performed. In cases of extensive lesions and those in
which complete removal of the cyst lining is challenging,
­sclerotherapy with tetracyclines can be considered.

­Malignant Melanoma
Melanoma is the most common malignant neoplasia in
the canine oral cavity. In a retrospective study of 338
canine oral melanomas, chow chows, golden retrievers,
and Pekingese/poodle mixes were overrepresented, and
the gingiva and labial mucosa were the most commonly

affected sites. Melanomas can be amelanotic in some
cases, posing a diagnostic challenge. However, Melan A
is a specific and sensitive marker for canine melanoma.
Dogs with melanomas of the labial mucosa may have an
increased survival time (310 days) compared to those
with oral melanomas at other sites (123 days). This dif­
ference was, however, not statistically significant. In this
same study, postsurgical survival time was 173 days.
Survival was significantly associated with the presence of
KIT anywhere in the section of a melanoma. This also
becomes important when considering the use of c‐kit
inhibitors such as toceranib phosphate (Palladia®, Pfizer
Animal Health) in the treatment of oral melanomas.
When evaluating the effects of multimodal therapy with
adjuvant treatment with carboplatin, the median overall
survival for all dogs was 440 days. In a study evaluating
the use of radiation therapy with an alternate‐day sched­
ule of 4 Gy/fraction for a total of 48 Gy over four weeks,
8% of dogs had acute reactions, and 7.6% of dogs showed
chronic effects including osteonecrosis and the develop­
ment of fistulae. Local efficacy was determined by tumor
size, and systemic metastasis influenced long‐term sur­
vival in patients with tumor recurrence.
Antiangiogenic therapies have also been evaluated after
the discovery of higher vascular endothelial growth factor
(VEGF) levels in the plasma and serum of dogs with malig­
nant melanomas than in a control population. In a study
describing the effect of radiation on the expression of
VEGF and VEGF receptor in the canine melanoma cell line
TLM 1, radiation induced significantly higher VEGF pro­
duction in the 8 and 10 Gy group, which may have contrib­
uted to tumor resistance. The enhanced secretion of VEGF
may increase survival by decreasing apoptosis, stimulating
proliferation, and increasing angiogenic potential.
When evaluating the efficacy of a xenogenic vaccine
targeting tyrosinase as an adjuvant treatment, results
have been contradictory. One study found no difference
between progression‐free survival, disease‐free interval
or median survival time in dogs that received this treat­
ment. A study evaluating the safety of administration of
this vaccine in cats revealed side‐effects of grade 1–2 in
11.4% of cats, suggesting a minimal risk of adverse effects.
Oral melanoma is highly metastatic and recurrent, with
age, size, site, and stage being reliable prognostic indicators.
A subset of well‐differentiated melanocytic neoplasms in
dogs has been described, and these tumors have shown a
mean survival of 23.4 months and a median survival of 34
months after local excision without adjuvant therapy.

­Squamous Cell Carcinoma
Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common
oral tumor in domestic cats and the second most

540

­common oral tumor in dogs. This tumor can vary in
appearance and may present as an ulcerated area or a
mass. In cats, sometimes the ulcerated area appreciated
on oral examination may represent the “tip of the i­ ceberg”
(Figure 50.5).
Although historically, the sublingual/lingual region
has been reported to be the most commonly affected
site, recent reports show the gingiva on the mandible and
maxilla to be most often involved. Metastasis to man­
dibular lymph nodes in these cases, as evaluated by fine
needle aspiration cytology, has been documented to be
as high as 31–36%. A significant association between
mandibular lymph node metastasis and survival time has
not been found. Evidence of pulmonary metastasis,
which had been evaluated by three‐view thoracic radiog­
raphy or necropsy, was present in 10% of cases but was
not a significant negative prognostic factor. Interestingly,
tumor volume appeared not to be a predictor for regional
and distant metastasis, as no significant association was
seen between tumor size and metastasis.
Feline oral SCC is generally considered to carry a poor
prognosis, and outcome has been largely dependent on
the degree of primary tumor invasion at diagnosis. Most
cats with oral SCC succumb to the effects of progressive
local disease and treatment failure. The prognostic
impact of completeness of surgical margins is unclear,
and studies evaluating multimodal treatment have
shown improved survival times compared to monother­
apy. A study evaluating multimodal therapy for nonre­
sectable tumors found survival times with complete
remission of up to 759 days. Twenty‐one cats treated
with 10, once‐daily fractions of 4.8‐Gy showed a median
overall survival of 174 days.
Squamous cell carcinoma in dogs commonly arises in
dentate areas, although well‐differentiated tumors have
been reported to arise more commonly in edentulous areas
and the tongue. A retrospective study evaluating 84 dogs
with a diagnosis of oral and oropharyngeal SCC reported

(b)

different subtypes, including conventional (well differenti­
ated, moderately differentiated, and poorly differentiated),
papillary, basaloid, adenosquamous, and spindle cell carci­
noma. Neutered female dogs, dogs aged 10–15 years,
English springer spaniels and Shetland sheepdogs were
overrepresented in this retrospective study.
Papillary SCC is the term used for a well‐differentiated
variant of this tumor that grossly as well as microscopi­
cally shows papillae or fronds on the surface. Papillary
SCC appears to carry the best prognosis. Thought to be
a tumor of young dogs, papillary SCC has recently been
shown to be a tumor of adult dogs as well, with a retro­
spective study revealing that more than 75% of the
affected canine population was older than 6 years of age.
In this study, two distinct histologic presentations were
described that correlated with the appearance on imag­
ing studies: the cavitating and noncavitating patterns.
Predominance of large breeds and the rostral maxilla
as the most common location in dogs with papillary SCC
have also been reported. In this study, surgical excision
with 1–2 cm margins allowed for a mean tumor‐free
interval of 12.1 months. Neither study found regional or
distant metastasis. A hemangiosarcoma‐like mass com­

­Eosinophilic Granuloma
Eosinophilic granuloma is a disease that results from
underlying antigenic stimulation. The eosinophil is one
of the players in type I inflammatory reactions. The most
commonly identified underlying causes in cats include
ectoparasites and other insects, environmental allergens
(i.e., atopic dermatitis), and food hypersensitivity.
Eosinophilic granulomas are exfoliative, and thus diag­
nosis can be reached through fine needle aspiration or
impression smears. However, histopathologic examina­
tion is useful to rule out other differential diagnoses such
as neoplasia or infection. Distinctive histopathologic
features of eosinophilic granuloma are small foci of

resulting in flame figures. Clinically, these lesions are
characterized by a proliferative or ulcerative component
with yellow pinpoint areas consistent with sulfur gran­

palate and/or glossopharyngeal arches (Figure 50.6).
Indolent ulcers, also known as rodent ulcers, another
presentation for this type of inflammatory process, are
commonly seen near the midline of the (usually) upper
lip but can also be seen on the lower lip. A puffy lip or a
diffuse, firm sublingual swelling are rare manifestations
of this disease. Some cats are asymptomatic, and in some
the disease may be self‐limiting.
Ulcerative eosinophilic palatitis has been described in
Cavalier King Charles spaniels. Some can have full or
near resolution of lesions with glucocorticoid therapy
whereas others may resolve spontaneously. Eosinophilic
granuloma has also been reported in the Siberian husky
in which a hereditary cause has been proposed.
Treatment involves removing the underlying cause by
recommending flea prevention, a hypoallergenic diet,
and switching to stainless steel bowls. Additionally,
immunosuppressive therapy with prednisone or predni­
solone at 0.5–1 mg/kg q24h PO may be necessary.
Recently, a study evaluating the efficacy of treatment
with amoxicillin‐clavulanic acid in cats for 21 days
showed a 42.6% reduction in mean lesion size for lip
ulcers and a 96.2% reduction in skin plaques. If the area
shows evidence of chewing trauma or exposure to for­
eign objects, debulking may be considered as well as
intralesional glucocorticoid injections (e.g., triamci­

(PLR120), a downregulator of mast cell degranulation,
showed clinical improvement in 67% of affected cats. For
cats with severe ulcerative cutaneous or oral lesions that
are unresponsive to glucocorticoid treatment, FHV‐1

­Foreign Body
A retrospective study evaluating gastrointestinal foreign
bodies in dogs and cats showed that 63% of linear foreign
bodies originated from the base of the tongue in cats as
opposed to 3% in dogs. English bull terriers and springer
spaniels were overrepresented in this study. The most
common types of foreign object recovered from cats
were string, rope, or fishing lines. Burdock and fox tails
can also become entrapped in the oral mucosa, and in
dogs they have been reported to elicit a type of granular
stomatitis. These oral lesions most often occur on the tip
and lateral edges of the tongue and the rostral portions of
the gingiva, usually at the mucogingival junction and the
labial mucosa of the upper lip. Occasionally, the philtrum
is involved. Initially, they appear as small papules that
can then coalesce, and eventually a necrotic center may
develop. Removal of the foreign body along with thor­
ough debridement and flushing of the wound is the treat­
ment of choice. Oral antibiotics and soft food may also
be considered.
Oropharyngeal and esophageal stick penetration inju­
ries in dogs can pose a challenge, as studies have shown
that foreign bodies can be found in only about half or less
of the affected patients. Surgical exploration, local
debridement, and thorough lavage, however, have shown
a favorable outcome in both studies. Esophageal pene­
tration injuries carry the worst prognosis, and thus a
ventral medial surgical approach has been recommended
in cases where cervical emphysema is seen radiographi­
cally. Advanced diagnostic imaging with magnetic reso­
nance imaging and/or computed tomography may
improve the rate of recovery of patients with such for­
eign bodies.

­Immune‐Mediated and Autoimmune
Diseases
Failure of desmosomal adhesion can result from genetic,
autoimmune, or infectious causes. Pemphigus repre­
sents the most common autoimmune blistering derma­
tosis in domestic animals. Pemphigus vulgaris (PV) is a

deep, acantholytic dermatosis. It is rare in cats, with an
estimated incidence of one per 10 000 veterinary derma­
tology cases per year. It is more commonly seen in mature
cats. This condition is also rare in dogs, with no age pre­
disposition but a predilection for certain breeds such as
German shepherds and collies, and a predisposition for
males. PV can have mucosal and mucocutaneous mani­
festations. In most dogs, lesions first develop in the oral
cavity or mucocutaneous junctions. Lesions on haired
skin predominate over pressure points. Presentation can
be acute or chronic, and the direct Nikolsky sign is usu­
ally positive. Lesions can present as erythemas, erosions,
ulcerations, scales, and crusts. Light microscopy shows
suprabasal acantholysis and cleft formation. Erosive
lesions are preferentially located in the oral cavity and
mucocutaneous junctions. Oral involvement may also
include gingivitis, stomatitis, or glossitis. Most patients
with PV show signs of systemic disease such as anorexia,
lethargy, weight loss, and fever. Spontaneous resolution
of cases has been reported. However, 40% of dogs were
reported to have a fatal outcome due to either their local
disease or systemic manifestations.
Of the autoimmune subepidermal blistering derma­
toses, 80% of patients with bullous pemphigoid develop
oral lesions at the initial onset of disease or later during
its course. Bullous pemphigoid represents 50% of subepi­
dermal autoimmune blistering dermatoses in cats and
26% in dogs. As opposed to PV, this disease can afflict
animals of any age, even before puberty. Lesions consist
primarily of turgid vesicles, erosions, ulcers, and crusts.
Oral lesions can be seen in 60% of dogs, but in cats few
lesions are present. In cats as well as in horses, sub­
epithelial vesicles exhibit fewer inflammatory cells, and
special stains are needed to visualize degranulating
eosinophils. Long‐term remission of bullous pemphigoid
has been seen in one cat treated with corticosteroids.
Mucous membrane pemphigoid, although uncom­
mon, has been reported in at least two cats, and the
authors have witnessed one additional case. Laminin 5
and 6, collagen XVII, and integrin alpha‐6/beta‐4 have
been implicated as autoantigens in both humans and
dogs. However, only laminin‐5 has been recognized in
the feline homologue of this disease.
Canine systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) occurs
mainly in pure‐breds including spaniels, pointers,
retrievers, German shepherd dogs, and Doberman pin­
schers ranging from 2 to 6 years of age. SLE has been
reported in at least two cats with palatine and glossal
ulceration. Behavioral changes, nonerosive polyarthritis,
fever, lymphadenomegaly, weight loss, and leukopenia
are primarily seen with this condition, and dogs tend to
have one or two systemic signs. The oral ulceration is
likely a complication of the systemic vasculitis that
occurs.

Erythema multiforme (Figure 50.7) accounts for 0.11%
of dermatology cases seen in the feline population at an
academic institution. In this report, only 38% of dogs
showed oral lesions, and no oral lesions were reported in
the only cat described. In a case report of erythema mul­
tiforme in a cat, lesions first developed on the face and
head, but there were no visible lesions in the oral cavity.
This patient did not respond to withdrawal of current
medications, but a significant improvement was noted
approximately one week after treatment with human
immunoglobulin. Toxic epidermal necrolysis and idio­
pathic vasculitis have also been reported to occur in a
small number of cats and dogs.
The diagnosis of these disorders is based on both mor­
phologic and immunologic criteria. Proper site selection,
biopsy technique, and sample handling are extremely

important to reach a definitive diagnosis. Biopsy of the
leading edge of a lesion when an intact blister is not
found may be sufficient. Preserving the samples in
Michel’s solution is also preferred by some pathologists.
This is a transport medium that preserves tissue anti­
genicity at ambient temperatures.
Treatment for these conditions should be considered
life‐long, and owner commitment for periodic monitor­

with complete blood counts and serum chemistry pan­

successful in treating most of these conditions, some
cases require other forms of immunosuppressive or
immune‐modulating therapy. Some immune‐mediated
skin diseases have also been treated with tetracycline,

immune‐modulating and antiinflammatory effects.
Antibiotics should be prescribed in cases with a second­
