including nutritional support and pain control until
long‐term therapy takes effect. Idiopathic vasculitis can
also cause oral ulcerations.

­Metabolic Disease
Nutritional deficiencies, although uncommon, can have
oral manifestations. In the acute setting, tacky mucus
membranes can indicate dehydration or hypovolemia,
and pale mucus membranes can indicate shock or ane­
mia. Oral manifestations of metabolic disease may resur­
face with the recent increase of owners opting to feed
their pets home‐cooked diets. Protein deficits can cause
ulceration of the dorsal surface of the tongue. Severe nia­
cin deficiency can cause hyperemia and ulceration of
mucosal surfaces, especially the tongue. Severe biotin
deficiency causes salivation and scaling of the lips.
Hypervitaminosis A can lead to gingival enlargement
and delayed development and early exfoliation of incisor
teeth. Primary or secondary hyperparathyroidism can
lead to a condition known as “rubber jaw” which is char­
acterized by a diffuse decreased radiographic density in
the bones, primarily of the lower jaw.
Acute uremia is defined as a rapid decline in renal
function leading to retention of uremic wastes. The inci­
dence of acute uremia in animals is unknown, but in
humans it accounts for 1% of hospital admissions.
Uremic halitosis and oral ulcerations are common find­
ings on physical examination of severely affected
patients. This occurs especially at the labial and buccal
mucosa, lateral margins of the tongue, sublingual
mucosa, lateral lip frenula, and lip commissures. Uremic
vasculitis and thrombosis lead to necrosis and sloughing
of the mucosa. Hypothyroidism can also lead to vasculi­
tis and petechiation on the gingiva and tongue. Halitosis
is often a feature of this syndrome, as the lesions become
secondarily infected. In severe cases, there may be exten­
sive necrosis that leads to sloughing of the tip of the
tongue. The lesions are often very painful and contribute
to the anorexia often observed in animals with kidney
disease. Any condition that can produce a hypercoagula­
ble state may lead to thrombi formation and subsequent
sloughing of the affected areas.
Treatment for these conditions is symptomatic until the
inciting cause can be removed or resolved. Symptomatic
treatment includes pain management (buprenorphine
0.01 mg/kg q8–12h, IV), bypassing the mouth with
­supplemental enteral or parenteral nutrition, and use of
gastric protectants (sucralfate 0.5–1 g q4–6h, PO). Topical
mouthwashes such as a mixture of diphenhydramine,

sucralfate or aluminum and magnesium hydroxide
(Maalox®, Novartis), and lidocaine may provide some
local pain control. Dilute (0.12%) chlorhexidine rinses
also play a role in preventing secondary infection of the
necrotic areas. Other metabolic disease such as diabetes
mellitus, liver failure, and respiratory disease as well as
immunosuppressive medications have also been reported
to lead to oral ulceration and necrosis.

­Burns
Burns can be caused by electricity, chemicals, heat, fric­
tion or radiation (Figure 50.8).
Chewing on household power cords is the most com­
mon cause of electric burns in dogs and cats, and these
are likely low‐voltage injuries. The electrical current can
cause damage through its direct effect as well as via
transformation of electric energy into heat. The pet
should be evaluated for cardiac arrhythmias and neuro­
genic pulmonary edema prior to evaluating the oral cav­
ity under sedation or anesthesia. Edema and necrosis are
typically seen in the tongue, palate, and lip commissures.
Discoloration of adjacent teeth secondary to pulpitis can
also be seen. Some of the long‐term effects of electric
burns include development of an oronasal fistula and
sloughing of necrotic portions of the tongue. Patients
should be treated symptomatically for at least 7–10 days
or until the tissues fully claim themselves. Until defini­
tive surgery can be performed, antibiotics and pain med­
ication should be instituted. Nutritional supplementation
should be considered when patients refuse to eat soft
food. Definitive therapy consists of debridement of the
lesions unless these are superficial enough to heal by
contraction and reepithelialization.
Chemical burns can result from exposure to house­
hold cleaning products, phenolic compounds, essential
oils, heavy metal (thallium) or plant toxins (i.e.,
Diffenbachia). The rostral and dorsal aspects of the
tongue and the palate are usually affected. The poison
control center should be contacted in these cases for
treatment of any ingested substances. Similar to electric
cord injuries, treatment should be symptomatic, but
debridement is less often necessary. Patients should be
evaluated for esophagitis and gastritis and treated
accordingly. The hair of affected patients should be
clipped or washed with dish detergent if grooming
caused the chemical to contact oral mucosa. Thermal
injuries can be encountered in animals that are fed
home‐prepared diets or heated milk. Injuries are like
those seen with chemical burns, with the lips and nasal
plane also being affected. With both chemical and elec­
tric burn injuries, symptomatic treatment and client
education are necessary.

­Salivary Gland Disease
The prevalence of salivary gland disease in dogs and cats
in a retrospective study was 0.3% , with dogs accounting
for two‐thirds of the population studied. Salivary gland
neoplasia accounted for 30% of the cases seen, followed
by, in order of decreasing frequency, sialadenitis (26%),
degenerative or fibrotic lesions (11%), sialoceles (9%),
and infarction (8%).
Salivary gland neoplasia appears to have different
behaviors in the dog and cat. Cats tend to have more
advanced disease at the time of diagnosis. A possible
familial predisposition in Siamese cats has also been
reported. Despite this, survival times in dogs and cats
appear to be similar, at 500–550 days. Masses are
usually detected by owners, although halitosis,
­
dysphagia, and exophthalmia have been reported.
­
Adenocarcinoma is the most common histologic type
of tumor seen. A sialolipoma of a minor salivary gland
and lymphosarcoma of major salivary glands have also
been reported.

Sialadenosis typically is a bilateral and painless enlarge­
ment of the salivary glands. Although the exact cause of
this disease is unknown, concurrent gastrointestinal dis­
ease, certain medications, hormonal disorders or primary
disorders affecting the sympathetic innervation to the
glands have been implicated. Retching and gulping are
the most common clinical signs seen with this condition.
Differential diagnoses for this disease include inflamma­
tory variants including necrotizing sialometaplasia, gran­
ulomatous giant cell sialadenosis, and spirocercosis. Both
sialadenosis and necrotizing sialometaplasia have shown
response to treatment with phenobarbital at an anticon­
vulsant dose (starting at 2 mg/kg, PO BID). Cases of spi­
rocercosis also respond to phenobarbital treatment, but
this is in addition to macrocyclic lactones used to elimi­
nate the microorganism. Granulomatous disease has
responded to treatment with glucocorticoids at an anti­
inflammatory dose. Necrotizing sialometaplasia has been
reported in a few cats. In contrast to dogs, excision of the
affected salivary glands in cats provided resolution of
signs with no recurrence reported.

Salivary mucoceles, also known as sialoceles, are swell­
ings created by the extravasation of saliva from the ducts
or salivary glands themselves. Extravasation of saliva can
not only cause a localized swelling, but also the inflam­
mation that results can lead to signs of discomfort.
Although trauma, foreign bodies, sialoliths, aberrant
parasite migration, and neoplasia have been reported to
lead to sialocele formation, sometimes the exact cause
for these swellings cannot be determined. With these
differentials in mind, advanced diagnostic imaging such
as CT or ultrasound should be considered for evaluation.
A difference in the imaging characteristics of these
lesions can be found when comparing acute with chronic
cases, and dystrophic mineralization can occur in very
long‐standing cases. In dogs, sialoceles arise more com­
monly in the cervical and sublingual regions. However,
the sublingual area seems to be more commonly affected
in cats. Sialoceles in the cervical, sublingual, and pharyn­
geal regions can all lead to difficulty swallowing and
breathing. Surgical removal of the glands involved is the
treatment of choice, and different approaches have been

described for the resection of mandibular/sublingual
and zygomatic glands to increase exposure and also
decrease the morbidity that can be associated with these
surgeries.

­Conclusion
Examination of the oral tissues and dental structures is
an essential component of physical examination. Dental
and oral disease is very commonly seen in our pets. The
systemic health of the patient should be thoroughly
assessed before attributing a presenting complaint of
anorexia to dental and oral disease alone. The anamnesis
will also prove to be helpful in guiding your treatment
approach when dealing with patients with concurrent
conditions. Staging treatment and triaging are at times
favorable for these patients to prevent very prolonged
anesthetic episodes that may endanger the health of our
compromised patients.

Gastritis and Gastric Ulceration in Dogs and Cats
Katie Tolbert, DVM, PhD, ADCVIM (SAIM) and Emily Gould, DVM, MS
College of Veterinary Medicine, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA

­Normal Gastric Mucosal Barrier
Function
The gastric mucosal barrier is provided by the luminal
production and secretion of protective factors, an intact
epithelial lining, and a rich mucosal blood supply.
Mucosal secretions including bicarbonate, mucus,
immunoglobulins, and anti-bacterial substances p
­ romote
the integrity of the mucosa and protect the underlying
epithelium from noxious insults. Potential insults to the
gastric mucosa include diffusion of luminal acid and
pepsin, fluctuations in temperature and osmolality, and
translocation of ingested bacteria. The gastric mucosal
barrier is bolstered by a single layer of epithelial cells
which is capable of rapid repair following injury. The
local production of prostaglandins acts to stimulate
bicarbonate and mucus secretion, decrease gastric acid
secretion, and promote a healthy gastrointestinal
mucosa. The total flow of blood through the gastric
mucosa can be increased to clear noxious substances
produced during the inflammatory response and deliver
oxygen and bicarbonate to injured epithelium.
Breakdown of the gastric mucosal barrier is a primary
source or consequence of nearly all causes of gastritis
and gastric ulceration.

­Etiology and Pathophysiology of
Gastritis
Canine and feline gastritis is defined as inflammation of
the stomach and occurs in response to many stimuli.
Gastritis can be classified by duration of clinical signs
(acute or chronic) and by histopathologic changes
(e.g., lymphoplasmacytic, eosinophilic, fibrosis, atrophy).
The release of a variety of inflammatory mediators,

including pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines,
eicosanoids (prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and thromboxanes), neuropeptides, nitric oxide, peroxidases, and
proteinases, perpetuate gastritis through increasing
exposure of the denuded epithelium and underlying
mucosa to toxic insults (e.g., gastric acid, bile acids,
­pepsin). As well as exerting direct effects on the gastric
mucosal cells, many of these mediators act to alter
mucosal permeability and blood flow.
Gastric ulceration, which can be a sequel of severe or
prolonged gastric inflammation and ischemia, is defined
as a defect in the gastric mucosa extending to the muscularis mucosa or through the muscularis propria. Ulcers
can be full thickness (perforating) or partial thickness.
Perforating ulcers can be associated with hemorrhage
and septic peritonitis and therefore are considered life
threatening when left untreated. Gastric ulceration is
more frequently reported in the dog than the cat, but as
observed with gastritis, toxic agents, drug‐induced reactions, neoplasia, severe systemic illness, and infectious
organisms can be injurious to the gastric mucosa in both
species.
A variety of etiologies have been implicated in the
development of canine and feline gastritis and gastric
ulceration (Tables 51.1 and 51.2). These include mechanical irritants, drugs, systemic illness, infections, breed‐
associated diseases, motility disorders, and occupational
and exercise‐related stressors.
Gastric foreign bodies and dietary indiscretion are
common causes of acute gastritis in dogs and cats.
Although the stomach is not the primary site of protein
absorption, dietary protein intolerance and food responsive disease can also be linked with gastritis in both dogs
and cats, albeit less frequently. The presentation of food
antigens to the gut‐associated lymphoid tissue in the
small intestine can initiate immediate or delayed hypersensitivity reactions capable of inducing vomiting with

­secondary gastritis. Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)
is considered to be a predisposing factor for gastric
ulceration, but this is a relatively uncommon complication of IBD.
Invasive gastric and nongastric tumors resulting in
gastric hyperacidity cause physical damage to the gastric
mucosal barrier that can incite the development of secondary gastritis and gastric ulceration. Primary gastric
neoplasms represent 1% of all cancers diagnosed in companion animals. Gastric carcinoma (most common in the
dog), lymphoma (most common in the cat), leiomyomas,

leiomyosarcomas, and mast cell tumors are the most frequently reported in association with gastritis. Mast cell
tumors, systemic mastocytosis, and pancreatic gastrinomas increase the risk of ulceration due to the overproduction of histamine and gastrin, respectively. Mast cell
tumors and gastrinomas were overrepresented in one
large literature review of cats with gastroduodenal
ulceration.
Nonneoplastic, proliferative masses associated with
gastritis include gastric polyps and benign gastric
­hypertrophy or hyperplasia with accompanying gastritis.

VetBooks.ir

51 Gastritis and Gastric Ulceration in Dogs and Cats

Chronic hypertrophic pyloric gastropathy has been
­documented in many breeds and usually manifests with
clinical signs of pyloric outflow obstruction.
Drugs, household chemicals, and plants are also a
­frequent cause of gastritis in dogs and cats. A list of
common plants and household chemicals associated
­
with gastritis may be found in an excellent review by
Webb and Twedt (see Further Reading list).
Nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), a
leading cause of gastritis and gastric ulceration in companion animals, are both directly and indirectly injurious
to the gastric epithelium as a result of being weak
acids and via their inhibitory effect on prostaglandin
production, respectively. Aspirin, flunixin meglumine,
indomethacin, ibuprofen, acetaminophen, ketorolac,
deracoxib, and carprofen have all been associated with
the development of gastric lesions. Nonselective COX
NSAIDs (e.g., aspirin) are the most ulcerogenic and
should be used with caution. NSAID‐induced ulcers are
often localized to the pyloric antrum and pylorus. COX‐2
selective NSAIDs (e.g., meloxicam) are considered less
ulcerogenic than nonselective inhibitors, but careful
monitoring is still advised as all NSAIDs can be ulcerogenic as well as delay healing of epithelial injury. NSAIDs
should be considered contraindicated and used sparingly
in companion animals that have concurrent diseases
with ulcer‐­inducing potential.
Corticosteroids at high doses can cause gastritis, but
they are unlikely to be the sole cause of gastric ulceration
except when given concurrently with an NSAID or in the
presence of other risk factors. Other drugs commonly
associated with gastritis in either ­species include some
antibiotics (e.g., penicillins, chloramphenicol, lincosamides, tetracyclines) and chemotherapeutic agents.
Ingestion of noxious chemicals (e.g., phenols/alcohols),
toxic substances (e.g., lead, Dieffenbachia), foodstuffs
capable of producing thermal damage and foreign bodies
has also been reported to cause gastritis and ulceration.
Systemic illness (e.g., hepatic, renal, neurologic or endocrine disease) and/or conditions causing poor gastrointestinal (GI) perfusion (e.g., hypoadrenocorticism,
gastric dilation‐volvulus, thromboembolic disease) can
trigger gastric inflammation and/or gastric ulceration.
Ulcer development in animals with hepatic dysfunction
most commonly results from compromised hemodynamics. Although severe renal dysfunction results in
decreased elimination of uremic toxins and gastrin, gastric ulcers are uncommonly documented in dogs and
cats with end-stage renal failure.
Infectious causes of gastritis include a variety of bacterial species, helminths, oomycetes, fungi, and viruses.
Most infectious agents rarely cause gastric signs alone,
however, and therefore are not discussed in detail in this
chapter. Although uncommon, infectious and parasitic

etiologies (e.g., pythiosis, gnathostomiasis, Aonchotheca
putorii, Toxocara cati) have also been associated with
gastric ulceration. In cats, heartworm infection may
cause vomiting and gastritis, while this is uncommon
in dogs.
Bilious vomiting syndrome, a frequently encountered
yet poorly understood gastric motility disorder in dogs,
can induce gastritis through reflux of injurious bile salts
into the stomach. Affected dogs generally vomit early in
the morning following an overnight fast.
Other less commonly encountered causes of gastritis
and gastric ulceration include occupational stress (e.g.,
racing Alaskan sled dogs) and breed‐related gastropathies, including atrophic gastritis in the Norwegian
lundehund and immunoproliferative enteropathy
­
in basenjis. Hypereosinophilic syndrome, particularly in
Rottweilers, and both hypereosinophilic syndrome and
feline gastrointestinal eosinophilic sclerosing fibroplasia (FGESF) in cats can cause severe gastritis and g­ astric
ulceration. Hospitalization and postoperative stress
may be a more common cause of ulceration in cats than
in dogs.
Helicobacter pylori and Related Organisms
The relationship between colonization with Helicobacter
spp. in canine and feline patients and the occurrence of
gastritis and gastric ulceration is unclear. Helicobacter
pylori is an important cause of gastritis and ulceration in
humans but not in companion animals, and the role of
other Helicobacter species as gastric pathogens in dogs
and cats is less well defined. Multiple Helicobacter spp.
(H. heilmannii, H. pylori, H. felis, H. bizzozeronii) have
been isolated in both dogs and cats with varying degrees
of gastritis. Thus, Helicobacter infection should only be
considered as a cause of clinical signs in dogs and cats
when associated with histopathologic evidence of gastric
inflammation, and after other causes have been excluded.

­Epidemiology of Gastric Disease
Consideration of the animal’s signalment aids in the
prioritization of differentials for gastritis and gastric
­
ulceration. For example, foreign body ingestion, dietary
indiscretion, and infectious causes of gastritis are more
commonly identified in younger animals. Dachshunds
and other chondrodystrophic breeds predisposed to
intervertebral disc disease might be at higher risk for
subclinical gastric ulceration with concurrent steroid
and/or NSAID therapy. German shepherd dogs have
been reported to be at greater risk for gastric ulceration
­following ibuprofen administration.

Gastritis resulting from inflammatory bowel d
­ isease,
systemic disorders, and neoplasia is more common in
middle‐aged to older companion a­ nimals. Breed‐related
gastritis, however (seen in Norwegian lundehunds,
Rottweilers, and basenjis) can occur at any age.
Adenocarcinomas develop in middle‐aged dogs (<10
years) more frequently than other gastric neoplasms,
and are usually located in the pyloric antrum or gastric
body (greater curvature). Collies, German shepherd
dogs, Staffordshire terriers, Bouviers des Flandres,
Norwegian elkhounds, and Belgian shepherds have
been identified as breeds at higher risk for developing
gastric carcinoma. Male dogs are overrepresented
among dogs with gastric neoplasms in some reports,
although a sex predisposition is not yet widely recognized. The Norwegian lundehund is at higher risk for
development of neuroendocrine carcinoma secondary
to chronic, severe atrophic gastritis. Lymphoma is
more prevalent in older cats, while middle‐aged cats
are more likely to be diagnosed with inflammatory
bowel disease. No breed predispositions are recognized for primary gastric cancer in cats, but one report
exists of two related Persians with confirmed gastritis
and adenocarcinoma.
Large‐breed, deep‐chested and working dogs (Great
Danes, standard poodles, Irish wolfhound, Newfound­
land, Weimaraner, mastiff and hound breeds, German
shepherd dogs) are at higher risk for gastric dilation‐­
volvulus (GDV) and secondary ulceration.
Young to middle‐aged, spayed female dogs are more
likely to develop hypoadrenocorticism and gastritis secondary to vomiting. Breeds such as the standard poodle,
Novia Scotia duck tolling retriever, Rottweiler, Great
Dane and Portuguese water dog are overrepresented.
Geographic location influences the risk of development
of fungal gastritis. Histoplasma capsulatum is one of the
most common canine mycotic pathogens in the United
States and manifests primarily with signs of gastrointestinal disease in young to middle‐aged dogs. Histoplasma
spp. infection should be ruled out in dogs displaying signs
of gastrointestinal disease that are living in endemic
regions such as the mid‐western, southern, and Gulf
Coast regions of the US, as well as Central America.
There is a higher prevalence of histoplasmosis in males
compared to females, with pointers, Weimeraners, and
Brittany spaniels identified as predisposed breeds.
Pythium insidiosum has been documented in dogs with a
travel history to or residing in tropical regions, the Gulf
Coast and mid‐western states, and northern California.
Male Labrador retrievers and German shepherd dogs are
overrepresented. Dogs infected with parvovirus, distemper virus, and coronavirus are often younger (less than
3 years of age), unvaccinated and from multidog environments (kennels, shelters).

Environmental history may also give clues towards
identification of uncommon causes of feline gastritis.
The nematode Ollulanus tricuspis is found in cats
throughout the US, whereas Aonchotheca putorii is more
common in tropical, temperate areas worldwide. Feline
dirofilariasis occurs more commonly in the mid‐west
and south‐east, with a higher prevalence also reported in
northern California and Florida.

­History and Clinical Signs of Gastritis
The duration (acute versus chronic) and severity of signs
in dogs and cats with gastritis and gastric ulceration vary
depending on the underlying etiology. Clinical signs can
range from overt gastrointestinal signs to only weight
loss. For animals with “garbage gut” or those that have
ingested caustic substances, toxins, ulcerogenic medications or foreign bodies, the onset of clinical signs is often
rapid (usually within a few hours). Clinical signs in
patients with gastric foreign body obstruction often
include lethargy, inappetence, vomiting, and antisocial
or “hiding” behavior. Owners should be questioned
regarding the possibility of exposure to yarn, string,
tinsel, needles or hair ties accessible in the house.
­
Intoxications secondary to chocolate (theobromine),
macadamia nuts, mycotoxins (e.g., mushrooms, sago
palms, blue‐green algae, molds), and marijuana should
be considered in dogs exhibiting vomiting in association
with an acute onset of neurologic abnormalities.
Viral etiologies should be suspected when there is an
outbreak of gastrointestinal signs in multiple dogs from
the same shelter or household. Viral gastroenteritis can
cause inappetence, fever, lethargy, vomiting, and small
bowel diarrhea. Distemper is known to cause severe
­neurologic signs, but manifests as gastrointestinal (inappetence, vomiting, diarrhea) and respiratory signs early
in the course of infection.
As the vast majority of episodes of drug‐induced gastritis and GI ulceration in the dog are caused by NSAID
use (with or without steroids), a full drug history should
be obtained for any dog (or cat) presenting with signs of
gastric disease. Dogs receiving chronic NSAID therapy
with gastrointestinal signs should be regularly evaluated
for gastritis. A change as subtle as hyporexia should raise
concern. A recent history of antibiotic administration
preceding development of clinical signs should raise
­suspicion for an adverse reaction to medication.
Infectious gastritis should be suspected if there is
travel history to an endemic area or there has been ingestion of uncooked or raw foods. Vomiting in animals with
pythiosis or histoplasmosis is often accompanied by
other clinical signs including diarrhea, cutaneous
lesions, lymphadenopathy, and ocular abnormalities

VetBooks.ir

51 Gastritis and Gastric Ulceration in Dogs and Cats

(uveitis, retinal lesions). Dogs suffering from fungal
mycosis may also exhibit anorexia and rapid weight loss,
and succumb quickly to their disease. Puppies or younger
dogs, especially those that have not received a broad‐
spectrum anthelminthic, are at higher risk for parasitic
disease.
Animals with neoplasia‐induced gastric disease may
have a more chronic history, with progressive signs of
gastrointestinal disease (e.g., weight loss, lethargy, anorexia, ptyalism, vomiting, diarrhea). Clinical signs of
lymphoma in cats are often protracted and mimic those
of inflammatory bowel disease, although cats with
lymphoblastic lymphoma often exhibit a more rapid
deterioration. Some gastric neoplasms can lead to gastroesophageal reflux, thus these animals can present
with signs of esophagitis including regurgitation or ptyalism following meals (see Chapter 52). Animals with
mastocytosis or gastrinomas can have evidence of
hematemesis, depending on the severity of gastric
lesions. Cutaneous lesions can also accompany systemic
mastocytosis and fungal disease.
Inflammatory bowel disease and food responsive gastroenteritis are two of the most common causes of gastritis in young and middle‐aged dogs. Common clinical
signs in animals with IBD can include weight loss (with or
without good appetite), lethargy, hyporexia or anorexia,
intermittent vomiting and either large or small bowel
diarrhea with large bowel diarrhea being more common.
Beef, wheat, lamb, egg, chicken, soy, and wheat are common dietary allergens, but any protein or carbohydrate
source is capable of eliciting an immune reaction.
Younger dogs that are presented with mild clinical signs
and predominantly diarrhea of large bowel origin are
more likely to have food‐responsive disease. Cats with
inflammatory bowel disease often exhibit weight loss,
hyporexia, anorexia, ptyalism, vomiting, and diarrhea.
Cutaneous lesions, lower airway abnormalities
(­coughing, tachypnea) and palpably thickened intestinal
loops on exam should increase the clinical suspicion
for eosinophilic gastroenteritis or hypereosinophilic
syndrome in cats.
Dogs and cats that develop gastritis secondary to systemic disease often have other clinical signs related to
the primary system involved. Hepatic dysfunction can
result in polyuria and polydipsia (PU/PD), petechiae or
ecchymosis secondary to coagulopathy, and neurologic
signs indicative of encephalopathy in severely affected
cases. Portosystemic vascular anomalies should be ruled
out in younger dogs with chronic or intermittent gastrointestinal and neurologic signs and inability to gain
weight. Suspicion of a shunt is particularly high if the
animal’s owners report a history of worsening neurologic
signs following ingestion of a meal. Vomiting secondary
to advanced kidney disease should be suspected in dogs

with PU/PD, weight loss, and a poor hair coat. Dogs with
hypoadrenocorticism commonly present for waxing and
waning lethargy, hyporexia, vomiting and soft stools or
small bowel diarrhea.
Cats with secondary causes of gastritis (e.g., hyperthyroidism, chronic kidney disease [CKD] or liver disease)
also typically display extragastrointestinal clinical signs.
Owners might note hyperactivity, weight loss, dull hair
coat, alopecia, and occasionally aggression in hyperthyroid cats. Clinical signs of renal and liver disease mimic
those seen in dogs, although uremic ulceration of the
tongue and palate might be noted more frequently in
cats. Uremic gastropathy, characterized by erosive or
ulcerative gastritis, has been a previously reported sequel
of renal dysfunction. Recent studies, however, suggest
this is not a common finding in cats with CKD.
Physical exam findings in companion animals with
gastritis or gastric ulceration are variable and depend on
the underlying etiology. Slightly thickened or “ropey”
small intestinal loops are often appreciated in both dogs
and cats with inflammatory bowel disease. Many of these
patients are moderately to severely underweight.
Abdominal lymphadenomegaly might be noted on
abdominal palpation in cats with IBD or GI lymphoma.
Pruritus and/or signs compatible with allergic dermatitis
might be noted in patients with food‐responsive gastritis. Cranial abdominal pain might be appreciated on
physical examination in cases of foreign body ingestion,
pancreatitis, gastric neoplasia, and/or severe GI ulceration. These animals might also be febrile. Linear foreign
bodies may become anchored to the base of a cat’s
tongue, so careful inspection of this area on physical
examination is critical. Depending on the severity and
chronicity of disease, patients can exhibit signs of dehydration, hyperthermia, and/or hypovolemic or septic
shock. Cardiac arrhythmias can also be noted secondary
to hypovolemia and ischemia. Frank blood or tarry stools
may be identified on rectal examination, but the absence
of these signs does not rule out gastric bleeding. Severe
or prolonged blood loss is often associated with pale
mucous membranes.
Neurologic abnormalities (e.g., myoclonus, nystagmus, tremors, seizures or inappropriate mentation, head
pressing, star gazing) are often observed in animals with
distemper virus, intoxications or hepatic dysfunction.
Pyrexia, cutaneous lesions, lymphadenopathy, and ocular lesions (uveitis, tapetal hyper‐ or hyporeflectivity,
fundic lesions) can occur with fungal infections. Tapetal
hemorrhage or a detached retina might be visible (secondary to systemic hypertension) during the fundic
exam of patients with renal dysfunction.
Cutaneous lesions such as edema, ulceration, and
abscessation are often found in dogs with systemic
­mastocytosis and fungal disease.

­Diagnostic Approach to Suspected
Gastritis
Clinicopathologic Examination of the Gastritis
Patient
A minimum database of clinicopathologic testing,
including a complete blood count, serum chemistry,
urinalysis, and total thyroxine (in middle‐aged to older
cats), is typically recommended for dogs and cats being
presented with moderate to severe signs and/or a
chronic history of disease, prior to more invasive testing. Clinicopathologic abnormalities vary depending
on the underlying etiology, duration, and severity of
disease. Patients with peracute causes of gastric
­inflammation or ulceration (e.g., foreign body ingestion, intoxication or GDV) can lack bloodwork
­abnormalities in the early stages of the disease. However,
baseline bloodwork and imaging are recommended as
they can demonstrate evidence of GI bleeding or other
co‐morbidities or reveal an underlying predisposing
cause. Anemia is the most common laboratory finding
in dogs and cats with gastroduodenal ulceration.
Depending on the severity and chronicity of gastric
bleeding, the anemia can vary from regenerative to
nonregenerative with clinicopathologic features of
iron deficiency (e.g., microcytosis, hypochromasia).
Peripheral eosinophilia may be observed in dogs or cats
with infectious causes of gastritis or gastric ulceration,
hypoadrenocorticism or the eosinophilic enteropathies
such as hypereosinophilic syndrome or eosinophilic
IBD. Neutrophilic leukocytosis can be observed in
patients with hyperadrenocorticism, IBD or infectious
diseases.
An elevated blood urea nitrogen:creatinine ratio in the
presence of anemia strongly argues for further assessment of possible GI bleeding. Electrolyte derangements
may be present as a result of gastrointestinal losses (vomiting, diarrhea). The absence of a stress leukogram, with
or without altered serum sodium and potassium ratios
(<27:1) and/or hypoglycemia, hypocholesterolemia, and
hypoalbuminemia would support pursuit of additional
testing for hypoadrenocorticism.
Coagulation testing should be included as part of
the minimum database in patients with unidentified
causes of GI bleeding. Common causes of prolonged
clotting times in dogs with clinical signs of gastric
­disease include septicemia, hepatic failure, and rodenticide intoxication.
Fecal flotation, examination of vomitus, and empirical
anthelminthic treatment are recommended in animals
where parasitic disease is likely or before pursuing more
invasive diagnostic testing such as gastroscopy or exploratory laparotomy.

Diagnostic Imaging in Gastric Disease
Survey radiographs and abdominal ultrasonography
(AUS) can have variable results in patients with gastritis
and gastric ulceration. Neither condition should be
excluded on the basis of normal abdominal imaging.
Abdominal radiographs performed in patients with signs
of gastric disease can reveal radiopaque foreign bodies,
gastric and extragastric neoplasms (if large enough to distort normal anatomy) and/or other causes of inflammation and ulceration (e.g., pancreatitis, GDV). Gastric
neoplasms in both cats and dogs are rarely identified with
radiographs alone, except in cases of calcified (­radiopaque)
carcinomas. Abdominal effusion and pneumoperitoneum
are not specific for gastric perforation, but signal the need
for urgent exploration with additional imaging modalities
or exploratory surgery in a patient with compatible clinical signs. Mediastinal and esophageal masses can be
observed in dogs with pythiosis, so thoracic radiographs
are recommended for dogs with compatible clinical signs.
Ultrasonographic abnormalities observed in some
patients with gastric disease, particularly gastric ulceration, include disruption of normal wall layering and/or
focal gastric wall thickening. Hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and abdominal lymphadenopathy can be present in
dogs with neoplastic and/or infectious causes of gastric
disease. Gastric masses are often visible on AUS, but the
absence of a mass does not rule out infiltrative neoplasia.
Most commonly, changes on abdominal ultrasound are
nonspecific with abnormalities suggestive of, but not
diagnostic for, gastritis or gastrointestinal disease.
Gastric Histopathology
Histopathologic evaluation of biopsies (endoscopic or
full thickness) is required for the definitive diagnosis
of gastritis while diagnosis of ulceration is generally
made by visualization of the ulcerated mucosa and acquisition of biopsies with endoscopy or exploratory surgery.
However, the underlying cause is often not identified on
evaluation of gastric tissue, thus correct diagnosis often
requires consideration of the patient’s signalment, history, clinical signs, bloodwork, and imaging.
Gastroscopy or abdominal exploratory surgery are
the only antemortem methods for obtaining a definitive
diagnosis of gastric ulceration and gastric mucosal
biopsy specimens for histopathologic examination.
Animals with very diseased, friable tissue or preexisting
ulceration are at greater risk for endoscopic‐induced
perforation, so caution is warranted with gastroscopy in
patients where there is a suspicion of gastric ulceration.
Ulceration secondary to NSAID administration is found
more often in the pyloric antrum than other sites of the
stomach. Mastocytosis typically causes multiple diffuse

VetBooks.ir

ulcerative lesions in dogs. Gastrointestinal disease secondary to infectious etiologies often requires histopathologic or immunohistochemical identification of the
organism. Helicobacter‐associated gastritis in cats and
dogs is definitively diagnosed by identification of the
organism in gastric biopsies using fluorescence in situ
hybridization (FISH) or polymerase chain reaction
(PCR). Increased tissue urease activity and positive urea
breath tests have been correlated with the presence of
Helicobacter, but are also identified in the presence of
other urease‐producing bacteria and thus lack specificity. Special staining methods (Steiner staining) and
immunohistochemistry methods can aid in species
differentiation.
Gastritis and/or gastric ulceration secondary to gastric
neoplasms (carcinomas, lymphoma, mast cell tumors) or
gastrinomas can be identified via histopathologic
­examination of tissue (e.g., stomach, pancreas) biopsies.
Serum gastrin measurement provides a noninvasive test
when gastrinoma is suspected. Marked hypergastrinemia in the presence of gastroduodenal ulceration is suggestive of a pancreatic gastrinoma. Thus, a serum gastrin
measurement should be performed in any patient presenting for chronic gastritis and gastroduodenal ulceration where other systemic diseases are eliminated as
causes. Serum gastrin concentration should be interpreted cautiously in the face of acid suppressant treatment, which can result in ­
increased serum gastrin
concentrations.
Ancillary Diagnostic Testing in Gastric
Disease Patients
Testing for the presence of bacterial enteropathogens
such as E. coli, Clostridium, Campylobacter and
Salmonella spp. might be considered as an ancillary
diagnostic test for dogs ­presenting with fever, acute hemorrhagic diarrhea, and vomiting. However, results should
be interpreted with caution, as these organisms have
been isolated from the feces of healthy dogs and cats.
In cases where there is a high suspicion of gastrointestinal mycosis or oomycete disease, multiple diagnostics
are available for antemortem diagnosis. Pythium testing
includes serology, enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assay
(ELISA), PCR or immunohistochemistry (IHC) of
infected tissues or blood. A quantitative urine antigen
enzyme immunoassay is available for Histoplasma
­detection. Pyogranulomatous lesions and visualization
of fungal organisms can be noted in biopsies obtained
from dogs with fungal gastritis within the liver, spleen,
­ iopsies
lymph nodes, or gastrointestinal tract. If present, b
of cutaneous lesions should be submitted for histopathology and fungal culture. Gastritis in the Norwegian
lundehund is often secondary to lymphangiectasia (diag-

nosed by endoscopic visualization and histopathology).
Evidence of protein‐losing enteropathy is variably
­present on bloodwork. It has been hypothesized that
this syndrome can also lead to development of gastric
carcinoma as a result of chronic, severe gastritis.

­Treatment of Gastritis and Gastric
Ulceration
The best course of therapy for animals with gastritis or
gastric ulceration is removal of the offending agent, if
possible, and amelioration of mucosal injury. Specific
therapies will depend on the identified cause (e.g., azole
treatment for Histoplasma infection, chemotherapy/­
surgery for neoplasia).
Nonspecific, supportive treatment for animals with
gastritis and vomiting should begin with restoration of
fluid deficits and normalization of electrolyte imbalances, if present. A list of commonly used medications
for gastritis and gastric ulceration is provided in
Table 51.3.
Acid suppressants (e.g., histamine‐2 receptor antagonists [H2RAs] and proton pump inhibitors [PPIs]) are
recommended in vomiting animals with clinical signs of
vomiting‐induced esophagitis but should not be used
prophylactically. H2RAs are competitive inhibitors for
the interaction of histamine with its receptor on the gastric parietal cell but differ in potency (famotidine > ranitidine > cimetidine). In contrast, PPIs (e.g., omeprazole,
pantoprazole, esomeprazole) are inactivators of the proton pump and are more effective than H2RAs in raising
both feline and canine intragastric pH. Thus, PPIs,
administered twice-daily, are considered the treatment
of choice when concern for acid‐induced tissue injury
exists. Preliminary evidence suggests that PPIs are more
effective when given alone than in combination with
H2RAs in dogs for the treatment of upper GI ulceration.
Antiemetics (e.g., 5‐HT3 and neurokinin receptor antagonists) may be administered to vomiting animals once
mechanical obstruction has been ruled out as a cause of
the clinical signs.
Cytoprotective agents (e.g., sucralfate) can be given,
once vomiting is controlled, if there is evidence or suspicion of gastrointestinal bleeding. Sucralfate is most
effective at an acidic pH and can interfere with appropriate absorption of pH‐dependent drugs. Thus,
sucralfate should be administered as a slurry at least
1–2 hours before or after administration of meals and
other medications. The PGE1 analog misoprostol is
indicated for use in NSAID‐induced toxicoses but does
not promote healing in non‐NSAID‐induced causes of
GI ulceration.

­Prognosis
The prognosis for patients with gastritis and/or gastric
ulceration ranges from excellent to guarded depending
on the underlying etiology, severity of disease at
presentation, and individual response to therapy.
­
Uncomplicated, acute disease in younger, otherwise

healthy animals without significant co‐morbidities is
usually associated with a good prognosis. In contrast,
onset of significant gastric disease and ulceration in
older animals with chronic histories of gastrointestinal
disease or other co‐morbidities is often associated with
progression of an underlying disease process and can
carry a more guarded prognosis.

Disorders of the Esophagus
Silvia Funes, DVM, MS, DACVIM (SAIM)1 and Craig Ruaux, BVSc (Hons), PhD, MACVSc, DACVIM (SAIM)2
1
2

VCA Bay Area Veterinary Specialists and Emergency Hospital, San Leandro, CA, USA
School of Veterinary Science, Massey University, Palmerston North, New Zealand

­Normal Esophageal Anatomy
and Physiology
The esophagus is a readily distensible, muscular tube
that transports ingested material from the oropharynx to
the stomach. It is divided into three sections –the cervical, thoracic and abdominal segments – and enclosed at
each end by a muscular sphincter (the upper and lower
esophageal sphincters).
The esophageal wall has four distinct layers: adventitia, muscularis, submucosa, and mucosa. The entire
muscularis layer in the canine esophagus is composed of
skeletal muscle, whereas the distal one‐third of the feline
esophagus consists of smooth muscle. This difference in
muscular structure may partly explain the differing prevalence of esophageal disease in dogs and cats, with cats
relatively rarely presenting with esophageal diseases
other than foreign bodies or squamous cell carcinoma.
The upper esophageal sphincter is composed of fibers
from the cricopharyngeus muscle and thyropharyngeus
muscle. In dogs, the lower esophageal sphincter is
­composed of an outer layer of striated muscle and an
inner layer of smooth muscle, while in cats the lower
esophageal sphincter consists of smooth muscle only.
Swallowing is a complex motor reflex requiring coordinated action of the tongue, oropharynx, upper esophageal sphincter, and esophagus to ensure that food
enters the gastrointestinal tract and not the upper airways. When swallowing is not occurring, the upper and
lower esophageal sphincters are tightly closed and the
esophagus is relaxed. During swallowing, the upper
esophageal sphincter relaxes and the food bolus is
pushed into the cervical section of the esophagus. A primary peristaltic wave is generated, transferring the
bolus to the stomach. This primary peristaltic wave will
be followed by secondary waves if the esophagus is not

cleared of material. Relaxation of the lower esophageal
sphincter accompanies the primary peristaltic wave,
allowing entry of the food bolus into the stomach.
The most common esophageal disorders encountered
in private practice include esophagitis, megaesophagus,
esophageal strictures, and esophageal foreign bodies.
Less commonly encountered disorders include great
vessel anomalies, lower esophageal hiatal disorders,
esophageal neoplasia, spirocercosis, cricopharyngeal
dysphagia, esophageal diverticulae, and esophageal
fistulae.

­Recognition of Esophageal
Disorders
Common clinical signs of esophageal disease include
regurgitation, dysphagia (difficult swallowing), ptyalism
(excessive salivation), extension of the head and neck,
repeated swallowing attempts, and pain. Regurgitation is
a hallmark sign of esophageal disease and needs to be
­differentiated from vomiting. Regurgitation is defined as
the passive retrograde expulsion of material from the
esophagus while vomiting is an active process mediated
by a central reflex. Vomiting is usually associated with
abdominal contractions and might show prodromal signs
of nausea (lip smacking, increased salivation, discomfort
or anxiety) or the presence of bile in the ejected material.
Oropharyngeal dysphagia, a less common clinical
syndrome, should be differentiated from regurgitation.
­
Clinical signs of oropharyngeal dysphagia include multiple
swallowing attempts with a single bolus, dropping food or
water from the mouth or nostrils, and difficulty drinking.
When possible, having the owner video record the episodes may be helpful in distinguishing oropharyngeal
swallowing disorders from esophageal motility disorders.

One of the most frequent complications of esophageal disorders is aspiration pneumonia; this is the most
common cause of death in animals with esophageal
motility disorders. Dogs with aspiration pneumonia
secondary to esophageal disease can present with fever,
inappetence, coughing, mucopurulent nasal discharge,
and pulmonary crackles. Dogs with chronic and severe
esophageal dysfunction may present with weight loss
and poor body condition scores secondary to
­inadequate food intake. Dogs with foreign bodies or
esophagitis are usually painful during swallowing.
Foreign bodies are often associated with an acute onset
of regurgitation. The presence of esophageal disease at
the time of weaning is more commonly seen with congenital idiopathic megaesophagus, vascular ring anomalies or congenital stenosis. The history may indicate a
recent anesthetic procedure that could cause reflux
esophagitis and potential stricture, exposure to caustic
medications (e.g., doxycycline) or foreign bodies. Signs
of concurrent neuromuscular disease can be seen in
dogs with megaesophagus secondary to myasthenia
gravis.

­Diagnostic Approach to Esophageal
Disease
Plain thoracic and cervical radiographs are the initial
step in all animals with clinical signs and histories consistent with esophageal disease. Radiographs are useful
in the identification of megaesophagus, radiopaque foreign bodies, and hiatal defects. In addition, the lungs and
mediastinum can be evaluated for any evidence of aspiration pneumonia or pneumomediastinum associated
with esophageal perforation.
A contrast esophagram should be considered when
plain radiographs do not identify a lesion. The contrast
study can be performed under fluoroscopy or using
plain radiography (see Chapter 53). The use of fluoroscopy helps in the evaluation of esophageal motility.
Contrast studies can be useful in the identification of
radiolucent foreign material, strictures or neoplasia.
Contrast esophagram studies are usually contraindicated in animals with megaesophagus because of the
high risk of aspiration pneumonia. A water‐soluble iodinated contrast agent is preferred if esophageal perforation is suspected.
Esophagoscopy can be useful for the diagnosis of
esophageal neoplasia, esophagitis, strictures, and perforation. This minimally invasive procedure allows the
direct visualization of the esophageal mucosa and lumen
and can be used to obtain biopsies, retrieve foreign bodies, balloon esophageal strictures or deploy esophageal
stents.

­Specific Esophageal Disorders
Megaesophagus
Congenital Megaesophagus

Megaesophagus is a condition characterized by diffuse
esophageal dilation and decreased or absent esophageal
motility. Megaesophagus may be a congenital or acquired
(adult‐onset) disease. A familial predisposition has been
identified in several breeds including the Great Dane,
German shepherd, Irish setter, Chinese shar‐pei,
Newfoundland, miniature Schnauzer, Labrador retriever
and fox terrier breeds, as well as Siamese cats. In the
wirehaired fox terrier, congenital megaesophagus is
inherited as a simple autosomal‐recessive trait, while in
miniature Schnauzers it is transmitted as either a simple
autosomal‐recessive or dominant trait. Affected dogs
usually start having clinical signs of regurgitation at or
shortly after weaning.
The main differential diagnosis that should be considered in young dogs with regurgitation at the time of
weaning is a congenital vascular ring anomaly. Plain
radiographs are usually sufficient to differentiate between
these disorders, although contrast studies are necessary
in some cases.
The etiopathogenesis of congenital megaesophagus is
unclear. Esophageal motility and nerve stimulation studies in dogs with megaesophagus indicate a defect in the
afferent neural pathway, while the efferent neural pathway appears to be intact.
The prognosis for congenital megaesophagus is
guarded to poor. Some dogs can be managed for months
to years while others rapidly succumb due to uncontrolled regurgitation and aspiration pneumonia.
Breeding of affected patients is not recommended.
Treatment details for megaesophagus are discussed
below.
Acquired Megaesophagus

Acquired megaesophagus can occur in any breed or age.
Acquired megaesophagus may be primary (idiopathic)
or secondary to multiple disorders, particularly diseases
causing neuromuscular dysfunction.
The most common cause of secondary acquired megaesophagus in dogs is myasthenia gravis(MG). MG may
be congenital (rare) or acquired. Acquired MG is an
autoimmune disorder characterized by autoantibodies
directed against the acetylcholine (Ach) receptors of
skeletal neuromuscular junctions. These antibodies bind
to the Ach receptors, reducing the number of receptors
available for normal neuromuscular transmission. When
acetylcholine is released from presynaptic vesicles at the
nerve terminal, it is unable to bind to the receptors on
the postsynaptic muscle fiber membrane. Depending on

VetBooks.ir

52 Disorders of the Esophagus

the clinical presentation, MG can be classified as generalized, focal or acute fulminant. Generalized MG usually
presents with generalized muscular weakness that worsens after exercise; megaesophagus has been well documented in these cases. Acute fulminant MG usually
presents as a flaccid tetraparesis and acute respiratory
distress.
The gold standard for the diagnosis of acquired MG is
the detection of serum autoantibodies directed against
Ach receptors. An Ach receptor antibody concentration
of ≥0.6 nmol/L is considered positive. Approximately
2% of dogs with generalized MG, however, are negative
for Ach receptor antibodies. A presumptive diagnosis
can be made by a positive response to an ultra short‐acting anticholinesterase agent (Tensilon test: edrophonium chloride IV at 0.1–0.2 mg/kg). This test can lead to
a cholinergic crisis in nonmyasthenic patients or if accidentally overdosed, producing bronchoconstriction,
bradycardia, salivation, lacrimation, retching, diarrhea,
and vomiting. In this situation, atropine sulfate should be
administered IV (0.02–0.04 mg/kg IV). Dogs with focal
or generalized MG are treated with anticholinesterase
agents such as pyridostigmine bromide (1–3 mg/kg PO
q8–12 h or 0.01–0.03 mg/kg/h as a constant rate IV
­infusion) or neostigmine bromide (2 mg/kg/day PO in
divided doses to effect or 0.04 mg/kg IM q6h).
Focal MG usually affects the motor fibers of cranial
nerves innervating the larynx and pharynx.
Megaesophagus associated with focal MG can be misdiagnosed as idiopathic acquired megaesophagus, and
assessment of anticholinesterase antibody titers is
strongly recommended in the work‐up of the great
majority of dogs with esophageal motility disorders.
Endocrine diseases such as hypoadrenocorticism and
hypothyroidism have historically been associated with
megaesophagus. Megaesophagus has been reported in
dogs with primary, secondary and atypical hypoadrenocorticism. Proposed causes include altered muscle carbohydrate metabolism due to a lack of physiologic
cortisol production, and the effects of abnormal sodium
and potassium concentrations on membrane polarization. An adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulation test is necessary for the diagnosis. Although a
definitive association between hypothyroidism and megaesophagus has not been proven, there are reports of
dogs with hypothyroidism and megaesophagus. There is
also an association between MG and hypothyroidism
and thyroid function should be evaluated concurrently
with diagnostic testing for MG.
Megaesophagus has also been described as a paraneoplastic syndrome. According to one study, megaesophagus was present in 40% of dogs with thymoma. Thymoma
also has been associated with MG in dogs and cats.
Complete thymus resection can result in resolution of

megaesophagus. However, nonresectable thymoma in
dogs with megaesophagus has a poor prognosis.
Idiopathic megaesophagus is the most common cause
of megaesophagus in dogs. It usually affects large‐breed
dogs between 5 to 12 years old. The etiopathogenesis is
unknown. There is no sex or breed predilection. Many
dogs affected with idiopathic megaesophagus have a very
dilated and aperistaltic esophagus.
Treatment of Megaesophagus
The treatment of dogs with idiopathic megaesophagus is
entirely supportive and symptomatic, while animals with
acquired megaesophagus should be treated specifically
for the underlying disease. Thoracic radiographs are
recommended to monitor and document esophageal
­
dilation and evaluate for aspiration pneumonia.
Frequent feeding of small, high‐calorie meals with the
patient in a cranially elevated position will help meet
nutritional requirements and reduce regurgitation.
Upright feeding, holding the dog in vertical position, or
using “Bailey” chairs are often effective strategies for
controlling regurgitation in many dogs. Very weak
patients or those in whom the regurgitation is uncontrollable might benefit from placement of a gastrostomy
tube. The optimal food consistency depends on the
patient and should be tailored to each individual dog.
The most common complications of megaesophagus
are aspiration pneumonia and esophagitis. Aspiration
pneumonia should be treated using broad‐spectrum
antibiotics. Culture and sensitivity testing of a transtracheal wash or bronchoalveolar lavage sample is useful to
guide antibiotic choice. Esophagitis can also worsen
megaesophagus and lead to strictures.
The use of prokinetic medications in dogs with megaesophagus has not been shown to have any benefit.
Metoclopramide and cisapride exert their actions on
smooth muscle and do not have any action on skeletal
muscle, thus they are not useful in dogs with esophageal
hypomotility. These medications may also increase the
tone of the lower esophageal sphincter, decreasing
esophageal emptying. In cases of esophageal reflux,
however, these medications might be useful because they
decrease the episodes of reflux and esophagitis.
Bethanecol binds and stimulates cholinergic (muscarinic) receptors and may be helpful in stimulating
esophageal propagating contractions.
Prognosis for Animals with Megaesophagus
The prognosis for patients with megaesophagus depends
on the underlying disease and the presence of secondary
complications such as aspiration pneumonia. In dogs
with MG, resolution of megaesophagus can occur within

559

VetBooks.ir

560

Section 6 Gastrointestinal Disease

the first six months. Dogs with congenital megaesophagus have a more guarded prognosis. Some dogs can
recover and acquire normal esophageal function if
­dietary management is begun early. The prognosis for
idiopathic megaesophagus in adult dogs is poor and
spontaneous recovery rarely occurs. Most dogs eventually die due to aspiration pneumonia.

­Esophagitis
Esophagitis can be defined as chronic or acute inflammation of the esophageal mucosa. Esophagitis can be
caused by a chemical or caustic injury (acid, drug‐
induced), esophageal foreign body, gastroesophageal
reflux, radiation, or food retention secondary to megaesophagus. The degree of inflammation can be mild, with
lesions localized in the mucosa, or severe, affecting the
muscularis layer.
The administration of oxytetracycline and doxycycline
has been associated with esophagitis in cats. Other orally
administered medications including clindamycin, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, and bisphosphonates
can also produce esophagitis.
Esophageal foreign bodies can cause severe esophageal
inflammation in dogs and cats. They are usually located
in the thoracic inlet, at the base of the heart or the lower
esophageal sphincter.
Gastroesophageal reflux is a consequence of movement of gastric content into the esophagus. Exposure of
the mucosa to the refluxed gastric acid, digestive
enzymes, and bile acids can rapidly induce inflammation. Gastroesophageal reflux has been associated with
anesthesia, hiatal hernias, neoplasia affecting the distal
esophagus or lower esophageal sphincter, and delayed
gastric emptying. Anesthesia is a known risk factor for
gastroesophageal reflux. The duration of the anesthesia
and preanesthetic agents used appear to influence the
risk of gastroesophageal reflux. Medications that
decrease the lower esophageal tone, such as thiopentone,
propofol, morphine, xylazine, and atropine, can increase
the risk of reflux. Prolonged fasting (24 hours) before
anesthesia is associated with a higher risk of gastroesophageal reflux.
Clinical signs of esophagitis include decreased appetite, odynophagia (painful swallowing) or dysphagia, ptyalism, coughing, and regurgitation. Some animals only
show subtle signs with decreased appetite and increased
salivation. Clinical signs consistent with esophagitis 1–4
days after an anesthetic procedure are suggestive of
esophageal reflux, and should be managed aggressively
to decrease the risk of esophageal stricture formation.
Dogs with chronic vomiting should be monitored closely.
The final diagnosis of esophagitis is done by direct

­visualization of the esophageal mucosa via endoscopy.
Focal or diffuse mucosal erythema with increased friability is often seen.
Treatment
Treatment of esophagitis is focused on the elimination
of the underlying cause and allowing inflammation to
resolve. Esophageal foreign objects need to be treated
as an emergency and retrieved as soon as possible.
Administration of drugs associated with esophagitis
(doxycycline, oxytetracycline, clindamycin) should be
discontinued. The main cornerstones of the treatment
of esophagitis are acid suppression, mucosal protection
via sucralfate administration, and supportive care. In
some cases, supportive care may require interventions
to provide nutritional support, such as percutaneous
endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube placement. The
use of prokinetic medications is controversial, but is
recommended when reflux esophagitis is suspected.
The most common acid suppressants used in dogs
and cats are proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and histamine‐2 receptor antagonists (H2‐blockers). Proton
pump inhibitors covalently bind to and irreversibly
inhibit the H+‐K+‐ATPase proton pumps. PPI medications are available in both oral (omeprazole) and parenteral (pantoprazole, esomeprazole, lansoprazole)
formulations. H2‐blockers act by blocking the action
of histamine on parietal cells in the gastric mucosa,
decreasing the production of acid by these cells.
PPIs have proven to be more effective at raising intragastric pH than histamine‐2 receptor antagonists.
Administration of PPIs twice daily (0.7–1 mg/kg q12h)
rather than once daily is recommended to effectively
increase the intragastric pH in both dogs and cats. The
combination of PPIs and H2‐blockers is not superior to
the administration of a PPI alone.
Sucralfate is an aluminum salt of a sulfated disaccharide that, when activated in an acidic environment, forms
a paste‐like material that binds to and protects exposed
submucosa and the mucosa from acid exposure.
Sucralfate is generally administered as a slurry 3–4 times
per day, separate from food and other medications.
Prokinetic medications such as metoclopramide and
cisapride are useful to increase the tone of the lower
esophageal sphincter and enhance gastric motility. In
cases of gastroesophageal reflux, the use of metoclopramide (2 mg/kg q24h as a constant rate infusion [CRI]) or
cisapride (0.5 mg/kg q8h PO) is recommended.
Anesthesia is the main cause of gastroesophageal
reflux and esophagitis in dogs and cats. The position
during anesthesia has not been identified as a risk factor.
The frequency of reflux is greatest in abdominal procedures. When acid reflux is confirmed, esophageal lavage

VetBooks.ir

52 Disorders of the Esophagus

with water, followed by 20 mL of 4.2% bicarbonate, is
recommended.
In severe cases of esophagitis, placement of a gastrostomy tube may be indicated to ensure adequate caloric
intake, while also reducing esophageal pain and further
irritation of the esophageal mucosa.

­Esophageal Strictures
Esophageal strictures arise as the result of severe esophageal inflammation affecting the muscularis layer. During
the healing process of these lesions, intramural fibrous
contraction may occur, leading to a band of scar tissue
that produces a circumferential narrowing of the esophageal lumen.
The main clinical signs associated with esophageal
strictures are regurgitation, weight loss, coughing, salivation, anorexia, odynophagia, and vomiting. Benign
esophageal strictures are usually a consequence of severe
esophagitis due to esophageal reflux secondary to anesthesia or foreign bodies. Malignant esophageal strictures
are associated with neoplasia. Strictures secondary to
gastroesophageal reflux are often located between the
thoracic inlet and the diaphragm, whereas strictures
­cranial to the thoracic inlet are usually associated with
foreign body injuries.
Clinical signs and the history of the patient will typically suggest the presence of an esophageal stricture.
Barium contrast studies, using conventional radiography
or fluoroscopy, are useful diagnostic tools. Endoscopic
visualization of esophageal stricture is the most reliable
method of diagnosis, and has the advantage that treatment can be immediately initiated. Circumferential narrowing of the esophagus, with intraluminal fibrous tissue
bands, is usually visualized.
Treatment
There are two preferred techniques typically used for the
treatment of benign esophageal strictures: bougienage
and ballooning.
Bougienage involves the use of rounded, rigid or semirigid instruments that are pushed through the esophagus
to progressively stretch the stricture. Different sizes are
used serially to gradually open the stricture. The bougienage technique applies both radial and shearing forces
to the fibrous tissue at the site of the stricture. Wire‐
guided bougienage appears to be safe and is commonly
associated with a good outcome.
Esophageal ballooning is performed by passing an
inflatable balloon into the stricture. The balloon dilates
and becomes rigid when inflated, applying a radial force
to the stricture. The balloons are positioned into the

lumen using endoscopy or fluoroscopy guidance. Balloon
dilation does not apply shearing forces to the stricture
tissue.
Esophageal ballooning and bougienage are reportedly
equally safe and effective. The number of repetitions of
the dilation necessary varies between patient (with most
requiring 1–4 sessions); both methods have success rates
of 70–88%. The interval between dilation attempts is
usually 7–10 days. Both methods have been associated
with complications, including mucosal tearing, hemorrhage, and esophageal perforation. When dilating an
esophageal stricture, the aim is to return the patient to
normal or at least manageable swallowing function that
will allow sufficient nutritional intake. Dilation of the
esophagus to the prestricture diameter is usually unnecessary, as many animals will show marked improvement
in swallowing function with less than complete dilation
of the esophagus.
During the series of dilation treatments, it is critical to
aggressively manage esophagitis and prevent further
damage from gastroesophageal reflux. Sucralfate suspensions, antacids (PPIs), and prokinetics (cisapride,
metoclopramide) are generally indicated to protect the
mucosa, reduce acid secretion and increase the tone of
the lower esophageal sphincter. The use of systemic
­corticosteroids is controversial in these patients and further studies are necessary to evaluate their efficacy.
Intralesional corticosteroid injection using triamcinolone can be used instead of systemic corticosteroids.
Mitomycin‐C can also be used topically at the stricture
site, after dilation, to reduce collagen formation and the
risk of recurrence of the stricture.

­Esophageal Foreign Bodies
Esophageal foreign bodies are more common in dogs
than in cats. The most common foreign bodies in dogs
are bone fragments and rawhide type chews. In cats,
string or linear foreign bodies attached to the base of the
tongue are the most frequently encountered. Esophageal
foreign bodies are most commonly found between the
base of the heart and the diaphragm.
Clinical signs associated with foreign bodies include
regurgitation, gagging, anorexia, and retching. The
severity of esophageal damage depends on both the type
and duration of the obstruction. Animals with esophageal perforation or aspiration pneumonia commonly
present obtunded, febrile, anorectic, and with coughing.
Radiopaque foreign bodies can be diagnosed using
thoracic radiographs. Thoracic radiographs are also useful to rule out the presence of aspiration pneumonia or
esophageal perforation. Contrast radiography is useful to
reveal radiolucent foreign material. Direct visualization

561

VetBooks.ir

562

Section 6 Gastrointestinal Disease

of the foreign body using esophagoscopy confirms the
diagnosis, and is typically a prequel to treatment.
Treatment
Esophageal foreign bodies are considered medical emergencies. Esophagoscopy can be used to confirm and
retrieve the foreign material using a variety of grasping
instruments. Foreign bodies located close to the lower
esophageal sphincter may be able to be pushed into the
stomach. The long‐term prognosis is usually excellent
although short‐term complications are common. The
most common complications include esophagitis, aspiration pneumonia, and esophageal perforation (pneumothorax). Dogs with moderate and severe esophagitis
are more prone to develop strictures.
When extensive esophageal perforation or necrosis is
present, surgical removal is recommended. Esophageal
surgery has been associated with a higher risk of esophageal dehiscence due to the segmental blood supply, the
absence of a serosal layer and the movement and tension
of the surgical site. The most common complications
include dehiscence, pyothorax, and pleuritis. Transthoracic
esophagostomy retrieval of foreign bodies has been associated with a survival rate of 77–93%.
Medical treatment for esophagitis is necessary after
retrieving the foreign material. Recheck thoracic radiographs are useful to identify pneumothorax and/or
pneumomediastinum secondary to esophageal perforation. Small esophageal perforations may be able to be
medically managed with antibiotics and supportive care.
In cases of severe esophageal injury, after retrieval of the
foreign body, the placement of a gastrostomy tube should
be considered.

­Vascular Ring Anomalies
Vascular ring anomalies (VRAs) are congenital malformations of the embryonic aortic arches that affect both

dogs and cats, producing esophageal constriction.
Persistent right aortic arch (PRAA) is the most common anomaly in dogs and cats; this anomaly is associated with entrapment of the thoracic esophagus. PRAA
occurs when the aorta develops from the embryonic
right fourth aortic arch rather than the left fourth aortic arch. As a consequence, the esophagus is constricted
between the ligamentum arteriosum (LA) dorsally,
pulmonary artery on the left, aorta on the right, and
the heart ventrally. Although VRAs have been reported
in many breeds of dogs and cats, German shepherds,
Irish setters and the Labrador retriever may be
predisposed.
Regurgitation and failure to thrive are the most common clinical signs and are often present at the time of
weaning. Thoracic radiographs often reveal dilation of
the esophagus cranial to the base of the heart; plain radiography is also useful to screen for concurrent aspiration
pneumonia. When plain radiographs are nondiagnostic,
a barium contrast study may aid in visualization of
esophageal obstruction at the base of the heart. Direct
visualization of the esophageal mucosa via esophagoscopy may be useful to differentiate between extraluminal
and intraluminal compression.
Treatment
Definitive treatment of PRAA involves surgical ligation
and transection of the ligamentum arteriosum via thoracoscopy or thoracotomy. Esophageal hypomotility and
regurgitation may persist after surgical ligation and the
risk of this outcome increases with the duration of clinical signs. In a recent study evaluating the short‐ and
long‐term outcome following surgical repair of PRAA,
the long‐term outcome for dogs was excellent in 30%,
good in 57%, and poor in 13%. Patients with persistent
regurgitation after surgery are treated supportively as
described for idiopathic megaesophagus, with upright
feeding, small, frequent meals, and restraint of the
­animal in a “Bailey” type chair.

Gastrointestinal (GI) motility disorders are a diagnostic
and therapeutic challenge. They can consist of delayed or
accelerated transit times as well as impaired or inappropriate relaxation anywhere in the GI tract. Delayed transit is the most common form. This may be a primary
localized neuromuscular disorder, part of a more generalized GI motility disturbance (e.g., dysautonomia) or
secondary to systemic health problems (metabolic, toxic,
inflammatory, neoplastic, obstructive, etc.).

­Motility Disorders of the Esophagus
Physiology of Esophageal Motility
The esophagus acts as a simple tube for the transport of
food from the oral cavity to the stomach. Between swallows, it is collapsed but can distend markedly to accommodate a food bolus. Structurally, it is of similar
composition to the remainder of the GI tract, but it lacks
a serosa. In dogs, the muscular layer (responsible for the
motor function) is composed of two layers of striated
muscles spiraling in oblique bundles and crossing each
other at right angles. In cats, there is a transition zone
from striated to smooth muscle at the level of the heart.
There are two sphincters: the upper esophageal
sphincter (UES), consisting of the cricopharyngeus muscle, and the gastroesophageal sphincter (GES), which is a
thickening of the esophageal muscle at the junction to
the stomach.
Esophageal transport of a food bolus – as part of the
complicated swallowing act – is under complete autonomic neuronal control. Efferent neurons from the
nucleus ambiguous in the medulla oblongata innervate
the striated muscle (dogs and cats) and the smooth
­muscle (cats) via the vagus nerve. Once the food bolus
is voluntarily pushed caudally into the oropharynx,

a ­
complex reflex is instituted, that starts with cricopharyngeal relaxation. The food bolus is then passed
through the UES into the cervical esophagus. Immediately
thereafter, the UES closes, preventing material from
entering the trachea or being pushed back into the pharynx. Continuous peristaltic contractions move the food
aborally, where it passes through the relaxed GES (primary esophageal peristalsis). In a case where the first
peristaltic wave is inadequate for complete transport,
secondary esophageal peristalsis occurs, where local
esophageal distension generates another peristaltic wave.
Clinical Signs of Esophageal Motility Disorders
The classic clinical sign of esophageal disease is regurgitation. Additional common complaints are dysphagia,
hypersalivation, retching and gagging, odynophagia, and
repeated swallowing attempts. Less common signs are
anorexia and lethargy. Both dogs and cats can show signs
of aspiration pneumonia (fever, tachypnea, coughing,
dyspnea).
On physical examination, low body condition score/
weight loss or poor growth might be apparent. Rarely, a
dilated esophagus can be palpated in the cervical region.
Bradycardia, loss of pupillary light reflexes, decreased
tear production (demonstrated by a Schirmer tear test),
dry mucous membranes, and constipation/diarrhea in
combination with megaesophagus are indicative of a
dysautonomia.
Causes of Esophageal Motility Disorders
In small animals, primary esophageal motor dysfunction
is poorly defined and infrequently recognized, except for
idiopathic megaesophagus and esophageal diverticula in
dogs. A high prevalence of subclinical primary esophageal dysmotility has been reported in certain dog breeds
