(Chinese shar‐pei, bouvier des Flandres) and in young
dogs (up to 2 years of age). The reported prevalence of
abnormal esophageal motility in cats is 0.05%.
Secondary esophageal dysmotility is seen in most animals with obstructive or inflammatory esophageal disease; these will not be covered in detail in this chapter
(see Chapter 52). Obstructive disorders can be grouped
into intraluminal (foreign body), intramural (neoplasia,
granuloma, stricture) or extraluminal (vascular ring
anomaly, mediastinal mass), whereas inflammation
(esophagitis) is frequently due to gastroesophageal reflux
disease (GERD).
Megaesophagus

Megaesophagus is defined as generalized esophageal
dilation with hypo‐ or amotility and can be primary
­(idiopathic) or secondary (acquired). It has to be differentiated from localized esophageal dilation, which can
be frequently observed proximal to obstructive disorders. However, early cases of megaesophagus might have
only segmental dilation, which may become generalized
with time. In addition, not all dogs with abnormal esophageal motility progress to megaesophagus.
Idiopathic megaesophagus may be congenital or
acquired. In some dog breeds (Great Dane, German
shepherd, Irish setter, golden retriever, Labrador
retriever, greyhound, Newfoundland, shar‐pei), a familial predisposition is reported, while in others (miniature
schnauzers and fox terriers) an autosomal dominant
inheritance trait has been discovered. In cats, megaesophagus is uncommon. The acquired adult‐onset form
is most commonly idiopathic (>70%) or secondary to
other systemic disorders, especially those causing neuromuscular dysfunction.
The pathogenesis of megaesophagus in dogs is still
poorly understood, but defects in afferent neural pathways have been suggested, while efferent neuromuscular
pathways seem to be intact. Decreased motor responses
of the UES and GES to intraluminal stimuli have been
reported.
Ancillary diagnostic tests are performed in dogs with
megaesophagus with the intent to detect an underlying
cause (e.g., myasthenia gravis), as treatment of the underlying disorder might lead to complete resolution of
esophageal dilation, and to identify co‐morbidities such
as aspiration pneumonia. Initial tests can include a
complete blood count (CBC) and determination of
­
C‐reactive protein (or other acute phase proteins) as a
measure of the severity of secondary inflammation/
infection. Measurement of acetylcholine receptor antibody (AchRA) titer by an accredited laboratory can aid
the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis and should be done in
all dogs with megaesophagus. Focal myasthenia gravis
occurs in the absence of muscle weakness and is the

­second most common cause (≈25% of cases) of acquired
megaesophagus. Endocrinopathies such as hypoadrenocorticism and hypothyroidism have frequently been
implicated as a cause of megaesophagus in the dog.
However, the association of megaesophagus with
hypoadrenocorticism is rare. In almost all dogs that
simultaneously suffered from hypoadrenocorticism and
megaesophagus, Na:K ratios were abnormally low.
Consequently, an adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)
stimulation test is only indicated in these dogs if electrolyte abnormalities (hyponatremia and hyperkalemia with
a Na:K ratio <27) are observed.
Other potential tests that could be considered in dogs
with megaesophagus, on an individual basis, include
blood lead concentrations (lead poisoning), edrophonium
chloride challenge test (generalized myasthenia gravis) or
electromyography in a dog with generalized muscle
­weakness (polyradiculoneuritis, polymyositis, etc.).
Diagnostic Tests to Assess Esophageal
Motility
Survey radiographs do not assess esophageal motility,
but can be informative regarding luminal obstructions,
dilation/ diverticula, strictures, and megaesophagus.
The esophagus is not visible in its physiologic state as
it has the same opacity as the surrounding soft tissue. A
mildly air‐filled esophagus or small “pockets” of air can
be present due to physiologic transient dilation, aerophagia (anxiety, dyspnea) and during sedation/anesthesia.
Both left and right lateral radiographic views might
be necessary in some cases to diagnose esophageal
dilation.
Megaesophagus is characterized radiographically via
visualization of a dilated, enlarged, air‐filled esophagus
(sometimes also filled with fluid or ingesta). The trachea
can show some ventral deviation. The caudodorsal
­thorax might appear hyperlucent.
If plain radiographs are inconclusive, contrast studies
(esophagrams) can be helpful. They should not be performed if the cause of regurgitation is already clear on
the plain radiographs. The use of barium sulfate in cases
where perforation cannot be excluded/is suspected
(pneumomediastinum) or where the risk of immediate
regurgitation is high should be avoided. Ideally, contrast
studies of the esophagus should be limited to the use of
iodine‐containing media.
Immediately after oral administration of contrast
(10–20 mL/animal at a time), a few longitudinal parallel
esophageal folds outlined by barium can be visible in the
normal canine esophagus, while cats show additional
transverse mucosal folds in the caudal third of the esophagus (so‐called “herringbone” pattern). To assess subtle
motility disorders limited to the passage of solid food,

VetBooks.ir

53 Motility Disorders of the Alimentary Tract

contrast can be mixed with food and the radiographs can
be repeated.
To diagnose functional cricopharyngeal and esophageal dysmotilities that do not lead to dilation (achalasia,
cricopharyngeal bars), a sliding hiatal hernia (type I) or
GERD, contrast‐enhanced videofluoroscopic esophagography (fluoroscopy) is the imaging modality of choice,
as it provides continuous, dynamic and real‐time assessment of the entire swallowing process. Conscious animals are placed in lateral or sternal position. Neat liquid
barium, barium paste, barium mixed with canned food
(all administered via syringe) or barium‐soaked kibble
(in animals willing to eat) can be used. Three to five swallows are observed in real time with at least one followed
all the way into the stomach.
Esophagoscopy is rarely useful to investigate functional dysphagia as esophageal motility cannot be
assessed under general anesthesia, but it can be performed to remove esophageal foreign bodies, detect
esophagitis/GERD, esophageal tumors or hiatal hernias.
Esophageal mucosal biopsies can be useful in the diagnosis of GERD, esophagitis, and neoplasia, but can be
­difficult to retrieve due to the firmness of the mucosa
and the difficulty in achieving an oblique or 90° angle.
Esophageal manometry allows assessment of the intraesophageal pressure generated by peristalsis and provides
clinically important information on esophageal motor
function. Recently, high‐resolution impedance manometry
has become the standard for the evaluation of esophageal
function in humans. This technique has recently been used
in dogs (Figure 53.1) and while technically demanding and
limited to a research setting at the moment, it gives an overall highly informative assessment of esophageal motility.
Treatment of Esophageal Motility Disorders
Medical treatment of esophageal dysmotility in dogs qnd
cats is typically unrewarding. Management of megaesophagus is directed towards treating the inciting cause
(e.g., use of pyrido‐ or neostigmine in myasthenia gravis)
and based on the optimization of feeding regimens.
Feeding from an elevated position, sometimes aided by
using specialized feeding chairs, and the attempt to avoid
complications like aspiration pneumonia are the most
important measures. The ideal type of food (kibbles, gruel,
homogenized food, etc.) for individual patients has to be
found in a “trial‐and‐error” fashion. If an underlying disease process is suspected, empirical treatment is often initiated until test results (e.g., AchRA titer) are available.
Aspiration pneumonia has to be treated aggressively, usually with intravenous fluids and antibiotics, coupage, and
potentially secretolytics. If esophagitis is suspected or
proven, oral sucralfate s­uspension and proton pump
inhibitors (to avoid GERD) should be prescribed.

­Motility Disorders of the Stomach
Gastric motility is a highly coordinated process involving
neuromuscular and hormonal signals and is triggered as
a response to either the presence of food in the stomach
or a range of different local (mechanical or functional) or
systemic diseases. There are three separate types of gastric motility disorders: accelerated gastric emptying, retrograde transit (reflux), and delayed gastric emptying.
Physiology of Gastric Motility and Emptying
Functionally, the stomach can be divided into the proximal (consisting of cardia, fundus, first third of the corpus) and distal (distal two thirds of the corpus and
antrum) compartments. The proximal compartment is
responsible for the accommodation of food and liquids
and characterized by slow tonic contractions. The distal
compartment is characterized by phasic propagating
contractions generated by pacemaker cells (interstitial
cells of Cajal [ICC]) that lead to mechanical milling of
gastric contents (called trituration) and their final expulsion through the pylorus. Pressure and amplitude of
these contractions increase in an aboral direction.
Digestive motility resulting in gastric emptying occurs
in three consecutive phases:
1) propulsion (proximal part of the antrum contracts)
2) emptying and mixing (pylorus opens partially and
duodenal peristalsis is momentarily halted while particles up to 2 mm pass the pylorus)
3) retropulsion (larger particles are propelled back into
the corpus).
Interdigestive motility occurs to empty nondigestible
food particles/foreign bodies, swallowed saliva, and
small amounts of mucus and cellular debris. In the dog,
this motility pattern is called the migrating motor complex (MMC) and starts with intense contractile activity
in an aboral direction (“clean sweep”) followed by a
period of relative quiescence and a short phase of irregular undirectional contractions. Interdigestive motility in
the cat is uniquely associated with long fused migrating
spike burst contractions interspersed with short periods
of irregular activity.
Clinical Signs of Gastric Dysmotility
In dogs with delayed gastric emptying, clinical signs can
include gastric distension and vomiting of undigested or
partially digested food >8 h after feeding (when the
stomach should be empty). In cats, the importance of
gastric emptying disorders remains unclear. Clinical
signs include anorexia, vomiting, regurgitation, and
weight loss.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease is detected more frequently in dogs than cats. It can occur spontaneously or
be related to general anesthesia. In both species, it can
result in ptyalism, retching, regurgitation or vomiting,
pain when swallowing and dysphagia (see Esophageal
Dysmotility, earlier). Occasionally, excessive grass eating
and cough are also reported in dogs.
The frequency of duodenogastric reflux in dogs is
unclear. However, it has been proposed to lead to bilious
vomiting syndrome (BVS), which is characterized by
vomiting of bile and mucus after a prolonged fasting
period.
Accelerated gastric emptying is rarely a problem leading to clinical signs in dogs, but is hypothesized to be the
cause of vomiting in hyperthyroid cats. Acute infectious
or obstructive diseases of the gastrointestinal tract can
also lead to secondary hyperperistalsis of the stomach,
but hypoperistalsis, vomiting/retching, and diarrhea are
more frequent presenting complaints.
Other signs of gastric dysmotility or its underlying
causes can include anorexia, belching, pica, weight loss
or abdominal pain. In animals with dysautonomia,
­gastric hypomotility is one of many problems due to denervation of the autonomous nervous system. Hence,
other clinical signs typically associated with this disease,
such as dry eyes and nose, mydriasis, regurgitation, and
constipation, are often predominant.
Physical examination findings can range from no
detectable abnormalities to the presence of an enlarged
abdomen (gastric distension), decreased or increased
bowel sounds, and nonspecific/cranial abdominal pain.
Rarely, neuromuscular abnormalities may also be
observed if severe metabolic or systemic derangements
(electrolyte abnormalities, dysautonomia) are present.
Causes of Gastric Dysmotility
Delayed Gastric Emptying

Delayed gastric emptying is probably underdiagnosed in
both dogs and cats, especially in cases where no obvious
obstruction of gastric outflow is present. Mechanical
obstructions (gastric neoplasia, hyperplasia, polyps, foreign material) are usually easy to diagnose based on
history, physical examination and diagnostic imaging
­
procedures and are not further discussed in this chapter.
However, diagnosis of functional problems (due to either
local or systemic disorders) is not as straightforward.
A number of primary causes of functional gastric stasis
have been described in the dog, including infectious and/
or inflammatory diseases, peptic ulcers, and following
surgical procedures. Systemic disorders suspected to
affect gastric motility include electrolyte disturbances
(especially hypercalcemia, hyper‐ or hypokalemia), disorders of acid–base balance, septicemia, pancreatitis,

peritonitis, systemic inflammatory response syndrome
(SIRS), dysautonomia, and metabolic diseases such as
diabetes mellitus
Gastric dilation‐volvulus (GDV) in large and giant dog
breeds has been speculated to be caused by delayed gastric emptying, but evidence for the influence of size or
weight on gastric emptying times and the presence of
gastric dysmotility in dogs with GDV is controversial.
Diseases of the large intestine (e.g., colitis, constipation) can potentially also delay gastric emptying via
reflex mechanisms.
The clinical importance of gastric emptying disorders
in the cat is unknown. There are a few case reports of
delayed gastric emptying in cats with rare conditions
such as pylorospasm, hyperplastic gastropathy, and
dysautonomia. Delayed or dysfunctional gastric emptying is suspected in conjunction with conditions like diabetes mellitus, pancreatitis, and inflammatory bowel
disease (IBD) but specific investigations into these diseases as causes of gastric dysmotility in cats are lacking.
Retrograde Transit

Gastroesophageal reflux disease and duodenogastric
reflux are retrograde transit disorders. Neither of these
conditions has been extensively investigated in small animals. GERD is more often associated with diseases of the
esophagus or the distal esophageal sphincter, and occurs
most commonly during or after general anesthesia.
Duodenogastric reflux can lead to BVS (also called
fasting vomiting) in dogs. Clinical signs of BVS improve
in most cases by changing the feeding regimen (frequent
feeding of small meals) and administration of prokinetics
and gastroprotectants. This suggests an underlying
abnormality in gastrointestinal motility, but no further
investigations have been performed to date. No reports
exist of duodenogastric reflux in cats apart from its
occurrence with experimental devascularization and
ulceration of the stomach.
Accelerated Gastric Emptying

Accelerated gastric emptying (for example, in acute
infectious or obstructive disease) is usually associated
with hypermotility of the entire GI tract; hence diarrhea
can be the predominant problem, or occur alongside
other clinical signs. Isolated hypermotility of the stomach has not been reported in dogs.
Diagnostic Tests to Assess Gastric Motility
and Emptying
Several methods have been used to assess gastric motility – especially gastric emptying times – in small ­animals.
Their diagnostic usefulness and availability for the practitioner are summarized in Table 53.1.

Diagnostic Imaging for Gastric Motility Disorders
in Routine Veterinary Practice

Plain abdominal radiographs showing liquid or solid gastric contents after a fasting period of >6–8 hours in the
dog and >4 hours in the cat should raise the suspicion of
delayed gastric emptying. If no obvious cause can be
identified, serial radiographic imaging after oral administration of contrast media (i.e., liquid barium sulfate,
iodinated contrast) can be performed (for the full protocol see section on small intestinal dysmotility later).
This method only evaluates emptying of liquid contents, which is less relevant, and can appear normal even
though emptying of solids is impaired. Liquids (including neat barium) should be emptied from the stomach
within three hours in dogs and within 60 minutes in cats
(50–70% of cats have an empty stomach at 15 and 30
minutes, respectively). Completion of gastric emptying
when barium is mixed with food can be variable in both
dogs and cats (4–16h), and barium can separate from the
food, making this method unreliable to assess solid‐
phase gastric emptying in small animals.
Barium‐impregnated polyethylene spheres (BIPS)
were originally designed to mimic solid‐phase gastric
emptying and to detect GI obstructions. They are commercially available in two sizes (1.5 and 5 mm diameter),
with the smaller theoretically being emptied with
­digestive contractions and the larger with interdigestive
­motility. Attempts have been made to assess gastric emptying times using BIPS in both dogs and cats, but the
data are not reliable. In one study using dogs, the time to
emptying of half the administered BIPS from the stomach was nearly twice as long as that of simultaneously
administered, radiolabeled food. In cats, gastric emptying

of 1.5 mm BIPS also did not parallel “true” gastric emptying of a solid radiolabeled meal, but rather assessed
interdigestive motility. Therefore, interpretation of solid‐
phase gastric emptying with BIPS cannot be recommended in small animals.
Technologic advances have facilitated the availability
and feasibility of using abdominal ultrasonography to
assess gastric emptying. Even though gastric motility can
be visualized with ultrasound and the frequency of antral
contractions has been reported in healthy dogs (4–6/min
during emptying), no standardized protocol to assess
gastric emptying is available. Also, as this method is
based on the estimated change in antral volume, it might
not accurately reflect gastric emptying if antral contents
are moved into the fundus by the antral contractions.
This procedure requires a skilled operator and the
administration of a test meal or liquid of a defined volume, which can be challenging in veterinary patients. At
this stage, ultrasound cannot be recommended to assess
gastric emptying in a routine setting.
Diagnostic Tests Currently Restricted to Referral
Centers or Research Facilities

Radioscintigraphy is considered the gold standard
method to assess gastric emptying and has been used in
a number of studies to determine physiologic gastric
emptying times and validate new tests. Due to the need
for special facilities and equipment, this technique is not
often applied in small animal patients. Most commonly,
99m
technetium bound to tracer substances to avoid GI
absorption (i.e., albumin colloid) is used. “Dual isotope”
methods where solid‐ and liquid‐phase gastric emptying
are assessed simultaneously (using both 99mtechnetium

VetBooks.ir

53 Motility Disorders of the Alimentary Tract

and 111indium) have also been described. Typical gastric
half‐emptying times when using canned food are around
70 minutes in dogs and 2–4 hours in cats.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed
tomography (CT) imaging have so far not been used in
veterinary patients to assess gastric emptying, although
these modalities have been used in human patients. One
complicating factor might be the need for sedation or
general anesthesia, which can influence GI motility.
Some protocols for sedation have been evaluated regarding their influence on gastric emptying, but the results
are inconsistent, especially in cats. In dogs, a combination of acepromazine and butorphanol was shown to significantly prolong GI tract emptying times and decrease
motility.
Noninvasive methods to detect smooth muscle
contractions based on measurement of changes in
electrical resistance across the epigastric region after
ingestion of a test meal using standard ECG electrodes have been assessed in dogs. Because of the
sensitivity of these methods to artifacts induced by
even slight body movements, their future application
in dogs and cats is probably confined to research
purposes.
Methods that might have potential to be used in a routine clinical setting involve plasma or breath tracers. The
paracetamol (acetaminophen) absorption test has been
described for assessment of liquid‐ and solid‐phase gastric emptying. Plasma drug concentrations are measured
in serial blood samples after ingestion of paracetamol in
solution, and the rate of gastric emptying is related to the
appearance of paracetamol in the blood, as it is poorly
absorbed from the stomach but rapidly from the
­duodenum. However, this test has so far only been used
in a research setting and not been validated against
scintigraphy.
Breath tests have been studied comparatively well to
assess gastric emptying in dogs and to a lesser degree in
cats. These tests involve the ingestion of a stable 13C‐
labeled substrate which is rapidly absorbed (e.g., octanoic acid or sodium acetate) and metabolized to 13CO2,
which is then detectable in exhaled breath. The test protocol is simple, labelled tracers are comparably cheap
and no special equipment or expertise is required. Breath
samples can be collected from animals with a facemask,
which does not involve excessive restraint. Samples can
be stored for up to 60 days in sealed containers and can
be sent to the laboratory for analysis, where the 13C:12C
ratio is determined by infrared or mass spectrometry.
From these data plotted against time, gastric emptying
times and coefficients can be calculated. Normal gastric
half‐emptying times determined by breath test are
around 2.7–3.4 hours in dogs and four hours in cats. 13C‐
breath tests show acceptable to good correlation to

­scintigraphy and ultrasonography, respectively, in dogs
and good correlation compared to scintigraphy in cats.
Treatment of Gastric Dysmotility
No guidelines for the appropriate indication, combination, and duration of motility‐modifying therapies for
gastric emptying disorders are available. Due to the diagnostic challenges discussed above, correct assessment of
most gastric motility disorders or any therapeutic effect
is difficult. It is important to investigate, diagnose, and
treat any underlying disease leading to dysmotility before
motility‐modifying drugs are administered (Table 53.2).

­Motility Disorders of the Small
Intestine
Small intestinal (SI) motility ensures the efficient absorption of nutrients (mixing of chyme with digestive
enzymes, optimal contact of ingesta with the intestinal
mucosa) and orderly aboral movement of content,
including indigestible residues. Motility is also critical in
preventing bacterial translocation, which is achieved by
constant net aboral flow of luminal contents and the unidirectional “valve” function of the ileocecal junction,
preventing backflow of cecal contents.
Physiology of Small Intestinal Motility
Similar to gastric motility, physiologic motility of the SI
in dogs consists of digestive contractions (uncoordinated
circular segmentation and highly coordinated propulsive
peristalsis) and interdigestive motility (interdigestive
migrating motility complexes [IDMMCs]). In cats,
IDMMCs do not exist; instead, they show migrating
spike complexes that are less vigorous than the canine
counterpart.
Dogs have been extensively used to understand the
physiology of intestinal motility, the importance of neurotransmitters, hormones, and other polypeptides and
the effect of different dietary components on GI transit
times. Very little of the information gained from experimental studies in dogs can be directly translated into
v­ eterinary practice.
There is evidence for breed and/or size differences in
GI transit times in dogs, with larger breeds showing
longer transit times compared to miniature breeds. This
might be partially due to the relative size of the GI tract
compared to body weights: the GI tract of dogs >60 kg
comprises 2.8% of their total body weight, compared to
7% in small‐breed dogs (<5 kg). Hence, breed and age
characteristics must be taken into account when assessing SI or total GI transit times.

Clinical Signs of Hypo‐ and Hypermotility
of the Small Intestine
Clinical signs of small intestinal dysmotility can be variable, and heavily depend on the underlying cause.
Assessing the animal’s signalment and taking a thorough
history including any drug administration, potential for
accidental ingestion of medication(s), toxins or foreign
material, vaccination status, contact with other animals,
recent surgical procedures, etc. can help to initially classify the possible problem.
Local diseases (within the abdominal cavity or the GI
tract) are more likely to cause clinical signs obviously
associated with intraabdominal organs, ileus or GI
obstruction (abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, but
also anorexia, constipation) whereas systemic diseases
can present with a variety of signs not necessarily immediately associated with the GI tract (e.g., mydriasis, dry
nose and eyes, and prolapse of the third eyelid in dysautonomia or generalized neuromuscular signs in muscular dystrophy).
Physical examination in patients with signs of GI dysmotility can be variable and depend on the underlying
problem. Signs can be unspecific (lethargy, poor body
condition), point towards a local intraabdominal process
(nausea, abdominal pain, distension, mass, fluid‐filled
intestines) or be suggestive of a more generalized systemic problem (generalized weakness, neurologic abnormalities). Depending on the severity of fluid losses
through vomiting and/or diarrhea, clinical signs can also
be dominated by dehydration or hypovolemia (circulatory shock) or even SIRS.
Diseases Associated with Dysmotility
of the Small Intestine
Most reports regarding SI motility focus on functional or
mechanical GI ileus. Ileus is defined as the inhibition of
propulsive bowel activity, irrespective of the pathogenic
mechanism.
In small animals, SI ileus due to a primary (systemic or
local) neuropathy or neuromuscular disease is much less
common than secondary ileus, for which the causes are
multiple.
Dysautonomia and Other Neuromuscular Diseases

Dysautonomia is a generalized neuropathy first described
in cats in the United Kingdom. Subsequently, this disease
has been documented worldwide in dogs and cats. It is
characterized by generalized autonomic dysfunction
with megaesophagus/esophageal hypomotility, gastric
and small intestinal distension/hypomotility, and urinary
bladder distension. Degenerative lesions are found in
autonomic ganglia, the spinal cord and axons, but the

cause for these changes is unknown. Diagnosis is based
on typical clinical signs, ophthalmic pilocarpine test and
(postmortem) histopathology. Supportive care (with or
without chronic topical piloacarpine) is the only treatment option. Prognosis is grave in most cases.
Muscular dystrophy has been described in the golden
retriever (X‐linked genetic disorder), rarely other dog
breeds and cats, and is primarily characterized by progressive muscular weakness. It is typically caused by
mutations in the dystrophin gene responsible for muscle
structure and metabolism. Affected dogs and cats show
hypertrophy of skeletal musculature, tongue, diaphragm,
esophagus and sartorius muscle and atrophy of others.
Clinical signs apart from muscle weakness and tremor
include dysphagia, gastroparesis, abdominal pain, and
intestinal distension. In one postmortem canine study,
petechial hemorrhages, ecchymosis, and ulceration of
the gastric mucosa and generally dilated intestinal loops
were described, which was suggested to be indicative of
decreased intestinal transit. Most dogs die of cardiac or
respiratory failure within 8–9 months.
One case of visceral myopathy in a 6‐month‐old
domestic shorthair kitten with a six‐day history of anorexia, vomiting, and diarrhea has been reported. Severely
dilated loops of hypomotile intestine were found and
20 cm of jejunum was resected. On histopathology, the
distal jejunum showed a markedly atrophic longitudinal
muscle layer with focal degeneration, calcification, loss
of myocytes, and replacement by fibroblasts. The cat was
alive and doing well 20 months after surgery.
Postoperative Ileus and Short Bowel Syndrome

Postoperative ileus, defined as “ileus that develops following abdominal surgery, typically resolving spontaneously with 2–3 days,” is more frequent in humans than
dogs and has not been reported in cats. Laparotomy and
manipulation of the viscera are the main postulated etiologies but other factors, such as anesthetic agents or
postoperative opioid administration, can contribute.
Diagnosis can be based on clinical signs such as nausea,
vomiting, intestinal distension and abdominal pain and
via the exclusion of other causes of functional ileus (e.g.,
metabolic disorders, renal injury, septic peritonitis, pancreatitis, obstruction) postoperatively. Treatment consists of intermittent orogastric or permanent nasogastric
tube placement to empty the stomach of excess fluid and
gas, early postoperative (“trickle”) feeding, as this might
stimulate coordinated propulsive activity of the GI tract,
and the administration of prokinetics. Prognosis is generally good to excellent.
Short bowel syndrome is defined as malabsorption due
to insufficient intestinal surface area to an extent that
fluid and nutrients to sustain life cannot be absorbed
without specific nutritional support. There is evidence of

VetBooks.ir

53 Motility Disorders of the Alimentary Tract

dysmotility of the remaining parts of the GI tract, with
reduction of slow waves and disappearance of interdigestive motility. Clinical signs usually consist of watery diarrhea, steatorrhea, polyphagia, and weight loss. Total
parenteral nutrition and aggressive medical management are often necessary in the early postoperative
period, until oral feeding can counterbalance the nutritional needs. Stabilization of intestinal function should
start within 1–3 months after surgery. Complete recovery occurs within 3–12 months, but depends on the
extent of surgical removal of intestinal segments, with
early reports demonstrating a poor prognosis in some
cases with massive resections (74–88%).
Intestinal Pseudoobstruction

Intestinal pseudoobstruction or functional paralytic
ileus is characterized by the presence of chronic intestinal dilation and dys‐ or amotility in the absence of
mechanical obstruction. Only 12 cases of chronic intestinal pseudoobstruction have been reported in small animals (10 dogs and two cats) that showed clinical signs of
chronic intestinal disease (anorexia, intermittent vomiting, diarrhea). Diagnosis was based on abdominal imaging with radiographs showing generalized intestinal
dilation but no evidence of mechanical obstruction.
Histopathology showed some recurrent common features in dogs such as atrophy or complete loss of smooth
muscle fibers (n = 10), moderate to severe lymphoplasmacytic or mixed inflammation of the muscular layers (n
= 7) with predominantly T cells being present (n = 4),
and varying degrees of fibrosis/sclerosis (n = 6). In one
dog, severely hyperplastic smooth muscle of the lamina
propria and thickening of the muscularis mucosae were
reported. In cats, the histologic picture was somewhat
different: even though muscle atrophy was present, this
was true only for the longitudinal muscle layers in certain segments of the jejunum in one cat. Seven out of the
10 dogs were euthanized due to progressive disease
within days to five weeks after diagnosis.
Secondary Small Intestinal Hypomotility

Dogs and cats frequently suffer from obstructive intestinal diseases (foreign bodies, bezoars, neoplasia, volvulus), hence these conditions – together with neoplasia
and intussusceptions – should always be considered as
potential cause of dysmotility.
Few large‐scale reports examining clinical abnormalities, causes, prognostic factors, and outcome in small
animals with mechanical ileus are available. Of 704
examined cases, the average age was 4 years for dogs and
3 years for cats, with 60% being male. Mean duration of
illness before presentation was four days and most common symptoms included inappetence, vomiting, lack of
defecation, and abdominal pain. Mechanical ileus due to

a solitary foreign body obstruction (plastic balls, stones,
textiles) was the most common cause (69 cats and 338
dogs) followed by a linear foreign body (35 cats, 43 dogs)
and neoplasia (24 cats, 195 dogs). Less common causes
were intussusception, ileal obstipation, intraabdominal
inflammatory or neoplastic adhesions, volvulus, incarcerations of intestinal loops, idiopathic intestinal paralysis, intestinal diverticula, and parasitic infections.
Diagnosis (history of foreign body ingestion, physical
examination revealing abnormal intestinal palpation,
diagnostic imaging confirming the suspicion of obstruction/ileus) is usually straightforward and the optimum
treatment depends on the localization, size, material or
underlying cause (i.e., neoplastic) of the obstruction. In
most cases (>90%), surgical intervention is necessary.
Long‐term‐survival can be achieved in >80% of patients.
A longer duration of clinical signs, presence of a linear
foreign body (as opposed to a discrete one), multiple
­surgical procedures/incisions of the intestine and intestinal perforation have been associated with increased
mortality, whereas neither the degree of obstruction
(partial or complete) nor the location of the foreign body
had an effect on survival.
Obstruction due to neoplasia carries a much graver
prognosis, with median survival times of six months for
dogs and seven days for cats.
Intussusception is frequently found in young animals
and often associated with parvoviral enteritis or other
forms of acute gastroenteritis. There is some evidence
for a breed predisposition in the German shepherd dog
and pure‐breed/pedigree cats. Prognosis is good if surgical reposition or resection is successful.
Functional SI dysmotility can be secondary to any type
of infection or inflammation of the GI tract or within the
abdominal cavity. Both hypo‐ and hyperperistalsis can
occur, but reports of hyperperistalsis are scarce.
Parvoviral enteritis is the classic example of functional
ileus secondary to infection. Generalized atony of the
intestinal tract with distended and fluid‐filled intestinal
loops is a frequent finding on ultrasonography (75%) and
weak peristaltic contractions indicative of functional
ileus were observed in most of the remaining cases.
Sepsis or other serious medical illnesses requiring
hospitalization in the intensive care unit (ICU) are
­
known to be associated with gastrointestinal dysfunction
in people. Both gastric and small intestinal motility is
delayed in human ICU patients, which may lead to intolerance of enteral nutrition and increased risk of aspiration. Additionally, acute stress‐induced gastropathy and
ischemic colitis (both associated with risk of hemorrhage) is a common finding in human ICU patients. In
the authors’ experience, similar syndromes and complications also exist in small animals admitted to the ICU.
We routinely and regularly assess the grade of gastric

571

VetBooks.ir

572

Section 6 Gastrointestinal Disease

­filling in our ICU patients (especially patients with sepsis, SIRS, on mechanical ventilation, and those with
increased risk of aspiration pneumonia) semiquantitatively via ultrasonography. If there is sufficient suspicion
of GI hypomotility (gastric distension), prokinetic drugs
like prucalopride or erythromycin are administered
early. If oral medication is not tolerated, rectal administration can be tried. Even though the authors subjectively
think this type of management decreases the risk of aspiration pneumonia and other complications, there is at
this time no objective evidence that these interventions
influence outcome of small animal ICU patients.
Acute pancreatitis causes substantial damage to the GI
tract in people and rodent models. Usually, this is associated with acute necrosis, ischemia, and bleeding, but
varying degrees of dysmotility have also been documented, likely due to cytokines being produced as part of
the local inflammatory process. In dogs, the typical clinical signs associated with acute pancreatitis (vomiting)
and the severity of abdominal inflammation in some
patients suggest that GI dysmotility or ileus is commonly
present. However, no data regarding GI dysmotility in
pancreatitis in small animals are available.
There is some evidence that both acute kidney injury
(e.g., in leptospirosis) and chronic kidney disease have an
inhibitory function on orderly intestinal motility. In
other conditions, GI dysmotility is suspected but not
proven. One example is diabetes mellitus, where altered
levels of neuropeptides have been documented in experimental animals. However, even in humans, the exact
mechanism for small intestinal dysmotility in this endocrinopathy is not well understood. So far, no consistent
correlation between changes in enteric neurotransmitters, numbers of ICCs (decreased markedly in one
­neuroanatomic human case report) and manometric or
transit observations has been detected.
It is likely that (gastro)intestinal dysmotility is also
­present in other chronic conditions such as IBD, canine
idiopathic large bowel diarrhea (CILBD), hepatitis/
hepatopathies, etc. Unfortunately, no study investigating
GI motility in these conditions in dogs and cats is
available.
Iatrogenic and Toxic Causes of Gastrointestinal
Ileus

Intestinal dysfunction is a common side‐effect when
­opioid mu‐ and delta‐agonists are administered as analgesics. Most commonly, constipation and vomiting are
observed. This can occur immediately after the first dose
and persist for the duration of therapy. In most cases,
discontinuation of opioid treatment is sufficient to
improve intestinal function. Occasionally, laxatives and
other therapies may be used additionally to treat
constipation.

A variety of toxins (e.g., mercury, thallium, lead), pharmaceuticals (antibiotics like lasalocid, nitrofurantoin,
salinomycin), pesticides (e.g., organophosphates),
organic solvents and other chemicals (e.g., acrylamide,
hexacarbons) have been reported to cause peripheral
neuropathies, which might include ileus or other forms
of dysmotility of the GI tract (i.e., megaesophagus, etc.)
although these are infrequently seen and poorly
documented.
Diagnostic Tests to Assess Small Intestinal
Motility or Transit Times
The outcome of SI motor activity depends on the patterning of contractions in both space and time; that is,
where and when do the contractions occur with respect
to each other? Methods to assess these relationships
must address substantial technical challenges to gather
functionally relevant information.
Diagnostic Imaging Procedures for Small Intestinal
Transit Studies

Contrast studies of the SI are the most commonly used
method to assess transit time or to search for intestinal
obstruction in small animals. Neat liquid barium sulfate,
ionic or nonionic organic iodine contrast media or, less
frequently, contrast mixed with semisolid food is administered orally. The recommended dosage for liquid barium is 6–16 mL/kg body weight, with the high end of the
dose range for cats and small dogs and the lower end for
large dogs. The protocol for performing a contrast study
of the GI tract in dogs and cats is summarized in Box 53.1.
Usually, the final radiograph is taken after 12 hours to
check the complete gastric and SI evacuation of contrast.
Barium‐impregnated polyethylene spheres (see above)
have also been used for SI transit studies. The sensitivity
and specificity of this method, however, is low.
Contrast fluoroscopy is used in human medicine to
detect mucosal disease and stenoses that may induce
secondary changes in motility, transit, and absorption.
However, this technique is insensitive for the direct
detection of abnormal transit times. Observation times
are limited (radiation exposure) and once the majority of
contrast has entered the small intestine, overlying loops
of bowel hinder the interpretation. Fluoroscopy has not
been reported for assessment of small bowel transit in
small animals.
Ultrasonographic assessment of small intestinal motility is challenging due to observer variability, interference
from intraluminal gas and the difficulty of finding objective measures to assess contractions. Even though two
studies found that Doppler ultrasound techniques
(pulsed‐wave and duplex Doppler, respectively) allow
graphic visualization and qualitative and quantitative

analysis of intestinal motion in dogs, these procedures
are rarely used in routine practice.
Scintigraphy can potentially be used to assess small
intestinal transit times. However, unless the test substance is delivered past the pylorus, this technique also
includes gastric emptying. Therefore, scintigraphy is
usually imprecise about actual small intestinal transit
time and more accurately assesses orocecal transit time.
In small animals, scintigraphy has rarely been used for
assessing small bowel transit alone. Dual‐scintigraphy
(using 99mtechnetium and 111indium) can be used to
assess whole‐bowel transit times. More recently, scintigraphy has been used to assess GI motility in comparison
to a wireless motility capsule, which gives accurate information about whole‐intestinal transit times and their
respective subsets.
Recording of Small Intestinal Muscle Contractions

These procedures are usually of an invasive nature
(implanted strain gauges or luminal manometers) or can
be used ex vivo only. As far as the authors are aware, no
attempts at noninvasive detection of electrical potentials
created by intestinal muscle contractions (as done with
moderate success for gastric emptying) have been reported
in small animals. It can be assumed, however, that they are
extremely prone to artifacts created by patient movement.
Breath Tests and Other Tracer Tests

The lactulose or hydrogen breath test, which is the breath
test most widely used to assess SI transit in humans, has
also been applied to dogs. Nonabsorbable lactulose is
fermented, yielding H2 on reaching the colon. This
hydrogen gas is rapidly absorbed and exhaled.
Interpretation of hydrogen breath test results can be
complicated if carbohydrate malabsorption is present.
Additionally, the effect of diet is not entirely clear, hence
this test is not currently recommended for routine use.
Salicylazosulfapyridine has been administered orally,
intraduodenally or intracecally in experimental dogs as a
SI tracer substance; the detection of its metabolite sulfapyridine in plasma correlates with SI transit time. Apart
from drug metabolism studies, this tracer has not been
used in a clinical setting or in dogs with GI diseases.
Treatment of Small Intestinal Dysmotility
Treatment of small bowel dysmotility is usually targeted
to the specific etiology. Intestinal obstruction should be
relieved surgically as soon as the patient is stable enough
for general anesthesia. If infection, inflammation or sepsis is suspected, a search for the underlying cause,
depending on the predominant clinical signs, followed
by appropriate treatment should be initiated. If intestinal
hypomotility is suspected to be drug induced, any

medication with the potential to adversely affect GI
­
motility should be discontinued.
Supportive treatment is mandatory to maintain fluid
and electrolyte balance and perfusion of vital organs.
Prokinetics (Table 53.2) should be used cautiously and
only if elimination of the inciting cause and supportive
treatment is not sufficient to restore SI motility. Especially
in severe infectious enteritis, prokinetics are not recommended, as they might increase the risk for intussusception or volvulus. In postoperative ileus, however, or in
patients requiring long‐term intensive care, prokinetic
agents have a place to decrease hospitalization time and
co‐morbidities such as aspiration pneumonia. Intestinal
stasis in severely ill patients increases the risk of intestinal
bacterial translocation, hence cautious feeding of small
energy‐dense meals (depending on what the primary condition is and what the patient tolerates) and prokinetic
treatment can aid in maintaining small bowel function.

­Motility Disorders of the Large
Intestine
Physiology of Large Intestinal Motility
The large intestine is mainly responsible for the absorption of water and electrolytes, and storage of intestinal
content, as feces enter the colon in a liquid state. There
are three prominent patterns of colonic motility:
segmentation contractions which separate and mix the
ingesta, increasing the contact time with the mucosa
for absorption
●● antiperistaltic contractions propagating ingesta back
toward the ileum, again slowing down intestinal transit and allowing additional time for absorption
●● mass movements, which are unique to the large intestine. Also known as giant migrating contractions
(GMCs), the mass movement consists of strong and
prolonged peristaltic aboral contractions, which
­evacuate the entire large intestinal content.
●●

In contrast to the interdigestive phases, when the colon
shows no considerable motility, colonic contractions
increase significantly following a meal. These so‐called
gastrocolic and duodenocolic reflexes are controlled by
the enteric nervous system and ensure coordinated
movement and orderly evacuation of the GI tract with
the ingestion of a “new” meal.
Clinical Signs of Hypomotility
and Hypermotility of the Large Intestine
Large intestinal (LI) diarrhea is a manifestation of colonic
hypermotility and hypersecretion, typically characterized

Large intestinal hypomotility results in constipation,
which is defined as absent, infrequent or difficult

­defecation (tenesmus). In its most severe form, constipation leads to obstipation where impacted, hard and dry
feces make normal defecation impossible. Typically owners observe frequent attempts to defecate, tenesmus and
dyschezia (difficult or painful defecation) with little or

no feces produced. Animals might vocalize during
attempts at defecation. Other possible signs are anorexia,
lethargy, vomiting, and an abnormal stance (hunched
up). Infrequent passage of watery material and mucus,
which has bypassed the impacted feces, might be wrongly
interpreted as diarrhea.
Animals with LI diarrhea will frequently be normal on
physical examination, even though in some cases rectal
palpation might reveal irregular mucosal surface or rectal masses. Impacted feces and, depending on the severity of the problem, dehydration, abdominal pain, and
debilitation are findings in animals with decreased
colonic motility or obstruction resulting in constipation,
obstipation or even megacolon.
Diseases Associated with Dysmotility
of the Large Intestine
Increased Large Intestinal Motility

As increased LI motility is part of the manifestation of
every type of “colitis” (acute or chronic), the number of
underlying diseases is manifold. In dogs, this includes
infectious (e.g., Trichuris vulpis, toxins from Clostridium
perfringens infection, Prototheca zopfii) and noninfectious (e.g., food hypersensitivity) causes, diseases with
inflammatory (IBD, granulomatous colitis [GC] of boxers and bulldogs) or neoplastic infiltration of the colonic
wall, as well as a number of “idiopathic” disorders where
hypermotility is implicated as a primary cause; these
include fiber‐responsive colitis and CILBD. The latter is
also often called irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), spastic
colon, nervous/stress‐induced colitis or mucoid colitis.
In these dogs, inciting stressors can sometimes be identified (travel, changes in daily routine, loss of other pets or
family members). They can show submissive or anxious
behavior (urination, separation anxiety, fear of noise),
but tend not to be aggressive.
Canine idiopathic large bowel diarrhea is defined by
colonic dysfunction in the absence of identifiable structural, biochemical, or microbiologic abnormalities and
thus is a diagnosis of exclusion. While no studies have
shown a pathophysiologic mechanism in dogs, abnormal
myoelectrical activity leading to abnormal LI motility is
likely part of this disease in humans, in combination with
psychosocial factors, altered pain, and visceral reception.
The prevalence of CILBD ranges from as low as 5% to
26% in dogs. It is more commonly found in large breeds
and those under stress (police/customs, guide dog for
the blind, herding) or dogs that are easily overexcited.
Decreased Large Intestinal Motility

Constipation can be due to intestinal or systemic
problems. Intestinal causes are mostly obstructive
­
­(intraluminal [stricture, fecolith, tumor] or extraluminal

[prostatomegaly, pelvic fracture, perianal tumor, pseudocoprostasis]) or dietary (foreign material [bone, stones,
garbage, hair]) in origin. Systemic problems can be
caused by external factors (long inactivity, confinement
[hospitalization]), drugs (opioids, barium, sucralfate,
­calcium channel blocker, anticholinergic) or be part of
metabolic problems (dehydration, hypokalemia, hypercalcemia). Finally, neuromuscular dysfunction may also
result in decreased LI motility. Here, colonic hypomotility is frequently associated with lumbosacral spinal cord
problems (Manx cat deformity, neoplasia, degenerative
disease, injury) and feline idiopathic megacolon, and less
frequently with ganglioneuritis (one dog reported),
dysautonomy (Key–Gaskell syndrome), and canine
hypothyroidism.
Megacolon is more commonly seen in cats than dogs.
It is defined as persistently increased large bowel diameter, often as an end‐result of chronic constipation.
Idiopathic megacolon accounts for about two‐thirds of
all feline cases of constipation. Its etiopathogenesis is
incompletely understood, but dilation of the colon
appears to be due to functional disturbances of the
colonic smooth muscle cells. Lesions seem to begin in
the descending colon and then progress to involve the
ascending colon. Affected cats are usually middle‐aged
(mean 5–6 years) with males (70%) more commonly
affected. Repeated episodes of obstipation are often
reported. Diagnosis is reached when all other causes
(mechanical obstruction, inflammation, neoplasia) have
been excluded and typically involves neurologic assessment, diagnostic imaging studies (with and without
­contrast), and histopathology.
Assessment of Large Intestinal Motility or
Transit Times
Real‐time assessment of LI motility is difficult to perform and thus complete GI or orocecal transit times are
usually investigated.
Diagnostic Imaging Procedures Available
in Routine Practice

On survey radiographs, size and opacity of the LI are
extremely variable and formed feces are of a heterogeneous opacity. Nevertheless, a ratio of the maximal diameter of the colon to L5 length >1.48 is a good indicator of
feline megacolon (sensitivity 77%, specificity 85%).
Contrast radiographs after rectal administration of positive (barium) or negative (air) contrast media or their
combination (double contrast studies) might be indicated in animals with LI diarrhea or constipation to
exclude an obstruction but they do not show true LI
motility. The LI should not be assessed on a SI contrast
study as LI filling is incomplete and there is overlap with

VetBooks.ir

53 Motility Disorders of the Alimentary Tract

parts of the SI. LI contrast studies should also not be
done two hours after a cleansing enema, 6–12 hours
after colonoscopy and 3–4 days after full‐thickness
colonic biopsies. Ultrasound has so far not been investigated to evaluate LI motility.
Measurement of Gastrointestinal Transit Times

Different ways to assess LI motility or whole‐intestinal
transit have been employed, but are so far limited to
research purposes or require special equipment. The
simplest way to assess oroanal transit time is to feed plastic markers of different colors and recover them from the
feces. Different radiopaque markers have been used in
healthy dogs as well. Similar to assessment of gastric
emptying (see earlier), radioscintigraphy has also been
used to determine LI motility (e.g., with 111In). Recently,
total GI transit times and LI transit times were measured
with a wireless motility capsule system in dogs. Other
tests used in human medicine, such as colonic manometry or MRI, have so far only been used in experimental
dogs to assess LI motility and are not useful for routine
diagnostics.
Treatment of Large Intestinal Dysmotility
Treatment of Idiopathic Colitis and CILBD

Treatment of LI dysmotility secondary to infectious or
inflammatory colitis, neoplasia or mechanical impairment is directed towards the underlying cause.
Treatments for IBD with LI involvement, food hypersensitivity, fiber‐responsive colitis and CILBD overlap
­frequently, as all involve some form of dietary modification (see later). This also explains why definitive diagnosis and accurate separation of these disease entities can
be difficult.
Dietary modifications often include the change to a
novel protein (and possibly carbohydrate) source or a
hydrolyzed protein diet. Alternatively, increasing the
amount of dietary fiber or adding bulk‐forming agents
(e.g., a commercial high‐fiber diet or the addition of
­psyllium 1–3 tbsp/day or unprocessed wheat bran 1–5
tbsp/day) to the food also frequently leads to clinical
improvement.
Antibiotics usually have no place in treating “idiopathic” colitis. However, the authors have noticed that
some dogs improve with the administration of metronidazole or tylosin, similar to antibiotic‐responsive chronic
enteropathy/IBD, even if constipation or LI diarrhea are
the only presenting complaints.
Antiinflammatories can aid in controlling LI symptoms in some dogs. As in small intestinal forms of IBD,
this might include the administration of steroids (if all
other causes of clinical signs, especially infectious diseases, have been excluded), for example prednisolone

(1–2 mg/kg SID to BID) or budesonide (0.05–1 mg/kg/
day with the total dose not exceeding 3 mg q8h).
Alternatively, sulfasalazine (15–30 mg/kg BID to TID,
maximum 6 g/day) has been particularly useful in controlling idiopathic colitis in some dogs. However, this is
usually done on an empirical basis, and the decision
regarding which dogs can or need to be treated with
either of those antiinflammatory compounds is often
arbitrary.
When CILBD is suspected (and all other causes of colitis have been ruled out), treatment should start with
dietary modifications (fiber supplementation; see earlier). The remainder of treatment depends on the nature
of clinical signs (intermittent, alternation between constipation and diarrhea, abdominal pain/cramping) and
their suspected inciting cause. Different types of bulking
agents (psyllium, kaolin, pectin) can help in times of
diarrhea. Alternatively, motility modifiers or antispasmodics may be tried (Table 53.3). Antispasmodic drugs
might relieve some pain and sedatives reduce stress
effects. Most dogs only require treatment for a day to
two weeks, with some requiring long‐term treatment.
Stressors should be avoided and behavioral therapy can
be considered. Drugs modifying behavior, including amitriptyline, can be tried in refractory cases of CILBD (see
Table 53.3). The prognosis of CILBD is good, particularly
for dogs that respond to fiber supplementation.
Treatment of Constipation

Management of constipation depends on the severity
and the underlying cause, which should be addressed
first (mechanical obstruction, pelvic fracture, neurologic
disorder, etc.). If possible, drugs that may cause constipation (opioids, diuretics, antispasmodics, anticonvulsants,
sucralfate, NSAIDs) should be minimized or discontinued. In overweight animals, weight loss should be
encouraged and their activity increased. Cat litter boxes
should always be kept clean, to encourage defecation,
and water intake should be increased (availability of
water bowls, addition of water to food).
In addition, or as sole treatment in mild cases, dietary
modification is recommended. This can again consist of
bulk‐forming agents (high‐fiber diet, added psyllium or
bran) or the administration of lactulose or other laxatives
(see Table 53.3). A single enema or rectal suppository on
an outpatient basis can also be considered.
In more severe or refractory cases, manual removal of
impacted feces and several warm water enemas (in many
cases requiring general anesthesia) are necessary.
Adequate amounts of intravenous fluids need to be
administered to correct dehydration and possible electrolyte abnormalities and to prevent worsening of obstipation. Constipation is most commonly a recurring
problem and long‐term prophylactic measures (dietary

Chronic treatment of constipation and idiopathic
megacolon might require prokinetic treatment. Drugs
that show some effect on colonic motility include
cisapride and prucalopride. The influence of H2
receptor antagonists on colonic motility is not entirely
clear. Newer drugs that might have some positive
effect on colonic motility in dogs (lubiprostone, mirtazapine) have not been thoroughly tested in clinical
cases.
Subtotal colectomy should be considered in cases of
feline idiopathic megacolon refractory to conventional
(diet, laxatives) and prokinetic treatment.

­Prokinetics
Prokinetic drugs are divided into serotonergic 5‐HT4
agonists, motilin‐like drugs, dopaminergic D2 antagonists, H2‐receptor antagonists, and novel compounds
(see Table 53.2).
5‐HT4 Agonists
Drugs acting on gastrointestinal 5‐hydroxytryptamine
(5‐HT4 or serotonin) receptors have potent prokinetic
effects. Of the various 5‐HT4 agonists, cisapride has
been most extensively studied, but was withdrawn from
most of the European and US markets due to lethal
­cardiac side‐effects (torsade de pointes tachycardia) seen
in humans. Other 5‐HT4 agonists include mosapride
(available in Japan), prucalopride (available in the USA
and Europe), and tegaserod (also removed from the
­market for similar reasons as cisapride).
The gastric prokinetic properties of cisapride have
been documented in many experimental settings, but in
some studies, no effect on gastric emptying in dogs was
observed. In high doses (3 mg/kg), it can even slow emptying of solids.
Mosapride has been shown to restore gastric motility
in dogs with vincristine‐ or prednisolone‐induced g­ astric
hypomotility in healthy experimental dogs, but seems to
have no effect on the distal intestinal tract.
Prucalopride stimulated gastric emptying in a dose‐
dependent manner at relatively low doses (0.01–0.16 mg/
kg), stimulates physiologic gastrointestinal peristalsis/
defecation at higher doses (approximately 0.6 mg/kg)
and induces MMCs at still greater doses (around 1 mg/
kg) in dogs.
Naronapride (ATI‐7505) is marketed as a selective 5‐
HT4 agonist without the cardiac side‐effects in humans,
but only one study has assessed its gastric prokinetic
properties in dogs so far. It was found to be orally

bioavailable in dogs with an increase in coordinated
­
antral and small bowel contractility but little effect on
colonic motor activity.
Motilin‐Like Drugs
The antibiotic drug erythromycin accelerates gastric
emptying by inducing phase III contractions of the interdigestive MMCs, even when used in a subantibiotic
­dosage. These contractions are similar to those induced
by the endogenous gastrointestinal hormone motilin.
Several synthetic erythromycin derivates have been
developed; for example, EM574, which is 250 times more
potent than erythromycin itself in inducing MMCs and
has no antibacterial properties. Similarly, mitemcinal
(GM‐611) has been shown to accelerate gastric emptying
in healthy dogs as well as to improve delayed gastric
emptying in a canine model of diabetic gastroparesis.
Another synthetic erythromycin derivative, ABT‐229,
accelerates gastric emptying, motility index, and gastroduodenal coordination in a dose‐dependent manner.
This compound is around 40‐fold more potent than
erythromycin.
One potential complication that can arise from the
stimulation of interdigestive motility is that it can lead to
“dumping” of gastric contents into the duodenum before
they have been acidified and denatured appropriately.
This can then lead to inadequate absorption of nutrients
and osmotic diarrhea.
Dopaminergic D2 Antagonists
There is no convincing evidence that dopaminergic
D2 antagonists like metoclopramide and domperidone have prokinetic effects on the canine stomach,
even though metoclopramide in particular has been
advocated for this purpose for years. Consequently,
these drugs should not be used solely for this indication in dogs.
Metoclopramide has no effect on complete gastric
emptying times or corporeal contractions in experimental dogs. Regarding its effects on MMC disruption or
inhibition as well as antral contractions, study results are
inconsistent. When emptying of solid and liquid contents were assessed separately, metoclopramide slowed
solid gastric emptying (cooked liver), while accelerating
emptying of liquids (5% dextrose). There is some potential evidence from several studies that metoclopramide
might improve antropyloroduodenal coordination and
the frequency of pyloric and duodenal contractions in
experimental settings, possibly by enhancing acetylcholine effects. However, there was no acceleration of gastric
emptying in dogs after GDV surgery. Effects of metoclopramide might be dose dependent, as the standard dose

579

VetBooks.ir

580

Section 6 Gastrointestinal Disease

(0.2–0.4 mg/kg) did not reduce gastroesophageal reflux;
however, a high dose (1 mg/kg followed by a CRI with
1 mg/kg/h) reduced reflux. Thus, metoclopramide might
not be harmful in a dog with suspected gastric hypomotility, especially as nausea and vomiting might also be
present and its antiemetic effects via 5‐HT3 antagonism
are undisputed, but metoclopramide cannot induce a
strong prokinetic effect, particularly in cases with complete gastric atony.
Domperidone decreases the frequency of corporeal,
pyloric, and duodenal contractions and deteriorates
antropyloroduodenal coordination by decreasing the
frequency of contractions spreading from the antrum or
pylorus to the duodenum. It is therefore not indicated as
a prokinetic agent in the dog.
Itopride (Ganaton®, Abbott) is used to treat functional
dyspepsia in people. It is a prokinetic benzamide derivate, unlike metoclopramide and domperidone. This
drug has both antidopaminergic and antiacetylcholinesterase actions. Its gastroprokinetic dose, when administered intraduodenally in healthy experimental dogs, was
1–3 mg/kg while at doses of 10–100 mg/kg it inhibited
apomorphine‐induced vomiting. It seems to have similar
prokinetic effects to cisapride and mospride when given
orally.
Histamine H2‐Receptor Antagonists
Some H2‐receptor antagonists (ranitidine and nizatidine,
but not cimetidine or famotidine) have prokinetic effects
mediated by cholinergic mechanisms, especially on gastric smooth muscle or, in the case of ranitidine, also on
isolated small intestine.
The gastric prokinetic properties of ranitidine have
been assessed in both rodents and humans. However,
neither in healthy subjects nor in various diseases (gastric stasis in intensive care patients, peptic ulcers, and
others) have the effects on gastric emptying, gastric volume/retention or pH been consistent. Some studies
suggest acceleration of liquid gastric emptying times as
well as faster passage of a motility capsule, possibly
based on an increase in phase III motor activity. Other
studies show no effect on gastric motility, and two studies even demonstrate a dose‐dependent delay in gastric
emptying. In dogs, only a few studies are available
assessing the effect of ranitidine of gastroesophageal
reflux during anaesthesia (where it had no apparent

effect) or on GI transit times using a wireless motility
capsule (also no effect).
Nizatidine has also been studied extensively regarding
its gastric prokinetic properties in experimental rodents
and humans. Most studies seem to agree that it has more
consistent gastroprokinetic effects than ranitidine or
famotidine. In addition, it also enhances colonic peristalsis in humans. In experimental dog models, it was as
potent as cisapride in accelerating solid‐phase gastric
emptying, but clinical studies or extensive in vivo studies
in dogs are lacking.
Novel Prokinetic Compounds
Several new drugs and compounds have been tested
for their prokinetic properties in dogs. Some have a
defined mechanism of action, some are herbal extracts
where the principal component is not identified. This
includes DA‐9701 (marketed as Motilone® in Korea),
which is an extract from Corydalis tubers (a genus of
plants in the Papaveraceae family with about 470 species, also sometimes known as Chinese poppy) and
Pharbitis seeds (plants belonging to the Convulvulaceae
family and often used synonymously to morning glory,
which is another genus [Ipomoea]of this family). This
substance lead to improvement of gastric accommodation and increased postprandial volume in healthy
experimental dogs, but the effects on gastric emptying
are unclear.
Lubiprostone (Amitiza®, Mallinckrodt) is used in the
management of chronic idiopathic constipation or
inflammatory bowel disease with constipation in
humans. It is a selective type‐2 chloride channel (ClC‐2)
activator and hence increases chloride ion transport and
fluid secretion into the intestinal lumen. This compound
has been shown to accelerate gastric emptying in healthy
experimental dogs, as well as small bowel and colon
transit and interdigestive motility.
Mirtazapine (several brand names) is a noradrenergic
and serotonergic antidepressant used in small animals as
appetite stimulant. One study in healthy experimental
dogs has shown that it can accelerate gastric emptying
times when given at a high dose, but it is unclear if this
translates to a clinical setting yet.
To the authors’ knowledge, none of the drugs mentioned above have been used outside a research setting
or in spontaneously occurring disease in dogs.

Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency in Dogs and Cats
Panagiotis G. Xenoulis, Dr Med Vet, PhD
College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX

Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI) results from an
inadequate production of pancreatic enzymes from pancreatic acinar cells, leading to maldigestion and clinical
signs of weight loss, polyphagia, and diarrhea. There are
currently no studies estimating the prevalence of EPI in
the general canine and feline population, but EPI is considered the second most common disease of the exocrine
pancreas in small animals (after pancreatitis). Although
EPI is considerably more common in dogs than in cats, in
the past few years EPI has been diagnosed with increasing frequency in the feline population, likely due to
increased awareness of this condition in cats and the
availability of better tests for its diagnosis.

­Pathogenesis
In humans, it has been estimated that EPI occurs when
more than 90% of the exocrine pancreas (i.e., pancreatic acinar cells) is destroyed. When that happens, the functional
capacity of the remaining exocrine pancreas is inadequate
for the production and secretion of sufficient amounts of:
enzymes for the digestion of protein, fat, and
carbohydrate
●● bicarbonate for neutralization of gastric acid entering
the duodenum
●● pancreatic intrinsic factor for the absorption of
­cobalamin in the ileum
●● antimicrobial proteins for regulation of small intestinal microbiota.
●●

Therefore, EPI has multiple consequences.
The main consequence of EPI is deficient intraluminal
digestion of nutrients. This is mainly the result of
insufficient production and secretion of pancreatic
­
­proenzymes and enzymes by an inadequate number of
pancreatic acinar cells. However, this is not the only
mechanism leading to nutrient maldigestion and malabsorption in EPI. Studies have shown that there is also

altered a­ctivity of intestinal mucosal enzymes and
impaired intestinal function. In some cases, these
­functional abnormalities are accompanied by mucosal
pathology. Although the exact reason for these abnormalities is unknown, it is speculated that the lack of
trophic ­influence of pancreatic secretions, as well as bacterial overgrowth in the small intestine, may play a role.
In addition, acid injury of the intestinal mucosa may
occur, as a result of lack of neutralization of gastric acid
entering the duodenum.
Another major consequence of EPI is related to cobalamin absorption. The exocrine pancreas is a major source of
intrinsic factor in the dog and the main one in the cat.
Therefore, EPI leads to a significant reduction in or even
total absence of intrinsic factor in the intestinal lumen,
which in turn leads to cobalamin malabsorption and
cobalamin deficiency at both the intracellular and extracellular level. Overgrowth of cobalamin‐binding bacteria in
the small intestine may also be a contributing factor. Severe
cobalamin deficiency is typically recognized by low serum
cobalamin concentrations. Cobalamin deficiency has been
shown to have major biochemical implications (e.g., defective amino acid metabolism and DNA synthesis) and has
also been shown to be a negative prognostic factor in animals with gastrointestinal diseases, including EPI.
Alterations in the intestinal bacteria and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth are likely common in animals
with EPI due to the lack of antibacterial properties of
pancreatic secretions. Intestinal dysbiosis is believed to
contribute to clinical signs of EPI and might often be a
reason for treatment failure, especially when proper
antibiotic treatment is not used.

­Etiology
Current studies on the etiology of EPI in dogs have investigated specific canine breeds predisposed to developing
this disease. Therefore, information from those studies

Clinical Small Animal Internal Medicine Volume I, First Edition. Edited by David S. Bruyette.

Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/bruyette/clinical

VetBooks.ir

584

Section 6 Gastrointestinal Disease

involves certain breeds and may or may not hold true for
other breeds.
Most studies available to date have investigated the etiology and pathogenesis of EPI in German shepherd dogs
(GSD) and rough‐coated collies, and in those breeds EPI
is most commonly the result of pancreatic acinar atrophy
(PAA). In those breeds, PAA likely is the result of an
immune‐mediated condition resulting in atrophic lymphocytic pancreatitis, as evidenced by histopathology of
the pancreas in dogs during the development of PAA.
Eventually, this chronic inflammation, which is limited
to the exocrine portion of the pancreas, leads to total
destruction of pancreatic acinar tissue and PAA. In those
breeds, PAA is most likely acquired and almost certainly
has a genetic basis. The earlier belief that EPI in these
breeds has an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance
has been largely abandoned, and a polygenic inheritance
pattern is currently suggested. Genome‐wide association
studies in GSD have failed to identify any specific genes
or major loci associated with EPI, suggesting that EPI in
this breed might have several different genetic causes or
might be the result of multiple loci with small effects.
Further studies are required to identify the genes
involved in the development of PAA in GSD and other
dog breeds. In addition, the roles that various environmental factors might play in association with a predisposing genetic background have not been investigated.
Pancreatic acinar atrophy is typically considered to be
by far the most common etiology of EPI in the overall
canine population. Although PAA can be the cause of
EPI in any canine breed, other etiologies might be more
common in certain breeds. End‐stage chronic pancreatitis leading to pancreatic fibrosis is likely the most important etiology after PAA, and it has been reported as a
cause of EPI in several studies. Chronic pancreatitis can
be especially difficult to diagnose in dogs and cats and,
therefore, in most cases a diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis has not been reached by the time EPI is diagnosed. In
chronic pancreatitis, both endocrine and exocrine pancreatic cells may be destroyed and therefore EPI may be
accompanied by diabetes mellitus in some cases.
Recently, isolated pancreatic lipase deficiency has been
reported as a cause of EPI in dogs. In these cases, all other
pancreatic enzymes and proenzymes are synthesized and
secreted normally. Isolated pancreatic lipase deficiency
causes severe lipid maldigestion and malabsorption, leading to the typical signs of EPI despite the fact that there is
no deficiency in other pancreatic enzymes. The cause of
isolated pancreatic lipase deficiency in dogs is unknown.
Other possible causes of EPI in dogs include pancreatic duct obstruction, pancreatic hypoplasia or aplasia,
and pancreatic neoplasia. All of these are extremely rare
causes of EPI in dogs.
Chronic pancreatitis is believed to be the most common cause of EPI in cats. PAA has been reported in three

cats with EPI and is therefore believed to be a considerably less common cause of EPI in this species compared
to dogs. Other causes of EPI in cats may include pancreatic aplasia or hypoplasia, pancreatic tumors, isolated
deficiencies of pancreatic enzymes, and pancreatic duct
obstruction (for example, as a result of neoplasia,
Eurytrema procyonis infestation, and complications
from cholecystoduodenostomy surgery).

­Signalment
Dogs and cats of any breed can develop EPI. However,
certain groups are clearly predisposed. The most well‐
described breed predisposition for EPI involves the GSD.
Studies in North America and Europe have shown that
GSDs have increased prevalence of EPI, with this breed
representing approximately 60% of all cases of EPI. Other
breeds predisposed to EPI include rough‐coated collies,
Cavalier King Charles spaniels, cocker spaniels, West
Highland white terriers, and chow chows. No breed predispositions have been described for cats.
Dogs of almost any age can develop EPI, with a reported
age range extending from 3 months to 17 years. When
considering all dogs with EPI, the disease more commonly
appears in young adult dogs (median age 3 years). However,
within the group of dogs with EPI, there are subgroups
that have different ages of onset. Specifically, the onset of
the disease might be at an earlier age in certain breeds
(median 18 months for chow chows; median 3 years for
GSDs and rough‐coated collies) compared to other breeds
(median 7 years for Cavalier King Charles spaniels). These
differences may in part reflect differences in the etiology of
EPI; for example, EPI as a result of PAA typically develops
in young adult dogs (usually by the age of 5 years). EPI that
develops in older dogs (such as Cavalier King Charles
spaniels) might be more likely to be the result of chronic
pancreatitis rather than PAA, because more time is
believed to be required until pancreatic acinar cells are
destroyed as a result of chronic low-grade inflammation.
Cats of any age can develop EPI, with some cats diagnosed at less than 1 year of age. However, EPI is more
commonly diagnosed in middle‐aged to older cats, with
a mean age of 8 years.
Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency can occur in both
male and female dogs. Most studies agree that females
are slightly predisposed compared to males. No sex predilection has been reported for cats.

­Clinical Features
The classic and most common presentation of dogs with
EPI involves a chronic history of weight loss (Figure 54.1),
a normal or increased appetite, and diarrhea, which is

Figure 54.1 This dog presented with significant weight loss due
to EPI. The dog had lost 10 kg during the last few months. This is a
