might be seen. Other possible clinical signs include
coprophagia, borborygmus, flatulence, abdominal discomfort, and a poor hair coat. In some cases, EPI may be
subclinical and those cases can only be diagnosed with
appropriate laboratory testing (see section on Trypsin‐
Like Immunoreactivity). Dogs may remain in the subclinical phase for years or sometimes for life.
Cats with EPI have a similar presentation to dogs. In a
retrospective study of 150 cases of feline EPI, the most
common clinical sign was weight loss (which was often
the only clinical sign), followed by loose stools, poor hair
coat, anorexia, increased appetite, depression, watery
diarrhea, and vomiting. It is likely that many of these
clinical signs reflect concurrent diseases such as chronic
pancreatitis and inflammatory bowel disease. In cases
where chronic pancreatitis is the cause of EPI, polyuria
and polydipsia may be seen as a result of concurrent diabetes mellitus.

­Diagnosis
The diagnostic evaluation of animals suspected of having
EPI should always take into consideration the clinical
presentation, general clinicopathologic findings, and the
results of diagnostic modalities used to specifically assess
pancreatic structure, function, and pathology.
Routine Clinical Pathology
Findings of complete blood count (CBC), chemistry profile, and urinalysis are typically unremarkable in animals
with EPI. When present, routine blood test abnormalities (e.g., increased hepatic enzyme activities, hypoalbuminemia, hyperglycemia) reflect concurrent diseases
such as inflammatory bowel disease and diabetes
mellitus.
Trypsin‐like Immunoreactivity

Figure 54.2 The feces from the dog in Picture 1. The feces are
large in volume and semi-formed. This is a common finding in
dogs with EPI.

usually characterized by passage of large volumes of
semiformed feces (Figure 54.2). However, it is not
uncommon for some dogs with EPI to present with a
clinical picture that deviates from the classic presentation. In those cases, periods of anorexia, absence of
diarrhea, and occasionally watery diarrhea or vomiting

Trypsin‐like immunoreactivity (TLI) measures serum
concentrations of trypsin and trypsinogen and is the test
of choice for the diagnosis of EPI in dogs. This test is
highly sensitive and specific for the diagnosis of EPI.
Animals with EPI produce and secrete lower than n
­ ormal
amounts of trypsinogen in serum and therefore a subnormal TLI concentration (usually defined as <2.5 μg/L)
in an animal with compatible clinical signs is sufficient to
make a diagnosis of EPI. A TLI result well within the reference range is sufficient for excluding EPI in the vast
majority of cases, and a normal TLI result should direct
clinicians towards the investigation of other disorders
as the cause of the observed clinical signs.
One exception to this rule is the case of isolated pancreatic lipase deficiency, where the patient has EPI but

585

VetBooks.ir

586

Section 6 Gastrointestinal Disease

secretion of trypsin and trypsinogen is normal and
therefore serum TLI concentrations are also normal.
In these cases, the diagnosis of EPI is quite challenging.
The current assays for the measurement of pancreatic
lipase concentration (i.e., Spec‐cPL) are not suitable for
the accurate measurement of pancreatic lipase concentrations at very low concentrations, and therefore isolated pancreatic lipase deficiency cannot be diagnosed
using these assays. Although epidemiologic studies are
lacking, isolated pancreatic lipase deficiency in dogs is
considered to be an uncommon cause of EPI.
Single TLI results within the equivocal range (usually
between 2.5 and 5.7 μg/L) in dogs with clinical signs of
gastrointestinal disease need to be interpreted with
­caution. In these patients, subsequent retesting of serum
TLI may show either a normal concentration or progression to EPI. Therefore, patients with canine TLI (cTLI)
results in the equivocal range should be investigated for
chronic intestinal disease, while cTLI concentrations
should also be measured a few weeks later.
Some dogs with no clinical signs characteristic of EPI
have repeatedly subnormal (<5.7 μg/L) cTLI concentrations. These dogs have been shown to have subclinical
EPI and some, but not all, are expected to develop clinical EPI in the future. The time of progression from the
subclinical to the clinical disease varies greatly and
might be from a few months to years. Thus, these
patients should be closely monitored for the development of clinical signs of EPI and cTLI testing should be
repeated periodically. It should be noted that a single
serum cTLI concentration is not sufficient for diagnosing subclinical EPI.
Because renal disease might increase serum cTLI concentrations and obscure a diagnosis of EPI, reevaluation
of nondiagnostic serum cTLI concentrations in azotemic
dogs suspected of having EPI is recommended. Similarly,
concurrent pancreatitis might falsely increase the serum
cTLI concentration.
Due to the fact that EPI appears to be less common in
cats than in dogs, diagnosis of this disease has been less
well investigated and is more challenging in this species.
Similar to dogs, the feline TLI (fTLI) test appears to be
the most reliable test for the diagnosis of EPI in cats with
a specificity of at least 85%. The sensitivity of this assay
for the diagnosis of feline EPI has not been evaluated
to date. Although there are currently two assays that
measure fTLI in serum (one radioimmunoassay that is
available in the USA and one ELISA available in Europe),
only one of those assays (the radioimmunoassay) has
been reported to be analytically validated; this test is
available through the Gastrointestinal Laboratory at
Texas A&M University. Similar to dogs, it can be recommended that nondiagnostic serum fTLI concentrations
in azotemic cats suspected of having EPI be reevaluated,
because renal disease might falsely increase serum fTLI

concentrations. The same is true for cats with concurrently increased serum feline pancreatic lipase (fPLI,
Spec‐fPL) concentrations indicating pancreatitis.
Trypsin‐like immunoreactivity testing can be performed in animals that are already on enzyme supplementation without this affecting the results. TLI assays
are species specific and do not measure trypsinogen and
trypsin of other species.
Pancreatic Fecal Elastase
An ELISA for the measurement of pancreatic elastase in
feces is commercially available and is marketed in Europe
(Shebo Biotech, Germany) for the diagnosis of canine
EPI. It is considered to be specific for EPI, although a
recent study reported false‐positive results in 23.1% of
cases and the sensitivity of this test has not been sufficiently evaluated. The fact that this test is easy and quick
to perform might make it a reasonable initial approach
for dogs with suspected EPI, but a positive test result
must be verified by measurement of a serum TLI concentration. This test might also be useful for EPI cases
that are due to pancreatic duct obstruction. However, to
date such cases have only been anecdotally reported in
the veterinary literature.
Other Tests
Serum amylase and lipase activities have been shown to
have no value in the diagnosis of EPI in either dogs or
cats. Canine pancreatic lipase immunoreactivity concentrations are low or undetectable in most dogs with EPI,
but commercial assays for the measurement of serum
PLI concentration (Spec‐cPL and Spec‐fPL) are not useful for the diagnosis of EPI in dogs and cats, respectively,
because they have been optimized to detect changes in
the higher levels of their respective working ranges.
Measurement of the fecal proteolytic activity has been
used in the past for the diagnosis of EPI in dogs and cats.
A plethora of other tests, including microscopic examination of feces and the bentiromide absorption (BT‐
PABA) test, have also been used for the diagnosis of EPI.
These tests often give false‐positive and/or false‐negative results, and many of them are impractical, expensive
or of limited availability, and thus are not recommended
for the diagnosis of canine or feline EPI. However, these
tests may be useful in special cases where serum TLI
concentration is in the normal range (e.g., EPI due to
pancreatic duct obstruction) but EPI is heavily suspected
based on the clinical picture.
Histopathology
Exocrine pancreative insufficiency is a functional and
not a histopathologic diagnosis, and thus histopathology

VetBooks.ir

54 Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency in Dogs and Cats

is not indicated for the diagnosis of EPI in dogs and cats.
While it is believed that more than 90% of the pancreatic
parenchyma needs to be destroyed in order for clinical
signs of EPI to develop, it is almost impossible to accurately determine the extent of pancreatic atrophy either
grossly or histopathologically, and thus whether acinar
cell loss is leading to EPI. The utility of histopathology is
limited to determination of the underlying cause of EPI
(PAA or pancreatitis). Even then, in dog breeds that have
been shown to be predisposed to EPI due to acinar atrophy (i.e., German shepherds, rough‐coated collies), histopathology is redundant. Therefore, histopathology
should only be used in atypical cases where the cause of
EPI needs to be determined.

­Treatment
The vast majority of animals with EPI require lifelong
treatment with pancreatic enzyme supplementation,
with or without other treatments. Although pancreatic
enzymes are essential for digestion, alternative pathways
for digestion of some nutrients do exist and therefore
rare animals may compensate for the loss of pancreatic
enzymes and display only minimal clinical signs without
treatment.
Table 54.1 summarizes the treatment options for dogs
and cats with EPI.

Pancreatic Enzyme Supplementation
Pancreatic enzyme supplementation is the cornerstone
of EPI treatment in the vast majority of cases. There are
several different types of products that can be used for
the management of EPI in animals and differences in
efficacy may exist among them. Options generally
include enteric‐coated preparations, uncoated enzyme
powder (as powder or in capsules), and raw pancreas.
Most commercially available products contain pancreatic enzymes and proenzymes that are derived from porcine pancreas (in the form of dried extracts), while raw
pancreas (which also contains pancreatic enzymes and
proenzymes) is usually obtained from cattle or pigs.
Only a small proportion of the orally administered
pancreatic enzymes remains functionally intact by the
time they reach the small intestine. It has been reported
that up to 85% of pancreatic enzyme activity can be lost
in the stomach due to the acid pH and/or the action of
gastric pepsins. Therefore, enteric‐coated preparations
have been developed to protect the enzymes from degradation in the stomach. There has been considerable discussion regarding the comparative efficacy of different
products for the treatment of EPI. To add to the confusion, results of available studies have been conflicting.
An early study suggested that enteric‐coated preparations were less effective than uncoated preparations,
while a more recent study suggested that there was no

However, these studies were retrospective and uncontrolled. A more recent blinded, randomized, controlled
trial showed that dogs receiving an enteric‐coated pancreatic enzyme product responded better to treatment
compared to dogs receiving identical but uncoated product. Therefore, enteric coating seems to be beneficial,
although the results of this study may not be applicable
to all preparations of enteric‐coated pancreatic enzymes.
In a recent retrospective study of 150 cats with EPI, there
was no difference in the efficacy of different pancreatic
enzyme products suggesting that all products might be
similarly effective.
Fresh raw pancreas contains pancreatic enzymes and
can be used to effectively manage animals with EPI. Raw
pancreas should be fresh‐frozen in aliquots, and each aliquot should be used with one meal. Raw pancreas is
likely the most economical option for pancreatic enzyme
supplementation but it is also associated with certain
limitations. First, it can be difficult to obtain and inconvenient for most owners to process raw pancreas. More
importantly, raw animal tissues might be contaminated
with important pathogens (e.g., Salmonella spp.,
Campylobacter spp.) and may pose a risk for infection to
both humans and animals. For these reasons, raw pancreas is not commonly used for the treatment of EPI in
animals.
All dogs and cats with clinical EPI should receive pancreatic enzymes. Regardless of the product used, pancreatic enzymes are added to each meal. Preincubation of
the food with pancreatic enzymes is not necessary. The
starting dose varies depending on the manufacturer but
is usually titrated to individual patients after initial treatment and resolution of clinical signs. In many animals,
doses can be significantly reduced long term to the lowest effective dose. Enzyme supplementation therapy is
required for the rest of the animal’s life. Side‐effects from
pancreatic enzyme use are rare but may include oral
bleeding and irritation that typically resolve with dose
reduction.
Antibacterials
Some animals with EPI do not respond to pancreatic
enzyme replacement therapy alone. In a large percentage
of animals with EPI, this is believed to be partially due to
small intestinal dysbiosis and/or bacterial overgrowth
(SIBO), which might be present as a result of loss of the
bacteriostatic effects of pancreatic secretions and the
presence of excess undigested substrates that can be
used by intestinal bacteria. However, studies of antibacterial use in dogs with EPI have not shown improved
treatment response or prognosis consistently. In ­addition,

no studies have compared the efficacy of different
­antimicrobial agents in the treatment of dogs and cats
with EPI.
Because small intestinal dysbiosis/SIBO is believed to
be common in dogs with EPI and is notoriously difficult
to confidently diagnose, antimicrobials are usually used
in conjunction with pancreatic enzyme supplementation at the beginning of EPI treatment. Alternatively,
antimicrobials can be added to the treatment regimen
if there is poor response to treatment with pancreatic
enzymes alone. Antimicrobials commonly used
include metronidazole, tylosin, and oxytetracycline,
and are typically used for a minimum of 2–4 weeks
(see Table 54.1). Some animals might need multiple
courses of antibiotics throughout their lives. The role of
intestinal bacteria and dysbiosis is much less clearly
defined in feline EPI. Choices for antibacterial treatment in this species are similar to those in dogs, and
can be used in cases that do not respond to treatment
with pancreatic enzyme and cobalamin supplementation (see Table 54.1).
Cobalamin Supplementation
As mentioned previously, hypocobalaminemia and
cobalamin deficiency are especially common (>80% of
cases) in dogs and cats with EPI. Therefore, serum cobalamin concentrations should be measured in all animals
with EPI. Cobalamin deficiency can lead to various gastrointestinal and systemic complications, and severe
hypocobalaminemia has been reported to be a negative
prognostic factor in dogs with EPI and cats with chronic
gastrointestinal disease, that often co-exists with EPI in
this species. Cats with cobalamin deficiency have been
shown to have abnormalities in amino acid metabolism.
In a recent publication reviewing 150 cats with EPI,
cobalamin supplementation favorably affected the
response to treatment, even in cats with normal serum
cobalamin concentrations. Therefore, correction of
cobalamin deficiency is important in both dogs and cats
with EPI.
Because cobalamin deficiency can lead to cobalamin
malabsorption, oral supplementation of cobalamin was
considered not to be effective in dogs and cats with EPI.
However, recent evidence suggests that oral supplementation of cobalamin might be equally effective in these
cases. Cobalamin should be administered subcutaneously using the following dosage regimen: 250–1250 μg
(depending on the size of the animal) once a week for six
weeks, followed by an injection one month after that.
Oral cobalamin should be administered at 250 μg (cats)
or 250–1250 μg (dogs, depending on the size), daily,
for 8 weeks. Serum cobalamin concentrations should

VetBooks.ir

54 Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency in Dogs and Cats

be checked one month after the last dose and then
­monitored periodically (e.g., every six months) as some
animals may require repeated cycles or life‐long cobalamin supplementation.
Dietary Modification
There are two major dietary factors believed to be important in the management of dogs with EPI: the fat content
of the diet and the amount and type of dietary fiber.
Historically, it has been suggested that a fat‐restricted
diet should be offered to dogs with EPI because adequate
fat digestion and subsequent resolution of clinical signs
may not be achieved with enzyme replacement therapy
alone. One of the problems encountered with the use of
low‐fat diets in dogs with EPI is that weight gain could be
difficult and slow to achieve, especially in large‐breed
and cachectic dogs. In addition, low‐fat diets may contribute to deficiencies of fat‐soluble vitamins given the
fact that fat digestibility does not normalize after enzyme
supplementation.
Studies in dogs with EPI failed to show a clear benefit
of any diet (including low‐fat diets) over another. In fact,
different diets appeared to be more suitable for different
dogs, suggesting that several diets should be tried in
patients with EPI until the most appropriate one for a
specific animal is identified. Therefore, the routine and
exclusive use of fat‐restricted diets in all dogs with EPI is
not currently recommended. High‐fat diets should probably be avoided, however, at least during the initial stabilization phase. In some cases, there might be no need to
change the animal’s original diet, if it is complete and
balanced. The type of fat (e.g., long‐chain vs medium‐
chain triglycerides) also does not seem to play a crucial
role in the response to treatment.
It has been suggested by some authors that high‐fiber
diets should be used in dogs with EPI. However, there is
no convincing evidence in the literature for such recommendation. High‐fiber diets might prohibit weight gain in
hyporexic animals as a result of low caloric density.
In addition, certain types of fiber can impair the activity of
pancreatic and brush border enzymes, potentially leading
to reduced digestibility of nutrients. Therefore, high‐fiber
diets are currently not recommended in dogs with EPI.
No studies have evaluated the use of specific diets in
cats with EPI. Therefore, dietary recommendations are
based mainly on clinical experience and extrapolation
from clinical experience with dogs. Fat‐restricted diets
should be avoided if possible, for the same reasons mentioned above for dogs. In addition, cats are strict carnivores and protein and fat are their main energy sources,
while carbohydrates (which are often increased in fat‐
restricted diets) should be generally kept at low levels.

As in dogs, high‐fiber diets should probably be avoided
in cats with EPI.
Histamine‐2 Receptor Antagonists and Proton
Pump Inhibitors
Histamine‐2 receptor (H2 receptor) antagonists and proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) have been recommended by
some as adjunctive treatment in animals with EPI. A large
proportion of pancreatic enzymes, especially lipase, is
inactivated in the stomach due to low pH. It has been
hypothesized that acid‐suppressing medications may
reduce the hydrolysis of pancreatic enzyme supplements
in the stomach through the increase of gastric pH, thus
increasing efficacy. Obviously, this applies only to uncoated
enzyme supplements and raw pancreas. However, no
studies have evaluated the efficacy of acid suppression in
the treatment of EPI in dogs and cats, and therefore their
usefulness is questionable. In addition, the potential problem of reduced efficacy of enzyme ­supplements due to
hydrolysis in the stomach could be overcome by increasing the dose of enzymes or by using products with enteric
coating. Therefore, the routine use of acid suppression
medications is currently not recommended.

­Prognosis
Although clinical improvement is noted in the vast
majority of dogs and cats treated appropriately for EPI, a
percentage do not respond well to treatment for reasons
that have not been clearly defined. Good initial response
to treatment is seen in approximately 60% of dogs and
cats with EPI, with the remaining animals showing either
partial (~20%) or poor (~20%) response. Partial or poor
response is usually indicated by the animals remaining
underweight or having soft stools.
Median survival time for dogs with EPI has been
reported to be approximately five years. The most
important parameter that affects survival seems to be
initial response to treatment, with animals that have a
good ­initial response surviving on average almost eight
times longer than those with poor response. Therefore,
animals that respond well to initial treatment seem to
survive for long periods. As mentioned above, hypocobalaminemia has been shown to be a negative prognostic factor, and animals with severe hypocobalaminemia
survive half as long as animals without severe hypocobalaminemia. The nature and severity of clinical signs,
signalment, and different therapeutic interventions do
not seem to have important prognostic significance.
No data are available for survival and prognosis in cats
with EPI.

Pancreatitis in the Dog
Caroline Mansfield, BSc, BVMS, MVM, PhD, MANZCVS, DECVIM-CA
Melbourne Veterinary School, University of Melbourne, Melbourne, Australia

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Pancreatitis in the dog includes an array of presentations,
from low‐grade inflammation incidentally discovered to
animals with severe, life‐threatening systemic disease.
Clinically, veterinarians often use the term chronic pancreatitis (CP) to describe instances where the clinical
signs are mild, whereas acute pancreatitis (AP) is the
term used when there is greater severity and a rapid onset
of clinical signs. This clinical classification, h
­ owever, does
not always correlate with the histologic classification.
Histologically, AP is defined as neutrophilic inflammation, without fibrosis or exocrine atrophy, which is usually present within the body of the pancreas and/or
peripancreatic fat. There have been extensive experimental studies, predominantly in rodent models, of initiating events of AP. In essence, AP develops when inert
zymogens (precursors of digestive enzymes) are activated within pancreatic acinar cells rather than within
the duodenal lumen. If this occurs at a low level, safeguards such as pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor
(PSTI) come into play and mop up the activated pancreatic enzymes within the body of the pancreas. Once PSTI
is overwhelmed, there is an influx of proinflammatory
cytokines (especially interleukin‐8) and neutrophils.
Other inflammatory pathways are then also stimulated
including the complement, kallin‐kallikrein, and nitric
oxide pathways. Circulating anti-inflammatory mediators (such as alpha‐macroglobulins) can initially counteract this inflammatory state, but in many situations are
themselves overwhelmed. When pro-inflammatory
pathways overcome defences, there is reduced pancreatic
microcirculation, as well as ongoing inflammation and
necrosis within the pancreas due to neutrophil migration
and adherence. This inflammation and necrosis theoretically therefore starts in the pancreatic acinar cells, but
when severe spills out into the peripancreatic fat.

Although some dogs with AP may have self‐limiting
disease or mild clinical severity (mild abdominal pain,
vomiting), others develop systemic complications due to
activation of the multiple inflammatory cascades. The
cause of abdominal pain is considered to be distension of
the pancreatic capsule, or via stimulation of mesenteric
pain receptors by inflammatory exudate. The pathophysiology of pain is quite complex: the nociceptive (ascending) pathway travels via the dorsal horn, and is mediated
by amino acid (glutamate and aspartate) and neuropeptide (substance P, neurokinin A, and calcitonin gene‐
related peptide) release. If there is ongoing nociceptive
input, activation of N‐methyl‐D‐aspartate (NMDA)
receptors may occur, which is considered a key step in
the development for central sensitization. Vomiting
occurs due to both central and peripheral stimulation of
vomiting pathways, but the exact mechanism has not
been confirmed for AP. Systemic effects of AP relate
both to the clinical signs (hypovolemia, etc.) and the
presence of circulating proinflammatory mediators.
There are many potential factors that may initiate or
trigger the initial activation of pancreatic zymogens within
the acinar cells. Experimentally, it has been shown that
co‐localization of lysosomal granules and zymogen granules leads to zymogen activation. This effect appears to be
amplified by a reduction in acinar cell pH, and is considered to be the mechanism by which activation occurs in
people with sudden increases in intracellular calcium (as
can occur during cardiopulmonary bypass). In dogs, the
most commonly implicated causes of AP include dietary
indiscretion, drugs, trauma, and unknown (or idiopathic).
High‐fat, low‐protein diets in particular are clearly implicated in causing AP in dogs and rodent models; clinically
this is typically in association with long‐term feeding of
urolithiasis diets. There is a large list of drugs that may
cause idiosyncratic pancreatitis, but the most frequently
implicated drugs include azathioprine, potassium

­bromide, and o
­ rganophosphates. Onset of pancreatitis
can occur immediately after starting these medications. In
some cases, there is delayed onset of drug‐induced pancreatitis, particularly in humans; this would make the link
more difficult to prove in dogs. Trauma is also well recognized as a cause of AP but the pancreatic trauma is usually
one of a constellation of abnormalities. Often, no inciting
cause is identified; however, unobserved dietary indiscretion may still occur in these cases.
Chronic pancreatitis (CP) is defined histologically as
lymphocytic‐plasmacytic inflammation of the pancreas
and peripancreatic area with presence of concurrent
fibrosis. Although pancreatic function is generally preserved, dogs with CP can develop diabetes mellitus or
exocrine pancreatic insufficiency associated with the
fibrosis. The etiology of CP is poorly understood in dogs.
The currently accepted rationale for CP in humans is
called the sentinel acute pancreatitis event (SAPE)
hypothesis. With the SAPE hypothesis, pancreatic acinar
cells initially come under some type of oxidative stress
(e.g., fats, alcohol, oxidative products in the bile), but do
not develop any inflammation or fibrosis. When the
­acinar cells are sufficiently stimulated by the oxidative
stress, a pro-inflammatory response occurs (the acute
pancreatitis event). If the oxidative stresses are removed
at this point, the pancreas generally heals with no ongoing consequences. However, if there is perpetuation of
low‐grade inflammation in response to continued oxidative stresses, stellate cells that migrate to the pancreas in
response to secretion of proinflammatory cytokines are
stimulated, leading to periacinar fibrosis. It is not certain
if SAPE occurs in dogs, as many or most of the oxidative
stressors do not generally occur chronically in the canine
population, but the rationale appears logical to apply.
There are also multiple genetic abnormalities that predispose humans to CP, including mutations of cationic
trypsinogen, which cause spontaneous production of
trypsin in the acinar cells. To date, no similar genetic
mutation has been identified in dogs, although investigations are still ongoing. Additionally, autoimmune disease
is strongly suspected to occur in cocker spaniels, and
may be similar to the autoimmune form of pancreatitis
identified in people. Obstructive causes of CP are not
common in dogs, and dietary indiscretion is not thought
to be as important a trigger for CP as it is for AP.

­Epidemiology
The true incidence of pancreatitis is difficult to determine, as definitive antemortem diagnosis is often problematic. In one study assessing dogs submitted for
postmortem at a first opinion practice, the prevalence of

CP was 34%, with over half of those classified as having
moderate or marked pancreatic inflammation. Similarly,
inflammation or fibrosis was identified in approximately
50% of dogs in a postmortem study at a referral institution. There appears to be a breed predisposition for
spaniel breeds, particularly cocker spaniels. This may
reflect the dog population in the study region, but anecdotal evidence would support this statement to hold in a
wider dog population. These prevalence studies raise
two major points. Firstly, CP is probably grossly underrecognized due to the difficulties in diagnosing the
condition antemortem. Secondly, histologic changes
­
may not be clinically important, and postmortem studies
may actually overemphasize the importance of CP or the
sensitivity of various tests.
The incidence of AP is similarly difficult to determine,
although it is a condition that occurs worldwide.
Anecdotal reports would suggest that AP is the most
commonly diagnosed emergency presentation of the
gastrointestinal system in dogs. In most reports, middle‐
aged, overweight dogs appear to be predisposed.

­History and Clinical Signs
Acute Pancreatitis
The clinical presentation of AP is initially related to the
development of gastrointestinal clinical signs: vomiting,
anorexia, and abdominal pain. Abdominal pain may be
subtle or difficult to determine initially but can be manifested as severe (e.g. crouching in prayer position and
excessive restlessness). The severity of these clinical signs
along with the duration of onset also determines the findings. Animals may be weak or obtunded and in hypovolemic shock if there is a rapid reduction in circulating
blood volume and vasoconstriction due to systemic inflammation. This spectrum of clinical signs is incorporated in
Table 55.1. Rectal temperature can be increased (due to
inflammation) or decreased (due to shock), and some
dogs may also present with neurologic signs. Roughly one‐
third of dogs will also reportedly have diarrhea or melena.
Co‐morbidities such as diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
may be present. It is considered probable that DKA develops secondary to overwhelming destruction of the pancreatic tissue; however, it is also possible that the acidotic
state in DKA leads to pancreatitis. However, with preexisting or undiagnosed diabetes, dogs can be expected to
also have a history of polyuria/polydipsia and weight loss.
The systemic nature of severe inflammation also
means that animals may have respiratory signs (due to
develop­ment of acute lung injury and/or pleural effusion), neurologic abnormalities (due to thromboembolic

Local complications can also occur, such as extrahepatic bile duct obstruction (EHBDO); EHBDO may
develop due to physical obstruction of the bile duct by an
enlarged and inflamed pancreas, or due to decreased
motility of the bile duct mediated by local peritonitis.
Regardless, dogs with EHBDO are jaundiced, although as
a complication it generally occurs late in the progress of
disease and often the dog appears to be recovering.
Another local complication is the development of fluid‐
filled regions within the pancreas, often associated with
necrosis (Figure 55.1). These acute fluid collections may
be incidental findings, but often are associated with a sudden increase in abdominal pain. True pancreatic abscessation is extremely unlikely in dogs, and pseudocysts
develop weeks following an acute episode of pancreatitis.
Chronic Pancreatitis
Chronic pancreatitis is generally a milder presentation
than AP. In some circumstances, there may be no associated detectable clinical signs. In other dogs, there may be
a single episode or waxing and waning loss of appetite,
mild vomiting, and abdominal pain. Diabetes mellitus
may occur in conjunction with CP, and so flares of pancreatic inflammation may coincide with periods of insulin resistance. Similarly, CP may be concurrent with
exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and the clinical signs of
the latter may predominate.

­Diagnosis
Routine Laboratory Tests
Routine hematology is fairly nonspecific in pancreatitis,
although a stress leukogram is usually present. As AP is a
systemic inflammatory condition, there may also be
changes in other white blood cell concentrations.
Biochemical changes reflect the degree of dehydration
and hypovolemia present (increased total protein,
azotemia, electrolyte derangements, etc.) but are not
pathognomonic for pancreatitis. Total lipase and amylase
activities can be markedly increased in AP, but can also be
normal in severe AP and increased with nonpancreatic
disease. Both renal disease and administration of dexamethasone can increase serum lipase and/or amylase
activities, without primary pancreatitis being present.
Due to the inherent issues with sensitivity of routine
lipase assays, a catalytic assay utilizing a more selective
lipase substrate (1,2‐o‐dilauryl‐rac‐glycero‐3‐glutaric
acid‐{6′‐methylresorufin} ester [DGGR]) has been
recently assessed. The DGGR assay appears to have higher
sensitivity than routine lipase assays, and has similar findings to ELISA‐based measurements of specific pancreatic
lipase concentrations (details of this test are given later).
Often dogs with AP have grossly lipemic serum, and
although this may be a consequence of fat saponification
during the disease, fasting serum cholesterol and triglycerides should be measured 1–2 weeks after recovery to
ensure that hyperlipidemia is not an inciting factor.

There have been a number of studies evaluating cPL
for the diagnosis of pancreatitis (Table 55.2). Overall,
cPL should be considered highly specific for pancreatitis.
Sensitivity of the cPL assay appears to be high in animals
with AP, but less so for CP. When interpreting cPL, it
should be remembered that pancreatic inflammation
may be present, but not be the cause of the clinical presentation. The most relevant application of this is when
there are duodenal foreign bodies or septic peritonitis
that can cause “bystander” pancreatic inflammation.
Misdiagnosis in this situation could fail to identify that
surgical correction is required.
Pancreatic elastase (PE‐1) is another enzyme considered to be pancreas specific. There is a commercially
available canine PE‐1 (cPE‐1) ELISA (ScheBo.Elastase
1‐Canine, ScheBo Biotech AG, Giessen, Germany). It
appears that PE‐1 has wide variation in healthy dogs, and
similar sensitivity and specificity to cPL when assessing
dogs with severe AP (see Table 55.2). However, this
premise should be tested in a larger cohort of dogs.

Pancreas‐Specific Biochemistry
Until the past decade, pancreas‐specific enzymes such as
trypsin‐like immunoreactivity or trypsinogen activation
peptide have not been considered useful in diagnosing
either AP or CP. Canine pancreatic lipase (cPL) has been
developed into a commercially available ELISA test
(Spec‐cPL), and is now used widely in veterinary practice. It is thought that cPL is only produced in the pancreas, and is affected less by non-pancreatic disease than
total lipase. There have been some studies that show
clearance of cPL is not affected by acute or chronic
reductions in glomerular filtration. The reference interval for the laboratory ELISA is <200 μg/L in healthy dogs,
with results >400 μg/L considered consistent with a diagnosis of pancreatitis in dogs with compatible clinical
signs. There is also an in‐clinic rapid semiquantitative

Diagnostic imaging is an important component of the
investigation of dogs presenting with signs of abdominal
disease. The major indication for abdominal radiographs
is to rule out the presence of surgical disease such as
intestinal obstruction or gallbladder rupture. The
changes associated with AP are nonspecific on radiographs and include loss of detail in the cranial abdomen,
and on the VD view, pushing of the proximal duodenum
laterally (Figures 55.2 and 55.3).
Ultrasound is generally accepted as the most useful
diagnostic imaging modality to evaluate the pancreas in
clinical practice. Full abdominal ultrasound is recommended to assess for the presence of free fluid or other
diseases. Changes described in CP are fairly vague, and it
is considered that this diagnosis is difficult to make
definitively via ultrasound. Pathognomonic signs of AP
include an enlarged, hypoechoic pancreas surrounded
by bright, hyperechoic fat and mesentery (Figure 55.4).
To date, more advanced imaging modalities such as
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT) are infrequently performed in dogs with AP,
due to the prolonged anesthesia required and the
accepted sensitivity of ultrasound. The use of CT imaging in people is more frequently done, and can identify
infected necrosis and other changes with a high degree
of sensitivity.

Cytology and Histology
Cytology is not used frequently in evaluating dogs with
AP. However, abdominal fluid analysis should form part
of the work‐up to ensure that a septic or neoplastic process is not missed. Dogs with AP will generally have a
suppurative, non-septic exudate present. A recent study
in a small number of dogs with AP determined that
measurement of cPL in peritoneal fluid had a sensitivity
of 100% when using a cut‐off value >500 μg/L. Caution

should be applied before relying extensively on this, as

Aspiration of fluid‐filled collections within the pancreas may have a therapeutic benefit (described later).
Fine needle aspirates (using a 25 G needle) can safely be
obtained from the pancreas and may be beneficial in
some cases of CP. Cytology is generally considered of
marginal utility in AP, as there is often such a large
degree of necrosis and inflammation that the samples
are ­nondiagnostic and/or cellular criteria overlap with
malignancy.
Histologic evaluation of pancreatic biopsy is considered the gold standard for diagnosis of pancreatic pathology. This is seldom obtained in dogs with AP, due to the
morbidity associated with this procedure. The most
common finding in dogs with AP is widespread necrosis
of pancreatic and peripancreatic tissue. In dogs with
milder, more intermittent clinical signs, exploratory
­laparotomy is more commonly indicated. The stomach,
intestines (distal and proximal small intestine), mesenteric lymph nodes, and liver should all be sampled in
addition to the pancreas.
A summary of the diagnostic approach recommended
when dogs present with severe signs compatible with
AP is shown in Figure 55.5.

­Therapy
Acute Pancreatitis
Treatment of AP is generally supportive and nonspecific.
The major “triad” of treatment is IV fluids, analgesia, and
nutritional support. Fluid therapy should be tailored to
the individual dog, with correction of electrolyte losses
and restoration of circulating blood volume and acid–
base balance being of the utmost importance. A recent
study in humans suggested that using alkalinizing fluids
(Hartmann’s solution) produced a better response than
acidifying solutions (saline) and so extrapolation would
suggest that this (or alternatively, lactated Ringer’s solution) would be a good first‐line fluid choice in dogs. The
volume of IV fluids required to correct blood volume
may be higher than can be tolerated, and potentially lead
to pulmonary edema or other signs of volume overload.
In those circumstances, the use of colloid therapy may be
of benefit. There is little to no evidence that using plasma
will be beneficial in dogs with AP unless they have overt
coagulation disorders.
Analgesia is essential in dogs that have AP, even if little
pain is observed. Abdominal pain can be categorized as
mild, moderate or severe (see Table 55.1). The principle
behind analgesia in these situations is to start with the

maximal combination/dose considered necessary for the
level of pain and then titrate down (rather than starting
low and titrating up if ineffective). Ideally, analgesic
­protocols in AP should avoid the use of drugs such as
fentanyl that dramatically reduce gastrointestinal
­motility. However, if pain is not controlled by the recommended protocols, then using fentanyl as a constant rate
infusion (CRI) should be considered. The addition of
methylnaltrexone may mitigate the decreased GI motility in those circumstances.
A partial mu‐agonist such as buprenorphine or full mu‐
agonist such as methadone should be considered as the
baseline therapy (starting at maximum doses and intervals: 10–40 μg/kg q6–8h and 0.1–0.5 mg/kg q4–6h
respectively, then tapering down). If pain is moderate then
ketamine (5–20 μg/kg/min) and lidocaine (25–50 μg/kg/
min) CRIs should be started at the higher dosage end.
Once pain is well controlled, the ketamine should be
reduced first, followed by lidocaine and then tapering of
the opioid. With severe pain, epidural morphine (0.1 mg/
kg q12–24h) or a fentanyl CRI (0.2–0.8 μg/kg/min)
should be given, along with the lidocaine and ketamine
as above. Once pain is controlled, the epidural/CRI is
swapped for intermittent opioid, then all are tapered as
previously described.
If possible, oral gabapentin (10 mg/kg q12–24h) could
also be administered. If there is a sudden relapse of pain,
the pancreas should be reexamined via ultrasound for
the presence of a fluid collection. In people, aspiration of
fluid collections is recommended when they are sterile,
in preference to surgical debridement. Even in infected
necrosis, control with antibiotics is undertaken before
any surgical procedures. As virtually all the fluid collections in dogs will be sterile, and pancreatic surgery is
associated with high morbidity and mortality rates, percutaneous drainage of fluid‐filled areas is advocated for
dogs as well. This can be performed using mild sedation
and fine needle aspiration.
Nutritional support is the third major component of
management. In people and dogs with critical illness,
lack of enteral nutrition has been shown to perpetuate
systemic inflammation as well as leading to mucosal
atrophy and other changes. In mild‐to‐moderate cases of
AP, the current rationale is to start enteral feeding if
there has been no/little enteral nutrition for more than
five days. In severe cases of AP, the earliest possible
enteral nutrition is advocated. Dogs with severe AP can
tolerate esophageal tube feeding, and so surgery or prolonged anesthesia to insert jejunostomy tubes is not
essential. If the animal is moribund or unable to withstand a general anesthesia, then nasoesophageal tube
feeding should be started as soon as possible. Once they
are able to have GA safely, then an esophageal (E) tube
should be inserted. Dogs can still be offered food by

mouth, and can be sent home with an E tube in place
if necessary.
The biggest complications associated with interventional enteral nutrition are aspiration pneumonia and
tube site infection. Close attention should be paid to the
tube site to avoid the latter. To avoid regurgitation and
development of aspiration pneumonia, it is not recommended to feed full resting energy requirements (RER)
unless the feeding is extremely well tolerated. Rather, the
first 24 hours should be 25% RER and titrate up slowly
each day. Similarly, there is no evidence that a specific
diet will result in improved outcome or speed of recovery, and as such any balanced convalescent diet for dogs
is generally well tolerated.
Another important aspect of management of AP is to
reduce vomiting and control nausea. Due to the role of
substance P in mediating abdominal pain and vomiting,
maropitant should be considered a first‐line antiemetic
drug. If vomiting is poorly controlled, or the dog appears
to have severe nausea, then additional medications such
as ondansetron (0.5 mg/kg IV then q12–24h) can be
added. There is a theoretical disadvantage in using metoclopramide as it inhibits dopamine in rodent models.
Due to the potential prokinetic benefits of metoclopramide a CRI should still be considered if decreased GI
motility is thought to be contributing to nausea/
inappetence.
There is little to no evidence that administering gastric
acid suppressants does anything to reduce morbidity of
AP in dogs. However, if there is melena or hematemesis
then use of a proton pump inhibitor should be considered. The presence of any systemic complications such
as pleural effusion or ventricular tachycardia should be
assessed and treated as required. Antibiotics are not necessary unless bacterial translocation is considered likely.
The area most likely to undergo investigation in the
future is targeted antiinflammatory therapies and
analgesic agents. Similarly, the use of corticosteroids
­
may be further evaluated, particularly when hypotension
appears to be nonresponsive to fluid therapy.
Follow‐Up

If an inciting cause (such as drug or food) is known, then
this should be removed. Dogs can be discharged with
feeding tubes in place if required, and a low‐fat diet is
currently recommended. This should generally be fed for
1–2 weeks and then the dog should be reevaluated and
fasting serum triglyceride and cholesterol concentration
measured. If these are high, investigations should be
undertaken for underlying causes of hyperlipidemia and
treatment, including diet, continued as appropriate. If
there is no hyperlipidemia, dogs can be transitioned back
to their regular diet. Analgesia may be necessary in the

early stages following hospitalization, and medication
such as tramadol or gabapentin dispensed.
Anecdotally, tramadol may cause inappetence and so
gabapentin may be a better alternative. In people, after a
bout of severe AP subclinical EPI exists for approximately four weeks following resolution. It is not certain if
this occurs in dogs, but it may be therapeutically useful
to supplement pancreatic enzymes for a short period
after discharge. Animals should not be discharged if they
still need antiemetic therapy.
Chronic Pancreatitis
Unfortunately, treatment options for CP are poorly
explored, and the benefit of proposed treatments is
unsupported. It does make sense to look for underlying
causes of CP that can be corrected, such as hyperlipidemia. If there is hyperlipidemia, then an underlying
endocrinopathy should be considered, particularly hypothyroidism. If both triglycerides and cholesterol are
increased, then an inherent defect in lipid metabolism is
more likely. In the absence of an endocrinopathy, treatment should initially consist of feeding a low‐fat diet,
with <15% dry matter as fat. Other treatments such as
omega‐3 fatty acid supplementation (20–30 mg/kg day)
can also be used, but should be gradually introduced as
they can cause gastrointestinal signs in their own right. If
triglycerides (TG) alone are high and do not decrease
with dietary management then gemfibrosil (7.5–10 mg/
kg PO q12h) may be used. Other less well‐established
treatments such as chitin (binds lipids in the diet) and
niacin (to reduce liver TG synthesis) may also be beneficial. For treatment of high cholesterol (with normal TG)
when dietary treatment is ineffective, a statin (HMG
CoA‐reductase inhibitors) may be used. Safety margins
are high for this group of drugs in dogs, and a dosage of
10–20 mg PO once daily is currently recommended for
lovastatin. If the animal is not hyperlipidemic, there is no
evidence for benefit from feeding a low‐fat diet. However,
this is frequently done in practice and if the diet is
well balanced, long‐term feeding of it is unlikely to
cause harm.
If no underlying cause is diagnosed and CP is confirmed or strongly suspected, then the dilemma is
whether to treat with analgesia alone or with additional
antiinflammatory/immune suppression. Ideally, immune
suppression should be used only when there is histologic
confirmation of lymphocytic inflammation within the
pancreas. If the dog is not diabetic, prednisolone is the
drug of choice for both immune suppression and to treat
inflammation/fibrosis, albeit at different dosages for the
different effects. Prednisolone has been removed
from the register of drugs that can potentially cause

599

VetBooks.ir

600

Section 6 Gastrointestinal Disease

­pancreatitis in people, and studies have shown that glucocorticoids do not cause any histologic changes in dogs.
If the dog is diabetic, it is not appropriate to use prednisolone due to increased insulin resistance. Ciclosporin is
a viable treatment option for CP in diabetic dogs, but it is
expensive in medium to larger breeds. Azathioprine has
been implicated as causing pancreatitis in dogs, but this
is a weak association. More importantly, it has not been
shown that dogs with preexisting idiopathic or dietary‐
induced pancreatitis are more likely to develop reactions
to azathioprine.
The pathogenesis of pain in CP is complex and multifactorial. Studies in humans have shown that the degree
of fibrosis is not related to the degree of pain, and that
interaction between the nervous system and inflammatory process is crucial. Major mediators of pain in CP
appear to be calcitonin gene‐related peptide (CGRP) and
substance P, acting through the neurokinin‐1 receptor.
Therefore, during acute bouts of inflammation, treatment with a NK1 receptor antagonist such as maropitant
may be of benefit in multiple ways (antiemetic, reducing
pain and potentially directly attenuating the systemic
inflammatory response). Additionally, the concept of
neuronal plasticity suggests that the longer inflammation has been present, the more severe the pain associated with it will be. The most effective method of
long‐term analgesia that can be administered at home in
dogs is probably tramadol, and/or gabapentin.

­Prognosis
The reported mortality rate for AP in dogs ranges from
27% to 58%. This reported rate may not reflect the mortality in general veterinary practice, as the reports originate from referral centers, and euthanasia for
non-medical reasons (i.e., financial) may also exert an
influence. Even taking these factors into account, there
apparently is a higher mortality rate in dogs with AP than
the 5–15% reported in human studies. Chronic pancreatitis is unlikely to carry a high mortality rate if it occurs
in isolation, but as a co‐morbidity it may exert a negative
prognosis on other co‐existing diseases.

­Conclusion
The pancreas should be considered in a similar light to
the liver, in that many intraabdominal diseases can cause
secondary inflammation and changes within the pancreas. To attribute clinical signs in a dog to pancreatitis,
all other abdominal diseases such as septic peritonitis or
intestinal foreign body obstruction, for instance, should
be excluded. Treatment of acute and chronic pancreatitis
is nonspecific and supportive. This too suggests that
exclusion and management of concurrent or primary
disease are often more important than a definitive diagnosis of pancreatitis in itself.

Pancreatitis in the Cat
Craig Ruaux, BVSc (Hons), PhD, MACVSc, DACVIM (SAIM)
School of Veterinary Science, Massey University, Palmerston North, New Zealand

In the veterinary profession, attitudes to pancreatitis in cats
have undergone a massive shift in relatively recent times.
From an earlier perspective that pancreatitis was an uncom­
mon disease in the cat, recent findings and the introduction
of new diagnostic testing modalities have led to the under­
standing that pancreatitis is actually common in the feline
patient. Pancreatitis may actually be one of the most com­
mon diseases of the domestic cat, and is often an important
co‐morbidity with other diseases. This is particularly true of
diseases of the gastrointestinal tract and liver. The actual
importance of pancreatitis in the overall health of the
domestic cat remains somewhat unclear, in part due to the
very different pathology of most cases of pancreatitis in this
species and the markedly different way in which cats tend to
manifest this disease when compared to dogs.
In large part, this relatively recent change in attitudes to
feline pancreatitis has arisen with the development and
ready availability of much more sensitive and specific diag­
nostic tests for this disease. Advances in the resolution and
availability of ultrasound imaging, new noninvasive diag­
nostic tests for specific markers of pancreatic tissue integ­
rity and increased willingness to obtain pancreatic biopsies
and histopathologic assessment have all been extremely
valuable in advancing our knowledge of this disease.
The purpose of this chapter is to provide an overview
of the presenting signs and histories, diagnostic approach
to, and current recommendations for the management of
pancreatitis in the domestic cat.

­Clinical Signs and Symptoms
of Pancreatitis in Cats
History and Physical Examination Findings

A quite remarkable difference between companion ani­
mal species is seen in the way that pancreatitis manifests.
While specific reporting of clinical signs seen in cats

with either suspected or actually confirmed pancreatic
disease is uncommon in the veterinary literature, aggre­
gation of results from several studies has provided data
on clinical signs and owner complaints in 136 cats; these
findings are summarized in Table 56.1.
One remarkable observation from the aggregated data
in Table 56.1 is that the most common clinical sign in
cats with pancreatitis, across a variety of studies span­
ning several decades, is decreased appetite, followed
closely by lethargy. Vomiting and abdominal pain, both
frequent clinical signs of pancreatitis in dogs, were
reported in less than 50% of feline patients. The actual
case outcomes and severities of clinical presentations in
the cats aggregated for Table 56.1 range from mild dis­
ease with “incidental” findings of pancreatic disease
through to objectively severe, life‐threatening or termi­
nal disease. Based on clinical signs alone, there is no way
to distinguish the severity of pancreatic disease or pre­
dict the histopathologic findings if biopsies are to be
taken. While some authors have suggested that chronic
pancreatitis in the cat is a less severe disease, this is prob­
ably an unfounded belief; cats with chronic pancreatitis
can present with objectively severe presenting signs
(most likely associated with an acute worsening of their
disease, or an “acute on chronic” disease presentation).
Given that both decreased appetite and lethargy are
nonspecific signs, and are also common reasons for pres­
entations of feline patients for veterinary care, it is not
surprising that pancreatitis is becoming a much more
common diagnosis in feline medicine. In light of these
data, pancreatitis should be considered a reasonable and
important differential diagnosis for any cat presenting
with vague, nonspecific clinical signs.
Physical examination findings in cats with pancreatitis
are also often unrewarding. Clinical signs such as cranial
abdominal pain and guarding, commonly encountered
in canine patients, are uncommon in cats with diagnoses

nature of pain manifestation in many cats, and a ten­

a normal response on the part of feline patients. Often,
the most important findings on physical examination in
feline patients with pancreatitis are signs and symptoms
of co‐morbid disease (palpably thickened gastrointesti­
nal tract, icterus, poor body condition), or findings that
are important in the assessment of the overall state of
health of the patient (state of hydration, presence of free
abdominal fluid, alterations in body temperature). As
with the histories of cats with pancreatitis, these vague,
diffuse, and nonspecific findings in most cats with pan­
creatic inflammatory disease mean that pancreatic dis­
ease is a reasonable differential diagnosis in essentially
any cat that presents unwell.
Characterization of Pancreatitis in the Cat
Typically, pancreatitis has been divided into acute and
chronic diseases, based on histologic differences in
human and canine patients. Generally speaking, “acute
pancreatitis” is either neutrophilic or hemorrhagic and is
associated with rapid onset of severe symptoms, marked
abdominal pain and potentially life‐threatening acid–
base and electrolyte disturbances. By comparison,
“chronic pancreatitis” is typically associated with fibrous
replacement of pancreatic tissue and the presence of a
lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate. Although chronic
pancreatitis is being recognized more frequently in
canine patients, most clinicians consider acute pancrea­
titis to be the most common form of the disease in dogs.
In cats, chronic pancreatitis is the most commonly
diagnosed disease following histologic assessment of
pancreatic biopsies. As in humans and dogs, this diagno­
sis is based on the presence of lymphocytic or plasma­
cytic cellular infiltrates and, typically, some degree of
fibrosis. In some studies, >80% of cats with pancreatic

disease show this form of pancreatic infiltrate.
Remarkably, at least one necropsy‐based study of cat
pancreata has suggested that signs of pancreatic inflam­
mation, including lymphocytic‐plasmacytic infiltration
and fibrotic change, are common in cats with no history
suggestive of pancreatic disease.
One problem with the terminology of pancreatitis,
particularly the distinction of acute vs chronic pancreati­
tis, is the implication of differing chronologies of the dis­
ease. This is particularly problematic in the feline patient.
While it is generally safe to assume that cats with longer
histories of recurrent clinical signs such as lethargy,
decreased appetite, and recurrent vomiting do indeed
have chronic pancreatitis, the converse is not necessarily
true. Given the subtle nature of clinical signs and histori­
cal complaints in many cats with pancreatic disease, and
the waxing/waning nature of clinical signs in most
chronic lympho‐plasmacytic diseases, it is not valid to
assume that a cat with a new presentation of relatively
acute clinical signs actually has “acute pancreatitis” as
defined histologically. As discussed earlier, there is no
reliable way to distinguish necrotizing or hemorrhagic
pancreatitis from lympho‐plasmacytic disease in feline
patients. Therapeutic decision making should be based
on assessment of the overall state of health of the patient
on presentation, rather than assumptions that a patient
may or may not have a particular form of the disease.

­Noninvasive Diagnostics for Feline
Pancreatitis
Routine Clinical Chemistries
Routine clinical chemistry and complete blood count
(CBC) evaluations are a critical part of the approach to
any unwell feline patient. In the context of cats with a
suspicion of pancreatitis, the most important aspect of
the routine chemistry panel and CBC is the assessment
of the overall physiology of the patient. There are very
few to no findings on routine clinical pathology panels
that can be considered highly sensitive or specific for
pancreatitis in the cat. One exception to this would be
the “pancreas‐specific lipase” assays that are beginning
to be promoted more heavily in some routine chemistry
panels, and are discussed in more detail later.
In the dog and human patients, traditionally we have
relied on the measurement of serum amylase and lipase
activities to establish a diagnosis of pancreatitis, with the
expectation that these activities will be markedly elevated.
While these tests are admittedly low sensitivity and speci­
ficity in both dogs and people, marked elevations in
patients with compatible clinical signs are at least strongly
supportive of the clinical suspicion of pancreatitis.

VetBooks.ir

56 Pancreatitis in the Cat

In the cat, a long‐standing belief in veterinary medicine
is that amylase and lipase activities have essentially no
diagnostic utility, with unacceptably low sensitivity and
specificity in this species. While there is a large element of
truth to these assertions, these opinions are based on a
limited number of publications that assessed a small num­
ber of cats, and all dated from a period before the veteri­
nary profession came to truly appreciate the very different
manifestations of this disease in the cat. The low specific­
ity reported for these tests may owe as much to false‐­
negative diagnoses based on an incorrect understanding
of the way in which this disease presents in the cat.
Common clinical pathology abnormalities encoun­
tered in cats are related to organ systems that are com­
monly compromised or involved in co‐morbid diseases.
Abnormalities in liver enzyme activities (both alanine
aminotransferase [ALT] and alkaline phosphatase
[ALKP], suggesting both hepatocellular compromise and
cholestasis), azotemia, alterations in acid–base status,
hypocalcemia, and inflammatory leukograms (typically
left‐shift neutrophilia) are all encountered relatively
commonly. Some studies have suggested that marked
hypocalcemia is a negative prognostic factor, likely due
to sequestration of calcium in saponified abdominal fat,
a phenomenon that tends to accompany hemorrhagic
and necrotizing pancreatic pathology.
Specialty Diagnostic Tests
Noninvasive diagnostic testing relies on the use of
marker compounds, detectable in the serum or some
other sample such as urine, that are specific to the organ
of interest and are altered in disease states of that organ.
Ideally, the marker compound will be altered with dis­
ease of the primary organ, but unaltered by changes in
other organ systems or by concurrent medical therapy.
In the case of pancreatic disease, these marker com­
pounds are usually digestive enzymes of some type. The
use of typical amylase and lipase activity assays has
already been discussed. More recent diagnostic tests that
have been investigated include serum concentrations of
trypsin‐like immunoreactivity (fTLI), feline pancreatic
lipase (now offered as the Spec‐fPL™ assay), and activity
tests using more “pancreas‐specific” lipase substrates,
particularly DGGR‐lipase activity.
While trypsinogen/fTLI is pancreas specific, and is
released in conditions of pancreatic disease, the peak
changes in this enzyme are relatively short and soon after
the onset of disease, and some other diseases (specifi­
cally small intestinal disease and severe azotemia) can be
associated with elevations in fTLI without histologic
evidence of pancreatic disease. This combination of
­
transient changes in serum concentrations and minor
alterations with other, nonpancreatic diseases results in

fTLI testing having only moderate sensitivity and speci­
ficity for the diagnosis of pancreatitis in the cat. The
greatest utility of fTLI testing lies in the ruling in or out
of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency in feline patients
(see Complications of Pancreatitis in Cats, later).
Serum concentrations of feline pancreatic lipase (Spec‐
fPL) and lipase activity assays using more highly selective
assay substrates both show greater utility than routine
amylase/lipase activities and the fTLI test; these tests are
discussed in greater detail later.
Specific Pancreatic Lipase Test

Feline‐specific pancreatic lipase (fPLI) refers to a par­
ticular protein, a lipase enzyme, synthesized and released
solely by the pancreas in cats. This particular enzyme’s
concentration in serum is measured using the serum
Spec‐fPL assay, available either as a “cage‐side” SNAP
test or via specialty clinical pathology testing. This assay
relies on monoclonal antibodies directed against the
feline protein which are highly species specific. The use
of canine PLI tests with feline samples can result in a
false‐negative rule‐out of pancreatic disease in the cat.
As the fPLI protein is specifically and exclusively
­synthesized in the exocrine pancreatic tissue, the con­
centrations in the serum are dependent on the rate of
synthesis and the “leakage” of the protein into the inter­
stitial space and then the circulation. Conditions associ­
ated with increased cellular leakage (generally, some
form of pancreatitis) are associated with increased serum
concentrations of this protein, so the detection of
increased circulating fPLI protein (i.e., a high Spec‐fPL
test result) is suggestive of pancreatic disease, particu­
larly in cats with compatible clinical signs.
The sensitivity and specificity of fPLI testing have been
investigated in several studies. Reported sensitivities and
specificities for this test are 67–100% and 67–82%,
respectively. In one moderately large study (n = 182 cats)
using the Spec‐fPL assay, the overall sensitivity for this
test was 79%, with a specificity of 82%, for detection of
pancreatitis in this group. Overall, the Spec‐fPL has the
highest reported sensitivity and specificity (at the time of
writing) of any diagnostic modality for the detection of
pancreatitis in the cat.
The use of Spec‐fPL measurement as a prognostic
marker and monitoring parameter for recovery has also
received some attention. Marked elevation of Spec‐fPL
(values >20 μg/L) has been associated with a poorer
prognosis in cats hospitalized with pancreatitis. There
are no data in the literature suggesting that greater eleva­
tions in Spec‐fPL are associated with poorer response to
therapy in cats with chronic pancreatitis, assuming ade­
quate management of co‐morbidities. A much greater
factor influencing response to chronic pancreatitis in
cats is adequate management of chronic enteropathy and

603

VetBooks.ir

604

Section 6 Gastrointestinal Disease

the identification and treatment, if present, of cobalamin
deficiency in these cats.
Pancreas‐Specific Lipase Assays

The lipase activity assays used in most commercial labo­
ratories and bench‐top analytic systems rely on lipase
within the serum sample cleaving a substrate of some
sort; this cleavage then results in a change in the test
solution (such as changing pH or color) that can be
measured, giving a value for lipase activity. There is a
large number of lipase activity substrates that can be
used, and the substrates typically used by high‐through­
put commercial laboratories are different from those
used in the bench‐top systems. Even within bench‐top
systems, there are differences in substrates between dif­
fering manufacturers. For this reason, the comparison of
lipase activity assays between two different systems is
generally fruitless and does not yield any useful data.
Many tissues in the body contain quite high amounts of
lipase. Obviously, the exocrine pancreas is very rich in
these enzymes but other organs, including the liver,
gastric mucosa, and duodenal mucosa, contain lipase
­
activity. These lipases can be released from these other
organs in disease states, and contribute to the total circu­
lating lipase activity. The specificity of a lipase assay for
detection of pancreatic disease thus depends on the speci­
ficity of the substrate used for pancreatic lipase. This sub­
strate specificity varies markedly between s­ ubstrate types.
One substrate with greater specificity for pancreatic
lipase that has undergone some investigation in cats
is 1‐2‐o‐Dilauryl‐rac‐glycero‐3‐glutaric acid‐(6’‐methyl­
resorufin) ester (DGGR). A DGGR‐based clinical chem­
istry assay has been validated for use in feline serum
samples, and the sensitivity and specificity of the test
compared with the use of both Spec‐fPL testing and
abdominal ultrasonography. The DGGR‐based assay had
similar, if slightly lower, sensitivity and specificity to the
Spec‐fPL assay in the assessment of cats with clinical
signs compatible with pancreatitis. In a similar follow‐up
study, the DGGR‐based assay was found to show the best
agreement with both Spec‐fPL and abdominal ultra­
sonography in cats with hypo‐ or mixed‐echoic pancre­
atic parenchyma, findings that are generally considered
consistent with acute pancreatic disease.
Overall, DGGR‐based lipase activity assays likely have
clinical utility in feline patients, and an elevated activity
value in an unwell feline patient should prompt further
assessment for the presence of pancreatic disease.
However, this approach is reliant on the use of this spe­
cific substrate in whichever analytic system is being
employed. Information regarding the actual substrates
used by the various reference laboratories and in‐house
chemistry systems commonly found in veterinary prac­
tice is not readily available at this time.

Pancreatic Biopsy and Histology
Pancreatic biopsy and histologic examination is gener­
ally considered the “gold standard” for the detection of
pancreatic disease, including pancreatitis. Unfortunately,
pancreatic biopsy is still a relatively uncommon part of
the approach to feline patients, for a variety of reasons.
Chief among these is likely cost to the client and the
invasive nature of celiotomy to obtain biopsies. Recently,
however, the use of laparotomy and laparoscopy‐assisted
biopsy techniques has provided a lower cost, less inva­
sive method for obtaining pancreatic biopsies, usually in
concert with liver and intestinal biopsy procedures.
Surgical biopsy of the feline pancreas has been shown
to have a low risk for complications such as postsurgical
pancreatitis, assuming that the patient is adequately
hydrated and hemodynamically stable at the time of sur­
gery. Side‐effects and postsurgical morbidity are uncom­
mon in cats undergoing surgical biopsy of the pancreas
using punch biopsy instruments or crush‐fracture tech­
niques using hemostats. Pancreatic biopsy, particularly
in cats undergoing assessment for gastrointestinal dis­
ease, is justified in many cases and should be considered
part of the routine samples collected during exploratory
celiotomy or laparoscopic exploratory procedures.
While biopsy samples are rightly considered the most
effective way of assessing pancreatic disease, a number of
shortfalls of this technique must be recognized. Even
with laparoscopic procedures, the collection and assess­
ment of histologic samples are still more expensive and
have higher risk to the patient than the use of noninva­
sive testing such as clinical chemistries. In addition,
pathology within the pancreas is often heterogeneous in
distribution, and differing areas may show differing cel­
lular infiltrates or levels of activity. This may lead to
incorrect diagnosis of the overall state of the pancreas
when only a single sample is taken, as is often the case
with laparoscopic biopsies of the pancreas in the cat.
Finally, there is a well‐recognized variability between
individual pathologists with respect to assessment and
description of pancreatic samples. Histologic scoring
systems for pancreatic disease have been proposed and
published, including for the cat, but the use of these sys­
tems is generally limited to research publications and
retrospective case series descriptions. It is uncommon
for histopathologists to report pancreatic biopsy samples
using these scoring systems in veterinary medicine.
Interpretation of Specialized Tests
Interpretation of the specialized tests used for the diag­
nosis of pancreatic disease in cats is sometimes compli­
cated, particularly if the test is part of a broad‐ranging
panel used in the initial assessment of a patient if there
is no clear initial diagnosis being assessed. Part of the

VetBooks.ir

56 Pancreatitis in the Cat

­difficulty of assessing these tests comes from the obser­
vation that we do not truly know the prevalence of pan­
creatic disease in the feline population. While at least
one study suggests that pancreatic pathology is quite
common in the feline population (approximately 60% of
cases necropsied, where the patient was not suspected to
have pancreatic disease), one caveat about this study is
that these were still, largely speaking, unwell cats that
were necropsied. If the true prevalence of pancreatic dis­
ease in the feline population is as high as 60%, then an
unexpected finding of a high Spec‐fPL concentration or
DGGR‐lipase activity on sentinel chemistry panels may
be a true indication of pancreatic disease. While the pan­
creatic disease present may not be an important clinical
finding, this does not mean that this is an incorrect diagnostic finding. This is particularly true when the clinical
chemistry panel is being run on an apparently healthy
patient as part of a health monitoring or wellness
program.
An additional important factor in the interpretation of
these tests is the very variable, and often subtle, clinical
signs and histories of this disease, as previously dis­
cussed. When clinical chemistry panels and Spec‐fPL
tests are being run as part of a broad‐ranging assessment
in a cat that is known to be unwell, but with no clear ini­
tial indication of why, abnormalities in these tests are a
strong indication of likely clinically significant disease. It
is inappropriate to discount these findings in these
patients, and important to consider that pancreatic
­disease is, to all indications, common in the sick cat pop­
ulation and also a common co‐morbid condition with
other diseases.
Diagnostic Imaging
Along with the specialized noninvasive testing methods
discussed above, diagnostic imaging is commonly used
in the assessment of pancreatic disease in the cat. Of the
various methodologies available, high‐resolution
abdominal ultrasonography typically has the greatest
diagnostic yield. It also allows further assessment of
other abdominal organs that may be involved in co‐mor­
bid diseases, such as the hepatic parenchyma, biliary
tree, and intestinal walls.
Plain abdominal radiography, while commonly used
in cats with suspected abdominal disease, has a very
low diagnostic yield in cats with pancreatitis. The pan­
creas is not visible on plain abdominal radiographs, and
changes commonly seen in dogs with pancreatitis
(“ground glass” appearance, loss of local contrast, wid­
ening pyloric angle) are infrequent in cats due to the
differing underlying pathology in most cases. While
abdominal radiography has some possible advantages
in terms of lower cost and greater availability, the very

low diagnostic yield is a contraindication for its use in
most cases.
The increasing availability of high‐resolution abdomi­
nal ultrasonography in companion animal practice has
dramatically improved the use of diagnostic imaging to
characterize pancreatic disease in the cat. Observation
of pancreatic enlargement, hyperechoic mesentery and
abdominal fat, altered parenchymal echogenicity (most
commonly hypoechogenicity or a mixed pattern),
abdominal effusions, pancreatic cysts or pseudocysts,
corrugation of the duodenum, and dilation of the pan­
creatic duct are all considered consistent with pancreati­
tis in cats with consistent clinical signs. These findings
are specific indicators of the presence of pancreatic
pathology, but their sensitivity for accurate diagnosis in
cats with histologically confirmed pancreatitis is quite
variable, with reported sensitivities ranging from ~11%
to 80%. Sensitivity of abdominal ultrasound for the
detection of feline pancreatic disease is highly dependent
on operator skill and equipment resolution. Given the
variable and often low sensitivity of abdominal ultra­
sound examination in the diagnosis of pancreatitis in
cats, this modality cannot be reliably used as a “rule‐out”
test for this disease. However, significant additional
information useful for management of these cases is
often obtained, particularly when screening for co‐
morbid conditions such as cholangitis/cholangiohepati­
tis or the presence of extrapancreatic disease that
could explain the clinical signs. Therefore, abdominal
ultrasonography, carried out by a well‐trained and experi­
enced ­operator, is recommended in all cats where there
is a clinical suspicion of pancreatitis.
In humans, the use of abdominal computed tomogra­
phy (CT) examination is considered highly useful in the
assessment of pancreatic disease. This modality allows
the assessment of pancreatic architecture, presence and
severity of fibrotic change and detection of both com­
mon inciting causes for pancreatitis in humans (such as
gallstones) and other co‐morbid diseases. The utility of
abdominal CT for the assessment of feline pancreatic
disease is much lower than in humans. This is due to
the much smaller mass of pancreatic tissue in the cat,
and less common presence of severe architectural dis­
tortions due to fibrosis. Additionally, abdominal CT
examination of cats typically requires general anesthe­
sia, which may be contraindicated in severely unwell
cats and also leads to significant additional cost. CT
examination has been reported in cats in a small num­
ber of publications; the overall sensitivity and specific­
ity were not higher than those seen with less invasive
testing such as Spec‐fPL or abdominal ultrasonography,
and thus abdominal CT cannot be recommended as a
part of the diagnostic approach to pancreatic disease in
the cat at this time.
