­
manganese, systemic inflammation, altered gamma‐
aminobutyric acid (GABA, an inhibitory neurotransmitter), benzodiazepine receptor signaling and altered
catecholaminergic signaling due to changes in branched
chain aromatic amino acid profiles. Whatever the
­underlying cause, the overall result is a disruption of
brain function, typically leading to waxing and waning
clinical signs.
Gastroduodenal Ulceration
Patients with hepatobiliary disease are predisposed to
gastric and duodenal ulceration for a number of reasons.
Portal venous hypertension is an important risk factor
resulting in vascular stasis and venous congestion, which
together increase the risk of mucosal ulceration due to
reduced mucosal blood flow and secondarily reduced
bicarbonate and mucus secretion. This risk is further
increased in anorexic animals or those exposed to nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs or potentially corticosteroids. Gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding is an
important consideration in any patient with HE that
suddenly deteriorates or in any patient with liver disease
that becomes more subdued or develops a reduced
appetite.

The liver is involved in the manufacture of the majority
of the coagulation factors, including fibrinogen (factor I),
prothrombin (factor II) and factors V, VII, IX, X, XI, and
XIII. The site of factor VIII production is controversial,
but it is likely that the liver plays an important role in its
production. It is also the site of the vitamin K‐dependent
activation of factors II, VII, IX, and X and protein C. In
addition to this, the liver is involved in the clearance of
activated clotting factors and the production of clotting
factor inhibitors (e.g., antithrombin and alpha‐1‐antitrypsin) and fibrinolytic proteins such as plasminogen.
Hence, in liver disease there is the potential for disrupted
production of coagulation factors and their inhibitors
along with impaired clearance of both activated coagulation factors and the products of the fibrinolytic system.
The extent of the resulting abnormalities reflect the
severity of the underlying liver disease, ranging from
individual factor deficiencies to disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
A study of 42 dogs with histologically confirmed liver
disease demonstrated that one or more coagulation
abnormalities was present in 57% of the dogs. These
abnormalities ranged from single factor deficiencies in
four of the dogs to DIC in three dogs. An older study suggested a figure of 93% of dogs with liver disease having
abnormal coagulation parameters, although this study
involved more severely affected cases. A study of 45 cats
with liver disease showed that 98% of the cats had one or
more abnormality detected. What is important to recognize clinically is that, whilst spontaneous hemorrhage
may be rare in animals with hepatic disease, hemostatic
abnormalities occur commonly. Hence, the clinician
needs to exercise caution when considering interventional diagnostic procedures and a coagulation profile
should be performed in all such cases.

­Signalment
Patient signalment is very important when approaching
the patient with hepatobiliary disease. There are a variety of known or suspected breed predispositions to
hepatic disease which can be helpful to consider, particularly in view of the occult nature of many cases of early
liver disease. Congenital portosystemic shunts (CPSS)
have worldwide breed predispositions including Irish
wolfhounds, cairn terriers, Labrador retrievers, dachshunds, Yorkshire terriers, Australian cattle dogs, Maltese
terriers, and miniature schnauzers. In cats, the condition
is seen most frequently in mixed‐breed cats, although
Persian and Himalayan breeds are also overrepresented.
Additionally, copper‐associated hepatitis has been

VetBooks.ir

60 Approach to the Patient with Liver Disease

described in several breeds, including the Bedlington terrier, Dalmatian, Doberman pinscher, Labrador retriever,
West Highland white, and Skye terriers. A recent study
documented breeds at risk of developing chronic hepatitis in the UK (see Chapter 64). These included three
breeds in agreement with a previous, older study from
Sweden: the American and English cocker spaniel,
Doberman pinscher and Labrador retriever, and additionally highlighted an increased risk in the cairn terrier,
English springer spaniel, Great Dane, and Samoyed.
However, it should be recognized that the gene pools in
different countries can vary, such that certain breed characteristics and predispositions may be more regional.
In addition to the breed, the age at onset of clinical
signs can be very helpful in aiding diagnosis of some
hepatobiliary conditions. For example, animals with
CPSS typically present at a younger age. This has classically been described to be less than 1 year of age, although
increasingly older dogs seem to be recognized, presumably as clinicians are looking more widely for the condition. There have been reports of increasing numbers of
miniature schnauzers not being diagnosed until they are
over 7 years, presenting with only mild signs. Reports
looking at the age and gender distribution of dogs presenting with chronic hepatitis have shown the mean age
at diagnosis to be approximately 8 years when all breeds
were considered together, although some breeds tended
to present at a younger age (e.g., English springer spaniel). In general, females are overrepresented, although
again there are occasional breeds where this does not
appear to be the case.

access to toxins and a history of any recent drug administration are extremely relevant. The clinician should
maintain a high index of suspicion whenever a patient
develops new clinical signs within four weeks of starting
a new drug. There are many known potentially hepatotoxic drugs, common examples being phenobarbital
and itraconazole, but most drugs have the potential
for an idiosyncratic reaction in an individual patient.
Consumption of a hepatotoxin is also possible, such as
certain mushrooms, xylitol (contained in sugar‐free
sweets) or even herbal/dietary supplements that the
owner might be administering.
Hepatobiliary disease can result in a very broad range
of clinical signs reflecting both the sheer variety of functions the liver performs and the central role it plays in
many metabolic and detoxifaction pathways. This central role means that hepatic disease can result in the secondary dysfunction of other organs, as in HE. It also
places the liver in a position where it can itself become
secondarily affected, for example with hyperadrenocorticism or hepatic lipidosis. The net result is that the clinician needs to be alert to this when approaching a case,
aiming to first decide if hepatobiliary disease could be
present in an animal but then, importantly, whether this
represents a primary or secondary phenomenon. These
key ­questions sound very straightforward, but they can
be challenging to address in many patients and will be
reconsidered as different aspects of the investigation of
liver disease are explored.

­Diagnosis
­History and Clinical Signs
A thorough history with good attention to detail is key to
approaching any clinical case. This is particularly pertinent with potential hepatobiliary cases for a variety of
reasons. As outlined in the introduction, the large
hepatic functional reserve means that in order to diagnose diseases before there is significant, irreversible loss
of healthy liver tissue, the clinician needs to identify
cases with subtle and often vague clinical signs.
Symptoms such as anorexia, vomiting, lethargy or mild
polyuria/polydipsia, which are often waxing and waning,
should alert the clinician that liver disease is a potential
differential diagnosis. The onset of clinical signs may
­initially appear acute in nature but careful discussion
with the owner might elucidate a more chronic background than initially described. Box 60.1 summarizes
clinical signs that may be observed in animals with
liver disease.
The potential for toxin exposure should always be considered so a detailed description of the animal’s potential

Biochemical Evaluation
The employment of clinical pathologic testing is central
to the approach to animals with hepatobiliary disease.
In many cases, recognition of abnormal test results often
provides the first indication that liver disease may be
present. It is not uncommon to detect high liver enzyme
activities as the only abnormality on preanesthetic or
health screens, prompting further investigation. In addition, as outlined above, in view of the typical presentation of hepatobiliary cases, it is important to use clinical
pathology to aid in the diagnosis is liver disease early on
in the disease process. Often at this stage the clinical
signs may be vague and nonspecific with clinical pathology aiding greatly in the decision making and further
defining of such cases.
The laboratory evaluation of hepatobiliary patients has
several broad aims: to determine/confirm the presence
of hepatobiliary disease and assess hepatic function, to
aid in distinguishing primary or secondary hepatic
disease and to contribute to diagnostic planning or

certain hormones or drugs, such as corticosteroids, to
induce production of particular liver enzymes and the
presence of isoenzymes within tissues other than liver.
The clinical interpretation of the significance of liver

considered in the context of the patent, its history, and
the full clinical pathology results.

offer any indication of liver function. In an animal with a
primary hepatopathy, the magnitude of hepatocellular
enzyme release may broadly relate to the number of
hepatocytes affected, particularly in the acute setting.

Enzyme Markers of Liver Disease

The liver enzymes evaluated can be divided into two
main groups dependent on their cellular location and
clinical utility. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and
aspartate aminotransferase (AST) are the two most commonly measured markers of hepatocellular injury and
are found primarily within the hepatic cytosol. Alkaline
phosphatase (ALP) and gamma‐glutamyl transferase
(GGT) are the most commonly measured biliary

VetBooks.ir

60 Approach to the Patient with Liver Disease

important to appreciate that in severe chronic disease,
such as cirrhosis, the liver enzyme release may be
minimal due to reduced hepatic synthetic capacity.
­
In addition, the serial evaluation of serum enzyme
­activities can be more useful than a single time point in
determining the importance of liver enzyme elevation
and the likely prognosis in a patient. It is generally considered a favorable sign if values continue to fall gradually after a single liver insult whereas ongoing persistent
elevation may indicate a chronic hepatopathy and the
requirement for further investigation.
The serum enzyme activity at any point in time is
dependent on the overall hepatic activity of the enzyme
or the capacity for de novo synthesis (in response to cholestasis or drug induction), the serum half‐life of the
enzyme, and the cellular location of the enzyme (determining the ease of release of the enzyme, e.g., “leakage”
of cytosolic enzymes). These factors vary not only
between different enzymes but also between species, as
will be discussed below. Hence, it is important to ensure
species‐specific criteria are being used when interpreting the values in a given patient. When evaluating the
liver enzymes, it is important to consider the pattern of
enzyme increase (hepatocellular or cholestatic), the
magnitude of this change and the temporal pattern of the
enzyme changes over time. For example, are they
decreasing gradually, fluctuating or progressively
increasing? The reference intervals for liver enzymes
vary considerably between laboratories due to different
assay methods. In view of this, it is more appropriate to
consider the magnitude of increase in relation to the
upper limit of the reference interval when comparing
values between labs.
Hepatocellular/Leakage Enzymes

Alanine aminotrans­ferase is a cytosolic enzyme that is
released into the serum from hepatocytes with increased
hepatocyte membrane permeability or following hepatocellular necrosis. This enzyme is considered to be a sensitive indicator of hepatocellular injury in dogs and cats
and is also considered to be the most liver‐specific
enzyme in these species. Although ALT is also found in
cardiac and skeletal muscle and the kidneys, this is not
generally of clinical significance as the isoenzymes found
in these other locations either have short half‐lives or are
present at low concentrations. However, occasionally
severe muscle injury can result in ALT elevation.
The half‐life of ALT in the dog is controversial, with
reports ranging from about six hours to 2.5 days. What is
clear is that the half‐life is considerably shorter in the cat,
with the result that smaller elevations are far more clinically significant in this species. The highest increases in
ALT activity, in either species, are seen during acute
hepatic inflammation or necrosis, the magnitude of

­elevation, in this setting, being roughly proportional to
the number of hepatocytes affected but providing no
insight into the severity of injury or its reversibility.
Rapid elevations in enzyme activity occur following
changes in hepatocyte membrane permeability.
Following experimental toxin administration, values
rise sharply within 24–48 hours, peaking at values up to
100 times normal within approximately five days and
then falling back to normal within 2–3 weeks. In general,
with hepatic injury, a reduction in the enzyme activity of
approximately 50% every 2–3 days would be viewed as a
good prognostic sign. Elevated ALT activity can also
occur with cholestasis due to the damaging effect of
accumulated bile acids on hepatocyte membranes. The
elevations that occur in this setting are typically more
gradual in onset and are not as dramatic overall. Certain
drugs can also result in ALT enzyme increases, for
­example anticonvulsant drugs or corticosteroids. These
elevations tend to be dose dependent but also show considerable inter individual variation. The elevations seen
with phenobarbital administration would typically be
within the 4–5‐fold range compared to a 10‐fold or
higher elevation occurring in animals with hepatotoxicity. However, the results need to be interpreted in light of
the overall clinical picture and in combination with liver
function evaluation where there is any concern.
The interpretation of ALT elevation in the clinical setting frequently poses a diagnostic challenge. Persistent
elevations of ALT are characteristic of canine chronic
hepatitis and can be the only abnormality noted on a
blood panel in animals in the early stages of the disease.
Hence, elevations in excess of twice the upper limit of the
reference range occurring over 1–2 months are potentially significant and should not be disregarded. However,
frequently up to five‐fold elevations in ALT are observed
in dogs with primary gastrointestinal diseases such as
inflammatory bowel disease or pancreatitis. In addition,
hemolytic anemia or cardiovascular disease can cause
significant elevations in ALT secondary to hypoxia.
Endotoxemia or sepsis can cause secondary hepatic
changes, as can many endocrinopathies. These examples
demonstrate the limitations of ALT; while it is very sensitive for the detection of hepatocellular insult and hence
cases with potential primary hepatopathies, it is equally
sensitive for the detection of secondary hepatopathies
and “reactive” liver changes occurring in response to
other systemic illness or drug exposure. In view of this,
the clinician should interpret ALT activity in combination with the remainder of the clinical biochemistry,
knowledge of the animal’s breed and history along with
maintaining an awareness of the potential interference of
extrahepatic disease.
Aspartate aminotransferase is also a marker of hepatocellular damage within the group of “leakage” enzymes,

647

VetBooks.ir

648

having a predominantly cytosolic location within hepatocytes. However, there is in addition a mitochondrial
fraction, comprising about 30% of the total hepatic
enzyme activity, which is only released during hepatocellular necrosis. The half‐life of AST is about 4–20 hours
in the dog and one hour in the cat. In general, in acute
liver injury, elevations of AST mirror those of
ALT although the overall values tend not to be as high
(10–30‐fold increases in the dog and up to 50‐fold in the
cat). Following the insult, the AST values should return
to normal more quickly than ALT reflecting its shorter
half‐life. Hence, it has been suggested that persistent
AST elevation in this setting is a poor prognostic sign. In
cats, AST has been shown to be more sensitive than ALT
for the detection of hepatobiliary diseases, with sensitivities reported to be approximately 83% and 76% sensitivity respectively in one report. Elevations in AST also
occur with skeletal muscle disease so any elevation
occurring in the absence of ALT elevation should be
cross‐referenced with creatinine kinase measurement to
exclude this possibility. In general, most biochemical
profiles offer only one hepatocellular enzyme measurement, typically ALT, and the measurement of AST in
addition to this is unlikely to offer a marked clinical
advantage.
Biliary Enzymes

Alkaline phosphatase is a membrane‐bound enzyme that
has been shown to have a high sensitivity (85%) but low
specificity (51%) for the detection of hepatobiliary disease in dogs. The converse is true for cats, with reported
values of 48% sensitivity and 93% specificity. These performances reflect differences in the half‐lives and overall
enzyme activity in the two species along with differences
in the isoenzymes and their potential for induction (discussed further later).
In dogs and cats, there are a variety of tissues known to
exhibit ALP activity, including intestinal mucosa, renal
cortex, placenta, liver, and bone. There are two genes
encoding ALP in the dog with post-translation modifications resulting in different isoforms of the enzyme. The
tissue nonspecific ALP gene is responsible for the transcription of liver ALP (L‐ALP), bone ALP (B‐ALP), and
kidney ALP (K‐ALP), whereas the second gene encodes
intestinal ALP (I‐ALP). An additional isoenzyme, glucocorticoid‐induced ALP (G‐ALP), is important in the dog
and is thought to represent a post-translational modification of I‐ALP. In the dog, the total serum ALP (T‐ALP)
measured on clinical biochemistry profiles reflects the
combination of L‐ALP, B‐ALP, and G‐ALP; other isoenzymes fail to contribute to this measurement due to a
combination of their short half‐life and/or low overall
tissue activities. In the cat, T‐ALP comprises L‐ALP and
B‐ALP due to a lack of G‐ALP in this species, although

placental isoenzyme has also been detected late‐term
in this species.
An appreciation of the contributions of these isoenzymes is important when interpreting biochemistry
results. For example, B‐ALP increases with osteoblastic
activity and hence its contribution to T‐ALP varies with
age. In view of this, in young growing animals T‐ALP is
approximately twice the normal adult reference range
purely as a result of increased B‐ALP. In addition, elevations may occur in adult dogs with active bone lesions,
such as osteomyelitis or osteosarcoma, but these are
rarely more than five‐fold increases. Where there is concern in interpretation, it may occasionally be helpful to
look at an additional enzyme, such as GGT, with no bone
isoenzyme, to clarify the situation. The isoenzyme that
causes far more problems for interpretation is G‐ALP, as
discussed later.
Liver ALP is found predominantly within the periportal zone of the liver, bound to hepatocyte canalicular and
sinusoidal membranes. The serum activity of this enzyme
is increased in response to cholestasis (intra‐ and extrahepatic) and induction of de novo synthesis. ALP is
released into the circulation by enzyme‐induced solubilization from the hepatocyte membranes, a process that is
enhanced by bile salts and hence increases with cholestasis. In the latter situation, accumulated bile salts also
induce production of L‐ALP, significantly enhancing the
resultant increase in serum ALP activity. The half‐life of
L‐ALP is approximately 70 hours in the dog and six hours
in the cat. This short half‐life in the cat, combined with a
lower ALP activity in feline liver, is important practically.
Clinically significant elevations of ALP activity in the cat
are considerably smaller than those seen in the dog. Cats
with hepatic disease may have ALP elevations two‐ or
three‐fold higher than normal as opposed to dogs where
values are often more than four‐ or five‐fold normal. This
situation, in combination with the lack of G‐ALP enzyme
in the cat, results in the far lower ­sensitivity of ALP for
liver disease in the cat (48%) but enhanced specificity
(93%). In view of this, the interpretation of ALP elevation
in dogs and cats differs considerably.
In dogs, ALP induction occurs in response to endogenous and exogenous corticosteroids and phenobarbital.
The response to corticosteroids is rapid (increased ALP
mRNA within 24–48 hours) and may occur following
oral, topical (including ear/eye preparations) and parenteral exposure, with elevations in serum enzyme activity
persisting for up to six weeks after exposure has ceased.
In addition, a vacuolar hepatopathy, with glycogen accumulation within hepatocytes, occurs with exposure to
excessive corticosteroid levels. This too may contribute
to ALP elevation by generating intrahepatic cholestasis.
The overall ALP elevations can be dramatic and complicate the interpretation of ALP activity in the dog. G‐ALP,

VetBooks.ir

60 Approach to the Patient with Liver Disease

as outlined earlier, is the product of the I‐ALP gene. As
with L‐ALP, the hepatocyte is the site of de novo synthesis of G‐ALP, with membrane accumulation and elution
occurring in the same way. Exposure to endogenous or
exogenous corticosteroids results in G‐ALP induction
and hence increased serum activity. It was hoped that
measurement of the distinct isotypes of ALP within
a serum sample would aid the interpretation of serum
T‐ALP, but this has not been found to be the case
­clinically. While normal dogs have low G‐ALP (<15%
T‐ALP) and dogs exposed to corticosteroids have much
higher G‐ALP, the specificity of G‐ALP for corticosteroid exposure is low. Elevations in G‐ALP are observed in
dogs with primary liver disease, diabetes mellitus, and
other chronic illnesses. G‐ALP synthesis is also induced
in addition to L‐ALP by phenobarbital.
In a published series of 270 dogs with histopathologically confirmed hepatobiliary disease, the most marked
elevations of T‐ALP were documented in dogs with
cholestasis (median 10‐fold increase) followed, in order
of magnitude, by steroid‐induced hepatopathy, chronic
hepatitis, and hepatic necrosis (all medians approximately six‐fold increase or slightly less). Periportal injury
tends to result in more marked increases in T‐ALP activity than centrilobular pathology. Hepatocellular and
­biliary carcinomas have also been documented to show
increases in serum ALP activity, as have some nonhepatic tumors. Metabolic diseases with fatty infiltration of
the liver, such as diabetes mellitus and hepatic lipidosis,
are also associated with significant elevations in ALP. In
general, extrahepatic causes of ALP elevation are less
important in the cat and corticosteroid‐induced ALP
elevations do not occur in this species. As with ALT, the
level of ALP elevation observed does not correlate with
the underlying disease process and persistent elevation is
a source of more concern than a single abnormal value.
Elevations of ALP, like any clinical pathology test, must
be interpreted in the context of other laboratory findings
and in light of the patient’s signalment and history.
For example, Scottish terriers are known to have higher
ALP activities than other breeds with an, as yet, poorly
characterised ­underlying cause.
Gamma‐glutamyltransferase is also a membrane‐
bound biliary enzyme. The serum GGT activity is largely
derived from liver sources of the enzyme, with increased
activity resulting from, as with ALP, de novo synthesis or
increased elution from biliary membranes in response to
cholestasis. In general, GGT elevations parallel rises in
ALP. GGT also shows corticosteroid induction but,
unlike ALP, has no bone isoenzyme and shows less
induction with phenobarbital administration.
The relative diagnostic performances of GGT and ALP
were compared in a study of 270 dogs with confirmed
hepatobiliary disease. GGT was found to be more

­specific for liver disease than ALP (87% compared to
51%), but it showed considerably less sensitivity (46%
compared to 85%). In this study, it was suggested that the
diagnostic value of the enzymes could be increased by
considering the two enzymes in series, first looking at
ALP and then GGT. In this setting, the positive predictive value and specificity were improved without a major
decrease in the negative predictive value. The specificity
of increased ALP and GGT activity used in this series
was 91%. When comparing the relative performance of
the two enzymes in cats, the converse is true: GGT is
more sensitive but less specific than ALP. In a study of
54 cats with hepatic disease, the sensitivity and specificity of GGT were found to be 83% and 67% respectively,
compared to 48% and 93% for ALP. There was, however,
one notable exception to this situation. In cats with
hepatic lipidosis, ALP is more sensitive than GGT, with
the latter within the reference interval or only mildly
elevated in a number of cases.
In summary, the measurement of ALP is probably
preferable to GGT in the dog but the converse is true for
the cat. However, there are likely to be some additional
benefits from the measurement of both enzymes.
Markers of Liver Function
Plasma Proteins

The liver is the exclusive site of albumin production and
hence liver disease is an important differential diagnosis
to consider in an animal with hypoalbuminemia. The
liver’s reserve capacity for albumin production is large
and the half‐life of albumin in the circulation is in excess
of a week. In view of this, hypoalbuminemia tends to
occur in animals with chronic hepatic disorders, such as
cirrhosis, or with , where liver synthetic capacity is
severely compromised. Hence, serum albumin measurement is a relatively insensitive measure of hepatic insufficiency. In addition to this, hypoalbuminemia is not
specific for hepatic disease. It can occur with protein‐
losing enteropathies and nephropathies, exudative skin
conditions, vasculitis, third space loss, acute blood loss,
and secondary to inflammation, reflecting albumin being
a negative acute‐phase protein.
The liver produces alpha‐ and beta‐globulins, whereas
lymphoid cells produce gamma‐globulins, meaning
that the liver is not the exclusive source of the globulins
measured on a biochemistry profile. Whilst hepatic synthetic failure may result in hypoglobulinemia, reflecting
the liver’s role in production, more commonly hyperglobulinemia occurs with acquired liver disease. This can
result from a variety of causes including an underlying
inflammatory disorder with enhanced gamma‐globulin
production, the generation of increased quantities of
acute phase reactants (within the alpha‐ and beta‐­
globulin fractions) or as a result of systemic immune

649

VetBooks.ir

650

Section 7 Diseases of the Liver, Gallbladder, and Bile Ducts

stimulation following decreased antigen clearance by
Kupffer cells. It is important to note that in some cases,
the globulin elevation may be sufficient to mask hypoalbuminemia if only the total protein concentration is
measured on a blood panel.
Coagulation Factors

The role of the liver in the production of coagulation
­factors and the frequency with which coagulation parameter abnormalities occur were discussed earlier. As with
albumin, whilst reduced coagulation factor production
can result from hepatic synthetic failure, it is an insensitive indicator of dysfunction. In addition, the overlap
between the liver’s role in factor production, activation
and clearance, along with fibrinolysis, make interpretation of the results of hemostatic testing challenging.
From a clinical perspective, the evaluation of a coagulation profile is important in any patient suspected to have
liver disease that is scheduled to have further invasive
diagnostic procedures, such as a liver biopsy.
Protein Catabolism

The liver produces urea from ammonia, releasing it into
the systemic circulation for renal excretion. The serum
urea concentration may be close to or below the reference interval in patients with hepatic insufficiency, PSS,
and urea cycle abnormalities. Reports have suggested
that approximately 65% of dogs and cats with PSS
have low blood urea levels, reflecting reduced synthetic
capacity. However, as with other tests, this finding is not
specific to liver disease. Serum urea concentrations may
also be decreased by diuresis and medullary wash‐out,
malnutrition or a protein‐restricted diet. Conversely,
gastrointestinal bleeding can result in a disproportionately high serum urea concentration relative to serum
creatinine and should alert the clinician to this possibility
if observed on biochemistry results.
The catabolism of dietary amino acids and urea by
bacteria within the gastrointestinal tract produces
ammonia, which is normally cleared from the portal circulation by the liver. The bulk of this ammonia is then
converted within the liver to urea during the urea cycle.
In view of this, hyperammonemia can result from hepatic
insufficiency, portosystemic shunting or dysfunction of
the urea cycle. The latter group includes rare genetic
cycle abnormalities, cobalamin deficiency or arginine
deficiency (cats). The large reserve capacity of the urea
cycle makes hyperammonemia a relatively insensitive
test of liver function. The measurement of blood ammonia concentration is far more sensitive for the detection
of acquired and CPSS, which effectively short‐circuit the
liver, with reported sensitivities ranging between
80–100% in dogs and just over 80% in cats. These values
are increased further by the measurement of postprandial

blood ammonia levels, with one paper showing
­sensitivities of 81% and 91% in pre‐ and postprandial
samples. The reported sensitivity of ammonia for the
detection of hepatocellular dysfunction in this paper
was 36%, highlighting its limitation.
Another paper compared the diagnostic utility of
plasma ammonia and fasting serum bile acids in the
diagnosis of PSS in dogs. They found bile acids to be a
little less sensitive, but considerably less specific than
ammonia measurement, although the use of postprandial samples would have been likely to improve the sensitivity (see later). With adjustment of the cut‐off value
for the ammonia level to 75 μmol/L, the sensitivity and
specificity for the detection of congenital or acquired
PSS were optimized at 92% and 98% respectively.
Hence, it can be very useful for the diagnosis of these
conditions.
One of the limiting factors for ammonia measurement
is the sample handling requirements. Samples should be
collected immediately onto ice, the plasma separated
from erythrocytes rapidly and the assay performed
within 30 minutes, rendering measurement in a practice
setting challenging. This problem is further compounded
by the fact that the results of dry chemistry tests have
frequently been shown to be unreliable. More recently,
however, point‐of‐care analyzers have become increasingly available, offering a viable, more reliable option.
Carbohydrate Metabolism

The liver plays a central role in variety of pathways
involved in carbohydrate metabolism, but from a diagnostic standpoint, the main assay relating to these functions is blood glucose. Hypoglycemia can occur with
liver ­disease, although again this is a very insensitive test
reflecting the significant reserve capacity for glucose
production. Some cases of CPSS can present with hypoglycemia, as can animals with severe hepatic compromise such as massive hepatic necrosis or severe c­ irrhosis.
Hepatic neoplasms can occasionally result in hypoglycemia due to either the release of insulin‐like factors (e.g.,
IGF‐2) or excessive glucose consumption. Glycogen
storage diseases and rare congenital hepatic enzyme
deficiencies can also result in hypoglycemia, as can a
variety of extrahepatic diseases. Hence hypoglycemia is
neither sensitive nor specific for the identification of
hepatic disease.
Lipid Metabolism

The liver is involved in a variety of metabolic pathways,
with the synthesis of cholesterol and lipoproteins most
relevant from the point of view of laboratory results.
The serum cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations
observed in animals with liver disease vary considerably
from normal to increased or decreased. Since these

VetBooks.ir

60 Approach to the Patient with Liver Disease

analytes are also affected by a variety of other extrahepatic causes, neither test offers utility as a specific
marker for liver disease. They are, however, useful in
contributing to the overall clinical picture and may aid
in the identification of relevant extrahepatic illnesses.
Hypercholesterolemia occurs with severe hepatic
insufficiency or in animals with congenital or acquired
PSS, but can occur with a variety of conditions, including
gastrointestinal disease and hypoadrenocorticism.
Hypercholesterolemia may occur with cholestasis, but
again is not specific for liver disease as it can occur
with endocrinopathies, protein‐losing nephropathies,
pancreatitis, and primary hyperlipidemias. A mild
hypertriglyceridemia may occur with cholestasis.
In addition, hypertriglyceridemia has been associated
with a proportion of dogs with biliary mucoceles.
Others

Bilirubin metabolism was discussed in an earlier section.
From a diagnostic standpoint, it is helpful to consider the
potential causes of hyperbilirubinemia by dividing the
causes into prehepatic, hepatic, and posthepatic. The former can be quickly identified by significant anemia and
enhanced erythrocyte breakdown and once excluded, the
presence of hyperbilirubinemia becomes far more specific
for liver disease than many of the other clinical pathology
analytes. Despite this, bilirubin measurement still has
important limitations. As with other parameters, it is still
a relatively insensitive measure of hepatic insufficiency,
becoming elevated only once significant hepatic reserve is
exhausted, for example with end‐stage cirrhosis patients.
In addition, hyperbilirubinemia does not distinguish
between primary and secondary hepatopathies. Sepsis
can cause significant cholestasis and hyperbilirubinemia,
and many of the causes of posthepatic jaundice are extrahepatic, such as pancreatitis and pancreatic or duodenal
neoplasia. In cats, hyperbilirubinemia is a more sensitive
indicator of hepatobiliary disease than it is in dogs, reflecting the increased proportion of liver diseases in the cat
that involve biliary disease.
When approaching a patient with hyperbilirubinemia,
having excluded prehepatic jaundice, the next stage is to
try to establish whether hepatic or posthepatic pathology
is most likely. Evaluation of the remainder of the biochemistry panel is important to establish if there are
other features suggestive of hepatic insufficiency, for
example hypoalbuminemia, and to examine the hepatic
enzyme activities. Typically, with posthepatic jaundice
there is dramatic elevation of the cholestatic liver
enzymes, more so than the hepatocellular leakage
enzymes, hypercholesterolemia and no evidence of
hepatic insufficiency. However, the picture is often not
clear‐cut, with hepatocellular enzyme activities increasing in patients with posthepatic cholestasis over time

due to the toxic effects of accumulated bile salts, and
markers of hepatic insufficiency unchanged due to their
lack of sensitivity. Abdominal ultrasound is the next step
in examining such a patient, and is typically the most
useful method to distinguish between hepatic and posthepatic jaundice (see later). In some patients, the distinction between hepatic and posthepatic disease is blurred
with their presentation involving components of each,
for example cholangitis.
Bile Acids

Bile acids are steroid acids that are a normal constituent of
bile and function in fat digestion within the intestine. The
two primary bile acids, cholic and chenodeoxycholic, are
synthesized in the liver from cholesterol and are then conjugated, mainly with taurine, before being excreted in bile
for release into the gut or storage in the gallbladder. These
conjugated bile acids are ionized at intestinal pH and
function in fat digestion by aiding the formation of
micelles. Intestinal bacteria metabolize some of the primary bile acids to the secondary bile acids, deoxycholic
and lithocholic acid, within the gut lumen. Once in the
ileum, primary and secondary bile acids bind to specific
receptors, allowing their reabsorption and enterohepatic
circulation. This system sees a maximum of approximately
5% fecal loss per day of bile acids, with the remainder
returned to the liver in the portal circulation for removal
and reexcretion. The daily losses are replaced by liver
manufacture of new bile acids, maintaining a constant bile
acid pool in the normal animal. This low‐level replacement is not affected by reduced liver function.
This enterohepatic circulation of bile acids forms the
basis of the serum bile acid assay, a dynamic liver function
test. The rationale for this test is that reduced liver function
or impairment of the enterohepatic circulation, due to
either reduced biliary excretion or disruption of the portal
circulation, results in elevation of the serum bile acid concentration measured in peripheral blood. The indications
for its use are in the diagnosis of PSS and the assessment of
liver function in cases where liver disease is suspected but
hyperbilirubinemia is not present. The latter is a less sensitive indicator of hepatic dysfunction; once hyperbilirubinemia is present in a patient, the measurement of serum
bile acids offers no further information.
A fasted serum bile acid is obtained after a 12‐hour fast
and assesses enterohepatic circulation in the fasted state.
A postprandial sample taken two hours after feeding provides an endogenous challenge. The rationale for the latter is that feeding stimulates gallbladder contraction with
release of stored bile and hence increased quantities of
bile acids for enterohepatic circulation, thus providing an
additional challenge for the assessment of liver function.
It has been shown that a proportion of PSS cases have
results within the reference interval for fasting bile acids

651

VetBooks.ir

652

Section 7 Diseases of the Liver, Gallbladder, and Bile Ducts

but abnormal results on a postprandial sample. However,
rather than the postprandial sample specifically providing additional information over the fasting sample, use
of the paired pre‐ and postprandial samples together
increases the overall sensitivity of the test. The postprandial bile acid value may be the lower of the two values in some cases, potentially reflecting factors such as
gallbladder contraction during the fasting period,
incomplete gallbladder contraction, delayed gastric
emptying, altered intestinal motility, and decreased bile
acid absorption. When interpreting these paired samples, the higher value should be interpreted. Most veterinary laboratories utilize enzymatic fluorimetric or
spectrophotometric methodologies for the assay, which
means that lipemia and hemolysis can affect the results.
The reference intervals provided by individual labs vary
based on their individual methodology but are generally
very approximately <5 μmol/L and <10 μmol/L for pre‐
and postprandial values, respectively. However, some
normal animals have values within these intervals,
­necessitating adjustment of the cut‐off values used for
interpretation.
Serum bile acid assays (SBA) represent one of the
more sensitive measures of liver function available at
this time. Their utility relies on the fact that they give
an indication of liver function whereas liver enzymes
offer markers of liver insult or drug induction. In general, the lower sensitivity of bile acids for the detection
of hepatobiliary disease makes them poor screening
tests. They are more appropriately employed as a function test to evaluate patients prescreened by routine
biochemistry, with the aim of identifying those patients
in whom a liver biopsy should be considered. One
exception to this situation is their performance in
patients with PSS. Sensitivity of 100% for the detection
of PSS in cats and dogs has been quoted using cut‐off
values of 20 μmol/L and 25 μmol/L respectively, for
postprandial samples. The sensitivities noted in these
papers for the identification of other causes of hepatic
dysfunction were considerably lower than these values,
as has been noted elsewhere.
The values gained for SBA provide no indication of the
underlying cause of hepatic dysfunction, do not differentiate between primary and secondary hepatopathies, and
provide no information about disease severity or overall
prognosis. An early paper identified 100% specificity for
the presence of histopathologic abnormalities on hepatic
biopsies using cut‐off values of 20 μM/L for preprandial
and 25 μM/L postprandial samples. These results were
gained in a highly prescreened population, suspected by
experts to have liver disease based on clinical findings
and routine clinical pathologic testing. Hence, the prevalence of hepatobiliary disease in this population was
high. This fact affects the test performance considerably

and should be remembered when tests are being utilized
in very different clinical situations. When SBA have been
present on biochemistry panels and used more as screening tests, some spurious high values have been observed
in animals with no other evidence of liver disease.
Research suggests that these values may relate to bacterial overgrowth and the measurement of increased concentrations of deconjugated bile acids in some patients.
In other animals, extrahepatic disease is likely to be
resulting in high values and secondary hepatopathies.
The point is that care must be taken to consider the
context in which test results are gained; the specificity of
the test will be lower in a population with a lower prevalence of hepatobiliary disease. Using increased cut‐off
values for the assay will increase the specificity of the
test, but this is usually at the expense of sensitivity.
Values above 40 μmol/L are more likely to indicate
­primary hepatic dysfunction unless underlying causes
such as hyperadrenocorticism are identified. In view of
this, the author typically takes this value as more indicative of the need for further evaluation, such as a liver
biopsy. However, values between 20 and 40 μmol/L represent an important “gray‐zone” and warrant critical evaluation in relation to the patient, its clinical signs, and the
potential for extrahepatic causes. The evaluation of pre‐
and postprandial samples may aid clarification, if not
already performed, and the test should be repeated after a
period of time where there is any uncertainty. It should
always be remembered that the test, while helpful and
better than most measures of liver function, still has limitations. Where there is persistent liver enzyme elevation
over time, even without elevation of SBA, a liver biopsy
may well be indicated on a case‐by‐case basis (see later).
Patients with values in the “gray‐zone” with clinical signs
suggestive of liver disease or those without clinical signs
in which elevations persist with no other explanation are
also likely to warrant a liver biopsy. The measurement of
urine bile acids has been investigated but does not appear
to offer particular advantage over the SBA.
Hematology
Mild to moderate anemia is common in patients with
liver disease. The more common causes include anemia
of chronic disease and gastrointestinal bleeding. Acute
bleeding following liver biopsy, rupture of neoplasm or
hepatic rupture, resulting from trauma or pathologic
processes such as peliosis or hepatic amyloidosis, can
also occur, as can hemostatic disorders. Morphologic
changes in erythroctes (poikilocytes) are seen in some
dogs with chronic liver disease. These include irregularly
speculated cells, or acanthocytes and target cells, both of
which are thought to result from altered phospholipid
­ eoplasia
metabolism. In addition, microangiopathy with n

VetBooks.ir

60 Approach to the Patient with Liver Disease

or DIC may result in the generation of schistocytes.
A frequent finding in dogs with CPSS is microcytosis,
thought to reflect altered iron metabolism.
There are no specific leukocyte changes seen with liver
disease. An inflammatory leukogram may occur with
any inflammatory, infectious (e.g., leptospirosis) or neoplastic process. In one report, 16 out of 36 dogs (44%)
with chronic hepatitis were found to have an inflammatory leukogram. Thrombocyte changes may also be seen
in dogs with liver disease, although again the changes are
nonspecific. Thrombocyte counts may be reduced in
animals with DIC and significantly lower thrombocyte
counts were reported in dogs with chronic hepatitis and
cirrhosis.
Urinalysis
Ammonium biurate crystals have been reported to occur
in 40–70% of dogs with CPSS and may provide an early
clue to diagnosis in such patients, although they are not
a specific finding. Bilirubinuria can also be an important
finding. Since cats have a high renal threshold for bilirubin and their renal tubules do not make bilirubin, its
presence is always significant in this species. In dogs,
lower levels of bilirubin are a normal finding, particularly
in male dogs. High levels suggest hemolytic or hepatobiliary disease and discolored urine may be one of the
first reasons an owner seeks veterinary attention for a
jaundiced pet. Urine specific gravity may be reduced in
animals with CPSS and hepatic insufficiency in line with
the observed polyuria/polydipsia in these cases.
Serology
Dependent on the geographic location, serologic testing
for a variety of infectious agents may be appropriate, for
example Leptospira, Neospora, Toxoplasma, Rocky
Mountain spotted fever, Dirofilaria, Ehrlichia, and
­systemic mycoses.
Genetic Tests
The deletion mutation that causes copper hepatotoxicosis in the majority of Bedlington terriers has been identified and is now available as a genetic test for the disease
in this breed (www.vetgen.com). This test is run alongside a previously identified linkage marker to identify
any dogs in the breed that are affected by copper toxicosis but do not have this specific deletion mutation.
The occurrence of many chronic hepatopathies in specific breeds and the recognition of inheritance patterns
in some of the breeds make it likely that more genetic
tests will become available as the genetic bases of these
diseases are identified.

Newer Tests
There are a variety of newer assays being investigated,
for example, 13C‐labeled galactose breath test for
­assessment of liver function and serum protein C for
the ­
differentiation of portal vein hypoplasia without
­portal hypertension (formerly known as microvascular
­dysplasia) from PSS.
Summary of the Interpretation of Clinical
Pathology
As discussed, there is no one clinical pathology finding
that defines a specific diagnosis of hepatobiliary disease
in dogs and cats. The clinician needs to interpret all the
tests together in the context of the patient and its clinical
presentation. Consideration of patterns of abnormalities
in the clinical pathology tests rather than individual tests
in isolation can be helpful in increasing or decreasing the
index of suspicion of different conditions, as outlined in
Table 60.1. Once this type of interpretation has been
considered, the use of diagnostic imaging allows further
refinement and direction towards either the pursuit of
potential extrahepatic causes of the animal’s signs and
laboratory findings or more specific hepatic testing such
as cytology or biopsy.
Diagnostic Imaging
Diagnostic imaging is a very important component of
the investigation of a patient with suspected hepatobiliary disease, typically performed in combination with
clinical pathology evaluation. Imaging can aid directly in
the identification of hepatobiliary disease and the presence of any extrahepatic conditions that may be of
­relevance or directly contributing to the generation of
secondary hepatopathies. In some situations, imaging
may allow direct identification of the specific cause of
the hepatobiliary disease, for example congenital PSS,
although more typically it adds pieces to the overall clinical picture being built up for a given case. In some situations, prognostic information may be contributed, for
example the finding of a very nodular and irregular liver
in a dog suspected to have cirrhosis.
Abdominal ultrasound is particularly useful in guiding the approach to jaundiced patients, as outlined
earlier, and the identification of biliary tract abnormalities such as biliary mucoceles or cholecystitis. It
can also be ­helpful to establish if hepatic lesions are
localized or generalized within the parenchyma and to
provide guidance in gaining targeted biopsies or bile
samples as indicated. Further detail on imaging in the
investigation of hepatobiliary disease is covered in
Chapter 61.

Cytologic and Histopathologic Evaluation
in Liver Disease
The results gained from diagnostic imaging and clinical
pathology testing do not typically provide a definitive
diagnosis in patients with liver disease, except in cases
such as CPSS. The gold standard for diagnosis in these
patients is usually histopathologic evaluation of a liver
biopsy. The liver biopsy can provide a definitive diagnosis in some situations, for example neoplasia. In other
cases, while a specific diagnosis may not be made, the
biopsy provides important information about the pathologic reaction pattern observed, including the location of
lesions, cell types involved, and the chronicity of the
changes. This information is invaluable in guiding therapeutic intervention and providing prognostic information. In addition, follow‐up biopsies offer an important
guide to the clinician when assessing the response to
therapy. Cytologic evaluation of samples may be considered in some situations and is discussed below. In general, liver histopathology offers significant diagnostic
advantages over cytologic samples.
Cytologic Evaluation

It is possible to gain cytologic samples from liver patients
by performing percutaneous ultrasound‐guided fine
needle aspiration of liver parenchyma or bile by cholecystocentesis. Percutaneous aspiration of ascitic fluid
can also provide useful information. These techniques
are minimally invasive and are associated with a low risk
of complications. The clinician should exercise caution
when approaching patients with hemostatic disorders,
although the risk is far less with a fine needle aspiration
compared to liver biopsy.
In general, the indications for fine needle aspirates of
hepatic parenchyma are the same as those outlined later
for liver biopsy. However, the main disadvantage of fine
needle aspirates and cytologic evaluation is the limited
diagnostic accuracy of this approach. The sample size
gained provides a limited number of cells to evaluate,
hemodilution may cloud interpretation and in addition,
no morphologic information about the lesion is provided, as it is with histopathology.
Studies that have compared results gained with fine
needle aspiration and histopathology have generally
shown poor concordance rates. One study evaluated
56 dogs and 41 cats and showed agreement between fine
needle aspirates and histopathology in approximately
30% of dogs and 50% of cats. The greatest agreement was
seen with vacuolar hepatopathies, largely accounting for
the higher accuracy in cats. However, this category also
had a high rate of misdiagnosis as the primary underlying lesion was missed on cytologic examination in many
cases. Since hepatic lipidosis in cats is frequently a sequel

to an underlying disease rather than a primary diagnosis,
this would place important limitations on cytology as a
sole means of diagnosis. With diffuse or focal neoplastic
disease, aspirates can prove useful; for example, a diagnosis of lymphoma may alleviate the need for a biopsy.
However, this is not the case in all situations; the
­differentiation of nodular hyperplasia and hepatoma is
not possible cytologically. In addition, the performance
for canine inflammatory liver diseases is generally poor.
This relates to both the importance of liver architecture
in the categorization of the diagnosis (e.g., chronic
­hepatitis versus cirrhosis) and the chances of missing
inflammatory cells where there are areas of fibrosis.
Occasionally, infectious agents such as histoplasmosis
can be diagnosed by fine needle aspiration.
Overall, the clinician must be aware of the limitations
of fine needle aspirates of liver parenchyma and regard
them more as a contributor of information rather than
providing a definitive diagnosis in most situations. The
main advantages are the safety aspects in high‐risk
patients and the general requirement for only limited
sedation. They can also be performed quickly, contributing to patient planning and even a final diagnosis in some
cases.
Cytologic evaluation of ascitic fluid in combination
with analysis of the total protein content and cell count
allows determination of the nature of the ascites, for
example whether it is a transudate, modified transudate
or exudate. In general, accurate categorization of the
ascites aids in diagnostic planning by narrowing
down the potential differentials considered in a case. For
example, demonstration of an exudate with a bilirubin
concentration greater than twice that of the serum would
suggest bile peritonitis and should prompt surgical intervention. More frequently with liver disease, a modified
transudate is obtained, resulting from portal hypertension and increased hepatic lymph leakage.
Bile cytology can also provide important information
where clinical signs are suggestive of cholestasis or gallbladder abnormalities are detected ultrasonographically.
These samples can be gained by cholecystocentesis
either percutaneously by ultrasound guidance or directly
during laparoscopy or laparotomy. The finding of bacterbilia and/or neutrophils within the bile supports a diagnosis of bacterial cholecystitis, or cholangitis if there is
histopathologic evidence to support hepatic changes. In
addition to cytologic evaluation, anaerobic and aerobic
bacteriologic culture of bile should be performed. In the
author’s experience, bacteria are evident within bile far
more frequently than inflammatory cells and occasionally provide evidence of a bacterial etiology in patients
where bile culture proves negative due to antibiotic
administration. In other patients, bacterial culture may
be positive in the absence of any cytologic abnormalities.

655

VetBooks.ir

656

Section 7 Diseases of the Liver, Gallbladder, and Bile Ducts

In general, bacteriologic culture of bile yields far more
positive results than culture of liver parenchyma.
Histopathologic Evaluation
Indications

As discussed earlier, the laboratory tests for liver disease
rarely identify a specific etiology. Having employed clinical pathology and ultrasonography as diagnostic tests to
identify potential liver disease, evaluation of a liver
biopsy aids the provision of a diagnosis and prognosis
and in guidance of therapeutic intervention. In general, a
liver biopsy is indicated in the following circumstances.
Asymptomatic patients with persistent, serial elevations in liver enzyme activities.
●● Asymptomatic patients with abnormal hepatic function tests (e.g., fasting serum bile acid or postprandial
serum bile acid).
●● Where hepatic parenchymal abnormalities are identified ultrasonographically.
●● Where there is unexplained hepatomegaly.
●● To assess response to therapeutic intervention.
●● Evaluation of animals with potential breed‐specific
hepatopathies.
●● Any animal with progressive signs of liver disease.
●●

It is important to recognise the potential for the occurrence of liver enzyme elevation and secondary “reactive”
hepatopathies as a result of extrahepatic causes.
Consideration of and, if appropriate, evaluation for the
presence of potential extrahepatic causes, such as hyperadrenocorticism in dogs, hyperthyroidism in cats and
gastrointestinal or pancreatic disease, is important
before pursuing a liver biopsy, particularly where only
liver enzyme elevation is noted on a biochemistry panel.
The consideration of more than one liver enzyme activity, evaluation of results on more than one occasion and
performing a liver function test, such as pre‐ and postprandial bile acids, can be helpful to clarify the situation
where there is any doubt.
Prebiopsy Considerations

When planning liver biopsy, there are several important
factors to consider, including risk to the patient and the
type of biopsy procedure to be used. The main types of
biopsy approaches available are ultrasound‐guided needle biopsy, laparoscopic biopsy, and surgical biopsy. The
most important potential complications of liver biopsy
are hemorrhage, trauma to adjacent organs, and infection, the relative risks of which vary with the technique
used and are discussed further later.
It is important to evaluate the overall clinical stability
of a patient and hemostatic function prior to obtaining a
liver biopsy. The circulatory status and potential for
hemorrhage should be considered in addition to how

well the animal will tolerate sedation or general anesthesia. The latter is particularly a consideration in patients
with signs of HE where medical management to stabilize
the patient prior to more invasive procedures is often
necessary. A minimum database to screen hemostatic
function should include a platelet count, prothrombin
time (PT), and partial thromboplastin time (PTT). The
measurement of buccal mucosal bleeding time (after
establishing a normal platelet count on a blood smear) is
also recommended due to some reports of increased
complications due to primary hemostatic abnormalities
(platelet dysfunction) rather than secondary hemostatic
(coagulation factor) abnormalities. Measurement of
fibrinogen along with fibrin degradation products (FDPs)
and D‐dimers to assess for increased fibrinolysis might
also be considered. However, it should be noted that
there is often poor correlation between coagulation
parameters and major complications at liver biopsy.
Although there is little veterinary literature published in
the area, one study suggested that a platelet count below
80 × 109/L, a PTT more than 1.5 times the reference
interval in cats and a PT above the reference interval in
dogs were all associated with an increased risk of minor
complications in animals undergoing ultrasound‐guided
needle biopsies.
Some clinicians suggest administration of vitamin K 24
hours prior to biopsy in all cases. It is certainly appropriate to treat any patients with prolonged coagulation
screens, as administration has been shown to improve
clotting times in many patients. The administration of
vitamin K to all hyperbilirubinemic patients, particularly
cats, is probably prudent in view of the role of bile in the
adsorption of fat‐soluble vitamins and the insensitivity
of PT and PTT in detecting bleeding diatheses. The use
of fresh‐frozen plasma to deliver coagulation factors to
patients with mildly increased PT and PTT is also an
option. Following a liver biopsy, it is essential that
patients are closely monitored over at least 12 hours for
clinical signs of postbiopsy hemorrhage. Evaluation of
heart rate, mucous membrane color, abdominal size, and
mentation is important. Measurement of total protein
and packed cell volume does not provide useful information when monitoring for acute hemorrhage.
Ultrasound‐Guided Biopsy

Ultrasound‐guided biopsies involve the use of a cutting‐
type needle which is ideally automated or semiautomated. These are spring‐loaded needles similar to the
manual Tru‐cut style and help when coordinating operation of the ultrasound probe with one hand and the
biopsy gun with the other. The fully automated devices
initially fire the inner part of the needle containing the
biopsy channel and then the outer cutting device rapidly
afterwards. The semiautomated ones allow the operator

VetBooks.ir

60 Approach to the Patient with Liver Disease

to position the inner part of the needle and then fire the
outer section. There are advantages to each type but the
semi-automated ones probably offer greater accuracy in
positioning the needle for more precise sampling. There
are reports of increased risk of fatal complications when
using the fully automated Tru‐cut biopsy needle in cats
so its use in this species is not recommended.
The advantages of ultrasound‐guided biopsy are the
less invasive nature of the procedure compared to laparotomy and the need for sedation rather than general
anesthesia in most patients. Multiple sites may be sampled along with the additional advantage of targeting
potentially abnormal areas identified ultrasonographically. The relatively low cost to the owner and reduced
recovery times are also beneficial. However, there are
significant limitations to the technique. The risk of hemorrhage is important and is greater with this technique
than with laparotomy or laparoscopy where there is
more scope for both the detection of hemorrhage and
intervention where necessary. Large‐volume ascites is a
contraindication for this type of biopsy technique as it
may increase the risk of significant hemorrhage.
Microhepatica is also a contraindication due to the risk
of inadvertent damage to other tissues.
Another important limitation of Tru‐cut style biopsies is the small sample size and hence the diagnostic
accuracy of samples gained. A study looking at biopsy
samples from 98 dogs and 26 cats compared the results
gained by three different pathologists evaluating two
needle biopsies (18 gauge automated string‐triggered
needle) and a wedge biopsy from the same animal. All
three pathologists agreed on the morphologic diagnosis
for a given patient 44% of the time using needle biopsies
and 65% of the time when relying on evaluation of the
wedge biopsies. Overall, the results gained from the
needle biopsies concurred with those gained from
the wedge biopsies in only 47% of dogs and 50% of cats.
The discordance rate increased still further when
patients with inflammatory or vascular disease or those
with significant fibrosis were considered separately.
The use of a 14 or 16 gauge needle rather than an 18
gauge needle is likely to increase the accuracy of diagnosis by increasing the average number of portal triads
sampled. However, the risk of hemorrhage is increased
with increased needle size. The use of a 16 gauge needle
for dogs and 18 gauge for cats is often most practical,
taking a larger number of needle biopsies (3–5) from
multiple sites so that the risk of missing a lesion due to
patchy distribution or small sample size is further
reduced. Despite this approach, with the ultrasound‐
guided approach there is often a tendency to biopsy a
more limited number of liver lobes than with surgical
approaches due to the limitations of access and ease of
imaging.

Surgical Biopsy

A wedge biopsy gained at laparotomy is another method
for obtaining a liver biopsy. This may be performed by
performing a random biopsy from the edge of a liver lobe
using a guillotining suture or in a more directed way in an
abnormal area using transfixing ligatures or a biopsy
punch (see surgical texts for more detailed information
about biopsy method). This approach offers the advantage
of the clinician being able to grossly examine the liver and
extrahepatic biliary tract along with other intraabdominal
organs that may impact the liver, for example the pancreas
and duodenum. There is also the option to biopsy other
organs and gain bile samples for cytology and culture.
Multiple, large biopsies may then be taken from areas the
clinician identifies to be abnormal, potentially finding
smaller lesions that may not have been apparent at ultrasound. This significantly reduces the problems of sampling error and allows samples to be gained from multiple
liver lobes. This approach is not affected by liver size and
allows attention to hemostasis with use of direct manual
pressure and/or topical hemostatic agents (e.g., Gelfoam®).
The main disadvantages of surgical biopsies are the more
invasive nature of the procedure, the increased recovery
time, and requirement for general anesthesia. The cost to
the owner is also significant.
Laparoscopic Biopsy

Laparoscopic biopsy of the liver affords many of the
advantages of surgical liver biopsies but is far less invasive
and allows faster patient recovery. The clinician is able to
grossly inspect the entire liver and extrahepatic biliary system, again taking bile samples as indicated. Surrounding
structures can also be examined and in some cases biopsied, although the latter is more straightforward with laparotomy. The biopsy samples are taken using specially
designed forceps and can be taken easily from multiple
regions with clear visualization allowing attention to
hemostasis. As with laparotomy, local pressure, hemostatic agents or electrocautery may be employed to limit
any hemorrhage. The sample size gained is good, again
reducing problems with sampling error. The main disadvantages of laparoscopy are the cost of equipment and the
need for significant training. As with surgery, there is a
need for general anesthesia and the cost is higher than
ultrasound‐guided sampling. A recent retrospective paper
showed low complication rates, although potential complications, other than hemorrhage, include air embolism,
damage to viscera with trocar placement and the potential
for seeding of neoplastic cells through port sites. The latter would also be a potential complication with needle
biopsies. Approximately 4% of cases in this study required
conversion to a laparotomy.
Overall, there are significant advantages provided
by surgical or laparoscopic biopsies and these are the

preferred choice of the author if the pet owner is willing
to take this approach. When approaching cases with
jaundice, it is important to utilize clinical pathology findings in combination with ultrasound to try to establish if
jaundice is hepatic or posthepatic in origin (having
excluded prehepatic – see earlier). If extrahepatic bile
duct obstruction is suspected, laparotomy and laparoscopy allow direct visualization of the extrahepatic biliary
system and local organs, evaluation of patency of the bile
duct, bile sampling and, if necessary, cholecystectomy.
Surgical intervention, such as biliary diversion or resection of a mass, is also possible with a laparotomy.
Ultrasound‐guided liver biopsy should be avoided in this
situation due to risks of rupture to the biliary tree. The
author still prefers the surgical or laparoscopic approach
even in cases of suspected intrahepatic jaundice due to
the advantages offered in examining and sampling the
gallbladder and local organs. Ultrasound has been shown
to be insensitive in diagnosing gallbladder rupture in
dogs with both gallbladder mucoceles and cholecystitis.
In addition, the sensitivity of ultrasound for detection of
cholecystitis is not 100%. In view of this, direct evaluation can be useful.
In acute cases where ultrasound is suggestive of pancreatitis, surgical intervention should be avoided while
initial symptomatic management is evaluated. Many
such cases will improve without further intervention and
the attendant risks of anesthesia and reduced pancreatic
perfusion. Only if the jaundice persists despite this management is surgery indicated.
Liver Histopathology

There are a variety of additional stains that can be used
along with the standard hematoxylin and eosin for further evaluation of liver histopathology. When a clinician
performs a liver biopsy, they should be ready to work
with the pathologist reading the biopsy. Providing a clear

clinical history is imperative. Understanding that the
biopsy represents only a small fraction of the overall liver
is key. The clinician should always relate the information
gained to the patient’s clinical picture and bloodwork,
remembering that there is the possibility of significant
sampling error, as discussed in the sections above. The
biopsy results should be used to guide the treatment by
defining the disease processes noted within the sample
(e.g., inflammation, vacuolation) rather than necessarily
providing a definitive diagnosis.
In breeds in which copper‐associated hepatopathies
are known to occur, the measurement of hepatic copper
is important. Ideally semiquantitative copper staining of
biopsy samples and quantitative copper analysis of tissue
should both be performed. The latter requires adequate
sample size, which typically entails a wedge biopsy.
Information for individual cases is probably best discussed with the pathologist involved.

­Conclusion
Patients with hepatobiliary disease pose many diagnostic
challenges to the clinician. The vast array of liver functions and its tremendous functional reserve mean that
patients with significant disease can present in very
diverse guises and often very late in the overall disease
process. The challenge for the clinician is to become adept
at identifying patients with liver disease early on, when
they may have vague or minimal clinical signs, as these
patients are the ones more likely to benefit from treatment. Diagnostic tests, such as clinical pathology, rarely
offer a definitive diagnosis in patients with liver disease.
Instead, they should be used to build up an overall picture
guiding a rational approach to the patient. A liver biopsy is
often necessary, providing the most accurate indication of
the underlying disease process, severity, and prognosis.

Imaging in Hepatobiliary Disease
Esther Barrett, MA, VetMB, DVDI, DECVDI, MRCVSt
Wales and West Imaging, Chepstow, UK

The aim of diagnostic imaging in hepatobiliary disease is
to provide information about the structure and, to a certain extent, the function of the hepatobiliary system. In
common with the diagnostic imaging of all other organ
systems, the imaging findings are rarely specific for a single disease process and it is not possible to exclude disease on the basis of apparently normal imaging findings.
Hepatobiliary imaging should therefore be considered
not as an isolated process but as an important part of the
overall diagnostic work‐up, with the imaging findings
always interpreted in the light of all the other available
information (patient history, findings on physical examination, results of laboratory investigations, etc.).
Radiography and ultrasonography are the techniques
most commonly used in the diagnostic imaging of the
hepatobiliary system. Although much less widely available, scintigraphy (nuclear medicine) is also a well‐established hepatobiliary imaging technique, useful in
providing functional as well as anatomic information.
More recently, the advanced cross‐sectional imaging
techniques of computed tomography (CT) and magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) have become increasingly useful, especially in the anatomic mapping of complicated
vascular anomalies and in the evaluation of, and potential surgical planning for, patients with liver masses.

­Classification of Hepatobiliary Disease
In 2006, the WSAVA published the outcome of its hepatic
standardization project, an initiative started in July 2000
with the aim of describing universally accepted standards and criteria for the diagnosis of all known liver diseases of dogs and cats. In establishing the recommended
classification of different hepatobiliary diseases, ultrasonographic findings were considered an important feature, alongside clinical pathologic and histologic findings.

As a result of this work, four main groups of liver disease
have been established: parenchymal disorders, neoplastic disease, biliary tract disorders, and vascular disorders. In this chapter, the WSAVA classification system is
used as a basis for describing the imaging features of
commonly encountered hepatobiliary diseases.

­Normal Hepatobiliary Anatomy
The canine and feline liver is the largest soft tissue organ
in the abdomen and is divided by deep fissures into left
and right, quadrate and caudate lobes. The left and right
hepatic lobes are further divided into lateral and medial
sublobes. The liver is located almost completely within
the costal arch, with a convex cranial surface lying immediately adjacent to the diaphragm and an irregularly concave caudal surface lying in contact with the stomach,
pancreas, duodenum, and right kidney. On the ventral
aspect of the liver, the proximal aspect of the fetal falciform ligament usually remains as an irregular fat‐filled
fold (falciform fat).
The Biliary System
The canine gallbladder is typically pear shaped and lies
between the quadrate and right medial lobes. The feline
gallbladder, which is sometimes folded or bilobed, usually lies between two parts of the right medial lobe. The
common bile duct is formed by the confluence of the
cystic duct (from the gallbladder) with the hepatic duct/s
(directly from the liver). The common bile duct leaves
the liver at the porta hepatis, where it lies ventral to the
hepatic arteries and the hepatic portal vein, and enters
the proximal duodenum at the major duodenal papilla.
In cats, the pancreatic duct usually joins the common
bile duct before emptying via the major duodenal papilla
into the proximal duodenum. In dogs, although both the

pancreatic duct and common bile ducts empty at the

additional accessory pancreatic duct empties further
­distally, via the minor duodenal papilla.

Radiologic Evaluation

Hepatic Vasculature

Normal Findings

The liver is unique in having a dual blood supply. The
proper hepatic arteries, which arise from the abdominal
aorta via the celiac artery and enter the liver at the porta
hepatis, supply approximately one‐fifth of the blood
­supply. The remaining four‐fifths of the blood supply is
provided by the hepatic portal vein. The portal vein
arises in the midabdomen, where it is formed by the
­confluence of the larger cranial mesenteric and smaller
­caudal mesenteric veins. It is joined by the splenic vein
and gastroduodenal vein, before entering the porta hepatis, where it lies ventral to the hepatic arteries and dorsal
to the ­common bile duct. On entering the liver, the portal vein divides into a smaller right portal branch, which
arborizes into the right medial and lateral lobes, and a
larger left portal branch, which arborizes throughout the
remaining liver. Venous drainage from the liver is
through several (usually three) short hepatic veins and
multiple tiny tributaries, which empty into the caudal
vena cava as it crosses the liver on the right dorsal aspect
of the midline.
Lymphatic Drainage
Lymphatic vessels from the hepatic parenchyma and the
gallbladder anastomose and drain together into the
hepatic and splenic lymph nodes. Variable numbers (typically between one and five) of hepatic lymph nodes lie to
the right and left of the hepatic portal vein, just caudal to
the porta hepatis, and receive lymphatic drainage from
the liver, stomach, duodenum, and pancreas. The splenic
nodes are located along the course of the splenic artery
and vein and receive lymphatic drainage from the esophagus, stomach, pancreas, spleen, omentum, and diaphragm, as well as the liver. Together with the gastric
lymph nodes, which drain the liver mesentery, and the
pancreaticoduodenal lymph nodes, the hepatic and
splenic lymph nodes form the celiac lymph center.

­Hepatobiliary Radiography
Radiographic Technique
A minimum of two orthogonal views, a ventrodorsal and
either a right or left lateral recumbent view, is recommended for evaluation of the liver. Good radiographic
technique is essential in order to obtain images of high
diagnostic quality.

The radiologic assessment of the hepatobiliary system
relies on the logical evaluation of liver position, size,
shape, opacity, and margination.
The normal liver is of homogenous soft tissue opacity,
merging with the soft tissue opacities of the diaphragm
and gallbladder to form the “hepatic silhouette.” On a lateral view (Figure 61.1a), the hepatic silhouette is approximately triangular in shape, with a sharply pointed
caudoventral angle.
The liver lies within the cranial abdomen, immediately
caudal to the diaphragm, with the right kidney and stomach lying against its caudal border. The “stomach axis” is
an imaginary line running from the fundus to the pyloric
antrum of the stomach. This axis, which is most easily
recognized when a small amount of gas is present in the
stomach lumen, provides a useful reference point for
evaluating liver size. In most dogs and cats, the liver is
almost entirely contained within the costal arch, and the
gastric axis lies approximately parallel to the ribs; however, normal variations, both in the position of the caudoventral hepatic angle with respect to the costal arch
and in the orientation of the gastric axis, may be seen
between different dog breeds and ages. Deep‐chested
dogs typically have a relatively cranially located liver,
with a more upright gastric axis, while the liver of barrel‐chested dogs and puppies tends to extend further
caudally and may protrude beyond the costal arch,
resulting in caudal displacement and anticlockwise rotation of the gastric axis.
The caudoventral angle and ventral border of the liver
are often highlighted against the relative radiolucency of
the adjacent falciform fat on a lateral abdominal radiograph; this provides a clearly defined ventral margin,
especially in cats, where the gallbladder is occasionally
identified as a soft tissue bulge along the ventral hepatic
border. The position of the cranial and caudal hepatic
margins is inferred from the location of the diaphragm
and stomach respectively. Dorsally, the caudate lobe of
the liver lies adjacent to the right kidney; in most dogs,
these two soft tissue structures merge into a single soft
tissue opacity, and the caudodorsal margin of the liver
cannot be seen. Cats typically have a larger amount of
retroperitoneal fat, usually separating the caudodorsal
liver from the right kidney and allowing the two structures to be identified separately.
The hepatic silhouette is less easily appreciated on a
ventrodorsal radiograph (Figure 61.1a); while the position of the cranial margin is demarcated by the location
of the diaphragm, the caudal margins are poorly defined
and can only be inferred from the location of the
stomach.
