Changes in Position

Displacement of the liver from its normal subcostal position in the cranial abdomen is almost always due to
abnormalities of the adjacent organs and structures
rather than primary hepatobiliary pathology. Examples
include the cranial displacement of the liver through a
ruptured diaphragm and the caudal displacement of the
liver due to increased thoracic volume.
Changes in Liver Size and Shape

Generalized hepatomegaly (Figure 61.2) is an increase in
overall liver size, recognized on a lateral radiograph as
caudal extension, and usually rounding, of the caudoventral hepatic margin beyond the costal arch, together with
caudal displacement and anticlockwise rotation of the
gastric axis.

Localized hepatomegaly (Figure 61.3) is usually more
challenging to identify and in some cases may be difficult
to differentiate from diffuse hepatic enlargement.
Lesions bulging from the surface of the liver will cause
distortion of the normally smooth hepatic margins and
are most easily recognized where they bulge from the ventral or caudal hepatic surfaces. Asymmetric displacement
of organs caudal to the liver may be seen in patients with
large unilateral lesions: a left‐sided liver mass may cause
caudal displacement of the stomach and spleen, while a
right‐sided mass may cause caudal displacement of the
right kidney, pylorus and proximal duodenum, together
with displacement of the stomach across to the left.
A small liver (microhepatica) (Figure 61.4) is usually
completely contained within the costal arch and is recognized by cranial displacement of the stomach and clockwise rotation of the gastric axis.
An apparently small liver is often a normal finding in
deep‐chested dogs and may be difficult to differentiate
from genuine microhepatica.
Changes in Opacity

Hepatobiliary mineralization is uncommon. Focal or
multifocal mineralized areas are occasionally seen due to
dystrophic mineralization of chronic parenchymal
­disease (see Figure 61.3). Dystrophic mineralization of

branching lucencies due to gas migrating throughout the
biliary tree (e.g., due to emphysematous cholecystitis) or,
very rarely, throughout the portal venous system.
Changes in Margination

Clearly defined ventral and caudoventral hepatic margins rely on the presence of abdominal fat highlighting
the soft tissue opacity of the liver; loss of this clear
­margination may be seen in patients with ascites and in
very young or emaciated patients.

­Hepatobiliary Ultrasonography
Ultrasound Technique
The location of the liver within the costal arch limits the
availability of acoustic windows from which the liver can
be evaluated without interference from the ribcage. The
use of a transducer with a relatively small contact area is
therefore recommended; a curvilinear or microconvex
probe operating at frequencies of 5–12 MHz is ideal,
with the higher frequencies being used for cats and
small‐to‐medium dogs and the lower frequencies for
large‐ and giant‐breed dogs.
Careful patient preparation is important in optimizing
image quality. An overnight fast is strongly recommended, as the presence of gas and ingesta within the
stomach lumen often reflects and/or attenuates the
sound waves, hindering detailed examination. Although
not always necessary, sedation will usually facilitate an
easier and more thorough examination, especially in
deep‐chested or tense patients who may resent the firm
pressure of an ultrasound probe around their ribcage. A
clipped area extending cranially to the level of the xiphisternum and extending dorsally two‐thirds of the way up
the abdominal wall on either side is required, together
with the generous application and reapplication of ultrasound gel to optimize acoustic transmission.
The liver is fixed within the costal arch by a number of
ligamentous attachments. This fixed location facilitates a
systematic approach to the ultrasound examination. In
cats and small‐to‐medium dogs, it is often possible to
examine the entire liver from a subcostal window, ­usually
with the patient in right lateral or dorsal recumbency:

the ultrasound probe is placed in the midline just caudal
to the xiphisternum and the ultrasound beam is “swept”
through the liver in both sagittal and transverse planes.
In patients where the liver lies well within the costal margins (typically deep‐chested patients and those with a
small liver), it can be challenging to get a good image
from a subcostal window, and it is often easier to examine each side of the liver by obtaining dorsal and transverse plane images through the adjacent intercostal
spaces. The gallbladder, common bile duct, and caudal
vena cava all lie to the right of midline; for this reason,
evaluation of the biliary tract and screening for possible
portosystemic shunts are often performed with the
transducer positioned on the right side, either just caudal
to the costal arch or within the caudal intercostal spaces.
Recognizing Artifacts
Several artifacts are commonly encountered during
hepatic ultrasound. The “mirror‐image” artifact (Figure 61.5)
is seen as a reflection of the liver beyond the diaphragm,
and is caused by the highly reflective interface between
the liver and lung. “Acoustic enhancement” is caused by
the fact that fluid results in less attenuation of the ultrasound beam than soft tissues, and is recognized as the
tissues deep to a fluid‐filled structure, such as the gallbladder, appearing artificially echogenic relative to the
adjacent tissues.

Figure 61.5 A sagittal plane ultrasound image of a normal canine
liver. The diaphragm is seen as a curved hyperechoic line (blue
arrows) demarcating the cranial hepatic margin. The normal
hepatic parenchyma (pink arrow) is of medium echogenicity with
a coarse but even echotexture. In the near field, the ventral border
of the liver is separated from the coarser appearing falciform fat
(green arrow) by a fine hyperechoic line representing the hepatic
capsule. A “mirror‐image” of the liver is seen beyond the
diaphragm (yellow arrow).

“Acoustic shadowing” occurs when highly attenuating
structures (such as bone and calculi) leave the deeper tissues relatively devoid of echoes, appearing artificially
hypoechoic or anechoic. In the normal liver, acoustic
shadowing may be recognized deep to the ribs when
scanning through an intercostal space. “Reverberation” is
recognized as a closely spaced series of parallel hyperechoic bands running across the screen and is caused by
sound waves reverberating between the transducer and a
very reflective gas interface. When examining the liver,
this artifact is most frequently identified deep to a gas‐
filled stomach.
Ultrasound Evaluation
A consistent, logical approach to ultrasound evaluation
is recommended, with an initial assessment being made
of the position, size, and shape of the liver, followed by
more detailed evaluation of the parenchymal structure,
vasculature, biliary system, and lymph nodes.
The position of the liver is most easily evaluated relative to the position of the surrounding organs. The diaphragm should be seen as a curved hyperechoic line on
the cranial aspect of the liver, demarcating the interface
between liver and air‐filled lung, with a mirror‐image
artifact sometimes seen beyond the diaphragm. Caudally,
the normal liver is in contact with the spleen on the left,
the stomach centrally and the right kidney on the right.
Changes in position are more commonly encountered
due to changes in the adjacent organs or structures (e.g.,
rupture of the diaphragm) than due to abnormalities of
the liver itself.
Although radiography is usually more useful in evaluating the overall size and shape of the liver, ­caudal extension of the liver beyond the costal arch and rounding of
the normally sharply pointed caudoventral margin in
patients with generalized hepatomegaly may also be
identified on ultrasound. Localized hepatomegaly is usually easier to identify with ultrasound than with radiography, and is recognized by distortion and/or bulging of
the hepatic margins, often together with a localized
change in the appearance of the hepatic parenchyma.
Parenchymal Structure

The normal liver (see Figure 61.5) is of medium echogenicity with a slightly coarse but uniform echotexture,
interrupted only by the hepatic vasculature and gallbladder. Although the hepatic margins are generally well
defined, the liver lobes are not usually individually identified unless they are separated out by the presence of
free abdominal fluid. The liver is bordered on the ventral
aspect by variable amounts of falciform fat. This fat is
coarser in appearance than the normal hepatic parenchyma and is usually demarcated from the liver by the

fine hyperechoic line of the hepatic capsule; however, in
some patients the demarcation between fat and liver is
not as clear and the falciform fat may be misdiagnosed as
hepatomegaly.
Biliary System

The normal gallbladder is seen just to the right of midline
as a rounded fluid‐filled structure with a thin well‐defined
echogenic wall. Normal gallbladder size varies widely and
is larger in fasted or anorexic patients. The normal gallbladder wall measures up to 1 mm across in cats and up
to 2–3 mm in dogs. Gallbladder sludge is a common and
often incidental finding, recognized as echogenic, nonshadowing material settled dependently within the
­gallbladder lumen. The normal intrahepatic biliary tree
cannot be identified, although in some patients, especially cats, it is possible to identify the normal common
bile duct leaving the porta hepatis ventral to the hepatic
portal vein and entering the proximal duodenum at the
major duodenal papilla.
Vasculature

Normal hepatic arteries are not identified on ultrasound.
The hepatic portal vein enters the liver at the porta hepatis before branching into left and right portal veins and
arborizing throughout the liver. The portal vasculature is
seen as branching, tapering anechoic tubes with characteristically echogenic walls. The caudal cava enters the
liver dorsal to the portal vein, receiving venous drainage
via the hepatic veins as it crosses the right side of the
liver. Unlike the portal veins, the walls of the hepatic
veins cannot usually be seen.
Hepatic Lymph Nodes

The hepatic and splenic lymph nodes receive the majority of lymphatic drainage from the liver and are located
respectively at the porta hepatis and along the course of
the splenic vein. The normal lymph nodes are small,
ovoid, isoechoic to the surrounding mesentery and
­usually not identified. Enlarged lymph nodes are typically hypoechoic and rounded or irregular.

­Imaging Features of Hepatobiliary
Disease
Parenchymal Disease
Conditions classified as parenchymal disorders include
vacuolar diseases (e.g., steroid hepatopathy, hepatic lipidosis), amyloidosis, acute and chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, hepatic abscessation, granulomatous disease, and
hepatic necrosis (e.g., due to toxic, ischemic or immune‐
mediated disease).

VetBooks.ir

61 Imaging in Hepatobiliary Disease

The radiologic assessment of hepatic parenchymal disease is limited to the evaluation of overall hepatic size
and shape; ultrasound assessment provides additional
valuable information about parenchymal echotexture
and echogenicity and is therefore more sensitive in the
detection of parenchymal abnormalities. Hepatic parenchymal disease may be described as diffuse, focal or
multifocal, depending on the distribution of changes
­
identified on ultrasound.

(a)

Diffuse Parenchymal Disease

Diffuse parenchymal pathology is usually due to generalized infiltrative disease, typically affecting all liver lobes.
Unless the disease process results in a fairly marked
change in liver size and/or shape, the liver may appear
normal on abdominal radiographs. However, in many
cases, changes in hepatic echogenicity and/or echotexture can be identified on ultrasound.
Accurate evaluation of hepatic echogenicity is challenging, as apparent echogenicity is influenced by
machine settings and transducer choice; this makes the
identification of uniform alterations in hepatic echogenicity especially difficult. Comparison of the liver with
adjacent organs imaged at the same depth is useful: the
normal canine liver is coarser than and hypoechoic to
the spleen, but usually isoechoic, or slightly hyperechoic,
to the kidneys. A diffusely hyperechoic liver is likely to
be similar in echogenicity to the spleen, with decreased
contrast between abnormally hyperechoic parenchyma
and the hyperechoic portal vessel walls blurring the normally clear definition of these walls. A diffusely hypoechoic liver may be recognized by the unusual
prominence of the portal vessel walls, which become
highlighted by the abnormally hypoechoic background.
Diffuse parenchymal disease may also be seen as an
abnormally heterogenous liver of mixed hyper‐ and
hypoechogenicity. This can be difficult to differentiate
from a poorly defined multifocal disease process. It is
also important to remember that it is possible for significant infiltrative disease to be present without any obvious abnormalities identified on ultrasound examination.
Due to the nonspecific nature of the imaging findings,
cytologic and/or histopathologic evaluation of tissue
will almost always be required to provide a definitive
diagnosis.
Vacuolar Disease

Vacuolar hepatopathy (Figure 61.6) is most commonly
associated with steroid hepatopathy and hepatic
lipidosis.
The liver typically appears diffusely enlarged, with
caudal extension of a rounded caudoventral hepatic
margin recognized on both abdominal radiography and
ultrasound. On ultrasound, the liver is typically hypere-

Amyloidosis

Amyloidosis may cause hepatomegaly, with diffusely
heterogenous hepatic parenchyma characterized by
mixed hyperechoic and hypoechoic foci described in
cats. Spontaneous hepatic rupture may occur in patients
with severe amyloidosis, resulting in hemabdomen. This

of normal serosal detail and on ultrasound as the presence of free abdominal fluid. A breed predisposition to
amyloidosis is reported in Shar Peis, Abyssinian and

Acute Hepatitis

Although acute hepatitis may cause diffuse hepatic
enlargement, this is often not obvious on abdominal
radiography or ultrasound. A diffusely hypoechoic liver
with unusually prominent portal vessel walls may be
recognized but in some patients the liver may appear
ultrasonographically unremarkable. In cats, there may
be evidence of concurrent biliary tract disease (see
later).
Chronic Hepatitis and Cirrhosis

Chronic hepatitis (Figure 61.7) is usually associated
with a mixed pattern of hepatic fibrosis, inflammation, and hyperplasia; this appears on ultrasound as
heterogenous hepatic parenchyma of mixed
echogenicity.
Cirrhosis is the end‐stage of chronic hepatitis; a
small, irregularly marginated liver may be identified on
both abdominal radiography and ultrasound; extensive
hepatic fibrosis may result in diffusely increased
hepatic echogenicity, often with hypoechoic regenerative nodules scattered throughout the parenchyma and
bulging from the hepatic margins. Portal hypertension
is a common sequel to hepatic fibrosis, resulting in
abdominal ascites and the development of acquired
portosystemic shunts.

Figure 61.7 Sagittal plane ultrasound image showing the liver of
a patient with chronic hepatitis. The liver is small and irregularly
marginated (blue arrows).

Hepatocutaneous Syndrome

Hepatocutaneous syndrome (Figure 61.8), also known as
superficial necrolytic dermatitis, is occasionally seen in
older dogs, where it is associated with ulcerative skin
lesions.
The hepatic parenchymal lesions are seen as multiple
hypoechoic nodules, giving the liver a “honeycomb”
appearance. There are no marked changes in hepatic size
or shape, making this condition impossible to diagnose
from abdominal radiographs.
Focal or Multifocal Parenchymal Disease

Focal or multifocal parenchymal lesions are more easily
recognized than diffuse parenchymal infiltration on
ultrasound examination and are typically seen as areas of
altered echogenicity and/or echotexture that are highlighted by the surrounding normal parenchyma. Large or
peripheral lesions may be identified on abdominal radiographs if they result in localized hepatomegaly or distortion of the hepatic margins. The imaging features
described are not specific and it is not possible to accurately differentiate the different lesions on imaging
appearance alone.
Hepatic Abscesses

Hepatic abscesses are rare in cats and dogs. Although
multiple lesions may be seen, solitary lesions, often at
least 3 cm in diameter, are more common. On ultrasound, the typical appearance is of a rounded or irregular
cavitated lesion, with a relatively echogenic and variably
thick capsule around a hypoechoic central area. There

Cystic Lesions

Hepatic cysts are recognized as well‐circumscribed,
single or multiple, uni‐ or multilocular, thin‐walled
­

enhancement. Congenital cystic diseases of the dog and
cat are occasionally seen and may be associated with
polycystic kidney disease. These congenital cysts typically arise from congenital dilation of the intrahepatic
bile ducts, and strictly speaking should be classified as a
biliary disorder. Differential diagnoses include parasitic
cysts, focal areas of necrosis, and cystic tumors (e.g., biliary cystadenoma). Cystic lesions that do not distort the
hepatic margins will not be recognized on abdominal
radiographs.
Hepatic Granulomas and Hematomas

Hepatic granulomas and hematomas are uncommon.
Granulomas are occasionally identified in association
with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, fungal diseases,
migrating parasites and, in cats, feline infectious peritonitis. They are usually multifocal and typically appear
hyperechoic and well marginated on ultrasound.
Abdominal radiographs are often unremarkable but may
occasionally show evidence of dystrophic mineralization, with hepatomegaly and possible distortion of the
normally smooth hepatic margins seen in patients with
extensive disease. Hematomas may be seen following
trauma or biopsy procedures, typically appearing anechoic or hypoechoic on ultrasound until an echogenic
clot has formed. The subsequent retraction and lysis of
the clot results in a variable pattern of mixed echogenicity whose appearance cannot be differentiated from an
abscess or necrotic tumor.

due to the presence of free fluid. Depending on the volume of fluid, it may also be possible to appreciate alteration of the normal hepatic shape.
Neoplastic Disease
The WSAVA classification of neoplastic disorders
includes primary neoplasia, usually arising from the
hepatocytes (hepatocellular adenoma/carcinoma) and/or
the biliary system (e.g. cholangiocellular adenoma/carcinoma), primary vascular neoplasia (most commonly
hemanigosarcoma), diffusely infiltrative hematopoietic
neoplasia (e.g., lymphoma, malignant histiocytosis, and
malignant mastocytosis) and metastatic neoplasia.
Although benign, nodular hyperplasia, commonly seen in
older dogs but less frequently identified in cats, is also
included in the classification of neoplastic disease.
Primary Focal Neoplasia

Primary liver tumors arising from the hepatocytes or the
biliary system are typically seen as focal, or occasionally
multifocal, masses. A wide variety of imaging features
may be recognized and it is not possible to differentiate
between benign and malignant lesions or between tumor
types based on imaging appearance. On ultrasound,
lesions are variably well defined and vary in size, shape,
and echogenicity (Figure 61.9).
Biliary cystadenomas are uncommon benign tumors
of older cats. These lesions, which have a wide range of
possible sizes and may be solitary or multifocal, are characterized by the presence of a variable cystic component
(Figure 61.10).

Liver Lobe Torsion

Liver lobe torsion is a rare cause of acute abdominal pain
and abdominal effusion in the dog. On ultrasound, the
affected lobe is typically seen as a hypoechoic mass,
often surrounded by free fluid, with color Doppler demonstrating reduced or no blood flow into the area. A loss

Benign Nodular Hyperplasia

Hepatic hemangiosarcomas often also have a cystic
component and, in cases of rupture, will be accompanied
by the presence of free abdominal fluid. Liver tumors will
only be recognized radiographically where they cause
localized hepatomegaly and/or distortion of the normal
hepatic shape (see Figure 61.3). The oral administration
of barium may be useful in determining the location of
the gastric axis in cases with suspected localized hepatomegaly. Pedunculated liver tumors can be confusing and
may be seen as a cranioventral soft tissue abdominal
mass, which is not obviously connected to the liver. In
patients with tumor rupture and subsequent hemoperitoneum, abdominal radiographs will show loss of serosal
detail.

Benign nodular hyperplasia, also referred to as regenerative nodular hyperplasia, appears on ultrasound as multiple nodules of variable size, shape, echogenicity, and
definition. It is not possible to distinguish between
benign nodular hyperplasia and primary or metastatic
neoplasia from the ultrasound appearance. Mild
­generalized hepatomegaly may occasionally be radiographically apparent in patients with benign nodular
hyperplasia.
Disease of the Biliary System
Important disorders of the biliary tract include cholestasis, due to either primary liver disease or obstruction of
the (usually extrahepatic) biliary tract, and cholangitis
(most commonly neutrophilic or lymphocytic). Diseases
affecting the gallbladder include gallbladder mucoceles
and cholecystitis (frequently seen in cats, sometimes in
association with neutrophilic cholangitis).

Infiltrative Neoplasia

Lymphoma, histiocytic tumors, and mast cell tumors are
typically diffusely infiltrative. On ultrasound, these
tumors are most commonly recognized as diffusely
hypoechoic or heterogenous hepatic parenchyma, or as
multifocal parenchymal nodules or masses. Less
­commonly, the hepatic parenchyma appears diffusely
hyperechoic or, occasionally, ultrasonographically normal. Evaluation of the area around the porta hepatis is
important for the identification of hepatic lymphadenopathy, which is often identified in association with
infiltrative hepatic neoplasia. Diffuse neoplastic infiltration often results in generalized hepatomegaly, which
may be apparent on abdominal radiographs.
Metastatic Neoplasia

Metastatic hepatic disease is most likely to be recognized on ultrasound as multifocal nodules or masses.

Extrahepatic Cholestasis

Causes of extrahepatic biliary obstruction (EHBO)
include inflammation or neoplasia of the common bile
duct, pancreas or duodenum and obstruction of the duct
lumen by choleliths (choledocholithiasis). Dilation of the
common bile duct (>5 mm in cats and >4 mm in dogs) is
the most consistent ultrasound finding in acute EHBO
(Figure 61.12).
Dilation of the extrahepatic and intrahepatic bile ducts
may be seen in patients with obstruction of at least 5–7
days duration; these dilated ducts are recognized as the
presence of multiple slightly tortuous anechoic tubes
with hyperechoic walls, which do not show any evidence
of flow on Doppler. Dilation of the gallbladder is an
inconsistent finding and the absence of a distended gallbladder does not exclude the possibility of EHBO.
Detailed evaluation of the common bile duct is required
to identify possible causes of obstruction; obstructive
choleliths are most commonly located in the distal common bile duct, highlighted by the dilated bile duct proximal to the obstruction, with an empty bile duct seen
distally. In patients with inflammatory or neoplastic disease, an extraluminal mass may be identified causing
obstruction; however, it is not possible to determine the
nature of the mass (inflammatory or neoplastic) from the
ultrasound appearance. Although mineralized choleliths
may be identified on abdominal radiographs, EHBO will
not be seen.

lymphocytic cholangitis are both commonly diagnosed
in cats, but less frequently reported in dogs. On ultrasound, cholangitis is most commonly recognized as
­diffusely hypoechoic hepatic parenchyma, which highlights the echogenic walls of the portal vasculature
(Figure 61.13).
These changes are nonspecific, and it is not possible to
make a definitive diagnosis or to distinguish between
neutrophilic and lymphocytic disease without tissue
sampling. Cholangitis cannot be diagnosed from abdominal radiographs. Concurrent cholecystitis (see later) is
identified in a significant number of cats and occasionally dogs with cholangitis.

Gallbladder mucoceles occur in dogs and are caused by
an abnormal accumulation of inspissated mucus and bile
within the gallbladder lumen, leading to progressive
luminal distension and potentially to necrosis and ultimately rupture of the gallbladder wall. Typical mucoceles
have a distinctive ultrasound appearance, described as
“kiwi‐like” or “stellate,” with immobile hyperechoic striations seen radiating from a central point (Figure 61.14).
Variations in the appearance include a “mosaic‐like”
pattern of mixed echogenicity; unlike gallbladder sludge,
which is a common and often incidental finding, the contents of a gallbladder mucocele are immobile and do not
move with gravity when the patient changes position.
Gallbladder wall thickness is variable, although inflammation and/or necrosis may result in wall thickening.

Cholecystitis

Cholecystitis is more commonly identified in cats than
dogs, and is usually associated with bacterial infection.
Typical ultrasound features of acute cholecystitis include
gallbladder wall thickening (Figure 61.15) (>1 mm in
cats, >2–3 mm in dogs), together with thickening of the
wall of the common bile duct.
The thickened gallbladder wall may be diffusely
hyperechoic or may have a layered appearance, with a
hypoechoic central layer sandwiched between hyperechoic layers. Differential diagnoses for gallbladder wall
thickening include acute cholecystitis, edema (e.g., in
patients with hypoalbuminemia or portal hypertension), cystic mucinous hyperplasia and, rarely, neoplasia. Although commonly considered to be an incidental
finding, biliary sludge, sludge balls, and choleliths may
be associated with cholecystitis, especially in cats.
Biliary sludge is recognized as mobile echogenic nonshadowing debris within the gallbladder lumen. Sludge
balls are mobile, rounded, echogenic, nonshadowing
luminal structures composed of thick bile. Choleliths
are seen as hyperechoic foci of variable size, shape, and
number, often casting an acoustic shadow. Ultrasound‐
guided aspiration of bile (cholecystocentesis) is useful in
providing material for bacterial culture in patients with
suspected cholecystitis.
Radiographic abnormalities associated with cholecystitis are unusual; however, choleliths may occasionally be
identified as small mineralized foci in the area of the gallbladder and/or common bile duct and, rarely, patches

gallbladder wall (blue arrows) in a 10‐year‐old ME cross‐bred dog
diagnosed with cholecystitis.

and streaks of gas opacity may be seen in patients with
emphysematous cholecystitis.
Hepatic Vascular Disorders
The largest group of hepatic vascular disorders consists
of the circulatory disorders, which are subdivided into
congenital portosystemic shunts, hepatic congestion due
to outflow disturbances, and disorders due to portal
hypertension. Other vascular disorders include peliosis
hepatis and portal vein thrombophlebitis.
Congenital Portosystemic Shunts (CPSS)

Congenital portosystemic shunting occurs due to an
anomalous connection between the portal vasculature
and systemic venous system, which allows blood to
bypass the hepatic sinusoids. CPSS are usually
described according to their location (extrahepatic or
intrahepatic) and can be further classified by their anatomic configuration. Extrahepatic CPSS are most commonly identified in smaller breed dogs and in cats,
while intrahepatic CPSS are most commonly identified
in larger breed dogs. Although studies have demonstrated more than 90% accuracy for experienced operators, the identification of CPSS with ultrasound is
challenging.
In addition to evaluating the liver from the standard
subcostal acoustic window, the use of a high right dorsal

VetBooks.ir

61 Imaging in Hepatobiliary Disease

acoustic window, located just cranial to the right kidney,
with the patient positioned in left lateral recumbency, is
recommended for visualization of the caudal vena cava
(CVC) and the hepatic portal vein (HPV) as they enter
the liver; in most patients with an extrahepatic CPSS,
this window allows identification of the shunting vessel
itself. Subcostal, right dorsal intercostal, and left ventral
intercostal windows are all recommended for evaluation
of the liver in patients with a suspected intrahepatic
CPSS. In anesthetized patients with a very small liver,
positive pressure ventilation may be useful in improving
visualization by displacing the liver caudally. Although
not essential, color and spectral Doppler allow the determination of flow direction, the identification of turbulence and the measurement of hepatic portal velocity,
and are therefore very useful in the ultrasound assessment of patients with suspected CPSS.
The majority of extrahepatic CPSS in dogs originate
from the splenic or left gastric veins and terminate in the
caudal vena cava (usually at the level of the epiploic foramen), the left phrenic vein (at the level of the oesophageal
hiatus) or, less commonly, in the azygos vein. In cats, portocaval shunting via the left gastric vein is most frequently
reported but cats also appear to have a higher incidence
of more unusual shunting loops, which may arise caudal
to the confluence of the mesenteric veins. Regardless of
the precise anatomy, the ultrasound appearance of an
extrahepatic CPSS is usually of a relatively short, dilated
and sometimes tortuous vessel, diverting blood away
from the hepatic portal vein (Figure 61.16).

Figure 61.16 Color Doppler ultrasound image showing an
extrahepatic portocaval shunt (blue arrows) in a 6‐month‐old ME
Bichon × Yorkshire terrier. The blue color indicates that the
direction of blood flow is away from the hepatic portal vein.

Comparison of the diameter of the portal vein at the
porta hepatis with the diameter of the aorta and caudal
vena cava at the same level is very useful; a portal
vein:aortic ratio ≤0.65 is predictive for the presence of an
extrahepatic shunt. Conversely, an extrahepatic shunt is
considered unlikely with a portal vein:aortic ratio >0.8
and a portal vein:caval ratio >0.75.
Intrahepatic CPSS may be classified as left, central or
right divisional. The left divisional shunt, which represents a patent ductus venosus and joins the left portal
branch to the intrahepatic caudal vena cava, is the most
common (Figure 61.17).
Both right and central divisional shunts arise from the
right portal branch; right divisional shunts are long
shunts, whereas the central divisional shunt is usually a
short aneurysm‐like dilation joining the right portal
branch with the intrahepatic caudal vena cava.
Microhepatica is common in dogs with both extrahepatic and intrahepatic CPSS, but is less commonly
reported in cats. Urolithiasis and mild renomegaly are
also fairly common in dogs, but infrequently identified
in cats.
Potential abnormalities identified on survey radiographs of patients with CPSS include microhepatica,
renomegaly, and limited serosal detail due to poor body
condition. In cases with portoazygos shunting, a dilated
azygos vein is occasionally recognized as a soft tissue
band crossing the thorax adjacent to the aorta. Although
hematogenous osteomyelitis of the lumbar vertebrae has
occasionally been reported in patients with CPSS, this is
not a common finding. The uroliths associated with CPSS
are ammonium biurate and are typically radiolucent.

Figure 61.17 Color Doppler ultrasound image showing a left
divisional intrahepatic portocaval shunt in a 6‐month‐old FE
golden retriever. The mosaic pattern of the color Doppler indicates
turbulence at the point that the shunt joins the intrahepatic
caudal vena cava.

Historically, mesenteric portovenography was widely
used for the definitive confirmation of a suspected portosystemic shunt and for the differentiation between intra
and extrahepatic shunts. The most popular technique for
portovenography is the intravenous injection of nonionic iodinated contrast media through a catheter preplaced into a mesenteric vein. This involves a laparotomy
and is an invasive procedure. Alternative and potentially
less invasive, but less commonly used, techniques for
contrast administration include percutaneous ultrasound-guided catheterization of the splenic vein, catheterization of the cranial mesenteric artery via the femoral
artery and transvenous retrograde portography. In many
cases, mesenteric portovenography has been superseded
by contrast Computed Tomographic examination.
However, during surgical occlusion of a shunt, portovenography is still used to verify that the correct vessel has
been occluded, to check that there are no additional
shunting vessels and to assess the degree of portal vascularization post-ligation. Fluoroscopic imaging of the contrast injection provides useful real time information (Fig
61.18): if this is not available, then standard radiographic
views (ideally both lateral and VD views, each exposed at
the end of a separate contrast injection) should be taken.
Hepatic Congestion

Disturbance of the normal venous outflow results in passive hepatic congestion. Causes include right‐sided heart
failure and obstruction or compression of the cranial part

of the caudal vena cava (between the hepatic veins and
right atrium), for example by thrombosis, neoplasia or
inflammation. Ultrasound findings include hepatomegaly,
reduced hepatic echogenicity, dilation of the hepatic veins
and caudal vena cava and, in some cases, the presence of
free abdominal (+/− pleural) fluid. Radiographs may show
hepatomegaly and loss of serosal detail in patients with
ascites, possibly with evidence of a pleural effusion and
cardiomegaly in patients with right‐sided heart failure.
Portal Hypertension

Chronic portal hypertension resulting in the development of portosystemic collaterals (acquired portosystemic shunts) is relatively common in dogs, but rarely
identified in cats. Causes of portal hypertension include
advanced chronic liver disease (cirrhosis), intrahepatic
arterioportal fistulae, congenital hypoplasia of the portal
vein and portal vein obstruction. Ultrasound evaluation
of patients with portal hypertension will typically demonstrate ascites, often with edema of the gallbladder wall
and pancreas. Spectral Doppler is useful in measuring
portal velocity; the identification of reduced flow velocity (from a normal velocity of approximately 17+/5cm/s to <10 cm/s in the dog), and occasionally reversed
portal flow, is very suggestive of portal hypertension.
The portosystemic collaterals open in response to sustained portal hypertension and connect the portal system directly to the systemic circulation. These acquired
shunting vessels can be challenging to identify on ultra-

sound; in dogs, the opening of splenorenal collaterals,

left kidney, has been most commonly documented.
Ultrasound examination may be useful in documenting the cause of portal hypertension. A small, hyperechoic, irregular liver with multiple hypoechoic
regeneration nodules may be identified in patients with
cirrhosis. Intrahepatic arterioportal fistulae are direct
connections between the hepatic arteries and the portal
vessels. These vascular anomalies may be congenital or
acquired and may be seen on ultrasound as distended,
tortuous intrahepatic vessels. The high arterial pressure
results in portal hypertension and dramatic ascites, with
spectral Doppler demonstrating reversed, often pulsatile
flow within an enlarged hepatic portal vein. Congenital
hypoplasia of the hepatic portal vein is thought to affect
both extrahepatic and intrahepatic portal vasculature
and includes the condition of portal vein hypoperfusion
previously referred to as microvascular dysplasia.
Although hypoplasia of the extrahepatic portal vein
may be seen as a reduction in vessel diameter, the lack of
objective measurement criteria makes this difficult to
identify definitively. A small liver may be identified in
patients with mild portal vein hypoplasia; ultrasound
examination is often otherwise unremarkable. However,
evidence of portal hypertension and acquired portosystemic shunting may be identified in patients with more
severe changes. The most common cause of portal vein
obstruction is portal thrombosis, which may occur secondary to hypercoagulability, vascular stasis or damage
to the vascular endothelium (for example, due to local
neoplasia or inflammation). Portal thrombosis is recognized as an intraluminal immobile echogenic structure,
with color Doppler highlighting the thrombus as filling
defects in the normal pattern of flow (Figure 61.19).

Figure 61.19 Color Doppler ultrasound image highlighting a
portal thrombus as a filling defect within the hepatic portal vein
(blue arrows).

Larger thrombi can extend from the extrahepatic portal vein into the portal branches, resulting in portal
hypertension and acquired shunting.
Radiographic examination of patients with portal
hypertension is often unrewarding. Many will have
­evidence of ascites, obscuring the serosal detail of the
abdomen. In patients with chronic liver disease, it may
be possible to identify microhepatica, even in the
presence of ascites, by the cranial displacement and
­
clockwise rotation of the gastric axis.
Peliosis Hepatis

Peliosis hepatis is seen as randomly distributed cystic and
blood‐filled spaces within the liver, thought to be formed
due to either focal hepatocytic necrosis or local obstruction of small portal branches with hepatic atrophy and
subsequent sinusoidal dilation. The condition is rare in
dogs and more commonly identified in older cats. On
ultrasound, the the abnormal sinusoidal dilation may be
seen as multiple cystic lesions that may mimic vascular
tumors, such as hemangioma or hemangiosarcoma.

­Advanced Imaging Techniques
Contrast‐Enhanced Ultrasound
Contrast‐enhanced ultrasound is a non-invasive imaging technique that enables the functional assessment of
organ perfusion patterns. The contrast media consist of
microscopic (2–6 μm) inert gas‐filled microbubbles that
are injected intravenously. When subjected to ultrasound waves, these bubbles respond with a nonlinear
oscillation, generating strong harmonic ­frequencies that
can be detected using specialized transducers and dedicated contrast imaging software. In the liver, two phases
of contrast enhancement may be recognized: the early
phase of enhancement is equivalent to the blood pool
phase and is composed of arterial (wash‐in) and portal
(wash‐out) stages, with the enhancement peaking at the
same time as peak portal blood flow (typically 15–60
seconds in dogs), and disappearing by 150–200 seconds
in most dogs. This early phase allows the detection of
hepatic arteries and small vessels that would not be
apparent with conventional gray‐scale B‐mode imaging.
The late phase is only recognized with contrast media
that are able to leave the blood pool; this phase corresponds to intracellular contrast uptake and enables the
assessment of parenchymal perfusion.
Contrast‐enhanced ultrasound has been demonstrated
as a safe and accurate technique for differentiating
between benign and malignant liver lesions. Malignant
lesions do not have a portal venous supply and are
­perfused only via the hepatic arterial supply. At peak

673

VetBooks.ir

674

Section 7 Diseases of the Liver, Gallbladder, and Bile Ducts

(portal) early phase enhancement, malignant nodules
therefore appear show hypoenhancement in comparison
to the surrounding liver, while benign nodules typically
show isoenhancement or slight hyperenhancement. A
similar pattern is reported during late‐phase enhancement, with most malignant lesions appearing relatively
hypoechoic.
Nuclear Scintigraphy
Although nuclear scintigraphy is a well‐established imaging technique, its availability is limited by the strict regulation of radiopharmaceuticals. Nuclear medicine is most
widely used as a very sensitive and minimally invasive
technique for the diagnosis of PSS. The best documented
protocol involves the per‐rectal administration of 99mtechnetium pertechnetate (99mTc), which is rapidly absorbed
from the colonic mucosa. The 99mTc subsequently enters
the mesenteric vessels, from where it should pass through
the hepatic portal vein into the hepatic parenchyma before
filtering through the hepatic microcirculation to enter the
hepatic caudal vena cava and then the heart. In a patient
with a PSS, the 99mTc bypasses the liver and is delivered
directly to the heart. Regions of interest (ROIs) drawn
over the heart and liver are used to calculate the shunt
fraction by comparing the intensity of radioactive counts
over the heart with the intensity of counts over the liver.
Shunt fraction
Total heart counts over first 12 seconds
Total heart and liver counts over first 12 seconds
A normal shunt fraction is less than 15%. In dogs with
PSS (extra‐ or intrahepatic), shunt fractions of 80%+ have
been reported; lower shunt fractions (approximately 50%)
have been reported in cats with PSS. Unfortunately, there
does not appear to be a good correlation between the calculated shunt fraction and the physical size of the shunt.
Direct ultrasound‐guided injection of the 99mTc into the
splenic parenchymahas been described as an alternative
to per‐rectal administration; this results in significantly
decreased radiation exposure and provides superior
image quality, in many cases allowing the differentiation
between single congenital and multiple acquired shunts.
Although useful both in confirming the presence of a PSS
and identifying the presence of continued shunting after
an unsuccessful or partial surgical ligation, disadvantages
of nuclear scintigraphy include the lack of specific
­anatomic information (especially with per‐rectal scintigraphy), as well as the potential inconvenience and hazards
of working with radioactive isotopes. Portal vein hypoplasia (microvascular dysplasia) will not be identified
with nuclear scintigraphy.

Following the intravenous administration of the radiopharmaceutical 99mTc‐mebrofenin, hepatobiliary scintigraphy may also used for the evaluation of liver function,
detection of cholestasis and biliary tract obstruction, and
diagnosis of cholecystitis. In the normal patient 99mTc‐
mebrofenin is extracted from the blood pool by the liver,
with peak liver radioactivity observed 6–8 minutes after
injection. The hepatic extraction fraction (HEF) is used as
a measure of hepatocyte function. Following extraction by
the hepatocytes, the radiopharmaceutical is excreted into
the biliary tree with a half‐life of 19 minutes, resulting in
detectable radioactivity in the gallbladder and small intestines within one hour of injection. A prolonged clearance
time indicates extrahepatic biliary obstruction and in dogs
may allow the detection of abnormalities before any ultrasound changes are identified.
Computed Tomography
Computed tomography (CT) is an increasingly widely
available, rapid and noninvasive diagnostic imaging technique that is especially useful in the evaluation of hepatic
vascular abnormalities and hepatic mass lesions.
Multidetector row CT angiography enables very detailed
anatomic evaluation of the hepatic arterial, portal and
venous architecture and should facilitate the identification of both intra‐ and extrahepatic portosystemic
shunts, arterioportal fistulae, and portal vein obstruction. Using three-dimensional reconstructions, it should
be possible to accurately identify and trace the hepatic
­portal vein and its tributaries and to accurately identify
the ­origin and termination of both intra‐ and extrahepatic shunts.
In patients with hepatic masses, CT provides important information about the exact size and extension of a
mass, allows identification of significant vascular
involvement, and facilitates evaluation of the rest of the
abdomen and the thorax for the presence of metastatic
disease; this information is invaluable both in determining the feasibility of surgical resection and in planning
surgical margins. More recently, the use of dynamic contrast CT in dogs has shown potential in the differentiation of benign and malignant hepatic masses.
Disadvantages of CT include its relatively limited availability, the requirement for general anesthesia, and the
relatively high doses of ionizing radiation involved.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Contrast‐enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI),
usually referred to as magnetic resonance angiography
(MRA), is routinely used in humans for imaging the
­portal venous system. Although the acquisition of good‐
quality images is technically difficult and accurate
interpretation of the images requires experience, this

VetBooks.ir

61 Imaging in Hepatobiliary Disease

technique is being successfully used in dogs and cats and
can provide a rapid and accurate diagnosis with excellent
anatomic resolution. In dogs with liver masses, MR
imaging findings have also been successful in differentiating benign and hepatic lesions.

­Image‐Guided Sampling
Although diagnostic imaging provides useful information,
the imaging features of canine and feline hepatobiliary disease are rarely specific for a single disease process. Despite
the potential offered by newer techniques such as contrast‐enhanced ultrasound, CT and MRI, in most cases it
is still not possible to definitively characterize the underlying disease process or to differentiate benign from malignant disease from the imaging appearance alone.
Obtaining samples of material for cytology and/or histopathology is therefore important in providing additional
information and, in many cases, a definitive diagnosis.
The most commonly used image‐guided sampling
techniques are percutaneous ultrasound‐guided aspiration and tissue‐core biopsy. These well‐established techniques are routinely used in dogs and cats, and are
considered safe and minimally invasive. Fine needle aspiration (FNA) is cheaper, easier and has fewer potential
complications than tissue‐core biopsy. However, cytopathologic (FNA) and histopathologic (core biopsy)
diagnoses from the same tissue do not always agree.
FNAs inevitably result in disruption of the normal structural relationship between cells within a tissue and are
therefore most useful in diagnosing diseases that can be
identified from individual cells (e.g., lymphoma) and in
differentiating between inflammatory, neoplastic, and
degenerative/necrotic change. In conditions where preservation of tissue architecture is more important, for
example vascular disorders and chronic hepatopathies, a
tissue‐core biopsy is more likely to provide useful diagnostic information.

When obtaining samples, the most important guidelines are to use the shortest distance and the safest path
to reach the site of interest. The needle should not pass
through more than one body cavity or more than one
organ and for both FNA and tissue‐core samples, it is
important to visualize the needle tip as it is advanced
into the tissue, keeping the entire needle length visible
within the plane of the ultrasound beam. Accurate needle placement is usually easier using a curvilinear (or
micro‐convex) transducer. For superficial lesions, linear
transducers have the advantage of superior near‐field
resolution, but needle placement may be more challenging. 1” or 1.5” 20–22 ga standard injection needles are
most commonly used for FNA, with 2.5” or 3.5” spinal
needles occasionally used for sampling deeper lesions.
For tissue‐core biopsies, either manual or automated
biopsy devices may be used. A 14, 16 or 18 ga needle
(depending on the size of the patient and of the liver) and
a 2 cm tissue sample notch are usually selected.
Depending on the patient’s clinical status and the tissue
being sampled, a coagulation profile is not usually
required before obtaining FNAs; however, it is strongly
recommended prior to tissue‐core biopsy.
Although many conscious patients will tolerate ultrasound‐guided FNAs, sedation is recommended and general anesthesia is indicated for patients undergoing
tissue‐core biopsy. When obtaining FNAs, the skin overlying the aspiration site should be clipped and cleaned
prior to sampling; ultrasound gel can confuse the cytologic interpretation and should be avoided. For a tissue‐
core biopsy, aseptic preparation is required. Ultrasound
gel may be used, but should be sterile.
Serious complications associated with FNAs are rare, but
include hemorrhage, tumor seeding, and, following gallbladder aspiration, bile leakage and potential peritonitis.
The risk of hemorrhage is increased with tissue‐core biopsy;
however, although small amounts of free fluid are not
uncommon post biopsy, in patients with normal coagulation status any bleeding should be self‐limiting.

Metabolic, Toxic, and Neoplastic Diseases of the Liver
Jan Rothuizen, DVM, PhD, Dip ECVIM-CA
Department of Clinical Science of Companion Animals, Utrecht University, Utrecht, The Netherlands

­Metabolic Diseases
The liver displays a multitude of metabolic functions,
which may fail when the liver becomes diseased. The
most important functions which may cause immediate
clinical signs with a failing, diseased liver are bilirubin
metabolism and metabolism of neurotransmitter precursors. Failing liver function may then lead to hyperbilirubinemia with icterus, and hepatic encephalopathy,
respectively. Furthermore, the liver is involved in many
metabolic and detoxification processes, and may therefore be the principal organ to develop secondary damage. The most important examples are secondary
nonspecific (reactive) hepatitis, steroid or vacuolar
hepatopathy, and hepatotoxicity of drugs such as acetaminophen, carprofen, and sulfonamides. Hepatic lipidosis (steatosis) in cats deserves specific mention, as this is
the most common metabolic disorder of the liver in cats.
The final group of metabolic liver diseases are the inherited metabolic diseases. Some are very frequent, such as
copper storage diseases in many dog breeds, while others
are rare (amyloidosis) or very rare (lipoprotein lipase
deficiency, lysosomal storage diseases).
Vacuolar Hepatopathy, and Liver Changes
in Cushing Disease
Etiology/Pathophysiology

Both spontaneous hyperadrenocorticism (Cushing disease) and the administration of glucocorticoids cause
specific abnormalities in the liver. A similar hepatic
change may occur without any known cause. There is
glycogen accumulation in the hepatocytes that results in
large vacuoles (ballooning). This leads to varying degrees
of hepatomegaly. These changes can cause elevation
of the plasma levels of liver enzymes, mainly alkaline

phosphatase (ALP), and bile acids. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) may be elevated but usually much less than
the cholestasis indicators. Increased ALP is caused not
only by hepatocellular damage but also by induction of
an isoenzyme of ALP by glucocorticoids.
History and Clinical Signs

The clinical signs are those of Cushing disease if this is
the underlying cause. Steroid hormones other than cortisol may also cause these liver effects. The above‐mentioned changes in the liver can result in hepatomegaly,
which may be detectable by abdominal palpation. The
histologic changes occur long before signs suggestive of
Cushing disease, as do the elevations of ALP and ALT. It
is important to remember that a number of signs that
occur in Cushing disease also occur in primary liver diseases: lethargy, exercise intolerance, polydipsia, hepatomegaly, and elevated ALP, ALT, and bile acids.
Diagnosis

It is important to know whether elevated liver enzyme
levels and bile acids are due to exogenous corticosteroid
use or Cushing disease. The typical liver changes can
always be determined by histologic examination of a liver
biopsy; the histologic changes are specific. These diffuse
changes are also detectable in cytologic smears taken by
way of fine needle aspiration. The corticosteroid‐induced
ALP isoenzyme can be distinguished because most of it
is still active after heating the plasma to 65° for 2 minutes.
Readers are referred elsewhere for discussions on the
diagnosis and management of Cushing disease.
Therapy

The glucocorticoid‐induced changes in the liver are
reversible within a few weeks to months after removing
the cause. However, in other cases, the prognosis depends

Clinical Small Animal Internal Medicine Volume I, First Edition. Edited by David S. Bruyette.

on the cause of the glucocorticoid excess. In cases in
which it is not possible to identify the cause of glucocorticoid excess, over time fibrosis may develop, leading to
worsening liver disease.
Hepatic Lipidosis Secondary to Diabetes
Mellitus
Etiology/Pathophysiology

The liver plays a central role in fat metabolism. In diabetes mellitus, there is increased lipolysis in adipose tissue
and therefore increased delivery of fatty acids to the liver,
while the production of triglycerides is also increased.
Fat accumulates in the liver cells and in the dog it is
microvesicular, mainly caused by accumulation of triglycerides. This fatty change begins around the central
veins and progresses toward the periphery of the lobule.
This results in the development of hepatomegaly.
Sometimes there is cholestasis, which can be quite
severe. There is much more severe liver dysfunction with
fatty change than with glycogen accumulation. In
humans, the chronic fatty change that occurs in diabetes
mellitus can lead to hypertrophic liver cirrhosis, but in
dogs and cats this is very rare.
History and Clinical Signs

Fatty change in the liver is usually present in diabetes
mellitus and it can occur without causing clinical signs.
It can also cause mild to severe intrahepatic cholestasis.
In this case, physical examination reveals hepatomegaly
and icterus. All of the liver enzymes can be mildly to
severely increased. The clinical signs are those related to
diabetes mellitus, namely polyuria, polydipsia, weight
loss, and an increased appetite.
Diagnosis

Liver histology demonstrates the fatty change, which is
confirmed in combination with the diagnosis of diabetes
mellitus (persistent hyperglycemia, glucosuria).
Therapy

Therapy of fatty change in the liver of dogs is not necessary. Regulation of the diabetes mellitus leads to a gradual disappearance of the fatty change.
The Liver in Hyperthyroidism
Hyperthyroidism is associated with fatty infiltration of
the hepatocytes. This does not cause clinical signs of
liver dysfunction, but in many cases the liver enzymes
and bile acid levels are abnormally high. The fatty
changes are not severe and there is no liver enlargement.
A number of clinical signs associated with hyperthyroidism mimic those of primary liver diseases: polyuria,
vomiting, diarrhea, and weight loss.

Hepatic Lipidosis (Steatosis) in Cats
Etiology/Pathophysiology

One important difference between dogs and cats is the
relatively low capacity of the liver enzymes responsible
for conjugation of cholephilic substances, used to make
them more polar prior to biliary or urinary excretion, in
the cat. The low hepatic glucuronyl transferase capacity
is important for the metabolism of endogenous products
such as bilirubin and exogenous compounds, either
drugs or toxins. The elimination of drugs like chloramphenicol, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs and anticonvulsants depends on this function. Hence, toxic
side‐effects develop much more easily in cats in cases of
overdosage or reduced liver function.
Cats also have different amino acid requirements from
dogs, as they cannot synthesize a sufficient number of
the essential amino acids (arginine, taurine, and carnitine). Arginine is an important intermediate metabolite
in the hepatic urea cycle in which ammonia is being converted into urea. This causes a relatively high susceptibility
to develop hyperammonemia and hepatic encephalopathy in cases of inadequate protein intake, for example
anorexia. Cats, unlike dogs, may have hepatic encephalopathy with parenchymal liver disease without portosystemic collateral circulation. Arginine and taurine are
involved in the hepatic production of apoproteins, which
are used to form the very low‐density lipoproteins. These
lipoproteins are the form in which the liver can secrete
triglycerides into the circulation for further metabolism.
Insufficient availability of arginine and taurine may lead
to accumulation of triglycerides in the liver, for example
in the case of fasting. Taurine also plays a role in detoxification, as it is used by the liver as a conjugating group to
make substances such as bile acids more hydrophilic.
Taurine is also involved in glutathione metabolism,
which is one of the major routes of hepatic detoxification. Carnitine is an intermediate enabling beta‐oxidation of long chain fatty acids in mitochondria, and this
function may be impaired in anorexia.
Fat accumulation in the liver occurs in different species, as a result of metabolic conditions in which there is
increased deposition or impaired removal of triglycerides in the liver. Clinically, this may be of importance in
diabetes mellitus as discussed for dogs. Subclinical fat
accumulation, only detectable with histologic examination of the liver, occurs in many other conditions such as
high intake of calories, hypoxia of the liver and induction
by a number of toxic substances. Cats, however, display
an idiopathic form of hepatic lipidosis that may become
life‐threatening. Accumulation of triglycerides is the
result of a disturbed balance between triglyceride uptake
by the liver and their removal. The latter is normally
achieved by formation of lipoproteins (especially very

VetBooks.ir

62 Metabolic, Toxic, and Neoplastic Diseases of the Liver

low‐density lipoproteins, VLDL), which allows for secretion of fatty acids into the circulation for further metabolism in other tissues. Another route for the liver to
metabolize fatty acids is via beta‐oxidation.
Fat cats seem to be predisposed, but lean cats may also
develop lipidosis. It is generally appreciated that prolonged fasting is the most important factor inducing lipidosis. Fasting may affect hepatic fatty acid metabolism in
three ways. First, fasting induces peripheral lipolysis and
increased delivery of fatty acids to the liver. The intake of
essential amino acids may also become inadequate.
Deficiency of arginine and taurine may inhibit the apoprotein formation necessary to form resulting in the
accumulation of triglycerides. Finally, carnitine deficiency
may result in impairment of beta‐oxidation, which is a
major pathway for hepatic fatty acid catabolism.
Most cats with lipidosis have slight hyperglycemia as a
result of impaired glucose tolerance. It is not known
what underlying mechanism leads to deranged glucose
metabolism. There is no tendency to develop overt diabetes mellitus. There is no consistency with respect to
the level of insulin and glucagon; both high and low values have been reported. In cats with concurrent diabetes
mellitus, very high doses of insulin are required to lower
the blood glucose in these cats, suggesting insulin resistance. We have measured high growth hormone concentrations in a few patients, which could explain insulin
resistance, but this could not be related to progestin
administration or other factors known to induce growth
hormone excess. Whatever the cause, hyperglycemia is a
possible factor further contributing to accumulation of
triglycerides.
Lipidosis results in hepatomegaly with yellow discoloration and a friable texture. As in all types of hepatomegaly, the margins of the lobes become rounded.
Accumulated fat is concentrated in micro‐ or macrovesicular vacuoles in the hepatic cytoplasm. Swelling of
cells can easily produce intrahepatic cholestasis.
Reduced liver function and fasting may trigger hepatic
encephalopathy.
Signalment

Lipidosis may occur at any age in both males and females,
although there seems to be an increased incidence in
middle‐aged cats. There appear to be individual differences in susceptibility; some cats sustain prolonged fasting without developing lipidosis, and others develop
recurrence with every episode of prolonged fasting. It is
interesting to note that hepatic lipidosis occurs regularly
in the United States but less frequently in Europe, and is
very uncommon in the United Kingdom. It is not known
whether these regional differences reflect variations in
genetic make‐up of the populations or differences in
composition of cat food.

History and Clinical Signs

Cats often present with anorexia and lethargy. There
may be occasional vomiting, and icterus is a common
finding. Clinical signs consistent with hepatic encephalopathy may also occur. Clinical signs related to an
underlying disease resulting in anorexia may also be
present.
Diagnosis

The clinical signs and findings on physical examination
(icterus and hepatomegaly) are not specific, and neither
are elevated serum bile acids and liver enzymes. Slight or
moderate hyperglycemia is often present but this is not
diagnostic. Remember that stress during blood sampling
often results in hyperglycemia in cats. On ultrasonographic examination, an enlarged and obviously hyperechoic liver is commonly seen. The diagnosis can only be
made by evaluation of liver tissue. However, due to the
diffuse nature of the disease, fine needle aspiration cytology is usually diagnostic.
Therapy

The most important management strategy is to get the
cat out of the catabolic condition, and to supply the
amino acids essential to prevent further fat accumulation
and development of hepatic encephalopathy. Forced
feeding of semiliquid food may be required, and this can
be achieved in most cases by slow oral feedings with a
syringe. However, this method of feeding is unsuitable
for the long term and can be very difficult in some cats.
Other forms of enteral feeding are therefore preferred,
and esophagostomy or gastrostomy tubes are sensible
first choices. These feeding tubes can be left in situ for
prolonged periods, and also enable sufficient calories to
be fed to meet the cat’s daily need. Alternatively, a nasoesophageal feeding tube can usually be placed with relative ease, although these are not suitable for the long
term, nor adequate for meeting the daily nutritional
requirements.
Since protein is the most important component in the
treatment of the metabolic derangements leading to lipidosis, 30–40% of the total calories should be administered as protein. Moreover, diets should contain the
essential amino acids arginine and taurine. Recovery formula commercial diets are available to meet these
requirements. It may be advisable to give vitamin B12
supplementation as well. There is little indication for the
use of glucose as an energy source, since cats tend to
have glucose intolerance and cannot adequately utilize it.
So‐called lipotrophic compounds, such as methionine,
are also not recommended. It also is not recommended
to administer insulin, because of the risk of life‐threatening hypoglycemia, whereas hyperglycemia appears to be
a secondary instead of a primary phenomenon.
