Supportive care includes restoration of the fluid and
electrolyte balance. Ammonia (if available), electrolytes
(sodium and especially potassium), and pH should be
monitored to permit supportive care directed at hepatic
encephalopathy if indicated.

resulting from liver dysfunction depend on the extent of
liver necrosis, and vary from general illness and lethargy
to hepatic encephalopathy. Anorexia and vomiting may
occur as a result of impaired detoxifying function of the
liver.

Prognosis

Diagnosis

Owners need to be warned that the prognosis is generally guarded, with roughly half of cats surviving.
Moreover, therapy can be prolonged, sometimes consisting of several weeks to months of enteral nutrition. The
prognosis is quite good if the condition is diagnosed and
treated early. However, cats with severe hepatic encephalopathy have a worse prognosis.

The presence and severity of any liver changes can only
be confirmed by histologic examination of a liver biopsy.
These changes are specific and therefore confirmatory.
An impression of the severity and course of the liver
necrosis is provided by measurements of the liver
enzymes and bile acids in serum, but they may also be
elevated in any other hepatobiliary disease and are by no
means specific. The diagnosis of the underlying disease
causing anemia or shock is not discussed here.

Liver Changes Due to Anemia and Shock
(Acute Hypoperfusion)
Etiology/Pathophysiology

Liver degeneration or necrosis can occur with acute
hypoxia of the liver. In this context, it is important to
remember that the blood supply of the liver is predominantly venous and therefore any adaptation to hypoxia
requires time. Possible causes for such lesions are acute
hemolysis or massive blood loss. Histologically, there is
necrosis of the centrilobular zone 3 (the oxygen‐poor
part of the liver lobule). Extensive necrosis may occur in
rare cases with confluent and bridging necrosis, forming
connections between necrotic centrilobular areas.
Necrosis induces a secondary inflammatory reaction of
polymorphonuclear cells, and there is usually widespread cholestasis. In cases of hemolysis, there is erythrophagocytosis and/or accumulation of iron pigment in
the reticuloendothelial system, and sometimes extramedullary hematopoiesis is seen. In addition to the general
illness and icterus, hepatic encephalopathy can also
occur in severely affected cases.
These changes explain why hemolytic anemia is so
often accompanied by an increase in conjugated bilirubin, and this is sometimes marked. It is the cholestasis,
rather than the hemolysis, that determines the degree of
icterus. Hence, bilirubin is predominantly the conjugated direct reacting type. ALT, AST, ALP, and gamma‐
glutamyl transferase (GGT) can be severely elevated.
Sometimes, the liver dysfunction is so severe that, in
spite of adequate treatment of the hemolysis, it leads to
death.
History and Clinical Signs

Clinical signs are usually acute in onset, and a history of
recent shock may be present. In hemolytic anemia, the
mucous membranes may be jaundiced and are usually
pale. Clinical signs are in part those of anemia, namely
lethargy and exercise intolerance. Subsequent signs

Therapy

Management primarily involves treatment of the underlying cause of hypoxia. There is no specific treatment
possible for the hepatic lesions, and the liver will recover
spontaneously in most cases after resolution of the
underlying condition. In cases of severe damage, the
impaired liver function may become life‐threatening.
Only symptomatic supportive therapy for liver dysfunction can be given, to allow time for the liver to regenerate. Specific measures to prevent or reduce hepatic
encephalopathy may be important. Remember that the
course of liver regeneration cannot be evaluated by the
degree of icterus.
Prognosis

The prognosis is very variable and primarily depends on
the underlying cause of hypoxia. If the underlying cause
can be addressed, hepatic changes are likely to be
reversible.
Amyloidosis
Etiology/Pathophysiology

Amyloidosis of the liver is very rare in dogs or cats.
Amyloidosis is often a systemic disease involving a number of organs. In cases of generalized amyloidosis, there is
usually also deposition of amyloid in the liver and kidneys,
but this seldom leads to clinical signs relevant to the liver.
The severe glomerular damage leading to urinary protein
loss is almost always the most important clinical phenomenon. In the liver, deposits of amyloid are visible as amorphous hyaline and eosinophilic material in the space of
Disse when Congo red staining is used. Depending on the
amount of amyloid, the liver may be enlarged on abdominal palpation. However, it is often a normal size. Liver
enzymes and bile acids may be increased, although sometimes they are within the normal reference interval.

VetBooks.ir

62 Metabolic, Toxic, and Neoplastic Diseases of the Liver

Signalment

Amyloidosis is frequently identified in the shar‐pei dog,
although other breeds can be affected. In cats, the
Siamese, Oriental shorthair, Devon Rex and Burmese are
predisposed.
History and Clinical Signs

Overt liver dysfunction is rare in amyloidosis, even when
the liver is grossly enlarged. Nephrotic syndrome is the
most common finding in these patients due to severe and
prolonged proteinuria resulting from renal amyloidosis.
Other possible signs of renal dysfunction are vomiting,
anorexia, and polyuria. Spontaneous rupture of the liver
may occur in severe cases, resulting in acute blood loss,
shock, and death.
Diagnosis

The deposition of amyloid can only be detected by cytologic or histologic examination of relevant biopsy material (liver or kidney). Taking biopsies is not without risk
as the liver may rupture, resulting in severe abdominal
hemorrhage.
Therapy

There is no specific treatment available for amyloidosis.
The deposition of amyloid is progressive and in animals
with end‐stage disease, the prognosis is very poor.
Copper Storage Diseases Leading to Chronic
Hepatitis and Cirrhosis
The accumulation of copper in liver tissue has been
described in several breeds of dog. Excessive accumulation includes that seen in true “copper storage” disease,
where the primary initiating event is a defect in copper
excretion leading to secondary hepatocyte damage, and
“copper‐associated” disease, in which copper accumulates secondary to an underlying inflammatory liver
disease.
Copper storage diseases probably occur in several
breeds of dog, although there appear to be differences in
prevalence between countries. Copper storage disease
was suspected in about 30% of all dogs with hepatitis in
one study from The Netherlands, but is relatively uncommon in the UK. The Bedlington terrier, Labrador
retriever, Dalmatian, Anatolian shepherd, Airedale terrier, and spaniel breeds appear to be predisposed.
In primary copper storage disease, copper accumulates in the liver when the excretion of excessive copper
into the bile is deficient. This is a gradual process and
usually toxic levels leading to chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis are reached at an age of 4–7 years. Copper first
accumulates in the centrolobular region of the liver (zone
3 around the central vein); in later stages, zone 2 and

zone 1 (periportal zone) may also become gradually
affected. This differs from copper‐associated disease,
which is the predominant form in all dogs, in which cholestasis causes periportal copper accumulation (zone 1),
with copper later accumulating in zones 2 and 3.
Copper Storage‐Induced Hepatitis and Cirrhosis
in the Bedlington Terrier
Etiology/Pathophysiology

This disease occurs in Bedlington terriers, resulting in an
accumulation of copper in the liver, usually due to an
autosomal recessive mode of inheritance. In many
affected dogs, the disease is caused by a deletion in the
COMMD1 gene, resulting in lack of production of a specific protein. This protein is an important chaperone for
the copper‐transporting protein ATPase 2, encoded by
the human Wilson disease gene ATP7B, the principal
hepatocyte exporter of copper into bile. Only homozygotes become ill; heterozygotes have a normal liver.
Normally, some of the copper ingested is absorbed in
the intestine and transported to the liver in the portal
blood, where it is loosely bound to albumin. Most of this
is taken up by the hepatocytes and excreted in the bile via
the liver cell lysosomes. A small part is incorporated in
ceruloplasmin in the liver, and copper incorporated in
this protein is released in the plasma. Copper in ceruloplasmin is used for incorporation in a number of enzymes
and proteins, essential for normal function. Most of the
copper is bound to the protein metallothionein. Copper
then moves to the lysosomes of the hepatocytes and is
excreted into the bile bound to an unidentified protein.
In this form, it leaves the body in the feces. In Bedlington
terriers with copper storage disease, the hepatocytes are
almost completely unable to excrete copper in the bile
and hence there is an increasing accumulation of copper
in the liver. The exact nature of the defect is not known,
but it is a lysosomal disorder. Because the copper accumulation begins gradually, the clinical signs usually only
begin to appear after around 4 years of age. The increased
copper concentration in the liver can be confirmed after
1 year of age; before then, some dogs with the disease
have not yet stored sufficient copper to distinguish them
from normal animals.
There is a chronic form in which the copper accumulation leads to liver cell necrosis and secondary hepatitis,
cumulating in cirrhosis. Some dogs also have an acute
form of copper storage disease, with a hemolytic crisis.
The hemolysis is probably the result of a sudden release
of a large amount of copper from hepatocytes into the
blood. The mechanism for this is not clear. The sudden
increase in blood copper concentration causes acute
hemolysis, and because liver function is already reduced,
this leads to severe icterus. Tubulonephrosis may occur
and can lead to uremia. The hemolysis in turn results in

681

VetBooks.ir

682

Section 7 Diseases of the Liver, Gallbladder, and Bile Ducts

centrilobular liver necrosis as a result of hypoxic damage. In dogs surviving the hemolytic crisis, cirrhosis
occurs much more often than in other animals.
History and Clinical Signs

With chronic copper accumulation, the clinical signs are
those of chronic hepatitis or cirrhosis. The reader is
therefore referred to the relevant sections for further
details. In the acute form there is acute hemolysis, anemia, severe icterus, and sometimes uremia. The acute
form is often lethal within a few days.
Diagnosis

Laboratory examination may reveal any of the changes
seen in chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis, such as increased
ALT, ALP, GGT, bile acids, and bilirubin. Hypoalbuminemia
and hepatic encephalopathy with increased ammonia concentrations occur only in late stages. There are no specific
laboratory parameters that are specific for copper accumulation. Ceruloplasmin and free copper concentrations are
not different from healthy dogs, whereas Wilson disease in
humans is associated with decreased ceruloplasmin levels.
On the basis of the clinical examination and result of
blood tests, it is not possible to differentiate copper storage disease from chronic hepatitis or cirrhosis. The diagnosis can only be made by demonstrating increased
copper accumulation in a liver biopsy in animals older
than 1 year. Histologically, copper in a liver biopsy may be
detected with specific stains such as rubeanic acid. The
same staining may be used on cytologic preparations collected by fine needle aspiration. Copper accumulation
begins in hepatocytes around the central veins (zone 3)
and gradually spreads outwards toward the portal areas.
The copper is stored in the hepatic lysosomes. The copper‐induced liver cell damage only occurs when a certain
level is exceeded. The damage leads to ongoing liver cell
necrosis and secondary inflammation that can eventually
result in fibrosis and cirrhosis. The normal concentration
of copper in the canine liver is between 50 and 300 μg/g
dry weight. Dogs with copper accumulation have levels
exceeding 1000 μg/g dry weight at 1 year of age, but most
cases have higher concentrations. With time, levels of
12 000 μg/g dry weight may be reached. At 1 year of age, a
few dogs have concentrations between 300 and 1000 μg/g
dry weight, and most of them appear not to accumulate
when reexamined later.
A genetic test for the mutated COMMD1 gene is available, although not all dogs with the disease have this
defect. However, heterozygote carriers cannot be distinguished from homozygote healthy animals. A few decades
ago, the incidence of the disease in Bedlington terriers was
about 30–50%. However, with the availability of a reliable
genetic test, the incidence of the disease has dramatically
declined, with clinical cases becoming quite rare.

Therapy

Once signs of chronic hepatitis or cirrhosis are present,
or those of an acute hemolytic crisis have developed,
specific therapy is usually not possible. Symptomatic
and supportive care is therefore important. In chronic
hepatitis or cirrhosis, management of hepatic encephalopathy, portal hypertension, and ascites is vital.
Readers are referred to Chapter 65 for further details
regarding therapy.
Hemolytic crisis is a very serious event. Administration
of penicillamine, which is a chelating drug that binds
metals, preferentially copper, is indicated. The penicillamine–copper complex is excreted from the kidneys
into urine, resulting in free copper being removed from
the circulation. Intravenous infusion of fluids with diuresis may also be helpful to enhance urinary copper
excretion.
It is important to try to prevent the development of
clinical signs in dogs at risk for copper storage disease.
Hence, asymptomatic dogs should be examined at a
young age, and if there is copper accumulation, life‐long
medication with drugs that prevent further accumulation of copper is essential. There are two drugs available,
and both are given orally in a capsulated form.
Penicillamine may be given 30 minutes before each meal
at a total daily dose of 25 mg/kg. Penicillamine binds
copper in the circulation and the bound complex is
excreted in the urine. Another drug is zinc, which may be
given as zinc gluconate at a dosage of 30 mg/kg/day in
divided doses immediately before each meal. The action
of zinc is at the level of the intestinal mucosa, as it induces
the formation of copper‐binding metallothionein, thus
preventing the absorption of copper. The two drugs
should not be combined since they form complexes and
inactivate each other. These medications are unable to
reduce hepatic copper levels in most cases, but they prevent further accumulation and development of the
symptomatic stage. Another measure to prevent further
accumulation is to reduce the copper content of the food.
Commercial foods have been developed to treat and prevent copper storage diseases, and have been proven to be
very effective. These are veterinary‐formulated liver
diets containing low copper and high zinc.
Copper Storage‐Associated Hepatitis and Cirrhosis
in Labrador Retrievers

Since 2006, Labrador retrievers have been reported to
have a form of copper storage disease causing hepatitis,
which if untreated results in cirrhosis. Much of the
description pertaining to the Bedlington terrier applies to
the disease in Labradors. Like all forms of copper s­ torage,
the disease develops gradually due to the slow accumulation of copper in the centrilobular area of the liver.
Therefore, the typical age of onset of clinical signs in this

VetBooks.ir

62 Metabolic, Toxic, and Neoplastic Diseases of the Liver

breed is also 4–7 years. The copper concentrations in
Labrador retrievers remain much lower than in Bedlington
terriers (by a factor of 10), and liver samples from Labrador
retrievers usually do not exceed 2000 μg/g dry weight,
whereas Bedlington terriers may have concentrations
exceeding 15 000 μg/g dry weight. Another difference is
that Labrador retrievers do not develop a hemolytic crisis
as easily as Bedlington terriers. The hepatitis may remain
“hidden” for a long period since the most sensitive marker,
ALT, may stay within normal limits for years, even when
copper accumulation and hepatitis are already present. In
more advanced cases, fibrosis and cirrhosis may develop,
similar to other breeds with copper storage disease.
The diagnosis is made in the same way as the
Bedlington terrier, and prevention and therapy are also
comparable. Commercial hepatic diet has proven very
effective in this breed. Although it is a proven genetic
disease, it appears to be much more complex than in the
Bedlington terrier, and as such a reliable genetic test is
not yet available. Due to the complexity of the disease, it
is difficult to give good advice to breeders to aid in prevention of the disease.

­Toxic Diseases
Nonspecific Reactive Hepatitis
Due to Endotoxins
Etiology/Pathophysiology

Nonspecific reactive hepatitis is a diffuse or focal liver
disease with secondary inflammatory reaction resulting
­
from toxemia or sepsis. Reactive hepatitis can occur with
every toxemia, sepsis, inflammation, and necrotizing process (including necrosis in tumors). When the process is in
tissues drained by the portal system, toxins are transported
exclusively to the liver. Toxins and bacteria from processes
elsewhere are first diluted in the general circulation before
reaching the liver. It is therefore logical that reactive hepatitis is most often caused by processes within the abdomen.
Reactive hepatitis develops in most cases of gastroenteritis and extensive gastric or intestinal tumours (e.g.,
lymphoma), as a result of increased endotoxin absorption.
It also develops in peritonitis, including local peritonitis
resulting from abdominal surgery, and in other inflammatory processes in the organs drained by the portal vein.
Reactive hepatitis is thus most often caused by gastrointestinal disorders. On the other hand, vomiting and/or
diarrhea often occur with primary liver disorders. Hence,
when a patient with gastrointestinal problems is found to
have high liver enzyme levels, the classic chicken‐or‐egg
situation is encountered, and this problem may only be
solved with liver histopathology. However, the reaction
pattern in the liver to endotoxins primarily involves the

development of canalicular cholestasis, and therefore the
cholestatic enzymes ALP, GGT, and bile acids are the most
important markers. In many primary liver diseases, the
hepatocellular enzymes ALT and AST are the predominant markers, with cholestatic markers less affected.
However, there are many exceptions to this general rule.
The circulating toxins, inflammatory mediators, and
microbes cause reticuloendothelial proliferation and
infiltration of neutrophils into the liver. There can also
be focal liver necrosis. In chronic cases, there is also lymphocytic and plasmacytic inflammation. There can be
mild to severe cholestasis in the canaliculi. In some cases
associated with sepsis, there are diffuse foci of necrosis,
microabscesses, or granulomas (e.g., infection with
Herpes canis, toxoplasmosis, brucellosis, tuberculosis,
E. coli and migrating larvae of Toxocara canis).
Hepatocellular functions usually remain intact in this
group of secondary liver diseases. Therefore, hypoalbuminemia, coagulopathies and hepatic encephalopathy are
not seen in animals with nonspecific reactive hepatitis.
History and Clinical Signs

The clinical signs are often determined by the primary
disorder. Hence, there is often vomiting and/or diarrhea,
and sometimes fever. When reactive hepatitis is severe,
there can be icterus, general lethargy, and sometimes
reduced exercise intolerance.
Diagnosis

Differentiation between primary liver diseases and reactive hepatitis is only possible by histologic examination
of a liver biopsy. The abnormalities described under
pathogenesis are characteristic. Once the diagnosis of
reactive hepatitis is made, it can be very difficult to localize the primary process. Further examination and investigation of the gastrointestinal system are usually
therefore indicated.
Therapy

Therapy and prognosis depend on the primary disorder.
Reactive hepatitis itself requires no treatment, since it
resolves spontaneously after removal of the cause. The
underlying, likely gastrointestinal disease should therefore be treated.
Drug Toxicity
Many toxins and drugs are concentrated in the liver and
may cause direct toxic damage (intrinsic toxicity), and
rarely cause idiosyncratic (very acute and severe) toxicity.
Direct toxic damage may primarily involve the hepatocytes, causing necrosis and/or steatosis, or bile canaliculi,
causing intrahepatic canalicular cholestasis. In veterinary
medicine, documented idiosyncratic liver toxicity is

683

VetBooks.ir

684

Section 7 Diseases of the Liver, Gallbladder, and Bile Ducts

restricted to sulfonamides causing severe intrahepatic bile
duct necrosis and irreparable cholestasis. Anecdotally,
although not well documented, liver toxicity has also been
reported for azathioprine, ketoconazole, fen/oxibendazole,
phenobarbital, halothane, methoxyflurane, cephalexin,
amoxicillin, oxacillin, nafcillin, erythromycin, clindamycin,
and several other drugs. The hepatic lesions may include
canalicular cholestasis and/or liver cell vacuolization and
in severe cases liver cell necrosis. There are no large
studies to document the true risk and toxicity of these
drugs. Relatively well‐documented toxicity is reported for
diazepam (cats), acetaminophen (paracetamol) in dogs
and cats, and carprofen in dogs.
Specific Toxins
Diazepam Toxicity in Cats

This toxicity has all the features of an idiosyncratic reaction, and has only been reported in cats receiving several
doses of diazepam. Toxicity results in severe necrosis of
the entire liver lobule, leading to fulminant liver failure
and severe signs including inappetence, vomiting, severe
lethargy, hepatic encephalopathy, coagulopathy, and
jaundice. Liver enzymes, including the transaminases
ALT/AST, and also ALP and bile acids are significantly
elevated. Only symptomatic treatment is possible and
the prognosis is poor in most cases.
Acetaminophen (Paracetamol) Toxicity in Dogs and Cats

Too high a dose of acetaminophen may cause severe oxidative hepatic damage. The result is hepatocellular
necrosis which, depending on the dose, may involve the
entire liver lobule and cause complete liver failure.
Acetaminophen has been used as an experimental drug
to induce reproducible acute liver failure in dog models,
and it is one of the most used suicide drugs in humans.
If acetaminophen toxicity is suspected, antioxidative
drugs such as SAM‐e and N‐acetylcysteine are advised.
However, the proven effect of these drugs was tested in
experimental situations in which the drug was given
together or before the toxic drug. Treatment after the
occurrence of the toxicity, as occurs naturally, may be
less successful. The most important treatment is immediate gastric lavage. Supportive care with intravenous
fluids and enteral feeding may also be required. If hepatic
encephalopathy with severe hyperammonemia is present, the prognosis is often very poor.
Carprofen Toxicity in Dogs

This nonsteroidal antiin­flammatory drug (NSAID) may
cause idiosyncratic hepatic toxicity. The toxicity usually
occurs after prolonged or repeated treatments, and may
cause very severe liver damage. Immediate drug withdrawal and supportive care, with intravenous fluids and
intensive therapy, result in a favorable outcome for
most cases, although several weeks of treatment may be

required. Carprofen may also cause simultaneous renal
toxicity. Carprofen toxicity causes marked elevation of
all liver enzymes, bile acids, and bilirubin. It is not known
if other NSAIDs can cause similar hepatotoxicity.
Sulfonamide Toxicity in Dogs and Cats

Repeated or prolonged treatment with sulfonamides
(including trimethoprim/sulfa) may occasionally lead to
an idiosyncratic toxicity of the liver in both dogs and cats.
The intrahepatic bile ducts appear to be targeted, especially the collecting bile ducts receiving bile from the
smaller liver lobules. In most cases, these intrahepatic
components of the biliary tree undergo complete necrosis,
leading to very severe intrahepatic cholestasis. The degree
of cholestasis is comparable to that of complete extrahepatic bile duct obstruction. Clinical signs include a sudden
onset of anorexia, depression, vomiting, polyuria, and
occasionally acholic stool, in combination with marked
icterus. Sometimes the liver is moderately enlarged. The
resulting clinical signs are those of severe cholestasis with
preservation of liver function. At ultrasonography, the
gallbladder may be entirely empty. The diagnosis requires
careful histologic examination of the liver, since the lesions
have a specific pattern. Management includes immediate
withdrawal of the drug, and therapy with the choleretic
drug ursodeoxycholic acid. Complete recovery has never
been documented and surviving cases need to be treated
lifelong with ursodeoxycholic acid.
Biologic Toxins

Amanita mushrooms and blue algae are the two important producers of biologic toxins, which may cause very
severe liver damage. Both toxic mushrooms and blue algae
cause severe necrosis of hepatocytes, and this is dose
dependent. In most cases, the damage is very severe and
associated with complete liver necrosis (fulminant hepatitis). This leads to massive increases of all liver parameters
(enzymes, bile acids, ammonia, etc.). Clinical signs are
comparable to those of the drug toxicities, and may include
hepatic encephalopathy, jaundice, spontaneous bleeding,
and severe lethargy. Therapy is supportive, with antiemetics and intravenous fluid administration, and normalization of blood pH and electrolytes. Forced diuresis may
help to relieve the signs of hepatic encephalopathy.

­Neoplasia
Primary Tumors
Hepatocellular Carcinoma
Etiology/Pathophysiology

Among epithelial tumors, hepato­
cellular carcinoma
(HCC) occurs more frequently than hepatocellular adenoma. Both tumors are usually solitary and can become

VetBooks.ir

62 Metabolic, Toxic, and Neoplastic Diseases of the Liver

very large, leading to focal enlargement of a liver lobe.
Hepatocellular carcinomas do not commonly metastasize and they grow slowly. They seldom lead to reduced
liver function as they only arise from one liver lobe, leaving the rest of the liver intact. Hepatocellular carcinoma
is associated with chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis in
humans, but such a relation does not appear to exist
in dogs though they appear to occur more frequently in
Scottish terriers with hyperphosphatemia.
Signalment

Hepatocellular carcinomas are generally seen in older
dogs, and some studies have shown a breed predisposition in the poodle, fox and Scottish terrier, and Labrador
retriever.
History and Clinical Signs

Hepatocellular carcinomas lead to the development of
clinical signs only when they have attained a significant
size, at which time they may be palpable. With increasing
size, they can also displace the stomach and cause vomiting. Abdominal palpation reveals a mass in the cranial
abdomen in most cases, and the tumor may be so big that
the abdomen is distended. It may be difficult to distinguish such masses from those arising from the spleen.
Hypoglycaemia occurs relatively commonly (about
50% of cases), and may be a paraneoplastic phenomenon
due to tumor production of insulin‐like peptides (IGF‐2).
In some cases, hypoglycemia induces exercise intolerance or episodic weakness.
Diagnosis

The liver enzymes are variably elevated, and sometimes
may be within the reference interval. Focal enlargement
of the liver, often combined with displacement of the
stomach, can often be identified on plain abdominal
radiographs. Ultrasonography reveals a mass with an
echogenicity similar to that of normal liver, although
sometimes echogenicity is abnormal. Histology of a liver
biopsy may be diagnostic, but sometimes these tumors
are well differentiated and may be very hard to distinguish from normal liver or an adenoma. Cytologic diagnosis is therefore impossible in most cases.

Bile Duct Carcinoma
Etiology/Pathophysiology

This is a relatively infrequent primary tumor of the biliary epithelium. In the dog, it usually arises from intrahepatic bile ducts and readily metastasizes to the liver
parenchyma and other organs. The multiple metastases
throughout the biliary system often lead to signs of cholestasis. In the cat, bile duct carcinomas occur more often
in the large bile ducts and result in obstruction. The disease tends to be rapidly progressive.
History and Clinical Signs

Icterus is a common clinical sign. Other clinical signs
depend on the amount of hepatic involvement, and signs
may be those of acute or chronic liver disease. There is
often widespread infiltration of the tumor in the liver
and thus hepatomegaly.
Diagnosis

Physical examination and laboratory findings usually only
indicate extrahepatic cholestasis. Fine needle aspiration
cytology is generally not useful for diagnosis. Bile duct
carcinoma is best diagnosed by liver biopsy, either under
ultrasound guidance or at laparotomy/laparoscopy.
Therapy

The tumor usually is usually very infiltrative. However, if
localized to a single liver lobe, lobectomy of that lobe can
be curative. In most cases, no treatment is possible by
the time clinical signs occur. Moreover, no anticancer
chemotherapeutic drugs have been shown to be effective
in the management of this tumor type.
Hemangiosarcoma
Etiology/Pathophysiology

This is the only common mesenchymal type of hepatic
tumor. They are usually smaller (up to a few centimeters)
and multiple. Because they occur as multiple masses,
their presence often results in more extensive hepatic
dysfunction and cholestasis than are seen with epithelial
tumors. Apart from being primary liver tumors, they
may also be metastatic from other organs such as the
spleen, kidneys, and skin.

Therapy

Signalment

Surgical removal of the affected liver lobe is the only definite treatment. This may be successful if the tumor is
not located near the hilus, the large hepatic vessels or
major bile ducts. Peripherally located carcinomas are
resectable, and in most cases, resection is curative. It is
important to monitor the blood glucose concentration
during or directly following surgery. Moreover, no anticancer chemotherapeutic drugs have been shown to be
effective in the management of this tumor type although
tyrosine kinsase inhibitors are being investigated.

History and Clinical Signs

Hemangiosarcomas usually occur in older dogs and
there appears to be a breed predisposition in the German
shepherd dog, golden retriever, boxer, Great Dane and
English setter.
Mesenchymal tumors usually have a severe and rapid
course, with anorexia, vomiting, weight loss, and sometimes icterus. Abdominal distension and hemorrhagic
ascites due to ruptures of the tumor may be present.

685

VetBooks.ir

686

Section 7 Diseases of the Liver, Gallbladder, and Bile Ducts

Diagnosis

There may be palpable liver enlargement but this is not
always the case. Biochemical examination usually reveals
high liver enzymes and bile acids but this is nonspecific.
Ultrasonography allows visualization of any tumors, and
these appear as dark hypoechogenic masses due to their
rich vascularization. The diagnosis may also be confirmed by laparoscopy/laparotomy. Ultrasound‐guided
biopsy can be used in diagnosis, although there is a risk
of bleeding and also tumor seeding. Fine needle aspiration cytology is not recommended for diagnosis.
Therapy

Mesenchymal tumors are usually inoperable and rapidly
progressive. See discussion of hemangiosarcoma in
Chapter XX. Survival times are usually in the area of
weeks to months, and the owner should be warned about
the risk of acute bleeding into the abdomen.
Secondary Tumors (Metastatic)
Etiology/Pathophysiology

Tumors of organs in the portal drainage area usually
metastasize to the liver in the course of the disease.
Hemangiosarcomas of the spleen are by far the most frequent, followed by pancreatic carcinomas and gastrointestinal tumors. Tumors from outside the portal drainage
area can also metastasize to the liver. Tumor metastases
are almost always multiple and distributed throughout
the liver. Depending on their number and size, there can
be varying amounts of liver damage.
History and Clinical Signs

The clinical signs may originate chiefly from the primary
organ: vomiting in the case of gastric tumors, extrahepatic cholestasis with pancreas tumors, and ascites
resulting from hemorrhage from splenic hemangiosarcoma. The main clinical signs caused by liver damage
from metastatic disease include lethargy, anorexia, vomiting, and icterus. There may also be palpable hepatomegaly, although this depends on the number and size of
masses.
Diagnosis

Physical and laboratory signs of liver damage and/or
cholestasis are not specific. The diagnosis is made by his-

tologic examination, although this may be missed by a
percutaneous liver biopsy. The chances of a representative liver biopsy are increased when this procedure is
performed under ultrasound guidance.
Therapy

Because of the multiple sites of metastases, surgery is
virtually never possible and the prognosis is extremely
guarded.
Generalized Systemic Tumors: Malignant
Lymphoma
Etiology/Pathophysiology

Hepatic lymphoma is relatively commonly seen in dogs
and cats, usually as part of a generalized disease. However,
in some cases lymphoma may only be present in the liver.
Infiltration of tumor cells causes hepatomegaly, and
intrahepatic cholestasis can also occur. Because the liver
damage is diffuse and widespread, there is often severe
liver dysfunction. The tumor infiltration is usually more
severe in the portal areas and around the central veins,
which sometimes causes severe portal hypertension.
Portal hypertension then results in the development of
ascites and acquired portosystemic shunting vessels. In
such cases, hepatic encephalopathy may develop.
History and Clinical Signs

The signs are highly variable, depending on the organ
systems involved. With respect to the liver, clinical signs
of icterus, lethargy, anorexia, and vomiting may occur.
Sometimes there is ascites and hepatic encephalopathy.
Hepatomegaly and splenomegaly may result in abdominal distension.
Diagnosis

The diagnosis can always be confirmed by a percutaneous liver biopsy. The diffuse hepatic involvement also
means that the diagnosis can usually be made by fine needle aspiration cytology; this is one of the few indications
for performing this test for the diagnosis of liver disease.
Therapy

A variety of anticancer chemotherapy protocols for
­lymphoma are available, and the reader is referred to
Chapter 134 for details of these.

Feline Inflammatory Liver Disease
Nicki Reed, BVM&S, Cert VR, DSAM (Feline), DECVIM-CA, MRCVS
VeterinarySpecialists, Scotland 1Deer Park Road Livingston West Lothian

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Inflammation of the liver in cats may occur with infectious diseases such as feline infectious peritonitis, toxoplasmosis or bartonellosis although other systems may
be more significantly affected than the liver. Hepatitis
may also be seen in association with toxic damage from
drugs such as diazepam, paracetamol (acetaminophen),
methimazole and carbimazole, potentiated sulfonamides, tetracyclines, griseofulvin, and phenobarbitone.
Most commonly, however, feline inflammatory liver
disease refers to the cholangitis/cholangiohepatitis complex, which is primarily an inflammatory disease of the
biliary system. When the inflammation breaches the
fibrous tissue of the periportal limiting plate, the term
cholangiohepatitis may be used. However, as this is
uncommon, cholangitis is usually the more correct term.
Cholangitis may be further classified, according to the
WSAVA Liver Standardisation Group, into neutrophilic
cholangitis (NC), lymphocytic cholangitis (LC), and
chronic cholangitis associated with liver fluke infestation.
The last of these is due to ingestion of raw fish containing
metacercariae of the family Opisthorchiidae, and is associated with mixed inflammation around dilated bile ducts
and development of periductal and portal fibrosis.
Neutrophilic cholangitis is proposed to be due to
bacteria ascending into the biliary system from the intestines, as common bacteria identified include E.coli and
Enterococcus. Acute neutrophilic cholangitis (ANC) shows
a predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate in the epithelium
and lumen of the bile ducts, and edema may be present in
the portal areas. In more severe cases, the inflammation
extends into the hepatic parenchyma and may potentially
lead to development of hepatic abscesses. In more chronic
cases (chronic neutrophilic cholangitis – CNC), the infiltrate becomes more mixed in nature, comprising lymphocytes, plasma cells and fibrosis in addition to neutrophils.

Concurrent inflammation is commonly identified in
other organs such as the pancreas (60%), intestines (50%),
and kidneys (60%). The combination of cholangitis, pancreatitis, and inflammatory bowel disease is commonly
known as triaditis, and occurs in approximately 25% of
NC cases.
Lymphocytic cholangitis is attributed to an immune‐
mediated process although some authors have suggested
that it may be a more chronic form of NC. The inflammatory infiltrate is predominantly T lymphocytes in the
portal region, and in some cases the biliary ductular
­epithelium. With chronicity, portal bridging fibrosis can
develop, severe forms of which have been referred to as
sclerosing cholangitis. Proliferation of bile ducts or ductopenia can develop and ductopenia is also considered to
reflect an immune‐mediated process.
The pathogenesis of this disease complex is incompletely
understood. Recent work has suggested that bacteria may
play a role in LC, as bacterial DNA has been found in the
bile of 38% of cats affected with LC. Although this may
support the theory that this is a chronic form of NC, it
could also be the consequence of the disease, with dilation
of the bile ducts and decreased peristalsis p
­ ermitting retrograde ascent of bacteria from the duodenum. Whether
or not Helicobacter spp. play a role in triggering initiation
of this disease also remains speculative. Another recent
study has also documented bacteria within the hepatic
parenchyma but not the bile ducts in cats with NC, questioning the traditional hypothesis of ascending infection
and suggesting hematogenous entry via the portal vein.

­Epidemiology
Cholangitis‐cholangiohepatitis was first described in
cats in the 1980s. It is the second most common feline
hepatic disorder after hepatic lipidosis in the USA, with

hepatic lipidosis being diagnosed twice as often as
­cholangitis, although prevalence within a necropsy population is only documented at 0.86%. The prevalence of
the different forms of cholangitis is difficult to establish,
due to different classifications in older publications.
In the UK, cholangitis anecdotally may be more common
than hepatic lipidosis.

­Signalment
Neutrophilic cholangitis has been reported in a wide age
range, although most commonly young to middle‐aged
cats are affected and a recent study documented a
median age at diagnosis of 110 months (9.2 years). No
breed or sex predispositions are reported. LC was previously reported to affect primarily young cats, and
Persians were suggested to be overrepresented. More
recent studies, however, have suggested that this disease
affects mainly middle‐aged to older cats, with a median
age of around 10.5–11 years. Again, no breed or sex predisposition has consistently been identified.

­History and Clinical Signs
Cats suffering from NC often present more acutely ill
with a shorter history than those with LC. Signs reported
by owners include anorexia or inappetence, vomiting
and/or diarrhea, lethargy, weight loss, and ptyalism
(excessive production of saliva). Physical examination
findings can include dehydration, icterus, hepatomegaly,
abdominal pain, and pyrexia.
Cats suffering from LC often remain bright, and some
may show polyphagia rather than anorexia, although
either is possible. Vomiting and diarrhea tend to be more
intermittent, hence a more insidious history prior to seeking veterinary attention. Acholic feces can occur in cats
with biliary obstruction, for example from cholelithiasis or
with ductopenia due to sclerosing cholangitis (Figure 63.1).
Pyrexia is less common on physical examination
although hepatomegaly and, in advanced cases ascites
can be present.
It is not possible to differentiate the two conditions
based on history and physical examination findings
alone, as there can be significant overlap in presentation.

­Diagnosis
Routine hematology is often nonspecific. Neutrophilia
may be more commonly seen with NC than LC, and neutrophils can have a toxic appearance. Lymphopenia is
also a nonspecific finding. While significant (10–40× ref-

erence range) increases in alanine aminotransferase
(ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and gamma‐glutamyl transferase (GGT)
can be seen, not all cases of cholangitis (NC or LC) will
have elevated values. Hyperglobulinemia may be seen
with LC. Electrolyte abnormalities, most commonly
hypokalemia, may be present as a consequence of vomiting and/or diarrhea.
Bilirubin is frequently, but not always elevated. The
effect on bile acids is likely to be similar to bilirubin, as
both substances are excreted in bile and affected by cholestasis (see Figure 63.1). Intrahepatic cholestasis results
with reduced flow of bilirubin from the hepatocytes into
the bile canaliculus, as a result of periportal edema and
inflammation. Obstruction of larger bile ducts due to
inflammation or cholelithiasis also causes extrahepatic
cholestasis.
Urinalysis should be performed to add further information. The specific gravity can be useful to assess for
concurrent renal involvement if azotemia is identified. In
acutely ill patients it is often high due to dehydration.
The finding of bilirubinuria is abnormal in cats, so if
identified, it reflects hyperbilirubinemia. It does not help
differentiate between the causes of icterus, but if urobilinogen is absent, this may indicate abnormal enterohepatic recirculation, suggestive of extrahepatic bile duct
obstruction (see Figure 63.1).
Although imaging can add further information, findings may be normal or nonspecific for cholangitis.
Radiography can identify hepatic enlargement, and with
chronic inflammatory changes, mineralization of the biliary system can be seen. Presence of ascitic fluid will
reduce the utility of this imaging modality.
On ultrasonographic examination, the liver often
appears normal although it may be enlarged and have a
normal, hypoechoic or hyperechoic texture. Due to the
potential for “triaditis,” it is also important to evaluate
the remainder of the abdomen fully, especially the pancreas, intestines, and kidneys. Free fluid may be sampled
for biochemical analysis, cytology, and culture to rule
out some other differential diagnoses such as feline
infectious peritonitis or neoplasia.
The biliary system should be closely evaluated,
although no differentiation can be made between NC
and LC based on ultrasound findings. The gallbladder
can contain echogenic debris, although this may be seen
in normal cats as well. If the common bile duct is found
to be distended (>4 mm), it should be checked closely
for intraluminal (e.g., choleliths) or extraluminal (e.g.,
pancreatic mass effect) obstructive lesions that require
surgical correction (Figure 63.2). Thickening of the gallbladder wall (>1 mm) is suggestive of cholecystitis.
Ultrasound guidance may be used to obtain bile for
culture, although this can be problematic if the bile is

With complete obstruction of the biliary system, urobilinogen will not be available for urinary excretion, and stercobilin will not be
present in the feces (acholic feces). Bacteria are responsible for deconjugation of bile acids and bilirubin, therefore these processes may
also be affected by abnormal gut flora.

inspissated, requiring use of a larger gauge needle and
hence potentially increased risk of bile peritonitis.
Coagulation times may be prolonged due to vitamin K
deficiency, both as a result of anorexia but also because
cholestasis reduces passage of bile acids into the intestine
where they are required for absorption of this fat‐soluble
vitamin. Coagulation times should therefore always be
evaluated prior to liver biopsy. Liver biopsy is required for

a definitive diagnosis. Due to the patchy distribution of
lesions, the larger samples obtained via laparoscopy or
surgical wedge biopsies may be preferable to needle
(“Tru‐cut”) biopsies. Ideally, both liver and bile should be
cultured, as different organisms may be cultured from
each site, although culture of bile yields higher recovery
of organisms than culture of liver. Anaerobic as well as
aerobic culture should be performed.

­Therapy
If chronic cholangitis is identified to be due to liver
flukes, treatment involves the administration of praziquantel (30 mg/kg PO q24h for 5–10 days). Treatment of
necroinflammatory hepatitis primarily involves withdrawal of any hepatotoxic drugs and use of supportive
and hepatoprotective therapies as described later.
Patients with ANC can be seriously ill, potentially in
septic shock from bacteremia. Fluid therapy should
therefore be administered at rates appropriate to the

degree of dehydration or shock present. Potassium supplementation at 20 mmol/L fluid is likely to prevent
development of hypokalemia with rehydration; however,
if hypokalemia is already documented, higher rates may
be required.
Analgesia should be administered as abdominal pain is
a common finding in these patients. Opioids are preferred over nonsteroidal antiinflammatories, especially
in hypovolemic patients.
Antibacterial therapy should ideally be based on culture and sensitivity results, but pending these, empiric
choices may be made based on the likely bacteria present
(gram negative and anaerobes – see Table 63.1).
Combination therapy may be required (e.g., fluoroquinolone plus metronidazole). Intravenous antibacterial
therapy should be used initially in systemically ill
patients. Antibacterial therapy is typically administered
for a minimum of four weeks, or until values of hepatic

Surgery may be required to manage biliary obstruction, if identified. The above treatments should be initiated first to stabilize the patient as biliary surgery is
complex and may require prolonged general anesthesia.
Surgical procedures such as stenting of the bile duct,
cholecystectomy, cholecystotomy or biliary bypass
(cholecystoduodenostomy, cholecystojejunostomy) may
be required.
Nutritional support is very important as, if hepatic
lipidosis is not already present, these anorectic patients
are at risk of developing it. Placement of a feeding tube is
recommended. A nasoesophageal tube may be placed in
the first instance, especially if prolonged clotting times
are identified, but an esophagostomy tube is preferred.
The wider bore of these tubes increases the range of diets

that may be administered as well as enabling some medications to be given via this route. In addition, the chance
of removal is reduced, and owners often can manage
these tubes at home. Gastrostomy tubes may be placed at
time of surgical intervention if required.
“Critical care” diets are generally appropriate as they are
highly digestible, can be administered via feeding tubes and
are supplemented with arginine, taurine, and antioxidants.
Hepatic encephalopthy (HE) is usually a contraindication to
feeding a high‐protein diet but in this population of cats,
signs of HE are generally attributable to arginine deficiency
from anorexia and will correct with feeding protein. An
exception to this is if HE is present due to development of
acquired portosystemic shunts subsequent to severe fibrosis, although significant hepatic fibrosis is uncommon in
cats. Longer term dietary management should consider the
presence of concurrent diseases and be chosen accordingly.
A diet for inflammatory bowel disease may be more appropriate than a “hepatic” diet, for example.

Vitamin supplementation is usually beneficial in anorectic cats. B vitamins become rapidly depleted and thiamine deficiency can contribute to neurologic signs, while
cobalamin deficiency can exacerbate anorexia. Vitamin E
is an antioxidant that also has antiinflammatory properties. Vitamin K supplementation may be required to correct coagulopathies (Table 63.2).
Symptomatic therapy can include antiemetics (e.g.,
metoclopramide or maropitant) and gastroprotectants
(e.g., H2 blockers, proton pump inhibitors, sucralfate).
Control of vomiting is important for patient comfort and
to reduce the risk of feeding tubes becoming dislodged.
Gastroprotectants may be beneficial due to the presence
of concurrent inflammatory bowel disease and to address
gastritis induced by persistent vomiting (see Table 63.2).
S‐adenosyl‐L‐methionine (SAM‐e) has a number of
hepatoprotectant effects: it is a glutathione precursor
(hence antioxidant properties), it stabilizes cell membranes, and it modulates inflammatory cytokines. As low
glutathione levels are present in a high percentage of cats
with hepatobiliary disease, administration of SAM‐e
should be beneficial, although no published data exist to
support this claim (see Table 63.2).
Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) is a hydrophilic bile
acid that has a number of benefits: choloresis, that is,
making the bile more liquid and promoting bile flow;
replacement of more toxic, hydrophobic bile acids; antiapoptosis; antioxidant; and immunomodulation (see
Table 63.2). It has been used as the sole therapy for treatment of primary sclerosing cholangitis in people, but its
use as sole therapy for treatment of LC in cats did not
compare favorably to prednisolone.
Immunosuppression is considered important for the
management of LC, but should only be commenced once
NC has been ruled out. Prednisolone is typically
employed, starting at higher, immunosuppressive doses
and tapering to as low a dose as possible once in remission (see Table 63.2). Some authors have also advocated
the use of methotrexate or chlorambucil.

Development of fibrosis is seen with progression of the
disease. While the use of colchicine to reduce fibrosis has
previously been advocated in dogs, there are no studies
to demonstrate benefit. Moreover, its use can be associated with significant side‐effects. Current medical advice
suggests that it not be recommended, although silymarin
and UDCA may have potential antifibrotic effects.
Our poor understanding of the etiopathogenesis of the
cholangitis‐cholangiohepatitis complex, and lack of controlled clinical trials, combined with an inability on occasions to obtain diagnostic samples before antibacterial
therapy, can often result in initiation of therapy with an
antibacterial along with other supportive therapies as
indicated. If a diagnosis of NC has been made, and
improvement has plateaued, prednisolone at antiinflammatory doses could be introduced as this may be beneficial in attenuating the inflammatory response.

­Prognosis
Prognosis will depend on the severity of the disease.
Obstruction of the bile duct, necessitating surgical intervention, has a guarded prognosis, particularly where biliary diversion surgery is required. Cats with ascites
similarly have a guarded prognosis as this is likely to represent the presence of significant fibrosis. However, cats
that survive the initial acute phase of NC or that are diagnosed with LC often go on to live for several years.
Relapses are possible, especially if there is a concurrent
condition such as pancreatitis that may be difficult to
control.
Lymphocytic cholangitis is likely a progressive disease,
and dilation of the bile ducts may be irreversible. This has
been proposed to increase the risk of these cats developing ascending infections and potentially cholecystitis,
therefore although recurrence is not inevitable, periodic
monitoring of liver parameters +/‐ ultrasonographic evaluation of the biliary system may be warranted.

Canine Inflammatory Liver Disease
Nick Bexfield, BVetMed, PhD, DSAM, DECVIM-CA, PGDipMEdSci, FHEA, MRCVS
Department of Veterinary Medicine, Queen’s Veterinary School Hospital, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK

The most frequently identified inflammatory liver diseases in dogs are nonspecific reactive hepatitis, acute
hepatitis (AH), and chronic hepatitis (CH) and their histologic appearance has been standardized by the World
Small Animal Veterinary Association’s (WSAVA) Liver
Standardization Group. Nonspecific reactive hepatitis
represents a nonspecific response to a variety of extrahepatic disease processes, especially febrile illnesses and
inflammation somewhere in the splanchnic bed.
Histologically, it is characterized by an inflammatory
infiltrate in portal areas, and sometimes in the parenchyma, without evidence of hepatocellular necrosis or
apoptosis. It results from a disease occurring outside the
liver, so will not be discussed further. AH is characterized
by a combination of inflammation and hepatocellular
apoptosis and necrosis, with the specific features varying
according to the cause. The majority of AH cases occur as
a result of toxin or drug ingestion, and are discussed further in Chapter 62.
Acute hepatitis can sometimes be caused by infection
with certain bacteria or viruses, and these are detailed
below. CH is defined histologically by the presence of
hepatocellular apoptosis or necrosis, a variable mononuclear or mixed inflammatory cell infiltrate, regeneration,
and fibrosis. It is the most frequently identified canine
inflammatory liver disease and so will be the focus of most
of this chapter.

­Chronic Hepatitis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
The development of fibrosis is the key pathologic change
that leads to the development of CH. The hepatic stellate
cell, also known as the Ito cell or lipocyte, is central in the
development of fibrosis in humans and rats, and evidence also suggests its involvement in the pathogenesis

of hepatic fibrosis in dogs. Hepatic stellate cells reside in
the space of Disse, between the sinusoidal endothelial
cells and the hepatocytes. In the healthy liver, they are
the major storage site of vitamin A, but in chronic liver
injury they are stimulated to transform into collagen‐
secreting, activated cells that express smooth muscle‐
specific alpha‐actin and secrete high‐density matrix and
collagen into the space of Disse. The secretion of collagen and formation of fibrous tissue from activated
­stellate cells are believed to be indirect via the release
of cytokines from inflammatory cells, although some
inflammatory mediators act on them directly. Fibrous
tissue within the liver leads to the development of intrahepatic portal hypertension by altering sinusoidal tone
and blood flow. The development of portal hypertension
results in many of the complications of chronic liver disease such as ascites and gastrointestinal (GI) ulceration.
The known or postulated causes of CH are listed below,
although the majority of cases have no identifiable cause
and thus are termed idiopathic.
Infectious Causes
Canine Acidophil Cell Hepatitis Virus

A potential viral cause of AH and CH was identified in
1985 and named “canine acidophil cell hepatitis virus”
although no specific agent was isolated. Histopathologic
examination revealed an inflammatory infiltrate with
areas of hepatocyte necrosis and scattered numbers of
large cells with acidophilic cytoplasm, termed “acidophil cells.” When liver homogenate and serum from
affected dogs were injected into naive animals, this
resulted in the development of clinical and pathologic
changes of AH that in some dogs progressed to CH.
However, no further work to identify the potential
transmissible hepatitis‐causing agent was performed,
nor have further reports emerged.

Canine Adenovirus‐1

Adenoviruses are medium‐sized viruses, two of which
are known to infect dogs: canine adenovirus type 1
(CAV‐1) and canine adenovirus type 2 (CAV‐2). CAV‐1
is well known as a cause of AH in nonimmune dogs, but
CH has also been experimentally reproduced in partially
immunized dogs challenged with CAV‐1. However, several studies have failed to identify CAV‐1 in liver tissue
from large numbers of clinical cases of CH.
Canine Hepacivirus

A novel virus, canine hepacivirus (CHV), was recently
identified in outbreaks of respiratory illness in dogs from
animal shelters in the USA. CHV was also identified at
low levels in hepatocytes dogs that died of “unexplained
GI illness” although the results of liver histology were not
reported. Despite CHV being identified in canine liver
tissue, it is unclear if this virus is hepatotrophic or if it
causes disease. However, in two recent studies, there
was no evidence of exposure to, or a carrier state of, CHV
in large cohorts of dogs with CH, suggesting that the
virus is probably not associated with canine CH.
Hepatitis Viruses A, B, C, E, and GBV‐C

Although hepatitis B (HBV) and C viruses (HCV) are by
far the most frequent causes of human chronic viral hepatitis, several other viruses are implicated. The more frequently described include hepatitis A (HAV) and E
viruses (HEV), and GB virus‐C (GBV‐C), although these
are generally associated with the development of AH.
However, previous attempts using polymerase chain
reaction (PCR)‐based approaches have failed to identify
HAV, HBV, HCV, HEV, and GBV‐C in liver tissue from
large numbers of dogs with CH.
Bacteria

Infection with leptospires is a well‐known cause of AH,
as detailed later in this chapter. Infection with leptospires
can also cause CH, with histologic changes consisting
mainly of lymphoplasmacytic, portal and intralobular
inflammation, hepatocyte necrosis, and biliary stasis.
The organisms are relatively sparse and difficult to find
with conventional staining techniques, so it is possible
that CH associated with leptospirosis is underrecognized. Using nested PCR, a recent study failed to detect
Leptospira spp. DNA in 98 dogs with CH.
Infection with other bacteria is a relatively uncommon
cause of CH. Bacillus piliformis, Helicobacter canis,
Ehrlichia canis and Bartonella spp have also been identified in dogs with CH, but causality has not been clearly
established. Dogs do develop cholangitis or cholangiohepatitis, and this is covered in further detail in
Chapter 67. Additionally, granulomatous hepatitis is an
unusual presentation, in which the predominant cell

type present is the macrophage. Lesions are usually multifocal and have been associated with numerous bacteria,
including Nocardia, Mycobacterium, Rhodococcus,
Bartonella, and Borrelia. Chronic hepatic leptospirosis is
a particular concern in these cases and should be ruled
out with fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH). In
addition, several fungi have been associated with this
specific histologic diagnosis.
Autoimmunity
An immune-mediated aetiology to human liver disease is
well recognised, and the criteria for its diagnosis are well
established. Diagnosis is based on increased serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) activity, presence of positive serum autoantibody titres, increased serum IgG
concentration, characteristic histopathology findings,
and exclusion of other aetiologies. However, there is only
anecdotal evidence for an immune-mediated cause to
canine CH. Circulating autoantibodies were present in
the serum of dogs with a variety of liver diseases, and
antiliver membrane protein antibodies have been identified in serum of dogs with CH. However, the question
that remains from all these studies is whether these
autoantibodies are the primary cause of the disease, i.e.
suggestive of an autoimmune aetiology, or whether they
are a secondary phenomenon. Peripheral blood mononuclear cell proliferation in response to liver membrane protein was also significantly higher in dogs with CH
compared to control dogs. Moreover, high numbers of
CD3+ lymphocytes are found in the liver of dogs with
CH, again suggesting the involvement of the immune system in the etiology of the disease. An immune-mediated
aetiology to CH in some dogs is also suggested by the fact
that there is a female gender predilection, along with
clearly defined breed predispositions. In addition, the
association of certain susceptibility and resistance MHC
class II haplotypes with CH indicates a role of the immune
system in disease development, although this does not
necessarily point to an autoimmune aetiology.
Copper
The accumulation of copper in liver tissue has been
described in several breeds of dog. Excessive accumulation includes that seen in copper-associated hepatitis,
sometimes known as true “copper storage” disease,
where the primary initiating event is a defect in copper
excretion leading to secondary hepatocyte damage, and
the copper accumulation which occurs secondary to an
underlying inflammatory liver disease. Copperassociated hepatitis was first described in the Bedlington
terrier over three decades ago. Since then, many studies
have detailed its clinical course and pathologic features,

VetBooks.ir

64 Canine Inflammatory Liver Disease

including the progressive accumulation of copper in
hepatocytes starting in zone 3 and leading to the development of CH. Copper‐associated hepatopathies have
been reported in several breeds of dog including the
Dalmatian, Labrador retriever, Skye terrier, West
Highland white terrier, and Doberman pinscher. These
may not be true copper storage diseases as copper does
not build up throughout life, and the amount of copper
stored is often not correlated with the severity of the
underlying disease. Although uncommon in the United
Kingdom, copper‐associated hepatopathy is increasingly
seen in other countries, especially The Netherlands.
Disorders associated with excess copper accumulation
are covered in more detail in Chapter 62.
Epidemiology
Historically, the term canine CH was poorly defined
and used to describe a variety of inflammatory liver diseases. The terms chronic active hepatitis and chronic
lobar hepatitis were used early in the description of the
disease, although these names have now largely been
abandoned in favor of CH. Improvements in the classification of canine CH were brought about by the
WSAVA Liver Standardization Group which established standardized histologic criteria for diagnosis.
Since the publication of these criteria, one study has
demonstrated a postmortem prevalence of 12% in a
first opinion practice setting in the UK. Data to assess
the prevalence of the disease in other countries are not
available, although anecdotally CH appears to be the
most frequently identified inflammatory liver disease in
dogs worldwide.
Signalment
Chronic hepatitis typically affects middle‐aged to
older dogs, with the median age for all breeds in a recent
study being 8 years (range, 7 months to 16 years). Females
appear to be predisposed, with a female to male ratio of
1.5:1.0 in one study. Several reports detail breed predispositions to CH. The first of these was performed on a
Swedish population of dogs, and demonstrated that the
American and English cocker spaniel, West Highland
white terrier, Labrador retriever, Doberman pinscher,
and Scottish terrier had an increased risk for CH. In this
study, the disease was reported to occur more commonly
in middle‐aged to older animals and there was a gender
predisposition in male English and American cocker
spaniels and female Labrador retrievers. A recent study
performed in the UK assessed the breed distribution by
comparing the signalment of 551 cases with a histologic
diagnosis of CH to that of a large control population.
From a total of 61 breeds, the American cocker spaniel,

History and Clinical Signs
Clinical signs in dogs with CH vary, and are usually
nonspecific and insidious in onset. Sometimes another
disease, stress or therapy causes sudden decompensation. The liver has tremendous functional and structural reserve, and a significant loss of normal hepatic
tissue can occur with minimal or no change in clinical
signs. In addition, the liver has a remarkable capacity to
regenerate following hepatic injury, providing the damage is not too severe or ongoing. Overt liver failure does
not develop until at least 70–80% of functional capacity
is lost, so the development of clinical signs implies
marked impairment of liver function. In addition, some
dogs with advanced CH or cirrhosis can be asymptomatic, or alternatively may present with signs of “acute”
liver disease.
The clinician should pay particular attention to subtle
waxing and waning GI signs, depression, lethargy, anorexia, weight loss, and polyuria and polydipsia. Additional
signs that may be more suggestive of CH, although still
not specific, include jaundice, ascites, coagulopathy, and
neurologic signs caused by hepatic encephalopathy.

VetBooks.ir

698

Section 7 Diseases of the Liver, Gallbladder, and Bile Ducts

Clinical signs of hepatic encephalopathy, which are often
intermittent, include behavioral changes, hypersialism,
head pressing, circling, ataxia, temporary blindness, seizures, and coma. In one study of 101 dogs with both AH
and CH, the most commonly identified clinical signs were
lethargy (56/101), anorexia (56/101), vomiting (48/101),
polyuria and polydipsia (47/101), and weight loss (28/101).
Physical examination findings are generally relatively
unremarkable. Poor body condition is often seen in animals with CH. With progressive disease and the further
development of fibrosis, liver size reduces in dogs with CH.
Ascites and icterus may also be seen with chronic disease.
Diagnosis
Clinical Pathology

Clinical pathology is usually the next step in the investigation of a dog with suspected CH. Sometimes, results
of clinical pathology performed for another reason, for
example as a preanesthetic blood screen, may fortuitously reveal the presence of CH. Clinical pathology
findings include elevations of liver enzymes, especially
hepatocellular enzymes released as a result of liver cell
damage, namely ALT and aspartate aminotransferase
(AST). Increased ALT activity is the primary clinical laboratory finding in dogs with CH, and is raised in over
90% of cases. In addition, the markers of cholestasis,
alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and gamma‐glutamyl transferase (GGT), are invariably elevated. It is important to
remember that liver enzyme activity is not a test of liver
function, and very occasionally a dog with advanced CH
may have liver enzymes within the reference interval. In
addition, elevations in liver enzymes are not an uncommon reaction to many other diseases and these elevations can sometimes be marked.
While liver enzymes do not give any indication of liver
function, there are other tests on the biochemistry panel
which provide some information about liver function.
Due to the development of fibrosis, liver function in dogs
with CH is progressively compromised, and so these
markers are particularly useful in diagnosis. With progressive liver dysfunction, levels of albumin, urea, glucose
and coagulation factors decrease, while the concentration of bile acids, ammonia, and bilirubin increases.
Hypoalbuminemia occurs in about 40% of cases, although
with advanced disease (cirrhosis), this increases to 75%.
None of these tests are completely specific for liver disease, so they should always be interpreted in the light of
other clinical and clinicopathologic findings.
Both qualitative and quantitative abnormalities in
erythrocytes may also be present in dogs with CH, in
combination with alterations in white cell and platelet
numbers. The more frequently encountered abnormalities in dogs with CH include mild nonregenerative anemia

of chronic disease, which is normocytic and normochromic. Sometimes abnormal red cells including acanthocytes (irregular large surface projections) and/or target
cells (codocytes), which are dense‐centered cells surrounded by a clear area, can be identified on a blood
smear. Dogs with CH may have a neutrophilic ­leukocytosis,
although this is a nonspecific change. Thrombocytopenia
may develop due to platelet sequestration or increased
destruction, and alterations in platelet function (thrombocytopathies) may also occur.
Abnormalities may be present in the urine of dogs with
CH, including a low specific gravity (<1.030), bilirubinuria, increased urobilinogen, urate crystals, and occasionally urate calculi. Approximately 10% and 60% of dogs
have prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and partial
thromboplastin time (PTT) respectively.
Diagnostic Imaging

Diagnostic imaging is usually the next step after clinical
pathology in the assessment of the dog with suspected
CH. Abdominal radiography can be used to assess liver
size, as dogs with CH may have a reduced liver size.
However, the liver may appear normal on routine radiographic evaluation, even when severely diseased. Ultra­
sonography is the preferred imaging modality for the
investigation of liver disease. In one study of 67 dogs
with CH, only 15 had no identifiable ultrasonographic
abnormalities. Hepatic size was assessed as normal in
26, enlarged in eight and small in 26. Hepatic structure
was found to be normal in 27, irregular in 31, and 11
had increased echogenicity. Nodular processes were
observed in 16 dogs and ascites was present in 18. The
reader is referred to Chapter 61 for further details on
diagnostic imaging in the investigation of liver disease.
Liver Biopsy

It is not possible to make a definitive diagnosis of CH from
the results of clinical pathology or diagnostic imaging. In
some cases, a tentative diagnosis can be made but definitive diagnosis ultimately relies on histologic examination
of liver tissue. Moreover, descriptors of severity of inflammation and the amount of fibrosis are provided, and these
can be used prognostically and therapeutically. Liver histology will give vital information to help establish the most
appropriate therapy. Without a biopsy, therapy of CH will
be at best nonspecific and at worst counterproductive.
Many methods are available for collection of liver tissue,
and the method used will depend on clinician preference,
availability of equipment, technical skill, type of lesion
present, location, and clinical stability of the patient.
Further details about the methods for collection of liver
tissue are detailed in Chapter 60. The recently published
ACVIM Consensus statement on the diagnosis and treatment of chronic hepatitis in dogs, recommends a wedge

VetBooks.ir

64 Canine Inflammatory Liver Disease

biopsy taken at laparoscopy or laparotomy because trucut
biopsies produce misleading results 50% of the time and
also carry an increased risk of haemorrhage. Needle aspiration cytology is not reliable for the diagnosis of CH and
is therefore not recommended.
The only real absolute contraindication for liver biopsy
is severe coagulopathy. Prior to biopsy, coagulation status should be checked, by way of platelet count, measurement of PT, PTT, and ideally thromboelastography.
In humans, thromboelastography can predict bleeding
tendencies in cirrhotic patients, but data does not exist
in dogs to determine how reliable this is as an assessment
of bleeding tendencies. However, assessment of coagulation status should not be a substitute for proper technique and adequate postoperative care. If coagulation
times are prolonged, vitamin K can be given by injection
24 hours prior to biopsy and then coagulation times
retested. An alternative approach, if available, is the use
of fresh‐frozen plasma to assist in replenishing deficient
coagulation factors. All animals should be hospitalised
and monitored carefully for signs of hemorrhage for at
least 12 hours after biopsy.
As detailed previously, standardized criteria for the histologic diagnosis of CH exist. The standard histochemical stain used in the assessment of liver tissue is
hematoxylin and eosin, but consideration should be
given to the use of additional stains for specific features
such as reticulin (connective tissue), Perls’ Prussian blue
(ferritin), Fouchet’s (bile pigments) and periodic acid–
Schiff (polysaccharides). In addition, specific histochemical stains for copper, such as rubeanic acid or
rhodanine, should be consider in at‐risk breeds (see earlier) (Figure 64.1).
