Therapy
Therapy for CH is aimed at the underlying cause, if known.
However, as the etiology of most cases is currently not
understood, specific therapies are usually not possible.
Hepatocytes have a remarkable capacity for regeneration,
which means that early diagnosis and therapy have the
potential to reverse disease mechanisms. It is also important to initiate therapy as early as possible in an attempt to
inhibit fibrosis, which will ultimately lead to functional
impairment. Therapy aimed at addressing clinical signs of
liver disease, including ascites, GI ulceration leading to
melena, and hepatic encephalopathy, is also an important
part of therapy of the dog with CH. Copper chelators are
important in dogs with copper-associated hepatitis.
Careful dietary management to support the liver is essential too. Unfortunately, in veterinary medicine there is a
lack of controlled ­studies on clinical efficacy and pharmacokinetics of the drugs commonly used in canine CH. As
a result, many of our current therapeutic protocols are
either derived from human hepatology or anecdotal
reports or originate from low‐quality veterinary clinical
studies. The following refers to the recommended therapy
of a dog with CH.
Corticosteroids

Corticosteroids have antiinflammatory, immune‐modulating, and antifibrotic properties. They have a potent
indirect antifibrotic action via reducing prostaglandin
and leukotriene production from inflammatory cells,
and a weak direct antifibrotic action by inhibiting
mRNA and enzymes. Corticosteroids are indicated in
the therapy of CH where there is biopsy evidence of
ongoing inflammation, when there is mild to moderate
fibrosis associated with an inflammatory infiltrate, and
when infectious causes have been ruled out as far as possible. However, steroids are not without adverse effects,
and these can be very severe and potentially life‐threatening in some dogs with CH. Adverse effects include
increased protein catabolism, fluid retention, GI ulceration, and risk of infections. Their use in humans with
ascites, GI ulceration, and encephalopathy has been
shown to decrease survival time, and the same is likely
to be true in dogs. These are patients with portal hypertension. As advanced bridging fibrosis or cirrhosis is
likely to be associated with portal hypertension,
­corticosteroids are therefore contraindicated if there is
biopsy evidence of these changes. Dexamethasone tends
to cause more adverse effects than prednisolone and
should be avoided.
There have been limited numbers of studies evaluating
the use of corticosteroids in dogs with CH. In an early
study, prednisolone was used in 151 dogs at a dose of
2.2 mg/kg/day for 7–14 days, and resulted in increased

699

VetBooks.ir

700

Section 7 Diseases of the Liver, Gallbladder, and Bile Ducts

survival from a median of ten months to thirty months,
and complete remission was reported in some dogs
with no relapse. However, the diagnosis of CH was not
made according to our current histologic criteria. In a
more recent study of 36 dogs with idiopathic CH treated
with prednisolone at 1 mg/kg/day for at least six weeks,
at follow‐up 11 dogs were in complete remission, eight
dogs had recurrent clinical signs, and 17 had residual
disease. In a prospective study of CH in English Springer
spaniels, 14 dogs were treated with prednisolone at a
mean dose of 1.2mg/kg/day. These dogs all demonstrated improved survival over a historical control
group, and there was improvement in liver enzyme
activity and bilirubin in all. Finally, a retrospective
study demonstrated that when 13 Cocker spaniels were
treated with prednisolone 0.5-1.25mg/kg/day, in combination with azathioprine, there was a longer survival
than a historical control group. . In these reports, some
dogs with CH demonstrate an improvement in clinical
signs, laboratory data or histopathology, inferring an
immunomodulatory or anti-inflammatory benefit.
However, limited conclusions can be drawn from most
of these studies, as the underlying cause of CH wasn’t
often known. In addition, variable doses of immunosuppressive drugs were used, and dogs usually received
concurrent therapies. If there is strong evidence for an
immune-mediated causes to CH (see earlier), the clinical should consider using an immunosuppressive dose
of corticosteroids. However, if infectious causes have
not been ruled out, and especially if hepatic histology is
not typical for an immune-mediated aetiology, a lower
dose should be used.
The duration of corticosteroid therapy, or method
of dose reduction in dogs with CH is also not known. In
human patients, corticosteroids are continued for at
least six months beyond remission, and in some cases
life‐long. It is often difficult to assess remission in dogs,
particularly as corticosteroids induce hepatic enzymes
and so confuse attempts to follow the disease clinicopathologically. Repeat liver biopsy can be very useful,
although sometimes results are nonrepresentative if the
disease is patchy in distribution. The length of therapy
therefore remains empiric and some animals remain on
life‐long therapy. In this situation the aim is to use a low
alternate‐day dose. Using an additional immunosuppressive alongside corticosteroids may enable a more
rapid tapering of the corticosteroid.
Ciclosporin has also been used as an additional, or
alternative, immune‐modulating drug in canine CH. . In
a retrospective study 48 dogs with suspected idiopathic
CH were treated with 5.0mg/kg BID cyclosporine; 79%
of dogs achieved biochemical remission, although no
follow-up biopsies were taken to determine the effects of
therapy on hepatic histology.

Antifibrotics

Progressive fibrosis in CH ultimately leads to reduced
function and many of the clinical consequences of
advanced liver disease. The most effective ‘anti-fibrotic’
in chronic liver disease is to remove the underlying cause.
In addition to the antifibrotic action of corticosteroids,
more specific antifibrotics exist. Colchicine, an alkaloid
that binds tubulin, may be useful in some dogs with CH
and moderate to marked fibrosis on biopsy, although it is
not licensed for use in animals. Although it may improve
survival in some human patients with advanced fibrosis,
there are very limited reports of its use in dogs. If used,
care should be exercised as adverse effects, including
marrow suppression, anorexia and diarrhea, are seen relatively commonly. Again, it is very difficult to judge how
long to treat for and a follow‐up liver biopsy is necessary
to assess response. The author does not use colchicine.
Cholerectics and Bile Acid Modifiers

Ursodeoxycholic acid (ursodiol, UDCA) is a hydrophilic
bile acid that displaces toxic hydrophobic bile acids and
also stimulates bile flow (it is a cholerectic). These two
actions reduce cell damage and oxidative stress resulting
from retention of bile acids in the liver. It has also been
shown to have immunomodulatory actions by reducing
immunoglobulin and interleukin production and expression of MHC‐1 on hepatocytes. Recent studies show an
additional antioxidant activity with a synergistic action
with S‐adenosyl‐L‐methionine (SAM‐e) and vitamin E.
No data on its use in canine CH are available, although
because biliary stasis is invariably present, it is probably
indicated in all cases. It also appears to be well tolerated
with no significant adverse effects reported to date.
Antibiotics

The majority of dogs with CH do not appear to have an
underlying bacterial etiology, and so do not require antibiotics. Having said that, due to compromised reticuloendothelial function, bacterial infections may be a secondary
complication of many liver diseases, including CH, and so
their use may be justified. Moreover, antibiotics should
also be used if the patient has signs of hepatic encephalopathy. Because of their efficacy against enteric organisms and
ability to concentrate in bile, suitable antibiotics include
ampicillin, amoxicillin, cephalexin, fluoroquinolones, and
metronidazole. Note that, because of its reliance of hepatic
clearance, metronidazole should be used at half the routine
dose in dogs with liver disease to avoid toxic adverse effects.
The use of antibiotics in dogs with bacterial cholangitits/
cholangiohepatitis is discussed in Chapter 67.
Antioxidants

These include vitamin E, zinc, silymarin (milk thistle),
and SAM‐e. Oxidant stress is likely to be increased due

VetBooks.ir

64 Canine Inflammatory Liver Disease

to the effects of inflammation, reduced blood flow, and
mitochondrial damage by refluxed bile acids. Oxidation
is a significant mechanism of hepatic damage, therefore
antioxidant therapy is reasonable. SAM‐e increases
hepatic and red blood cell levels of glutathione, a potent
antioxidant, and is also a critical enzyme in transmethylation, transsulfuration, and aminopropylation pathways. As part of these pathways, SAM‐e is essential to all
cells and is particularly important in hepatocytes because
of their central role in metabolism. It is widely available
as a neutraceutical for dogs, sometimes in combination
with silymarin. Although no experimental data exist,
antioxidants are likely of benefit in CH. However, not all
antioxidants are necessarily innocuous in liver disease;
for example, ascorbate may increase liver damage by
accumulating iron, so it is best to avoid supplementing
vitamin C.
Copper Chelators

Copper chelators include 2,3,2‐tetramine tetrahydrochloride (2,3,2‐T), 2,2,2‐tetramine tetrahydrochloride
(2,2,2‐T), penicillamine, and zinc. 2,3,2‐T is the more
potent chelator but is not widely available in a drug formulation. Penicillamine is an alternative copper chelator, but significant adverse effects can be associated
with its use. Copper chelators should be reserved for
dogs in which significant copper accumulation has been
identified in liver tissues, primarily those animals with
copper storage disease. Zinc is used as prophylaxis in
dogs with copper storage disease, and commercially
produced hepatic support diets often contain increased
zinc for this reason. The use of copper chelators for the
management of copper-associated hepatitis is discussed
in Chapter 62.
Diuretics

Ascites in CH is usually due to portal hypertension,
although in some animals hypoalbuminemia may contribute to the pathogenesis. If blood albumin is normal or
near normal in the ascitic dog, portal hypertension is
likely to exist. Portal hypertension leads to splanchnic
pooling of blood with subsequent reduction in systemic
arterial pressure and activation of the renin‐angiotensin‐
aldosterone system (RAAS). RAAS activation then leads
to further fluid retention and more ascites. Spironolactone,
an aldosterone antagonist, is therefore the drug of choice
in ascitic patients with portal hypertension, although it
can take 2–3 days to work. For this reason, spironolactone combined with a thiazide diuretic or furosemide
can be used in an attempt to increase its speed of action.
Spironolactone also has the advantage that it does
not induce hypokalemia, which can precipitate hepatic
encephalopathy (HE) (hypokalemia allows ammonia to
enter cells more easily).

Gastroprotectives

Portal hypertension is common in dogs with CH and
leads to gut wall edema and potentially ulceration. This is
one of the most common causes of death in dogs with
chronic portal hypertension. Sudden GI bleeding can
precipitate an acute encephalopathic crisis due to the
high protein content of blood. An important way to
reduce the incidence of GI tract ulceration is to ensure
adequate enteral nutrition (see later), as anorexia predisposes to GI ulceration. H2 receptor antagonists, or proton pump inhibitors, are often used in the prevention and
therapy of ulceration. However, there is some evidence
that gastric pH is actually elevated in human CH, and,
moreover, many ulcers are duodenal rather than gastric,
so the rationale for these drugs is unclear. Traditionally,
ranitidine is preferred as an H2 receptor antagonist in
liver disease as it does not affect the cytochrome P450
system, and sucralfate should probably be used also.
Dietary Management

Appropriate dietary management is as important as drug
therapy in the dog with CH. Each case is individual and
the diet should be adjusted accordingly, so clinicians
should resist the temptation to think that “one diet fits
all.” In particular, many dogs with CH are fed diets with
inappropriate and excessive protein restriction, which
may restrict hepatic regeneration and result in protein‐
calorie malnutrition. Specific recommendations include
the following.
Feed a palatable diet little and often (4–6 times a day)
as many dogs with CH may be inappetent. Frequent
feeding also reduces the development of HE.
●● Feed highly digestible, high‐quality protein in normal
amounts whenever possible. Good‐quality commercial diets are acceptable. Examples of high‐quality
proteins include soya and these can be supplemented
if weight or blood albumin decreases. If signs of HE
are suspected, feeding a normal amount of high quality digestible protein little and often is recommended.
Excessive protein restriction may result in protein‐
calorie malnutrition and the breakdown of highly
ammoniagenic endogenous proteins.
●● Dogs with CH may have impaired carbohydrate metabolism, so a diet containing highly digestible, complex
carbohydrates should be fed.
●● Normal amounts of fat should be fed, although fat can
be restricted if steatorrhea develops.
●● Fermentable fiber is helpful in dogs with HE as it acidifies the colon and traps ammonia. It also increases
nitrogen incorporation into bacteria and reduces
­bacterial ammonia production. Nonfermentable fiber
is helpful in preventing constipation, a predisposing
­factor for hepatic encephalopathy.
●●

701

VetBooks.ir

702

Section 7 Diseases of the Liver, Gallbladder, and Bile Ducts

Zinc deficiency is common in human CH and is thought
to also occur in dogs with CH. Supplementation reduces
HE and decreases copper absorption from the GI tract
and copper availability in the liver. Zinc may also have
antiinflammatory, antifibrotic, and antioxidant effects.
●● In dogs with excessive hepatic copper accumulation,
primarily those with a primary copper storage disease,
copper intake should be restricted. This includes not
providing water from copper pipes in soft water areas.
●● Fat‐soluble vitamins include A, D, E, and K. Vitamin E
is an antioxidant and can be supplemented in dogs
with CH. Vitamin K supplementation may occasionally be necessary if clotting times are prolonged, especially preceding biopsy. Vitamins A and D should not
be supplemented as vitamin A can cause hepatic damage and vitamin D can cause calcification in tissues.
●● Vitamin B, a water‐soluble vitamin, can also be supplemented, as there may be increased loss associated
with polyuria.
●●

The effectiveness of dietary therapy should be monitored
by the assessment of clinical signs and making sure that
the patient maintains body weight and blood protein
­levels. Consideration should also be given to the use of
enteral feeding methods in the anorexic dog with CH.
Prognosis
The prognosis for CH is variable, and likely dependent
on multiple factors, especially the underlying etiology
and stage of disease. The presence of advanced fibrosis
and cirrhosis is strongly associated with a reduced survival time in humans with CH, and the same appears to
be true in dogs. In one study, the median survival time of
a variety of breeds of dogs with CH was 18.3 months.
Other studies have demonstrated mean survival times of
approximately 18 months and 16 months, again in a variety of breeds of dog with CH. In Labrador retrievers with
CH, the median survival was 374 days (range, 1–2645
days), whereas in English springer spaniels it was 189
days (range, 1–1211 days).
One of the most important individual prognostic
indictors in CH appears to be the presence of ascites; the
time from onset of clinical signs to death was two months
for dogs with ascites, compared to 33 months for those
without. Total serum bilirubin has also been shown to be
significantly negatively correlated with a reduced survival time in dogs with CH. Other parameters associated
with a shorter survival time in dogs with CH include
anorexia, prolonged prothrombin time, prolonged partial thromboplastin time, thrombocytopenia, hypoalbuminemia, and hyperglobulinemia. Caution should,
however, be employed when interpreting these data in
the individual dog with CH, as prognosis is likely dependent on multiple variables.

­Acute Hepatitis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
The majority of cases of AH are idiopathic. Of the known
causes, toxin or drug ingestion is thought to be most
common, and is discussed further in Chapter 62. Other
causes of AH are discussed here.
As detailed previously, a potential viral cause of AH
and CH was identified some 30 years ago and named
“canine acidophil cell hepatitis virus.” However, no specific agent was isolated, nor have further reports
emerged. CAV‐1 is probably the best known infectious
cause of AH, particularly in non‐Immune dogs, but it
can occasionally cause disease in partially immune dogs.
However, the use of widespread vaccination against this
disease has significantly reduced its incidence, so cases
of clinical disease are now uncommon.
Probably the most frequently implicated infectious
cause of AH is due to Leptospira spp. The characteristic
hepatic lesions in acutely infected dogs include edema
and sinusoidal congestion, perivascular inflammation,
hepatocyte necrosis, and cholestasis. Some animals
also present with signs of renal dysfunction. Widespread
vaccination has significantly reduced the incidence of
disease although, at least in the UK, the majority of
dogs are only vaccinated against two serovars. Clinical
cases of leptospirosis due to infection with other serovars occur, so the use of vaccines providing protection
against these additional serovars is recommended.
Infection with other bacteria is a relatively uncommon
cause of canine AH, although dogs do develop cholangitis or cholangiohepatitis.
Defects in copper metabolism leading to the development of AH have also been described in several breeds of
dog. In one study of 21 dogs with AH, five had histologic
evidence of increased copper accumulation and were
diagnosed with copper‐associated hepatopathy.
Epidemiology
Few data exist to determine the prevalence of AH in
dogs. In part, this likely represents the failure to achieve
a histologic diagnosis in many animals. In one study of
101 cases of primary hepatitis, AH was diagnosed in 21
dogs and CH in 67. Improvements in histologic classification of canine liver diseases, including that of AH, may
therefore result in future prevalence studies.
Signalment
Acute hepatitis, like CH, typically affects middle‐aged to
older dogs, and females appear to be predisposed. In a
study of 21 dogs diagnosed with AH, the mean age of

VetBooks.ir

64 Canine Inflammatory Liver Disease

affected dogs was 7.8 +/− 4.1 years, with a range of 2.4–
14.5 years. No comprehensive study has been performed
to determine the breed predispositions to AH, although
in this same study, Jack Russell terriers may have been at
increased risk.
History and Clinical Signs
Clinical signs in dogs with AH are usually nonspecific and
similar to those described for CH. Interestingly, in one
study of dogs with AH, clinical signs had been present for
10.0 weeks (range, 0.5–52 weeks) before diagnosis. Again,
the clinician should pay particular attention to subtle waxing and waning GI signs, depression, lethargy, anorexia,
weight loss, and polyuria and polydipsia. Clinical signs of
HE may also occur in the patient with AH. Physical examination findings are generally unremarkable, although the
liver is occasionally palpably enlarged in the dog with AH.
Dogs with an infectious etiology may also be pyrexic and
show other signs of systemic disease.
Diagnosis
As discussed earlier, clinical pathology is usually the
next step in the investigation of a dog with suspected
AH. Clinical pathology findings include elevations of
liver enzymes, including ALT, AST, ALP, and GGT. In
one study, there was no significant difference in any routine biochemical or hematologic variable between dogs
with AH and CH. However, if liver function is assessed,
it is more likely to be within the reference range in dogs
with AH.
Diagnostic imaging is often performed after clinical
pathology in the assessment of the dog with suspected
AH. Abdominal radiography can be used to assess liver
size, although as detailed earlier, ultrasonography is
the preferred imaging modality for the investigation of
liver disease. In one study of 21 dogs with a histologic
diagnosis of AH, all apart from two had abnormalities
detected on ultrasonographic examination of the liver.
Hepatic size was assessed as normal in seven
dogs, enlarged in eight, and small in six. The hepatic

parenchyma was found to be normal in seven dogs,
irregular in 11, and to have increased echogenicity in
three. Interestingly, three dogs with AH had evidence of
ascites on ultrasonographic examination.
It is not possible to make a definitive diagnosis of AH
based on results of clinical pathology or diagnostic
imaging. Definitive diagnosis ultimately relies on histologic examination of liver tissue. However, as animals
with AH may be systemically unwell, liver biopsy is
often not performed in the acute setting, with patient
treatment based on a tentative diagnosis. Fine needle
aspiration cytology is not reliable for the diagnosis of
AH, and is not recommended.
Therapy
Therapy for AH is aimed at the underlying cause, if
known. However, as the etiology of most cases is currently not understood, treatment is generally symptomatic and supportive. In one retrospective study, dogs
with AH were treated with antibiotics (5/16), hepatic
support diet and ursodeoxycholic acid (7/16), and 5/16
dogs were not treated. Due to the potential for an underlying infectious cause, corticosteroids are usually avoided
in dogs with AH . The use of antiviral drugs in dogs with
CAV‐1 infection has not been studied. Fluid therapy is
required if the dog is anorexic, and short‐term nutritional support by methods of assisted enteral nutrition is
sometimes also required.
Prognosis
The prognosis for AH is variable, and likely dependent
on multiple factors, such as the etiology, severity of disease, and how early treatment is instigated. In a previous
study, the median survival time of dogs with AH was 34.9
months. It is also possible that AH progresses to CH in
some dogs. For instance, in a study of 12 dogs with AH
that had a repeat liver biopsy performed after approximately six weeks, histopathology revealed complete
remission of inflammatory and degenerative changes in
six dogs, no changes in one dog, and progression from
AH to CH in five dogs.

Cirrhosis and its Consequences
Katherine Scott, DVM, DACVIM (SAIM)
VCA Alameda East, 9770 East Alameda Ave, Denver, CO, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Cirrhosis
Development of hepatic fibrosis and subsequent cirrho­
sis is a common complication of chronic hepatitis (CH).
Cirrhosis is defined histologically by the presence of dif­
fuse bridging fibrosis and regenerative hepatic nodules.
CH can be caused by a variety of different initial insults
that include toxins or drugs, breed‐associated metabolic
errors, including disorders of copper metabolism, and
infections, although the majority of cases are idiopathic.
Regardless of the underlying cause, fibrosis may develop
when CH is severe and/or is present for an extended
period of time.
Fibrosis develops when hepatic myofibroblast‐like cells
become activated secondary to hepatic injury. These cells
produce factors including transforming growth factor‐
beta (TGF‐beta), which upregulate hepatic extracellular
matrix components such as collagen and glycoaminogly­
cans. TGF‐beta also upregulates inhibitors of metallopro­
teinases, resulting in decreased extracellular matrix
breakdown. In CH, these changes result in progressive
accumulation of extracellular matrix in the liver. Cirrhosis
develops with the diffuse accumulation of fibrous tissue
in the liver, resulting in conversion of normal hepatic
architecture into structurally abnormal hepatic nodules
(Figure 65.1). With the development of cirrhosis, a variety
of adverse consequences develop, and these are predomi­
nantly related to the development of portal hypertension
and progression of hepatic dysfunction.
Portal Hypertension
Portal hypertension (PH) is an increase in blood pres­
sure within the portal vasculature, the vessels responsi­
ble for providing venous drainage to the intestines and
spleen. The hypertension can be caused by any disease

that results in obstruction of venous return of portal
blood. PH can be classified according to location of the
increase in blood pressure, including prehepatic, intra­
hepatic, or posthepatic causes. The type of portal hyper­
tension caused by cirrhosis is an intrahepatic form of PH,
as opposed to prehepatic PH that occurs in disorders of
the portal vein itself, or posthepatic PH that occurs with
right‐sided heart failure or caudal vena cava disorders.
With cirrhosis, hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cells have
lost normal fenestrae and acquired a collagenous base­
ment membrane in their place. This change, as well as
other remodeling changes in the liver such as regenera­
tive nodules and microthrombi, results in distortion of
sinusoids and increases intrahepatic venous resistance,
with resultant PH.
Ascites

Once PH is present, ascites may also develop as, accord­
ing to Starling’s law, the increased venous resistance and
increase in portal venous hydrostatic pressure drive fluid
out of the vasculature and into the interstitial space.
Lymphatic drainage of the interstitial space may be able
to deal with this extra fluid for some time, but when the
regional lymphatics become overwhelmed and unable to
control this increase in interstitial fluid, ascites will
develop.
Additionally, ascites may develop as a result of hypoal­
buminemia secondary to severe liver disease. Albumin is
a plasma protein normally produced by the liver, and
significant hepatic dysfunction may result in a clinically
important decrease in albumin concentration. Albumin
is the most important blood protein responsible for
maintenance of normal plasma colloid oncotic pressure.
If serum albumin levels decrease to less than approxi­
mately 1.6 g/dL, plasma colloid oncotic pressure will
become too low to maintain intravascular volume and
fluid will enter the interstitial space. Animals with cir­
rhosis will often develop both portal hypertension and

Acquired Portosystemic Shunts

Portosystemic shunts are anomalous venous vessels
that join the portal blood with the systemic vasculature,
while bypassing the liver. They can be congenital in ori­
gin or acquired secondary to cirrhosis/fibrosis or other
causes of PH. If PH develops and does not resolve
quickly, the development of multiple acquired porto­
systemic shunts (aPSS) may occur. Acquired shunts
are thought to develop in an attempt to decrease PH.
Experimentally, it takes 5–14 weeks of PH before
acquired shunts develop. This continued increase in
hepatic venous portal pressure results in the opening of
embryonic vessels that arise between the portal vascu­
lature and the cranial and caudal vena cava, resulting in
the formation of multiple aPSS. These shunts vary in
anatomic location, but are most commonly visualized
as a plexus of small vessels found caudodorsal to the left
kidney. They connect the portal vasculature with the
vena cava, allowing for venous blood to bypass the liver.
This blood remains unfiltered and enters the systemic
circulation.
Hepatic Encephalopathy

One of the most important consequences in the develop­
ment of aPSS is hepatic encephalopathy (HE). In the
­presence of aPSS, toxins normally filtered by the liver are
transported from the gastrointestinal (GI) tract to the
rest of the systemic circulation, including the central
nervous system (CNS). While many toxins are involved
in this process, ammonia is thought to be one of the most

Gastrointestinal ulceration is another possible complica­
tion of severe hepatic disease or cirrhosis. In humans, GI
ulceration is thought to be related to impaired gastric
mucosal defense secondary to alterations in GI motility
and circulation, and bile acid secretion. While this con­
dition has been described in people, the etiology has not
been evaluated in dogs and cats. Portal hypertension also
likely contributes to the development of GI ulceration.
Regardless of cause, GI ulceration is a recognized com­
plication of liver disease in animals. If GI bleeding occurs
as a result of ulceration, this can acutely increase the risk
of HE. Blood is a highly ammoniagenic protein, and may
result in a rapid increase of serum ammonia levels when
absorbed following the digestion of blood. This rapid
increase in ammonia may cause a sudden onset of signs
related to HE.
Coagulation Disturbances
The liver is responsible for the production of coagulation
factors, recycling and activation of vitamin K‐dependent
factors and protein C, production of thrombopoietin,
and removal of clotting factors from the circulation. In a
liver which is severely diseased from cirrhosis, coagula­
tion abnormalities are likely to be present to some degree.
Studies have shown that anywhere from 57–93% of dogs,
and 82–98% of cats with liver disease have at least one
alteration in coagulation parameters. Decreased factor
production appears to play the most significant role in
secondary hemostatic abnormalities, but consumption
of factors due to disseminated intravascular coagulation
(DIC) may also occur.
Thrombocytopenia may also occur secondary to liver
disease in dogs, but is uncommon in cats. Thrombo­
cytopenia is usually mild, and may occur secondary
to decreased thrombopoietin production by the liver,
increased sequestration in the spleen as a result of splenic
congestion secondary to liver disease, increased con­
sumption from low‐grade DIC, and increased destruc­
tion due to autoantibodies.

­Signalment
Signalment of an animal with cirrhosis largely depends on
the underlying cause of liver disease, but cirrhosis is much
more common in dogs than in cats. This may be due to a
slower accumulation of fibrosis in cats, or development of
more severe complications of hepatic failure before
advanced fibrosis occurs. Males and females are likely to be
equally affected, and dogs with breed‐related risk of CH
are more likely to be affected. For further details of dog
breed predilections to CH, the reader if referred to
Chapter 62. Dogs with ­idiopathic CH and copper‐associ­
ated CH are often middle‐aged to older, while dogs with
lobar‐dissecting h
­ epatitis are usually young, around 2 years
of age. Dogs or cats with a history of hepatotoxicity sec­
ondary to environmental toxins or drugs may be of any age.

­History and Clinical Signs
The presenting clinical signs in chronic liver disease are
often vague in nature, and include a history of inappe­
tence, lethargy, vomiting, polyuria/polydipsia, weight loss,
and/or diarrhea. Melena may be observed if GI ulceration
is present. Ascites and icterus are more specific clinical
signs that may be noted. Neurologic abnormalities such as
depressed mentation, circling, ptyalism in cats, star‐gaz­
ing, seizures, stupor or coma may also occur secondary to
HE. These neurologic changes may be intermittent in
nature, and frequently occur shortly following ingestion of
a meal containing protein. Signs have usually been present
for weeks to months, and are often progressive in nature.
Physical examination findings are also often nonspe­
cific, and may only include weight loss or muscle wast­
ing. If ascites is present, abdominal distension and a
palpable fluid wave may be apparent. Splenomegaly may
also occur in the presence of PH and pooling of blood in
the spleen. Icterus may be visualized on the skin, sclera,
or mucous membranes as a result of accumulation of
bilirubin. Less commonly, petechiae or ecchymosis may
be observed on the skin or mucous membranes second­
ary to thrombocytopenia or thrombocytopathy. Melena
may be observed on rectal examination. If HE is present,
neurologic examination abnormalities localizing to the
forebrain may be present.

­Diagnosis
Laboratory Testing
The most common laboratory abnormalities in patients
with cirrhosis are alterations of liver‐related enzymes.
Patients with cirrhosis will often have a known history of

elevated liver enzymes, including alanine aminotrans­
ferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alkaline
phosphatase (ALP), and gamma-glutamyl transpepti­
dase (GGT). However, in occasional cases of severe
hepatocellular loss, liver enzymes may be within normal
limits simply due to the low number of remaining hepat­
ocytes. Liver pseudofunction tests may also be abnor­
mal, and suggest some degree of liver dysfunction. It is
estimated that a reduction of approximately 70–80% of
overall hepatic function must be present before these
alterations occur. Pseudofunction tests include decreased
albumin, BUN, cholesterol, and/or glucose, and an
increase in ­bilirubin. All of these pseudofunction com­
pounds are produced or metabolized normally by the
liver, and will be altered in states of liver dysfunction.
On a complete blood count, microcytosis may be noted
in patients with acquired or congenital PSS, secondary to
a deficiency in mobilization of iron stores. Anemia may
occur from GI ulceration and blood loss or bleeding sec­
ondary to coagulopathy. Mild thrombocytopenia may be
present due to decrease in hepatic synthesis of throm­
bopoietin. Leukocytosis is nonspecific, but may occur
secondary to stress, inflammation, or infection.
Urinalysis is often normal in patients with cirrhosis,
but may demonstrate dilute urine as a result of decreased
BUN concentration. Urea is a major component of the
renal medullary concentration gradient, and, when
decreased, may lead to the development of dilute urine.
Bilirubinuria may be observed, and is always significant
in the cat, and if 2+ or greater is also significant in the
dog. Urate crystals may be observed in as many as
40–70% of dogs with canine PSS, and secondary urinary
tract infections are possible as a result of dilute urine.
Coagulation testing should be undertaken if hepatic
biopsy is to be performed, or if any clinical signs of
­bleeding are observed. Prothrombin time (PT) and partial
thromboplastin time (PTT) may be increased, and anti­
thrombin, fibrinogen, and protein C levels are decreased
in dogs and cats with cirrhosis due to poor production of
coagulation factors and/or decreased recycling of vitamin
K. Vitamin K deficiency may be especially important in
cats with severe liver disease. Evaluation of platelet func­
tion testing via buccal mucosal bleeding time may also be
abnormal secondary to a thrombocytopathy.
Hepatic function testing can be performed by measur­
ing pre‐ and postprandial bile acid concentrations or
blood ammonia levels. Both tests may be elevated in the
face of significant liver dysfunction or aPSS secondary
to cirrhosis. Postprandial bile acids are considered to
be more sensitive for detection of PSS but elevated
ammonia may be more specific. Additionally, ammonia
is ­currently the only measureable HE toxin, so the find­
ing of hyperammonemia may also suggest a higher risk
of clinical signs related to HE. However, ammonia sam­

ples are labile, and must be placed on ice and analyzed

For further details of laboratory testing in patients
with liver disease, the reader is referred to Chapter 60.
Imaging
Imaging modalities most commonly utilized for further
evaluation of cirrhosis and its complications include
abdominal radiographs and abdominal ultrasound.
Abdominal radiographs are the most commonly avail­
able imaging modality, but are relatively nonspecific for
hepatic disease. Cirrhosis may result in microhepatica,
which can be visualized on abdominal radiographs.
However, this is a change that may be seen in other
hepatic diseases such as congenital PSS. Ascites sec­
ondary to PH or hypoalbuminemia may be visible radi­
ographically as loss of abdominal serosal detail.
Abdominal ultrasound is a very useful noninvasive
imaging modality that can be utilized to further diagnose
liver disease and its complications (Figure 65.2).
Ultrasound can evaluate hepatic parenchymal echo­
genicity and uniformity, overall hepatic size, biliary
structures, hepatic and portal vessels, and identify very
small volumes of ascites that might not be visible radio­
graphically. It can also be utilized to identify multiple
aPSS­. Ultrasound is also useful in guiding safe ­collection
of samples of ascites or bile for fluid analysis, or ultra­
sound‐guided “Tru‐Cut” biopsies.
Unfortunately, while ultrasound is a very useful nonin­
vasive test, it does not identify changes pathognomonic
for a specific liver disease, and should never be used to

rule out the possibility of liver disease. Many dogs and
possibly cats without sonographic abnormalities may still
have important liver abnormalities on histopathology.
Ultrasound is also not a reliable method to diagnose
­cirrhosis. In a study evaluating ultrasound findings with
histopathologic diagnoses, there were no sonographic
features significantly associated with cirrhosis, and it was
concluded that ultrasound could not reliably be used to
detect the presence, absence, or severity of fibrosis. In
fact some animals with cirrhosis had ultrasonographi­
cally normal appearing livers. But sonographic findings
may still be useful in suggesting the possibility of cirrhosis
and its consequences. Findings that would be most sug­
gestive of cirrhosis and subsequent PH include identifica­
tion of multiple aPSS, a small liver with irregular margins,
presence of ascites, and a hyperechoic echotexture. But
ultimately, biopsy and histopathology are required to
obtain a definitive diagnosis of cirrhosis.
Other imaging modalities may also be useful in diag­
nosing the cause or complications of cirrhosis. Computed
tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI) may provide a more complete evaluation of hepatic
vasculature than abdominal ultrasound. When utilized
with contrast, CT and MRI may also provide further eval­
uation regarding location of neoplasia and possible
metastasis. Rectal or transsplenic nuclear scintigraphy
can be useful in the diagnosis of PSS, when ultrasound is
inconclusive, although scintigraphy may not be able to
distinguish congenital versus aPSS. Further details of
diagnostic imaging in the investigation of cirrhosis and its
complications can be found in Chapter 61.
Cytology and Fluid Analysis
Fine needle aspiration cytology is an inadequate method
to diagnose cirrhosis. While cytology may help identify
the underlying cause of cirrhosis, it cannot confirm the
presence or absence of fibrous tissue
Cytology of ascitic fluid may be utilized when attempt­
ing to identify whether the ascites is caused by PH, infec­
tious disease, or neoplastic disease. Typically, ascites
secondary to PH is a modified transudate (also refereed to
as a protein-rich transudate), or possibly a pure transu­
date. PH ascites is nonneoplastic, and noninflammatory
in origin. Cytology and culture of bile may also be impor­
tant in diagnosing the underlying cause of cirrhosis. Biliary
cultures have been shown to yield a ­significantly higher
rate of positive growth than hepatic tissue cultures.
Histopathology

Figure 65.2 Ultrasonographic image of a cirrhotic liver. Note the
presence of large‐volume ascites, a small liver with irregular
hepatic margination, and mottled echogenicity.

The gold standard diagnosis of cirrhosis is liver biopsy
with histopathology that identifies the presence and
extent of fibrosis. Not only is it important to document

VetBooks.ir

65 Cirrhosis and its Consequences

the presence and severity of cirrhosis, but it is crucial
to attempt to identify the underlying disease that has
resulted in the development of fibrosis/cirrhosis. This
will allow for specific treatment to be directed at the
underlying cause.
Due to the risk of coagulopathy in dogs with hepatic
­disease, coagulation testing including PT, PTT, platelet
count, and possibly buccal mucosal bleeding time (BMBT)
should always be performed prior to liver biopsy.
Interestingly, results of these parameters do not consist­
ently predict risk of bleeding after liver biopsy in human
patients with chronic liver disease. Fibrinogen concentra­
tion should also be evaluated if possible, as it may be
decreased in cirrhosis. In humans, thromboelastography
(TEG) analysis can predict bleeding tendencies in cir­
rhotic patients, but the value of TEG in predicting bleed­
ing in our canine and feline patients with liver disease is
unknown. In cases of hypofibrinogenemia or other coagu­
lopathy, transfusion with cryoprecipitate or fresh frozen
plasma should be performed prior to biopsy. Vitamin K1
therapy (1–1.5 mg/kg q12–24h for three doses) prior to
biopsy may also be necessary, e­ specially in cats.Assessment
of coagulation status should, however, not be a substitute
for proper technique and adequate post-operative care.
Biopsy may be obtained through ultrasound‐guided
“Tru‐Cut” needles, laparoscopically, or via exploratory
laparotomy. Each method has practical advantages and
disadvantages when it comes to cost, time involved,
invasiveness, and availability. But collection of a wedge
biopsy via laparoscopy or exploratory laparotomy is
­generally considered to be a superior method of sample
collection. It has been shown that morphologic diagnosis
of needle biopsy specimens and wedge biopsies (consid­
ered the gold standard) only agreed in 40% of animals
with liver disease. If the “Tru‐Cut” biopsy method is
­utilized, two or more samples should be collected to
minimize sampling error. Further details on the methods
to collect liver tissue can be found in Chapter 60.

­Treatment
Cirrhosis is considered irreversible. Therefore, the
most important aspect of treatment is addressing the
underlying cause of liver disease as early as possible to
prevent further development of fibrosis/cirrhosis, and
to minimize the risk of cirrhosis‐associated complica­
tions. Corticosteroids have been shown to have positive
long‐term effects in the treatment of idiopathic chronic
­hepatitis, and may have minor antifibrotic properties
(see Chapter 62). Copper‐chelating medications such
as D‐penicillamine or trientine should be utilized in
cases where primary copper‐associated chronic hepati­
tis is diagnosed. In cases of previous toxic hepatopathy

or idiopathic disease, specific treatment may not be
possible. In all cases of cirrhosis, treatment must also
include management of any important complications of
cirrhosis.
Colchicine (0.03 mg/kg/day) is the only specific drug in
veterinary medicine currently used to stop the formation
of fibrosis. It is thought to stimulate collagenase activity,
increasing the breakdown and decreasing the formation
of collagen. Colchicine is reported to have important and
common side‐effects, including vomiting, diarrhea, and
neurologic signs. Additionally, there are no large studies
that have shown positive benefit from this medication, it
has not been evaluated in cats, and it is currently cost‐
prohibitive for many pet owners. As a result of these
problems, most clinicians do not currently recommend
its use, even in documented cases of hepatic cirrhosis.
Glucocorticoids may be beneficial in some cases of
cirrhosis. Steroids interact with TGF‐beta signaling
pathways and may reduce fibrotic progression, although
this effect may be relatively weak. More importantly,
prednisone/prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day) may be useful
in inhibiting hepatic inflammation, if present. This
decrease in inflammation will result in decreased activ­
ity of hepatic stellate cells, responsible for formation of
further fibrosis. Glucocorticoids may be most benefi­
cial for treatment of dogs and cats with active hepatic
inflammation that have not yet developed fibrosis/cir­
rhosis. Evidence supporting use of glucocorticoids in
the absence of hepatic inflammation is lacking, so their
use may or may not provide additional benefit in treat­
ment of cirrhosis alone. Moreover, the adverse effects
of steroids in animals with advanced fibrosis can be
very significant. Due to their ability to cause gastric
ulceration, they should be used with extreme caution in
animals with , as these animals already have a compro­
mised GI tract blood flow. Steroids cause muscle break­
down so may also potentiate HE.Further details on the
use of corticosteroids in dogs with chronic liver disease
can be found in Chapter 62.
Losartan is another medication that shows promise for
fibrosis/cirrhosis but has not yet been evaluated for this
purpose in small animals. Losartan is an angiotensin II
receptor antagonist that has been shown in rodent mod­
els to inhibit hepatic stellate cell activation and attenuate
hepatic fibrosis. It is currently utilized in veterinary
medicine for its effects on proteinuria. No studies have
shown if losartan may be an effective therapy in prevent­
ing fibrosis development in dogs or cats.
Ascites
Ascites may spontaneously improve with specific
treatment of the underlying liver disease. Reducing
hepatic inflammation, when present, may decrease PH

709

VetBooks.ir

710

Section 7 Diseases of the Liver, Gallbladder, and Bile Ducts

and therefore decrease the volume of ascites. If this
is ineffective, treatment with diuretics is indicated.
Spironolactone is the drug of choice in these cases due
to its sodium‐wasting but potassium‐sparing effects,
with a starting dose of 1–2 mg/kg/day. Aldactazide, a
combination of spironolactone and hydrochlorothi­
azide, may also be administered. Low‐dose furosemide
(1-2 mg/kg PO q12h) can also be utilized, but carries a
risk of worsening HE due to its acidifying effects.
Therefore, it should only be added to therapy when
other diuretics fail to fully control the ascites. Dietary
sodium restriction may also be beneficial to help
decrease volume of ascites. Diets with <0.05 g/100 kcal
of sodium have been recommended. It is important to
monitor electrolytes and renal values while on these
medications, and taper to lowest effective dose to con­
trol clinical signs of ascites.
Abdominocentesis may be performed when necessary
for severe abdominal distension resulting in patient
­discomfort or respiratory difficulties. Removing large
volumes of ascites may result in cardiovascular collapse
and poor perfusion, in addition to lowering body protein
levels, so it is recommended to only remove 20–50% of
the total volume of effusion in one procedure.
Hepatic Encephalopathy
In treating HE, efforts are classically focused on lowering
the amount of encephalopathic toxins in the colon. This
can be performed by both dietary changes and adminis­
tration of lactulose and/or antibiotic therapy. Because
ammonia is derived from protein sources, historically a
protein-restricted diet with reduction in aromatic amino
acids has been recommended in dogs with HE secondary
to cirrhosis. However, protein restriction is controversial,
and evidence from human medicine actually suggests
that patients with cirrhosis require additional, not
reduced, amounts of protein. What is probably more
important is to ensure that the protein content of the diet
is highly digestible and is fed little and often. Dairy and
soy proteins have been found to promote less HE com­
pared to meat protein. Commercial hepatic diets are
available for dogs, although in some dogs the protein level
may be too low, and muscle catabolism may occur. In
these dogs, supplementation with highly digestible, high‐
quality protein in limited amounts may be necessary.
Lactulose is a nonabsorbable disaccharide that acidi­
fies the colonic lumen, converting ammonia (NH3) into
ammonium (NH4+). The positively charged ammonium
is membrane impermeable, compared to the neutral
charge of ammonia. Lactulose is also a cathartic, decreas­
ing GI transit time for production and absorption of
ammonia. Lactulose dosing starts at 0.25 mL/kg PO

q8–12h, with adjustments in dose as needed to achieve a
goal of 2–3 soft, but formed stools daily.
Antibiotics have also been used for HE in an effort to
decrease the volume of colonic urease‐producing bacteria
responsible for production of ammonia. The two most
commonly utilized antibiotics are neomycin (22 mg/kg
q8h) and metronidazole (7.5 mg/kg q12h). Neomycin is an
oral aminoglycoside. Aminoglycosides are very poorly
absorbed by the GI tract, so it is thought that the effects
will usually remain within the GI tract. However, neomycin
carries a risk of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, even when
given orally, so acute kidney injury can occur. Metronidazole
may result in vomiting, diarrhea, or neurotoxicity, espe­
cially when administered at high doses or chronically.
Alternatively, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid can be used at
standard doses to decrease in the patient with HE.
Emerging evidence also suggests that inflammatory
cytokines are synergistic with ammonia in precipitating
HE. Treating concurrent inflammatory and infectious
disease in other organs is therefore an important part of
managing the patient with HE.
Emergency treatment of HE is warranted if a patient
presents with seizures or coma, or otherwise is severely
neurologic and unable to safely receive oral medica­
tions. A warm water cleansing enema (10–15 mL/kg
water) should be given to remove fecal material and
allow for a retention enema with lactulose. Lactulose
(5–10 mL/kg) should then be infused at a 30% dilution
and allowed to remain in the colon for 10–15 minutes.
Flumazenil is an antagonist for benzodiazepine recep­
tors and is used as a reversal agent for benzodiazepines.
Because HE may cause stimulation of GABA/benzodi­
azepine receptors, flumazenil (0.01–0.02 mg/kg IV)
may also provide acute improvement in neurologic
depression in cases of HE.
If seizures are present, diazepam or other benzodiaze­
pine medications should not be administered as these
may increase the stimulation of GABA/benzodiazepine
receptors and risk worsening neurologic depression.
Instead, levetiracetam (20 mg/kg) may be given IV for
acute seizure control. Phenobarbital may also be utilized.
If prolonged seizure activity has been present or there
are clinical signs of cerebral edema, mannitol infusion
may also be necessary.

Gastrointestinal Ulceration
Gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding can increase
the risk of HE due to digestion of blood proteins and
absorption of ammonia. Therefore, aggressive treatment
is warranted in cases of GI ulceration. Proton pump
inhibitors such as omeprazole (1 mg/kg q12–24h) have

VetBooks.ir

65 Cirrhosis and its Consequences

been proven to have superior acid‐blocking effects com­
pared to H2 blockers in dogs and should be utilized in
these cases. Sucralfate may also be of benefit in rapid
healing and prevention of continued bleeding.
Coagulation Disturbances
Disturbances in coagulation will usually only need to be
treated in the face of active bleeding, or if a biopsy is to
be pursued. Vitamin K1 therapy may also be beneficial
either for acute hemorrhage or prior to biopsy, especially
in cats. For active bleeding, cryoprecipitate (1 unit/10 kg)
should be administered for hypofibrinogenemia, as it
provides the most concentrated source of fibrinogen.
Fresh‐­frozen plasma (10–20 mL/kg) may also be utilized
for fibrinogen and other factor replacement.
Hepatoprotectants
The evidence regarding hepatoprotectant therapy in vet­
erinary medicine is generally lacking. It is unclear when
and which hepatoprotectant might be most beneficial for
specific hepatic diseases in dogs and cats. Therefore, it is
difficult to make recommendations regarding their use in
animals with cirrhosis. However, the use of ursodeoxy­
cholic acid, S‐adenosyl‐L‐methionine (SAM‐e), silymarin,
N‐acteylcysteine, and vitamin E have all been anecdotally
or experimentally recommended as potentially beneficial
in the treatment of severe liver disease.
One of the more promising hepatoprotectant medica­
tions is ursodeoxycholic acid (ursodiol, UDCA). Ursode­
oxycholic acid is a synthetic hydrophilic bile acid that is
thought to provide a cholerhetic effect, decreasing l­evels
of more “toxic” hydrophobic bile acids. It is also thought
to have immunomodulatory and antioxidant effects. It has
been advocated for use in CH and gallbladder mucoceles.
Its utility in the treatment of cirrhosis is unknown.
S‐adenosyl‐L‐methionine has also been advocated for
use in cases of hepatic disease. It is thought to increase
available levels of glutathione, an important antioxidant
of the liver, by increasing levels of the glutathione pre­
cursor methionine. Glutathione production may become
inadequate in cases of chronic inflammation and con­
tinuous oxidative stress. SAM‐e was reported to be
effective in veterinary medicine in a case of acetami­
nophen toxicity, and may provide protection against
steroid hepatopathy. It is unknown if it provides benefit
in cases of cirrhosis.
Silymarin, silybinin, or milk thistle, is another antioxi­
dant and free radical scavenger that increases levels of

superoxide dismutase (SOD). It has proven efficacy in
veterinary medicine against hepatic toxicity from
Amanita mushroom and acetaminophen toxicity. It was
also shown to decrease CCNU‐induced hepatotoxicity
when used in combination with SAM‐e. Again, its use
for treatment of cirrhosis has not been evaluated.Further
details on the use of hepatoprotectants in dogs with
chronic liver disease can be found in Chapter 62.

­Monitoring
The frequency of monitoring depends on the severity of
illness and the underlying disease. Rechecking electro­
lytes and renal parameters is of the utmost importance
when utilizing and adjusting doses of diuretic therapy.
Liver enzymes, most importantly ALT, should be evalu­
ated every 2–4 weeks in animals being treated with glu­
cocorticoids for inflammatory liver disease. If HE is
present, monitoring fasting ammonia levels may provide
useful information regarding response to HE treatment.

­Prognosis
Prognosis for cirrhosis is generally guarded, as cirrhosis is
an irreversible condition. Prognosis may also vary widely
based on whether or not the underlying hepatic disease is
treatable, and the severity of cirrhotic complications such
as HE and PH. One study evaluated dogs diagnosed with
CH with and without cirrhosis, and found that noncir­
rhotic dogs with CH had a median survival time (MST) of
33 months, compared to cirrhotic dogs MST of only 1.3
months. Ascites has been reported to be a negative prog­
nostic indicator in dogs with CH, with survival time from
onset of clinical signs to death of only two months, when
compared to dogs with CH and no ascites.

­Conclusion
Cirrhosis is a severe, irreversible condition that occurs as
a consequence of underlying liver disease. It often leads
to additional complications including portal hyperten­
sion, ascites, multiple aPSS , HE, gastric ulcers, and coag­
ulopathy. Early recognition and diagnosis of liver disease
followed by specific treatment are always warranted to
prevent the development of cirrhosis. Once cirrhosis and
its complications are present, supportive care is the only
treatment option and prognosis is guarded to poor.

Portosystemic Shunts and Microvascular Dysplasia
Geraldine Hunt, BVSc, MVetClinStud, PhD, FACVSc
School of Veterinary Medicine, University of California Davis, Davis, CA, USA

­Etiology
Portosystemic shunting refers to a condition where
blood bypasses the liver and travels from the hepatic
portal circulation to the systemic circulation through
one or more connections that can occur at a microvascular or macrovascular level.
Congenital portosystemic shunts (CPSS) occur as a
result of an error in embryonic development where
­primordial vessels either develop abnormal connections
or fail to undergo atresia. This has been shown to have a
genetic basis in some breeds, including the Maltese, Irish
wolfhound, and Cairn terrier. Inheritance, as assessed by
pedigree analysis and test‐mating, appears to be c­ omplex –
either digenic or polygenic with variable expression.
Rarely, intrahepatic shunts may result from failure of
the ductus venosus to close. This is most commonly
reported in Irish wolfhounds (considered to be digenic in
this breed). Left‐divisional shunts may be encountered in
any breed, but it is unclear how often these represent
failure of the ductus venosus to close, versus other vascular malformations.
Acquired shunts develop as a result of increased
­vascular resistance within the portal system, the hepatic
sinusoids or the hepatic veins (in the face of normal
­central venous pressure). The most common cause is
hepatic fibrosis/cirrhosis, although other conditions
such as portal vein thrombosis, periportal neoplasia,
hepatic arteriovenous fistula, and dynamic hepatic
­vascular occlusion are sometimes encountered.
Microvascular dysplasia (MVD, which has more recently
been termed portal vein hypoplasia (PVH) without portal
hypertension, refers to abnormal development or absence
of the portal microvasculature within the liver. As different
authors use different terminology, this spectrum of conditions will be referred to henceforth as PVH‐MVD. PVH‐
MVD may occur with or without CPSS. Dogs and cats

with primary PVH‐MVD (but no CPSS) may develop
acquired shunts within the first few years of life due to
chronic portal hypertension, in which case they fall into a
category termed “noncirrhotic portal hypertension.”
Classification and Anatomy
Portosystemic shunts are classified according to three
criteria:
congenital versus acquired
single versus multiple
●● macroscopic versus microscopic.
●●
●●

Congential portosystemic shunts are further classified
according to their point of origin as either extrahepatic
(originating from the hepatic portal vein or one of its
source vessels) or intrahepatic (originating from one of the
hepatic branches of the portal vein). Extrahepatic shunts
are described by their origin and insertion (e.g., portocaval,
splenoazygous). A subset of extrahepatic shunts that insert
into the phrenic or hepatic vein has recently been characterized in various countries. Intrahepatic shunts are typically described according to the division of the portal vein
from which they arise (left, central, and right‐divisional).
A subset of dogs with CPSS have portal aplasia and no
demonstrable portal circulation to their liver. In these
cases, the shunt represents the only outlet from the portal circulation, inserting directly into the systemic venous
circulation. Unfortunately, there is no surgical option for
these patients. This anatomic variant may be associated
with other malformations such as interruption of the
caudal vena cava with azygous continuation, abdominal
situs inversus, and segmentation of the spleen.
Acquired shunts are usually multiple and generally
extrahepatic. Multiple intrahepatic shunts have been
identified in patients following thrombogenic coil occlusion of intrahepatic shunts but it is not yet known

Neurologic perturbations caused by the liver dysfunction resulting from portosystemic shunting leading to
neurologic abnormalities are termed hepatic encephalopathy (HE) (see description later).
It is becoming increasingly recognized that infection
and inflammation also play a role in development of
encephalopathy in laboratory animals and humans.
Circulating blood levels of C‐reactive protein (a marker
of inflammation) have relatively recently been shown to
be elevated in dogs with HE, suggesting that this is also
likely to be an important mechanism in dogs. HE may be
complicated by hypoglycemia in patients that are inappetent or being fasted, as a result of low hepatic glycogen
reserves in the hypoplastic or damaged liver.
Circulating levels of these substances will fluctuate

other factors affecting gastrointestinal transit time, bacterial flora or the production of ammonia within the gut.
Gastrointestinal hemorrhage is a known risk factor for

ulceration (see later).

Polyuria and polydipsia are common in patients with
portosystemic shunts. The mechanism is not completely
understood but is probably multifactorial. Contributing
factors include low plasma BUN and poor renal concentrating ability, and increased thirst resulting from systemic inflammation and fever.

­Pathophysiology
Dogs and cats with portosystemic shunting usually have
low functional hepatic mass. The liver either fails to grow
normally as it is deprived of its normal blood supply,
trophic factors (such as insulin and hepatic growth factor) and nutrients, or liver function is impaired as a result
of a primary hepatopathy (in cases with acquired portosystemic shunts).
The major clinical signs associated with portosystemic shunting result from failure of the liver to metabolize substances being absorbed from the
gastrointestinal tract, receive pancreatic hormones,
and metabolize other circulating hormones. There is
deranged nitrogen metabolism and the capacity of the
liver to produce urea is diminished, leading to elevated
levels of circulating ammonia and low blood urea
nitrogen (BUN) levels. Serum bile acids, which normally undergo almost complete enterohepatic circulation, are also elevated in systemic samples. Abnormal
filtering or metabolism of a variety of other substances
absorbed into the portal venous blood (branched chain
and aromatic amino acids, bacteria and bacterial tox-

has been observed in some patients with CPSS, but is far
more likely to be seen in patients with acquired portosystemic shunts resulting from end‐stage hepatopathy of

Pathophysiology of Portal Hypertension
Portal hypertension (leading to acquired portosystemic
shunts) is by definition an increase in portal venous
pressure above the expected normal of 8–12 mmHg
(note that patients with CPSS will usually have portal
pressures comparable or slightly higher than central
venous pressure (typically 4–8 mmHg). Portal hypertension occurs when the resistance to vascular flow
within the hepatic portal vein or sinusoids increases,
causing sequestration of blood within the viscera.
Reduction in the arterial to venous pressure gradient
across the capillary beds of the gut causes reduced
blood flow and hence reduced oxygen delivery to tissues. Alteration of hydrostatic pressure, often accompanied by reduced plasma oncotic pressure resulting
from the patient’s underlying liver disease, allows fluid
to leak from the capillaries into both the intestinal
lumen and the peritoneal cavity, resulting in ascites and
diarrhea. In acute, severe portal hypertension, frank
blood may leak into the lumen of the bowel, resulting in
hematemesis and hematochezia. Edema and swelling of
the intraabdominal organs causes stretching of the capsules and peritoneum, and hence this condition can be
quite painful.
Reduction in blood flow through the hepatic sinusoids
results in lower venous return to the right atrium, with a
resultant fall in cardiac output and the compensatory
changes of tachycardia and reduced stroke volume.
Hypovolemic shock will eventuate if the compensatory
mechanisms are not sufficient to assure adequate tissue
oxygen delivery, or if ongoing fluid losses into the bowel
and peritoneal cavity cannot be replaced.
In patients that are able to compensate for mild to
moderate portal hypertension, small veno‐venous
communications open within a few days. These take
the path of least resistance from the portal circulation
into a nearby branch of the systemic venous system,
and therefore tend to occur where the vascular systems are in closest proximity to one another (root of
the mesentery, esophageal hiatus, perianal region).
These vessels are thin‐walled and tortuous and usually
cluster in plexi.

Although congestive heart failure or caudal vena caval
obstruction causes hepatic venous distension, this does
not result in acquired portosystemic shunting because the
hydrostatic pressure is increased within the caudal vena
cava as well as the hepatic sinusoids and there is hence no
hydrostatic drive for the portosystemic shunts to occur.
Ascites resulting from increased hydrostatic pressure
within the caudal vena cava (caval tumors, right‐sided
congestive heart failure) tends to be a modified transudate due to leakage of protein‐rich hepatic lymph,
whereas ascites resulting from mild to moderate
­portal hypertension tends to be a transudate. Ascites
occurring in fulminant portal hypertension may also be
sanguinous if the capillaries or splenic capsule rupture.
Portal hypertension is likely to result in splenomegaly,
with a normal to small‐sized liver, unless the obstruction
occurs at the level of the hepatic venules or hepatic
veins (Budd–Chiari syndrome).

­Epidemiology
Signalment
Acquired shunts may be seen in any species or breed of
patient in which diseases causing hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis occur. A good example of such a disease in dogs is
chronic hepatitis. A subset of patients with acquired
shunts resulting from portal hypertension caused by
congenital PVH‐MVD will present before the age of 3
years and may be ­indistinguishable from patients with
CPSS (see further discussion in Diagnosis section).
Congenital shunts are seen most commonly in pure‐
breed dogs, or cross‐bred dogs with parents of breeds that
are overrepresented amongst the shunt population. Many
breeds have been reported as predisposed around the
world, the most notable being a number of terriers
(Yorkshire, cairn, Maltese, Jack Russell), Chihuahuas, miniature schnauzers, pugs, toy poodles, Australian c­ attle dogs,
Labrador and golden retrievers, and Irish wolfhounds.
In general, extrahepatic shunts are more common in
terriers and other small‐breed dogs, whereas intrahepatic shunts are more common in medium‐ to large‐
breed dogs. However, exceptions occur (e.g., toy and
miniature poodles) and some form of shunt imaging is
recommended prior to surgical exploration. Patients
from breeds that are not known to be predisposed to
CPSS are more likely to “break the rules” and should be
evaluated especially carefully.
PVH‐MVD tends to occur in similar breeds to those
affected with CPSS, and has been best characterized in
the terrier‐type breeds such as Maltese, Yorkshire and
cairn terriers.

History and Clinical Signs
Patients with portal vascular abnormalities may be clinically asymptomatic (abnormality detected after routine
wellness screening, or preanesthetic blood testing), ­display
vague and self‐limiting clinical signs, or present with
severe neurologic abnormalities associated with HE.
Common clinical signs include a picky appetite or pica,
failure to thrive, hypersialism (most evident in cats), sporadic vomiting, polyuria and polydipsia, urinary irritation and obstruction caused by ammonium biurate
calculi, episodes of abnormal mentation accompanied by
ataxia, and amauratic (apparent) blindness. Cats with
CPSS may have copper‐colored irises, although this is
not always the case, and it is not pathognomonic .
Dogs with CPSS sometimes present with a history of
generalized motor seizures, although in a subset of cases
the seizures are caused by a co‐morbidity such as idiopathic epilepsy or granulomatous meningoencephalitis
(more recently referred to as meningoencephalitis of
unknown etiology), rather than the shunt itself (see
Prognosis section). Behavior changes including aggression may occasionally prompt presentation. Dogs with
CPSS may have other intermittent problems that seem to
result from systemic debility, such as coughing, ocular
discharge, and urinary tract infection.
Ascites is very uncommonly seen in dogs with CPSS
unless they have been on a restricted protein diet for an
extended period of time. Ascites is more common in
cases of portal hypertension accompanying end‐stage
liver disease or portal venous hypertension/dysplasia.

­Diagnosis
There are a number of diagnostic methods, including
demonstration of liver dysfunction, confirmation of portosystemic shunting, imaging of the shunt, and histologic
evaluation of the liver.
Clinical Pathology
Biochemical abnormalities typically include low to low‐
normal BUN, cholesterol, albumin, glucose and protein C,
andelevatedliverenzymes(alanineaminotransferase[ALT],
alkaline phosphatase[ALP]). Serum bile acid activity is
measured before (resting) and after eating (post prandial),
to gauge the degree to which bile acids leak into the systemic circulation from the portal vein, rather than being
extracted by enterohepatic circulation. Serum bile acid
activity should be elevated in animals with portosystemic
shunts, and the post prandial sample is more frequently
abnormal than the resting sample. Plasma ammonia levels
can also be measured before and after administration of

an ammonium chloride solution per rectum (ammonia
tolerance test). Ammonia is labile in serum, and the
ammonia ­tolerance test is somewhat more invasive and
can be very d
­ angerous, and thus serum bile acids are preferred over ammonia as a clinical screening test.
Hematologic a­ bnormalities include anemia with microcytosis and often a mature neutrophilia.
Confirmation of Portosystemic Shunting
This is most easily done using nuclear scintigraphy; imaging the patient following rectal or transsplenic administration of technetium pertechnetate. Contrast portography,
following injection of radiographic contrast agent through
a catheter placed in the jejunal vein or percutaneously by
means of splenic injection (­splenoportography), provides
another mechanism for confirmation that portal blood is
passing directly into the caudal vena cava and bypassing
the liver. Contrast portography also provides a mechanism for determining the anatomy of the portosystemic
shunt, if a good‐­quality study is achieved. Chapter 61 provides further details on the methods to image the animal
with a portosystemic shunt.
Imaging of the Portal Vasculature
Abdominal sonography is the least expensive and invasive modality, but confidently finding a portosystemic
shunt can be difficult in very small dogs, dogs with intestinal gas or ingesta, or with shunts that are in unusual
locations. Even in the hands of an experienced sonographer, shunts may not be located in up to 25% of patients.
Even when the vessel is not identified, circumstantial
evidence for CPSS may include turbulence within the
prehepatic caudal vena cava, renomegaly, microhepatica,
and urinary calculi.
Three‐dimensional imaging using computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is
becoming the “gold standard” of diagnosis. Dual‐phase
CT angiography (DPCTA) allows confirmation of
­portosystemic shunting, clarification of the exact shunt
anatomy, identification of other congenital abnormalities, calculation of liver volume, assessment of hepatic
perfusion in both the arterial and venous phase, and
identification of urinary calculi. DPCTA is essential for
planning transvenous coil embolization.
Differentiating CPS from PVH‐MVD
Dogs with these two conditions may present in exactly
the same way, although dogs with PVH‐MVD are less
likely to demonstrate overt signs of HE. Confirmation by
nuclear scintigraphy, or advanced imaging, that there is
no macroscopic shunt, and identification of the histologic

VetBooks.ir

66 Portosystemic Shunts and Microvascular Dysplasia

features on liver biopsy in the absence of another hepatopathy that could explain the biochemical p
­ erturbations are
required for definitive diagnosis of PVH‐MVD.

­Therapy
Medical Therapy
Medical therapy is aimed at ameliorating the signs of
HE by reducing the amount of ammonia (and other substances) produced in the gut, and the degree to which
they are absorbed. Medical management is often
employed in those animals that show few clinical signs on
presentations, are older, in which financial or owner-lead
reasons limit surgery, or which have a shunt that is not
amenable to ligation. The main aims of therapy are to
decrease the formation of gut derived encephalotoxins,
especially ammonia. Therefore the mainstays of current
therapy are a combination of dietary alterations, oral antibiotics to suppress bacterial populations that produce
encephalopathic toxins and local acting agents to reduce
gastrointestinal uptake of ammonia (e.g. lactulose).
Controlled trials have not been performed in animals to
determine the optimal treatment for HE and so current
recommendations are based on anecdotal evidence.
Feeding a high‐quality digestible diet is the mainstay of
management of the stable patient. Protein restriction is
controversial, and generally not recommended, as some
authorities report that dogs with CPSS actually have normal to increased requirements. If protein restriction is
required, a commercial restricted protein diet is the easiest to prescribe. For clients who wish to formulate their
own diet, protein sources should be easily digestible and
metabolizable. Vegetable and dairy proteins tend to be
better tolerated than meat‐based ones, with cottage
cheese being a palatable option for many patients. Cats
have more stringent dietary requirements than dogs, and
this should be taken into account when choosing a diet.
Patients with reduced hepatic mass will have poor glycogen reserves and a tendency toward hypoglycemia, so
meals should be given frequently.
Lactulose is prescribed for symptomatic patients, with
the goal of reducing intestinal pH and thereby trapping
ammonia within the gut, and by virtue of its action as an
osmotic cathartic, hastening intestinal transit time and
reducing the time available for absorption of ammonia.
In patients that are actively encephalopathic and unable
to tolerate oral medication, lactulose may be administered rectally.
Antibiotics may also be prescribed, with a view to
reducing the intestinal bacterial population and thus
reducing ammonia production. Further details about
medical management of the patient with liver disease
can be found in Chapter 65.

There is evidence that patients with liver disease are at
increased risk for gastrointestinal ulceration, and anecdotal reports of this being a particular problem in dogs
with intrahepatic shunts. Therefore, many clinicians
include some type of antacid medication (H2 receptor
antagonist or protein pump inhibitor such as famotidine
or omeprazole) as part of the standard medical management protocol. Finally, emerging evidence also suggests that inflammatory cytokines are synergistic with
ammonia in precipitating HE and that controlling
inflammation in other organs is an important part of
managing the patient with HE.

Surgical Therapy
Surgical therapy is indicated for patients with CPSS, or
hepatic arteriovenous fistulae, where the primary problem can be resolved. Patients with acquired shunts secondary to end‐stage liver disease or PVH are unlikely to
benefit from surgical attenuation of their shunts as the
­ echanism for decompressing
shunts are providing a m
the portal system and reducing portal hypertension.
Dogs with PVH-MVD, and those with portal vein aplasia, are also not candidates for surgical intervention.
However, the results of liver biopsy may inform medical
management in patients with acquired liver disease, and
this often provides justification for surgical exploration.
Surgical therapy for CPSS is aimed at identifying the
shunt and attenuating it. As most patients have poorly
developed hepatic portal circulation and relatively high
portal vascular resistance, total immediate occlusion of
the shunt is highly likely to result in life‐threatening portal hypertension. Therefore, surgical methods aim either
to provide partial occlusion (which may be increased in
stages by subsequent procedures) or application of a
device to promote slow occlusion. The goal of slow or
staged occlusion is to allow the intrahepatic portal circulation time to regenerate, with reduction in vascular
resistance, at the same time as the shunt is being slowly
or incrementally occluded.
The main techniques used for slow occlusion of extrahepatic shunts are cellophane bands and ameroid constrictors. Cellophane bands promote occlusion by
stimulating a foreign body reaction and fibrosis between
the band and the shunt wall. Ameroid constrictors produce some mechanical occlusion as the ameroid clay
takes up fluid, but also cause local inflammation with
fibrosis and thrombosis of the shunt vessel. More recent
reports have described the use of a variety of other clear
films for shunt occlusion in dogs and cats, including
polypropylene and polyethylene. These seem to be as
effective as cellophane, probably due to the chemicals
incorporated during the manufacturing process.

VetBooks.ir
