Intrahepatic shunts were historically addressed by surgical attenuation using either extravascular dissection or
a transvenous approach under partial venous inflow
occlusion. In recent years, minimally invasive procedures have become more common, with an expanding
body of international experience in interventional techniques such as percutaneous thrombogenic coil embolization (PTCE). This technique results in much less
morbidity. The downsides are the need for advanced
equipment (including fluoroscopy) and expertise, and
the likelihood that repeated procedures will be required
for complete shunt occlusion (see Prognosis section).
Surgical Attenuation

Surgical exploration is performed through a ventral
­midline celiotomy, which may be extended cranially by
transdiaphragmatic incision or median sternotomy.
Combination of a paracostal incision with a ventral midline celiotomy is also an effective way of exposing the
craniodorsal abdomen, but is rarely required for shunt
surgery. A standard exploration should be performed to
evaluate the portal vasculature and identify the portosystemic shunt. If present, acquired shunts will usually be
visible around the cranial aspect of the left kidney.
Perioperative Monitoring and Treatment

Serum glucose concentration should be monitored
­regularly due to the tendency for hypoglycemia. Albumin
levels may drop markedly when intravenous crystalloid
is administered at surgical rates, and plasma transfusion
is sometimes required. However, serum albumin
increases relatively little following plasma transfusion,
and therefore human albumin solutions are an alternatively way to increase serum albumin. Hemodynamic
parameters should be measured regularly during and following surgery to gauge trends and allow early detection
of developing portal hypertension. Patients can be
severely polyuric prior to surgery and may require
increased fluid rates to avoid dehydration postoperatively. Potassium supplementation may be required.
Complications of Surgery

A large range of complications have been reported following surgery for CPSS. Anesthetic‐related complications include hypotension (mainly in cats), hypothermia
due to small body size and poor body condition, and
hypoglycemia for reasons previously described.
Intraoperative hemorrhage is not usually a major issue
unless tearing of the vessels occurs during dissection.
This is more likely during treatment of intrahepatic
shunts, but unlikely if careful technique is used when
dissecting extrahepatic vessels. Although some perturbations in coagulation parameters have been reported in
dogs with CPSS, most patients do not experience clini-

cally significant problems with coagulation. This is much
more likely to be a problem in patients with end‐stage
liver disease.
The major life‐threatening complications that occur
perioperatively are portal hypertension and postligation
neurologic dysfunction. The incidence of portal hypertension has been greatly reduced by adoption of the slow
occlusion techniques, and publication of guidelines for
safe shunt attenuation. Mild to moderate portal hypertension may not cause life‐threatening problems; affected
patients may have inappetence or diarrhea for a short
period of time, or develop ascites. Assuming they are
able to compensate hemodynamically for the reduced
central venous return, and the bowel does not become
critically hypoxic, they will eventually develop acquired
shunts and a consequent return of portal pressure
towards normal. Early published reports suggested that
up to 20% of patients can be expected to develop acquired
shunts but more recent studies, in which patients underwent postoperative evaluation using DPCTA, showed
that the incidence is probably less than 10%, with an
additional 10% of patients experiencing ongoing shunting as a result of misplacement or failure of the attenuating device to promote complete occlusion.
Postoperative neurologic sequelae range from blindness or muscle twitching, through disorientation, to
generalized motor seizures and status epilepticus.
­
Hypoglycemia and HE may also produce signs that can
be difficult to distinguish from true postligation neurologic dysfunction . In addition, patients experiencing seizures preoperatively may continue to have seizures
postoperatively if the seizures were caused by something
other than their CPS.
Hypoglycemia, HE, and the seizures of idiopathic epilepsy should be manageable by evaluating the patient
and relevant bloodwork, and treating accordingly.
Postligation neurologic dysfunction seizures and status
epilepticus constitute a much more serious problem with
a guarded prognosis. The cause of these seizures is still
not well understood, but may include factors such as
imbalance of neurotransmitters, cerebral edema, and
derangements in cerebral blood flow. Historically, seizures were considered to occur acutely, with patients
found when they were already in status epilepticus.
Closer observation of patients following surgery has
shown that in many cases, the condition is progressive.
Patients start behaving abnormally, vocalizing and showing signs of disorientation and inappropriate mentation.
They do not interact appropriately when being handled.
They are ataxic and often display compulsive movements. Left untreated, they will develop facial twitches
that progress to generalized motor seizures and status
epilepticus. Several studies have shown an incidence of
seizures in up to 5% of dogs following surgery for CPSS.

VetBooks.ir

66 Portosystemic Shunts and Microvascular Dysplasia

Anecdotal experiences suggest that older dogs and pugs
may be at greater risk for seizures, but this has not been
definitively proven. Cats seem at greater risk for neurologic sequelae, including blindness and twitching, in
addition to seizures. Preoperative treatment with phenobarbitol and levetiracetam (Keppra®) has been shown to
significantly reduce the incidence of seizures, although
published reports and anecdotal experience suggest that
the risk is not completely abolished.
Therapeutic Decision Making
In light of the fact that many patients have mild clinical
signs, and surgical shunt attenuation has a significant
morbidity/mortality rate, owners are sometimes faced
with a difficult choice between long‐term medical management and surgical correction. Some dogs live apparently normal lives with no management at all, whereas
others develop severe clinical signs within the first few
months of life. On risk–benefit analysis, a young puppy
with obvious HE is more clearly a candidate for surgery
than an 8‐year‐old dog in which CPSS is detected on a
routine wellness check. An exception would be the older
male dog in which CPSS is diagnosed following urethral
obstruction with ammonium urate calculi. Medical management in these patients may not control stone formation, and as urethral obstruction is, in itself, potentially
life‐threatening, many owners will opt for surgical
­correction of the CPSS. Likewise, patients with severe
polyuria/polydipsia may be generally happy but present
unacceptable management issues, making surgery an
attractive option.
Many dogs with severe clinical signs will become near‐
normal on medical management, prompting the owners
to question the necessity for surgery. The choice then is
between lifelong dietary management and other therapies, weighed against a high probability for return of liver
function to normal following CPSS attenuation.
Ongoing Evaluation
There are two main factors that should be considered
when determining a patient’s progress, either with
­medical or surgical management: liver function and the
presence and degree of portosystemic shunting.
Biochemical Evaluation

Liver function is usually monitored indirectly by measuring blood levels of the products of hepatic metabolism
including albumin, cholesterol and BUN . Return of cholesterol and BUN to reference levels is a good indicator
that liver function is returning to normal. Serum bile
acid levels are a sensitive indicator of macroscopic or
microscopic portosystemic shunting. Postoperatively,

patients may have normal serum biochemistry and a
normal technetium scan in the face of continuing mild
elevations in serum bile acids. The significance of these
mild elevations to long‐term prognosis is not yet known.
Protein C has been proposed as a useful monitoring tool
but the assay is not offered widely, and results from different laboratories may differ, making interpretation of
single results difficult.
Nuclear Scintigraphy

Per rectal scintigraphy provides an estimate of shunt fraction and is helpful in determining the degree of shunt closure following surgery. It does have some interobserver
variation, and we reported some dogs with normal technetium scans following surgery that had persistent shunting through small tributary vessels. Therefore, the results
of scintigraphy should be interpreted in the context of
other measures such as serum biochemistry and imaging.
Percutaneous transsplenic scintigraphy is more accurate
and may provide information about shunt anatomy in the
hands of an experienced operator, but is more invasive
and not yet performed routinely.
Abdominal Sonography

Assuming that the shunt was sonographically visible
before surgery, postoperative sonography is a mechanism
for confirming closure of the shunt, increase in liver volume, and decrease in kidney size. It is also useful for identifying or monitoring development of urinary calculi.
Computed Tomography

Dual‐phase CT angiography is emerging as the most
reliable way to evaluate patients postoperatively, ­allowing
calculation of liver volume and perfusion, and evaluation
of shunt anatomy, presence of persistent shunting
through the original shunt or acquired vessels.
Interpretation of Surgical Outcomes

Historically, patients have undergone minimal objective
follow‐up after surgical attenuation, making interpretation of published outcomes difficult. Patients with
­persistently abnormal blood values may have persistent
shunting, acquired shunts, PVH-MVD, or some other
hepatopathy. Persistently abnormal technetium scans
are now recognized to occur in a variety of scenarios,
including failure of the occlusion device to promote
complete occlusion, malpositioning of the occlusion
device, and development of acquired shunting. Clearly,
neither of these techniques is able to identify the etiology
for the abnormal result, and thus inform the most appropriate management plan.
Imaging using sonography may be helpful if the abnormal vessel(s) are visible. The ideal strategy for evaluation
would include serial serum biochemistry including

719

VetBooks.ir

720

Section 7 Diseases of the Liver, Gallbladder, and Bile Ducts

serum bile acids and protein C, nuclear scintigraphy, and
DPCTA. This battery of tests should be used as the gold
standard for future research studies attempting to evaluate surgical outcomes, but is not realistic for clinical
patients, many of whom have shown resolution of their
clinical signs and for whom the risk of anesthesia and
contrast imaging is not warranted. Advanced imaging
should, however, be considered for patients displaying
persistent biochemical or scintigraphic abnormalities six
months following surgery.

­Prognosis
While medical management can be successful for a prolonged period in many patients, the published literature
suggests that outcomes following surgery are better, as
long as the surgery is performed before severe secondary
changes in liver function occur. A more recent study has
shown that those undergoing surgical ligation of the shunting vessel have a longer median survival time, and a lower
frequency of ongoing clinical signs. The mortality rate following correction of CPSS (including PTCE) is less than
5%. Up to 80% of patients receiving slow occlusion devices

for extrahepatic CPS can be expected to regain normal
liver function, with a median survival of 152 months. The
mortality and morbidity rates are higher for surgical correction of intrahepatic shunts, and for cats with CPSS of
any anatomic type, and the chance of return to liver function is lower than for dogs with e­ xtrahepatic CPSS.
The prognosis for patients undergoing PTCE has not
yet been established definitively. However, early reports
suggest that the mortality and morbidity rates are low,
and patients are highly likely to show substantial clinical
improvement, although complete closure of the shunt is
unlikely.
Regardless of the technique used, the clinical impact of
residual flow through the original shunt has yet to be
determined. Intuitively, a reduction in shunt fraction
should improve hepatic function, but the actual shunt
fraction at which a patient might resume a normal diet
and not show clinical signs is not known.
Approximately 10% of patients will never return to
normal liver function even following complete shunt
occlusion and will likely require lifetime medical management, although interestingly, they are often less
severely affected clinically once acquired shunts have
developed than they were with a single shunt.

Diseases of the Gallbladder and Extrahepatic Biliary Ducts
Ben Harris, MA, VetMB, CertSAM, MRCVS
Northwest Veterinary Specialists, Sutton Weaver, Cheshire, UK

The gallbladder is a bladder‐like organ possessing a thin,
mucosa‐lined wall with a muscular layer and an outer
serosal layer. Its function is to store, modify, and secrete
bile, which is synthesized in the hepatocytes and reaches
the gallbladder via bile canaliculi, lobar bile ducts, and
eventually the cystic bile duct. During its time stored in
the gallbladder, bile becomes concentrated (up to 10
times) and mildly acidified. Gallbladder contraction pro­
pels bile into the common bile duct (CBD) and then via
the sphincter of Oddi into the proximal duodenum at the
major duodenal papilla. Gallbladder contraction is stim­
ulated by cholecystokinin, gastrin, and motilin, which in
turn are released in response to fatty acids, peptides, and
amino acids in the stomach and duodenum.
In cats, the CBD joins the pancreatic duct, sharing a
common opening into the duodenum at the duodenal
papilla. In dogs, the pancreatic and CBD meet only at the
papilla; in many dogs, an additional separate pancreatic
duct enters the duodenum more distal to the papilla.

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Disorders of the canine and feline biliary tract are more
frequently acquired than congenital, although congenital
biliary cysts, malformations, and biliary atresia have
been reported. The flow of bile from the gallbladder to
the duodenal papilla, as well as the chemical character of
bile and the mucosal immunity (secretory IgA and
mucosal mononuclear cells), serves to reduce the risk of
biliary bacterial infection. In vivo studies and molecular
techniques have detected transitory bacteria in bile of
normal dogs. Interruption or obstruction to flow may
allow these transitory bacteria to colonize the tract,
causing bacterial cholangitis.
Trematode infections (Platynosomum fastosum and
other Platynosomum spp.) of the biliary tract are found
occasionally in cats in the southern USA, in South

America and Asia, with clinical disease ranging from
asymptomatic to severe obstructive cholangitis or subse­
quent neoplastic transformation to cholangiocarcinoma.
Mucosal resistance to the extreme chemical nature of
bile is afforded by secretion of mucin from mucous
glands within the biliary tract. Hypersecretion, possibly
as a result of inflammatory stimuli or transporter defects
(ABCB4 phosphatidylcholine translocator mutation in
Shetland sheepdogs), may result in accumulation of
mucin within the gallbladder in dogs, leading to the for­
mation of a biliary mucocele (Figure 67.1). Untreated
­biliary mucoceles may rupture, as the gallbladder wall
becomes necrotic under pressure from the accumulating
concretion of mucus. Bile is a highly irritating substance,
so leakage into the abdomen results in a chemical perito­
nitis (“bile peritonitis”). Cholecystocentesis is contrain­
dicated in biliary mucocele patients because of the risk of
gallbladder rupture.
Biliary obstruction may be either intrinsic to the bil­
iary tract or outside it. Blockage of biliary flow results in
posthepatic jaundice. One of the more common causes
of biliary obstruction is acute pancreatitis. This occurs
due to the intimate association of the body of the pan­
creas with the CBD near the duodenal papilla – the point
of entry of the CBD into the small intestine. Pancreatic
carcinoma or biliary carcinoma similarly may result in
complete bile duct obstruction. Inflammation or neo­
plastic infiltration of and around the duodenal papilla
(e.g., duodenal lymphoma, carcinoma) is an occasional
cause of jaundice.
Choleliths are uncommon in cats and dogs but may
cause bile duct obstruction or rupture. Most canine and
feline choleliths contain some bile pigments, rather than
being pure cholesterol liths such as those commonly
found in humans. A predisposition to cholelithiasis may
occur due to gallbladder motility disorders, endocrine
disease, cholestasis, cholangitis or supersaturation of the
components of bile (cholesterol, pigments).

not reported in dogs, inflammation around the duodenal
papilla can alter bile flow and may encourage bacterial
colonization of the biliary tract. Likewise, intestinal
motility disorders or small intestinal bacterial over­
growth may augment infection risk by increasing
numbers of potentially pathogenic bacteria that may
­
ascend the biliary tract.
Biliary flukes are not prevalent in Europe, but are more
commonly found in the southern USA, South America,
and Asia. Infection requires ingestion of a secondary
intermediate host such as a frog or lizard.

Primary biliary neoplasia ranges from benign chole­
dochal cysts and biliary cystadenoma to biliary carci­
noma, which may originate in the intrahepatic or
extrahepatic biliary system. Biliary neoplasia occurs more
commonly in cats. The gallbladder is susceptible to infarc­
tion if the cystic artery – the sole arterial blood supply to
the organ – is compromised by trauma or thrombosis.
Bacterial cholangitis may occur due to ascending bac­
terial infection from the gastrointestinal tract, hematog­
enous spread or colonization by the aforementioned
transitory bacteria.

­Epidemiology
Arguably, the most common disorders predisposing to
biliary tract disease are endocrine diseases such as
hyperadrenocorticism, diabetes mellitus, and hypothy­
roidism. Of these, hyperadrenocorticism increases risk
of gallbladder mucocele by up to 29 times; the associa­
tion with hypothyroidism and diabetes mellitus is less
concrete.
Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a common co‐
morbidity with cats with cholangitis, just as there is a

Particular species and breed associations are found for
certain biliary disorders. Neoplasia occurs more com­
monly in middle‐aged to older cats and dogs, but benign
and cystic disorders may be acquired even in individuals
less than 2 years of age. Biliary flukes are reported in cats
but are far less common in dogs. Mucocele formation is
more common in Shetland sheepdogs, border terriers,
miniature schnauzers and cocker spaniels and become
increasingly common in dogs beyond middle age.
Mutation of a phosphatidylcholine translocator (ABCB4)
has been identified in affected Shetland sheepdogs.
Choleliths are more commonly found in miniature
schnauzers and miniature poodles, particularly in older
females.
Pancreatic neoplasia does not have a strong breed pre­
disposition, but pancreatitis is more commonly associ­
ated with cocker spaniels and miniature schnauzers. Of
note is the often marked inflammatory swelling of the
pancreas in cocker spaniels with pancreatitis, which may
be erroneously described as a pancreatic tumor based on
diagnostic imaging findings. Those breeds with predis­
positions towards endocrine disease (e.g., hypothyroid­
ism, hyperadrenocorticism) may be more commonly
affected by bile stasis, cholangitis, and biliary mucocele.

­History and Clinical Signs
Nonobstructive biliary tract disease may be insidious in
onset, with vague clinical signs such as lethargy, pyrexia,
anorexia, and vomiting. Pyrexia is more likely to be pre­
sent with florid inflammation, bile peritonitis or bacterial
biliary infection but can also be seen with cholelithiasis,
presumably due to secondary bacterial infection. Clinical
signs may be mild and therefore present for weeks or
months before veterinary attention is sought.

VetBooks.ir

67 Diseases of the Gallbladder and Extrahepatic Biliary Ducts

Vomiting may be a clinical sign associated with biliary
disease itself or caused by an underlying associated prob­
lem such as pancreatitis. A history of dietary indiscretion
or ingestion of fatty foods may be relevant in cases of acute
pancreatitis. Abdominal pain may result from the obstruc­
tion or distension of the bile ducts or gallbladder or from
inflammation of the biliary tract and surrounding area
(e.g., local peritonitis). Patients with biliary mucocele may
also exhibit abdominal pain and, if significantly obstruc­
tive, may become jaundiced. Jaundice (icterus) becomes
clinically evident as yellow discoloration of the mucus
membranes, skin, and sclera when the serum bilirubin
exceeds around 2 mg/dL. The exact concentration at
which icterus becomes clinically visible will depend upon
the patient’s own pigmentation and hemoglobin concen­
tration (mucous membrane p
­ allor makes icterus more
evident). Total biliary obstruction prevents pigmentation
of the feces, resulting in pale “acholic” feces.

­Diagnosis
Clinical Examination
It should be apparent from clinical examination if the
patient is jaundiced, but jaundice is only clinically evident
when serum bilirubin levels exceed 2 mg/dL. As previ­
ously mentioned, how evident hyperbilirubinemia is will
depend upon multiple factors. Examination of the sclera
or internal aspect of the pinna (the latter particularly in
cats) may display more obvious evidence of icterus.
Cranial abdominal pain may manifest as a hunched
posture, “prayer posture” or via the patient’s response to
palpation. Once again, how evident this subjective find­
ing is will depend upon patient factors and also concur­
rent problems such as pancreatitis. Pancreatic pain
usually localizes to the right cranial abdominal quadrant,
but may be more diffuse. In some patients, pancreatic
pain does not manifest until pressure is placed directly
upon the pancreas during ultrasonography. A very dis­
tended gallbladder might be palpable beyond the hepatic
margin in some patients, but this is unusual. If rupture of
the biliary tract has occurred then an abdominal effusion
may be present, potentially resulting in a fluid wave on
ballottement. Often, however, patients with bile perito­
nitis have tensed abdominal muscles, because of the
associated pain, which limits clinical examination.

Blood biochemistry in biliary tract disease varies
depending upon the degree of biliary obstruction as well
as the accompanying hepatic and pancreatic disease.
In an icteric patient, total bilirubin will be increased. If
the patient has significant cholestasis, then bile acids will
also be increased. If total bilirubin is increased then
nothing additional may be inferred from measurement
of bile acids or performing a bile acid stimulation
test – the patient has either significant hepatic functional
compromise or bile duct obstruction.
Increases of the concentration of biliary canalicular
enzymes in the blood are expected (alkaline phosphatase
[ALP], gamma‐glutamyl transferase [GGT]) with choles­
tasis or biliary tract inflammation. Bile acids are toxic to
hepatocytes, so it is extremely common for animals with
bile stasis to have elevation in hepatocellular enzymes
(alanine aminotransferase [ALT], aspartate aminotrans­
ferase [AST]). Patients with concurrent hepatic paren­
chymal disease may also have increased hepatocellular
enzymes. If hepatic disease is advanced enough to impair
hepatic function, then urea and albumin may be reduced
due to poor hepatic synthesis and conversion. Similarly,
coagulation factors may be depleted due to reduced
recycling of the vitamin K‐dependent factors (II, VII, IX,
X), resulting in prolonged coagulation times (prothrom­
bin time, activated partial thromboplastin time).
The inflammatory response may cause increased
­synthesis of globulins. Pancreatitis may be reflected by
elevations of amylase and lipase, due to leakage from the
pancreas, but these enzymes have poor specificity and may
be spuriously elevated in hemoconcentrated patients and
patients with other diseases. Amylase and lipase are even
less sensitive and specific in cats than in dogs. Pancreatic
species‐specific lipase is a more sensitive and specific test,
but it must be remembered that a positive result does not
necessarily indicate that pancreatitis is the primary prob­
lem as gastrointestinal disease, peritonitis, or pancreatic
neoplasia can also result in increased pancreatic specific
lipase. Additonally, a normal value does not exclude pan­
creatitis as a possible differential diagnosis.
Hematology
The complete blood count can reflect the inflammatory
disease by revealing increased numbers of neutrophils
which, in marked inflammation or infection, may exhibit
a left shift or toxic changes.

Blood Chemistry

Urinalysis

Following centrifugation, the plasma or serum of a jaun­
diced patient’s blood will appear deep yellow (icteric).
This interferes with some colorimetric blood biochemis­
try tests.

Icteric patients are, by definition, hyperbilirubinemic,
which results in bilirubinuria, imparting a deep yellow
color to the urine. On microscopic examination of urine
sediment, bilirubin crystals may be evident.

Section 7 Diseases of the Liver, Gallbladder, and Bile Ducts

Diagnostic Imaging
Radiography

Radiography may give an overall impression of the size of
the liver but usually does not give information regarding
structure. It may identify the presence of radiodense
choleliths within the biliary tree or gallbladder. Rarely,
the gallbladder may be visible as a “porcelain gallblad­
der” with a fine mineral opacity delineating the gallblad­
der wall. This may be caused by dystrophic mineralization
due to neoplasia of the gallbladder. If peritonitis has
developed subsequent to biliary rupture, then effusion
will cause loss of radiologic contrast in the cranial abdo­
men or a “ground glass” appearance.
Ultrasonography

Transcutaneous abdominal ultrasonography is the main­
stay of imaging of the biliary tract. It affords assessment
of the bile ducts within and outside the liver, ensuring
that the ducts are patent and not distended. The gall­
bladder may be examined and measured, noting any
material within the lumen as well as the wall thickness.
The common bile duct should be followed from the gall­
bladder to the point of entry into the duodenum at the
major duodenal papilla. Intestinal gas may impede this
examination. The normal common duct may measure
3 mm diameter in dogs or up to 4 mm diameter in cats.
Choleliths appear as hyperechoic structures with distal
acoustic shadowing. If a cholelith is causing complete
obstruction then the bile duct may appear dilated proxi­
mally. Choleliths do not commonly cause obstruction,
but may be associated with nonobstructive bile duct
­dilation. In humans and most likely in dogs, such nonob­
structive dilation may be associated with bacterial infec­
tion of the bile duct. In this circumstance, it is ­difficult to
determine whether the cholelithiasis is the cause or the
consequence of cholangitis.
Complete bile duct obstruction does not necessarily
result in gallbladder distension but often causes dilation
of the major bile ducts, sometimes giving a very tortuous
appearance on ultrasonography.
Echogenic sediment or “sludge” is a normal finding in
many dogs and cats but should be dependent (i.e.,
affected by gravity) and not obscuring the lumen. “Sludge
balls” are echogenic, roughly spherical accumulations of
bile and mucus that move depending upon patient posi­
tion. They may pose a risk for bile duct obstruction.
Gallbladder mucoceles classically have a hyperechoic
stellate appearance on ultrasound, with strands of the
echogenic material extending to the gallbladder wall.
Early or incipient mucoceles may have a more subtle
appearance, but the main feature is of immobile non­
dependent sludging occupying the majority of the
gallbladder.

Advanced Imaging

Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imag­
ing may yield more detailed information about the
extrahepatic biliary ducts and gallbladder. They can be
useful for detecting neoplasia, characterizing anatomic
anomalies and detecting choleliths. The main advan­
tage of advanced imaging above abdominal ultrasound
is that regions of the abdomen are usually not missed
on advanced imaging, though methodical radiologic
review is essential and time‐consuming. Whereas gas­
trointestinal gas may obscure the bile ducts by reflect­
ing ­ultrasound, this is not a problem with advanced
imaging. When assessing the abdomen for neoplasia on
computed tomography, the thorax may also be scanned
to assess for possible metastasis. Intravenous contrast
may be used to assess the vascularity of a structure to
assist in diagnosis. The requirement for sedation, anes­
thesia, and exposure to ionizing radiation must be
considered.
Endoscopy
The duodenal papilla may be assessed during endoscopy,
which affords the opportunity for gastrointestinal biop­
sies. Some small studies of endoscopic retrograde chol­
angiography and cholangiopancreatography in cats and
dogs have documented that this procedure is feasible,
but there is no tangible benefit over advanced imaging.
Cholangiopancreatography has been used historically to
induce pancreatitis for experimental purposes in
dogs – this in itself casts doubt over its diagnostic utility
and safety. Using a similar procedure employing a side‐
angled endoscope, it is feasible to cannulate and there­
fore stent the common bile duct in the case of functional
obstruction (e.g., acute pancreatitis, pancreatic mass).
Cholecentesis
If inflammatory or bacterial cholangitis is suspected
then bile sampling is indicated. This may be performed
under ultrasound guidance or during a laparotomy or
laparoscopy. While potential complications include bile
leakage and subsequent peritonitis and vagal‐induced
arrhythmias, most samples taken in this way do not
cause complications. The gallbladder should be emptied
as much as possible during the procedure to reduce the
pressure of the residual contents and the risk of leakage.
Bile obtained should be examined cytologically and
should also be submitted for gram staining and bacterial
culture and sensitivity (the author prefers to submit two
transport charcoal swabs of bile – one for aerobic and
one for anaerobic culture conditions). Ideally, both aero­
bic and anaerobic culture should be performed. In a
study of patients with hepatic inflammation, nearly one

VetBooks.ir

67 Diseases of the Gallbladder and Extrahepatic Biliary Ducts

quarter had positive bile culture whereas 6% had positive
culture of liver tissue. In patients with confirmed chole­
cystitis, more than half had a positive bile culture.
Laparotomy and Laparoscopy
Direct examination of the extrahepatic biliary system and
gallbladder affords an opportunity for biopsy, cytology,
and potentially palliative and curative surgical interven­
tion. Complete bile duct obstruction is an indication for
surgical intervention. Bile ducts may be stented for short‐
or long‐term management of obstruction, to allow reso­
lution of the underlying disorder (e.g., acute pancreatitis
causing complete extrahepatic bile duct obstruction).
Surgical exploration may be done via laparotomy or
laparoscopy. Whichever technique is adopted, the
opportunity should be taken for biopsy of the liver and
pancreas, cholecentesis, and possibly intestinal biopsy.
Surgery is required for assessment and potentially repair
of the b
­iliary tract in cases of bile peritonitis.
Cholecystectomy is indicated in the case of gallbladder
mucocele.
Cytology
Fine needle aspirates may be taken, under ultrasound
guidance, from the liver, pancreas, and associated lymph
nodes. Similarly, cholecentesis and abdominocentesis
may be performed to investigate potential inflammatory
or infectious processes. As previously mentioned, chole­
centesis is contraindicated if biliary mucocele is
­suspected – diagnosis may be confirmed at surgery.

(e.g., cholelith). One large retrospective study of bile and
liver culture in dogs and cats with hepatobiliary disease
found that Escherichia coli, Enterococcus spp., Bacteroides
spp., Streptococcus spp., and Clostridium spp. were the
most common isolates. This study suggests that empiri­
cal antibiotic choice for hepatobiliary infection could
include a fluoroquinolone for gram‐negative cover
alongside a penicillin or metronidazole for gram‐positive
and anaerobic organisms. It cannot be stressed enough,
however, that responsible antibiotic usage demands cul­
ture and sensitivity testing, particularly before employ­
ing antibiotics such as fluoroquinolones. Repeating bile
culture to monitor response to treatment should be con­
sidered, as significant antibiotic resistance can develop
during the course of treatment.
Cholerectics
Sludging and stasis of bile promote biliary inflamma­
tion and infection. Additionally, hydrophobic bile
acids are cytotoxic and damage cell membranes.
Ursodeoxycholic acid (ursodiol, UDCA) is a hydro­
philic bile acid, which exerts cytoprotective and anti­
oxidant effects and induces choleresis (increased bile
flow). The recommended dose is 10–15 mg/kg once daily.
In addition to using this drug in cholangitis, it may
have some efficacy in treating early mucoid bile accu­
mulation (early gallbladder mucocele). Ursodeoxycholic
acid is contraindicated in complete bile duct obstruc­
tion and is not an alternative to s­ urgery for gallbladder
mucocele.
Antioxidants

­Therapy
Surgery
The patient should be stabilized first as biliary surgery is
complex and may require prolonged general anesthesia.
As detailed above, dogs with gallbladder mucoceles are
treated surgically by way of cholecystectomy with or
without biliary bypass (cholecystoduodenostomy, chol­
ecystojejunostomy). Surgery is often required for ani­
mals with extrahepatic bile duct obstruction, especially if
this is complete or persistent. Rupture of the biliary tract,
resulting in bile peritonitis, is another indication for
s­ urgical intervention.
Antibiotics
Antibiotic choice for biliary infections should be ideally
based upon results of culture and sensitivity. A 4–6‐week
course is advisable in the absence of a nidus for infection

In addition to the antioxidant effects of ursodeoxycholic
acid, other antioxidant drugs are commonly used
in hepatobiliary disease. S‐adenosyl‐L‐methionine
(SAM‐e) increases glutathione production in cat and
dog livers, assisting conjugation and acting as an anti­
oxidant. SAM‐e has been shown to reduce hepatotoxic­
ity following acetaminophen administration. Milk
thistle‐derived silymarin has strong antioxidant proper­
ties and has been shown to exert hepatoprotective
effects when administered alongside some chemother­
apy drugs. Those formulations which complex silymarin
with phosphatidylcholine have much improved bioa­
vailability. Vitamin E is a widely available antioxidant
that also reduces transcription of proinflammatory
cytokines.
Parasiticides
Praziquantel or fenbendazole may be used as flukicidal
therapy.

­Prognosis
Biliary neoplasia bears a grave prognosis as resection is
rarely achieved and metastasis is common. Stenting of the
bile duct may be of palliative use and can be performed at
endoscopy, laparotomy or as a laparoscopy‐assisted proce­
dure. Bacterial cholecystitis and cholangitis bear a favora­
ble prognosis if the infection is identified and treated.
Gallbladder mucocele has an excellent prognosis following

successful surgery, but the perioperative period carries
risks such as bile peritonitis and inducing pancreatitis.
Rupture of the biliary tract of any cause bears a guarded
prognosis, particularly if bacterial infection is present.
There is a broad spectrum of prognoses with pancreatitis
with extrahepatic bile duct obstruction, depending upon
the severity and complications. Acute pancreatitis carries a
guarded prognosis, but may reach a successful outcome in
a good proportion of cases with intensive management.

The Neurologic Examination
Alexander de Lahunta, DVM, PhD, DACVIM (Neurology), DACVP
College of Veterinary Medicine, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY, USA

­Anatomic Diagnosis
What is the most important first step in evaluating a
patient presented for a neurologic disorder? It is making
the anatomic diagnosis based on the results of your
neurologic examination. Did you ever think about who
first made these correlations between the neurologic
signs exhibited by a patient and the location of the lesions
responsible for these clinical signs? Based on textbook
publications that were available to me, you have to credit
the keen observations of two veterinary pathologists for
this: Jack McGrath at the University of Pennsylvania
School of Veterinary Medicine and Anthony Palmer at
the Cambridge University School of Veterinary Medicine.
These two astute veterinarians both published a textbook
in 1956 and 1965 respectively that recorded their observations of the location and character of nervous system
lesions with the clinical observations supplied to them by
the clinicians that examined the patient prior to its death.
Thus began the concept of an anatomic diagnosis.
I was a veterinary student at the College of Veterinary
Medicine at Cornell University from 1954 to 1958. The
majority of my clinical neurology education took place in a
course in Applied Anatomy in my third year of college.
This course taught the clinical signs associated with cranial
nerve abnormalities and the effects of specific nerve dysfunction on the gait of the animal. I joined the faculty of the
Department of Anatomy at this college in 1963 and was
given the responsibility of teaching the new course in neuroanatomy to first‐year veterinary students in their second
semester. As a rule, veterinary students have a need to
understand the reason why they must study a subject.
When a course in clinical neurology does not exist or is a
brief exposure in the third year, most students will find it
difficult to concentrate on neuroanatomy in their first year.
If you agree with this, then you will understand that
combining the teaching of neuroanatomy and clinical neurology in one course is the solution and the foundation for

making an appropriate anatomic diagnosis. The first‐year
student is readily able to handle this. Now, in the 21st century, when the need for teaching time is so critical, it should
be recognized that the most effective teaching of neuroanatomy and clinical neurology is as a vertically integrated
course taught by a board‐certified veterinary neurologist
ideally in the first year of the curriculum. Most veterinary
neuroanatomy courses are taught by nonveterinarians and
as a result there is no correlation to clinical disorders.
As an example of how far we have come, consider this.
Prior to the mid‐1960s, there was no understanding of
the pathogenesis of what was known as coonhound
paralysis then and is now known as polyradiculoneuritis.
There had been a few case studies published that suggested that these dogs became paralyzed following the
trauma to their cervical spinal cord caused by their continual jumping up on the trees where they had followed a
raccoon. Now, you should recognize the fallacy of this
observation because you understand that a cervical spinal
cord lesion cannot cause the diffuse lower motor neuron
disorder that is present in these paralyzed dogs. Hopefully,
your education has taught you how to distinguish tetraplegia caused by a lower motor neuron disorder from one
caused by an upper motor neuron disorder.
Fifty years ago, we were just learning the importance of
making an anatomic diagnosis and how to do it. Now, we
are faced with how to select the most useful diagnostic
procedure to support our most presumptive clinical
diagnosis from a plethora of diagnostic instruments.
Issues of expense and patient safety are most prevalent.
However, all of these ancillary procedures are meaningless without an accurate anatomic diagnosis.
I was asked to write about the approach to a neurologic
patient. This must be a compassionate hands‐on approach
that requires your utmost patience as well as that of your
patient so that a thorough physical neurologic examination can be performed. An accurate anatomic diagnosis
will be dependent on this cooperation between you and

your patient. It is perfectly appropriate to make a fool of
yourself as you attempt to gain the cooperation needed
from your patient. When you think about this, you are
asking this patient to perform movements never asked of
it before. It is really remarkable how well most of them
cooperate. The reward will be as accurate an anatomic
diagnosis as possible.
Examination of a patient with signs of a neurologic
disorder should include a review of the history, a complete physical examination, a neurologic examination,
and appropriate ancillary procedures. The purpose of
the neurologic examination is to determine the neurologic abnormalities and, based on that, the location of
the lesion or lesions in the nervous system responsible
for causing these abnormalities. The location is the
anatomic diagnosis. The continual use of a routine systematic procedure will provide you with the experience and
confidence to make an accurate anatomic diagnosis.
The differential diagnosis must be based on the anatomic
diagnosis, and the order of significance of these disorders
will depend on your evaluation of the signalment and

history. Be sure to consider all five major kinds of lesions
in your differential diagnosis or a list of these with which
you are comfortable. My list includes malformation, injury,
inflammation, neoplasia, and degeneration (MIIND). Your
experience with the anatomic diagnosis together with the
signalment and history will often lead to a presumptive
clinical diagnosis. Further examination of the patient with
ancillary procedures must depend on your differential
diagnosis and what you consider to be the most likely
clinical diagnosis. Many factors will be considered in this
selection, including the cost to the owner.
Be sure to record carefully all your observations from the
neurologic examination, and never rely on your memory.
Many forms are available for recording your observations.
Some of these forms list in detail every possible response
that is present or absent, with numbers to estimate the level
of response. The considerable variation between individual
patients of the same species makes the recording of the
degree of a response less reliable and often misleading. I
prefer a less time‐consuming form that is easier to follow
and adaptable to all species. An example of this follows.
