Tetanus and Tetany

Tetanus is a continuous sustained extensor muscle
­contraction. The cause is the tetanus toxin released by
Clostridrium tetani bacterial infection of domestic
­animals. The disease occurs when the tetanus spores
localized to an anaerobic environment, such as a necrotic
wound, transform into the toxin‐producing form. The
exotoxin, tetanospasm, travels from the infected site via
peripheral nerves to the central nervous system. The
toxin prevents the release of the inhibitory neurotransmitter glycine from interneurons in the spinal cord and
brain, resulting in excessive excitation of brainstem and
motor neurons.
Both cats and dogs are fairly resistant to tetanus.
When infected, they can exhibit an extreme stiffness
progressing to extensor rigidity of all limbs, spastic facial
muscles and trismus within 5–10 days of infection. A
“grimacing” expression with the ears pulled back is usually seen. Occasionally, localized tetanus may affect only
a single limb or be confined to the facial muscles. Many

VetBooks.ir

70 Seizures and Movement Disorders

animals are hypersensitive to external stimuli. The diagnosis is based predominantly on a history of recent
wounds and clinical signs. Initial treatment consists of
aggressive wound debridement, parenteral penicillin
or metronidazole treatment, muscle relaxant therapy
(diazepam constant‐rate infusion at 0.3 mg/kg/h or
pentobarbital 3–10 mg/kg IV to effect) and nutritional
support. Tetanus antitoxin (100–1000 IU/kg IV) has
been reported to reduce the duration of clinical effects.
A test dose of 0.2 mL SC should be given first to test for
anaphylactic reaction. Careful attention should be given
to hydration and nutritional support, as the trismus can
prevent adequate fluid and food intake. Complete remission of clinical signs will usually occur within several
weeks to months.
Tetany is a variable and intermittent extensor muscle
contraction. It may accompany both central and peripheral nervous system diseases. In dogs, tetany is most
commonly seen with hypocalcemia‐associated parturition or hypoparathyroidism. Total calcium is typically
below 7.0 mg/dL. Dogs will often suffer from an inability
to rise, extensor muscle contractions, and hyperthermia
(from muscle contractions). Secondary hypoglycemia
may also be seen due to the excessive muscle movements. Treatment is focused on initial muscle relaxation
with benzodiazepines, followed by calcium and vitamin
D supplementation.

obese animals. One can usually detect a fine ­“rippling”
movement of the muscle as a sign of fasciculation.
The differential diagnoses of muscle fasciculations
range from the benign to the more severe neuromuscular disease. Benign, or contraction, fasciculations can be
seen after strenuous exercise and possibly in very tense
animals. Other transient muscle fasciculations can be
associated with hypercalemia, hypomagnesemia, and
certain toxic drug reactions, to include theophylline,
terbutaline, caffeine and methylxanthine (chocolate toxicity), and anticholinesterase agents (i.e., pyridostigmine
and neostigmine used for the treatment of myasthenia
gravis). Fasciculations associated with neuromuscular
disease are most likely to be present after the onset of
clinical signs of weakness. Degenerative feline and canine
motor unit disease and more advanced cases of distal
axonopathy in the dog are conditions that are more likely
to be associated with muscle fasciculations.
Myokimia is a pattern of abnormal muscle contraction
that produces a “rippling” or “writhing” appearance of
the area involved. The change is the result of spontaneous discharges of large motor units. Myokimia is an indication of neuronal disease followed by sprouting of the
motor unit territory in response to the denervation.
Myokimia or myokimia‐like syndrome has been
described in Jack Russell terriers and is associated with
hyperthermia and collapse.

Myoclonus

Tremor Syndromes

Myoclonus is defined as a sudden, rapid, involuntary
muscle movement of short duration caused by active
muscle contractions (positive myoclonus) or pauses in
muscle activity (negative myoclonus). Classification can
be by clinical presentation, site of origin, or etiology.
Reflex myoclonus to auditory stimuli has been reported
in the retriever dog breeds. Spinal myoclonus arises from
abnormal neuronal discharges originating in the spinal
cord and is of two main types: segmental and propriospinal. Segmental myoclonus can occur in canine distemper‐infected dogs, producing a repetitive, myoclonic jerk
motion of one or more limbs, even during sleep. Epileptic
and drug‐induced myoclonus in dogs are examples of an
etiologic classification.

A number of tremor syndromes have been described in
affected humans that are also seen in small animals.
Tremor is defined as a rhythmic oscillation of a body part
and classified according to its anatomic distribution, frequency (tremors/s, or Hertz) amplitude (fine or coarse
with increasing severity), presence at rest, standing (posture), or movement or performance of specific tasks
(intention), The degree of tremor (amplitude) is often
variable, and can be exacerbated with emotional (anxiety)
and physical activity and stimulant drugs (e.g., caffeine).
The two main types of tremor are known to occur either
at rest or with action. Rest tremor describes an involuntary, rhythmic oscillation of a body part completely supported against gravity. This tremor could be seen in a leg
with the animal lying down and not supporting weight.
Action tremor occurs during voluntary contraction of
skeletal muscle and is classified as postural, kinetic, isometric or task‐specific. Kinetic tremor describes oscillation during guided voluntary movement, also known as
an intentional tremor, and is the most common type seen
with cerebellar disease in small animals.

Fasciculations and Myokimia

Muscle fasciculations are spontaneous contractions of
muscle fibers within a motor unit and arise from ectopic
electrical activity in the distal axons. Fasciculations typically are the manifestation of irritability of the neuronal
cell body (motor neuron) or its accompanying axons. As
such, they are most often associated with motor neuron
disease and peripheral nerve disorders. Fasciculations can
be more readily observed in the distal appendicular muscles and the tongue but can be difficult to detect in more

Essential Tremors

Physiologic and essential tremor syndromes are the
most common in people and can occur in older dogs, in

769

VetBooks.ir

770

Section 8 Neurologic Disease

particular aging terrier breeds. In dogs, it is a pure clinical syndrome characterized by progressive action tremor
of pelvic limbs, starting with posture that worsens with
activity and excitement. Severity can range from barely
perceptible tremor to altered gait and balance problems.
Signs can progress as the dog ages.
Tremor Associated with Neuromuscular Disease

Tremor attributed to weakness is almost always associated with underlying nerve disease. Most likely, this type
of tremor is an exaggeration of the normal physiologic
tremor that results from the synchronized discharge of
enlarged motor units in patients with a reduced number
of surviving motor neurons. Dogs with advanced peripheral neuropathies can present with this type of tremor in
the pelvic limbs. The tremor is exaggerated after exercise
and while standing. Other conditions that directly affect
nerve function with this type of tremor include compressive neuropathy from lumbosacral disk disease or stenosis, nerve sheath tumors, and other mass effects or
entrapment syndromes involving the nerve.
Drug‐Induced Tremors

Drug‐induced tremor has been reported in the cat and
dog. Predictable tremor can be seen with stimulant toxicity (e.g., caffeine, amphetamines, cocaine, etc.). Other
potential drugs that have induced tremor in humans
include valproic acid, amiodarone, procainamide, and
lithium. Tardive dyskinesia represents a wide variety of
involuntary movements in humans, including chorea,
dystonia, akathisia, myoclonus, tremor, and stereotypies.
Stereotypy, or rhythmic involuntary movements, is the
most common manifestation resulting from exposure to
dopamine receptor‐blocking agents, such as phenothiazine (e.g., acepromazine) or antiemetic drugs (e.g.,
metoclopramide).
Cerebellar‐Related Tremors

By far the most common cause of tremor in small animals is cerebellar syndromes and disease. Cerebellar diseases are often associated with a conglomeration of signs
related to abnormal motor activity to include any or all of
the following: tremors, bilaterally symmetric ataxia without paresis, dysmetria, vestibular signs (head tilt, nystagmus, falling), absent menace with preservation of vision,
and pupillary changes. An altered resting posture is often
present, with affected animals demonstrating truncal
ataxia (swaying of the body back and forth or side to side)
and compensatory broad‐based stance for balance,
known at titubation (cerebellar postural tremor).
Cerebellar tremors are associated with diffuse cerebellar
cortical diseases. These intention tremors are characterized by a fine head tremor that worsens with initiation
of voluntary head movements. The more acute‐onset

diseases affecting the cerebellar cortex usually result in
more pronounced tremor disturbances. Severe action‐
related tremors may affect the entire body, with complete loss of all muscular coordination, and failure to
posture and prehend food. Ensuing hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, and related complications from continuous
muscle activity require that these patients be aggressively
treated on an emergency basis (see later). Fortunately,
many “pure” cerebellar diseases can be treated and/or
compensated for by the patient.
Cerebellar syndromes associated with tremor can be
divided into congenital and acquired diseases (see
Box 70.2). Congenital neonatal syndromes represent diseases of the newborn animal in which the clinical signs
are present from birth and nonprogressive. In contrast,
the clinical signs of congenital postnatal diseases begin
in the pediatric animal after birth and are slowly progressive. Acquired cerebellar diseases can be either acute or
chronic in onset, with rapid progression most commonly
seen with inflammatory diseases and toxic exposures
(e.g., mycotoxins, metaldehyde, macadamia nuts).
Diagnosis
The diagnostic approach to an animal with AIMs starts
with an evaluation of whether the movement disorder is
hyperknetic, hypokinetic or paroxysmal (Figure 70.2).
The next step is to determine if the animal exhibits any
signs of tremor of the head, neck or other areas of the
body. Animals without tremor should then be evaluated
for signs of excessive rigidity or stiffness. Constant extensor muscle rigidity is more likely to be a sign of tetanus,
while variable extensor muscle rigidity is associated with
tetany. An initial metabolic evaluation of a complete
blood count, serum chemistry panel, ionized calcium,
and creatine kinase should be performed. Tetanus is
diagnosed predominantly on clinical signs and history,
while tetany is diagnosed typically on the presence of
hypocalcemia or other metabolic disorder.
If no extensor muscle rigidity is detected, then signs of
abnormal muscle movement of myotonia, fasciculation,
or myokimia should be suspected. These signs are all
indicators of underlying neuromuscular disease, and as
such merit further specific diagnostic testing for either
peripheral neuropathy or myopathy. Again, an initial
metabolic evaluation of a complete blood count, serum
chemistry panel, ionized calcium, and creatine kinase
should be performed. The next level of testing would be
electrodiagnostic evaluation with electromyography and
nerve conduction testing. Electromyography (EMG)
tests the stability of the muscle membrane.
If tremor is present as part of the history or clinical
examination, then the next step is to determine if any
paresis is present. Care must be taken not to confuse

weakness with falling from incoordination. A reliable
test is to hop an animal on each leg individually to see if
it will collapse on that leg during testing. A weak animal
will not be able to support weight on that limb, while an
uncoordinated one will. If paresis is present, then one
should consider either a multifocal or noncerebellar central nervous system disease. A history of possible toxicity

advanced testing. If the metabolic evaluation is normal
as stated above, then a MRI scan of the brain and/or spinal cord with possible cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis
is warranted to evaluate for the underlying etiology.
If paresis is not present with the tremor syndrome,
then it is most likely that the animal is suffering from a
pure cerebellar disease process. Acute onset of clinical
signs is now more suggestive of either a toxic reaction or
inflammatory disease process. If toxicity is documented,
then no further diagnostic testing may be needed, and
symptomatic therapy can be instituted. If toxicity cannot
be documented, then a CSF analysis is recommended. If
the CSF is normal, then MRI scanning of the brain may
be necessary. If the disease process is more chronic and
progressive in nature, then the patient should be evaluated for a possible mass lesion of the cerebellum with an
MRI scan prior to collection of CSF for analysis.

Treatment
The goal for the control of tremors in small animals is
to determine the etiology, remove any inciting cause
(toxin or iatrogenic), and provide immediate and
­prolonged symptomatic relief for acquired diseases.
A number of treatments for essential tremor have
been proposed for people, with varying results. First‐
line treatments useful in the dog include phenobarbital at 2.5 mg/kg PO BID, or a beta‐adrenergic
antagonist (propranolol 2.5–10 mg PO BID to TID).
Benzodiaze­pines appear not be effective in humans or
dogs (personal experience). Topiramate, has recently
been shown to be efficacious in refractory essential
tremor cases in humans at a dose range of 100–200
mg/day.
Recommended emergency treatment for acute onset
of suspected acquired tremor disease should be based
on an IV loading dose of diazepam or midazolam at 0.5
mg/kg IV followed by constant‐rate infusion (CRI) of
either drug at 0.5 mg/kg/h in 0.9% saline at 1.5 times the
maintenance fluid rate. This situation can be life‐threatening and requires a rapid therapeutic approach.
Adjuvant therapy to stabilize hyperthermia should be
given.

Disorders of the Forebrain
Sam N. Long, BVSc, PhD, DipECVN
Centre for Animal Referral and Emergency, Melbourne, Australia

­Anatomy/Function
The forebrain, also known as the prosencephalon,
encompasses the two cerebral hemispheres, together
with the diencephalon (the most rostral part of the brainstem, itself consisting of the thalamus, hypothalamus,
and epithalamus). It is regarded as a region of the brain
separate from the rest of the brainstem because it is
separated in part by the tentorium cerebelli from the
other main compartment within the cranial vault, the
caudal fossa. In addition, the forebrain is responsible for
those functions in both animals and humans which are
commonly thought of as the “higher” functions: memory, behavior, personality, learning, and integration. It is
the forebrain that receives information from the outside
world, integrates it with memory and other functions,
makes decisions based on this information and predicts
the outcomes of those decisions in order to select the
most appropriate one. Anatomically, this occurs within
what are known as the association areas. Rather than
being a distinct area of the brain, the association areas
are a dense, interconnecting network of interneurons
with short axons and widespread dendrites that essentially have no beginning and no end. In dogs and cats, the
association areas represent approximately 20% of the
cerebral cortex compared with approximately 85% in
humans.
The other main areas within the cerebral cortex are the
projection areas. These regions are the primary sensory
and motor cortex (responsible for receiving sensation
and generating motor program output), the primary visual
and auditory centers (for receiving vision and hearing),
and the rhinencephalon (responsible for receiving
olfactory information – evolutionarily this is the most
primitive part of the brain).

Sitting between and below the cerebral hemispheres,
and connecting them to the rest of the brainstem, is the
diencephalon. The most important functional components of the diencephalon are the thalamus, a major
gateway for all information entering and leaving the
cortex, and the hypothalamus, which houses higher
control over the major endocrine systems such as the
pituitary–adrenal axis and thyroid function, amongst
others, as well as regulating temperature, appetite, and
sodium homeostasis.
The clinical significance of these anatomic structures
is that disorders affecting the forebrain result in the
clinical signs detailed in Table 71.1.

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Lesions within the forebrain can arise as one of a number
of pathologic processes, often categorized using the
DAMNIT‐V system (Degenerative, Anomalous, Metabolic,
Neoplastic/Nutritional, Inflammatory, Traumatic/Toxic
and Vascular). A complete list of differential diagnoses is
provided in Box 71.1.
It is important to note that clinical signs are dependent
not on the nature of the lesion/disease, but on where it
arises (and how rapidly). A patient presenting with signs
of right‐sided forebrain disease (e.g., circling, unilateral
blindness in the left eye with normal pupillary light
reflexes, left‐sided proprioceptive deficits) may be
­suffering from any one of the following diagnoses: an
ischemic infarct, a primary brain tumor, granulomatous
meningoencephalitis, or a bacterial abscess. For this reason, details of history and signalment are extremely
important to collect since they provide the only way of
narrowing this list of differentials.

­Degenerative and
Developmental Causes
Storage Diseases
There are a large number of diseases caused by congenital
deficiencies in the enzymatic pathways that are involved
in degrading lysosomal waste products within cells. The
biochemical pathways involved are complex but the
majority of described storage diseases involve a deficiency of a lysosomal acid hydrolase enzyme. A deficiency
in any one enzyme leads to a build‐up of undegraded
products within lysosomes in the cell’s cytoplasm which
ultimately enlarge and cause the death of the cell.
Although cells in all body organs are affected, neurons are
especially vulnerable since they are postmitotic, permanent cells. Most of these conditions affect young animals
at early ages, affect both males and females, and are
autosomal recessively inherited. Most commonly, the initial clinical signs are referable to cerebellar dysfunction
but two in particular, alpha‐fucosidosis and ceroid lipofuscinosis, may show up with signs of forebrain disease
initially, including behavioral changes, dullness and vision
abnormalities (typically abnormal depth of vision or inability to focus rather than blindness), followed by generalized ataxia, dementia, tetraparesis, tremors, and seizures.
Affected breeds include border collies, Tibetan terriers,
English setters (ceroid lipofuscinosis), and springer spaniels (alpha‐fucosidosis).
In alpha‐fucosidosis, the diagnosis can occasionally be
made on hematologic examination (40% of lymphocytes
may have cytoplasmic vacuoles) or genetic testing. In
ceroid lipofuscinosis, skin biopsy and demonstration of
autofluorescent pigment may confirm the diagnosis.
Imaging studies and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) taps are
typically normal and CSF may be normal or show vacuolated macrophages (alpha‐fucosidosis). Generally, these
diseases are progressive and nontreatable, with death
occurring by the second or third year of life, although
gene therapy has been shown to reverse clinical signs in
a feline model of alpha‐mannosidosis, suggesting gene
therapy may one day become available.
L2‐Hydroxyglutaric Aciduria
This is a poorly characterized condition reported over
the past 10 years in young to middle‐aged Staffordshire
terriers. Initially reported in the UK, the disease has now
been seen worldwide. Clinical indications include vague
prosencephalic signs – abnormal behavior, anxiety, difficulty/slowness in learning (owners may describe these
dogs as dull), and an abnormal, ataxic gait (difficult to
localize). Signs may also include seizures in some cases.
The onset of the condition is from 6 months onwards,

Figure 71.1 Histopathology of the cerebellum of a dog with L2‐
hydroxyglutaric aciduria. Note the vacuoles in the Purkinje cell layer
and molecular layer as well as the deep cerebellar white matter.

with both males and females affected and with some
dogs presenting in middle age.
The condition is caused by an inborn error of metabolism leading to widespread vacuolation within neurons
in the brain with excess secretion of L2‐hydroxyglutaric
acid in the urine (organic acid). Diagnosis may be
suggested by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) finding
(lack of distinction between gray and white matter on
T2‐weighted MRI scans with diffuse cerebral atrophy)
and demonstration of excess organic acid in the urine,
and genetic testing is now available (Figure 71.1). Overall,
the long‐term prognosis is guarded as the condition is
untreatable but some dogs with mild signs may live a
relatively normal life if seizures are controlled with anticonvulsant medication.

­Anomalous Causes
Hydrocephalus
Hydrocephalus is a pathologic enlargement of the ventricles as distinct from ventriculomegaly which describes
enlargement of the ventricles which may or may not be
pathologic (there is considerable breed‐related variation
in ventricular size, with brachycephalic dogs such as
boxers and bulldogs often having larger ventricles than
other breeds). True hydrocephalus may occur due to
obstruction in the ventricular system (obstructive or
noncommunicating form; most common) or overproduction of CSF from tumors of the arachnoid granulations
and choroid plexus (nonobstructive or communicating
hydrocephalus; less common).

775

VetBooks.ir

776

Section 8 Neurologic Disease

Causes of obstruction may be either congenital (stenosis of the mesencephalic aqueduct, failure of opening of
the lateral apertures of the fourth ventricle) or acquired
(secondary to inflammatory disease or neoplasia or other
cysts obstructing part of the system). Dilation of the ventricular system upstream of the obstruction results in
clinical signs. In mature animals with acquired hydrocephalus, the cause may not be determinable and is often
presumed to be the result of clinically inapparent inflammation or hemorrhage within the ventricular system.
Enlargement of the ventricular system can also occur
with age – as the cerebral cortex tissue volume decreases,
so ventricles get larger to take up the extra space available (this is also known as hydrocephalus ex vacuo).
Clinical signs predominantly refer to the area affected,
most commonly the forebrain but potentially also hindbrain if the fourth ventricle is affected. Seizures,
behavioral changes, cortical blindness, dullness, head
pressing, and circling are all reported in association
with this condition. Occasionally vestibular signs are
also present. Diagnosis requires imaging – either MRI
or CT, or ultrasound in dogs where an open fontanelle is
present for placement of the ultrasound probe. This
applies to congenital cases in particular, and often the
skull is abnormally large and dome‐shaped with divergent strabismus as a result of displacement of the orbits.
On all imaging modalities, the lateral ventricles appear
abnormally enlarged, and in congenital cases a very thin
rim of cerebral cortex may surround these (Figure 71.2).
Depending on the level of obstruction, the third and/or

fourth ventricle and mesencephalic aqueduct may also
be enlarged. MRI may reveal the presence of increased
fluid signal (on T2‐weighted or FLAIR scans) in the
periventricular tissue if the development of the hydrocephalus is acute. The septum pellucidum which
­normally separates the lateral ventricles on midline may
be absent.
Treatment is either medical or surgical; reasonable
long‐term management is possible with corticosteroid
therapy at antiinflammatory doses. Carbonic anhydrase
inhibitors have also been used in acute stages of disease
but cause significant electrolyte disturbances in the long
term so are not recommended for chronic management.
Recently, some authors have described omeprazole in
some cases of acquired hydrocephalus based on experimental studies that suggest it may reduce CSF production by 26% but no evidence supports its use in dogs with
hydrocephalus. Surgical treatment is also commonly
performed which involves placement of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt via a small craniotomy which transfers
fluid via a one‐way, pressure‐sensitive valve into the
abdominal cavity for absorption by mesentery.
Long‐term prognosis is generally good, with approximately 75% of cases improving or resolving following
shunt placement. However, up to 22% may require subsequent revision to deal with blockage or infection which
are common complications

­Metabolic Causes
Hepatic and Uremic Encephalopathy

Figure 71.2 Dorsal plane CT scan of the brain of a dog with
obstructive hydrocephalus. Note the extreme paucity of cerebral
cortex.

The pathogenesis of hepatic encephalopathy (HE) is
poorly understood. Hepatic insufficiency from a number
of causes, including acute liver failure, chronic liver
failure (including cirrhosis), congenital portosystemic
shunts and congenital urea cycle enzyme abnormalities,
can all result in secondary prosencephalic disease. As a
consequence, various substances pass from the portal
circulation directly into the systemic circulation without
undergoing detoxification. These include ammonia
(probably integral to the pathogenesis of dysfunction),
various amino acids (especially the aromatic amino acids
phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan), short‐chain fatty
acids, mercaptan and various biogenic amines, indoles
and skatoles, incriminated in causing HE. Increased intracellular osmolality from too‐rapid glutamine accumulation (ammonia is metabolized by astrocytes to glutamine)
may result in cerebral edema, which also may play a role
in development of cerebral hyperemia and increased
intracranial pressure. Glutamine, short‐chain fatty acids,
aromatic amino acids, and mercaptans are sodium/
potassium ATPase inhibitors.

VetBooks.ir

71 Disorders of the Forebrain

Other theories pertaining to the pathogenesis of HE
include perturbed monoamine neurotransmission as a
result of altered plasma amino acid metabolism; imbalance between excitatory amino acid neurotransmission
(glutamate) and inhibitory amino acid neurotransmission (gamma‐aminobutyric acid, GABA); and increased
cerebral concentration of an endogenous benzodiazepine‐like substance.
Clinical signs relate to prosencephalic disease:
behavioral changes (vocalizing, aggression), dullness,
ataxia, circling, aimless wandering, blindness, seizures,
and head pressing. In severe cases this can progress to
stupor or coma. Diagnosis is made on biochemistry
panels together with pre‐ and postprandial bile acid
tolerance tests. Ammonia levels can also be measured
but are very labile and should only be relied on if quality control standards associated with performing the
test are high. If imaging studies are performed, MRI
may show (precontrast) T1‐weighted hyperintensities
in the caudate nucleus, amgydala and hippocampus
and/or cingulate gyrus. Treatment is directed at the
underlying hepatic disease. Ligation of portosystemic
shunts (or coil embolism) is the treatment of choice for
animals with congenital shunts.
It is also important to note that when treating animals
with seizures secondary to hepatic insufficiency, anticonvulsants that are metabolized by the liver should be
avoided (e.g., phenobarbitone, diazepam). Potassium
bromide or levetiracetam are preferable as first‐line
therapy. In addition, animals that have portosystemic
shunts ligated may develop seizures shortly postoperatively, for reasons that are poorly understood (and independent of whether the patient has HE prior to shunt
ligation). Various causes have been postulated, including
the existence of endogenous benzodiazepine‐like ligands
within the brain of these patients. These seizures are frequently very difficult to control if they occur; potassium
bromide at 100 mg/kg PO QID for 24 hours followed by
30 mg/kg PO SID dosing has been recommended but is
not always effective, and levetiracetam has also been
proposed as a useful treatment. Propofol constant‐rate
infusions (CRIs) have also been reported to be effective.
In addition to HE, a rare encephalopathy associated
with end‐stage renal disease is also reported, with clinical
signs including depression or stupor, seizures, muscle
fasciculations, and myoclonic head‐bobbing movements.
The diagnosis is usually straightforward, with profound
uremia evident on biochemistry panels, usually with
accompanying hyperphosphatemia. The underlying
cause is unknown, with suggested mechanisms including
depressed cerebral oxygen consumption, cerebral
hypoxia, increased brain calcium levels, and increased
blood levels of parathyroid hormone (PTH). In experimental uremia, the electroencephalogram (EEG) changes

associated with disease can be abolished if parathyroidectomy is performed before induction of uremia.
Prognosis is poor as a result of the underlying renal disease but treatment with calcitriol (1.5–3.4 ng/kg/day
PO) can reduce signs of neurologic depression in animals
with chronic uremia, as long as phosphate levels are normal to prevent renal mineralization.
Electrolyte Disturbances
Hypoglycemia

There are two main causes for hypoglycemia: insulin‐
secreting tumors (insulinomas) of the pancreas, and
overdosage of diabetic patients with insulin (especially
when not eating). Young puppies (less than 3 months of
age) are also prone to hypoglycemia in association with
cold, starvation or gastrointestinal (GI) disease, and
hypoglycemia may also be seen in animals with portosystemic shunts. Clinical signs associated with hypoglycemia include behavioral changes, weakness, ataxia,
collapse, transient blindness, and seizures. Signs are
often intermittent, becoming more frequent as the disease progresses, and may be associated with periods of
fasting, exercise or excitement. Rarely, polyneuropathies
may also occur with hypoglycemia; tetraparesis/plegia,
facial nerve signs, hyporeflexia, and hypotonia are the
most commonly seen signs associated with these. Central
nervous system (CNS) signs occur because neurons are
unable to synthesize or store glucose and rely almost
entirely on glucose derived from the blood.
Diagnosis of hypoglycemia secondary to insulinoma
requires demonstration of hypoglycemia in a fasting
blood sample, together with elevated insulin levels (from
paired samples). Treatment is directed at removing the
underlying cause of hypoglycemia plus administration of
dextrose solutions (5%). In animals with inoperable
insulinomas, prednisolone and diazoxide can be used
but the prognosis is guarded to poor, with survival of
90 days only (vs 12–14 months for resectable tumors).
Sodium Abnormalities

Neurologic signs may be seen in association with both
hypernatremia and hyponatremia.
Hypernatremia

Hypernatremia occurs with sodium >156 mEq/L (dogs)
or >161 mEq/L (cats). Causes include:
●●

excess water loss: diabetes insipidus (central or nephrogenic), burns, fever, osmotic diuresis (acute/chronic
renal failure, diabetes mellitus, diuretics, or IV solute
administration such as mannitol, glucose or urea),
osmotic diarrhea (lactulose therapy, malabsorption
syndromes, infectious enteritides), hot weather

777

VetBooks.ir

778

Section 8 Neurologic Disease

excess salt intake: salt poisoning, administration of IV
hypertonic solutions (NaCl), sodium bicarbonate, or
saline emetics
●● insufficient water intake: lack of access, inability to
drink, CNS disease resulting in primary adipsia (absence
of thirst), mental depression, congenital adipsia.
●●

Marked hypernatremia may induce cerebral signs,
such as depression, weakness, irritability, uncharacteristic aggression, confusion, propulsive circling, dementia, seizures, coma, and death as the result of cellular
dehydration of neurons. Neurologic signs may not
occur until serum Na levels exceed 170–175 mEq/L
(>350 mOsm/kg), although the severity of neurologic
signs depends especially on the rate of increase, with
signs being most severe in animals with rapidly developing hyperosmolality.
Treatment depends on the rate at which hypernatremia
develops; overrapid correction can lead to worsening
clinical signs (due to a relative hyponatremia and movement of water from the vascular spaces into the brain).
Replacement of the water deficit should be undertaken
using 5% dextrose with the aim of correction of the deficit
over 24 hours (or longer). In animals with acute‐onset
hypernatremia, correction of Na levels at a rate of 1.0
mEq/h is acceptable. However, if the hypernatremia is
more chronic, Na levels should not be allowed to change
at more than 0.5 mEq/h. In animals with excess salt
intake, diuretics should be given in conjunction with fluid
therapy to avoid pulmonary edema.
Hyponatremia

Hyponatremia occurs when serum Na levels are less than
146 mEq/L in dogs (151 mEq/L in cats). Hyponatremia
can be further divided into true hyponatremia (associated with total body water in excess of Na – serum osmolality is low, <290 mOsm/L) and pseudohyponatremia
(low Na with normal or increased serum osmolality).
Clinical signs of hyponatremia relate primarily to the
rate of onset of hyponatremia. In acute hyponatremia,
sodium levels within the brain are relatively normal
while sodium levels within the vascular spaces are low.
Water flows down its concentration gradient into the
brain, producing cerebral edema and raised intracranial
pressure (ICP). Signs include generalized weakness,
depression, stupor, coma, seizures, and dementia.
Treatment is aimed at increasing sodium levels: use
hypertonic saline (3–5%) when serum Na <115 mEq/L.
The Na deficit is calculated using:
Defect mEq /l

140 measured Na

bodyweight kg

0.3

The replacement fluid should be given slowly over
12–24 hours. For animals with hypovolemic hyponatremia, normal isotonic saline can be used. For animals

with normovolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia
associated with excessive water intake or renal retention, water restriction (i.e., limiting water intake to less
than urine output) can be performed. In instances where
severe neurologic signs are seen associated with normal
or excessive intravascular fluid, frusemide (2–4 mg/kg
IV) can be used to promote renal water excretion.
Chronic hyponatremia may be more difficult to treat
since overrapid correction of the deficit can result in a
worsening of clinical signs associated with central pontine myelinolysis. Lesions appear in white matter
associated with death of oligodendrocytes and loss of
myelin, resulting in bilaterally symmetric lesions in the
pons and rarely (10% of cases) thalamus, subthalamic
nuclei, striatum, internal capsule, amygdala, lateral
geniculate body, white matter of the cerebellum and deep
layers of the cerebral cortex. The postulated hypothesis
is that with chronicity, cells within the brain extrude
intracellular electrolytes followed by organic osmolytes
(“idiogenic osmoles”), in order to reduce the risk of brain
edema. When sodium is replaced intravascularly as part
of fluid therapy, osmotic attraction of water out of cells
in the brain results in dehydration of brain tissue. Clinical
signs occur several days after fluid treatment: ataxia,
weakness, hypermetria, visual deficits, depressed menace response (with normal pupillary light response
[PLR]), reduced proprioception, exaggerated licking
movements, episodic myoclonus, whole‐body spasms,
obtundation, and tetraparesis. Prognosis for recovery is
reasonable; in one study of two dogs, one died but the
other recovered over 4–7 weeks. As a result, it is important to stick to the guideline of replacing Na at a rate no
greater than 0.5 mEq/L/h.

­Neoplastic Causes
Brain Tumors
Tumors affecting the brain can arise as one of several
forms.
Primary tumors arise from cells and structures of the
brain itself.
●● Secondary tumors arise from cells and structures adjacent to the brain.
●● Metastatic tumors arise from spread of a tumor at a
distant site.
●●

The most common tumors that affect dogs (and humans)
are primary tumors. They occur with a slightly greater incidence than in people (14–15 per 100 000 dogs vs 8–9 per
100 000 people at risk). The most common types include:
●●
●●

meningiomas
astrocytomas

VetBooks.ir

71 Disorders of the Forebrain

oligodendrogliomas
choroid plexus papillomas
●● pituitary macroadenomas
●● ependymomas
●● primitive neuroectodermal tumors (PNETs).
●●
●●

Meningiomas are the most common brain tumors seen
in both dogs and cats (approximately 45% of all primary brain tumors in dogs). They are thought to arise
from arachnoid cap cells of the meninges and occur
anywhere along a meningeal surface (e.g., cerebral convexity, falx cerebri, at the cerebellopontine angle, in the
olfactory lobe), or within a ventricle. They can occur as a
discrete focal mass, as an en plaque form or with large
cystic components within them. On imaging, they have a
broad‐based dural attachment and are often associated
with hyperostosis of the overlying bone (approximately
50% of the time in cats). Contrast enhancement is typically homogenous. Noncontrast‐enhancing areas associated with necrosis are not uncommon in dogs.
Histopathologically, they appear benign; in cats, they are
often well encapsulated and removable surgically but in
dogs tend to creep into the Virchow‐Robin spaces
­surrounding meningeal vessels so microscopic disease
usually remains after debulking.
Astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas together are
often referred to as gliomas. Astrocytomas are thought
to arise from an astrocyte precursor cell while oligodendrogliomas are thought to arise from an oligodendrocyte
precursor, although this is by no means certain. They
occur with approximately equal frequency – approximately 17% and 14% of all primary brain tumors in dogs,
respectively. Astrocytomas in humans are graded using a
four‐grade classification scheme created by the World
Health Organization, WHO Grade I being a very small
subset (pilocytic astrocytomas), grade II encompassing
most astrocytomas, Grade III anaplastic astrocytoma,
and Grade IV glioblastoma multiforme.
Oligodendrogliomas may occur more frequently in
boxers and more commonly in periventricular white matter. They can also spread along CSF pathways. Imaging
features of both types suggest an intraaxial tumor (arising
from within the brain tissue). On MRI, oligodendrogliomas are frequently hypointense on T1‐weighted scans
and hyperintense on T2‐weighted scans, as befitting their
gross mucinous appearance. Astrocytomas tend to be
more solid in appearance on imaging with greater and
more heterogenous contrast uptake.
Choroid plexus papillomas arise from the choroid
plexus of the lateral, third or fourth ventricles. Since they
arise from essentially a collection of blood vessels, they
tend to enhance very strongly and uniformly following
contrast administration on imaging studies. Most are
histologically benign but a few can be anaplastic (choroid

plexus carcinoma). They can also seed along CSF pathways and implant in other parts of the neuraxis.
Pituitary macroadenomas arise from the hypophyseal
stalk and expand dorsally into the thalamus/hypothalamus, and on imaging appearance commonly look like
“mushroom clouds.”
Ependymomas and PNETs occur relatively uncommonly; ependymomas arise from ependymal cells lining
the ventricular system, whilst the PNET’s origin is currently unknown.
Secondary tumors most commonly include adenocarcinomas arising from the nasal epithelium and invading
the brain, and osteosarcomas, fibrosarcomas or multilobulated tumors of bone arising from the skull that
compress the brain.
Metastatic tumors arise from tumors that spread hematogenously (since there is no lymphatic drainage within
the brain). Common candidates include lymphoma, metastatic carcinoma (from mammary gland, lung, and GI
tract, most commonly) and hemangiosarcoma.
Histiocytic sarcoma can also occur in the brain (both as a
metastatic tumor and as a primary brain tumor).
Clinical signs associated with tumors reflect their site
of origin. In the case of meningiomas, it is common for
tumors to have been present for several months before
the onset of clinical signs as these tumors grow slowly,
allowing the brain to accommodate. Tumors arising in
the prosencephalon often cause seizures and cortical
blindness. Seizures without interictal abnormalities may
be seen with tumors arising on the ventral midline or in
the rostral parts of the prosencephalon.
Diagnosis requires either MRI or computed tomography (CT) scanning. CSF taps may show albuminocytologic dissociation (increased protein with normal cell
counts) in tumors with significant necrosis, and very
occasionally may reveal neoplastic cells (with lymphoma
most commonly, but also metastatic carcinomas and
very occasionally with oligodendrogliomas or choroid
plexus papillomas).
Treatment requires surgical debulking (where location allows) followed by irradiation with megavoltage
sources. Typical hyperfractionated dose schedules
include 2–3 Gy daily doses up to a maximum of approximately 50 Gy. Survival times in dogs are reported to
approach a median of two years, with some patients living three or four years following diagnosis. At present,
there is little evidence to support different treatment
modalities for different tumor types, with the exception
of meningiomas in cats, for whom surgical debulking
alone often results in survival times of up to 4–5 years.
However, in people some tumor types (particularly oligodendrogliomas) are chemosensitive, associated with particular patterns of genetic rearrangements in these tumors
(loss of heterozygosity of the short arm of chromosome

779

VetBooks.ir

780

Section 8 Neurologic Disease

1 and the long arm of chromosome 19) and it may be
that in the future the same features may be identified in
canine oligodendrogliomas.

­Nutritional Causes
Thiamine Deficiency
Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency occurs sporadically in
dogs and cats either if commercial rations are naturally
low in thiamine or if food is treated with excessive heat
or sulfites/sulfur dioxide preservatives. One recent
report also describes a series of cats fed a commercial
dry‐food diet without any obvious problems in formulation. All‐fish diets in particular are a risk factor since
many species of fish contain thiaminases. Thiamine is
essential for carbohydrate metabolism (especially glucose) via the Krebs cycle and deficiency leads to increased
levels of pyruvate and lactate, together with reduced red
blood cell transketolase activity. The brain is particularly
susceptible since it is dependent on glucose or lactate‐
pyruvate for energy.
Clinical signs of thiamine deficiency include anorexia,
vomiting, depression, wide‐based hindlimb stance,
ataxia, progressive paraparesis, crouching hindlimb
gait, torticollis, head ventroflexion, circling, generalized
tonic‐clonic seizures, weakness, opisthotonus, coma,
and death. Proprioceptive and menace deficits may be
seen, along with tremors and occasionally nystagmus.
Some dogs show signs of hysteria. In cats, vestibular
signs, head tremors, dilated poorly responsive pupils
and absent menace response are common. With severe
lesions, semicoma, persistent crying, opisthotonus, limb
spasticity, and death may occur. Lesions consist of polioencephalomalacia, bilaterally symmetric in periventricular gray matter, brainstem nuclei (the red nucleus
and vestibular nuclei are commonly affected), cerebellar
peduncles, and cerebral cortex.
Treatment requires prompt administration of thiamine hydrochloride 25–50 mg/day IM in dogs (10–20
mg IM cats) over several days. Complete remission of
clinical signs usually occurs if treatment is initiated
promptly, although some cats have been reported to
have residual visual and proprioceptive deficits.

­Inflammatory/Idiopathic Causes
Noninfectious Inflammatory Diseases
Meningoencephalomyelitis of Unknown Origin

Meningoencephalomyelitis of unknown origin (MUO)
in the dog comprises a variety of conditions that are
thought to be immune mediated in nature and which

involve inflammation of the brain, meninges, and/or
spinal cord. MUO is the umbrella term used to encompass granulomatous meningoencephalomyelitis (GME),
necrotizing leukoencephalitis (NLE), and necrotizing
meningoencephalitis (NME). GME is an angiocentric,
mixed lymphoid, infiltrative process that predominantly
affects the CNS white matter and leptomeninges. The
clinical signs of all these conditions vary depending on
those parts of the nervous system where the lesions are
most severe. Commonly, however, the clinical picture is
one of multifocal, asymmetric, intracranial disease seen
in a young to middle‐aged (or older) small‐breed dog.
Granulomatous Meningoencephalitis

Three forms of GME have been described based on morphologic and clinical characteristics: disseminated, focal,
and ocular. The disseminated form typically manifests
with acute onset of rapidly progressive clinical signs suggestive of a multifocal CNS disorder whereas focal GME
is associated with clinical signs suggestive of a single
space‐occupying mass with an insidious onset and slowly
progressive course. The ocular form of GME manifests
with acute onset of visual impairment and dilated nonresponsive pupils caused by optic neuritis. Dogs with the
ocular form can subsequently develop CNS lesions.
The cause of GME is unknown, with immune‐mediated,
infectious, and neoplastic causes proposed as possible
etiologies. Historically, GME was once classified within a
group of conditions known as reticulosis, the neoplastic
form of which has since been reclassified as B cell lymphoma occurring within the brain, suggesting that
there are features of the disease which are common to
cancer. Other investigations have focused on the nature
of the immune system attack on the brain which appears
to be similar to a delayed‐type hypersensitivity and
which involves antibodies directed at astrocytes. So far,
efforts to identify an underlying infectious trigger for the
immune response have been unsuccessful.
Necrotizing Leukoencephalitis and Necrotizing
Meningoencephalitis

Necrotizing leukoencephalitis and NME both started
out as conditions identified in certain breeds, with NLE
being called Yorkshire terrier encephalitis and NME
called pug encephalitis. Since these early reports in
specific breeds, an increasing number of dogs of other
(and mixed) breeds have been identified with these conditions, including Yorkshire terriers with pug encephalitis and vice versa. The necrotizing meningoencephalitides
differ from those in GME in distribution and severity.
Both are characterized by extensive necrosis and nonsuppurative inflammation. In NME, the lesions tend to
involve more of the cerebral gray and subcortical white
matter. The neurologic signs are acute and progressive

VetBooks.ir

71 Disorders of the Forebrain

and reflect a forebrain disorder, with seizures observed
in most dogs. NLE is characterized histologically by multifocal areas of extremely severe mononuclear inflammation surrounding a large malaciac gliotic center,
predominantly affecting the brainstem and periventricular cerebral white matter. Brainstem signs with central
vestibular dysfunction predominate, although a mixture
of forebrain and brainstem signs also occurs.
The etiopathogenesis of GME, NME, and NLE likely is
multifactorial: familial predisposition, infectious agents,
and immunopathologic mechanisms all may play roles in
disease pathogeneses. GME is responsible for up to 25%
of canine CNS disease.
Diagnosis and Treatment

A female predisposition for GME has been reported and
the disease is most common in young to middle‐aged dogs.
Most cases of the necrotizing meningoencephalitides
described so far have occurred in young and adult animals
(6 months to 7 years) with no gender predisposition.
Confirmation of a diagnosis of GME, NME, and NLE
requires histopathologic confirmation, and as such is
infrequently achieved antemortem. Extraneural signs
such as hyperthermia are rare. Blood examination may
be normal or reveal a stress leukogram. CSF findings
include a pure mononuclear pleocytosis or a mixed cell
population (particularly in acute cases), bearing in
mind that cytology cannot discriminate between
immune‐mediated, infectious, and neoplastic considerations for canine meningoencephalitis. Similarly, the
absence of CSF abnormality does not rule out the possibility of GME, particularly in dogs pretreated with
corticosteroids or where the lesions are not in close
proximity to the ventricular system and subarachnoid
space. CSF findings in dogs with NME or NLE reveal a
moderate pleocytosis with mononuclear cells or mixed
cell pleocytosis and mild to marked elevation of protein
concentration.
Imaging findings in MUO are nonspecific but can help
to support the suspected clinical diagnosis. CT scan may
reveal hyperdense lesions after injection of contrast
medium intravenously. Most frequently, the diagnosis is
made following MRI scans. The most consistent MRI
finding in dogs with the multifocal form of GME is the
presence of multiple hyperintense T2‐weighted (T2W)
and fluid‐attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) lesions
scattered throughout the cerebral white matter. Contrast
enhancement may be present and may be strong (occasionally with ring enhancement) or mild. Central nervous system lymphosarcoma and, less commonly, glial
neoplasms and metastatic neoplasia can present with
similar clinical and imaging findings and should therefore be part of the differential diagnosis list. The focal
form of GME presents on CT or MRI as a nonspecific

single space‐occupying mass. The more characteristic
distribution of the lesions observed in breed‐specific
meningoencephalitis (NLE or NME) may aid in the
imaging diagnosis of these conditions.
At present, immunosuppression is the mainstay of
therapy for MUO. Most clinicians treat with corticosteroids together with adjunctive immunosuppression,
although whole‐brain radiation therapy has also shown
promise in the treatment of GME in some cases (supporting the hypothesis that neoplasia might be part of
the etiopathogenesis). Response to corticosteroids
is variable and may be temporary, but dogs often have
a favorable initial response to steroid monotherapy.
Typically, secondary immunomodulatory agents are
added once negative serology and PCR results have
ruled out other disease.
In a clinical setting, steroid monotherapy may resolve
signs associated with MUO in some dogs, but insufficiently or only transiently provides resolution in others.
Most studies suggest that longer survival is achieved
with additional therapy. The most commonly used
additional immunomodulatory drugs include cytosine
arabinoside (CA) at 50 mg/m2 q12h SC for two days
(using a regime that involves therapy initially at three‐
weekly intervals, then reducing to every four weeks,
every five weeks, and continuing every six weeks thereafter), ciclosporin at 5–10 mg/kg q12h PO, procarbazine at 25–50 mg/m2 q24h PO, azathioprine at 2 mg/
kg q24h PO for 14 days before tapering to every other
day, mycophenolate 10–20 mg/kg q12h PO, and leflunomide at 2–4 mg/kg q24h PO. A prednisone/vincristine/cyclophosphamide (COP) protocol has also been
described, although this has not been shown to provide
longer survival than a prednisone/CA protocol and is
associated with more adverse effects. Treatment is
monitored by clinical response and regression of neurologic deficits and occasionally repeated CSF analysis
and MRI.
The prognosis for long‐term remission in proven cases
of GME and the breed‐specific meningoencephalitides
has been reported as being poor. However, such reports
have been limited to histopathologically confirmed cases
of GME that died or were euthanized as a result of the
severity of their disease, so the poor prognosis in these
studies may be biased. Most recent studies have reported
several years survival in dogs with MUO with aggressive
immunosuppression, and potentially cure, although ultimately other side‐effects (predominantly hepatic failure)
may be life‐threatening.
Infectious Diseases
Encephalitis and meningitis often exist concurrently in
dogs and cats with infection of the CNS. Numerous

781

VetBooks.ir

782

Section 8 Neurologic Disease

infectious agents have been incriminated and include
viruses (distemper, rabies, parvovirus, parainfluenza,
herpes, feline leukemia, feline immunodeficiency virus),
bacteria, rickettsia (Ehrlichia, Rocky Mountain spotted
fever), protozoal (Toxoplasma, Neospora), fungi (blastomycosis, histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, aspergillosis,
coccidioidomycosis), and spirochetes (Lyme disease,
leptospirosis). Adding to this list, a number of parasites
have been reported to affect the brain during aberrant
migration (Toxocara, heartworm, Cuterebra larvae) and
the incidence of these depends mainly on geographic
location. CSF and infectious titers or DNA testing
­performed on serum or CSF are the most reliable antemortem diagnostic tests for identifying infectious CNS
diseases.
Canine Distemper Virus Encephalomyelitis

Canine distemper virus (CDV) is a paramyxovirus that
commonly infects the CNS of dogs and other carnivores.
Unvaccinated and vaccinated dogs are at risk for this
disease, and although the prevalence of infection seems
to be decreasing in some countries, sporadic outbreaks
have been reported in several countries, particularly
where vaccination coverage is incomplete. Systemic
signs of disease such as respiratory and gastrointestinal
involvement are reported to precede the neurologic signs
by 2–3 weeks. However, many dogs have no previous
history of disease prior to the onset of neurologic signs.
Many dogs probably develop transient CNS infections
without concurrent clinical signs. Lesions may be found
in gray (polioencephalomyelopathy, PEM) and/or white
matter (leukoencephalomyelopathy, LEM). Since the
lesions are predominantly demyelinating in nature, it has
been proposed as a model for the study of multiple sclerosis. PEM is more frequently seen in immature dogs
while a combination of PEM and LEM is more common
in mature animals.
Infected dogs can present with a variety of neurologic
signs that tend to be progressive. Clinical signs in dogs
with chronic CDV encephalomyelitis may have a chronic
insidious or waxing and waning course, and are often not
associated with systemic signs of CDV. The classic syndrome of distemper myoclonus (repetitive and continual
myoclonic jerks that affect the whole body or just one
body part with a characteristic 1 Hz frequency) can be
pathognomonic.
The diagnosis of CDV can be difficult. CSF analysis is
often the most helpful diagnostic test. However, an
inflammatory response is often lacking in the acute
stage of the disease, with mononuclear pleocytosis
more often observed in the chronic stage.
Immunofluorescent staining of conjunctival tissues,
urine sediment, tracheal wash or CSF leukocytes for
CDV antigen is variably successful, but positive results

are occasionally obtained in dogs with chronic CDV
encephalomyelitis. Identification of neutralizing CDV
antibodies in serum is of questionable value in previously vaccinated dogs, and demonstration of CDV antibodies in CSF can be complicated if CSF is contaminated
with peripheral blood. Several PCR techniques have
been described for the detection of CDV in various tissues and body fluids, some of which are now commercially available, and these can be applied to CSF; this is
probably the most specific and sensitive test for the
antemortem diagnosis of CDV encephalomyelitis
regardless of the clinical form of disease present.
The chronic form of the disease is typically slowly
progressive, although clinical signs may be well tolerated
for long durations. Therapy is mainly supportive and
symptomatic. Overall, prognosis is poor although the
disease is not fatal in all dogs and some may recover.
Feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP)

Two biotypes of feline coronavirus (FCoV) exist: feline
infectious peritonitis virus (FIPV) that causes FIP, and
feline enteric coronavirus (FECV) that induces mild
enteritis from which cats typically recover. FIPV has
been shown to arise within individual patients from a
spontaneous mutation of existing FECV infection. FIP
is a clinical disease that arises due to infection of macrophages by FIPV, which subsequently results in the
immune‐mediated formation of pyogranulomatous
lesions with an affinity for serosal, pleural, uveal,
meningeal, and ependymal membranes (surface‐related
disease).
The neurologic clinical variant of FIP is the most common infectious cause of meningoencephalomyelitis in
the cat, as well as being the most prevalent spinal cord
disease of cats. Although the effusive form is about four
times more common than the noneffusive form, neurologic involvement is more common with the noneffusive
(or “dry”) form of the disease and develops in cats with
humoral immunity, but with partial cell‐mediated
immunity (immunity sufficient to induce granulomatous inflammatory reaction around virus present in
macrophages, but not quite adequate to eliminate the
infection). The pathogenesis involves FIP virus inducing
a pyogranulomatous and immune complex‐mediated
vasculitis involving the meninges, ependymal lining,
periventricular brain tissue, and choroid plexus of the
CNS. As a result, clinical signs most commonly arise as
a result of hydrocephalus secondary to obstruction of
the ventricular pathways.
Cats with FIP are typically young (<3 years of age),
pure‐bred, from multiple cat households and the disease
is more common in sexually intact males. The main
route of infection with FCoV is oronasal from contact with
infected feces. Asymptomatic carriers are not common.

VetBooks.ir

71 Disorders of the Forebrain

Clinical signs most commonly relate to hydrocephalus
and associated forebrain syndrome (seizures, cortical
blindness, obtundation) although central vestibular
signs are often also reported, as the meningitis caused
by FIP may be more severe in the ventral brainstem
and at the base of the cerebellum, and choroid plexitis
and ependymitis are frequently severe in the caudal
fossa.
The diagnosis of FIP is challenging, especially when
signs are restricted to the CNS. Hematology findings
may include anemia, leukocytosis, and hyperglobulinemia. Serum tests for anticoronavirus antibodies have a
low specificity and a negative serum titer does not
exclude the possibility of FIP‐associated neurologic disease because soluble antibodies can form immune complexes and escape detection by standard tests. There is
also considerable overlap in titers in cats with and without FIP (some cats with FIP have low titers, while many
cats with high titers never develop FIP). The CT and MR
abnormalities present in the brains of cats are well
described and include meningeal contrast enhancement,
choroid plexitis (contrast enhancement), ependymitis,
granuloma formation, and obstructive hydrocephalus,
most commonly due to blockage of the mesencephalic
aqueduct. CSF analysis may reveal a predominantly neutrophilic or mixed cell pleocytosis, but can be normal.
CSF total protein concentration is often markedly elevated (>200 mg/dL). Documentation of elevated coronaviral antibody concentrations, especially in cerebrospinal
fluid, confirms exposure and is supportive of the diagnosis. However, this result must be interpreted with respect
to the integrity of the blood–brain barrier. Positive coronavirus‐specific PCR performed on CSF can be used as a
relatively reliable antemortem diagnostic tool.
Treatment of FIP is immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory in nature, but the disease should be
considered terminal in virtually all affected cats.
Corticosteroids, chlorambucil, cyclophosphamide, and
interferons have been used with variable efficacy in FIP
cases.
Protozoal Encephalitis

Toxoplasmosis and neosporosis are polysystemic protozoal diseases capable of causing heterogeneous signs
of peripheral and CNS dysfunction. Natural infection
with Toxoplasma gondii is more common in cats, but
also occurs in dogs. Ingestion of tissue from infected
intermediate hosts (ingestion of encysted bradyzoites)
is the most common cause of infection in both species.
Other forms of infection include fecal contamination
and in utero infection. With Neospora caninum, dogs
are affected, most commonly via in utero transmission,
although they may also be infected by ingestion of
intermediate host tissue.

Following acute systemic infection in intermediate
hosts in which the organism can be disseminated to
many body organs (this phase may be subclinical), tissue
cysts form most commonly in the CNS, skeletal muscle,
and heart muscle. The parasites are mainly intracellular
and subclinical infection may persist for the life of the
host, although activation of toxoplasmosis may occur in
association with severe immunosuppressive disorders.
These protozoal organisms have the potential to cause
an extremely variable number of clinical neurologic syndromes. Two main forms are observed:
encephalomyelitis – neurologic signs associated with
protozoal encephalomyelitis are variable and may
reflect a focal or multifocal disease process
●● Neospora myositis‐polyradiculoneuritis – this is probably the most commonly reported infectious myositis
in dogs and presents with severe pelvic limb paresis
and skeletal muscle fibrosis in young dogs, especially
those less than six months of age.
●●

A tentative antemortem diagnosis of toxoplasmosis is
established in dogs most commonly through elevated
IgM titers, IgG seroconversion, or documentation of a
positive clinical response to an antiprotozoal treatment
regimen. In cats, an elevated serum or CSF IgM titer is
considered diagnostic for toxoplasmosis. However, a
positive titer can be found in animals previously subclinically infected with either organism and demonstration
of a rising titer with serial (monthly) testing may be
required to confirm a diagnosis of active disease.
Neosporosis is diagnosed by serologic detection of indirect fluorescent antibody titers in dogs. Demonstration
of tachyzoites of either organism in various tissues or
body fluids is also diagnostic but rarely achieved. CSF
analysis typically demonstrates pleocytosis with a mixed
population of neutrophils and the presence of small and
large mononuclear cells. Eosinophils may also be seen.
Sensitive PCR assays have been reported for the detection of both Neospora caninum DNA and Toxoplasma
gondii DNA in biological samples. Muscle biopsy is
indicated in dogs with polyneuropathy/polymyositis and
may reveal nonsuppurative inflammation and tachyzoites within myocytes.
Treatment for both diseases is identical. Clindamycin
(10–15 mg/kg PO q812h for a minimum of 12 weeks) is
the preferred therapy. However, TMS (15 mg/kg PO
q12h) in combination with pyrimethamine (1 mg/kg/day
PO) may also be effective. Folic acid or brewer’s yeast
supplementation should be considered (5 mg/dog/day)
in animals receiving this latter therapy. The prognosis for
survival is fair to good, but recovery of neurologic function may be incomplete in those animals with severe
clinical signs. In the author’s experience, some cases may
require long‐term (a year or possibly longer) therapy,

783

VetBooks.ir

784

Section 8 Neurologic Disease

suggesting selective immunodeficiency in some animals
contributing to the presence of infection.
Bacterial Meningoencephalitis

Bacterial infection of the CNS is a relatively rare cause of
encephalitis and/or meningitis in dogs and cats compared
with other species. Bacterial infection of the brain can be
the consequence of hematogenous spread (metastasis
from distant foci of infection), penetrating injury to the
skull (bite wound, bullet, surgery) or direct extension of
infection from the middle/inner ear, eyes or nasal sinuses.
Infection of the CNS may result in an abscess and/or, much
less frequently, collection of pus (empyema) in subdural or
epidural locations. Brain abscesses are life threatening due
to systemic and local toxicity (in the early stages of cerebritis) and increased intracranial pressure (during/after capsule formation). Clinical signs are largely the result of the
inflammatory reaction that the bacteria provoke.
Affected animals can present with a wide variety of
neurologic signs of intracranial disease that reflect a
focal anatomic diagnosis suggesting a space‐occupying
lesion or a multifocal syndrome associated with many
small microabscesses. These signs are usually rapidly
progressive and frequently fatal if left untreated. Fever is
present in approximately 50% of cases at presentation.
Hematology usually reflects an inflammatory process
(leukocytosis with or without left shift) or can be normal.
Imaging of the brain (CT or MRI) may be suggestive of
an inflammatory process and may reveal a defect in the
skull suggestive of a penetrating injury or signs suggestive of otitis media/interna.
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis usually reveals an elevated
nucleated cell count, with the majority of cells being
degenerate neutrophils, and marked elevation in total
protein concentration. Bacteria may be visible in the spinal fluid. In some cases, CSF can be normal or may show
nonspecific inflammatory changes. CSF should be cultured if it contains degenerate neutrophils although it is
uncommon for culture to be positive. Urine and blood
culture should also be considered in animals in which
there is no obvious source of infection.
Treatment of abscesses centers around antibiotic therapy, often for long periods, based on culture and drug
sensitivity testing of organisms isolated from the abscess.
When cultures cannot be obtained, a broad‐spectrum
antibiotic, such as third‐generation cephalosporins and
enrofloxacin or metronidazole, can be used. In the early
stages antiinflammatory doses of corticosteroids to
reduce surrounding edema are indicated, and seizure
control with anticonvulsants may be required. Antibiotic
therapy should be maintained for several weeks after
clinical signs have resolved. Surgical decompression by
craniectomy is indicated in cases of brain abscess that do
not respond to medical management.

Mycotic Meningoencephalitis

Fungal CNS infections other than cryptococcosis are
uncommon in dogs and cats. Small animals with mycotic
CNS infections can have neurologic signs that range
from peracute in onset to insidiously progressive, and
lesion localization is often suggestive of multifocal
disease.
Cryptococcus neoformans is the most commonly implicated systemic mycotic agent causing CNS signs in both
dogs and cats. Extraneural organ involvement is often
present, but may be clinically occult, or absent in some
cases. Brainstem disease resulting in signs of vestibular
dysfunction is frequently reported. Peripheral vestibular
disease has also been reported to be a sequel of cryptococcosis in cats.
The diagnosis of cryptococosis is best established
by cytologic or histologic demonstration of the organism, with its characteristic capsule, from tissue aspirates or biopsies, or in body fluids, such as urine or CSF;
organisms can be identified in the CSF of more than
90% of dogs with CNS signs. In cases in which organisms cannot be demonstrated, serologic testing using
the latex agglutination procedure that identifies cryptococcal capsular antigen is recommended. Serologic
testing can be performed on blood or CSF, although
CSF is preferred. Latex agglutination testing is generally considered to be both highly sensitive and specific.
CT and MRI imaging of the brain in cats and dogs with
cryptococcosis have demonstrated numerous and
­variable abnormalities including single or multifocal
mass lesions, meningeal enhancement, intraparenchymal ring enhancement associated with “punch hole”
lesions in the gray matter, and choroid plexus
enhancement.
The recommended therapy for CNS cryptococcosis is
fluconazole (5 mg/kg PO q12h), as this agent effectively
penetrates CNS tissues. Intrathecal administration of
amphotericin B has also been described. The length of
therapy required is often protracted, and serial serologic
monitoring has been recommended. Treatment should
ideally be continued until clinical signs have resolved,
CSF analysis has normalized, and two consecutive titers
performed one month apart have been negative.
However, relapses have occurred after consecutively
negative serum titers, and it has been suggested that
when possible, treatment should continue until the
patient is seronegative and all previously documented
intracranial MR abnormalities have resolved. Newer
antifungal agents, such as voriconazole, offer advantages including excellent CNS penetration, a broader
antifungal spectrum, and greater potency than either
fluconazole or itraconazole, and thus may prove to be
beneficial for the treatment of CNS cryptococcosis in
dogs and cats.
