­Vascular Causes
Cerebrovascular Accidents
Cerebrovascular accident (CVA), also known as stroke,
is defined as a sudden onset of nonconvulsive and nonprogressive focal brain signs secondary to cerebrovascular disease (any pathology affecting the blood supply of
the brain). By convention, these signs must remain for
more than 24 hours to qualify for the diagnosis of CVA;
if the clinical signs resolve within 24 hours, the episode is
called a transient ischemic attack or TIA.
Causes and Pathophysiology

Ischemic strokes result from occlusion of cerebral blood
vessels by a thrombus or embolism while hemorrhagic
strokes result from rupture of blood vessel walls within
the brain parenchyma or subarachnoid space.
Ischemic Stroke

Ischemic strokes have been reported infrequently in the
veterinary medical literature when compared with the
human medical literature. Suspected underlying causes
identified in histopathologically confirmed cases include:
septic thromboemboli associated with bacterial endocarditis or other sources of infection
●● atherosclerosis associated with primary hypothyroidism
and miniature schnauzers with hypertriglyceridemia
●● aberrant parasite migration (Cuterebra) or parasitic
emboli (Dirofilaria immitis)
●● embolic metastatic tumor cells
●● intravascular lymphoma
●● fibrocartilaginous embolism
●● aortic or cardiac embolism.
●●

However, in those cases which are not severe enough to
warrant admission to the postmortem room, a concurrent medical condition can be found in just over 50% of
dogs. The most commonly encountered conditions are:
hyperadrenocorticism
chronic kidney disease
●● hypothyroidism
●● hypertension.
●●
●●

Chronic kidney disease and hyperadrenocorticism were
the most commonly suspected underlying causes for the
hypertension in one study. No underlying cause could be
identified antemortem in nearly half of the dogs; this type
of infarct of unknown origin is referred to in humans as
cryptogenic. No age, sex or breed predisposition has been
identified in dogs but Cavalier King Charles spaniels
(CKCS) and greyhounds appear to be overrepresented.
Reports of ischemic stroke in cats are scarce. The term
feline ischemic encephalopathy (FIE) has been used to

describe cases of peracute onset of clinical signs consistent with a unilateral cerebral or brainstem problem caused
by ischemia. Although the cause remains unknown in
most cases, some of them have been linked to Cuterebra
migration. It is believed that the migrating parasite, or
the host response to it, leads to vasospasm in the cerebral
vasculature (typically middle cerebral artery).
Failure of blood supply (which results in decreased
perfusion pressure within one area of the brain) leads to
the development of ischemia, progressing to infarction if
this is severe and persists. An infarct describes the area
of compromised brain parenchyma that results from this
process. The initial drop in perfusion pressure may occur
either secondary to vascular obstruction that develops
within the occluded vessels (thrombosis) or due to
obstructive material that originates from another vascular bed and travels to the brain (thromboembolism). Two
distinct regions of an infarct can be distinguished: the
core, where ischemia is severe and infarction develops
rapidly; and the penumbra surrounding the core, which
shows a more moderate decrease of cerebral blood flow
(CBF), allowing longer durations of ischemic stress to be
tolerated. Tissue within the penumbra has the potential
for recovery and therefore is the target for interventional
therapy in acute ischemic stroke.
Hemorrhagic Stroke

In contrast to the high incidence in humans, intracerebral hemorrhage resulting from spontaneous rupture of
vessels is considered rare in dogs and cats. Secondary
hemorrhage has been reported in dogs in association
with:
rupture of congenital vascular abnormalities
primary and secondary brain tumors
●● inflammatory
disease of the arteries and veins
(vasculitis)
●● intravascular lymphoma
●● brain infarction (hemorrhagic infarction)
●● impaired coagulation.
●●
●●

Nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage has been
reported in dogs but remains very rare when compared
to its occurrence in humans, where aneurysmal rupture
is the most common underlying cause.
In hemorrhagic stroke, blood leaks from the vessel
directly into the brain, forming a hematoma within the
brain parenchyma, or into the subarachnoid space. The
mass of clotted blood causes physical disruption of the
tissue and pressure on the surrounding brain. This alters
CNS volume/pressure relationships with the possibility
of increasing intracranial pressure and decreasing cerebral blood flow. In addition, the tissue downstream of the
ruptured vessel(s) undergoes ischemia as a result of the
loss of blood supply. As the volume of the hematoma

785

VetBooks.ir

786

Section 8 Neurologic Disease

initially develops, ICP typically remains constant due to
a system of compensation known as cerebrovascular
autoregulation. However, with progressive expansion of
the hematoma, these mechanisms become exhausted,
after which further increases in the volume of the clot
become associated with a dramatic increase in ICP.
In severe cases, this increase in ICP causes a decrease in
perfusion of the brain and ultimately fatal herniation of
the brain at the level of the foramen magnum.
Clinical Presentation

Neurologic signs seen in stroke patients are characteristically peracute or acute in onset and nonprogressive or
regressive in their evolution. Initially, deficits observed
are usually focal, often asymmetric and ultimately related
to the area of the brain involved. The combination of
abrupt onset and focal, often asymmetric localization
should raise the index of suspicion for vascular disease.
The initial signs are then followed by an arrest and
regression of the neurologic deficits in all except the fatal
strokes, although worsening of edema (associated with
the secondary injury phenomena) can result in progression of neurologic signs for a short period of 24–72
hours. In addition, intracranial hemorrhage can present
with progression of signs for up to 24–72 hours before
regression as a result of reorganization of the hemorrhage and edema resorption.
Neurologic deficits usually reflect a focal anatomic
diagnosis and depend on the location of the vascular
insult (telencephalon, thalamus, midbrain, pons, medulla,
cerebellum). Infarction of an individual brain region is
associated with specific clinical signs that reflect the loss
of function of that specific region.
Diagnosis

Advanced imaging (CT, conventional and/or functional
MRI) is a prerequisite for confirming a diagnosis of
stroke, for defining both the vascular territory involved
and the extent of the lesion, as well as distinguishing
between ischemic and hemorrhagic disease. Imaging
studies are also necessary to rule out other causes of
neurologic deficit such as tumor, head trauma, and
encephalitis.
Computed tomography images are frequently normal
during the acute phase of ischemic stroke, making the
diagnosis of ischemic stroke using CT an exercise in the
exclusion of other differential diagnoses. In part, this is
due to the relatively noisy CT images of the brain in
animals with a large skull to brain ratio, compared with
people. Early CT signs of ischemia can be subtle and
difficult to detect even by very experienced readers and
include parenchymal hypodensity, loss of gray–white
matter differentiation, subtle effacement of the cortical
sulci, and local mass effect. By way of contrast, CT is

exquisitely sensitive for the detection of acute hemorrhage in hemorrhagic stroke. Acute hemorrhage is evident as a hyperdensity on CT due to hyperattenuation
of X‐rays by the globin portion of blood, particularly for
the first eight days following onset. The attenuation
decreases until the hematoma is isodense about one
month after the event. The periphery of the hematoma
contrast enhances from six days to six weeks after onset,
due to revascularization.
Magnetic resonance imaging can be used to identify
ischemic stroke within 12–24 hours of onset and to
distinguish hemorrhagic lesions from infarction. T2‐
weighted and FLAIR images are particularly useful in
imaging of ischemic stroke since they allow correlation
of the lesion with anatomic structures and vascular
­territories. With these sequences, ischemic infarction
appears as a hyperintense lesion. The conformity of an
infarct to a vascular territory is an important element in
the diagnosis that helps in distinguishing these lesions
from other differentials. Ischemic infarcts are limited
to the region of the brain vascularized by the affected
vessel, and are often wedge‐shaped in appearance with
resultant sharply demarcated borders. There is minimal
to no mass effect associated with these lesions. Changes
are best appreciated in the gray matter and are well visualized in deep gray matter structures such as the thalamus and basal ganglia due to their selective vulnerability
to ischemia. Contrast enhancement (associated with
reperfusion) is not usually seen until at least 7–10 days
but the inverse is a useful indicator – lack of contrast
uptake in the ischemic region often results in a noticeably darker area on postcontrast T1‐weighted scans.
In the case of hemorrhagic stroke, particular characteristics of hematoma evolution are useful in making the
diagnosis with conventional sequences. As the hematoma
ages, oxyhemoglobin sequentially breaks down into several paramagnetic products – first deoxyhemoglobin, followed by methemoglobin, and finally hemosiderin. The
earliest possible detection of hemorrhage depends on the
conversion of oxyhemoglobin to deoxyhemoglobin which
occurs after 12–24 hours. Whilst oxyhemoglobin provides a signal similar to that of normal brain parenchyma,
the iron exposed to surrounding water molecules in the
form of deoxyhemoglobin creates a signal loss, making it
easy to identify on T2‐weighted and susceptibility‐
weighted sequences. Gradient echo (T2‐weighted)
sequences are exquisitely sensitive to the disruption of
the local magnetic field that this creates and show hemorrhage as dense hypointense regions.
In addition to conventional MRI sequences, several
functional MRI (fMRI) techniques have been developed
for the early diagnosis of stroke. These include diffusion
and perfusion imaging and magnetic resonance angiography (MRA). Diffusion‐weighted imaging (DWI) is

VetBooks.ir

71 Disorders of the Forebrain

used commonly in humans in the diagnosis of acute
stroke. DWI sequences detect the random diffusion of
water molecules through tissues. When brain parenchyma loses its blood supply, energy delivery to neurons
fails and water becomes trapped within cells by cell
membranes. This can be detected on DWI sequences as
a hyperintense region within the brain representing
brain parenchyma in which water diffusion is restricted
as a result of this energy failure. In addition to DWI, perfusion‐weighted imaging is employed to depict regions
of hypoperfusion in the brain and can document the tissue “at risk” (i.e., penumbra) by comparing the results
with the findings on DWI. In addition, MRA can noninvasively assess the intracranial vessels of stroke patients.
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis is unlikely to confirm a
diagnosis of CVA but helps to rule out inflammatory
CNS disease. CSF is variable in dogs and cats with CVA.
In most cases, it is either normal or reflects a mild mononuclear or neutrophilic pleocytosis. CSF proteins are
occasionally elevated.
Identification of Underlying Causes of Stroke

In the case of presumptive or confirmed ischemic stroke,
ancillary diagnostic tests should focus on evaluating the
animal for hypertension (and its potential underlying
causes), endocrine disease (hyperadrenocorticism,
hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, diabetes mellitus),
kidney disease (especially protein‐losing nephropathy),
heart disease, and metastatic disease. Diagnostic tests in
presumptive or confirmed cases of hemorrhagic stroke
should focus on screening the animal for a coagulopathy,
hypertension (and potential underlying causes), and
metastatic disease (particularly hemangiosarcoma).
Treatment and Prognosis

Once the diagnosis of a stroke has been made, any potential underlying or associated disease should be identified
and treated accordingly. Generally, treatment of these
patients aims to provide supportive care, maintain adequate tissue oxygenation, and manage neurologic and
nonneurologic complications. Nursing management of a
recumbent dog will be vital to the success of more specific therapies. Such management includes attention to
the prevention of decubital ulceration, aspiration pneumonia, and urine scald, in addition to physical therapy
and enteral nutrition provision. More specific therapies
are aimed at preventing further neurologic deterioration.
Most cases of ischemic stroke recover within several
weeks with only supportive care. Potential underlying
causes should be investigated and treated accordingly to
limit the risk of recurrences. Definitive therapy in people
involves thrombolytic therapy in an attempt to salvage
the ischemic penumbra – tissue surrounding the
ischemic core in which rapid restoration of the blood

supply may reverse the initial damage. However, the window of opportunity for this to occur is approximately
six hours, making it very rarely achievable in animals.
Monitoring and correction of basic physiologic variables
are important, as is maintaining normal blood pressure.
The most important consideration in hemorrhagic
stroke is maintenance of cerebral perfusion by treatment
of hypotension and elevated ICP, as well as treating the
underlying cause if one has been identified. The medical
management of dogs with intracranial hemorrhage commonly includes:
stabilization of the patient (airway protection, monitoring and correction of vital signs)
●● assessment and monitoring of the neurologic status
●● determination and treatment of potential underlying
causes of the hemorrhage
●● assessment of the need for specific treatment measures, including management of increased ICP.
●●

The risk of neurologic deterioration and cardiovascular
instability is highest during the first 24 hours after the
onset of an intracranial hemorrhage, as the space‐occupying lesion slowly expands and cerebral vasogenic
edema develops. During this phase, if the neurologic status deteriorates, aggressive therapy to control ICP with
mannitol (0.25–1 g/kg administered IV over 20 min) or
other agents may need to be considered, and in rare cases
craniotomy to alleviate cerebral edema.
The prognosis for ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke
depends overall on the initial severity of the neurologic
deficit, the initial response to supportive care, and the
severity of the underlying cause if one has been identified.
Most cases of ischemic stroke recover within several
weeks with only supportive care and there appears to be
no association between the region of the brain involved,
the type of infarction (territorial or lacunar), and outcome. However, dogs with a concurrent medical condition have a significantly shorter survival time than those
with no identifiable medical condition. Dogs with a concurrent medical condition are also significantly more
likely to suffer from recurrent neurologic signs due to
subsequent infarcts.
Feline Ischemic Encephalopathy
Feline ischemic encephalopathy (FIE) represents a
peculiar variant of cerebrovascular disease. FIE is an
ischemic necrosis of cerebral tissue that has been
reported sporadically in male and female cats of all ages,
especially in summer months in the US. Clinical signs
are usually acute in onset, nonprogressive, and variable,
and typically suggest unilateral cerebral or brainstem
involvement. Signs may include depression, head tilt,
anisocoria, circling, seizures, and changes in attitude/

787

VetBooks.ir

788

Section 8 Neurologic Disease

behavior. Clinical signs may be modified or disappear
with time and, unlike other forms of cerebrovascular
accident, multiple episodes may occur. Hematology,
blood chemistries, and skull radiographs are usually
normal while MRI reveals classic signs of a major
ischemic infarct. CSF analysis may be normal or show
mild to moderate elevations in cell numbers (usually
monocytic) or protein levels. Lesions are usually unilateral and may involve up to 75% of one cerebral and/or
cerebellar hemisphere. The major area of infarction is
frequently in the distribution of the middle cerebral
artery.
The cause of this enigmatic ischemic condition has
been uncertain but clinical similarities between FIE and
Cuterebra infection of the brain have historically been
noted. Intriguingly, at postmortem some of these cats

have been found to harbor Cuterebra larvae within the cranial vault (commonly within the olfactory bulbs and
optic nerves following migration through the cribiform
plate) – and some of the changes visualized are associated with the migration track of the parasite. However,
much of the vascular compromise occurs in locations
distant to the parasite, suggesting an elaborated toxic factor
causing disseminated vasospasm and consequent
ischemia. It should be noted that although this association
has been noted in the US, some cats in other countries in
which Cuterebra is not found can also be affected with similar ischemic lesions.
Treatment is largely supportive. Prognosis is often
favorable since many of the signs seen initially will ameliorate; however, behavioral changes and uncontrollable
seizures may persist.

Vestibular Disease
Tammy Stevenson, DVM, DACVIM (Neurology)
Veterinary Specialty Hospital, San Diego, CA, USA

The term vestibular disease is used to describe a neuro­
anatomic localization within the vestibular system of any
cause, and therefore, is not a specific diagnosis.
The purpose of the vestibular system is to provide
balance by adjusting limb extensor/flexor tone to accom­
modate for changing head and body positions. This results
in controlled and coordinated eye‐head‐trunk‐limb
movement with proper postural support.
The structures of the vestibular portion of the inner ear
include semicircular canals that are responsible for con­
veying information regarding acceleration in angular
planes, and the utriculus and sacculus which convey infor­
mation regarding linear acceleration and static head posi­
tion (relative to gravity). Information from these receptor
organs travels via the vestibular portion of the vestibuloc­
ochlear nerve (CN VIII) to the vestibular nuclei (four on
each side of the brainstem – rostral, caudal, medial, and
lateral), through the caudal cerebellar peduncle, to the
flocculonodular lobes of the cerebellar hemisphere. The
dorsal spinal nerves of C1–3 provide input to head posi­
tion and balance and can also cause vestibular signs when
dysfunctional.
Dysfunction of one or more parts of the vestibular
system may result in the signs we classically recognize as
“vestibular disease” – a head tilt, nystagmus, walking in
circles, ataxia/falling or even rolling, abnormal limb
extensor tone, and nausea/vomiting. These signs are due
to the vestibular system’s extensive connections with
various parts of the central nervous system (CNS).
Projections via the medial longitudinal fasciculus to
the nuclei of CN III, IV, and VI which control the
extraocular eye muscles. In homeostatic conditions,
these connections result in normal physiologic nystag­
mus (oculocephalic reflex), and with dysfunction,
pathological nystagmus.
●● Projections via the vestibulospinal tract, to the neck,
trunk, and limbs, resulting in appropriate head/neck
●●

position relative to gravity and with movement, and
appropriate limb tone and position relative to gravity
and head position. Dysfunction results in head tilt, and
imbalance in extensor tone such that the animal leans
or circles to the side with less tone.
●● Projections to the vomiting center (in the reticular for­
mation) leading to ptyalism, inappetence, and vomiting.
●● Projections to the cerebral cortex to provide conscious
awareness of the body’s position in space via the
thalamus (pathway not well identified), and awareness
of dysfunction such that the patient may “feel bad.”
●● Projections to the cerebellum (via the caudal cerebellar
peduncle, in the vestibulocerebellar tracts) which may
result in decreased extensor tone on one side of the
body and increased tone on the other (leaning).
As with all problems involving the CNS, the location of
the lesion, not what caused the lesion(s), determines the
signs you see. Therefore, a thorough neurological exami­
nation is critical to proper localization and an accurate
differential list which, in turn, guides the diagnostic plan.

­Peripheral versus Central Disease
For vestibular disease, the first step is differentiating
peripheral from central disease. Peripheral vestibular
disease is characterized by a head tilt and circling towards
the side of the lesion, and pathological nystagmus with
the fast phase away from the lesion. Unfortunately, cen­
tral vestibular disease cannot be definitively ruled out on
exam alone. However, any of the following abnormalities
can lead to a confident central localization.
●●

Cranial nerve deficits other than VII or VIII. Deficits
associated with VII or VIII alone can be seen with both
peripheral and central disease, as can sympathetic dys­
function (Horner syndrome). Involvement of other

Clinical Small Animal Internal Medicine Volume I, First Edition. Edited by David S. Bruyette.

Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/bruyette/clinical

VetBooks.ir

790

Section 8 Neurologic Disease

cranial nerves is typically due to brainstem involve­
ment where the cranial nerve nuclei are situated and
there may also be concurrent mentation changes due
to the diffuse projections of the reticular activating
system (RAS) in this location.
●● Cerebrothalamic dysfunction – mentation changes,
seizures, head turn +/− wide circles, visual deficits,
proprioceptive deficits, etc. Signs are due to multifo­
cal/diffuse disease or increased intracranial
pressure.
●● Cerebellar signs – intention tremors, hypermetria,
truncal sway, absent menace with intact vision.
Cerebellar lesions produce ipsilateral signs (or bilateral
if diffuse/multifocal cerebellar involvement).
●● Proprioceptive deficits +/− paresis – proprioceptive
deficits may come from a lesion interrupting the flow
of information anywhere along the pathway from the
cortex through the thalamus and brainstem (which
may result in varying degrees of paresis) or from the
cerebellum (no paresis).
The presence of one or more of the above signs, by defi­
nition, localizes the problem to the CNS. Central disease
may be due to a multifocal problem (i.e., infections,
inflammatory disease, lymphoma, multiple metastatic
lesions), from increased ICP leading to compression of
adjacent vestibular structures, or from direct involve­
ment of the central vestibular system.
Examination of the vestibular patient can be challeng­
ing, making localization difficult. For example, patients
that are profoundly affected by nausea and imbalance
often feel/act mentally dull and lethargic. Supporting
patients to assess proprioception can be futile when they
are rolling and flailing. Finally, it is important to consider
any preexisting disease that may suggest two localiza­
tions or multifocal disease, such as a history of cervical
pain or seizures.
Nystagmus has been classically used to localize ves­
tibular disease as peripheral versus central, but this
should be undertaken with caution. Vertical nystagmus
is strongly suggestive of, but not definitive for, central
disease. Constant, unchanging horizontal nystagmus is
associated with peripheral disease.
Paradoxical vestibular disease is associated with
lesions in the rostral and medial vestibular nuclei, the
caudal cerebellar peduncle, or the flocculonodular lobe
of the cerebellum, and therefore it is always central in
origin. Lesions associated with any of these neuroana­
tomic localizations should produce lateralizing signs.
Once the side is determined (i.e., side of proprioceptive
deficits, hypermetria), if the head tilt/circling is away
from the lesion, +/− the fast phase of the nystagmus
towards the lesion, then it is considered paradoxical ves­
tibular disease.

­Etiology
To ensure a complete list of differential diagnoses,
breaking down differentials into larger categories and
then fitting specific differentials into those categories
will help limit oversights.
Degenerative

In general, acute versus chronic history should help
with ranking differentials. Acute histories are more com­
monly associated with idiopathic disease, vascular
events (ischemic vs hemorrhagic), toxin exposure (met­
ronidazole, ronidazole) +/− otitis interna (usually
with an associated chronic otitis externa/media).
Thiamine deficiency is often acute and can progress
rapidly in cats. Of course, there are always exceptions.
Peripheral Vestibular Disease
Anomalous/Congenital

Some animals are born with signs of peripheral ves­
tibular disease, either unilateral or bilateral. Bilaterally
affected animals are commonly deaf as well. The exact
cause is unknown, although both degeneration of the
vestibular nerve and inflammation of the labyrinth
have been described. Recent research suggests a possible
genetic mutation in a doberman puppy. The signs are
often noted when the animal first becomes mobile. Head
tilt and ataxia, +/− circling are seen. Bilaterally affected
animals may look more “cerebellar,” swinging the head
back and forth, and have a more generalized appear­
ance to the ataxia. Often pathological nystagmus is not
appreciated and physiological nystagmus is frequently
decreased/absent in these bilaterally affected patients.
Most animals will remain static or improve with time,
but deafness is typically permanent. Congenital ves­
tibular disease and deafness are possible in any breed,
but reported breeds include Siamese, Burmese, and
Tonkinese cats, Dobermans, cocker spaniels, akitas,
German shepherds, beagles, and smooth fox terriers.
Primary secretory otitis media is a disease most com­
monly seen in Cavalier King Charles Spaniels and less
commonly in other brachycephalic breeds, such as
french bulldogs. It results in a collection of mucoid effu­
sion in the tympanic bulla presumably due to these
breeds extreme nasopharyngeal confirmation compro­
mising normal drainage. It is rarely associated with ves­
tibular signs.

VetBooks.ir

72 Vestibular Disease

Idiopathic

Canine idiopathic vestibular disease is common in
older dogs. The history is often an acute onset of head
tilt, nystagmus (fast phase away from the head tilt),
ataxia/falling/rolling, drooling/nausea, inappetence,
and vomiting. The severity can be quite variable, from
mild to extreme. There is no specific treatment, but
symptomatic therapy with antinausea/antiemetic medi­
cations for apparent nausea, fluid support to maintain
hydration until they are eating, +/− diazepam (GABA
modulator acting centrally to suppress vestibular
responses) can help the patient feel better during recovery.
Appropriate recumbent care is necessary in nonambu­
latory patients, especially since they will often lie only
on one side. Improvement can be quick (hours) but
more commonly takes 1–3 weeks and often there is a
residual head tilt. Signs are exacerbated in the dark
since visual compensation is the primary means for
improved function. It is uncommon, but possible, for
idiopathic vestibular disease to recur. However,
repeated events should encourage diagnostic testing to
exclude other causes.
Feline idiopathic vestibular syndrome can occur in
cats of any age and affects outdoor cats more fre­
quently. It appears to be more common in the summer
and fall months in the northeastern United States,
although this timing is not appreciated in other parts
of the country. Clinical signs are similar to canine
idiopathic disease, but vomiting is less common.
­
Diagnosis is based on exclusion of other causes of
peripheral vestibular disease. Cats also spontaneously
recover within a few weeks.
Infectious
Otitis Media/Interna

Ascending infection via the auditory tube can result in
otitis media/interna in the absence of otitis externa.
Otoscopic exam may not be conclusive in these cases
unless there are obvious changes to the tympanic mem­
brane (bulging, rupture). Otitis externa is often present
without concurrent otitis media/interna. Therefore,
definitive diagnosis of otitis media/interna typically
requires advanced imaging. This may not be practical in
all cases. Cats with otitis media may also have evidence
of Horner’s syndrome as the sympathetic fibers pass
through the bullae in this species. Since the facial nerve
travels near the horizontal external ear canal and by the
bulla, severe and chronic ear disease may also result in
signs of facial paresis/paralysis if the periauricular tissues
are involved. Depending on the severity of the problem,
treatment may involve medical or surgical management.
Typically, the outcome is better for surgical management
with antibiotic/antifungal therapy based on culture and
sensitivity results. Clinical signs may still be present after

resolution of infection due to permanent nerve damage,
including deafness.
Inflammatory
Nasopharyngeal Polyps

A polyp is a fleshy mass composed of granulation tissue
covered with respiratory epithelium, that originates from
the lining of either the auditory tube or the middle ear.
The primary etiology is unknown, but viral and/or chronic
inflammatory processes are suspected to play a role. They
are most common in cats 1–5 years of age but have been
documented in much older cats as well, with an equal dis­
tribution in males and females. Polyps can also lead to sec­
ondary infection or inflammation of the middle and inner
ear, and therefore, patients may present with vestibular
signs. Since the mass can also grow into the pharyngeal
area, signs of sneezing and gagging may be the presenting
clinical complaint. Polyp removal is typically via traction
or surgical approach (ventral bullae osteotomy) but recur­
rence is possible. Rarely dogs are affected.
Cholesteatoma

A cholesteatoma is a nonneoplastic concretion of keratin
debris, keratinizing epithelium, and epidermoid cystic
structure(s) that is thought to be a rare sequela of chronic
inflammation and is reported infrequently in dogs with
otitis media. The cholesteatoma results in bullae expan­
sion and secondary osteolysis. Patients often present for
pain on opening the mouth, pain on palpation of the ear,
+/− peripheral vestibular signs. Surgical intervention is
necessary, so it should not be mistaken for primary infec­
tious otitis and managed medically. There are imaging
characteristics that can help differentiate it from primary
infectious otitis which should prompt surgical interven­
tion. Risk of recurrence after surgery is high. Monitoring
with advanced imaging every 6–12 months should be
considered.
Neoplasia

Any neoplastic process adjacent to the vestibular anatomy
(such as squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, oste­
osarcoma, fibrosarcoma, chondrosarcoma) can potentially
result in peripheral vestibular signs. The mass may track
along the skull base where cranial nerves exit their respec­
tive foramina, resulting in one or more of the following in
addition to vestibular signs: facial paralysis, change in
voice, stridor, difficulty swallowing, and tongue deviation
or dimpling/contracture. If there are no changes in menta­
tion and no proprioceptive deficits or paresis, localization
to the peripheral vestibular system would still be suspected
(i.e., the process has not yet invaded the cranial vault to any
appreciable degree on exam). Advanced imaging and
cytology/biopsy would be needed to determine the extent
of the disease, treatment options, and prognosis.

Toxicity

Drug toxicity (topical, intravenous, and inhaled drugs)
can result in both deafness and vestibular signs by
damaging the hair cells or the vestibulocochlear nerve
itself. Antibiotics (aminoglycosides, erythromycin,
minocycline, topical choramphenicol, etc.), antiseptics
(chlorhexidine), diuretics (furosemide), and miscellaneous
other agents (salicylates, propylene glycol, ceruminolytic
agents, lead, mercury, etc.) are all recognized as causes of
ototoxicity in veterinary patients, with aminoglycoside
being the most commonly reported cause. NSAIDs are
a well‐recognized cause of reversible toxicity in people.
Early recognition and withdrawal of the medication may
limit damage, but by the time signs are recognized, the
damage may be permanent. Even when animals do not
recover fully from peripheral disease due to ototoxicity,
they usually compensate adequately to maintain a good
quality of life.

sive dilation of the fourth ventricle. Arachnoid divertic­
uli within the quadrigeminal cistern are more
commonly associated with seizures if clinical signs are
present at all, but vestibulocerebellar signs may be noted.
Caudal occipital malformation syndrome (also called a
Chiari‐like malformation) that leads to a degree of obstruc­
tive hydrocephalus and dilation of the fourth ventricle or
bulbomyelia may result in central vestibular signs. Severe
generalized hydrocephalus can occasionally be associ­
ated with vestibular signs because of fourth ventricle
involvement, but this would be an uncommon clinical
sign. Malformations leading to high cervical instability
(i.e., atlantooccipital or atlantoaxial subluxation/luxa­
tions) can rarely lead to secondary edema and inflamma­
tion extending cranial to involve the vestibular nuclei but
caudal nuclei involvement would also be present.
Infection

Since the vestibular apparatus is housed in the hardest
bone in the body, the petrous temporal bone, trauma is
not a common cause of vestibular disease. However,
blunt trauma, typically hit by car, can result in skull/bulla
fractures, hemorrhage in the soft tissues of the middle
and inner ear and lead to vestibular disease. Horner’s
syndrome and facial paralysis may also result from direct
trauma or soft tissue swelling/hemorrhage involving the
adjacent tissue as they are in close proximity to CN VIII.
Treatment for the vestibular signs would be supportive
care and time. Resolution of vestibular signs may be
incomplete.

Otitis can extend through the internal acoustic meatus
and result in intracranial disease with compression of
the brainstem from abscess formation or even active
meningitis/encephalitis, although this is less common.
Infectious agents are usually bacterial, but fungal dis­
ease is also possible.
Systemic infections involving the CNS or infections
apparently isolated to the CNS are uncommon in dogs,
with the exception of certain signalments and geographic
locations: Cryptococcus on the west coast, coccidiodio­
mycosis in desert locales, histoplasmosis and blastomy­
cosis in the Midwest, to name a few. Infections typically
cause multifocal signs that may include the vestibular
system.
Young dogs and cats are at higher risk for viral dis­
eases, with distemper and FIP being the most commonly
diagnosed.
Neospora and distemper appear to have a predilection
for cerebellar involvement which may result in vestibular
signs.

Central Vestibular Disease

Vascular

Metabolic

Hypothyroidism is often linked to peripheral vestibular
disease, although the association is tenuous. If hypothy­
roidism is detected in a patient with peripheral vestibu­
lar disease, treatment should be considered.
Trauma

Brain tumors, stroke‐like events, drug toxicities (such as
metronidazole and ronidazole), nutritional deficiencies
(thiamine), infections (such as distemper, feline infec­
tious peritonitis, Toxoplasma gondii, Neospora caninum,
and fungal infections) or diseases that cause inflammation
of the brain (such as granulomatous or necrotizing
meningoencephalitis) may all lead to central vestibular
disease in both the dog and the cat.
Anomalous/Congenital

Malformations resulting in central vestibular signs may
be present at birth but can progress over time due to
obstruction of CSF flow either within cystic structures
(i.e., arachnoid cysts/diverticuli) or leading to progres­

Vascular events (ischemic vs hemorrhagic) typically
have an acute onset, but may appear progressive over a
24‐hour period. Causes of vascular events often do not
have an underlying identifiable cause, but screening for
causes of thromboembolic disease, +/− bleeding disor­
ders, is warranted.
Hypertension, primary or secondary, can lead to ves­
tibular episodes. Many of these cases mimic idiopathic
vestibular disease in history and examination findings,
but the events will often recur, similar to TIAs in people,
and only resolve or improve once hypertension is
­controlled. In cases where there is an acute onset of ves­
tibular signs that clearly localize to the central vestibular
system, the cerebellum is most commonly involved, in

VetBooks.ir

72 Vestibular Disease

the author’s experience. MRI may be normal or show
evidence of ischemia within the vestibular system.
A normal MRI cannot exclude an ischemic event as the
area of compromised tissue may be smaller than the
resolution of the MRI (especially in small patients and
low field magnets), or sequencing that best highlights
tissue ischemia may not be available (software limita­
tions). MRI done in close temporal relationship to the
onset of signs could miss lesions that may be evident if
done a few hours to days later. Very small hemorrhages
or ischemic areas may be missed if gradient echo or dif­
fusion‐weighted sequences are not pursued.
Hypothyroidism can result in the formation of athero­
sclerosis, leading to vascular thrombosis and signs men­
tioned earlier.
Hemorrhagic vascular events are less common and
underlying causes such as thrombocytopenia, clotting
deficiencies (rodenticide toxicity, liver disease, etc.),
metastatic hemangiosarcoma, and hypertension should
be investigated.
Inflammatory

Inflammatory CNS disease (i.e., granulomatous meningo­
encephalitis, necrotizing meningoencephalomyelitis,
and breed‐specific encephalitides) is one of the more
common diseases neurologists diagnose. Young to
middle‐aged toy‐breed dogs are typically affected, but
any age and breed are susceptible. It usually presents as
multifocal disease and the patient may have one or more
of the following clinical signs: vestibular signs, cervical
pain, paresis, cranial nerve deficits, circling, obtunda­
tion, seizures. The cause is unknown but may be a com­
bination of genetic predisposition and an antigenic trigger
(recent illness, vaccination/medication, environmental
antigenic stimulation) resulting in an inappropriate
immune system attack on nervous tissue. MRI and spinal
fluid analysis are needed at a minimum to determine a
diagnosis. Often ruling out infectious disease (i.e., PCR
on CSF, serology, cultures, etc.) is necessary as the inflam­
mation may be secondary to another cause. Biopsy
would be needed for a definitive diagnosis and, given the
invasiveness, risk and cost associated, is not often pursued.
Therefore, treatment is based on the signalment, history,
and collection of diagnostic results supporting a sterile
inflammatory disease process.
As with other immune/inflammatory diseases, treatment
involves immunosuppression with one or more medica­
tions (i.e., prednisone, cytosar, azathioprine, cyclosporine,
etc.) for a prolonged period of time, often months, some­
times years. Response to treatment can be quite varia­
ble, but in the author’s experience many patients can be
weaned off drugs with the less severe forms of disease.
Inflammatory granulomas can cause mass lesions that
may be mistaken for neoplasia. These granulomas seem

to have a predilection for the cerebellar pontine angle,
leading to vestibulocerebellar signs, but can occur in
other locations as well.
Neoplasia

Neoplastic processes that affect the central vestibular sys­
tem include those that are commonly found at the cere­
bellar pontine angle (CPA), such as malignant peripheral
nerve sheath tumors of the trigeminal nerve that extend
intracranially, meningiomas, chorioid plexus tumors,
or ependymomas. Meningiomas, gliomas, round cell
tumors, and metastatic disease involving the cerebellum
(flocculonodular lobe) or brainstem vestibular nuclei can
also result in vestibular signs. Changes in intracranial
pressure due to neoplastic mass lesions elsewhere can
result in vestibular signs due to brainstem or cerebellar
compression (including cerebral herniation under the
tentorium cerebelli or cerebellar herniation from the
foramen magnum). MRI, +/−CSF, and surgical or CT‐
guided biopsy are necessary to confirm an antemortom
definitive diagnosis of neoplasia. However, most diagnoses
of intracranial neoplasia are made on imaging character­
istics and treated as such with radiation therapy, +/−
chemotherapy with definitive diagnosis only confirmed
after necropsy.
Nonneoplastic Mass Lesions

Epidermoid cysts, dermoid cysts, and teratomas are
thought to arise from trapped ectodermal embryonic
tissue as the neural tube is closing and therefore could be
included in the anomalous category. When found intrac­
ranially, they appear to have a predilection for the caudal
fossa and thus can produce vestibular signs. Other
nonneoplastic mass lesions that could produce vestibular
signs include arachnoid cysts/diverticuli, inflammatory
granulomas, cholesterol granulomas, infectious abscesses/
granulomas, parasitic cysts, and hematomas.
Nutritional

Thiamine deficiency (vitamin B1) in carnivores often
includes signs of central vestibular disease in addition
to cerebrothalamic signs (mental dullness, seizures) and
postural changes, cervical ventroflexion (in cats in par­
ticular), and paraparesis in dogs. Cat are more commonly
affected than dogs and signs can progress rapidly.
Unconventional diets (raw fish diets, diets cooked at very
high temperatures, diets with sulfur dioxide preserva­
tives) are typically the cause, but even commercial diets
can lead to thiamine deficiency. Bilaterally symmetric
changes on MRI (most apparent on FLAIR and gradient
echo sequences) within the brainstem nuclei (caudal
colliculi are most affected) are classic for thiamine
­
­deficiency. Histologic changes include petechial hemor­
rhages, edema, and neuronal necrosis.

793

VetBooks.ir

794

Section 8 Neurologic Disease

Ideally, patient thiamine levels +/− diet thiamine levels
would be pursued. Often, supplementation with thia­
mine and resolution of signs may be the only option. The
signs are completely reversible if treated in a timely
­manner and fatal if untreated.
Metronidazole and Ronidazole Toxicity

Toxicity associated with metronidazole is most often
found with high doses (15–30 mg/kg BID) or prolonged
therapy even at more conservative doses. Signs vary in
severity and often appear more cerebellar than vestibular,
but may include vertical nystagmus or ocular tremors,
intact vision with absent menace, mild to severe general­
ized ataxia, possibly progressing to a nonambulatory
state with decerebellate posturing, hypermetria in ambu­

latory patients (sometimes more severe in the PL), kypho­
sis, and proprioceptive deficits without loss of strength.
Discontinuation of the medication will result in resolution
of signs over days to weeks, but treating with IV or oral diaz­
epam (0.5 mg/kg TID 3–5 days) can expedite recovery.
Ronidazole is most commonly used for the treatment
of tritrichomonas foetus in cats and toxicity results in
similar signs as above.
The mechanism of toxicity is not known. In people,
changes on MRI show bilaterally symmetric alterations
in the cerebellar dentate nuclei signal intensity and often
the vestibular nuclei as well. There is speculation that it
may be mediated by thiamine deficiency due to similar
MRI changes in patients diagnosed with Wernicke
encephalopathy.

Meningoencephalitis and Meningomyelitis
Christopher L. Mariani, DVM, PhD, DACVIM (Neurology)
College of Veterinary Medicine, NC State, Raleigh, NC, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
The meninges comprise three connective tissue layers
that surround the brain and spinal cord: the pia mater,
arachnoid mater (these collectively known as the
­leptomeninges), and the dura mater (or pachymeninx).
Inflammation of the meninges, known as meningitis,
may remain confined to these structures, or may also
involve the underlying brain and/or spinal cord, termed
meningoencephalitis and meningomyelitis respectively.
There are a whole host of infectious diseases that can
cause inflammation of the meninges or underlying
­central nervous system (CNS) in small animals. These
include viral, bacterial, fungal, rickettsial, protozoal, and
parasitic organisms (Table 73.1). These organisms may
infect the CNS as part of a systemic, multiorgan process
(e.g, Rickettsia rickettsia, canine distemper, Blastomyces
dermatitidis) although some agents display a notable
neurotropism with CNS entry via the bloodstream or nasal
passages (e.g., Cryptococcus neoformans, Cladophia­
lophora bantiana). Within the CNS, these infectious
agents may cause clinical signs through a variety of
mechanisms. Their presence often results in an immune
response with resulting inflammation. Such an inflammatory response can occasionally involve the vasculature supplying the CNS, leading to vascular injury and
resulting ischemic or hemorrhagic disease. Inflammation
of the ependymal surface and changes in the viscosity of
the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) can result in disruption of
CSF flow and obstructive hydrocephalus (e.g., with feline
infectious peritonitis [FIP]). Some organisms can infect
neurons or glia, causing direct dysfunction or death of
these cells (e.g., canine distemper virus).
Despite this large number of organisms that can cause
CNS disease, documented infections comprise a very
small proportion of small animal meningoencephalitis
and meningomyelitis cases. Cats are generally considered

more likely to develop infectious CNS disease than dogs,
although documentation of infectious agents is still difficult in this species. In dogs, the vast majority of meningoencephalitis and meningomyelitis cases appear not to
have a direct infectious cause, and are often termed “sterile” as a result. In these animals, invading immune cells
lead to CNS inflammation and resulting clinical signs.
Whether these represent a response to an as yet undetected infectious organism, an overactive immune‐mediated response to an unknown environmental trigger or a
true autoimmune process remains to be determined.
However, broad screening studies aimed at detecting previously unknown infectious agents have thus far been
relatively unrewarding, and an immune‐mediated process appears more likely for the majority of canine cases.
There are several well‐recognized syndromes that occur
in dogs where infectious agents have not been identified
(Table 73.2). Many of these conditions are highly breed
associated and a genetic role in their pathophysiology has
long been suspected. Such a role has been best investigated in pug dogs with necrotizing meningoencephalitis
(NME). Several studies in this breed have shown a strong
association of disease with a specific haplotype localized
in the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) II region
of chromosome 12. This finding resembles what is seen in
many immune‐mediated diseases in humans, including
multiple sclerosis. How­
ever, this association probably
does not identify a strictly causative mutation, but likely
confers an increased risk of disease development, and it is
suspected that other factors, such as the presence of a
“trigger” to set the disease in motion, also play a role.
Interestingly, other dog breeds with NME that develop a
histologically identical lesion do not seem to share the
same at‐risk haplotypes as pugs and clearly more work to
define these underlying susceptibilities needs to be done.
The pathophysiology of most canine and feline
meningoencephalitides is relatively poorly understood,

­Epidemiology
Environmental conditions and exposures play an important
role in the transmission of many of the infectious organisms that cause meningoencephalitis or meningomyelitis.
These include housing density and animal‐to‐animal
transmission (e.g., canine distemper virus, FIP), transmission via wildlife bites (e.g., rabies, feline immunodeficiency virus [FIV]), exposure to soil or stagnant water
sources (e.g., Blastomyces dermatidis, Cryptococcus
neoformans, Entamoeba histolytica), or transmission
from insect or arthropod vectors (e.g., Dirofilaria immitis,
Ehrlichia canis, Rickettsia rickettsia). As mentioned
above, most of the CNS inflammatory diseases seen in

73 Meningoencephalitis and Meningomyelitis

dogs have no known infectious etiologies, and are likely
immune‐mediated processes that occur in individuals
with a genetic predisposition after some sort of antigenic
“trigger.” Such triggers remain unknown at this time but
might be related to exposure to environmental antigens
or to antigens from infectious agents not involving the
CNS (e.g., respiratory or gastrointestinal infection).

­Signalment
Although dogs and cats of any age or breed can be affected
by inflammatory CNS disease, certain populations are
predisposed to its development. Infectious diseases
occur more frequently in younger animals, which may be
related in part to maturation of the immune system or
vaccination failures. As mentioned above and detailed in
Table 73.2, many of the apparent noninfectious canine
meningoencephalitides have strong breed predispositions, and these diseases also have fairly consistent ages
of onset. As a general rule, meningoencephalitis occurs
more frequently in young to middle‐aged animals.
Gender seems to play a minor role in most of these diseases, although some early reports of GME and a more
recent study of NME have described a female predominance. In contrast, most of the dogs reported to develop
eosinophilic meningoencephalitis have been male.

­History and Clinical Signs
The history may reveal important predisposing factors
for some of the infectious diseases, including vaccination
history, exposure to ticks or mosquitoes, animal bites,
ingestion of raw food or carrion, and exposure to soil or
stagnant water. Obtaining a thorough travel history may
elucidate additional potential differential diagnoses as
some of the tick‐borne and fungal diseases have clear
geographic distributions.
Clinical signs of meningoencephalitis and meningomyelitis typically have an acute onset with progression
over time; chronic infection or inflammation of the CNS
is unusual. The signs seen are dependent on the region
of the nervous system that is involved. Animals with
meningitis (including SRMA) typically present for pain,
particularly cervical pain, and neurologic deficits are
frequently absent or subtle. Patients with forebrain
involvement may present with seizures, altered mentation, depressed consciousness, visual deficits, and compulsive pacing or circling. Brainstem disease can result
in cranial nerve deficits such as vestibular dysfunction,
facial nerve paralysis, pupillary abnormalities, strabismus,
dysphagia, megaesophagus or tongue atrophy together

with ataxia and paresis of all four limbs. Myelitis also
results in ataxia and paresis, together with spinal pain
and possibly deficits in segmental spinal reflexes.
Postural reaction deficits may be seen with lesions in
any of these regions. One hallmark of inflammatory
disease of the CNS is that it frequently results in a
­multifocal distribution of signs (i.e., multifocal lesion
localization), which is uncommonly seen with other
disease processes.
Occasionally, signs that are very characteristic for a
specific disease may be noted, such as distemper
“myoclonus” or rigid limb extension due to muscle
contractures in dogs with Neospora caninum infection.
In addition, some infectious diseases may involve multiple organ systems, producing signs referable to the
respiratory system (e.g., canine distemper, blastomycosis),
bone (Coccidioides immitis), integument (canine distemper, blastomycosis), gastrointestinal tract (canine distemper, Prototheca) or other systems. Involvement of
other systems is not typical for the “sterile” meningoencephalitides, although occasionally polyarthritis is seen
in dogs with SRMA.

­Diagnosis
A complete blood count may show abnormalities with
certain infectious agents, such as thrombocytopenia
with rickettsial infections or eosinophilia with some
parasite or protozoal diseases. If CNS inflammation is
part of a multisystemic infectious or inflammatory process, then a neutrophilic or monocytic leukocytosis may
be evident. Serum chemistry may similarly show abnormalities in certain conditions such as hyperglobulinemia
with FIP or Ehrlichia canis infections or changes indicative of renal or hepatic dysfunction in multisystemic
infections. However, in most animals with inflammatory
CNS disease, the complete blood count (CBC), serum
chemistry, and urinalysis are relatively unremarkable.
Although infrequently analyzed, acute phase proteins
may show changes in some animals, such as elevations in
serum C‐reactive protein, fibrinogen or serum amyloid
A protein.
A diagnosis of meningoencephalitis or meningomyelitis is most commonly made with advanced diagnostic
imaging and analysis of CSF. Conventional imaging tests
such as radiography or ultrasound have little role in the
diagnostic process outside of screening other organs
within the thoracic and abdominal cavities for disease.
Myelography is a technique that involves the injection of
contrast material into the subarachnoid space, followed by radiography of the vertebral column.
Interruptions in the flow of contrast material can result
in several imaging patterns indicating mass lesions in

797

VetBooks.ir

798

Section 8 Neurologic Disease

extradural, intradural‐extramedullary or intramedullary
locations. Although myelography may be abnormal with
meningomyelitis if a mass effect or spinal cord swelling is
a component of the disease process, these abnormalities
are nonspecific and rarely facilitate a definitive diagnosis.
In addition, myelography itself results in inflammation
of the meninges and spinal cord, which can worsen clinical signs, and so this intervention must be pursued with
caution. Therefore, more advanced imaging modalities
are preferred for patients with potential inflammatory
CNS disease, if available.
Computed tomography (CT) is a technique that utilizes X‐rays to produce cross‐sectional images of desired
anatomic structures. Software packages allow manipulation of images to highlight tissues of varying densities
(“windowing”) and images can be obtained both before
and after the administration of intravenous contrast
material, which can highlight areas within the CNS
where normal vascular barriers are compromised (e.g.,
neoplastic tissue, areas of inflammation). Computed
tomography can also be combined with myelography to
improve visualization of contrast within the subarachnoid space, which increases the diagnostic utility of this
latter technique. In animals with meningoencephalitis
or meningomyelitis, CT may show areas of hypodensity
within the brain or spinal cord parenchyma respectively,
corresponding to inflammation and associated edema;
these areas often show enhancement after contrast
administration. Meningeal enhancement, either occurring alone or in conjunction with parenchymal enhancement, may also be noted. There are some limitations
associated with CT imaging, including a relative lack of
sensitivity for inflammatory lesions when compared
with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and the occurrence of a phenomenon known as beam hardening
artifact, which compromises imaging of the medulla
oblongata due to the thick nature of the adjacent petrous
temporal bone.
Magnetic resonance imaging is currently the gold
standard for visual evaluation of CNS anatomy and associated disease states. Compared with CT, it has improved
sensitivity for the detection of most CNS pathology,
including inflammatory diseases. It utilizes a completely
novel technology that does not rely on ionizing radiation
but rather on placing the patient in a high magnetic field
and delivering radiofrequency pulses, which change the
movements and behavior of hydrogen atoms (protons)
within the patient. As these protons move, they create a
magnetic signal that is captured to generate images.
As protons are primarily concentrated within water in
biologic tissues, the differences in water content between
different tissues and different pathologic processes are
what determine the contrast within the images generated.
The parameters controlling delivery of the radiofrequency

pulse and capture of the resulting signal can be adjusted
to create many different sequences, which can highlight
or remove signals associated with certain tissues or
pathologies. Inflammatory lesions generally appear as
hypointense on T1‐weighted images and hyperintense
on T2‐weighted images, with some degree of enhancement after contrast administration. Enhancement of
both parenchymal lesions and meninges can be seen
after intravenous contrast administration. This enhancement varies in intensity and uniformity, and may be
influenced by a variety of factors including the degree of
inflammatory cell infiltrate, associated tissue edema and
the presence of necrotic tissue within the lesion.
The analysis of CSF is an integral part of the diagnostic
process for patients with inflammatory CNS disease.
Cerebrospinal fluid can be collected from the cerebellomedullary cistern or the lumbar subarachnoid
space. Normal CSF has very few leukocytes (0–5/μL), an
absence of erythrocytes, and a low protein concentration
(0–20 mg/dL). Meningeal, brain or spinal cord inflammation usually leads to increases in leukocytes (pleocytosis)
and protein concentration within the CSF. Occasionally,
an infectious (e.g., canine distemper) or noninfectious
meningoencephalitis or meningomyelitis will lead to an
increased protein without a corresponding increase in
white blood cell numbers, which is known as albuminocytologic dissociation. Cytologic evaluation of the CSF
can also provide valuable information to the clinician.
The composition of leukocytes within the CSF can
provide clues to an infectious etiology in some cases
(e.g., eosinophilic pleocytosis with parasitic and some
fungal infections, lymphocytic pleocytosis with viral
infections) or can be associated with presumed immune‐
mediated conditions in others (e.g., neutrophilic pleocytosis with SRMA, mononuclear pleocytosis with NME).
In rare cases, infectious organisms can be visualized on
CSF cytology (e.g., Cryptococcus neoformans).
It must be noted that CSF pleocytosis is not exclusive
to inflammatory disease, as such a pattern can also
be seen with other conditions, including neoplasia or
acute trauma. In addition, albuminocytologic dissociation is a common and relatively nonspecific change
seen with compressive, vascular, neoplastic, and
degenerative CNS diseases. As a result, CSF evaluation
is ideally performed in conjunction with advanced
diagnostic imaging (preferably MRI) in order to rule
out these other conditions.
Despite utilizing both CNS imaging and CSF analysis,
the diagnosis can remain elusive in some cases. The most
common scenario is difficulty in distinguishing inflammatory from neoplastic disease. In these situations,
obtaining meningeal and/or brain tissue for histologic
evaluation may be the best way to arrive at a definitive
diagnosis. Brain biopsy is rarely performed for suspected

VetBooks.ir

73 Meningoencephalitis and Meningomyelitis

meningoencephalitis, although advances in stereotactic
biopsy systems and minimally invasive methods may
help in making such an option more acceptable to both
clinicians and the owners of affected animals. As GME,
NME, and NLE are diagnoses that can only be made with
histopathology, many clinicians will refer to cases of
inflammatory CNS disease diagnosed with imaging and
CSF analysis as meningoencephalitis of unknown etiology
(MUE) or unknown origin (MUO). This designation
typically does not include dogs with SRMA, eosinophilic
meningoencephalitis, or greyhound meningoencephalitis as these patients have distinctive signalments, clinical
syndromes, imaging findings, and/or CSF abnormalities
(see Table 73.2).
A variety of assays are available to identify infectious
agents within the blood, CSF or other body fluids. These
include assays for organism antigens (e.g., Cryptococcus
neoformans), antibodies generated against the organism
(e.g., IgG and IgM for canine distemper or Toxoplasma
gondii), and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for organism DNA or RNA. Cytologic findings associated with
other body systems (e.g., inclusion bodies in cells from a
conjunctival swab in animals with canine distemper)
may also aid in the diagnosis of certain infectious
­diseases and prompt additional testing for suspected
organisms.

­Therapy
Therapy for meningoencephalitis and meningomyelitis
depends on the underlying etiology causing the inflammation, but typically involves antimicrobial, antiinflammatory or immunosuppressive medications. There are
no antiviral medications known to be effective or currently recommended for use in small animals with CNS
viral infections, and treatment for these patients remains
largely supportive. Animals with a documented or suspected bacterial meningoencephalitis are ideally treated
with an antibiotic that shows good penetration of the
blood–brain and blood–CSF barriers (Table 73.3).
Antifungal medications are indicated in some patients,
and these also vary in their ability to penetrate the CNS.
Doxycycline not only has antibacterial activity with
good CNS penetration, but also is the drug of choice for
animals with rickettsial infections. Animals with T. gondii
or N. caninum infections may respond to sulfa antibiotics, clindamycin and/or pyrimethamine. Animals with
infectious meningoencephalitis often benefit from
short‐term, antiinflammatory doses of glucocorticoids,
although immunosuppressive doses and prolonged
administration of these medications should be avoided
as they can impair clearance of the infecting organisms
and substantially worsen clinical signs.

Treatment of the “sterile” meningoencephalitides
focuses on the control of inflammation and suppression
of the immune system with glucocorticoids and in
some cases additional immunosuppressive medications.
Prednisone or dexamethasone is often started at antiinflammatory doses after imaging studies and CSF collection, pending the results of infectious disease testing.
Antimicrobial drugs are usually indicated while awaiting
these results. When the clinician has ruled out infectious
causes, the patient is reassessed and their response to
therapy is evaluated. Some animals will respond fully to
antiinflammatory glucocorticoids. However, those with
an absent or partial response will often benefit from
escalation to an immunosuppressive dose (Table 73.4).
If remission is achieved, this dose is continued for an
extended period and then the dose is slowly reduced over
a period of weeks to months. Some animals are eventually
able to have their glucocorticoid therapy discontinued,

although they must be monitored closely for relapse of
clinical signs. Conversely, many patients require long‐
term and often life‐long therapy.
Some conditions, such as SRMA, generalized tremor
syndrome and idiopathic eosinophilic meningoencephalitis, can typically be managed with glucocorticoids
alone. This strategy can also work for patients with
GME, NME or NLE although anecdotal evidence suggests that these dogs do not respond as well, and may
benefit from additional immunosuppressive therapy. This
benefit may occur due to additional mechanisms of
immunosuppression (typically interference with lymphocyte proliferation) or by allowing a decreased glucocorticoid dose, which reduces adverse effects and
improves overall management. Several different immunosuppressive drugs have been utilized in this scenario
(see Table 73.4), and choice is based primarily on clinician preference, as rigorous studies demonstrating a

clear benefit of these medications have not yet been published. The use of other immunomodulatory interventions,
such as intravenous immunoglobulin and plasmapheresis, is an intriguing possibility that has yet to be investigated in small animal patients. Anticonvulsant therapy is
utilized in animals with seizures. Dogs with generalized
tremor syndrome may also benefit from concurrent diazepam therapy. Although the pain associated with meningoencephalitis or meningomyelitis usually improves
dramatically with glucocorticoid therapy, additional analgesics such as gabapentin or opioid medications may
prove beneficial until the inflammation subsides.
The primary means of monitoring response to therapy
in animals with inflammatory CNS disease is assessment
of clinical signs based on examination and questioning of
the owners. Although complete normalization is ideal and
achievable in many patients, some animals are left with
residual deficits. A significant challenge for the clinician is to determine if such deficits are the result of active
inflammation or permanent damage (i.e., loss of cells or
tissue) to the CNS. Periodic monitoring with a CBC and
serum biochemistry is indicated in patients receiving glucocorticoids or other immunosuppressive drugs to detect
adverse effects associated with therapy (e.g., myelosuppression, hepatic failure) as well as infections occurring
secondary to immunosuppression. Monitoring of serum
drug concentrations is not routinely performed, although
some clinicians will utilize this for ciclosporin A. Similarly,
repeat CNS imaging and/or CSF evaluation can be helpful
in some patients to assess the degree of ongoing inflammation and other pathology, although this is not routinely
performed by all clinicians and is obviously dependent on
the owner’s financial means. Serial monitoring of antibody or antigen titers can be useful in the monitoring of
some infectious diseases.

­Prognosis
The prognosis for animals with inflammatory CNS
­disease is highly variable, and depends on both the
underlying etiology as well as an individual’s response
to therapy. Some animals with viral disease may clear
the virus, and the prognosis depends on the amount
of damage that occurred to the CNS while infected
(e.g., canine distemper). These animals may survive,
although often with residual deficits (e.g., distemper
“myoclonus”). Conversely, some viral diseases such as
rabies, pseudorabies, and FIP are invariably fatal.
Fungal disease typically requires long‐term and often
life‐long therapy. Animals with bacterial or protozoal
diseases can be treated successfully although they may
be left with residual deficits and the prognosis is typically guarded.
Dogs with SRMA, generalized tremor syndrome, and
idiopathic eosinophilic meningoencephalitis, usually
have a good prognosis, with full resolution of clinical
signs and long‐term remission after therapy, although
relapses are possible. The prognosis for dogs with
GME, NME, and NLE is much more variable. Although
some of these patients may respond fully to treatment,
life‐long therapy is typical, and many dogs will have an
incomplete response. In addition, some dogs progress
and die in spite of aggressive treatment. However, the
prognosis for cases cited in the literature is likely to be
overly pessimistic, as there is a bias towards dogs that
have had disease confir­
mation via histopathology.
Finally, the prognosis for animals with greyhound
meningoencephalitis has been suggested to be poor,
although aggressive therapeutic intervention has not
yet been described in the literature.

Diseases of the Neuromuscular Junction
David Lipsitz, DVM, DACVIM (Neurology)
Veterinary Specialty Hospital, San Diego, CA, USA

The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) consists of the
efferent nerve terminals, the neuromuscular cleft, and
the postsynaptic membrane. As an action potential
reaches the presynaptic nerve terminal, voltage‐gated
calcium channels open, allowing Ca2+ ion efflux into the
presynaptic nerve terminal. This Ca2+ influx allows synaptic vesicles containing neurotransmitter to dock and
fuse with the sarcolemma in the process of exocytosis,
thereby releasing the neurotransmitter acetylcholine
(ACh) into the synaptic cleft. Fusion of the vesicular
and plasma membranes is mediated by SNARE (soluble
N‐ethylmaleimide‐sensitive fusion) proteins. Some of
the SNARE proteins that are used for synaptic vesicle
exocytosis include synaptobrevin (VAMP1), syntaxin 1a,
and synaptosome‐associated protein 25 (SNAP‐25).
These SNARE proteins may be the target of many disease
processes and toxins.
The ACh released from these vesicles then diffuses
through the synaptic cleft and binds to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) located on the specially
folded postsynaptic muscle fiber sarcolemma. The adult
nACHR has been shown to have four different protein
subunits (α, β, δ, ε). The receptor is arranged in the fashion
of five subunits: 2 α1, β1, δ, ε. These subunits span the
lipid bilayer, creating a water‐filled pore which forms a
“hydrophobic girdle” that acts as a barrier to ion permeation. When ACh binds to the receptor, it undergoes
conformational change that allows a preferential influx
of Na+ > Ca++ and an efflux of potassium. This region is
also closely associated with a high density of sodium
channels in order to promote and amplify the signal to
assure the propagation of an action potential to generate
muscle contraction. As the sodium ions move into the
muscle membrane, local depolarization occurs in what is
termed an endplate potential (EPP) which spreads across
the surface of the sarcolemma, with the ensuing excitation‐contraction coupling allowing the muscle fiber to
contract. The magnitude of the EPP is dependent on the

amount of ACh released and the amount of nAChRs but
there is normally an abundance of both, resulting in a
large safety factor for neuromuscular transmission.
Acetylcholinesterase then breaks down the ACh (producing choline and esterase) and the ACh diffuses away
from the synapse, allowing the sodium channels to close.
New ACh molecules are synthesized when the choline
is transported, through reuptake into the presynaptic
terminal.
The clinical presentation in animals with neuromuscular transmission disease is very similar regardless of
whether the disorder is presynaptic (i.e., botulism) or
postsynaptic (i.e., myasthenia gravis). There is usually a
symmetric progressive generalized weakness in all limbs.
Exercise intolerance is often seen as well. Tendon reflexes
may or may not be intact. There is often facial muscle,
laryngeal, pharyngeal or esophageal weakness associated
with these disorders. Sensory function is unaffected, as
would be expected.

­Myasthenia Gravis
Myasthenia gravis (MG) is a neuromuscular transmission disorder caused by a reduction in the number of
functional nAChRs on the postsynaptic membrane. It is
usually the result of an acquired autoimmune disease
and much less commonly a congenital disorder.
Clinical Presentation
Myasthenia gravis should be a consideration in any animal
being examined for focal or generalized neuromuscular
weakness. The clinical signs may be focal in nature and
limited to esophageal dilation leading to regurgitation,
pharyngeal dysfunction causing dysphagia and laryngeal
paresis/paralysis causing dysphonia (voice change).
Multiple cranial nerve abnormalities may also occur in

VetBooks.ir
