Section 9 Infectious Disease

months after infected tick exposure, starting with a four‐
day episode of self‐limiting anorexia, fever, lameness,
and local lymphadenopathy in the leg closest to tick
attachment, followed sometimes by several additional
short episodes in the same or different leg(s) every two
weeks, resolving without treatment. Older exposed pup­
pies (13–26 weeks old) showed fewer signs and episodes,
and adult dogs (>26 weeks old) seroconverted without
illness. Antibiotic therapy cleared 85–90% (but not all)
experimental dogs, based on skin biopsy culture and
PCR test results.
In clinical cases in the field, dogs with suspected Lyme
arthritis may show lameness in one leg with a hot swol­
len painful joint and joint effusion. Dogs with polyar­
thropathy (e.g., hocks/carpi) may have co‐infections,
immune‐mediated arthritis or perhaps had multiple tick
attachment sites affecting multiple limbs/joints. Dogs
with Lyme arthritis typically respond quickly (within 1–2
days) to antibiotics, and if they do not, other causes of
signs should be sought. Response to treatment may be
coincidental, due to responsive co‐infections (e.g., ana­
plasmosis), or due to the antiarthritic, antiinflammatory
properties of doxycycline.
Lyme Nephritis
There is no experimental model for Lyme nephritis so
the incubation, progression, best treatment, or whether
Lyme vaccine prevents or promotes aggravates the ill­
ness are unknown. It is suspected to be a chronic mani­
festation, since it is associated with seropositivity and
circulating immune complexes at presentation. Retriever
dogs are predisposed, so an underlying genetic immuno­
dysregulation and/or podocytopathy may exist. Dogs
with early or mild glomerulonephritis may have occult
proteinuria; more severely affected dogs present with
signs of protein‐losing nephropathy (PLN), such as
edema/effusions, thromboembolic events (e.g., pulmo­
nary, saddle, portal, neurovascular), hypertensive dam­
age (e.g., blindness, epistaxis, neurovascular events), and
eventually renal failure (e.g., anorexia, weight loss, eme­
sis, polyuria/polydipsia, and potentially oliguria/anuria).

­Diagnosis
Serology
The organism migrates interstitially (exception: B. mayonii,
a cause of Lyme borreliosis in humans, may travel hematog­
enously) and is difficult to find by cytology with special
stains, culture, or PCR testing, so serologic testing is used for
antibodies directed against natural exposure antigens. Older
tests such as whole‐cell enzyme‐linked i­mmunosorbent

assay (ELISA), indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA),
immunoglobulin (Ig) G, IgM, and western immunoblot
show cross‐reactivity with antibodies from vaccines and
other infections, and are no longer preferred.
The C6 peptide antibody test is sensitive and specific
for natural exposure antibodies against part of the VlsE
antigen, which is only expressed by the spirochete after
infecting the host and is not in Lyme vaccines. Antibodies
against the C6 peptide rise 3–5 weeks after infection and
persist in carriers. Qualitative in‐house C6 peptide
­testing is combined with tests for heartworm antigen
and antibodies against multiple Anaplasma and
Ehrlichia spp. (e.g., SNAP‐4Dx Plus, IDEXX Reference
Laboratories). Quantitative C6 peptide antibodies (Lyme
Quant C6, IDEXX) usually wane 50% by six months post
treatment. The new baseline result is useful for com­
parisons should future signs of illness suggest relapse or
reinfection. The AccuPlex®4 test (Antech Diagnostics
Reference Laboratories) tests for heartworm antigen
and antibodies against Anaplasma phagocytophilum
and Ehrlichia canis; its qualitative Lyme antibody test
uses an algorithm comparing the magnitude and
responses to five markers, including those usually found
in vaccinates (ospA) vs after natural exposure (ospC,
VlsE, ospF), and for recent exposure (ospC antibody
rises 2–3 weeks post exposure and wanes within 3–5
months) vs past/chronic infection (ospF antibody rises
6–8 weeks post exposure and persists). The Multiplex
test (Cornell University) quantitates ospA, ospC, and
ospF antibodies. The in‐house Abaxis/Zoetis qualitative
tests for only Lyme (VetScan) or for Lyme/A.
phagocytophilum/E. canis/heartworm (FLEX4) tests for
Lyme antibodies directed against proprietary antigens
mimicking VlsE, ospC, and p41 (flagellin).
Compromised interpretation of the Lyme test results
above may be due to ospA antibodies possibly present in
nonvaccinates after natural exposure (acutely or in carri­
ers), ospC antibodies induced by new Lyme vaccines
(bacterins and chimeric recombinant), and cross‐react­
ing flagellin antibodies from other infections/vaccines.
The magnitude of any natural exposure Lyme antibody
titer does not predict illness, but may validate exposure.
Lyme Arthritis
Many causes for lameness or inability to rise need to be
considered. Overdiagnosis is a problem; one study
showed that 40% of Lyme arthritis cases were misdiag­
nosed and signs were due to other causes – for example,
Lyme seropositivity was coincidental. Blood tests
­(complete blood count [CBC]/biochemical profile) are
not abnormal but other tick‐borne or other illnesses may
cause changes such as cytopenias, hypoalbuminemia,
hyperglobulinemia, azotemia, etc. All seropositive dogs

VetBooks.ir

100 Lyme Borreliosis

should be checked for proteinuria. Joint tap cytology
shows a neutrophilic inflammatory response without
bacteria, but morulae may be seen due to co‐infections.
Lyme Nephritis
Abnormalities may include elevated blood pressure
measurement, proteinuria/cylindruria, ± glucosuria, ±
decreased concentrating ability, hypoalbuminemia,
hypercholesterolemia, azotemia, hyperphosphatemia,
anemia, thrombocytopenia, and abnormal (hypercoag­
ulable) thromboelastography. Diagnostic work‐up
of PLN also includes screening for other infectious,
inflammatory, genetic, and neoplastic diseases that
cause proteinuria (e.g., serologic testing, urine culture,
chest radiographs, abdominal ultrasonogram). Renal
imaging is usually unremarkable. Renal biopsy by
­experienced personnel with thin section light micros­
copy, special stains, immunofluorescence, immunohis­
tochemistry, and transmission electron microscopy
shows immune‐complex glomerulonephritis (staining
techniques for Lyme‐specific complexes are not vali­
dated), and possible secondary tubular necrosis/regen­
eration and interstitial nephritis.

­Therapy
Therapy for nonclinical nonproteinuric dogs is not war­
ranted. For Lyme arthritis signs, doxycycline (10–20 mg/
kg/day for 30 days) or minocycyline is recommended
because of possible responsive co‐infections. Other
antispirochetal antibiotics include amoxicillin, erythro­
mycin, azithromycin, cefovecin, and ceftriaxone. Mana­
gement for Lyme nephritis includes longer antibiotic
regimes (perhaps until the Quant C6 result has waned), a
modified low‐protein diet, renin‐angiotenin‐aldosterone
system inhibitors (e.g., angiotensin‐converting inhibitors
and/or angiotensin receptor blockers), omega‐3 fatty
acids, antithrombotics, antihypertensives, drugs for renal
failure (e.g., antiulcer medications, phosphate binders),
and possibly immunosuppressives if renal biopsy shows
glomerular immune‐complex deposition or, in rapidly
progressive cases, even without biopsy confirmation
(compassionate care). The best protocol is unknown but
may include single or combined mycophenolate, cyclo­
phosphamide, steroids, chlorambucil, cyclosporin, and/
or azathioprine.

­Prognosis
The prognosis for Lyme arthritis is excellent as the
course is self‐limiting or responsive to antibiotics within

1–2 days. If unresponsive, consider other causes. The
prognosis for Lyme nephritis is guarded to poor if the
dog presents in renal failure, but may be better in earlier
stages. Monitoring abnormalities frequently with treat­
ment adaptation is essential.

­Prevention
Tick control year round (ticks are active when tem­
perature is >40 °F or 4 °C) is most important, since
ticks in Lyme‐endemic areas may transmit borreliosis
as well as anaplasmosis, babesiosis, ehrlichiosis,
mycoplasmosis, and Rocky Mountain spotted fever,
and possibly bartonellosis. Some of these are trans­
mitted within the first day of tick attachment so prod­
ucts which ­prevent tick attachment (e.g., permethrins
or amitraz) or kill ticks fast after attachment (e.g.,
isoxazolines) are preferred.
There are five Lyme vaccines available: three killed
adjuvanted bivalent bacterins (LymeVax, Zoetis;
Duramune Lyme, E
­ lanco; Nobivac Lyme, Merck Animal
Health) including ospA and ospC, a nonadjuvanted
recombinant subunit ospA vaccine (Recombitek Lyme,
Merial), and a chimeric recombinant adjuvanted vac­
cine which includes ospA plus ospC from seven strains
(Vanguard crLyme, Zoetis). Even in endemic areas,
Lyme vaccination is controversial because:
tick control is important to protect dogs from other
tick‐borne diseases in these areas
●● most exposed dogs do not become ill or they respond
quickly to commonly used antibiotics
●● Lyme vaccines may interfere with some diagnostic
tests
●● Lyme vaccines are costly, have inconsistent efficacy,
produce weaker/shorter duration of immunity
that may require six-month boostering, and cause
more postvaccinal adverse events than other canine
vaccines.
●● the most serious forms of Lyme disease have an immune‐
mediated pathogenesis, so theoretically it may not be a
good idea to introduce Lyme antigens to genetically
predisposed dogs, lest sensitization or aggravation
of immune‐complex deposition in glomeruli or joints
may occur.
●●

These last possibilities may not appear temporally asso­
ciated with vaccination and are difficult to study without
an experimental model of Lyme nephritis. Most con­
cerns are anecdotal and theoretical, and because owner
compliance to using adequate tick control may be prob­
lematic, many veterinarians recommend Lyme vaccina­
tions in addition to tick control.

­Public Health Implications
A seropositive dog has exposure to wildlife, may be a car­
rier for infection with other tick‐borne diseases or lepto­
spirosis, and is a sentinel for Lyme exposure in the environs.

Educate owners about landscaping, tick prevention on
their pets and themselves, and that physicians in Lyme‐
endemic areas may prescribe humans a single day’s pre­
ventive dose of doxycycline to be taken within 72 hours of
removing an engorged Ixodes tick.

Leptospirosis
Katharine F. Lunn, BVMS, MS, PhD, MRCVS, DACVIM (SAIM)
College of Veterinary Medicine, NC State, Raleigh, NC, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology

­Epidemiology

Leptospirosis is a zoonotic bacterial disease affecting the
health of animals and humans throughout the world. In
small animals, clinical leptospirosis is a significant problem
in dogs, but the role of leptospires in feline disease is still
poorly understood. Leptospiral organisms are typically
divided into serovars, based on antibody responses to surface proteins. Serovars are further classified into antigenically related serogroups. Canine leptospirosis is caused by
several serovars of the pathogenic species Leptospira
interrogans sensu latu. Examples of serovars that have
been implicated in canine disease include Grippotyphosa
(serogroup Grippotyphosa), Pomona (serogroup Pomona),
and Bratislava (serogroup Australis).
Leptospiral organisms enter the host through intact
mucosal surfaces or damaged skin. During the first week of
infection, organisms multiply and spread throughout the
vascular space, leading to vascular damage and invasion of
many organs and tissues. During this initial leptospiremic
phase, organisms can be isolated from the blood. The
immune phase of infection begins in the second week, with
the appearance of serum antibodies. This leads to clearing
of leptospires from the blood and many organs; however,
organisms may be protected from the systemic antibody
response in sites such as the renal tubules and the eye.
Leptospiruria develops in the second week after infection
and can persist for days to months, depending on the species of the mammalian host and the infecting serovar.
Pathologic changes associated with leptospirosis
include vasculitis and endothelial cell damage. The precise mechanisms by which leptospires cause tissue damage and disease are not well understood, but several
toxins and enzymes produced by the organisms likely
contribute to disease pathogenesis. The pathogenicity of
leptospires may also be related to their motility and their
ability to adhere to, and penetrate, cells.

Pathogenic leptospires are maintained in the environment
through the shedding of organisms in the urine of a wide
variety of endemically infected mammalian reservoir
hosts. These reservoir hosts usually do not develop clinical
disease, but serve as a source infection for incidental hosts,
such as dogs and humans. In some locations, there appears
to be an increased incidence of leptospirosis in late summer and fall, perhaps associated with weather conditions
and wildlife behavior. Leptospires survive, but do not replicate, in warm and wet environments, whereas freezing,
ultraviolet radiation, and dehydration all reduce survival.
Transmission to incidental hosts is usually indirect, through
exposure to contaminated water, soil, food or bedding,
although direct contact through ingestion, bite wounds, or
direct contact with urine is possible.
Reservoir hosts that likely contribute to environmental
contamination include the raccoon, opossum, fox, skunk,
mouse, rat, vole, squirrel, and deer. Clinicians should note
that many of these reservoirs co‐exist with humans in
urban, suburban, and periurban environments, thus leptospirosis is not confined to large‐breed, working, predominantly outdoor dogs or rural dogs. Many clinicians
routinely diagnose leptospirosis in small‐breed indoor
dogs. Indeed, two different recent studies have demonstrated that dogs in some urban areas are at increased risk
for leptospirosis, and that small dogs (<15 lb) were more
likely to be diagnosed with the disease. Case reports and
serologic surveys have demonstrated both clinical leptospirosis and subclinical exposure to the organisms in dogs
from many locations in the US and Canada, and it is likely
that only desert regions are truly free of the disease.
Unfortunately, it is difficult to determine which serovars
predominate in different geographic regions, as diagnosis
is usually based on antibody titers, and these cannot identify the infecting serovar. Further studies are needed to

Clinical Small Animal Internal Medicine Volume II, First Edition. Edited by David S. Bruyette.
© 2020 John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Published 2020 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc.
Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/bruyette/clinical

VetBooks.ir

Section 9 Infectious Disease

isolate and genetically type the organisms in order to better understand the epidemiology of leptospirosis in different hosts and regions of the world.

­Signalment
Any age, breed, and sex of dog is susceptible to leptospirosis, and the diagnosis should not be ruled out on the
basis of signalment. A recent study of the Veterinary
Medical Database demonstrated signalment changes in
canine leptospirosis from 1970 to 2009. In the most
recent decade studied, the highest prevalence of disease
was in the 7–9.9 year age group, and in dogs <15 lb. The
terrier group had the highest prevalence in this decade,
and Yorkshire terriers had the highest prevalence among
small breeds. Other sources have suggested an increased
susceptibility in German shepherd dogs, although this
has not been rigorously evaluated.
There are few reports of clinical leptospirosis in cats,
but it has been shown that cats can seroconvert to leptospiral organisms, and there is some evidence that cats
may shed leptospires in the urine. However, it has not
been clearly demonstrated that leptospirosis is a significant clinical problem in domestic cats.

­History and Clinical Signs
The manifestations of leptospirosis in dogs range from
peracute disease to subclinical infection, and include
sudden death, acute kidney injury (AKI), liver disease,
vasculitis, and uveitis. Because this is a zoonotic disease,
it is essential that veterinarians maintain a high index of
suspicion for this infection, particularly in cases with
atypical clinical signs.
Typical clinical signs in acute or subacute leptospirosis
include lethargy, anorexia, fever, muscle pain, abdominal
pain, signs of shock, dehydration, vomiting, diarrhea,
bleeding, jaundice, polyuria, oliguria, and anuria. While
AKI has been the most common presentation for canine
leptospirosis in recent years, affected patients may also
present with a combination of renal and hepatic disease,
or hepatic disease alone.
Acute kidney injury in leptospirosis may be anuric,
oliguric, or polyuric. Dogs that survive AKI due to
­leptospirosis may progress to chronic kidney disease
(CKD). Acute kidney injury may be undetected in subclinically infected animals, and those patients may eventually be diagnosed with CKD of unknown cause.
Leptospirosis should also be considered in any dog with
previously diagnosed CKD that develops unexplained
“acute‐on‐chronic” kidney disease. Other manifestations

of renal disease in canine patients with leptospirosis
include glucosuria in the absence of hyperglycemia,
nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and renal tubular acidosis. Liver disease associated with leptospirosis is predominantly cholestatic in nature, with minimal histopatho­logic
changes.
Clinicians should be aware that patients with leptospirosis may present with unusual signs, including respiratory distress, bleeding disorders, effusions, and uveitis.
Pulmonary disease in dogs with leptospirosis is probably
more common than previously suspected, and has been
attributed to pulmonary hemorrhage, a known serious
complication of leptospirosis in people. Bleeding disorders may manifest as petechiae, epistaxis or gastrointestinal bleeding, and are most likely due to vasculitis,
although the mechanisms are poorly understood.

­Diagnosis
Common but nonspecific laboratory findings in dogs
with leptospirosis include azotemia, hyperphosphatemia,
metabolic acidosis, hyper‐ or hypokalemia, hyperbilirubinemia, increased serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
activity, and increased serum alanine aminotransferase
(ALT) activity; the latter is usually less markedly
increased than ALP activity. Mild to moderate thrombocytopenia is relatively common, although the platelet
count is seldom low enough to directly cause spontaneous bleeding. Urine specific gravity can be hyposthenuric in patients with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; it may
also be isosthenuric or concentrated, depending on the
extent of renal involvement. Urinalysis may reveal hematuria, cylindruria, proteinuria, or glucosuria.
Imaging findings are also nonspecific, and may include
reticulonodular pulmonary interstitial or alveolar opacities on radiographs, and ground‐glass nodules or diffuse
opacity and peribronchovascular interstitial thickening
on thoracic computed tomography (CT). Abdominal
ultrasound examination has been reported to reveal
renal and hepatic changes, perirenal and peritoneal effusions, intestinal wall thickening, and lymphadenopathy.
Diagnostic tests for leptospirosis rely on detection of
the organism, or detection of an antibody response in the
infected patient. It is recommended that both types of
tests be utilized to maximize the chance of diagnosing
this zoonotic disease. It is essential that the results of any
diagnostic test be interpreted in light of the patient’s
clinical signs, clinicopathologic findings, and vaccination
history.
The microscopic agglutination test (MAT) is still the
most widely used antibody detection test for the diagnosis of leptospirosis. Advantages of this test are that it is
widely available and provides a numerical titer that allows

VetBooks.ir

101 Leptospirosis

comparison of paired acute and convalescent titers. Most
authors recommend that an initial titer of ≥1:800 is consistent with a diagnosis of leptospirosis in an unvaccinated dog. If initial titers are low, or the patient has an
unknown vaccine history, convalescent titers can provide
further information. Although a 2–4‐week period
between acute and convalescent titers is often recommended, it is not always necessary to wait that long.
When performing paired acute and convalescent titers, a
fourfold change (usually an increase) in titer supports the
diagnosis of leptospirosis. Most laboratories that perform
the MAT will test patient sera against multiple serovars
(representative of serogroups) and often report seropositivity to more than one serogroup, due to significant
cross‐reactivity. For this and other reasons, it should be
noted that MAT results cannot identify the infecting
leptospiral serovar in an individual patient. However, for
most clinicians this is of little importance, as there is currently no evidence that clinical signs, treatment, or prognosis are serovar or serogroup specific. When paired
titers are performed, the MAT is a highly sensitive and
specific test for leptospirosis.
More recently available serologic tests for the diagnosis of canine leptospirosis include an enzyme‐linked
immunosorbent assay (ELISA) test that detects antibodies to the lipoprotein LipL32 found on the surface of
pathogenic leptospires, available both at a reference laboratory and as a point‐of‐care test (SNAP® Lepto Test,
IDEXX), and a patient‐side lateral flow device test that
detects IgM antibodies to a whole‐cell antigen from
Grippotyphosa and Bratislava serovars (WITNESS®
Lepto, Zoetis). These tests give qualitative positive or
negative antibody results, with proposed advantages
including lower cost and shorter turn‐around time, compared to the MAT. In one study, SNAP Lepto demonstrated similar performance to the MAT for the detection
of antibodies to Leptospira spp., with agreement being
greater in MAT‐positive samples with higher titers. In a
more recent study comparing MAT, SNAP Lepto, and
WITNESS Lepto in experimentally infected dogs, the
WITNESS test detected seroconversion to common
leptospiral serovars in all 32 dogs by day 10 after infection, the MAT detected seroconversion in 30 of 32 dogs
by day 14, and the SNAP test detected antibodies in only
three of 32 dogs in the 14‐day follow‐up period. However,
it is important to note that the challenge infection in
these dogs did not result in clinical illness, and the comparative performance of these tests may be different in a
clinical setting in which patients are sick and potentially
presented later in the course of infection.
Advantages of the point‐of‐care tests include that they
potentially allow earlier diagnosis of leptospirosis, thus
facilitating early institution of safe patient handling protocols and appropriate medical therapy. However, these

tests cannot reliably distinguish vaccinal titers from natural infection, and they do not provide numerical titers
to allow comparison of acute and convalescent titers.
These disadvantages are particularly important in dogs
with low initial titers, vaccinated dogs, or dogs with an
unknown vaccination history.
If a negative result is obtained on either point‐of‐care
test, additional serum samples should be obtained for
acute and convalescent MAT titers (or the point‐of‐care
test can be repeated in 1–2 weeks), polymerase chain
reaction (PCR) testing should also be performed (see
later), and leptospirosis should not be ruled out unless an
alternate diagnosis is confirmed, or acute and convalescent serologic tests are negative. If a positive result is
obtained on a point‐of‐care test and the patient is vaccinated, or has an unknown vaccine history, acute and
convalescent MAT titers should be performed to distinguish between vaccinal titers and natural infection.
Bacterial culture of pathogenic leptospires is very
rarely used as a diagnostic test in dogs, because it is technically demanding, of limited availability, and requires
several months of incubation. Dark‐field microscopy and
fluorescent antibody tests have been used to demonstrate the presence of organisms in urine samples but
sensitivity is poor, and these tests have largely been
replaced by PCR‐based assays. Blood or urine samples
from canine patients can be tested by PCR for the presence of DNA from pathogenic leptospires.
A variety of different PCR tests are available, with
quantitative tests such as real‐time PCR likely to be more
sensitive. Despite the wide availability and frequent use
of PCR‐based assays, there are relatively few published
studies that evaluate their sensitivity and specificity.
Potential causes of false‐negative results include low
leptospire numbers in the sample collected, intermittent
shedding of organisms in the urine, or the presence of
PCR inhibitors in the sample. False‐positive results on
the PCR assay may be due to sampling from a subclinically affected carrier, the presence of dead organisms, or
contamination of the sample during collection, handling,
or processing in the laboratory. If leptospirosis is suspected, obtaining both blood and urine samples for PCR
testing may increase the chances of detecting the organism. Positive or negative results from the PCR should be
further followed up with acute and convalescent MAT
titers, and should always be interpreted in light of the
patient’s clinical signs.

­Therapy
There are no prospective studies that provide data
regarding the best antibiotic protocols for treatment of
leptospirosis in dogs. There are many studies that address

947

VetBooks.ir

948

Section 9 Infectious Disease

antibiotic therapy in other species, including experimental models of leptospirosis, and large animals such as pigs
and cows. Antibiotics used to treat leptospirosis should
terminate leptospiremia and eliminate the carrier state.
Doxycycline is often used as it is generally believed to
achieve both of these goals. Doxycycline is also used prophylactically in humans who have a high risk of exposure
to leptospirosis. Penicillins are often used to clear leptospiremia, which should also reduce the risk of organ
damage. Penicillin, ampicillin, and amoxicillin all appear
to be effective.
The choice of antibiotic to be used in the acute phase
of the disease is generally dictated by the clinical status of
the patient. In general, injectable antibiotics are used in
acutely ill patients that are vomiting or not eating.
Patients that tolerate oral medications may be started on
amoxicillin and then changed to oral doxycycline, or oral
doxycycline may be used as the sole therapy if the patient
tolerates it. Again, there are no published data that
address the duration of antibiotic therapy in dogs with
leptospirosis. Most clinicians treat with a penicillin for
1–2 weeks, followed by doxycycline for two weeks, or
treat with doxycycline alone for 2–3 weeks.
For dogs with AKI due to leptospirosis, supportive
care is essential for a successful outcome. Patients with
leptospirosis that remain oliguric or anuric are candidates for extracorporeal therapies such as hemodialysis.

­Prognosis
The prognosis for dogs with leptospirosis likely depends
on which body systems are affected, and the extent and
severity of organ damage. If suspected or diagnosed
promptly, and appropriate specific and supportive therapy is initiated, the majority of dogs with leptospirosis
will recover from the disease. The prognosis is expected
to be guarded for patients with oliguric or anuric AKI,
unless renal replacement therapy is initiated. Patients
with less severe AKI may progress to CKD or return to
normal. In a recent German study of 99 dogs with leptospirosis, dogs that did not survive were more likely to
have severe dyspnea, oliguria, azotemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and severe radiographic pulmonary changes,
with the latter being specifically associated with high
mortality.

­Vaccination
Most of the canine leptospirosis vaccines currently used
in the US include the serovars Icterohaemorrhagiae,
Canicola, Pomona, and Grippotyphosa. It is not known

whether these vaccines protect against additional serovars. Contemporary vaccines are purified by subunit
technology or microfiltration processes, and they appear
to be associated with fewer vaccine reactions compared
to the whole‐cell cultures that were commonly used in
the past.
Vaccination against canine leptospirosis continues to
be an area of controversy, despite a growing body of work
regarding vaccine efficacy in dogs. In particular, it has
been convincingly shown in several studies that vaccination against leptospirosis confers protection against
challenge for at least one year, and also confers significant protection against urine shedding. It should be
noted that there is little correlation between protection
against clinical disease and antibody titers in vaccinated
dogs. Postvaccination MAT titers generally fall by four
months after vaccination, and rarely persist for one year.
This should be kept in mind when interpreting MAT
titers in vaccinated dogs. It has been shown that vaccination does not cause false‐positive results in a PCR‐based
assay for canine leptospirosis.
As noted above, leptospirosis is not a disease that is
confined to large‐breed, outdoor, rural, or working dogs.
This author recommends that the risks and benefits of
vaccination against leptospirosis be discussed with every
dog owner. It is important to bear in mind that leptospirosis is one of the most commonly diagnosed causes of
canine AKI, and that the disease can be seen in dogs of
any age, breed, sex, or lifestyle. It is also important to
bear in mind that currently available vaccines appear to
be both safe and efficacious.

­Public Health Implications
Leptospirosis is a zoonotic disease. It is essential that veterinary personnel understand how the organism is spread
and that infection can occur through damaged skin or
intact mucus membranes. In this author’s opinion, all
dogs with unexplained acute azotemia (including acute‐
on‐chronic) should be treated as leptospirosis suspects
until an alternate diagnosis is obtained. It is not necessary to place these dogs in isolation, but it is essential to
avoid human and animal contact with the urine of suspects. Direct contact with blood should also be avoided.
Leptospirosis suspects should have a urinary catheter
placed, or should only urinate in a dedicated area that
can be cleaned and disinfected. Dogs that urinate in their
cages should have a urinary catheter placed with a closed
collection system. This is also often a valuable procedure
in the management of AKI patients. If placement of a urinary catheter is not possible, for example in a small dog,
absorbent pads can be used in the cage to collect urine.
These can also be weighed to monitor urine output.

VetBooks.ir

101 Leptospirosis

All personnel nursing a dog with leptospirosis should
wear gowns, gloves, and shoe covers while handling the
patient. Immunosuppressed individuals should not handle leptospirosis suspects. Facemasks and eye protection should be worn when cleaning cages or runs, or
handling wet bedding. Laboratory personnel should
wear gloves and a mask when handling body fluids from
a leptospirosis suspect. Gloves should always be worn
when handling canine urine, as dogs can be asymptomatic carriers of leptospirosis. Fortunately, leptospires

are sensitive to most detergents and disinfectants, and
are also killed by drying and sunlight. Owners of dogs
with leptospirosis should be advised to avoid contact
with the dog’s urine. If the dog urinates in the house,
they should wear gloves and use household detergents
or disinfectants to clean up the urine. How long these
dogs will shed leptospires is unknown, but appropriate
antibiotic therapy should reduce the risk. Owners should
contact their own physician with questions about human
leptospirosis.

Yersiniosis
Maria Grazia Pennisi, DVM, PhD
University of Messina, Messina, Italy

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Yersinia pestis is the agent of a rare, highly contagious,
and often fatal zoonosis. Known since ancient times as
plague or “black death,” Y. pestis devastated medieval
Europe with widespread epizootics. Today, Y. pestis is
enzootic in some foci in the Americas, Africa, the Middle
East, and Asia.
Yersinia pestis is a gram‐negative, facultatively anaero­
bic coccobacillus that belongs to the family Enterobacte­
riaceae. The bacterium can survive for weeks in the
environment as it is resistant to low temperatures and
freezing. However, it is sensitive to high temperatures and
desiccation. Yersinia pestis is a vector‐borne pathogen
transmitted by many flea species. Xenopsylla cheopis
(Oriental rat flea) and some other flea species such as
Oropsylla montana (the ground squirrel flea) are very effi­
cient vectors whereas others, such as the dog and cat fleas
(Ctenoceph­alides spp.), are much less efficient. Fleas
acquire the organism from bacteremic mammals. Yersinia
pestis can infect a wide range of mammals, including
humans. Host species have variable susceptibility to devel­
opment of the disease due to various factors. Less suscep­
tible hosts such as mice, rats, squirrels, and prairie dogs
usually develop prolonged bacteremia and therefore act as
natural reservoirs. Due to high flea infestation rates and a
communal lifestyle, burrowing mammals facilitate trans­
mission of the organism by fleas to a high number of hosts.
Within the flea midgut, the bacterium replicates.
Aggregates of the organism block the digestive tract,
which causes the flea to suck blood with increased effort
and regurgitate organisms into the bite wound it inflicts
on subsequent hosts. Cats and dogs can acquire the
infection from fleas but they may also become infected
by ingesting infected prey. Although less common, trans­
mission through aerosolization or contact with mucous
membranes or skin wounds also occurs.

In susceptible mammalian hosts like the cat, Y. pestis is
able to evade host innate immune defenses. It can infect
macrophages wherein it abundantly multiplies inside
phagolysosomes, causing cell lysis. In more resistant
hosts such as dogs, Y. pestis is susceptible to macrophage
killing inside phagolysosomes. When transmitted by a
flea bite, the bacterium is carried by mononuclear cells to
regional lymph nodes where it causes a suppurative lym­
phadenitis with a marked lymph node swelling (the
bubo). Fistulae drain thick purulent exudate from the
affected lymph nodes. When transmission occurs via
ingestion of infected prey, mandibular and retropharyn­
geal lymph nodes are involved. Clinical disease charac­
terized by lymphadenitis is called bubonic plague.
Dissemination via lymphatic vessels or the bloodstream
can follow lymphadenitis. After bacteremia, other lymph
nodes, the lungs, and many other organs and t­ issues can
be affected. Abscesses, hemorrhagic and necrotic lesions
may occur in many organs. Sepsis may also occur.
Bacteremia and multiple organ involvement is referred to
as septicemic plague. Dissemination occurs more quickly
after ingestion of infected prey or inhalation of the organ­
ism from contaminated aerosol droplets. The pulmonary
form, known as pneumonic plague, can occur in cats due
to hematogenous spread or inhalation of organisms.
It has been established that cats are the domestic spe­
cies most susceptible to plague. Reinfection is possible
and seropositive cats are not protected from bacteremia
or death but may have a more prolonged course of the
disease.
Similar to the presentation in cats, three different clin­
ical forms of plague are described in humans: bubonic,
pneumonic, and septicemic. Bubonic plague is the con­
sequence of flea transmission while pneumonic plague
develops after inhalation of the bacterium or hematoge­
nous spread. Septicemic plague may arise from the other
two forms.

Section 9 Infectious Disease

­Epidemiology
One of the oldest diseases known to man, plague is still
endemic in many natural foci in the Americas (western
USA, Peru, Brazil, Argentina, Ecuador), Africa (Algeria,
Libya, Congo, Madagascar, Malawi, Mozambique,
Uganda, Tanzania, South Africa) and Asia (China,
Mongolia, Vietnam, India, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Iran).
Recent outbreaks have occurred in previously endemic
areas after prolonged periods of absence. Countries
belonging to the World Health Organization are obliged
to notify officials when plague is diagnosed in humans,
but underreporting likely occurs.
Each endemic focus is linked to the presence of a spe­
cific mammalian reservoir and flea vector. Variability in
annual incidence is linked to climatic variability, specifi­
cally to rainfall because humidity favors both flea repro­
duction and increased food availability for rodent hosts.
Enzootic hosts of Y. pestis are resistant to the develop­
ment of disease and have prolonged bacteremia, thereby
maintaining the flea–host–flea cycle in the wild. In
endemic areas, outbreaks of recurrent or sporadic plague
epizootics rapidly involve individuals of a particularly
susceptible (epizootic) host species. These animals are
easily infected when a highly competent flea vector spe­
cies is more abundant.
Most cases of human plague result from exposure to
fleas or activities that result in contact with reservoir
hosts, such as skinning rabbits. Exposure to domestic
cats accounts for approximately 10% of human plague
cases. Veterinary staff and owners of free‐roaming cats
are at increased risk for Y. pestis infection in endemic
areas. In some cases, human patients reported being bit­
ten or scratched by infected cats but sometimes just han­
dling or caring for a sick cat was the only contact
reported. In one human case, the infecting scratch was
obtained by a healthy cat which had fought with a cat
suffering from bubonic plague. Importantly, human
infection from cats commonly results in the pulmonary
form of the disease (pneumonic plague) which is associ­
ated with rapid progression and a higher fatality rate.
Dogs rarely develop clinical signs. Infection results in
people primarily due to contact with the Yersinia‐
infected fleas they carry. Dogs and other carnivores may
serve as sentinels for Y. pestis because infection results in
the transient production of antibody, peaking 3–4 weeks
post exposure and lasting 4–8 months.

­Signalment
Yersiniosis is diagnosed in dogs much less frequently
than in cats. The disease is reported in cats (3 months to
15 years old) and dogs (1–14 years) of any age, but it

seems to be more frequent in adults. No gender or breed
predilection is known.

­History and Clinical Signs
Free roaming in rural areas and hunting activity are the
main risk factors for dogs and cats in endemic areas. In
experimental infections, the incubation period lasts
24–48 hours but after natural exposure it may be up to a
few days.
Fever, lethargy, and anorexia occur in cats associated
with the development of the “bubo,” a swollen painful
lymph node. This swelling can be confused with abscesses
that commonly arise from cat fights. Buboes may involve
any superficial lymph node but mandibular and ret­
ropharyngeal nodes are more frequently affected because
infection is commonly acquired by the oral route as a
result of predation. Ulcerative or necrotic lesions may be
observed on lips or oral mucosa. The white blood cell
count is usually elevated with increased neutrophils and
bands. In benign cases, drainage of the primary bubo is
followed by resolution of fever and progressive recovery.
In other cases, fatal septicemia rapidly occurs and may
evolve to distributive shock and multiple organ dysfunc­
tion syndrome (MODS). MODS associated with Y. pestis
is manifested by persistently high fever, depression,
hypotension, rapid capillary refill time (CRT), bradycar­
dia, hypodynamic peripheral pulses, hypoalbuminemia,
hypoglycemia, and increased bilirubin, liver enzymes,
blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and creatinine. Oliguria and
metabolic acidosis are also observed. Disseminated
intravascular coagulation (DIC) may also occur and is
responsible for a hemorrhagic diathesis. Suspicion of
DIC is increased in patients with thrombocytopenia,
prolongation in activated partial thromboplastin time
(APTT) and prothrombin time (PT), increased fibrin
degradation products (FDPs) and/or D‐dimer, and
decreased antithrombin. In some septicemic cases a pri­
mary bubo is not found.
Primary pneumonic plague is not a typical presenta­
tion in cats because infection is rarely caused by
­inhalation. Pulmonary involvement is usually due to dis­
semination from a bubonic primary lesion. Cough and
dyspnea represent the clinical manifestation of a pulmo­
nary disease and thoracic radiographs may show the
presence of poorly defined focal patchy and coalescing
opacities due to pulmonary abscessation. Pleural effu­
sion may also be found.
Few case reports of plague in dogs have been docu­
mented. Clinical signs include mild to severe hyperther­
mia, lethargy, anorexia, stomatitis, painful enlargement
of the superficial lymph nodes (mandibular, retropharyn­
geal, superficial cervical or inguinal), vomiting, diarrhea,

VetBooks.ir

102 Yersiniosis

respiratory signs, and abscesses. Leukocytosis and neu­
trophilia are often recorded.

­Diagnosis
In endemic areas, bubo‐like lesions and hyperthermia
should immediately prompt consideration of Y. pestis in
free‐roaming or hunting cats and dogs. Public health
officials should be notified immediately. Standard oper­
ating procedures for handling potentially infectious ani­
mals or materials should always be followed. Such
procedures include isolation of the patient, and wearing
surgical masks, gloves, and eye protection when per­
forming physical examination and any clinical or labora­
tory procedures. Laboratories should be contacted for
proper collection and submission protocols prior to col­
lecting and submitting samples from an animal sus­
pected of being infected.
Cytologic evaluation on both Gram‐ and Giemsa‐
stained smears from draining lesions may quickly show
the presence of a large number of monomorphic Gram‐
negative (Gram staining) organisms with a bipolar safety
pin shape (Giemsa staining). The diagnosis is confirmed
by culture, direct fluorescent antibody test (DFA) or pol­
ymerase chain reaction (PCR). The DFA is performed by
approved laboratories on tissue imprints on slides,
smears of lymph node aspirate, or samples from draining
pharyngeal or cutaneous lesions. Isolates can be made
from cultures of oral swabs, blood or swollen lymph
nodes if samples are obtained before starting antibiotic
therapy. However culture can be insensitive, and takes
several weeks. It should be noted that culture of Y. pestis
can only be performed at approved laboratories due to
its zoonotic potential, and public health authorities
should be contacted to obtain information on collection
and submission guidelines. Molecular diagnostic meth­
ods from clinical samples are also available from select
laboratories. Negative immunofluorescence assay (IFA),
culture or PCR does not rule out infection.
Diagnosis can also be confirmed by serologic methods.
Antibodies against the organism’s F1 capsular antigen
can be detected many days after the onset of clinical
signs and last many months after the infection. Dogs and
cats may test seronegative at presentation, as illness may
occur prior to seroconversion. A fourfold or more rise in
antibody titer against F1 antigen (15 days minimum
apart) or a single titer of 1:32 or more by hemagglutina­
tion in a cat or dog with signs suggestive of plague is
diagnostic. ELISA tests or semiquantitative rapid lateral
flow immunochromatographic tests using recombinant
antigens have also been developed for humans and mam­
mal reservoirs. Tests for antigen detection in mammals,
fleas, and environmental samples are also available.

­Therapy
Rapid appropriate therapy should be started as soon as
possible without waiting for the confirmatory test result
when infection is suspected. Strict isolation measures
and personal protection measures should be followed
and antiflea treatment applied. Public health authorities
should be contacted immediately for notification and
guidelines. Treated cats and dogs are considered nonin­
fectious after three days of therapy when fever wanes and
clinical recovery occurs but a minimum of three weeks of
therapy is required. Many antibiotics have in vitro effi­
cacy or are effective in experimental mouse studies.
Gentamicin is a first‐choice antibiotic for dogs and cats
at a dose of 6–8 mg/kg q24h IM, SC or IV. Doxycycline is
a second choice for less severe cases. Oral administration
of this antibiotic poses a higher risk for caretakers and
should be avoided in the initial treatment period.
Draining of buboes is recommended (adopting the
appropriate operating procedures for avoiding infection
as explained earlier). Chlorhexidine is used for flushing
fistulae.

­Prognosis
In an experimental trial which reproduced oral transmis­
sion, 37% of 16 infected cats died. A minority of cats
(19%) experienced a subclinical infection and 44% recov­
ered after a clinical disease. Poor prognosis was associ­
ated with persistently high fever ( ≥40 °C, 105 °F). None of
the cats in this experimental trial were treated with anti­
biotics or other measures and in natural disease a fatal
course is observed in about half of feline clinical cases.
Most cats promptly treated with antimicrobial drugs
survive and drainage of cutaneous abscesses improves
prognosis. Conversely, abscess development in the lung
is considered a negative prognostic factor in cats.
Experimental studies show that dogs have only a mild
febrile syndrome and a benign course with no fatality,
and this appears to be the case in naturally infected dogs
as well. Co‐infection with other agents such as Ehrlichia
canis may result in more severe clinical manifestations.
In treated dogs, clinical cure is obtained in 1–21 days.

­Prevention
Several types of vaccines have been produced for use in
people at risk who are exposed to Y. pestis due to profes­
sional activities. However, these vaccines are no longer
available in the US. Under experimental conditions, vac­
cination with a killed vaccine did not protect cats from

953

VetBooks.ir

954

Section 9 Infectious Disease

infection or death. This is consistent with the fact that
after infection, seropositive cats are not protected from
bacteremia or death.
Doxycycline (10 mg/kg SID PO for seven days) is
administered to exposed animals to prevent develop­
ment of disease.

­Public Health Implications
Humans can acquire Y. pestis from cats through bites,
scratches or aerosolization of respiratory secretions.
Fleas on pets also expose humans to the disease.
Personnel working in veterinary practices where plague
is enzootic should be aware that plague occurs in cats
and dogs. Veterinary staff handling potentially infectious

animals or materials should be adequately protected
from Y. pestis infection by wearing a well‐fitted surgical
mask, gloves, and eye protection. Exudates should be
considered infectious, and any material used for treating
suspect cats should be disinfected, autoclaved, or
incinerated.
In plague‐affected areas, owners should be advised to
prevent their cats and dogs from roaming freely and to
strictly follow flea control programs. Other general
advice includes avoiding sleeping with pets, avoiding
handling sick or dead animals without adequate protec­
tion, and preventing rodent infestations by eliminating
food sources and available shelter. Owners of an animal
diagnosed with plague should be instructed to contact
their physician immediately for prophylactic antibiotics
and other treatment as indicated.

Tularemia
Linda Kidd, DVM, PhD, DACVIM
College of Veterinary Medicine, Western University of Health Sciences, Pomona, CA, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Tularemia is a rare but severe zoonotic illness caused by
Francisella tularensis, a small gram‐negative non-sporeforming, aerobic coccobacillis bacterium. The organism
infects a number of mammals although some, such
as rabbits and hares, rodents, cats and sheep, appear
to be particularly susceptible to disease. The organism
is ­classified into subspecies (also referred to as types),
with F. tularensis tularensis (type A) and F. tularensis
­ olarctica (type B) causing most disease in cats and
h
­people. Disease caused by type A appears to be more
severe and is diagnosed more commonly in cats and
­people than that caused by type B.
Francisella tularensis is very stable in the environment
and is transmitted to people and other mammals by a number of mechanisms. These include through biting flies,
mosquitoes, fomites, aerosols, and water. Aquatic protozoa
may also play a role in transmission. Fleas are considered
potential but inefficient mechanical vectors. Several tick
species also transmit F. tularensis. Transstadial and transovarial transmission have been documented in ticks so they
are true biologic rather than mechanical vectors.
Francisella tularensis readily infects macrophages and
cells of the reticuloendothelial system. It can also infect
hepatocytes and other cells. In macrophages, it survives by
inhibiting phagolysosomal fusion and the respiratory burst.
After replicating, it induces a form of apoptosis known as
pyroptosis. This releases the bacterium and allows it to be
taken up by other phagocytic cells. Severe inflammatory
responses in the host can cause serious morbidity.
After cutaneous infection, the bacteria may replicate
locally and then migrate to local lymph nodes. Further
dissemination and septicemia can follow. Lesions in the
lungs, spleen, liver, lymph nodes, and skin may result.
Systemic infection may also occur without prior localized

infection. Pulmonary infection may also result directly
from aerosolization. Infection may also be introduced by
the oral or gastrointestinal route.
Immunity is T cell mediated, and natural killer cell
secretion of interferon‐gamma and subsequent activation of macrophages appears important in immunity.

­Epidemiology
Type A occurs in North America, whereas type B occurs
throughout the northern hemisphere. Types A and B
cause disease in both cats and people. Type A is subdivided into types I and II, which appear to have relatively
distinct geographic distributions and differences in
­pathogenicity, with type I causing more severe disease.
F. tularensis is a reportable disease in the US, occurring
in every state except Hawaii. The prevalence of the disease in people is highest in the south central US, the
Pacific Northwest, and Massachusetts (Figure 103.1).
The incidence of tularemia has been decreasing overall
in the US in recent years.
In people, tularemia has classically been referred to as
rabbit fever, because many reports of the disease have
been associated with contact with rabbits. These include
an outbreak associated with aerosolization of the organism while skinning rabbits after a hunt, and running over
a rabbit nest with a lawn mower, among others. Recently,
however, the importance of cats as a source of human
infection has been illustrated. Due to predation on rabbits and rodents, and exposure to environmental sources
such as water and ticks, free‐roaming cats are believed to
be at particular risk for exposure. In one serosurvey in
the US, 12–24% of cats were seropositive. Alarmingly,
it was recently reported that 48% of human cases in
Nebraska were cat associated.

Because of its pathogenicity, the potential for aerosol
transmission and other factors, F. tularensis is considered
a Tier 1 bioterrorism agent. This is important for veterinarians to consider, as cats and possibly dogs could
potentially serve as sentinels if such an attack were to
occur.

­Signalment
Infection in young adult cats and dogs has been reported
most frequently, with natural infection in cats reported
much more commonly than in dogs.

­History and Clinical Signs
Clinical signs can range from minimal to severe disease
and death. Severity of illness is likely determined by type
and subtype of the organism and host immunity.
Different clinical categories of disease, including ulceroglandular, glandular, pneumonia, and tonsillitis or pharangitis with cervical lymphadenopathy, are described in
people. These disease manifestations are determined in
part by route of inoculation.
Manifestations in cats appear to be similar to those found
in people. In cats, clinical findings may include a more

localized form that includes chronic subcutaneous draining
abscesses, or generalized severe disease. In the severe form
of the disease, fever, depression, lethargy, jaundice, splenomegaly, lymphadenomegaly, and hepatomegaly occur. Oral
and lingual ulcerations may be present and might indicate
ingestion as a route of infection. Embolic pneumonia associated with oral or gastrointestinal exposure has been
described. Fever, lethargy, anorexia, lymphandenopathy,
ocular changes, and tonsillitis have been described in dogs.

­Diagnosis
Tularemia should be a differential diagnosis in cats with
fever of unknown origin, chronic draining lesions/
abscesses, lymph node enlargement and hepatosplenomegaly and oral ulcerations. Free roaming and hunting
behaviors, especially predation of rabbits or rodents,
should increase the index of suspicion for infection.
Plague is an important differential diagnosis for tularemia.
Guidelines have been established by the European
Advisory Board on Cat Diseases (www.abcdcatsvets.
org/) for tularemia in cats. They state:
When handling animals with suppurative or draining skin or lymph node lesions in endemic areas,
gloves and goggles should be worn. Gloves should

VetBooks.ir

103 Tularemia

also be worn when there is any direct contact with
the oral mucosa. Handling of diagnostic samples by
laboratory staff should follow biosafety procedures.
In addition to taking in‐clinic precautions, laboratories
and couriers should be warned that tularemia is a differential diagnosis before diagnostic specimens are submitted and appropriate precautions taken. Veterinarians
should notify and consult public health authorities for
guidance when tularemia is suspected.
Complete blood count may reveal thrombocytopenia,
leukocytosis or leukopenia. Toxic change may be present
in neutrophils. Serum chemistry may reveal elevations in
alanine aminotransferase (ALT), alkaline phosphatase
(ALP), and bilirubin. Lymph node aspiration may show
reactive changes, pyogranulomatous inflammation or
neutrophilic inflammation.
Pathologic findings include multiple foci of necrosis in
lymph nodes, spleen, liver, and lung. Fibrinosuppurative
to granulomatous inflammation may be present in many
organs. It is difficult to demonstrate the organism in tissues with routine staining.
A fourfold increase in titer demonstrates acute infection, although it is important to note that animals may be
seronegative early in the course of disease. Therefore, a
negative titer does not rule out infection. Because antibody can be long‐lived, a single positive titer is not diagnostic for active infection.
Antibodies may be used to directly demonstrate the
presence of the organism in lymph node aspirates and
tissue samples using direct immunofluorescent antibody
assays. PCR verifies active infection. Culture is also a
diagnostic method that demonstrates the presence of the
organism. The laboratory must be notified that tularemia
is a differential to protect laboratory workers and because
the organism is fastidious and requires special media to
grow. A negative result for immunofluorescent antibody
assays, PCR or culture does not rule out infection.

­Therapy
Aminoglycosides are the treatment of choice. Doxycycline
and fluoroquinolones are also effective treatments but
may be associated with relapse, which may be ameliorated with a longer course of treatment (three rather than
two weeks).

­Prognosis
Specific information about prognosis in dogs and cats
has not been published.

­Public Health Implications
Public health authorities should be notified immediately when tularemia is suspected. Infected cats may
transmit tularemia by bites, scratches or contact with
or aerosolization of fluids or tissue specimens or
potentially fur. Veterinary and laboratory personnel
should take appropriate precautions as detailed earlier.
To prevent tularemia, owners should be advised to
keep cats from roaming and hunting, provide appropriate ectoparasite control and to seek medical care if
they feel ill or if they have been scratched or bitten by
a cat with suspected infection.
According to the US government, “an urban cluster of
tularemia cases among persons with a common natural
exposure could be the first sign of a bioterrorist attack.”
Cats may serve as sentinels for such an attack due to
their apparent disease susceptibility and exposure to
environmental sources of the organism. Veterinarians
should be vigilant in considering tularemia as a differential diagnosis in cats or dogs with compatible clinical
signs.

Q Fever
Linda Kidd, DVM, PhD, DACVIM
College of Veterinary Medicine, Western University of Health Sciences, Pomona, CA, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Q fever is caused by the gram‐negative bacterium
Coxiella burnetii. Coxiella burnetii is a gamma‐proteobacteria currently classified in the order Legionellales.
The organism exists in two forms: a large‐cell variant
that is the metabolically active form, and a small‐cell
variant which is spore‐like. The small‐cell variant is
released into the environment where it is very resistant
to destruction by chemicals, light, and desiccation, and
can survive for long periods of time. The target cell of
this obligately intracellular organism is the macrophage.
Host factors may contribute to its ability to survive
intracellularly as interleukin (IL)‐10, an antiinflammatory cytokine, appears to inhibit phagosome maturation, while intracellular killing appears to be facilitated
by interferon (IFN)‐gamma. Cell‐mediated immunity
is important in controlling infection. Granulomatous
inflammation occurs in infected hosts. In animals, the
uterus and mammary glands are the most common sites
of infection. The organism concentrates in the placenta
during parturition, and large numbers of the organism
are aerosolized from these membranes and also carried
by dust and other environmental sources once contamination has occurred.

­Epidemiology
Coxiella burnetii has a worldwide distribution. Many
species of mammals, birds, and arthropods, including
ticks, can be infected. Infection of mammalian hosts may
occur through aerosolization, oral (ingestion) or tick
transmission. In mammals, the organisms concentrate in
placenta and are excreted in milk, urine, saliva, and feces.

Cattle, sheep, and goats are the most important reservoirs for the organism. Serosurveys suggest free‐roaming
rural cats and dogs are at increased risk. Exposure to raw
meat, particularly raw kangaroo meat, has been implicated as a possible risk factor in cats. Recently, infections
have been identified in United States soldiers returning
from Iraq where Q fever is endemic. In a recent serosurvey, 5% of wild canines in Iraq were seropositive, while
no military working dogs (MWDs) in the region were
seropositive. Diligent use of flea and tick control, and the
fact that the MWDs in this study did not have access
to local farm animals or food were hypothesized to
­contribute to the discrepancy. Serosurveys have shown
that exposure in cats is common in many areas of the
world, ranging from 2% to 61%. Interestingly, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) failed to amplify DNA from the
organism from the vaginas of 50 intact female Colorado
shelter cats while 4/47 uterine biopsy samples from client‐owned cats were positive. A follow‐up study showed
a similar PCR‐positive prevalence rate of 8.1% in the
uterine tissues of cats with and without reproductive
abnormalities.
Coxiella burnetii is primarily of importance in small
animal medicine due to its zoonotic potential. Clinical
disease in dogs and cats is not commonly recognized.
Multiple reports of infection in people after exposure to
periparturient cats and dogs have been described.
Despite these reports, a study on pet ownership was not
associated with increased risk of antibody formation in
people. Cats and neonatal kittens have been reported as
a source of infection in people more often than dogs.
A recent report of an outbreak in a small animal veterinary hospital was associated with a female cat undergoing C‐section; 8/9 infected personnel working at the
veterinary hospital worked the day of the C‐section while
the ninth person cleaned equipment the morning after.

Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/bruyette/clinical

Section 9 Infectious Disease

­Signalment
Because infection is usually asyptomatic, a study on signalment of naturally infected cats and dogs has not been
described. Most cases in the literature describe intact
female dogs and cats undergoing parturition as a source
of exposure. MWDs deployed in Iraq may be at increased
risk for infection especially if they have exposure to farm
animals.

­History and Clinical Signs
Disease is usually subclinical in dog and cats. Fever, anorexia, and lethargy have been described in experimental
infection. Abortion or neonatal death has been associated with infection but the organism’s role in causing
reproductive abnormalities in dogs and cats is not fully
elucidated. In one report, lesions in affected kittens
included granulomatous myocarditis, hepatitis, nephritis, and pneumonia.

­Diagnosis
Serology has been used to document exposure, while
isolation, histopathology, immunohistochemistry, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), and PCR can
­document infection. Public health authorities should
be contacted for guidance on sample submission for
suspected cases. Animals may be seronegative in the
acute phase of disease prior to seroconversion.
Sensitivity also varies depending on the serologic
assay, and assays are species specific. The inability to
demonstrate the organism using PCR, culture, FISH,
and histologic methods does not rule out infection.
Because the organism is highly infectious to people
and stable in the environment, taking precautions to
prevent infection in clinical and laboratory workers
and owners is important.

­Therapy
Studies investigating efficacy of treatment in cats
and dogs have not been reported. Doxycycline is the

treatment of choice in people with acute infections.
Doxycycline in combination with hydroxychloroquine
is recommended for chronic infections in people.
Doxycycline and chloramphenicol are suggested for
treating cats by the European Advisory Board on Cat
Diseases (www.abcdcatsvets.org/coxiellosis‐q‐fever/).

­Prognosis
Because naturally infected dogs and cats are asymptomatic, prognosis for survival in these species is thought
to be good. The possibility of chronic asymptomatic
infection and reservoir potential should be considered.

­Public Health Implications
Q fever is a reportable disease in the United States.
Humans are very susceptible to Q fever. Farm workers,
laboratory workers, and veterinarians are at increased
risk. Acute and chronic infections occur in people and
are associated with significant morbidity and mortality.
Exposure to parturient cattle, sheep, and goats, and aerosolization of the organism from environmental contamination by their fluids and tissues has historically been the
primary route of infection in people, although exposure
to periparturient cats has been the primary risk in some
studies. Human infection associated with exposure to
cats and dogs is usually in the context of aerosolization of
high concentrations of organisms in placental tissues
during parturition.
Guidelines for prevention and management of C. burnetii in cats have been established by the European
Advisory Board on Cat Diseases (www.abcdcatsvets.org/
coxiellosis‐q‐fever/). Wearing gloves and masks during
parturition of ALL cats and dogs, diligent use of tick control and preventing cats and dogs from roaming have
been recommended. Direct mouth‐to‐mouth resuscitation of kittens and puppies after C‐section should be
avoided. More extensive guidelines to prevent infection
in people, which include additional recommendations
such as avoiding the consumption of raw milk or raw
milk products, are available from the United States
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (www.cdc.
gov/qfever/).

Brucellosis
Erin E. Runcan, DVM, DACVT and Marco A. Coutinho da Silva, DVM, MS, PhD, DACT
Department of Veterinary Clinical Sciences, Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology

­Epidemiology

Canine brucellosis is caused by the aerobic, gram‐negative, coccobacillus species Brucella. The most clinically
relevant infection in dogs is caused by Brucella canis,
although reports exist of infection with B. abortus,
B. melitensis, and B. suis in individual animals. The bacterium is highly contagious, and often spreads rapidly in
breeding kennels. Transmission is also possible via frozen semen and artificial insemination as the bacterium is
resistant to cryopreservation.
The organism is best known for being venereally
transmitted via vaginal and seminal secretions in sexually mature animals. Transmission also occurs in utero,
at parturition, or during abortion through oronasal,
­conjunctival, or transdermal contact of aborted fetal tissues, placental tissues, urine, milk, or vulvar discharge.
Aborted tissues are highly infectious, containing high
numbers of organisms, and abortion often results in persistent vaginal discharge that can last for 4–6 weeks.
Infection can also occur via artificial insemination with
infected semen, and via fomites such as contaminated
food and water bowls, equipment, and clothing. The
bacterium is highly stable and can survive for months in
moist soil in the environment.
Following contact, invading bacteria are able to survive
phagocytosis and are taken up by lymphatic and genital
organs where they rapidly reproduce. Bacteremia occurs
1–4 weeks post infection and can persist for up to six
months. Bacteria can be intermittently detected in tissues and secretions for up to 64 months post infection.
While the bacteria reproduce best in reproductive
­tissues, a variety of clinical signs can manifest as a result
of hematogenous transmission to the eye, kidneys, and
vertebrae.

Canine brucellosis is widespread in domestic and feral
dog populations throughout the southern United States,
in Central and Southern America, and Asia. It is unclear
how important wild canids or stray dog populations
are in disease transmission. Sporadic cases have been
reported in Europe. Recently, the disease has become
more prevalent in breeding kennels due to their growing
number, ease of buying/selling and trading infected dogs,
and increased international semen shipment.

­Signalment
There are no current recognized breed or age predispositions. As venereal transmission is most significant, sexually
intact, reproductively mature dogs are most likely to become
infected, but the disease has been readily identified in both
neutered and intact individuals. There has been a case report
of a child becoming infected as a result of contact with an
infected 8‐week‐old puppy and thus, the disease is zoonotic,
especially in immunocompromised individuals.

­History and Clinical Signs
The majority of individuals infected with B. canis are
asymptomatic. Fever is uncommon and there are no clinical signs that are pathognomonic. The classic clinical
sign is late‐term abortion in bitches, with abortion
occurring at 45–55 days gestation. Deceased pups are
often autolysed, and surviving pups are often weak,
have peripheral lymphadenopathy, and may die months
later as a result of bacteremia. A greenish‐gray vulvar

Clinical Small Animal Internal Medicine Volume II, First Edition. Edited by David S. Bruyette.
© 2020 John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Published 2020 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc.
Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/bruyette/clinical

VetBooks.ir

964

Section 9 Infectious Disease

discharge may persist in aborting bitches for up to six
weeks. Some bitches may have perceived infertility due
to early embryonic loss.
Males develop a characteristic epididymitis approximately five weeks after infection. Increased presence of
neutrophils and teratozoospermia with sperm agglutination is often seen 18 weeks post infection. Over 90% of
sperm are morphologically abnormal by week 20 post
infection. The enlarged epididymis is often painful and
scrotal dermatitis may also be seen due to increased
­licking of the scrotum because of discomfort. Chronic
infection often leads to testicular atrophy. Concurrent
prostatitis is common.
Dogs with systemic infection may also present with
clinical signs outside the reproductive tract, depending
on the site of infection. Discospondylitis, lymphadenitis,
lameness, ataxia, recurrent anterior uveitis, and low‐
grade meningitis have all been reported in B. canis‐
infected animals.

­Diagnosis
Direct detection of the organism in culture remains the
only definitive diagnostic method available; however, the
slow growth rate, intracellular location, and previous
antibiotic therapy may affect the results. Therefore, a
negative culture does not rule out disease. Positive blood
cultures may occur starting at 2–4 weeks post infection
up to several years following infection due to intermittent shedding of the organism. Placenta, fetus, lymph
nodes, bone marrow, prostate, spleen, urine, vaginal
­discharge, and semen may all be potential sites for culture of organisms.
Due to the difficulty in growing the organism in
­culture, serology can be a helpful screening tool for the
disease. Antibodies can be detected 3–4 weeks post
infection and serology is most accurate as a screening
test 8–12 weeks post infection. Serologic testing is highly
sensitive, but has low specificity due to cross‐reactivity
with other bacterial species. Serologic tests include the
rapid slide agglutination test (RSAT), which is available
as a commercial, cage‐side screening test, with or without the addition of 2‐mercaptoethanol (2‐ME). If a sample tests positive with the RSAT test, 2‐ME should be
added to prevent cross‐reactivity with IgM antibodies to
other bacteria species and increase the specificity of the
test. A second serologic test, the tube agglutination test
(TAT), is similar but is quantitative. Titers less than
1:200 should be retested approximately two weeks later.
Any positive agglutination test should be validated with

ancillary testing before the animal is considered to be
truly positive.
Agar gel immunodiffusion (AGID) assays are frequently used as the confirmatory test of choice for other
serologic assays, although positive cross‐reactions are
common. Enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assays
(ELISAs) detect antibodies to the organism and may be
more rapid and specific than agglutination or AGID
assays. Positive dogs can be detected within 30 days of
infection using this test, but current availability of this
test is limited commercially.
Most recently, real‐time polymerase chain reaction
(PCR) testing has become available as a rapid, sensitive,
and specific assay for Brucella species. It also has the
benefit of being able to directly detect Brucella canis
DNA in blood and tissues. It is likely that PCR will be the
diagnostic test of choice in the future as it becomes more
widely available.

­Therapy
Due to the intracellular location of Brucella bacteria,
antimicrobial treatments are challenging. There is no
vaccine currently available. While it is possible for aborting females to subsequently carry and produce litters
without treatment, infection is likely to be transmitted to
offspring and infected dogs remain a risk to other dogs
and humans.
Infected animals should be quarantined and removed
from the breeding population via surgical sterilization. In
kennel situations where infected animals are i­dentified,
euthanasia may be recommended to prevent transmission of disease and resident animals should be tested
monthly. New animals introduced to the kennel should be
isolated until two negative screening tests are obtained at
least 30 days apart. Breeding animals should be screened
serologically every six months prior to breeding.
No single antimicrobial protocol has been shown to consistently eliminate the disease long term. Many believe
that permanent cures may not be possible even with
surgical sterilization and antimicrobial treatment.
­
Combination protocols with aminoglycosides and tetracyclines (gentamicin 5 mg/kg SC q24h for seven days,
repeated every three weeks for three months, and doxycycline 10 mg/kg orally q12h), or tetracyclines and streptomycin (tetracycline 30 mg/kg orally q12h for 28 days and
streptomycin 20 mg/kg IV q24h for 14 days) show the
most success, but even with treatment, titers may reappear much later after infection, especially d
­ uring times
of stress. A protocol using twice‐daily oral e­ nrofloxacin

VetBooks.ir

105 Brucellosis

(5 mg/kg q12h for 30 days) has been described as successful in preserving fertility in a kennel outbreak situation,
although some dogs had persistently elevated antibodies
and subsequent treatments were required.

­Prognosis
As infected dogs rarely show clinical signs, prognosis for
survival is excellent. However, since infected dogs remain
a potential source for infection for other dogs and immunocompromised humans, they should be kept in isolation from these individuals. Infected dogs should not be
used for breeding and infection may be devastating to a
breeding kennel due to its rapid spread.

­Public Health Implications
Due to zoonotic concern, B. canis is a reportable disease
in most states. Human case reports are often limited to
laboratory workers and immunocompromised individuals. Most infections in people are mild although serious
illness can occur. The disease may be underreported in
humans due to varying clinical symptoms, which may
mimic other diseases. Krueger and workers showed in a
2014 study that based on serologic testing, kennel
employees and dog breeders are most likely to be exposed
and many may have experienced Brucella‐associated illness without diagnosis. Fortunately, humans respond
well to antibiotic therapy and the disease is cleared when
treated appropriately long term.
