Tetanus and Botulism
Andrea Fischer, DVM‚ Dipl. ECVN, Dipl. ACVIM (Neurology)
Department of Veterinary Clinical Sciences, Ludwig‐Maximilians University, Munich, Germany

­Tetanus
Etiology and Pathophysiology
Tetanus results from the effects of tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin) which is released by the anaerobic bacillus
Clostridium tetani. Spores of C. tetani are ubiquitous,
survive in soil, and can contaminate and infect wounds.
Thus, tetanus is a true toxicoinfection in which the toxin
is produced and released within the infected wound.
Following binding to peripheral nerve surface ganglioside
receptors, the toxin (L‐chain of tetanospasmin) is
internalized into the peripheral nerve terminals.
­
Tetanospasmin undergoes retrograde axonal transport to
the spinal cord or brainstem, where it migrates transsynaptically to its site of action, inhibitory interneurons
which utilize glycine or gamma‐aminobutyric acid
(GABA) as neurotransmitters. Tetanospasmin acts as a
metalloproteinase which cleaves and inactivates a vesicle‐associated membrane protein (VAMP) called synaptobrevin. Synaptobrevin mediates fusion of vesicles
with the neuronal membrane and release of neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft. Interference with the release
of glycine from inhibitory neurons in the spinal cord and
brainstem results in stimulus‐sensitive muscle rigidity
and spasticity worsened by touching, stretching or noise.
Tetanus can be localized or generalized. With localized tetanus, the toxin migrates only to the inhibitory
interneurons in the spinal cord segments which are closest to the injury site and there is no hematogenous spread
to distant synapses or further transsynaptic migration as
in generalized tetanus.
Epidemiology
Tetanus occurs in a worldwide distribution. Dogs
are less sensitive to the effects of tetanus toxin than
horses or humans, and cats are more resistant than

dogs. Consequently, localized tetanus is more frequently
reported in cats than in dogs.
Signalment
Any dog or cat of any breed or age can be affected, but
younger animals appear to be more susceptible.
History
Many patients have a history of an infected wound within
the previous 10 days (up to three weeks). Draining
wounds, tracts or wounds of the feet are frequent causes.
Rarely, tetanus may occur following non-sterile surgical
procedures, intraabdominal (female reproductive tract)
or dental infections. Occasionally, the initial site of infection may not be detectable. Previous paw wounds may be
diifucult to detect and only mild swelling may be evident
despite ongoing infection. Radiographs of the paws are
often indicated to identify foreign bodies and ongoing
osteomyelitis which may require surgical management.
Clinical Signs
Localized tetanus presents with rigidity or stiffness,
often resulting in rigid extension of one or both limbs,
usually the ones next to the infection site or injury.
Generalized tetanus causes signs of generalized muscle
stiffness and rigidity, which are exacerbated by excitement, touch, or noise. Generalized tetanus is always
associated with characteristic head muscle spasms
resulting in trismus, erect ears, which are drawn together,
excessive wrinkling of the forehead‚ drawn‐back muzzle
(risus sardonicus), and episodic prolapse of the third
eyelid. Initially, only salivation, miosis, enopththalmos,
risus sardonicus, erect ears or trismus may be present
(severity class I), but these may progress to severe tris­ysphagia, and generalized extensor rigidity
mus, d

Clinical Small Animal Internal Medicine Volume II, First Edition. Edited by David S. Bruyette.
© 2020 John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Published 2020 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc.
Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/bruyette/clinical

VetBooks.ir

968

Section 9 Infectious Disease

­presenting as a stiff gait and sawhorse stance (severity
class II), or recumbency with rigid extension of all limbs,
muscle f­ asciculations, spasms, seizures, and opisthotonus
(severity class III). Severity class IV involves autonomic
dysregulation of heart rate and blood pressure. Mental
status is usually normal unless severe hyperthermia or a
seizure develops. Trismus, pharyngeal and laryngeal
muscle spasms impair food and water intake and increase
the risk for aspiration pneuomonia. Complications in
severely affected animals are respiratory distress and
aspiration pneumonia, hyperthermia, gastrointestinal
ulceration, multiple organ failure, and autonomic failure.
Hiatal hernia, megaesophagus, and urethral sphincter
spasms may occur. Autonomic failure results in bradyarrhythmias and blood pressure variability.
Diagnosis
Tetanus is one of the rare diseases in which diagnosis is
solely based on a combination of characteristic clinical
signs and history. Attempts to culture C. tetani from the
wound are often not successful and do not prove toxin
production. Real‐time polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
for detection of the neurotoxin gene fragments of C. tetani
has been used to support the diagnosis in humans.
Continuous motor unit activity in antagonistic flexor and
extensor muscles and repetitive discharges following
peripheral nerve stimulation during electromyography
may suggest tetanus but these findings are not specific.
Therapy
Routine first line management consists of application of
tetanus antitoxin, metronidazole TID, sedatives and
thorough investigation for an infected wound, especially
on the paws. Equine tetanus antitoxin (median dosage
100–300 U/kg IV, range up to 1000 U/kg, higher dose
given to smaller patients, not to exceed 20 000 units)
should be given once immediately upon hospital admission slowly over 5–10 minutes and also prior to any
wound management. Tetanus antitoxin will neutralize
any free unbound toxin in the circulation but is not effective against the toxin once it has been internalized.
Intravenous administration of equine tetanus antitoxin is
preferred to intramuscular application of human tetanus
immunoglobulin. Intravenous administration achieves a
rapid increase in circulating antitoxin, but is associated
with risk of anaphylaxis. An intradermal or subcutaneous test dose is routinely recommended but its predictive
value is poor. The antihistamine diphenhydramine may
be given prior to tetanus antitoxin administration.
Tetanus antitoxin (500–1000 units) should also be
injected locally proximal and around the wound and
prior to any surgical exploration. Intrathecal injection
into the subarachnoid space (1000 units preservative‐
free antitoxin) has been beneficial in human patients.

Metronidazole 10 mg/kg TID IV is the preferred drug
for treatment of clostridial infection. Penicillin G is also
an appropriate choice, although the fact that it is a GABA
antagonist should be considered. Antimicrobial treatment should be continued for 7–10 days. Surgical wound
debridement may be necessary.
It is of the utmost importance to keep the animals in a
quiet noise‐protected environment and to avoid any
unnecessary manipulations. Ear plugs should be considered. Diazepam, acepromazine (0.005 - 0.02 mg/kg/h
CRI or repeated injections as needed), chlorpromazine
or methocarbamol (5 - 10 mg/kg/h CRI or 30 - 60 mg/kg
QID IV) alone or in combination may achieve sufficient
muscle relaxation and sedation in milder affected cases
(class I). Dexmedetomidine CRI (25 µg/m2/h) is very
effective to provide a continuous state of sedation.
Diazepam or midazolam constant rate infusion (CRI)
and phenobarbital CRI, or even general anesthesia may
be necessary to achieve muscle relaxation in severe generalized tetanus. Propofol or pentobarbital CRI may also
be used. Magnesium sulfate CRI has been beneficial as
an adjunctive treatment. Pain should be addressed
aggressively. Opioids are preferred to non-steroidal analgesics e. g. butorphanol (0.1 - 0.2 mg/kg/h CRI) or fentanyl CRI. Rescue therapy in humans consists of intrathecal
baclofen, anesthesia with neuromuscular blockade, and
positive pressure ventilation.
Management of severe generalized tetanus requires
intensive supportive care in the intensive care unit for up
to three weeks. This is an essential part of the management
of generalized tetanus and needs to be communicated to
the clients. Parenteral nutrition or an esophagostomy tube
may be necessary to address caloric needs and keep the
animal hydrated if trismus develops. Urinary catheterization may be necessary. Patients need to be closely monitored for signs of autonomic failure (heart rate, blood
pressure regulation) including life‐threatening bradyarrhythmias and signs of aspiration pneumonia.
Glucocorticoids are contraindicated in the management of tetanus.
Prognosis
Patients can completely recover within 4–6 weeks.
Published survival rates are from 50% to 80%. Prognosis
varies with tetanus severity classification. Sleep disturbances are reported following recovery from tetanus.
Public Health Implications
Body fluids and tissues, urine, and feces should be
handled with care and appropriately labeled before
­
­submitting to the laboratory as they may contain toxin.
Animals with tetanus have the potential to cause bite
wounds as well.

106 Tetanus and Botulism

­Botulism
Etiology and Pathophysiology
Botulism results from ingestion of spoiled food or dead
carcases which have been contaminated with bacteria of
the species Clostridium botulinum. Clinical signs of botulism are due to the effects of C. botulinum neurotoxins
which are already present in the food. Unlike tetanus,
botulism is a true intoxication, in which the preformed
toxin is ingested with the food, rather than an infection.
Up to now, seven types of neurotoxin have been identified (botulinum toxins A–G). In people, types A and B
are identified in most intoxications, while type C remains
the most commonly reported toxin in dogs and also in
one case series describing occurrence of botulism in
cats. Toxicoinfection, in which the toxin forms secondary to bacterial growth in the gut or a wound, is recognized in people (wound botulism in drug abusers) but
has not been described in dogs.
Once the ingested toxin passes the gastrointestinal (GI)
barrier and gains access to the systemic blood circulation,
it binds to surface ganglioside receptors on the peripheral
nerve endings of motor nerves, which utilize acetylcholine
as the neurotransmitter. Following internalization, the L‐
chain of botulinum neurotoxin remains in the presynaptic
motor nerve terminals. Unlike tetanospasmin, botulinum
neurotoxin does not undergo retrograde axonal transport.
Each type of botulinum toxin (L‐chain) targets specific
proteins of the SNARE protein family, which mediate neurotransmitter release in the synaptic cleft. Thus, all types
of botulinum toxins result in a similar functional deficit,
namely impaired release of acetylcholine into the synaptic
cleft in response to arriving action potentials and influx of
calcium. Functionally, botulism represents a presynaptic
neuromuscular transmission disorder.
Epidemiology
Botulism can occur worldwide. Groups of animals may
be affected if they share feeding habits, such as several
dogs eating from a large animal carcase or when spoiled
contaminated food is fed to several dogs. Outbreaks may
also occur around polluted lakes when dogs ingest dead
waterfowl harboring C. botulinum in their guts.
Nevertheless, isolated cases of botulism may also occur
Signalment
Any dog of any age can be affected. There is only one
report of botulism in cats.
History and Clinical Signs
A thorough dietary history is essential. Botulism is considered if ingestion of dead fish, dead waterfowl, other

animal carcases or rotten meat is reported. Feeding a raw
food and bones diet should be considered a risk factor.
Botulism has a rapid onset of action. Intoxicated animals present with acute onset of generalized lower motor
neuron paresis or paralysis. In many cases, peak paralysis
will be reached within a day. Uncommonly, a more
­protracted onset over several days has been reported.
Neurologic examination shows normal mentation, flaccid generalized lower motor neuron paresis or paralysis
with absent spinal reflexes of all limbs. Additional cranial
nerve signs such as mydriasis, facial nerve paralysis, and/
or tongue paralysis may occur in more severely affected
dogs. Respiratory movements may be impaired due to
diaphragmatic or intercostal muscle paralysis. Laryngeal
paralysis may co‐exist. There is no evident hyperesthesia
on palpation of the spine or muscles. In people, prolonged autonomic impairment following recovery from
botulism is a concern but has not been described in dogs.
Diagnosis
Clinical suspicion of botulism is based on the neurologic
signs of acute lower motor neuron paresis or paralysis
and a history suggestive of possible toxin uptake in the
absence of other causes such as polyradiculoneuritis,
raccoon bites, tick paralysis, myasthenia gravis (crisis),
coral snake poisoning, and ionophore toxicity.
Confirmation is obtained by the detection of botulinum
neurotoxin (direct evidence) or botulinum toxin producing Clostridia (indirect evidence) in the serum or feces
by mouse bioassay. Toxin‐specific enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) or PCR are increasingly available for toxin detection, but their sensitivity may be
lower than the mouse bioassay. Serum antibodies against
botulinum neurotoxins may appear during the recovery
phase. Unless seroconversion or a significant rise in titers
is demonstrated, they can only be considered as a rather
nonspecific indicator of exposure because antibody may
also be present in normal dogs. Notably, results of confirmatory tests (toxin assays, toxin‐specific antibodies)
are usually obtained with a significant time delay for up
to seven days or more, and thus offer little help for the
initial emergency management of the patient.
Electrodiagnostic examinations may facilitate diagnosis , because they offer a readily available bedside test.
When performed within the first days after onset, EMG
will be remarkably unremarkable. Distal peripheral nerve
stimulation results in a compound action potential of
normal morphology but with a reduced amplitude and
area. Nerve conduction is commonly normal. In contrast
to polyradiculoneuritis there is no temporal dispersion.
Repetitive stimulation may show a decrement or increment or be normal. Consequently, high‐frequency repetitive stimulation has been recommended. However,
examination in normal dogs showed variable results,

969

VetBooks.ir

970

Section 9 Infectious Disease

limiting the value of this test due to a lack of specificity.
Botulism may result in mild spontaneous electric activity
from denervation in the second week after onset and also
a mild decrease in nerve conduction velocity, but electrodiagnostic examination is rarely performed at that
time due to the early disease peak followed by gradual
recovery starting at day 5–7 after onset.
Therapy
The focus of therapy is to provide supportive care to the
patient. Clinicians should not be reluctant to provide
ventilator support if there is obvious respiratory impairment. Especially during the first two days after onset, the
dog’s respiration needs to be carefully monitored.
The use of botulinum antitoxin is controversial. First,
botulinum antitoxin needs to be directed against the specific toxin type, which suggests that antitoxin CD should
probably be used in dogs. There is a risk for anaphylaxis
but this appears to be low. A subcutaneous test dose may
be applied 30–45 minutes prior to IV application and pretreatment with diphenhydramine considered. Botulinum
antitoxin will only be able to neutralize the free unbound
fraction of toxin in the systemic circulation but not the
bound and internalized toxin which is responsible for the
observed clinical signs. Consequently, the goal behind the
application of toxin type‐specific botulinum antitoxin is
to prevent further progression of the paralysis and specifically to avoid respiratory paralysis and the need for
ventilatory support in cases with large amounts of circulating unbound toxin or ongoing GI absorption.

Supportive care should include adequate bedding,
­frequent turning, and intravenous fluids. Nutritional
support is also needed if the dogs are unable to eat or
drink on their own. Application of an eye lubricant is
indicated if facial movements and lid closure are
impaired. Any dog with botulism needs to assessed
carefully for the presence of megaesophagus.
Prolonged autonomic dysfunction as a consequence of
botulism is a concern in humans, thus bladder emptying and GI motility should be closely monitored. Drugs
that can impair neuromuscular transmission (clindamycin, aminoglycosides, neuromuscular blocking
agents) and glucocorticoids should be avoided. In
severely affected animals with respiratory distress,
early intubation and ventilation should be considered
as a life‐saving tool.
Prognosis
Most dogs recover from botulism within 2–3 weeks if
they do not die from respiratory arrest at the peak of the
paralysis.
Public Health Implications
Botulism cannot be transmitted directly from dogs and
cats to people but body fluids and tissues, urine, and
feces should be handled with care and appropriately
labeled before submitting to the laboratory as they may
contain toxin.

Anthrax
Wayne E. Wingfield, MS, DVM, DACVS, DACVECC1 and Jerry J. Upp, DVM2
1
2

Department of Clinical Sciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
Midtown Animal Hospital, Gering, NE, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Anthrax is a life‐threatening infectious disease that normally affects animals, especially ruminants (such as goats,
cattle, sheep, and horses). Both the dog and cat appear to
be relatively resistant to the inhalational and cutaneous
forms of anthrax, but clinical disease associated with
ingestion of contaminated carcases is reported. Because
dogs and cats may theoretically act as sentinels for infection in people during bioterrorist attacks, familiarity with
the disease is important for the small animal clinician.
The agent of anthrax is a bacterium called Bacillus
anthracis and it possesses three known virulence factors:
an antiphagocytic capsule and two protein exotoxins,
called the lethal and the edema toxins. The role of the
capsule in pathogenesis was demonstrated in the early
1900s, when anthrax strains lacking a capsule were
shown to be avirulent. The capsule is composed of a polymer of poly‐D‐glutamic acid, which confers resistance
to phagocytosis and may contribute to the resistance of
anthrax through lysis by serum cationic proteins.The
anthrax toxins, like many bacterial and plant toxins, possess two components: a cell‐binding, or B, domain necessary for entry into the host cell, and an enzymatically
active, or A, domain that has the toxic and, usually, the
enzymatic activity. The two toxins are unusual in that the
B protein, called protective antigen (molecular weight
[MW] 83 000), is shared by both toxins. Thus, the lethal
toxin is composed of the protective antigen combined
with a second protein, which is known as the lethal factor
(MW 90 000). The lethal toxin is lethal for experimental
animals and also has been shown to possess similar
structure and activity to metalloproteases, although no
direct enzymatic activity has yet been discovered.
The edema toxin, consisting of the same protective
antigen together with a third protein, edema factor (MW

89 000), causes edema when injected into the skin of
experimental animals. The edema factor is a calmodulin‐
dependent adenylate cyclase, which elevates intracellular
cyclic adenosine monophosphate, and which is likely to
be responsible for the marked edema often present at the
site of bacterial replication.
Each of the three toxin proteins – the B protein and
both A proteins – individually is without biologic activity.
The critical role of the toxins in pathogenesis was established when it was shown that deletion of the toxin‐
encoding plasmid or the protective antigen gene alone
attenuates the organism. The lethal toxin also appears to
be more important for virulence in a mouse model than
the edema toxin.
Anthrax can infect humans in three ways. The most common is infection through the skin, which causes an ugly sore
that usually goes away without treatment. Humans and animals can ingest anthrax from carcases of dead animals or
contaminated soil/plant materials that have been contaminated with anthrax. Ingestion of anthrax can cause serious,
sometimes fatal disease. The most deadly form is inhalation
anthrax. If the spores of anthrax are inhaled, they migrate to
lymph nodes in the chest where they proliferate, spread,
and produce toxins that often cause death. Interestingly, the
dog is quite resistant to inhalational anthrax. Experimental
studies have shown it required over 150 times the dosage in
dogs as compared to humans. Likely it is the long nose of
the dog which serves as an effective filtration system in preventing the usual fatal inhalational form of anthrax.
Infection is initiated with the introduction of the spore
through a break in the skin (cutaneous anthrax), through
entry through the mucosa (gastrointestinal anthrax), or
inhalation of spores 1–2 μm in diameter. After ingestion
by macrophages at the site of entry, germination to the
vegetative form occurs, followed by extracellular multiplication and capsule and toxin production. In the lungs, the

be washed using a 0.5% hypochlorite solution. Wounded
or discharged victims will create a possible vector if they
are not properly decontaminated. Anthrax does not
readily transfer from one person to another unless the
spores are in the clothing/shoes and there is some
method of moving the spores to another person. Once a
rescuer walks in the anthrax, then the threat of “movement” to other areas is very real.
Bodies that are not immediately recoverable pose little
threat. Anthrax doesn’t “jump up and bite you or me”! As
long as the bodies are not disturbed and/or wind movement is low, the anthrax will stay inside the bodies or in
the clothing.

­Signalment
Anthrax occurs throughout the world. B. anthracis exists
in the soil as a spore. The question remains unsettled as
to whether its persistence in the soil is due to significant
multiplication of the organism in the soil or if it is due
solely to cycles of bacterial amplification in infected animals whose carcases then recontaminate the soil. The
form of the organism in infected animals is the bacillus.
Only when the organism in the carcass is exposed to oxygen does sporulation occur.
Anthrax is most common in agricultural regions where
it occurs in animals. It is primarily a disease of herbivores
(Table 107.1); carnivores and humans are incidental
hosts. Animals, domestic or wild, become infected when
they ingest spores while grazing on contaminated land or
eating contaminated feed. Environmental conditions
such as drought, which may promote trauma in the oral
cavity during grazing, are thought to increase the chances
of acquiring anthrax. It is spread from animal to animal
by mechanical means and biting flies. Spread from one
environmental site to another appears to occur via
nonbiting flies, rodents, and carrion‐eating birds. Free
anthrax spores can also be spread by water and wind.
Human anthrax victims can also theoretically spread
anthrax spores that landed on their clothing and external
body surfaces. Therefore, each victim should be decontaminated and issued new clothes before leaving the
scene. Estimates have shown that ~90% of anthrax will

­History and Clinical Signs
Anthrax in veterinary species may be peracute, acute or
subacute, or chronic. The peracute form most frequently
affects cattle, sheep, and goats. The acute or subacute
form is common in cattle, sheep, and horses. Chronic
anthrax is most often seen in less susceptible species
such as swine but may also be seen in cattle, horses, dogs,
and cats. Suspicions of anthrax are raised when livestock
are found dead, bloated, and without rigor mortis. Blood
is usually evident at body orifices.
Dogs and Cats
Both the dog and cat appear to be relatively resistant to
anthrax. Dogs are supposedly 500–1000 times more
resistant to anthrax infection than humans. The gastro-

intestinal form is most common. In most cases, consumption of tissue from infected livestock is considered
the source of the infection. Inhalational and cutaneous
anthrax have not been reported in dogs and cats. Their
longer noses and dense hair coats are possible reasons
for this.
Clinical signs of anthrax include respiratory distress
and dysphagia resulting from swelling of the neck secondary to regional lymphadenopathy, hemorrhagic and
ulcerative inflammation of the oral cavity and pharynx,
hemoptysis, lingual swelling, enteritis, and enlargement
of the kidneys, spleen, and liver. Sudden death with few
premonitory signs has also been reported. The incubation period in naturally infected carnivores is often difficult to determine, but it is believed to be approximately
3–7 days with a range of 1–14 days.
Pets exposed to anthrax will likely be subject to the
gastrointestinal problems listed above but may complicate matters for their owners/rescuers with their thick
fur harboring B. anthracis spores. When petted or handled, these spores can be aerosolized and expose the pet
owner or rescuer. Additionally, dogs and cats “wash”
their feet/bodies with their tongue, which transfers the
anthrax directly into the pet (possibly initiating either
pharyngeal or gastrointestinal anthrax). These facts
would seem to favor early decontamination and quarantine of exposed animals.
Birds
Birds are usually highly resistant to anthrax. Buzzards,
vultures, and other carrion‐eating birds may transmit
the spores on their talons and beaks.

standard still being the direct identification of the

­Therapy
Anthrax is a reportable disease. That means that local or
state health agencies must be notified if a case of anthrax
is diagnosed in dogs, cats, and other veterinary species.
Treatment for anthrax in small animals is undocumented at this time. Natural strains of B. anthracis are
usually susceptible to several antibiotics; most but not
all natural strains are susceptible to penicillin (dogs:
penicillin G potassium 20 000 U/kg IV, IM, SC q4h).
Some strains, particularly those used in bioterrorist
attacks, may be resistant to penicillin. For this reason, the
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends other antibiotics (Table 107.2) as the initial treatment, particularly for systemic disease, until antibiotic

Bacillus anthracis is a large, gram‐positive, encapsulated, spore‐forming, nonmotile bacillus (1–1.5 μm ×
3–10 μm), grows readily on sheep blood agar aerobically,
and is nonhemolytic under these conditions. The colonies are large, rough, and grayish‐white, with irregular,
curving marginal outgrowths. Both in vitro in the presence of bicarbonate and carbon dioxide, and in tissue in
vivo, B. anthracis forms a prominent capsule. In tissue,
the encapsulated bacterium occurs singly or in chains of
two or three bacilli. The organism does not form spores
in living tissue; sporulation occurs only after the infected
body has been opened and exposed to oxygen. Remember

effective only against the vegetative stage of B. anthracis,
and not against spores. Treatment is continued for at
least 60 days in people with inhalational anthrax, as
spores may remain dormant in the lungs and germinate
during that time.
The pulmonary form of anthrax in people is a medical
emergency. Early and continuous intravenous therapy
with antibiotics may be life‐saving and ventilator support
is often required. In a bioterrorism attack, humans
exposed to anthrax will be given antibiotics before they
become sick. A vaccine exists but is not yet available to
the general public. Most experts think that the vaccine
will also be given to exposed individuals who are victims
of a bioterrorist attack. Supportive therapy may also be
necessary, particularly for the inhalational and gastrointestinal forms.
Effective treatment depends on early recognition of
the symptoms. Treatment for cutaneous anthrax is usually effective, but the inhalational and gastrointestinal
forms are difficult to recognize early and the mortality
rates are higher.

­Public Health Implications
Anthrax in humans is associated with agricultural, horticultural, or industrial exposure to infected animals or
contaminated animal products, and as a weapon of mass
destruction disseminated by terrorists. In less developed
countries, primarily in Africa, Asia, and the Middle East,
anthrax occurs from contact with infected domesticated
animals or contaminated animal products. This includes
handling contaminated carcases, hides, wool, hair, and
bones, and ingesting contaminated meat. Cases associated with industrial exposure are rarely seen today but
may occur in workers processing contaminated hair,
wool, hides, and bones. Direct contact with contaminated material leads to cutaneous disease, while ingestion of infected meat gives rise to oropharyngeal or
gastrointestinal forms of anthrax. Inhalation of a sufficient quantity of spores, usually seen only during generation of aerosols in an enclosed space, is associated with
processing contaminated wool or hair, or opening
anthrax‐laced letters, giving rise to inhalational anthrax.
In mail‐handling sites, B. anthracis spores may be aerosolized during the operation and maintenance of high‐
speed mail‐sorting machines, potentially exposing
workers and other mail. In addition, these spores could
get into heating, ventilating, or air‐conditioning systems.
Unreliable reporting makes it difficult to estimate with
accuracy the true incidence of human anthrax. It was estimated in 1958 that worldwide between 20 000 and 100 000
cases occurred annually. In more recent years, anthrax in

animals has been reported from 82 countries, and human
cases continue to be reported from Africa, Asia, Europe,
and the Americas. In the United States, the annual incidence of human anthrax had steadily declined, from about
127 cases in the early years of this century to about one
per year over the past 10 years. The vast majority of cases
were cutaneous. Under natural conditions, inhalational
anthrax is exceedingly rare, with only 18 cases having
been reported in the United States in the 20th century.
Outbreaks of Weaponized Anthrax
Weaponized anthrax has caused two outbreaks of disease (key points from each are outlined in the sections
below).
Sverdlovsk Outbreak – 1979

This outbreak in the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
resulted from accidental release of anthrax spores from a
military microbiologic facility where weaponized
anthrax was being produced.
Seventy‐seven human cases were reported and 66 of
the patients died, for a case–fatality rate of 86%; 75 cases
were inhalational and two were cutaneous (one on the
back of the neck and one on the shoulder). A recent statistical analysis of available data suggests that 250 cases
with 100 fatalities may actually have occurred. The mean
patient age for males was 42 and for females was 55 years,
and interestingly no cases were reported in children.
United States – 2001

This outbreak predominantly involved direct exposure
to mail that was deliberately contaminated with anthrax
spores. Several contaminated letters were sent and one
was reported to contain 2 g of powder, with 100 billion to
1 trillion anthrax spores per gram.
Twenty‐two cases (11 inhalational and 11 cutaneous)
were identified. Five of the patients with inhalational
anthrax died, for a case–fatality rate of 45% among that
group. The outbreak demonstrated several important
points about weaponized anthrax: mail can be an effective vehicle for disseminating anthrax spores; cross‐contamination of mail likely can occur within postal facilities;
and persons who handle or process unopened contaminated mail are at risk of acquiring anthrax. Substantial
environmental contamination can occur in facilities handling contaminated mail or in offices where contaminated mail is opened.

­Prevention
Public health measures to prevent contact with infected
animals are invaluable. There is a vaccine available for

VetBooks.ir

107 Anthrax

people at high risk (such as veterinarians, laboratory
technicians, employees of textile mills processing
imported goat hair, and members of the armed forces).
The Department of Defense and the Centers for Disease
Control and Prevention are working hard to prevent a
bioterrorist attack and to be prepared to deal with the

consequences if one occurs. For anthrax, vaccines
with greater efficacy and fewer side‐effects are under
development. Currently, most vaccines are given by
injection. Early studies in experimental animals are
showing promise for an oral vaccine for anthrax.

Actinomycosis, Nocardiosis, and Mycobacterial Infections
Joanna Whitney, BSc, BVSc, PhD, MVetStud, MACVS (SMAnimMed, ECC)1 and Vanessa R. Barrs, BVSc (Hons),
MVetClinStud, MACVSc (Small Animal), FACVSc (Feline), GradDertEd (Higher Ed)2
1

Small Animal Specialist Hospital, North Ryde, NSW, Australia
University of Sydney, Sydney, Australia

­Actinomycosis

Actinomyces form histopathologic lesions characterized
by pyogranulomatous inflammation with areas of central
necrosis surrounded by macrophages, neutrophils, and
plasma cells. Subacute and chronic infections result in
granulation tissue formation, extensive fibrosis, and sinus
tracts. Exudates and effusions are often malodorous.
Actinomyces may form bacterial colonies in infected body
fluids, commonly referred to as “sulphur granules,” that
grossly appear tan or white.

Etiology/Pathophysiology and Epidemiology

Signalment

Actinomyces spp. are facultatively anaerobic or microaerophilic, Gram‐positive, nonacid‐fast, nonsporulating, and
nonmotile bacilli. These opportunistic pathogens are commensals of the mucous membranes, especially the oral cavity
but also the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts.
Actinomyces are often involved in polymicrobial infections
that enhance their pathogenicity. A. viscosus, A. hordeovuln­
eris, A. bowdenii, A. canis, A. catuli, A. turicensis, A. weissii,
and A. odontolyticus have been isolated from canine infections. A. viscosus, A. meyeri, A. odontolyticus, A. hordeovuln­
eris, and A. bowdenii have been isolated from infections in
cats. Actinomyces pyogenes was recently reclassified based
on 16S rRNA gene sequencing to be included in the genus
Arcanobacterium. This organism has been reported to produce actinomycosis‐like infections in both dogs and cats.
Actinomyces cause disease following inoculation of
body tissues, frequently in conjunction with other bacteria. Portals of entry include oral mucosa damaged by
chronic gingivitis and periodontal disease, foreign body
migration, subcutaneous inoculation via bite wounds or
plant material, and aspiration of oropharyngeal material
or grass awns. Infections occur primarily in immunocompetent individuals.

Young, male, large‐breed outdoor dogs are overrepresented. Hunting and working animals are often affected,
particularly with soft tissue abscesses or pyothorax associated with plant material foreign bodies. Young, male
cats are also at increased risk from aggressive interactions involving scratches and bite wounds resulting in
inoculation of oral bacteria.

Actinomyces, Nocardia, and Mycobacteria belong to the
order Actinomycetales. All are bacilli that form branching
filaments and cause pyogranulomatous infections. However,
differences in antimicrobial susceptibility patterns, zoonotic
implications, and prognoses make an understanding of
how the organisms are differentiated clinically important.

History and Clinical Signs
In both dogs and cats actinomycosis is most commonly
associated with subcutaneous and soft tissue abscesses
and intrathoracic disease. Clinical findings may include
pneumonia, lymphadenopathy, intra‐ or extrapulmonary
masses or pyothorax. Central nervous system (CNS),
periodontal, ocular, peritoneal, urinary bladder, cardiac,
and orthopedic infections have also been reported in
dogs. In cats, less common presentations include abdominal granulomas, intracranial/spinal empyema, and
cholecystitis.
Cervicofacial actinomycosis occurs in both cats and
dogs associated with extension of oral bacteria into the
soft tissues of the head and neck secondary to periodontal

disease, oral trauma, and bite wounds. Lesions most commonly develop around the jaw and neck.
Cutaneous and subcutaneous actinomycosis manifests
as flocculent to firm masses often with draining sinus
tracts typically on the thoracic wall, flanks or limbs.
These lesions in dogs are often secondary to migrating
grass awns. In cats, they are associated with bite wounds.
Thoracic actinomycosis can present as pneumonia, lymphadenopathy, intra‐ or extrapulmonary masses or pyothorax. Thoracic actinomycosis in cats occurs secondary
to aspiration of oral flora whereas canine infections are
secondary to inhalation and migration of grass awns.
Clinical signs may be nonspecific, such as lethargy and
weight loss, or can include tachypnea, dyspnea, and coughing. Foreign bodies in dogs can migrate further into the
retroperitoneum, resulting in abscessation in this area.
Abdominal, visceral, and central nervous system infections can develop from extension of subcutaneous infections, foreign body migration or hematogenous spread.
Osseous infections can result from extension from other
locations or contamination of orthopedic implants.
Diagnosis
A provisional diagnosis of actinomycosis is based on the
identification of Gram‐positive, nonacid‐fast filamentous
organisms on cytologic examination of fluid or tissues
from suspicious lesions using a modified Ziehl–Neelson
(Kinyuon) method. A definitive diagnosis requires either
isolation and phenotypic identification of the causative
agent using biochemical methods, chemotaxonomy, and
serology or identification using molecular methods.
Molecular methods, most commonly 16S rRNA gene

sequencing, are now the diagnostic techniques of choice
for identifying the infecting species as they provide accurate and rapid results. It is important to note that culture
and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) can be negative in
some cases. Furthermore, culture or detecting organisms
using PCR without compatible clinical signs may not be
clinically significant since Actinomyces are commensals.
Therapy
The combination of surgery and antimicrobial treatment
is generally superior to antimicrobial treatment alone in
resolving Actinomyces infections in which a foreign body
is suspected. Thoracotomy and debridement are recommended in dogs with pyothorax, while cats generally
require only tube thoracostomy in addition to medical
therapy. This likely reflects the difference in etiologies in
which canine infections generally result from foreign body
migration and feline infections are caused by aspiration of
oral flora. Prolonged antimicrobial therapy for several
months is often required to resolve infection. Actinomyces
spp. are susceptible to high doses of penicillins as well as
other antibiotics (Table 108.1). As actinomycosis often
occurs as a component of a mixed bacterial infection,
identification, susceptibility testing, and treatment of the
co‐infectious agents are also imperative for resolution.
Prognosis
The prognosis for dogs and cats with subcutaneous and
soft tissue actinomycosis and for cats with pyothorax is
generally good when treated for sufficient time. However,
reported survival rates in dogs with thoracic disease are
variable and CNS actinomycosis is invariably fatal.

108 Actinomycosis, Nocardiosis, and Mycobacterial Infections

Public Health Implications
Humans bitten by dogs or cats can develop actinomycosis. However, there have been no reports of transmission
from infected animals to humans.

­Nocardiosis
Etiology/Pathophysiology and Epidemiology
The genus Nocardia consists of filamentous, branching,
Gram‐positive, variably acid‐fast, catalase‐positive,
nonmotile aerobic bacilli. Unlike commensal Actino­
myces, Nocardia species are ubiquitous soil saprophytes,
involved in plant decomposition. Pathogenic species
have been isolated from house dust, garden soil, beach
sand, swimming pools, and tap water in different geographic regions. Pathogenic Nocardia species in dogs
include N. caviae, N. asteroides, N. abscessus, N. otitidis‐
caviarum, N. brasiliensis, N. cyriacigeorgica, and N. vet­
erana, while those in cats include N. tenerifensis,
N. africana, N. nova, N. farcinica, N. cyriacigeorgica,
N.brasiliensis, and N. elegans. The virulence of Nocardia
spp. varies with the phase of growth associated with
changes in composition of the cell wall.
Infection with Nocardia species occurs after inhalation of aerosolized environmental organisms or inoculation via puncture wounds. The host T cell response is
essential in limiting dissemination of nocardial infection
following inoculation, but it is also responsible for the
development of the characteristic suppurative to granulomatous lesions of nocardiosis.
Nocardiosis is less common than actinomycosis and in
contrast to Actinomyces, Nocardia infections are most
common in immunosuppressed patients.
Signalment
Localized infections, particularly abscesses of the subcutaneous tissues, are most frequently seen in young outdoor dogs secondary to foreign body migration and
inoculation during puncture wounds. Similarly, cats of
any age with outdoor access more commonly develop
superficial lesions.
Disseminated or systemic nocardiosis develops in young
and immunosuppressed dogs and cats. The increasing use
of immunosuppressive medications in veterinary patients
has resulted in an increase in the incidence of such
infections.
History and Clinical Signs
Nocardiosis is typically classified as subcutaneous,
pulmonary and systemic, or disseminated. In
­

immunocompetent companion animals, especially cats,
­
disease most commonly manifests as cutaneous and pulmonary lesions. Disseminated disease, often involving
the CNS, has been reported more commonly in young
and immunosuppressed dogs. Nocardia spp. have been
isolated sporadically from cases of hepatitis and cystitis.
Cutaneous nocardiosis is the most common manifestation of disease in cats, associated with inoculation
via scratches from cat fights and punctures from plant
material.
Dogs and cats with disseminated or systemic disease
typically have a history of immunosuppressive disease or
administration of immunomodulating drugs. In particular, nocardiosis has been shown to occur currently with
canine distemper virus infection in endemic areas.
Pulmonary nocardiosis may occur in isolation associated with wound inoculation or foreign body migration,
or as a component of disseminated disease. In dogs, the
most common clinical signs of pneumonia include dyspnea, nasal discharge, fever, weight loss, and anorexia.
Diagnosis
A presumptive diagnosis of nocardiosis may be made
based upon macroscopic and microscopic examination
of clinical specimens. Organisms on Gram‐stained slides
will appear as Gram‐positive, thin filamentous organisms
within a background of lymphocytes and macrophages.
Acid‐fast stains may be used to demonstrate acid‐fastness in samples that have revealed filamentous organisms
with Gram staining. However, this reaction is unreliable
in direct clinical samples and may be dependent on the
growth media used and age of culture samples. Species
identification has traditionally been performed based on
biochemical methods, chemotaxonomy, and serology.
Molecular methods, most commonly 16S rRNA gene
sequencing, are now used preferentially for bacterial
identification as these provide accurate and rapid results.
Due to the ubiquitous nature of Nocardia spp., the significance of isolation of these organisms from clinical
samples should be assessed in light of the clinical findings. Identification of the sample organism in multiple
samples also aids in determining significance.
Therapy
Treatment of nocardiosis relies upon debridement and
drainage of the lesion and prolonged antimicrobial therapy.
Most Nocardia spp. are susceptible to sulfonamide antimicrobials and these often form the basis of medical
therapy. However, species differences in susceptibility
have been reported and in vivo response to treatment
does not always reflect in vitro results. In humans, a
range of other antimicrobials (see Table 108.1) are efficacious

979

VetBooks.ir

980

Section 9 Infectious Disease

with protocols based on established species‐specific susceptibility patterns advocated for treatment of persistent
or disseminated infections. Six to 12 months of antimicrobial therapy is required in most cases for optimal
results. Alternatives to sulfonamides should be considered for prolonged treatment of nocardiosis to minimize
the risk of adverse drug reactions.
Prognosis
While cases of superficial nocardiosis may show initial
response to treatment, most patients are euthanized due
to deterioration or disease recurrence. Disseminated
nocardiosis, especially with CNS involvement, has a
grave prognosis. The poor outcome for these patients is
likely associated with the underlying immunosuppressive disease.
Public Health Implications
There have been no cases of acquired infection from
infected animals, but cat scratches have caused cutaneous nocardiosis in people. Immunocompromised individuals should take special precautions when interacting
with infected dogs or cats.

­Mycobacteriosis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Members of the genus Mycobacterium are intracellular,
aerobic, acid‐fast, nonspore‐forming, environmentally
resistant bacilli. Mycobacteria spp. are generally saprophytic and nonpathogenic, but several are primary
or opportunistic pathogens in dogs cats, and humans.
Infecting bacteria are phagocytosed by host macrophages
within which the organism replicates. Infected macrophages produce proinflammatory mediators and
attract monocytes and other inflammatory cells to the
site of infection, resulting in focal or disseminated granulomatous to pyogranulomatous disease.
Mycobacterial infections are recognized increasingly
in companion animals because of improved diagnostic
techniques and increased use of immunosuppressive
medications. Recent evidence suggests that the prevalence of mycobacteriosis in companion animals, particularly in the United Kingdom, is underestimated due to
nonspecific signs, a low index of suspicion, and difficult
antemortem diagnosis.
The mycobacteria that cause companion animal infections are generally divided into tuberculous, saprophytic
or opportunistic, and lepromatous groups. Generally,
the tuberculous group includes members of the

Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) complex, the saprophytic group includes members of the M. avium complex (MAC) and other nontuberculous bacteria, and
the lepromatous group includes bacteria that cause
feline leprosy and canine leproid granuloma syndromes
(Table 108.2). However, there is much overlap in these
categories since different organisms cause similar clinical lesions and there is disagreement in the grouping of
organisms. Organisms from all groups can cause cutaneous lesions whereas systemic or disseminated disease
results from infection with tuberculous or saprophytic/
opportunistic agents.
Epidemiology
Tuberculosis is caused by infection with members of the
MTB complex, all of which are obligate pathogens (see
Table 108.2). The prevalence of disease within a region
and the causative agent are dependent on the presence of
the primary host species. Humans are the reservoir host
for M. tuberculosis so the incidence of M. tuberculosis
infection in dogs follows the distribution reported for
people, and includes areas of the US, Africa, France, and
Switzerland. M. bovis infections in people occur in Great
Britain and New Zealand and consequently most feline
infections are also reported in these regions.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection typically results
from close contact with infected humans. Disease transmission occurs via inoculation, ingestion or inhalation.
Organisms in sputum and respiratory secretions are aerosolized and inhaled or ingested by in‐contact pets.
However, due to the chronicity of disease and potential
for hematogenous dissemination, the route of infection
may not be identifiable at the time of diagnosis. Although
there are minimal reports of transmission of M. tubercu­
losis from pets to their owners the zoonotic potential of
infected animals is of major concern, particularly for
immunocompromised owners.
The primary reservoir of M. bovis is domestic cattle,
with transmission to dogs and cats thought to be due to
ingestion of contaminated meat or milk. Cats and dogs
are considered to be potential amplifier hosts of M. bovis
in endemic areas, meaning that they may act as a source
of infection for other animals and people. Rodents, feral
pigs, wild deer, badgers, and opossums are established
reservoir hosts for M. bovis and/or microti.
The occurrence of peripheral primary cutaneous
lesions in cats suggests that some infections may develop
following inoculation of organisms via bite wounds.
Hunting and catching small rodents are risk factors for
M. microti infection in cats.
The saprophytic mycobacteria are the most common
causes of mycobacteriosis in cats and dogs. This group
includes the rapid‐growing mycobacteria (RGM) and

VetBooks.ir

108 Actinomycosis, Nocardiosis, and Mycobacterial Infections

slow‐growing mycobacteria (SGM) groups, including
the M. avium‐intracellulare complex (see Table 108.2).
The saprophytic mycobacteria are widely distributed in
the environment. They have variable geographic prevalence likely associated with environmental factors such
as warmer temperatures that support their growth.
Infection with RGM usually follows cutaneous, pulmonary or gastrointestinal inoculation. Disseminated disease may develop in immunosuppressed animals.
Canine and feline leproid syndromes are characterized
by discrete cutaneous lesions. The causative agents are
fastidious and cannot be cultured readily. Feline leprosy
results from infection with one of a number of saprophytic species (see Table 108.2). M. lepraemurium infection is thought to be transmitted to cats by rodent bites.
Insect vector transmission has also been proposed but is
unverified.
It is not clear whether canine leproid granuloma syndrome results from infection with one or more species.
Partial characterization using gene sequencing has
shown that genetically identical organisms have been
associated with the disease worldwide; however, the
causative species remains incompletely defined due to
inability to culture it in the laboratory. Transmission of

the canine agent via insect vectors seems likely. Case
clusters of disease in related foxhounds suggest additional environmental or genetic factors may be involved.
Signalment
Younger animals tend to be more commonly affected by
mycobacteriosis, particularly cutaneous forms of the disease. This may be associated with increased exposure to
environmental organisms and precipitating injuries that
allow infection. Patients that develop disseminated disease are often suspected to be immunocompromised
although supportive evidence for this may not be apparent. Tuberculosis is most commonly observed in animals
with prolonged close contact with an infected primary
host. Adult nonpedigree cats with outdoor access are
most commonly affected, although Siamese cats are also
overrepresented. Feline leprosy is most common in
young cats and in older cats that are immunosuppressed.
Canine leproid granuloma syndrome is most common in
large‐breed, short‐haired dogs, especially boxers. Bassett
hounds, schnauzers, and Abyssinian cats are overrepresented in disseminated saprophytic mycobacteriosis,
suggesting genetic immunodeficiencies in these breeds.

History and Clinical Signs
Cutaneous lesions in mycobacteriosis vary. Leproid
granulomas can be single or multiple nodules with or
without ulceration and frequently occur on the head and
limbs. The most common manifestation of tuberculosis
and saprophytic mycobacterial infections in cats is the
cutaneous form that results in the development of subcutaneous masses, often with draining sinuses and a
regional lymphadenopathy. Skin lesions are usually
mobile, firm, raised, moist, and without odor. The saprophytic mycobacterial agents have a predilection for
adipose tissue and often cause a panniculitis of the ventral abdomen and inguinal area in cats (Figure 108.1).
Ocular lesions are frequently reported in cats with the
leproid syndrome. Pulmonary, gastrointestinal or
disseminated granulomatous lesions can result from
­
infection with tuberculous and saprophytic group organisms. Abdominal and pleural effusions often develop
with progressive disease.
Diagnosis
Clinical pathologica results are generally nonspecific, and
may include a neutrophilia with a left shift, nonregenerative anemia, decreased albumin:globulin ratio, and hypercalcemia. Where there is systemic involvement, diagnostic
imaging findings are consistent with nonspecific infiltrative disease of the abdominal and/or thoracic cavities
with possible organ and lymph node mineralization.
Tuberculin intradermal testing in dogs and cats is generally unrewarding. However, immunodiagnostic assays for
diagnosis of M. bovis in cats, including semiquantitative
interferon‐gamma production and point‐of‐care qualitative antibody detection tests, have shown positive results,
although further evaluation is required.

Figure 108.2 Acid‐fast bacilli in a sample from a cat with feline
leprosy.

Suspicion of mycobacteriosis should be raised in
­animals with consistent presenting signs whenever pyogranulomatous inflammation is identified on cytologic or
histopathologic examination. Provisional diagnosis is
based on the identification of acid‐fast bacilli within tissue samples, exudates or blood smears (Figure 108.2).
Definitive diagnosis requires organism identification and
is imperative in mycobacterial infections in connection to
their treatment and zoonotic potential. Like acid‐fast
staining, culture for mycobacteria must be specifically
requested from the laboratory.
While RGM are often difficult to identify cytologically
due to the scant number of organisms seen, they can
generally be cultured within seven days. Conversely,
SGM may be abundant on tissue cytology but cannot be
cultured readily, if at all. Molecular techniques, particularly
16S rRNA sequencing, provide rapid and accurate identification of mycobacteria which is of particular importance in potential zoonotic infections. However, bacterial
culture and susceptibility testing should still be attempted
to determine appropriate antimicrobial therapy.
Therapy and Prognosis

Figure 108.1 Inguinal panniculitis in a cat.

The zoonotic potential and implications of treating
infected animals must be considered before treatment
(see later). Recommendations for treatment of tuberculous and saprophytic infections include triple agent antimicrobial therapy (a fluoroquinolone, a macrolide, and
rifampicin) for three months followed by continued
administration of two of these agents for an additional
six months (see Table 108.3). Other antimicrobials,
including doxycycline, aminoglycocides, third‐generation
cephalosporins, and chloramphenicol, have been
reported to have been used in combination protocols or

Public Health Implications
Although the risk of transmission from dogs and cats to
humans is low, members of the tuberculosis complex and
MAC have zoonotic potential. Infected animals may
excrete organisms in sputum and respiratory secretions
that are aerosolized and can be inhaled or ingested by humans
in close contact. Euthanasia or aggressive treatment of

983

VetBooks.ir

984

Section 9 Infectious Disease

dogs and cats infected with these organisms is imperative
to eliminate the risk of zoonotic transmission.
Infection of veterinary personnel with M. tuberculosis
has been reported following necropsy of infected dogs.
In one case, the organism may have been aerosolized during use of an electric saw. Cutaneous inoculation of
mycobacterial bacilli has also been reported associated
with needle sticks contaminated by laboratory and
patient samples. Care should be taken in specimen handling

and appropriate personal protective equipment must be
worn to avoid aerosolization, inhalation, and inoculation
of organisms.
Tuberculosis is reportable or notifiable in a number of
countries. Regional and national health authorities
should be consulted when tuberculous infections are
suspected or diagnosed in dogs and cats to allow thorough
epidemiologic investigation.

Fungal Infections
Jane E. Sykes, BVSc, PhD, DACVIM (SAIM)
Department of Medicine and Epidemiology, University of California‐Davis, Davis, CA, USA

­General Features of Fungal
Infections
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Fungal infections can be classified as superficial (cutane­
ous) mycoses or deep mycoses. Superficial mycoses are
limited to the skin and include dermatophytosis and
Malassezia infections. Deep mycoses can be caused by:
organisms that exist as molds (hyphal forms) in the
environment, the conidia (spores) of which are typi­
cally inhaled by mammalian hosts and then transform
into replicating yeasts in tissues (dimorphic fungi)
●● organisms that exist as spore‐producing molds in the
environment, are inhaled by mammalian hosts and
then continue to grow as molds in tissues, such as
Aspergillus
●● Candida, which is a commensal of mucous mem­
branes and invades opportunistically.
●●

With the exception of Sporothrix, infections caused
by dimorphic fungi and molds are acquired from the
environment, and disease transmission from one affected
animal to another does not occur. Incubation periods
are often several weeks to months in duration, because
of the slow replication rate of many fungi.
Epidemiology and Signalment
In general, dogs and cats of any age, breed, and sex can
develop deep mycoses, but dogs are often young adult,
pure‐bred dogs, suggesting that genetic factors predis­
pose to infection. Most cats with deep fungal infections
test negative for retroviruses, but some animals have
concurrent diseases such as malignancy or a history of
treatment with immunosuppressive drugs, including
chronic low‐dose glucocorticoid therapy. Some dogs

and cats have evidence of concurrent opportunistic
infections such as toxoplasmosis, neosporosis or papil­
lomavirus. Cats housed exclusively indoors can develop
soil‐borne fungal infections such as histoplasmosis or
cryptococcosis.
History and Clinical Signs
Many infections with dimorphic fungi are probably
subclinical. Animals that develop systemic disease
­
are often evaluated for vague signs such as lethargy,
weight loss, inappetence, weakness, and low‐grade fever,
together with signs of respiratory involvement and/or
dissemination to sites that commonly include the skin,
bone, eye, and brain. Findings on routine hematologic
and biochemical testing are also nonspecific and include
nonregenerative anemia, mild leukocytosis, hypoalbu­
minemia, and hyperglobulinemia. In a smaller pro­
portion of dogs with systemic mycoses, hypercalcemia
secondary to granulomatous inflammation may be pre­
sent. Although most infections are acquired through
inhalation, radiographic evidence of pulmonary involve­
ment can be absent in some dogs and cats with dissemi­
nated disease.
Diagnosis
Persistent disease in the face of antibacterial therapy, or
progression in the face of glucocorticoid therapy, should
raise suspicion for a fungal infection. Definitive diagno­
sis is based on clinical suspicion combined with cytology
and/or histopathology, fungal culture, antibody or anti­
gen testing, and/or real‐time polymerase chain reaction
(PCR) assays. Cytology and histopathology have variable
sensitivity and specificity and a limited ability to identify
fungal pathogens. The use of special stains such as peri­
odic acid–Schiff or Gomori’s methenamine silver can

Clinical Small Animal Internal Medicine Volume II, First Edition. Edited by David S. Bruyette.
© 2020 John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Published 2020 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc.
Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/bruyette/clinical

VetBooks.ir

Section 9 Infectious Disease

highlight fungal elements in tissues. Most fungi grow
within seven days in the laboratory, but occasionally
­several weeks elapse before growth occurs. Some dimor­
phic fungi (Blastomyces, Histoplasma, Coccidioides)
grow as a mycelial form in the laboratory, which repre­
sents a laboratory health hazard. For these pathogens,
culture should only be performed if a diagnosis cannot
be established through other methods, and the labora­
tory should be warned that infection with a dimorphic
fungus may be present, so that appropriate precautions
are taken. Culture also allows antifungal susceptibility
testing, although at this time, the clinical relevance of
susceptibility test results is unclear for many fungi.
Antigen testing can be helpful for diagnosis and
­therapeutic monitoring of histoplasmosis (urine), blasto­
mycosis (serum), cryptococcosis (serum or cerebrospi­
nal fluid [CSF]), and disseminated aspergillosis (serum),
although serologic cross‐reactivity with other fungal
pathogens is common with all assays except those for
cryptococcosis. Serum antibody testing is helpful for
diagnosis of coccidioidomycosis and pythiosis. At the
time of writing, more information is needed on the
­clinical sensitivity and specificity of real‐time PCR assays
that are available for detection of fungal pathogens,
but these may be useful when a fungal pathogen is
­suspected but cannot be detected or identified using
other diagnostic tests.
Therapy
Treatment of fungal infections most often involves the
use of orally administered azole antifungal drugs such as
itraconazole capsules (usually 5 mg/kg PO q24h for
dogs) or fluconazole tablets (5–10 mg/kg PO q24h). In
general, fluconazole is less active than itraconazole, and
itraconazole is preferred as first‐line treatment for most
infections, with the exceptions of Cryptococcus and
­
Candida. Most molds are resistant to fluconazole.
Topical antifungal drug preparations that contain azole
drugs may be sufficient for treatment of the superficial
mycoses. Liver enzyme activities should be monitored
monthly during systemic treatment with azole antifun­
gals in order to monitor for hepatotoxicity. Itraconazole
solution (10 mg/mL) has higher bioavailability than the
capsules and is administered at a lower dose (3 mg/kg
PO q12h) and on an empty stomach. If itraconazole cap­
sules are used, they should be administered with food.
Compounded formulations of itraconazole should be
avoided.
If clinical signs do not improve with azole treatment,
measurement of serum drug concentrations could be
considered. Serious systemic infections may require
treatment with intravenous amphotericin B, with careful
monitoring for evidence of nephrotoxicity before each

infusion. Lipid complex amphotericin B preparations
are not necessarily more effective than deoxycholate
amphotericin B but are less nephrotoxic. Deoxycholate
amphotericin B is administered to dogs at 0.5 mg/kg in
250–1000 mL of 5% dextrose over 4–6 hours on a
Monday‐Wednesday‐Friday basis; the dose for cats is
0.25 mg/kg, which is given in 30 mL of 5% dextrose over
one hour. Administration of 0.9% NaCl at 1.5–2 times
maintenance for one hour prior to and after administra­
tion is recommended. Electrolytes cause amphotericin
to precipitate so the line must be flushed with D5W prior
to administration of the drug. Lipid complexed ampho­
tericin B is administered to dogs at 3 mg/kg and cats at
1 mg/kg over two hours.
Voriconazole or posaconazole could also be consid­
ered for treatment of refractory deep fungal infections if
client finances permit their use. Voriconazole (4–5 mg/
kg PO q12h) has excellent central nervous system (CNS)
penetration and so represents an option for dogs with
fungal meningoencephalomyelitis. However, virtually all
cats do not tolerate voriconazole due to gastrointestinal,
neurologic, and cardiac adverse effects, so until a safe
dose is known, voriconazole should not be administered
to cats.
Other treatments that may be required for dogs or cats
with serious pulmonary infections with or without dis­
semination are supplemental oxygen, nebulization and
coupage, fluid therapy, and, in some cases, mechanical
ventilation. Initially, clinical signs may worsen with
­treatment, possibly as a result of organism death and an
associated inflammatory response. Nonsteroidal antiin­
flammatory drugs such as carprofen could be considered
to control pyrexia, and systemic glucocorticoids may be
required to control brain inflammation and edema in
dogs and cats with CNS infections, although this is con­
troversial. Topical antiinflammatory and antiglaucoma
agents may be indicated if ocular involvement is present.
In animals with endophthalmitis, enucleation may be
necessary to control ocular pain and eliminate infection.
Surgery may also be required for treatment of refractory
fungal osteomyelitis (amputation) or large pulmonary
granulomas (lung lobectomy).
Prognosis
Most fungal infections require several months of treat­
ment at a minimum. Typically, treatment is continued
until there is no evidence of disease remaining based on
serial physical examinations, imaging, and antigen or
antibody testing. Animals with disseminated fungal
infections often require more than a year of treatment, or
lifelong therapy. The prognosis is often poor when severe
immunosuppression and dissemination are present at
the time of diagnosis, but if immunosuppression can be

VetBooks.ir

109 Fungal Infections

reversed and aggressive antifungal drug treatment is
­initiated promptly, complete recovery is possible.
Public Health Implications
Direct inoculation of yeast forms of fungi can potentially
cause infection. The mycelial form of dimorphic fungi
can pose significant zoonotic risk, although these are
typically only present when the organisms are cultured
in the laboratory. Appropriate precautions such as avoid­
ing needle sticks and other traumatic wounds when
working with animals that have deep fungal infections
should be followed. Caution when performing necrop­
sies, and cremating, rather than allowing burial of
deceased patients are also important to prevent zoonosis
from mycelial forms.

­Dermatophytosis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Dermatophytosis is caused by fungi that belong to the
genera Microsporum, Trichophyton or Epidermophyton.
These organisms secrete proteases that allow them to
invade macerated or traumatized keratinized tissue.
Infectious arthrospores persist in the environment for
more than a year given optimal temperature and humid­
ity, and are transmitted by close contact with other
infected animals or contaminated fomites. The most
common dermatophyte species that infect dogs and cats
are Microsporum canis, Microsporum gypseum, and organ­
isms that belong to the Trichophyton mentagrophytes
­species complex (especially Arthroderma benhamiae).
Microsporum canis and organisms that belong to the
T. mentagrophytes species complex are zoophilic derma­
tophytes (adapted to animal hosts), whereas M. gypseum
is a geophilic dermatophyte (soil saprophyte).
Epidemiology and Signalment
Cats are more susceptible than dogs to dermatophytosis.
The prevalence of infection is highest in regions with
warm, humid climates. The risk of infection is higher
in young animals and animals with concurrent immuno­
suppressive disorders, such as hyperadrenocorticism.
Dogs that burrow in soil may also be at increased risk.
Persian and Himalayan cats and Yorkshire and Jack
Russell terriers appear to be predisposed.
History and Clinical Signs
Classically, dermatophytosis is characterized by one or
more circular lesions of alopecia with an erythematous

Figure 109.1 Fox terrier with dermatophytosis caused by
Trichophyton mentagrophytes species complex organisms. Source:
Image courtesy of the University of California, Davis Veterinary
Dermatology Service.

margin, superficial scale and crusts, and follicular pap­
ules and pustules. In dogs, lesions are most often on the
face, distal limbs, and tail. When the claw is involved,
there may be thickening of the ungual fold and deformity
of the claw. Infection by T. mentagrophytes may result in
widespread lesions with scar formation (Figure 109.1).
Lesions in cats are extremely variable. In long‐haired
cats, dermatophytosis may simply be manifested as a
poor hair coat with excessive shedding.
Other forms of dermatophytosis include nodular inflam­
matory lesions known as kerions, and dermatophytic
mycetomas, which are nodular lesions that ­coalesce and
drain fluid. Persian and Himalayan cats appear to be prone
to dermatophytic mycetomas.
Diagnosis
Diagnosis of dermatophytosis is based on clinical suspi­
cion together with Wood’s lamp examination, identifica­
tion of hyphae and spores using skin and hair cytology,
histopathology of skin biopsy specimens, and/or fungal
culture. A positive Wood’s lamp examination occurs
when some strains of M. canis fluoresce within infected
hair shafts. The sensitivity of Wood’s lamp examination
is low and false positives can occur when fluorescence of
keratinized debris is misinterpreted as fungal fluores­
cence. The gold standard for diagnosis of dermatophyto­
sis is fungal culture of hairs plucked from the edge of
lesions, scrapings of crusts, or brushings of the haircoat
(using a new toothbrush). Use of a microbiology labora­
tory is recommended whenever possible in order to
properly distinguish dermatophyte growth from that of
saprophytic molds and to prevent contamination of the
practice environment.

Therapy
Dermatophytosis often resolves spontaneously within
three months in otherwise healthy animals. Treatment is
recommended for animals that are immunosuppressed,
those that live in multipet households, and those that
live with immunocompromised owners or children.
Treatment should consist of systemic antifungal drugs
(itraconazole is the drug of choice, but fluconazole, keto­
conazole, griseofulvin or terbinafine also have activity
against dermatophytes), with or without twice‐weekly
topical treatment (preferably a 1:16 dilution of lime
­sulfur) and environmental decontamination. Ideally, all
in‐contact animals should be examined and cultured
using a toothbrush technique. Animals with positive
­cultures (and those with clinical signs) should be treated
both systemically and topically. All unaffected, culture‐
positive animals should be treated topically along with
any in‐contact animals. Long‐haired cats should be
clipped in order to remove contaminated hair and facili­
tate penetration of topical treatments, although this is
controversial because of the potential for contamination
of the environment and for disruption of the skin.
Clippers must be disinfected with 10% bleach afterwards.
Potential fomites (bedding, collars, grooming equip­
ment) should be discarded if possible. Disinfection of
hard surfaces should be performed with a 1:10 dilution
of bleach, 0.2% enilconazole, or an enilconazole fogger
(if available). Carpets and furniture should be thoroughly
vacuumed and then steam cleaned, after which vacuum
cleaners may need to be replaced.
Treatment is usually needed for at least 10–12 weeks.
Animals should be examined and a culture performed
monthly (and no earlier than weekly) during treatment.
Treatment should be continued until lesions resolve and
two successive cultures are negative. For group‐housed
animals, at least three successive negative cultures are
recommended. If serial cultures are not possible because
of financial limitations, treatment should be continued
for 2–4 weeks after clinical signs resolve.
Prognosis
The prognosis for resolution of clinical signs is generally
good, especially in households with one or only a few ani­
mals. Dermatophytic mycetomas may require long treat­
ment durations; in some cats, surgery may be required for
lesion resolution.
Public Health Implications
Dermatophyte species that cause disease in dogs and
cats have the potential to cause disease in people. Young
children and immunocompromised people are most
­susceptible. Protective gloves and clothing should be

worn when handling infected animals. Young children
and immunocompromised people should avoid any
contact.

­Malassezia Infections
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Malassezia spp. are lipophilic yeasts that normally colo­
nize animal and human skin. Malassezia pachydermatis
is the most commonly isolated yeast species from the skin
and ears of healthy dogs and cats, and is most commonly
found in the ear canals, lips, axillae, interdigital spaces,
anal sacs, and occasionally the nose and vagina. Other
species can also colonize the skin of healthy cats.
Malassezia proliferate opportunistically, and com­
monly contribute to chronic dermatitis and otitis externa
in dogs, and to a lesser extent in cats. Underlying
­diseases that predispose to proliferation of Malassezia
spp. include allergic dermatitis, endocrinopathies, inter­
trigo, primary keratinization/cornification disorders, a
history of prolonged treatment with antibacterial drugs
or ­glucocorticoids, and, in cats, underlying neoplasia or
retrovirus infections. In some animals, hypersensitivity
reactions to yeast antigens may contribute to the inflam­
matory response that results.
Epidemiology and Signalment
Predisposed dog breeds include American cocker
­spaniels, West Highland white terriers, basset hounds,
poodles, and Australian silky terriers. Sphynx and Devon
Rex cats have high rates of Malassezia spp. colonization
when compared with domestic short‐hair cats.
History and Clinical Signs
Clinical signs of Malassezia infection include erythema,
pruritus, alopecia, scaling, and a greasy exudate. The
most commonly affected sites are the ear canals, ­skinfolds
(periocular and perioral skin, ventral neck, axillae, ingui­
nal regions, and perineum) and interdigital skin. Chronic
infections can result in hyperpigmentation, lichenifica­
tion, and stenosis of the ear canal, and affected animals
may emit a pungent odor.
Diagnosis
The diagnosis of Malassezia infection is usually based on
cytologic examination of tape preparations. The yeasts
stain darkly basophilic and exhibit wide‐based budding,
resembling “footprints.” Mean counts of ≥1 yeast per oil
immersion field (1000× magnification) for dermatitis
and ≥5 organisms per oil immersion field for otitis are

VetBooks.ir

109 Fungal Infections

considered abnormal in dogs. More than 12 yeasts/high
dry field is considered abnormal in feline ear canals.
The ear canals of healthy dogs and cats have mean counts
of ≤ 2 yeasts/high dry field (400× magnification).

conidia that are aerosolized and inhaled by the host,
where they transform into yeasts, trigger a pyogranu­
lomatous inflammatory response, and produce localized
pulmonary or disseminated disease.

Therapy

Epidemiology and Signalment

Therapy of Malassezia spp. infections requires identifi­
cation and treatment of the underlying cause, in addition
to antifungal drug treatment. Topical therapy is adequate
for many infections. Topical otic preparations for treat­
ment of Malassezia otitis are used twice daily until there
is cytologic resolution of infection, typically 2–4 weeks.
These contain antifungals such as clotrimazole, micona­
zole or posaconazole, which are usually combined with a
glucocorticoid and an antibacterial compound. Some
antiseptic ear cleaners, such as Epi‐Otic, also have activ­
ity against Malassezia and should be considered as an
alternative to reduce unnecessary use of antibacterials.
Cleaning is performed on a 12‐ or 24‐hour basis for
5–7 days, and then every second or third day until
­clinical signs resolve. Subsequently, weekly maintenance
cleaning may reduce the risk of recurrence. Malassezia
dermatitis can be successfully treated with twice‐weekly
shampooing with a 2% miconazole/2% chlorhexidine
shampoo for three weeks, which also serves to prevent
recurrence. Systemic antifungal drugs such as ketocona­
zole, itraconazole, fluconazole or terbinafine (30–40 mg/
kg PO q24h) may be needed to treat more severe
­infections or infections of the claw bed.
Treatment should be monitored through serial derma­
tologic examinations and cytologic evaluation of tape
preparations, and at least three weeks of treatment is
usually required.

Blastomyces dermatitidis prefers warm, moist, sandy soil
that is rich in organic debris such as decaying vegetation.
The fungus is primarily found in North America around
the Great Lakes, along the Ohio and Mississippi river
valleys, and in the southeastern states. A smaller focus of
endemicity exists in the northeast that extends into
Ontario, Canada. Occasionally disease appears in
­nontraveled dogs that reside in nonendemic parts of the
United States.
Young adult, large‐breed (>15 kg) dogs are predis­
posed. Most affected dogs are apparently immunocom­
petent. Overrepresented breeds include coonhounds,
pointers, Weimaraners, retrievers, and Doberman pin­
schers. Residence close to water sources and exposure to
sites of soil disturbance also increase the risk of infec­
tion. Blastomycosis is rare in cats.
History and Clinical Signs

­Blastomycosis

Infection with Blastomyces may result in disease that is
localized to the lungs and associated lymph nodes, or
signs that are severe and progressive with dissemination
to extrapulmonary sites, which include the skin, eye,
bone, prostate, and testes, and the CNS. Infection has
also been reported in the mammary glands, nasal or oral
cavities, cardiac tissues, and very rarely in the kidneys,
liver, spleen, peritoneum, gastrointestinal tract, and
­urinary bladder. Neurologic involvement secondary to
extension of intranasal Blastomyces granulomas through
the calvarium has also been described.
In addition to nonspecific signs of illness, affected dogs
may show signs that include cough, exercise intolerance
and tachypnea, peripheral lymphadenopathy, ocular
manifestations such as uveitis, chorioretinitis or pano­
phthalmitis, nodular or ulcerated cutaneous or mucocu­
taneous lesions, and lameness due to fungal osteomyelitis
or arthritis. Gastrointestinal signs, polyuria or ­polydipsia,
nasal discharge, sneezing and/or epistaxis, mammary or
testicular masses, facial distortion, cardiac arrhythmias,
and neurologic signs due to meningoencephalitis or
ependymitis are less common. Clinical signs of blasto­
mycosis in cats resemble those in dogs.

Etiology/Pathophysiology

Diagnosis

Blastomycosis is caused by the dimorphic fungus
Blastomyces dermatitidis, which grows as a thick‐walled
budding yeast in tissues. Hyphae within soil produce

Prognosis
If the underlying cause can be resolved and there is
good client compliance, the prognosis for resolution of
Malassezia infections is generally good.
Public Health Implications
Malassezia pachydermatis can occasionally be carried
on human skin. The risk of disease transmission appears
low, although it may occur. Hand washing may theoreti­
