alveolar‐interstitial patterns, pulmonary mass lesions,
tracheobronchial lymphadenopathy, and/or single or
multiple pulmonary nodules that resemble pulmonary
neoplasia. Radiographs of affected bone typically show
osteolytic lesions, often accompanied by periosteal
­proliferation and soft tissue swelling.
A diagnosis of blastomycosis is often confirmed
through cytologic examination of affected tissues, lung
washes or body fluids. The yeasts are 8–15 μm in ­diameter,
have a thick, refractile cell wall, and exhibit broad‐based
budding, although occasionally organisms are not visual­
ized. The organisms are usually accompanied by pyo­
granulomatous inflammation (Figure 109.2).
Other methods of diagnosis include histopathology
(e.g., of bone or tissue biopsies), fungal culture, antigen
testing, and molecular diagnosis with PCR‐based assays.
Serologic tests for blastomycosis that detect antibody
currently have poor sensitivity and specificity, and so the
use of these tests is not recommended for routine diag­
nosis. When performed on urine, assays for Blastomyces
cell wall galactomannan antigen (MiraVista Diagnostics,
Indianapolis, IN) have high sensitivity (93.5%) and speci­
ficity (98%) for diagnosis of canine blastomycosis, but
due to serologic cross‐reactivity, results may also be
­positive in dogs with other fungal infections, especially
histoplasmosis.
Therapy
The most widely used specific therapy for blastomycosis
in dogs is itraconazole or fluconazole. The duration of
treatment should be based on serial monitoring of
­clinical signs, radiographic lesions, and urine antigen
titers (i.e., every 4–8 weeks). For dogs with pulmonary

involvement, radiographic lesions and clinical signs may
initially worsen with treatment. Initial worsening of radi­
ographic lesions does not appear to affect survival. Urine
antigen concentration declines with effective treatment.
Although a positive residual urine antigen titer at the
time treatment is discontinued does not necessarily pre­
dict that relapse will occur, a negative urine antigen test
is recommended before treatment is discontinued. Most
dogs require at least 4–6 months of treatment, and some
dogs may require treatment for more than one year,
especially those with osteoarticular infections or wide­
spread dissemination. Treatment with amphotericin B
could be considered for dogs with severe disease with
widespread dissemination, followed by azole therapy
after there has been a satisfactory clinical response to the
amphotericin B.
Prognosis
Cure rates of 50–75% have been reported in dogs with
blastomycosis; an additional 20–25% of dogs experience
disease recurrence after treatment is discontinued,
which can occur as long as a year later. The most com­
mon radiographic sequelae to pulmonary blastomycosis
are pulmonary bullae and persistent focal interstitial pat­
terns, presumably as a result of pulmonary fibrosis.
Involvement of the CNS, severe lung disease, and a high
band neutrophil count are negative prognostic factors.
Public Health Implications
Blastomyces dermatitidis causes disease in people. Direct
transmission between mammalian hosts does not occur,
with the exception of inoculation of yeast via bite wound
or needle sticks. Laboratory personnel are at risk if
­samples are cultured and should be warned that blasto­
mycosis is suspected prior to submission. Bodies of
deceased pets should be cremated rather than buried.
Dogs are sentinels for human exposure.

­Histoplasmosis
Etiology/Pathophysiology

Histoplasma capsulatum is a dimorphic, soil‐borne
­fungus. Microconidia produced by the fungus are inhaled
by mammalian hosts, and within the lungs transition to
the yeast phase, which replicates by budding within
­alveolar macrophages. Some animals control the initial
infection but remain latently infected with small num­
bers of yeasts. Subsequent immune suppression can lead
to reactivation years later. Replication of H. capsulatum
leads to a granulomatous inflammatory response, which

VetBooks.ir

109 Fungal Infections

is sometimes accompanied by fibrosis. When a cell‐
mediated immune response is defective, yeast forms
migrate to local lymph nodes (such as the tracheobron­
chial lymph nodes) and other tissues that contain mono­
nuclear cells, such as the liver and spleen. Other common
sites of dissemination include the bone marrow, small
and/or large intestinal tract, pancreas, the skin, bones,
central nervous system, and eyes.
Epidemiology and Signalment
Histoplasma capsulatum is found worldwide, but espe­
cially along the Mississippi, Missouri, Tennessee, and
Ohio river valleys of the United States as well as in Latin
America. H. capsulatum can be found in the intestinal
tract and guano of bats, which constitute the primary
reservoir of the organism and disseminate it geographi­
cally. H. capsulatum can also be found in high concentra­
tions in decaying avian guano, but it is not shed in the
feces of birds.
Cats are as susceptible, or slightly more susceptible,
to histoplasmosis as dogs. Affected dogs and cats can be
as young as several months of age, but most are middle
aged, and geriatric animals can also be affected.
History and Clinical Signs
Approximately 40% of cats with histoplasmosis show res­
piratory signs such as dyspnea and tachypnea, and to a
lesser extent cough and nasal discharge. Ocular signs
such as chorioretinitis and/or uveitis occur in approxi­
mately one‐quarter of cats, and around 20% of cats have
evidence of osteomyelitis. Nodular or ulcerated and
draining skin lesions, peripheral lymphadenopathy, vom­
iting, diarrhea, oral ulceration, and myelopathy have also
been described.
Dogs appear to be particularly predisposed to
­gastrointestinal tract histoplasmosis. Involvement of the
small and large intestines may result in malabsorption,
diarrhea, dramatic weight loss, melena, dyschezia,
tenesmus, and hematochezia. Profuse diarrhea may be
chronic and persist for several months. Tracheobronchial
lymphadenopathy is common and may contribute to
­
cough through airway compression. Other signs include
respiratory difficulty, icterus, vomiting, hepatomegaly,
­lymphadenomegaly, nasal discharge, ocular signs, ­polyuria
and polydipsia, lameness due to osteomyelitis, ­cutaneous
nodules, and neurologic signs such as ­seizures or paraly­
sis/paresis.
Diagnosis
As with other deep mycoses, findings on routine labora­
tory testing are typically nonspecific and suggestive of

inflammation. Dogs with acute progressive disseminated
histoplasmosis may have increased band neutrophils,
lymphopenia, monocytopenia, and thrombocytopenia.
Increased liver enzyme activities, hyperbilirubinemia,
and evidence of coagulopathies may be present in ani­
mals with hepatic involvement. In cats, plain thoracic
radiographs can reveal diffuse, linear, nodular or miliary
interstitial patterns. Alveolar, interstitial, and/or bron­
chial patterns, tracheobronchial lymphadenopathy, lung
lobe consolidation, and/or rarely pleural effusion can be
seen in dogs. Lesions in dogs can sometimes calcify.
Abdominal imaging may show hepatomegaly, spleno­
megaly, abdominal lymphadenopathy or ascites. A thick­
ened intestinal wall with architectural disruption of the
bowel wall may be identified on ultrasound examination.
Colonoscopic findings in dogs with colonic histoplasmo­
sis include irregularity, ulceration, increased granularity,
and friability of the colonic wall.
Cytologic examination of affected tissues or body ­fluids
reveals pyogranulomatous or granulomatous inflamma­
tion. H. capsulatum yeasts are usually seen extracellularly
and within mononuclear phagocytes, although they may
not be identified within chronic, fibrosing lesions. The
yeasts are 2–4 μm in diameter, oval, have a basophilic
center and are surrounded by a clear halo due to shrink­
age artifact (Figure 109.3).
Antibody assays for H. capsulatum have had poor clin­
ical sensitivity and specificity, so are not recommended
for routine diagnosis. An enzyme‐linked immunosorb­
ent assay (ELISA) for H. capsulatum antigen (MiraVista
Diagnostics, Indianapolis, IN) is widely used in human
patients for diagnosis of histoplasmosis, and as with
blastomycosis, urine is the preferred specimen for t­ esting

capsulatum organisms within the cytoplasm of a circulating
monocyte from a dog with disseminated histoplasmosis.

(sensitivity 95%). False positives occur as a result of sero­
logic cross‐reactivity in human patients with other dis­
seminated mycoses, especially blastomycosis. Antigen
levels become undetectable with successful treatment.
This assay appears to have a similar performance in cats
and dogs with histoplasmosis, although studies that
­evaluate large numbers of cats and dogs with confirmed
histoplasmosis are required to fully establish the sensi­

Therapy
In human patients, itraconazole has consistently been
more effective than fluconazole for treatment of histo­
plasmosis. Nevertheless, some animals can be cured
with fluconazole monotherapy, so if funds or patient fac­
tors do not permit itraconazole treatment, fluconazole
can be used. Amphotericin B should be used to treat
dogs or cats with severe acute pulmonary, acute dissemi­
nated, or CNS disease, after which treatment should
be continued with an azole. The decision to discontinue
treatment should be based on lesion resolution and prob­
ably serial monitoring of urine antigen titers, although
this requires further study.
Prognosis
The length of treatment and prognosis for histoplasmo­
sis depend on the severity and chronicity of disease and
the immune status of the host. At least six months of
treatment is generally required. Many animals require
treatment for 12 months or longer, and those with
chronic disease may require treatment for more than
two years.
Public Health Implications
Humans can be infected with H. capsulatum but direct
transmission from cats and dogs has not been reported.
Remains of infected animals should be cremated rather
than buried.

­Cryptococcosis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Cryptococcosis is caused by dimorphic, basidiomycet­
ous fungi that belong to the genus Cryptococcus. Cry­
ptococcus neoformans and C. gattii cause the vast
majority of infections. A filamentous form that produces
basidiospores is thought to exist in the environment.
Mammalian disease is believed to occur when basidio­
spores are inhaled, typically after an incubation period of

several months, although in some cases, reactivation of
subclinical infections may occur years after exposure. In
animal tissues, the basidiospores are thought to convert
to the yeast form, which is round to oval with a charac­
teristic, variably sized polysaccharide capsule. Within
tissues, Cryptococcus reproduces by narrow‐based bud­
ding. After infection is established within the lung or
nasal cavity, the organism can spread hematogenously to
other sites, particularly the lymph nodes, eye, skin, and
CNS. Cryptococcus has a predilection to invade the
meninges, and typically causes meningitis or menin­
goencephalitis. In animals with nasal cavity involvement,
extension of infection into the brain may also follow
osteomyelitis of the cribriform plate.
Epidemiology and Signalment
Based on molecular methods such as multilocus
sequence typing, cryptococcal strains worldwide have
been divided into eight molecular types: VNI, VNII,
VNIII, and VNIV (C. neoformans) and VGI, VGII, VGIII,
and VGIV (C. gattii). Differences in epidemiology, path­
ogenicity, clinical features, and drug susceptibility have
been associated with each molecular type. The environ­
mental niche for C. neoformans is thought to be weath­
ered bird (especially pigeon) guano, whereas C. gattii has
been associated with Eucalyptus trees in Australia and a
variety of other tree species on the west coast of North
America.
The incidence of cryptococcosis in cats is eightfold
higher than that in dogs. Siamese, Birman, and ragdoll
cats have been predisposed in Australian studies but
were not found to be at risk in the US. Similarly, German
shepherd dogs, Doberman pinschers, and Great Danes
appear to be predisposed in Australia, whereas American
cocker spaniels are predisposed in the US.
History and Clinical Signs
Cryptococcosis is often a chronic infection in cats. Upper
respiratory tract signs due to nasal cavity involvement are
common, sometimes with associated mandibular lym­
phadenopathy. Single or multifocal ulcerated or nonul­
cerated cutaneous or mucocutaneous masses may also be
present. Lower respiratory tract signs are uncommon, but
can occur as a result of pleural effusion or severe medias­
tinal lymphadenomegaly. Neurologic signs vary depend­
ing on the location of lesions in the CNS. Optic neuritis
and chorioretinitis develop in as many as one‐third of
affected cats, and almost always indicate CNS involve­
ment. Other signs include peripheral lymphadenomegaly,
lameness due to osteoarticular infection, and swollen
­digits. Rarely, involvement of the abdominal lymph nodes,
kidneys, spleen, liver, and thyroid can occur in cats.

VetBooks.ir

109 Fungal Infections

In contrast to cats, dogs often develop widespread
­dissemination with neurologic involvement. They may
also present with signs relating to gastrointestinal or
pancreatic involvement. Cryptococcal rhinosinusitis
may be subclinical in dogs or may result in sneezing and
mucopurulent nasal discharge. Cutaneous involvement
is uncommon but, as in the cat, may be a marker for dis­
seminated disease. Other clinical signs that are occasion­
ally present in dogs include peripheral lymphadenomegaly
or lameness (due to osteomyelitis or arthritis).
Diagnosis
Thoracic radiographs in dogs and cats with cryptococ­
cosis are often normal, although interstitial to alveolar
infiltrates or small nodular lesions may be present.
Occasionally, pulmonary nodules, tracheobronchial
lymphadenopathy, mediastinal masses, or pleural effu­
sion are found.
Definitive diagnosis of cryptococcosis is based on eval­
uation of representative tissue specimens or body fluids
(including cerebrospinal fluid) with cytology, culture,
and occasionally histopathology (Figure 109.4), with or
without serologic detection of cryptococcal antigen.
Latex agglutination assays for detection of cryptococ­
cal polysaccharide capsular antigen are widely used in
veterinary patients and are very (>85%) sensitive and
specific, although false‐negative and false‐positive
results can occur. ELISAs are also available. Serum anti­
gen testing provides a rapid diagnosis when organisms
cannot be visualized or cultured, and may prove advan­
tageous when CSF collection is unacceptably risky. Even
a titer as low as 1:2 can indicate cryptococcal infection.

Because false‐positive latex agglutination titers of up to
1:200 have been detected in cats, attempts to confirm
infection using other diagnostic tests are recommended
in animals that have titers <1:200. For dogs and cats sus­
pected to have cryptococcal meningoencephalomyelitis
that have negative serum antigen titers, CSF should be
submitted for cytologic examination, antigen titers, and
fungal culture.
Therapy
Some dogs and cats with cryptococcosis, especially
those with lesions restricted to the skin, can be treated
successfully with azole antifungal drug monotherapy.
Fluconazole is a reasonable initial choice, because of its
good penetration of the brain and eye. Generally, cats
improve within 1–2 weeks of starting therapy. Treatment
should be continued until there is complete lesion
­resolution and the cryptococcal antigen titer becomes
negative. This typically takes 2–12 months, although
longer periods of therapy may be required. For recovered
animals that achieve an antigen titer of 0, the titer can be
monitored every 3–6 months, so that relapse is diag­
nosed early. Some cats (especially those in California
infected with molecular type VGIII) fail to respond com­
pletely to treatment, antigen titers persist at high levels,
and relapse occurs after an initial treatment response. In
some of these cats, prognosis is guarded and treatment
with other azoles or combination therapy with ampho­
tericin B may be necessary.
For cats with CNS cryptococcosis or those that fail
to respond to azole antifungal drugs, a combination
of amphotericin B and 5‐flucytosine (250 mg PO q8h) or
amphotericin B and fluconazole is recommended. Dogs
with disseminated disease or CNS involvement should
be treated initially with amphotericin B and fluconazole,
because those treated with flucytosine often develop
cutaneous necrosis 1–2 weeks after starting therapy.
Treatment with 5‐flucytosine and amphotericin B is con­
tinued for 2–4 weeks or until azotemia develops, after
which treatment is continued with an azole. Anecdotally,
administration of terbinafine to some dogs and cats that
have failed azole or amphotericin B treatment has led to
clinical improvement.
Prognosis

Figure 109.4 Histopathology showing large numbers of
Cryptococcus organisms within the meninges of a 3‐year‐old
domestic short‐hair that died of disseminated cryptococcosis.

In studies from Australia, approximately 75% of cats with
cryptococcosis were treated successfully. In one study,
the median survival time of cats with CNS cryptococco­
sis was only 13 days (0–4050 days), but outcomes were
more favorable if cats survived at least three days after
diagnosis. The prognosis is guarded for dogs, with suc­
cess rates that range from 30% to 55%. The median survival

time for dogs with CNS cryptococcosis in North America
was seven days (0–3680 days).
Public Health Implications
Humans can develop cryptococcosis through environ­
mental exposure. Notably, it is an important infection in
people with AIDS. Direct transmission from animals to
people has not been reported, but contaminated needle‐
stick injuries may transmit the organism. Cryptococcus
grows on routine fungal laboratory media as a yeast, so is
less likely to represent a hazard to laboratory personnel
than dimorphic fungi that grow as molds.

­Coccidioidomycosis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Coccidioides spp. (Coccidioides immitis and C. posa­
dasii) are dimorphic fungi that exist in soil as chains of
barrel‐shaped arthrospores. The arthrospores are aero­
solized and inhaled by animal hosts. This may be fol­
lowed by localized pulmonary disease or dissemination
to the tracheobronchial lymph nodes and then other
anatomic sites in the face of an inadequate immune
response. Infections often follow a pattern of moist con­
ditions (required for growth of Coccidioides spp. in the
soil), a dry period, then soil disruption, such as may
occur with heavy rainfall, dust storms, or construction.
After inhalation, arthrospores are phagocytosed by
alveolar macrophages. They then enlarge into a spherule
(8–100 μm in diameter). Hundreds of endospores
develop within the spherule, which are released when
the spherule ruptures. This is associated with a pyogran­
ulomatous inflammatory response.
Epidemiology and Signalment
In the environment, Coccidioides spp. are distributed in
regions with arid soils, low elevations above sea level, and
hot summers. Infections occur primarily in the south­
western United States, Mexico, and parts of Central and
South America. In southwestern USA, highly endemic
regions include the south‐central valley of California
(“Valley Fever”) and Arizona. Latent i­nfections occur in
dogs and these can reactivate after treatment with immu­
nosuppressive drugs. Coccidioidomycosis is rare in cats.
History and Clinical Signs
Development of clinical signs often follows a subacute to
chronic course. Many dogs continue to otherwise appear
healthy, with occasional periods of inappetence. Clinical
signs of respiratory tract involvement include cough,

tachypnea, and/or exercise intolerance. Rarely, diffuse
pneumonia follows a more fulminant course, as reported
in immunocompromised humans.
A small percentage of infected dogs develop dissemi­
nated infections. Sites of dissemination often include
osteoarticular sites, the CNS, skin, peripheral lymph
nodes, eye, testes, prostate, and pericardium. Rarely,
other sites, such as abdominal organs, are affected. Dogs
with skin involvement may have ulcerated skin lesions
that drain serosanguinous fluid, or subcutaneous mass
lesions. Neurologic signs result from fungal meningoen­
cephalitis and include obtundation, blindness, nystag­
mus, ataxia, placing deficits, circling, cervical pain,
tetraparesis, and seizures. Ocular manifestations include
chorioretinitis, uveitis, optic neuritis, and endophthal­
mitis. Pericarditis may lead to signs of right‐sided cardiac
failure, with development of ascites and pleural effusion.
Diagnosis
Thoracic radiographs in dogs with disseminated coc­
cidioidomycosis are often unremarkable. The most
common radiographic finding in dogs with pulmonary
coccidioidomycosis is tracheobronchial lymphadeno­
megaly. Although this may be the only finding, most
dogs also have mild to moderate interstitial infiltrates.
Nodular interstitial, interstitial‐alveolar, bronchointer­
stitial infiltrates, and/or sternal lymphadenomegaly
may also be present. Dogs with pericarditis may have
cardiomegaly and pleural effusion, with hepatomegaly
and decreased abdominal detail. Echocardiography in
these dogs may reveal thickening and mass lesions of
the ­pericardium, pericardial and pleural effusion, and
­cardiac tamponade.
A diagnosis of coccidioidomycosis is typically con­
firmed using serology for antibodies to Coccidioides spp.,
because of the low sensitivity of cytology and the fact
that culture is hazardous to laboratory personnel and
can have a long turnaround time. Cytologic examination
of specimens from affected tissues or body fluids reveals
granulomatous or pyogranulomatous inflammation.
Occasionally, spherules can be identified as round, baso­
philic, double‐walled, crinkled structures (8–70 μm in
diameter) (Figure 109.5). Sometimes endospores (2–5 μm
in diameter) can be seen in association with ruptured
spherules.
Most diagnostic laboratories detect antibodies to
Coccidioides using gel immunodiffusion. False‐negative
serologic test results are rare in dogs with coccidioido­
mycosis. Antibody titers typically range from 1:2 to
1:256. Dogs with active infection may have titers as
low as 1:2, and healthy dogs in hyperendemic areas
in Arizona have had titers as high as 1:16. As a result,
positive titers of 1:16 or lower should always be
­interpreted in light of clinicopathologic abnormalities

109 Fungal Infections

VetBooks.ir

from inhalation of the mycelial form, which can develop
in tissues if they are stored for long periods after death of
an infected animal. Physicians should be notified imme­
diately in the case of inoculation or possible inhalation of
a mycelial form. Necropsies should be performed with
appropriate precautions and take place soon after death
to prevent mycelial form growth. Bodies of infected
­animals should not be buried but should be cremated
as soon as possible. Laboratories should be warned if
coccidioidomycosis is suspected.

­Aspergillosis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Figure 109.5 Cytology of a tracheal wash specimen showing a
Coccidioides spherule surrounded by pyogranulomatous
inflammation.

and, in hyperendemic areas, other diagnostic tests (such
as cytology, histopathology or culture) should also be
used to confirm the diagnosis.
Therapy
Dogs with pulmonary coccidioidomycosis often respond
well to azole monotherapy with fluconazole or itracona­
zole. Treatment with amphotericin B is recommended
either alone or in combination with an azole antifungal
for dogs with refractory disease or those with severe
­clinical signs. Successful treatment of Coccidioides peri­
carditis has been reported after subtotal pericardiectomy
and epicardial excision in conjunction with antifungal
drug therapy. Referral to a specialist surgeon with expe­
rience in the technique is strongly recommended.
Prognosis
The prognosis for resolution for coccidioidomycosis
depends on the severity of infection and the extent of
dissemination. The duration of treatment ranges from
six months (localized pulmonary coccidioidomycosis) to
many years, and in some cases, life‐long treatment is
needed. IgG antibody titers decrease with successful
treatment, which in general should be continued until
lesions resolve and the titer is 1:2 or lower.
Public Health Implications
Coccidioidomycosis is an important and serious
­infection in people that is generally acquired from envi­
ronmental exposure. Disease and death may occur from
direct inoculation from needle‐stick injuries and also

Aspergillus are hyaline molds, the conidia of which are
found commonly in soil, water, air, and decaying vegeta­
tion. Aspergillus spores are inhaled, and in the absence of
adequate immune defenses, enlarge and germinate to
form hyphae, subsequently leading to a variety of nonin­
vasive to invasive disorders that include keratomycosis,
fungal otitis externa, sinonasal aspergillosis (SNA),
sinoorbital aspergillosis, bronchopulmonary and dissem­
inated aspergillosis. Keratomycosis, otitis externa, feline
sinoorbital aspergillosis, and bronchopulmonary asper­
gillosis in dogs are relatively rare conditions, and beyond
the scope of this chapter. A variety of other molds less
commonly cause infections in dogs and cats, including
nonpigmented molds such as Penicillium, Paecilomyces,
Pseudallescheria, and Geotrichum (hyalohyphomycoses);
pigmented molds such as Alternaria, Exophiala, and
Cladophialophera (phaeohyphomycoses); and zygomy­
cetes such as Basidiobolus, Conidiobolus, and Mucor. The
reader is referred elsewhere for detailed discussions of
these pathogens.
Sinonasal aspergillosis is a subacute to chronic disease
of the nasal cavity and sinuses that is most often caused
by organisms that belong to the A. fumigatus complex.
In most cases, affected dogs have no evidence of immune
compromise, but sometimes SNA occurs as a result of
implantation of a foreign body or other preexisting nasal
disease, such as nasal neoplasia. SNA is a noninvasive
disease, and the fungus does not extend beyond the
mucosal epithelium. Production of toxins by the fungus
and a profound host inflammatory response are thought
to lead to extensive turbinate and bony destruction.
Disseminated (invasive) aspergillosis in dogs is most
often caused by A. terreus or A. deflectus, although other
Aspergillus species have also been isolated.
Epidemiology and Signalment
Sinonasal aspergillosis in dogs is most common in large,
nonbrachycephalic breeds. SNA uncommonly occurs in

995

VetBooks.ir

996

Section 9 Infectious Disease

cats, but diabetes mellitus has been identified in some
affected cats.
Disseminated aspergillosis in dogs likely occurs as a
result of an uncharacterized genetic immunodeficiency,
because young adult female German shepherds are
strongly predisposed, and immunosuppressive drug
treatment is rarely present in the history of affected dogs.
Disseminated aspergillosis is extremely rare in cats.
History and Clinical Signs
Clinical signs of SNA in dogs and cats consist of sneez­
ing, serous to mucopurulent nasal discharge, depigmen­
tation of the nasal planum (Figure 109.6), and, less
commonly, epistaxis.
Nasal pain may be manifest in dogs as pawing at the
face or withdrawal. Nasal airflow is usually normal or
increased. Serous ocular discharge may occur as a result
of destruction of the bones of the orbit. Rarely, palpation
of the nasal bones or the hard palate reveals defects.
Osteolysis of the cribriform plate occasionally leads to
meningitis with neurologic signs such as obtundation or
seizures.
Sites often involved in dogs with disseminated asper­
gillosis include the vertebral endplates and discs, renal
pelvis, long bones, and lymph nodes. However, any organ
may be affected, including the spleen, liver, heart, cardiac
valves, pancreas, eyes, lungs, brain, meninges, small
intestine, skin, spinal cord, thyroid, adrenal glands, pros­
tate, and trachea. The most frequent clinical signs are
lethargy, inappetence, pain, lameness, and ataxia and
paresis secondary to discospondylitis.
Diagnosis
Imaging of the nasal cavity of dogs with SNA using plain
radiography (open mouth view), computed tomography

Figure 109.6 Nasal depigmentation and ulceration in a dog with
sinonasal aspergillosis.

(CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can reveal
loss of turbinates, defects in the nasal septum, and/or
increased soft tissue opacity within the nasal cavity. CT
and MRI have increased sensitivity over plain radiogra­
phy, and are the preferred imaging modalities. Osteolysis
of the cribriform plate, orbit, and frontal bones may be
identified using advanced imaging. In some animals,
lesions are limited to the frontal sinus. Visualization of
fungal plaques by rhinoscopy and sinuscopy confirms
the diagnosis. Trephination or surgical exploration of the
frontal sinuses may be necessary to visualize (and treat)
this region. Cytologic examination of mucosal swabs,
brush specimens of the nasal cavity, or nasal biopsies can
reveal hyphae, which are septate and branch at 45°
angles, and sometimes also conidia. Culture of Aspergillus
from nasal biopsies supports the diagnosis, although
negative culture results do not rule out SNA.
Disseminated aspergillosis may be suspected on the
basis of signalment and clinical findings. In some cases,
hyphae are visualized in tissue aspirates or urine sedi­
ment from affected dogs. Growth of a typical Aspergillus
species (most commonly A. terreus or A. deflectus) from
a normally sterile site confirms the diagnosis.
Both serum antibody and antigen assays have been
evaluated for diagnosis of SNA and disseminated asper­
gillosis in dogs. Assays that detect serum antibodies to
Aspergillus include ELISA and gel immunodiffusion (ID)
assays. Different antibody assays vary in their sensitivity
and specificity for diagnosis of SNA but in general, posi­
tive results suggest a diagnosis of SNA, but negative
results do not rule out SNA. Dogs with disseminated
aspergillosis frequently test negative, and so serum
­antibody testing is not recommended for diagnosis of
this disease.
The sensitivity and specificity of serum Aspergillus
galactomannan antigen ELISA (Platelia®) for diagnosis of
SNA are low, and its use is not recommended for this
condition. However, serum or urine antigen testing has
high sensitivity for diagnosis of disseminated aspergillo­
sis in dogs, and a high specificity when using a cut‐off
galactomannan index of 1.5. High‐level false positives
(>1.5) appear to occur only in dogs with other fungal
infections, especially those caused by Penicillium or
Paecilomyces, and dogs treated with Plasmalyte® fluid
therapy.
In summary, a strong positive assay result in a dog with
clinical abnormalities consistent with disseminated
aspergillosis and no history of Plasmalyte administration
supports a diagnosis of a mold infection, but fungal cul­
ture is required to confirm that Aspergillus is the causa­
tive agent. A negative result in a dog with disseminated
disease suggests that Aspergillus is not the cause, but
does not rule out the possibility of infection by another
fungal species.

109 Fungal Infections

Therapy
Treatment of SNA requires thorough mechanical
debridement of plaques with endoscopic biopsy forceps
under anesthesia, followed by topical antifungal drug
therapy. Frontal sinus trephination and curettage or
open surgical debridement of the frontal sinus may be
required. Provided the cribriform plate is intact, debride­
ment is followed by lavage with 0.9% saline and suction,
followed by topical therapy with clotrimazole or enilcon­
azole. Several protocols for topical antifungal drug
administration have been described. The reader is
referred elsewhere for description of these protocols.
Debridement and a second treatment are then per­
formed one month later; sometimes, a third treatment
may be necessary. Additional systemic treatment with
antifungal drugs could also be considered, but it is not
clear whether this improves outcome. Systemic azole
antifungal drug therapy could be considered as an alter­
native to topical therapy in dogs with cribriform plate
destruction, when topical treatment has the potential to
lead to death or life‐threatening neurologic signs.
Canine disseminated aspergillosis is treated with itra­
conazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, and/or ampho­
tericin B. Terbinafine has been used in addition to azole
therapy with limited success. At best, treatment leads to
remission for months to more than a year, but usually
antigen titers remain high and eventually relapse occurs,
leading to euthanasia or death. Although expensive, vori­
conazole is a treatment of choice in humans with inva­
sive aspergillosis, and has led to remissions of many
months’ duration in some dogs. A. terreus is resistant in
vitro to amphotericin B, but clinical improvement still
occurs after treatment of some dogs with lipid com­
plexed amphotericin B. Caspofungin is also used to treat
invasive aspergillosis in humans, but expense and the
need for daily intravenous administration have limited
its use in dogs.
Prognosis
Success rates for treatment of SNA have varied from less
than 30% to 100%. Low success rates reflect extensive
disease that is often present at diagnosis, together with
irreversible turbinate loss. Dogs with turbinate loss are
predisposed to recurrent bacterial infections of the
nasal cavity, which lead to persistent nasal discharge
and sneezing. Therefore, attempts should be made to
reach a diagnosis as early as possible when SNA is on
the differential diagnosis list. Treatment with antibacte­
rial drugs without pursuing a diagnosis only leads to
disease progression, and is inappropriate because pri­
mary bacterial infections of the nasal cavity are rare in
adult dogs.

Many dogs with disseminated aspergillosis have
advanced disease at diagnosis, sometimes with respira­
tory distress, pathologic fractures, vertebral subluxa­
tions, and cord compression. The prognosis for these
dogs is poor.
Public Health Implications
Aspergillosis occurs in people who have significant
immunosuppressive disorders, such as transplant recipi­
ents, and is usually due to Aspergillus fumigatus complex
organisms. Infections are acquired from the environ­
ment, and transmission from dogs and cats has not been
described.

­Candidiasis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Candida species are yeasts that belong to the normal
gastrointestinal, urogenital, and cutaneous flora but can
invade tissues and cause disease as a result of disruption
of normal host defenses. Candida species can also be
isolated from soil, inanimate objects, and hospital
­environments. The yeasts are small (3–6 μm), ovoid and
reproduce by budding. Budding results in the formation
of new yeast cells, pseudohyphae (chains of elongated
yeast cells), and true septate hyphae.
Disease syndromes caused by Candida spp. that
occur in dogs and cats include keratitis, cutaneous or
mucocutaneous candidiasis, otitis, urinary tract infec­
tions (UTIs), gastrointestinal candidiasis, peritonitis,
and disseminated infections. The most commonly iso­
lated species is Candida albicans, and only C. albicans
appears to cause disseminated disease in dogs and cats.
Epidemiology and Signalment
Predisposing factors in dogs or cats with local or dissem­
inated candidiasis have included diabetes mellitus, treat­
ment with immunosuppressive drugs or broad‐spectrum
antibacterial drugs, a history of gastrointestinal surgery,
parvoviral infections, and/or underlying malignancy.
Disseminated candidiasis has also been described in
apparently immunocompetent animals, which may
reflect an underlying genetic immunodeficiency.
Urethrostomy or cystostomy tube placement may be in
the history of some animals with Candida UTIs.
History and Clinical Signs
Lower urinary tract candidiasis may be subclinical or asso­
ciated with signs of lower urinary tract disease. Cutaneous
candidiasis may manifest as erythema, ­alopecia, erosions,

997

VetBooks.ir

998

Section 9 Infectious Disease

and crusting, often where disruption of cutaneous or
mucocutaneous regions has occurred (such as a previ­
ous surgical site or around a feeding tube or cystotomy
stoma). Candida peritonitis can follow intestinal sur­
gery, treatment with broad‐spectrum antibacterial
drugs, and subsequent enterotomy site dehiscence.
Mixed infections with Candida and intestinal flora may
develop. Affected dogs are febrile, have abdominal pain,
and may have other gastrointestinal signs such as vom­
iting and diarrhea.
Dogs with disseminated candidiasis frequently develop
rapidly progressive clinical signs that include fever, inap­
petence, weight loss, and other clinical signs that reflect
the specific organs involved. The latter can include the
pancreas, liver, mesentery, spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs,
lymph nodes, and less often the bone, intestinal tract,
eyes, meninges, thyroid, and/or prostate gland. Ocular
signs include keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis, and
endophthalmitis. Thromboembolic disease may compli­
cate disseminated infections.
Diagnosis
Definitive diagnosis of candidiasis requires visualization
of Candida blastospores, pseudohyphae, and true
hyphae within lesions by cytologic or histopathologic
examination, as well as confirmation of its identity using
fungal culture. Because Candida can be isolated from
the skin and mucous membranes of healthy dogs and
cats, infection must be confirmed with cytology or histo­
pathology when Candida is isolated from these sites.
A diagnosis of disseminated candidiasis should be
­considered whenever Candida is isolated from the eye,
skin, or urinary tract of an animal that develops systemic
illness, and aggressive treatment instituted without delay.
Isolation of Candida allows antifungal susceptibility
testing. Some isolates (especially C. glabrata and C. krusei)
are resistant to multiple antifungal drugs.
Therapy
Treatment of candidiasis should involve management of
underlying immunosuppressive disorders and specific
antifungal drug treatment. Systemic antibacterial drugs
should be discontinued if not clearly indicated, or the
spectrum of activity should be narrowed. Cutaneous and
corneal infections are usually treated with a combination
of topical antiseptics or antifungal medications and sys­
temic antifungal drugs until lesions resolve. Dogs and
cats with Candida UTIs should initially be treated with
fluconazole, which concentrates in urine. Intravesicular
treatment with 1% clotrimazole under anesthesia may
be necessary in animals that fail to respond to treat­
ment. Intravesicular treatment is continued weekly until

Candida can no longer be isolated from the urine.
Typically 1–4 treatments, spaced one week apart, are
required.
Systemic candidiasis is treated aggressively with
­systemic antifungal drugs, especially fluconazole, and
supportive care. One dog with Candida peritonitis was
treated successfully with surgical lavage of the abdo­
men, abdominal drain placement, and intravenous
­fluconazole. Antifungal drugs other than fluconazole
with activity against Candida include amphotericin B
and caspofungin, both of which must be administered
parenterally.
Prognosis
The prognosis for successful resolution of local Candida
infections is good, but successful treatment of systemic
candidiasis in dogs or cats is rarely described.
Public Health Implications
Human infections with Candida species result primarily
from invasion by normal flora.

­Sporotrichosis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Sporothrix species are dimorphic, saprophytic fungi that
cause disease that often results from cutaneous or
subcutaneous inoculation of the organism through a
­
puncture wound, but can also follow inhalation of the
fungus. Direct contact with cats that have sporotricho­
sis, without an apparent break in the skin, can also result
in transmission.
Sporothrix species prefer moist soil that is rich in
decaying vegetation. The fungus is distributed world­
wide in tropical and temperate zones, but is most preva­
lent in tropical or subtropical regions of the Americas.
The S. schenckii species complex includes multiple
Sporothrix species, the epidemiology of which is still
incompletely understood.
Epidemiology and Signalment
Cats are more susceptible to sporotrichosis than dogs
and are thought to facilitate spread of organisms in the
environment. Contaminated claw or bite wounds are
thought to be important modes of transmission. Male
cats have been overrepresented. Sporotrichosis in dogs is
uncommon, but tends to occur in hunting breeds.
Introduction of the organism with plant foreign bodies
may lead to infection in some dogs.

VetBooks.ir

109 Fungal Infections

History and Clinical Signs

Therapy

In dogs and cats, Sporothrix spp. most often cause focal
or multifocal cutaneous lesions. These are crusted,
thickened or nodular lesions that often ulcerate or drain
serosanguinous fluid. Most cats have multiple cutaneous
lesions. These lesions may develop as a result of autoin­
oculation during grooming or they may be a manifesta­
tion of a disseminated infection.
Transmission by inhalation is thought to occur in some
cats that develop pulmonary and nasal cavity disease.
Respiratory signs include sneezing, cough, tachypnea,
increased respiratory effort, stertor, and/or nasal dis­
charge. Cats also can develop generalized disease, with
involvement of the lungs, liver, spleen, kidneys, lymph
nodes, and/or testicles. Clinical signs of systemic involve­
ment include fever, generalized lymphadenomegaly,
anorexia, vomiting, and weight loss. Osteoarticular
­sporotrichosis has rarely been described in dogs.

The treatment of choice for most dogs and cats with
sporotrichosis is itraconazole. Alternative antifungal
drugs for refractory disease include supersaturated
potassium or sodium iodide, terbinafine, or ampho­
tericin B. Unfortunately, potassium iodide formulations
often lead to adverse gastrointestinal signs in cats.
Localized hyperthermia has been used as adjunct ther­
apy to treat fixed cutaneous lesions, because most strains
of Sporothrix survive poorly at high temperatures. In this
case, a thermal bag at a temperature of 40–42 °C is
applied at least twice daily to lesions for 15 minutes.

Diagnosis
Cytologic examination or histopathology of affected tis­
sues from cats reveals pyogranulomatous inflammation
with large numbers of round to cigar‐shaped yeasts,
which can be found intracellularly within neutrophils
or macrophages and extracellularly (Figure 109.7).
The yeasts are 4–6 μm in diameter and typically exhibit a
single bud with a narrow base.
Dogs tend to have very low numbers of organisms in
skin lesions, which may not be readily detected. Definitive
diagnosis of sporotrichosis can be made by fungal ­culture
of aspirates or biopsies from lesions. Use of molecular
assays to identify Sporothrix could also be considered.

Prognosis
In general, the prognosis for cure of sporotrichosis is
good. Treatment durations of at least 4–6 months are
generally required, but some cats require more than a
year of treatment. Treatment should be continued for a
month after complete resolution of lesions.
Public Health Implications
Inoculation from cat scratches, bites or direct contact
with infected cats are important means by which people
acquire sporotrichosis. Sporotrichosis should be consid­
ered as a differential diagnosis for any cat with a draining
cutaneous lesion, and such cats should be handled with
gloves and hands washed after contact. Owners of
infected animals should minimize contact, and if contact
is necessary, it should be recommended that they wear
gloves and wash their hands immediately after handling
the animal. Owners should also be warned of the risk of
exposure to the organism in the environment. Needle‐
stick injuries should be avoided and laboratory person­
nel warned of suspect cases.

­Miscellaneous Fungus‐Like Infections
(Pythiosis and Rhinosporidiosis)
Etiology/Pathophysiology

Figure 109.7 Cytology of an impression smear of a skin lesion
from a cat with cutaneous sporotrichosis. Large numbers of
intracellular pleomorphic yeasts are present.

A variety of fungus‐like organisms that reside in
aquatic environments and are thought to invade dam­
aged host tissues can cause disease in dogs and cats.
These include Pythium insidiosum, Lagenidium spp.
and Rhinosporidium seeberi. Pythium insidiosum
and Lagenidium are oomycetes (water molds), whereas
R. seeberi is an aquatic protistan parasite (class Meso­
mycetozoea) that is taxonomically located between
­animals and fungi. Pythium insidiosum causes severe,
progressive gastrointestinal or cutaneous disease in dogs

999

VetBooks.ir

1000

Section 9 Infectious Disease

and rarely cats that is often fatal. In the US, pythiosis
most often occurs in the Gulf Coast states but has also
been recognized in other parts of the USA, including
California and Arizona. Lagenidium is found primarily
in the southern United States and causes ulcerative
cutaneous lesions or systemic lymphadenopathy in dogs.
Rhinosporidium seeberi is most often found in warm,
wet environments such as the southeastern and south‐­
central USA, where it causes polypoid masses in the
­rostral nasal cavity of dogs and rarely cats.
Epidemiology and Signalment
Pythiosis, lagenidiosis, and rhinosporidiosis most
­commonly occur in young, large‐breed dogs that are
apparently immunocompetent.
History and Clinical Signs
Gastrointestinal pythiosis in dogs is characterized by
severe, focal intestinal wall thickening, often with mes­
enteric lymphadenopathy. Clinical signs include weight
loss, anorexia, vomiting, diarrhea, and sometimes hema­
tochezia. Cutaneous pythiosis in dogs occurs most often
at the base of the tail, on the extremities, or the peri­
neum, and is characterized by ulcerated mass lesions
with draining tracts. Generally, gastrointestinal and
cutaneous pythiosis do not occur concurrently.
Dogs with lagenidiosis are typically evaluated for cuta­
neous lesions that resemble those of cutaneous pythio­
sis. Local lymphadenopathy occurs in some dogs, and
may occur in the absence of obvious cutaneous lesions.
Dogs with lagenidiosis may also have intrathoracic or
intraabdominal lesions, which may involve the great ves­
sels, tracheobronchial, sublumbar and/or inguinal lymph
nodes, lung or cranial mediastinum.
In dogs and cats, infection by R. seeberi leads to forma­
tion of pedunculate to sessile masses within the rostral
third of the nasal cavity. The polyps range in size from a
few millimeters to several centimeters. Clinical signs
consist of subacute to chronic progressive sneezing with
or without epistaxis, snuffling, and sometimes a serous,
mucoid or serosanguinous unilateral nasal discharge.

Cytologic examination of smears, brushings or biopsies
of R. seeberi polyps reveals pyogranulomatous inflamma­
tion with numerous R. seeberi endospores. Histopathology
reveals abundant sporangia in various stages of develop­
ment (Figure 109.8).
Therapy and Prognosis
Aggressive surgical resection is the treatment of choice
for these infections. A combination of high‐dose itracon­
azole (10 mg/kg PO q24h) and terbinafine (5–10 mg/kg
PO q24h) should be used to treat dogs with nonresecta­
ble pythiosis or lagenidiosis, or when there is concern
that not all margins have been cleared of disease. Dogs
with nonresectable gastrointestinal pythiosis may also
benefit from treatment with antiinflammatory doses of
glucocorticoids. Prognosis is guarded to poor, but some
dogs can be cured with aggressive therapy. To monitor
for recurrence, ELISA serology can be performed at sur­
gery and 2–3 months later. If serum antibody levels drop
by more than 50% within three months, medical therapy
can usually be discontinued.
Because Rhinosporidium polyps are often rostrally
located, surgical excisions can often be extended caudally
from the nares in order to remove the polyps. Many dogs
have no recurrence of clinical signs thereafter, but some
experience disease recurrence within months of surgery.
Public Health Implications
Human infections with P. insidiosum are rare and are
acquired from the environment. However, routine pre­
cautions when handling infected tissues or exudate
should be followed.

Diagnosis
Diagnosis of pythiosis, lagenidiosis, and rhinosporidiosis
is often initially based on the results of cytology or histo­
pathology, which reveals broad, poorly septate hyphae
that resemble zygomycete hyphae. Culture and/or PCR
and sequencing can be used to distinguish between these
organisms. Serologic assays that detect antibody are also
available to assist diagnosis, but these do not discrimi­
nate between pythiosis and lagenidiosis.

Protozoal and Protozoa‐Like Infections
Gad Baneth, DVM, PhD, DECVCP1 and Laia Solano‐Gallego, DVM, PhD, DECVCP2
1
2

School of Veterinary Medicine, Hebrew University, Rehovot, Israel
Facultat de Veterinaria, Universitat Autonoma de Barcelona, Barcelona, Spain

Parasites are responsible for some of the most important
and widespread diseases of domestic dogs and cats.
Some of these parasitic infections are also zoonotic and
can infect humans. A thorough understanding of the
pathogenesis and epidemiology of these parasitic diseases is required in order to treat infected pets and prevent the spread of disease efficiently. This chapter focuses
on important protozoal diseases in dogs and cats with
emphasis on etiology, pathophysiology, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention.

­Toxoplasmosis
Etiology and Pathophysiology
Toxoplasma gondii is a tissue coccidian protozoon with a
sexual life cycle in the intestine of felids, the definitive
host, and an asexual phase in intermediate hosts. The
intermediate hosts of T. gondii include all warm‐blooded
vertebrates including humans. Cats and intermediate
hosts can be infected by bradyzoites in meat or by sporulated T. gondii oocysts from cat feces. Cats shed T. gondii
oocysts in their feces within 3–10 days after infection by
bradyzoites from tissue cysts and excretion continues for
approximately 7–21 days (median eight days) with massive shedding which can reach hundreds of millions of
oocysts per cat during the shedding period. After that
initial period, risk of further oocyst shedding is limited.
Oocysts in cat feces undergo sporulation in the environment and develop sporocysts containing infective
sporozoites within 1–5 days in appropriate humidity,
temperature, and oxygenation conditions [1].
After oral infection, T. gondii sporozoites release from
the oocysts and can invade the gut, multiply as tachyzoites, disseminate systemically and localize in internal
organs, the nervous system, and muscle tissues. In most

cases, infection is subclinical and parasites are eventually
encysted as tachyzoites in tissues, but severe and fatal
disease can occur due to acute infection or reactivation
of parasites in tissue cysts. In addition, in some host species and in humans, infection can cross the placenta and
infect embryos intrauterinely.
Several T. gondii genotype strains have been described
with variable virulence and host predilection. These
include the more common genotypes I, II, and III described
in North America and Europe as well as ­several atypical
genotypes [2].
Epidemiology
Exposure to T. gondii in cat populations is widespread and
positive serology may be detected in up to 74% of cats in
domestic feline populations worldwide. Dogs have also
been reported to have high exposure to T. gondii with
seroprevalence rates ranging from 30% to 64% in different
countries and populations. Most T. gondii infections are
subclinical and hosts may remain chronically infected
without developing clinical disease. Cats are often infected
by preying on infected rodents and it has been shown that
T. gondii infection can alter rodent behavior and make
them less alarmed, consequently increasing their likelihood of falling prey to domestic cats. Toxoplasmosis is
one of the most common zoonotic infections in humans
and is responsible for human ­abortions, birth defects,
encephalitis, and generalized disease [1,3].
Signalment
Cats and dogs of any age or gender can be affected.
Young and immunosuppressed animals tend to develop
more severe disease. Congenital infection is usually associated with more severe disease than infection of adult
cats, often affecting the liver and respiratory tract.

History and Clinical Signs
Clinical signs in cats are rarely related to the gastrointestinal stage of T. gondii development which is usually subclinical. Cats affected by systemic infection may show a
variety of clinical signs including fever, anorexia, abdominal pain, respiratory distress, ocular inflammation, lethargy, and central nervous system disorders. These are
associated with tachyzoite dissemination and their cytotoxicity with generation of local and systemic inflammation. Acute disease in dogs may be accompanied by
neuromuscular, central nervous system (CNS), respiratory, gastrointestinal, hepatic, and more rarely ocular
manifestations. Myositis and myocarditis are also prevalent in canine toxoplasmosis. Disease in both cats and
dogs may result from new infection or from reactivation
of latent infections by immune suppression such as
cyclosporin treatment, distemper infection in dogs or
feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV) in cats [4].
Diagnosis
Cats and dogs with acute systemic toxoplasmosis may
develop nonregenerative anemia, leukopenia with lymphopenia, or neutrophilic leukocytosis, monocytosis,
and eosinophilia. Serum biochemistry abnormalities
during acute toxoplasmosis may include hypoproteinemia with hypoalbuminemia. Increased activities of alanine aminotransferase (ALT), creatinine kinase (CK),
and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) are found in animals with hepatic or muscle necrosis.
Excretion of oocysts by cats during the limited shedding period can be detected by fecal examination or polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Oocysts are relatively
small (10 μM) and can be concentrated by fecal flotation

with centrifugation using sugar solutions such as Sheather’s
sugar solution. Hammondia hammondi and Besnoitia
spp. produce oocysts which are morphologically indistinguishable from T. gondii occysts in cat feces.
Diagnosis of clinically ill cats and dogs is based on
compatible clinical signs and laboratory abnormalities
and by the detection of specific serum antibodies, demonstration of parasite DNA by PCR, or visualization of
tachyzoites by cytology in clinical samples. T. gondii tachyzoites may be detected by cytology during acute toxoplasmosis in peritoneal and ascitic fluids, and more rarely
in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), blood and bronchoalveolar
lavage washings or other tissues. PCR performed on CSF,
aqueous humor, or any other body fluid or internal organ
tissue is confirmative of infection with T. gondii.
Serology is carried out by the enzyme‐linked immunoabsorbent assay (ELISA), immunofluorescence assay
(IFA) (Figure 110.1), agglutination assays, and immunochromatographic kits.
Subclinically infected animals may display antibody
levels, and therefore positive serologic results may only
indicate previous infection, which is not necessarily
acute. The demonstration of increased IgG levels by at
least fourfold in paired sera taken at least two weeks
apart or high IgM levels suggests active acute infection,
although this is often not observed. Immunoblotting and
ELISA assays have been developed for the measurement
of specific T. gondii IgM, IgG, and IgA antibody classes in
an effort to discern the kinetic pattern of antibody formation in feline infection.
About 80% of healthy cats experimentally infected with
T. gondii develop detectable specific IgM antibodies
within 2–4 weeks post infection and most become IgM
seronegative by 16 weeks. However, some cats, particularly those with FIV or ocular toxoplasmosis, may have

Figure 110.1 A positive indirect fluorescent
antigen test serologic response to Toxoplasma
gondii antigen. Source: Courtesy of Dr Monica
Leszkowicz Mazuz, Kimron Veterinary Institute,
Israel.

VetBooks.ir

110 Protozoal and Protozoa‐Like Infections

persistent IgM levels. Since some cats never develop a
detectable IgM response and others have persistent IgM
antibodies, it is not possible to accurately use IgM serology to predict recent infection, although a positive antibody titer can be suggestive of it. Furthermore, T.
gondii‐specific IgG can be detected by serum ELISA in
healthy cats from 3–4 weeks after experimental infection.
By this time, oocyst shedding has usually been completed
and therefore IgG seropositive cats are usually considered
of low risk to public health. However, T. gondii‐IgG antibodies usually persist in the sera of infected cats for years
or even for their lifetime due to the persistence of tissue
infection.
In addition, anti‐T. gondii antibodies can be measured in
the CSF and aqueous humor to demonstrate local production of antibodies as an indication of organ infection. This
local antibody production can be compared to the serum
antibody concentration using an antibody coefficient to
differentiate whether local production of antibodies is present or if antibodies have diffused from the circulation.
Therapy
Clindamycin is the current treatment of choice in dogs
and cats with clinical toxoplasmosis. It is administered at
10–20 mg/kg PO q12h for at least two weeks to dogs
and at 12.5 mg/kg PO q12h for 2–4 weeks to cats.
Azithromycin at 10 mg/kg PO q24h for four weeks is an
additional treatment choice for cats and trimethoprim‐
sulfonamide at 15 mg/kg PO q12h for 2–4 weeks is an
alternative treatment for animals with intolerance to
clindamycin. Uveitis due to toxoplasmosis is treated with
1% prednisolone acetate ophthalmic drops.
No vaccine is currently available commercially for the
prevention of T. gondii infection in cats and dogs, or the
prevention of oocyst shedding in cats. Avoiding exposure of cats and dogs to T. gondii infection includes
prevention of hunting and feeding of raw or undercooked meat. Cat feces should be discarded properly
every day to prevent exposure to sporulated oocysts.
Prognosis
Acute toxoplasmosis often starts improving 24–48 hours
after initiation of clindamycin treatment. Ocular and
CNS infections tend to respond more slowly and disease
in immunocompromised patients usually has a poorer
prognosis.

­Neosporosis
Etiology and Pathophysiology
Neospora caninum is a coccidian parasite which is an
important cause of abortion in livestock worldwide and
can also cause neurologic disease in dogs. Neospora caninum

can infect several domestic animal species including
dogs, cattle, sheep, goats, horses, and chickens, and wild
animal species including deer, rodents, rabbits, coyotes,
wolves, foxes, and birds. Dogs, wolves, coyotes, and foxes
are the definitive hosts of N. caninum [5].
The sexually reproductive stage of the parasite’s life cycle
occurs in the intestine of a canine definitive host which
passes unsporulated oocysts in the feces. Infective oocysts
are ingested by an intermediate host, such as cattle, following sporulation in the environment which happens within
24 hours. Tachyzoites of N. caninum develop in the infected
intermediate host during acute infection followed by the
development of bradyzoites walled off in tissue cysts as
infection becomes chronic. Dogs acquire the infection
mainly by ingesting parasite cysts from ­tissues of infected
intermediate hosts, in particular cattle, and shed oocysts
approximately five days after bradyzoite ingestion. In addition, transplacental transmission during pregnancy has
been shown to occur in dogs, sheep, and cattle.
Epidemiology
The prevalence of N. caninum varies in different dog
populations and has been reported to be associated with
the dog’s environment and lifestyle. Free‐roaming dogs
living in rural areas are more likely to be seropositive
than urban dogs with less access to infected prey, bovine
placentas, aborted fetuses or other potentially infected
tissues. High seroprevalence rates of above 50% have
been reported in beef farm dogs in South America,
whereas populations of healthy dogs in Europe and the
USA typically have seroprevalence rates below 15%.
Signalment
Dogs of any age or gender can be affected by N. caninum
but disease is more common in dogs under the age of
1 year.
History and Clinical Signs
The clinical manifestations of canine neosporosis are due
to inflammation and necrosis caused by cellular destruction induced by tachyzoites. As for T. gondii, disease by N.
caninum can be caused by new infection, or by reactivation of parasites in cysts during host stress or immune
compromise. Immune‐suppressive treatment for other
disease by cyclosporin, steroids or azathioprine may activate latent N. caninum infection. Neospora caninum may
replicate in the lower respiratory system, skin, liver, and
nervous system. Disease is mostly associated with the
neuromuscular predilection of this parasite. Neurologic
disease is especially severe in congenitally infected puppies and may be apparent shortly after birth or delayed
and manifested months after birth, usually before the age

Therapy
