­History and Clinical Signs
Dogs and cats with glomerular disease can present with
a variety of clinical signs, determined by the severity of
proteinuria or renal disease and the presence or absence
of any systemic disorders. They may be asymptomatic,
have nonspecific signs (e.g., anorexia, weight loss, lethargy)
or have signs of more advanced renal disease (e.g., polyuria, polydipsia, vomiting, diarrhea, halitosis). Animals
with severe urinary protein loss may develop nephrotic
syndrome and have evidence of fluid retention (e.g.,
abdominal enlargement consistent with ascites, peripheral edema). Animals also may develop clinical signs
from thromboembolism (e.g., dyspnea, loss of limb function), or hypertension (e.g., acute blindness, or recent
onset of neurologic signs or cardiac murmur). When glomerular disease is suspected, the history should include
questions about the environment, possible exposure to
infectious diseases as well as relevant drug or dietary
exposure.
Complete physical examinations should be performed
on dogs and cats with suspected glomerular disease,
including body condition score, retinal and rectal examinations. Physical examination is often unremarkable.
Poor body condition or poor hair coat may be nonspecific evidence of systemic disease. Animals with advanced
renal disease may have oral ulcerations, pale mucous
membranes, or dehydration. Subcutaneous edema or

ascites, or both, are sometimes noted and consistent
with nephrotic syndrome. Occasionally, there is physical
evidence of thromboembolic disease, such as dyspnea or
a decreased or absent peripheral pulse. Evidence of a
predisposing inflammatory, infectious, or neoplastic
process may be detected during the physical examination. The kidneys of affected animals are variable in size.
Animals with chronic kidney disease often have small,
firm, irregularly shaped kidneys, whereas those with less
severe or long‐standing disease often have normal‐sized
or, occasionally, enlarged kidneys.

­Diagnosis
When proteinuria is detected, there are three key elements that need to be assessed: localization, persistence,
and magnitude. Although proteinuria is the hallmark
of glomerular disease, it can also occur secondary to
prerenal, postrenal or renal tubular causes. The magnitude of proteinuria is generally assessed via the urine
protein:creatinine ratio (UPC). Persistent renal proteinuria that is of high magnitude (i.e., UPC >2) is most
likely of glomerular origin; however, there is no range of
numbers that is diagnostic for any one renal disease and
the overlap in expected ranges is too broad to be clinically reliable. In fact, glomerular lesions have been seen
in dogs without proteinuria. Urine albumin can also
be used to assess proteinuria. Microalbuminuria may
develop before the UPC is increased. It therefore seems
reasonable to conclude that a dog or cat with persistent
microalbuminuria of increasing magnitude should be
assessed as having an injurious process to the glomerular
filtration barrier and may eventually develop overt
proteinuria.
Once glomerular disease is suspected, a comprehensive diagnostic evaluation is recommended for all dogs
and cats which includes urinalysis, serial UPC measurements, completed blood count, biochemical profile, and
blood pressure measurement. Urine culture is warranted
if there is pyuria, hematuria, bacteriuria, dilute urine
(e.g., urine specific gravity <1.025) or concurrent diseases which might predispose the patient to urinary tract
infection (e.g., hyperadrenocorticism). Animals with
potential exposure to infectious diseases should undergo
the appropriate testing. Any concominant extrarenal
disease should be evaluated further (e.g., aspriation
cytology of cutaneous masses, appropriate testing for
hyperadrenocorticism). If proteinuria is of high magnitude (i.e., UPC >3.5), associated with hypoalbuminemia,
azotemia, or hypertension, or progressive or nonresponsive to treatment, additional diagnostics including
but not limited to abdominal ultrasound, thoracic
­radiographs, more extensive evaluation for infectious

VetBooks.ir

121 Glomerular Disease

diseases, and assessment of the coagulation system are
indicated.
The results of this comprehensive evaluation will
vary considerably in affected animals. Hypoproteinemia
due to hypoalbuminemia develops in many dogs and
cats with glomerular disease but is more likely in animals with heavy proteinuria. Azotemia, hyperphosphatemia, and metabolic acidosis, consistent with renal
failure, may be present in animals with severe disease,
although as many as 50% of affected animals will be
nonazotemic. Nonregenerative anemia, secondary to
renal failure or a systemic disease, is observed in many
affected animals.
Other hematologic abnormalities also may reflect concurrent and possibly underlying systemic diseases.
Thrombocytosis and hyperfibrinogenemia are common
findings in dogs with glomerular disease. The nephrotic
syndrome of hypoalbuminemia, proteinuria, hypercholesterolemia, and edema, although pathognomonic for
glomerular disease, will only be present in a small proportion of dogs with glomerular disease (i.e., 10–15%).
Because fluid retention can sometimes be cavitary, thoracic radiographs and abdominal ultrasound can be used
to help detect edema. However, incomplete nephrotic
syndrome (i.e., without edema or ascites) occurs in about
half of affected dogs. The nephritic syndrome is a term
that has primarily been used in people to describe a set
of signs that develop secondary to renal inflammation,
generally acute, that extends into the glomeruli. In people, this syndrome is characterized by hematuria and
red blood cell (RBC) casts with one or more of the following: subnephrotic proteinuria, edema, hypertension,
azotemia, oliguria. Although the nephritic syndrome has
not been fully characterized in dogs, perhaps because of
the probable low prevalence of acute glomerulonephritides in dogs, it is possible that dogs with acute inflammatory glomerular diseases (e.g., Lyme nephritis) may
present with a nephritic‐like syndrome. Isosthenuria is a
variable finding in dogs and cats with glomerular disease
and as many as 40% of affected dogs with glomerular disease will maintain renal concentrating ability, achieving
urine specific gravities in excess of 1.035.
The finding of concurrent renal azotemia, concentrated urine, and proteinuria is indicative of glomerular
disease. Cylindruria is common in dogs with glomerular
disease; casts are most often hyaline but can be granular, waxy, or fatty. When affected animals are imaged,
the kidneys may appear normal or small and irregular;
some animals may have abnormally enlarged kidneys.
Increased echogenicity of the cortex and loss of corticomedullary distinction may also be noted during
abdominal ultrasound. The renal pelvis may be mildly
dilated if polyuria is present or if fluids are being
administered.

Renal biopsy should be considered under certain circumstances: proteinuria is of high magnitude (UPC >3.5,
with or without concurrent hypoalbuminemia), progressive, or unresponsive to standard therapy; immunosuppressive therapy is being considered; medical
con­traindications to biopsy are not present; the renal
biopsy can be collected, prepared and interpreted by
experienced personnel; and, the sample can be submitted for evaluation using standard light microscopy but
also electron microscopy and immunofluorescence.
Medical contraindications to biopsy include advanced
chronic kidney disease (i.e., IRIS stage 4), coagulopathy,
cystic disease, hydronephrosis, pyelonephritis, perirenal
abscess, uncontrolled hypertension, severe anemia, and
pregnancy.
Electron microscopy is essential if a renal biopsy is to
be evaluated and was required to confirm or rule out
ICGN in 27.4% and 23.1% of biopsies, respectively, from
one study. Light microscopy alone was 94% sensitive and
77% specific in identifying ICGN when specimens were
evaluated by highly experienced nephropathologists; it is
unlikely that pathologists without nephropathology
training would achieve these same results.

­Therapy
Standard Therapy
Standard therapy is the foundation for the care that
should given to all dogs with glomerular disease, regardless of the inciting cause, and includes inhibition of
the renin‐angiotensin‐aldosterone system (RAAS), and
management of dietary intake, hypercoagulability, systemic hypertension, and body fluid volume (Box 121.1).
Evidence suggests that UPC >1.0 is associated with
negative patient outcomes and when the UPC is reduced
to <0.5, the outcome is improved. Therefore, it is recommended that standard therapies be considered when the
UPC is persistently >0.5. However, standard therapy
rarely leads to complete resolution of the renal lesions.
Inhibition of RAAS

Hemodynamic forces influence the transglomerular movement of proteins. The RAAS can be therapeuti­cally targeted to alter renal hemodynamics, leading to a reduction
in proteinuria. Decreased efferent glomerular arteriolar
resistance leads to decreased glomerular transcapillary
hydraulic pressure, which ideally leads to a reduction in
proteinuria. Other proposed mechanisms include reduced
loss of glomerular heparan sulfate, decreased size of the
glomerular capillary endot­helial pores, improved lipoprotein metabolism, slowed ­glomerular mesangial growth and
proliferation, and i­nhibition of bradykinin degradation.

Angiotensin‐converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEi; e.g.,
enalapril, benazapril), angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB;
e.g., telmisartan), and aldosterone receptor blockers (e.g.,
spironolactone) are the agents that target RAAS.
For most dogs with glomerular‐range proteinuria,
an ACEi is the initial agent used. Typically, an ACEi is
given once daily initially, but more than half of the dogs
will eventually need twice‐daily administration and perhaps additional dosage escalations. Although worsening
azotemia is a concern regarding the use of ACEi, severe
worsening (i.e., >30% increase from baseline) due to
ACEi administration alone seems uncommon and dogs
that are dehydrated may be at highest risk. Less is known
about the use of an ARB in dogs with glomerular disease
although they have been extensively studied in people.
The ARB that has historically been used in dogs with glomerular disease is losartan, although it has not always
been effective. Recently, telmisartan has been shown to
be very effective in some dogs and may prove useful as
the initial line of therapy. Telmisartan has a more profound effect on lowering blood pressure than ACEis and
should be used carefully in dogs that have low basal blood
pressures (e.g., systolic <140 mmHg).

Because neither an ACEi nor an ARB as a single agent
provides complete blockade of the RAAS, there may be
an added benefit to combined therapy; however, this
approach should be used with caution as it has been
associated with a higher risk of kidney failure and death
in people. Serum aldosterone increases over time (i.e.,
aldosterone escape) in people treated even with maximal
dosages of ACEi and ARB; prolonged hyperaldosteronism may have adverse effects on the heart, systemic
blood vessels, and glomeruli. People with hyperaldosteronism may have a greater reduction in proteinuria when
an aldosterone receptor antagonist is added to their therapy. Spironolactone has been used most commonly in
dogs; however, there are few data that support the efficacy of this drug in dogs in the management of glomerular disease. Spironolactone should only be effective if
serum aldosterone concentrations are increased. This
drug could be tried in animals that have high serum
aldosterone concentrations and persistent proteinuria in
spite of treatment with an ACEi, ARB or both, with the
understanding that its efficacy in reducing proteinuria
has not been established.
All dogs that are being treated for glomerular disease
via RAAS inhibition should be monitored at least quarterly by a minimum of UPC, urinalysis, systemic arterial
blood pressure and serum albumin, creatinine and potassium concentrations. The UPC, serum creatinine, serum
potassium, and blood pressure should be evaluated 1–2
weeks after an ACEi or ARB has been added or altered.
The desired therapeutic effect is a reduction in proteinuria without a severe worsening of renal function (i.e.,
>30% increase in serum creatinine), a critical increase in
serum potassium or the unlikely development of hypotension. Changes in the magnitude of urine protein are most
accurately measured by assessing trends in the UPC over
time. Day‐to‐day variations in the UPC occur in most
dogs with glomerular proteinuria, with greater variation
occurring in dogs with UPC >4. Consideration should be
given to either averaging 2–3 serial UPC or measuring a
UPC in urine that has been pooled from 2–3 collections.
The target for reduction is a UPC of <0.5 without inappropriate worsening of renal function; however, when
that is not possible, a partial response with a reduction in
the UPC of 50% or more is the alternative target.
Dogs with serum potassium concentrations of >6 mEq/L
should be monitored closely and therapy should be modified when serum potassium concentrations are >6.5 mEq/L.
Before modifying treatment, pseudohyperkalemia, due to
the high potassium content of some blood cells which may
occur in dogs with glomerular disease, should be eliminated as a cause by measuring the potassium concentration in lithium heparin plasma. True hyperkalemia can be
managed by reducing the ACEi or ARB drug dosage, discontinuing spironolactone ­administration, or by feeding

VetBooks.ir

121 Glomerular Disease

diets that are reduced in potassium or administering an
intestinal potassium binder (e.g., kayexelate). If the target
reduction in UPC is not achieved and the dog does not
have the before mentioned adverse effects, the dosages
may be increased every 4–6 weeks.
Modified Dietary Intake

Modification of dietary intake has a central role in the
management of all dogs with kidney disease and has
been associated with delaying spontaneous progression
of kidney disease and reducing the magnitude of proteinuria. It is well known that fat content of a diet can affect
renal outcome. Most commercially available renal diets
are modified with respect to polyunsaturated fatty acids
(PUFA) content with the goal of slowing progression and
reducing proteinuria. The consensus recommendation is
that dogs with glomerular disease should be fed a diet
with a reduced n‐6:n‐3 PUFA ratio of approximately 5:1.
It is unknown if there is any additional benefit of supplementing n‐3 PUFA when this ratio is already being provided via the diet. If supplementation is chosen, care
should also be taken to provide adequate antioxidants
(e.g., vitamin E). Dogs with glomerular disease should be
fed modified protein diets because this has been shown
to reduce proteinuria and slow progression.
Lastly, the sodium chloride content should be reduced
in diets fed to dogs with glomerular disease. Salt restriction may enhance the beneficial effects of agents used to
inhibit RAAS and help reduce fluid retention.
Antithrombotic Therapy

Hypercoagulability is a complication of protein‐losing
glomerular diseases and thromboembolism can occur in
as many as 25% of dogs with glomerular disease. The
pathogenesis of hypercoagulability in glomerular disease
is complex and incompletely understood. Urinary loss
of antithrombin has long been given as the explanation
but in reality, the pathogenesis is more complex than
this and probably includes vascular stasis as well
as increased platelet aggregation, plasma procoagulant
factors, and fibrinogen concentrations. Unfortunately,
serum albumin concentrations, antithrombin activity,
and UPC cannot be used in isolation to predict hypercoagulability in individual patients. It follows then that it
remains unclear when to implement thromboprophylaxis. Consensus recommendations call for the daily
administration of low‐dose aspirin (1–5 mg/kg/day) in
dogs with protein‐losing glomerular diseases. Clopidogrel
may be an effective alternative.
Antihypertensive Therapy

All dogs with glomerular disease should undergo repeat
evaluation for systemic hypertension. This evaluation
should not only include measurement of systemic blood

pressure but also assessing the patient for target organ
damage, evaluating for conditions that may contribute to
hypertension and determining if any concurrent conditions that may complicate antihypertensive therapy are
present. Personal preference and experience should dictate how the blood pressure is measured; however, the
substaging by arterial blood pressure system that has
been proposed by the International Renal Interest Society
(IRIS) should be used to guide therapy (Table 121.2).
Antihypertensive therapy should be initiated when the
blood pressure exceeds 160 mmHg systolic or 100 mmHg
diastolic (i.e., AP2 or above). The goal of therapy is to
reduce the blood pressure to less than 150 mmHg systolic or 96 mmHg diastolic (i.e., AP0). Lowering the
blood pressure is not an emergency unless there is severe
ocular or central nervous system target organ damage. In
most cases, blood pressure reduction can be achieved
gradually over a period of several weeks. Effective treatment of hypertension should lead to a concomitant
reduction in the magnitude of proteinuria in dogs with
glomerular disease. Feeding a salt‐restricted diet alone
will not lower the blood pressure into the target range
but it may enhance the antihypertensive effects of the
inhibitors of RAAS, generally ACEi. However, ACEi are
generally only associated with a 10–15% reduction in
blood pressure. This reduction may be all that is needed
for dogs that are only moderately hypertensive (i.e.,
AP2). Dogs that are severely hypertensive (i.e., AP3)
should have a calcium channel blocker (i.e., amlodipine)
added to their RAAS inhibition therapy. Alternatively,
telmisartan can be used as a single agent to manage
hypertension and proteinuria.
The consensus recommendation is that dogs with IRIS
chronic kidney disease stages 1 or 2 should have blood
pressure evaluated 3–14 days after any change in antihypertensive therapy whereas those in stages 3 or 4 should

be evaluated 3–5 days after making any change. Dogs that

The purpose of these evaluations is not only to assess
effectiveness of the antihypertensive therapy but also to
evaluate for exacerbation of azotemia. Dosages should be
reduced if the serum creatinine has increased more than
30% from baseline or if the blood pressure is reduced to
less than 120–mmHg systolic or 60–mmHg diastolic.
Once target blood pressure is achieved, the dogs should
be evaluated at 1–4‐month intervals, depending upon the
stability and severity of the renal disease.
Body Fluid Volume

Dogs with glomerular disease may have fluid excesses,
deficits or maldistribution, which may need to be corrected if the dog has decompensated or is being prepared
for anesthesia. Correcting body fluid imbalances in dogs
that are hypoalbuminemic from glomerular disease is a
very difficult therapeutic challenge. Fluid therapy can
exacerbate edema and hypertension and diuretics can
exacerbate azotemia or uremia. As such, those who have
experience and expertise in critical care are the best people to deliver these therapies to dogs with glomerular
disease.
Fluid therapy should be given only when needed to
help control clinical signs or provide support to those
dogs that have inadequate fluid intake. Both colloids and
crystalloid can be used. However, the decision to use colloids should not be based on the presence of hypoalbuminemia or decreased colloidal oncotic pressure alone.
Colloids should be considered when crystalloids have
failed to bring about the desired result. The fluid status
of affected dogs should be assessed before and during
fluid therapy on the basis of serial body weight and other
physical examination findings (e.g., skin turgor, appearance of mucous membranes, capillary refill time, pulse
rate and quality, arterial blood pressure). When the
serum albumin decreases below 2 g/dL in people, the
plasma oncotic pressure is sufficiently reduced to allow
for transudation of fluid from the vascular compartment
into the interstitial space. Dogs may be more resistant to
the formation of edema, which does not generally occur
until the serum albumin concentration is below 1.5 g/dL.
Plasma volume may be reduced at this point, making the
use of diuretics in the management of edema relatively
ineffective and also dangerous because of the increased
risk of acute kidney injury and vascular stasis leading to
thromboembolism.
Diuretics should be avoided unless needed to control
respiratory distress. When needed, furosemide is the
drug of choice for pulmonary edema but spironolactone
may be best for pleural or abdominal effusion. Provision
of adequate exercise also may help reduce the formation
of edema or ascites.

Immunosuppressive Therapy
Immunosuppressive therapy should be considered in
dogs that have severe, persistent or progressive glomerular disease and ICGN documented via appropriate evaluation of a renal biopsy specimen. However, there are
many practical and medical reasons why a biopsy might
not be performed. In addition, financial limitations may
prevent biopsy. The end‐result is that sometimes veterinarians must decide about the use of immunosuppressive
therapy in dogs with glomerular disease without a pathologic diagnosis. In these situations, immunosuppressive
therapy should not be administered if there is any doubt
that the proteinuria is of glomerular origin, administration of the specific drug is medically contraindicated, or
there is a high index of suspicion that the dog has a nonimmune‐mediated familial disease or amyloidosis.
Immunosuppressive drugs should be considered without a pathologic diagnosis when standard therapy has
been implemented but the azotemia is progressive or the
serum creatinine is >3.0 mg/dL or serum albumin is
<2.0 g/dL. Because ICGN is the disease process in approximately 50% of dogs with glomerular disease, using
immunosuppressive agents in these dogs without a renal
pathologic diagnosis has a 50:50 chance of being appropriate. The risks associated with such therapy need to be
clearly communicated to the pet owners.
Even with biopsy‐proven ICGN, the profession does not
have data regarding the expected outcomes of the various
possible protocols. Therefore, specific drug recommendations are difficult to formulate. The immunosuppressive
protocol should probably vary based on the severity of
clinical signs and the rate of progression of the glomerular
disease. More aggressive protocols that use rapidly active
agents are probably best for dogs with severe and rapidly
progressive disease. The rapidity with which the drug
becomes active is of less concern in dogs with more slowly
progressive disease. Drugs that could be considered are
glucocorticoids, mycophenolate, cyclosporine, cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil and azathioprine. Likewise,
combined therapy of mycophenolate and prednisolone,
cyclophosphamide and prednisolone or chlorambucil and
azathioprine could be considered. There is only weak evidence that supports worse outcomes when dogs with glomerulonephritis are managed with glucocorticoids and
more evidence is needed before the use of these drugs is
discarded. However, it is clear that glucocorticoids will
increase proteinuria; UPC monitoring is best performed
in samples collected on days when glucocorticoids are not
administered in patients receiving alternate‐day therapy.
Glucocorticoids should also be used with caution in dogs
that are receiving concurrent aspirin therapy.
Patients receiving immunosuppressive drugs should
be monitored for drug‐specific adverse effects as well as

VetBooks.ir

121 Glomerular Disease

a therapeutic response. Dogs should be thoroughly evaluated 1–2 weeks after starting therapy and every two
weeks after for the first 4–6 weeks of treatment, then
every four weeks for the next three months and then
quarterly until disease resolution.
A therapeutic response is viewed as a reduction in the
magnitude of proteinuria with improvement or stabilization of renal function and increases in serum albumin
concentration. A reduction in proteinuria is as described
earlier (see Inhibition of RAAS). Improvement or stabilization in renal function is defined as a sustained reduction in serum creatinine to less than 1.4 mg/dL (complete
response) or by >25% of baseline (partial response). A
meaningful increase in serum albumin is defined as a
sustained increase to >2.5 mg/dL (complete response) or
either to 2.0–2.5 mg/dL or by >50% of baseline (partial
response). Secondary goals include improved blood
pressure regulation, resolution of edema, and stabilization of body weight. If there are no unacceptable adverse
drug effects, treatment should be continued for 8–12
weeks before changing the regimen or discontinuing
treatment. Those demonstrating a partial or complete
response should have therapy continued for at least
12–16 weeks. If partial or complete responses are not
evident by the end of 8–12 weeks, the immunosuppressive protocol should be changed or discontinued. If there
is no response by 3–4 months, all immunosuppressive

therapy should be discontinued following appropriate
drug tapering.

­Prognosis
The prognosis for dogs and cats with glomerular disease is
variable and probably based on a combination of factors.
The prognosis is expected to differ with the various diseases. Although progressive disease can be expected to
occur in a large percentage of animals with glomerular disease, spontaneous remission and response to specific therapy can also be expected. Furthermore, disease progression
can be slow enough for the animals to lead relatively normal lives, especially when the diagnosis is established early
in the disease process. In humans, azotemia, severe proteinuria, systemic hypertension, and marked tubulointerstitial lesions at presentation are the most significant
predictors of an unfavorable outcome in most forms of
glomerular disease. In dogs, the presence of nephrotic
syndrome or azotemia is a negative prognostic indicator.
Median survival time for dogs with nephrotic syndrome
was only 12.5 days versus 104.5 days for dogs without
nephrotic syndrome. When only nonazotemic dogs were
considered, (i.e., serum creatinine <1.5 g/dL), the median
survival for those with nephrotic syndrome was 51 days
versus 605 days for those without nephrotic syndrome.

­Urethral Obstruction
Etiology/Pathophysiology
There are a number of potential etiologies for urethral
obstruction (UO), with important differences between
dogs and cats. For dogs, the most common cause is uro­
lithiasis, with neoplasia, prostatic disease, trauma, and
stricture as additional considerations. Calcium oxalate
and struvite stones occur most commonly in dogs, fol­
lowed by ammonium biurate and cystine stones. Urethral
strictures develop secondary to chronic urethritis,
trauma during prior urethral catheterization, damage to
the urethral epithelium from urolith passage, urethral
tear or avulsion secondary to trauma, or as a result of
exuberant healing following surgical urethral incision.
Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder trigone and
prostatic carcinoma are the urothelial neoplasms most
commonly associated with urethral obstruction.
For feline UO, urolithiaisis (predominantly calcium
oxalate) represents a smaller proportion of cases, with
the presence of a urethral plug and/or functional obstruc­
tion from urethral spasm/edema recognized more com­
monly. In any of these circumstances, it is thought that
the presence of feline idiopathic cystitis (FIC), and asso­
ciated inflammation of the lower urinary tract, may set
the stage for obstruction. Much less commonly, though
for reasons similar to those seen in dogs, cats may have
obstruction caused by neoplasia or urethral stricture.
Regardless of underlying cause, complete obstruction
of the urethra results in a similar pathologic progression.
Urine will accumulate within the urethra and urinary
bladder until those tissues can no longer distend. Once
this occurs, intraluminal pressure builds, resulting in
mucosal injury. The intraluminal pressure is then trans­
mitted up the ureters to the kidney and Bowman’s

­capsule with subsequent reduction of glomerular filtra­
tion. As a result, there will be accumulation of normal
­excretory products such as blood urea nitrogen, creati­
nine, phosphorus, potassium, and hydrogen ion within
approximately 24–48 hours. These then combine to cre­
ate the expected clinical course associated with UO.
Uremia can have a number of effects including depres­
sion, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia. The resulting
decreased intake and ongoing losses can cause the patient
to become dehydrated. Retention of organic and inor­
ganic acids can result in severe metabolic acidosis with
severe implications. Normal protein and enzyme func­
tion can be pH dependent, as well as responsiveness to
catecholamines and the ability to maintain cardiovascular
homoestasis. Finally, the development of severe hyper­
kalemia contributes significantly to the life‐threatening
nature of this disease process. Hyper­kalemia affects elec­
trical conduction and ultimately leads to bradycardia,
atrial standstill, and eventually cardiac arrest (particularly
at potassium levels above 9 or 10 mEq/L). As a result of
this combination of factors, without intervention com­
plete urethral obstruction will lead to significant illness
within 24–48 hours, and m
­ ortality within 3–5 days.
Epidemiology and Signalment
Given their long and narrow urethra (compared to females),
males are much more likely to develop UO. Among cats,
there do not appear to be specific breed predispositions for
UO in general, though Himalayan and Persian cats may
have an increased risk of urolithiasis. There is some evi­
dence to suggest indoor‐only cats, and cats fed an exclu­
sively dry food diet, may have an increased risk of UO.
Dogs that have a predisposition for stone formation
have a greater risk for developing UO. This includes older
castrated males and small‐breed dogs (bichon frise,

Pomeranian, shih tzu, etc.) at risk for calcium oxalate
stones. Because of their strong association with urinary
tract infection (UTI), female dogs are much more likely
to have struvite urolithiasis. Dalmatians and breeds pre­
disposed to portosystemic shunts (e.g., Yorkshire terri­
ers) should be considered for the potential of urate stones.
Lower urinary tract neoplasia is reported to have a higher
prevalence in Scottish terriers, Shetland sheepdogs, wire‐
haired fox terriers, and West Highland white terrier.
History and Clinical Signs
Feline UO typically involves demonstration of lower uri­
nary tract signs: vocalizing and straining unproductively
in the litter box. Cats with FIC may present similarly,
which could serve to complicate the diagnosis based on
these signs alone. Signs of systemic illness (vomiting, leth­
argy, anorexia, changes in mentation) in conjunction with
lower urinary tract signs should point more strongly to
UO than FIC. Owners may not be aware of lower urinary
tract signs when litter boxes are kept in isolated areas, or
the cat is indoor‐outdoor. These patients will present for
their systemic signs, and so UO might not be considered
as quickly. Along those lines, UO should be considered as
a differential for any sick male cat that presents.
Dogs may present for signs consistent with lower uri­
nary tract disease leading to obstruction, including fre­
quent trips outside, stranguria/dysuria, and pollakiuria.
Once obstruction occurs, owners might report unpro­
ductive attempts to urinate, abdominal distension, and
abdominal discomfort.
Clinical signs will depend on duration of obstruction
and degree of systemic impact by the time of presenta­
tion. A firm, distended urinary bladder will be the most
prominent feature for patients early in the disease pro­
cess. In dogs, it may be possible to palpate the presence
of a stone in the pelvic urethra, or prostatomegaly, when
performing a rectal exam. If the obstruction has been
present for greater than 24 hours, the patient may display
signs of systemic illness. Systemic signs include dehydra­
tion, dull mentation, bradycardia, and hypothermia.
Hyperkalemia should be considered for any ill patient
that presents with bradycardia as the normal stress
response to hospital presentation is tachycardia (though
patients with a primary conduction disturbance or cats
with septic or cardiogenic shock can also demonstrate
bradycardia). For cats with UO, the combination of brad­
ycardia (HR <140) and hypothermia (T <96.6 °F) strongly
suggests a serum potassium level greater than 8 mEq/L.

Point‐of‐care diagnostics are especially important in
the initial stages of assessing the sick obstructed patient.
This should include packed cell volume and total pro­
tein, as well as assessment of electrolyte, acid–base
status, and/or kidney values (if available). Expected
­
abnormalities include azotemia, hyperkalemia, and met­
abolic acidosis. An ECG should be placed to evaluate the
effects of hyperkalemia on electrical conduction in the
heart, even if the patient is not demonstrating bradycar­
dia. Progressive changes that can be seen associated with
hyperkalemia include prolonged P‐Q interval, dimin­
ished to absent P‐waves, widened QRS and tall, tented
T‐waves (Figure 122.1). Eventually, ECG changes can
progress to atrial standstill, ventricular fibrillation or
asystole. In cats, it is important to note that wide com­
plex tachycardia, rather than the expected bradycardia,
has been reported in the setting of severe hyperkalemia.
Once stabilized, more complete systemic bloodwork
(complete blood count, biochemical profile) should be
performed if clinically indicated. Urinalysis is typically
performed in dogs with UO to assess urine pH, presence
of crystalluria, and evidence for UTI. As cats are much
less likely to have a UTI, and the clinical importance of
crystalluria is unclear, the diagnostic value of urinalysis
is questionable. Similarly, given evidence that the inci­
dence of UTI at the time of presentation is very low in
cats, urine culture should not be performed. However,
dogs with UO are much more likely to have concurrent
UTI and a culture is more likely indicated.
Diagnostic imaging of some form should be performed
in any patient with UO. Typically, abdominal radio­
graphs are a first step to assess for the presence of cystic
and/or urethral calculi. Calcium oxalate and struvite
stones are radiopaque and should be evident on radio­
graphs. However, ammonium biurate and cystine may
be radiolucent and so an apparent absence of stones
does not rule out urolithiasis. The entire lower urinary
tract should be included (Figure 122.2), and the patient
positioned to help minimize superimposition of the pel­
vis or hindlimbs (Figure 122.3). Common sites where
stones lodge include the base of the os penis for dogs and

Diagnosis of UO is largely based on history, clinical signs,
and physical exam. However, further diagnostics are help­
ful to assess the systemic compromise of the patient as
well as to determine the underlying cause of obstruction.

Male dogs should be assessed for prostatomegaly and/

abdominal detail may suggest uroabdomen secondary to
bladder leakage/rupture. In some cases, it may be useful
to perform a positive or negative contrast cystourethro­

thral tear are suspected. Abdominal ultrasound may also
be of benefit in patients with radiolucent stones, pros­
tatic disease, or lower urinary tract neoplasia.

Intravenous catheter placement and fluid therapy should
be initiated immediately in the “sick” UO patient. This
will serve to begin rehydration/volume repletion, as well
as have a dilutional effect on the serum potassium level.
There is some debate as to the optimal fluid to use.
Traditionally, 0.9% NaCl has been considered the fluid of
choice because it has a greater dilutional effect on potas­
sium. However, 0.9% NaCl is an acidifying solution which
could exacerbate metabolic acidosis. Conversely, bal­
anced electrolyte solutions are alkalinizing but contain
small amounts of potassium (4–5 mEq/L) and therefore
may have less of a dilutional effect. It has been demon­
strated that between 0.9% NaCl and a balanced electro­
lyte solution (Normosol R®) there were no differences in
outcome (survival, length of stay) or in reduction of
serum potassium levels, though acid–base abnormalities
corrected more rapidly in the Normosol R group. If car­
diovascular collapse is present, it may be necessary to

administer crystalloid “shock doses” (80–90 mL/kg dog,
40–60 mL/kg cat) in bolus fractions (1/4 to 1/3 shock
dose over 15–30 minutes, repeated as necessary) to rap­
idly restore vascular volume. If resuscitation is not nec­
essary, fluid rate should be based on replacement of
dehydration added to the maintenance fluid require­
ment. If time does not allow more accurate determina­
tion of fluid rate, it is reasonable to start at a rate of
10 mL/kg in the initial stages and then reassess. Care
must also be taken with the amount of fluids given, espe­
cially in cats, as a recent study has shown that cats with
UO are at risk for volume overload.
While urinary catheter placement and IV fluids will be
important in addressing the underlying cause, there is a
significant delay for glomerular filtration rate (GFR) to
resume and for potassium excretion to occur. Calcium
gluconate is the most immediate way to offset the effects
of hyperkalemia on electric conduction, though this
medication does not decrease the potassium itself. In
addition, medications that promote intracellular shift of
potassium include regular insulin, dextrose, terbutaline,
and/or sodium bicarbonate (see Table 122.1 for dosing
recommendations).
Generally, if it was deemed necessary to give calcium
gluconate, then one or more of these medications should
also be given. It should be noted that dextrose should
always be given with insulin to prevent the development
of hypoglycemia.
There is also consideration of cystocentesis as part of
initial management. On the one hand, it may allow for
more immediate relief of bladder pressure compared to
urinary catheter placement (particularly for those with
limited experience in deobstructing). In addition, rela­
tively less sedation is typically needed to perform cysto­

centesis. Cystocentesis can allow an uncontaminated
urine sample to be obtained for urinalysis and/or urine
culture. Finally, it is speculated that decreasing intralu­
minal pressure may make for easier passage of a urinary
catheter. The major counterargument against the use of
cystocentesis is related to the concern for bladder tear or
rupture. While this is a known potential side‐effect
whenever cystocentesis is performed, it is believed by
some that a distended and friable bladder present with
UO is associated with increased risk. There is evidence
to suggest that development of clinically significant
abdominal effusion, as shown by abdominal ultrasound
or radiographs, occurs very uncommonly after cystocen­
tesis in cats with UO and that this procedure can be
safely performed. Similar information regarding cysto­
centesis in dogs with UO is currently unavailable.
Urethral catheterization

Urinary catheter placement is an important step in the
management of UO. In this process, every effort should
be made to minimize the risk of urethral trauma and
optimize the likelihood of successful catheterization.
Along these lines, UO patients should receive appropri­
ate sedation and pain medication, with consideration of
coccygeal epidural and/or general anesthesia. In addi­
tion to impacts on patient comfort and standard of care,
inadequate analgesia and sedation may be associated
with urethral spasm and urethral injury. If the patient is
still reactive to effort (vocalizing, moving), additional
medications should be given; alternatively, general anes­
thesia should be performed.
For cats, the perineal region should be clipped, prepped,
and draped in order to minimize risk of contamination.
An open‐ended semi‐rigid catheter (polypropylene or

the obstruction. Given the very rigid nature of polypro­
pylene catheters, care should be taken not to use too
much force in advancing. For comfort, as well as associ­
ated inflammation and irritation, these catheters should
also not be left in place. With regard to optimal catheter
size, there is some evidence to suggest that use of a 3.5 Fr
urinary catheter may be associated with less risk of
immediate reobstruction compared to 5 Fr. However,
another study failed to show this association.
When passing the catheter, aggressive flushing (rather
than force) should be utilized to dilate the urethra and
retropulse/break down any physical component of the
obstruction. For the flush solution, adding sterile lubri­
cant to sterile saline and mixing across a three‐way stop­
cock (in a ratio of 10:1) may help to decrease urethral
injury by allowing lubricant to be deposited throughout
catheter placement (rather than just lubricating the end
of the catheter). Another helpful technique is to pull the
prepuce dorsal and caudally after the catheter is intro­
duced into the penile urethra (Figure 122.5). Elevating
the natural downward angle of the urethra as it passes
out of the pelvic canal may facilitate catheter placement.
Once the initial catheter is in place, the urinary bladder
can be emptied and flushed. A sterile closed collection
system should be connected to allow for urine produc­
tion to be quantified, and decrease risk of ascending
infection.
(a)

For catheterization and deobstruction in dogs, general
anesthesia can be especially important to ensure optimal
urethral relaxation. The prepuce or vulva should be
cleaned and flushed to decrease risk of contamination. A
red rubber or Foley catheter is typically used, though in
some circumstances a more rigid catheter may be needed
(with potential increased risk of urethral trauma). Similar
to the process described for cats, hydropulsion with
lubricated saline should be the primary means of retro­
pulsing any physical obstruction. In male dogs, it is help­
ful to pinch the urethral orifice to prevent antegrade
movement of flush solution. An additional useful trick
(in either male or female dogs) is to have an assistant rec­
tally apply pressure to the pelvic urethral during hydro­
pulsion. This allows a build‐up of pressure which, when
released, can help dislodge a luminal obstruction.
If urethral catheterization fails due to urethral trauma,
rupture, or persistent partial obstruction, antegrade ure­
thral access can provide a means to deobstruct the
patient and facilitate catheterization (Figure 122.6).
Briefly, percutaneous access into the bladder is achieved
with an 18 gauge over‐the‐needle catheter by palpation
or ultrasound guidance. Through the catheter, a hydro­
philic wire is directed toward the bladder trigone and out
the urethra. As the tear or trauma is usually created from
a retrograde direction, the wire finds the true urethral
lumen easily and often can be directly advanced out the
penile urethra. Once wire access is achieved in this man­
ner, the open‐ended urinary catheter is advanced over
the wire into the bladder lumen. The access catheter and
wire are then removed and the urethral catheter sutured
in placed and cared for routinely. Ideally, this procedure
is performed under fluoroscopic guidance to visualize
the path of the wire and appropriate positioning of the
catheter.
Postobstructive Care

(b)

Figure 122.5 Once the catheter is seeded in the distal urethral,
the prepuce is pulled dorsal and caudal to straighten the urethra
and facilitate passage.

One major facet of postobstructive care is careful moni­
toring of urine output and maintaining fluid balance.
Some patients may experience a postobstructive diuresis
which can lead to significant quantities of urine produc­
tion. Proposed mechanisms for this diuresis include
accumulation of osmotically active substances in the
blood, pressure necrosis, medullary washout and/or
antidiuretic hormone resistance. Likely owing to these
mechanisms, it has been demonstrated that up to 50% of
cats may have increased urine production after deob­
struction. However, in some circumstances it is unclear
whether the initial rates of fluids administered may have
also been contributing to increased urine production.
Similar data are not available for dogs.
Given the potential to produce significant quantities of
urine (>5–10 mL/kg/h), it is very important to keep up
with urinary losses to prevent dehydration and hypov­

resultant rate could be very high). In the postobstructive
period there is also the potential concern for inadequate
urine production (<1 mL/kg/h). Major concerns in this
setting would be obstruction of the collection system,
dehydration, or oliguria from acute kidney injury.
The obstructive process and urethral catheter place­
ment are painful and stressful, and could add to postob­
structive morbidity. As such, provision of adequate
analgesia and sedation is also important for managing
these patients. For cats, buprenorphine (0.01–0.02 mg/kg
q8h) generally provides sufficient pain control. If buprenor­
phine is not sufficient, a fentanyl continuous rate infusion
(CRI) (2–4 μg/kg/h) or intermittent methadone (0.2–
0.3 mg/kg q6h) is recommended. Because of the potential
to cause excitability and hyperthermia, hydromorphone is
typically avoided. For dogs, fentanyl or methadone (similar
doses as cats) or hydromorphone (0.05–0.1 mg/kg) typi­
cally provide adequate analgesia. Acepromazine (0.05 mg/

kg IV/IM/SC or 0.5 mg/kg PO) can provide adequate seda­
tion to decrease stress and agitation, so long as the patient
is stable. Given the potential functional nature of feline
UO, the alpha‐antagonist effects of acepromazine might
promote urethral relaxation and decrease risk of reob­
struction once the urinary catheter is removed.
Another important consideration is whether UO
patients should be placed on antibiotics after catheter
placement. This may be done with concern for existing
UTI, or for introducing a UTI secondary to catheter
placement. For cats, it has traditionally been accepted
that the incidence of bacterial infection in lower urinary
tract disease is very low. There is also evidence that pro­
phylactic antibiotics do not prevent development of
catheter‐associated UTI. Therefore, antibiotic therapy is
not recommended for UO in cats while the urinary cath­
eter is in place unless bacteriuria and pyuria are docu­
mented. Dogs with evidence of UTI (based on urine
cytology or positive culture) should be placed onto
appropriate antibiotics.

Electrolytes and renal values should be monitored
every 12–24 hours (or more frequently depending on
patient severity at presentation) and should rapidly cor­
rect to normal. If there has not been a significant reduc­
tion in renal values within 24 hours, complications (such
as uroabdomen) may have occurred. Given the potential
for potassium wasting secondary to diuresis in the pos­
tobstructive period, supplementation may be needed,
even for patients that initially presented with life‐threat­
ening hyperkalemia.
Further Therapeutic Considerations

For cats with UO not secondary to urolithiasis, medical
management is typically sufficient. The urinary catheter
should remain in place until bloodwork abnormalities,
gross urine changes (major debris, clots or plugs), and
postobstructive diuresis have resolved in order to help
minimize the risk of immediate reobstruction. Performing
a urine culture and susceptibility after catheter removal
(sample obtained by cystocentesis) is recommended to
determine if a UTI has been introduced. Observation for
12–24 hours after catheter removal will help to ensure
effective spontaneous urination prior to discharge. In
order to improve comfort and potentially decrease risk
of reobstruction, continued analgesia and sedation after
discharge may be helpful. While buprenorphine was
previously recommended for oral administration in cats,
its bioavailability has been called into question and it
may not be effective. Instead, gabapentin (10 mg/kg) has
potential as an oral analgesic, and could be given in con­
junction with continued administration of acepromazine
(0.5 mg/kg) for 5–7 days. As an alpha‐1 antagonist and
urethral relaxant, prazosin (0.25–0.5 mg per cat q12h)
has also been suggested to decrease urethral spasm.
However, a recent study failed to show an impact of pra­
zosin administration on the overall risk of reobstruc­
tion. Antibiotics should only be dispensed based on
results of urine culture taken after catheter removal.
Other recommendations which may help to decrease
the risk of reobstruction include increasing water intake
by switching to wet food, flavoring the water, or using a
running‐water bowl. In order to decrease stress, and
thereby potentially reduce risk of reobstruction, envi­
ronmental enrichment may be of benefit.
Urethral obstruction caused by urolithiasis often
requires surgical intervention for stone removal. In most
circumstances, successful catheterization is associated
with retrohydropulsion of stones into the urinary blad­
der, which can be removed by subsequent cystotomy. If
catheterization and deobstruction was not successful, it
may be necessary to perform a urethrotomy, but this can
be associated with significant risk of urethral stricture.
For more distally lodged stones, penile amputation and
perineal or scrotal urethrostomy may be preferred.

Minimally invasive techniques for stone removal, includ­
ing laser lithotripsy, percutaneous cystolithotomy, and
cystoscopic‐guided stone basket retrieval, are available
in some centers. Stones should always be submitted for
analysis to determine composition, with subsequent die­
tary management to decrease risk of recurrence.
Historically, dogs that presented with complete UO
secondary to neoplasia were euthanized, managed by
indwelling urinary catheters until NSAIDs (piroxicam),
chemotherapy or radiation therapy alleviated the obstruc­
tion, or underwent urinary diversion procedures that
are invasive and associated with moderate to severe
rates of morbidity. In the last decade, intraluminal
stenting for malignant urethral obstruction has been
employed with increasing frequency as a mechanism
to palliate the disease and restore urethral patency
(Figure 122.7).
In the largest series to date on urethral stent implanta­
tion, involving 42 dogs, the obstruction was relieved in
41 dogs and median survival was reported as 78 days,
with some dogs living for over a year after stent implan­
tation. The most common complication associated with
the procedure was urinary incontinence, graded as
severe in approximately 25% of the dogs. While place­
ment of a urethral stent for urothelial malignancy pro­
vides a minimally invasive option for animals with
complete urethral obstruction, it is solely a palliative
procedure and further tumor growth and/or spread
should be expected unless additional chemotherapy or
radiation therapy is pursued.
Surgical therapy is often advised for patients with ure­
thral stricture if the animal is stranguric or oliguric and
can result in an excellent outcome if the stricture is in the
penile urethra and either a perineal urethrostomy (feline)
or scrotal urethrostomy (canine) can be performed.
Treatment of urethral strictures is complicated when
they occur within the pelvic urethra as this will require
surgical exposure to the pelvic canal and resection of the
stricture. Additionally, surgical resection and anastomo­
sis to remove a urethral stricture may induce develop­
ment of a stricture at the anastomotic site as the tissues
heal. Options in these cases include urinary diversion
procedures such as a cystostomy tube, which are associ­
ated with a high rate of complications, balloon dilation of
the stricture, or placement of an intraluminal stent.
Urethral stenting for the palliation of urethral strictures
has been reported with good to excellent results in both
the dog and cat (Figure 122.8).
While effective in many cases, there is a risk of urinary
incontinence with stent implantation that is higher in
female dogs and in animals with greater amounts of ure­
thral coverage (e.g., longer stents). Anecdotally, stric­
tures have been observed to grow through the interstices
of bare‐metal stents. Consequently, covered stents may

Alternative Management Protocols for Feline UO

Unfortunately, the ability to provide the optimal treat­
ment course (close monitoring, IV and urinary catheteri­
zation) may be limited by owner financial constraints.
Predicated on the notion that there is a component of
functional obstruction (urethral edema and spasm), it
has been demonstrated that pharmacologic manipula­
tion (buprenorphine and acepromazine +/‐ dexmedeto­
midine), a low‐stress environment, and intermittent
cystocentesis can result in spontaneous urination with­
out the need for catheterization. This approach was
­successful in achieving spontaneous urination in approx­
imately 75% of cats in one study. However, while a rea­
sonable alternative to euthanasia, this protocol cannot
be recommended in lieu of traditional management
(which carries a reported success rate of 91–94%) as
no direct comparison between the two has been made.
Further, severely debilitated cats in need of emergency
stabilization, based on significant physical exam/meta­
bolic derangements, should be excluded from this
protocol.
In some cases, financial limitations might preclude the
ability to hospitalize for treatment. Under those circum­
stances, it may be necessary to offer euthanasia, ­especially
for severely affected patients (hypothermia, bradycardia,
lateral recumbency, etc.). For those patients presenting
in the earlier stages of obstruction that are not yet sig­
nificantly ill, it may be possible to provide care on an out­
patient basis, though this should be reserved as a last
resort. One option would be to provide sedation and
analgesia (acepromazine and buprenorphine) and blad­
der decompression through either passage of a urinary
catheter or cystocentesis. Catheterization would offer
the benefit of removing any physical obstruction within
the urethra but could also result in damage or irritation
to the urethral and an increased risk of reobstruction.
Cystocentesis would likely be less expensive to perform
and less injurious to the urethra, but might only provide
temporary relief if a significant physical obstruction
is present.
In either approach, the patient would be discharged in
the hopes that continued analgesia and sedation will
allow for spontaneous urination to occur. Aside from
anecdotal reports and clinical experience, there is no evi­
dence to support the merits of either of these approaches,
nor is there information regarding the likelihood of suc­
cess or recurrence. The client would have to be well
informed of the potential for treatment failure, and fol­
low‐up phone calls to determine response would be
strongly recommended.

Prognosis
Depending on the underlying cause, there is an approxi­
mately 15–40% incidence of recurrence with feline UO.
With repeated obstructive episodes, it may be necessary
to consider perineal urethrostomy (PU). This procedure
will decrease risk of UO, though will not impact underly­
ing FIC if present. In addition, patients with a PU may be
at increased risk for UTI.
Prognosis for UO in dogs is even more dependent on
the underlying cause. Obstruction secondary to urolithi­
asis is generally very good with successful catheteriza­
tion and stone removal, though there is potential for
recurrence. Proper dietary management to decrease
stone formation may help decrease this risk. Prognosis
for bladder/urethral/prostatic neoplasia is guarded, with
palliative efforts (chemotherapy, radiation, urethral
stenting) only providing temporary relief. Reported
median survival for dogs with urothelial malignancy
varies from days to nearly one year after diagnosis,
­
depending on the severity of disease and the treatment
pursued.

­Ureteral Obstruction
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Ureteral obstruction in small animals results from uro­
lithiasis, stricture, blood clots, congenital anomalies
(ureteropelvic junction stenosis), neoplasia, external
compression, severe ureteritis, or as a functional conse­
quence of urethral obstruction. In nearly all cats and
most dogs, urolithiasis is identified as the underlying
cause. A rare cause of ureteral stricture is the presence of
a circumcaval ureter, reported in four of 10 cats with
strictures in one series and also reported in case reports
of dogs. The consequences of ureteral obstruction vary
depending on several factors: whether one or both kid­
neys are affected, the acuity versus chronicity of the dis­
ease, whether the obstruction is partial or complete, and
the presence of any complicating co‐morbidities, such as
infection.
Ureteral obstruction may be complete or partial,
depending on whether any urine is able to flow beyond
the site of obstruction. The degree of obstruction dic­
tates the severity of any rise in hydrostatic pressure
exerted upstream of the obstruction – to the proximal
ureter, renal pelvis, and renal parenchyma. The effect of
this increased pressure on the proximal ureter and renal
pelvis is passive dilation of these structures, which can
become profound (Figure 122.9).
Similar to UO, the increased pressure upstream of a
ureteral obstruction is transmitted from the renal pelvis
to the renal parenchyma, specifically to the nephron and

Figure 122.9 Ultrasound images of ureteral obstruction in a dog (a) and cat (b). In both images, moderate to severe dilation of the renal

Bowman’s space, resulting in impairment or even cessa­
tion of glomerular filtration. With experimental acute
ureteral obstruction, renal blood flow initially increases,
but gradually declines as ureteral hydrostatic pressure
rises and the obstruction is not alleviated. Permanent
damage to the kidney occurs within days to weeks after
ureteral obstruction though if the obstruction can be
alleviated rapidly, there may be no permanent effect on
renal function. Experimental studies in dogs suggest the
obstructed kidney will recover only a fraction of its ini­
tial, normal GFR after weeks of complete obstruction
even if the obstruction is completely alleviated at that
time. In the setting of bilateral ureteral obstruction, the
effect on GFR is even more dramatic. This implies that
diagnosis of ureteral obstruction is an urgent problem
that requires rapid deobstruction to preserve renal func­
tion, particularly as animals with ureteral obstruction
often are older and likely have a degree of renal compro­
mise prior to the development of the obstruction.
Epidemiology and Signalment
Large‐scale epidemiologic studies of ureteral obstruction
in veterinary medicine are lacking. As described above, the
cause in most feline cases appears related to ureterolithia­
sis while the cause in dogs is often related to ureterolithiasis
or urothelial malignancy. The epidemiology of urolithiasis
(both upper and lower urinary tract) in small animals sug­
gests that from the 1980s to the early 2000s, there was an
increasing frequency of this condition in both dogs and
cats, concurrent with an increased proportion of calcium
oxalate calculi compared to struvite. This trend for increas­
ing calcium oxalate calculi in cats appears even more dra­
matic when only upper urinary tract stones are considered.
In dogs with ureterolithiasis, struvite and calcium oxalate
calculi seem to be found in a comparable proportion.

Breed predilections are observed in dogs with upper
urinary tract calculi, with miniature schnauzers, Lhasa
apsos, shih tzus, and Yorkshire terriers affected with
greater frequency than other breeds. No consistent
breed differences have been reported in cats specific to
ureterolithiasis. There are breeds of dog that are recog­
nized to have a greater incidence of urothelial malig­
nancy than others. Specifically, the Scottish terrier,
Shetland sheepdog, beagle, wire‐haired fox terrier, and
West Highland white terrier are reported to have an
increased risk.
The effect of gender on prevalence of ureterolithiasis is
unclear. It has been suggested that male cats are more
frequently affected by urolithiasis in general than
females, though reports evaluating solely ureteral stones
suggest a higher proportion of female cats. In dogs with
ureterolithiasis, there are fewer cases reported, but a
female majority was also observed. Female dogs have
been recognized as having a higher prevalence of urothe­
lial neoplasia compared to males; additionally, castrated
dogs of both sexes are at higher risk for transitional cell
carcinoma compared to sexually intact dogs.
History and Clinical Signs
The signs of ureteral obstruction are often nonspecific,
with vomiting, lethargy, and inappetence commonly
reported. Abnormalities in urination, such as pollaki­
uria, hematuria, or stranguria, can also be seen, which
may be related to concurrent lower urinary tract
­uroliths, lower urinary tract infection, or ureteral irri­
tation. Weight loss may be reported if the animal
has a chronic course of disease with compromised
renal function. Increased urination and thirst may also
be observed, associated with renal dysfunction if
present.

VetBooks.ir

122 Obstructive Uropathy

Diagnosis
Abdominal pain may be the only finding associated with
unilateral ureteral obstruction, as the animal’s renal
function from the contralateral kidney should be suffi­
cient to maintain renal values in a normal range.
Abdominal discomfort appears to be a more easily rec­
ognized sign in the dog than the cat. On physical exami­
nation, a poor body condition may be observed if the
obstruction has been chronic and renal dysfunction is
long‐standing. It is relatively common to observe cats
with marked discrepancy in renal size on abdominal pal­
pation, the so‐called “big kidney, little kidney” syndrome.
This is theorized to occur secondary to prior chronic
obstruction of the little kidney, which led to a reduction
in glomerular filtration and renal blood flow, progressive
nephron loss, renal fibrosis, and compensatory hyper­
trophy of the unobstructed big kidney.
Diagnostic testing involves arterial blood pressure
measurement, serum biochemical analyses to investigate
the degree of renal dysfunction and concurrent disease, a
complete blood count to screen for anemia or leukocyto­
sis, urinalysis and urine culture, and imaging. Abdominal
radiographs are advised to look for evidence of urolithi­
asis as most, at least in the cat, are calcium oxalate and
therefore radiopaque. However, radiography is imperfect
as small stones may be missed or findings interpreted as
stones may not be within the urinary tract. The presence
of calculi in the kidneys, bladder, or urethra as well as the
relative size of each kidney can also be investigated with
survey radiographs. For dogs with urothelial neoplasia,
an increased soft tissue opacity may be observed at the
bladder trigone or prostate. Confirmation of ureteral
obstruction, however, typically requires ultrasound (see
Figure 122.9). Ultrasound should be utilized to quantify
the magnitude of renal pelvic and ureteral dilation, the
presence, number, and location of uroliths throughout
the urinary tract, the existence of a stricture or area of
ureteral thickening, the location of a trigonal or other
extramural lesion compressing the ureter, an assessment
of renal blood flow, and the presence of any free abdomi­
nal fluid.
Therapy
Treatment is directed at providing the animal comfort
and alleviating the obstruction. Analgesia should be
given due to the pain associated with ureteral obstruc­
tion, related to stretch of the ureteral wall and renal cap­
sule resulting in activation of mechanoreceptors. Medical
therapy should be initiated as soon as a diagnosis of ure­
teral obstruction is made as it will be necessary to help
stabilize the animal and may aid in alleviating the
obstruction in a small proportion of cases. However,

medical therapy is typically insufficient to cure most ure­
teral obstructions, as the physical barrier (stone, tumor,
stricture) must be addressed.
Upper urinary tract calculi are typically calcium oxa­
late, particularly in the cat, and dietary dissolution will
therefore not be effective in most cases. Furthermore,
there is insufficient time to allow dissolution to take
place in the setting of a complete ureteral obstruction in
which rapid nephron loss is occurring. In the patient
with ureterolithiasis, intravenous fluid therapy should be
initiated as the animal is often dehydrated and an
increase in urine flow may help to move the calculus into
the bladder.
Ureteral relaxation and reduced ureterospasm can be
achieved by administration of an alpha‐receptor antago­
nist such as prazosin (0.25–0.5 mg per cat q12h) or the
smooth muscle relaxant amitriptyline (1 mg/kg PO
q24h). There are additional medications with greater uri­
nary selectivity now available on the human market,
such as tamsulosin, though there is only anecdotal evi­
dence of their use in animals. An additional strategy to
facilitate movement of ureteroliths is a mannitol infusion
(0.25‐0.5 g/kg over 20 min, followed by CRI at 1 mg/kg/
min) to promote an osmotic diuresis. Mannitol should
be given with caution in these animals, however, as
hypervolemia can develop – particularly in cats or dogs
with bilateral ureteral obstruction. In the dog, broad‐
spectrum antibiotics should be initiated as canine upper
urinary tract calculi are more likely to be infected than in
cats, which are typically sterile.
While medical therapy should be initiated once a diag­
nosis of ureteral obstruction is made, it must be recog­
nized that medical therapy is effective in only a small
portion (reported as less than 15%) of cats with obstruc­
tive ureteroliths. Medical therapy should be attempted
for no more than 12–48 hours in animals with ureteral
obstruction secondary to urolithiasis, depending on the
stability of the patient, with serial monitoring to evaluate
for progressive renal decline or movement of the stone. If
medical therapy is unsuccessful, or in the setting of ure­
teral obstruction secondary to urothelial malignancy
that will not respond rapidly to medical therapy, inter­
vention by surgery or minimally invasive therapy is
advised.
Currently, noninvasive therapy for ureteral obstruction
secondary to urolithiasis involves the use of extracorpor­
eal shock wave lithotripsy. This treatment modality
employs high‐energy shock waves directed through the
body and focused at the site to pulverize the urolith into
sufficiently small particles that can be safely passed out of
the body. This is the standard of care in the treatment of
human upper urinary tract calculi, but has not gained
wide use in veterinary medicine. Few veterinarians
employ this therapy in cats as the small size of the feline

ureter makes even small stone fragments problematic
and even in dogs there is risk of ureteral obstruction after
shock wave therapy of nephroliths. The likelihood of
ureteral obstruction following shock wave therapy can be
limited if a ureteral stent is implanted at the time of the
shock wave treatment. Extracorporeal shock wave litho­
tripsy is a consideration for dogs and appears well toler­
ated, though transient hematuria or shock wave‐induced
pancreatitis may occur.
In dogs, surgical ureterotomy for an obstructive uro­
lith is typically associated with a favorable outcome in
the hands of an experienced surgeon. In cats, however,
major complications were reported in a significant num­
ber of the cases, with a mortality rate of 18% in the larg­
est series from a highly experienced center. In light of
these figures, alternatives to surgical ureterolith removal
have been developed in recent years, including ureteral
stenting (Figure 122.10) and subcutaneous ureteral
bypass (Figure 122.11).

An indwelling ureteral stent is composed of a flexible
polymeric compound that has a loop at each end, which
help maintain the stent’s position throughout the ureter,
with one loop in the renal pelvis and the other in the
bladder. Ureteral stents may be placed endoscopically,
though this is most feasible in female dogs where a rigid
cystoscope and a comparatively larger urethra facilitate
the procedure. For cats, the stents are typically placed via
an open abdominal procedure with fluoroscopic guid­
ance. The stent may be placed antegrade through the
renal parenchyma after needle access into the renal pel­
vis, or retrograde through a cystotomy incision and visu­
alization of the ureterovesicular orifices. Reports of
ureteral stents in both dogs and cats suggest successful
implantation in greater than 95% of cases with low com­
plication or reintervention rates. The cat shown in
Figure 122.10 presented with a BUN of 280 mg/dL (refer­
ence interval, 13–30 mg/dL) and a creatinine of 20.5 mg/

In the authors’ experience, ureteral stents in cats pro­
vide acute resolution of the obstruction but have a mod­
erate risk for ureteral irritation and pollakiuria that can
be challenging to manage. Studies suggest one‐third of
cats with a ureteral stent will have dysuria either tran­
siently or permanently and that 19% of feline ureteral
stents will become obstructed. There is also an increased
risk of ascending urinary infection with a stent in place.
In human medicine, ureteral stents are left in place for
only 3–4 months in most cases to avoid stent encrusta­
tion and calcification. However, stents have been left
indwelling in cats for greater than five years that were
seemingly well tolerated (see Figure 122.10). In dogs,
ureteral stents for benign ureteral obstructions are well
tolerated, can be placed cystoscopically, and are often
removed once the obstructive stone has passed, avoiding
long‐term risk for stent dysfunction. The presence of a
ureteral stent induces passive ureteral dilation which
may allow a previously obstructive urolith to pass, after
which the stent can be removed via an outpatient cysto­
scopic procedure. Currently, the authors monitor ani­
mals with ureteral stents every 3–4 months by imaging
and urine culture. If stent malfunction develops, evi­
denced by recurrent infection, pollakiuria, obstruction,
abdominal pain, or stent migration/fracture, then the
stent is removed via cystoscopy or cystotomy.
To avoid eventual dysuria and potential complications
of a ureteral stent in cats, or for those animals in which a
stent cannot be placed, subcutaneous ureteral bypass
(a)

(b)

devices are commercially available. Subcutaneous ure­
teral bypass employs a nephrostomy tube and a cystos­
tomy tube, which are connected to a dual‐lumen vascular
port that is attached under the skin to the ventral body
wall. This port allows the system to be flushed at regular
intervals to avoid obstruction and facilitates urine sam­
pling (see Figure 122.11). At many centers, subcutaneous
ureteral bypass devices are now the treatment of choice
for obstructive urolithiasis in cats but are rarely implanted
in dogs where conventional surgery or temporary ureteral
stenting are often effective. Long‐term complications of
ureteral bypass devices include infection and biofilm for­
mation, encrustation and obstruction, and rarely signs of
dysuria. The rate of complications appears lower in cats
with a subcutaneous ureteral bypass device than was
observed with ureteral stents but routine surveillance
(imaging, system flushing, urine culture) is still required.
For animals with ureteral obstruction secondary to
urothelial malignancy, ureteral stenting is advised to
deobstruct the kidney and restore urine flow. In the dog,
this is done via percutaneous transabdominal access to
the dilated renal pelvis with a small needle, through
which a wire is advanced under fluoroscopic guidance to
the site of obstruction (Figure 122.12).
The wire is manipulated through the obstruction, into
the bladder, and out the urethra. The stent is then
advanced over this wire and into place within the renal
pelvis proximally and the bladder distally and urine now
flows through the stent lumen, bypassing the neoplastic
obstruction. A small series of 12 cases found that percu­
taneous stent implantation for trigonal urothelial carci­
noma was feasible in all dogs and the stents remained
patent for the remainder of the animals’ lives, which
ranged from 0.25 to 11 months.

Prognosis
The prognosis for ureteral obstruction is fair, dependent
on the chronicity of the obstruction, the ability of the
veterinarian to alleviate the obstruction, and the under­
lying disease process. If the obstruction has been in place
for some time, a return to normal renal function after
ureteral patency is restored is unlikely. In the setting of

urolithiasis, recurrence of stones and progression of
intrinsic renal dysfunction are common, but typically
manageable. In dogs with urothelial malignancy, the
prognosis by the time they have developed ureteral
obstruction is typically poor. However, ureteral decom­
pression in this disease can allow an improved quality of
life and give the patient additional time until conven­
tional therapy (e.g., chemotherapy) has an impact.

­Overview
Definition
Urine is a complex solution that contains multiple crystal
components. The ionic elements of crystals in urine are
referred to as crystalloids, which can be organic or inor­
ganic. Uroliths are organized assemblages of crystalloids,
combined with a small amount of organic matrix, located
within the urinary tract.
Urolith Formation
Formation of urinary calculi (uroliths) has been hypoth­
esized to occur through multiple mechanisms or pro­
cesses. Three of the more common of these theories are:
the precipitation‐crystallization theory: supersaturation
of urine with crystalloids is followed by growth of calculi
●● the matrix‐nucleation theory: an abnormal substance
in the urine is responsible for calculi development
●● the crystallization‐inhibition theory: the absence of a crit­
ical inhibitor (or the presence of a promoter) of crystal
formation is the primary factor in calculi development.
●●

All three of the above theories (individually or in combi­
nation) likely contribute to development of individual
uroliths.
Urine is commonly supersaturated with crystalloids,
and this is a prerequisite for urolith formation (Figure
123.1). Supersaturation of urine with crystalloids depends
on urine crystal volume, renal crystal excretion, urine
concentration, urine pH, and the presence of urolith
promoters or lack of inhibitors. Following establish­
ment of these supersaturation criteria, and dependent on

numerous patient‐related factors, urine crystals may
begin to aggregate into a nucleus. The crystal nucleus,
commonly referred to as the nidus, can then develop into
a urolith, aka the “stone.”
Additional theories regarding urolith development
have been postulated. One of these, homogenous nuclea­
tion, refers to the spontaneous precipitation of crystals
from a pure solution. This process is considered uncom­
mon in urine, and urine crystal formation is believed to
occur through heterogenous nucleation. This theory is
similar to the matrix‐nucleation theory, whereby another
substance (e.g., bacteria, inflammatory cells or debris)
acts as a nidus for crystal precipitation. Once again, after
the crystal nidus has formed, it may develop into a uro­
lith dependent on the following: degree and duration of
urine supersaturation, and sufficient time for the nidus
to remain in the urinary tract without being flushed out.
Factors that predispose to urine stasis also play an
important role in urolithiasis formation. Consequently,
factors that induce frequent and regular voiding of urine
may be protective and aid in prevention of urolith devel­
opment and progression.

­History and Physical Examination
History
Dogs and cats with uroliths may present for a variety of
animal owner concerns. Most commonly, dogs and cats
present with lower urinary tract signs (i.e., pollakiuria,
hematuria, stranguria) related to the irritating presence of
uroliths in the bladder or urethra. In patients with upper
urinary tract uroliths (i.e., nephroliths, ureteroliths), signs

in clinical signs related to uremia, unless there is con­
tralateral kidney disease.
Systemic disease signs, such as fever, weight loss or
dehydration, associated with uremia may be present
dependent on functionality of the renal parenchyma and
the presence of infection. Flank pain may be present with
ureteral obstruction or infection.

­Patient Signalment Related
to Specific Stone Types
In dogs and cats, signalment (breed, sex, age) and geo­
graphic region can provide clues to urolith composition
(Tables 123.1, 123.2).
Figure 123.1 One canine oxalate urolith from a 12‐year‐old
