of systemic disease may be noted (e.g., vomiting, lethargy,
anorexia, polyuria‐polydipsia secondary to uremia, etc.),
which can range in severity, as related to secondary infec­
tion or complete urethral obstruction. Other patients
may have subclinical disease, that is, no signs, and either
upper or lower urinary tract uroliths are discovered inci­
dentally, for example via radiographs, ultrasound, etc.
Physical Examination Findings
Physical examination is frequently normal but dependent
on stone type and, more importantly, location, abnor­
malities associated with either the lower or upper urinary
tract can occur and are detailed below. Systemic signs
(i.e., fever, dehydration, etc.) can be found in patients
with secondary infections or obstructive disease.
Lower Urinary Tract Urolith Physical Exam Findings

Palpation of urinary calculi can be challenging, particu­
larly in overweight or tense patients. If the bladder is
empty and there are multiple stones, a crepitant sensa­
tion may be noted on bladder palpation. Urethral stones
can sometimes be palpated rectally or via palpation of the
perineum or penile urethra. A large firm bladder may be
suggestive of urethral obstruction. However, in the case
of uroabdomen, the bladder may be empty (not palpable),
and the patient may have a tense and painful abdomen.
Upper Urinary Tract Urolith Physical Exam Findings

The patient may be subclinical. An enlarged kidney may
be palpated with hydronephrosis associated with ure­
teral obstruction in dogs and cats; however, most cats
have chronically small kidneys, even with obstruction.
Unilateral renal or ureteral obstruction should not result

Oxalate Urolithiasis
Calcium oxalate uroliths are usually composed of 100%
calcium oxalate, although some also contain varying
amounts of calcium phosphate. Additionally, concurrent
infection can change the composition of the stone, for
example calcium oxalate nidus encased in struvite shell.
Two crystalline forms of calcium oxalate uroliths can
occur: calcium oxalate monohydrate (whewellite) and
calcium oxalate dihydrate (weddellite). Calcium oxalate
monohydrate is more frequent in canine uroliths than
calcium oxalate dihydrate.
The surface characteristics of oxalate uroliths can vary
widely; uroliths may be smooth, mulberry shaped or have
sharp projections (Figure 123.2; see also Figure 123.1).
Epidemiology and Risk Factors

Calcium oxalate uroliths represented 48.1% (49.5%
including mixed stones) of all canine and feline uroliths
submitted to the Canadian Veterinary Urolith Centre
(CVUC) from 2009 to 2014 (see Table 123.2). Most upper
urinary tract uroliths in cats (98%) and half of those
found in dogs are composed of calcium oxalate.
Although calcium oxalate stones are not considered
infection induced, they may be associated with secondary
urinary tract infections (UTI). This is because the presence
of the uroliths is believed to affect the patient’s local immune
defenses. In one study, 52% of female dogs and 31% of male
dogs with calcium oxalate urolithiasis were found to have
concurrent bacteria present, that is, positive urine or uro­
lith cultures. However, other studies have not supported an
association between calcium uroliths and UTI.
Risk factors for calcium oxalate uroliths in dogs include
sex, and they occur more commonly in male than female
dogs. Additionally, neutered male dogs have an increased
risk of calcium oxalate uroliths compared with intact
males. Obese dogs are more likely to form calcium oxa­
late uroliths, which is similar to cats and humans.

Excessive urinary excretion of calcium (hypercalciuria) or

saturation of calcium oxalate than equivalent increases in
urinary calcium concentration on a molar basis.

recently been demonstrated that the absence of enteric
colonization of O. formigenes is a risk factor for CaOx
urolithiasis in dogs.

In humans, the mineral content of water may play a role
in calcium oxalate urolith formation. It is also thought
that increased sodium content can increase water intake
and offset its calciuretic effect. Increased water sodium,
calcium, or the absence of trace minerals such as zinc,
which chelates calcium, may increase the risk of calcium
oxalate urolithiasis. However, in cats, the source of water
(bottle, municipal, etc.) did not appear to affect the risk
of calcium oxalate urolithiasis. A similar study has not
been conducted in dogs.
Modifiers of Calcium Oxalate Crystal Formation

In humans, urine normally contains several natural
inhibitors of urolith formation and growth. Inhibitors
can be either organic or inorganic substances in urine
that reduce crystal formation, aggregation, or growth. A
defect or deficiency in these inhibitors may contribute to
urolith formation. Inhibitors of calcium oxalate include
citrate, magnesium, pyrophosphate, glycosaminogly­
cans, nephrocalcin, and Tamm–Horsfall mucoprotein.
Although little is known about these inhibitors in dogs, it
is suspected they may play a similar role as in humans.

Hyperadrenocorticism is associated with calcium oxalate
urolithiasis in humans and dogs. In humans, glucocorti­

mobilization of calcium from bone. Glucocorticoid‐

induced decreases in tubular resorption of calcium,

A recent study in humans demonstrated an association

explain why this breed is at high risk of calcium oxalate

Struvite Urolithiasis
Epidemiology

Struvite uroliths are typically composed of 100% magne­
sium ammonium phosphate hexahydrate. Struvite stones
may also contain varying amounts of calcium phosphate
(termed calcium apatite) or calcium carbonate phos­
phate (termed carbonate apatite). These uroliths are
commonly referred to as “infection stones” or “urease
stones” because, in dogs, they are primarily due to the
presence of urease‐producing bacteria. Struvite stones
are often multifaceted or pyramidal in appearance, espe­
cially when multiple urocystoliths are present, because
the adjacent surfaces are smooth and flattened. If soli­
tary, struvite may have sharp spiculated projections
(Figure 123.3). Struvite uroliths represented 35.5%
(43.6% including mixed stones) of all canine and feline
uroliths submitted to CVUC from 2009 to 2012 (see
Table 123.2). More recently, struvite urolith submissions
have increased and have exceeded the calcium oxalate

Figure 123.3 Bladder struvite uroliths retrieved from a 10‐year‐
old female spayed golden retriever. Source: Courtesy of Andrew
Moore, Canadian Veterinary Urolith Centre.

urolith submissions for small animals (2018 Minnesota
Urolith Center [MUC] Global Data generated by
Minnesota Urolith Center, February 2019).
Struvites are most commonly located in the lower uri­
nary tract (LUT) (95%). Risk factors appear related to sex
and associated higher bacterial infection risk, as they are
more frequent in female dogs (71–85% of struvite sub­
mitted to urolith centers) than male dogs (15–29%).
Certain breeds are predisposed to struvite uroliths (see
Table 123.1).
Etiopathogenesis

The majority of canine struvite uroliths are due to urinary
tract infection, most commonly related to bacterial infec­
tion with urease‐producing organisms. However, sterile
struvite urolithiasis has been reported in related cocker
spaniels. In dogs, Staphylococcus pseudintermedius is
cited as the most common urease‐producing bacterium
associated with struvite uroliths. Other less common
urease‐producing organisms include Pseudomonas spp.,
Klebsiella spp., Proteus, and Corynebacterium urealyticum. Urease‐producing mycoplasmas (termed urea­
plasma) such as Ureaplasma urealyticium may also cause
struvite urolithiasis.
Infection‐based struvite uroliths form when urease
cleaves urea to form ammonia and bicarbonate. The
available ammonium then combines with magnesium
and phosphate, normally present in urine, to form mag­
nesium ammonium phosphate hexahydrate (struvite)
crystals. Bicarbonate increases the urine pH (i.e., urine
becomes more basic), which then decreases the solubil­
ity of struvite crystals. Ammonium also damages the
urothelial glycosaminoglycan layer by acting as an irri­
tant. This allows struvite crystals and bacteria to adhere
to the urothelium and may promote production of an
organic matrix for the crystal–matrix interaction, lead­
ing to stone formation. Unlike in cats, where sterile stru­
vite urolithiasis may occur solely because of excess
mineral intake in the diet, infection with a urease‐pro­
ducing bacterium is associated with struvite urolithiasis
in most dogs.
Infection‐induced struvite uroliths may contain viable
bacteria trapped in the interstices of the stone layers.
Bacteria have been cultured from the core of struvite
uroliths that have been stored in formalin for years.
Dissolution or fragmentation of struvite uroliths may
release viable bacteria into the urinary tract and this may
cause reinfection unless appropriate antimicrobials and
duration of therapy are provided. If the bacteria isolated
from the urine and the urolith differ, a change in antimi­
crobial is only necessary if poor clinical response is
observed. If a nonurease‐producing bacterium is isolated
and subclinical bacteriuria is suspected, an antimicrobial

1127

VetBooks.ir

1128

Section 10 Renal and Genitourinary Disease

is rarely indicated. If a urease‐producing bacterium is
isolated, antibiotic therapy should be continued as long
as struvite uroliths are present. If therapy duration is
insufficient, UTIs will not resolve or a relapse of infec­
tion will likely occur.
Purine Urolithiasis
Epidemiology

Naturally occurring purine uroliths consist of uric acid
(and its various salts) and xanthine. Xanthine and uric
acid are successive biodegradation products in the
metabolism of purines (Figure 123.4). Purine uroliths
may be pure (100%) in composition, or less commonly,
may contain varying amounts of other minerals. The
term “urate” includes uric acid, ammonium urate, and
the other salts of uric acid, mostly sodium acid urate,
sodium calcium urate, and ammonium calcium urate.
Ammonium urate accounts for 86% of urate uroliths.
Urate uroliths are typically small, round, smooth
stones that are greenish‐brown in color (Figure 123.5).
There are often multiple urate uroliths present. Cross‐
sections of urate uroliths reveal a concentric appearance.
Xanthine uroliths are typically similar in size and shape
to urate uroliths but are usually yellow to brown
(Figure 123.6).
Purine uroliths accounted for 6.4% of canine uroliths
analyzed at the MUC between 1981 and 2007, making it
the third most common type of canine urolith in this
region. In Canada, purine uroliths represented 3.44% of
canine and feline uroliths submitted to the CVUC between
2009 and 2012 (see Table 123.2). The majority of urate
(97%) and xanthine (94%) uroliths that are submitted for

Risk factors for purine uroliths (and types of these)
include species, breed, age, and sex. Ammonium urate is
the most common (approx. 95%) naturally occurring
purine urolith in cats. Xanthine uroliths are uncommon
specimens submitted to the CVUC, having been diag­
nosed in only five cats and five dogs (0.02% of uroliths in
cats and 0.09% of uroliths submitted in dogs) from 2009
to 2012 (see Table 123.2). Uroliths composed of hypox­
anthine have not been recognized in cats.
Urate stones may be found in dogs of any age but are
most frequently retrieved from young to middle‐aged
dogs (see Table 123.1). Pure urate uroliths occur more

VetBooks.ir

123 Urolithiasis in Small Animals

often in males than in females. Female dogs may sponta­
neously void urate uroliths without being detected. In
dogs, urate uroliths are most commonly retrieved from
Dalmatians (61% of ammonium urate and 91% of sodium
and calcium urate uroliths). In cats, the typical patient
with urate uroliths is a pure‐bred neutered cat, 4–7 years
old, with uroliths in the bladder or urethra. The Siamese
breed seems to be overrepresented, along with the
Egyptian Mau and Birman breeds. Cat breeds that
had lower odds for urate urolith submission than
mixed breeds included Abyssinian, American shorthair,
Himalayan, Manx, and Persian. There is no sex predispo­
sition in cats.
Naturally occurring xanthine uroliths are rare and are
frequently retrieved from dogs that have been treated
with allopurinol.
Etiopathogenesis in Dogs

The purine metabolites, uric acid and xanthine, have
much lower solubility than that of allantoin. Consequently,
if urine is oversaturated with these substances, uroliths
can form. A high dietary intake of purines and purine
precursors, along with acidic urine, aids in urolith for­
mation. Infection with urease‐producing bacteria may
also promote formation of urate uroliths by increasing
ammonium ion concentration from the breakdown of
urea (see Figure 123.6).
Dalmatian Dogs

Dalmatian dogs are predisposed to the development of
urate uroliths because of their reduced transport of uric
acid into hepatocytes. This results in decreased conver­
sion of uric acid to allantoin, a subsequent moderate
increase in serum uric acid concentration (hyperurice­
mia), and then hyperuricosuria. The inheritance of
hyperuricosuria in Dalmatians is via a simple autosomal
recessive gene. The missense mutation in the SLC2A9
gene that encodes for a urate transporter is responsible
for this defect, and all Dalmatians are homozygous.
Despite excretion of relatively large quantities of uric
acid, not all Dalmatians form urate uroliths. It is esti­
mated that 25% of male Dalmatians will have urolithiasis
and it is suspected that other risk factors play a role in
dogs who become urate stone formers.
Non‐Dalmatian Dogs

Dogs other than Dalmatians accounted for approxi­
mately 30–60% of urate uroliths submitted for analysis.
Similar to Dalmatians, urolith‐forming bulldogs and
black Russian terriers have been shown to be homozy­
gous for a mutation in SLC2A9. However, the reasons for
development of urate uroliths in these non‐Dalmatian
breeds is unknown and does not appear associated with
hepatic dysfunction.

Hepatic Dysfunction

Hepatic dysfunction is associated with a reduced ability
to convert ammonia to urea and uric acid to allantoin.
Therefore, dogs suffering from hepatic dysfunction may
develop hyperammonuria and hyperuricuria, which
may result in urate urolith formation. The incidence of
urate urolithiasis appears to be higher in dogs with por­
tal vascular anomalies than with other causes of hepatic
dysfunction.
Xanthine

Xanthine is an important mediator in purine metabolism;
the drug allopurinol binds rapidly to (and inhibits the
action of ) xanthine oxidase, thereby decreasing conver­
sion of hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric
acid. The result is a reduction of serum and urine concen­
trations of uric acid, with an increase in serum and urine
concentrations of xanthine. As such, most xanthine uro­
liths in dogs form secondary to therapy with allopurinol
via this mechanism. This is particularly true when a diet
high in purines (meat based) is fed to these at‐risk dogs.
Naturally occurring xanthinuria has been reported in
Cavalier King Charles spaniels and dachshunds, and is
thought to reflect an inborn error of xanthine oxidase
activity.
Etiopathogenesis of Urate Urolithiasis in Cats

The pathophysiology of urate urolith formation in cats is
unknown. Ammonium urate uroliths have been recov­
ered from cats with portovascular anomalies. Such con­
genital anomalies can be found in male and female cats
and are typically are detected when cats are <12 months
of age. As Siamese cats are overrepresented among those
with portosystemic shunts, it is recommended to evalu­
ate them for underlying liver pathology when this breed
is presented with calculi. However, most cats with urate
stones do not have portovascular anomalies, and risk
factors for urate lithogenesis in cats are thought to
include an increase in renal excretion and urine concen­
tration of uric acid, the potential presence of promoters,
or the absence of inhibitors of urate urolith formation.
Xanthine urolithiasis is considered rare in cats, and
only five cats have been reported with spontaneous
xanthine urolithiasis and hyperxanthinuria in the last
20 years.
Calcium Phosphate Urolithiasis
Calcium phosphate uroliths are commonly called apa­
tite uroliths. Most pure calcium phosphate uroliths in
dogs are composed of hydroxyapatite. Brushite (cal­
cium hydrogen phosphate dehydrate) stones are less
common and whitlockite (calcium orthophosphate)
uroliths are rare.

Epidemiology and Risk Factors

Epidemiology

Pure calcium phosphate uroliths are rare in dogs, com­
prising only 0.3–0.6% of uroliths submitted to the MUC
per year and 2% of uroliths submitted to the CVUC (see
Table 123.2). Most calcium phosphate uroliths are mixed
in composition and are predominantly (≥70%) struvite or
calcium oxalate. Mixed stones are very common in cats
and dogs.
Risk factors for these uroliths vary based on stone con­
tent and sex, as pure hydroxyapatite uroliths occur
slightly more in male dogs (52%) than female dogs (48%)
whereas with brushite uroliths, male dogs (75%) are
more commonly affected than female dogs (24%).

Geographic location of the dog or cat plays a large role in
the prevalence of cystine urolithiasis. In the USA, urolith
prevalence has been reported as 1–2%. This is in con­
trast to parts of Europe where cystine urolithiasis has
been reported as 8% in Sweden and 26% in central Spain.
In Canada, cystine uroliths submitted to the CVUC rep­
resented 0.6% and 0.1% of all canine and feline stones,
respectively, between 2009 and 2012 (see Table 123.2).
Risk factors for cystine urolithiasis in dogs include age,
breed, and sex. Most affected dogs are males (98%),
although the disease is not genetically sex linked, and
young to middle‐aged (3–8 years). The exception to
these risk factors is the Newfoundland breed, where
these stones occur in both genders and often at a younger
age. Newfoundland dogs also appear to have an increased
incidence of cystine nephroliths.
Breed predisposition has varied widely over the last
15 years and urolith risk may depend on the dog’s geo­
graphic location. Unfortunately, most studies do not
compare breed distribution to the national registry for
dog breeds, nor are dog health insurance numbers,
which have provided the information for these studies,
common everywhere. Bull mastiff, Scottish deerhound,
English bulldog, Newfoundland, Chihuahua and dachs­
hund are the most common breeds affected in North
America, while terrier breeds (Yorkshire, Jack Russell,
and West Highland white) are the most affected in
the UK.

Etiopathogenesis

Several factors may influence urine calcium phosphate
saturation including urine concentration of calcium and
phosphate, urine pH, and the presence or absence of
inhibitors of calcium phosphate crystal formation.
Alkaline urine pH decreases the solubility of hydroxyapa­
tite and likely contributes to calcium phosphate uroliths.
Excessive urinary excretion of calcium (hypercalciuria)
and phosphate (hyperphosphaturia) may also induce cal­
cium phosphate urolith formation.
Co‐morbidities such as primary hyperparathyroidism
and hypercalcemia may influence stone formation, and
up to 30–40% of dogs with primary hyperparathyroidism
present with calcium‐containing uroliths. However,
hypercalcemic cats are more likely to have calcium oxa­
late rather than calcium phosphate uroliths.
It has been reported that some dogs with urinary tract
hemorrhage can develop blood clots mineralized with
calcium phosphate. These stones are not considered true
calcium phosphate uroliths as they do not contain the
same matrix proteins or ultrastructure as typical calcium
phosphate uroliths.
Cystine Urolithiasis
Dogs that develop cystine uroliths excrete an increased
amount of cystine (and to a variable extent other amino
acids) in their urine, a condition called cystinuria.
Cystine is composed of two cysteine amino acid mole­
cules linked by a disulfide bond. Urine solubility of cys­
tine is low, and dogs with cystinuria are predisposed to
urolith formation.
Canine cystine uroliths are typically pure, but a few
contain struvite, urate, silicate, oxalate or calcium apa­
tite. Typically, urolith appearance is smooth, oval and
light yellow to reddish‐brown. The size of cystine uro­
liths varies, but small and multiple stones are common.
The cystine uroliths submitted to urolith centers have
usually been retrieved from the LUT.

Etiopathogenesis

In normal dogs, cystine is freely filtered at the glomeru­
lus and then actively reabsorbed in the proximal tubules.
Cystinuria is a limited hereditary renal transport d
­ isorder
involving cystine and the dibasic amino acids ornithine,
lysine, and arginine, collectively known as COLA.
Instead of the normal >99% reabsorption in the proximal
renal tubules, these amino acids are lost in the urine;
however, only cystine causes a problem. In cystinuric
patients, the carrier proteins responsible for reabsorp­
tion are defective. The type of amino acids lost and their
quantity vary depending on the case. The low solubility
of cystine in acidic urine predisposes to the formation of
cystine crystals and uroliths in the urinary tract.
Cystinuria in humans and dogs is classified into several
distinct types depending on age of onset, severity, sex,
inheritance, and mutant gene. In dogs, type I‐a cystinu­
ria is an autosomal recessive disease caused by a SLC3A1
gene mutation common in the Newfoundland, Landseer,
and Labrador retriever breeds.
A nonsense mutation in exon 2 of the SLC3A1 (amino
acid – aa‐transport) gene has been identified as a
­molecular basis of the defect but the underlying genetic

VetBooks.ir

123 Urolithiasis in Small Animals

defect(s) in most cystinuric breeds of dogs have yet to be
identified. More recently, Labrador retrievers were found
to have a different mutation in the same gene, encoding
for a renal basic amino acid transporter. DNA‐based
genetic tests are available to detect abnormal cystine
excretion for some breeds of dogs.
Type II cystinuria is an autosomal dominant disease
that has been reported in Australian cattle dogs, border
collies (type II‐a) and miniature pinscher (type II‐b). In
the latter, the mutation affects the SLC7A9 gene and
encodes for intramembrane transporter protein.
The molecular basis for androgen‐dependent type
(type III) cystinuria is unknown. Type III cystinuria
regroups several breeds of dogs such as the English bull­
dog, English mastiff, French bulldog. Type III cystinuria
is typically detected later in life, is less severe clinically,
and appears to involve only males. Castration seems to
lower cystine excretion, therefore the mode of inherit­
ance is unclear. No gene mutation has been identified as
the cause of type III cystinuria.
Etiopathogenesis of cystine in cats is not well charac­
terized, but one study recently reported an SLC3A1
mutation causing cystinuria in a cat as well as three dif­
ferent SLC7A9 gene variants in four cats.
Resources for cystinuria testing (urine nitroprusside/
genetic testing) can be found at PennGen Laboratories:
http://research.vet.upenn.edu/penngen

crops. Plant sources implicated in silicate urolithiasis
include rice and soybean hulls and corn gluten feed.
Silicates may be high in certain home‐made diets and in
some groundwater from aquifers. In certain regions, soil
may contain high concentrations of silicate so consump­
tion of dirt and grass (pica) should be discouraged.
Experimentally, beagle dogs consuming large quanti­
ties of antacids containing magnesium trisilicate were
predisposed to silica uroliths. Homeopathic, other medi­
cations and vitamin‐mineral supplements may contain
silica, for example silica is used in anticaking materials
added to tablets.
Other Types of Urolithiasis
In dogs, mixed composition uroliths comprised 2.3% of
uroliths submitted to the MUC, with an additional 8.8%
of uroliths being described as compound. Compound
uroliths are likely to form when factors initially promot­
ing precipitation of one type of mineral are replaced by
factors promoting precipitation of a different mineral.
This can make compound uroliths poorly responsive to
medical management due to the need to treat each min­
eral type separately for dissolution or prevention.
The list below includes uncommon types of uroliths
submitted to major urolith centers.
Suture induced: some stones can be induced by residual
or retained suture material. Uroliths typically have a
piece of suture contained within the stone, or have a hole
where the suture was located (Figures 123.7 and 123.8).
●● Dried solidified blood calculi: calculi composed solely
of dried solidified blood have been removed from the
urinary tract of cats.

Silicate Urolithiasis
Epidemiology

Silica (silicon dioxide) uroliths are infrequently diag­
nosed. They account for 0.9% of specimens submitted to
the MUC and 0.7% of specimens submitted to the CVUC
between 2009 and 2012 (see Table 123.2). Silica‐contain­
ing nephroliths are rarely submitted to urolith centers,
but have been reported in native Kenyan dogs.
Some silica uroliths are pure, while others are composed
of different layers, with oxalate and struvite being the most
commonly associated minerals. Most silica uroliths have a
“jackstone” appearance; however, an outer layer (coating)
of another mineral type may mask this configuration.
Typically, multiple silica uroliths present and cross‐sec­
tion of the urolith usually reveals laminations.
The majority of dogs with silica uroliths are male, with
a mean age of 7.2 +/‐ 3.1 years (range 1–17 years).
Etiopathogenesis

Silica uroliths are thought to form due to individual ani­
mal increase in consumption of this mineral. Animal
protein contains very low concentrations of silica and
consumed dietary sources are likely plant origin, such as
direct ingestion of soil or ingestion of contaminated

Urine Sediment

Urolithiasis typically induces inflammatory urine sedi­
ment, such as pyuria (presence of white blood cells),
hematuria (red blood cells), and proteinuria. Bacteria may
also be present if there is a primary or secondary UTI,
(i.e., infection induced by urolith‐associated trauma).

●●

Urine pH

The urine pH of dogs and cats depends on many factors
and can be affected by method of measurement. A study
in dogs found that urine dipstick tended to overestimate
pH, in some cases yielding an alkaline result for a sample
that had a mildly acidic urine as determined by the refer­
ence method. As such, if accurate measurement of urine
pH is important, a pH meter should be used. Relatively
inexpensive hand‐held instruments are commercially
available.
Certain minerals are more soluble in acidic or alkaline
pH. For these reasons, some minerals tend to precipitate
and form stones in acidic (e.g., cystine, purine, calcium
oxalate) or in alkaline pH (e.g., struvite, calcium carbon­
ate, and calcium phosphate stones). At present, research
indicates conflicting results regarding the role urine pH
plays in the formation of calcium oxalate stones.
Crystals

Crystals may indicate the presence of uroliths or be nor­
mal, that is, no urolith. As such, specific therapy for crystal­
luria is not indicated unless a urolith is documented
through imaging, the patient has a history of urolithiasis or
urethral plugs (cats), and/or specific crystal types are noted.
In order to correctly identify crystalluria, urine should
be analyzed within one hour of collection. This is advised
because both calcium oxalate and struvite crystals can
form in vitro if there is a delay prior to analysis or due to
refrigeration. Crystal types that are not normally present
in the urine, and demand attention regardless of urolith
presence, include cystine, xanthine, and urate (excluding
Dalmatians).
Urine Culture

Figure 123.9 Melamine cyanuric acid removed from the bladder

Urine culture and susceptibility should be performed in
all patients with urolithiasis in order to detect infections
and start appropriate antibiotic treatment if necessary,

that is, there are concurrent clinical signs of infection.
Urinary tract infections can be the primary cause of uro­
lith formation (e.g., struvite uroliths in dogs), or they can
be secondary to urolith‐induced irritation of the urinary
tract. If the urine culture is negative despite a high suspi­
cion of UTI in a patient (i.e., a dog with struvite stones),
culture of the bladder wall and stone nidus, at the time of
stone removal, is strongly advised in order to accurately
direct any needed antimicrobial therapy.
Bloodwork
Complete blood count (CBC) is usually normal in
patients with urolithiasis. A left shift may (or may not) be
present with pyelonephritis or pyonephrosis. A serum
biochemistry may show evidence of liver dysfunction in
a dog with hepatic vascular abnormalities (portosys­
temic shunt [PSS]), microvascular dysplasia (portal
hypoplasia), or severe hepatic disease. The lab changes
can include increased alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
and alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and with hepatic dys­
function there can be low albumin, urea, and glucose.
Bile acid (pre‐ and postprandial) measurement is
strongly recommended if a young dog or cat presents
with bladder stones and clinical signs compatible with
PSS (i.e., signs of hepatoencephalopathy, polyuria/poly­
dipsia [PU/PD], poor growth) or increased liver enzymes.
Dogs with portovascular abnormalities are more likely to
have urate uroliths than those with other types of hepatic
dysfunction. Middle‐aged, small‐breed dogs with a por­
tovascular anomaly and good portal perfusion can have
normal chemistry panels with urate stones, making bile
acid testing indicated.
In cases of ureteral calculi resulting in urinary tract
obstruction, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine
may or may not be increased. This will depend on the
laterality (unilateral or bilateral obstruction) and under­
lying intrinsic renal damage due to the calculi. Azotemia
will not be present if the contralateral (nonobstructed)
kidney is normal. Most cats (88%) with unilateral ure­
teral calculi are azotemic (>90%), indicating the presence
of intrinsic renal disease in the contralateral kidney.

example of this is a calcium oxalate stone forming in an
at‐risk breed of dog after an incidence of struvite uro­
lithiasis due to bacterial infection.
Stone Layers

When a urolith is analyzed, it is named according to the
constituents making up the majority of the “stone”
(Figure 123.10). These layers consist of the following.
Nidus (center of the urolith): this may or may not be
composed of crystalline material and/or a foreign
body, such as suture material.
●● Stone: the stone may or may not be composed of the
same minerals as the nidus.
●● Shell: the layer(s) that surround the stone. The shell is
the outermost complete layer on the urolith.
●● Surface crystals: these may or may not be present on
the outermost surface of the urolith. They do not com­
pletely encase the urolith (incomplete layer).

●●

Ideally, all four layers of the urolith should be analyzed
separately and their respective mineral amounts listed.
Only quantitative analysis ensures that all urolith layers
are examined and provides an estimate of the mineral
content of each visible layer. This is important since con­
fusion over urolith content and therapy and prevention
can occur when only the outer layer is analyzed. This type
of confusion can also occur when using the qualitative

Imaging of the Urinary Tract
Radiography

Specific Tests to Detect Cystinuric Dogs

Most uroliths are radiopaque on survey abdominal radi­
ographs. Radiopaque uroliths include calcium p
­ hosphate,
calcium oxalate, struvite and silicate (Figures 123.11 and
123.12). Survey radiography is suitable for identification
of these radiopaque uroliths, ­provided they are greater
than approximately 2–3 mm in diameter. However, urate,
cystine, and xanthine uroliths are generally character­
ized as radiolucent or only slightly radiopaque on survey
radiographs. The failure rate for detection of uroliths by
survey radiography was 2–27% dependent on urolith
size and composition.
Clinicians may try to guess the chemical composition
of a urolith based on the density, shape, and number of
uroliths on radiographs. One aid for this type of “guessti­
mate” is the pneumonic POCUS, which is used by clini­
cians to remember the order of the stones that are most
radiodense to radiolucent: calcium phosphate, calcium
oxalate, struvite, silicate, cystine, and urate calculi.
Contrast‐enhanced radiographic procedures or ultra­
sound are needed to identify uroliths composed of com­
pounds similar to the radiographic density of soft tissue.
Double‐contrast cystography has been associated with
high sensitivity and low false‐negative detection rates
(Figure 123.13). Small uroliths are detected more reliably by
double‐contrast cystography or ultrasonography. However,
ultrasound is superior to double‐contrast cystogram in
experienced hands and for very small stones and sand.

On average, dogs with type I cystinuria have a several‐
fold higher urinary COLA excretion than non‐type I
cystinuric male dogs. A simple urinary screening test to
determine if a dog is cystinuric is available through the
Metabolic Screening Laboratory, Section of Medical
Genetics, at the University of Pennsylvania (http://
research.vet.upenn.edu/penngen). This test can detect
any type I cystinuric animal, but not necessarily all dogs
with non‐type I cystinuria. High‐performance liquid
chromatography can be further used to determine the
amount of cystine and other amino acids in urine.
However, this form of quantitative amino acid analysis is
currently restricted to a few laboratories (PennGen and
LaboKlin) and is relatively expensive. Based on studies,
dogs with either cystine levels of >200 μmol/g creatinine
or COLA values of >700 μmol/g creatinine are consid­
ered cystinuric. Moreover, for Newfoundlands and
Labrador retrievers, a breed‐specific mutation test is
available that detects not only cystinuric dogs but also
asymptomatic carriers. Finally, in mastiffs, a preliminary

Stone Characterization

Uroliths are defined based on their mineral composi­
tion as noted earlier. The following terms are used to
identify type.
Pure urolith: when 70% or more of the urolith is com­
posed of one type of crystalloid, it is named for that
crystal type. In dogs and cats, most stones have one
major crystal component.
●● Mixed urolith: when less than 70% of the urolith is
composed of one mineral, it is called a mixed urolith.
This means that the urolith does not contain one pre­
dominant mineral type but is a combination of two or
more types.
●● Compound urolith: this is a urolith in which each layer
is composed of a different mineral. Uroliths that have
formed around foreign material in the urinary tract are
often classified as compound. Suture material, urinary
catheter, metal pellets, plant material, hair strands,
and other foreign objects (ex. porcupine quill) have all
been reported to be a part of uroliths of various min­
eral types.

more sensitive than survey and contrast cystography

Ultrasonography allows simultaneous evaluation of
the upper urinary tract for nephroliths and ureteroliths.
Therefore, radiography combined with ultrasonogra­
phy are preferred over contrast radiography alone.
Ultrasound can detect upper urinary tract obstruction
that is characterized by renal pelvis dilation >13 mm.
However, pelvis dilation can be iatrogenic (diuresis) or
secondary to different diseases such as chronic kidney
disease or pyelonephritis. Although a renal pelvis
>13 mm may indicate ureteral obstruction, the absence
of dilated renal pelvis does not rule out an upper urinary
tract obstruction. The combination of proximal ureteral
dilation and normal kidney pelvis diameter can be asso­
ciated with ureteral obstruction in cats. In a recent study,
25% of cats with confirmed ureteral obstruction had a
renal pelvis <13 mm but a proximal ureteral dilation. In
25% of cats with ureteral obstruction, ureteropyelog­
raphy is necessary to determine the cause of the
obstruction.
Computed Tomography

Determination of urolith composition using computed
tomographic (CT) peak attenuation measurement has
been described in vitro. In humans, this technique is
preferentially used in order to detect uroliths and also to
predict their composition. CT may be more specific for
ureteral calculi than either radiography and/or ultra­
sonography in cats.

Ultrasonography

Ultrasonography is a cost‐effective tool in the diagno­
sis of urolithiasis but it may overlook some important
aspects of the stones that can help the clinician predict
the nature of the uroliths, such as surface contour and
shape. One limitation of ultrasound is that it often
overestimates urolith size, so radiographs should be
used for determining size when possible. Ultrasound is
also less reliable than radiography for predicting the
number of stones and their location. Finally, ultra­
sound only provides evaluation of the most proximal
portion of the urethra and therefore cannot replace
radiography.
Ultrasonographic examination can detect radiopaque
and radiolucent uroliths. One study compared survey
and contrast radiographs, pneumocystography, double‐
contrast cystography, and ultrasound using a 7.5 MHz

Educated Guess
Determining the type of urolith based on imaging stud­
ies alone is very risky. This type of “guesstimate” of uro­
lith composition based on the radiolucency of a stone
and its shape can lead the clinician to misdiagnosis
(Figure 123.14). In certain scenarios the chemical com­
position of uroliths may be predicted based on patient
signalment, in combination with the results of urinalysis,
urine culture, and radiographs. However, it must be
understood that this technique can lead to error and is
not advised as the best method of urolith identification.
In situations where uroliths are not available for analysis
or are pending analysis, the guesstimate may need to be
used; however, communication to clients that errors may
be made with this technique and verification of stone
type (when practical and possible) are ideal. Unfortunately,
this verification cannot be made until stone analysis
occurs. For example, the clinician can make an educated
guess as to the likelihood that a given stone is com­
posed of struvite based on finding a urease‐positive

breed (ex. female bichon frise). Certain breeds are also
predisposed to a specific type of urolith which makes
guesstimating a bit less risky, for example Dalmatians
(see Table 123.1).
As mentioned, there are multiple “traps” or pitfalls to
avoid when guesstimating the chemical composition of
a urolith. Areas where errors can occur include urine
pH, urinalysis and crystalluria, urine culture results,
and radiographic density of the stone. Urine pH can be
influenced by meals and time of day. First morning pre­
prandial urine is typically the most acidic and concen­
trated sample of the day. After eating, the pH will
become more alkaline, often referred to as the “alkaline
tide.” Urine pH is also affected by stress and hyperventi­
lation, leading to respiratory alkalosis and consequent
urine alkalinization, for example a stressed dog panting
in clinic. Additionally, an acidic pH does not rule out
the presence of struvite stones. One example of this
would be a compound urolith made of a struvite core
surrounded by an oxalate shell. The pH may also be
alkaline if there is concurrent infection with urease‐
producing bacteria, while the predominant urolith
type may be unrelated to infection, for example a cal­
cium oxalate stone and concurrent Staphylococcus spp.
infection.
Similarly to urine pH pitfalls, crystalluria is not a con­
sistent feature of the urinalysis in dogs and cats with uro­
liths. For example, in one study of 30 cats with struvite
urocystoliths, struvite crystals were only detected in 17
patients. Additionally, dogs and cats may have a small
number of struvite or calcium oxalate crystals, but other
types of crystals do not typically form in vitro.

­Medical Management of Lower
Urinary Tract Stones
It is ideal to identify urolith type prior to initiation of dis­
solution protocols, and if uroliths are small enough,
voiding or catheter retrieval may be possible and allow
for this. Unfortunately, stone composition identification
is rarely possible prior to the need to make therapy deci­
sions, and best “guesstimate” strategies are warranted in
most cases. As such, it is imperative to perform diagnos­
tic studies (urinalysis, urine culture, radiography) to
evaluate urolith size and location and to provide the
most information to guide therapy as available.
Attempts to medically dissolve uroliths are not always
the least expensive method of management, nor is medi­
cal dissolution an option for all stone types, such as cal­
cium oxalate. For other urolith types (e.g., struvite), the
cost of diet and antimicrobial therapy along with the cost
of the recheck appointments and imaging should be dis­
cussed thoroughly when considering medical dissolu­
tion. Similarly, animal owner communication to ensure
compliance is essential in order for medical dissolution
strategies to be successful.
Rationale for Medical Dissolution
Medical dissolution of amenable urolith types consists of
reducing the concentration of the calculogenic material
in the urine and increasing its solubility.
Regardless of urolith type, increasing water intake
through diet and via increased water consumption will
assist in dilution of urine crystalloids and help prevent
ongoing crystal formation. This may also aid in flushing
existing stones from the bladder in female dogs. The aim

VetBooks.ir

123 Urolithiasis in Small Animals

of water increase strategies is to obtain a urine specific
gravity of <1.020.
Indications for (and Limitations of) Medical
Urolith Dissolution
Urolith Type

Struvite, urate, and cystine stones in dogs may be amena­
ble to medical dissolution; however, the uroliths must be
located in undersaturated urine for this to occur. This
requires intervention with diet and urine dilution strate­
gies, along with appropriate therapy of concurrent bacte­
rial infections. Dissolution success is much lower for
urate and cystine stones than struvite, and in cats, only
struvite uroliths are responsive to medical dissolution. In
cats, low‐protein diet and allopurinol has been reported
as effective in urate stone dissolution; however, until fur­
ther studies looking into safety and efficacy of this treat­
ment are performed, mechanical removal of bladder or
urethral urate uroliths is advised. Mechanical urolith
removal is recommended for bladder or urethral cystine
stones in cats, in part because 2‐MPG (Thiola®, t­ iopronin)
is toxic in cats, and is only effective about 60% of the time
in dogs.
Urolith Location

Medical dissolution for specific stone types can be suc­
cessful, but is more efficient when uroliths are located in
an area where they are in constant contact with urine,
such as the bladder. Suspected struvite nephroliths or
ureteroliths should be medically dissolved unless they
are too large to be effectively bathed in urine.
If uroliths are obstructive, relief of obstruction with a
minimally invasive approach and rapid control of infec­
tion should preserve kidney function.
Obstructive ureteroliths cannot be dissolved by medi­
cal or dietary protocols unless a ureteral stent is placed
concurrently. Urethroliths are typically not amenable to
dissolution, although they may be flushed into the blad­
der by retrograde hydropulsion and then dissolution can
be attempted.
Calcium oxalate uroliths are not amenable to medical
dissolution regardless of location, and must be removed
from the urinary tract mechanically. In cats, because
more than 90% of feline upper urinary tract stones are
composed of calcium oxalate, dissolution should not be
attempted with obstructive nephroliths or ureteroliths.
Silica uroliths are also thought to be unresponsive to
medical dissolution.
Size and Number of Uroliths

The size and number of the stones will influence rapidity
of dissolution but do not dictate the likelihood of ther­
apy success in stones that are amenable to dissolution.

Since the rapidity of dissolution is related to the size and
surface area of the urolith being exposed to urine, one
large urolith will take longer to dissolve than multiple
small uroliths. An analogy for this is that one large ice
cube will dissolve more slowly than an equal volume of
crushed ice. The rate of dissolution is influenced by the
surface area of the urolith exposed (“bathed”) in under­
saturated urine.
Presence of Obstruction

Medical dissolution is contraindicated in patients with
obstruction of the urinary tract. Relieving urinary tract
obstruction in those cases is mandatory in order to avoid
consequences such as postrenal azotemia, irreversible
renal damage, bladder rupture, and death.
Risk of Obstruction in Males

Medical dissolution of urocystoliths in male dogs is asso­
ciated with a risk of urethral obstruction once the uro­
cystoliths are small enough to pass into the urethra. The
risks and clinical signs of urethral obstruction should be
explained to the owner if medical dissolution is elected
in male dogs, and regular monitoring of urination is rec­
ommended. Medical dissolution should only be tried in
male dogs after clear owner communication and assur­
ance of owner compliance and ability to observe and act
on clinical evidence of obstruction.
Infection‐Induced Urolith

If the urease‐producing bacterium is isolated from uro­
lith culture, appropriate antibiotic therapy based on
urine culture and susceptibility must be administered
during the entire urolith dissolution period. Otherwise,
the persistence of infection with a urease‐producing
organism will confound dissolution of the stones. Despite
diet change, concurrent urinary tract infection will
maintain alkaline urine and promote urolith formation
and growth.
Dietary Factors

Limitations of medical dissolution are inherent to the
diet and medical therapy needed for the given urolith; for
example, an acidifying diet with low protein and caloric
content should not be fed to a pregnant or lactating
bitch. Similarly, thoughtful consideration of nutritional
growth requirements in young dogs and kittens needs to
occur when a diet lower in purines (protein) is indicated
for medical urolith dissolution (e.g., urate uroliths).
Similarly, a diet with a high salt or fat content should be
avoided in a patient with congestive heart failure or pan­
creatitis, respectively, as these patients may require vary­
ing levels of sodium or fat restriction for their concurrent
medical condition.

Protocol for Medical Management
and Prevention of Individual Urolith Types
Calcium Oxalate Uroliths
Dissolution of Calcium Oxalate Uroliths

At present, calcium oxalate stones cannot be dissolved
through medical (nutritional) means in dogs and cats. As
such, removal or bypass of these uroliths by different
interventional methods is recommended. As upper uri­
nary tract stones in cats are predominantly composed of
calcium oxalate (>98%), medical dissolution is also not
recommended in these patients.
Follow‐Up and Prevention of Calcium Oxalate Uroliths

Dietary therapy has been recommended to help prevent
recurrence of calcium oxalate stones. Nutritional strate­
gies to aid prevention of calcium oxalate stones in cats or
dogs primarily focus on increasing water intake via feed­
ing canned or wet food or by adding water to dry food.
These techniques help to increase dilution of urine and
flush crystals from the urinary tract, and one study
showed that feeding canned food to a group of dogs
decreased their risk of calcium oxalate compared to
feeding a dry diet.
Medical management that is believed to prevent recur­
rence of calcium oxalate urolithiasis includes the follow­
ing factors.
Increased water content of food (>75% water: high
moisture).
●● Avoidance of dietary urinary acidification (pH <6.25
cats and <6.6. dogs).
●● Correction of underlying hypercalcemia. In cats with
recurrent CaOx stones and idiopathic hypercalcemia,
there may be a benefit to feeding a high‐fiber diet in
association with potassium citrate therapy.
●● Dietary sodium increase. Controversial at this time.
Feeding high‐sodium diets (3.5 g/1000 kcal) is not a
substitute for increased dietary moisture, as had been
previously thought, and any benefit of dietary increase
in salt is believed to be short‐lived.
●● Management with potassium citrate in cats and dogs
with persistence of acidic urine, and consideration
of thiazide diuretics if recurrence despite other
interventions.
●● Dietary protein restriction. At present, the recommen­
dation to restrict dietary protein in these patients is
controversial and it is very difficult to reduce dietary
protein without concurrent dietary phosphorus reduc­
tion. Unfortunately, lower phosphorus has been asso­
ciated with a higher risk of calcium oxalate uroliths.
This is due to low diet phosphorus leading to increased
intestinal absorption of calcium and increased calci­
triol production, which then leads to further calcium
gastrointestinal absorption and calciuresis.
●●

Avoidance of calcium‐containing supplements in at‐
risk patients.
●● Reduction in foods rich in oxalate precursors.
Examples of these include chocolate, nuts, beans,
sweet potatoes, wheatgerm, spinach, rhubarb. For a
complete list of the oxalate content in foods, please
visit the Oxalosis and Hyperoxaluria Foundation web­
site: www.ohf.org.
●●

In dogs, the diets recommended to achieve the above
goals are those that have undergone specific urinary test­
ing (i.e., CORI, RSS, Activity Product Ratio) to reduce
risk of calcium oxalate formation. Examples of these
diets include Hill’s c/d, Purina St/Ox, and Royal Canin
S/O. Unfortunately, the ideal diet to prevent calcium
oxalate urolith recurrence remains unknown.
Despite diet modification, recurrence in animals with
CaOx is high: 33% at two years in cats and up to 57% at
three years in dogs. If calcium oxalate uroliths recur
despite dietary therapy, the use of medications such as
thiazide diuretics or potassium citrate may benefit spe­
cific patients.
Potassium citrate supplementation has been shown to
reduce recurrence of calcium oxalate uroliths in humans.
In veterinary patients, there are conflicting opinions on
the utility of potassium citrate for prevention of calcium
oxalate urolithiasis. In normal dogs, potassium citrate
supplementation did not significantly increase the mean
citrate excretion, although in three miniature schnauzers
supplementation did increase urinary citrate excretion
and lower relative calcium oxalate supersaturation. In
another study, potassium citrate did not increase mean
urinary citrate concentration but did cause a dose‐
dependent increase in urine pH. If calcium oxalate crys­
talluria is persistent or calcium oxalate uroliths recur,
potassium citrate is commonly recommended to achieve
a urine pH of 6.5–7.0 using a dose of 150 mg/kg PO q24h.
The serum potassium should be initially monitored
monthly during potassium citrate supplementation and
the dose reduced if hyperkalemia occurs.
Thiazide diuretics are proven to reduce the recurrence
of calcium oxalate urolithiasis in humans by reducing
urinary calcium excretion. However, there are conflict­
ing results for dogs, and in normal dogs, administration
of chlorothiazide did not reduce urinary calcium excre­
tion. In contrast, administration of hydrochlorothiazide
decreased urinary calcium excretion and urine calcium
concentration in dogs with calcium oxalate urolithiasis.
Reduction in urinary calcium was greatest in dogs with
the highest pretreatment urine calcium concentrations
when combined with using Hill’s Prescription Diet u/d.
As thiazide diuretics contribute to urine acidification,
concomitant administration of potassium citrate may be
recommended. Hydrochlorothiazide (2 mg/kg PO q12h)

VetBooks.ir

should be considered in dogs that have persistent cal­
cium oxalate crystalluria or recurrence of calcium oxa­
late urolithiasis despite dietary therapy. This drug can
cause severe gastrointestinal (GI) side‐effects.
Decreased serum vitamin B6 concentrations were
detected in a small number of oxalate stone‐forming
dogs compared to nonstone formers. Based on this study,
supplementation of vitamin B6 (2–4 mg/kg PO q24–48h)
could be considered in repeat stone formers. Vitamin C
is converted to oxalate, so vitamin C supplementation
may contribute to hyperoxaluria and increased risk of
calcium oxalate urolithiasis. Vitamin D supplementation
increases intestinal absorption of calcium, thereby pro­
moting hypercalciuria and increased risk of calcium oxa­
late urolithiasis.
Dietary recommendations for prevention of calcium
oxalate uroliths in cats are thought to be similar to those
in dogs, although higher salt levels are sometimes used
to aid increased urination. In addition, one two‐year
study in cats showed no significant difference between
two diets that differed in calcium and magnesium con­
tents and in urinary pH potential. Primary hyperoxaluria
can occur in cats. Examples of diets that have undergone
urinary testing for reduction of calcium oxalate include
Hill’s c/d Multicare (canned and dry), Purina UR St/Ox
(canned and dry), and Royal Canin S/O (canned, chunks
and gravy, and dry).

to eradicate UTI throughout the diet treatment and is
likely the most important facet of medical dissolution of
struvite uroliths. The average time of dissolution of
canine infection‐induced struvite urocystoliths on the
Hill’s s/d diet was approximately 2–3 months in dogs.
This diet should not be continued beyond this time as it
is not meant to be a long‐term diet.
Feeding small meals throughout the day rather than
one or two large meals may prevent postprandial alkaline
tide and is associated with more acidic urine production
and less struvite crystalluria.
The use of urinary acidifiers has been suggested in
dogs because struvite and hydroxyapatite are most solu­
ble in acidic urine (pH 6.0–6.5). In most dogs with infec­
tion‐induced struvite uroliths, eradication of the UTI
with dietary modification will return urine pH to the
acidic range. Use of urine acidifiers in these cases is not
indicated.
Most clinical symptoms of lower urinary tract inflam­
mation resolve after the first 10 days of antibiotic and
diet therapy. However, antibiotic and diet therapy should
be continued for one month beyond radiographic evi­
dence of urolith dissolution or one month beyond stone
removal. Although feeding a dissolution diet is advised,
struvite uroliths have been managed with effective con­
trol of the underlying UTI alone.

Struvite Uroliths
Dissolution of Struvite Uroliths in Dogs

Examination of urine pH, specific gravity, sediment, and
culture is recommended at 5–7 days after starting
­therapy, and then every four weeks until the stones are
dissolved (Table 123.3). Once dissolution (based on radi­
ographic evidence) or removal is accomplished, a urine
culture should be obtained at four and eight weeks later,
with cessation of antibiotic and dietary therapy four
weeks after resolution. Urine culture and radiographs
should then be repeated every three months for one year
and then every six months thereafter. The goal is to
maintain the average urine pH 6–6.5, the average urine
specific gravity <1.020, the sediment free of significant
crystalluria, and the dog free of bacterial infection.
In dogs with a history of urinary tract infections, pro­
active and routine urine culture and susceptibility is rec­
ommended. This is particularly important if co‐morbid
situations arise (e.g., hyperadrenocorticism, renal dis­
ease) that may predispose to the development of a uri­
nary tract infection.
The need for specific ongoing dietary therapy for pre­
vention of struvite uroliths in dogs is unknown. Since the
majority of dogs have infection‐induced struvite uro­
liths, it is likely that effective control and prevention of
infection alone would be sufficient to prevent recur­
rence. However, dietary therapy to lower urine concen­
tration (canned food or addition of water) or minimize

Struvite uroliths in dogs are almost always due to infec­

The calculolytic diets most commonly advised for

Medical Management of Struvite Uroliths in Cats

Struvite uroliths in cats are typically sterile. Since stru­
vite is more soluble in acidic urine, any factors that may
contribute to urine alkalinization should be assessed
(e.g., vegetable protein diet, familial history, obesity/
inactivity leading to urine stasis). Although struvite
stones in cats are generally sterile, lower urinary tract
infection can occur and predispose to alkaline urine.
Urinary tract infections are more common in cats <1
year and >10 years, as well as in those with compro­
mised host defenses (e.g., diabetes mellitus, perineal
urethrostomy, renal disease, urinary tract neoplasia,

upper urinary tract stone disease, etc.). A thorough urine
assessment and culture should not be omitted in at‐risk
patients. Upper urinary tract stones in cats are almost
never struvite.
The calculolytic diets most commonly advised for
struvite stone dissolution in cats are Hill’s s/d and Royal
Canin S/O. Hill’s Feline s/d diet has been used success­
fully to dissolve stones in cats with struvite urolithiasis.
The average time for dissolution of sterile struvite cysto­
liths in cats fed this diet was about 30 days. Dissolution
of feline infection‐induced struvite stones, which are
uncommon, took 60–90 days. Urinary acidifiers are not
useful or advised in cats fed Hill’s c/d, s/d, or soft‐moist
diets because these foods are already acidifying.
Dissolution of feline struvite stones in cats eating Royal
Canin Urinary SO (canned and dry) occurred in a median
of 18 days (range, 10–55 days) in 31 of 39 cats.
Prevention and Follow‐Up of Struvite Uroliths in Cats

Radiographs are recommended after stone removal or
dissolution to ensure all uroliths have been eradicated.

After this time, examination of urine pH, specific gravity,
and sediment is recommended at two weeks, four weeks
and then every three months for one year. The aim is to
maintain the average urine pH <6.5, the urine specific
gravity <1.030 and the sediment free of significant crys­

significant crystalluria and uroliths, rechecks may be
decreased to twice yearly.
For cats with infection‐induced struvite uroliths, fol­

one week after the end of the antibiotics. Further assess­
ment is recommended in cats that have repeat urinary
tract infections and struvite crystalluria.
Examples of diets recommended for use in struvite
prevention due to their known efficacy in reducing mag­
nesium and phosphorus levels and urinary acidification
properties include Hill’s c/d Multicare (canned and dry),
Purina UR St/Ox (canned and dry), and Royal Canin S/O
(canned, chunks and gravy, and dry). Many of the lifes­
tage diets from Hill’s, Purina, and Royal Canin are also
aimed at concurrent struvite urolith prevention. It is par­
ticularly important in cats that therapy is directed at
reduction of urine concentration, and thus a high‐mois­
ture diet is advised.
Ammonium Urate Uroliths
Dissolution of Ammonium Urate Uroliths in Dogs

Medical dissolution of urate can be achieved, although it
may not always be in the patient’s best interest, such as
urinary tract obstruction.
Dissolution of urate is only indicated in patients with
an underlying defect in purine metabolism and not in
cases of liver dysfunction. Nutritional therapy for urate
dissolution is achieved with a combination of the
following.
Urine alkalinization: alkaline urine contains low
amounts of ammonia, which subsequently reduces
ammonium urate. Feeding a low‐protein (purine) diet
and/or with potassium citrate supplementation pro­
duces alkaline urine.
●● Increase in urine volume: a canned diet (or addition of
water to the diet) is preferred for this reason. A low‐
protein diet also decreases the concentration of urine
by “wash‐out” of the medullary concentration gradient
(via low urea). The goal is a urine specific gravity of
<1.020.
●● Decreasing the excretion of ammonium ions: feeding a
diet low in protein‐purines decreases urea production
and consequently ammonium and its ions.
●● Decreasing the excretion of uric acid: feeding a diet low
in purines and their precursors will aid in this. The
purine content of proteins varies (e.g., it is high in
organ meats and fish), and by using selected protein
●●

sources (plant, egg white), severe protein restriction is
not mandatory to achieve a low urinary urate level.
●● The desired urine pH for urate dissolution is approxi­
mately 7.0. Targeting a higher urine pH (>7.5) could be
detrimental because it could favor the formation of
calcium phosphate urolith. Potassium citrate (50–
150 mg/kg q12h) may be needed to alkalinize the urine
if diet alone is not enough to sustain an average urine
pH of approximately 6.8–7.0. Obtaining both a fasting
and postprandial (2–6 hours after a meal) urinary pH
will allow for consistent and accurate medical titration
of potassium citrate. The patient should be monitored
for hyperkalemia when higher doses of potassium cit­
rate are used.
Hill’s Prescription Diet canine canned u/d (the most
purine‐restricted diet currently commercially available)
and allopurinol (30 mg/kg/day, divided q8–24h) has been
recommended for medical dissolution of urate stones.
This diet is very low in protein‐purine and contains
potassium citrate and calcium carbonate for urinary
alkalinization. In a clinical study of 25 dogs with ammo­
nium urate uroliths fed this diet and treated with allopu­
rinol, complete urolith dissolution occurred in nine dogs
(36%), partial dissolution in eight (32%), and no dissolu­
tion in eight (32%). The mean time for urate urolith dis­
solution was 3.5 months. Similar results were reported
when this diet was used for dissolution of sodium urate
uroliths. Owners must be fully compliant (i.e., no other
food or treats should be given) if this option is selected.
Careful patient monitoring is necessary as these uroliths
are prone to migrating into the urethra where lower uri­
nary tract obstruction can occur. However, Hill’s u/d is
contraindicated in dogs prone to pancreatitis or hyper­
lipidemia due to its high fat content.
Allopurinol is a specific enzyme inhibitor that causes
partial blockage of the purine degradation pathway
above the level of uric acid (see Figure 123.6). Allopurinol
inhibits the enzyme xanthine oxidase. As a result, hypox­
anthine, xanthine, and urate are all excreted in the urine.
Each of these purine metabolites has a different urinary
solubility; hypoxanthine is very soluble, whereas xan­
thine and urate are only poorly soluble. Allopurinol will
reduce the oxidation of xanthine to urate. Consequently,
xanthine concentration in the urine increases.
The dose of allopurinol recommended is variable
(5–30 mg/kg/day, divided q8–24h). It has a dose‐depend­
ent half‐life of 2.5–3 hours in dogs. For dissolution of
ammonium urate stones, the higher dose is recom­
mended (15 mg/kg q12h). Allopurinol and its metabo­
lites are excreted via the kidney, therefore the dose
should be reduced in patients with renal failure. In addi­
tion, any medications the dog is receiving need to be
carefully assessed. For example, allopurinol can inhibit

1141

VetBooks.ir

1142

Section 10 Renal and Genitourinary Disease

metabolism of azathioprine, and can reduce metabolism
of anticoagulants, theophylline or aminophylline. Ciclo­
sporin (Atopica®) increases uric acid levels in urine and
should not be used in dogs with urate urolithasis.
There is a risk of xanthine stone formation with allopu­
rinol use. Careful monitoring for the presence of xan­
thine is strongly advised in all patients on allopurinol, as
it is likely to occur in patients treated with allopurinol
while fed a nonpurine‐restricted diet. This may also
occur in patients treated for leishmaniosis with allopuri­
nol. Clinicians may be able to dissolve xanthine uroliths
by discontinuing allopurinol and starting a low‐purine
diet. Alternatively, a preliminary study evaluating a low‐
purine, moderate‐protein diet evaluated the reduction of
xanthine calculi in dogs on allopurinol for long‐term
support of leishmaniasis therapy and appears to be
promising. Control of concurrent urinary tract infection
with appropriate antibiotics based on culture and sensi­
tivity is also essential for both dissolution and prevention
of urate uroliths.
Follow‐Up and Prevention of Ammonium Urate
Uroliths in Dogs

A low‐purine diet is advised (Hill’s Prescription Diet u/d
or Royal Canin UC Low Purine). Diets that contain lean
meat and glandular organs are high in purines, thus
avoidance of meat‐based protein (diet or treats) is recom­
mended. Acceptable treats include carrots, apple slices,
and air‐popped popcorn. Urine alkalinization to decrease
the production of ammonia and ammonium ions by the
kidneys is also recommended. The goal of urinary alka­
linization is to keep the urine pH around 6.8–7.0.
Allopurinol is only recommended for urate prevention
if urate crystals persist despite dilute and alkaline urine.
If urate crystals persist despite these interventions, the
lowest dose of allopurinol that prevents crystals is
advised, to avoid risk of xanthine stones.
For all urolith types, increasing water consumption
decreases supersaturation of urine with crystals through
dilution. Ideally, a urine specific gravity <1.020 in the
morning is desired. Dry food may be soaked with water
(aka “swim the kibbles”) or canned food may be fed to
help increase water consumption. Multiple water bowls,
small feedings, and ice cubes are all potential ways to
encourage drinking. Control of urinary tract infections
with appropriate antibiotics (based on culture and sensi­
tivity results) is essential in prevention.
The risk of recurrence is high for metabolic uroliths.
Owner compliance is essential to reduce risk, and aware­
ness of the genetic (breed) predisposition must be
encouraged.
The recommended follow‐up for these patients is
examination of urine pH, specific gravity and sediment
at two weeks, four weeks, and then every three months

(see Table 123.3). Double‐contrast cystography or ultra­
sonography should be performed every two months. If
the dog remains urolith free, free of clinical signs, and
significant crystalluria, rechecks may be decreased to
every 2–4 months for the first postoperative year, and
then twice yearly.
If the urate uroliths are secondary to a PSS, correction
of the portal vascular anomaly is expected to resolve
hyperuricuria and hyperammonuria followed by disso­
lution of ammonium urate uroliths. The frequency of
successful dissolution post attenuation of the shunt has
not been reported. Similarly, there is no study evaluat­
ing the success rate of a low‐protein diet alone to dis­
solve urate stones in dogs with a PSS. Stones can and
should be removed during correction of the PSS.
Nephroliths typically dissolve after PSS attenuation, so
they do not need to be removed unless problematic
(obstruction).
Prevention of Ammonium Urate Uroliths in Cats

Similar to dogs, the features of a balanced diet designed
to prevent recurrence of ammonium urate and uric acid
urolithiasis in cats are high moisture, low purine (low‐
protein or vegetable‐based protein), and the ability to
produce a urine pH of 6.8–7.0. For example, Hill’s
Prescription Diet k/d (wet) would be recommended.
Anecdotally, a commercially available hydrolyzed soy
protein diet has been fed to cats to provide an adequate
protein intake in a low purine form.
Calcium Phosphate Uroliths

Calcium phosphate uroliths are frequently multiple
small uroliths, and their removal by surgical or nonsurgi­
cal methods is recommended to avoid urethral obstruc­
tion. Dissolution of calcium phosphate has been reported
following parathyroidectomy for treatment of hyperpar­
athyroidism in dogs.
Prevention of stone recurrence includes identification
and therapy of any underlying disorder that causes an
elevated calcium or phosphorus level or alkaline urine
pH. Examples of these include primary hyperparathy­
roidism, disorders that predispose to hypercalciuria
(hypercalcemia, excess vitamin D, systemic acidosis,
excess dietary calcium), disorders that predispose to
hyperphosphaturia (excess dietary phosphorus), and
decreased urine volume.
Dietary manipulation that increases moisture and sub­
sequent polyuria (e.g., canned formula or moderate
sodium supplementation), and also provides the targeted
calcium and calcium:phosphorus ratio is also recom­
mended to prevent recurrence. A diet that avoids exces­
sive acidification (to prevent calcium oxalate risk) or
excessive alkalinization of urine is desired. The features
of a diet designed to prevent recurrence of calcium

phosphate urolithiasis in cats are thought to be similar to
those in dogs.
Cystine Uroliths
Cystine Uroliths in Dogs

Medical dissolution of cystine in dogs consists of reduc­
ing cystine concentration in the urine and increasing its
solubility. As with all uroliths, increasing urine volume is
beneficial for dilution of crystalloids. The solubility of
cystine can be increased by making the urine pH alkaline
(approximately 7.0–7.5), either by feeding a specific diet
or by treatment with potassium citrate.
Features of a diet thought to help recurrence of cys­
tine are:
urine dilution
low protein/purine levels (low protein or vegetable
protein)
●● alkalinize urine – target pH of 6.8–7.0
●● limit sodium intake
●● taurine and carnitine supplementation.
●●
●●

Hill’s Prescription Diet Canine u/d and Royal Canin UC
Low Purine have been recommended because they alka­
linize the urine and reduce urine concentration. They are
also markedly protein restricted (low in s­ ulfur‐containing
amino acids), which decreases cystine excretion by
20–25% via reduction of cystine precursors.
Some dogs with cystinuria have increased renal excre­
tion of carnitine, and low‐protein diets increase the risk
of carnitine deficiency and associated dilated cardiomy­
opathy in cystinuric dogs. As such, carnitine supplemen­
tation may be indicated. In addition, cystine is a precursor
for taurine synthesis, and taurine supplementation may
be warranted in these patients.
Dissolution of cystine urolithiasis has been reported
by treating patients with a thiol‐containing drug without
feeding a protein‐restricted diet. Thiol‐containing drugs
react with cystine, resulting in its conversion to a more
soluble compound by a disulfide exchange reaction.
Thiol‐containing drugs include D‐penicillamine and 2‐
mercaptopropionylglycine (2‐MPG) (tiopronin, Thiola®,
Mission Pharmaceuticals). Although both drugs are
effective, metal chelation and gastrointestinal side‐
effects of D‐penicillamine make it a less desirable choice.
2‐MPG, at a dosage of 15–20 mg/kg of body weight
divided and given orally twice daily, is the treatment of
choice, in combination with dietary modifications for
dissolution and prevention of cystine calculi. Use of this
protocol resulted in dissolution of 60% of uroliths in one
study within 1–3 months and was effective in 18/18 dogs
in another. This drug has been reported to be associated
with side‐effects in dogs such as aggression, myopathy,
anemia, proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, elevations of
liver enzymes, and dermatologic changes.

Prevention of Cystine Uroliths

Diets used for dissolution of cystine uroliths are appro­
priate for cystine urolith prevention. Thiol‐containing
drugs have been used to prevent recurrence of cystine
uroliths in dogs, at doses similar to those used for disso­
lution. Older dogs are less likely to form cystine uroliths
and it may be possible to stop or taper therapies as
patients mature. The risk of recurrence of these uroliths
is high because cystinuria is an inherited defect in some
affected dogs. Giger et al. observed that castration of
mastiffs, Kromfohrlanders, and Irish terriers with non‐
type I cystinuria drastically diminished the excretion of
cystine and dibasic amino acids. Maintaining a negative
cyanide‐nitroprusside test may be used to monitor and
adjust therapy. In the subset of dogs with androgen‐
dependent cystinuria, castration can resolve cystinuria.
If cystinuria decreases two months after castration com­
pared to baseline measurement (before castration), the
patient is less likely to have recurrence of cystine uro­
liths. If cystinuria persists four months after castration, it
was probably not androgen dependent. Nitroprusside
test and cystine crystalluria are less reliable tests than
urine cystine measurement to detect persistent risk of
cystine uroliths formation.
