Silica Uroliths in Cats and Dogs

Effective dissolution protocols have not been reported
for silicate stones in small animals. The risk of silica uro­
lith recurrence is not well documented. In one study of
silica uroliths, 12% of dogs had a previous episode of uro­
lithiasis, but in most cases it was not known whether the
previous urolith was also composed of silica.
To reduce the risk of silica stone recurrence, it is rec­
ommended to change the diet to one in which the vege­
table content is limited. The recommendation is to avoid
diets containing soybean hulls and corn gluten feed, and
to avoid the ingestion of soil. As with all uroliths,
increased water intake should be promoted to decrease
the resulting concentration of calculogenic material in
urine.
Mixed and Compound Uroliths

The management of compound uroliths is challenging
because they consist of layers containing different mineral

1143

VetBooks.ir

1144

Section 10 Renal and Genitourinary Disease

compositions. Theoretically, the objective of compound
urolith dissolution is to design a protocol to dissolve the
outer layer of the urolith first, and then change the pro­
tocol to address each successive outer layer. Serial reeval­
uation of the size of the compound urolith by an
appropriate imaging technique is recommended. Once
the urolith does not decrease in size, medical therapy
may be adjusted to attempt dissolution of suspected
minerals in the inner layers. An alternative to the above
consists of dissolving the outer layer of the urolith to
reduce its size, followed by removing the remaining
smaller portion by voiding urohydropropulsion. Neither
of these techniques is usually possible in practice given
the inability to predict each layer of the compound uro­
lith and then adjust medical therapy as each layer dis­
solves. As such, mechanical removal is recommended for
the majority of compound stones.
Compound uroliths may also contain layers that are
not amenable to dissolution (i.e., calcium oxalate). For
example, dissolution of an outer layer (i.e., struvite) may
lead to a smaller size of urolith, which will then not dis­
solve any further as the underlying layer is calcium oxa­
late. This may increase the risk of urinary tract
obstruction in male dogs. For this reason, most com­
pound uroliths are removed either surgically or using a
minimally invasive method (see later). Following removal
of the compound urolith, the specific management strat­
egy is aimed at prevention of the inner layer (nidus) of
the compound urolith (i.e., the first layer to form).
Suture‐associated stones have become more common.
In one study they accounted for 0.6% of all canine uro­
liths and 9.4% of recurrent uroliths from 1999 to 2006.
Suture‐induced stones were more likely to be compound
uroliths and often had a calcium phosphate nidus. Suture
material that dissolves rapidly (like poliglecaprone ver­
sus polydioxonone) is recommended, in case bladder
mucosal penetration occurs during closure.

­Removal of Lower Urinary
Tract Uroliths
Lower urinary tract calculi should be removed if they are
not amenable to medical dissolution and if they are caus­
ing, or may cause, clinical signs, urinary tract obstruc­
tion, inflammation, or recurrent infection.
Surgical Removal
In small animals, surgical removal of uroliths by cystot­
omy or urethrotomy was the traditional standard of care
for many years. However, urethral surgeries may result
in permanent alterations of the anatomy and function of
the urethra. For this reason, urethral surgeries are now

discouraged and minimally invasive management of
urethral stones has become the standard of care (see
later).
Calculi remained in the bladder after cystotomy in up
to 20% of dogs and cats. When removing cystic calculi,
the urethra should be catheterized and flushed to ensure
that it is free of calculi. Postoperative radiographs of the
entire urethra are indicated as well to ensure that all cal­
culi have been removed. A 2008 study reported that 9.4%
of recurrent stones in dogs were suture induced. Luminal
penetration is common in thin‐walled bladders, but this
is not believed to be associated with formation of calcu­
lus if absorbable monofilament suture is used.
Complications of cystotomy include a high recur­
rence rate of calculi, the need for serial surgeries that
can lead to suture‐induced stones, strictures, adhesions,
bleeding, uroabdomen, pain, and other life‐threatening
complications.
Nonsurgical Treatment Options
In humans, minimally invasive treatment options have
mostly replaced traditional surgical stone removal. In
2002, open surgical removal of uroliths was described in
only 0.3–4% of human patients. In small animals, mini­
mally invasive treatment options are now considered the
standard of care to manage lower urinary tract stones.
They consist of voiding urohydropropulsion (VUH),
intracorporeal lithotripsy, extracorporeal shock wave
lithotripsy (ESWL), cystoscopic stone basket retrieval,
percutaneous cystolithotomy (PCCL), and laparoscopic‐
assisted cystotomy.
All minimally invasive stone retrieval procedures
should ideally be performed after a negative urine cul­
ture has been documented, or the patient has been
placed on an appropriate antibiotic for at least 24 hours.
Voiding Urohydropulsion

Voiding Urohydropulsion consists of removing small
bladder calculi by inducing voiding while the dog or cat
is positioned vertically or laterally (Figure 123.15). This
procedure was first described by Lulich et al. and can be
successfully performed in dogs and female cats but not in
male cats as their narrow urethra may become obstructed
by the stones.
Stone size is the most important criterion in deciding
if VUH is an appropriate treatment option. Stones
smaller than 3–4 mm can typically be voided respectively
by small and small‐medium female dogs. In female ultra‐
small breeds (such as Pomeranian, Chihuahua), careful
evaluation of the size of the urethra in relation to stone is
indicated. We recommend passing an 8 Fr urinary cath­
eter before doing a VUH while the dog is under anesthe­
sia and choosing an alternative stone removal method if

VetBooks.ir

123 Urolithiasis in Small Animals

(a)

(b)

Figure 123.15 (a) Vertical positioning of a female dog to perform voiding urohydropulsion. (b) Container with cystic calculi removed by
voiding urohydropulsion.

the urethra is smaller than 8 Fr. Stones smaller than 3 mm
can be voided by male dogs weighing 10–25 kg. In male
dogs weighing 5–10 kg, stones smaller than 2–3 mm may
be voided. The clinician needs to try to catheterize the
urethra first to evaluate its size. A catheter that is 3 Fr is
equivalent to 1 mm, so that if an 8 Fr urinary catheter can
be passed through the urethra, a 3 mm stone can be
voided.
For VUH, the patient is placed under general anes­
thesia. The urethra is catheterized and the bladder is
distended with warm sterile saline. The capacity of
the bladder is typically 10–15 mL/kg. Once the bladder
is fully distended, the patient is positioned vertically
and then the urinary catheter is removed (see
Figure 123.15a). The bladder is agitated so that gravity
causes the stones to fall into the trigone. With strong,
steady bladder expression while pulling the bladder cra­
nially to straighten the urethra, the intravesicular pres­
sure will maintain a strong urine stream as small
fragments of stone material are voided into a container
(see Figure 123.15b). General anesthesia is mandatory
for this procedure, as the bladder can rupture if the
patient does not have a relaxed, unobstructed urethra.
The procedure is repeated until no calculi or stone

fragments are passed for two expressions. Radiography,
with or without positive or negative contrast (depend­
ing on the lucency of the stones), or cystoscopy, can be
performed after the procedure to confirm complete
urolith removal. VUH can also be used to obtain a few
small stones for analysis to determine whether medical
dissolution is an option for the remaining stones.
Empiric antibiotics should be given during the proce­
dure and for 3–5 days afterward. Broad‐spectrum anti­
biotics such as amoxicillin or cephalexin are usually
prescribed. To minimize discomfort during urination,
NSAIDs or opioids are administered for 1–4 days as
needed and based on clinical signs.
Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy (Box 123.1)

Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy uses an external
unit guided by fluoroscopic visualization to create shock
waves that pass through the soft tissue of the patient. It is
typically used for the fragmentation of upper urinary
tract calculi from a renal pelvis or ureter, which are then
left to pass spontaneously through the ureter, bladder,
and urethra. It has also been used to fragment bladder
stones in some dogs. However, the movement of stones
within the bladder during treatment limits the repeated

Intracorporeal Lithotripsy

Electrohydraulic lithotripsy (EHL) and laser (Ho:YAG:
holmium:yttrium, aluminum, garnet) lithotripsy were
developed in the 1970s to fragment bladder uroliths in
humans, with success rates reported to exceed 90%. Both
types of intracorporeal lithotripsy have been described
in veterinary patients. To date, the Ho:YAG laser is the
most commonly used device for intracorporeal litho­
tripsy in veterinary and human medicine.
During laser lithotripsy, the patient is placed under
general anesthesia as for routine cystoscopy. Once the
urolith is visualized with the cystoscope, a small‐­
diameter flexible quartz laser fiber (200, 365, or 550 μm)
is guided through the working channel. The tip of the
fiber is placed in direct contact with the surface of the
urolith at a 90° angle, and pulsed laser energy is trans­
mitted from the energized crystal to the urolith via the
fiber (Figure 123.16). The stone is fragmented by a ther­
mal drilling process, in which the pulse of energy trave­
ling through the fiber creates a microscopic vapor bubble
on the surface of the calculus. The closer the fiber tip is
to the target, the larger the effect, having its greatest
effect in contact mode. The energy is absorbed in
<0.5 mm of fluid, making it safe to fragment uroliths in
tight locations, such as within the urethra, ureter, renal
pelvis, or urinary bladder, with limited risk of adjacent
urothelial damage.

(b)

Figure 123.16 Visualization of bladder stones (oxalate) before (a) and after (b) fragmentation with the Ho:YAG laser in a female dog.

VetBooks.ir

123 Urolithiasis in Small Animals

Stones are typically fragmented until the pieces are
small enough to be voided using VUH or manually
extracted from the bladder using a stone retrieval basket.
This technology is considered the standard of care in
human medicine and is currently being utilized for lower
urinary tract stones in many veterinary hospitals in
North America.
The Ho:YAG laser has been reported to be effective on
all stone types. Adams et al. reported that laser litho­
tripsy resulted in complete fragmentation of all uroliths
in 100% of females (28/28 dogs) and 86.7% of males
(39/45 dogs). In the literature, complete urolith removal
is typically achieved in 100% of dogs with urethroliths,
83–96% of female dogs with cystoliths, and 68–81% of
male dogs with cystoliths. In the Adams et al. study,
the complication rate reported with laser lithotripsy
was 17.9% in female dogs and 13.3% in male dogs.
Complications were typically minor and shortterm,
including urethral swelling, edema, and mild hematuria,
which were medically managed. Shortterm complica­
tions were most commonly related to urethral mucosal
swelling from serial passage of the cystoscope in female
dogs and resolved with the placement of an indwelling
urinary catheter for 12–24 hours. Short‐term complica­
tions were reported in 5/28 (17.9%) of female dogs and
6/45 (13.3%) male dogs in this study. In comparison,
Thierman‐Mankin et al. reported short‐term complica­
tions in 37–50% of 144 dogs using traditional surgical
cystotomy.
In another canine study in which laser lithotripsy was
retrospectively compared with traditional cystotomy,
both methods were considered equally effective. Complete
urolith removal rate was not significantly different
between dogs in the cystotomy group (86%) and those in
the lithotripsy group (89%). There were no significant
differences in complications evaluated between the
groups and patients undergoing lithotripsy were dis­
charged from the hospital 12 hours earlier than those
having a cystotomy. Adams et al. reported that of 73 dogs
with uroliths treated by laser lithotripsy, only 19% (14/73)
had stone recurrence after approximately 12–24 months
of follow‐up, which is less than that previously reported
with cystotomy (42%).
The greatest challenge of both laser and EHL litho­
tripsy is the removal of small stone fragments from the
bladder following fragmentation, which can take
extended periods of time and result in urethral trauma/
edema during repetitive endoscope passage. Grant et al.
identified female sex as a positive predictor of success
(complete stone removal). They reported that smaller body
weight, large urolith burden, and increasing urolith size
significantly increased the time required to perform laser
lithotripsy. This has made the use of other procedures, like

PCCL, appealing for smaller dogs and cats with a large
bladder stone burden, regardless of size or sex.
Cystoscopic‐Guided Basket Removal

Another option for stones that are too large for VUH but
small enough to fit through the urethra with gentle trac­
tion is stone basket retrieval. A variety of stone baskets
are available from several manufacturers. Basket retrieval
is usually performed under cystoscopic guidance,
although fluoroscopy can also be used. Typically, the size
of the stone is the limiting factor. Basket retrieval can be
considered in female dogs with stones <4–5 mm, male
dogs with stones <3 mm, and female cats with stones
<3 mm.
Percutaneous Cystolithotomy (PCCL)

This minimally invasive approach has been reported in
27 dogs and cats with excellent complete stone removal
rates (96%), short procedure times (40–75 min), and
similar hospitalization times as those seen with transure­
thral lithotripsy, regardless of patient sex, size, stone
number, or species. This procedure can be an alternative
in animals in which transurethral lithotripsy is a chal­
lenge (small male dogs, male dogs with a large stone bur­
den, male and female cats, rabbits, guinea pigs, etc.) or if
lithotripsy is unavailable.
For this procedure, a single small incision (approxi­
mately 1–1.5 cm) is made into the abdominal cavity just
over the apex of the urinary bladder. Once the bladder is
palpated digitally, stay sutures are used to hold the blad­
der up to the incision while a laparoscopic screw‐tip
cannula or port is inserted into the bladder at the apex.
Surgical aspiration is usually used while fluid is flushed
into the bladder with a urethral catheter, as the best
visualization is achieved with a saline‐filled bladder.
The bladder is typically not fully exteriorized
(Figure 123.17a,b). A small, rigid cystoscope is inserted
through this port into the bladder, and stones are iden­
tified and removed with a stone retrieval basket through
the working channel of the cystoscope (Figure 123.17c–e).
If the stones are very small, they can be flushed out
of the port in a retrograde manner with a urinary cath­
eter in the urethra flushing fluid into the bladder while
a suction device is placed into the port suctioning out
the fluid and small fragments. If the stones are larger
than the port, they can either be fragmented by litho­
tripsy or manipulated through the small incision with
the stone basket. It is very rare that lithotripsy is needed
concurrently. After all calculi are removed from the
bladder, the entire urethra is examined with a rigid cys­
toscope (female dogs) or a flexible ureteroscope (male
dogs) to ensure that all fragments have been removed
and the small incision is sutured closed. A basket

Laparoscopic‐Assisted Cystoscopy

Laparoscopic‐assisted cystoscopy is performed via a
mini laparotomy. In this technique, the abdomen is
insufflated with carbon dioxide and the bladder is iso­
lated. Another trocar is inserted into the abdomen at the
level of the bladder apex, and the bladder is exteriorized
at this access point using a laparoscopic Babcock forceps.
The incision is enlarged, creating a mini laparotomy, to
pull the urinary bladder. A small cystotomy is performed
and the bladder wall is sutured to the skin of this small
abdominal incision. A rigid cystoscope is then inserted
into the bladder for calculus retrieval. The use of a basket
passed through the working channel or a grasping for­
ceps next to the cystoscope aids in removal of the stones.
The cystotomy incision is closed routinely. This proce­
dure makes it difficult to maintain bladder distension for
the best visibility.
Laparoscopic‐assisted cystoscopy can circumvent
some of the limitations associated with laser lithotripsy,
but it does require creating a pneumoperitoneum, mak­
ing the alternative PCCL very appealing.

­Removal of Upper Urinary
Tract Uroliths
The incidence of nephroliths and ureteroliths in cats has
increased as much as 50‐fold since the early 1980s.
Calcium oxalate is the most common (>98%) type of
stone found in the upper tract of cats, followed by cal­
cium phosphate, in the form of apatite, or urate.
Approximately 30–60% of ureteroliths in dogs are com­
posed of calcium oxalate.
Indications for Upper Urinary Tract
Urolith Removal
Nephroliths

Many canine and feline nephroliths remain static in size
and clinically silent for years. Some controversy exists
as to whether nonobstructive kidney stones worsen
underlying kidney disease. Most recent studies in human
and cats show that the presence of nephroliths (vs no

nephroliths) seems to worsen renal disease and outcome.
For this reason, removal of nephroliths in people is
encouraged. In small animals, because of the challenges
associated with removal of nephroliths and the lack of
evidence that nephroliths are a cause of renal disease
progression rather than a marker for more aggressive
renal disease, it is not yet recommended to remove neph­
roliths that are not complicated. Nephrolith removal is
not indicated unless uroliths are increasing in size and
compressing the renal parenchyma, causing recurrent
infections despite appropriate duration of medical man­
agement, or if the patient has a partial or complete uret­
eropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction resulting in
hydronephrosis, renal parenchymal loss, worsening renal
function, chronic hematuria, or pain.
Ureteroliths

If one or more ureteroliths are obstructing urine flow,
causing hydroureter and/or hydronephrosis, or are asso­
ciated with discomfort, hemorrhage, or concurrent pye­
lonephritis, management for medical stone passage or
interventional urinary diversion is indicated immedi­
ately, regardless of stone composition, as time is critical.
The presence of a hydroureter without renal pelvic dila­
tion greater than 5 mm is sufficient to suspect ureteral
obstruction. If the ureteral obstruction is complete,
decompression of the renal pelvis becomes urgent to
preserve the function of the ipsilateral kidney. The longer
the ureter remains obstructed, the more significant and
irreversible the damage. In one study, after seven days of
obstruction, the GFR was permanently diminished by
35% after relief of the obstruction, and recovery took five
weeks to occur. When the obstruction lasted for 14 days,
the GFR was permanently diminished by 54%, with
recovery taking four months to occur. These studies
were performed in dogs without preexisting renal or ure­
teral disease, so a worse outcome might be expected in
feline and canine patients with chronic obstructions,
previous and/or exhausted renal hypertrophy compen­
sation, and preexisting renal insufficiency. These data
suggest that aggressive and timely intervention is neces­
sary when a ureteral obstruction is diagnosed and that
the “watch and wait method” should be avoided when­
ever possible.
Medical Management
Medical management of upper urinary tract stones
includes dissolution (nephroliths), aggressive diuresis, or
intermittent hemodialysis (IHD).
More than 50% of dogs with ureteral obstructions have
been reported to have urinary tract infection. For that
reason, any patient with ureteral obstruction should
have a urine culture performed and should be given the

1149

VetBooks.ir

1150

Section 10 Renal and Genitourinary Disease

appropriate antimicrobials. For dissolution to occur, the
uroliths must be surrounded by undersaturated urine to
allow them to go back into solution. For these reasons,
urocystoliths and nephroliths are amenable to dissolu­
tion but ureteroliths and urethroliths are not. Dissolution
of struvite nephroliths has been reported in six dogs that
had bacterial pyelonephritis and impaired urine‐concen­
trating ability. An average of 184 days of treatment
(range, 67–300 days) with a calculolytic diet (Hill’s
Prescription Diet Canine s/d) and antibiotic therapy was
required for radiographic dissolution of the stones in
these dogs. In the author’s experience (AB), ureteroliths
should be dissolved within 2–6 weeks and nephroliths
should be decreased in size (<75 % initial size) by three
months. It can take up to nine months to dissolve large
nephroliths. Increasing the number of walks per day
should be encouraged to improve stone elimination.
Aggressive diuresis has been effective at helping move
ureteroliths down into the bladder and in resolving
azotemia in 8–14% of cats with ureteroliths. This lim­
ited success rate of diuresis may be explained by the high
percentage of ureteral obstruction secondary to stric­
ture in cats.
Surgical management was effective in 101 cases, but
has a high postoperative complication rate (31% in cats
and ~35% in dogs) and perioperative mortality rate (18%
in cats and 25% in dogs). Medical management should be
considered prior to surgical intervention; however, more
aggressive management should be considered if the
patient fails to improve with medical management alone
for 48 hours, or if the patient is anuric/oliguria, hyper­
kalemic, overhydrated or if there is progressive renal pel­
vic dilation.
In the authors’ experience, aggressive diuresis in cats
appears to be more effective for small stones (<1–2 mm)
in the distal third of the ureter compared to larger stones,
or those in the proximal ureter. Aggressive diuresis con­
sists of aggressive IV fluid therapy while monitoring
­central venous pressure, body weight, electrolyte con­
centrations, and hydration status. One recommended
fluid therapy protocol includes administering 0.45%
saline mixed with 2.5% dextrose at a maintenance rate
(e.g., 50–60 mL/kg/d). Additionally, a replacement fluid
such as Plasma‐Lyte® (Abbott Animal Health) or lactated
Ringer’s solution (avoiding saline, if possible, to reduce
sodium load) is administered to correct dehydration and
promote diuresis (e.g., 45–75 mL/kg/d). The maximum
combined fluid rate should not exceed 120 mL/kg/day. In
patients without cardiac compromise, mannitol is
administered as a bolus at 0.25–0.5 g/kg over 20–30 min­
utes followed by a constant rate infusion of 1 mg/kg/min
for 24 hours. If, after 24 hours, there is no evidence of
improvement based on imaging and serial bloodwork,
the mannitol infusion is discontinued. Other medical

alternatives include amitriptyline, alpha‐adrenergic
antagonist therapy (prazosin or tamsulosin), or glucagon
therapy.
Intermittent hemodialysis has been reported to resolve
acute kidney injury secondary to obstructive uretero­
liths. Thirteen cats did not have any surgical intervention
and eight of these 13 survived 365 days or longer past
discharge; all of these cats had a degree of renal recovery
sufficient for discontinuation of IHD prior to hospital
discharge.
If medical management fails or the patient is unstable
(e.g., hyperkalemic, overhydrated, oligo‐/anuric, devel­
oping progressive hydronephrosis), or if IHD is not
available at the institution, immediate renal decompres­
sion should be considered. If minimally invasive urolith
extraction or bypass is not possible, then the two best
options are to (1) place a nephrostomy tube or (2) initi­
ate IHD or continuous renal replacement therapy
(CRRT), for stabilization. Immediate renal pelvis
decompression is recommended over hemodialysis or
CRRT if the patient is stable enough to undergo anes­
thesia and the operator is comfortable with the proce­
dure. Renal pelvis decompression halts the damage
being done by the increased hydrostatic backpressure,
whereas hemodialysis stabilizes a patient while the ure­
teral obstruction persists, resulting in ongoing renal
injury. A short delay in treatment in a stable patient is
preferred over immediate treatment by an inexperi­
enced operator, as the complication rates with any of the
decompression procedures are high if experience is lim­
ited. Partial obstructions allow a longer window of
opportunity for treatment without such dramatic renal
damage as seen with complete obstructions, allowing
time to arrange referral to a facility with experience in
these procedures. Over 75% of obstructed feline patie­
nts have a partial ureteral obstruction based on
ureteropyelography.
Many patients with ureteral obstruction have concur­
rent urinary tract infections (75% of dogs and 10–30% of
cats) so broad‐spectrum antimicrobial therapy is recom­
mended for all patients, and a urine culture and sensitiv­
ity should be part of the work‐up.
Surgical Removal of Upper Urinary
Tract Uroliths
Nephroliths

In small animals, traditional intervention for treatment
of nephrolithiasis involves a nephrotomy, pyelotomy, or
salvage ureteronephrectomy. Complications can be
severe and life‐threatening after a nephrotomy, including
hemorrhage, decreased renal function, ureteral obstruc­
tion by remaining nephrolith fragment passage, and uri­
nary leakage into the abdomen from the renal incision.

VetBooks.ir

123 Urolithiasis in Small Animals

In a study of normal cats, the GFR of the ipsilateral kid­
ney decreased by 10%–20% after a nephrotomy. This was
clinically insignificant in normal cats but in a clinical
patient with maximally hypertrophied nephrons due to
prior nephrolith‐induced damage, the significance could
be dramatic. Therefore, feline patients with an already
compromised GFR from chronic stone disease may
develop a clinically significant decline in renal function
after nephrotomy. Since over 30% of adult cats eventually
develop chronic kidney disease associated with a 75%
decline of renal function, a 10–20% further decline in
GFR from a nephrotomy may be poorly tolerated. Hence,
nephrotomy should be avoided when possible in all cats,
especially those with existing renal disease. In dogs
undergoing traditional surgery for nephrolithiasis, there
was a very high complication rate (23%) following the
procedure, as well as remaining fragments in more than
40%. In addition, 67% of dogs undergoing nephrectomy
developed renal azotemia.
Typically, unless the stone results in a ureteral obstruc­
tion or severe perisitent hematuria, is the cause of
chronic UTIs, or is so large that it is overtaking the renal
parenchyma, nephroliths remain clinically silent for the
life of the dog or cat and removal is currently not being
recommended. The 2016 ACVIM consensus statement
on the management of urinary tract stone disease rec­
ommends management of upper urinary uroliths by
minimally invasive techniques rather than standard sur­
gery when possible.
Ureteroliths

Traditional surgical intervention to address ureteroliths
includes ureterotomy, neoureterocystostomy, ureterone­
phrectomy, or renal transplantation. Kyles et al. reported
procedure‐associated complication and mortality rates
of >30% and 18–38%, respectively, in more than 150 cats
that underwent at least one of these procedures. These
cases were seen at two universities where microsurgical
expertise was available and a renal transplant program
existed. The morbidity and mortality rates may be
higher in environments where operating microscopes
and microsurgical experience and expertise are not
available.
Many of the complications associated with surgery are
due to site edema, recurrence of stones that then pass
from the renal pelvis to the surgery site, stricture forma­
tion, persistent obstructions, missed ureteroliths, and
ureterotomy‐associated or nephrostomy tube‐associated
urine leakage. In the Kyles et al. study, patients that
underwent a ureterotomy for treatment of a ureteral
obstruction (the most commonly performed procedure
in practice) had a perioperative mortality rate of 25%.
Uroabdomen occurred in 15% of cats in which a uretero­
neocystotomy was performed.

When ureterotomy or ureteroneocystotomy is unsuc­
cessful, a ureteronephrectomy may be required, which is
not ideal due to the high risk of subsequent stone‐
induced obstruction of the contralateral kidney and the
majority of cats being azotemic at the time of diagnosis
with a unilateral ureteral obstruction. Chronic kidney
disease is common in cats when a ureteral obstruction
is diagnosed, with 75–97% of cats with a unilateral
obstruction reported to be azotemic. For this reason,
removing a kidney for a diseased ureter should never be
encouraged.
Another major concern is that in one study, 40% of cats
developed a second ureteral obstruction over a 1–2‐year
follow‐up, and of these cats, 62% had evidence of neph­
rolithiasis documented at the time of the first surgery.
Unfortunately, removing a nephrolith in a cat is chal­
lenging and potentially harmful, and it is impossible to
predict whether a nephrolith will become an obstructive
ureterolith, so nephrotomy should not be encouraged.
Results after ureterotomy, pyelotomy, and/or uretero­
nephrectomy have been reported in 16 dogs. The mor­
tality rate (death related to azotemia or to clinical signs
related to the urinary system) in this study was 25% (4/16
dogs). Of the 12 dogs that were followed, 17% required
an additional surgery within four months for ureteral
stricture or recurrent ureteroliths. Most dogs (88%) had
urinary tract infections at diagnosis, and 50% had con­
current nephrolithiasis. Ten (62.5%) dogs presented to
the hospital with elevated blood urea nitrogen and/or
creatinine concentrations and 50% remained elevated
after successful surgery. Postoperatively, two dogs had
worsening azotemia.
Minimally Invasive Management
of Nephroliths and Ureteroliths
In humans, minimally invasive procedures are the treat­
ment of choice for nephrolithiasis and ureteroliths
due to the high complication rates and morbidity asso­
ciated with traditional surgery (Table 123.4). These
procedures include ESWL for nephroliths <1–2 cm and
endo­scopic nephrolithotomy (percutaneous nephroli­
thotomy [PCNL] or surgically assisted endoscopic neph­
rolithotomy [SENL]) for nephroliths >1–2 cm. Open
surgery and laparoscopy are typically only considered
after other less invasive options have failed or been deemed
inappropriate.
Over the last 10 years, evidence‐based data support
that minimally invasive treatment of upper urinary tract
uroliths in dogs and cats is associated with a lower mor­
bidity and mortality rate compared to surgical proce­
dures. Selection of the most kidney‐sparing procedure
should always be a priority to treat upper urinary tract
uroliths in small animals.

Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy

Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy is used to fragment
uroliths fixed in one location. It has been successfully used
to fragment nephroliths and ureteroliths in dogs and uret­
eroliths in cats. The patient is placed under general anes­
thesia to permit positioning and provide analgesia.
Fluoroscopy is used to position the ESWL unit to target
the urolith. If compromised renal function is of concern, or
if bilateral ESWL is to be performed concurrently, limiting
treatment to a maximum of 2000–2500 shock waves per
kidney is recommended. For uroliths in the distal ureter or
urinary bladder, higher doses are possible because the kid­
ney is not within the treatment focal zone and collateral
damage to surrounding tissues seems to be minimal.
Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy is most com­
monly recommended for the treatment of nephroliths and
ureteroliths in dogs, rather than cats, for two reasons.
First, the feline ureter does not routinely accommodate
nephrolith fragment passage. Therefore, a nonobstructive

nephrolith could become an obstructive ureterolith after
ESWL. Post ESWL, nephrolith fragments are typically
≥1 mm in diameter, and the typical unstented feline ureter
is 0.3–0.4 mm in diameter. Second, there is some concern
that feline kidneys are more sensitive than canine kidneys
to shock waves and could experience bleeding.
Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy treatment was
reported to be successful in approximately 85% of dogs
with calcium‐containing nephroliths and ureteroliths.
Successful fragmentation of renal stones was achieved
in 90% of dogs, but some dogs required multiple treat­
ments. Overall, 30% of dogs required more than one
ESWL treatment for adequate fragmentation of neph­
roliths when lithotripsy was used; when an older model
dry unit (Modulith SL‐20) was used, up to 50% of dogs
required more than one treatment. Success rates
approach ~85% with one treatment when ureteral
stenting is concurrently performed. In one study of five
cats with ureterolithiasis treated by ESWL (wet unit),

VetBooks.ir

123 Urolithiasis in Small Animals

only one cat had complete resolution of the ureterolith,
and partial fragmentation occurred in two other cats;
however, these fragments were still too large to pass
down the ureter. In the authors’ (AB) experience, suc­
cess in stone fragmentation and passage was seen in
two of an additional five cats, suggesting an approxi­
mate 30% passage rate overall (3/10). However, larger
studies are needed to confirm these results and this
procedure is not currently recommended in cats by the
authors.
Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy is believed to be
safe and well tolerated by canine kidneys. In a series of
140 dogs with nephroliths or ureteroliths treated by
ESWL, the most common complication was ureteral
obstruction by stone fragments, which occurred in
approximately 10% of dogs. With the advocacy of ure­
teral stent placement for larger nephroliths (>10–20 mm)
before ESWL, this risk has declined. In dogs, it has been
shown that the renal changes observed after ESWL typi­
cally result in minimal decreases in GFR and renal blood
flow during the first 24 hours of treatment, and both
return to baseline within one week. Extrarenal complica­
tions with ESWL include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and
pancreatic injury (i.e., increased enzymes levels not asso­
ciated with clinical signs). Shock wave‐induced dysrhyth­
mias have been described in a few human patients (<8%).
Hospitalization typically ranges from eight to 24 hours
to monitor for the passage of urolith fragments and to
allow postprocedure analgesia and diuresis with intrave­
nous fluid therapy. Stone fragments may be voided 1–2
(a)

days after the procedure and collected in a strainer or
cheesecloth to be analyzed. Animals with ureteral stents
often require shorter hospital stays, as the concern for
post‐ESWL ureteral obstruction is diminished. Patients
are discharged with instructions for monitoring urina­
tion and urine appearance, lethargy, abdominal pain, or
vomiting. Follow‐up radiography and ultrasonography
are typically recommended one day after treatment, then
in 2–4 weeks, and then every month thereafter until all
stones are passed. If fragments that have passed into the
urinary bladder are not voided within 1–2 months after
ESWL, VUH or cystoscopic stone basketing is recom­
mended. If stone fragments remain in the kidney or ure­
ter after 2–3 months, repeat ESWL is suggested as long
as there is no concurrent ureteral obstruction. A second
treatment is required in 15–35% of cases to achieve
effective fragmentation if the remaining fragments
appear too large to safely pass through the ureter. In
cases of ureteral obstruction, placement of a ureteral
stent would be recommended.
Ureteral Stents

The use of ureteral stents in dogs and cats has been
investigated for the last 14 years as a less invasive alter­

invasive techniques (endoscopy and fluoroscopy in most
dogs) or surgically assisted (nephrostomy access in most
cats), can circumvent many of the perioperative compli­
cations of surgery (e.g., leakage, stricture, reobstruction)

and include reocclusion, migration, or dysuria. In dogs,
ureteral stents have replaced standard surgery to
decompress upper urinary tract obstruction. Long‐
term complications include urinary tract infection
(26%), occlusion of the stent (9%), ureteritis (5%), stent
migration (5%), encrustation (2%), and hematuria (7%).
More than three‐quarters of the patients were able to
clear the infections if present before ureteral stent
placement. In cats, ureteral stent placement can be
challenging and is associated with a 38% rate of long‐
term dysuria (responsive to steroid therapy). Since sub­

lower complication rates (see later) than ureteral stent­
ing in cats, it is now considered the treatment of choice

Endoscopic Nephrolithotomy

In humans, PCNL is typically performed for large or
embedded nephroliths (>15–20 mm). In small animals,
PCNL/SENL is considered if ESWL fails or is not avail­
able, cystine stones (which are resistant to EWSL) are
present, or the stone is >15–20 mm (depending on
patient size).
Typically, a combination of ultrasonographic, endo­
scopic, and fluoroscopic guidance is used for both PCNL
and SENL. PCNL has been performed in 11 dogs and
one cat to date. The smallest patient to date having a
PCNL/SENL was 5 lbs (2.3 kg), making patient size less
of an issue than other alternatives.
Typically, for PCNL, a renal access needle is used
to access the renal pelvis through the greater curvature
of the kidney under ultrasonographic guidance.
Subsequently, a nephroscope is inserted through a sheath
and into the renal pelvis to visualize the stone. If the lat­
ter is small enough, a stone retrieval basket is used to
remove the stone. If the stone is larger than the sheath,
intracorporeal lithotripsy (ultrasonic, pneumonic, elec­
trohydraulic, or Ho:YAG laser) is used to fragment it.
Once the stone fragments are small enough to fit through
the sheath, they are removed and a locking‐loop nephros­
tomy tube (5 or 6 Fr) is left in place to allow the small
hole to seal and form a nephropexy.
Surgical‐assisted endoscopic nephrolithotomy can be
performed similarly to that described for PCNL, only the
abdomen is opened to assist in nephrostomy access
­closure, to prevent the need for a nephrostomy tube.
For both PCNL and surgical‐assisted endoscopic
nephrolithotomy, because a balloon is used to dilate the
renal parenchyma (no incision is performed), minimal
nephron loss occurs. PCNL and SENL are considered
the most “kidney‐sparing” procedures with the highest
urolith‐free rate and minimal effect on GFR. For these
reasons, they are recommended as the first treatment for

patients with staghorn calculi according to the American
Urologic Association Guidelines.
The author (AB) has performed endoscopic nephroli­
thotomy in 11 dogs and one cat (16 renal units) using the
PCNL approach (n = 4 renal units) or SENL (n = 12 renal
units) to remove complicated nephroliths (median diam­
eter 2.5 cm; range, 0.5–5.7 cm). No kidney required
conversion to traditional surgical nephrotomy or
­
nephrectomy. Median procedure time was 180 minutes
(range, 90–270 minutes). Patients were discharged
within 48 hours (range, 48–144 hours). The procedure
was successful (resolution of complicated nephroliths) in
14 renal units. Ureteral stents were placed in all cases
during the PCNL/SENL and removed after 1–20 weeks
minimally invasively. No recurrence was reported during
the follow‐up period (median duration 557 days).
Owners tolerated recovery from the SENL better than
the PCNL because a nephrostomy tube was not required.
Overall, this series of cases demonstrates that PNCL
and SENL have a greater stone‐free rate (93% vs 85%)
and lower recurrence rate (0% vs 10%) than ESWL for
large problematic nephroliths. The results of this study
suggest that the median survival time is higher for dogs
with IRIS stage 1, 2 or 4 disease treated with ENL com­
pared to previously reported survival times for the same
IRIS stage diseases. However, further prospective studies
are required to draw conclusions as this was only a small
number of cases.
Ureteroscopy

Contrary to human medicine, ureteroscopy is rarely per­
formed in veterinary patients. For minimally invasive
treatment, dogs with a ureteral obstruction could have
an endoscopic ureteral stent placed and/or may also
undergo ESWL. If the patient is large enough (at least
39.6–44 lb [18–20 kg]), ureteroscopy can be considered.
However, most dogs with ureterolithiasis are small ter­
rier or toy breeds, making this an uncommon procedure.
If this is to be performed, then the preplacement of a ure­
teral stent to allow for passive ureteral dilation, prior to
ureteroscopy, is typically recommended.
Subcutaneous Ureteral Bypass

Feline ureteroliths are typically more frustrating than
canine ureteroliths due to the small diameter of the feline
ureter (<0.4 mm) and the endoscopic and surgical limita­
tions. In cats, ESWL is not typically advised and ureter­
oscopy is not possible.
A subcutaneous ureteral bypass (SUB) involves the
placement of a nephrostomy tube and a cystostomy tube
that are connected subcutaneously to a shunting port,
allowing for urine drainage from the kidney directly to
the bladder, bypassing the ureter (Figure 123.19). Initially,
this procedure was primarily performed for cats with

1155

Section 10 Renal and Genitourinary Disease

VetBooks.ir

1156

Figure 123.19 Lateral radiographs of a feline patient following
the placement of a subcutaneous ureteral bypass.

ureteral strictures, very proximal ureteral obstructions,
or in which stent placement was unsuccessful. Based on
experience in over 300 cats in the authors’ practice, it is

now preferred over the feline ureteral stent due to the
minimal complications both shortterm and longterm.
Over 93% of cats survived to hospital discharge after
admission. The longest period for which an SUB device
has remained in place is nine years (personal communi­
cation AB), and the short‐ and long‐term complications
seen with this device are fewer and less severe than those
seen with ureteral stents in cats (see Table 123.5).
The use of a SUB device to treat cats with ureteral
obstruction has been associated with the highest sur­
vival rate to date. In that study, 135 out of 144 (94%)
cats survived to hospital discharge, and 90%, 83%, 80%
and 74 % of cats were alive after one, three, and six
months and one year respectively after SUB placement.
The most common complication was stent obstruction
(25%) requiring SUB system replacement. However,
with the use of tetrasodium ethylenediaminetet­raacetic
acid (tEDTA) solution, the rate of reobstruction declined
to 4.5%.

Prostatic Diseases
Serge Chalhoub, DVM, PhD, DACVIM (SAIM)
Department of Veterinary Clinical and Diagnostic Sciences, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, University of Calgary, Calgary, AB, Canada

Both male dogs and cats have prostate glands, but cats
rarely develop prostatic diseases. Prostatic diseases are
relatively common in middle‐aged to older, intact male
dogs and rare in neutered males, with a higher reported
frequency in medium‐ and large‐breed dogs. Most companion male dogs and cats are neutered, which prevents
the majority of prostatic diseases.
The prostate is the only accessory sex gland in male
dogs, and it surrounds the urethra in the pelvic region
caudal to the trigone of the bladder and distal to the
internal urethral sphincter. It is oval in shape and bilobed,
with the two lobes separated by a prominent median
septum (Figure 124.1). The size of the prostate is greatly
influenced by hormonal stimulation. Castration of dogs
removes the important trophic f­actors necessary for
­prostatic growth and function, estrogen and testosterone, and leads to prostatic ­atrophy (Figure 124.2).
The prostate itself is an exocrine gland that produces
continuous secretions that flow into the urethra through
multiple prostatic ducts. These secretions make up
the largest component of spermatic ejaculate (90–95%).
Normal prostatic acini are lined with tall columnar to
cuboidal epithelium. The prostate reaches normal size by
age 2, but it continues to grow with age in the intact
male.
Most problems associated with the prostate result in
prostatomegaly, but many of the diseases do not result in
pain upon palpation of the prostate or lower urinary
tract signs. The most common prostatic diseases are
benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), bacterial acute and
chronic prostatitis, prostatic abscesses, prostatic and
paraprostatic cysts, and prostatic neoplasia (discussed in
further chapters).

­Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
and Prostatic Cysts
Etiology
Benign prostatic hyperplasia is by far the most common
prostatic disease in intact male dogs, and it develops due
to long‐term exposure of the prostate trophic hormone
testosterone’s active metabolite dihydrotestosterone
(DHT). Over time, an imbalance in the ratio of androgens to estrogens develops, and there is also both an
increase in prostatic tissue sensitivity to androgens and
an increase in androgen receptors. Over 50% of intact
male dogs will develop symptoms from BPH by age 5,
and by the age of 6 years 80% will manifest symptoms.
Fluid‐filled cysts may develop within the prostate and
are secondary to the hormonal influences that also cause
BPH. Theses cysts may not cause clinical signs until either
they get infected and develop into an abscess, or affect the
flow of urine through the urethra due to their size.
History and Clinical Signs
Not all dogs with BPH develop clinical signs. In others,
as the prostate becomes enlarged, observed clinical signs
with BPH include intermittent or continuous serosanguinous discharge or hematuria, and less commonly
straining to defecate, and lower urinary tract signs. Dogs
may experience pain upon ejaculation, and BPH can lead
to infertility in some cases. Dogs with BPH are not usually systemically ill but they do have a higher incidence of
developing prostatitis, prostatic abscesses, and urinary
tract infections.

Diagnosis
With all suspected prostatic diseases, it is important to
put the entire clinical picture together: history, clinical
signs, physical exam, imaging results, laboratory results,
and cytology or histopathology.
Performing a rectal examination is of the utmost
importance. Neutered males rarely develop prostatic
­diseases but they can still develop prostatic neoplasia, so
it is important not to rule out prostatic diseases in castrated males. In most patients, the caudal portion of the
prostate can be palpated on the ventral floor of the colon.
This may be difficult in larger dogs. The normal prostate
should not be painful and should be soft. With BPH, the

prostate tends to feel enlarged but it is smooth, symmetric, and rarely painful. The median raphe may not be as
obvious to palpate. The enlargement may cause the prostate to move cranially into the abdominal cavity, and
therefore can be difficult to palpate rectally without the
help of concurrent abdominal palpation. Prostatic cysts
can rarely be identified. Rectal palpation should also
include the dorsal portion of the distal colon to feel for
enlarged iliac lymph nodes. With BPH, lymphadenopathy should not be present. Constipation may be possible,
but the rest of the physical exam is usually within
normal limits.
Complete blood count (CBC) and chemistry panel are
unremarkable in dogs with BPH and noninfected prostatic cysts. Human prostate‐specific antigen (PSA) has
not been shown to correlate with prostatic disease in
dogs. Abdominal radiographs may reveal an enlarged
soft tissue opacity in the caudal abdominal region usually near or within the pelvic canal and caudal to the
bladder, especially on a lateral radiograph. Radiographs
are not very sensitive or specific for identifying the
­etiology of prostatic disease but they do give a good indication of size and shape of the prostate. Prostatic mineralization can be seen in both neutered and intact dogs. In
neutered dogs, mineralization strongly indicates neoplasia, whereas in intact dogs, mineralization can indicate
neoplasia, prostatitis, BPH, and prostatic cysts.
Constipation can be noted on radiographs. The prostate
is harder to recognize on abdominal radiographs in a
neutered male.
Retrograde contrast urethrocystography can aid in
the diagnosis of prostatic and urethral disease. Prostatic
disease may result in the uptake of contrast into glandular tissue, and the degree of uptake can correlate with
severity of disease. With BPH, there should be minimal
to no contrast uptake. It may be possible to appreciate a
narrowed prostatic urethral diameter due to compression by an enlarged prostate.
Ultrasonography has become the gold standard for
visualizing the prostate. In the intact male, the normal
prostate usually appears as a bilobed structure on short
axis and oval on long axis, its architecture uniform and
with a homogenous echogenicity similar to the spleen. In
BPH, the prostate appears enlarged and there may be a
loss of visualization of the median septum. Echogenicity
should not differ from the normal prostate or the
­prostate may be slightly more hyperechoic (Figure 124.3).
Prostatic cysts can be seen within the parenchyma and
usually contain anechoic fluid (Figure 124.4). Cysts may
vary in size and number.
For a specific diagnosis of prostatic disease, a sample
of prostatic cells, fluid, or tissue is recommended.
Often with typical clinical signs and diagnostic results,
BPH can be tentatively diagnosed and treated, but it is
important to note that other diseases cannot be excluded.

therapy to treat BPH.

Prognosis

Diagnosis

Prognosis from uncomplicated BPH causing clinical
signs is excellent with surgical castration as treatment is
curative, and good with medical therapy depending on

Abdominal ultrasound is the modality of choice
for detection of these cysts (Figure 124.5). They often
­resemble a second urinary bladder.

­Paraprostatic Cysts
Etiology
Paraprostatic cysts are fluid‐filled structures that
develop beside and outside the prostate secondary to the
retention of the embryonic muellerian duct system
(uterus masculinus). These cysts may become quite
large, usually are thin‐walled, and contain anechoic to
debris‐filled fluid.
History and Clinical Signs
These cysts often do not cause appreciable clinical signs,
or they may grow large enough to compress and obstruct
the urethra or the colon.

History and Clinical Signs

Figure 124.5 Paraprostatic cyst as seen on sagittal ultrasound

Therapy
Surgery is required to completely or partially remove
these cysts. Concurrent castration is recommended.

Acute prostatitis is usually a very painful condition and
these patients tend to have a greater frequency of systemic signs: depression, dehydration, anorexia, abnormal discharge, painful gait, difficulty urinating, inability
to mount or ejaculate, and trouble defecating. Lower
urinary signs such as stranguria, purulent urethral
­
discharge, hematuria, pollakiuria, and abnormal dis­
charge are often present. Patients may also vocalize when
attempting to urinate or defecate. Stool quality may
change due to compression of the colon. Other common
clinical signs and physical examination findings include
fever, vomiting, diarrhea, dehydration, tenesmus, and
constipation. Abscesses may rupture within the abdominal cavity and cause symptoms of acute abdomen,
­endotoxemia, sepsis, and peritonitis.
Dogs with chronic prostatitis may sometimes have no
evident clinical signs. History may include decreased
mounting behavior, decreased sperm count or quality,
recurrent and chronic urinary tract infections, lethargy,
decreased appetite, intermittent urethral discharge, and
potentially other vague and nonspecific clinical signs.

Prognosis

Diagnosis

Prognosis is good to excellent depending on the ability to
surgically remove the cysts.

Rectal palpation usually reveals either an enlarged and
symmetric prostate or the prostate can be abnormally
shaped, especially when abscesses are present. Acute
prostatitis may be very painful on palpation. Iliac lymph
node enlargement is possible.
With acute bacterial prostatitis, the CBC may be normal or may display a neutrophilic leukocytosis of varying
severity with a left shift. The biochemistry panel
may reveal azotemia of varying degrees which may be
a combination of postrenal (secondary to prostatic
enlargement and urethral obstruction), intrinsic renal
(ascending pyelonephritis) or prerenal (dehydration) factors. Hepatic enzymes, especially alkaline phosphatase
enzyme, may be elevated. Urinalysis collected by cystocentesis may reveal hematuria, proteinuria, and an
active sediment but this is not sensitive or specific for
diagnosing prostatitis. Urine culture is usually positive.
Abdominal radiographs may indicate an enlarged and
irregular prostate, and mineralization is possible.
Peritonitis is sometimes noted caudal to the bladder
due to inflammation and secondary to abscess rupture.
The bladder may also be pushed cranially into the
abdominal cavity. Abdominal ultrasound findings
include an enlarged and sometimes irregular prostate
that is diffusely heterogenous with or without abscesses,
sometimes giving the appearance of being mottled
(Figure 124.6). Contrast urethrocystogram may indicate
prostatic contrast uptake of varying degree.

­Prostatitis and Prostatic Abscesses
Etiology
Bacterial prostatitis is usually the result of an ascending
infection via the urethra and into the communicating
prostatic ducts. The presence of other prostatic conditions such as BPH, prostatic cysts, or prostatic neoplasia
may increase the incidence of prostatitis. Alterations in
urine flow and urinary tract infections also increase the
risk of prostatitis in intact males. Hematogenous infection is also possible but less likely. Prostatitis is reported
in all age groups in intact males and is exceedingly rare in
neutered males.
The most common bacterial organism to cause prostatitis is Escherichia coli. Other common infectious
­etiologies include Staphylococcus spp., Streptococcus
spp., Mycoplasma spp., Pseudomonas spp., and Proteus
spp. Brucellosis is possible secondary to venereal and
hematogenous transmission. Prostatic abscesses can
develop secondary to prostatitis or within prostatic
cysts. Chronic prostatitis is reported to be more ­frequent
than acute prostatitis but with less evident clinical
signs.

Cytology is necessary for a diagnosis and for targeted
therapy, but caution must be exercised in obtaining samples (see Table 124.1). Typical cytology findings include
free and phagocytosed bacteria, intact and degenerate
neutrophils, macrophages, necrotic debris, and hyperplastic epithelial cells with mild anisokaryosis.
Therapy
Targeted antibiotic therapy is indicated in both acute and
chronic prostatitis and prostatic abscesses. Antibiotics
must be chosen based on culture and sensitivity results
as well as their ability to penetrate prostatic tissue. The
ideal antibiotic needs to be lipid soluble and have lower
serum protein binding to be able to cross into the ­prostate
(Table 124.2). If higher protein binding is a characteristic
of a particular desired antibiotic, using a higher dosage
range is necessary. While awaiting cytology and culture
results, therapy should be started with enrofloxacin.

Figure 124.6 Prostatic abscess and prostatitis as seen on
ultrasound transverse image plane. Note the mottled appearance
of the prostate surrounding the abscessed region. Source: Image
courtesy of Dr Tim Spotswood.

There are unfortunately very few clinical data or trials in
veterinary medicine looking at the efficacy of specific
antibiotics and their effectiveness in crossing into the
dog prostate and treating prostatitis. In the presence of
sepsis, the antibiotic spectrum should be broadened
(beta‐lactam, third‐generation cephalosporin, aminoglycosides, imipenem). The blood–prostate barrier is compromised in these situations and antibiotics that would
not generally penetrate the prostate will do so.
Ciprofloxacin is not indicated in infectious prostatitis
as not only does it have poor oral bioavailability in dogs
and cats, it also does not penetrate the prostate as well
as enrofloxacin. Antibiotic therapy should be continued
for a minimum of 4–6 weeks, and prostatic culture should
be rechecked 3–5 days after discontinuation of antibiotics. Specific treatment for sepsis and peritonitis is detailed
elsewhere, as is the treatment for acute azotemia.
Surgery may be necessary for prostatic abscesses.
Medical drainage of abscesses by percutaneous ultrasound‐guided aspiration combined with targeted
antibiotic therapy rarely results in the resolution of
­
abscesses. However, ultrasound‐guided drainage may
facilitate stabilization of a patient if surgery is delayed.
Multiple surgical techniques have been described
­including omentalization, marsupialization, placement
of drain tubes, and partial or total prostatectomy, with
omentalization seeming to offer the best results and
fewer complications.
It is always recommended to neuter dogs with prostatitis and prostatic abscesses as this can accelerate recovery and also prevent recurrence. Finasteride therapy may
be used in breeding dogs to shrink the prostate but its
efficacy in prostatitis is unknown.
Prognosis
Prognosis is good to guarded in acute prostatitis without
abscessation or sepsis. Chronic prostatitis may be more

­Squamous Metaplasia of Prostatic
Epithelial Cells
This condition is quite rare and usually develops
­secondary to exogenous estrogen administration (such

as to treat BPH or transdermal patches and creams used
as hormone replacement therapy in women) or to an
estrogen‐secreting tumor such as a Sertoli cell tumor.
Dogs may be asymptomatic or develop clinical signs similar to dogs with prostatitis. Diagnosis is obtained via
biopsies. Treatment involves antibiotic therapy for
potential secondary prostatitis, identifying and treating
the cause of the metaplasia (surgery and potentially
chemotherapy for Sertoli cell tumors, discontinuation of
estrogen compounds). Prognosis is guarded as chronic
prostatitis may develop.

Management of Chronic Kidney Disease
Jessica Quimby, DVM, PhD, DACVIM (SAIM)
Department of Veterinary Clinical Sciences, Ohio State University Veterinary Medical Center, Columbus, OH, USA

Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is defined as the presence of structural or functional abnormalities in one or
both kidneys that has been present for three or more
months. In most cases with renal dysfunction, this is a
progressive disease, and currently no treatment short of
renal transplantation has been shown to reverse or halt
declining renal function for any significant period of
time. Renal transplant and dialysis are less widely available and are expensive therapies. Additionally, not all
CKD patients are acceptable candidates for transplantation or dialysis. Medical management therefore is the
mainstay of treatment and can help patients cope with
metabolic complications of the disease and improve
quality of life.

­Disease Staging
The severity of signs associated with kidney disease varies depending on the degree of kidney dysfunction. In
order to better tailor therapy to the individual patient
and to provide some assessment of prognosis, staging of
disease is recommended. The International Renal
Interest Society (IRIS), a panel of experts in veterinary
nephrology, has developed a staging system for chronic
kidney disease in dogs and cats (www.iris‐kidney.com)
that has been accepted by the American and European
Societies of Veterinary Nephrology and Urology. With
this system, once diagnosed with CKD, animals are
grouped into four stages (IRIS 1–4) based on serum creatinine, as well as substages based on proteinuria and
blood pressure. The recent guidelines also incorporate
SDMA results. Assessment of kidney function is based
on fasted serum creatinine measurements assessed on at
least two occasions in a stable, hydrated patient (Table
125.1). Caution should be exercised in staging elderly

patients in poor body condition as muscle mass contributes
to daily creatinine production; very thin animals may
have lower than expected serum creatinine concentrations. The biomarker SDMA is correlated with glomerular
filtration rate (GFR) and as it is not affected by muscle
mass, has been incorporated into the IRIS guidelines to
help determine staging in patients with muscle loss.
Due to variability in normal ranges for serum creatinine, some patients staged as IRIS 1 or 2 may have serum
creatinine within the reference range. The patient’s overall clinical status should be taken into account and serum
creatinine should not be interpreted without a concurrent
urine specific gravity. For example, creatinine >1.6 mg/
dL in a feline patient with a urine specific gravity <1.035
may be indicative of kidney disease even though it is
within a published reference range.
Substaging is performed to further characterize the
disease based on the measurement of arterial blood
pressure and proteinuria, both of which are a concern as
they potentially hasten disease progression. Classification
of proteinuria is determined by measuring urine
protein:creatinine ratio (UPC) in a culture‐negative sample with an inactive sediment (Table 125.2). Unless the
UPC is markedly elevated or less than 0.2, classification
should ideally be based on multiple UPC determinations
(2–3) over at least a two‐week period.
Blood pressure substage is determined by incorporating both arterial blood pressure measurement and
assessment of the presence of end‐organ damage such as
retinal lesions and neurologic signs (Table 125.3). With
the exception of animals who have a blood pressure
>200 mmHg and/or evidence of end‐organ damage,
blood pressure classification should be determined
based on at least three independent measurements, ideally over several days to weeks. The lowest measurement
is the one utilized.

­Medical Management of Chronic
Kidney Disease
Medical management of CKD consists of treatments
designed to provide supportive and symptomatic care
for the animal, with the goal of correcting nutritional,
fluid, electrolyte, endocrine, and acid–base imbalances.
These treatments aim to minimize the clinicopathologic
and pathophysiologic effects of kidney dysfunction.
Unfortunately, medical management is not expected to
halt, reverse or cure kidney dysfunction or any associated renal lesions. If any treatable underlying cause of
disease is identified, such as infection or obstruction, it is
imperative that it be addressed. The management guidelines presented in this chapter are intended for animals
with stable chronic disease, not those currently undergoing a uremic crisis.
Nutrition and Dietary Therapy
Several studies have documented the therapeutic value
of specially formulated diets in the management of CKD,
including evidence of decreased incidence of uremic crisis and increased survival and modulation of biomarkers.
It is perhaps a common misconception that the sole purpose of these diets is protein restriction. Other modifications present in these diets are as important, or potentially
even more important than protein restriction. In com-

parison to a maintenance diet, renal diets are typically
formulated to contain modified amounts of high‐quality
protein, increased caloric, soluble fiber and B vitamins,
omega‐3 polyunsaturated fatty acid and antioxidant content, reduced amounts of phosphorus and sodium, and
to have a neutral effect on acid–base balance. In addition,
feline renal diets are supplemented with potassium.
Recently, early‐stage renal diets that are phosphorus
restricted but with less restricted protein content have
also become available for cats.
The greatest clinical challenge with recommending a
renal diet is acceptance by the animal. The failure of the
patient to eat the formulated diet negates the benefit of
dietary management, and therefore a key therapeutic
target for these patients is the maintenance of appetite
and food intake. Poor body condition is associated with
decreased prognosis in several species and it also has a
negative effect on owner perception of quality of life. As
animals with CKD often suffer from poor appetite, this
should be actively addressed in a management plan.
Nonacceptance of renal diets can potentially be overcome by addressing underlying metabolic complications
of CKD as well as gradually introducing the renal diet
over several weeks. Many animals will readily accept and
continue eating a renal diet provided the transition
period is adequately slow. Other tips to encourage
acceptance of renal diet include increasing owner compliance with education regarding the benefits of the diet,
avoiding transitioning to the renal diet during a uremic
crisis event to prevent food aversion, trying different
temperatures, textures and brand formulations of food,
and medically managing nausea and inappetence associated with uremic syndrome.
It is particularly important that the patient eat sufficiently to satisfy caloric requirements. A nutritional
assessment should be performed at each visit including
body weight, body condition score, muscle mass score,
and a thorough nutritional history (www.wsava.org/
nutrition‐toolkit). Insufficient caloric intake could
potentially lead to protein malnutrition as evidenced by
decreased muscle mass, anemia and decreased serum
albumin or total protein concentrations.
If caloric requirements are not being met, yet m
­ etabolic
complications are controlled and medical management
of inappetence is unsuccessful, supplementation with a
diet palatable to the animal or assisted feeding should be
considered. Assisted feeding options include placement
of an esophagostomy or percutaneous gastrostomy tube
for long‐term nutritional management. Tube feeding has
the additional advantage of allowing the owner to deliver
oral water and medications to the patient and can be a
valuable tool for long‐term management of CKD.
Disadvantages of tube feeding include the anesthesia
required for placement and tube site complications.

Antinausea and Appetite Stimulant Therapy
Patients with CKD can suffer from nausea, vomiting, and
inappetence likely as a result of uremic toxins that are
sensed in the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the brain.
Several potent antiemetic/antinausea therapies are now
available. These include the 5‐HT3 receptor antagonists
ondansetron and dolasetron and the NK1 receptor
antagonist maropitant citrate. These drugs work at the
chemoreceptor trigger zone and vomiting center in the
brain, as well as receptors in gastrointestinal tract, and
can be given orally or as an injection.
Maropitant is commonly used for acute vomiting but a
pharmacokinetic and toxicity study in cats indicated that
longer‐term usage appears safe and it is often used for
long‐term therapy in chronically ill patients. When given
daily for two weeks at a dose of 4 mg/cat, maropitant was
demonstrated to palliate vomiting associated with CKD
in cats with stage II and III CKD. Maropitant citrate is
administered at 1 mg/kg.
Ondansetron has been documented to be twice as
effective as metoclopramide in palliating uremic nausea
and vomiting in human CKD patients. Ondansetron and
dolasetron are frequently used as antiemetics, but recent
studies have called into question their efficacy at currently recommended doses in cats (0.5 mg/kg BID).
Pharmacokinetic studies in cats have demonstrated that
oral bioavailability of ondansetron is poor in this species
(~35%) and the half‐life is very short (approximately one
hour), making it most appropriately a q8h medication.
Subcutaneous ondansetron had a slightly longer half‐life
of three hours. Ondansetron is also not appropriate as a
transdermal medication as a recent paper assessing
transdermal absorption in cats demonstrated no clinically relevant blood levels after administration. The ideal
dosing regimen of ondansetron for dogs is also unknown
and there is some evidence that oral bioavailable in dogs
is extremely poor (<10%). However, a recent study demonstrated that ondansetron had superior antinausea
effects in comparison to maropitant in a cisplatin model.
Dolasetron has traditionally been recommended as a
once‐daily medication at doses of 0.5–1 mg/kg; however,
a recent paper demonstrated that after a 0.8 mg/kg

­subcutaneous dose the drug is not detectable in the
serum at 12 hours and does not palliate xylazine‐induced
emesis.
Although more commonly used as an appetite stimulant,
mirtazapine also demonstrates antiemetic properties,
acting at the 5‐HT3 receptor similar to ondansetron. In
cats, mirtazapine has been shown to significantly reduce
vomiting associated with CKD.
Limiting gastric acidity with the use of H2 blockers like
famotidine or proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole anecdotally appears to palliate inappetence in some
CKD patients. However, these medications have never
been evaluated in a clinical trial despite famotidine being
one of the most commonly prescribed medications in
CKD cats. Recent studies of the effect of omeprazole on
the gastric pH in normal cats indicate that at 1 mg/kg
twice daily, it is superior to famotidine in its ability to
inhibit acid production, but again no clinical trials have
been performed in CKD cats and CKD cats do not
appear to experience hyperacidity as previously assumed.
Additionally, proton pump inhibitors have recently been
linked to an increased risk of kidney disease in humans.
The applicability of this finding to veterinary patients is
entirely unknown, and a recent retrospective study found
no correlation between acid‐suppressing medications
and increased risk for kidney disease or progression of
disease. Due to lack of evidence for a high incidence of
ulcerative gastritis associated with CKD, sucralfate is
recommended only if gastric ulceration and hemorrhage
are suspected as it is sometimes poorly tolerated and
may lead to further inappetence.
In addition to addressing uremic nausea and vomiting,
appetite stimulants can also be used to encourage food
intake, particularly in late‐stage patients. Cyproheptadine
has been used for some time as an appetite stimulant and
has anecdotal efficacy in many patients, although its efficacy has never been scientifically evaluated. Mirtazapine
has become more commonly used, particularly in cats,
and recent exploration of its pharmacodynamics and
pharmacokinetics has provided information for more
effective use in animals. Pharmacodynamic studies in
cats have illustrated that it can be a potent appetite

­stimulant, but higher doses are more commonly associated with side‐effects (hyperexcitability, vocalization,
agitation). Smaller, more frequent doses are recommended: 1.88 mg q48h orally in cats with CKD and
0.6–1 mg/kg once to twice daily in dogs. In dogs, twice‐daily
dosing may be required due to relatively shorter half‐life
than in other species. Mirtazapine is also amenable to
transdermal administration, and has recently become
FDA approved for use in cats (Mirataz®, KindredBio).
Owners should be aware that mirtazapine and cyproheptadine cannot be administered concurrently; cyproheptadine is used as an antidote for serotonin effects of
mirtazapine overdose and thus negates the efficacy of
the latter.
Capromorelin (Entyce®, Aratana Therapeutics), a ghrelin agonist, has recently become FDA approved as an
appetite stimulant for dogs.
Systemic Hypertension
Systemic hypertension appears to be common in dogs
(31–54%) and cats (20–65%) with CKD, but the exact
pathophysiologic relationship is unknown. Systemic
hypertension can have deleterious effects such as retinal
hemorrhage and detachment, neurologic and cardiac
impairment. Therefore, the diagnosis and treatment of
hypertension are important in this patient population.
Once hypertension has been classified (see Table
125.3), the decision to initiate therapy is based on the
degree of hypertension and the animal’s IRIS stage.
Patients with CKD stage 2–4 and blood pressure persistently over 160 mmHg are candidates for treatment.
Antihypertensive therapy should be considered for IRIS
1 patients with arterial blood pressure persistently
greater than 180 mmHg. It is unknown what the optimal
arterial blood pressure is for patients with CKD. A general guideline is to reduce the blood pressure to between
100 and 160 mmHg. Aggressive reduction of blood pressure is only necessary in patients experiencing ocular
and neurologic complications and otherwise it may take
weeks, particularly in dogs, to achieve adequate control.
Treatment strategies for cats and dogs differ slightly
based on the efficacy of currently available antihypertensive
medications for each species. Currently utilized antihypertensive medications in dogs include angiotensin‐converting
enzyme (ACE) inhibitors (enalapril and benazepril), calcium channel blockers (amlodipine) or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) such as telmisartan. These medications
are thought to be most effective at reducing hypertension in
dogs although most patients require multiple medications
and few studies have been done in this area. ACEI and
ARB are also used for the management of concurrent proteinuria. Typical starting doses of ACEI are 0.25–0.5 mg/kg
every 12–24 hours with increases based on effect on blood

pressure up to 2 mg/kg/day. In dogs, amlodipine doses
range from 0.1 to 0.5 mg/kg/day and are typically combined
with an ACEI. Recommended dose for telmisartan is 1 mg/
kg once daily.
Amlodipine is documented to be an effective treatment for hypertension in the cat and has traditionally
been the drug of choice in this species. ACEI have not
been demonstrated to adequately reduce blood pressure
in cats when used as sole therapy. Amlodipine is prescribed at an initial dose of 0.625 mg/cat <5 kg and
1.25 mg/cat >5 kg. Alternative formulations of the drug
have been explored including transdermal amlodipine
and a chewable form which may provide some degree of
efficacy. Amlodipine has also been documented to
decrease proteinuria in cats. Telmisartan is also an effective antihypertensive medication in cats and has recently
become approved for this indication in cats (United
States) as well as an antiproteinuric (UK and Europe).
For all antihypertensive therapy, blood pressure should
be rechecked within 7–10 days after initiating treatment.
Monitoring renal values and electrolytes is also important; ACEI can decrease GFR and result in increasing
azotemia, in which case therapy should be reassessed.
Hyperkalemia is also a common side‐effect of ACEI and
ARB in dogs and may limit the dose that can be administered. Additional guidelines for the use of ACEI and ARB
can be found in the consensus statement for the standard
treatment of proteinuria.
Proteinuria
Proteinuria is associated with poorer prognosis in several species. The renal tubular epithelial cells are responsible for processing protein and this increases their
metabolic load and oxidative stress. Although reducing
proteinuria has been demonstrated to significantly slow
disease progression in humans, studies in dogs and cats
have documented decreased proteinuria secondary to
ACEI administration, but results so far are only suggestive of long‐term benefit. Nonetheless, it is considered
standard of care that dogs and cats with stage 2, 3 and 4
CKD with UPC greater than 0.5 and 0.4 respectively, and
cats and dogs with stage 1 CKD and UPC greater than
2.0 be treated with antiproteinuric drugs such as ACEI or
ARB. Additionally, systemic hypertension exacerbates
proteinuria and should be addressed as previously
described. Therapeutic renal diets are considered to be
standard of care and have been demonstrated to be helpful in the management of proteinuric CKD and typically
are restricted in phosphorus, contain conservative
amounts of high‐quality protein, adequate nonprotein
calories, as well as omega‐3 fatty acids, antioxidants, and
buffers to help control acidemia. Management of nutrition to meet caloric intake is a key goal.

Angiotensin‐converting enzyme inhibitor or ARB
therapy is instituted with a therapeutic goal of normalizing (<0.5) or, when impossible, at least reducing the
UPC by 50% (Figure 125.1). Dosing, side‐effects, and
monitoring for ACEI are as described for antihypertensive therapy; starting at the low end of the range and cautiously increasing the dose to maximize effect on
proteinuria while monitoring for adverse effects is recommended (see Figure 125.1). Unacceptable side‐effects
of ACEI or ARB therapy include an increase in serum
creatinine >30% in IRIS 1–2 dogs, >10% in IRIS 3 dogs or
any increase in creatinine in stage 4 dogs; serum potassium >6.0 mmol/L; blood pressure <120 mmHg. Extreme
caution should be used in prescribing ACEI or ARB in
dogs with IRIS stage 4 disease. In these patients, side‐
effects may outweigh benefits at this stage of disease
progression.
Additional guidelines for the use of ACEI and ARB can
be found in the consensus statement for the standard
treatment of proteinuria.
Protein‐losing nephropathies are associated with an
increased risk for thromboembolism and the prevalence

in dogs has been reported to be as high as 25%. Few studies
have assessed the efficacy of antithrombotic therapies
specifically in glomerulonephropathy (GN) patients.
Currently consensus recommendations consist of 1–5 mg/
kg low‐dose aspirin daily for thromboprophylaxis.
Clopidogrel (1.1 mg/kg daily) is likely similarly effective
to low‐dose aspirin. No studies have demonstrated
superior efficacy to justify the higher cost.
Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are antiinflammatory and the underlying process in CKD is inflammatory in nature; supplementation is thought to be
beneficial. Several studies have demonstrated evidence of benefit in human CKD patients and rodent
models demonstrate decreased oxidative stress,
inflammation, and scarring. Many renal diets are now
supplemented with PUFAs in appropriate ratios. The
need to supplement omega‐3 fatty acids beyond that
present in renal diets is not fully known at this time.
However, supplementation at 0.25–0.5 g of omega‐3
PUFA/kg containing eicosapentaenoic acid and
docosahexaenoic acid has been described as a dose
extrapolated from human literature.
