1170

Section 10 Renal and Genitourinary Disease

Approximate 50% of dogs with protein‐losing nephropathy have immune‐mediated disease. The goals of performing a renal biopsy are to identify subtypes of GN
that involve immune complexes, guide the decision
regarding the necessity of immunosuppressive therapy,
and assess prognosis. Renal biopsy should be avoided in
patients with bleeding disorders, uncontrolled hypertension, chronic end‐stage disease and in very small patients
(cats and dogs <5 kg). It is highly recommended that if
taking the time and trouble to biopsy, samples are sent to
a nephropathologist (International Veterinary Renal
Pathology Service, Ohio State University, https://vet.osu.
edu/vmc/international‐veterinary‐renal‐pathology‐
service‐ivrps). Immune suppression is indicated when
electron‐dense deposits are seen on electron microscopy
or if there is positive immunofluorescent staining. A typical therapeutic regimen is mycophenolate 10 mg/kg BID
and adding prednisolone when rapidly progressing
(1 mg/kg BID). Steroids should not be used as monotherapy and the goal in using them is to taper relatively
quickly. If biopsy is not possible or safe, empiric immunosuppressive therapy can be considered in patients
where standard therapy is not effective, serum creatinine
is >3 mg/dL, and there is rapid progression of disease or
severe hypoalbuminemia. It is generally considered that
if a response to immunosuppressive therapy is not seen
in eight weeks, it is unlikely to occur.
Fluid Therapy
As CKD progresses, GFR decreases and azotemia worsens, yet the patient is not able to compensate by concentrating urine and maintaining hydration. Dehydration is
therefore a common complication of CKD and can lead
to inappetence, lethargy, weakness, constipation, and
increased susceptibility to uremic crisis. Owners should
be aware that concurrent illness, vomiting and diarrhea,
household changes/stress or inadequate water sources
promote dehydration and can have more serious effects
in CKD patients, potentially precipitating a uremic crisis.
Maintaining hydration by administering subcutaneous
balanced electrolyte solutions appears to anecdotally
improve appetite, activity, and quality of life and reduce
constipation in CKD patients, although no clinical trials
have been performed. Subcutaneous fluid administration
is generally feasible in cats and small dogs and can be a
very helpful tool for owners in management of disease,
particularly in stage 3 and 4. With instruction, many owners find the procedure to be feasible, and tolerated by the
patient. Additionally, feeding canned food instead of dry
kibble, or adding water to food is another way to increase
water consumption. Paying special attention to water
sources in the house – fresh, accessible, water fountains
for cats, etc. – is also an important tip for owners.

Anemia
As kidney disease progresses, renal production of
erythropoietin decreases and anemia can result. Other
factors that can contribute to anemia include poor nutrition, blood loss, concurrent infection, and reduced red
blood cell lifespan. Anemia may exacerbate the hypoxic
environment in the kidney by reducing oxygen delivery
to the area, thus potentiating oxidative stress, renal damage, and progression of disease. Anemia has been identified as a negative predictor of survival in CKD.
Therapeutic action should be taken when hematocrit
nears or drops below 20%. Although gastric ulceration is
thought to be relatively uncommon with CKD, chronic
gastrointestinal hemorrhage is suspected when melena,
elevated BUN, iron deficiency or anemia disproportionate to level of azotemia is noted. Empiric treatment with
antacid and sucralfate with an increase in hematocrit
supports the diagnosis.
Hormone replacement therapy is the most effective
treatment for anemia secondary to CKD and can be
addressed with artificial products such as recombinant
human erythropoietin (Epogen®, Amgen) or darbepoetin
alpha (Aranesp®, Amgen). Epogen is given as a SC injection and is effective in treating anemia secondary to
CKD. However, as it is a foreign protein, approximately
one‐third of animals will develop antibodies against both
the foreign erythropoietin and their own, and potentially
become transfusion dependent. For this reason, the
product is not recommended until packed cell volume
(PCV) falls below 20% and owners should be informed of
this risk. Close monitoring of hematocrit is crucial so
that possible antibody formation and subsequent drop
in hematocrit are caught quickly. If therapy is stopped
appropriately, suppressed erythropoiesis may be reversible.
Darbepoetin is a longer‐acting form of erythropoietin
and appears to have less association with anti‐epo antibodies. It is currently the product of choice, but expense
can limit its use for some owners. Therapy with darbepoetin consists of an induction phase and a maintenance
phase. Initially, darbepoetin is administered 0.5–1.0 μg/
kg subcutaneously once weekly. Blood pressure as well as
PCV should be checked weekly during the initiation
period; hypertension associated with too quick an
increase in PCV is the main side‐effect. Other reported
side‐effects include pure red cell aplasia, arthralgia, fever,
seizures, polycythemia, and iron deficiency. Previous
estimates of treatment success have been 60–65% in cats
(multiple concurrent disease) and 85% in dogs. Typical
response time is 2–4 weeks.
Once the hematocrit has reached the lower end of the
normal range, the frequency of administration can be
decreased to every other week to maintain the animal
long term. Stimulating erythropoiesis is associated with

VetBooks.ir

125 Management of Chronic Kidney Disease

a high iron demand and due to the functional iron deficiency associated with CKD, iron supplementation is
recommended when therapy is initiated, as well as every
few months through the course of therapy. Iron injections (iron dextran 50 mg/cat IM, 10–20 mg/kg dogs IM,
typically well tolerated) are considered better that oral
iron supplementation as the latter tends to be bitter and
likely to exacerbate an already poor appetite, as well as
being poorly absorbed from the GI tract. B vitamins are
necessary for red blood cell (RBC) synthesis and the
degree to which they are deficient in CKD patients and
an active contributor to anemia is poorly understood.
Given their benign nature, supplementation is unlikely
to be harmful but no information about efficacy currently exists. However, B vitamins are not considered
effective as sole therapy for anemia.
Hypokalemia
Hypokalemia is a common finding in cats with stage 2
and 3 CKD likely due to a combination of increased urinary loss, inadequate dietary intake, and activation of the
renin‐angiotensin‐aldosterone system. Hypokalemia is
less common in stage 4 cats due to markedly decreased
glomerular filtration, and less common in dogs due to
ACEI therapy. In cats, common presenting signs of profound hypokalemia are hypokalemic myopathy and constipation. Fortunately, profound hypokalemia is less
common since the advent of renal diets supplemented
with potassium. Hypokalemia is associated with development and worsening of CKD in humans and appears
to exacerbate damage to tubular epithelial cells.
Potassium supplementation may be provided orally as
potassium gluconate (1–4 mEq/cat twice daily), or potassium citrate (40–75 mg/kg PO divided twice daily), to
effect. Various forms of potassium supplements are
available including pill, powder, and gel. Potassium citrate has the added advantage of being an alkalinizing
agent, but the degree to which this is effective for treatment of metabolic acidosis has not been evaluated.
Potassium chloride is not recommended as an oral supplement because it is acidifying and unpalatable, but may
be added to subcutaneous fluids at concentration up to
30 mEq/L (higher concentrations can be associated with
irritation).
Serum potassium levels are not representative of systemic tissue potassium levels and animals with low normal serum potassium may be systemically depleted,
which is exacerbated by metabolic acidosis. Some clinicians advocate prophylactic supplementation even when
serum potassium is in the low normal range, with a goal
of maintaining serum potassium levels above 4 mg/dL.
The value of prophylactic potassium supplementation
has not yet been established.

Mineral and Bone Disorder:
Hyperphosphatemia
The disturbances in calcium, phosphorus, and magnesium,
and associated clinical syndromes in CKD are referred
to as CKD‐mineral and bone disorder (CKD‐MBD).
Renal secondary hyperparathyroidism is a major component in this process involving excess phosphorus,
parathyroid hormone (PTH), and fibroblast growth
factor (FGF)23. The kidneys are the main route of
phosphorus excretion and as kidney function declines,
hyperphosphatemia develops. Hyperphosphatemia is
detrimental because it contributes to renal secondary
hyperparathyroidism, ­
tissue mineralization, and progression of CKD. Thus, controlling phosphorus intake
through diet and phosphate binders is an important part
of CKD management. Feeding a phosphorus‐restricted
diet is the first recommended step for managing CKD‐
MBD and studies have demonstrated efficacy in decreasing serum concentrations of phosphorus, PTH, and
FGF23 as well as improved outcome. Evidence suggests
that feeding a phosphorus‐restricted diet even if serum
phosphorus is normal is potentially beneficial. If a renal
diet is initiated and phosphorus is still elevated after 4–6
weeks, then a phosphate binder is recommended with the
goal of keeping serum phosphorus in the low normal
range if possible (Table 125.4). These medications bind
the phosphorus in the food, making it less bioavailable,
so it is critical that the medication is given with each
meal. Several different phosphate binders are available,
including aluminum hydroxide, calcium carbonate, and
lanthanum carbonate, but the main problem with administration is palatability.
Therapy is initiated with a starting dose of 30–100 mg/
kg/day for aluminum hydroxide, 150 mg/kg/day for
calcium carbonate, and 30 mg/kg/day for lanthanum
­
­carbonate. Doses are to effect, and generally therapy
begins at the lower end of the dose range and is increased
every 4–6 weeks until serum phosphorus concentrations
are within the desired range. Use of calcium‐containing
phosphate binders is potentially associated with the
development of hypercalcemia, particularly if calcitriol is
also being administered. Serum ionized calcium should
be monitored during use.

Calcitriol
Calcitriol, the active form of vitamin D, is produced in
the kidney. Production is decreased in CKD and hyperphosphatemia further inhibits its synthesis. Calcitriol is
an important inhibitor of parathyroid hormone and low
levels lead to renal secondary hyperparathyroidism
which has multiple deleterious consequences. In early
CKD, controlling phosphorus levels may be sufficient to
maintain levels. As kidney disease progresses, supplementation of calcitriol may be necessary. In dogs and
people, supplementation of calcitriol has been shown to
be beneficial, resulting in slower progression of disease;
however, a preliminary study performed in cats was not
supportive of supplementation. Further evaluation of
calcitriol therapy, or other types of vitamin D analogs is
necessary to determine efficacy.
When prescribed, calcitriol therapy is initiated at a dosage of 2.0–2.5 ng/kg daily and should not exceed 5 ng/kg/
day. Calcitriol should be given on an empty stomach as
administration with food increases calcium absorption
and the risk of hypercalcemia. Cost may be a concern for
many owners as the drug and required monitoring are
costly; careful monitoring of ionized calcium, phosphorus, and PTH levels is required as hypercalcemia can
result from oversupplementation. If hypercalcemia
results, the daily dose can be doubled and given every
other day to decrease intestinal absorption of calcium.
Alkalinization Therapy
Metabolic acidosis is common in animals with overt
signs of uremia and may promote progression of disease.
In humans with CKD, bicarbonate therapy has been
demonstrated to slow progression and improve nutritional status. Blood gas analysis should be used to
determine acid–base status and whether treatment is
warranted. Therapy is initiated when blood pH and
bicarbonate concentration drop below the normal range.
Changing to a renal diet may improve acid–base balance
as these diets are pH neutral. Potassium citrate administration has the advantage of serving both as an alkalizing
agent and a potassium supplement; typical doses are
40–60 mg/kg two to three times daily, but degree of efficacy has not been demonstrated.
Antioxidant Therapy
The kidney is the site of substantial aerobic metabolism that
results in the production of reactive oxygen species.
Additionally, several processes in the diseased kidney potentially result in increased oxidative stress, including hypoxia,
anemia, proteinuria, and inflammation. Oxidative stress has
been documented in humans with CKD and potentially

contributes to the progression of disease. Oxidative stress
and decreased antioxidant capacity have been demonstrated
in cats with CKD, and vitamins E, C, and B‐carotene have
been shown to decrease oxidative stress in CKD cats. Animals
with CKD may benefit from antioxidant therapy, but randomized clinical trials are needed to determine the effect on
progression and survival.
Fatty Acid Therapy
Omega‐3 fatty acids are antiinflammatory and the
underlying process in CKD is inflammatory in nature, so
supplementation is thought to be beneficial. Several
studies have demonstrated evidence of benefit in human
CKD patients and rodent models demonstrate decreased
oxidative stress, inflammation, and scarring. Many renal
diets are now supplemented with fatty acids.
Enteric Dialysis and the Microbiome
Alterations in the gut microbiome and increased production of uremic toxins have been associated with CKD
in several species, including cats. Enteric dialysis refers
to the oral administration of prebiotic‐probiotic bacteria
which metabolize urea, creatinine, indoles, and phenols
in the gut, preventing absorption and therefore decreasing azotemia (Azodyl®). Enteric dialysis has some demonstrated efficacy in humans and rat models and it is a
popular supplemental therapy in feline CKD. A recent
study demonstrated that sprinkling the pill in the food,
contrary to manufacturer’s instructions, negated any
potential benefit. Controlled clinical studies are still
needed to determine the effect of enteric dialysis on
serum creatinine or uremic toxins in dogs and cats.

­Monitoring CKD Patients
Chronic kidney disease is progressive and as such,
patients’ metabolic state, clinical signs, and supportive
care needs change over time. Factors such as hypertension and proteinuria may not initially be present at diagnosis, but can develop later in the course of the disease.
Patients in stage 1 and 2 CKD are typically monitored
every 4–6 months once stable kidney function has been
established. Patients in stage 3 and 4 require more frequent monitoring, especially if metabolic complications
are present, and should be assessed minimally every 3–4
months. A typical visit should include clinical history,
medication review, physical examination, nutritional
assessment, and labwork consisting of CBC, serum biochemistry, urinalysis, and blood pressure. Urine cultures
and UPC are performed at regular intervals as well.
Establishing a relationship and providing client education

VetBooks.ir

125 Management of Chronic Kidney Disease

regarding the importance of monitoring and follow‐up
will improve compliance.

­Prognosis
Predicting prognosis in CKD can be somewhat challenging as the progression of disease varies substantially
between individuals. Poor body condition, proteinuria,
hypertension, hyperphosphatemia, and anemia have all

been associated with a poorer prognosis and should be
targets for disease management to maximize survival.
Typically, CKD progresses much more slowly in cats
than in dogs. Dogs with stage 3 and 4 CKD quickly
­progress and within months to a year or two may be
euthanized due to the disease. Cats with early CKD can
have stable disease, typically for years, and may die of
another disease process. Cats with stage 3 and 4 typically
­progress more slowly than dogs at a similar disease stage
and may still live months to years.

The Role of Dialysis
Adam E. Eatroff, DVM, DACVIM (SAIM)
ACCESS Specialty Animal Hospitals, Los Angeles, CA, USA

Peritoneal dialysis, intermittent hemodialysis, and
­continuous renal replacement therapy are being used in
companion animal medicine with increasing frequency
for the treatment of both acute kidney injury and chronic
kidney disease. Peritoneal dialysis, intermittent hemodialysis and hemofiltration, and continuous renal replacement therapy (the three modalities are hereafter referred
to as “dialysis,” unless they are discussed as separate
­entities) are employed with the goals of removing accumulated uremic toxins and fluid and reestablishing physiologic acid–base and electrolyte balance when the kidneys
are damaged to an extent that renders them incapable of
performing these duties. The goal of this chapter is to
introduce the reader to the indications, treatment goals,
complications, and prognostic considerations relevant to
dialysis. A discussion of the technical aspects of each
therapeutic modality is beyond the scope of this chapter,
but excellent resources exist for the ­interested reader.

­Dialysis Modalities
Renal replacement therapy is a term used to describe
various treatment modalities designed to perform the
excretory, regulatory, and, in some cases, synthetic
responsibilities of the kidney. Renal replacement therapies can be classified as intracorporeal (e.g., renal transplantation, peritoneal dialysis) and extracorporeal (e.g.,
intermittent hemodialysis and hemofiltration, continuous renal replacement therapy). Renal transplantation
relies on the provision of a donor kidney graft intended
to perform the function of the native kidneys, and is
reserved for cases of end‐stage kidney disease. This
modality is not discussed further here.
The remaining modalities are based on the principles of
diffusion, convection, and adsorption for uremic solute

clearance and restoration of acid–base and ­electrolyte
balance. Diffusion occurs when uremic solutes redistribute in solution from areas of higher concentration (blood)
to lower concentration (dialysate). The use of a semipermeable membrane to separate the dialysate from the
blood allows for the restriction of movement of larger
substances (protein and cellular components), while
smaller substances (uremic toxins) are able to redistribute
freely through the pores of the membrane. Convection
utilizes the application of a hydrostatic or osmotic force to
blood to promote fluid (plasma water) movement across a
membrane. Any substances dissolved in the plasma water
that are small enough to pass through the pores of the
membrane are removed. When the removal of fluid,
rather than solute, is the primary indication for convective
clearance, this modality is referred to as ultrafiltration.
Adsorption, which quantitatively contributes the least to
uremic solute removal, occurs when s­ ubstances adhere to
the membrane due to physiochemical interactions.
Peritoneal dialysis is performed by infusion of a solution (dialysate) into the peritoneal cavity. The peritoneal
membrane serves as a membrane across which uremic
solutes diffuse from the blood into the dialysate; solutes
(e.g., bicarbonate) of which the patient is deficient can
be administered via diffusion from the dialysate across
the peritoneal membrane into the patient’s blood.
Convective clearance of uremic solutes and excess fluid
can be achieved by use of hypertonic dialysate, which
exerts an osmotic force, drawing plasma water across
the p
­ eritoneal membrane into the dialysate. Dialysate is
intermittently infused and removed from the peritoneal
cavity in cycles during peritoneal dialysis. Intermittent
hemodialysis and continuous renal replacement rely on
the movement of blood through fibers composed of a
semipermeable membrane housed in a cartridge (dialyzer for intermittent hemodialysis; filter for continuous

Clinical Small Animal Internal Medicine Volume II, First Edition. Edited by David S. Bruyette.
© 2020 John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Published 2020 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc.
Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/bruyette/clinical

VetBooks.ir

Section 10 Renal and Genitourinary Disease

renal replacement therapy). The fibers are bathed in
dialysate, thus providing an arrangement analogous to
peritoneal dialysis, with three major exceptions: solute
and fluid exchange occur outside the body, the membrane across which exchange takes place is not native to
the patient, and blood and dialysate are typically moved
in countercurrent directions (as opposed to dialysate
remaining stagnant in the peritoneal cavity) to maximize
the concentration gradient for diffusion. For intermittent
hemodialysis and continuous renal replacement therapy,
convective clearance is achieved by application of negative hydrostatic pressure, which draws plasma water
across the dialyzer or filter membrane.

­Dialysis for Acute Kidney Injury
In companion animal medicine, dialysis is most frequently employed to treat acute kidney injury of various
etiologies, including leptospirosis (dogs), ureteral
obstructions (cats), and nephrotoxicity (dogs and cats).
However, in a recent publication, the etiology was undetermined in 43 of 93 (46%) dogs treated with intermittent
hemodialysis for acute kidney injury. While the high proportion of undiagnosed cases was likely due, in part, to
an inability to obtain a serologic diagnosis of leptospirosis or confirm the presence of the organism in tissue or
fluid, this statistic underscores the degree of prognostic
uncertainty that is frequently present when dialysis is
initiated in cases of acute kidney injury. The same study
reported ureteral obstructions as the most common
underlying etiology in cats undergoing intermittent

hemodialysis. Figure 126.1 demonstrates the use of intermittent hemodialysis for the treatment of a cat with
bilateral ureteral obstruction, and Figure 126.2 demonstrates the use of continuous renal replacement therapy
for the treatment of leptospirosis.
Regardless of the underlying cause of acute kidney
injury, the decision to implement dialysis is made based
on a multitude of factors, all of which are discussed below.
Azotemia/Uremia
Historically, severe uremia (e.g., blood urea nitrogen and
creatinine concentrations of ≥100 mg/dL and ≥10 mg/dL,
respectively) was considered a major indication for dialysis. However, recent trends favor initiation of dialysis at
less severe degrees of azotemia. The reasons for the lessening of this threshold are twofold. First, as the veterinary community gains experience and proficiency with
dialytic techniques, the safety and feasibility of this treatment have improved significantly. Consequently, the
value in preventing severe complications (e.g., gastrointestinal, neurologic, pulmonary) of uremia has become
evident, and favorable outcomes have become more
likely when dialysis is initiated in efforts to prevent these
complications, rather than reverse them. The window
for prevention of severe uremia usually is present at less
severe degrees of azotemia than the thresholds reported
above. Therefore, the degree of azotemia should be
assessed every 24–48 hours, so that dialysis can be initiated when consecutive days of worsening renal function
are documented, despite appropriate conventional medical and/or surgical therapy. Second, analogous to the
Figure 126.1 This cat had hyperkalemic
acute kidney injury secondary to bilateral
ureteral obstruction. Prior to surgical
intervention, the patient was given three
intermittent hemodialysis treatments
which resulted in resolution of
hyperkalemia and azotemia.

VetBooks.ir

Figure 126.2 This dog was diagnosed
with leptospirosis and was initially treated
with conservative medical management.
Worsening azotemia and volume
overload, however, prompted initiation of
continuous renal replacement therapy.

decision to administer a packed red blood cell ­transfusion
(i.e. the “transfusion trigger”), the decision to implement
dialysis is based on a variety of factors in addition to the
degree of azotemia (the correlate of azotemia, in the
transfusion example, would be the hematocrit). These
factors include co‐morbid conditions, such as cardiovascular disease, pulmonary disease, or a low seizure threshold, which may be exacerbated with less severe degrees
of renal dysfunction.

­Fluid Overload/Oliguria/Anuria
Parenteral fluid administration is considered a cornerstone of treatment for acute kidney injury and a variety of
other kidney diseases. However, misconceptions regarding the potential benefits and adverse effects of aggressive fluid administration are widespread. In cases of
severe renal dysfunction, aggressive fluid therapy with
the goal of achieving a positive fluid balance has not been
shown to improve renal clearance of uremic solutes.
While the serum or plasma creatinine concentration may
improve with achievement of a positive fluid balance, this
improvement is more likely related to accumulation of
fluid in the extracellular compartment, which results in
an increase in the volume of distribution of creatinine
and a dilutional effect on the serum or plasma creatinine
concentration. In human patients with acute kidney
injury (AKI), a decrease in serum or plasma ­creatinine
concentration has been shown to be directly proportional
to the degree of fluid accumulation. Fur­thermore, fluid
overload has been associated with negative outcomes,

including increased mortality and decreased renal recovery. Additional data suggesting the association between
fluid overload and outcome exists in a canine intensive
care unit (renal and nonrenal cases) are emerging. While
fluid overload can occur in a patient with normal urine
production or polyuria, this complication is most frequently encountered in oliguric or anuric patients. Even
restriction of all parenteral fluid therapy cannot prevent
fluid overload in anuric patients, due to the obligate fluid
load administered with medications and nutrition.
Once fluid overload occurs and manifestations, such
as pulmonary, gastrointestinal, and neurologic complications, are recognized, restoration of normal fluid balance
can be difficult to achieve. Diuretic therapy (e.g., loop or
osmotic diuretics) is frequently ineffective at promoting
fluid excretion in severely compromised kidneys, and
some diuretics (e.g., mannitol) may even be contraindicated due to the obligatory solute load that accompanies
administration. Therefore, dialysis (ultrafiltration) may
be the only effective means of removing excess fluid.
Hyperkalemia
Hyperkalemia is frequently the most immediate life‐
threatening complication of severe acute kidney injury.
Arrhythmias that negatively affect cardiac output or
result in death can occur when the serum or plasma
potassium increases above 6 mmol/L. The likelihood of a
clinically significant arrhythmia is increased when acidemia, uremia, or fluid overload is severe. While there
are several pharmacologic approaches to the treatment
of hyperkalemia in AKI (e.g., intravenous dextrose ±

1177

VetBooks.ir

1178

Section 10 Renal and Genitourinary Disease

­regular insulin and intravenous calcium gluconate, β2
agonists), the effects of these treatments are typically
modest and transient when renal function is severely
compromised. In these cases, rapid restoration of renal
function (e.g., surgical removal of ureteral obstructions)
or provision of dialysis are frequently necessary to
­normalize serum or plasma potassium concentration.
It should be noted, however, that restoration of renal
function is superior to intermittent forms of dialysis in
restoring whole‐body potassium balance, due to the
­predominantly intracellular distribution and slow redistribution of potassium when it is removed from the
extracellular space (as is the case in dialysis).
Severe Acidemia
In humans, provision of supplemental sodium bicarbonate in solution has not been proven to be of benefit in
cases of severe acidemia accompanying acute kidney
injury. Furthermore, in cases of oliguria or anuria, the
fluid volume administered once sodium bicarbonate has
been diluted to a physiologically tolerable osmolality
may result in complications associated with fluid overload. Bicarbonate, however, can be administered in therapeutic concentrations as an alkali buffer to patients
without an obligatory fluid load when the bicarbonate is
a component of the dialysate. During dialysis, bicarbonate diffuses from a medium in which it has a high concentration (the dialysate) to a fluid with a lower
concentration (the patient’s plasma water), resulting in
administration of sodium and bicarbonate ions without
fluid. The provision of alkali without a concomitant fluid
load can safely restore the extracellular pH to within the
normal range, allowing for normal function of metabolic
machinery in various tissues.
While these four factors are commonly encountered in
cases of AKI, the decision to employ dialysis does not
only depend on each factor’s presence but its degree of
severity. In human medicine, the optimal timing of initiation of dialysis for acute kidney injury has been vigorously
debated, and no consensus has been reached regarding
the benefit of early versus late initiation of therapy. The
data presented in the human literature likely cannot be
extrapolated to veterinary patients because the degree of
renal dysfunction that falls into the “late” category (typically defined as serum creatinine concentrations in the
range of 3.5–5 mg/dL and urea concentrations in the
range of 60–100 mg/dL) would be considered “early” or
“mild to moderate” dysfunction by most veterinarians. It
is the author’s impression that in veterinary cases of AKI
for which dialysis is initiated early, when the serum creatinine concentration is in the mild to moderate range,
outcomes are much improved compared to when dialysis

is initiated later (serum ­creatinine concentration >10 mg/
dL). Earlier initiation of dialysis allows for the prevention
of the sequelae of fluid overload, hyperkalemia, and
severe acidemia. Preventing these complications provides
the patient with optimal metabolic stability to facilitate
renal recovery and reduces the costs associated with
measures required to address complications such as pulmonary edema and cardiac arrhythmias. Initiation of
dialysis prior to decompensation of the patient may even
allow for a rapid transition to outpatient dialysis treatments, which can reduce client costs even further and
extend the client’s available financial resources.

­Dialysis for Chronic Kidney Disease
Although chronic kidney disease is an infrequent indication for dialysis, compared with acute kidney injury, dogs
and (less frequently) cats have been treated successfully
with chronic intermittent hemodialysis for prolonged
periods of time, ranging from a few months to over a
year. For patients with end‐stage chronic kidney disease,
dialysis may be thought of as analogous to palliative
chemotherapy or radiation therapy for patients with
oncologic diseases. The goals of treatment are maintenance of an acceptable quality of life, rather than the
metrics of tumor response in the case of cancer treatment or precise regulation of uremic, acid–base, electrolyte, and fluid balance in the case of chronic dialysis.
Patients that receive the greatest benefit from chronic
hemodialysis are typically those with International Renal
Interest Society (IRIS) stage 4 chronic kidney disease
(CKD) that are free of co‐morbidities (e.g., significant
cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, neurologic, or orthopedic disease). Dogs that weigh greater than 5 kg typically
tolerate chronic treatment better than smaller dogs or
cats. The reason for smaller animals’ inability to tolerate
chronic hemodialysis as well as larger patients has not
been determined. However, the author speculates that
this difference may be due two possible factors: (1) the
large volume of blood, relative to the body mass, that
must be outside the patient’s systemic circulation at any
given time to fill the dialysis circuit, and (2) the repeated
loss of blood endured by the patient, caused by residual
blood trapped in the dialysis circuit that cannot be
returned at the end of each treatment. Despite treatment
with erythropoiesis‐stimulating agents, smaller patients
are reliant upon multiple red blood cell transfusions that
must be administered before, during, or after some or all
dialysis treatments. The repeated administration of red
blood cell transfusion in such a short period of time (the
first 2–3 weeks of treatment) can lead to an increasing
probability of clinically devastating transfusion reactions
during the subsequent weeks/months of treatment. An

VetBooks.ir

126 The Role of Dialysis

additional limitation of chronic hemodialysis is the
financial and logistic responsibility of the owner. Not
only can chronic hemodialysis be cost prohibitive for
most owners, but the practical considerations may be
overwhelming. Patients treated with chronic hemodialysis typically require treatments, lasting as long as six
hours, three times per week. If a scheduling conflict prevents as few as one treatment from being performed, the
patient may have a high probability of suffering from
severe uremic complications (e.g., nausea), fluid overload, or hyperkalemia. Despite these limitations, a properly selected patient and its owner can enjoy an excellent
quality of life for several months to years when treated
with chronic hemodialysis.

­Alternative Indications for Dialysis:
Acute Intoxications and Therapeutic
Plasma Exchange
An additional, often overlooked indication for dialysis is
decontamination following acute toxin exposure. There
are a variety of intoxications that can be treated effectively with dialysis. However, treatment success is highly
dependent on the pharmacokinetic properties of the
toxin and timing of treatment in relation to ingestion/
exposure. Small (<500 daltons), freely circulating toxins
are efficiently removed from the blood compartment
with conventional hemodialysis, which utilizes diffusion
as the predominant clearance mechanism. Toxins with
small volumes of distribution are typically retained in the
vascular or extracellular compartment, and are more
efficiently accessed for clearance. However, retention of
toxins within the vascular compartment is typically a
result of a high degree of protein‐binding.
Because dialysis employs membrane‐based separation
techniques that, for most dialyzers and filters, exclude
the movement of proteins across the membrane, alternative techniques must be employed for toxins that are
highly protein bound. Charcoal hemoperfusion and
therapeutic plasma exchange are alternatives to conventional dialysis modalities, and can be employed to circumvent the limitations associated with dialytic removal
of protein‐bound toxins. Charcoal hemoperfusion
employs a large cartridge that, rather than housing membrane‐bound fibers bathed in a dialysate solution, contains activated charcoal around which blood percolates
as it is moved through the dialysis circuit. Binding interactions between toxins and the activated charcoal are
stronger than between the toxins and plasma proteins,
resulting in the transfer of the toxin from the plasma protein to the activated charcoal (adsorption). The large volume of blood that is required to fill the commercially

available charcoal columns, along with hematologic
changes associated with interactions of cellular blood
components with the charcoal, are sources of possible
adverse effects of this treatment (e.g., hypotension and
thrombocytopenia, respectively). There are multiple
hemoperfusion columns in the development of veterinary patients that utilize a more biocompatible substrate
for adsorption of exogenous toxins. These columns are
also of smaller volume than the previous charcoal
­cartridges, making them an attractive alternative to the
existing charcoal cartridges. Therefore, both the potential harm posed to the patient by the toxin to which it has
been exposed and the possible adverse effects of charcoal
hemoperfusion must be considered if this ­treatment is
to be employed.
Therapeutic plasma exchange may be considered in
lieu of charcoal hemoperfusion due to the smaller dialysis circuit size required and the avoidance of exposure of
cellular blood components to a substance as reactive as
charcoal. Therapeutic plasma exchange employs the
same equipment and convective clearance principles
described above to remove an offending substance from
the blood. However, it differs from conventional dialysis
in that semipermeable membranes have pores that are
large enough to allow passage of plasma proteins.
Therefore, therapeutic plasma exchange allows for
removal of a protein‐bound toxin, along with its carrier
protein. Disadvantages of this technique include the
requirement for replacement of the removed plasma
with a fluid that has a similar oncotic pressure to the
removed plasma and, if the protein composition of the
replacement fluid differs significantly from the removed
plasma, the potential for coagulopathy associated with
clotting factor depletion.
With regard to the financial considerations of these
two treatments, the cost is comparable. Charcoal hemoperfusion and therapeutic plasma exchange have been
used most commonly by the author for blood purification following ingestion of massive quantities of various
nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. The reader is
referred elsewhere for an extensive listing of intoxications that can be treated with dialysis.
In addition to blood purification for the treatment of
acute intoxication, therapeutic plasma exchange may
also be of benefit for a variety of immune‐mediated
­diseases. Due to the large pore size of the membranes
used, blood components as large as immunoglobulins
and immune complexes are easily cleared with convection using these membranes. Historically, therapeutic
plasma exchange was performed with dedicated equipment that utilized a centrifugal technique for blood
­component separation. Availability of this equipment is
still limited in veterinary medicine. However, the development of dialysis equipment with a wide selection of

1179

VetBooks.ir

1180

Section 10 Renal and Genitourinary Disease

­interchangeable filters and software has provided the
capability to perform this procedure with devices primarily designed for renal replacement therapy. In the
past several years, reports of therapeutic plasma
exchange performed for the treatment of diseases such
as myasthenia gravis and immune‐mediated hemolytic
anemia have appeared in the veterinary literature, heralding a new era in the evaluation of this modality for the
treatment of immune‐mediated diseases.

­Availability of Dialysis and Prognosis
for Dialysis Patients
The veterinary community has witnessed exponential
growth in the number of facilities offering dialysis for
small animal patients. Peritoneal dialysis requires equipment that is readily available, and this modality is performed in many emergency and specialty hospitals that
offer 24‐hour care. Effective implementation of intermittent hemodialysis and continuous renal replacement
therapy is limited to hospitals that not only have the
proper equipment but also employ properly trained individuals. Nonetheless, due to the low cost and ease of
acquisition of the necessary equipment, many veterinary
facilities now offer intermittent hemodialysis and continuous renal replacement therapy.
Despite the paucity of literature available describing
outcome, it appears that the prognosis for veterinary
patients treated with dialysis is variable, and dependent
on the underlying disease etiology, severity of illness, and
co‐morbid conditions. In cases of acute kidney injury of
any etiology, the survival to hospital discharge for both

dogs and cats is approximately 50% with the use of intermittent hemodialysis. When considering all possible
­etiologies, choice of modality does not appear to dramatically affect survival rate. Certain etiologies of acute kidney
injury treated with dialysis, such as leptospirosis in dogs
and ureteral obstructions in cats, have higher survival
rates, reaching 80–90%. In contrast, the prognosis for
acute kidney injury secondary to ethylene glycol intoxication is poor, with only 20% of dialysis patients regaining
sufficient renal function to allow discontinuation of
dialysis.
While the current overall success rate for treatment
of acute kidney injury with dialysis appears disappointing, closer evaluation of the situation provides cause for
optimism. The survival rates achieved in veterinary
medicine are similar to those achieved in human medicine. This accomplishment is likely due, in large part, to
the etiologic differences between human and veterinary
acute kidney injury. Human acute kidney injury most
commonly arises as a complication of disorders (e.g.,
sepsis, advanced cardiac disease) that alone carry a
poor prognosis. Therefore, when acute kidney injury
does occur, the likelihood of a poor outcome is multiplied. In veterinary medicine, however, many dialysis
candidates presented for acute kidney injury secondary
to leptospirosis or select intoxications have no preexisting co‐morbid conditions that may affect prognosis.
Therefore, if the potential benefit of dialysis is recognized early, and these patients are treated with dialysis
prior to the onset of severe complications, there is the
potential for the veterinary community to significantly
improve the current success rate for treatment of acute
kidney injury.

Micturition and Associated Disorders
Julie K. Byron, DVM, MS, DACVIM (SAIM)
College of Veterinary Medicine, Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA

­Physiology of Micturition
The primary purpose of the lower urinary tract is to store
urine and facilitate its elimination at an appropriate time.
The bladder is in storage phase 99% of the time and in
emptying phase only 1% of the time. Coordination of
both storage or filling and emptying requires a complex
interaction between the somatic and autonomic nervous
systems, as well as normal function of the tissues involved.
The three divisions of the peripheral nervous system
innervate the urethra. The pudendal nerve carries
somatic signals to the striated muscle that makes up the
outer layer of the urethral muscles. The pelvic nerve,
which is parasympathetic, and the hypogastric nerve,
which is sympathetic, innervate the two smooth muscle
layers that surround the urethra. Both the somatic and
parasympathetic innervation arise from the sacral spinal
cord segments, while the sympathetic innervation arises
from the lumbar spinal cord. Local reflex arcs exist as
well as central controls. Signals are processed in the pon­
tine micturition center of the brainstem and the cerebral
cortex to sense bladder distension and determine con­
scious control of voiding (Figure 127.1). The primary spi­
nal segments involved in micturition are L1–L2, S1–S2
(storage phase), and S1–S3 (emptying phase).
During the normal storage phase, stretch receptors in
the bladder wall send afferent signals along the pelvic
nerve, which activate a reflex arc through the hypogas­
tric nerve to the urethra. Norepinephrine (NE) is released
by postganglionic neurons to activate beta‐adrenergic
receptors in the bladder wall, allowing for relaxation and
continued filling. NE also stimulates alpha‐1‐adrenergic
receptors in the urethra and causes contraction of the
smooth muscle surrounding the urethra, thus preventing
urine leakage.
An additional urethral reflex, called the guarding reflex
in humans, is the somatic‐mediated contraction of the

striated muscle surrounding the urethra in response to a
sudden increase in abdominal pressure, such as during a
cough or sneeze. Afferent signals travel up the pelvic
nerve and initiate efferent signals down the pudendal
nerve, releasing acetylcholine (ACh) and activating nico­
tinic cholinergic receptors, causing contraction of the
striated muscle.
In addition to normal neurologic mechanisms, several
other factors are important for maintenance of urinary
continence. The integrity of the smooth muscle of the ure­
thra, normal urethral mucosa which creates a watertight
seal, associated vasculature, and the support of connective
tissues are also key. In females, estrogen appears to have a
significant impact on these tissues. Its withdrawal after
neutering appears to play a role in urethral sphincter
mechanism incompetence seen in neutered female dogs.
During initiation of voiding, stretch receptors send
afferent signals along the pelvic nerve to the pontine
micturition center. Signals from the cerebral cortex and
the hypothalamus are processed to determine if the situ­
ation is appropriate for initiation of micturition. If so,
signals are sent down the pelvic nerve, leading to ACh
release at the postganglionic parasympathetic neurons.
ACh binds to receptors and stimulates bladder smooth
muscle contraction. At the same time, inhibitory signals
are sent to the hypogastric nerve and the urethra relaxes,
allowing normal emptying.
Micturition disorders can be divided into those
­primarily related to storage and those related to e­ mptying
of urine.

­Disorders of Storage
Storage disorders primarily result in the leakage of urine
without intent by the animal. These may result from an
anatomic or developmental abnormality or acquired

Urethral Sphincter Mechanism Incompetence
Urethral sphincter mechanism incompetence (USMI) is
the most common storage disorder in dogs. The urethral
sphincter mechanism involves the smooth muscle of the
urethra as well as the surrounding support tissues, sub­
mucosal vasculature, and urothelium. USMI is thought
to result from a breakdown in this complex through

reduced muscular responsiveness and tone, and
­structural changes in the periurethral tissues. In female
dogs, these changes appear to be associated with a
­reduction in estrogen and alterations in follicle‐stimulat­
ing hormone and luteinizing hormone after neuter­
ing – thus the term “hormone‐responsive incontinence.”
Previously thought to be distinct processes, it is now
understood that USMI and hormone‐responsive incon­
tinence are the same entity. The pathophysiology of its
development in male dogs is poorly understood, but
there may be a relationship to decreased testosterone

VetBooks.ir

127 Micturition and Associated Disorders

levels, and increased follicle‐stimulating hormone and
luteinizing hormone, since it appears more frequently in
neutered than in intact males.
Urethral sphincter mechanism incompetence is most
common among neutered female dogs. It is less common
in neutered males and rare in cats. It appears to affect up
to 20% of neutered females and up to 30% of large‐breed
dogs over 20 kg. Several breeds have been found to have
increased risk including the Doberman pinscher, giant
schnauzer, Old English sheepdog, Rottweiler, Weima­
raner, and boxer, but any breed may be affected. Recent
literature has demonstrated an increased risk of develop­
ment of USMI in dogs neutered either before 3 months
of age or after the first estrus. In addition, it appears that
dogs over 15 kg have an increased risk of USMI the ear­
lier they are neutered. It is possible that this is related
to the development and sensitivity of the sphincter
mechanism tissues to estrogen and other hormones, but
the mechanism is incompletely understood. Predisposing
factors such as a pelvic bladder, short urethra, or recessed
vulva may also be associated with increased risk of devel­
oping USMI, but the presence of one of these does not
necessarily lead to incontinence.
Signs of incontinence may begin at any time, but
appear most often within a few years of neutering. Dogs
with USMI usually have normal bladder capacity and are
able to urinate normally with complete emptying of the
bladder. While most of these dogs are otherwise healthy,
clinical signs can worsen dramatically if co‐morbidities
develop, leading to polyuria or difficulty posturing to
urinate. The increased volumes of urine in the bladder,
and for longer periods of time, may lead to increased
pressure on the already weakened sphincter mechanism
and leakage. Lower urinary tract infection can also lead
to increased frequency of clinical signs. It is suspected
that USMI, and urinary incontinence of any cause, is
associated with increased risk of urinary tract infection
(UTI), but no studies have been conducted to fully evalu­
ate this.
Owners often seek veterinary care when the frequency
becomes bothersome, although on further questioning,
it is apparent the signs have been occurring for months
or years. It is essential to establish that the animal is pass­
ing urine unconsciously. Many owners will complain of
“incontinence” when the animal is demonstrating sub­
missive urination or is otherwise consciously urinating
in inappropriate places. Dogs with USMI may leak urine
when recumbent, sleeping, or after exertion. Although
the passage of urine is involuntary, dogs may increase
grooming of the perivulvar or preputial area to remove
the urine. USMI is an acquired condition, so questioning
of the owner regarding the onset of clinical signs is
important. Animals that have been incontinent from
birth or prior to neutering should be assessed for con­

genital malformations such as ectopic ureters, prior to
making a diagnosis of USMI.
Physical examination of these animals is often nor­
mal, with the exception of perivulvar or preputial urine
staining. As mentioned above, the conformation of the
vulva should be noted, although its contribution to
USMI is unclear. The presence of perivulvar dermatitis,
regardless of conformation, may increase the risk of uri­
nary tract infection. Rectal examination and palpation
of the urethra are normal. Urination is observed to be
normal and complete, with little or no residual volume.
The assessment of residual urine is essential in male
dogs to differentiate USMI from detrusor urethral dys­
synergia, a disorder of incomplete bladder emptying
(see later).
The presence of urinary incontinence in an otherwise
healthy neutered female dog that was previously conti­
nent is often adequate for presumptive diagnosis of
USMI and a trial of empiric therapy. Due to its lower
incidence, intact females, males, and cats with similar
histories and clinical signs require additional evaluation
before making a diagnosis of USMI (Figure 127.2).
The animal should be observed urinating, if possible.
Normal posturing and a full stream without stranguria
should be noted. Assessment of residual urine volume
may be made by bladder catheterization or estimated
using abdominal ultrasound of the bladder. A urinalysis
and urine culture should be performed. The presence of
isosthenuria or hyposthenuria may contribute to sever­
ity of incontinence and may require additional evalua­
tion for an underlying cause. Animals with polyuria may
not respond to medical treatment as well as those mak­
ing normal volumes of urine. As noted above, the risk of
urinary tract infection in animals with USMI has not
been evaluated, but its presence may lead to worsening
signs. Therefore, screening for and treatment of an
infection may increase therapeutic success. A complete
blood count and serum biochemistry panel may be indi­
cated but are not always necessary for diagnosis of
USMI, although they may be helpful when making ther­
apeutic choices, and are important in evaluating animals
with polyuria.
If anatomic abnormalities are suspected, imaging such
as contrast radiography, abdominal ultrasound, or con­
trast computed tomography is indicated. Cystoscopic
evaluation of the lower urinary tract allows assessment
of the entire urethra, ureter placement, and bladder
mucosa. Advanced diagnostics, such as urodynamic
studies, are designed to quantify the pressure produced
along the urethra and the compliance and detrusor func­
tion of the urinary bladder. These are available at many
referral institutions and are most often indicated in
patients with equivocal signs and poor response to ther­
apy, as well as in urologic research.

Medical treatment of USMI in the neutered female dog
consists of increasing number and sensitivity of alpha‐
receptors in the urethral sphincter with estrogen, or by
stimulating those receptors with an alpha‐agonist
(Table 127.1).
The most commonly used estrogens are diethylstilbes­
trol (DES) and estriol (Incurin™). DES is not available
commercially so it must be compounded. Adverse effects
associated with estrogen use include mammary gland
development, vulvar swelling, and attractiveness to
males. These are usually dose related and subside with

dose reduction. The more serious adverse event associ­
ated with estrogen use is irreversible bone marrow
­suppression, although the doses most associated with
bone marrow suppression are much higher than those
recommended to treat USMI.
Phenylpropanolamine (PPA, Proin™) is the alpha‐­
agonist most widely used for the treatment of USMI. It is
commercially available in sizes designed for use in dogs.
The dose and frequency needed for each animal tend to
vary widely and may need to be increased over time to
maintain continence. Adverse effects associated with
PPA include restlessness, aggression, changes in sleeping
patterns, and gastrointestinal signs. These are also
­usually alleviated by a reduction in dose or frequency.
Frequently, both an estrogen and PPA are used in the
same patient for severe or refractory incontinence. There
is little evidence supporting a synergistic increase in
efficacy, but there are anecdotal reports of greater
­
improvement than on a single medication regimen.
Phenylpropanolamine is also frequently used in male
dogs and cats with USMI. In addition, neutered male
dogs may be treated with testosterone cypionate as
monthly injections, although its efficacy is not well doc­
umented. Although male dogs with USMI are most
responsive to PPA, only 43% show good to excellent
response, much lower than in female dogs. Estrogen
compounds should not be used in males and are rarely
used in cats. Care should be taken to monitor the mam­
mary glands for neoplasia in cats receiving estrogens.
In patients that fail medical therapy, surgical options
may be necessary. These are generally only pursued if
the animal does not respond to, or cannot tolerate, medi­
cal treatment. A number of surgical procedures have
been used to treat USMI, many based on the theory of
increasing the transmission of abdominal pressure to the
proximal urethra. These include colposuspension, tran­
sobturator vaginal tape, and urethropexy. These have
had variable outcomes and are considered to have poor
long‐term efficacy. The most promising surgical proce­
dure for USMI is placement of an artificial urethral
sphincter which may be adjusted via a subcutaneous
port. Recent studies have shown it to lead to a significant
increase in continence in female dogs that had failed
medical therapy for USMI. In addition, it has been suc­
cessfully placed in male dogs and, recently, a female cat.
Lower Motor Neuron Bladder
Incontinence as a disorder of storage can also occur sec­
ondary to spinal cord injury or disease. Lesions in the
S1–S2 region will lead to weakness of the striated mus­
cular sphincter. Disruption of the local reflex arc at these
segments leads to an easily expressible bladder which
may empty with minor increases in abdominal pressure.

These animals are identified by decreased anal tone and
a poor perineal reflex as well as their easily expressible
bladder. Most of these animals are unable to voluntarily
void and require intermittent catheterization or manual
expression by the owner. Correction of the underlying
cause may lead to some return to normal function.
Because of the tendency to have incomplete emptying of
the bladder with manual expression, these animals are at
increased risk of developing urinary tract infection and
appropriate monitoring must be in place.
Detrusor Hyperreflexia/Overactive Bladder
Detrusor hyperreflexia/overactive bladder (OAB) is the
most common form of urinary incontinence in people,
but it has been poorly characterized in domestic species.
The true incidence of OAB and its importance as a cause
of urinary incontinence in dogs and cats are unknown. In
people, it is characterized by sudden urgency to urinate
and involuntary loss of urine associated with bursts of
detrusor contractions at bladder volumes far below capac­
ity. In dogs, it may manifest as an animal that loses blad­
der compliance and capacity and thus may need to urinate
more often than before without an increase in urine pro­
duction or inflammation of the lower urinary tract. OAB
may be a cause of treatment failure in some dogs treated
for USMI, and should be considered in these cases.
Diagnosis of OAB in animals can be challenging and is
only definitively made using urodynamic studies such as
cystometrography. Response to therapy with antimus­
carinic drugs is often used to presumptively diagnose
OAB in veterinary species. The most commonly used
include oxybutynin and imipramine, the latter of which
also has alpha‐agonist effects. Adverse effects of these
medications include gastrointestinal abnormalities such
as diarrhea and constipation, as well as parasympatholy­
tic signs like tachycardia and hyposalivation.

­Disorders of Emptying
The inability to completely empty the bladder during a
normal void can result from either a functional or
mechanical obstruction of the outflow tract and urethra,
or an abnormality of the detrusor which impairs its com­
plete contraction. Overflow incontinence can result
from the lack of complete emptying, often when the ani­
mal is at rest. An owner may not be able to differentiate
this from an animal with a storage disorder (e.g., USMI),
and it is up to the clinician to determine the underlying
process so that appropriate therapy can be instituted.
Inability to completely empty the bladder is a risk factor
for UTI, and these animals should be monitored for
infection.

Detrusor Atony
Complete emptying of the urinary bladder is dependent
on normal contraction of the detrusor muscle. In the
normal animal, the bladder relaxes during filling with
only small increases in intravesical pressure. As the blad­
der continues to fill, the pressure increases to a threshold
which triggers a detrusor contraction and emptying.
Loss of adequate detrusor contraction can result from
neurogenic or nonneurogenic abnormalities. Injury to
the sacral spinal cord S1–S3 or pelvic nerves can lead to
bladder atony, and is often associated with weakened
urethral tone. These animals often have decreased per­
ineal reflexes and easily expressed bladders.
Treatment of the underlying lesion, if possible, may
lead to improved voiding function. However, until nor­
mal function returns, careful management of urination
must be followed. Male dogs are usually aseptically cath­
eterized 2–4 times a day either in the hospital or at home,
and cats and female dogs are often manually expressed.
Parasympathomimetic drugs such as bethanechol are
not useful in these animals as they require a functional
pelvic nerve and associated spinal segments for clinical
efficacy.
Direct damage to the detrusor muscle can occur from
overdistension due to mechanical or functional outflow
obstruction of acute or chronic nature. The muscle fibers
of the detrusor transmit action potentials which initiate
contraction via tight junctions. With overdistension,
these tight junctions are interrupted, leading to an absent
or ineffective contraction. The overdistension may be
acute, as with obstructive feline idiopathic cystitis in a
male cat, or chronic, as with a dog with a functional
obstruction of the urethra. Relief of the obstruction and
maintenance of a small bladder volume for up to two
weeks may allow the junctions to reestablish and the
return of coordinated detrusor function. This is usually
managed by either indwelling or frequent sterile cathe­
terization of the bladder. Bethanechol may be used in
these patients to enhance stimulation of the detrusor
contraction since the pelvic nerve is intact. Other medi­
cations that have been shown to enhance detrusor func­
tion are cisapride and metoclopramide. It is essential
that relief of any urethral obstruction, functional or
mechanical, be attained before starting medical therapy
to enhance detrusor contraction.
Functional Obstruction – Detrusor
Urethral Dyssynergy
Functional urethral obstruction, or detrusor urethral
dyssynergy (DUD), arises from an abnormality in the
reflex arc at the neurologic or muscular level which
allows the urethral sphincter to relax at the initiation of

VetBooks.ir

127 Micturition and Associated Disorders

detrusor contraction and urination. It may affect the
smooth muscle internal urethral sphincter, the striated
external sphincter, or both. It is possible that the lesion is
cranial to the associated spinal segments and involves
the loss of inhibitory signals to the pudendal and
hypogastric nerves, but may be a more local lesion to the
nerves, the neuromuscular junction, or the sphincter
itself. Unlike the “upper motor neuron bladder” seen in
animals with thoracolumbar intervertebral disc disease
and other spinal cord lesions, these animals typically
have an otherwise normal neurologic examination.
The disorder affects primarily middle‐aged, large‐ and
giant‐breed male dogs. One case series of 22 dogs
reported a mean age of 4.9 years. Clinical signs are simi­
lar to those of mechanical obstruction. The animal often
postures to urinate and is able to produce a urine stream
that quickly becomes attenuated or stops completely.
The animal may continue to posture to urinate or make
several attempts without fully emptying the bladder. The
presence of large amounts of residual urine typically
leads to overflow incontinence and may be mistaken for
USMI. This leakage can occur because the hypertonicity
of the involved sphincter is often dynamic and is trig­
gered by the act of voiding. In chronic cases, bladder
overdistension and subsequent atony may develop.
Unlike animals with mechanical obstruction, these dogs
are typically easy to catheterize and usually do not show
increases in urethral pressure on urodynamic evaluation
unless actively voiding. Contrast urethrography may be
normal or reveal areas of narrowing of the urethra
(urethrospasm).
Presumptive diagnosis of DUD is often made by
observing the dog urinate with a typical interrupted pat­
tern, documentation of a large residual urine volume,
easy passage of a urinary catheter, and ruling out of a
mechanical obstruction. Normal residual urine volume
in 48 normal dogs was reported to be 0.1–3.4 mL/kg
body weight with a mean of 0.2 mL/kg. The author uses
<0.5 mL/kg as a general guideline. Ultrasonography is
recommended to assess the ureters and renal pelves for
dilation secondary to chronic obstruction and ureterore­
nal reflux of urine. Additional diagnostics, including
contrast urethrography, urethroscopy or urodynamic
evaluation, may be necessary to verify the diagnosis in
patients who fail to respond to medical therapy.
Treatment of the hypertonic urethral sphincter
­generally consists of alpha‐adrenergic blockade with
prazosin, an alpha‐1‐specific antagonist with demon­
strated effects on both the internal and external ure­
thral sphincter. Tamsulosin, which is specific for the
alpha‐1A ­subtype found in the internal urethral sphinc­
ter, has also been successful in these dogs. Some dogs
will require additional therapy if the striated muscle is
more ­significantly affected. Benzodiazepines, such as

midazolam, or other skeletal muscle relaxants, includ­
ing ­acepromazine and methocarbemol, may be more
effective if the external urethral sphincter is involved.
Midazolam or diazepam is typically administered 30
minutes before voiding to decrease external urethral
sphincter pressure. Dantrolene and baclofen have been
used in the past as skeletal muscle relaxants; however,
the potential for adverse effects has decreased their use
in veterinary patients. In severe and refractory cases,
intermittent sterile catheterization by the owner at
home may be necessary. Medical therapy of associated
bladder atony should only be started after adequate
relief of the functional urethral obstruction has been
reached. Close monitoring of these patients for residual
urine volume and UTI is needed to assess efficacy of
treatment and prevent complications.
It is possible that patients with controlled DUD will
experience relapse in times of stress such as hospitaliza­
tion or boarding. These animals may need periodic addi­
tional therapy or catheterization even if usually able to
urinate normally.
Prognosis for recovery of normal voiding is good, but
most dogs will require life‐long therapy for DUD.
Attempts to taper medications to the lowest effective
dose may be hampered by relapse of clinical signs after
months of normal voiding. Prognosis appears to be
worse in patients with bladder atony or UTI secondary
to urine retention. Anecdotally, urethral stenting may
improve clinical signs, but this is considered a salvage
procedure with several potential complications, and
indicated only in the most refractory of cases.
Functional Obstruction – Neurogenic
Neurogenic functional urethral obstruction is generally
caused by spinal cord lesions cranial to the sacral seg­
ment. This leads to loss of inhibitory signals to the
hypogastric and pudendal nerves which prevents sphinc­
ter relaxation upon voiding. This is the classic “upper
motor neuron bladder” in which the patient is unable to
urinate normally and is difficult to express manually. The
most commonly affected patients are those with interver­
tebral disc disease and associated paresis. These animals
typically have additional neurologic deficits, including
paresis and nociceptive loss. Treatment of the underly­
ing lesion typically leads to partial or complete return to
normal voiding function after days to weeks. Until nor­
mal voiding resumes, the patients are managed as for
DUD with alpha‐adrenergic blockade, and manual
expression or catheterization. Monitoring for overdis­
tension and UTI is critical in these patients, as is nursing
care, particularly since the overflow incontinence that
can accompany this process may lead to skin breakdown
in these recumbent patients.

Dysautonomia
Dysautonomia is a rare condition involving degeneration
of the neurons of the autonomic nervous ganglia, leading
to sympathetic and parasympathetic dysfunction. It has
been most commonly reported in both dogs and cats in
the UK and Scandinavia, but small clusters of cases in
both species have been seen in the US. Its underlying
cause is unknown, but neurotoxin exposure is strongly
suspected.
In addition to the classic findings of unresponsive
mydriasis and prolapsed nictitans, the abnormalities
seen with dysautonomia can range from ileus and consti­
pation to decreased systolic function of the heart. These

dogs and cats often have significant voiding dysfunction
and urine retention due to bladder atony and overflow
incontinence secondary to urethral sphincter incompe­
tence. There is no specific treatment for dysautonomia
and spontaneous remission is uncommon.
The prognosis is related to the severity of the clinical
signs and the specific organ functions affected.
Management of the urinary complications is usually
possible, involving bladder expression and/or urethral
catheterization, along with parasympathomimetic
agents. It is the challenging management of the gastro­
intestinal components of the disease which often leads
to euthanasia.

Urinary Tract Infections
Nicole Smee, DVM, MS, DACVIM
Las Vegas Veterinary Specialty Center, Las Vegas, NV, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
The most common isolate from canine urine is Escherichia
coli which accounts for one‐third to half of all positive
urine cultures. The next major group of uropathogens
includes gram‐positive cocci, Staphlyoc­occus, Streptoc­
occus, and Enterococcus. Remaining uropath­ogens include
Proteus, Klebsiella, Pasteurella, Mycoplasma, Enterobacter,
and Pseudomonas. These 10 genera accounted for 95%
and 97% of all urinary isolates in male and female dogs,
respectively. A retrospective analysis of feline urine cultures submitted to a teaching hospital also found E. coli
to be the most common pathogen (47%), followed by
Staphlyococcus (18%), Streptococcus (13%), and Klebsiella
(4%). In both dogs and cats with bacterial urinary tract
infection (UTI), 75% of the time there is a single pathogen, in 20% of cases there are two pathogens and ≤5% of
the time there are three species. Multiple organism infections are more commonly observed in female dogs.

­Epidemiology/Signalment
Bacterial UTI is common; approximately 5–27% of dogs
will experience infections of the urinary tract at some point
during their lifetime. Female dogs are more commonly
affected than males. In contrast to dogs, bacterial UTI is
relatively rare in cats. In young, otherwise healthy cats with
signs of lower urinary tract inflammation, bacterial UTI is
rare (<2%). Incidence of bacterial UTI in cats increases
with age and occurs more often in cats older than 10 years.
Urinary tract infections are common in dogs and cats
with systemic diseases that may compromise normal
antimicrobial defenses. In a retrospective study of 101
dogs with diabetes mellitus (DM) or hyperadrenocorticism or both, 42 (41.6%) had a UTI. Dogs receiving long‐
term glucocorticoids are also at risk with a reported

incidence of 18–39%. Similarly, systemic disease can predispose cats to UTI. In retrospective studies evaluating
known predisposing conditions in cats, positive urine
cultures were found in 17–30% of cats with chronic kidney disease (CKD), 12–13% of cats with DM, and 12–22%
of cats with hyperthyroidism. In one of these studies,
decreasing urine specific gravity (USG) was not associated with positive urine culture; however, pyuria and
hematuria were associated with positive urine cultures.
In addition, Persian breed, females, increasing age, and
decreasing body weight were associated with positive
cultures.

­History and Clinical Signs
Clinical signs associated with a UTI depend on bacterial
virulence, status of the host immune system, duration of
the infection, and site or sites of infection. The most common clinical signs associated with lower UTI include pollakiuria, stranguria, dysuria, hematuria, and inappropriate
urination or periuria. If a UTI occurs secondary to a micturition disorder, such as an ectopic ureter, urethral sphincter mechanism incompetence (USMI), or urine retention,
clinical signs associated with the primary condition may
predominate. Similarly, in dogs and cats with systemic disease and compromised host defense mechanisms, clinical
signs associated with the underlying disease may predominate and the UTI may be relatively asymptomatic.
Dogs with uncomplicated UTI often have unremarkable physical examination findings. Predisposing causes
such as vulvar involution, severe perivulvular dermatitis,
vaginal stenosis, cystic or urethral calculi, or urethral
thickening may be identified in patients with a complicated UTI. Whenever possible, female dogs that present
with a UTI should have a digital vaginal examination
performed in order to identify an anatomic abnormality

Section 10 Renal and Genitourinary Disease

that may alter normal host defense mechanisms. For
example, palpation of a persistent paramesonephric
remnant may prompt further investigation for ectopic
ureters and palpation of vaginal strictures may prompt
further investigation for urine retention. Rectal examination may also identify abnormalities such as pelvic
trauma, urethral stones, or urethral thickening associated with neoplasia or granulomatous urethritis.
Acute bacterial pyelonephritis, prostatitis, and metritis are often associated with systemic signs such as fever,
an inflammatory leukogram, lethargy, and anorexia. In
contrast, patients with chronic prostatitis and pyelonephritis may not exhibit systemic signs and therefore it
may be more difficult to localize the infection.

­Diagnosis
Urinalysis may be helpful in differentiating a UTI from
other disorders causing lower urinary tract signs (e.g.,
bladder neoplasia), making initial antibiotic recommendations, and in some cases identifying potential predisposing disorders (e.g., glucosuria and crystalluria). Urine
specific gravity can be variable in patients with a UTI.
Dilute or minimally concentrated urine may be observed
in patients with concurrent disease predisposing to UTI
(e.g., DM or hyperadrenocorticism), or may be observed
if the infection involves the upper urinary tract. With a
UTI, hematuria and proteinuria are frequently observed
on dipstick analysis. The dipstick analyses for nitrite
(bacteria) and leukocyte esterase (white blood cells
[WBCs]) are designed for use in people, and are not reliable tests for canine and feline patients.
A urine sediment examination should be performed to
identify pyuria and bacteriuria. If urine is dilute or the
patient is immunocompromised (e.g., suffers from
hyperadrenocorticism, or is receiving exogenous corticosteroids), it may be difficult to identify WBCs or bacteria on urine sediment examination. Air‐dried, stained
sediment evaluations were more accurate than wet,
unstained mounts for identification of bacteria when
urine culture results were used as the gold standard. This
air‐dried, stained technique is easily performed in practice by placing one drop of sediment on a glass slide,
allowing it to air dry without spreading, and then staining the sample with a commercially available modified
Wright’s stain. It is important to remember, however,
that a culture is required for definitive diagnosis, and
will provide additional information (e.g., bacterial
­identification, number of organisms/mL of urine, and
antimicrobial susceptibility results).
Cystocentesis is the method of choice for collection of
urine samples, especially if a urine culture is anticipated.
In patients presenting with lower urinary tract signs

(e.g., pollakiuria and stranguria), collection by cystocentesis may be difficult due to the small size of the urinary
bladder. Alternative methods of urine collection may be
acceptable if cystocentesis cannot be performed or is
contraindicated (e.g., thrombocytopenia, suspected
­transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) of the urinary bladder
or pyoderma of the ventral abdomen). Urethral catheterization provides a superior sample compared with a free‐
catch voided sample but requires more technical skill,
especially in female patients. Care should be taken during
catheterization to prevent contamination from external
structures by ­clipping surrounding hair and cleansing the
external genitalia prior to the procedure. Based on current recommendations, free‐catch urine samples are not
acceptable for culture. Urinalysis and urine culture results
should always be interpreted in light of the urine collection method.
Although clinical signs and urinalysis findings may
increase the index of suspicion for a UTI, a urine culture is
the definitive diagnostic test. Ideally, the urine sample for
culture should be obtained prior to starting treatment. In
patients already receiving antimicrobial therapy, it may
be necessary to discontinue treatment for 3–5 days before
collection of urine culture. It is also important to consider
storage and transport of samples for culture in practices
where immediate culture processing is not possible. Sterile
containers that do not contain ­additives or preservatives
should be used. Commercially available urine collection
kits may be acceptable for up to 72 hours if sample processing is delayed. Bacterial counts can increase in urine
stored at room temperature within a few hours. In refrigerated samples, quantitative bacterial counts differed after
six hours of storage; however, this was not associated with
a change in interpretation of the clinical significance. It is
recommended that urine samples be cultured immediately but it is acceptable for urine to be refrigerated in a
closed container for up to six hours prior to culture.
Alternatives to sending a urine sample to a commercial
laboratory for culture include using a calibrated bacterial
loop (0.01 or 0.001 mL volume) to inoculate blood or
MacConkey’s agar plates in‐house. Culture plates are then
incubated for 24 hours and if significant numbers of colonies are produced in light of the urine collection method,
the plate can be sealed and shipped to a microbiology
­laboratory for bacterial identification and a­ntimicrobial
sensitivity testing. Alternatively, products like UriCult® culture paddles may also be used. In most cases, a quantitative
urine culture will aid interpretation of results. In addition
to bacterial numbers/mL of urine, knowledge of the
­normal flora may also be helpful in determining contamination versus infection when methods other than
­cystocentesis are used.
Not all species of bacteria will induce clinical signs or
cause disease.

­Classification of Urinary Tract
Infections

Uncomplicated UTI

Asymptomatic Bacteriuria
Bacteriuria is expected in patients with UTI, but may also
be observed in healthy dogs and cats if the urine sample has
been contaminated with normal flora and/or pathogens from
the distal urethra/urogenital tract (voided sample or during
urethral catheterization) or if the sample contacts a contaminated surface (e.g., cage floor, examination table). It is
important to differentiate urine contamination from a UTI
since the former does not need to be treated. Certain organisms are known to be commensal within the lower urinary
tract (Table 128.1). There is, however, overlap between
­normal flora and potential pathogens. Contamination can
be ruled out by repeating a urinalysis with urine obtained
via cystocentesis or by performing a quantitative urine
­culture on a voided or catheterized sample. Depending on
the method of urine collection, the number of bacterial
colony‐forming units (cfu)/mL of urine will vary between
contamination and UTI (Table 128.2).

Uncomplicated UTI occurs in patients where no underlying structural, neurologic, or functional abnormalities
exist. A UTI becomes complicated when host defense
mechanisms are compromised (e.g., CKD, hyperadrenocorticism, DM, cystolithiasis, USMI). In addition, UTIs
are often considered complicated if they occur in cats,
male dogs, and intact female dogs, or if they involve the
kidneys or prostate.
Recurrent or Reinfection
Recurrent UTIs can be defined as either relapses or reinfections. A relapse is an infection caused by the same
bacteria that caused the original infection, and usually
occurs within days of cessation of treatment. Relapses
are most frequently associated with ineffective antimicrobial treatment. This may be due to improper antibiotic usage (inappropriate selection, dose, duration, or
poor owner compliance), emergence of drug‐resistant
pathogens, or failure to eliminate predisposing causes

that alter normal host defense mechanisms and allow the
