with a higher degree of antimicrobial resistance compared to the original infection.
Reinfections occur when the initial infection was effectively treated (documented by negative culture after
therapy and resolution of clinical signs) and repeat culture confirms another infection. Typically, the time
between reinfections is greater than the time between
relapses. Reinfections usually indicate that host defense
mechanisms are compromised.

­Therapy
Ideally, antimicrobial administration should be based on
results from culture and susceptibility. Unnecessary or inappropriate usage of antibiotics can lead to antimicrobial
resistance, or delay the diagnosis of noninfectious cause
of lower urinary tract signs (e.g., like identification of
underlying TCC). In addition to susceptibility results,
the route and ease of administration, potential adverse
effects, cost, and concentration in the urine (or other targeted tissues, e.g., prostate, kidney) should be considered
when choosing an antibiotic.
To determine the minimum inhibitory concentration
(MIC), serial dilutions of an antibiotic are used to discover the lowest concentration that will inhibit bacterial
growth. This concentration is the MIC and although
results are reported as susceptible, intermediate, and
resistant, they usually also include the actual MIC followed by the breakpoints used to determine susceptibility. The goal of the breakpoint is to predict clinical
outcome for an individual patient. Breakpoints are determined by a combination of information including the
species, bacteria, disease, antibiotic, dose, route, and frequency. It is important to keep in mind that there are

limited data available for veterinary medicine; therefore
breakpoints are often determined by using information
available from human breakpoints.
A result reported as “susceptible” indicates a high likelihood of treatment success (>80%) with most antibiotics; “intermediate” indicates possible success in treatment
with potential alterations in normal dosing; and a “resistant” result indicates that a clinical cure is unlikely to
occur with that antimicrobial. The result is considered
susceptible if the MIC is in the breakpoint range or
below, intermediate if it is at the high end of the breakpoint, and resistant if it is above the breakpoint.
Urine antibiotic concentrations are usually more
important than plasma concentrations when treating a
UTI. Minimum inhibitory antibiotic concentrations and
the anticipated urine antibiotic concentration may be
used to guide treatment choices. Clinical efficacy is
expected if urine concentration is maintained at greater
than four times the MIC of the pathogen between doses.
For example, the MIC of ampicillin for a Staphylococcus
organism is approximately 10 μg/mL. The expected
serum and tissue concentrations of ampicillin are 1–2 μg/
mL whereas the expected urine concentration of
­ampicillin is >300 μg/mL. Since the expected urine concentration is >4 times the MIC, sensitivity for a superficial UTI should exist. Minimum inhibitory antibiotic
concentration testing based on anticipated urine concentrations is not appropriate for deeper tissue infections (e.g., pyelonephritis, thickened bladder wall) where
serum and tissue antibiotic concentrations are expected.
Interpretation of Results
The Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI)
is a committee of experts that examines pharmacokinetics, microbiology, pharmacodynamics, bacterial
population, MIC distribution, and clinical trial results.

VetBooks.ir

128 Urinary Tract Infections

Recommendations from this committee are considered
the gold standard for breakpoint determination. Veterinary
laboratories (or human laboratories with appropriate
susceptibility panels for commonly used veterinary antibiotics) that follow CLSI guidelines should be used for
culture and sensitivity testing.
Depending on the laboratory, comparing antibiotics
with similar susceptibility (e.g., cephalexin and cefazolin)
may be necessary but requires making assumptions. For
example, when comparing cefazolin with cephalexin,
cefazolin is typically administered intravenously q6h
whereas cephalexin is typically administered orally
q8–12h. It is also important to remember that in vitro
culture and sensitivity results may not correlate with in
vivo efficacy. For example, regardless of the susceptibility
results for Enterococcus, certain antibiotics including
cephalosporins, trimethoprim‐sulfamethoxazole, clindamycin, and aminoglycosides should always be considered resistant since they are not effective clinically and
do not correlate with in vitro results.
In many cases, antibiotic sensitivity testing results provide a clear direction for treatment with an antibiotic
that is orally administered, has few potential adverse
effects, and reasonable cost. In some cases, sensitivity
results demonstrate a high degree of bacterial resistance,
and route of administration, high cost, or potential
adverse effects of the potentially effective antibiotic may
be a concern. Although MIC may be used as a guideline
for antibiotic selection, veterinary breakpoints for most
antibiotics in the urinary tract of dogs and cats have
not been determined. When intermediate results are
obtained, it may be possible to achieve a cure if no alternative antimicrobial exists. This would most likely be
achieved by using a higher dose of an antimicrobial that
is excreted in the urine. In resistant infections, requesting an expanded antimicrobial sensitivity profile (e.g.,
ceftazedime, carbenicillin) may suggest alternative treatment regimes. Most commercial bacteriology laboratories have a second and third tier of antibiotics for
expanded sensitivity testing; however, high cost and parenteral administration may be trade‐offs.
Inappropriate antibiotic dosages or unnecessary usage
can lead to resistant organisms, affecting not only the
individual patient but potentially bacterial resistance in
other veterinary patients and owners. Antimicrobials
that are excreted in the urine are the mainstay of UTI
treatment and initial antibiotic considerations should
include amoxicillin, cephalexin or trimethoprim‐sulfadiazine. When host defense mechanisms are compromised, previous or current sensitivity results indicate
potential resistance, or when the infection involves the
prostate or kidneys, second tier antibiotic choices
should be considered including potentiated beta‐lactams
(e.g., amoxicillin‐clavulanic acid), fluoroquinolones, or

extended‐release cephalosporins (e.g., cefovecin). Second‐
tier antibiotics are not recommended as a first‐line treatment for an uncomplicated UTI, without appropriate
culture and sensitivity results. However, these may be
considered when rapid treatment is necessary to return
to function, prevent systemic spread of bacteria, or when
penetration into a specific tissue, such as the prostate, is
needed. For penetration into prostatic tissue, antibiotics
should be lipid soluble, not highly protein bound, and
ionize at the pH of the prostatic tissue. Good prostate
gland penetration can usually be achieved with fluoroquinolones, trimethoprim‐sulfa, and chloramphenicol.
Uncomplicated UTI
Dogs and cats with uncomplicated are typically treated
with a 7–14‐day course of antibiotics. It is reasonable to
assume that shorter durations of appropriate antibiotics
(≤7 days) may be effective but clinical trials are needed to
further evaluate shorter duration treatments. It is always
ideal to treat on the basis of urine culture and sensitivity
results, although economic constraints may preclude this
in first‐time patients with suspected uncomplicated UTI.
In these cases, antimicrobial selection should be based on
bacterial characteristics observed in the urine sediment
(e.g., gram positive vs gram negative, cocci vs rods).
For example, if a gram‐negative rod or bacillus is seen
(e.g., E. coli, Enterobacter, Klebsiella, Proteus), cepalosporins would be a good option. With gram‐positive cocci
(e.g., Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Enterococcus), amoxicillin and cephalosporin would be options. Clinical signs
should resolve within 48 hours with appropriate treatment. Along with resolution of clinical signs, evidence of
inflammation in urine sediment should also resolve in 3–5
days of antibiotic treatment.
When empiric antibiotic treatment is used, instructions to owners regarding what to expect as well as follow‐up plans are critical. If presenting clinical signs do
not resolve quickly, owners should be aware of the need
for a follow‐up urinalysis and culture and sensitivity.
Owners should also be aware of the importance of completing the entire antibiotic regime, even if signs resolve
early in the course of treatment. Finally, owners should
be instructed to observe their pets closely for signs of
UTI recurrence after the treatment regime is complete.
Clear communication and understanding of the “game
plan” will result in improved treatment outcome and
increased client willingness to return in cases of empiric
treatment failures.
Short‐Course/High‐Dose Protocol

Due to concerns with owner compliance during longer
treatment protocols, short‐course/high‐dose protocols
have been proposed for the treatment of uncomplicated

1193

VetBooks.ir

1194

Section 10 Renal and Genitourinary Disease

UTI in dogs. In a recent study in dogs, a short‐course/
high‐dose protocol of enrofloxacin (18–20 mg/kg once
daily for three days) was as effective as traditional‐dose
amoxicillin‐clavulanate (13.75–25 mg/kg twice daily for
14 days) in treating uncomplicated UTI. Preliminary evidence suggests this may be an effective option but additional research may be necessary to incorporate this into
routine clinical practice.
Complicated UTI
Antibiotic treatment of complicated UTIs should be prolonged (typically four weeks) and always based on urine
culture and sensitivity results. It is possible that shorter
duration of therapy may be effective in some or all clinical situations, but further studies are needed to provide
more specific recommendations. One week into treatment and one week prior to discontinuing antimicrobials,
reevaluation of the urine sediment can help determine
response to therapy. When effective, no bacteria or white
cells should be observed on sediment exam. Recheck
urine culture is again recommended 5–7 days after completion of therapy to confirm successful resolution of the
UTI. Prolonged treatment of a complicated UTI may be
necessary to sterilize the urinary tract but “buying time”
for correction of host defense mechanism abnormalities
is another important consideration. If host defense
mechanism abnormalities are not corrected, it may be
difficult to clear the current infection or, more likely, the
patient will experience reinfections.
Ancillary Therapies
Ancillary therapies designed to prevent recurrent UTI
are considered in patients where breaches in host
defenses are present but are not correctable or in cases
where an underlying cause for reinfection is not identified. Care should be taken to treat any underlying infection prior to starting any prevention measures. Owners
should watch closely for clinical signs and be advised that
frequent rechecks will be necessary to detect and treat
any breakthrough infections.
Urinary Antiseptics

The most commonly used urinary antiseptic is methenamine which is converted to formalin in an acidic environment. Methenamine may be considered in patients
with recurrent infections or those with potentially
untreatable or unresolved breaches in immunity. Just as
with the use of cranberry extract, this prophylactic treatment is not recommended as a sole treatment for UTIs.
Methenamine should only be used in conjunction with
antibiotics for the treatment of current infections or as a
preventive once the previous UTI has been cleared. Use

should be avoided in patients on sulfonamides or medications that cause alkaline urine. Urine acidifiers added
to methenamine cause acidic urine that can also decrease
activity of fluoroquinolone and aminoglycoside antibiotics. High doses can cause irritation to bladder mucosa
but this is more common in people than dogs.
Prophylactic Antimicrobial Protocols

Prophylactic antimicrobial treatment involves long‐term
daily administration of low‐dose antimicrobials in order
to inhibit or minimize uropathogen growth, thus
decreasing the opportunity for bacterial adhesion and
colonization of the uroepithelium. Unfortunately, there
are no studies in dogs that have evaluated the efficacy
and adverse effects of these protocols. Due to the risk of
creating resistant infections, prophylactic, low‐dose
antibiotic administration should be reserved for refractory cases and then only after all attempts to resolve
­correctable problems have been exhausted.
Prophylactic, low‐dose antibiotic treatment should
only be initiated after standard‐dose antibiotic treatment
has been successful (negative urine culture). Best results
are expected with drugs that are excreted in the urine.
Other considerations should include potential side‐
effects of the drug and previous culture and sensitivity
results. Commonly used protocols include fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins, or beta‐lactam antimicrobials.
The dose used should be one‐half to one‐third the therapeutic daily dose administered immediately after the last
voiding before bedtime. This protocol is typically recommended for a minimum of six months and urinalysis and
culture should be performed every 4–8 weeks. If at any
point during the treatment a UTI occurs, it is treated as
a complicated UTI. Prophylactic, low‐dose therapy can
be restarted after the reinfection has been resolved.
Cranberry Extract

Proanthrocyanidins, specifically A‐type isoforms, found
in cranberry juice inhibit E. coli attachment by blocking
interaction of bacterial P‐fimbriae with the surface of
uroepithelial cells. Canine studies evaluating the efficacy
of cranberry extract (CE) are limited, but some in vitro
data show promising results. One study demonstrated
that E. coli in urine from dogs receiving oral CE had
decreased ability to agglutinate to human red blood cells.
Similarly, a second study demonstrated that E. coli in
urine from dogs receiving oral CE had decreased ability
to adhere to Madin‐Darby canine kidney (MDCK) cells.
Based on these in vitro studies, oral administration of CE
may help reduce E. coli reinfections in patients with
compromised host defense mechanisms. Due to large
variations of the active compound in over‐the‐counter
products, it may be of benefit to use canine products
dosed according to manufacturer recommendations.

Box 128.1 Ideal steps to follow in the management of UTIs in dogs and cats
1) Diagnosis should be determined on the basis of history, urine sediment, and, ideally, urine culture and
sensitivity results. Rule out contamination in voided/
catheterized samples with quantitative culture.
Cystocentesis is the ideal way to collect urine for culture.
2) Select an antimicrobial agent based on culture and sensitivity. Without culture and sensitivity results, use air‐
dried sediment findings to guide antibiotic choice (e.g.,
cocci vs rods).
3) Reculture urine (or at least examine the urine sediment)
in 3–5 days to ascertain effectiveness of selected antimicrobial agent. Urine culture should be negative and/or
there should be no white blood cells in the urine
sediment.

4) Examine urine sediment 3–4 days before discontinuing
antibiotic treatment.
5) Repeat urinalysis and culture 5–7 days after cessation of
antibiotic therapy. (Steps 4 and 5 are especially important for recurrent UTI.)
6) Patients with recurrent UTIs should undergo imaging
studies (e.g., plain and/or contrast‐enhanced radiography
and/or ultrasonography), a complete blood count, and
serum biochemistry profile to determine whether they
have local/systemic underlying predisposing factors.
7) Frequent reinfections may need to be treated with low‐
dose nighttime antibiotic regimes or cranberry extract
after the initial inflammation has been cleared up in
response to standard‐dose antibiotic treatment.

Approach to the Cancer Patient
Lisa DiBernardi, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology), DACVR (Radiation Oncology)
Gulf Coast Veterinary Specialists, Houston, TX, USA

The goal of this chapter is to present an overview of
current cancer terminology, patient evaluation, diagnostic techniques, management strategies, and treatment
options with emphasis on the application of radiation
therapy.
Cancer is a group of diseases that are defined by the
uninhibited growth and replication of cells. Cancer arises
from an abnormal single cell that has suffered a disruption in its regulatory mechanism for proliferation and
self‐elimination. Cancer biology will be discussed in subsequent chapters.
Unregulated cellular proliferation is a characteristic of
both benign and malignant tumors. Metastasis distinguishes a malignant from a benign tumor. Metastasis is
the spread of cancer from one location to a regional or
distant location. A tumor is named based on its cell of
origin. A cancer that initiates from embryologically
derived endoderm, more commonly termed skin or epithelium of the internal organs, is a carcinoma. Carcinoma
will have a descriptor, a prefix, based on histology. An
example of a carcinoma of the oral cavity is a squamous
cell carcinoma. A benign mass within skin or epithelium
may be an adenoma, cystadenoma or papilloma. A
malignancy of mesoderm – bone, muscle, fat, cartilage,
or other supportive structures – is termed a sarcoma.
Benign examples include fibroma, lipoma, hemangioma,
chondroma, and osteoma. Central nervous system cancers involve the brain and spinal cord and are named
after the cells lining the interior and exterior of the brain
(glial, meningeal, ependymal cells) or cells from vascular
structures (choroid plexus). Lymphoma (lymphosarcoma) and multiple myeloma are malignancies involving
immune regulatory cells.
Discrete cell tumor is a term applied to tumors that
exfoliate as individual (discrete) cells, which are generally round in shape. This category includes mast cell

tumor, plasmacytoma, transmissible venereal tumor,
lymphoma, and histiocytic tumors, but is not limited to
these tumors. Leukemia results from malignant blood‐
forming tissues of the bone marrow.
The terminology for some malignancies may be misleading. Examples include those used for lymphoma and
melanoma. Lymphosarcoma and lymphoma are terms
for the same malignant process. Melanoma may be
benign or malignant depending on location, level of
invasiveness, and species. A histopathologic description
will state malignant melanoma versus melanocytoma
(benign melanoma).
The overall mortality due to cancer in dogs is 20–30%,
approximately one in four. The dog breed with the highest cancer prevalence in the United States is the golden
retriever. Currently the Golden Retriever Lifetime Study
is underway in the United States. The study’s purpose is
to identify the nutritional, environmental, lifestyle and
genetic risk factors for cancer and other diseases in dogs
(https://www.morrisanimalfoundation.org/goldenretriever-lifetime-study). In Sweden, a retrospective
study found boxer and Bernese mountain dogs to be
overrepresented in cancer deaths compared with other
breeds, including the golden retriever. The selection of
desired traits may lead to breed‐specific risks for the
development of cancer. Boxers, bulldogs, and retrievers
are prone to cancer of the skin and subcutaneous tissues.
The Siamese cat is predisposed to the development of
cutaneous mast cell tumors. Osteosarcoma is historically
a cancer of large and giant breeds. The power to identify
hereditary influences lies in the pure‐bred dog’s reduced
genetic complexity (diversity). Identification of pathway
dysregulation(s) will elucidate potential upstream or
downstream therapeutic targets. Current multiinstitutional consortium research is focused on the rapid identification and translation of novel therapies to benefit

­Initial Assessment
History
Pertinent information should be obtained through
open‐ended questions using reflective listening and
­confirming the information by paraphrasing important
points. Taking a thorough history incorporates both
nonverbal and verbal communication skills. This should
include the onset of the current problem, the anatomic
location of the problem or body system affected,
descriptors of the nature of the problem such as quality,
quantity, severity, onset, duration, timing of occurrence, frequency, as well as inciting factors that trigger
the occurrence, alter the frequency and severity or
improve the event. The duration of the presence of a
mass and the rate of growth may facilitate differentiation between benign and m
­ alignant processes. Previous
medical and surgical conditions, vaccination and
administration location, allergies, exercise, travel history, housing, feeding practices, elimination details,
administration of medications, ­
vitamins, nutraceuticals, and supplements should also be investigated. This
information is vital and may ­circumvent adverse events
associated with p
­ olypharmacy. Once the information is
obtained and organized, the organ system affected
should become evident.
Patient Evaluation
The physical examination is an essential portion of every
patient evaluation and should include all major organ systems. Leaving the affected body system for the final portion of the exam may permit minimal patient resistance.
Attention should be paid to the demeanor and behavioral
responses of the patient for pain assessment, location of
primary and/or metastatic disease, site of surgical interventions, musculoskeletal conditions and mobility, neurologic function, and dermatologic conditions. Once the
history and physical examination data have been integrated, the subsequent chapters will guide the reader
through the most probable differential ­diagnoses. It is
important to bear in mind that the presenting problem
may not always reflect the origin of the tumor but rather
be a consequence of a tumor‐associated change(s) in
function. For example, a dog may present for polyuria and
polydipsia when the inciting factor is humoral hypercal­ araneoplastic syndrome
cemia of malignancy (HHM), a p
associated with particular tumors.

Diagnostic Testing
Based on the generated list of differentials, tailored diagnostic testing may be recommended to support or refute
a diagnosis. Clinical features suggestive of a malignant
tumor include rapid growth, invasion into deep tissues
or overlying skin, fixation, ulceration, and poorly defined
margins. If a tumor lacks these clinical features, it should
not be assumed to be benign as malignant mesenchymal
tumors may appear demarcated when surrounded by
compressed normal tissue (pseudocapsule). Through the
use of cytology or histopathology, sampling of a mass is
required for differentiation.
An open dialogue is paramount when faced with evidence of a malignancy. The general public often has
unrealistic expectations regarding the diagnosis and
treatment of cancer. It is important to discuss the likelihood of a malignancy versus other diseases, as some
families may not have the emotional or financial wherewithal to proceed. Once a diagnosis is made, the anticipated biologic behavior will influence further
gnostics to identify to what extent the body is
dia­
affected locally, regionally, and distantly. This process is
termed staging.
Staging
Staging is necessary prior to treatment for accurate
assessment of overall condition, prognosis, and treatment response. The following chapters will illustrate the
predicted biologic behavior for specific malignancies.
Clinical staging using the World Health Organization
(WHO) classification system of tumor‐node‐metastasis
(TNM) has been applied to many canine and feline
tumor types. This classification has proven useful in the
prognostication of many but not all malignancies.
Clinical stage of specific tumor types will include the
size of the primary tumor (T), the identification of
spread to regional lymph nodes (N), and the presence of
metastasis (M). The subsequent chapters will reveal the
tumor types for which stage has been shown to be predictive for prognosis. A few examples are canine oral
melanoma, apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma,
and lymphoma.
Grading
Grading of a tumor is based on the histopathologic features, in particular mitotic index, percent necrosis, invasiveness, nuclear size, overall cellularity, and the presence
of inflammation. Grading has also been shown to be predictive for particular tumors. The search for advanced
prognostic markers and predictive factors is currently
focused on molecular processes such as altered cell cycle
progression, cellular proliferation, programmed cell

VetBooks.ir

129 Approach to the Cancer Patient

death (apoptosis), and angiogenesis (generation of blood
vessels). Identification and understanding of the altered
molecular tumor processes will ultimately reveal reliable
markers for diagnosis, and predict the clinical behavior,
prognosis, and response to therapy.

­Diagnostics
Primary assessment should include evaluation of tumor
extent, by clinical examination and appropriate diagnostic imaging or endoscopic techniques. Baseline
blood testing and urinalysis rarely lead to a cancer diagnosis but may reveal any co‐morbidity, and so revise the
decision‐making process or prognosis. Species differences must be taken into consideration. A dog with
HHM may have lymphoma or an apocrine gland anal
sac adenocarcinoma. In contrast, the inciting cause of
feline hypercalcemia is more likely a direct action of
tumor‐induced bone destruction as in multiple myeloma or a carcinoma invading bone rather than HHM
which is the result of cytokine‐ or hormone‐induced
hypercalcemia. The baseline blood testing for felines
should always include retroviral testing. Cats with lymphoma and feline leukemia virus will likely have half the
anticipated survival time.
Imaging
Tumor imaging concentrates on assessing the essential
morphologic features. Radiography, sonography, computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are applied routinely to identify local tumor
extent and patient staging. When faced with a choice of
diagnostic testing, the sensitivity and specificity should
be considered. For instance, clinical examination of a
limping Rottweiler with localization of pain to the proximal humerus may suggest a less extensive bone tumor
where radiography may be adequate. However, radiography is less sensitive than CT, which is less sensitive than
MRI. Be mindful that unless the owner is interested in a
limb‐sparing procedure, a radiograph may offer enough
evidence to proceed with tissue sampling or surgery. Of
note is that regional accessible lymph node sampling
should be performed when malignant masses are suspected. Sampling completes staging and may assist in
establishing a diagnosis.
When a tumor is expected to metastasize through the
circulatory system to the pulmonary parenchyma, three‐
view thoracic radiographs are recommended. In tumors
likely to metastasize through lymphatics such as mast
cell tumors and lymphoma, ventral‐dorsal and right lateral views will often suffice. The importance of clinical
staging may be unintentionally disregarded, especially
when exploratory surgery uncovers a mass. Any

­suspicious lesion should be sampled through biopsy or
fine needle aspiration (FNA). As mentioned previously,
sampling of the regional lymph nodes should also be
­performed. Any instruments contaminated with tumor
or intestinal contents should be discarded. Fresh tissue
should be cultured if granulomatous disease is
anticipated.
Advanced Diagnostics
Recent advancement in veterinary oncology has provided us with insight into disease processes and an
e volution toward targeted treatments. Prognostic
­
­information regarding survival time and disease‐free
interval in canine osteosarcoma was identified through
monitoring of serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and
bone ALP. Diagnostic tests for specific tumors are
available: PetScreen® test for lymphoma, CADET®
BRAF, CADET® BRAF Plus and V‐BTA™ (urine test for
bladder tumor analytes/mutations) for bladder cancer
diagnosis and monitoring. CADET® HM is a diagnostic
test utilizing cytological preparations or formalin fixed
parrafin embedded tissue to identify histiocytic diseases. Tests evaluating antibodies for thymidine kinase
and serum levels of the protein lactate dehydrogenase
can identify an ongoing malignant process. Once sufficient data are accrued, mainstream implementation
such as screening, diagnostic, prognostic and as treatment management tools may become possible.
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and flow cytometry
have yielded prognostic ­information, and guided our
treatment choices in lymphoreticular cancers and mast
cell tumors. Please refer to these specific ­chapters for
more detail.

­Therapy
Curative techniques are treatments that are intended to
induce remission of the cancer and may include various
therapeutic options such as chemotherapy, surgical
extirpation, radiation therapy, and immunotherapy, all
with the goal of long‐term tumor control. Definitive
therapy will both accomplish tumor control and result in
alleviation or elimination of pain, whereas palliative
therapy is an important tool for control of oncologic pain
and improved function, generally with minimal control
over the tumor itself.
Ultimately, the treatment choice should be based on
several factors that will be individual to each family: time
available for hospital visits, feasibility of administering
in‐home medications, anticipated survival time with and
without treatment, acceptable side‐effect profile, emotional and financial wherewithal to tolerate treatment,
and disease‐related side‐effects.

Chemotherapy
Fundamentally, local disease requires a treatment to be
directed to a specific area, typically surgery or radiation
therapy. Chemotherapy is often indispensable when presented with widely disseminated but chemoresponsive
disease (lymphoma) or when the development of metastatic disease is highly anticipated (canine osteosarcoma). The application, administration, and response
rates achievable through the use of chemotherapy are
addressed in their respective chapters.
Treatment Advances
Recent treatment advances have provided the veterinarian with orally administered targeted treatments
for mast cell tumors (Palladia™ and Kinavet‐CA1®).
TANOVEA®-CA1 (rabacfosadine) is the first FDA conditionally approved drug for the treatment of lymphoma
in dogs. This drug is delivered intravenously and has
been found to inhibit the proliferation of lymphoma
cells in vivo. Inter­ventional radiology utilizes fluoroscopy and endoscopy, placing expandable metallic stents
in the urethra of dogs with neoplasia, resulting in
increased urine flow with tumor obstruction or near‐
obstruction. Chemoembolization refers to the angiography guided administration of a vascular occluding
substance and chemotherapy through a catheter into a
pinpointed vessel within the tumor. This technique has
shown promise for the treatment of unresectable liver
tumors. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HCT)
is available for dogs with hematopoietic malignancies.
Immunotherapy research collaboration has provided
the first USDA‐approved canine melanoma vaccine
(Oncept®) indicated for aiding in extending survival of
dogs with stage II or stage III oral canine melanoma.
Other available conditionally licensed vaccines include;
Canine Lymphoma Vaccine, a xenogeneic murine
CD20 DNA therapeutic vaccine for use in dogs with
B-cell lymphoma upon achieving remission through
chemotherapy. Canine Osteosarcoma Vaccine for the
treatment of dogs one year or older diagnosed with
appendicular osteosarcoma. The vaccine is a lyophilized formulation of a modified-live,attenuated, recombinant HER2/neu–expressing strain of Listeria that
activates cytotoxic T cells. Lastly for our felines, Feline
Interleukin-2 (IL-2) Immunomodulator Vaccine may
delay postsurgical recurrence of feline fibrosarcoma in
adult cats with stage I disease.
We have also had advancements in treatment‐related
side‐effects, with reports revealing protection from tissue necrosis associated with administration of dexrazoxane in patients with chemotherapy extravasation.
Entyce®, capromorelin is an orally active small molecule
that mimics the action of ghrelin, which causes growth

hormone secretion and appetite stimulation. This has
significant potential to treat inappetence related to
therapy and/or underlying cancer in dogs and
chemo­
possibly cats. Maropitant citrate (Cerenia®) offers an economical addition to the armament for the prevention
and treatment of chemotherapy‐induced nausea and
vomiting. In an effort to avoid chemotherapy related toxicity primarily found in herding breeds an assay is available. These breeds have a higher risk of toxicity from
chemotherapeutic agents that are actively transported by
the p‐glycoprotein pump (e.g., vinca alkaloids, doxorubicin, dactinomycin, taxanes). The assay is noninvasive,
and is simply performed through either a blood sample
or cheek swab. For more information visit www.vetmed.
wsu.edu/depts‐vcpl/.
Surgery
Surgical intervention is the backbone of localized cancer
treatment and is often used adjunctively in metastatic
cancers. Surgical oncology will be addressed in the
respective chapters for which is applies.
Interestingly, perioperative anesthetic and analgesic
practices, including administration of opioid analgesics
and nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), use
of local anesthetic techniques, precipitation of the neuroendocrine stress response, temperature regulation,
and transfusion of blood products may influence long‐
term outcomes such as recurrence and metastasis.
Radiation Therapy
Radiation therapy (RT) utilizes the delivery of radiation
from a distance. The delivery of radiation therapy in veterinary medicine is through the use of three machine
types: orthovoltage (infrequently employed), cobalt‐60
(widely used), and linear accelerators (most common).
Pedestal machines are limited to up‐and‐down
­movement while isocentric machines rotate around the
patient. The advantage permits treatment from a variety
of angles. The prescribed radiation dose is expressed as
­tissue absorbed dose in units of gray (Gy). The total
­prescribed radiation is delivered in small defined doses
called fractions. Radiation therapy is often employed
when surgical resection of a tumor is limited by normal
surrounding structures, and it is not possible to eliminate microscopic cells. In select cases when normal
­tissue structures preclude adequate surgical removal,
radiation may be performed prior to surgery (preoperative). The majority of radiation therapy is performed
10–14 days postoperatively.
It is important that the radiation oncologist be aware
of the original tumor site, including the dimensions and
extent of invasion, so as to include all the affected tissue in the planned radiation field. When microscopic

VetBooks.ir

129 Approach to the Cancer Patient

residual disease is outside the treatment field, it is left
untreated and recurrence is likely; this is referred to as a
geographic miss. The risk increases with multiple surgeries by means of distortion of normal tissue structures.
Placement of hemoclips (radiopaque clips) at the margins of the resected tissue benefits treatment planning,
decreasing the likelihood of a geographic miss. The
majority of radiation‐induced adverse effects are often
mild and self‐limiting. Advanced imaging developments
have enhanced our ability to delineate tumor tissue
extent and have led to improved treatment outcomes
and fewer patient side‐effects.

­several terms under the umbrella term SRT. SRS (stereotactic radiosurgery) treats the CNS, brain and spine.
Despite having surgery in the name, the procedure is
noninvasive,and no surgery is involved. SBRT (stereotactic body radiation therapy) treats all other structures
than the brain and spine. SRT is used to treat tumors that
would otherwise be considered inoperable and classically it is not used to address microscopic disease. At
present, SRT use in veterinary patients is expanding
beyond the initially treated bone tumors, central and
peripheral nervous system tumors.

Intensity‐Modulated Radiation Therapy (IMRT)

Radiopharmaceuticals are radioactive substances used to
image and/or treat particular cancers. One example is
iodine‐131, a frequently employed treatment of thyroid
adenoma/carcinoma in the cat. Samarium‐153 and
related compounds have been used for treatment of
­multilobular osteochondrosarcoma, and osteosarcoma.

The majority of radiation treatments in veterinary oncology are delivered with radiation beams of uniform intensity in a static field. Collimators are used to limit the
treatment beam and provide a rectangular treatment
field. Further development has led to the more complex
multileaf collimator (MLC) which is made of many metal
slats capable of independent movement to shape the
field. IMRT has the ability to specifically modulate the
weights of small segments within an individual radiation
beam. This is referred to as intensity distribution, and
allows the beam to conform to the three‐dimensional
shape of complex tumor target volumes. This technique
of RT delivers a nonuniform fluence (beam intensity) to
the patient, allowing optimization of dose distribution to
the target volume while sparing critical tissues. The
MLC uses the superimposition of many subfields that
deliver the prescribed dose. The use of IMRT has permitted the radiation oncologist to treat tumors (nasal
and prostate) that would otherwise be difficult to control
without significant patient side‐effects.
Stereotactic Radiation Therapy

Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) involves precision delivery of one or several high doses of radiation to the target
(tumor) by means of a linear accelerator with a sophisticated treatment planning system, delivery, and positioning device (frame). The conformal nature of SRS permits
avoidance of toxicity to normal surrounding tissues. The
CyberKnife® Radiosurgery System delivers radiation
through a manipulated robot‐mounted linear accelerator. At present, SRS is primarily utilized in select canine
osteosarcoma patients and veterinary patients with central and peripheral nervous system tumors. Stereotactic
radiation therapy (SRT) involves precision delivery of
one or several high doses of radiation therapy delivered
to the target (tumor) by means of a linear accelerator
with a sophisticated treatment planning system, delivery,
and positioning device(s). Most linear accelerators are
floor mounted and revolve 360 degrees around the
patient. The conformal nature of SRT permits avoidance
of toxicity to normal surrounding tissues. There are

Palliative Medical Care
Metronomic Chemotherapy

Metronomic chemotherapy, which is intended to prevent tumor angiogenesis, is based on frequent, low‐dose,
continuous cytotoxic drug administration lacking the
rest period included with conventional chemotherapy. It
results in minimal toxicity, is often cost‐effective, and
convenient. In veterinary medicine, metronomic therapy
has become an affiliate to many protocols and usually
combines an orally administered cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agent with an NSAID. It is most frequently applied
in the treatment of visceral hemangiosarcoma (HSA),
transitional cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder, nasal
tumors, and metastatic cancers.
Pain Management
It is often difficult for clients to recognize the signs of
pain or discomfort in their pets. Unrelieved pain is a
major cause of suffering in patients with cancer.
Veterinarians managing cancer patients must be vigilant
about monitoring for and providing relief from pain,
whether caused by the neoplastic process itself or coincidental in nature. Providing adequate management of
pain is central to oncologic care and will improve the
quality of life of the animal patient.
Palliative Radiation Therapy
Palliative radiation therapy (PRT) is the administration
of a radiotherapy dose in a smaller number of treatments
(fractions) than would be used in the delivery of curative
intent RT (CRT); however, the fraction dose is higher
and less percise than SRT. The appeal of PRT lies in

improved quality of life through symptom relief and
when compared to CRT, the cost incurred is minimal. The
mechanism of radiation‐induced pain amelioration is
currently undefined. Reduction of inflammatory cells
through irradiation inhibits the release of chemical pain
mediators and is probably responsible for the rapid
reduction in pain seen in some patients. Decreased activity of osteoclasts in the bone microenvironment reduces
bone destruction and predicts the relief of pain through
irradiation.
Most patients treated with PRT will not be afforded
long‐term survival. Symptom relief may last 1–3 months.
The common early side‐effects associated with RT are
often easily ameliorated and patient tolerated. While
uncommon, late reactions associated with PRT may be
undesirable and life‐threatening. Tumor reirradiation
may be possible but continued treatment will increase
the likelihood of deleterious late effects. Aside from the
successful alleviation of discomfort in bone tumors, PRT
may offer relief for a variety of tumor types especially in
patients with tumor‐induced pain and limited function.
Adjunctive Techniques
Complementary techniques including acupuncture,
massage, and herbal remedies are being evaluated. The
actual practice of acupuncture incorporates many forms,
including dry needling, laser acupuncture, and electroacupuncture, and may incorporate acupressure or herbal
medicine. Specific considerations for acupuncture in the
presence of cancer include avoidance of insertion of needles into or near tumors, and attention to the risk of
infection in patients who are immunocompromised.

­End‐of‐Life Management
The hospice movement originated in the late 1960s when
Dame Cicely Saunders established the first medical

hospice that focused on palliative care of the whole
­
patient in an attempt to control distressing symptomatology while also managing the psychosocial aspects of
dying for the patient and the patient’s family. These
ideas are quite applicable to veterinary medicine. The
American Veterinary Medical Association’s established
guidelines for hospice care are available at: www.avma.
org/public/PetCare/Pages/hospice‐care.aspx
Euthanasia is a valid therapeutic tool in the management of progressive and intractable pain or disease in
veterinary patients but it is not one that is applied easily
in most situations. Many owners have questions about
timing and fear making the wrong decision. The veterinarian managing a terminal patient must be prepared to
handle a wide range of physical, financial, and emotional
issues. The grieving process is an individual experience,
making it essential to be supportive, permitting clients
to grieve in a manner we may not understand. Clients
may also need encouragement to speak openly with
children.
Veterinarians must perform many functions during
the course of treatment and palliative care of the oncology patient:
listening to the goals, fears, and contextual experience
of the owners
●● demonstrating awareness of the difficult nature of
the situation; reflective listening and empathy
can help build trust between the client and the
veterinarian
●● guiding the owners through the expected course of the
disease and helping them define an appropriate quality
of life for the patient
●● providing a peaceful and dignified release from suffering through appropriate methods of euthanasia.
●●

Veterinarians have an inordinate amount of pressure to
provide for patients, especially those under protracted
care. Attention should be given to the internal struggles
that may ensue should compassion fatigue arise.

Biology of Cancer and Cancer Genetics
Mary‐Keara Boss, DVM, PhD, DACVR (Radiation Oncology)
Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA

Veterinary patients develop cancer in all tissues of the
body, and these neoplasms are characterized according
to their cell type of origin: carcinoma – epithelial;
­sarcoma – mesenchymal; round cell tumor – typically of
the hematopoietic system. Cells can transition from a
normal phenotype to malignancy through acquisition of
mutations of certain types of genes. Oncogenes are
defined as those which code for proteins that allow
­dysregulated tumor cell growth and proliferation, while
tumor suppressor genes, which normally restrain cell
growth, allow cancer cells to grow and divide indefinitely
when absent or inactivated by mutation. The abnormal
characteristics and behaviors of cancerous cells and
­tissues share commonalities, such that the neoplastic
transformations and progression pathways have been
defined according to various hallmarks of cancer.
In their 2011 review, Hanahan and Weinberg revised
and expanded upon their initially described hallmarks.
The original six hallmarks are:
enabling replicative immortality
evading growth suppressors
●● resisting cell death
●● sustaining proliferative signaling
●● inducing angiogenesis
●● activating invasion and metastasis.
●●
●●

As new developments in cancer biology were discovered,
emerging hallmarks that involve the complex tumor
microenvironment were added:
avoiding immune destruction
deregulating cellular energetics and enabling characteristics crucial to the acquisition of the original
­ allmark capabilities
h
●● genome instability and mutation
●● tumor promoting inflammation.
●●
●●

This chapter on the biology of cancer and cancer
­genetics is organized in accordance with the hallmarks
of cancer. Each section will review the cancer biology
and genetics underlying the particular neoplastic characteristic being discussed, followed by examples of the
­relevance of the abnormality in clinical small animal
oncology today. Topics were assigned to a particular
­hallmark, and although it is recognized that overlaps in
content exist, this organization allowed a concise but in
no way comprehensive account of how the biology and
genetics of veterinary cancer may be conceptualized.
Further, the hallmarks are organized in an order that
allows the topics to progress from cellular to microenvironmental effects. Clinical aspects of each category
will be highlighted; however, for more detailed discussions, see chapters devoted to specific tumor types.

­Enabling Replicative Immortality
Cancer cells require the ability to replicate unlimitedly,
uninhibited by normal space restrictions, to form a
­macroscopic tumor. Normal cells will progress through
a tightly regulated, limited number of cell divisions;
thereupon, they face either senescence, which is an
­
­irreversible, nonproliferative, viable state, or crisis (cell
death). Cancer cells do not respect the bounds of senescence or crisis, and attain a state of immortality.
The classic in vitro demonstration of unlimited replication is the ability to continuously grow and passage tumor
cells in cell culture in the laboratory setting. The development and maintenance of cancer cell lines in vitro have
allowed for molecular characterization of specific tumor
types and evaluation of therapeutic responses through
experimental manipulations at the cellular level. Recent
research utilizing veterinary cancer cell lines includes

Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/bruyette/clinical

­studies of canine osteosarcoma, B cell lymphoma, mammary carcinoma, prostate carcinoma, and mast cell tumors,
as well as feline vaccine‐associated fibrosarcomas.
There are several fields of study devoted to understanding the uncontrolled nature of tumor cell replication. An underlying mechanism by which a cell regulates
the number of divisions tolerable over time is through
the integrity of chromosomal telomeres. Telomeres are
specialized nucleoprotein complexes that “cap” and protect the end of every eukaryotic chromosome against
chromosomal fusion, recombination, and terminal DNA
degradation. Telomeres become progressively shorter
with each doubling until they reach a critically short
length and induce replicative senescence. The enzyme
telomerase maintains telomeres by synthesizing and
replenishing telomeric DNA. Cancer cells exploit this
function by expressing telomerase and perpetually
replace their telomeres. It is through this mechanism that
most cancer cells gain replicative immortality. It has been
shown in dogs that telomerase activity is upregulated in a
majority of cancers and is absent in normal adult tissue.
In fact, according to veterinary oncologic studies, telomerase is present in greater than 90% of canine cancers and
is absent from most normal tissues, with the exception of
germ cells. Further, it has been suggested that a different
form of telomere maintenance, known as alternative
lengthening of telomeres (ALT) via homologous recombination, may occur in canine osteosarcoma cells.
Important to the concept of replicative immortality,
there has been great interest in studying cancer stem
cells. The basis of the cancer stem cell model is that
tumor development relies on a subset of stem cells that
have the ability to self‐renew and generate the diverse
cells that comprise the tumor through differentiation.
As such, the tumor exists as a heterogenous structure,
maintained by cancer stem cells, which are inherently
resistant to traditional chemotherapy and radiotherapy.
Recently, cancer stem cells have been identified, isolated,
and characterized from canine osteosarcoma cells in vitro.

to the treatment during mitosis and most resistant when
in the S phase. If treated in or prior to G1 or G2 phase, a
temporary arrest or “block” in the cell cycle occurs. It is
felt that the G1 and G2 blocks are necessary in order to
repair damage done to fragile DNA prior to duplication of
a faulty template or distribution of defective genes to a
daughter cell in mitosis. These transient delays are also
known as checkpoints. These checkpoints exist as safety
mechanisms to limit the propagation of heritable errors
and promote the survival of the cell. A well‐known tumor
suppressor protein, p53, plays a critical role in the G1
checkpoint and controlling the fate of injured cells. It has
been determined that a majority of cancers are affected
with mutated p53, which allows cells that have been damaged to proceed through the cell cycle and replicate, creating daughter cells with flawed genetic content.
Chemotherapy drugs can be defined as cell cycle phase
specific or cell cycle phase nonspecific. Examples of
chemotherapeutics that are cell cycle phase specific
include antimetabolites (i.e., gemcitabine, cytosine arabinoside, 5‐fluorouracil), which are S phase specific, interfering with the incorporation of nucleotides during DNA
synthesis, and vinca alkaloids (i.e., vincristine, v­ inblastine)
which are M phase specific, as they disrupt the assembly
of tubulin into microtubules and inhibit cell division.
Understanding these interactions, combination treatment plans, in which chemotherapy and radiation therapy are administered concurrently, can exploit the
sensitive phases of the cell cycle, with the goal of improving therapeutic efficacy. A clinical illustration of this
practice is the combination of gemcitabine, which kills
cells specifically in S phase, with radiation therapy, where
cells in S phase are the most resistant. The chemotherapy
dose must be reduced with this approach to limit the
severity of normal tissue toxicity; however, the combination has been reported for treatment of canine sinonasal
carcinoma and feline oral squamous cell carcinoma.

­Evading Growth Suppressors

Conventional cancer therapeutics may kill cells by
­inducing a lethal, cellular division, known as mitotic
catastrophe, or triggering an organized, ­
controlled
cell death, known as apoptosis.
Playing a dual role, the p53 tumor suppressor gene,
which was described in the previous section as controlling the G1 checkpoint in managing the cell cycle, is also
critical in activating the apoptotic response following
cellular damage. As it is very common for malignancies
to exist with mutant p53, cancer cells are adept at
­avoiding death by apoptosis. For example, the incidence
of p53 mutations in canine osteosarcoma varies from
24% to 47%.

The cell cycle is an organized balance of signals promoting and restricting replication and division; however,
neoplastic cells exist with dysfunctional growth control
mechanisms. The basic phases of the cell cycle have been
defined as S phase (DNA synthesis), M phase (mitosis),
and gaps, G1 (between M and S), G2 (between S and M),
G0 (senescence).
When cells are exposed to damaging agents, such as
ionizing radiation or certain chemotherapy drugs, the
therapeutic efficacy varies with respect to the phase of the
cell cycle. For example, irradiated cells are most sensitive

­Resisting Cell Death

VetBooks.ir

An alternative mechanism of resisting cell death by
cancer cells is through manipulating antiapoptotic pathways. These antiapoptotic pathways are intended to
maintain the natural homeostasis of cellular proliferation and deletion within tissues. Widely studied inhibitors of apoptosis include members of the Bcl‐2 family
and survivin. The distribution of Bcl‐2 protein in normal
and neoplastic feline tissues has been studied, as well as
the expression of survivin in canine urinary bladder
transitional cell carcinoma.
In general, mitotic catastrophe is the primary method
of cellular killing by radiation exposure and a significant
component of cell death by certain chemotherapy
agents. A major mode of action of chemotherapy‐
induced death is the activation of apoptosis. To provide
a clinical example, a class of drugs incorporated in
­cancer therapy protocols which induces apoptosis in a
specific cellular population are the bisphosphonates.
Bisphosphonate drugs used in veterinary oncology
include pamidronate and zoledronate, and these are prescribed for patients that have developed malignancies
which involve the destruction of bone. Bone undergoes
constant turnover. Homeostasis of the tissue is maintained by the a­ ctivity of osteoblasts, which create bone,
and osteoclasts, which destroy bone. Bisphosphonates
inhibit the destruction of bone by reducing osteoclast
activities and stimulating these cells to undergo apoptosis. The therapeutic effect of osteoclast inhibition is to
slow the malignant destruction of the affected bone,
which results in alleviation of pain and improvement of
quality of life. Recent examples of clinical research utilizing bisphosphonate drugs for the treatment of veterinary cancer patients include the use of pamidronate in
the management of canine appendicular osteosarcoma
and ­zoledronate for treatment of oral squamous cell
­carcinoma in cats.

­Genome Instability and Mutation
In an established neoplasm, mutations have evolved to
circumvent effective cell cycle checkpoints and DNA
repair mechanisms. This allows the tumor to reproduce
in a state of genetic instability, further driving an aggressive phenotype. In veterinary oncology, such genetic
instability has recently been studied in canine mammary
tumors, where variable rates of microsatellite sequence
aberrations were documented among the mammary
cancer samples.
A given population of tumor cells is heterogenous by
nature, with variable distributions of genetic mutations
and phenotypic manifestations of these abnormalities.
Genetic and pathologic evaluations of tumors with the
same clinical diagnosis exhibit intertumoral h
­ eterogeneity

due to multiple mutations in oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes, varying environmental conditions, and
inherited germline variations. The combination of these
factors leads to immense natural heterogeneity in tumor
phenotypes, disease outcomes, and response to therapies. The development of new molecular biological tools
has expanded the understanding of genetics and the
pathophysiology of tumorigenesis.
Gene expression profiling with the use of microarray
technology has greatly improved our ability to classify
tumors by generating unique molecular fingerprints that
have delineated tumor subtypes. DNA microarray technology allows the study of gene activity and gene function at the genome level as a means to analyze the
molecular phenotypes and clinical heterogeneity of
tumors. The emergence of genome sequences for a variety of veterinary species has allowed for the development of new microarray‐based technologies that
facilitate whole genome, or gene‐targeted, profiling to be
performed at a considerably higher resolution and
throughput.
The use of microarray‐based technology in the veterinary field has become more prevalent. Recently, the
utility of gene expression analysis using a cDNA microarray to differentiate metastatic and nonmetastatic soft
tissue sarcomas in dogs was investigated. Further,
microarray technology was used to characterize the
gene expression profile of tumors in a population of
dogs with soft tissue sarcomas being treated with radiation therapy and hyperthermia to predict therapeutic
response. Comparisons were made between the gene
changes that occurred, tumor volume, and functional
MRI parameters. Significant correlations were identified between tumor responses and genes involved in telomerase ­activity, DNA repair, inflammation, and growth
factor signaling. In this cohort of canine sarcomas, the
gene expression of tumors was affected significantly,
but not uniformly, by the combination of radiation and
hyperthermia.

­Tumor Promoting Inflammation
While it is important to understand the cellular characteristics of a tumor, we must consider that the cells exist
in a complex microenvironment. Tumor cells are intimately associated with supporting stromal cells, immune
cells, and microvasculature. Solid tumors exist in a state
of active inflammation, and conventional cancer therapy
can both promote and reduce inflammation. Tumor
tissue reacts as a unit to therapeutic interventions;
­
­however, responses to treatments are not limited to the
neoplasm. There are unique localized and systemic
responses to chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and other

1207

VetBooks.ir

1208

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

treatments that can result in transient or chronic effects.
Clinical examples of local and systemic inflammatory
reactions to oncologic treatments in veterinary medicine
would include localized oral mucositis within the radiation field and generalized intestinal inflammation with
certain chemotherapeutic agents, respectively.
The association between chronic inflammation and
neoplasia is well established. Some recent interesting
examples of chronic inflammatory lesions that progress
to cancer in veterinary medicine include biliary tract
trematode infection leading to cholangiocarcinoma in
cats, superficial corneal squamous cell carcinoma occurring in dogs with chronic keratitis, and traumatic or
­surgical fracture‐associated osteosarcoma development
in dogs.
A nonspecific and complex host response to inflammation that has been investigated for its potential use as
a prognostic and monitoring tool is the formation of
acute phase proteins (APP). APPs are induced by proinflammatory cytokines, and tumor cells produce large
amounts of transforming growth factor beta, cytokines
including interleukins 6 and 10, and prostaglandin E2.
Veterinary studies evaluating the use of APPs include trials with canine and feline lymphoma, canine mammary
carcinoma, mast cell tumors, soft tissue sarcoma, and
combinations of tumor‐bearing dogs and cats.
A targeted approach to inhibiting the inflammatory
component of cancer that is commonly used in veterinary oncology is the use of cyclooxygenase (COX)
inhibitors, specifically those that inhibit the enzyme
­
COX‐2. Overexpression of COX‐2 in tumors drives
many cancer‐associated mechanisms and COX‐2 inhibitors are prescribed to prevent or reduce the neoplastic
proinflammatory state. The effects of the COX‐inhibitor piroxicam have been evaluated in the treatment of
canine urinary bladder transitional cell carcinoma, as
well as canine oral malignant melanoma, inflammatory
mammary carcinoma, prostatic carcinoma, and oral
­
­squamous cell carcinoma.

­Avoiding Immune Destruction
Cancer develops in the host through deception of the
immune system. The roles of the immune cells are
defined by their involvement in either innate or adaptive
immunity. Cells of the innate pathway include phagocytic, antigen‐presenting cells (APC), such as macrophages and dendritic cells, and those of the adaptive
pathway consisting of cells with randomly generated
antigen receptors, like B and T lymphocytes. Generally,
APCs are activated by immunogenic stimuli, migrate to
lymphoid organs to present antigen to T cells, and stimulate the adaptive immune response.

The function of effector T cells and APCs can be disrupted by a T lymphocyte type, known as regulatory T
cell (Treg). Treg cells are important for immune tolerance through downregulation of self‐reactive lymphocytes; however, suppression of antitumor immune
responses by Tregs can promote tumor progression and
development. Large populations of Tregs have been
shown to be present in various human cancers and to
correlate with poor prognosis. The involvement of
Tregs in veterinary oncology has been investigated in a
number of different canine tumor types. In these studies, the numbers of Treg cells in the peripheral blood
and tumor‐draining lymph nodes were increased in
dogs with ­cancer compared to healthy dogs. Further,
Treg cell infiltration was statistically correlated with
high histologic grade in canine mammary carcinoma.
Many therapeutic approaches have been developed
that utilize the immune system to target and treat cancer,
and these techniques have been explored in veterinary
oncology. Nonspecific tumor immunotherapies, including biologic response modifiers, such as bacterial strains,
oncolytic viruses, and recombinant cytokines, growth
factors, and hormones, have been used to treat several
veterinary malignancies. Also, specific targeted immunotherapies, such as cancer vaccines, where the immune
system detects tumors through tumor‐associated antigens, have been utilized for veterinary patients. Clinical
examples of veterinary cancer vaccines include the
­xenogeneic DNA vaccine for canine melanoma and the
autologous tumor RNA‐loaded, activated B cell vaccine
for canine lymphoma.

­Inducing Angiogenesis
Tumor vasculature is unique and abnormal. In order for
a developing solid tumor to grow into a macroscopic
mass, it must induce the surrounding normal tissue to
either share its oxygen and nutrient supply or create its
own vascular network. The processes by which a tumor
forms new blood vessels, known as vasculogenesis, and/
or remodels existing vasculature, known as angiogenesis,
involve highly integrated signaling and communication
between cells of the microenvironment. Tumors stimulate persistent angiogenesis through expression of many
factors, one of the most important being the family of
vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) proteins.
Vascular endothelial growth factor is a growth factor
and its signal is transmitted through the tyrosine kinase
activity of transmembrane VEGF receptors. Most cancer
cells and certain tumor stromal cells express VEGF, and
stimulation of VEGF leads to endothelial cell proliferation, migration, and survival. In veterinary oncology,
VEGF expression has been recognized as a negative

VetBooks.ir

130 Biology of Cancer and Cancer Genetics

prognostic marker for a number of tumors, such as
canine intracranial meningiomas, osteosarcoma, lymphoma, oral malignant melanoma, and feline invasive
mammary carcinoma.
Abnormal tumor vessel morphology includes aberrant
architecture and function of blood vessels which often
leads to low oxygenation within the tumor, known as
intratumoral hypoxia. Tumor hypoxia may stimulate
angiogenesis through expression of the transcription
factor hypoxia inducible factor‐1 (HIF‐1). HIF‐1 induces
several proangiogenic factors such as VEGF. Hypoxic
regions within tumors are a significant issue in radiation
therapy because hypoxic cells are more resistant than
oxygenated cells to treatment. Hypoxic cells are also
more resistant to chemotherapy as hypoxic cells are farther from the vasculature and may not be exposed to
lethal drug concentrations. Importantly, hypoxia may
increase the biologic aggressiveness of a tumor by HIF‐1
activation of several neoplastic pathways.
Targeted therapeutic approaches have been developed
recently which are intended to disrupt tumor angiogenesis. The use of continuous, low‐dose chemotherapy is
commonly referred to as “metronomic chemotherapy.”
Three aspects of angiogenesis that are affected by metronomic chemotherapy are direct cytotoxic effects on the
endothelial cells of the tumor blood vessels indirect
effect of tipping the influence from proangiogeneic
growth factors to inhibitors, thus preventing further
­vessel expansion, and reducing the recruitment of bone
marrow‐derived endothelial progenitor cells. The efficacy of metronomic chemotherapy protocols has been
studied in veterinary oncology through clinical trials
with canine patients treated for splenic hemangiosarcoma and soft tissue sarcoma with the drug combination
of cyclophosphamide and piroxicam.

­Sustaining Proliferative Signaling
In normal tissues, growth factors regulate cellular proliferation and differentiation. Cancer cells, however,
develop a reduced requirement for exogenous growth
factors as they become capable of autonomous activation
of autocrine and paracrine growth pathways. As the
goals for cancer therapy include tumor regression and
eradication, this aberrant proliferation must be inhibited
to prevent resistance and recurrence.
Some of the key proteins regulating cell survival and
proliferation are the transmembrane epidermal growth
factor receptor (EGFR) and ligand epidermal growth factor (EGF). EGFR is overexpressed in many tumor types
and is associated with aggressiveness and resistance to
therapies. EGFR and EGF have been studied in veterinary medicine as potential prognostic indicators and

possible therapeutic targets in canine mammary cancer,
glial brain tumors, nasal carcinomas, and feline oral
squamous cell carcinoma.
Epidermal growth factor receptor belongs to a group
of proteins that form the receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)
superfamily. Tyrosine kinases are transmembrane receptors that regulate normal cell signal transduction and
maintain cell growth and differentiation. Additional
examples of receptor tyrosine kinases include Kit, Met,
VEGFR, PDGFR, and FGFR. RTKs are commonly
­abnormally activated and dysregulated in human and
veterinary cancer. For instance, Kit is a receptor found
on mast cells, and mutations to Kit in canine mast cell
tumors (MCTs) have been shown to drive unregulated
proliferative signaling. Up to 30% of all canine MCTs are
affected with Kit mutations, and these have been shown
to be significantly associated with tumor grade, as the
more malignant tumors are more likely to have abnormal
Kit receptors. Further, canine gastrointestinal stromal
tumors (GIST) have also been characterized as carrying
Kit mutations.
Recently, a variety of small molecule inhibitors that
target tyrosine kinases, known as tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), have been approved for the treatment of
human cancer. The use of these inhibitors has resulted
in significant clinical efficacy, being used as sole
therapeutics or in combination therapy protocols.
­
Importantly, TKIs have now been incorporated into
veterinary oncology care. Examples of these drugs
include Palladia™ (toceranib), and Gleevec® (imatinib).
Gleevec has been used to treat cancers in dogs and cats,
and Palladia has undergone registrational studies in
dogs with MCTs. The molecular targets inhibited by
these drugs consist of Kit, VEGF, and PDGFR and
they have been used to treat MCTs and sarcomas in
dogs and cats, as well as carcinomas, melanoma, and
myeloma in dogs.

­Deregulating Cellular Energetics
It has been discussed with the preceding hallmarks that
tumors adapt and proliferate despite harsh conditions of
inflammatory stress and disorganized, ineffective microcirculation. The tumor microenvironment is not only
characterized by varying degrees of hypoxia, but also
nutrient deprivation and low extracellular pH. The unusual metabolism of cancer cells is intimately involved in
creating such an abnormal physiologic state.
Normal tissues are able to sustain routine cellular
functions through the oxidation of nutrients to provide
energy in the form of adenosine triphosphate (ATP).
Glucose metabolism is regulated in response to changes
in cellular oxygen levels. Initially, glucose is converted to

1209

VetBooks.ir

1210

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

pyruvate by glycolytic enzymes. Under well‐oxygenated
conditions, pyruvate is oxidized in the tricarboxylic acid
cycle to form water and a substantial amount of ATP
(oxidative phosphorylation); however, under hypoxic
conditions, lactate dehydrogenase A converts pyruvate
to lactate and generates very little ATP (glycolysis).
It has been shown that glycolysis, under aerobic conditions, is particularly high in aggressive tumors when
compared with benign tumors and normal tissues. This
discovery of tumor‐specific, oxygen‐independent glycolysis was labeled the Warburg effect. This peculiar metabolic preference of tumor cells drives a significantly
inefficient breakdown of glucose for ATP and creates an
acidic microenvironment through the build‐up of the
byproduct lactic acid.
The increased dependence of cancer cells on the glycolytic pathway provides a biochemical basis for the
functional imaging technique positron emission tomography (PET). PET imaging has become increasingly
invaluable in human and veterinary oncology. Using the
glucose analog fluorine‐18‐fluorodeoxyglucose (18FDG),
the detection of glucose metabolism with PET is associated with the presence of malignant tissue before anatomic evidence occurs. While traditional methods for
determining response to therapy in veterinary oncology
centers on anatomic changes in measurable target
­
lesions, 18FDG‐PET combined with a CT scan can
be used as a sensitive marker of tumor response to anticancer therapies via interrogation of cellular glucose
metabolism.
Positron emission tomography plays an important
role in the diagnosis, staging, image‐guided treatment
planning, and monitoring of malignant diseases.
A recent preliminary study described the use of serial
18
FDG‐PET/CT to assess the response to toceranib
­therapy in canine cancer. Multiple types of canine tumors
have been evaluated for their avidity for FDG, including
mast cell tumor, lymphoma, mammary carcinoma, and
hemangiosarcoma. FDG‐PET has identified the involvement of metastatic sites not detected on physical examination and has been reported to provide more accurate
disease detection for improved diagnosis, staging, and
restaging with treatment of companion animals with
cancer.

­Activating Invasion and Metastasis
The final hallmark to be reviewed is invasion and metastasis, the processes of which are incredibly convoluted
and intricate. The properties required to attain the phenotype of an invasive and metastatic neoplasm involve

the multistep, coordinated foundation of the previously
discussed hallmarks.
Experimental molecular oncology studies suggest that
the progression of a solid tumor to a metastatic phenotype is not simply the result of dysregulated signal transduction pathways, but instead is achieved through a
stepwise selection process. The adaptation of populations of neoplastic cells to their harsh microenvironment
facilitates cancer cell dissemination through the up‐ or
downregulation of critical metastasis‐associated genes,
such as E‐/N‐cadherin for epithelial‐mesenchymal transition (EMT), uPAR for degradation of the basement
membrane and extracellular matrix, HGF/MET for cell
motility, and VEGF for stromal interactions, intra/
extravasation, and angiogenesis. The systematic alteration of these phenotypic regulators allows cells to escape
the hostile microenvironment of the primary tumor and
colonize a secondary location.
The role of E‐cadherin in metastasis of veterinary cancer has been investigated. E‐cadherin is a transmembrane glycoprotein involved in cell‐to‐cell adhesions of
two adjacent cells and is typically expressed by epithelial
cells. Metastatic epithelial malignancies are associated
with loss of E‐cadherin expression and connectivity with
their neighboring cells; this leads to EMT, where epithelial tumor cells obtain mesenchymal characteristics, as
well as invasive and metastatic properties. In veterinary
medicine, studies that have investigated E‐cadherin
expression have evaluated canine mammary carcinoma
and anal sac gland adenocarcinoma for associations with
clinical malignancy.
Dissemination of primary tumor cells to a secondary
location may result in colonization of any number of
anatomic locations. One of the most common metastatic
sites is the first regional lymph node or nodes to which
the lymphatics from the primary tumor drain; therefore,
the disease status of what is known as this sentinel
lymph node (SNL) is important in cancer screening.
Lymphoscintigraphy, the injection of a radioactive tracer
at the tumor site to identify lymphatic drainage, and
intratumoral/peritumoral blue dye injection have been
used to locate SNLs in veterinary oncology. The SNL can
then be evaluated via histopathology for the presence of
metastatic disease. In veterinary practice, lymph nodes
are generally aspirated or biopsied if palpably enlarged;
however, since metastases occur in lymph nodes of normal clinical appearance and in lymph nodes other than
those routinely assessed according to the anatomic location of the primary tumor, this advanced technique for
metastasis identification has been recommended.
Reports describing SNL identification in veterinary
medicine include studies investigating canine head and
neck tumors and mammary carcinoma.

VetBooks.ir

130 Biology of Cancer and Cancer Genetics

­Conclusion
Hanahan and Weinberg’s hallmarks of cancer provides
an incredibly useful conceptual framework for understanding the complex biology of cancer, and it is evident
that intimate associations link each. The categorical
focus of these cancer principles allows the specialized
refinement of molecular mechanisms; however, the

appreciation that each hallmark operates as part of a
greater circuit will promote discoveries that further
advance the study of veterinary cancer and clinical oncology. The advancements made by veterinary researchers
and clinician scientists featured in this chapter have contributed to a greater understanding of translational
oncologic concepts between human and companion animal cancer patients.

Endocrine Manifestations of Cancer
Ectopic Hormone Production
Cory Brown, DVM, DACVIM (SAIM)
VetScan Mobile Diagnostics, Powell, OH, USA

Ectopic hormone production of endocrine origin from
nonendocrine tumors is a particular type of paraneoplastic syndrome. Some of the more common manifestations, such as hypoglycemia and hypercalcemia, are
covered in Chapter 132. Those more particular to the
endocrine system are covered in this chapter.

­Cushing Syndrome
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Corticotropin (also known as adrenocorticotropic hormone – ACTH) is produced by the anterior pituitary and
stimulates cortisol production by the adrenal cortex.
Corticotropin has been demonstrated to be produced by
a variety of tumors in human medicine, resulting in a
Cushing‐like syndrome. Although primarily reported
with small cell lung carcinoma, other tumor types
include carcinoid tumors of the thymus, gastrointestinal
tract, thyroid, pancreas, and adrenal medulla. Ectopic
production of corticotropin is not well described in veterinary medicine, although sporadic case reports exist. It
is theorized by some that ectopic corticotropin production is underestimated in animals due to diagnostic
­limitations. Routine pituitary imaging is not typically
pursued in dogs diagnosed with Cushing disease.
Therefore, dogs with ectopic production of the hormone
may be assumed to be pituitary dependent and treated
accordingly. Based on this assumption, ectopic corticotropin production may be more prevalent than is
­currently reported in the veterinary literature.
Diagnosis and Treatment
At a minimum, ectopic corticotropin production should
be considered in dogs with neoplastic disorders that
show concurrent symptoms of hyperadrenocorticism.

The diagnosis of ectopic ACTH production is based on
hormonal evidence of pituitary‐dependent hyperadrenocorticism (PDH), normal to high endogenous ACTH
levels, and normal pituitary imaging. Therapy for ectopic
corticotropin production has not been well defined in
animals, although treatment of the primary tumor
should be attempted. Treatment with trilostane, an adrenal enzyme blocker, resulted in adequate resolution of
symptoms in one dog.
Recently, production of sex hormone steroid precursors
from adrenal cortical tumors has been identified as a
source of Cushing symptoms. These animals may demonstrate typical signs of Cushing disease, including polyuria/
polydipsia, polyphagia, weight gain, potbellied appearance, thin skin, and alopecia. Despite the clinical findings
consistent with hyperadrenocorticism, these animals
test negative for hyperadrenocorticism by ­conventional
screening methods (ACTH stimulation, low‐dose dexamethasone suppression test). However, an assay for particular cortisol precursors (such as progesterone and
17‐OH‐progesterone) may reveal elevated concentrations.
Although this condition is classically related to the presence of an adrenal cortical tumor, cortisol precursors may
be noted with pituitary‐dependent disease as well. This is
considered eutopic hormone production as opposed to
ectopic, as the hormone produced by the tumor is a product of the tumor itself. However, as the particular hormone being produced is atypical for expected forms of
hyperadrenocorticism, it is worthy of mention.
In the presence of a cortical tumor, surgical excision is
generally recommended if presurgical staging allows.
Abdominal ultrasonography is particularly useful to
identify a tumor, local vascular invasion, and metastases.
Approximately 50% of adrenal cortical tumors are malignant, and presurgical screening may identify local
­vascular invasion, metastatic disease to distant organs
(particularly the liver), and irregularity of the affected

Clinical Small Animal Internal Medicine Volume II, First Edition. Edited by David S. Bruyette.
