gland. If surgery cannot be performed, clinical symptoms may be managed with trilostane (Vetoryl®) or op‐
DDD (Lysodren®). Trilostane is a competitive inhibitor of
3‐beta‐hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, thereby reducing
cortisol synthesis from the adrenal gland. The inhibition
of steroid production is rapidly reversible and dose
dependent. Effects on cortisol production will wane
within 10–20 hours after cessation of the drug. Lysodren
is directly cytotoxic to the cells of the zona fasciculata
and zona reticularis of the adrenal cortex. As approximately 50% of cortical adrenal tumors are malignant, op‐
DDD is the theoretical medical therapy of choice though
studies evaluating survival and disease‐free interval of
dogs with adrenocortical carcinoma treated with trilostane vs op‐DDD are lacking.
Management of symptoms may be made easier by the
use of trilostane, as the side‐effects are generally found to
be less severe. Lysodren may be difficult to administer in
a clinically ill animal, as it causes nonselective adrenal
cortical necrosis and could result in a relative hypoadrenocortical state. This could be difficult to manage in
the ill patient due to the length of time needed to recover
from excessive adrenal gland destruction. Trilostane,
however, will have no effect on delaying the progression
of metastatic disease.
Therefore, in the case of nonsurgical metastatic disease, Lysodren may be more effective at prolonging survival due to the cytotoxic effects on metastatic tissue.
Trilostane has been used successfully to control clinical
symptoms of Cushing disease caused by an adrenal
tumor in the absence of metastases. The use of trilostane
or op‐DDD for the medical management of an adrenal
tumor should be carefully considered by the clinician if
surgery is not feasible.

­Syndrome of Inappropriate
Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) is commonly discussed but rarely diagnosed in the small animal patient. Much more common
in human medicine, SIADH is frequently diagnosed in
patients with pulmonary cancer (oat cell carcinoma).
Excessive production of ADH by the tumor cells results
in inappropriate free water retention. This leads to one of
the hallmark signs of the disorder, hyponatremia. Due to
excessive volume expansion, many elements within the
blood may undergo dilutional effects, such as urea nitrogen and potassium. Serum osmolality is also low, but
urine osmolality may be higher than that of serum as free
water is being retained by the kidneys.

Diagnosis and Treatment
The finding of a urine osmolality higher than that of
serum in the face of hyponatremia is suggestive of
SIADH. Careful water restriction will improve clinical
symptoms while the cause is elucidated. Water restriction must be monitored closely to avoid rapid fluctuations in serum sodium concentrations. SIADH has been
described rarely with tumors in dogs (such as salivary
carcinoma). This condition is more common with systemic diseases, such as cholangiohepatitis, congenital
hydrocephalus, and meningitis. Therefore, water restriction could lead to dehydration if the patient is clinically
ill. With chronic hyponatremia, the serum sodium concentrations should not increase at a rate greater than
0.5 mEq/L/h or 8–10 mEq/day to avoid cerebral fluid
shifts. Due to the paucity of reports of this disease in the
veterinary literature, the prognosis is unpredictable and
dependent on the underlying condition.

­Erythrocytosis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Erythrocytosis is defined as an increase in red blood cell
parameters (hematocrit, red blood cell count, hemoglobin). It may also be referred to as polycythemia. This
condition may be classified as relative or absolute.
A relative polycythemia is an apparent increase in red
blood cell mass that is actually due to a decrease in
plasma volume. This is commonly noted with dehydration and may be treated with fluid therapy to offset the
reduction in plasma volume. A relative polycythemia
would be expected to be associated with normal (or low)
erythropoietin levels.
An absolute polycythemia may be subclassified as primary or secondary. Primary polycythemia is independent of erythropoietin influence and arises from
progenitor cells within the bone marrow. The expanded
red blood cell mass appears morphologically normal,
and bone marrow aspiration suggests erythroid hyperplasia. Primary polycythemia is classified as a myeloproliferative disease, and is often referred to as polycythemia
vera. It may rarely progress to leukemia.
An absolute polycythemia that is classified as secondary is dependent on erythropoietin influence. This may
be an appropriate response, as seen with altitude changes,
right‐to‐left cardiac shunting disorders and hereditary
methemoglobin reductase deficiency. An inappropriate
polycythemic response may be seen with certain tumors,
especially of the kidney.
These tumors may produce erythropoietin ectopically,
resulting in a paraneoplastic syndrome of erythrocytosis. Several other mechanisms have been proposed to

VetBooks.ir

131 Endocrine Manifestations of Cancer

explain the rise in hematocrit, including decreased
metabolism of erythropoietin and production of erythropoietin‐stimulating hormones. Renal hypoxia due to
thrombosis or tumor mass may also play a role. This condition is rarely reported with other tumors, but has been
described in a dog with cecal leiomyosarcoma.
Diagnosis and Treatment
Erythrocytosis may be approached first by physical
examination to assess hydration status, cardiac auscultation, abdominal palpation to screen for abdominal
masses, and complete blood count (CBC)/serum chemistry. If the examination and bloodwork suggest dehydration, a fluid therapy trial should result in resolution of
the polycythemia. If dehydration is not present, or if
fluid therapy does not result in resolution, an absolute
polycythemia is present.
In the absence of obvious causes of a secondary absolute polycythemia (including appropriate responses such
as right‐to‐left shunting disorders and altitude changes),
evaluation of serum erythropoietin levels will help to differentiate erythrocytosis secondary to a renal (or other)
tumor from polycythemia vera (absolute primary polycythemia). In the latter condition, the erythrocytosis is
independent of erythropoietin, and erythropoietin levels
may be low to normal. The diagnosis of primary erythrocytosis (polycythemia vera) is often performed by ruling
out all other causes of secondary absolute polycythemia,
as erythropoietin measurements are not often available
and the assay is not species specific. Bone marrow evaluation should be considered if an absolute primary erythrocytosis is suspected to rule out marrow neoplasia.
Erythrocytosis secondary to production of erythropoietin from a renal tumor or other neoplasm will demonstrate marked elevations of serum erythropoietin levels.
Abdominal radiology or, preferably, ultrasonography will
help to detect a neoplasm of the gastrointestinal tract or
renal system. Treatment for an absolute erythrocytosis
that arises as a manifestation of cancer involves identifying and removing the causative neoplasm (i.e., renal
tumor, cecal tumor, etc.). Removal of the tumor will
result in resolution of the polycythemia. Phlebotomy
may be necessary prior to surgery to relieve symptoms of
hyperviscosity and reduce risk for a vascular accident.
No more than 20 mL/kg of blood or 25% of blood volume
should be removed at a time. A more exact volume to be
removed may be calculated by the following formula:
Blood to be removed mL
body weight kg blood volume mL / kg
actualPCV desiredPCV
actualPCV

where PCV is packed cell volume. Blood volume for dogs
and cats is considered to be 90 and 70 mL/kg respectively.
If tumor removal is not feasible, periodic phlebotomy
may control signs of hyperviscosity. In the case of renal
tumors, surgical removal alone affects survival, and without surgical intervention the prognosis is poor. In one
study evaluating surgical intervention, median survival
for dogs with renal carcinoma was 16 months (range 0–59
months), for dogs with sarcomas nine months (range
0–70 months), and for dogs with nephroblastoma six
months (range 0–6 months). In the same study, dogs that
did not undergo surgery had a median survival of <1
month (range 0–32 months). Additionally, removal of a
renal tumor results in resolution of the paraneoplastic
polycythemia. For a dog with a reported cecal leiomyosarcoma, phlebotomy helped control clinical symptoms for
over two years. It is important to note that fluid replacement is not generally recommended post phlebotomy. In
the presence of right‐to‐left cardiac shunting disorders,
volume replacement may be poorly tolerated by the
­cardiovascular system. In the presence of polycythemia
vera, the animal is volume replete prior to phlebotomy.
Treatment for primary polycythemia or absolute secondary polycythemia related to an uncorrectable cause
(such as a right‐to‐left shunt) involves a combination of
phlebotomy and hydroxyurea, covered elsewhere.

­Zollinger–Ellison Syndrome
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Secretion of excessive gastrin by neoplastic delta cells of the
pancreas has been described (gastrinoma). Gastrin is also
produced by G cells of the gastric antrum and duodenum,
and continued secretion results in hyperacidity. Clinical
symptoms are related to excessive production of gastric
acid from the continued stimulation of gastric parietal cells.
The findings of melena with a microcytic, hypochromic
anemia should lead to suspicion for gastrointestinal hemorrhage. This may be accompanied by weight loss, anorexia, and/or vomiting. Dogs may present late in the course
of disease, and as such cancer cachexia may be present.
Additionally, gastric ulceration may be severe and may
­predispose to gastric perforation. Endoscopic evaluation
of the stomach may reveal an ulcer, which typically is
located along the lesser curvature. Although gastrinomas
tend to be slow growing, approximately 85% demonstrate
metastasis at the time of diagnosis.
Diagnosis
Diagnosis of a gastrinoma can be challenging. Serum
gastrin levels may be evaluated, and samples should be

1215

VetBooks.ir

1216

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

obtained prior to administration of gastroprotectants.
Antacids such as famotidine, ranitidine, and omeprazole
will artifactually raise serum gastrin levels. Abdominal
ultrasonography may identify a pancreatic mass, but as is
the case with insulinomas, gastrinomas are often too
small to detect. Ultrasonography can be useful to screen
for metastatic disease, due to the relatively high rate of
metastasis with this tumor. Radioactive scanning with
pentetreotide may be useful but has limited availability.
Surgical exploration with or without abdominal CT may
be necessary if presurgical screening does not identify a
mass or obvious metastatic disease. Histopathology is
required for an accurate diagnosis.
Treatment
Medical therapy alone may be employed if a patient is a
poor surgical candidate. Aggressive antacid therapy is
indicated. Often, the author will combine a proton pump
inhibitor (such as omeprazole) with an H2 blocker (such
as famotidine). In addition, sucralfate may be administered with antacids, preferably 30 minutes to an hour

apart. Sucralfate should be administered first, as it reacts
with hydrochloric acid to create a protective complex.
Administration of an antacid prior to sucralfate may
reduce its efficacy.
Motility modifiers may be necessary to control reflux
and vomiting. Metoclopramide should be used with caution if a stomach ulcer is present, as it may enhance the
potential for perforation. Centrally acting antiemetics,
such as ondansetron or maropitant, are preferred.
Finally, streptozocin has been advocated as adjunctive
chemotherapy to surgical intervention, but should be
used with caution due to its toxicity. The prognosis with
gastrinoma is typically guarded. Paraneoplastic effects,
such as gastric perforation and peritonitis, adversely
affect prognosis. However, with aggressive treatment,
including surgery, survival times have ranged from 4.5 to
18 months.
These above conditions are particular to ectopic
­hormone production resulting in endocrine manifestations. Further paraneoplastic syndromes are described
elsewhere in this text.

Paraneoplastic Syndromes
Cory Brown, DVM, DACVIM (SAIM)
VetScan Mobile Diagnostics, Powell, OH, USA

Many tumors produce effects on the body that are not
related to direct invasion or compression. These effects
have become widely recognized as paraneoplastic syndromes. Recognition and treatment of these conditions
may allow early detection of occult neoplasia, reduction
of morbidity, and prolonged survival. The effects of paraneoplastic syndromes are due to the production and
excretion of peptides and hormones as well as immune
cross‐reaction between tumor and normal cells. This
chapter describes the most commonly recognized
paraneoplastic syndromes and their treatment. It is
­
important to recognize that the most effective treatment for all paraneoplastic syndromes is removal of the
­underlying tumor.

­Hypercalcemia
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Hypercalcemia remains one of the most commonly
encountered paraneoplastic syndromes in the dog and
cat. Commonly termed “humoral hypercalcemia of
malignancy,” this condition must be differentiated from
other common causes of hypercalcemia. Although it is
often noted with lymphoma (particularly mediastinal
lymphoma), multiple myeloma and anal sac adenocarcinoma, it may be observed with a variety of tumors. The
most common mechanism resulting in hypercalcemia is
release of a peptide by the tumor cells closely resembling
parathyroid hormone (PTH), called parathyroid hormone‐related protein (PTH‐rp). PTH‐rp mimics the
activity of PTH by binding to PTH receptors within the
renal tubule and bone. This leads to decreased calcium
excretion from the kidney and increased bone resorption. Other factors involved in hypercalcemia not related
to humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy include direct

bone invasion resulting in increased osteolysis and
­production of osteoclast‐activating factor by tumor cells.
Diagnosis
Initial investigation should include a thorough physical
and rectal examination. Further diagnostic evaluation
should include thoracic radiographs and abdominal radiographs or ultrasonography. Ultrasonography is preferred to evaluate for diffuse infiltration of abdominal
organs as well as abdominal lymphadenomegaly, as these
may be difficult to appreciate radiographically. Aspiration
of peripheral lymph nodes may be useful, even when the
lymph nodes are not clinically enlarged. Bone marrow
aspiration may be considered, especially in the face of
peripheral cytopenias, and additional radiographs or
bone scintigraphy may be carried out based on the
­presence of lameness or discomfort encountered during
palpation of long bones. Confirmation of an elevated calcium secondary to malignancy may be attempted by
evaluating PTH, PTH‐rp, and ionized calcium levels in
the serum. It is important to note that the ionized
calcium level is increased in patients with humoral
­
hypercalcemia of malignancy, and this may be monitored for a more accurate assessment of bioactive calcium levels. Evaluation of PTH‐rp with ionized calcium
and PTH can also help differentiate humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy from other causes of hypercalcemia
(i.e., renal disease, hyperparathyroidism).
Treatment
Common symptoms of hypercalcemia include polyuria/
polydipsia, muscle tremors, neurologic abnormalities
(including coma), renal dysfunction, and inappetence.
Treatment is aimed at reducing the ionized calcium level

as cancer therapy is ongoing. Mildly elevated total calcium levels are generally left untreated as cancer therapy
is ongoing, but all treatment decisions should take into
account the patient’s neurologic and renal status. Total
calcium levels that approach or exceed 13.5 mg/dL may
benefit from saline diuresis and administration of a loop
diuretic such as furosemide. Furosemide should only be
administered in the volume‐replete patient. Therefore,
subcutaneous or intravenous saline administration may
be necessary if clinical dehydration is appreciated.
Glucocorticoids may reduce intestinal absorption of
­calcium but should only be used once a diagnosis is
obtained, as they are directly cytotoxic to lymphoma and
myeloma cells. Use of the drug prior to establishing
a diagnosis may preclude an accurate diagnosis or
require more invasive procedures to obtain an accurate
diagnosis.
Finally, total calcium levels that are markedly elevated
(>17 mg/dL) constitute a medical emergency and w
­ arrant
hospitalization for diuresis. Administration of calcitonin
may be attempted, although the effects are short‐lived.
Administration of calcitonin subcutaneously may be
considered for a longer acting effect. Bisphosphonates
(pamidronate and zoledronate) may be used for persistent hypercalcemia and bone pain. The author generally
prefers pamidronate given as an intravenous infusion
every 2–4 weeks. In select cases of lymphoma, a chemotherapy trial may be necessary if a diagnosis is elusive or
if patient status dictates rapid intervention as laboratory
tests are pending. This should be supported by clinical
suspicion and after exhaustion of all available diagnostic
methods. Serum should be drawn and saved prior to a
chemotherapeutic trial. The author prefers L‐asparaginase
when this approach is necessary.
In all cases, successful treatment of the underlying
neoplasm will result in resolution of the hypercalcemia,
and the prognosis is dependent on the tumor type and
stage. The decline in calcium can be rapid with successful treatment of lymphoma. Calcium levels may then be
used as an additional tool to monitor for recurrence of
the neoplasm.

­Hypoglycemia
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Hypoglycemia as a paraneoplastic syndrome may be
related to excessive production of insulin‐like substances,
direct consumption of glucose by tumor cells and
decreased gluconeogenesis due to hepatic parenchymal
involvement. Production of IGF‐2 (acting as an insulin‐
like substance) has been implicated as a source of hypoglycemia in nonpancreatic neoplasms. Paraneoplastic

hypoglycemia has been associated with tumors such as
lymphoma, hepatocellular carcinoma and leiomyosarcoma, as well as renal tumors, mammary carcinoma, oral
melanoma, multiple myeloma, splenic hemangiosarcoma, pulmonary carcinoma, and others. Glucose levels
may be severely and persistently decreased (20–40 mg/
dL) in many cases, and clinical symptoms are related
directly to the neurologic effects of the hypoglycemia
as well as the concurrent release of counterregulatory
­hormones such as catecholamines. Many times, the
symptoms of hypoglycemia are severe and may predate
the diagnosis of the causative tumor.
Common symptoms of paraneoplastic hypoglycemia
include ataxia, lethargy, weakness (polyneuropathy), nerv­ eurologic
ousness or collapse, hunger or anorexia, focal n
abnormalities, seizures, and/or coma.
Diagnosis
Discovery of a persistent hypoglycemia should lead to
investigation for underlying neoplasia. Other etiologies
of hypoglycemia, including hypoadrenocorticism, sepsis,
congenital and acquired hepatic disorders, insulinoma,
malnutrition and toxicity (such as xylitol), should also be
investigated. Serum insulin levels should be evaluated in
the face of hypoglycemia to assess for an insulin‐­
secreting neoplasm. Normal or elevated insulin levels in
the face of hypoglycemia is not a normal finding.
Secretion of an insulin‐like substance (such as IGF‐2)
will not be detected when measuring serum insulin levels. Therefore, insulin levels are most often useful in the
diagnosis of pancreatic beta‐cell neoplasia (insulinoma).
Insulin concentrations should be determined on the
same sample documenting hypoglycemia. Thoracic radiographs and abdominal ultrasonography are indicated to
screen for a pancreatic islet cell tumor as well as intestinal, hepatic, and round cell neoplasia. Abdominal radiographs may be able to identify large intestinal or hepatic
tumors. Often, islet cell neoplasms cannot be identified
via ultrasonography due to their small size. In these
instances, surgical exploration or contrast CT may be
required.
Treatment
Treatment of this paraneoplastic syndrome involves
controlling clinical symptoms of hypoglycemia as the
underlying neoplasm is addressed. Often, it is difficult to
obtain euglycemia in the face of extensive or metastatic
neoplasia. In this situation, controlling the clinical manifestations of hypoglycemia becomes more important.
Management strategies for neoplasia‐related hypoglycemia are covered elsewhere.

VetBooks.ir

132 Paraneoplastic Syndromes

­Anemia/Thrombocytopenia
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Anemia and thrombocytopenia can be grouped together
as hematologic paraneoplastic syndromes as they may
occur together due to a common pathophysiology.
Immune‐mediated destruction due to mimicry of cell
membrane‐associated receptors or other immune cross‐
reactions tends to be the most widely accepted etiology of
secondary immune‐mediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA)
and thrombocytopenia. Symptoms of anemia and thrombocytopenia are nonspecific to the cause and are covered
elsewhere.
Diagnosis
When anemia is considered individually, it must first
be determined to be regenerative or nonregenerative.
A nonregenerative anemia may suggest bone marrow
involvement, especially in conjunction with other cytopenias. Bone marrow disease must be differentiated
from an acute anemia in which a regenerative response
has not yet had time to develop. Typically, it will take an
average of 3–5 days to develop a moderate regenerative
response, depending on how suddenly the anemia developed and the degree of anemia. Additionally, clinical
signs of anemia tend to be more severe the more acute
the onset, as the body has time to adapt to a chronically
developing anemia.
A bone marrow biopsy and/or aspirate should be considered in the face of a chronic, nonregenerative anemia.
The author prefers to begin with a bone marrow aspirate.
If the aspirate is productive, a slide may be reviewed to
assess for cellularity. Bone marrow infiltration due to lymphoma or myeloma tends to be highly cellular, and assuming bone marrow elements are observed in a c­ellular
sample, an aspirate may suffice. If the aspirate is nonproductive (i.e., a “dry” tap), a bone marrow biopsy may be
obtained. A biopsy may be necessary to obtain a diagnosis
of myelofibrosis or other chronically progressive bone
marrow disorders. With these chronic ­conditions, bone
marrow elements are replaced by fibrosis and the aspirate
may be hemodilute or completely nonproductive.
As most animals present with a moderate to severe
anemia, these procedures are generally performed
shortly after a component blood transfusion to improve
the candidacy for anesthesia. It is important to remember that if a bone marrow aspirate or biopsy is deemed
necessary, it should be obtained before or within 12 hours
of beginning steroid therapy. Steroids, including prednisone and dexamethasone, are directly cytotoxic to
lymphoma and myeloma cells. These are two of the more
common cancers that may infiltrate the bone marrow.

Thrombocytopenia is not a contraindication to bone
marrow sampling, as the associated hemorrhage typically results in an autotransfusion into the marrow,
thereby remaining clinically silent. Prolonged external
pressure to the incision site within the skin may be necessary, however.
Classically, pancytopenia will develop with a leukopenia followed by thrombocytopenia. Anemia will develop
last due to the longer half‐life of red blood cells in relation to platelets and white blood cells. This may not be
the case in clinical practice, as multiple factors affect the
production and destruction of all bone marrow elements. It is not uncommon to encounter myelophthisis
in the face of thrombocytopenia alone, and any combination of cytopenias should raise suspicion for bone
­ arrow involvement.
m
If the anemia is determined to be regenerative, bone
marrow sampling is typically not necessary. Red blood
cell morphology may identify clues as to the source of the
anemia. A morphology review by an experienced pathologist or lab technician should be obtained. Specifically,
immune‐mediated disease may be confirmed by the
presence of a moderate to large amount of spherocytes.
Spherocytes are red blood cells that have undergone a
loss of membrane due to removal of antigen–antibody
complexes by the phagocytic portion of the immune system. This results in a loss of surface area with retention
of volume. The consequence of this is the red blood cell
changing its morphology from a biconcave disc to a
sphere, resulting in the term “spherocyte.” Immune‐
mediated hemolytic anemia may also be diagnosed by
identifying gross or microscopic autoagglutination. In
the absence of a significant number of spherocytes or
detectable autoagglutination, a Coombs test may be performed to identify an immune component to the anemia.
In the presence of visibly detectable autoagglutination, a
Coombs test is not necessary.
A schistocyte is a red blood cell fragment that may
develop due to shearing forces. These fragments do not
have a central pallor and are irregular. Schistocytes may be
noted in IMHA, but they are most commonly recognized
as a consequence of hemangiosarcoma. Red blood cells
may be damaged as they travel through the smaller blood
vessels and fibrin strands of the tumor, and as such
­schistocytes should prompt evaluation for an underlying
vascular neoplasm. Anemia due to damage to red blood
cells as they travel through the smaller capillary beds is
often termed microangiopathic anemia. Microangiopathic
anemia may be seen with any hypercoagulable disease,
and should also alert the clinician to the potential for
thrombosis. Fibrin strands and smaller blood clots may be
noted with hyperadrenocorticism, pancreatitis and other
nonneoplastic disorders, and these may all result in a
microangiopathic anemia.

1219

VetBooks.ir

1220

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

Anemia may result from nonparaneoplastic disorders,
such as gastrointestinal blood loss, iron sequestration,
and medication. Thrombocytopenia may also be present
due to increased utilization, poor bone marrow production and immune‐mediated destruction that is unrelated
to a neoplastic disorder. The presence of these hematologic disorders should prompt the evaluation of a paraneoplastic disease if the clinical history, signalment, and
physical examination are suggestive. As a paraneoplastic
syndrome, thrombocytopenia tends to develop due to
immune‐mediated destruction from mechanisms similar to the development of IMHA, or increased consumption due to large tumors such as hemangiosarcoma.
Treatment
Treatment of secondary IMHA and immune‐mediated
thrombocytopenia (ITP) is similar to that of primary
IMHA, with attention to dealing with the underlying
cause. Immune suppression with prednisone is indicated
once a diagnosis is established, and may be effective
at controlling the anemia as cancer therapy is ongoing.
A wide dose range is reported for these disorders (1–4 mg/
kg/day), and the author prefers 0.5–1 mg/kg of prednisone twice daily, or 0.3 mg/kg dexamethasone sodium
phosphate IV twice daily. A higher dose may be used if
steroids are to be employed as sole therapy. Antithrombotic
therapy may be initiated with low‐dose aspirin, unfractionated heparin or clopidrogel. It should be noted that
the use of low‐dose aspirin (0.5 mg/kg by mouth once
daily) in the dog is considered safe in conjunction with
immune suppressive doses of prednisone or dexamethasone. This is the author’s treatment of choice in the dog.
For cats, the author recommends one‐quarter of a 75 mg
tablet (18.75 mg) of clopidrogel by mouth once daily. The
use of heparin is considered more effective at preventing
thrombi, versus preventing the progression of a clot as
with aspirin. However, monitoring of heparin therapy is
difficult and often expensive. Heparin use should be considered if monitoring is a­ vailable and feasible. Component
blood therapy may be necessary with either disorder, and
should be tailored to the patient. Platelet transfusions
have typically been found to be ineffective at long‐term
management of ITP, but they may play a role in preventing active bleeding. This may be important if intracranial
hemorrhage is suspected.
Gastrointestinal hemorrhage may result in significant
and refractory anemia, especially in the face of thrombocytopenia. This is an unfortunate negative prognostic
indicator with ITP and should be differentiated from
gastrointestinal ulceration. In the latter scenario, gastroprotectants should be instituted, and any medication
that may result in ulceration should be reduced or
­discontinued if possible. The majority of gastric ulcers
will develop due to medication or neoplasia, so if the

clinical history does not identify an offending medication, cancer should become a primary differential. More
specific therapy for primary IMHA and ITP is covered
elsewhere.

­Hypertrophic Osteopathy
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Hypertrophic osteopathy (HO) is an uncommon paraneoplastic syndrome. The pathophysiology is unclear,
but afferent neurologic stimulation may alter blood flow
to long bones. This is supported by case reports demonstrating resolution of lesions following vagotomy. HO is
most commonly noted with pulmonary lesions including
heartworm disease, but has been reported with nonthoracic neoplasia as well, including transitional cell carcinoma and adrenocortical carcinoma. Typical findings
include periostosis and subperiosteal new bone formation along the shafts of long bones. This condition is
­frequently painful. Affected limbs may be warm and
swollen, and radiographs will typically demonstrate the
common features of the disorder. Finding radiographic
evidence of HO should prompt radiographic evaluation
of the thorax. Abdominal ultrasonography may be considered if pulmonary lesions are not identified.
Treatment and Prognosis
Treatment is directed at removal of the underlying neoplasm. Vagotomy has been described but is not typically
performed as the primary treatment is to address the
underlying etiology. If the neoplasm cannot be treated,
pain management must be addressed. Opiates, nonsteroidal medication, steroids, and bisphosphonates have been
used alone or in combination to control discomfort.
Localized palliative radiation has been described but is
not typically recommended due to lack of supportive
­evidence. If tumor removal is successful, HO lesions
may persist for several weeks and require continued
pain management during this time. The lesions should
resolve given time if a thoracic neoplasm is successfully
removed.

­Myasthenia Gravis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Myasthenia gravis is an immune‐mediated condition
that develops from production of antibodies to nicotinic
acetylcholine receptors located on the postsynaptic
neuromuscular junction. This prevents neurogenic
­
­signal transduction, leading to the hallmark signs of episodic weakness, exercise intolerance, megaesophagus,

VetBooks.ir

132 Paraneoplastic Syndromes

and regurgitation. Aspiration pneumonia is a common
complication of frequent regurgitation and may result in
respiratory symptoms. This paraneoplastic syndrome is
most commonly related to the presence of thymoma.
Myasthenia gravis may be focal, generalized or fulminant. As a paraneoplastic syndrome, a generalized form
is typically encountered. This type of myasthenia affects
skeletal muscle of the limbs, resulting in the aforementioned clinical signs. Ocular muscles may be affected,
resulting in a fatigue to repeated palpebral reflexes.
Myasthenia may be suspected based on clinical symptoms, and confirmed by evaluated serum levels of
anticholinergic receptor antibodies. Administration of
edrophonium chloride (“Tensilon test”) may provide
presumptive support for myasthenia gravis as serum
titers are pending. Both focal myasthenia and generalized myasthenia result in megaesophagus, which is easily
demonstrated radiographically.
Treatment
Treatment of thymoma can result in resolution of myasthenia, but at times the megaesophagus may be persistent. The reason for this is not known. Anticholinesterase
medication, such as oral pyridostigmine or injectable
neostigmine, may help ameliorate clinical symptoms. It
is important to note that injectable medication may be
necessary if severe megaesophagus with frequent regurgitation is present. Alternatively, many dogs may be
managed well with a supplemental gastrostomy tube.
This can allow delivery of medication and supplemental
nutrition into the stomach, thereby circumventing the
esophagus altogether. Gastrostomy tubes do not reduce
the overall frequency of regurgitation or the risk for aspiration pneumonia, however. Food should be delivered in
a standing position, and consistency of the food should
be experimented with. Some dogs will tolerate food in a
meatball, some as a slurry, and others in a gelatin. Use of
a Bailey chair, which encourages an upright position during feeding, may be considered as well. If possible, the
dog should be taken for a short walk after each feeding.

­Superficial Necrolytic Dermatitis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Superficial necrolytic dermatitis (SND, or hepatocutaneous syndrome) is a condition characterized by erythema,
alopecia, and crusts involving the eyes, nose/muzzle, and
extremities. A typical feature of this disorder is hyperkeratosis of the footpads with central necrosis affecting
one or multiple pads. Often, the footpads may be so
painful that the animal will refuse to walk. The disease
has been noted commonly with chronic hepatic disorders as well as chronic administration of large doses of

phenobarbital. As a paraneoplastic syndrome, SND may
be noted with glucagonoma. In the author’s experience,
chronic and fibrotic liver disease is the most common
disorder associated with SND.
Diagnosis
The finding of footpad hyperkeratosis with or without
concurrent clinical findings should prompt abdominal
ultrasonography to evaluate the pancreas and liver. An
experienced ultrasonographer should be used to evaluate the pancreas for a mass. The liver may have a typical
“Swiss cheese” appearance. A liver biopsy may be diagnostic but may need to be obtained via laparoscopy or
laparotomy due to hemorrhage risk. Animals with a
glucagonoma may have symptoms of diabetes, including
polyuria/polydipsia and weight loss (for further information refer to Chapter 144). A poor appetite is often
­associated with chronic liver disease. Measurement of
glucagon levels may be undertaken but the test is not
always available, and glucagon levels are not always elevated in the face of a glucagonoma. SND is often associated with a hypercatabolic state which may be manifested
with a hypoalbuminemia and/or hypoproteinemia. An
amino acid profile may reveal significant reductions in
serum amino acids, helping to confirm the diagnosis.
Skin biopsy may be characteristic if lesions are present.
Treatment
Treatment is aimed at the underlying cause. Surgical
resection of a glucagonoma is best if feasible. With
chronic liver disease or nonresectable neoplasia, administration of intravenous amino acids will often help skin
lesions to resolve. This may help to reduce discomfort.
10% Aminosyn® (or an equivalent solution) must be
administered via a central catheter and over 8–12 hours
due to its hypertonicity. It is typically administered
weekly until skin lesions resolve.
Skin and footpad lesions should be kept clean and dry.
A high‐protein diet may be prescribed with supplementation of egg whites or protein powder. Broad‐spectrum
antibiotics may be administered to control secondary
infections, and analgesics may be necessary if discomfort
is present. Zinc, omega‐3 fatty acids, and niacin have all
been suggested as adjunct therapies. These may be difficult to administer in the face of a poor appetite and are
considered supplemental therapy.

­Paraneoplastic Alopecia
Paraneoplastic alopecia is described in cats affected by
pancreatic carcinoma. It may occasionally be seen with
hepatic or biliary carcinomas, and is characterized by a

1221

VetBooks.ir

1222

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

noninflammatory alopecia. Hair may be epilated in
clumps, and the underlying skin is often thin and glistening. Affected areas may include the ventral abdomen,
thorax, limbs, pinnae, and periorbital region. The cause
is unknown, but theorized to be secondary to cytokine
production by the tumor resulting in follicular atrophy.
Most cats present systemically ill, as the skin lesions typically develop at a later stage of the disease process.
Metastases may be present within the liver and/or lungs,
and diagnosis may be achieved through imaging
(­
including abdominal ultrasound, abdominal/thoracic
CT, and/or thoracic radiographs) and appropriate tissue
sampling.

­Conclusion
Paraneoplastic syndromes are diverse in their presentation
and severity. In fact, many other paraneoplastic conditions
exist that are beyond the scope of this text. These include
thymoma‐related exfoliative dermatitis, peripheral neuropathies, nodular dermatofibrosis, and paraneoplastic
pemphigus. Other conditions, such as fever and cachexia,
are often considered paraneoplastic but are not specific or
unique in their presentation. Prompt identification and
treatment of these conditions will aid the clinician in additional diagnoses, maintain patient comfort, and prevent
life‐threatening sequelae as cancer therapy is ongoing.

Lymphoid Leukemias, Myeloid Neoplasia, and Myelodysplastic Syndrome
Angela R. Kozicki, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology)
Bluepearl Veterinary Partners, Southfield, MI, USA

­Lymphoid Leukemias
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Lymphoid leukemias are differentiated as either chronic
lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) or acute lymphoblastic leu­
kemia (ALL). CLL is a clonal, neoplastic proliferation of
small, mature‐looking lymphocytes that manifests as a
persistent, often severe lymphocytosis. Three subsets
have been recognized based on immunophenotyping.
The most common is granular T‐CLL which consists of
proliferations of cytotoxic (CD8+) T cells. Despite con­
ventional thinking that CLL is always a primary bone
marrow disease, granular T‐CLL is considered a primary
splenic disease which can be verified by expression of a
marker for splenic red pulp (CD11d). The second is B‐
CLL (CD21+, CD79a+) and the third is nongranular/
atypical T‐CLL (CD3+) in which no consistent pattern of
concurrent CD4 or CD8 expression is found. ALL is
defined by proliferation of immature lymphoblasts in the
bone marrow or peripheral blood. The immunopheno­
type of ALL is typically B cell (CD21+, CD3‐, CD4‐,
CD8‐) with an acute, immature lineage based on expres­
sion of CD34, a stem cell marker.
Classification of lymphocytes involves assessment of
cell surface antigen (marker) expression that pertains to
both lineage and function. This classification is usually
performed by immunophenotyping. Immunophenotyping
consists of the application of a­ ntibodies specific for dif­
ferentiation antigens of lymphocytes and other immune
cells to identify lineages of these cells present in neoplas­
tic or reactive diseases. Immunophenotyping can be per­
formed on cytology smears, blood smears, fluids (blood
or bone marrow), formalin‐fixed paraffin sections or
snap‐frozen tissue sections. Immunophenotyping tests
include immunohistochemistry (on tissue samples),
immunocytochemistry (on cytologic or fluid samples),

and flow cytometry in which cell suspensions are stained
with specific fluorochromes, analyzed by a focused laser
beam and sorted by size and DNA content (ploidy of
cells). Immunophenotyping can identify the presence of
different blood cell lineages but cannot predict clonality
(whether a population arises from a single cell).
It is important to know normal percentages of lym­
phocyte subsets found in the peripheral blood of dogs
and cats to be able to distinguish a benign or reactive
process from a malignant one. In general, peripheral
lymphocytes of dogs consist of ~80% T cells (CD3+ or
CD5+) with 45% being helper T cells (CD4+), 25% being
cytotoxic T cells (CD8+) and the remainder being dou­
ble‐negative T cells (CD4‐, CD8‐). Approximately 15%
are B lymphocytes (CD21+) and the remaining lympho­
cytes are natural killer (NK) cells. Cats are very similar
but have slightly fewer T cells (~75%) and a greater per­
centage of B cells (~25%) in the peripheral blood.
The etiology of lymphoid leukemias is largely
unknown. In people, there is no known association with
radiation, chemicals or alkylating agents and no viral
cause. Genetic factors are suspected in both humans and
dogs but immunophenotype of the neoplastic cells in
these species is different in that most human lymphoid
leukemias are B cell in origin. Therefore, it is unwise to
try to make direct correlations between species since dif­
ferent causative factors may be involved. In cats, retrovi­
ruses such as feline leukemia virus (FeLV) play a role
since ~60–80% of cats with ALL are FeLV+. There is no
known association between FeLV and CLL in cats and no
evidence of a retroviral cause in dogs.
Epidemiology
In people, CLL is an indolent disease of older adults (>60
years of age) and accounts for 25–30% of all adult leuke­
mias among white populations in North America and

Western Europe. Ninety‐five percent of CLL in people
are B cell in origin. ALL is most common in young
­children (peak between 2 and 5 years) with a second peak
in aged populations and is most commonly B cell. The
true incidence of lymphocytic leukemias in animals is
unknown. CLL is thought to be less common than ALL
but more common than myeloproliferative disorders.
Signalment
In the dog, both ALL and CLL are most commonly seen
in middle‐aged to older animals with a median age of 10
years. No sex predilection has been found. Golden
retrievers and German shepherds are overrepresented in
CLL. CLL is rare in cats but seems to occur in elderly
cats with a mean age of 14 years. Cats with ALL are usu­
ally young and FeLV positive.
History and Clinical Signs
Most CLL animals are asymptomatic and the diagnosis is
incidental. When clinical signs are present, they are gen­
erally attributable to the degree of lymphocytosis, bone
marrow involvement or other organ involvement and
may include lethargy, inappetence, and weight loss.
Physical exam may show hepatosplenomegaly and mildly
enlarged peripheral lymph nodes. Clinical signs of ALL
patients are similar to CLL although they are typically
more severe. On physical exam, splenomegaly is the
most common finding but hepatomegaly and lymphad­
enopathy can also be present. Signs of life‐threatening
cytopenias such as pale mucous membranes, pyrexia,
and/or petechial hemorrhages are also possible.
Diagnosis
Diagnosis of CLL is commonly made by examination of
the peripheral blood and bone marrow by a clinical
pathologist. A complete blood count (CBC) generally
reveals an absolute mild to marked lymphocytosis (6000
to >100 000 lymphocytes/μL) and cytologically the nuclei
appear small and mature with condensed chromatin
(Figure 133.1).
Other common hematologic findings include a mild
normochromic, normocytic, nonregenerative anemia, a
mild thrombocytopenia (>100 000/μL), and rarely neu­
tropenia. The hematologic abnormalities associated with
feline CLL have not been well characterized although
they are thought to be similar to dogs. A monoclonal
gammopathy or hyperglobulinemia in cats has been
reported but is uncommon since most CLL are T cell in
origin. Bone marrow aspirates show a significant prolif­
eration of small mature lymphocytes (usually >30%)
except in granular T‐CLL which demonstrates a

Figure 133.1 Photomicrograph of lymphocytes in the peripheral
blood of a dog that has CLL. The lymphoid morphology is
predominantly small and well differentiated. Wright Giemsa stain,
1000× magnification. Source: Courtesy of Dr Jan Andrews, Antech
Diagnostics.

marked splenic proliferation or infiltration of granular
­lymphocytes with minimal bone marrow involvement.
Other staging tests commonly recommended include
thoracic radiographs, abdominal ultrasound, and subse­
quent aspirate and cytology of any enlarged organ.
Immunophenotyping of blood, bone marrow or cytology
samples generally reveals the presence of a T cell lym­
phocyte population with no evidence of CD34 expression
(early hematopoietic stem cell marker), confirming the
maturity of the lymphocytes in question. The presence of
30% or more lymphoblasts in the bone marrow is consid­
ered diagnostic for ALL. Lymphoblasts are ­intermediate‐
to‐large sized lymphocytes with moderate amounts of
basophilic cytoplasm. Lymphoblasts are larger than neu­
trophils, have a condensed nuclear ­chromatin pattern,
and have a high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio (Figure 133.2).
Staging tests recommended for ALL are similar to
CLL; however, one of the principal goals is to differenti­
ate ALL from stage V lymphoma by degree of blood and
bone marrow involvement, lack of significant lymphade­
nopathy and, most importantly, its immunophenotypic
characteristics. Patients with stage V lymphoma can have
a better prognosis since their disease does not ­originate
in the bone marrow. Immunophenotyping, especially
flow cytometry, can be very useful in these cases
because ALL patients will be CD34+, confirming an early
­hematopoietic origin. Both stage V ­lymphoma and CLL
patients will be negative for this marker.

nonresponsive patients. Treatment of ALL requires
aggressive chemotherapy; CHOP‐based therapies like
those used in lymphoma are the most common proto­
cols. Remission rates of 25% have been reported but
remission times tend to be short.
Prognosis

Other causes of a lymphocytosis (chronic ehrlichiosis,
Rocky Mountain spotted fever, and severe babesiosis in
dogs; feline immunodeficiency virus [FIV], Toxoplasma
gondii, and chronic inflammatory bowel disease in cats)
should be ruled out if lymphocytic leukemia is not an
obvious conclusion.
Therapy
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia can have a protracted
clinical course and treatment is not usually instituted
until specific criteria are met: the presence of periph­
eral cytopenias (anemia, thrombocytopenia and/or
­neutropenia), clinical signs associated with the disease,
­peripheral lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, and/or a
peripheral lymphocytosis of >60 000 (although this is not
standardized). The standard treatment for CLL is a com­
bination of the oral alkylating agent chlorambucil and
prednisone. The dose and frequency of chlorambucil can
vary. In dogs it is typically given orally at 0.2 mg/kg or
6 mg/m2 orally once daily for 7–14 days, then reduced to
0.1 mg/kg or 3 mg/m2 every other day thereafter. In cats,
2 mg/cat every 48 hours is commonly used. Oral pred­
nisone is used concurrently with chlorambucil at 1 mg/kg
daily for 1–2 weeks, then 0.5 mg/kg every other day
thereafter. In cats, 10 mg/cat every 24 hours is commonly
used. The addition of vincristine or the substitution of
cyclophosphamide for chlorambucil has been used in

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a slowly progressive
disease and many patients are monitored for months
before any therapy is instituted. Remission rates with
treatment are ~70–75% with overall survival times of >1
year. Immunophenotype has been shown to be predic­
tive with survival times for dogs with granular T‐CLL,
B‐CLL, and atypical CLL of 930, 480, and 22 days respec­
tively. Although the prognosis is good in the short term,
ultimately, CLL patients can experience an acute blast
crisis in which lymphoblasts replace mature lympho­
cytes (ALL) and response to aggressive treatment is poor.
Prognosis for dogs and cats with ALL is very poor.
Median survival times of 3–128 days have been reported
in ALL dogs with a CD34+ phenotype treated with
CHOP‐based treatment protocols.
Hematopoietic peripheral blood stem cell transplanta­
tion (HSCT) is presently a viable treatment option
for dogs with leukemias. Although not widely available,
improved survival and cure are possible with this
ad­v anced form of therapy.

­Myeloid Neoplasia
Myeloid neoplasms arise from clonally proliferating cells
in the bone marrow and manifest as either accumulation
of neoplastic cells in the blood or lack of normal blood
cells. Myeloid neoplasms are divided into acute myeloid
leukemia (AML) and myeloproliferative neoplasms
(MPNs) which include chronic myelogenous leukemia
(CML), polycythemia vera (PV), basophilic/eosinophilic
leukemia, and essential thrombocytosis. (Box 133.1).
Acute Myeloid Leukemia
Etiology/Pathophysiology

Acute myeloid leukemia is defined by an abnormal pro­
liferation of clonal cells in the bone marrow and periph­
eral blood that arise from a single immature blast cell.
AML is divided into several subcategories based on
the Animal Leukemia Study Group’s 1991 proposal
which was modeled after the human leukemia French‐
American‐British (FAB) Cooperative Group classifica­
tions (see Box 133.1). In this system, myeloid leukemias
are divided into phenotypic subtypes based on morphol­
ogy and cytochemistry profiling using an alphanumeric

code of M‐#, with the M standing for myeloid. The most
commonly reported forms in the dog are acute myelo­
blastic leukemia (M1 and M2) and acute myelomo­
nocytic leukemia (M4). Monocytic leukemia (M5),
erythroleukemia (M6), and megakaryoblastic leukemia
(M7) are also recognized in dogs but promyelocytic leu­
kemia (M3) has not been reported.
In dogs, the etiology of AML along with the other mye­
loid neoplasms is unknown. Genetic and environmental
factors such as exposure to radiation, drugs or toxic
chemicals are thought to play a role. Defining genetic
factors in dogs is difficult because canine karyotyping is

an arduous process due to the large number and mor­
phologic similarities of chromosomes and their resist­
ance to banding. Recently, however, advancements in
molecular cytogenetic analysis have aided in the discov­
ery of canine chromosomal abnormalities that are simi­
lar to human AML which may serve not only as diagnostic
and prognostic factors but also as therapeutic targets.
Epidemiology

A lack of veterinary studies examining myeloid neoplasms
has led to a deficiency of uniform diagnostic criteria,
nomenclature, and ultimately accurate diagnosis. Because
of this, correct information regarding incidence and other
epidemiologic information cannot be verified until a
more uniform classification system is standardized.
Signalment

Acute myeloid leukemia is rare with a variable patient
age at diagnosis. Males are more commonly affected
than females and large‐breed dogs seem to be predis­
posed. Retrospective studies suggest an increased inci­
dence in German shepherds, golden retrievers, and
Labrador retrievers. Small‐breed dogs have been
­represented in single‐case reports. The majority of feline
AML patients are FeLV positive.
History and Clinical Signs

The clinical course of AML is rapid. Common clinical
signs include extreme lethargy, secondary infection, and
hemorrhage. Hematologic abnormalities can be severe
with a WBC count as high as 150,000 μ/L. Anemia, neu­
tropenia, and thrombocytopenia are also common.
Spleen, lymph nodes, and liver are frequently involved
but other sites such as heart, kidney or central nervous
system (CNS) may be infiltrated as well.
Diagnosis

It is important to understand that AML is a disorder
resulting from uncontrolled proliferation or decreased
apoptosis of cells incapable of maturation, leading to the
accumulation of poorly differentiated or “blast” cells.
This is different from other myeloid neoplasms which
result from unregulated proliferation of cells that exhibit
incomplete/defective maturation, leading to the accu­
mulation of well differentiated cells. The diagnosis of
AML is generally made by evaluation of peripheral blood
or bone marrow. Confirmation of AML should include
consistent hematologic and morphologic criteria,
­p ositive ­staining for myeloperoxidase which is a heme
protein synthesized during myeloid differentiation that
constitutes the major component of neutrophil azuro­
philic granules, a consistent pattern of beta‐2 integrin
expression and absence of lymphoid antigens by immu­
nocytochemistry or flow cytometry (Figure 133.3).

133 Lymphoid Leukemias, Myeloid Neoplasia, and Myelodysplastic Syndrome

VetBooks.ir

progression of the malignancy, treatment is often limited
to palliative cytoreductive chemotherapy with such
drugs as cytosine arabinoside, doxorubicin, vincristine,
and cyclophosphamide. Intensive supportive care is
commonly necessary and may include blood and/or
platelet‐rich plasma infusion along with aggressive anti­
biotic therapy for infection.
Prognosis

largely unrewarding due to inadequate or short‐term
responses. As with other forms of leukemia, HSCT is
becoming a viable treatment option for dogs with leuke­

The prognosis for AML is considered poor. In one study
of 16 dogs with confirmed AML, median and mean sur­

with a range of 2–138 days. Most of the dogs in the study
were treated with chemotherapy. However, protocols
were not consistent and some dogs were euthanized
before any treatment could be instituted due to rapidly
progressive clinical signs. There is one case report of a
dog with megakaryoblastic leukemia that demonstrated
a lengthy survival of 24 months with treatment so all
AML is not necessarily rapidly fatal. For some dogs,
HSCT may be feasible. For those animals, HSCT offers
the possibility of prolonged survival and cure.
Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) are defined as
overproduction of differentiated bone marrow cells which
results in the accumulation of the affected cell (granulo­
cytes and/or monocytes, erythrocytes or platelets).
Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia
Etiology/Pathophysiology

Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) in dogs is charac­
terized by a neoplastic proliferation of the neutrophil
series and is more similar to human chronic neutrophilic
leukemia than human CML. Human CML is associated
with the proliferation of several hematopoietic cell line­
ages due to the presence of a BCR‐ABL translocation
(Philadelphia chromosome) between chromosomes 9
and 22. The regions of human chromosomes 9 and 22 are
evolutionarily related to regions on canine chromosomes
9 and 26 and a canine equivalent to the BCR‐ABL muta­
tion (Raleigh chromosome) has been identified in three
cases of canine CML. The etiology of most canine and
feline CML is unknown.
Signalment

There is no known age, sex, or breed predilection in
canine CML. FeLV infection has been associated with
CML in cats.
History/Clinical Signs

Many patients have no clinical signs until significant
organ infiltration or myelophthisis of the bone marrow

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

occurs. If clinical signs are present, they are often non­
specific and may include lethargy, inappetence, organo­
megaly, pale mucous membranes, and hemorrhage
caused by severe thrombocytopenia.

Signalment

Diagnosis

The majority of clinical signs occur secondary to hyper­
viscosity syndrome which is the sludging of blood due to
increased red blood cell mass. These signs may include
hemorrhage, exercise intolerance, neurologic signs such
as seizures or ataxia, splenomegaly, hyperemic mucous
membranes, injected sclera/retinal vessels, and weak­
ness. Cardiac or renal disease may also occur.

At diagnosis, the peripheral white blood cell count
(WBC) count is commonly >100 000/μL. Neutrophils
and neutrophilic precursors accumulate in bone mar­
row, peripheral blood and other organs such as the
spleen, liver, and lymph nodes. Eosinophils and baso­
phils may also be increased. CML must be distinguished
from a leukemoid reaction caused by inflammation,
immune‐mediated diseases, and/or a paraneoplastic
syndrome. Staging tests such as three‐view thoracic radi­
ographs, abdominal ultrasound, and bone marrow cytol­
ogy can be helpful in making this distinction. Biopsy of
the liver or spleen may also be helpful in distinguishing
CML from a leukemoid reaction due to its invasiveness.
Therapy

Treatment of CML consists of the chemotherapy agent
hydroxyurea at 20–25 mg/kg PO twice daily until the leu­
kocyte count drops to 15 000–20 000 cells/μL. The dos­
age of hydroxyurea can then be reduced by 50% on a
daily basis or to 50 mg/kg given biweekly or triweekly.
Prognosis

Although responders can be managed for several months
with chemotherapy, most CML patients will enter a ter­
minal phase of their disease. HSCT offers the only pos­
sibility of cure for dogs but may not be feasible or
practical. Death is either due to infection or hemorrhage
caused by neutrophil dysfunction and thrombocytopenia
or secondary to a “blast crisis.” Response rates in patients
in a blast crisis are low and the prognosis is very poor.
It is unknown whether the subset of canine CML patients
that have a BCR‐ABL chromosome will respond to
BCR‐ABL kinase inhibitors which have become the
standard of care for human CML patients.
Polycythemia Vera
Etiology/Pathophysiology

Polycythemia vera (PV) is a clonal disorder of erythroid
precursors in the bone marrow, which leads to the over­
production of red blood cells independent of erythropoi­
etin. PV is rare in the dog and must be differentiated
from more common causes of polycythemia such as rela­
tive polycythemia which is a result of hemoconcentra­
tion or secondary polycythemia which is driven by
erythropoietin. Conditions associated with secondary
polycythemia include chronic pulmonary disease, con­
gestive heart failure, renal disease, renal neoplasia, and/
or right‐to‐left cardiac shunts.

Polycythemia vera generally affects middle‐aged dogs
and cats with no breed or sex predilection.
History and Clinical Signs

Diagnosis

Recommended diagnostic tests to rule out relative or
secondary polycythemia include thoracic radiographs,
abdominal ultrasound, bone marrow aspiration, arterial
blood gas measurements, and serum EP levels if possible.
The diagnosis of PV is made by the demonstration of sig­
nificant erythrocytosis (hematocrit of 60–75%) with
normal to decreased serum EP levels. Bone marrow
cytology in PV is consistent with erythroid hyperplasia
with normal patterns of maturation.
Therapy

Treatment of PV consists of decreasing the red blood cell
(RBC) volume and, ideally, suppression of erythroid pro­
duction in the bone marrow. Phlebotomy with reinfusion
of the patient’s plasma after removal of the RBCs or
administering colloid and crystalloid solutions to replace
lost electrolytes is recommended. The PCV should be
reduced to 50–60% or by one‐sixth of its starting value
(15–20 mL/kg body weight can be removed at one time).
The drug of choice to suppress erythroid production is
hydroxyurea which works by inhibiting DNA synthesis.
Hydroxyurea is instituted at 20–25 mg/kg PO given twice
daily in dogs (10–15 mg/kg in cats orally once daily).
Once the hematocrit is below 60%, hydroxyurea is main­
tained at every other day dosing with the goal of main­
taining a normal or close to normal packed cell volume
(PCV).
Prognosis

The prognosis of PV is good with a high response rate
and survival times of longer than a year for responders.
Basophilic and Eosinophilic Leukemia
and Essential Thrombocythemia
Etiology/Pathophysiology

Basophilic leukemia has rarely been reported in dogs and
is diagnosed by an increased WBC count with a high
proportion of basophils in bone marrow and/or periph­
eral blood. The etiology is unknown. It is unclear whether
dogs and cats develop eosinophilic leukemia. At this

VetBooks.ir

133 Lymphoid Leukemias, Myeloid Neoplasia, and Myelodysplastic Syndrome

time, due to lack of useful clonality assays, eosinophilic
leukemia and hypereosinophilic syndrome are difficult
to differentiate. Essential thrombocythemia has been
described in the dog and is characterized by persistent
thrombocytosis of >600 000/μL without evidence of cir­
culating blast cells.
Signalment

There is no known age, breed, or sex predilection in any
of these disorders.
History and Clinical Signs

A history of lethargy, inappetence, and/or weight loss is
common with any of the myeloid neoplasms. Clinical
signs are generally vague and may include fever, pale
mucous membranes, petechiation, hepatosplenomegaly,
and lymphadenopathy.
Diagnosis

Basophilic leukemia must be differentiated from masto­
cytosis based on morphology. Although these cells are
usually easily distinguished from each other, changes in
morphology of the nucleus and granules in basophilic
leukemia can make this distinction more difficult.
Infiltration into other organs is possible, including the
liver, spleen and lymph nodes, so evaluation of these
organs by abdominal ultrasound and/or cytology can
aid in the diagnosis. To make a diagnosis of eosinophilic
leukemia, disorders associated with eosinophilia such
as skin diseases, respiratory, and/or gastrointestinal
tract diseases and parasitism need to be ruled out before
considering a neoplastic leukemic etiology. Dogs with
essential thrombocythemia can present with hepatos­
plenomegaly, nonregenerative anemia, and neutro­
philia. On examination of bone marrow, megakaryocytic
hyperplasia is the most common feature. Diseases that
are known to cause secondary thrombocytosis such
as chronic inflammatory diseases, rebound from
severe hemorrhage and iron deficiency anemia need
to be ruled out before making a diagnosis of essential
thrombocythemia.
Treatment/Prognosis

Treatment for basophilic leukemia with hydroxyurea has
provided complete or partial remissions for several
months in case reports. The effective treatment of eosin­
ophilic leukemia is unknown but in one case report,
treatment with corticosteroids was effective. Information
on treatment for essential thrombocythemia is lacking
but in one case report, a dog was successfully treated
with a chemotherapy protocol consisting of vincristine,
cyclophosphamide, Ara‐C, and prednisone. As with all
forms of leukemia, HSCT can be considered for suitable
dogs if feasible.

­Myelodysplastic Syndromes
Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are a heterogeneous
group of acquired alterations of hematopoietic stem cells
that have been described in humans, dogs, and cats.
MDS can be primary or secondary/acquired. Primary
MDS result from clonal expansion of a defective pluripo­
tent stem cell and therefore are considered neoplastic.
Some refer to myelodysplasia as preleukemia since it can
progress to acute leukemia in some cases.
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Several different aberrations can result from a dysfunc­
tional hematopoietic system constituting MDS. In dogs,
there are usually cytopenias in 2–3 cell lines in the
peripheral blood due to cell death caused by ineffective
hematopoiesis. Other blood abnormalities may include
dysplastic changes in several cell lines, metarubricytosis,
and macrocytic erythrocytes. The bone marrow is usu­
ally normocellular or hypercellular. Blast cells in bone
marrow make up <30% of all nucleated cells but in peo­
ple this threshold has been changed to <20%.
Three subtypes of primary MDS have been proposed
for dogs and cats: MDS with excessive blasts (MDS‐EB),
in which blast percentages are >5% and less than 20%,
MDS with refractory cytopenia (MDS‐RC) with blast
percentages <5% and cytopenias in one or more
lineages, and MDS with erythroid predominance
­
(MDS‐ER) in which the myeloid:erythroid (M:E) ratio is
<1. Cases of canine secondary MDS consistently have
<5% myeloblasts in the bone marrow. Secondary MDS
in dogs has been associated with several conditions
including myelofibrosis, neoplasia (lymphoma and
multiple myeloma), immune‐mediated thrombocyto­
penia, immune‐mediated hemolytic anemia, drugs, and
ionizing radiation. In cats, secondary MDS can be
­associated with FeLV.
Epidemiology
Genetic abnormalities in hematopoietic cells such as
mutations in oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes
along with chromosomal deletions have been discovered
in human MDS patients and are thought to play a role in
veterinary patients.
Signalment
MDS‐EB is the most common type of primary MDS and
occurs most frequently in middle‐aged to older dogs.
Both MDS‐RC and MDS‐ER occur in older dogs. No
breed or sex predilection is known in any of the
subtypes.

VetBooks.ir

1230

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

History and Clinical Signs
The clinical signs of both MDS‐RC and MDS‐ER are
vague and commonly include lethargy and exercise intol­
erance. Physical exam generally reveals pale mucous
membranes and an anemia‐related heart murmur.
Clinical signs of MDS‐EB tend to be more severe and
include depression, anorexia, fever, and diarrhea. These
patients commonly have a history of illness that pro­
gresses over several months.
Diagnosis
Evaluation of blood and/or bone marrow is needed for
diagnosis of MDS. Because primary and secondary MDS
cannot be consistently differentiated cytologically, a
diagnosis of primary MDS should be made only if sec­
ondary causes have been ruled out. The most common
hematologic abnormalities in MDS‐RC and MDS‐ER are
nonregenerative anemias without any evidence of throm­
bocytopenia or leukopenia. MDS‐ER differs from MDS‐
RC by characterization of marked erythroid hyperplasia
and the presence of >5% rubriblasts in the bone marrow.
Patients with MDS‐EB have moderate to severe nonre­
generative anemia with evidence of neutropenia and
thrombocytopenia. Dysplastic features in all cell lines

are commonly found and a hallmark feature of MDS‐EB
is the presence of increased numbers of myeloblasts
(between 5% and 20% of total nucleated erythroid and
myeloid cells).
Therapy/Prognosis
There is no standard treatment for primary MDS. In
humans, patients commonly receive no treatment
because they often do not have clinical signs. Supportive
care such as blood transfusions and antibiotics for infec­
tions is used as necessary. Growth factors can also be
used. In one case report of a dog with MDS‐ER, human
recombinant erythropoietin was used to treat profound
anemia to promote terminal differentiation of dysplastic
erythrocytes. The hematocrit increased and that patient
remained in remission for >30 months. Dogs with MDS‐
RC and MDS‐ER can have prolonged survivals when
treated with chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide or cyto­
sine arabinoside is most common) and supportive care.
Patients with MDS‐EB can progress to AML and treat­
ment has been less rewarding, with survival times of days
to months. For suitable dogs, allogeneic HSCT can be
considered. The treatment and prognosis of secondary/
acquired MDS are dependent on the underlying cause.

Lymphomas
Kristine Elaine Burgess, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology)

­Canine Lymphoma
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Canine lymphoma is one of the most commonly encoun­
tered neoplasms in the dog and is most analogous to
non‐Hodgkin lymphoma in people. It includes multiple
disorders of the lymphoid system, which are character­
ized by a monoclonal expansion of lymphoid cells. The
etiology of lymphoma is currently unknown and is likely
to be multifactorial.
Recent advances in molecular cytogenetics have dem­
onstrated various chromosomal aberrations associated
with diagnosis and prognosis in canine lymphoma.
These results, while in the early phase of research, are
similar to those seen in human non‐Hodgkin lymphoma
with dysregulation of certain molecular pathways.

Epidemiology
The incidence of canine lymphoma has steadily increased,
with approximately 84 per 10 000 dogs diagnosed each
year. Certain breeds are considered to have a higher
overall lifetime risk of developing lymphoma, suggesting
a heritable genetic component. These include boxers,
golden retrievers, basset hounds, and bulldogs. Likewise,
certain breeds of dogs are considered to be at much lower
risk, including dachshunds and Pomeranians.
Signalment
Average age at diagnosis is between 5 and 10 years old
with no apparent sex predilection.
History and Clinical Signs

Clinical presentation of multicentric lymphoma is highly
variable and will depend on the anatomic location

The most common presentation is that of an asymp­
tomatic dog with nonpainful but markedly enlarged
peripheral lymph nodes which would be classified as
stage III, substage a (see Table 134.1).
In general, dogs with stage V lymphoma will present
with clinical signs related to the anatomic location of the
disease. For example, dogs with bone marrow infiltration
may present with cytopenias, fever, sepsis or hemor­
rhage. Dogs with marked pulmonary involvement may
present in respiratory distress.
As lymphoma has the potential to cause a wide array of
clinical syndromes, it should be considered as a potential
cause of any unexplained disorder in high‐risk breeds
until proven otherwise.
Diagnosis/Clinical Staging
A diagnosis of canine lymphoma can be achieved via fine
needle aspiration (FNA) and cytologic evaluation of
an enlarged peripheral lymph node or tumor tissue.
Cytology supportive of lymphoma will demonstrate a
population of large or intermediate‐sized lymphocytes
comprising the majority (>50%) of cells. Small cell lym­
phoma is an exception, as it may not appear cytologically
malignant.

It is important to note that the presence of an inflam­
matory process within enlarged lymph nodes may con­
found a diagnosis since reactive lymphoid hyperplasia
can be difficult to distinguish from lymphoma. This
occurs commonly in the mandibular lymph nodes (due
to dental disease or ear infections), and evaluation of
these nodes should be avoided if possible.
A definitive diagnosis of lymphoma may require
­further analysis to determine if a clonal population of
lymphocytes is present. This can be accomplished via
polymerase chain reaction‐based assay evaluating anti­
gen receptor rearrangements (PARR). The presence of a
clonally expanded population of cells strongly supports a
diagnosis of lymphoma as it is uncommon in a reactive
­process. It should be noted, however, that this test can
result in a high percentage (upwards to 25%) of false neg­
atives. An alternative to PARR is a diagnostic test called
flow cytometry. This assay relies on monoclonal anti­
bodies and fluorescent markers to help confirm a diag­
nosis of lymphoma by evaluating for aberrancies and
determining the phenotype of leukocytes within a fresh
sample of blood or tissue (e.g., lymph node, effusions).
Because flow cytometry requires living cells to complete
the assay, an abundance of dead or dying cells will
­confound a definitive result.
Ideally, cytology should be used as a first‐line test fol­
lowed by confirmation with histology. A biopsy of lymph
node or other affected tissue can be obtained surgically
or via needle core biopsy. An excisional biopsy is pre­
ferred, as it allows for a more thorough classification of
the type of lymphoma by preserving the architecture of
the affected tissue. Biopsy samples also provide adequate
tissue to perform immunohistochemical phenotyping
for prognostic information by distinguishing between B
and T cell forms.
Histologic Classification

Lymphomas are a complex group of diseases that vary
clinically from indolent to aggressive, and from poorly
controlled to manageable with treatment.
Indolent forms of lymphoma are uncommon and
poorly understood. These low‐grade forms of lymphoma
are relatively slow growing and are associated with long
survival times with limited or no therapy. Examples
include marginal zone lymphoma, follicular lymphoma,
B or T cell small cell lymphoma, and T zone lymphoma.
The majority of dogs have a multicentric intermediate
or high‐grade variety, with diffuse large lymphoblastic B
cell being the most common. While higher‐grade lym­
phomas tend to be more responsive to chemotherapy,
the duration of tumor control is short when compared to
animals with low‐grade lymphoma, in which long sur­
vival is often achieved with minimal to no treatment.

VetBooks.ir

134 Lymphomas

Immunophenotype

Immunophenotyping is commonly used to distinguish
the population of lymphoid cells that make up the tumor.
Cell surface markers, such as CD3 and CD79a, aid in
­differentiating T cell from B cell lymphomas. It is well
established that dogs with a B cell form of lymphoma
have better response rates and prognosis compared to
those with a T cell phenotype.
Staging

Minimum database including a complete blood count
(CBC) with differential blood cell count, serum bio­
chemistry profile, and urinalysis should be completed to
evaluate for the presence of paraneoplastic conditions
and rule out co‐morbid disease.
Potential abnormalities related to lymphoma noted on
a CBC include blood dyscrasias such as a nonregen­
erative anemia, thrombocytopenia, lymphocytosis or
presence of circulating lymphoblasts. Bone marrow
­
aspiration is indicated in dogs with blood dyscrasias to
confirm lymphoma and rule out an unrelated blood
­disorder. This may also help to differentiate between
multicentric stage V lymphoma and a primary lympho­
blastic leukemia, which carries a worse prognosis.
A chemistry profile that includes a serum ionized cal­
cium level is recommended to evaluate for the presence
of hypercalcemia of malignancy and to assess liver and
kidney function.
A urinalysis is helpful in evaluating renal function and
can rule out a subclinical urinary tract infection. It is
important to note that dogs with hypercalcemia of
­malignancy may present with azotemia and isosthenuria,
which may not represent primary renal disease but
instead is a consequence of the effects of hypercalcemia
on renal tubules.
Thoracic and/or abdominal radiographs or abdominal
ultrasound are recommended to determine the presence
and extent of disease within visceral organs. When pre­
sent, pulmonary infiltrates typically appear radiographi­
cally as diffuse interstitial and/or alveolar patterns. Rarely
are there nodules or bronchial changes. Widening of the
cranial mediastinum may indicate the presence of medias­
tinal lymphoma.
Because of the potential for cardiotoxic effects of
­certain chemotherapy drugs, thoracic radiographs are
also important for assessment of cardiac changes.
Therapy
After establishing a diagnosis of lymphoma, a compre­
hensive discussion with the owner should encompass
goals, prognosis, associated costs, and potential compli­
cations. It is important to note that many owners have a

preconceived notion of cancer and its treatment.
Therefore it should be made clear that the majority of
dogs who receive chemotherapy will respond to treat­
ment and can achieve a remission in which they are free
of clinical signs related to lymphoma. In the author’s
experience, most owners who decide to proceed with
chemotherapy are cooperative, realistic, and apprecia­
tive of the efforts made to help their pets.
Treatment options range from multiagent protocols to
single‐agent prednisone and will be determined by the
location of the disease, the overall health of the pet, and
the emotional/financial commitment of the owner.
A primary veterinarian can easily manage many dogs
with multicentric lymphoma. However, consultation
with an oncologist may be helpful in establishing a treat­
ment protocol. Referral to an oncology center may be
indicated for atypical cases or for patients that are refrac­
tory to treatment.
Multiagent Chemotherapy Protocols

Drugs with established activity include cyclophospha­
mide (C), doxorubicin (H, hydroxydaunorubicin or
­doxorubicin), vincristine (O, Oncovin®), and prednisone
(P). Protocols incorporating these drugs are called
CHOP‐based protocols. All CHOP‐based multiagent
chemotherapy protocols are believed to be superior to
any single‐agent protocol with respect to remission
duration and overall survival time. Multiple studies have
demonstrated that approximately 80–90% of all dogs
receiving a CHOP‐based chemotherapy protocol will
experience a clinical remission with an overall median
survival time of 10–12 months. While success of t­ reatment
is highly variable, the majority of multiagent protocols
induce a first remission of >6 months after chemotherapy
induction.
Multiagent protocols are typically discontinued
15–19 weeks after the start of therapy. Long‐term main­
tenance chemotherapy has not demonstrated benefit
with respect to remission duration or progression‐free
survival.
A commonly used and well‐studied chemothera­
py
protocol for dogs with newly diagnosed or naive
­multicentric lymphoma is the University of Wisconsin
19‐week discontinuous (short) CHOP protocol. This
protocol is simple to administer since it relies on single‐
agent treatment at each visit, allowing for an assessment
of tolerability and efficacy of each drug. At week 19,
chemotherapy is discontinued if the dog is in complete
remission (Table 134.2).
Single‐Agent Chemotherapy Protocols

As noted earlier, multiagent protocol drugs work best
when given in combination at the onset of therapy.
