If multiagent therapy is not an option, it is reasonable to
incorporate any number of the CHOP drugs and create
an individual protocol that suits the dog and the owner.
Doxorubicin as a single agent, administered every 2–3
weeks (up to five total treatments), can induce a remis­
sion in 50–75% of dogs for a median of 6–8 months. Care
must be taken to monitor for cumulative cardiotoxic
effects of this drug in the dog, which can result in dilated
cardiomyopathy (DCM). It is advisable to avoid this drug
in dogs with a preexisting heart condition or breeds that
are considered high risk for DCM (e.g., boxer, Doberman
pinscher, Great Dane, etc.). Other protocols with similar
success include cyclophosphamide, vincristine, and
prednisone (referred to as COP).
Dogs which are treated with a palliative protocol of
prednisone as a sole therapy can achieve a short‐lived
remission of approximately 1–2 months. It is important
to note that these dogs, when compared to dogs given

multiagent therapy from the outset, are more likely to
develop multidrug resistance and experience shorter
remission and survival times if any subsequent chemo­
therapy is administered.
Reinduction Chemotherapy Protocols

Reinduction with CHOP‐based drugs is recommended
provided that the recurrence is temporally far enough
from the conclusion of the initial protocol (i.e., ≥ 2
months). Typically, a second or even third remission is
achievable with a variable duration of response.
Rescue Chemotherapy

Inevitably, resistance to the CHOP‐based chemotherapy
drugs will develop, and it is unlikely that continued use
of the same drugs will provide a significant benefit. At
that point, drugs not used in the initial CHOP proto­
cols are recommended and are referred to as rescue

VetBooks.ir

134 Lymphomas

­chemotherapy agents/protocols. Successful induction of
an additional remission with rescue protocols varies
between 50% and 90% but the length of remission is
decreased, at 1.5–2.5 months.
A novel chemotherapy agent, rabacfosadine (Tanovea®),
has been conditionally approved for use in dogs with naive
or relapse lymphoma. This compound as a single agent has
demonstrated excellent efficacy for dogs with B cell form
of lymphoma and may be variably successsful for dogs
with a T cell variant. Other second‐line drugs often used
for rescue therapy include lomustine (CCNU), mechlore­
thamine (Mustargen®), vinblastine (Velban®), dacarbazine
(DTIC), and cytosine arabinoside (Cytosar‐U®). While
each of these drugs has a variable degree of efficacy against
lymphoma, the duration of response is considerably lower
when compared to standard multiagent protocols.

Cutaneous Lymphoma

A majority of dogs tolerate chemotherapy well. Potential
adverse effects include mild to moderate nausea, vomit­
ing, or diarrhea, all of which are easily treated with sup­
portive care or symptom management. In rare instances,
life‐threatening complications related to chemotherapy‐
induced myelosuppression can develop, requiring hospi­
talization and aggressive supportive care.
A CBC must be performed prior to every treatment to
ensure an adequate white blood cell count. It is generally
accepted that an absolute neutrophil count of >2000
cells/μL and >50 000 platelets/μL be present prior to
chemotherapy administration to minimize the risk of
sepsis or other complications.

A primary cutaneous form of lymphoma can develop
within the skin and/or the oral cavity (mucocutaneous).
Dogs may present with pruritus, scaling of the skin, and
alopecia that will progress to areas of ulceration, nod­
ules, and proliferative plaques. Lesions can be solitary or
can involve multiple skin sites. Oral involvement appears
as plaque‐like lesions or nodules associated with the
gums and lips. Multiple punch biopsies of the affected
areas are necessary to establish a diagnosis of lymphoma.
There are two types of cutaneous lymphoma distin­
guished histologically and phenotypically: epithelio­
tropic (T cell) lymphoma (also called mycosis fungoides)
and nonepitheliotropic (B or T cell) lymphoma.
Treatment of cutaneous lymphoma depends on the
extent and location of disease. Single lesions may be
appropriately treated with local therapy consisting of
surgery or radiation therapy. Diffuse cutaneous lym­
phoma is best treated with chemotherapy. B cell cutane­
ous lymphomas often respond better than T cell, but the
response rate with chemotherapy is less than that seen
with other forms of lymphoma.
CCNU or multiagent chemotherapy is the treatment
of choice, although a recent study has also supported the
use of Tanovea when treating dogs for cutaneous forms
of lymphoma. While many dogs have an initial response
to chemotherapy, the lesions often return or new lesions
develop within a short period of time (3–5 months).
Many dogs are euthanized within six months of diagno­
sis due to the discomfort associated with progressive
ulceration, bleeding, and pruritus.

Extranodal Forms of Lymphoma

Prognosis

There are instances where a dog will present with lym­
phoma isolated to a solitary site, such as the alimentary
tract, skin, central nervous system (CNS) or nasal cavity.
On rare occasions, local therapies such as surgery or
radiation therapy may be employed. Careful staging,
including bloodwork, thoracic radiographs, +/‐ abdomi­
nal ultrasound, +/‐ bone marrow aspiration, is essential
to ensure multicentric involvement is not present before
considering local therapy.

Response rates and remission duration for dogs with
newly diagnosed lymphoma will vary depending on the
clinical picture, biologic behavior, histologic classifica­
tion, immunophenotype, and treatment protocol. In
general, dogs with large B cell lymphoma have better
response rates to a CHOP‐based chemotherapy protocol
than dogs with T cell lymphoma. In fact, due to the vari­
able success in the treatment of dogs with T cell lym­
phoma, many oncologists are now relying on a modified
chemotherapy protocol that incorporates more alkylat­
ing agents (e.g., cyclophosphamide or lomustine). This
modification is based on the presumption that these
agents may be more effective agents for dogs with a T cell
form of lymphoma.

Complications of Chemotherapy

Alimentary Lymphoma

Alimentary lymphoma is an uncommon extranodal lym­
phoma. Dogs will present with nonspecific clinical signs
consistent with gastrointestinal (GI) disease, including
weight loss, anorexia, diarrhea, and vomiting. Limited
information in the veterinary literature suggests this
form of lymphoma is poorly responsive to chemother­
apy. In the author’s experience, a chemotherapy protocol
that incorporates CCNU can be more effective than a
multidrug CHOP‐based chemotherapy protocol alone.

Additional Treatment Strategies

Because most dogs ultimately will develop chemother­
apy resistance, other methods of lengthening a clinical
remission may be employed. These include total and
half‐body radiation therapy, hematopoietic stem cell

transplantation (bone marrow transplant), and immuno­
therapy. These treatment strategies have variable success
and continue to be an active area of investigation.

­Feline Lymphoma
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Lymphoma (LSA) is one of the most common neoplasms
in the cat and can present in a variety of ways, depending
on the organ(s) affected. An association with retroviral
infection has been firmly established, with approximately
25% of feline leukemia virus (FeLV)‐positive cats devel­
oping lymphoma during their lifetime. Feline immuno­
deficiency virus (FIV) has also been implicated in the
development of lymphoma, although its true contribu­
tion has been difficult to determine since it often occurs
in conjunction with FeLV. Chronic immunosuppression
secondary to retroviral infection is thought to play a role
in this association. This correlates with the increased
incidence of lymphoma in cats receiving chronic
immunosuppressive drugs after renal transplantation.
­
Collectively, these findings parallel an increased inci­
dence of lymphoproliferative cancers in humans with
human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or those receiv­
ing chronic immunosuppressive therapy.
The underlying cause of nonretroviral‐induced feline
lymphoma is not completely understood. It is likely
that chronic inflammation plays a role given that feline
lymphomas frequently arise in organs or sites affected
by chronic inflammation. For example, a correlation
between chronic inflammatory bowel disease and ali­
mentary lymphoma has been proposed. Comparatively,
humans with celiac disease have a similar predisposition
towards lymphoproliferative disorders and cancer.
Recent studies have also demonstrated that chronic
exposure to environmental tobacco smoke is associated
with an elevated risk for gastrointestinal lymphoma
in cats.
Epidemiology
Lymphoma is the most common neoplasm of the hemat­
opoietic system of cats, with an estimated incidence of
200 per 100 000 cats.
Studies have demonstrated that FeLV‐positive cats
have a 60‐fold or greater relative risk of the cancer. FIV
infection also increases the relative risk of lymphoma
5–6‐fold.
While the incidence of feline lymphoma has not
changed with the development of effective antiviral
­vaccines, the most common presentation of lymphoma
is now in older retrovirus‐negative cats.

Signalment
There is a bimodal distribution for feline lymphoma in
which retroviral‐positive cats present with lymphoma at
a young age (1–3 years) and virus‐negative cats present
at an older age (10–13 years). Currently, the median age
at presentation is approximately 11 years. There is no sex
predilection and any breed of cat can be affected,
although Siamese cats are overrepresented, suggesting a
genetic susceptibility to the disease.
History and Clinical Signs
Location of the tumor appears to be the determinant
of clinical signs and prognosis in feline lymphoma.
Consequently, the WHO staging system is not used.
Instead, lymphoma is generally divided into different
anatomic classifications: mediastinal, gastrointestinal,
multicentric, and miscellaneous sites (such as nasal and
renal).
Mediastinal Lymphoma

Young cats typically present with a mediastinal form of
lymphoma with acute‐onset dyspnea, which rapidly
­progresses as the tumor begins to occlude lymphatics,
leading to pleural effusion. Physical examination may
reveal a noncompressible cranial thorax and muffled or
caudodorsal displacement of cardiac sounds.
Alimentary Lymphoma

Alimentary lymphomas usually involve the stomach and
intestines of older cats. Gastrointestinal tumors may be
discrete or diffuse. The primary clinical signs are anorexia
and weight loss, although some cats may also ­present
with vomiting and/or diarrhea. With these ­clinical signs,
it is important, though often difficult, to differentiate
lymphoma from inflammatory bowel disease.
Extranodal Lymphoma

Cats with other forms of lymphoma (e.g., nasal, renal,
CNS, laryngeal) will present with clinical signs reflecting
the anatomic location.
Diagnosis
As described in dogs, a diagnosis of lymphoma can be
achieved via fine needle aspiration or surgical, endo­
scopic or needle biopsy of affected tissue. As noted
­previously, a definitive diagnosis via a fine needle aspi­
rate can be confounded by an insufficient or nondiag­
nostic sample, or if there is a significant component of
inflammation present. Because alimentary lymphoma is
easily confused with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD),
a full‐thickness tissue biopsy is often necessary to

VetBooks.ir

134 Lymphomas

­establish a definitive diagnosis. A histologic evaluation
of the diseased tissue will provide a more accurate evalu­
ation of tissue morphology and degree of invasion. If an
equivocal diagnosis is present, techniques such as immu­
nohistochemical or immunocytochemical analysis, flow
cytometric analysis and polymerase chain reaction‐
based clonality assays are available to characterize the
disease and refine the diagnosis.
Currently, a histologic classification scheme similar to
those described in humans and dogs does not exist for
feline lymphoma. There are two histologic forms: high‐
(or intermediate) grade lymphoma and low‐grade
(or small cell) lymphoma. These histologic distinctions
in combination with anatomic location are the most
prognostic and will determine treatment.
Immunophenotype

Immunophenotyping is not commonly used for prog­
nostication purposes in the cat as it is in dogs and
humans. It is employed, however, to confirm the p
­ resence
of a phenotypically identical population of l­ymphoid
cells that make up the tumor. This can be completed
on tissue samples via histochemical or cytochemical
staining for CD3 (T cell expression) or CD79a (B cell
expression). According to some studies, a T cell pheno­
type is more prevalent in cats with small cell or low‐grade
alimentary lymphoma and B cell phenotype is more
common in large cell or high‐grade lymphoma. As
mentioned previously, cell morphology (large cell vs
­
small cell) is used more commonly than a phenotypic
distinction to determine treatment and prognosis.
Alimentary Lymphoma

Cats with alimentary lymphoma are typically diagnosed
via abdominal imaging (e.g., ultrasound), which is abnor­
mal in approximately 60–90% of cats. The appearance is
variable, and may be of a circumferential mass with loss
of GI wall layering, or of a diffuse small intestinal wall
thickening of the muscularis, propria, and submucosa.
Mesenteric lymphadenopathy is also common and has
been reported in 45–80% of affected cats.
A cytologic or histologic assessment of a needle aspirate
or needle biopsy samples from intestinal masses, enlarged
lymph nodes or other abnormal‐appearing organs is
essential to establish a diagnosis. Endoscopic, laparoscopic
or incisional biopsy achieved by laparotomy may also be
performed. Full‐thickness GI biopsies best distinguish
inflammatory bowel disease from lymphoma and will
­differentiate a high‐ or low‐grade intestinal lymphoma.
Mediastinal Lymphoma

For cats with mediastinal lymphoma, a diagnosis can be
established via survey thoracic radiographs followed by
thoracocentesis with cytologic examination of the fluid.

The fluid lymphocyte count is usually greater than
4000/μL, with most appearing as intermediate or large
lymphoblasts. In cases where fluid cytology is not
­diagnostic, aspiration or biopsy of the mass itself can be
completed via ultrasound or computed tomography
(CT) guidance. Immunophenotypic and clonality assess­
ment may be helpful in equivocal cases.
Nasal Lymphoma

Nasal lymphoma differs from other sites in that it is often
non‐systemic and confined to the nose and/or sinuses.
Nasal CT or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), rhinos­
copy, and biopsy are necessary to establish a diagnosis.
Thorough staging with evaluation of regional lymph
nodes, thorax, and abdomen is recommended if local
radiation therapy is to be considered for sole treatment.
Renal Lymphoma

Renal lymphoma usually causes bilateral renomegaly
which may be detected on physical exam. Clinical signs
at presentation are a consequence of renal insufficiency.
Ultrasound‐guided renal biopsy or FNA is recommended
to confirm the diagnosis.
Central Nervous System Lymphoma

Spinal CNS lymphoma usually causes hindlimb paresis
or paralysis with or without back pain. Most tumors are
extradural, and occur in the thoracolumbar or lumbosa­
cral regions. Often there is no radiographic evidence of
disease. The clinical signs of brain lymphoma are attrib­
utable to the region of brain affected. Advanced imaging
with MRI or CT can be helpful in determining extent
and location of the lesion, and to evaluate for multifocal
disease. Because cerebral spinal fluid evaluation is not
always definitive for lymphoma, a diagnosis may be
attempted through cytologic evaluation of the bone
­marrow or kidneys since these organs are also involved
in up to 70% of cases.
Staging
As in canine lymphoma, beyond those initial diagnostics
performed to establish the diagnosis of lymphoma,
­additional diagnostics should be considered as part of
complete staging.
A complete blood work‐up including a CBC with dif­
ferential blood cell count, serum biochemistry profile,
urinalysis, and FeLV/FIV screen should be completed on
all cats. While most cats will have an unremarkable blood
profile, this is useful to evaluate for the presence of other
co‐morbid conditions.
A bone marrow aspirate is indicated in cats with blood
dyscrasias to confirm the presence of lymphoma and
rule out other etiologies. Results of a bone marrow

­aspiration may help guide treatment if blood dyscrasias
are present.
Thoracic +/‐ abdominal radiographs or preferably
abdominal ultrasound are recommended to determine
the presence and extent of disease within visceral organs.
Therapy
There is less known about multicentric lymphoma treat­
ment protocols in the cat relative to the dog. While suc­
cess of the various chemotherapy protocols is highly
variable, the majority are capable of inducing a first
remission of >6 months after induction. Protocol choice
is based on cell type/grade.

protocol incorporating a drug with CNS penetration
(such as CCNU) is recommended.
Central Nervous System Lymphoma

Central nervous system lymphoma should be treated
with chemotherapy or radiation therapy emergently as
clinical signs, particularly paralysis, may become perma­
nent if treatment is delayed.

Large Cell or High‐Grade Lymphoma

Nasal Lymphoma

If nasal lymphoma is confirmed to be nonsystemic, local

Other Anatomic Locations

Other infrequently encountered forms of lymphoma in
the cat include laryngeal or tracheal. Cats presenting
with disease isolated to these locations can respond
­positively to local radiation therapy +/‐ chemotherapy
for periods of 6–12 months.
Prognosis
Generally, the overall response rate and survival time in
cats are much lower than those achieved in dogs.
However, this varies and is determined by the anatomic
location at presentation, grade of tumor, and viral status
of the cat.
High‐grade tumors progress rapidly but are more
likely to respond to multiagent chemotherapy for a
finite period of time, whereas low‐grade tumors pro­
gress slowly and can be easily managed as chronic
diseases.
Cats with mediastinal lymphoma respond well to
chemotherapy initially, but the duration of response is
usually short‐lived (2–3 months).

Cats with high‐grade alimentary lymphoma treated
with a multiagent chemotherapy protocol can respond
with median survival times of 210 days. A positive
response to treatment is the best prognostic indicator.
Cats achieving a complete or partial remission have a
significantly longer survival time of >2 years.
Cats with nasal lymphoma can enjoy lengthy ­survival
times of 1–3 years or more with radiation therapy
+/‐ chemotherapy.
Central nervous system and renal lymphoma are
uncommon but when encountered, cats can experience a
short period of clinical benefit from ­chemotherapy and/
or radiation therapy for a median of 2–6 months.

­Conclusion
Cats and dogs with lymphoma can respond favorably to
chemotherapy +/‐ radiation therapy. The treatments are
generally well tolerated with most animals ­achieving a
clinical benefit for variable periods of time. Prognosis is
dependent on location, extent of disease, histologic
grade, and phenotype. Cancer treatment in pets can be a
rewarding experience. Most pet owners appreciate the
dedication of the veterinarian and the additional quality
time they gain with their pets.

Plasma Cell Disorders
Orna Kristal, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology)
Kfar Saba, Israel

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Plasma cell neoplasms develop from clonal proliferation
of terminally differentiated immunoglobulin‐producing B
lymphocytes. They typically produce a homogenous
monoclonal immunoglobulin which is why they are
thought to originate from a single cell. However, not all
neoplasms are secretory and some may be biclonal or
even polyclonal. Reported plasma cell disorders (PCD) in
dogs and cats include multiple myeloma (MM), cutaneous
and noncutaneous extramedullary plasmacytoma (EMP),
IgM (Waldenström) macroglobulinemia (WM), solitary
osseous plasmacytoma (SOP), and plasma cell leukemia.
The etiology of PCD in dogs and cats is largely unknown.
No retroviral association was found in cats. Chronic
immune stimulation in rodent models and chronic infec­
tions in people have been associated with MM. Exposure
to ionizing radiation is a well‐known risk f­ actor and agri­
cultural chemicals, benzene, and petroleum products
have been considered potential risk ­factors in humans.
Multiple myeloma usually originates from multiple
bone marrow sites in dogs. In cats, multicentric noncuta­
neous EMP with or without bone marrow involvement
may present as MM. The neoplastic plasma cells in MM
typically secrete abnormal amounts of a single whole or
partial (light or heavy chain) immunoglobulin called the
M component, or paraprotein. In dogs, the M component
is usually IgA or IgG with similar frequency. In cats, the
IgG class is four times more common than IgA. IgM over­
production is uncommon in both species and is more
often associated with WM, a form of lymphoplasma­
cytic lymphoma. The abnormal light chains are excreted
in the urine and are called Bence Jones proteins.
Uncommon presentations in both species include
biclonal gammopathies, nonsecretory MM, monoclonal
gammopathies without hyperglobulinemia and
cryoglobulinemia. Cryoglobulins are immunoglobulins

that precipitate in temperatures below 37 °C, so they are
usually lost in the clot when the blood is allowed to clot
at room temperature.
Multiple myeloma negatively affects many organ
systems as a result of tumor infiltration, high levels
­
of circulating or deposited M component, production of
cytokines by tumor cells or bone marrow microenviron­
ment and the effects on the immune system.
Abnormal immunoglobulins can lead to hyperviscos­
ity syndrome (HVS) when high protein levels are reached.
The incidence of HVS is highest with IgM (WM) which
is a pentamer and has a high molecular weight, followed
by IgA‐secreting myelomas which are dimers that can
polymerize. IgG‐associated HVS occurs less frequently.
Increased serum viscosity leads to “sludging” of blood in
the vasculature that results in hypoxia and bleeding
diathesis leading to organ damage. HVS occurs in about
30% of dogs with MM and most commonly affects the
central nervous system (CNS), eyes, cardiovascular sys­
tem, and coagulation system.
Bleeding disorders are common in dogs with MM and
the mechanism is likely multifactorial. Coating of plate­
lets with paraproteins leads to decreased adhesiveness,
failure to release platelet factor III, and thrombocy­
topathia. Paraproteins can also interfere with clotting
factors and lead to abnormal fibrin polymerization.
Thrombocytopenia due to bone marrow infiltration
(myelophthisis) or immune‐mediated disease may also
contribute to bleeding. Approximately 33% of dogs and
25% of cats with MM have clinical evidence of bleeding.
Nonregenerative normocytic normochromic anemia
is the most common hematologic abnormality in MM
patients, present in about 66% of dogs and cats. Etiologies
may include myelophthisis, decreased erythrocyte life
span due to coating with paraprotein, blood loss, pro­
duction of inhibitory cytokines by myeloma cells and
decreased erythropoietin production due to renal

­dysfunction. Thrombocytopenia and neutropenia may
also occur.
Suppression of normal immunoglobulin production is
common and is suggested to result from normal feed­
back inhibition induced by the monoclonal gammopa­
thy. In people, maturation of normal B cells to plasma
cells is suppressed as well as T helper cell number and
function. These abnormalities can lead to immunosup­
pression and, combined with neutropenia, increased risk
for bacterial infections.
Osteolytic bone lesions are induced by secretion
of osteoclast‐activating factors from the bone marrow
microenvironment and myeloma cells. These factors
include the cytokines interleukin (IL)‐1 beta, tumor
necrosis factor (TNF)‐beta, and IL‐6. Osteolytic lesions
may cause pain, lameness, spinal compression due to
extradural tumor masses, or vertebral fractures which can
lead to paresis or paralysis. Lytic bone lesions are detected
in 50–60% of dogs with MM. In cats, skeletal involvement
is more variable, noted to occur in 8% of cases in one case
series and in up to 58–67% in other reports.
Hypercalcemia occurs in 15–20% of dogs and 9–25% of
cats with MM. Hypercalcemia was present in 50% of dogs
with MM at diagnosis when ionized calcium rather than
total calcium was measured. The main proposed mecha­
nism is direct bone osteolysis, although skeletal lytic lesions
are more common than hypercalcemia. Hypercalcemia
may be worsened by concurrent renal disease.
Renal disease is one of the serious complications of
MM, reported in 30–50% of dogs and about 25% of cats.
Light chains that are filtered by the glomerulus precipi­
tate in the renal tubule, causing interstitial nephritis.
Hypercalcemia, infiltration of the kidneys by myeloma
cells, decreased renal blood flow secondary to hypervis­
cosity, amyloidosis, glomerulonephritis, and pyelone­
phritis following immunosuppression may also
contribute to renal dysfunction.
Cardiac disease, a less common complication, may be
explained by increased peripheral vascular resistance,
excessive cardiac workload, and myocardial hypoxia sec­
ondary to hyperviscosity.
Waldenström macroglobulinemia is a rare disease in
animals and is considered a form of lymphoplasmacytic
lymphoma involving the spleen, lymph nodes, and bone
marrow along with serum IgM‐related signs of hypervis­
cosity or cryoglobulinemia. Osteolytic bone lesions and
hypercalcemia are not present and Bence Jones protein­
uria is uncommon.
Solitary PCD include EMP and SOP. They are defined
as local accumulation of neoplastic monoclonal plasma
cells without evidence of systemic PCD. Canine EMPs
are distinct, usually solitary tumors unrelated to MM.
The skin, especially the head, and extremities are affected
most commonly, followed by the mucous membranes of
the oral cavity (Figure 135.1) and the colorectal junction.

Figure 135.1 Oral extramedullary plasmacytoma in the maxilla of
a dog.

Other sites such as gastrointestinal, trachea, larynx, eye,
genitalia, and others are rare and comprise 1% of all EMP
cases. Cutaneous, oral, and colorectal EMPs are usually
benign but can be locally invasive and cause bone destruc­
tion in the oral cavity. In humans, cutaneous EMP is
uncommon and is often part of a multicentric disease. In
dogs, MM rarely exhibits cutaneous involvement. Fewer
reports exist regarding solitary EMP in cats but their
behavior and site distribution appear similar to dogs. The
multicentric EMP as part of MM is more common in cats
than dogs although incorporating abdominal ultrasound
and cytology into the staging of MM may prove abdomi­
nal organ involvement is more common than previously
thought. A recent study showed that 57% of dogs with
MM that underwent abdominal ultrasound were cyto­
logically confirmed to have liver, spleen, or abdominal
lymph node involvement. Amyloid deposits of immuno­
globulin origin occur in 3–13% of EMPs.
Solitary osseous plasmacytomas have been reported in
the dog affecting the appendicular skeleton, zygomatic
arch, and vertebrae. In humans (and probably in dogs),
the prognosis is much better than for MM but about 50%
of SOPs will eventually develop into MM.

­Epidemiology
Multiple myeloma is uncommon in both dogs and cats,
representing less than 1% of all malignancies. It com­
prises about 8% of all hematopoietic tumors and 3.6% of
all primary and secondary bone tumors in dogs. The
incidence in both species is lower than in humans.

­Signalment
Multiple myeloma affects older animals with a median age
of 8–9 years (range, 2–15) in dogs and 12–14 years in cats

VetBooks.ir

135 Plasma Cell Disorders

(range, 4–18). There is no breed or sex predilection in dogs.
In cats, it is most common in domestic short‐hairs and a
slight male predisposition has been reported. EMPs usually
occur in middle‐aged to older dogs (median age 9–10
years). The cocker spaniel and West Highland white terrier
seem to be at increased risk. Solitary EMPs are less com­
mon in cats and SOP is rarely reported in both species.

­History and Clinical Signs
Clinical signs of MM are variable, with a median duration
of one month prior to diagnosis. In dogs, the most com­
mon presenting sign is lethargy and weakness (62%).
Skeletal lytic lesions lead to lameness, pain and paresis or
paralysis with vertebral involvement (47%). Bleeding disor­
ders most commonly present as epistaxis or gingival bleed­
ing (37%). Ocular and CNS abnormalities are caused by
HVS, systemic hypertension or both. Ocular signs include
retinal bleeding, enlarged tortuous retinal vessels, retinal
detachment (35%), and acute onset of blindness. Hyphema,
episcleral injection, corneal edema, and aqueous flare may
also occur. CNS signs include dementia, personality
changes, disorientation, and seizures (12%). Polyuria/poly­
dipsia (25%) may develop secondary to renal disease and
hypercalcemia. Cardiopulmonary signs (syncope, cyano­
sis, congestive heart failure [CHF]) are less common.
Vomiting, anorexia, and weight loss have been seen in dogs
with hypercalcemia and/or renal disease. Some dogs may
present with secondary infections such as cystitis.
Physical examination findings may include pale mucous
membranes, dehydration, fundic changes, neurologic
deficits, fever, and cranial organomegaly.
In cats, lethargy, anorexia, and weight loss are the most
common clinical signs. Vomiting and diarrhea, as well as
cranial organomegaly and cutaneous or subcutaneous
masses are more common than in dogs.
Cutaneous and mucosal EMPs usually appear as pink
or red, raised, alopecic and sometimes ulcerated solid
nodules, about 1–2 cm in diameter (see Figure 135.1),
but they can range from 0.2 to 10 cm in diameter. The
majority of tumors are single, but some dogs may develop
more than one tumor simultaneously or sequentially.
Oral EMPs can cause bleeding and decreased appetite.
Colorectal EMPs can lead to hematochezia, rectal bleed­
ing, tenesmus, and rectal prolapse. SOPs cause pain,
lameness, or neurologic symptoms.

Suspicion of MM usually arises in an animal present­
ing with appropriate clinical signs and hyperglobuline­
mia. Initial evaluation includes CBC, full chemistry
panel, and urinalysis. Additional findings on these

MM produces a biclonal gammopathy. A dog with MM
may still have a normal globulin level due to suppression
of normal globulin production. Therefore, if findings
support MM, SPE should be done even if total globulin
level is normal. When monoclonal gammopathy is dem­
onstrated, immunoelectrophoresis can determine the
antibody type.
Urinalysis provides information on renal function, uri­
nary tract infection, and proteinuria. However, urine
dipsticks only measure albumin. Special heat precipita­
tion methods are required to detect Bence Jones pro­
teins. This is a qualitative test associated with a high rate
of false‐positive and ‐negative results in people. Urine
electrophoresis or immunoelectrophoresis may be more
reliable.
Bone involvement may appear on radiographs as mul­
tiple osteolytic lesions affecting mainly the axial skele­
ton, or as diffuse osteoporosis (Figure 135.3). Plain
survey skeletal radiographs are recommended for detec­
tion of these lesions. It is best to start with thoracic, lum­
bar spine, and pelvic radiographs, unless pain is localized
to other bones. Skeletal CT can be more sensitive than
radiographs for detection of small lesions and spinal cord
compression. Radionuclide bone scans are not recom­
mended because MM lesions are primarily lytic and may
be undetectable. Abdominal ultrasound is recommended
in all cats and in dogs without bone marrow plasma­
cytosis. Most common abnormalities are splenomegaly,
hepatomegaly, and changes in echogenicity or nodules in
these organs.
Bone marrow aspiration is required for a definitive
diagnosis of MM and is taken from routine sites. In some
cases, aspiration or a needle core biopsy is taken directly
from a lytic lesion if it is large enough and accessible.
This is especially pertinent in cases of SOP. Normal bone
marrow contains less than 5% plasma cells. Finding of

Figure 135.3 Lateral radiograph showing well‐demarcated small
“punched out” lytic lesions and a “lacy” trabecular pattern in the
cervical vertebrae due to diffuse osteopenia in a dog with MM.

>10% plasma cells in the marrow, especially if cellular
atypia or clustering is present, is used to diagnose MM by
some investigators, while the majority agree that >20%
plasma cells is a more reliable value. The morphology of
neoplastic plasma cells varies from normal to large pleo­
morphic cells with large cytoplasm, high mitotic index,
and multinucleation (Figure 135.4). In cats (and less often
in dogs), bone marrow infiltration may not be severe
enough and visceral organ infiltration may be diagnostic
instead.
In patients with hypercalcemia, ionized calcium is
indicated for confirmation because binding of calcium to
paraproteins will increase total calcium while ionized
calcium remains normal. Hypocholesterolemia was
reported in 68% of cats with MM in one study. A possible
explanation is downregulation of cholesterol production
by the liver to maintain oncotic pressure in the face of
hyperglobulinemia. When HVS is suspected, serum vis­
cosity can be measured in relation to water. Normal
canine serum viscosity is 1.6–1.8 times that of water.
Clinical signs of HVS usually appear when serum viscos­
ity is greater than five times that of water.
Differential diagnoses for monoclonal gammopathy
include B cell lymphoma, mainly chronic but also acute
B cell lymphoid leukemia, WM, chronic infections such
as Ehrlichia canis and leishmaniasis in dogs, feline infec­
tious peritonitis (FIP) in cats, and monoclonal gammop­
athy of unknown significance (MGUS). The latter is a
benign process, well recognized in humans but only a
few cases have been reported in dogs and cats.
Diagnosis of EMP and SOP is made by tissue biopsy
or fine needle aspirate. Most EMPs are not well

­differentiated and can be difficult to differentiate from
other round cell tumors. Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
is sometimes utilized in these cases to detect light and
heavy chains. The majority of EMPs stain for lambda
light‐chains, similar to the physiologic distribution of
light chains in normal canine and feline plasma cells.
Staining for multiple myeloma oncogene 1/interferon
regulatory factor 4 (MUM1/IRF4) is highly sensitive for
EMPs but 21% of B cell lymphomas stain positive as well.
It is therefore recommended to use it in combination
with other round cell markers together with morphol­
ogy of the cells. SOP, GI EMP, and multiple cutaneous
EMPs in dogs can metastasize, or develop into MM.
Therefore, it is important to fully stage them at diagno­
sis. Staging includes SPE (even if total globulin level is
normal), bone marrow aspiration, survey skeletal radio­
graphs, and abdominal ultrasound.

­Therapy
Chemotherapy with melphalan and prednisone is the
treatment of choice for MM in dogs. Although cure is
unlikely, response to treatment is achieved in most dogs
often for relatively long periods of time. Melphalan is
prescribed at a dose of 0.1 mg/kg PO once daily for 10
days, then 0.05 mg/kg PO once daily continuously. An
alternate pulse protocol with melphalan at 7 mg/m2
(rounded to the nearest whole 2 mg tablet) given once
daily for 5 days every 21 days is also used. Prednisone is
given at a dose of 0.5 mg/kg PO once daily for 10 days,
then 0.5 mg/kg PO on alternate days indefinitely or
­discontinued after 60 days. These protocols are usually
well tolerated and the main toxicity of melphalan is mye­
losuppression, most commonly thrombocytopenia.
It is generally accepted that a reduction in serum levels
of the M component by at least 50% is a reasonable
­therapeutic goal. In addition, clinical signs and clinical
pathology abnormalities should also improve, usually
within 2–4 weeks. Radiographic improvement of skeletal
lytic lesions may take several months, and may only be
partial. Routine monitoring of response to treatment and
toxicity is usually done with a complete blood count
(CBC), total globulin level, and Bence Jones protein
(if originally present) every two weeks. A CBC should be
checked at least once on day 7 of the pulse protocol.
Once a good response is achieved and no cytopenias
have been identified, follow‐up can be done less often.
Melphalan and prednisone have also been used in cats
but melphalan is more myelosuppressive than in dogs,
and may cause prolonged neutropenias. Ideally, melpha­
lan should be compounded for cats to allow accurate
dosing and avoid hazardous exposure of humans. Use of
chlorambucil, cyclophosphamide, CCNU, or multidrug

therapy may be more suitable in cats with MM than
­melphalan and responses have been documented.
Chlorambucil has been recommended for the treat­
ment of WM at a dose of 0.2 mg/kg PO once daily,
although treatment with melphalan and prednisone may
be effective as well.
Rescue therapy after disease relapse may be attempted
with other alkylating agents including cyclophospha­
mide, chlorambucil, or CCNU. The VAD protocol which
includes vincristine, doxorubicin, and dexamethasone
has been extrapolated from humans, while others have
used CHOP‐based lymphoma protocols. There are only
anecdotal data regarding these rescue protocols, but it
appears that while response rate is quite high, most
responses are of short duration.
Symptomatic animals presenting with severe compli­
cations of MM require supportive care simultaneously
with diagnosis and initiation of antitumor therapy.
Animals with severe signs of HVS (altered mentation,
hemorrhage, retinal detachment, or CHF) can be treated
with plasmapharesis. Renal dysfunction, especially with
concurrent hypercalcemia, is treated with IV fluid diure­
sis until symptoms improve. Severe hypercalcemia can
be treated with calcitonin in addition to fluid diuresis or
with IV bisphosphonates if diagnosis is delayed.
Prednisone is highly effective in treating hypercalcemia
but it should not be started prior to making a definitive
diagnosis as it may obscure results. Hypercalcemia usu­
ally resolves quickly after starting chemotherapy. Dogs
with extensive lytic lesions should have exercise restric­
tion and analgesia.
Bisphosphonates (BP) inhibit osteoclast activity and in
human. They have been shown to reduce bone pain, the
incidence of pathologic fractures and prolong time to
first event. The more potent amino‐bisphosphonates
such as pamidronate or zoledronate also appear to have
antitumor activity and zoledronate has shown a survival
advantage over placebo and other BP in patients with
symptomatic MM. Pamidronate or zoledronate probably
have a role in the treatment of animals with osteolytic
MM, but they have not yet been critically evaluated.
Large lesions can be treated with radiation therapy
(RT). In addition, fractures in weight‐bearing bones or
vertebrae require surgical stabilization alone or com­
bined with RT. Healing can occur, although it can be very
slow and only if local tumor control is achieved. Patients
presenting with a fever, other evidence of infection, or
severe neutropenia should be treated with broad‐spec­
trum antibiotics. Samples for culture and sensitivity
prior to antibiotic therapy should be collected if infec­
tion is suspected.
The treatment of choice for EMPs is usually surgical
resection. The cutaneous and mucosal EMPs are usually
benign and complete surgical excision carries an

excellent prognosis. In some cases, RT has been used for
nonresectable or recurrent EMPs as well as melphalan
and prednisone alone, or combined with RT. In cases
with SOP, surgical excision when possible or RT is the
treatment of choice. Fracture repair, or spinal cord
decompression and vertebral stabilization, followed by
RT could be considered when appropriate. Chemotherapy
may be used when RT is not available. Both modalities
have resulted in prolonged local control that is not nec­
essarily accompanied with bone remodeling.

­Prognosis
Two larger case series of dogs with MM, treated with
melphalan and prednisone, have been published to date,
32 years apart. One compared continuous and pulse pro­
tocols and found no statistically significant difference in
any of the outcome variables, although a small cohort size
and high numbers of censored dogs could have impacted
the results. In both studies, some dogs received an initial
dose of cyclophosphamide as well. In the first study
(Matus et al), a complete response (undetectable serum
monoclonal Ig) was observed in 43% of dogs, partial
response (≥ 50% decrease in Ig) in 49% and no response in
only 8%. The median survival time (MST) of all 37 dogs
was 540 days and the addition of cyclophosphamide did
not affect survival. In the second study (Fernandez et al),
overall response rate was similar (86%), but most were
defined as having a complete response. Median survival
time for all 38 dogs was 930 days, almost double the time
in the first study. Additionally, twelve dogs in the first
study were treated with prednisone alone and their MST
was 220 days. Matus reported that a response to treat­
ment with chemotherapy was positively associated with
survival. Hypercalcemia, Bence Jones proteinuria and
extensive bone lesions were negative prognostic ­indicators

for survival. Fernandez showed that renal disease and a
high blood neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio around the
time of diagnosis also negatively impacts survival. Ionized
hypercalcemia and osteolytic lesions among other factors
evaluated were not prognostic.
In cats, data are based on small numbers. Overall
remission rate is lower and survival times shorter com­
pared to dogs. A MST of 9.5 months was reported in one
study and no cat lived more than six months in another.
The prognosis for solitary cutaneous and mucocuta­
neous EMPs in dogs is generally good. Surgical excision
is curative in most cases. Local recurrence rate is
reported to be approximately 5% (higher for oral tumors),
nodal or systemic disease develops in 2% and new cuta­
neous EMPs occur in less than 2% of dogs. Cell type, pro­
liferation rate, presence of amyloid, and cyclin D1
reactivity have no prognostic significance in dogs. Dogs
with multiple cutaneous EMPs in the absence of MM
have been assigned a diagnosis of cutaneous plasmacyto­
sis (CP) based on the rare syndrome in humans, that usu­
ally follows an indolent course. In the first reported
series, 21 dogs with CP were treated with chemotherapy,
most with melphalan and prednisone. The overall
response rate was 74%, complete response was 37%,
median progression free survival was 143 days, but
median overall survival was longer at 542 days. None of
the dogs progressed to develop MM. In cats, EMP behav­
ior is less predictable. Some remain localized and surgi­
cal excision can lead to long‐term control while others
progress rapidly to MM.
As in humans, veterinary patients with successfully
treated SOP eventually develop local failure, new lesions
or MM but they can enjoy long disease‐free periods until
progression. It is important to thoroughly stage them at
initial diagnosis and to monitor routinely for local and
systemic relapse with serum globulin levels, careful atten­
tion to bone pain, and additional diagnostics if indicated.

Central Nervous System Tumors in Dogs and Cats
David Ruslander, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology), DACVR (Radiation Oncology)
Veterinary Specialty Hospital of the Carolinas, Cary, NC, USA

­Etiology/Epidemiology/Signalment
Central nervous system (CNS) tumors are infrequently
seen in dogs and cats but with increased imaging capabilities (computed tomography, magnetic resonance
imaging [MRI], etc.) and increased awareness of specific disease entities, there appears to be a subjective
rise in the incidence of diagnosis. By definition, the
CNS includes intracranial structures (brain and pituitary gland) as well as spinal cord. In these locations,
tumors are typically classified as either primary or
metastatic.

Other mutations that are commonly seen in human
brain tumors, including abnormal chromosome copy
number aberration (CAN), have also been reported,
indicating a possible similar etiology.
Historically, metastatic lesions to the CNS were
regarded as uncommon but with improvement in treatment of primary tumors and increased diagnostic capabilities, there appears to be a subjective rise. It is now
estimated that up to 50% of intracranial neoplasia in
dogs are metastatic in origin. The most common tumor
types are carcinomas, malignant melanoma, hemangiosarcoma, and lymphosarcoma.

Intracranial

Spinal Cord

The incidence of primary intracranial neoplasia in veterinary patients has been estimated to be 14.5/100 000 in
dogs and 3.5/100 000 in cats. The most common type in
the dog is meningioma, but glial tumors (astrocytoma
and oligodendroglioma), histiocytic sarcoma, choroid
plexus tumors, primitive neuroectodermal tumors
(PNET), and lymphoma can also occur. Meningioma
and lymphoma, followed by pituitary tumors, are the
most common primary tumors in cats.
Most dogs with primary neoplasia are >5 years of age
with the exceptions of lymphoma, which can occur at
any age, and glial tumors, which can occur in young dogs
due to their purported genetic predisposition. In the cat,
lymphoma can occur at any age, especially in young
feline leukemia virus (FeLV)‐positive cats.
Some dogs appear to be at higher risk for glial tumors,
such as boxers and other brachycephalic breeds. In one
recent study, it was reported that boxers represented
50% of all dogs receiving radiation therapy for a brain
tumor. In dogs, genetic mutations have been identified in
glial tumors, including the P53 tumor suppressor gene.

The incidence of spinal cord neoplasia in both species
has not been reported. In general, spinal tumors can be
described in terms of their anatomic location: extradural,
intradural/extramedullary, intramedullary, or mixed
compartment. In one large retrospective study of 399 histopathologically confirmed spinal cord tumors in dogs,
48% were extradural, 13% were intradural/extramedullary, 6% were intramedullary, and 33% were mixed
compartment.
The most common extradural primary spinal cord
tumor in the dog is meningioma, whereas in the cat it is
lymphoma followed by meningioma. Intramedullary
­spinal cord tumors are more likely to be primary (glial)
than metastatic, especially in younger dogs. Metastatic
intramedullary tumors are reported in both species and
are more common in older animals.
Spinal nephroblastoma is a specific malignancy that
arises from the embryonic remnants of the immature
kidney and typically occurs in young dogs (<3 years of
age). This tumor has a predilection for golden retrievers,
German shepherd dogs, and arctic breeds. It is most

often intradural/extramedullary and is located in the
caudal thoracolumbar region.
Spinal lymphoma often affects young cats, is associated with FeLV, tends to occur in an extradural location
in the thoracic and lumbar spine, and is usually present
in multiple locations outside the CNS. In dogs, CNS
lymphoma is sporadically identified. It is most commonly the T cell phenotype and located extradurally but
can be seen in any location.
Solitary spinal plasmactyomas (benign and malignant
proliferation of plasma cells) have been described in both
dogs and cats. Some lesions will remain solitary although
progression to systemic or multiple myeloma is possible.
Please refer to Chapter 135 for more information.
Carcinomas and hemangiosarcoma are the most commonly reported secondary spinal cord tumors in dogs.
Osteosarcoma is the most commonly reported in cats.
While initially thought to be very rare, the incidence of
metastatic lesions in the CNS has risen as diagnostic
imaging capabilities and control of the primary disease
have improved.

­History and Clinical Signs
Intracranial
Most patients with CNS neoplasia will present with
altered neurologic function (dull, nerve deficits, paresis,
etc.) but this is not universal. Some present with only
subtle symptoms such as lethargy, depression or neck
pain. Headaches are a common presenting symptom in
humans but recognition of this symptom in veterinary
patients is extremely difficult. Seizure or seizure‐like
activity as a presenting clinical finding is more common
in dogs than in cats.
Cats and dogs with pituitary tumors may present with
a variety of symptoms, many of which are nonneurologic
and relate to the endocrine abnormalities of hyperadrenocorticism (polyuria/polydipsia). In cats, unregulated
diabetes secondary to acromegaly is common due to
excessive growth hormone production. Initially, neurologic abnormalities may be subtle and limited to mild
lethargy and disorientation but often progress to more
severe abnormalities (seizures, mentation changes, neurologic deficits) with time.
Spinal Cord
Spinal cord neoplasia should be suspected in any patient
with a history of forelimb or hindlimb paresis or paralysis. Those presenting with spinal pain should also be suspect as pain is a common presenting symptom in both
cats and dogs. Onset of signs may be acute, as with lym-

phoma, but may be slowly progressive with more slowly
growing neoplasia such as meningioma.

­Diagnosis
Intracranial
All patients with neurologic symptoms should be considered as possible oncology cases. As such, a stepwise
approach is encouraged to allow for accurate staging and
identification of a primary tumor, if one exists, prior to
surgical intervention, radiation therapy or chemotherapy. Full blood analysis, urinalysis, three‐view thoracic
radiographs, and abdominal ultrasound should be performed prior to or in conjunction with advanced imaging (CT/MRI/positron emission tomography [PET]).
Magnetic resonance imaging has dramatically changed
the ability of the clinician to identify small subtle lesions
and as such is the preferred method of diagnosing brain
and spinal cord neoplasia. Improvement in technology
has increased the utility of CT imaging but MRI is still
recommended if available. Involvement and consultation
with a radiation oncologist early in the process will allow
for proper positioning of the patient should radiation
therapy be pursued. With MRI, the majority of dogs and
cats will have a hypo‐ to isointense lesion on T1‐weighted
and hyperintense on T2‐weighted images with a variable
amount of peritumoral edema. Contrast enhancement
with gadolinium is variable and more common with
high‐grade neoplasia given the disruption of the vasculature. Cystic lesions are more common with meningioma.
The presence of a “dural tail” on contrast‐enhanced T1
images has historically been associated with meningioma but can be seen with any neoplasia. This finding
results from thickening and contrast enhancement of
dural tissue extending from the primary tumor in a tail‐
like fashion. Other MRI and CT features of specific brain
neoplasia types have been described but there is considerable overlap among tumors (Figures 136.1 and 136.2).
With the exception of lymphoma, cerebrospinal fluid
(CSF) analysis is rarely useful in distinguishing neoplastic intracranial/spinal cord disease from inflammatory
lesions as it rarely reveals neoplastic cells. Analysis
often reveals increased protein levels, sometimes with
elevated cell counts. If CNS lymphoma is suspected,
more advanced testing of CSF such as antigen receptor
gene rearrangement and/or flow cytometry should be
pursued.
Histopathologic diagnosis of intracranial tumors
requires biopsy and the use of stereotactic CT guidance
in obtaining the sample. This advanced procedure has
become more commonplace. Associated complication
rates are reported to range from 12% to 27% with a 5–9%

136 Central Nervous System Tumors in Dogs and Cats

VetBooks.ir

mortality rate, but will continue to decrease as experience with the procedure increases. Currently, not all
patients receive histopathologic confirmation due to the
cost and risk of potential complications. To mitigate
some risk, cytology can be considered instead but this
too is not commonly performed. Hence many patients
are treated without a true diagnosis.
Dogs with suspected hyperadrenocorticism and cats
with suspected acromegaly or insulin resistance should
be evaluated with CT or MRI. Small pituitary masses
may escape detection with CT but larger lesions can be
detected with CT especially with newer generation CT
imagers.
Spinal Cord

Figure 136.1 T1‐weighted post‐contrast (gadolinium) coronal
image of a frontal lobe mass in a 9‐year‐old, male, golden
retriever. Surgical excision was performed. Histopathology was
consistent with histiocytic sarcoma. The dog’s only symptom
was acute onset of seizures.

As with intracranial neoplasia, full staging including
three‐view thoracic radiographs, full blood analysis,
urinalysis, and abdominal ultrasound should be performed before or in conjunction with advanced imaging (CT/MRI/PET). Survey spinal radiographs should
be performed to evaluate for possible bony lysis.
Although rarely helpful, lysis may be present and may
indicate a neoplastic process is emanating from outside the CNS with secondary invasion to spinal cord, as
in the case of skeletal neoplasia (osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma) or rarely soft tissue tumors (soft tissue
sarcomas, carcinomas). As with intracranial tumors,
due to cost, need for advanced diagnostic equipment
and risk of potential complications, many patients
with spinal neoplasia are treated without a definitive
diagnosis.

­Treatment/Prognosis
Central nervous system neoplasia, like other tumors, can
be managed with a combination of surgery, radiation,
and chemotherapy. However, the veterinary literature is
limited to uncontrolled and retrospective studies based
on relatively small numbers of patients.
Medical Management

Figure 136.2 T1‐weighted postcontrast (gadolinium) sagittal
image of a cervical spinal cord tumor in an 11‐year‐old male
castrated boxer, presenting for acute tetraparesis with associated
neck pain. The mass is consistent with a meningioma given the
extraaxial location and presence of a dural tail at the caudal
extent of the mass. Surgical excision and biopsy were not
performed. The dog received 48 Gy radiation therapy (16 × 3 Gy)
and adjuvant hydroxyurea with nearly complete resolution of the
neurologic signs/neck pain and was alive two years following
treatment.

Nonspecific treatment options include antiinflammatory doses of corticosteroids for peritumoral edema and
anticonvulsant therapy if seizures are a component of the
clinical presentation. Phenobarbital, Keppra® (levetiracetam), and zonisamide are all options for control
of seizures. Unfortunately, supportive care alone is associated with a poor prognosis in the vast majority of
patients. Published survival times in such a group are
generally between one and 10 weeks but individual
patients may far exceed this.

VetBooks.ir

1250

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

Surgery
Intracranial

Depending on the location, surgical intervention is recommended as a sole therapy for well‐circumscribed
meningiomas or a prelude to postoperative radiation
therapy and/or chemotherapy. Surgery alone for meningioma in dogs is associated with a median survival time
of 4.5–7 months. Radiation therapy in the postoperative
setting has increased that median to 16–30 months.
Other surgical techniques such as ultrasonic aspiration
or endoscopic‐assisted surgical resection have resulted
in survival times of 41 and 70 months in dogs, demonstrating the utility of more aggressive approaches.
Surgery as sole therapy for nonmeningioma tumors is
more variable, case dependent, and generally results in
median survival times of months rather than years.
Meningioma in the cat is often less aggressive and
invasive compared to the dog. Hence, the prognosis with
surgery as sole therapy is good to very good with median
survival times of 23–28 months.
Surgical approaches to the pituitary gland (transsphenoidal hypophysectomy) have been described but management is usually accomplished with fractionated
external beam radiation therapy or more recently radiosurgical techniques in both dogs and cats.
Spinal Cord

Outcomes in dogs and cats with spinal cord neoplasia
are understandably highly variable and there is considerable perioperative mortality due to poor return to function. Overall median survival in one study of 37 dogs was
240 days if they survived 20 days following surgery, but
40% did not survive to that point. In a separate study
evaluating surgery for intraspinal meningioma, clinical
improvement was noted in all dogs surviving the perioperative period but recurrence of clinical signs was at a
mean of 19 months. Only a minority were disease free
long term, thus indicating the need for postoperative
radiation therapy. Postoperative radiation therapy did
appear to have a benefit based on time to neurologic
deterioration but recurrence of signs and/or tumor was
still noted anywhere from 18 to 36 months. In cats
undergoing surgical treatment of spinal cord tumors,
improvement was reported in 25/26 cases but the median
survival time for those with malignant neoplasms was
110.5 days, compared with 518 days for those with
benign tumors. In this study, the vast majority of cats
eventually succumbed to disease‐related problems.
Radiation Therapy
Radiation therapy has evolved over the past several decades from relatively unsophisticated planning techniques

to the current state utilizing 3D computer planning and
modern technology. Long‐term efficacy of radiation
therapy alone is limited given the tolerance of the brain
and as macroscopic tumor control is generally not as
rewarding as adjunctive treatment following cytoreductive surgery. Table 136.1 gives a summary of treatment‐
related outcomes of CNS tumors.
Recently, stereotactic radiosurgical (SRS) approaches
have been employed which allow for one or two fractions
of high‐dose radiation to be delivered rather than the
conventional 15–25 daily fractions of lower doses per
fraction. This high dose per fraction is limited to the
tumor and a small volume of normal surrounding tissue.
This form of treatment theoretically minimizes the risk
of complications to normal tissues while providing ablative doses to the tumor. SRS is still in the investigational
stage in veterinary oncology and direct comparison to
conventional fractionated radiation therapy has not been
performed. However, preliminary results in the literature
are encouraging and the shortened overall treatment
times and minimal dose to noninvolved tissues are
attractive to both clinicians and owners and SRS likely
represents the future of radiation therapy for brain
neoplasia.
Side‐Effects

Acute and late developing radiotherapy side‐effects vary
depending on total dose given, dose per fraction, and the
total volume and specific tissue type being irradiated.
Late‐term side‐effects are rare (<20%) but when they
occur, management is challenging as they are often life‐
threatening. Of the late effects, brain necrosis is the most
common but others including spinal cord myelopathy
can occur. Unfortunately, the clinical distinction between
these late side‐effects and tumor recurrence is difficult
and often requires histopathology.
Acute side‐effects of CNS irradiation are rare and
often limited to surrounding normal structures in the
treatment field such as the oral cavity, otic and ocular
structures, and gastrointestinal tract. A syndrome of
delayed acute CNS effects can be seen several months
after completion of radiation therapy and are manifested
by responsiveness to corticosteroids. This syndrome is
thought to be a transient demyelination of the white matter rather than true necrosis which is the more classic
delayed effect.
Intracranial

Due to the limitations of available veterinary clinical
studies, the prognosis following irradiation of many primary intracranial tumors, especially those of glial origin,
is largely unknown (see Table 136.1). Based on what has
been reported, median survival time following irradiation may range from four months to greater than four

Spinal Cord

Radiation therapy of spinal cord tumors has been
described in the veterinary literature but studies are limited by low case numbers and lack of histopathologic
confirmation in the majority of patients. As with intracranial irradiation, a similar limitation of dose is encountered in the spinal cord and control times are affected by
the spinal cord tolerance.
In one study, primary radiation therapy for spinal cord
tumors (no histopathologic confirmation) resulted in
median control of nine months. In a separate study evaluating surgery for spinal meningioma, those that underwent postoperative radiation therapy appeared to have a
benefit based on time to neurologic deterioration but
recurrence of signs and/or tumor recurrence was noted
anywhere from 18 to 36 months. It is important to recall
that deterioration of neurologic condition may be related
to tumor recurrence but may also be related to spinal
cord damage/necrosis. Therefore, documentation of
true tumor recurrence is recommended prior to considering repeat irradiation and/or surgical intervention.
Chemotherapy
There is very little in the veterinary literature regarding
chemotherapy for CNS neoplasia with the exception of
standard chemotherapy for canine and feline lymphoma.
The blood–brain barrier represents a significant obstacle to the delivery of chemotherapy to the brain and spinal cord. Survival times of dogs with unconfirmed (no
biopsy) brain tumors treated with lomustine (CCNU)
were very similar to patients treated with supportive care
alone (93 vs 60 days).

Hydroxyurea is an alkylating agent most commonly
used in veterinary medicine for the management of polycythemia. Recently, it has been used as an adjuvant to
surgery and/or radiation therapy for dogs with intracranial and spinal meningioma. In one such study, oral
hydroxyurea in combination with glucocorticoids was
administered to 33 dogs with MRI‐diagnosed meningioma, resulting in a significantly longer survival time than
observed in 10 dogs treated with glucocorticoids alone.
Temozolamide has recently been evaluated in management of canine glial tumors. Although the data in
veterinary oncology are preliminary and no strong
recommendations can be made regarding efficacy and
comparison with other chemotherapy approaches
­cannot be made, results in the human literature are
encouraging.
For patients with CNS lymphoma, options in addition
to standard chemotherapy include lomustine, hydroxyurea, and the antimetabolite cytosine arabinoside which
cross the blood–brain barrier. The role of chemotherapy
specifically for spinal cord neoplasia is not known, but
similar chemotherapeutics are recommended depending
on final diagnosis when possible.
Newer Therapies
With increased understanding of how the immune system functions in tumor environments, immunotherapy,
in particular tumor vaccination and gene therapy,
has recently been developed to aid in the treatment
of canine brain tumors but these approaches remain
investigational.

Cancer of the Nose and Mouth
Lauren Askin Quarterman, DVM, DACVR (Radiation Oncology)
PetCure Oncology, San Jose, CA, USA

­Oral Tumors
Etiology/Pathophysiology
A wide variety of malignant and benign cancers develop
in the oral cavity. In dogs, the most common malignant
oral tumors in order of frequency are malignant melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and fibrosarcoma. In
cats, squamous cell carcinoma is the most common oral
cancer, with fibrosarcoma second. Risk factors for the
development of oral squamous cell carcinomas in cats
include flea collars and high intake of either canned food
or, specifically, canned tuna fish.
Oral malignant melanoma (OMM) is a highly malignant tumor with frequent metastasis to regional lymph
nodes and lungs. Metastasis has been reported in
80–100% of cases, and is associated with site, size, and
stage of tumor. Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) frequently invades bone in both the dog and cat. The metastatic rate for nontonsillar SCC in the dog is approximately
20% but nearly 100% of cases with tonsillar SCC metastasize to the retropharyngeal lymph nodes. The metastatic
rate of oral SCC in the cat is unknown, as control of local
disease in cats is rarely achieved. Oral fibrosarcomas
(FSA) are locally invasive but rarely (<30%) metastasize
to regional lymph nodes or lungs. At times, these tumors
may histologically appear benign and may be reported as
a fibroma or low‐grade fibrosarcoma. A well‐described
syndrome in large‐breed dogs, occurring most commonly on the hard palate and maxillary arcade, has been
termed “histologically low‐grade, biologically high grade”
fibrosarcoma. Despite the benign histologic appearance
of these tumors, they tend to grow rapidly, metastasize,
and invade bone. Rapid recurrence is common.
Epulides are relatively common neoplasms in dogs, but
rare in cats. Epulides appear similar to gingival hyperplasia. In general, four types of epulides have been described

in the dog: fibromatous, ossifying, acanthomatous, and
giant cell. The nomenclature is unfortunately confusing
and varied, and the clinician is encouraged to speak
directly to the pathologist if there are any questions over
terminology. The term epulis strictly refers to expansile
gingival lesions; more recently, it has been shown that
some of these tumors do not involve the periodontal ligament, with many of the fibromatous and ossifying types
being derived from the gingiva only. Periodontal odontogenic fibroma has recently been accepted as the correct
terminology to use to classify both the fibromatous epulis
and ossifying epulis, as these epulides are variations of the
same lesion. Also, the acanthomatous epulis has recently
been renamed acanthomatous ameloblastoma. A study in
2011 characterized the clinicopathologic features in 153
dogs with oral tumors of possible ondontogenic origin
and found that the three most common lesions were
canine acanthomatous ameloblastoma, peripheral odontogenic fibroma, and focal fibrous hyperplasia which is a
reactive lesion resulting from chronic inflammation.
Acanthomatous ameloblastoma is a benign tumor with
aggressive local behavior and frequent invasion into underlying bone. The rostral mandible is the most common site.
Fibromatous and ossifying epulides, unlike acanthomatous
ameloblastoma, are noninvasive. They are slow‐growing,
firm masses and are usually covered by intact epithelium.
Ossifying epulides usually have a broad base attachment
and are less pendunculated than fibromatous epulides.
These two epulides vary histologically by the presence or
absence of bone formation within the tumor.
Epidemiology
The oral cavity is the site of approximately 6% of all
­neoplasms in dogs, and oral cancer is the fourth most
common cancer overall. In cats, cancer of the oral cavity
accounts for 3–12% of all cancers.

Signalment
In contrast to other malignant oral tumors, OMM tends
to occur in smaller breed dogs as well as some large
breeds, with an average age at presentation of 12 years.
Cocker spaniel, miniature poodle, Anatolian sheepdog,
Gordon setter, chow chow, and golden retriever are overrepresented. The average age of a dog presenting with an
oral SCC is 8–10 years, while the average age for a cat is
10–12 years. Oral FSAs tend to occur in large‐breed
dogs, particularly the golden and Labrador retriever. The
average age at presentation is 7–9 years and there appears
to be a male predisposition. Dogs presenting with
fibromatous and ossifying epulides are typically 8–9
years, and a male predisposition has been reported.
Shetland and old English sheepdogs are predisposed to
acanthomatous ameloblastomas. The average age at
presentation is 7–10 years, and a sex predisposition is
not reported.
History and Clinical Signs
Cats and dogs with rostral oral cancer commonly present for a mass noted by the owner. Cancer in the caudal
oral cavity is rarely noted by owners and the animals
often present at an advanced stage of disease, resulting in
fewer options for treatment. Clinical signs may include
hypersalivation, exophthalmos or facial swelling,
epistaxis, weight loss, halitosis, bloody oral discharge,
dysphagia or pain on opening the mouth. Occasionally,
cervical lymphadenopathy (especially in squamous cell
carcinoma of the tonsil) is also found. Complete oral
examinations should always be performed during health
exams as early intervention may allow for more treatment options and an improved prognosis.
Diagnosis
Due to the wide range of cancer behavior and recommended treatment options for oral cancers, diagnostic
evaluation is critical. A biopsy is required for the definitive diagnosis, and this will assist the clinician in determining the biologic behavior and prognosis of the tumor.
Impression smear or fine needle aspirate cytology preparations of the tumor are generally not rewarding, as
many oral tumors are associated with a high degree of
necrosis and inflammation. Most animals will require a
short general anesthesia for careful mass evaluation,
regional radiographs, and biopsy. An incisional biopsy of
the mass is recommended.
Advanced imaging is recommended for oral tumors
arising from the maxilla, palate, and caudal mandible.
Computed tomography (CT) scans are generally preferred to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) because of
