superior bone detail. Both provide more information on
the local extent of the tumor than regional radiographs.
Information obtained from CT or MRI is critical in the
planning of definitive surgery and radiation.
Regional lymph nodes should be carefully palpated for
enlargement or asymmetry. Caution should be exercised,
however, when making clinical judgments based on palpation alone, as lymph node size is not an accurate predictor of metastasis. Lymph node aspirates should be
performed in all animals with oral cancers, regardless of
their size or mobility. Three‐view thoracic radiographs
are recommended to evaluate animals for evidence of
pulmonary metastatic disease. Thoracic CT scans should
be considered for animals with highly metastatic tumor
types such as OMM, since CT scans are more sensitive
for detecting pulmonary metastatic lesions. Based on
these diagnostic steps, oral tumors are then staged
according to the World Health Organization’s staging
scheme (WHO) (Table 137.1).
Therapy
Surgery

Surgical resection is the gold standard for oral tumors
and is the most commonly used modality for achieving
local control. The surgical approach depends on tumor
type and location. The majority of tumors involving the
maxilla, mandible, and hard palate will have underlying
bone involvement so surgical resection should include
bony margins to increase the likelihood of complete
excision. Minimum margins of at least 2 cm, and preferably 3 cm, are recommended for malignant tumors such
as SCC, OMM, and FSA in the dog.
Radiation Therapy

Radiation therapy can be used with palliative or curative
intent, or as an adjunct to surgery for incompletely
resected tumors or tumors with aggressive local behavior. Radiation therapy can be considered a primary treatment of canine oral SCC, OMM, and some benign tumors
such as epulides. These tumors are radiation responsive,
even when treated in the setting of gross ­
disease.
Radiation protocols used for the treatment of these
tumors have involved daily or alternate‐day treatments

VetBooks.ir

137 Cancer of the Nose and Mouth

consisting of 2.7–4.2 Gy per fraction with a total dose
ranging from 48 Gy to 57 Gy. More recently, stereotactic
radiation is being used as treatment of non-resectable
oral tumors. Protocols typically consist of 1-3 high doses
of radiation precisely targeted at the tumor, with rapid
dose fall off outside of the tumor. These protocols are
proving to provide durable control of disease, with
decreased acute side effects when compared to traditional radiation protocols; however published studies are
still limited.
When using radiation therapy alone, tumor control is
better achieved with smaller lesions (T1 or T2 tumors).
With megavoltage radiation, local recurrence is reported
in up to 30% of cases. When compared to T1 tumors,
tumor progression is three times more likely with T2
tumors and 5–8 times more likely with T3 tumors. Local
tumor control and survival time, however, can be
improved by combining surgery and radiation therapy.
Acute radiation side‐effects are common during treatment of oral tumors, but these are generally self‐limiting.
They can include alopecia and moist desquamation, oral
mucositis, dysphagia and ocular changes such as blepharitis, conjunctivitis, keratitis, and uveitis. Late side‐effects
are rare (<5%), but are much more serious as they are
permanent. Late side‐effects include skin fibrosis, bone
necrosis and oronasal fistula formation, development of
a second malignancy within the radiation field, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, cataract formation, and ocular
atrophy.
Chemotherapy

Frontline treatment for most oral tumors is control of
local disease with surgery and/or radiation therapy.
Chemotherapy is indicated for some tumors due to their
high metastatic potential. OMM and tonsillar SCC are
both highly metastatic tumors, but unfortunately their
response to chemotherapy is low.
The nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drug piroxicam, a
COX‐2 inhibitor, has been shown to have some effect
against canine oral SCC. Expression of COX‐2 has also
been noted in feline oral SCC, but no improvement has
been seen in the management of these tumors when
piroxicam has been used.
Immunotherapy

A DNA vaccine against tyrosinase is now commercially
available for the adjunctive treatment of dogs with
OMM. To maximize chances of long‐term survival, it
has been found that the vaccine is most effective when
residual disease is minimized and local regional control
has been achieved. Adverse reactions following administration of the vaccine have been found to be minimal,
with the most notable side‐effects consisting of bruising
and hematoma formation.

Prognosis
Malignant Melanoma

The prognosis for dogs with oral malignant melanoma is
guarded. In one study, median survival time (MST) of
dogs with untreated oral melanomas was two months.
Aggressive resection by mandibulectomy or maxillectomy can be effective for control of these tumors but
postsurgical recurrence has been reported to develop in
8–85% of dogs and metastasis to regional lymph nodes,
lungs, or other viscera may develop in as many as 95%.
Metastasis, particularly to the lungs, is the most common cause of death, being reported in 15–67% of dogs.
Median survival times for dogs with OMM treated with
surgery are approximately 17–18 months, 5–6 months,
and three months with stage I, II, and III disease,
respectively.
Coarse fraction radiation treatment effectively
achieves local control in dogs with melanomas.
Reduction in tumor size is attained in 83–100% of dogs,
and a complete response rate has been reported to be as
high as 70%. In a retrospective study of 140 dogs with
OMM treated with radiation therapy, it was found that
systemic chemotherapy had no impact on the development of metastatic disease, time to first event, or survival. In the same study, tumor location, bone lysis, and
tumor volume were all variables identified to predict
time to first event and survival. If none of these risks
were present, median survival for dogs with malignant
melanomas treated with radiation therapy was 21
months, and if one, two, or three risk variables were present, median survival time was 11 months, five months,
or three months, respectively.
The use of immunotherapy for malignant melanoma is
showing some promise, but most results involve small
numbers of dogs in phase I trials. Xenogeneic vaccine
studies for dogs with stage I–III OMM report median
survival times of almost three years when local regional
control had been achieved and patients received vaccine
versus 1.5 years when patients were given the same
­vaccine, but failed locally.
Canine Squamous Cell Carcinoma

Following mandibulectomy for canine nontonsillar SCC,
the median survival ranges from 19 to 26 months versus
10–19 months following a maxillectomy. Tonsillar SCC
carries a graver prognosis. Due to higher local recurrence and metastatic rates, studies report one‐year
­survival times of only 10%.
Full‐course radiation therapy, either alone or as an
adjunct following incomplete surgical resection, is also a
successful treatment modality for the management of
oral SCC in dogs. With full‐course radiation, a study of
39 dogs reported an overall median progression‐free

1255

VetBooks.ir

1256

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

survival time of 36 months. Local tumor recurrence was
a more common cause of first treatment failure than
regional metastasis to lymph nodes. Dogs with T1, T2,
and T3 tumors had a progression free, one‐year survival
rate of 89%, 83%, and 41% respectively, and a three‐year
progression‐free survival rate of 74%, 53%, and 23%,
respectively. A study of 14 dogs treated with full‐course
radiation therapy as the primary treatment modality
reported median disease‐free interval and survival of 12
and 14 months, respectively. The median disease‐free
interval was 16 months in dogs 9 years or less, and seven
months in dogs older than 9 years of age.
Feline Squamous Cell Carcinoma

The prognosis for feline SCC is poor, as there is no
known consistent, effective treatment for gaining local
control. In one series of 52 cats, the one‐year survival
rate was less than 10% with median survival times of
three months for surgery, surgery and radiation therapy,
radiation therapy and low‐dose chemotherapy, and radiation therapy with hyperthermia. Other studies investigating surgery alone, have reported median survival
times of 5.5–7.5 months, but only tumors of the mandible were considered resectable. In a separate study the
combination of surgery and radiation reported a survival
time of 14 months. All cases were arising from the
mandible.
Radiation therapy alone is generally ineffective in the
management of cats with oral SCC. However, the combination of radiation with radiation sensitizers or chemotherapy has resulted in response rates from 70% to 100%
and median survival times of approximately 3–6 months.
A recent prospective study including 31 cases of oral
SCC in cats evaluated the effectiveness of an accelerated
radiation therapy protocol and concomitant carboplatin
for treatment. Median survival for all cats in this study
was 5.4 months, while cats with tumors of tonsillar origin or cheek responded best to therapy with a mean survival of two years.
Fibrosarcoma

The prognosis for dogs with oral fibrosarcoma is guarded.
Multimodal treatment with surgery and radiation therapy
of the local disease results in the best survival rates.
Following maxillectomy or mandibulectomy alone, local
recurrence is reported in up to 60% of dogs with a median
survival time of 10–12 months and a one‐year survival rate
of 50%. Oral fibrosarcomas are considered to be radiation
resistant. A smaller tumor size improves the outcome following radiation therapy, with the median progression‐free
survival time of 45 months for dogs with T1 tumors compared to 31 months and seven months for T2 and T3
tumors, respectively. When radiation therapy is used as an

adjunct to surgery, a median survival time of 18–26 months
is reported. A study completed in 2011 reported the outcome in 29 dogs with oral fibrosarcomas treated with surgical excision with or without adjuvant radiation. The
median survival time in this study was reported to be
approximately two years with a one‐ and two‐year progression‐free survival rate of 88% and 58%, respectively.
Epulides

The prognosis for dogs with epulides is excellent following treatment with either surgery or radiation therapy. In
contrast to fibromatous and ossifying epulides, wide
local excision of adjacent soft tissue and bone is necessary for cure of acanthomatous ameloblastomas. Local
recurrence rate following bone‐removing surgery is less
than 5%.
Radiation therapy is indicated for acanthomatous
ameloblastomas that are not curable with surgery alone.
In a prospective clinical trial, 47 dogs with acanthomatous ameloblastomas (39 dogs) or fibromatous or ossifying epulides (eight dogs) were treated with 12 fractions
of 4 Gy, three times a week to a total dose of 48 Gy.
Clinical stage was the only significant prognostic factor,
with dogs that had stage T3 tumors having a 7.9 times
higher risk of tumor recurrence than dogs with stage T1.
In a 2004 study of 57 dogs treated with radiation therapy,
the median overall survival time was four years.
Intralesional bleomycin has also been described for the
treatment of acanthomatous ameloblastomas. With this
treatment, a complete response was sustained in all four
dogs treated for greater than one year with no local
recurrence.

­Nasal Tumors
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Carcinomas, including adenocarcinoma, squamous cell
carcinoma, and undifferentiated carcinoma, comprise
nearly two‐thirds of nasal tumors in the dog while sarcomas, including fibrosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, and undifferentiated sarcoma, comprise the
bulk of the remaining tumors. In the cat, lymphoma and
carcinoma are the most common tumors of the nasal
cavity. It has been speculated that dogs living in urban
environments may be at higher risk for developing nasal
tumors, and some studies have also associated the exposure of environmental tobacco smoke as an increased
risk factor, but this finding is not consistent. Nasal lymphoma in cats is typically feline leukemia virus (FeLV)
antigen negative, and definite risk factors have not been
reported.

VetBooks.ir

137 Cancer of the Nose and Mouth

Nasal tumors are locally invasive tumors that carry a
relatively low metastatic rate. Metastasis at the time of
diagnosis is seen in approximately 10% of animals, but
may be as high as 40–50% at the time of death. Death,
however, is usually attributable to local disease progression rather than metastatic lesions. Most common sites
of metastasis are the regional lymph nodes and lungs.
Less common sites include bones, kidneys, liver, skin,
and brain.
Epidemiology
Nasal tumors account for approximately 1% of all neoplasms in dogs and cats.
Signalment
The average age at the time of diagnosis for canine and
feline nasal tumors is 10 years. It appears that medium‐
and large‐breed dogs may be more commonly affected.
Also, a slight male predilection has been suggested in dogs,
and dolichocephalic breeds may be at an increased risk.
History and Clinical Signs
The most common clinical signs associated with nasal
tumors include epistaxis, bloody or mucopurulent nasal
discharge, facial deformity, sneezing, dyspnea, stertorous breathing, exophthalmia, and ocular discharge secondary to obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct. The
average duration of clinical signs before diagnosis is
three months. All of these clinical signs can overlap with
other intranasal diseases, but a strong suspicion for cancer should be made in older animals with an intermittent
and progressive history of initially unilateral and/or
mucopurulent discharge.
Diagnosis
Definitive diagnosis of a nasal tumor requires a tissue
biopsy but historical information and diagnostic imaging
can be highly suggestive of cancer. Conventional radiography can be helpful in the diagnostic evaluation of dogs,
but CT is preferred as it provides improved anatomic
detail, determination of the extent of the tumor, and
identification of nasal cavity abnormalities. A CT scan
also allows for detection of CNS invasion. Certain findings on CT are correlated with a diagnosis of cancer in
dogs, but none of these alone or in combination are
definitively diagnostic. A tissue biopsy is always required.
Once a definitive diagnosis has been made, fine needle
aspirates of regional lymph nodes should be completed,
along with three‐view thoracic radiographs.

Several staging systems based on radiographic or
CT findings have been proposed in canine nasal
tumors but their prognostic significance remains
controversial. The Adams modified staging system
­
developed in 2009 is the most recent system that has
been adapted (Table 137.2). With this system, dogs
with unilateral intranasal involvement confined to the
nasal cavity had the longest median survival time of
23.4 months when treated with definitive radiotherapy. Those with cribriform involvement had the
­shortest median survival time of 6.7 months.
Therapy
Treatment of nasal tumors is directed primarily at the
control of local disease. Unfortunately, the disease is often
extensive. Curative surgery is not possible as bone invasion occurs early in the course of the disease. Hence, radiation therapy is the standard of care. The combination of a
cytoreductive surgery followed by radiation therapy for
the treatment of nasal tumors has been evaluated, but has
not been shown to improve clinical outcome in dogs when
compared to megavoltage radiation alone.
With definitive or curative intent radiation, the goal of
treatment is to deliver the maximum radiation dose to the
tumor while minimizing the dose to surrounding normal
tissues. Most radiation therapy done in veterinary medicine involves the use of conventional computerized treatment planning. However, with advances in the field of
radiation oncology, the use of intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) has proven to be a very good option
for the treatment of nasal tumors. IMRT allows for the
optimization of radiation dose delivery to complex tumor
volumes with rapid dose drop-off to surrounding normal
tissues. When IMRT is used, normal tissue toxicities are
greatly reduced while higher cumulative doses of radiation
are delivered to the tumor. Traditional definitive protocols
involve the administration of a total radiation dose of 40-57
Gy in 10-19 fractions of 3-4.2 Gy, over a 2-4 week period.

Computerized treatment planning using CT images of the
patient are recommended to enhance normal tissue sparing while ensuring appropriate dose distributions within
the tumor. For IMRT, CT and computer planning is
required. Stereotactic radiation, which is similar to IMRT,
is the specific treatment of choice for most nasal tumors.
Protocols consist of the precision delivery of curative intent
therapy in 1-3 high dose fractions.
With stereotactic and/or traditionally fractionated
IMRT, acute toxicities that effect the rapidly dividing tissue
of the oral cavity, nasal cavity, skin, and eye can be seen, but
are typically very limited. Oral antibiotics, analgesics, and/
or artificial tears can be used as needed to counteract and
support any treatment related side effect. Life limiting late
side effects such as bone or brain necrosis are possible, but
the risk is expected to be less than 5%.
Palliative radiation therapy can also be considered for the
treatment of nasal tumors. With palliative radiation protocols, side‐effects are limited. Alleviation of clinical signs has
been reported in up to 95% of dogs treated, with median
survival times reported to be approximately 4–6 months.
Chemotherapy has also been evaluated for the treatment of
nasal tumors in dogs. Clinical responses are seen with
chemotherapy, but the response is usually not durable.
Prognosis
Canine Nasal Tumors

The long‐term prognosis for dogs with nasal tumors is
very dependent on the treatment pursued. A retrospective study of 139 dogs with nasal tumor evaluated
those that did not receive therapy. Their overall median
survival time was approximately three months. This
study also found that dogs presenting with epistaxis
had a significantly shorter median survival time than
those without epistaxis. Surgery as the sole treatment
of nasal tumors results in a median survival time of
only 3–6 months, with a high rate of acute and chronic
morbidity. Curative‐intent, high‐energy megavoltage
radiation alone results in a median survival time of
8–19.7 months, with one‐ and two‐year survival rates
ranging from 43% to 60% and 11% to 44%, respectively.
The combination of surgery followed by postoperative
radiation reports survival times ranging from 4.1
months to 15.2 months, adding no benefit to radiation
therapy alone. In a small series of 13 dogs that underwent preoperative radiation followed by surgical exenteration of residual disease, a survival advantage was
demonstrated (MST 47 months). However, these

patients experienced significant late side‐effects
including rhinitis (bacterial and fungal), osteomyelitis,
and fistula formation. A study in 2011 evaluated definitive reirradiation of nine dogs with nasal tumors and
found that reirradiation is a viable treatment option for
canine nasal tumors with tolerable acute and late side‐
effects. The MST time for the patients in this study was
30 months.
Feline Nasal Tumors

Reports of treatment for feline nasal tumors are
­lacking. One study including 16 cats with nonlymphoproliferative neoplasms treated with a definitive
course of radiation to a total dose of 48 Gy reported
a MST of 12 months. This treatment resulted in
­minimal acute side‐effects and modest chronic ocular
side‐effects. When radiation therapy protocols are
used for the treatment of feline nasal lymphoma,
long‐term control of local disease is favorable and it
has been reported that higher total doses (greater or
equal to 32 Gy) of radiation therapy may confer an
additional survival benefit. The role of chemotherapy
for the treatment of feline nasal lymphoma is undefined. Median survival times for cats receiving radiation therapy +/‐ chemotherapy for the treatment of
nasal lymphoma range from 13 to 31 months.

­Cancer of the Pharynx
Pharyngeal tumors are rare and little information has
been reported in literature. In cats, lymphosarcoma
is the most commonly reported. In dogs, extramedullary plasma cell tumor, osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, fibrosarcoma, and carcinomas have all been
reported. Malignant tumors of the pharynx are more
common; however, benign tumors have been reported
in dogs. These include rhabdomyoma, angioleiomyoma, and oncocytoma. Rhabdomyomas are minimally invasive and have a predilection for young
male dogs.
Surgery is the treatment of choice for pharyngeal
tumors. Many benign tumors can be removed while
preserving function, while radical procedures such as
permanent tracheostomy and complete laryngectomy
are required for malignant tumors. Chemotherapy
and radiation therapy can also be considered. Surgical
removal of pharyngeal rhabdomyoma is often considered curative.

Tumors of the Eye and Ocular Adnexa
Erin M. Scott, DVM, DACVO1 and Paul E. Miller, DVM, DACVO2

Department of Small Animal Clinical Sciences, College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
Department of Surgical Sciences, School of Veterinary Medicine, University of Wisconsin‐Madison, Madison, WI, USA

­Tumors of the Ocular Adnexa
Tumors of the eye, orbit, or adnexa may be painful and
disfiguring, impair vision, and elicit concern that life‐
threatening disease may be present elsewhere in the
body. Even benign ocular tumors may cause blindness
and loss of the eye simply by virtue of their location.
Although both ocular and periocular tumors are reportedly uncommon, their actual frequency is undoubtedly
greater as most presumably benign ocular tumors,
especially those affecting the canine eyelid, are not histologically examined. Histopathologic examination, however,
is essential to ensure proper diagnosis and treatment.
Eyelids, Third Eyelid, Conjunctiva, and Cornea
The etiology of ocular adnexal tumors is poorly understood
but suspected causes include chronic inflammation, exposure to ultraviolet light, and viral infection (e.g., papillomavirus). In dogs, more than 85% of eyelid and conjunctival
neoplasms consist of sebaceous or meibomian gland adenomas and epitheliomas, papillomas, and melanomas. The
substantial majority of these tumors are benign. Even histologically malignant canine eyelid tumors rarely metastasize,
although they may be more locally invasive and likely to
recur after surgery. In cats, however, most feline eyelid and
ocular surface tumors are malignant.
Meibomian Gland Adenoma/Epithelioma

Although rare in other species, benign meibomian gland
adenomas and epitheliomas are the most common eyelid
margin tumor in middle‐aged to older dogs. They may
grow rapidly, first starting as a nodular swelling of the
meibomian gland and eventually appearing as a proliferative mass exiting the meibomian gland orifice on the
lid margin.

Papillomas

In contrast, viral papillomas appear as verrucous masses
originating from the conjunctiva in young dogs. They are
well demarcated, superficial, and grow rapidly. Surgical
manipulation has been reported to disperse new papillomas over the ocular s­urface. Papillomas, like histiocytomas, usually resolve spontaneously in young dogs,
although persistence in older dogs is common. Other
forms of benign papillomas in dogs include squamous
papillomas, which are of unknown etiology and occur
at any age, as well as reactive papillomas, which are seen
secondary to other conditions that result in chronic
irritation.
Squamous Cell Carcinoma

Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) has a predilection for
the lower eyelid and medial canthus of white cats, and
comprises the majority of feline eyelid and third eyelid
tumors. It is less frequently reported in dogs, however, in
both species it tends to affect older animals. Predisposing
factors include exposure to solar radiation, lack of
adnexal pigmentation, and chronic ocular surface irritation. Ocular surface SCC has a predilection for the limbus, although it may also invade the cornea. SCC appears
as a focally thickened, roughened, pink‐to‐red lesion or
as an ulcerated lesion which is slow to heal. Metastasis to
regional lymph nodes occurs late in the course of disease
and distant metastasis is uncommon. SCC of the third
eyelid tends to more readily invade the orbit than ocular
surface or eyelid SCC (Figure 138.1a).
Hemangioma/Hemangiosarcoma

Adnexal vascular endothelial tumors are uncommon in
dogs and rare in cats. As with ocular surface SCC, solar
radiation is believed to be a risk factor. They usually
arise from the nonpigmented conjunctiva of the lateral

relatively superficial, focal, raised, soft, red masses
with visible feeder vessels (Figure 138.1b). Ulceration
is common in larger masses. Metastasis of primary
­conjunctival vascular tumors, even when classified as
hemangiosarcoma, is rare although it may recur following simple excision. It is critical to differentiate a
primary ocular hemangiosarcoma from a metastatic
lesion.
Melanocytoma/Melanoma

Dermal melanocytic tumors of the eyelid are common
and typically benign in dogs, while in cats they are rare
and more malignant. Melanocytic tumors of the conjunctiva are infrequent and malignant in both species
(although distant metastasis tends to be uncommon).
Conjunctival melanomas involving the nictitating
membrane and superior palpebral conjunctiva may have
greater metastatic potential. In both cats and dogs,
conjunctival melanomas often locally recur following
surgical excision, and may invade the orbit and spread to
regional lymph nodes or lungs.

Adenoma/Adenocarcinoma

Adenocarcinomas are the most common tumor of the
gland of the third eyelid. They appear as a localized, firm,
smooth, pink swelling arising from the posterior surface
of the nictitans. They mimic prolapse of the gland of the
nictitans (i.e., cherry eye), but a key differentiating feature is their occurrence in older dogs and cats. Recurrence
is common if the entire gland is not removed, and metastasis, especially to the regional lymph nodes and orbit, is
possible.
History and Clinical Signs
In addition to a mass lesion, other clinical signs of eyelid
or ocular surface tumors may include epiphora, conjunctival vascular injection, ocular discharge, elevation of the
third eyelid, conjunctival/corneal erosion or ulceration,
and corneal vascularization or pigmentation. Palpebral
conjunctival masses often protrude when they no longer
can be accommodated by the space between the eyelid
and globe. Advanced tumors invading the orbit may
result in exophthalmia or enophthalmia, depending on
their location. Large tumors and sebaceous adenomas
often have a substantial inflammatory component and
may be secondarily infected.
Diagnosis
The extent of conjunctival involvement should be determined by everting the eyelid (and third eyelid if affected).
Careful palpation of the lesion by inserting a lubricated
finger in the conjunctival cul‐de‐sac can aid in determining the full extent of the tumor and whether bony
involvement has occurred. Nasolacrimal lavage and
possibly positive contrast dacryocystorhinography may
help characterize medial canthal masses. Fluorescein
staining should be used to determine the integrity of the
ocular surface.
Small eyelid and ocular surface tumors are best
diagnosed and treated by excisional biopsy. Fine
needle aspiration (FNA) or incisional biopsies of
larger tumors aid in determining prognosis and planning
definitive therapy. Orbital ultrasound, skull radiographs, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), regional lymph node cytology,
and thoracic radiographs may be required to localize
or clinically stage potentially malignant tumors such
as SCC, third eyelid adenocarcinomas, and conjunctival
melanomas.
Therapy
Specific therapy varies with tumor type, size, location,
and extent; whether the eye still has vision; the animal’s

VetBooks.ir

138 Tumors of the Eye and Ocular Adnexa

expected lifespan; the amount of discomfort due to the
mass; and any financial constraints of the owner. All eyelid tumors, whether benign or malignant, may affect
vision or ocular comfort. Excision is indicated for all
eyelid tumors in cats, rapidly growing masses, those irritating the eye or impairing eyelid function, if the owner
is concerned, or the mass is cosmetically unappealing. In
young dogs, even large papillomas or histiocytomas that
are nonirritating may be monitored as spontaneous
regression is common.
Tumors involving less than one‐fourth to one‐third
of the palpebral fissure length are best treated by a
V‐plasty (wedge) or four‐sided (house) excision. In
the latter technique, the incision is made perpendicular
to the eyelid margin (rather than obliquely), resulting
in superior apposition of the eyelid margins and
greater wound stability, especially in larger tumors. It
may be possible to shrink large tumors that are
infected or inflamed with antibiotic or antiinflammatory therapy such that a wedge or four‐sided excision
becomes possible. Electrosurgical excision may result
in substantial scarring of the eyelids. Carbon dioxide
(CO2) laser ablation may be appropriate for some
smaller tumors.
Tumors greater than one‐fourth to one‐third of the
eyelid typically require reconstructive blepharoplasty or
other therapeutic modalities. Depending on tumor type,
alternative therapies include systemic chemotherapy
(e.g., lymphoma, mast cell tumors), local infiltration with
chemotherapeutic agents (e.g., SCC), and/or local radiation therapy (e.g., SCC). These modalities may completely eliminate the tumor or reduce it so that a less
extensive surgical procedure is possible. Reconstructive
blepharoplasty, however, is the procedure of choice if
surgical cure is a possibility, other modalities are unlikely
to substantially reduce the tumor, or if the tumor type
requires extensive margins.
Liquid nitrogen cryosurgery may be an alternative
to extensive blepharoplasty for some eyelid and corneal
tumors. It is fast, technically simpler than reconstructive blepharoplasty, and usually allows the
nasolacrimal puncta and canaliculus to be preserved.
Often cryosurgery can be performed with only sedation or local/topical anesthesia, which is helpful in
older or debilitated patients. After sedation/anesthesia,
the mass is isolated with chalazion forceps and
debulked flush with the lid margin. Using a closed
probe that approximates the diameter of the mass as
much as possible, an iceball is formed and allowed to
extend 3–5 mm beyond the visible margins of the
mass in a double freeze‐thaw cycle. If the tumor is
large, the iceballs should overlap. If complete regression is not achieved 2–3 weeks after the first session,
additional treatments may be performed. Marked

postoperative swelling and usually transient depigmentation of the frozen tissue are expected.
Tumors involving the conjunctiva and third eyelid
(especially conjunctival hemangiosarcomas, melanomas, and third eyelid adenocarcinomas) are best
treated by wide surgical excision, sometimes to the
point of exenteration. Excision of the entire third eyelid may result in keratoconjunctivitis sicca. Cryosurgery
may allow the third eyelid to be spared in papillomas
and early SCC. It can also be a useful adjunct to excision
in advanced canine conjunctival melanomas and SCC.
Superficial keratectomy/sclerectomy, often followed
by cryosurgery, is preferred for many corneal and
scleral tumors, although some tumors require full‐
thickness corneal/scleral resection and placement of a
donor graft.
Prognosis
With treatment, the prognosis for most canine primary
eyelid tumors is excellent. Even histologically malignant
primary lid tumors rarely metastasize, and recurrence
rates are low. Recurrences, however, need to be differentiated from new primary eyelid tumors as these are common. The prognosis for feline eyelid tumors is guarded,
as most eyelid tumors in cats are malignant. Conjunctival
melanomas and adenocarcinomas of the third eyelid
­frequently recur even if all clinically visible tumor is
removed. Conjunctival hemangiosarcomas most likely
have a good prognosis because total excision may be
curative, although recurrence and loss of the eye may
occur.
Limbal (Epibulbar) Melanoma
Limbal melanomas are typically benign, sessile, heavily
pigmented masses originating from melanocytes in the
limbal sclera or subconjunctival connective tissue of
middle‐aged dogs and cats. The majority are located in
the superior limbal region, suggesting that solar radiation may be a risk factor. Growth is slow and confirmed
metastasis has not been reported. Clinical signs are generally mild and may include localized corneal invasion,
epiphora, and mild conjunctival irritation. Differential
diagnoses include conjunctival melanoma, uveal melanoma invading the sclera, metastatic melanoma, and
staphyloma or coloboma. Gonioscopy and ocular ultrasound aid in differentiating invasive intraocular tumors
from limbal melanomas.
Therapy should be considered if the tumor has invaded
the eye, the animal is painful, or if growth is rapid.
Observation alone is often an appropriate approach in
older dogs given the benign nature and usually slow

1263

VetBooks.ir

1264

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

growth rate of these tumors. If intervention is required,
lamellar keratectomy/sclerectomy with graft placement,
cryosurgery or laser photocoagulation may be curative
or reduce the size of the mass such that it no longer
threatens vision for the remainder of the animal’s life.
Cryotherapy or beta‐irradiation may also substantially
reduce the risk of recurrence following local excision.
Enucleation is curative and indicated if the mass has
entered the eye and there is ocular discomfort.

­Intraocular Tumors
Primary Tumors
Primary intraocular tumors occur more frequently than
metastatic intraocular neoplasms in dogs and cats. They
most commonly originate from the uvea, and their etiology is poorly understood.
Canine Anterior Uveal Melanocytoma/Melanoma

Intraocular melanocytomas arising from the iris or ciliary
body comprise the majority of canine intraocular tumors.
(a)

(b)

(c)

(d)

Most tumors are benign and detected in older dogs
(7 years of age or older) although more rapidly growing
pigmented iridal masses have been described in young
dogs. Malignant intraocular melanomas may be locally
invasive but distant metastasis (usually hematogenously)
is rare.
Ocular melanosis of cairn terriers is a distinct clinical entity that resembles a diffuse and benign form of
uveal melanoma. It is a bilateral disorder in which the
iris becomes thickened and more darkly pigmented,
followed by release of pigment into the aqueous and
pigment ­deposition in the sclera/episclera. Secondary
glaucoma is common. Some cairn terriers may have
overt uveal melanocytic tumors, but in most dogs the
pigmented cells are nonneoplastic (Figure 138.2).
Choroidal Melanocytoma/Melanoma

These rare melanocytic tumors generally originate
from the peripapillary choroid and appear as well‐
delineated, raised, subretinal pigmented masses. They
may remain virtually static for many years, although
others may extend into the overlying retina, sclera,

optic nerve, and orbit. Although usually considered
benign, such invasion warrants a more cautious
prognosis. Small tumors are typically asymptomatic
although larger tumors ­frequently present with chronic
uveitis, secondary glaucoma, retinal detachment,
intraocular hemorrhage, or blindness. Ocular ultrasonography may be required to identify the mass in
these patients. Therapy is usually enucleation if the
mass is progressive or the eye is painful. Diode laser
ablation is an alternative treatment for small masses
that do not involve the optic nerve.
Feline Diffuse Iris Melanoma

Diffuse iris melanomas are the most common primary
intraocular tumor in cats. Although the prodromal
period may be quite long, most cats are 9 years of age or
older at the time of diagnosis.
The most common clinical sign is slowly progressive
diffuse iridal hyperpigmentation. Occasionally, a pigmented iridal nodule or amelanotic mass is seen. The
diagnosis is generally made clinically, and is based on
the presence of progressive iridal hyperpigmentation
and thickening or irregularity of the iris surface or
(a)

(b)

pupil (Figure 138.3). Secondary glaucoma may occur.
Diffuse iris melanoma is differentiated from chronic
anterior uveitis with iridal hyperpigmentation by the
absence of other signs of uveitis and a more protracted
course.
Diffuse iris melanoma has the potential to distantly
metastasize, especially to the liver and lungs. Iris hyperpigmentation, however, is typically very slowly progressive, often requiring months to years to progress to the
point at which the eye must be enucleated, and an additional 1–3 years after that before metastatic disease may
become evident. No single morphologic feature is predictive of outcome, but metastasis has been linked to a
greater mitotic index, larger tumors, extension through
the iris into the ciliary body stroma, and involvement of
the scleral venous plexus.
The treatment of diffuse iris melanoma is controversial. Because these eyes initially retain vision and are
comfortable, in the ideal setting, enucleation would be
delayed until just prior to malignant transformation,
invasion into other ocular structures, secondary glaucoma, or metastasis. Such precise timing; however, is
seldom possible. Enucleation is recommended if iris
hyperpigmentation progresses to involve virtually all
of the iris surface, pigmented cells are present in the
aqueous humor and trabecular meshwork, the pupil
is distorted (indicating iridal stromal invasion), invasion into the ciliary body or scleral appears imminent,
or intraocular pressure is elevated. However, it is
unknown whether early enucleation leads to increased
survival.
As an alternative to enucleation, some veterinary
ophthalmologists have attempted to ablate small,
focal, hyperpigmented foci with a diode laser in an
effort to preserve vision and the eye. The long‐term
success rate and side‐effects of this procedure, however,
are unknown.
In practice, slowly progressing lesions, especially in
older cats with other life‐limiting disorders, are often
simply monitored, ideally by comparison to baseline
photographs. In many cats, the progression may be so
slow that the patient can be followed for many years to a
decade or more without apparent metastasis.

the ciliary body or the posterior iris epithelium

Most eyes are blind from the preceding trauma or

Clinical signs include a retroiridal mass that may displace
the iris or lens and in advanced cases, secondary glaucoma, intraocular hemorrhage, and ocular pain.
Tumors that invade the sclera are typically classified as
adenocarcinomas and have anaplastic features, but
metastasis is uncommon and occurs late in the course of
the disease, if at all. However, a few cases of truly malignant pleomorphic adenocarcinomas with fatal metastasis have been reported in dogs. Dogs affected with this
rare form usually have long‐standing ocular disease that
was initially thought to be inflammatory or traumatic in
origin.
Due to the possibility of malignancy, early enucleation
of ciliary body tumors has been recommended, although
benign adenomas may remain static for years. This
makes enucleation controversial for small tumors unassociated with secondary ocular disease. Local intraocular resection or laser photoablation in an effort to
preserve vision and ocular comfort has been described.
Feline Ocular Posttraumatic Sarcoma

A unique entity in cats, sarcomas following ocular
trauma are second only to melanomas in frequency as a
primary feline ocular tumor. Most cats are middle‐aged
to older and the latency period following ocular trauma
to tumor development averages six to seven years. There
are three morphologic subtypes: spindle cell sarcoma
(the most common), round cell, and osteosarcoma/

Common presentations of intraocular tumors include
a visible mass involving intraocular tissues, sclera or
occasionally the orbit, as well as glaucoma, hyphema,
or anterior uveitis. Intraocular neoplasia should
always be considered in animals with hyphema, glaucoma, or both when there is no history of trauma or
coagulopathy. Small masses frequently have no
clinical signs. Pigmentation is not a reliable indicator
of tumor type.
Diagnosis
Usually, the clinical or ultrasonographic appearance (if the
media are opaque) is strongly suggestive of intraocular neoplasia. It may be difficult to differentiate organizing blood
clots from neoplastic mass lesions and more invasive diagnostic procedures may be required. Because most anterior
uveal brown or black masses are cystic and not neoplastic,
transillumination or ultrasonography should be attempted
before resorting to more invasive procedures. Uveal cysts
typically are spherical, may be attached to the ciliary body
or free‐floating in the anterior chamber, and allow bright
light to pass through them (see Figure 138.2a). Once suspected, most primary canine intraocular tumors that are
not blinding nor causing discomfort are observed for
progression, although occasionally FNA (with its risks of
inflammation, infection, and hemorrhage), intraocular
resection, or enucleation are used for diagnostic purposes.
It is also important to rule out metastasis from another
primary site (e.g., oral cavity or nailbed) to the eye, or from
the eye to other organs (especially lungs and liver).
Therapy
Because the risk of metastasis is low and the ability of
enucleation to prevent metastasis in the few malignant

VetBooks.ir

138 Tumors of the Eye and Ocular Adnexa

tumors that have been reported is unproven, it is difficult
to automatically advise enucleation of normotensive,
noninflamed, visual eyes. Therefore, canine primary
intraocular tumors are generally photographed and carefully followed for progression. Enucleation is advised if
malignancy is a concern or if intractable uveitis, chronic
hyphema, or secondary glaucoma is present. Isolated
primary masses involving only the iris or a portion of the
ciliary body may be amenable to local resection by sector
iridectomy/cyclectomy with preservation of the globe,
but this procedure requires an accomplished ophthalmic
surgeon and often has unsatisfactory long‐term results.
Transscleral and transcorneal Nd:YAG or diode laser
therapy may induce remission in small to moderate‐sized
primary intraocular tumors while also preserving vision.
Prognosis
The prognosis for histologically benign intraocular
tumors is excellent. Enucleation is curative but blinding.
Attempts at local excision or laser photoablation may
only be palliative, especially if the ciliary body or trabecular meshwork is involved.
Secondary Uveal Neoplasms
Because the uveal tract is highly vascular, numerous
malignant tumors have been reported to metastasize
to the eye. Lymphoma is the most common secondary
intraocular tumor in the dog and cat, with ocular lesions
affecting approximately one‐third of dogs with the disease.
Common clinical signs include a severe uveitis, in which
the amount of anterior chamber cell/flare is disproportionally severe compared to the degree of conjunctival
hyperemia and pupillary miosis. Other clinical signs include
secondary glaucoma, retinal hemorrhage and detachment, hyphema, conjunctivitis, and keratitis characterized
by corneal infiltrates, edema, vascularization, and intrastromal hemorrhage. Exophthalmia from orbital invasion
and vision loss due to optic nerve or central nervous
system (CNS) disease may also occur. Dogs with intraocular
lymphoma survive only 60–70% as long as dogs without
ocular involvement when treated with cyclophosphamide,
vincristine, and prednisolone (COP), or with doxorubicin.
Ocular signs may be palliated by topical or systemic corticosteroid therapy, but the most effective therapy is systemic
chemotherapy directed at the cancer itself. Enucleation may
be necessary for pain relief in some patients.

­Tumors of the Orbit and Optic Nerve
Orbital neoplasia may be primary, secondary to extension of adjacent tumors into the orbit, or the result of

distant metastasis. In cats and dogs, 90% or more of
orbital tumors are malignant, and regional infiltration
(including into the CNS) or distant metastasis is common. Numerous types of orbital tumors have been
described in cats and dogs. Tumors involving the optic
nerve are rare, although secondary invasion of the nerve
may occur in feline posttraumatic sarcomas, feline SCC,
canine choroidal melanomas, and canine meningiomas.
Primary Orbital Tumors
Sarcomas

Mesenchymal tumors are among the most common
canine primary orbital tumors. These include osteosarcomas, fibrosarcomas, reticulum cell sarcomas, and
­neurofibrosarcomas. Orbital tumors should be histologically graded for a more accurate prognosis but most sarcomas are locally invasive and carry a poor prognosis.
Canine Lobular Orbital Adenoma

Lobular adenomas, perhaps originating from the lacrimal gland, may involve the anterior orbit in dogs. They
typically present as soft, smooth conjunctival swellings,
or space‐occupying orbital lesions that can cause either
enophthalmia or exophthalmia. Lobular orbital adenomas are composed of multiple friable lobules, making
complete surgical excision challenging. Although benign,
recurrence is common, often 1–2 years after excision.
Meningioma

Canine orbital meningiomas are uncommon tumors
which tend to grow slowly and rarely metastasize.
Invasion of surrounding tissues, including bone and the
CNS, is possible.
Glioma

Gliomas are rare primary optic nerve tumors in dogs.
The metastatic potential of gliomas appears to be low,
but invasion into the retina or the ventral aspect of the
brain is possible.
History and Clinical Signs
Orbital neoplasia is typified by slowly progressive
exophthalmia, absent to minimal pain on opening the
mouth, difficulty in retropulsing the eye, and deviation
of the globe. Nasal or sinus tumors that suddenly erode
into the orbit occasionally result in acute exophthalmia
and substantial orbital pain. If the mass is anterior to the
equator of the globe, enophthalmia may occur. Chronic
epiphora secondary to obstruction of the nasolacrimal
duct, exposure keratoconjunctivitis, palpable orbital
masses, or unexplained orbital pain also suggest orbital
neoplasia. Measurement of corneal diameters and

intraocular pressure (IOP) allows differentiation of
buphthalmia from glaucoma (large corneal diameter and
high IOP) and exophthalmia (normal corneal diameter
and IOP).
Optic nerve lesions may result in unilateral or bilateral
blindness (the latter if the optic chiasm is affected),
which may be sudden in onset, as well as optic nerve
head pallor, papilledema, or marked protrusion and congestion of the optic disc on ophthalmoscopy. Relatively
mild exophthalmia with vision loss suggests optic nerve
neoplasia because other orbital tumors typically cause
profound exophthalmos before visual loss. Tumors
affecting more posterior portions of the optic nerve may
not cause exophthalmia or a visible change in the optic
nerve head.

Diagnosis
Differential diagnoses include nonneoplastic orbital
inflammatory diseases such as granulomas, cellulitis,
abscesses, and myositis of the extraocular and masticatory
muscles. Inflammatory orbital disorders typically exhibit
marked pain on opening the mouth. The location of an
orbital mass can usually be determined by careful physical
examination, including determination of the direction of
malposition of the eye, retropulsion of the globe, palpation
of the orbit, and oral examination caudal to the last molar.
In addition to physical examination, cytology of regional
lymph nodes, orbital imaging (computed tomography,
magnetic resonance imaging, orbital ultrasound), thoracic
radiographs, and possibly abdominal ultrasonography
should be performed. In one study of cats with orbital
neoplasia, 59% had orbital bone lesions on skull radiographs and 15% had evidence of metastasis on thoracic
radiographs. CT or MRI offers far superior visualization
of the orbit and facilitates planning of either radiation
or surgical therapy (Figure 138.5).
Histologic characterization by FNA or needle core
biopsies (performed via the mouth or through the periocular skin), with ultrasound or CT guidance if necessary, is
essential for arriving at a definitive diagnosis. It is important to avoid the globe, major orbital blood vessels, and
optic nerve when collecting these samples. If less invasive
methods of obtaining specimens are nondiagnostic,
exploratory orbitotomy or exenteration may be required.
If the optic disc appears normal, electroretinography,
MRI, and cerebrospinal fluid taps may aid in distinguishing optic nerve neoplasia from sudden acquired retinal
degeneration syndrome and posterior optic neuritis.
Therapy
Primary orbital and optic nerve tumors that have not
disseminated elsewhere may be amenable to surgical

Figure 138.5 (a) Orbital mass in a dog with exophthalmos and

excision. If bony involvement is not present, orbital
exenteration by widely dissecting around the mass (stripping periorbita if necessary) is usually preferred, as the
advanced stage of the tumor at the time of diagnosis typically makes it impossible to completely excise the mass
and preserve a functional or comfortable eye. If periorbital bones are involved, a radical orbitectomy, which
resects the affected orbital tissues and surrounding
bones, may be considered. When treating optic nerve
tumors, as much of the orbital optic nerve as possible should be removed in an attempt to obtain clear
margins.
If preservation of a comfortable eye and vision appears
possible, a variety of orbitotomy techniques have been
described, ranging from small incisions through the eyelid or mouth to reflection of the zygomatic arch, temporalis muscle elevation, and zygomatic process osteotomy.
Postoperative complications are common and may
include secondary enophthalmia with entropion, diplopia (double vision), facial nerve palsy, and severe orbital
hemorrhage. Surgical debulking can be palliative in some
patients, and some dogs may survive a year or more with
minimal therapy.

VetBooks.ir

138 Tumors of the Eye and Ocular Adnexa

The value of chemotherapy and radiation therapy
(RT), either alone or as an adjunct to surgery, is unclear,
although chemotherapy for orbital lymphoma may be
effective. Systemic corticosteroids may reduce perineuronal swelling and permit some patients with optic nerve
meningioma to maintain vision for several weeks to
months. RT may be helpful in the case of nasal tumors
with orbital extension, in subtotally excised or recurrent
tumors, and in other select cases.
The ocular side‐effects of conventional external beam
RT for nasal and periocular tumors can have a substantial
impact on an animal’s quality of life. Common complications include keratoconjunctivitis sicca, corneal
ulceration, enophthalmia, entropion, cataracts, retinal
hemorrhages, retinal detachments, and blindness.
Intensity‐modulated RT (IMRT), which uses c­onformal
avoidance, significantly decreases the ocular toxicity seen
in dogs treated by RT for sinonasal and orbital tumors.

Prognosis
The prognosis for most tumors involving the orbit and
optic nerve is poor with conservative treatment, especially
if there is bony involvement. Recurrence at the original site
and involvement of adjacent or distant sites are common,
often occurring within weeks to a few months. Even
benign‐appearing tumors such as lobular orbital adenomas and orbital meningiomas may be locally invasive and
tend to recur following wide excision.
Secondary Orbital Tumors
Most feline orbital tumors are epithelial in origin, with invasive SCC being the most common. Lymphoma is another
common secondary orbital tumor affecting both cats and
dogs. Orbital lymphoma should be considered part of a
­systemic process, and further diagnostics are warranted.

Cancer of the Heart
Nick A. Schroeder, DVM, DACVIM (Cardiology)1 and Lisa DiBernardi, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology),
DACVR (Radiation Oncology)2
1
2

LeadER Animal Specialty Hospital, Cooper City, FL, USA
Gulf Coast Veterinary Specialists, Houston, TX, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Cardiac neoplasia in small animals is usually associated
with pericardial effusion. Most of the time, rupture of a
cardiac tumor occurs which leads to hemopericardium
and cardiac tamponade. In dogs, the majority of cases
are secondary to malignant hemangiosarcoma. Cats
most commonly have cardiac lymphoma. Diagnosis is
frequently based on echocardiographic location of the
mass lesion, taking into account the age and breed of the
animal, and only rarely is histopathologic confirmation
achieved via surgical biopsy. Given the current rate
of change in treatment modalities, consultation with a
­veterinary oncologist is recommended.
Tumors of the heart typically arise from the myocar­
dium, the heart base or the pericardium and are com­
monly associated with pericardial effusion. Pericardial
effusion is a relatively common condition in the dog, much
less so in the cat. Normally, there are only a few milliliters
of fluid present in the pericardial space, which serves
to lubricate the epicardial surface. The pericardium is a
tough, fibrous membrane. The purpose of the pericar­
dium is to stabilize the position of the heart within the
thorax and provide some diastolic function. When signifi­
cant amounts of fluid accumulate within the pericardial
space, cardiac function may be compromised, and affected
animals may start to show clinical signs as described
below. The most common causes of pericardial effusion
are cardiac neoplasia and idiopathic ­pericardial effusion.
Malignant transformation of vascular endothelial cells
results in hemangiosarcoma (HSA). Cardiac HSA typi­
cally arises from the tissue of the right atrium (RA) and/
or right auricle (RAu), though other regions of the heart
may occasionally be affected. Spontaneous hemorrhage
causes hemopericardium.

Heart‐based tumors (HBTs) constitute approximately 5%
of cases of cardiac neoplasia in the dog and up to 3% in cats
and are commonly identified as incidental f­ indings. Most of
these are aortic body tumors (ABTs, chemodectoma or par­
aganglionoma). These tumors arise from chemoreceptor
cells sensitive to blood oxygen and carbon dioxide tension.
Most ABTs are locally invasive and up to 21% are malignant,
metastasizing to lung, liver, left atrium, pericardium or
kidneys. Approximately 5–10% of all heart‐based tumors
are ectopic thyroid c­arcinomas or parathyroid tumors.
These are rarely secretory or functional. Hemopericardium
may be present due to spontaneous hemorrhage from
the mass itself. Alternatively, a hydropericardium with a
modified transudate may develop secondary to obstruction
of lymphatic drainage of the pericardial sac.
The myocardium may be infiltrated with neoplastic
lymphocytes (LSA), occasionally causing pericardial effu­
sion, typically a modified transudate. Cardiac l­ymphoma
may be primary or multicentric.
Pericardial effusion may develop secondary to pericar­
dial mesothelioma. Pleural effusion may also occur in
affected animals with mesothelioma, often concomitant
with pericardial effusion.
Other miscellaneous and rarely reported cardiac
tumors include intrapericardial lipoma, rhabdomyosar­
coma, cardiac mxymoma, and other sarcomas.

­Epidemiology
The prevalence of cardiac neoplasia in the dog has
been cited at 0.19% and is less than 0.03% in cats.
Primary ­cardiac neoplasia constitutes 84% of cases,
with 16% ­
representing metastatic lesions (most
­commonly ­hemangiosarcoma and adenocarcinoma).

Most of the information available is derived from small
case series and retrospective data.

­Signalment
Golden retrievers and German shepherds are predisposed
to cardiac HSA. Afghan hounds, English setters, American
cocker spaniels, Doberman pinschers, Labrador retriev­
ers and miniature poodles have been reported to be at
increased risk as well.
English bulldogs, Boxers, and Boston terriers are the
most common breeds diagnosed with HBTs. Brach­
ycephalic breeds are predisposed, but HBTs may develop
in other breeds.
Cats of all breeds may develop cardiac lymphoma.
Cardiac lymphoma is quite rare in the dog.

­History and Clinical Signs
Dogs that have acute cardiac tamponade from sudden
hemorrhage by RA/RAu HSA into the pericardial space
typically pant, may collapse or experience hemodynamic
shock. Cardiac tamponade occurs when the intraperi­
cardial pressure exceeds the diastolic right atrial and
ventricular pressures. This leads to collapse of the right
ventricular outflow tract, right atrium and right ventricle
(RV). Typically, the left atrial (LA) and left ventricular
(LV) pressure exceeds the intrapericardial pressure, pre­
venting collapse. Collapse of the right‐sided chambers
leads to impaired filling, decreased pulmonary blood
flow and decreased filling of the left atrium and ventricle.
Even a small amount of fluid, if it suddenly develops can
result in serious hemodynamic compromise, whereas
slow accumulation can lead to signs that are insidious in
onset. Chronic pericardial effusion leads to hepatic
venous congestion and functional right heart failure, and
may result in a large, pendulous abdomen from ascites as
well as dependent subcutaneous edema.
On physical examination, dogs classically have
decreased or muffled heart and ventral lung sounds as
well as weak pulses. Other potential findings include a
fluid wave on palpation of the abdomen, hepatomegaly
and pitting edema of the rear limbs. Beck’s triad of clini­
cal signs associated with cardiac tamponade is hypoten­
sion, distended jugular veins, and muffled heart sounds.
Attention should be paid to the quality of femoral pulses
as the pulses may noticeably get weaker with inspiration
and stronger with expiration. This phenomenon, due to
intrathoracic pressure changes and the subsequent
effects on the pulse pressure, is termed pulsus paradoxus
and is highly suggestive of pericardial effusion.

Many HBTs are discovered incidentally with no appar­
ent clinical signs. Patients that are symptomatic typically
have signs referable to pericardial effusion or outflow
obstruction to the right side of the heart, either of which
may result in ascites.
Patients with LSA may have weight loss or signs
­associated with pericardial effusion. Occasionally, the
patient may present with symptoms referable to conges­
tive heart failure. These include difficult or labored
­breathing, exercise intolerance, coughing, inappetence
or lethargy.
Most patients with mesothelioma have symptoms
associated with pericardial and/or pleural effusion. As a
result, many present with dyspnea or increased respira­
tory rate and effort. An abdominal component to the
­respiratory effort may be noted.
Rhabdomyosarcoma has been reported to be associ­
ated with right‐sided congestive heart failure (CHF)
but not pericardial effusion, and some patients may be
completely asymptomatic. Patients with intrapericardial
lipomas are typically asymptomatic.

­Diagnosis
Diagnosis of pericardial effusion can be made une­
quivocally with cardiac ultrasound (echocardiography).
Hemangiosarcoma is usually diagnosed via echocardiog­
raphy, revealing the presence of a mass lesion on the
RA/RAu or RV junction of mixed echogenicity with
irregular anechoic regions. Patients may be hypotensive.
Radiographs typically reveal a globoid cardiac silhouette
with pulmonary vascular underperfusion, but may be
deceivingly normal or only show mild cardiomegaly.
Electrocardiography (ECG) commonly reveals sinus
tachycardia. The QRS complex may be of lower ampli­
tude (low‐voltage QRS). These comprise the most com­
mon electrocardiographic abnormalities associated with
pericardial effusion. The R‐waves may vary in amplitude
from beat to beat, a phenomenon known as electrical
alternans. This occurs as a consequence of the heart
swinging back and forth in the fluid‐filled pericardium.
The angle of the vector of LV depolarization is varied due
to the positional changes, subsequently altering the
amplitude of the QRS complex. This generally happens
when the heart rate is between 90 and 140 bpm.
Ventricular premature complexes, accelerated idioven­
tricular rhythm, ventricular tachycardia, paroxysmal
atrial flutter or atrial fibrillation, atrioventricular block,
bundle branch blocks and other conduction system dis­
turbances may occasionally be encountered on ECG in
patients with cardiac neoplasia. The ECG may also be
completely normal. Often, physical examination is more
reliable than radiographs and ECG. Cardiac magnetic

VetBooks.ir

139 Cancer of the Heart

resonance imaging (MRI) has not been shown to improve
the diagnosis of cardiac neoplasia when compared to
conventional echocardiography.
Testing of the pericardial effusion tends to be of lim­
ited diagnostic utility. Cytology of hemorrhagic effusions
does not reliably differentiate between neoplastic and
nonneoplastic disease. Neoplastic effusions have been
associated with lower pH, bicarbonate and chloride lev­
els and higher lactate, hematocrit, and urea nitrogen as
compared with serum values. Serum cardiac troponin
I levels have been shown to be elevated in dogs with
­neoplastic pericardial effusions.
On necropsy, HSA appears as a red to black, blood‐filled
mass on the epicardium. Histopathologic confirmation is
rarely obtained antemortem but is marked by scattered,
elongated plump neoplastic endothelial cells. By the time
of diagnosis, most cases have associated metastasis and
in general HSA should be considered a systemic/dissemi­
nated disease. The clinician should always assume that
HSA is more advanced than what is evident based on
imaging modalities. Cardiac troponin I levels have not
been shown to be a reliable diagnostic screening tool.
Definitive diagnosis requires surgical biopsy.
Heart‐based tumors are most commonly diagnosed
via echocardiography. Typically, these are visualized as
masses of mixed or homogenous echogenicity immedi­
ately adjacent to the ascending aorta, aortic arch and
proximal branch pulmonary arteries. Thoracic radio­
graphs may show a ventral deviation of the caudal aspect
of the intrathoracic trachea, resulting in a “hook‐like”
appearance if a large HBT is present. Cytologic evalua­
tion of pericardial effusion when present is rarely
­diagnostic. Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic
evaluation of surgically obtained biopsies, often taken
during palliative pericardectomy.
It is common for cats affected with LSA to have large
amounts of pericardial effusion, requiring pericardio­
centesis. The pericardial effusion should be submitted
for fluid analysis/cytology as lymphosarcoma may be
easily diagnosed. Most often, lymphosarcoma of the
heart ­produces infiltrative myocardial lesions. Echo­
cardiography may reveal irregular mottling and echo­
texture to the myocardium with focal areas of thickening,
and concentric left ventricular hypertrophy may mimic
hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Grossly, white, pale
lesions arise from the myocardium.
Patients affected with pericardial mesothelioma may
reveal focal thickening and irregularity of the pericardial
sac on echocardiography. However, normal pericardial
adipose tissue may mimic infiltrative lesions. It is very
common to have associated pleural effusion, and the
presence of a modified transudate in the pleural and per­
icardial cavities for no obvious underlying reason should
alert the clinician to the possibility of mesothelioma.

Unfortunately, cytology of the effusion is rarely diagnos­
tic as nonneoplastic reactive mesothelial cells are diffi­
cult if not impossible to cytologically differentiate from
exfoliated neoplastic mesothelial cells. Pericardial and/
or pleural biopsies are typically required for confirma­
tion of diagnosis.
Pericardial lipomas may be diagnosed on thoracic
radiographs with the appearance of an adipose density
within the cardiac silhouette. Echocardiography gener­
ally reveals a homogenously echogenic mass within the
pericardial sac with variable degrees of compression of
the right heart chambers. Ultrasound‐guided fine needle
aspiration may be attempted, although definitive diagno­
sis generally requires surgical biopsy.
Cardiac myxomas, rhabdomyosarcomas and other
cardiac sarcomas require surgical biopsy for confirma­
tion of diagnosis.

­Therapy
Once hemodynamically important pericardial effusion is
confirmed, immediate pericardiocentesis is warranted.
Ideally, an intravenous (IV) catheter is placed and a
shock bolus of fluids is administered, but patients may
require immediate pericardiocentesis and a IV catheter
and fluids may need to follow.
Frequently, the fluid grossly resembles port wine
which appears similar to venous blood. The presence of
dark, hemorrhagic pericardial effusion is classically
seen with HSA, but its presence is not pathognomonic
for HSA or other cardiac neoplasia. Less commonly,
the fluid may be serosanguinous from CHF or neopla­
sia. Rarely, it may be grossly purulent from pericarditis.
Commonly, any residual fluid will leak into the pleural
cavity from the hole that has been created in the
­p ericardium. Complications associated with pericar­
diocentesis include puncture of a cardiac chamber,
­laceration of a cardiac tumor or coronary artery with
subsequent intrapericardial hemorrhage. Most com­
monly, transient arrhythmias may occur, though they
tend to be self‐­limiting and only rarely require antiar­
rhythmic therapy.
In select cases of cardiac HSA, surgical excision may
be attempted (RA appendectomy +/‐ inflow occlusion
via right thoracotomy or median sternotomy), but in
the majority of cases complete surgical excision is not
achieveable. Pericardectomy alone is not advised due to
the risk of exsanguination and dissemination of tumor
cells into the pleural cavity and has not been shown to
affect recurrence of clinical signs or survival. Various
chemotherapeutics (doxorubicin, dacarbazine, cyclophos­
phamide, vincristine) have been attempted with a posi­
tive trend in overall survival time and time to metastasis.

1273

VetBooks.ir

1274

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

Metronomic chemotherapy, which is intended to prevent
tumor angiogenesis, is based on more frequent and
low‐dose drug administration lacking a rest period com­
pared with conventional chemotherapy. Metronomic
chemotherapy lends itself to minimal toxicity and is
often cost‐effective and convenient.
One small study evaluating canine splenic HSA com­
pared the use of low‐dose chemotherapy in combination
with piroxicam versus the standard of care chemother­
apy, doxorubicin. This study found no statistical differ­
ence in survival between the groups, leading to the
conclusion that low‐dose orally administered chemo­
therapy may be an effective alternative to conventional
chemotherapy. A group at Washington State University
used daily dosing of an alkylating agent, lomustine,
with or without nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs
(NSAIDs) to evaluate the toxicity. The majority of the
81 dogs in this study had macroscopic tumor and/or
metastasis with osteosarcoma and visceral HSA most
prevalent. Thirty-six percent of dogs experienced stable
or improved disease. Although minimal, mild to moder­
ate adverse hematologic and gastrointestinal events
occurred and an unexpectedly higher number experi­
enced azotemia (13%). Currently, there are no placebo‐
controlled studies available for cardiac HSA. Tyrosine
kinase‐mediated proliferation inhibition has been
observed in cell lines of canine HSA when exposed to
dasitinib and imatinib alone and in conjunction with
doxorubicin. The use of tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy
alone or in combination with standard or metronomic
chemotherapy has yet to yield improved survival times in
the treatment of cardiac HSA.
Early surgical excision is the preferred method of treat­
ment for heart‐based tumors. However, in the majority
of cases complete surgical excision is not possible.
Palliative pericardiocentesis and partial pericardiectomy
are viable treatment options for patients with pericardial
effusion secondary to HBT. A retrospective study of 6
dogs treated with stereotactic body radiation therapy
(SBRT) for heart-base tumors confirmed or presumed to
be chemodectomas was performed at the North Carolina
State University Veterinary Hospital. Respiratory and
motion management was key to the accurate delivery of
a minimum of 30 Gray (Gy) delivered in three 10 Gy frac­
tions. Four tumors were assessed after SBRT; tumor vol­
ume decreased by 30-76%. Possible treatment-related
complications included cough, tachyarrhythmias, and
congestive heart failure. Two dogs experienced sudden
death 150 and 294 days after SBRT. Three dogs were
alive at the time of the report (408 and 751 days after
SBRT) and one dog died of unrelated disease 1,228 days
after SBRT. While this protocol offered rapid tumor
reduction, cardiac arrhythmias assumed to be tumor or
treatment related and sudden death commonly occurred

after SBRT. SBRT may be ideal for select patients and
likely not of benefit for dogs lacking cardiovascular
­disturbances and/or incidentally diagnosed. As the use
of SBRT evolves we will recognize appropriate candi­
dates, and better define the survival benefit. Standard
and metronomic chemotherapy alone or combined with
small molecule inhibitors may be attempted, especially if
metastasis is evident.
In patients affected by cardiac lymphoma with clini­
cally significant pericardial effusion, palliative pericardi­
ocentesis is required. Considered to be stage V, substage
B, cardiac lymphoma may be treated with CHOP‐based
chemotherapy protocols.
Mesothelioma patients may have a palliative pericard­
ectomy performed, but clinically significant pleural
­effusion typically develops, and pericardectomy has not
been shown to decrease the occurrence of clinical signs
or survival time. In patients affected with mesothelioma,
carcinomatosis or sarcomatosis (with or without malig­
nant effusion), short‐term benefit has been obtained
with intracavitary chemotherapy. Intracavitary carbopl­
atin and/or mitoxantrone yielded a 333‐day median sur­
vival time. Three dogs with pleural mesothelioma treated
with intracavitary cisplatin had complete resolution of
their effusions for 129, 289 and over 306 days. Resolution
of effusion occurred within one or two treatments for all
three dogs.
Intrapericardial lipomas may be addressed surgically if
clinically important right‐sided inflow obstruction of the
heart is documented.

­Prognosis
The prognosis for cardiac HSA is generally considered
to be grave. Median survival times (MST) with pallia­
tive pericardiocentesis alone have been reported at
11 days (range 0–208 days). A MST of 43 days was
achieved in eight dogs undergoing pericardiectomy
and surgical resection of a RA HSA. In eight dogs with
pericardiectomy and RAu masses, MST was 90 days.
This difference in MST may be explained by the smaller
size of auricular masses. In a separate report, 15 dogs
with pericardiectomy and RA mass resection experi­
enced a MST of 42 days. In eight postoperative patients,
the addition of doxorubicin‐based chemotherapy sig­
nificantly improved MST to 175 days. In nonsurgical
cases doxorubicin‐based protocols may offer MST of
120 days. Pericardiectomy may be performed by one
of two techniques: surgical (thoracotomy) or thoras­
copic‐assisted pericardiectomy. However, if mass
removal is intended, thoracotomy would be the
ideal approach based on the experience level of the
surgical team.

VetBooks.ir

139 Cancer of the Heart

Heart‐based tumors have a fair prognosis, but this is
highly dependent on the presence or absence of pericar­
dial effusion, secondary outflow obstruction, or other
cardiac function abnormalities. Patients having under­
gone palliative pericardectomy had a MST of 730 days
(42 days with palliative pericardiocentesis alone).
The prognosis for cardiac LSA is guarded, but variable
based on response and severity. Twelve dogs with car­
diac lymphoma were evaluated and dogs treated with
combination chemotherapy had a MST of 157 days com­
pared to a 22‐day MST in untreated dogs. Three of the
treated dogs survived >328 days. There is no evidence

that primary cardiac LSA should be treated differently
from other bulky aggressive lymphomas arising at other
anatomic sites.
Patients suffering from pericardial mesothelioma
­generally have a fair to guarded prognosis. Many patients
may survive months to years with palliative centesis +/corticosteroid administration alone.
A variety of primary and secondary cardiac tumors
have been reported in the veterinary literature. With
technologic advancement, we will gain a more detailed
picture and begin to unearth important factors regard­
ing biologic behavior, treatments and prognosis.
