Cancer of the Airway and Lung
Joanne L. Intile, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology)
College of Veterinary Medicine, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA

­Cancer of the Airway
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Tumors of the larynx and trachea are rare in dogs and
cats. The most common primary tumors of the canine
larynx are carcinomas, with squamous cell carcinoma
occurring most frequently, followed by oncocytoma and
rhabdomyoma. Other reported laryngeal tumors
include mast cell tumor, extramedullary plasmacy­
toma, chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, melanoma,
lipoma, adenocarcinomas, fibrosarcoma, and papil­
loma. Metastatic tumors from a distant site are rarely
reported.
Feline primary laryngeal tumors include lymphoma,
squamous cell carcinoma, and adenocarcinomas. Lei­
omyoma, basal cell carcinoma, and polyps are also
reported.
Secondary invasion of the larynx can result from ingrowth
of primary thyroid tumors or regional lymphoma.
The most common tracheal tumors in dogs include
benign tracheal osteocartilaginous tumors, leiomyoma,
adenocarcinomas, mast cell tumor, and extramedullary
plasma cell tumor. In cats, adenocarcinomas, squamous
cell carcinoma, and other carcinomas are the most com­
monly reported.
Epidemiology
There are no known etiologic or epidemiologic factors
predisposing animals to developing laryngeal and tra­
cheal tumors.
Signalment
Other than a predilection for younger dogs to develop
oncocytomas, for older cats to develop malignant

laryngeal tumors, and a possible overrepresentation of
Siamese cats developing tracheal tumors, there is no
typical age, breed, or sex predilection for laryngeal and
tracheal tumors in dogs and cats. However, younger
animals with active osteochondral ossification sites are at
in­creased risk for developing benign tracheal osteocarti­
laginous tumors.
History and Clinical Signs
Patients with laryngeal tumors typically present with
signs directly related to the primary tumor, including
stridor, dyspnea, change in bark or voice, exercise intol­
erance, weakness, or dysphagia. Ptyalism may also be
noted.
Patients with tracheal tumors present with similar
symptoms as those with largyneal tumors, but are more
likely to cough.
Diagnosis
The diagnosis of a laryngeal tumor is often made upon
direct visualization on awake or sedated oral exam. Oral
exam provides limited information regarding the exten­
siveness of the tumor, but the advantage is that tissue
biopsy samples can be obtained in a relatively noninva­
sive and economical manner.
Cervical radiographs are helpful in localizing tumors
of the distal portions of the larynx or trachea. Images
may show a discrete soft tissue mass within the lumen of
the trachea, and/or a calcified mass in cases of osteo­
chondromas/chondromas. Thoracic radiographs are
recommended to evaluate for the presence of metastatic
disease and also to assess for evidence of aspiration
pneumonia, which may occur secondary to laryngeal
dysfunction. Cervical ultrasound and tracheoscopy may be

Clinical Small Animal Internal Medicine Volume II, First Edition. Edited by David S. Bruyette.
© 2020 John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Published 2020 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc.
Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/bruyette/clinical

VetBooks.ir

1278

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

helpful to determine the extent of tumors and can also
be used to obtain histopathologic samples. Computed
tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI) provide three‐dimensional localization of the
tumor as well as its proximity to other vital structures
within the cervical region. This detailed imaging may
facilitate a diagnosis but is often required for treatment
planning.
Laryngeal/tracheal lymphoma should be considered
part of a systemic disease process, therefore warranting
complete staging as part of a diagnostic plan.
Therapy
There is limited information regarding the treatment
of laryngeal tumors in dogs and cats. In dogs, benign
tumors of the larynx such as a rhabdomyoma or cyst
can be removed surgically. Some cases require place­
ment of a temporary tracheostomy tube. Smaller benign
masses can be removed via a transoral approach or
through a ventral laryngotomy. Postoperative inflam­
mation and obstruction may necessitate temporary
tracheostomy. For larger and/or more invasive tumors,
a partial or complete laryngectomy with a permanent
tracheostomy can be considered. Permanent tracheos­
tomy, providing relief of upper airway obstruction, is a
form of treatment for humans but has limited use in
veterinary medicine.
Reported complications of complete laryngectomy
in dogs include stomal collapse, the formation of a
tracheoesophageal fistula, pharyngeal dehiscence,
and ablation of the parathyroid glands. Permanent
tracheostomy in cats carries a 67% complication rate
with 29% in‐hospital mortality. A temporary gastrostomy
tube should be considered for any patient undergoing
aggressive laryngotomy.
Radiation therapy is used for treating invasive or nonre­
sectable tumors and is effective for treating lymphomas
and plasma cell tumors. However, limited evidence‐
based information exists. Chemotherapy, with or with­
out surgery, may also be effective.
Tumors of the trachea should be treated with surgery,
which is curative for benign osteochondral tumors.
Experimental evidence indicates that up to 50% of the
length of the trachea can be removed with successful
closure. Tension on the site of anastomosis is the limiting
factor. Intraluminal stenting or bronchoscopic debulking
can be palliative measures for relieving obstruction. As
with laryngeal tumors, the efficacy of radiation and/or
chemotherapy for non-hematologic tumors remains
unproven but can be considered when surgery is not
feasible.

Prognosis
Benign tumors of the larynx and trachea have a good
prognosis when treated with surgical resection alone.
Long‐term survival is also expected with treatment of
extramedullary plasmacytomas and granular cell tumors.
Unfortunately, information is too limited to provide spe­
cific prognosis’ for dogs with other malignancies of the
airway.
Similar to dogs, little information is available regarding
the prognosis for cats. In one reported study, the median
survival time for 27 cats with a variety of laryngeal and
tracheal tumors was only five days, with only 7% of
patients alive 12 months after diagnosis.

­Cancer of the Lung
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Primary lung tumors are rare in dogs and cats c­ ompared
to humans. The most common primary lung tumor in
dogs is bronchoalveolar carcinoma, followed by adeno­
carcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and s­ quamous
cell carcinoma. Other primary lung tumors include his­
tiocytic sarcoma, neuroendocrine tumors, and primary
pulmonary sarcomas. Benign primary lung tumors
include adenomas and fibromas. The most common pri­
mary lung tumor in cats is adenocarcinoma, followed by
bronchoalveolar carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma,
and adenosquamous carcinoma.
In both cats and dogs, primary lung tumors can spread
via hematogenous or lymphatic routes. This may occur
regionally, to intrathoracic lymph nodes, other lung
lobes, and the pleura, or distantly throughout the body.
More than three‐quarters of cats with pulmonary tumors
will develop metastasis. Local invasion of tumors within
the adjacent pulmonary parenchyma can occur.
In some cases, it is difficult to determine if a p
­ ulmonary
tumor represents a primary cancer versus a metastatic
lesion from a distant site. Immunohistochemical stains
can be helpful in such cases, as can complete and thor­
ough staging to evaluate for disease at distant sites.
Epidemiology
The relationship between environmental carcinogens
and the development of lung tumors in dogs has been
studied. One study showed that 75% of dogs with primary
lung tumors live in urban environments, but the results of
two other studies did not support this finding. The risk of
exposure to second‐hand smoke and development of lung
cancer in dogs has also been evaluated with conflicting

VetBooks.ir

140 Cancer of the Airway and Lung

results. The association in natural settings appears to be
weak, but the risk may be increased in brachycephalic dogs
compared to dolichocephalic dogs. It is hypothesized that
dolichocephalic dogs possess greater surface area for fil­
tration of inhalant carcinogens.
There are no known epidemiologic factors influencing
the development of primary pulmonary tumors in cats.
Signalment
The average age of dogs with primary lung tumors is
approximately 11 years (range 2–18 years). The risk of
developing lung cancer rises after the age of 13. Males
and females are equally susceptible. Tumors occur more
frequently in larger dogs, with 60% of cancers developing
in dogs weighing 20–30 kg. In cats, the average age at
diagnosis is 12–13 years (range 2–20 years) with most
cats being >5 years of age. No breed or sex predisposition
is consistently found in felines.
History and Clinical Signs
Between 52–93% of dogs with primary lung tumors
present with a chronic nonproductive cough. Other
­
signs include dyspnea, lethargy, weight loss, tachypnea,
pyrexia, inappetence, and lameness. Many dogs are diag­
nosed with primary lung tumors without any obvious
clinical signs during routine geriatric screening tests
(e.g., thoracic radiographs). Pleural effusion may occur
secondary to direct invasion of the tumor into the pleura
or regional pulmonary lymphatics. This may occur with
primary or metastatic tumors within the lung tissue.
Pneumothorax and hemoptysis may rarely occur.
Signs related to the respiratory system are detected in
one‐quarter to two‐thirds of cats with lung tumors.
Vomiting is reported in 20% of cats. Cats with lung
tumors are more likely to show nonspecific signs such as
lethargy, malaise, and inappetence compared with dogs.
Hypertrophic osteopathy is a known paraneoplastic syn­
drome associated with primary and metastatic lung tumors
in dogs and cats. Animals present with lameness of one or
more limbs. Radiographs will show periosteal proliferation
occurring perpendicular to the shaft of the long bones.
Hypertrophic osteopathy can resolve following removal
of a primary lung tumor. Other known paraneoplastic
effects in dogs include hypercalcemia, polyneuropathy,
polymyopathy, fever, and ectopic adrenocorticotropic
hormone production leading to hyperadrenocorticism.
Metastasis to the digits is a well‐described clinical con­
sequence of primary pulmonary tumors in cats and some
feline patients are initially diagnosed with bony lesions
within the phalanges prior to diagnosis of a pulmonary

tumor. Metastasis occurs more commonly to the weight‐
bearing digits. Multiple digits and multiple limbs are
commonly affected.
Diagnosis
Many dogs with primary and metastatic lung tumors are
diagnosed via thoracic radiography. Most dogs will show
a solitary pulmonary mass that is well circumscribed and
located in the caudodorsal lung lobes. Diffuse and
­alveolar infiltrative forms are also described. Radiographs
may also show regional l­ymphadenopathy or extension
of tumor into the surrounding pulmonary parenchyma.
Computed tomography is being more frequently uti­
lized for the diagnosis of pulmonary neoplasia in dogs
and cats and is ideal for surgical planning. Thoracic
CT scan is superior to thoracic radiography for the
detection of tracheobronchial lymph node metastases
and for detecting pulmonary metastases. The accuracy
rate for thoracic CT in detecting tracheobronchial
lymph node metastases was 93%, compared to 57% for
radiographs. In another study, thoracic radiographs
detected only 9% of CT‐detected pulmonary metastases.
Twenty one of 33 (64%) dogs had pulmonary nodules
or masses detected on CT. Of the dogs that had positive
CT findings, 17 of 21 (81%) had pulmonary nodules or
masses detected on radiographs by at least one inter­
preter. In another study using CT as the gold standard
diagnostic tool, the sensitivity of radiography for
detecting pulmonary metastases ranged from 71% to
95%, and specificity ranged from 67% to 92%. Radiography
had a positive predictive value of 83–94% and a nega­
tive predictive value of 65–89%. This increased accu­
racy of CT for detecting lesions is likely, in part, due to
its higher resolution for identifying smaller lesions
(e.g., thoracic CT can detect lesions of 1 mm in size)
compared to radiographs (can detect lesions only when
>7 mm in size). MRI of the thorax is not recommended
due to excessive motion artifact.
Pleural effusion is more common in cats, and is identi­
fied in approximately one‐third of patients. The diagnos­
tic utility of cytology of pleural effusion in providing a
diagnosis of pulmonary neoplasia is variable, but if effu­
sion is detected, it is recommended to submit a sample
for analysis as this is a relatively noninvasive technique
that can provide significant information.
Bronchoalveolar lavage can be considered and has
been found to be superior to transtracheal wash for diag­
nosing lung cancer in dogs.
Fine needle aspiration of lung tumors is safe, but there
is a theoretical risk of seeding tumor cells within the tho­
racic cavity during this procedure. Studies indicate fine

VetBooks.ir

1280

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

needle aspirate cytology is diagnostically accurate in up
to 90% and 100% of dogs and cats with pulmonary
tumors, respectively. Ultrasound and/or CT‐guided aspi­
ration has been described, as well as techniques utilizing
thoracoscopic or keyhole lung biopsy methods.
Therapy
Surgery is the treatment of choice for solitary pulmonary
tumors in dogs and cats. For unilateral tumors, surgery can
be performed through either an intercostal thoracotomy or
median sternotomy approach. Thoracoscopic and keyhole
techniques have also been described. Complete lung lobec­
tomy is the preferred surgical approach, but techniques for
partial lung lobectomy are described. The use of automatic
stapling equipment allows for decreased surgical time with
minimal complications, but is more difficult in small
patients. It is important to note that biopsy of hilar lymph
nodes at the time of thoracic surgery should be performed
to complete staging.
Pneumonectomy is considered for lesions that have
extended to all lobes of one lung while the contralateral
side is unaffected. The resulting physiologic alterations
are much greater than performing a single lobectomy.
Dogs can survive a 50% decrease in lung volume, but not
75%. Therefore excision of all lung tissue on the left side
can be tolerated since it represents less than 50% of total
lung volume.
There is little information regarding the utility of
chemotherapy for treating primary lung tumors in dogs
and cats. In dogs, doxorubicin and mitoxantrone have
been shown to provide little to no response. Two of seven
dogs with measurable pulmonary tumors showed a par­
tial response to treatment with vinorelbine. Single‐agent
vinorelbine was also evaluated in the microscopic dis­
ease setting in three dogs, and survival time for those
patients was 112, 169, and >730 days.
Inhalational therapy has also been evaluated in dogs,
resulting in complete and partial responses for dogs with
metastatic tumors compared to stable to progressive dis­
ease for dogs with solitary ones.
Intracavitary chemotherapy with cisplatin, carbopl­
atin, or mitoxatrone, as well as sclerosing agents such
as talc, has been used to treat malignant effusions
in dogs.
In people with non-small cell lung cancer, treatment
benefits have been obtained using targeted therapy
with either monoclonal antibodies or tyrosine kinase
inhibitors directed against cell signaling pathways. The
role of such targeted therapy in veterinary patients is
unknown.

The role of radiation therapy, interventional radiology,
and regional chemotherapy remains relatively unexplored
for veterinary patients with pulmonary neoplasia.
Prognosis
Most information regarding prognosis for animals with
pulmonary tumors is derived from the behavior of epi­
thelial tumors.
The median survival time of 24 beagle dogs diagnosed
with pulmonary carcinomas treated with symptomatic
care alone was 10 months (range five days to 42 months).
The prognosis for dogs with pulmonary tumors treated
surgically is variable and depends on a number of fac­
tors, some of which can only be determined postop­
eratively (e.g., histologic grade and completeness of
excision). An older study reported a median survival
time of 13 months with lung lobectomy alone. For dogs
with incompletely excised tumors, median survival time
was only about 1–2 months compared to 11 months for
completely excised tumors.
Several specific prognostic factors have been identified
in dogs with pulmonary tumors (Table 140.1). Tumor stage
is prognostic: T1 (solitary tumor) = median survival time
of 26 months, T2 (multiple tumors) = median survival time
seven months, and T3 (invasive into surrounding tissue) =
median survival time of three months. The presence of
metastatic disease within intrathoracic lymph nodes is a
negative prognostic factor for dogs with primary lung
tumors (11–15 months if no metastatic disease present;
1–2 months if metastases are detected). The presence of
clinical signs at the time of tumor detection is also a nega­
tive prognostic factor: 18 months with no clinical signs
compared to eight months when clinical signs are present.
Tumor size and location are also prognostic. Dogs with
tumors <100 cm3 and those with peripherally located
tumors have longer survival times compared with dogs
with tumors >100cm3 or encompassing entire lung lobes.
Histologic grade is a prognostic factor for both dogs
and cats. The median survival time for dogs with well‐
differentiated, moderately differentiated, and poorly dif­
ferentiated tumors was 28 months, eight months, and
five days, respectively. The median survival time for cats
with well‐differentiated tumors treated surgically was 23
months, compared to 2.5 months for cats with poorly
differentiated tumors. Other prognostic indicators for
cats include the presence of clinical signs (median sur­
vival time of 4 days if present vs. 78 days if not), pleural
effusion (median survival time 2 days vs. 31 days), and
the presence of metastatic disease (median survival time
3 days vs. 60 days.)

Cancer of the Esophagus and Stomach
Avenelle I. Turner, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology)
Veterinary Cancer Group, Culver City, CA, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Esophageal sarcomas have been reported secondary to
infection with Spirocerca lupi, an esophageal worm
found sporadically in the tropic warm temperate areas
and throughout the United States. There is no known
cause for the more commonly seen esophageal carcinomas. In cats, squamous cell carcinomas (SCC) are located
in the middle third of the esophagus, just caudal to the
thoracic inlet. These tumors are locally invasive and
metastasis to regional lymph nodes occurs early.
No definitive etiology has been identified in the development of gastric cancer but experimentally, long‐term
administration of nitrosamines may induce carcinomas
in dogs.

­Epidemiology
Cancer of the esophagus and stomach is rare and
accounts for less than 0.5% and 1% of all malignancies
respectively.
Esophageal tumors can be primary or metastatic.
Metastatic tumors are three times more common than
primary esophageal tumors and occur through local
invasion from the stomach, thymus, thyroid, and heart
base as well as from mammary adenocarcinoma and
lymphoma. In dogs, the most common primary esophageal tumors are SCC, osteosarcoma (OSA), fibrosarcoma
(FSA), and leiomyosarcoma. Sarcomas are seen more
commonly in areas where Spirocerca lupi is endemic.
In cats, the most common primary esophageal tumor is
SCC which is seen more commonly in females.
The most common gastric tumor in the dog is
­adenocarcinoma. Belgian shepherds, chow chows, rough‐
coated collies, and Staffordshire bull terriers appear predisposed to gastric adenocarcinoma, implying a genetic

component. The average age of patients affected with
carcinoma is 8 years with a 2.5:1 male‐to‐female ratio.
Other tumors affecting the stomach are lymphoma
(LSA), leiomyoma, leiomyosarcoma, gastrointestinal
stromal cell tumor (GISTs), extramedullary plasmacytoma (EPC), mast cell tumor (MCT), and carcinoid.
Leiomyomas occur in older dogs (mean age >15) as a
discrete, often pedunculated lesion in the cardia or
­
gastroesophageal junction. Recent studies utilizing
­
immunohistochemistry to detect CD117 (c‐kit protein),
a transmembrane receptor with a tyrosine kinase
­component, have shown up to 50% of leiomyomas and leiomyosarcomas are reclassified as GISTs. Leiomyosarcomas
do not express the c‐kit protein.
Lymphoma is the most common gastric tumor in cats
and males are more commonly affected. Gastric LSA is
covered in more detail in another section. Chronic
g­ astritis, Helicobacter, and common heritage have been
implicated in feline gastric cancer.

­Signalment
Most animals with esophageal cancer are older and no
breed predilection is evident. The average age for dogs
diagnosed with gastric carcinoma is 8 years. Males are
diagnosed 2.5 times more often than females. Cats with
gastric carcinoma are typically older with mean ages
reported between 10.6 and 12.6 years.

­History and Clinical Signs
Clinical signs associated with esophageal cancer are generally noted late in the course of disease. Symptoms occur
when the tumor is large and has caused an obstruction or
motility dysfunction. This can result in dysphagia and

Clinical Small Animal Internal Medicine Volume II, First Edition. Edited by David S. Bruyette.
© 2020 John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Published 2020 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc.
Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/bruyette/clinical

regurgitation. Other symptoms include weight loss, anorexia, halitosis, pain, and aspiration pneumonia. In some
cases, respiratory signs may be the only symptom. The
paraneoplastic syndrome hypertrophic osteopathy has
been reported secondary to S. lupi‐induced sarcomas.
A history of progressive vomiting, often with digested
blood “coffee grounds” or tinged with fresh blood, is
common in cases of gastric cancer. Weight loss, anorexia,
and cachexia are often noted over a period of weeks to
months. Paraneoplastic hypoglycemia can be seen secondary to leiomyomas or leiomyosarcomas and is likely
due to the production of insulin‐like growth factors.
EPCs may be associated with hyperproteinemia, monoclonal gammopathy, and hypercalcemia. On occasion,
occult blood or melena can be documented in the feces.

­Diagnosis
Staging for tumors of the esophagus should include thoracic radiographs (three‐view), minimum database
(complete blood count [CBC], serum biochemistry profile, and urinalysis) and an abdominal ultrasound to rule
out a possible primary tumor when the esophageal tumor
is suspected to be metastatic.
Thoracic radiographs of the cervical region and thorax
may be helpful in localization of esophageal tumors and/
or secondary aspiration pneumonia. Esophageal tumors
appear as a homogeneous mass in the region of the
esophagus, with gas retention and dilation proximal to
the lesion. Some esophageal tumors may appear calcified. Positive contrast esophagrams with barium will
usually demonstrate the lesion with or without fluoroscopy. Lesions appear as a rounded or lobulated, smoothly
elevated filling defect.
When available, esophagoscopy is definitive because it
can locate the lesion and obtain diagnostic tissue samples for histopathology. Esophageal tumors are typically
submucosal over which the mucosa is usually freely movable. Narrowing of the lumen is common, while stenosis
and obstruction are rare. Computed tomography (CT) or
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may be helpful in
determining extent of involvement, location, and invasiveness. Leiomyoma can be presumptively diagnosed
based on endoscopic examination and CT results that
indicate a well‐defined, round‐to‐ovoid encapsulated
mass, with no ulceration of the overlying mucosa or evidence of local invasion. Endoscopic biopsies are contraindicated with leiomyomas, as they increase the risk
of complications and mucosal perforation during surgery. Endoscopic fine needle aspiration is effective for
obtaining a tentative diagnosis and does not affect surgical outcome. EPCs have a predilection for the terminal
esophagus and cardia. A thoracotomy or cervical exploration can be performed to obtain a biopsy.

Staging for gastric tumors includes abdominal ultrasound, thoracic radiographs (three‐view) and minimum
database. Abdominal radiographs rarely reveal gastric
tumors. Anemia is the most common laboratory abnormality. Paraneoplastic hypoglycemia can be seen with
leiomyomas or leiomyosarcomas. Sporadically, elevated liver enzymes and elevated gastrin levels can be
documented.
Grossly, there are three variations of gastric carcinoma
that have been identified. Diffuse neoplastic infiltration
of the gastric wall can produce a thickened, nondistensible stomach known as “leather bottle stomach.” Gastric
adenocarcinoma may also manifest as a discrete,
­polypoid lesion or as mucosal plaques with ulceration.
Histopathologically, gastric adenocarcinomas may be
classified as a diffuse type with randomly arranged,
malignant epithelial cells or an intestinal type with
neoplastic cells that are well organized into distinct,
­
glandular structures. The clinical significance of these
histopathologic types is not currently known.
Ultrasonography is a useful imaging modality.
Carcinomas tend to be sessile and occur most commonly
on the lesser curvature and gastric antrum. Benign
lesions are pedunculated or well circumscribed and
often occur at the cardia. Sometimes, it is easier to find
gastric lymphadenopathy secondary to metastasis than
the primary gastric lesion. An ultrasound‐guided fine
needle aspirate or Tru‐Cut biopsy can be utilized to
obtain a diagnostic sample.
Gastroscopy with a flexible endoscope is the most
­sensitive and specific noninvasive way to identify and
localize lesions and obtain biopsies. When obtaining
biopsies, multiple samples should be taken from multiple
sites because the majority of gastric tumors have significant necrosis, ulceration and inflammation, making
­histopathologic examination difficult.
Barium contrast gastrograms can often document
infiltrative disease of the gastric wall, but these contrast
studies are cumbersome and take a relatively long time
to perform. Poor motility, delayed gastric emptying time
and/or prolonged adherence of contrast material to
ulcerated tissue are common findings. It should be noted
that it could take over 24 hours for barium to completely
leave the stomach, which would delay the ability to perform gastroscopy.
Open surgical biopsy is the most definitive method of
diagnosis. Leiomyoma/leiomyosarcmas should be stained
with CD117 (c‐kit) to differentiate GISTs.

­Therapy
There are limited therapeutic options for esophageal cancer. Intrathoracic access is challenging and surgery usually results in tension on the anastomosis site and

VetBooks.ir

141 Cancer of the Esophagus and Stomach

postoperative complications. Esophageal surgery is prone
to serious complications, including stricture, dehiscence,
infection, regurgitation, esophagitis, and f­istula formation. This has been attributed to many f­ actors, including
esophageal movement during swallowing, high wound
tension, lack of a serosal layer and the presence of a segmental blood supply to the esophagus. After esophageal
surgery, use of a gastrostomy tube is recommended to
decrease the amount of motion occurring at the surgical
site and facilitate mucosal healing. En bloc resection is
associated with the best prognosis but submucosal resection to debulk the mass without a full resection and anastomosis can be an acceptable treatment with successful
outcomes for leiomyomas/low‐grade leiomyosarcomas.
Short‐term palliation can be achieved with placement of
a gastric or percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube.
In people, palliation is commonly achieved by the placement of an endoluminal stent. An interventional technique to perform this procedure in veterinary patients is
potentially possible.
Radiation therapy is of limited use due to the tissue
tolerance of the surrounding structures. In humans,
­
radiation therapy alone is used as a palliative treatment
for esophageal tumors or following surgery. Results
­following radiation therapy alone are short‐lived and
universally poor unless done in combination with
s­ urgery and chemotherapy.
Complete surgical excision is the treatment of choice
for gastric adenocarcinomas but is typically complicated
due to advanced disease, predilection for the lesser curvature, antrum and pylorus, extensive gastric involvement and/or metastasis to regional lymph nodes and
liver. Surgical approaches such as a Billroth I (partial gastrectomy and gastroduodenostomy) or Billroth II (partial
gastrectomy and gastrojejunostomy) can provide immediate relief of gastric outflow obstruction and clinical
improvement in the early postoperative period. Careful
staging prior to pursuing surgery is recommended to
insure the morbidity associated with the procedure can
be justified.
The beneficial effects of chemotherapy alone or in the
adjuvant setting for gastric adenocarcinoma are largely
unknown. Reported chemotherapy protocols utilizing
5‐fluorouracil, 5‐fluorouracil and cyclophosphamide,
5‐fluorouracil, doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide (FAC
protocol) or cis‐platinum appeared to provide some clinical benefit in a few cases. Comparatively, 80% of people

with metastatic or nonresectable GISTs had a favorable
response with the use of imatinib (Gleevec®), a selective
tyrosine kinase inhibitor. This resulted in stabilization or
resolution of disease for a median of 20 months. Two
tyrosine kinase inhibitors are currently approved for use
in veterinary medicine (Palladia™, Pfizer, and Kinavet‐
CA1®, AB Science) and may also prove to be effective
against GISTs in dogs.

­Prognosis
The prognosis for esophageal cancer is very poor. These
cancers are usually not diagnosed until they are advanced,
by which time they are typically difficult or impossible to
resect and often are metastatic. Photodynamic therapy
has been attempted, but with modest results. The median
survival for dogs with esophageal sarcoma following surgery and doxorubicin chemotherapy was 267 days.
Interestingly, in many cases, the cause of death was secondary to aspiration pneumonia due to abnormalities in
esophageal motility.
The prognosis for gastric adenocarcinoma is poor following the onset of clinical signs. Without treatment,
animals usually succumb to their disease within 1–3
months. Surgery affords the best chance for improving
the long‐term prognosis. Animals that survive the perioperative period have reported median survival times of
4–6 months but a small number of long‐term survivals of
greater than 36 months have been reported. Most
patients eventually succumb due to recurrent or metastatic disease. Leiomyosarcomas and GISTs have a
slightly better prognosis with reported median survival
times of 6–12 months. Surgery can be curative for benign
lesions that are completely resected. EPCs have an
excellent prognosis with surgery and chemotherapy.
­
Information on long‐term follow‐up is lacking in the literature, but a dog treated with surgery and doxorubicin
chemotherapy was alive and asymptomatic 30 months
post diagnosis. Less than 10% of cases of gastric MCT,
regardless of treatment(s) utilized, lived beyond six
months. Occasionally, there are cases of gastric MCT
that appear to do significantly better than this, suggesting there may be a less aggressive variant of this disease.
This supports the palliative use of systemic chemotherapy in patients with minimal clinical symptoms and a
reasonable quality of life.

Cancer of the Small and Large Intestine
Edwin Brodsky, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology)
Veterinary Medical Center of Long Island, West Islip, NY, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
The majority of canine intestinal lymphomas are primary in nature, although extension from multicentric
lymphoma can occur. Most intestinal lymphomas in
dogs are multifocal or diffuse throughout the intestinal
tract with lesions located in the mucosa, submucosa, and
lamina propria. The majority of intestinal lymphomas
in dogs have been found to be of T cell origin on
immunohistochemistry
Small intestinal adenocarcinoma is uncommon in dogs
and the small intestine in general is an uncommon site
for cancer in dogs and people. Some possible explanations for this include rapid transit times through the
small intestine decreasing exposure to carcinogens, large
volume of mucosal secretions diluting out carcinogens,
a microbial population incapable of activating carcinogens, and microsomal enzymes in the small intestine that
may detoxify some carcinogens.
Forty seven percent of intestinal adenocarcinomas
expres COX‐2 in the neoplastic epithelium. The presence of the COX‐2 enzyme has been found to c­ ontribute
to tumorigenesis in rodent models and is a potential target for nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
Leiomyosarcoma is a slow‐growing, locally invasive,
malignant tumor originating from smooth muscle and is
generally slow to metastasize. A recent study reclassified
some dogs previously diagnosed with intestinal leiomyosarcomas as gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs)
based on the expression of the tyrosine kinase growth
factor receptor, KIT. It is thought that activating mutations in c‐kit are involved in the pathogenesis of these
tumors. Differentiating between a leiomyosarcoma and a
GIST may have implications for both biologic behavior
and treatment of the neoplasia.
Both adenocarcinoma and leiomyosarcoma of the
small intestine have the potential to metastasize (43.5%

and 16–50%, respectively). The most common site of
metastasis for an adenocarcinoma is the regional lymph
node and the most common site for a leiomyosarcoma is
the liver or the mesentery. Russell et al. reported a metastatic rate of 7% for canine GISTs based on immunohistochemical staining for CD117.
Feline intestinal lymphoma is generally not associated
with feline leukemia virus (FeLV) infection. An increased
incidence of feline lymphoma, specifically nasal and
intestinal, was found in cats exposed to environmental
tobacco smoke. Another possible cause of intestinal
­lymphoma is chronic inflammation, as there has been an
association between low‐grade or small cell intestinal
lymphoma and inflammatory bowel disease. It is thought
that intestinal lymphoma derives from the mucosa‐­
associated lymphoid tissue (MALT). However, the tumor
can progress and invade the submucosa and muscularis
layers of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Lesions can be
solitary, multifocal or diffuse throughout the intestinal
tract. Involvement of mesenteric lymph nodes is common and dissemination to other organs such as the liver,
spleen, kidneys, mediastinal lymph nodes or bone marrow can occur as the disease progresses. Intestinal lymphoma may either be small cell/lymphocytic (low-grade)
or large cell/lymphoblastic (high-grade). Reports are
mixed regarding the prevalence of low‐ versus high‐
grade alimentary lymphoma in cats. Earlier reports
­indicate that high‐grade lymphomas were more common, but more recent reports indicate the low‐grade
lymphomas are more prevalent.
Feline small intestinal adenocarcinoma usually affects
the jejunum and ileum. Approximately 50% of cats
with intestinal adenocarcinoma experience metastasis.
The most common sites of metastasis include the
­ esentery,
regional lymph nodes, peritoneum, omentum, m
liver, and lungs. Ascites may be present secondary to
carcinomatosis.

The intestinal lesion with feline intestinal mast cell
tumor can be diffuse, solitary or multifocal. The neoplasia may be either intraluminal or intramural. The small
intestine is the most common location for feline intestinal mast cell tumor but colonic involvement can occur.
Widespread metastasis is common at the time of diagnosis. One study found that 64% of cats with intestinal mast
cell tumor had multiorgan involvement. The most common sites of metastasis include lymph nodes, liver,
spleen, and rarely lung. Intestinal mast cell tumors can be
difficult to diagnose because their cytoplasmic granules
may not stain. This may be due to their anaplastic nature
or degranulation. It has been suggested that mucosal
mast cells are different from mesenchymal mast cells and
require special fixation to enhance the metachromasia.
Diff‐Quik staining of feline mast cell tumors sometimes
fails to reveal cytoplasmic granules. Circulating mast
cells are uncommon with intestinal mast cell tumors,
although peripheral eosinophilia has been reported.
Adenomatous polyps and carcinoma in situ are usually
solitary. However, multiple and diffuse varieties have
been identified. Furthermore, malignant transformation
to invasive carcinoma has been reported.
Canine colorectal adenocarcinoma generally can be
grouped into three categories based on its gross appearance: pedunculated, cobblestone, and annular. When
metastasis does occur with colorectal adenocarcinoma,
it usually travels via lymphatics to the local lymph nodes
and may sometimes seed the peritoneum, leading to carcinomatosis. The metastatic rate for colorectal adenocarcinoma ranges from 0% to 80%. Malignant transformation
from in situ tumors has been reported in 17–50% of dogs.
Approximately 75% of cats with colonic adenocarcinoma have metastasis. Half have distant metastasis and
half are local. Metastatic sites included the colonic lymph
nodes, mesenteric lymph nodes, liver, omentum, and
lungs. Carcinomatosis may also occur.

pacemaker cells of the intestinal tract and regulate peristalsis. Tumors derived from these cells are called gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs). GISTs can be
distinguished from leiomyosarcomas based on the
expression of c‐kit (CD117). In one recent study, two‐
thirds of dogs diagnosed with intestinal leiomyosarcomas were reclassified as GISTs based on positive staining
for CD117. In this study, GISTs were most common in
the cecum and large intestine (64%) as compared to the
stomach and small intestine (36%). In oposition to
GISTs,leiomyosarcomas appear to develop more commonly in the stomach and small intestine (90%) and are
less common in the large intestine (10%).
It is reported that up to 60% of all intestinal tumors in
dogs are located in the colon and rectum. Dogs are typically middle‐aged to older with males reported to be
affected more frequently than females. Unlike in the
small intestine, adenomatous polyps and carcinoma in
situ are commonly identified in the large intestine.
Malignant tumors, such as those that develop in the
small intestine also occur.
Lymphoma is the most common intestinal neoplasia in
cats. It is the most common anatomic form of lymphoma
in cats since the advent of FeLV vaccine as well as routine
FeLV testing and separation of FeLV‐positive cats.
Anatomic forms of feline lymphoma ­generally associated
with FeLV infection, such as the mediastinal and nodal
forms, are becoming less prevalent. Adenocarcinoma is
the ­second most common small intestinal tumor in cats.
Siamese may be overrepresented. Intestinal mast cell
tumor is the third most common intestinal tumor in cats.
Colonic adenocarcinoma (along with lymphoma) is one
of the two most common neoplasias that develop in the
feline large intestine.
Other less common intestinal tumors include
extramedullary plasmacytoma, extraskeletal osteosarcoma, and hemangiosarcoma.

­Epidemiology

­Signalment

Small intestinal tumors are in general, uncommon in
dogs. According to most reports, lymphoma is the most
common specific type. The intestinal tract is the most
common extranodal site for this malignancy, affecting
5–7% of all dogs diagnosed. Intestinal adenocarcinoma
and leiomyosarcoma are the two most common nonlymphomatous small intestinal tumors in dogs. In particular,
leiomyosarcoma is the most frequently diagnosed intestinal sarcoma and it commonly involves the jejunum and
cecum.
Recently, it was found that tumors previously categorized as leiomyosarcomas were in fact derived from the
interstitial cells of Cajal. Interstitial cells of Cajal are the

The median age for dogs with all types of lymphoma,
including intestinal, is 6–9 years. Small i­ntestinal neoplasia should be considered a differential diagnosis in a
middle‐aged to older dog with signs ­
consistent with
intestinal obstruction. The median age of onset for
canine intestinal leiomyosarcoma/GIST is 10.5 years.
They are reportedly more common in female dogs. Dogs
with colorectal polyps have a mean age of 7–8 years.
Colorectal adenocarcinoma most commonly affects
older male dogs. Feline intestinal lymphoma is more
common in older cats with a median of age of 10–12
years. Domestic short‐hairs are more commonly
affected. The average age of cats with small intestinal

adenocarcinoma is 10–11 years. Siamese may be overrepresented. Feline intestinal mast cell tumors tend to
affect older cats with a mean age of 13 years. Feline
colonic adenocarcinoma generally affects older cats with
no discernible sex or breed predilection.

­History and Clinical Signs
Clinical signs for most small intestinal neoplasias in dogs
and cats are similar and include one or more of the
following: anorexia, vomiting, diarrhea, weight loss,
­
melena, and lethargy. Signs may be subacute, acute or
chronic in nature, depending on the underlying disease
process. A patient may present with acute vomiting, anorexia, and abdominal discomfort secondary to a gastric
or small intestinal obstructive lesion or with a history of
chronic weight loss, decreased appetite and intermittent
vomiting over the course of months if a low‐grade intestinal lymphoma is the underlying problem. Therefore,
the chronicity of signs should not dissuade the clinician
from keeping neoplasia on the differential list for many
common GI presentations. Some patients may present in
shock if a GI perforation occurs secondary to underlying
intestinal neoplasia. Dogs with intestinal leiomyosarcomas may present with signs secondary to paraneoplastic
hypoglycemia, such as weakness, ataxia, and seizures.
Some patients with intestinal tumors may present with
signs referable to anemia such as weakness and lethargy
secondary to gastrointestinal bleeding.

­Diagnosis
A complete blood count, biochemistry profile, and urinalysis are recommended as part of a minimum database
but are not helpful in establishing a definitive diagnosis.
Anemia can be seen in up to ~64% of dogs with intestinal
neoplasia and is associated with intestinal hemorrhage
or anemia of chronic disease.
The chemistry panel can reveal a paraneoplastic
­hypoglycemia in dogs with intestinal leiomyosarcoma.
When a dog presents primarily for signs secondary to
hypoglycemia, rather than gastrointestinal signs, a serum
sample should be held for simultaneous blood glucose
and blood insulin levels to rule out inappropriate insulin
secretion secondary to an insulinoma (beta‐cell tumor of
the pancreas). Hypoproteinemia is a common laboratory
finding secondary to malabsorption or intestinal loss
in dogs and cats with diffuse intestinal lymphoma.
Cobalamin and folate should be assessed to ­evaluate for
malabsorption and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.
Animals with intestinal extramedullary plasmacytomas
should be thoroughly staged for systemic disease with

serum electrophoresis, bone marrow aspiration/evaluation, abdominal ultrasound, and survey skeletal radiographs. In cats with intestinal lymphoma or intestinal
carcinoma, an abdominal mass can be palpated in over
50% of cases. Abdominal radiographs may show an
obstructive pattern or abdominal mass. Three‐view thoracic radiographs should be performed but are usually
negative for metastasis at the time of diagnosis.
The imaging test that will give the clinician the most
useful information is abdominal ultrasound which provides information regarding size and location of the mass
as well as evidence of metastatic spread. It also provides a
means to achieve a diagnosis through less invasive procedures such as ultrasound‐guided aspiration and ultrasound‐guided biopsy. Ultrasound‐guided aspirates and
biopsies both can result in a false negative if a cystic,
necrotic or inflammatory area of the tumor is sampled.
As with any neoplasia, biopsy and histopathology is
the preferred method of diagnosis. Occasional misdiagnosis of neoplasia can occur with aspiration/cytology,
where a tumor may be aspirated and the cytology is consistent with one type of neoplasia (i.e., carcinoma) but
when a biopsy and histopathology are performed, the
diagnosis changes to another tumor type (i.e., lymphoma). This can occur when the aspiration contains
cells which are not representative of the underlying
lesion, the tissue sampled does not exfoliate well or in
order to make a correct diagnosis of neoplasia the evaluation of the tissue architecture is needed, not just evaluation of the cell type. Endoscopy and colonoscopy may
be helpful in diagnosing proximal small intestinal lesions
and colorectal lesions respectively. However, endoscopic
biopsy may underdiagnose intestinal lymphoma in dogs
and cats. Ultimately, abdominal exploratory surgery with
either incisional or excisional biopsy and histopathology
may be necessary to obtain a definitive diagnosis.
Immunohistochemistry for the expression of c‐kit
(CD117) is recommended in dogs with intestinal sarcomas to differentiate between GISTs (CD117 positive)
and leiomyosarcoma (CD117 negative). The differentiation between GISTs and leiomyosarcomas can have both
prognostic and therapeutic implications.
Routine immunohistochemistry has identified that T
cell is the most common immunophenotype of intestinal lymphoma in dogs. Feline intestinal lymphoma can
be either T cell or B cell in origin.

­Therapy
Surgical excision via intestinal resection and anastomosis, with or without adjuvant chemotherapy, is the
­primary treatment for most animals with intestinal neoplasia. Intestinal lymphoma is the one notable exception,

1289

VetBooks.ir

1290

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

where chemotherapy is the primary treatment recommendation. Surgery is only recommended in patients
with intestinal lymphoma when there is evidence of
intestinal perforation or obstruction. It is recommended
that 5–6 cm of normal intestine on either side of the
tumor be excised. For animals with colonic tumors, subtotal colectomy may be necessary. One study found that
cats that had subtotal colectomy for colonic adenocarcinoma had improved survival times over cats that had just
mass resection or mass biopsy. The authors of the study
do not suggest that every cat with a colonic mass should
receive subtotal colectomy but wide surgical margins are
recommended. Biopsy of the local lymph nodes, liver,
and any other abnormal‐appearing abdominal organ is
recommended to assess for metastasis. For dogs and cats
with rectal tumors, a transanal pull‐through procedure
has been found to be effective. A combined abdominal‐
transanal approach may be necessary for tumors located
at the cranial extent of the rectum extending to the
descending colon.
The benefit of postoperative chemotherapy is unknown
for dogs with small intestinal adenocarcinoma. However,
due to the moderate to high metastatic rate, the inclusion of adjuvant chemotherapy with doxorubicin‐based
protocols would be l­ogical. Approximately 50% of intestinal adenocarcinomas in dogs expres COX‐2. The products of the COX‐2 enzyme have been associated with
protumorigenic effects such as angiogenesis, cell proliferation, and inhibition of apoptosis. Therefore, the
author recommends including NSAIDs in the treatment
protocol for dogs with intestinal adenocarcinomas as
they have antineoplastic activity that may help improve
response and survival. The metastatic rate of small
intestinal carcinoma in cats is also high. Postoperative
chemotherapy is recommended to help control metastasis and to prolong survival. A study evaluating cats with
large intestinal carcinoma did show a survival advantage
for those that received doxorubicin chemotherapy postoperatively. Whether this chemotherapy protocol is beneficial in cats with small intestinal carcinoma has yet to
be determined but it is a logical choice for postoperative
therapy.
As with small intestinal adenocarcinoma, the use of
postoperative chemotherapy in dogs with small intestinal leiomyosarcoma has yet to be investigated in a randomized clinical trial. However, based on the moderate to
high metastatic rate (16–50%), chemotherapy should be
included in the treatment protocol. Surgical removal
alone results in prolonged survival times (over three
years) for dogs with GISTs. However, for those few cases
in which GISTs are nonresectable or metastatic, adjuvant treatment with tyrosine kinase inhibitors may be
useful. In humans with nonresectable or metastatic
GISTs, treatment with tyrosine kinase inhibitors has

been shown to result in longer survival times compared
to other treatments. Therefore, the use of tyrosine kinase
inhibitors in dogs with nonresectable, recurrent or metastatic GISTs is reasonable as GISTs in both species
express KIT/CD117. Activating mutations have been
found involving c‐kit in both dogs and humans and are
thought to be the driving force for GIST development.
There are two oral tyrosine kinase inhibitors in veterinary medicine, toceranib phosphate (Palladia™) and
masitinib mesylate (Masi). Only Palladia, is approved for
use in dogs with mast cell tumors in the USA. Regardless,
both inhibit KIT but their use in dogs with GISTs has yet
to be investigated.
Chemotherapy is the primary treatment for intestinal
lymphoma in dogs due to the multifocal or diffuse nature
of the disease. Although CHOP (cyclophosphamide,
doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone)‐based protocols
are considered the standard of care for dogs with multicentric lymphoma, due to the poor response of dogs
with intestinal lymphoma other alkylating agent‐based
protocols, including MOPP (mechlorethamine HCL,
vincristine sulfate, procarbazine, prednisone), lomustine
or DTIC/lomustine, may provide improved survival
times.
In cats with intestinal lymphoma, the treatment protocol varies depending on whether they have low‐grade
versus intermediate to high‐grade lymphoma. The treatment of low‐grade lymphoma consists of the administration of prednisolone and chlorambucil. One study
evaluating cats with low‐grade intestinal lymphoma
found that 78% were cobalamin (vitamin B12) deficient,
thus requiring cobalamin supplementation. Cobalamin
is absorbed exclusively in the ileum, complexed with
intrinsic factor. Low cobalamin is associated with metabolic derangements and low concentrations of several
amino acids. Intermediate to high‐grade lymphomarequires more aggressive therapy. The best response,
remission duration, and survival time is generally
achieved with CHOP‐based chemotherapy protocols.
Eventually, most cats relapse and/or develop resistant
disease. If relapsing after completing their initial CHOP
chemotherapy ­protocol, it can be restarted. The second
remission is generally about half the duration of the first.
Once they fail CHOP, rescue chemotherapy can be
attempted. The most successful rescue chemotherapy
protocols include MOPP and lomustine.
If a solitary mass is present and there is no evidence of
metastatic disease, surgical removal can be attempted in
cats with intestinal mast cell tumors. Due to the high rate
of disseminated disease with intestinal mast cell tumors,
postoperative chemotherapy is recommended based on
the likelihood of residual micrometastasis. If the intestinal mast cell tumor is not resectable or metastatic disease is present at the time of diagnosis, chemotherapy

VetBooks.ir

142 Cancer of the Small and Large Intestine

can be attempted. A study evaluating lomustine for cats
with a variety of mast cell tumors (cutaneous, splenic,
intestinal) found that two cats with intestinal mast cell
tumors responded. Whether lomustine would be effective in a large population of cats with intestinal mast cell
tumors is unknown. Other chemotherapy agents used in
dogs with mast cell tumors include vinblastine, cyclophosphamide, hydroxyurea, and prednisone. Their effectiveness in cats with mast cell tumors is unknown.
Many cat mast cell tumors have mutations in the gene
c‐kit leading to constitutive activation of the tyrosine
kinase growth factor receptor KIT. Activating mutations
of c‐kit have been implicated in mast cell tumor development and progression in dogs. Small molecule targeted
therapies (toceranib phosphate and masitinib meslyate)
have been approved for use in dogs with mast cell tumors.
As mentioned previously only toceranib phosphate is
approved for use in the USA. These targeted therapies
inhibit the activation of the abnormal growth factor
receptor KIT, resulting in cessation of cell growth and
proliferation and potentially leading to cell death through
apoptosis. A recent study evaluating Palladia in cats with
mast cell tumors reported a clinical benefit in 76%
(13/17) of those with the gastrointestinal form. However,
further studies are necessary.
Aside from definitive treatment with chemotherapy
and/or a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, all patients with intestinal mast cell tumors should receive prednisolone or
prednisone as well as a histamine receptor 1 and 2
­
antagonist.
For dogs with colorectal polyps, the use of NSAIDs has
been found to be of benefit in reducing clinical signs and
may be an alternative treatment to surgical excision. The
author recommends placing dogs that have had surgical
removal of colorectal polyps on NSAIDs postoperatively
in an attempt to prevent local recurrence, development
of additional polyps or malignant transformation of polyps. Although there are no clinical studies evaluating the
use of NSAIDs in this particular setting, NSAIDs have
been found to have various antineoplastic properties.
Surgical excision of colorectal plasmacytomas is curative in most cases. Plasmacytomas of other areas of the
intestinal tract can have a high metastatic rate and if
metastasis is observed, follow‐up chemotherapy in the
form of prednisone and melphalan is recommended.
Extraskeletal osteosarcomas are both locally and systemically aggressive. Adjuvant chemotherapy has been
shown to help prolong survival in dogs with extraskeletal
osteosarcoma. Therefore, postoperative carboplatin is
recommended for intestinal extraskeletal osteosarcoma.
Visceral hemangiosarcoma is an aggressive disease with
a high rate of metastasis. Adjuvant doxorubicin chemotherapy is recommended after surgical resection of intestinal hemangiosarcoma.

Many animals with intestinal neoplasia need supportive medications for nausea, decreased appetite, gastrointestinal protection, and diarrhea. The most commonly
used antiemetics include maropitant, ondansentron,
dolasetron, and metoclopramide. Appetite stimulants
include capromorelin, mirtazapine, cyproheptadine, and
megestrol acetate. Effective gastroprotectants include
famotidine, omeprazole, and sucralfate. Common antidiarrheal medications include metronidazole, tylosin, sulfasalazine, and loperamide.

­Prognosis
The prognosis for dogs with intestinal lymphoma is
generally much worse than for dogs with multicentric
lymphoma. A recent study using a CHOP‐based protocol with consolidation resulted in a 56% response rate
(50% complete response, 6% partial response). The
median survival time for the entire study population
was 2.5 months. The response rate for dogs with multicentric lymphoma is up to 90–95% with median survival times of 12–18 months. Another study evaluating
dogs with intestinal lymphoma treated with multiple
treatment modalities revealed very poor survival, with a
median survival time of 13 days. In dogs with intestinal
lymphoma, the presence of diarrhea and lack of
response to chemotherapy were negative prognostic
factors
In dogs treated with surgical excision for small intestinal adenocarcinoma, the presence of metastasis at the
time of surgery is associated with statistically shorter
survival time (median survival time three months, 20%
survival at one year) when compared to dogs without
metastasis (median survival time 15 months, 66.7%
­survival at one year).
Long‐term survival has been reported in dogs with
metastatic intestinal leiomyosarcoma. In one study, 50%
of dogs with intestinal leiomyosarcomas had metastasis
at the time of surgery. The median survival time of the
entire study population was 21.3 months. Another study
revealed a median survival time of 1.1 years for dogs
with small intestinal leiomyosarcoma that survived the
immediate postoperative period, with 29% of the dogs
dying of leiomyosarcoma. The results of these historical
studies should be viewed ­in light that some might have
been GISTs that had been misdiagnosed. In one study
evaluating both GISTs and leiomyosarcomas, the median
survival time for dogs with GISTs that survived the perioperative period was 37.4 months, whereas the median
survival time for dogs with leiomyosarcomas was only
7.8 months. Further, 7% of the dogs with GISTs developed metastasis. There were no reports of metastasis in
those with leiomyosarcomas.

Recurrence of clinical signs is uncommon with removal
of colorectal adenomatous polyps (17%). However,
recurrence of clinical signs after removal of carcinoma in
situ is fairly common (55%). The presence of multiple
lesions was also associated with recurrence of clinical
signs. Malignant transformation has been reported with
rectal polyps, although more commonly with carcinoma
in situ (17–50%).
The prognosis for dogs with colorectal adenocarcinoma has been linked to the gross appearance of the
tumor. The mean survival time for those with pedunculated lesions is 32 months, cobblestone lesions 12
months, and annular lesions 1.6 months.
Cats with small cell, low‐grade intestinal lymphoma
treated with prednisone and chlorambucil have a good
prognosis with response rates of 69–95% and median
survival times of 18–24 months.
Cats with intermediate to high‐grade intestinal lymphoma have a worse prognosis compared to those with
the low‐grade intestinal type. When compared to other
anatomic sites, cats with intermediate to high‐grade
intestinal lymphoma tend to have the second best prognosis, after nasal lymphoma. ­However, the response
rate, remission duration, and survival time for cats with
intermediate to high‐grade intestinal lymphoma are generally less than dogs with multicentric intermediate to
high‐grade lymphoma. The response rate for cats treated
with multiagent (CHOP‐based) chemotherapy is 50–86%
(complete response rate of 50–70%) with a median
remission duration of 4–9 months and a median survival
time of up to 7–9 months. Response to therapy, FeLV

status, substage, anatomic site, and chemotherapy
­
­protocols that include doxorubicin have been linked to
remission duration and survival. Unlike dogs, immunophenotype (T cell vs B cell) is not a prognostic factor
in cats with lymphoma.
The prognosis can be fairly good for cats with small
intestinal adenocarcinoma that survive the postoperative period, with average survival times of 15 months
reported. In one study, even those that had lymph node
metastasis at the time of surgery and survived the perioperative period fared well (average survival time of 12
months). In the study, recurrent adenocarcinoma was
the cause of death in 50% of long‐term survivors.
The prognosis for intestinal mast cell tumor has
­historically been considered to be poor due to the high
percentage of patients that present with metastatic disease. However, a recent study of cats indicated that the
prognosis may be better than once thought (median survival time 531 days).
Reported cats that had subtotal colectomy for colonic
adenocarcinoma had significantly longer survival times
than cats with either mass resection or biopsy. Median
survival time with subtotal colectomy was 138 days versus 68 days and 10 days for mass resection and biopsy
respectively. In the study, the presence of metastasis was
also associated with a shorter survival time (median survival time 49 days) compared to those cats that did not
have metastasis (259 days). Finally, cats that receive doxorubicin chemotherapy appear to have a significantly
longer survival time (median survival 280 days) compared to those that do not receive doxorubicin (56 days).

Avenelle I. Turner, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology)
Veterinary Cancer Group, Culver City, CA, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology

­History and Clinical Signs

Nearly all cancers of the exocrine pancreas are epithelial
and most are adenocarcinoma arising from either the
ductal or acinar epithelium. This is in contrast to insulinomas which arise from the islet cells of the endocrine
pancreas. Insulinomas are covered in more detail in a
different section. There are no known causes for exocrine pancreatic cancer (EPC) in veterinary medicine.
Experimentally, intraductal administration of N‐ethyl‐
N’‐nitro‐N‐nitrosoguanidine induces EPC in dogs.

Exocrine pancreatic cancer is rare and accounts for less
than 0.05% of all cancers in the dog and cat. Older female
dogs, spaniels, and Airedales have been described in previous publications as being at higher risk. In humans,
EPC remains the fourth most common cause of cancer‐
related death in the United States and it occurs most
commonly in people who smoke or have chronic pancreatitis or diabetes mellitus. It is not clear if this is true
in veterinary medicine but recently there have been several published reports of diabetes mellitus and EPC in
cats which are suggestive of a possible association. It is
unknown whether diabetes mellitus develops secondary
to compression of islet cells by tumor, secondary to cortisol‐induced beta‐cell degeneration, or secondary to
decreased carbohydrate metabolism, which is common
in humans with pancreatic carcinoma.

Symptoms associated with EPC are nonspecific and may
mimic pancreatitis. Anorexia, weight loss, lethargy, weakness, vomiting, maldigestion syndrome, abdominal distension, abdominal effusion, and icterus are common findings.
In cats that presented with EPC, 75% had anorexia, 63%
vomiting, and 38% abdominal pain, a palpable abdominal
mass, and/or jaundice. Duration of clinical signs appeared
to be bimodal, with 50% of cats having signs for <7 days
and the other 50% having signs for >1 month.
Paraneoplastic alopecia is a rare syndrome seen in cats
with pancreatic neoplasms. The pathogenesis of this dermatologic disease is unknown. Alopecia begins acutely
and typically starts with loss of clumps of hair on the
ventrum, and then spreads to the legs and eventually the
face. Dorsal alopecia is uncommon. Other changes noted
are poor, dry, thinning hair coat and focal areas of
­erythema. Often, there is a characteristic appearance to
the skin and in areas where cats groom, the skin can
appear shiny. Lesions develop rapidly over 2–10 weeks
and spread over much of the body. They appear in association with the tumor and in one case resolved with
tumor removal.
Histopathologically, the skin changes are characterized by loss of the stratum corneum and severe follicular
atrophy with miniaturized hair bulbs. The majority of
cases die or are euthanized within eight weeks of development of lesions so the presence of this condition on
physical examination is highly suspicious for EPC and
appears to be a poor prognostic factor.

­Signalment

­Diagnosis

The median age at diagnosis is 10 years for dogs and 12
years for cats. It occurs almost equally in both sexes.

Staging for EPC includes radiographs of the thorax (three‐
view), abdominal radiographs (two‐view), ­minimum

database (complete blood count, biochemistry profile,
urinalysis) and abdominal ultrasound. In cases where an
aspirate is going to be obtained, a clotting profile is advisable as prolongation in partial thromboplastin time (PTT)
and clotting disorders have been described in cats and
people with EPC respectively. In cases where surgery is
being considered, a computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen may be
useful in preoperative planning and identifying metastatic disease.
Laboratory findings are generally nonspecific but can
include leukocytosis, anemia, hyperglycemia, and elevations in liver enzymes. Dogs with pancreatic neoplasia
may have significant elevations in serum lipase with only
minimal elevations of serum amylase, implying tumor
production of lipase. These findings are inconsistent,
however. In a small case series of eight cats with EPC,
50% had neutrophilia, 33% had elevations in serum alkaline phosphatase activity, and 57% had increased alanine
aminotransferase. Mild hyperglycemia was identified in
63% of cats.
Physical examination findings can include abdominal
pain, icterus, abdominal distension, and/or ascites. In
small dogs or cats, palpation of a cranial abdominal mass
can occasionally be appreciated.
Survey abdominal radiographs may show decreased
serosal detail or a cranial abdominal mass effect. The
sensitivity for the detection of pancreatic tumors in dogs
has been reported to be 19% for radiographs and 75% for
ultrasound. Abdominal radiographs were helpful in identifying abdominal disease in cats with EPC. In one study,
abdominal radiography was able to identify abdominal
disease in all cases of pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
Ultrasonography is superior to abdominal radiographs for detecting EPC in both dogs and cats. It is a
useful diagnostic tool for localization of the tumor,
confirmation of ascites, and documentation of lymphadenopathy and metastasis. In cats, the ultrasound
findings seen with nodular hyperplasia of the pancreas
are similar to changes seen with malignant pancreatic
neoplasms. There was a trend, however, for malignant
masses to appear as a single, larger lesion exceeding
2 cm in at least one dimension. Hyperplastic nodules
typically did not measure more than 1 cm in diameter
and were n
­ umerous. Differentials for masses of the
pancreas are insulinoma, gastrinoma, adenocarcinoma,
adenoma, pancreatic pseudocyst, abscess, pancreatitis,
and lymphoma.
When effusion is present, cytology and fluid analysis
may reveal a modified transudate and neoplastic cells
indicating carcinomatosis. Solitary masses can be diagnosed with cytology. Cytologic samples obtained with
ultrasound guidance correctly diagnosed EPC in 92%
of cases.

­Therapy
The majority of EPCs are diagnosed at an advanced
stage. Fifty to seventy percent of animals have metastatic
disease to regional lymph nodes and distant sites documented at the time of diagnosis. In a study where necropsy findings were documented in cats with EPC,
metastases to the liver, abdominal lymph nodes, lung,
heart, diaphragm, tracheobronchial and cranial mediastinal lymph nodes were found. The incidence of metastasis seemed to be unrelated to the duration of clinical
signs. Cats with the longest history of clinical signs were
equally likely to have metastasis noted at necropsy as
cats with short histories. This suggests that the duration
of clinical signs prior to diagnosis is not a negative prognostic indicator.
Complete pancreatectomy or pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure) has been described in
humans and in dogs but carries a high perioperative
morbidity and mortality without significant cure rates.
Chemotherapy and radiation therapy have shown limited value in humans and animals and information
regarding the use of chemotherapy in veterinary medicine is scarce. In humans, external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) alone does not provide optimal tumor
control and local failure rates are as high as 72%. These
dismal results have spawned efforts to improve outcomes
by the concurrent administration of drugs that act as
radiation sensitizers, including 5‐fluorouracil, gemcitabine, and, most recently, paclitaxel.
Palliative therapy to address effusions can be attempted
with regular, periodic abdominocentesis and intracavitary chemotherapy. Protocols utilizing cisplatin and
­carboplatin have been described and appear to provide
palliation for select patients. When effective, this can
result in temporary relief from discomfort, slow the reaccumulation of the effusion, and possibly delay progression of the disease. Palliative responses, when seen, are
generally short‐lived.

­Prognosis
The prognosis of EPC is generally poor, with few animals living beyond a year although a small percentage
of dogs and cats have experienced long‐term survival.
In dogs, a unique variant of EPC described as hyalinizing pancreatic adenocarcinoma appears to be biologically less aggressive. The neoplasm is generally a
solitary mass usually involving the right limb of the
pancreas. Dogs without postoperative complications
or concurrent life‐threatening diseases survived
longer than expected (four months, 16 months, and
>19 months).

VetBooks.ir

143 Exocrine Pancreatic Cancer

In a retrospective study evaluating 34 cats with EPC,
metastatic disease was confirmed in 11 cats and overall
median survival was 97 days. The median survival times
for patients who received chemotherapy or had their
masses surgically removed was 165 days. Patients with
abdominal effusion present at diagnosis had a median
survival of 30 days. Interestingly, however, three patients
survived over one year.
A cat with metastatic EPC to the spleen treated with
partial pancreatectomy and splenectomy was reported
to be alive and disease free >2 years later. Therefore, the
prognosis for EPC in select dogs and cats may not be as
dismal as previously reported.

Comparatively, about 45 220 people develop cancer of
the exocrine pancreas each year in the US, and almost all
are expected to die from the disease. The median survival is 8–12 months for patients with locally advanced
disease and less for those with metastatic disease at presentation. Five‐year survival rates are consistently <18%.
The majority of these tumors (85%) are adenocarcinomas arising from the ductal epithelium. Surgical resection offers the only chance of cure. However, only
15–20% of patients have resectable disease at diagnosis,
approximately 40% have metastatic disease, and another
30–40% have locally advanced unresectable tumors.

Pancreatic Endocrine Tumors
Karen Eiler, DVM, MS, DACVIM (SAIM)
VCA West Los Angeles Animal Hospital, Los Angeles, CA, USA

­Insulinoma
Etiology/Pathophysiology
The pancreas is made up of endocrine and exocrine tis­
sue. The endocrine pancreas is composed of islets of
Langerhans, which make up approximately 1–2% of the
mass of the pancreas. Within the islets there are four cell
types: alpha, beta, delta, and polypeptide cells. Beta‐cells
secrete various hormones, with insulin being the pri­
mary product. Approximately 60–75% of the islet cells
are of beta‐cell origin.
Insulin is the hormone that is primarily responsible for
regulating blood glucose concentration. Insulin does not
influence entry of blood glucose into beta‐cells, as in
other tissues. Entry of glucose into the beta‐cell is pro­
portional to the blood glucose concentration. Beta‐cells
are extremely sensitive to glucose concentrations and
therefore the regulation of insulin secretion.
The central nervous system (CNS) has limited glyco­
gen storage and is unable to use energy sources other
than glucose. Thus, it is dependent on blood glucose to
maintain its energy requirements. With hypoglycemia,
cells within the cerebral cortex are affected first due to
their higher metabolic rate. Counterregulatory hormones
such as catecholamine, glucagon, growth hormone, and
cortisol are secreted in response to hypoglycemia and aid
in recovery from the hypoglycemic episode.
Insulinomas (beta‐cell insulin‐secreting tumor, beta‐
cell adenocarcinoma/adenoma) are insulin‐secreting
tumors of the pancreatic beta‐cells. They are the most
common endocrine pancreatic tumor in companion ani­
mals and are usually malignant.
Insulinomas can be found in both the right and left
lobes of the pancreas with equal frequency. Occult insu­
linomas are most frequently found in the pancreatic body.

Epidemiology
Insulinomas are uncommon in dogs and rare in cats.
One estimated report cites an incidence of 17.8/100 000
patient‐years in the dog and 12.6/100 000 patient‐years
at risk in the cat. Insulinomas have been associated with
multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) type I in people.
This is an inherited disease that also results in parathy­
roid and pituitary tumors. Although we do not have a
clear understanding of the epidemiology of canine insu­
linomas, there have been rare cases of canine MEN that
involve an insulinoma.
Signalment
In dogs, middle‐aged to older, medium to large breeds
are predisposed. Large‐breed dogs are overrepresented.
Breed predispositions have not been noted in cats.
History and Clinical Signs
Clinical signs are predominantly related to hypoglyce­
mia, resulting in neuroglycopenic manifestations and,
less commonly, stimulation of the sympathoadrenal sys­
tem. The degree and onset of clinical signs are related to
the severity and rate of development of hypoglycemia.
Gradual or chronic hypoglycemia may go unnoticed.
When chronically affected by hypoglycemia, some ani­
mals adjust to blood glucose levels of 20–30 mg/dL.
Clinical symptoms consistent with hypoglycemia
include seizures, lethargy, weakness, coma, and ataxia.
Catecholamine release can cause tachycardia, muscle
fasciculations, hunger, and restlessness. Exercise causes
rapid consumption of glucose and may precipitate an
episode of collapse or seizure.

Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/bruyette/clinical
