Diagnosis
Differential diagnosis for other causes of hypoglycemia
include hypoadrenocorticism, juvenile hypoglycemia, sep­
sis, growth hormone deficiency, nonpancreatic tumors,
insulin overdose, hepatic disease, glycogen storage diseases,
artifacts related to sample handling, and toxins. Other
types of neoplasms that can lead to paraneoplastic hypo­
glycemia include hepatocellular carcinoma, hepatoma,
leiomyosarcoma, leiomyoma, lymphoma, myeloma, and
hemangiosarcoma.
A minimum database (complete blood count, serum
chemistry, urinalysis) should be collected to rule out
other causes of hypoglycemia. Nonspecific findings that
may be associated with insulinomas include elevated
liver enzymes, hypokalemia, and hypophosphatemia.
Radiographs may help rule out other causes of hypoglyce­
mia. However, radiographic changes directly related to
insulinomas should not be expected. Sensitivity of identi­
fying insulinomas with abdominal ultrasound can be as
low as 36%. It may be more beneficial in identifying metas­
tasis in the liver and local lymph nodes. Failure to identify
a pancreatic mass does not rule out an insulinoma. Serum
insulin concentrations that are normal to high in the pres­
ence of hypoglycemia support a diagnosis of insulinoma.
Insulin:glucose and glucose:insulin ratios have high false‐
positive rates and are not recommended. Rather, insulin
concentration should be measured on a serum sample
taken when the blood glucose is below 60 mg/dL. Insulin
concentrations should be low or undetectable at this blood
glucose concentration. The serum glucose and insulin are
evaluated as a pair. Animals may need to be fasted in order
to obtain the appropriate samples and serial samples may
need to be drawn every 2–4 hours until the blood glucose
concentration is below 60 mg/dL. Provocative testing is not
recommended as it has not been shown to be more sensi­
tive than paired insulin and glucose measurement and can
be dangerous due to potentiation of hypoglycemia.
Additional preoperative and intraoperative methods of
tumor identification may be utilized. Nuclear scintigra­
phy with indium 111‐labeled pentetreotide has been
used to image somatostatin receptors in dogs with insu­
linomas. Insulinomas express high‐affinity somatostatin
receptors of subtype sst2 (SST2), thus allowing abnormal
foci of activity to be detected. Direct intraoperative
ultrasonography and intravenous injection of methylene
blue may also be beneficial in identifying insulinomas.
Methylene blue concentrates in the neoplastic tissue.
However, side‐effects including Heinz body anemia and
renal failure have been reported to occur.
Therapy
Surgery is the mainstay of treatment. However, even
when resectable, a cure is still unlikely. Gross or occult

metastasis should be expected. Debulking of gross
­disease may significantly assist in controlling clinical
signs. The goal of surgery is to remove as much neoplas­
tic tissue as possible. Special attention should be given to
regional lymph nodes and the liver. Complications
include hyperglycemia (diabetes mellitus), continued
hypoglycemia, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, and
pancreatitis.
First‐line medical management is glucocorticoid ther­
apy. In particular, prednisone administered at 0.25–3 mg/
kg orally twice daily can be utilized. The dose should be
increased as needed to control hypoglycemia. Prednisone
is used with small frequent feedings (four times daily)
and limited exercise. Exercise leads to an increased
peripheral demand for glucose in spite of impaired glu­
coneogenesis and glycogenolysis. As a result, insulin
secretion continues even as blood glucose falls.
Diazoxide decreases insulin release from beta‐cells
and stimulates epinephrine release from adrenergic cells.
The result is decreased insulin release and increased
hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. It is effec­
tive in 64–85% of dogs. The recommended dose is 5 mg/
kg every 12 hours but may be increased up to 30 mg/kg
every 12 hours if necessary. Thiazide diuretics potentiate
the effects of diazoxide. The most common side‐effects
of diazoxide are gastrointestinal in nature.
Octreotide is a somatostatin analog that activates
somatostatin receptors resulting in the inhibition of
­synthesis and secretion of insulin. Octreotide is only
effective if the malignant beta‐cells are expressing soma­
tostatin receptors (~60% in people). It is given at a start­
ing dose of 2 μg/kg SC twice daily. The dose can be
increased to three times daily. Limited studies suggest
that long‐term efficacy is poor. Side‐effects are limited
but the drug is costly.
Streptozotocin is a chemotherapeutic agent that has
direct toxic effects on pancreatic beta‐cells. It is nephro­
toxic and therefore intravenous fluid diuresis is required.
It is administered once every 2–3 weeks at a dosage of
500 mg/m2 for five treatments. If diabetes mellitus
occurs, treatment is discontinued. In one study on the
use of streptozotocin in dogs with insulinoma, controls
lived for 90 days. Dogs had a median duration of normo­
glycemia of 163 days when given streptozotocin every
three weeks. In another study, streptozotocin was given
every two weeks and the average return of hypoglycemia
was 196 days.
Prognosis
The World Health Organization (WHO) classification
for tumor staging is prognostic for insulinomas. Factors
that affect prognosis include presence or absence of
tumor (T0 or T1), regional nodal involvement (N0 or

VetBooks.ir

144 Pancreatic Endocrine Tumors

N1), and distant metastasis (M0 or M1). Therefore, full
staging (thoracic radiographs, abdominal ultrasound,
serum chemistry, complete blood count, and urinalysis)
is recommended.
Overall, the prognosis is guarded because of the high
rate of metastasis and recurrence of clinical signs.
Approximately 36–51% of dogs have detectable meta­
static disease at the time of surgery. With surgery alone,
stage I (T1N0M0), II (T1N1M0), and III (T1N0M1 or
T1N1M1) dogs have an expected median survival of 19
months, nine months, and six months respectively.
Survival time for dogs treated medically is less than
when surgery combined with medical management is
used. In one study, medical management with pred­
nisone and dietary change alone resulted in a median
survival time (MST) of 74 days. In a separate study, the
median survival time for dogs that had a partial pancrea­
tectomy was reported at 496 days. In a subset of nine
dogs that received postsurgical medical treatment
(diazoxide and prednisone) at the time of relapse, the
median survival time was extended to 1316 days.
Streptozotocin therapy, especially as an adjunctive to
surgery, should be considered. Although data are lim­
ited, normoglycemia has been shown to be prolonged
with use of streptozotocin when compared to dogs that
were medically managed with diet and prednisone (163
versus 90 days respectively). In addition, reduction in
metastatic lesions and resolution of hypoglycemic poly­
neuropathy in dogs have been reported.
Persistent postoperative hypoglycemia has also been
reported to be prognostic. In one study, dogs that became
normoglycemic postoperatively had a median survival of
680 days compared to those that remained hypoglyce­
mic, which had a MST of 90 days.

­Glucagonoma
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Alpha‐cells secrete glucagon and constitute about
20–25% of the endocrine pancreas. Glucagon has a pro­
found hyperglycemic effect. In people, glucagonomas are
commonly associated with diabetes mellitus and severe
paraneoplastic dermatologic disease. Dogs with gluca­
gonomas can have a similar dermatologic syndrome
called superficial necrolytic dermatitis, necrolytic migra­
tory erythema, or metabolic epidermal necrosis. This
dermatologic disease has been identified in multiple
dogs with glucagonomas but it is more commonly asso­
ciated with liver disease and is not pathognomonic for a
glucagonoma.
Glucagon has catabolic effects and opposes the effects
of insulin. It causes gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, and
lipolysis that cause the conversion of glycogen to ­glucose,

resulting in elevation of blood sugar. The catabolic effects
of glucagon result in hypoaminoacidemia. Requirements
for histidine and lysine‐rich keratohyalin granules in the
stratum granulosum make the epidermis susceptible to
hypoaminoacidemia.
Epidemiology
Glucagonomas are rare in people (<250 reported) with
only a few case reports in dogs. They have not been
reported in cats.
Signalment
The typical signalment is an older dog. There are no
reported breed dispositions.
History and Clinical Signs
Dermatologic manifestations include lesions of the foot­
pad, pressure points, periocular area, and mucocutane­
ous junctions such as the perineum, genitalia, and
muzzle. Hyperkeratosis of the footpads also occurs.
Weight loss is associated with the catabolic effects of the
glucagon. Hyperglucagonemia can cause diabetes melli­
tus resulting in polyuria and polydipsia.
Diagnosis
An elevated plasma glucagon level in the absence of
hypoglycemia is supportive of the presence of a gluca­
gonoma. Histopathology of skin biopsies will be consist­
ent with superficial hydropic dermatitis and marked
parakeratosis. A definitive diagnosis is obtained through
histopathology of the pancreatic tumor. In animals with
skin lesions, elevations in liver enzymes and hypoalbu­
minemia may also be present.
Therapy
Surgical debulking or resection is the treatment of
choice. Octreotide may be helpful in animals that have
alpha‐cells that are expressing somatostatin receptors.
Streptozotocin has been used with limited success in
people for palliative treatment. When dermatologic
lesions are present, a high‐quality protein diet such, as
Hill’s Science Diet a/d should used in nonencephalo­
pathic animals. Supplementation with 3–6 egg yolks per
day may also be beneficial. Intravenous amino acid ther­
apy has been useful. A 10% crystalline amino acid solu­
tion (Aminosyn®, Abbott Labs) at 25 mL/kg over 6–8
hours repeated every 7–10 days has been used to treat
hypoaminoacidemia. Ideally, the hypertonic amino acid
solution is administered via a central vein to decrease

1299

1300

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

risks of thrombophlebitis. Supplementation with zinc
and fatty acids may also be indicated. Corticosteroids
should be avoided as development of diabetes mellitus
worsens the prognosis.
Prognosis
The prognosis for pancreatic glucagonomas is poor.

­Gastrinoma
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Gastrinomas in dogs and cats are nonislet cell pancreatic
tumors that secrete gastrin. In humans, the majority
arise in the duodenum and less commonly the pancreas.
There is only one report of a duodenal gastrinoma in
the dog.
Parietal cells are stimulated to release acid by gastrin,
acetylcholine, and histamine. The primary effect of
hypergastrinemia is acid hypersecretion resulting in gas­
trointestinal ulceration. In humans, it is referred to as
Zollinger–Ellison syndrome.
Epidemiology
Gastrinomas are rare in dogs and cats.
Signalment
Dogs are typically middle aged and cats are typically
older. No breed dispositions have reported.
History and Clinical Signs
Common clinical signs are vomiting and weight loss.
Other clinical signs may include hematemesis, diarrhea
or melena, lethargy, and pale mucous membranes.
Prolonged elevation of circulating gastrin can cause gas­
tric antral hypertrophy. Perforated ulcers can result in
shock and peritonitis.
Diagnosis
A minimum database should be collected. Abnormalities
are typically associated with gastrointestinal bleeding,
vomiting, and liver metastasis. Biochemical abnormali­
ties may include anemia, hypokalemia, hypochloremia,
hypoalbuminemia, hypoproteinemia, and increases in
liver enzymes and hyperbilirubinemia.

Unless a perforated ulcer is present, abdominal radio­
graphs are of limited use. Contrast may be useful in iden­
tifying areas of thickened gastric wall.
Transabdominal ultrasonography is of limited
use because the tumors are typically small in size.
Abnormalities that may be identified include a primary
pancreatic tumor, evidence of metastasis in the liver and
regional lymph nodes and a thickened gastric wall.
Endoscopic evaluation of the upper gastrointestinal
tract may reveal esophagitis, esophageal and gastroduo­
denal ulcerations, and a thickened pylorus. Biopsies may
reveal inflammation, gastric mucosal hypertrophy, and
loss of the mucosal barrier.
Serum gastrin concentrations are typically three times
the upper normal range. However, they can be in the
normal range. In cases of suspected gastrinoma with
normal gastrin levels, provocative testing can be used.
Intravenous secretin or calcium infusion can stimulate
gastrin release.
A definitive diagnosis is obtained via biopsy. His­
topathology and immunohistochemistry will confirm a
gastrinoma.
Therapy
Surgery is typically only palliative due to the high meta­
static rate. Surgical treatment may be limited by the small
size of the tumor making identification difficult. The
techniques used to identify the mass are similar to those
used for identification of insulinomas and include
transabdominal and intraoperative ultrasound, magnetic
resonance imaging, and computed tomography. Most
gastrinomas express somatostatin receptors on the cell
surface. Therefore, indium 111‐labeled octreotide nuclear
scintigraphy has been used. Methylene blue injection has
been used for tumor identification in humans.
The goal of medical management is gastric acid
­reduction and treatment of gastroduodenal ulceration.
Histamine receptor antagonists and proton pump inhibi­
tors are used. Proton pump inhibitors block all three gas­
tric acid secretory pathways. Octreotide has two
beneficial effects: it suppresses tumor gastrin release and
inhibits gastrin from stimulating the parietal cells.
Prognosis
The prognosis is guarded to poor as approximately 76% of
cases have metastatic disease at the time of diagnosis. In
animals that receive both surgical and medical manage­
ment, survival times range from one week to 18 months.

Liver and Biliary Tract Tumors
Amanda K. Elpiner, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology)
VCA Great Lakes Veterinary Specialists, Cleveland, OH, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
The etiology of hepatobiliary tumors in dogs and cats is
largely unknown although human cases are often linked
to infection with the hepatitis virus (B and C) and cirrho­
sis. Cirrhosis, which may be secondary to chronic disease
or alcohol consumption in people, is rare in dogs and a
viral etiology has not been documented in dogs or cats.
Other theories behind the development of hepatocel­
lular carcinoma (HCC) and other hepatobiliary tumors
include exposure to chemical carcinogens (aflatoxins or
nitrosamines, for example) and chronic infections or
inflammatory diseases of the liver. Trematodes are
thought to be involved in the development of bile duct
carcinomas in people and this link has also been explored
in dogs and cats but seems unlikely to be a major cause or
concern. More recently, somatic genetic alterations are
thought to likely play a role in tumor development, such
as mutations in p53, PIK3CA, beta‐catenin, and others
which have been documented in people.
There are four main histologic categories of primary
hepatobiliary tumors in both dogs and cats: hepatocel­
lular, bile duct, neuroendocrine (carcinoid), and mesen­
chymal (sarcoma). Within in each individual category is
an array of both malignant and benign tumors. In gen­
eral, dogs are thought to be more likely affected by
­malignant tumors whereas cats more often have benign
tumors.
Primary hepatobiliary neoplasms can also be described
using three morphologic subtypes: massive, nodular, or
diffuse. The definition of a massive liver tumor is a large,
solitary mass confined to a single liver lobe; nodular
tumors have discrete nodules scattered throughout mul­
tiple liver lobes; diffuse tumors consist of coalescing
nodules within all liver lobes or widespread infiltration
of the hepatic parenchyma by neoplastic cells. As we will
discuss further, the histologic and morphologic features

of hepatobiliary tract tumors help us to make determina­
tions about prognosis for both dogs and cats.
Hepatocellular Tumors
Hepatocellular tumors develop from the hepatocyte.
These tumors include hepatocellular adenomas and
hepatocellular carcinomas. Hepatocellular adenomas are
benign tumors and while they can be found in both dogs
and cats, they are more common in the cat. Hepatocellular
adenomas are typically considered incidental findings
and rarely cause clinical signs in affected patients.
Adenomas can, however, reach a large size, necessitating
surgical removal. These tumors are also difficult to
­clinically distinguish from a massive HCC without the
aid of a biopsy.
Hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common pri­
mary liver tumor in the dog and the second most com­
mon in the cat. The majority of HCCs are morphologically
massive (53–84%) followed by nodular (16–25%) and
­diffuse (0–19%) presentations. The left side of the liver is
more commonly affected than the right, with over two‐
thirds of tumors arising from the left lateral, medial, and
papillary process of the caudate lobe. HCCs have the
ability to metastasize but the likelihood of metastasis is
largely based on the morphologic subtype. Massive HCC
have a low reported rate of metastasis (0–37%) whereas
the nodular and diffuse subtypes have dramatically
higher metastatic rates of 93% and 100% respectively.
Metastasis is most commonly reported to the regional
lymph nodes, peritoneum, and lungs.
Bile Duct Tumors
There are two primary tumors that can arise from the
bile duct epithelium in dogs and cats: bile duct adenomas
and biliary carcinomas. Bile duct adenomas are also called

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

biliary cystadenomas or hepatobiliary cystoadenomas.
These are considered benign tumors and are the most
common hepatobiliary tumor found in the cat (account­
ing for 50% of all feline hepatobiliary tumors). Similar to
hepatocellular adenomas, biliary adenomas typically do
not cause clinical signs in affected patients unless they
reach a large enough size to cause abdominal discomfort,
necessitating surgical removal. Male cats are thought to
be overrepresented.
Bile duct carcinomas (also called cholangiocarcino­
mas) are malignant tumors in both dogs and cats. They
have an aggressive clinical course with metastasis
detected in 60–80% of affected patients. Metastasis to
the local lymph nodes and lungs is most common but
other intraabdominal sites have been reported. In cats,
metastasis resulting in diffuse carcinomatosis can occur
in 67–80% of cases. Bile duct carcinomas can be intrahe­
patic, extrahepatic, or occasionally within the gallblad­
der itself. Morphologically, bile duct carcinomas are
similar to HCC in that 37–46% are massive, 0–46% are
nodular and 17–54% are diffuse. In dogs, females and
Labrador retrievers are thought to be predisposed
whereas there is no sex or breed predisposition yet
­confirmed in cats.
Neuroendocrine Tumors
These tumors arise from the neuroectodermal cells.
They are considered rare tumors in both the dog and cat
and are often referred to as carcinoids. Carcinoids have
a tendency to occur in younger animals compared to
other hepatobiliary tumors. They have an aggressive
clinical course and carry a poor prognosis, primarily
due to the fact that early metastasis is found in >90% of
patients diagnosed. The most common sites of metasta­
sis were the peritoneum and lymph nodes. These
tumors are t­ypically intrahepatic and have a predilec­
tion for a nodular or diffuse presentation, making
­surgical resection often difficult or impossible. A small
number of extrahepatic neuroendocrine tumors of the
gallbladder have been reported for which surgical
­resection was performed but long‐term follow‐up is
unavailable.
Mesenchymal Tumors (Sarcomas)
Mesenchymal tumors, also called sarcomas, arise from
the stromal cells of the liver. They are considered rare,
making up less than 15% of all primary hepatic tumors.
There are several different subtypes of sarcomas that
have been reported in the canine and feline liver
­including hemangiosarcoma (most common in the dog),
­leiomyosarcoma (most common in the cat), fibrosar­
coma, osteosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, and liposar­
coma. Primary hepatic sarcomas carry a poor prognosis

due to their aggressive clinical course and high rate
of metastasis. Metastasis to the lungs and spleen is
most common and is reported in 86–100% of cases.
Morphologically, approximately 36% of mesenchymal
tumors are massive and 64% are nodular. Bear in mind
that the liver is also a common site for secondary
sarcomas including metastatic hemangiosarcoma and
­
disseminated histiocytic sarcoma.

­Epidemiology
As discussed earlier, liver tumors in the dog and cat can
be of either primary or secondary origin. In the dog, ret­
rospective studies have indicated that the prevalence of
primary hepatic neoplasia is low (0.6–1.5% of all canine
tumors). Secondary neoplasia, the result of metastasis to
the liver, is a much more common occurrence. Tumors
originating in the spleen, pancreas, and gastrointestinal
tract are the most likely to result in metastasis to the
liver. However, other systemic neoplasms such as lym­
phosarcoma, malignant histiocytosis or systemic masto­
cytosis often involve the liver as part of their widespread
clinical course.
In cats, the prevalence is similar, with 1.0–2.9% of all
feline tumors being of primary hepatic origin. However,
when one study excluded hematopoietic neoplasms, the
prevalence increased to 6.9%. There are currently no
studies documenting the frequency of metastatic disease
to the liver in cats.

­Signalment
Hepatobiliary tumors are most common in older animals
(over the age of 10), the exception to this being carci­
noids which are typically found in younger animals (71%
of dogs were under the age of 10). Some studies indicate
that miniature schnauzers may be overrepresented
for the development of HCC and Labrador retrievers
may be predisposed to bile duct carcinomas but there are
no other known breed propensities in either species.
One study documented a male predilection for canine
HCC and a female predilection for bile duct carcinoma.
In cats, some studies have indicated a male predomi­
nance for carcinoids and bile duct tumors.

­History and Clinical Signs
In dogs with hepatobiliary tumors, clinical signs are often
lacking or will be somewhat vague. These may include
things such as anorexia, weight loss, lethargy, and vomit­
ing. Less frequently, symptoms such as abdominal

VetBooks.ir

145 Liver and Biliary Tract Tumors

discomfort, polyuria, polydipsia, diarrhea, seizures,
­
weakness, ataxia, dyspnea, hematochezia or melena may
be observed. If neurologic symptoms do occur in an
affected patient, they may be caused by s­econdary
hepatic encephalopathy or paraneoplastic hypoglycemia.
Physical examination may reveal the presence of a cra­
nial abdominal mass affect in up to 75% of patients.
However, some massive tumors or nodular and diffuse
tumors may not cause any obvious physical exam changes
and can be easily missed. Occasionally, a patient may
become jaundiced secondary to a hepatobiliary tumor or
develop ascites. Overall, dogs and cats with malignant
tumors are more likely to become symptomatic than
those patients with benign tumors.

­Diagnosis
Laboratory Tests
There are no distinguishing complete blood count
abnormalities found in patients with hepatobiliary
tumors. Hematologic profiles most often show mild and
nonspecific changes such as anemia, leukocytosis, and
thrombocytosis. A mild, nonregenerative anemia is most
common (present in 20–53% of patients). The cause is
largely unknown but speculated to be secondary to ane­
mia of chronic disease, red blood cell sequestration,
microangiopathic destruction through torturous tumor
vessels, or iron deficiency. A leukocytosis may also be
present and can be caused by inflammation or necrosis
of any large tumor. Thrombocytosis has been reported in
approximately 50% of dogs diagnosed with a massive
HCC. The cause of this is not fully understood but is
speculated to be secondary to anemia, inflammatory
cytokine production, chronic iron deficiency, or a para­
neoplastic process.
Similarly, serum biochemical profiles often show non­
specific changes. Liver enzyme elevations are commonly
found in dogs with hepatobiliary tumors but there is no
association with the magnitude of elevation and the
severity of disease. These abnormalities are also in no
way specific to hepatobiliary neoplasia as many other
clinical conditions can affect these values. There are,
however, some trends that may be helpful. Alkaline
phosphatase (ALP) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
are the most common values to be elevated in dogs with
primary hepatic neoplasia whereas aspartate ami­
notransferase (AST) and bilirubin are more commonly
elevated in metastatic neoplasia, with >90% of dogs hav­
ing elevations in more than one liver enzyme. In cats,
one study showed that ALT, AST, and bilirubin were
higher in cats with malignant tumors compared to
benign tumors The ratio of liver values to one another
has also been examined. An AST:ALT ratio of less than 1

is most common with HCC or bile duct carcinoma
whereas a ratio greater than 1 is more likely with a neu­
roendocrine or mesenchymal tumor.
Other biochemical abnormalities commonly seen
with hepatobiliary neoplasia include hypoalbuminemia,
hyperglobulinemia, hypoglycemia, and elevated bile
acids. In cats, azotemia has been reported as the most
common biochemical abnormality. Studies have not
clarified the cause of the azotemia though it may repre­
sent concurrent and unrelated chronic renal disease.
Imaging
Abdominal radiographs may be helpful at confirming the
presence of a large hepatobiliary mass but can easily miss
small, nodular or diffuse tumors. In some cases, radio­
graphs may show the presence of mineralization within
the biliary tree of dogs with bile duct carcinoma although
this is a rare and nonspecific finding. Therefore, ultra­
sound is the recommended method of imaging for both
dogs and cats. Ultrasound also allows for the detection of
intraabdominal metastasis, ascites, and the location of
the disease and its relationship to other anatomic struc­
tures. Most importantly, ultrasound will allow us to
determine the morphologic features (massive, nodular,
or diffuse) of the tumor and help guide whether surgical
resection should be attempted.
Ultrasound images alone, however, are not adequate to
diagnose histologic tumor type. An ultrasound‐guided
fine needle aspiration (FNA) or needle biopsy is recom­
mended, and is especially useful in cases of nodular or dif­
fuse disease. An accurate diagnosis is possible using these
techniques in approximately 60% of FNA samples and
90% of needle biopsy samples. Both of these procedures
are considered minimally invasive. In some cases, laparo­
scopic biopsy may be considered more appropriate and is
also an excellent means of determining histologic tumor
type. In cases of massive tumors, it may not be clinically
warranted to know the histologic diagnosis of a particular
tumor prior to proceeding with exploratory surgery since
the mass will most likely be fully removed and biopsied
postoperatively anyway. Advanced imaging modalities
such as computed tomography (CT) and magnetic reso­
nance imaging (MRI) are the primary imaging modalities
utilized in human medicine for hepatobiliary tumors but
have not been fully evaluated in veterinary medicine.

­Therapy and Prognosis
Hepatocellular Carcinoma
The prognosis for patients with HCC is dependent
­primarily on the morphologic subtype. Massive HCC
generally carries a good prognosis as it is confined to one

1305

VetBooks.ir

1306

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

liver lobe and is therefore amenable to surgical resection.
In addition to surgical resectability, other prognostic fac­
tors for massive HCC include the side of the liver affected
(right side worse than left side), pretreatment ALT and
AST elevations, and ratio of ALP:AST and ALT:AST. In
a paper evaluating surgery in 42 dogs with massive HCC,
the median survival time after liver lobectomy was 1460
days versus 270 days for dogs managed medically only.
Many of the dogs that underwent liver lobectomy were
lost to follow‐up as they were still alive or went on to die
of other unrelated causes at the end of the study period.
Right‐sided liver tumors are considered to have a worse
prognosis because of their proximity to the caudal vena
cava, resulting in an increased risk of intraoperative
death. Massive HCC has a low metastatic potential
(0–37%) and a low recurrence rate (0–13%) after surgical
resection.
In contrast, the prognosis for dogs with nodular or dif­
fuse HCC is poor. This is primarily because that these
tumors are not typically surgically resectable due to the
involvement of multiple liver lobes and they have a high
metastatic rate (93% and 100%, respectively). It is often
not possible to clinically determine if nodular and diffuse
types of HCC are secondary to intrahepatic metastasis
prior to diagnosis or represent multiple foci of disease.
There is little information in the veterinary field about
chemotherapy for the treatment of nonresectable HCC.
In general, HCC is thought to represent a chemoresist­
ant cancer as response rates of less than 20% are reported
in the human literature. This is thought to be secondary
to the development of drug resistance within the hepat­
ocytes, owing to their role in detoxification, or through
the expression of P‐glycoprotein. A recent paper evalu­
ated the chemotherapy agent gemcitabine (2’,2’‐dif­
luorodeoxycytidine), which has been used in human
medicine for the treatment of solid tumors, including
HCC. This study did not find a statistical improvement
in survival time for those patients with nodular, diffuse
or nonresectable massive HCC with the use of gemcit­
abine but the overall survival time of this small patient
population was 983 days. Other treatment techniques
that have been explored more recently include arterial

chemoembolization, immunotherapy, and antiangio­
genic medications.
Bile Duct Tumors
Initial treatment for bile duct tumors should be surgical
resection if they are confined to one (or two) liver lobes
with no evidence of distant metastatic disease. The prog­
nosis for surgically excised adenomas is excellent with no
reports of local recurrence of metastasis. On the other
hand, bile duct carcinomas carry a guarded prognosis
even when surgically excised due to their high rate of
metastasis and local recurrence. The median survival
time for patients with bile duct carcinoma is less than six
months despite surgical removal. Chemotherapy can be
considered to slow disease progression but specific
chemotherapy protocols and recommendations have not
been effectively evaluated to date in veterinary medicine.
There is also no known effective treatment for nodular
or diffuse tumors which cannot be surgically excised.
Neuroendocrine Tumors
Neuroendocrine tumors carry a poor prognosis.
Metastatic disease is documented in greater than 90% of
patients at the time of diagnosis. These tumors are often
morphologically nodular or diffuse, limiting the ability to
surgically excise them. There is currently no known
effective treatment or chemotherapy protocol and the
role of these treatments is largely unknown.
Hepatic Sarcomas
Liver lobectomy is recommended if tumors are confined
to a single liver lobe. Hepatic sarcomas, however, carry a
poor prognosis despite surgical resection due to their
high metastatic rate (86–100%). The role of chemother­
apy is still under investigation but protocols utilizing
doxorubicin and ifosfamide as well as antiangiogenic
protocols should be considered to slow disease progres­
sion based on their use in sarcomas in other locations
such as the spleen.

Tumors of the Urinary Tract
Pedro A. Boria, DVM, MS, DACVIM (Oncology)
Blue Pearl Veterinary Partners, Northfield, IL, USA

­Tumors of the Urinary Bladder
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Tumors of the urinary bladder are uncommon in dogs
and rare in cats. Transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) is the
most common primary tumor of the urinary bladder in
both species. Other tumors reported include squamous
cell carcinoma, leiomyosarcoma, leiomyoma, undifferentiated carcinoma, lymphoma, hemangiosarcoma,
rhabdomyosarcoma, fibroma, and other mesenchymal
tumors.
Transitional cell carcinoma is most often located in the
trigone region of the bladder in dogs and at the apex in
cats. Mass lesions and thickening of the bladder wall can
lead to partial or complete urinary tract obstruction.
Urethral and prostatic involvement has been reported
in 56% and 29% of cases respectively. At the time of
­diagnosis, lymph node involvement is reported in 16% of
cases, with 14% demonstrating spread to distant sites.
The overall metastatic rate is 50%.
Epidemiology
The overall incidence of bladder tumors is 2% of all
reported malignancies in the dog. In cats, bladder cancer
is rarely reported. Risk factors associated with the development of TCC include exposure to older‐generation
topical flea and tick control products (i.e., flea and tick
dips), lawn herbicides and pesticides, obesity, female sex,
and a strong breed‐associated risk. The female:male
ratio of dogs with TCC has been reported to range from
1.71:1 to 1.95:1. The risk is higher in neutered dogs than
in intact dogs of both sexes. New‐generation spot‐on
flea control products do not appear to be associated
with TCC.

Signalment
Affected dogs and cats are usually older, with an average
age of 11 years and 13 years respectively. The most
commonly affected breeds include West Highland
­
white terriers, beagles, dachshunds, Shetland sheepdogs,
and Scottish terriers which have an 18‐fold risk of
­ eveloping TCC.
d
History and Clinical Signs
The most common clinical signs associated with TCC are
stranguria, pollakiuria, hematuria, dysuria, and urinary
incontinence. Urinary tract signs may present for weeks
to months prior to diagnosis. Temporary relief of these
signs may be a­ssociated with the use of antibiotics.
In more severe cases, abdominal palpation may reveal a
palpable caudal abdominal mass. Rectal examination
abnormalities include urethral thickening or sublumbar
lymphadenopathy. TCC can also metastasize to the inguinal lymph nodes, so palpation of the inguinal fat pads
may reveal firm masses. Other lower urinary tract conditions resembling bladder TCC include other types of neoplasia, ­cystitis, polypoid cystitis, polyps, granulomatous
­cystitis/urethritis, and cystic calculi. Rarely, dogs have
shifting leg lameness or warm, swollen, and painful limbs
due to paraneoplastic hypertrophic osteopathy.
Diagnosis
Diagnostic evaluation of a patient with suspected TCC
should include deep abdominal palpation and rectal
evaluation. Rectal examination may reveal thickening
of the urethra and enlargement of internal lymph nodes.
The complete blood count and serum biochemical panel
may reveal signs of renal involvement. Urine sediment

reveals malignant cells in only 30% of cases. In cases with
high index of suspicion for a bladder mass, cystocentesis
should be avoided to decrease the chance of tumor
­transplantation or bladder rupture. Concurrent urinary
tract infection is prevalent in TCC cases, therefore urine
culture is recommended.
Diagnostic imaging is essential for documentation of
a bladder mass. Abdominal radiographs are usually
unrewarding unless the lesion is mineralized. However,
radiographs may show sublumbar lymphadenopathy,
prostatomegaly, a caudal abdominal mass or bony metastases. Thoracic radiographs demonstrate pulmonary
metastasis in 17% of cases at the time of diagnosis.
Pulmonary changes may include nodular interstitial or
lobar interstitial opacities and alveolar infiltrates.
Ultrasonography is a sensitive diagnostic tool to evaluate the urinary tract and has largely replaced the use of
double‐contrast cystography. Ultrasonography can also
confirm ureteral obstruction when there is dilation of the
renal pelvis alone or accompanied by hydronephrosis.
Histopathology is the gold standard for the diagnosis
of TCC. However, cytology can also be utilized. There
are multiple methods for obtaining bladder tissue samples such as cystotomy, cystoscopy, and traumatic catheterization. Due to sampling size, multiple tissue samples
should be submitted to increase the diagnostic yield.
Most recently, A DNA based assay to detect genetic
mutations specifically in the BRAF gene has proven to be
highly sensitive and specific for the diagnosis of TCC
(CADET® BRAF, Sentinel Biomedical). The test evaluates
malignant cells naturally shed and is therefore p
­ erformed
on voided urine samples. However, the assay is limited
TCC and experimentally it has been found that up to
15% do not have the mutation.
Therapy
Because the trigone and urethra are most commonly
involved in dogs, complete removal of the tumor is
­usually not possible. In addition, many dogs develop
multifocal bladder lesions. As a result, most dogs with
bladder tumors are managed medically, with chemotherapy, radiation and/or photodynamic therapy.
If a patient is suffering from urinary obstruction, surgery may be considered to reestablish urine flow or place
a cystostomy tube. The most common disadvantages of
tube cystostomy are recurrent urinary tract infections
and premature removal of the tube by the patient.
Urethral stents are gaining favor over cystostomy tubes.
Stents are placed surgically and nonsurgically using
fluoroscopy. The most common indication for urethral
stenting is luminal obstruction secondary to tumor infiltration. In a series of 12 cases, urethral stents relieved
obstruction in all cases. The outcome was fair to excel-

lent in 10/12 cases. Urinary incontinence is the most
common complication.
The use of radiation therapy for the treatment of TCC
of the bladder is limited. The reported one‐ and two‐year
survival rates following intraoperative radiation therapy
were 69% and 23%, respectively. Therapy‐related complications include urinary incontinence, pollakiuria, and
stranguria, all of which affect the patient’s quality of life.
A report of weekly course fractional external beam radiation therapy in combination with mitoxantrone and
piroxicam was well tolerated but results were no better
when compared to medical therapy alone. However,
90% of the dogs had amelioration of their clinical signs.
The mainstay treatment of TCC in dogs is systemic
medical therapy with cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibitors
alone or in combination with chemotherapy. Cure rates
are relatively low but several different drugs can lead to
remission or stable disease. In dogs, single‐agent therapy
with piroxicam or cisplatin has shown a response rate of
20% with a median survival time of approximately six
months. Although the concurrent use of cisplatin and
piroxicam combination therapy has shown a response
rate of 70%, the high incidences of renal failure lead to
early termination of the protocol.
The most commonly used chemotherapy combination in dogs is mitoxantrone (5 mg/m2 IV q3 weeks) and
piroxicam (0.3 mg/kg once a day). This combination
has a documented response rate of 35% and median
survival of 291 days. Indications to continue therapy
include positive response such as complete or partial
remission. Stable disease is considered a positive
response as long as the patient has no detrimental
effects associated with chemotherapy administration
and a good quality of life.
Deracoxib (Dermaxx®, Novartis), a COX‐2 inhibitor, at
a dose of 3 mg/kg/day, has shown positive responses,
with 17% of dogs having a partial response and 71% of
dogs having stable disease.
Prognosis
The prognosis for TCC in dogs will largely depend on
tumor size, location, and metastasis at the time of diagnosis. Multiple different treatments have been identified
that result in remission and stable disease for several
months. Most of these patients will have an excellent
quality of life while on treatment. Prognostic factors
for survival are tumor stage at the time of diagnosis
(Box 146.1), younger age (increased risk of distant metastasis), prostate involvement (increased risk of distant
metastasis), and higher T stage (increased risk of nodal
and distant metastasis). Information regarding prognostic factors in other bladder tumors is limited. Prognostic
factors for bladder tumor in cats have not been well

Most renal tumors occur in older dogs (mean age 8 years)

been reported to be 1.2:1. In cats, the median age at

female cats.

­Urethral Tumors

History and Clinical Signs

Most tumors affecting the urethra are malignant.
Transitional cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma
are the most commonly reported tumor types. Smooth
muscle tumors (e.g., leiomyosarcoma) have been reported
less frequently. Granulomatous urethritis, a benign
­condition of the urethra, must be differentiated from
malignant tumors due to the different treatment
approaches and prognosis. Treatment recommendations
and response rates for urethral tumors are similar to
those of the bladder.

Clinical signs associated with renal tumors are not specific. Presenting complaints may include weight loss,
polyuria, lethargy, hematuria, abdominal pain or signs
suggestive of renal failure (vomiting, anorexia). Physical
examination may reveal a midabdominal mass and
­occasionally bilateral renal enlargement.

­Renal Tumors
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Primary renal tumors are uncommon in dogs and cats. The
majority of these tumors are malignant and more than half
are epithelial in origin. In cats, lymphoma is the most common renal tumor and can affect both kidneys. In a report of
54 dogs with renal tumors, the most common was renal
cell carcinoma. Other tumors that can occur in the kidney
include TCC, nephroblastoma, hemangiosarcoma, other
sarcomas, and lymphomas. An unusual syndrome in
female German shepherd dogs consists of slow‐growing
dermal fibrosis and fibromas, concomitant renal

Diagnosis
Clinicopathologic findings include mild anemia alone or
accompanied with marked neutrophilia, or abnormalities
consistent with renal azotemia. Paraneoplastic ­syndromes
such as polycythemia, neutrophilia, and hypertrophic
osteopathy have been reported.
Ultrasonography is highly sensitive for the diagnosis of
renal neoplasia. Tissue samples can be obtained by
­ultrasound‐guided percutaneous biopsy or at the time of
surgery.
Therapy and Prognosis
Nephrectomy is the treatment of choice for dogs with
unilateral renal tumors without evidence of azotemia
or distant metastasis. Excretory urography, computed
tomography (CT), and evaluation of glomerular filtration rate (GFR) via scintigraphy may also be useful,

1309

VetBooks.ir

1310

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

­especially for surgical planning. Evaluation of possible
tumor extension into the vena cava is important if surgery is considered.
The reported median survival time for dogs with
renal cell carcinoma treated with nephrectomy is eight
months. Standardized chemotherapy as an adjunct or in
the metastatic setting for renal carcinoma has not been
well defined. In humans, sunitinib, a multikinase receptor inhibitor, has shown antitumor activity against metastatic renal cell carcinoma. At this time, controlled
studies using tyrosine kinase inhibitors against renal

­carcinoma in veterinary patients are lacking. Toceranib
phosphate, a multikinase receptor inhibitor similar to
sunitinib, is approved for mast cell neoplasia in veterinary patients and may be considered for the treatment of
metastatic renal carcinoma.
Chemotherapy treatment for renal lymphoma is similar to protocols used to treat lymphoma in other organs.
Approximately 60% of cats achieve complete remission.
Negative prognostic factors included involvement of
other organ system (CNS), FeLV infection, and severity
of renal failure.

Tumors of the Male Reproductive System
Trina Hazzah, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology)
VCA West Los Angeles Animal Hospital, Los Angeles, CA, USA

­Testicular Tumors
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Testicular tumors are the most common cancer found in
the male reproductive tract and are typically considered
nonaggressive. Primary testicular neoplasia commonly
arises from three separate areas of the testis: the susten­
tacular cells of Sertoli (Sertoli cell tumors), interstitial
cells (Leydig cell tumors), and germinal epithelium (sem­
inoma). A recent study evaluated 345 testicular tumors;
seminomas (33.9%) were the most common followed
by interstitial cell tumors (33%), and lastly Sertoli cell
tumors (26.4%). Although less frequently seen, other tumor
types can be found such as lymphoma, hemangiosarcoma,
and others.
Epidemiology
The prevalence of testicular tumors in dogs is 27%, which
has increased from previous years. A cryptorchid testicle
has an approximately 10 times increased risk of develop­
ing cancer compared to a descended testicle. This effect
may be in part due to the higher temperature of the
retained testis within the body. Of retained testes tumors,
34% are seminomas and 54% are Sertoli cell tumors.
Other risk factors are age, breed, and exposure to envi­
ronmental carcinogens. In one study, intact dogs over 6
years of age had an increased incidence of testicular
tumors. Collies and Shetland sheepdogs were five times
more likely to develop testicular tumors, specifically
Sertoli cell tumors. Environmental carcinogen exposure
has also been a proven risk factor.
Military working dogs in the Far East that were exposed
to chemical sprays like Agent Orange, herbicides, and
dioxin demonstrated an increased risk of seminomas.

Signalment
Testicular tumors are diagnosed in older dogs, with a
median age of approximately 10 years. No specific breed
predilection has been consistently described.
History and Clinical Signs
Sertoli cell tumors are often large (1–5 cm). Atrophy of
the contralateral testicle is common. Dogs with Sertoli
cell tumors can present with bilateral dorsal alopecia,
hyperpigmentation of the skin or scrotum, enlarged nip­
ples, squamous metaplasia of the prostate, gynecomas­
tia, and thinning of the skin. Many of these clinical signs
are associated with hyperestrogenism which causes signs
of feminization and is found in approximately 20% of
cases. Severe bone marrow hypoplasia leading to life‐
threatening pancytopenia can result from the excessive
endogenous estrogen production from the tumor.
Leydig cell tumors are relatively small (usually under
2 cm) in size, and can be found as either solitary or mul­
tiple and unilateral or bilateral.
Seminomas are larger tumors (can be greater than
5 cm) and often appear as nodules. They can occur along
with interstitial and Sertoli cell tumors. Hyperestrogenism
is rarely seen with this tumor type although a recent case
study described a 5‐year‐old Yorkshire terrier with con­
firmed hyperestrogenemia and secondary alopecia.
Diagnosis
Staging with full blood analysis, urinalysis, thoracic radi­
ographs, and abdominal ultrasound should be performed
in all patients with testicular tumors. Results typically
reveal no abnormalities unless the presence of hyperes­
trogenemia results in blood dyscrasias or pancytopenia.

The metastatic rate for seminomas and Sertoli tumors
is approximately 10%. Metastasis occurs through lym­
phatic invasion. Therefore, evaluation for regional
metastasis is warranted prior to surgery. There are
reports of aggressive seminomas in dogs with distant
metastasis to the spleen, lungs, meninges, eyes, and skin.
Testicular ultrasound is recommended in dogs with clin­
ical signs of testicular neoplasia and nonpalpable disease.
For dogs with signs of feminization, obtaining serum lev­
els of estradiol‐17‐beta may help support a diagnosis of
functional testicular tumor. Paraneoplastic hypertrophic
osteopathy, although rare, has been reported in a dog
with a Sertoli cell tumor. Therefore, extremity radio­
graphs should be performed in dogs with Sertoli cell
tumors with concomitant lameness.
Therapy
Castration, including scrotal ablation, is considered the
treatment of choice for testicular tumors and is curative
for dogs with nonmetastatic disease. However, when
metastatic disease is present, adjunctive chemotherapy
or radiation therapy is necessary. The use of cesium‐137
external beam radiation therapy for regional lymph node
metastasis in four dogs with seminoma has been
described and shown to be 100% effective. There is lim­
ited information regarding the usefulness of chemother­
apy, but there is suggested efficacy with both cisplatin
and bleomycin. There is recent evidence that seminomas
and Leydig cell tumors express kit (CD117), making the
use of a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (such as Palladia™, or
Gleevec®) a reasonable treatment option for cases with
metastatic disease. The use of metronomic chemother­
apy for high‐grade seminomas is also a valid treatment
option, as one study found that seminomas demon­
strated increased angiogenesis.
Prognosis
The prognosis is excellent for nonmetastatic testicular
tumors and guarded for metastatic tumors or dogs that
have blood dyscrasia secondary to hyperestrogenism.
Also, seminomas with high mitotic index and increased
numbers of agyrophilic nucleolar organizer regions
(AgNORs) had increased risk of metastasis.

­Prostate Tumors
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Carcinomas are the most common prostatic tumor, with
transitional cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma being
the most frequent types. Other types such as squamous

cell carcinoma, undifferentiated carcinoma, and sarco­
mas are rarely found. In dogs, most prostatic carcinomas
are suspected to be ductal or urothelial in origin, rather
than acinar, as in humans. The absence of androgen
receptors in ductal epithelial cells suggests that canine
prostatic carcinoma formation is likely androgen inde­
pendent. Controversy still exists regarding the effects of
castration on the development of canine prostatic
­carcinoma. Regardless, three studies did reveal that cas­
trated dogs were at increased risk for developing prostatic
­carcinoma with odds ratios ranging from 3.86 to 4.34.
Epidemiology
Prostate tumors are rare neoplasms in dogs, having a
prevalence of less than 1% of all canine cancers. These
tumors are extremely uncommon in cats with only a few
reported cases.
Signalment
There is no known breed predilection and prostatic car­
cinoma typically affects older dogs, median age 10 years.
Although exceedingly rare, prostatic carcinoma can
occur in older cats.
History and Clinical Signs
The most common presenting clinical sign in a dog with
a prostate tumor is either tenesmus or dysuria, including
hematuria, stranguria or pollakiuria. Older, castrated,
male dogs presenting with any of the above clinical signs
should be evaluated for urogenital cancer as few other
diseases cause such signs. Other possible presenting
signs are anorexia, weight loss, acute lameness or back
pain which may indicate metastasis to the pelvis or lum­
bar spine.
In cats, clinical signs vary but include dysuria, urethral
obstruction, and obstipation. Physical exam findings and
diagnostics are similar to those for prostate tumors in
dogs.
Diagnosis
Physical exam findings are variable but the most com­
mon abnormality is prostatomegaly that can be palpated
as irregular, firm, and painful and/or demonstrates loss of
the median raphe. Complete blood count and serum bio­
chemistry rarely reveal any specific changes. Urinalysis
often indicates pyuria or bacteriuria as secondary bacte­
rial infection is commonly associated with this neoplasia.
Many owners report improvement of clinical signs if
treated with antibiotic therapy, but this improvement is
often short‐lived. Three‐view thoracic radiographs are

VetBooks.ir

147 Tumors of the Male Reproductive System

recommended, although pulmonary metastasis occurs in
<10% of dogs at the time of diagnosis. Abdominal radio­
graphs are helpful in identifying prostatomegaly, miner­
alization of the prostate, sublumbar lymphadenopathy,
and/or bony lesions of the lumbar spine or pelvis (typi­
cally osteoblastic [proliferative] in nature).
Metastatic, hormone‐refractory, androgen‐independ­
ent prostate cancer in men is similar in biologic behavior
to canine prostatic carcinoma. Eighty five to ninety per­
cent of those diagnosed with this form of prostate cancer
will have evidence of skeletal metastasis during the
course of disease. Skeletal metastasis has been reported
to occur in 22% of dogs, with the majority of these lesions
found in the axial skeleton.
Abdominal ultrasound is the most useful of all imaging
modalities as it can help confirm regional metastasis
which occurs in approximately 50% of dogs at presenta­
tion. Definitive diagnosis requires cytology or histopa­
thology. Fine needle aspiration, via ultrasound guidance,
has been shown to be 80% accurate in confirming a diag­
nosis of carcinoma. As an alternative, a prostatic wash
can be performed. Although less invasive, it is also less
sensitive.
In the published feline cases, metastatic disease varied
in location, but included pulmonary, pancreatic, renal,
and myocardial.

Palliative irradiation, urethral stenting, laser ablation
or cystostomy tube placement can be considered in dogs
with urethral obstruction. These options are palliative
and may only increase survival time minimally.
Treatment for cats with prostatic carcinoma is
unknown. One reported cat underwent a prostatectomy
and received doxorubicin (30 mg/m2) and cyclophospha­
mide (300 mg/m2) and was euthanized 10 months later
due to recurrent disease.

Therapy

­Penis, Prepuce, and Scrotum Tumors

There is limited information regarding treatment effi­
cacy for dogs with prostate tumors. Androgen ablation
therapy is ineffective in dogs, as tumors arise from
androgen‐independent regions. For tumors confined to
the prostate, total or partial prostatectomy can be con­
sidered. Due to persistent incontinence and recurrent
urinary tract infections, patient morbidity is high while
owner satisfaction is expectedly low. Radiation therapy,
an alternate local treatment option, was not found to be
useful in one series of dogs which received a palliative
protocol. However, a more recent study indicated a 60%
response rate and an extended survival time (median
survival time 645 days) when intensity‐modulated
and image‐guided radiation therapy (IM/IGRT) were
utilized.
Due to the high metastatic rate in dogs, local treatment
alone is not effective. Cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibitor
therapy is reported to be successful in treating various
types of urogenital carcinomas. Two studies indicated
that approximately 75–88% of canine prostate carcino­
mas express COX‐2. A previous publication indicated
that COX inhibitors were effective in the treatment of
canine prostatic carcinoma (MST 6.9 versus 0.7 months).
In a separate study, the addition of mitoxantrone chemo­
therapy to piroxicam did not increase survival.

Prognosis
The overall prognosis for prostate cancer is guarded to
grave as this tumor is both locally and distantly aggres­
sive. The rate of metastasis at the time of death is approx­
imately 80%, with the most common sites being the lungs,
regional lymph nodes, liver, and bone. Prognostic indica­
tors that have been found to be negatively associated with
survival include the presence of metastasis at diagnosis,
presence of clinical signs at diagnosis, and the lack of
nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drug (NSAID) therapy.
It is difficult to confirm treatment and prognostic
information for cats based on the limited reports availa­
ble. However, it would be reasonable to consider that
these tumors have a similar prognosis to their canine
counterparts as they also tend to be aggressive.

Etiology/Pathophysiology
Tumors of the penis, prepuce, and scrotum are rare in
dogs and even rarer in cats. The most common tumors
of the penis are transmissible venereal tumor (TVT) and
squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). The prepuce can also
be affected by TVT. Most tumors of the prepuce and
scrotum are those associated with skin, specifically SCC,
melanoma, and mast cell tumor (MCT). Other reported
tumors that can affect all three areas include hemangio­
sarcoma, lymphoma, lipoma, plasmacytoma, soft tissue
sarcoma, ossifying fibroma, chondrosarcoma, and osteo­
sarcoma of the os penis.
Epidemiology
Limited information is available for this group of tumors.
See the section on epidemiology for transmissible vene­
real tumors below and the respective chapters for spe­
cific tumor types.
Signalment
With the exception of TVT, tumors of the penis, pre­
puce, and scrotum are generally diagnosed in older dogs.

Presenting signs are dependent on tumor location and

Complete staging including abdominal ultrasound to

Epidemiology
There is a higher prevalence of TVT in warm climates
and in rural areas where there are large numbers of free‐

Signalment
Transmissible venereal tumor affects both female and
male dogs. There is an increased risk in young, sexually
active dogs.

Therapy
Surgery is the treatment of choice for the majority of
tumors in this group. The exception is TVT (see section
on TVT below). Penile amputation may be required
when tumors are invasive or when extensive prepuce
removal is performed. For scrotal tumors, castration
with scrotal ablation is recommended. Adjunctive ther­
apy relevant to the tumor type is warranted when metas­
tasis or recurrence occurs.
Prognosis
The reader is encouraged to refer to the specific tumor
type chapters for a more in‐depth review. Overall, the
prognosis for nonmetastatic tumors, that can be com­
pletely excised, is good to excellent. However, for meta­
static or recurrent tumors the prognosis is guarded to
poor. Osteosarcoma of the os penis may have a guarded
prognosis as this tumor has the potential to metastasize
similar to other axial forms.

­Transmissible Venereal Tumor
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Transmissible venereal tumor is often transmitted
through coitus but can also spread through close contact
such as sniffing or licking of the genitalia. The exact ori­
gin of this tumor is unclear but evaluation of antigen
expression suggests that TVT expresses similar markers
to histiocytes. Canine TVT can be observed in leishma­
niotic dogs, and amastigotes can be harbored in canine
TVT cells.
Transmissible venereal tumors can affect other mem­
bers of the canine family such as foxes, coyotes, and

Transmissible venereal tumor can present as solitary or
multiple nodules on the external genitalia that appear as
pedunculated or cauliflower‐like masses. In males, it
usually occurs on the bulbus glandis but can be seen on
the penis or prepuce. In female dogs, the lesions develop
in or around the vagina. Infected dogs can present with a
few weeks (or months) history of bloody discharge,
deformed external genitalia, ulceration or swelling of the
affected area. Differential diagnosis may include urinary
tract infections, prostatitis, other causes of paraphimosis
or phimosis or other malignancies (urogenital carcino­
mas, sarcomas, or other round cell tumors).
Rarely, dogs can have extragenital lesions without a
primary lesion. These ulcerative, hemorrhagic lesions
can occur in the mouth, nose, eyes or skin caused by bit­
ing or rubbing which can predispose the skin to implan­
tation of the TVT.
Diagnosis
Transmissible venereal tumor should be suspected if the
geographic location, history, lifestyle, and clinical signs
fit the diagnosis. To obtain a definitive diagnosis, either
cytologic or histopathologic confirmation is required.
Microscopically, the cells are large, discrete (round cells)
with abundant blue cytoplasm containing distinct clear
vacuoles. Single or multiple nucleoli and mitotic figures
may be seen (Figure 147.1).
Transmissible venereal tumors have the immunohisto­
chemical staining characteristics of histiocytes. They
stain positive to antibodies against vimentin, lysozyme,
­macrophage‐specific immunostain (ACM)1, and alpha‐1‐
antitrypsin (AAT). Therefore, the use of immunohisto­
chemistry may be helpful in cases where it is difficult
to confirm a diagnosis or if there are atypical metastatic
sites present.

Figure 147.1 Fine needle aspirate of a canine TVT. Note the
homogeneous population of discrete round cells with mild
anisocytosis and anisokaryosis. The cells have a moderate amount
of cytoplasm with multiple discrete clear cytoplasmic vacuoles.

Any dog with suspected TVT should undergo full
staging, including urinalysis, as there is evidence that
dogs with TVT are at high risk of developing urinary
tract infections. Although metastatic disease occurs in
less than 10% of reported cases, evaluating for local
metastasis with abdominal ultrasound and three‐view
thoracic radiographs is recommended. A differential for
suspected metastasis is transplantation (autologous or
allogeneic) of TVT from the primary genital lesion.
Therapy
There are multiple treatment options for TVT. The least
invasive, least expensive and most effective option is
the use of single‐agent vincristine chemotherapy. Admin­
istering vincristine at the recommended dose of 0.5–

0.7 mg/m2 IV once weekly for 3–6 treatments elicits a
complete response in over 90% of dogs. Other protocols
involving cyclophosphamide, vinblastine, doxorubicin,
and methotrexate have been used with less success.
However, for vincristine‐resistant tumors, doxorubicin
given at 30 mg/m2 IV every three weeks can be effective.
Radiation therapy is an effective treatment modality
for TVT. Orthovoltage radiation was evaluated in 18
dogs with solitary primary genital and cutaneous lesions.
All lesions were treated with a total dose of 10–30 Gy.
Seven dogs had a complete response to a single fraction
of 10 Gy. The remaining patients required an additional
2–3 fractions to achieve a complete response. In a sepa­
rate study, 15 dogs with primary genital TVT received
cobalt irradiation. A 100% complete response rate was
reported.
Surgery can be used in cases of primary or metastatic
lesions, but it is not typically recommended as the recur­
rence rate can be up to 70%.
Lastly, the use of immunotherapy with intralesional
bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG) has been shown to be
effective as a single agent and in combination with
­vincristine therapy.
Prognosis
The prognosis for TVT is good to excellent as some dogs
can experience spontaneous regression. The majority of
dogs that receive single‐agent vincristine therapy or radi­
ation therapy will be cured of their disease. The progno­
sis is, however, guarded for dogs that have ocular or
central nervous system invasion or evidence of dissemi­
nated metastasis. An increase in the AgNOR area in the
nucleus was found to be a negative prognostic indicator
in dogs with TVT.

Gynecologic Cancers
Trina Hazzah, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology)
VCA West Los Angeles Animal Hospital, Los Angeles, CA, USA

­Uterine Tumors
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Uterine cancer is extremely rare in dogs and cats. This is
in part because the overwhelming majority of pets are
spayed. Leiomyoma is the most common uterine tumor
in the dog, followed by leiomyosarcoma. Other types of
tumors have been reported such as fibroma, lipoma,
hemangiosarcoma, fibrosarcoma, angiolipoleiomyoma,
adenoma, adenocarcinoma, and extramedullary plasmacytoma. In women, estrogen is considered to be the
­primary factor in the development of uterine carcinoma.
It is believed that both endogenous and exogenous
­estrogen can result in endometrial hyperplasia. It also
potentiates the transformation of endometrial hyperplasia to endometrial carcinoma. Estrogen is not the underlying hormone responsible for endometrial changes in
dogs. In fact, it is progesterone that plays a large role in
both neoplastic and nonneoplastic gynecologic diseases
of the dog. Dogs develop cystic endometrial hyperplasia
which is much less likely to transform into carcinoma.
The most common uterine tumor in the cat is adenocarcinoma which arises from the endometrium. Although
much rarer, leiomyoma, leiomyosarcoma, hemangioma,
squamous cell carcinoma, and carcinosarcoma have
been reported. An association of feline l­eukemia virus
(FeLV) and the development of uterine adenocarcinoma
in cats have been reported.
Birt–Hogg–Dubé (BHD) syndrome is a rare inherited
condition that occurs in German shepherd dogs resulting from a mutation in the canine orthologue (folliculin)
tumor suppresser gene. It manifests in multiple uterine
leiomyomas, bilateral renal cystadenocarcinomas, and
nodular dermatofibrosis. A similar BHD syndrome has
been noted to occur in humans.

Epidemiology
The incidence of uterine tumors is less than 0.5% in dogs
and approximately 1% in cats. BHD is inherited through
an autosomal dominant pattern.
Signalment
Uterine tumors typically occur in middle‐aged to older
dogs and cats, but there are reports in dogs under 1 year
of age. These tumors are overwhelmingly more common
in intact females, but there are reports of uterine stump
carcinomas in spayed females. There is no s­ pecific breed
predilection.
History and Clinical Signs
Most dogs and cats with uterine tumors are asymptomatic. However, purulent to hemorrhagic vaginal discharge, lethargy, anorexia, constipation, and pyometra
can occur. Other signs may be associated with the
­metastatic lesions themselves.
Diagnosis
A minimum database including complete blood count,
biochemistry, and urinalysis is recommended for any
animal with potential gynecologic cancer. Abdominal
radiographs may reveal a mass effect in the caudal
­abdomen. To thoroughly evaluate the extent of disease
or for the presence of regional metastasis, an abdominal
ultrasound is required. Although the majority of uterine
tumors are benign in the dog, three‐view thoracic
radiographs should be performed. In cats, thoracic
­
­radiographs and abdominal ultrasound are mandatory
as malignant uterine tumors are associated with a high

metastatic rate (up to 50%). Definitive diagnosis
requires histology and is easily obtained at the time of
hysterectomy.
Therapy
Ovariohysterectomy is the treatment of choice in all
cases of uterine tumors, except in the setting of distant
metastasis or carcinomatosis. Surgical excision of any
regional metastatic foci is also recommended.
In women, adjunctive chemotherapy has been shown
to have a mild to modest benefit for metastatic leiomyosarcomas and carcinosarcomas when compared to surgery or radiation alone. Although there are no veterinary
reports on the use of chemotherapy for uterine tumors,
it is highly recommended in cases of malignant or
­metastatic tumors. Based on human data, it would be
reasonable to consider chemotherapeutics such as cisplatin, carboplatin, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, gemcitabine, and ifosfamide as viable therapeutic options.
A 2007 study evaluated the presence of estrogen and
progresterone receptors in smooth muscle genital
tumors. Estrogen receptor alpha (ERalpha) was found in
56.3% and progesterone receptor (PR) in 84.4% of canine
tumors. This finding makes hormone receptor antagonist therapy a reasonable treatment option.
Prognosis
The prognosis is excellent for dogs and cats with benign
tumors following complete ovariohysterectomy. For
malignant tumors localized to the uterus, the prognosis
can be good as many of these dogs can still be cured with
surgery. However, the prognosis is guarded for metastatic tumors. In cats with uterine adenocarcinomas, the
prognosis is guarded to poor as they often metastasize.

­Vaginal Tumors
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Vaginal tumors are the second most common tumor of
the female reproductive system. The most common
­histologic type is leiomyoma. These tumors, similar to
the uterine leiomyomas, are slow growing and do not
metastasize. Other less common tumors include fibroma,
polyp, lipoma, myxoma, lymphoma, liposarcoma, mast
cell tumor, adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma,
fibrosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, osteosarcoma, hemangiosarcoma, and TVT.
One study found that all pedunculated masses were
benign. And of the sessile, broad‐based masses, all were
malignant (with the majority being TVT).

Feline vaginal tumors are extremely rare, with most
being benign.
Epidemiology
In dogs, there is some evidence that vaginal neoplasia
may be associated with a history of mammary tumors,
ovarian cysts, pyometra or previous treatment with
reproductive hormones. One study found that the
­majority of dogs with vaginal cancer are sexually intact
and nulliparous.
Signalment
The mean age for dogs with vaginal cancer is 10.8 years.
Although there is no breed predilection, both boxers and
poodles have been reported to have an increased risk.
History and Clinical Signs
Common clinical signs reported include purulent to
hemorrhagic vaginal discharge, swelling of the vulva or
perineal region, a vulvar mass, constant licking of the
vulva, dysuria or tenesmus. Tumors typically arise from
the vulva, vestibule, or vaginal roof. There is no correlation between the location of the mass and histologic
tumor type.
Diagnosis
Definitive diagnosis of malignancy requires histology.
However, the presence of a vaginal mass is often easily
determined based on history, clinical signs, and physical
exam findings (including a digital vaginal exam). For
small lesions, vaginoscopy may be required. Full staging
is recommended for all animals with vaginal tumors:
complete blood count, biochemistry, three‐view t­ horacic
radiographs, and an abdominal ultrasound. Paraneoplastic
hypercalcemia has been infrequently reported to be
associated with older basset hounds with clitoral
adenocarcinoma.
Treatment
Surgical excision with dorsal episiotomy is the treatment of choice. Concurrent ovariohysterectomy is also
recommended as some malignancies such as leiomyomas may be hormone dependent. For highly invasive
vaginal tumors, either subtotal vaginectomy or a complete ­
v ulvovaginectomy and perineal urethrostomy
can be performed. It is advised that any metastatic foci
should be removed at the same time.
Adjunctive radiation therapy and chemotherapy can
be considered for animals that have incompletely excised

VetBooks.ir

malignant tumors or metastatic/high‐grade tumors,
respectively.
The use of carbon dioxide laser ablation in conjunction
with doxorubicin chemotherapy(at 30 mg/m2 intravenously) every four weeks for a total of two treatments has
been shown to provide long‐term control in one case
report of a poodle with vaginal fibrosarcoma.
Another potential treatment is the use of the progesterone receptor antagonist aglepristone, as neoadjuvant
therapy prior to surgery for large benign vaginal tumors.

Signalment

Surgery is often curative for benign tumors and the

The majority of ovarian tumors affect older dogs, with

cell tumors. German shepherds and poodles were
also reported to have a higher occurrence of ovarian
tumors.

­Ovarian Tumors
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Ovarian tumors can arise from different locations
within the ovary and are classified based on their origin,
such as epithelial cells, sex cord stromal elements of the
ovary and germ cells. Epithelial tumors are further characterized as adenoma, cystadenoma, adenocarcinoma,
and undifferentiated carcinoma. Tumors referred to as
sex cord stromal tumors are granulosa cell tumors,
­luteomas, and thecomas. Although more common in
the male, this group also includes Sertoli, Leydig and
Sertoli‐Leydig cell tumors. Lastly, the germ cell tumors
include dysgerminoma, teratocarcinoma, teratoma, and
choriocarcinoma. Other rare tumor types include
hemangiosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, fibrosarcoma,
and carcinosarcoma.
The majority of ovarian tumors, regardless of their histologic subtype, are unilateral. However, adenocarcinomas and mixed sex cord stromal tumors (specifically
Sertoli‐Leydig cell tumor) can occur bilaterally in about
30% of cases. The rates of occurrence for each type v­ aries
depending on the study, but granulosa cell tumors and
epithelial tumors account for most ovarian tumors in
dogs and granulosa cell tumors are the most common
ovarian tumor found in cats.
The overall metastatic rate for ovarian tumors in dogs
is approximately 25%, with a higher incidence, approximately 50%, in both adenocarcinomas and teratomas.
Sex cord tumors are the only histologic type that has the
potential of being hormonally active, as they arise from
gonadal tissue of the ovary and can produce steroid
hormones.
In cats, the most common ovarian tumor is granulosa cell tumor, followed by dysgerminomas. They are

Epidemiology
As ovarian tumors are extremely rare in both dogs and
cats, the true prevalence is unknown.

History and Clinical Signs
The clinical signs reported are variable but may include
vaginal discharge, distended abdomen, pyometra, and an
abnormal estrus cycle. If metastasis occurs, clinical signs
may be associated with the location of involvement, such
as ascites secondary to tumor effusion. As sex cord
tumors can cause hormonal dysfunction, signs associated with excess sex hormones (both estrogen and
progesterone) can be observed. Examples of such
­
changes include bilateral alopecia, vulvar enlargement,
vaginal bleeding, pyometra, and endometrial hyperplasia. Granulosa cell tumors rarely produce enough sex
hormone to cause bone marrow aplasia, but rare examples of sepsis or bleeding secondary to neutropenia and
thrombocytopenia have been reported.
Diagnosis
Although the metastatic rate for ovarian tumors is relatively low, it is still recommended that thorough staging
is performed including complete blood count, biochemistry, three‐view thoracic radiographs, and abdominal
ultrasound. An ultrasound is especially important to
help evaluate for local metastasis to regional lymph
nodes, surrounding organs, and peritoneum. It is not
recommended that ultrasound‐guided cytology/biopsy
be performed. If the tumor is malignant, seeding or
translocation of the tumor cells can occur. If histopathology cannot differentiate tumor type, the use of immunohistochemistry may be helpful. HBME‐1 (and cytokeratin
7) and inhibin‐alpha are useful markers to confirm epithelial and sex cord stromal tumor origin, respectively.

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

Many dogs with metastatic ovarian carcinoma can
present with secondary ascites. One study found that
the overall accuracy of using cytology to differentiate
ovarian carcinoma effusions from other types is approximately 95%.
Therapy
A complete ovariohysterectomy is the treatment of
choice for dogs with ovarian tumors that have no
­evidence of metastasis and typically results in a cure.
There are limited reports of dogs with metastatic
tumors. In one report, a dog was treated with cisplatin
50 mg/m2 intraperitoneally for ovarian carcinomatosis,
resulting in long‐term control. In humans, platinum
drugs, taxanes, and monoclonal antibodies are considered first‐line therapies. Based on human research and
success with chemotherapy, platinum agents should be
considered for metastatic ovarian tumors. In a recent

study, cyclooxygenase 2 (COX‐2) was found to play a
potential role in carcinogenesis and was expressed in
81% of canine ovarian carcinomas. Therefore, the use
of NSAID therapy, similar to what has been found in
other urogenital tumors, should be considered for
­ovarian carcinomas.
Prognosis
The prognosis is excellent for solitary ovarian tumors that
are completely excised with no evidence of metastasis. If
metastatic disease is present, the prognosis is guarded
to poor, depending on the response to c­hemotherapy.
The use of platinum drugs and COX‐2 inhibitors is
recommended.
Treatment and prognosis are similar in cats. Surgery is
the treatment of choice, and if metastatic disease is
present, carboplatin (intravenous or intraperitoneal)
­
and/or COX‐2 inhibitors are recommended.

Mammary Cancer
Julie Bulman‐Fleming, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology)
Veterinary Cancer Group, Tustin, CA, USA

­Canine Mammary Cancer
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Mammary tumors occur most commonly in intact
female dogs and in female dogs spayed later in life.
Hormone exposure, primarily during development of
the mammary glands, is the most significant risk factor.
Increasing age and breed are also consistently reported
risk factors. Obesity at 9–12 months of age and diets
high in red meat have also been associated with increased
risk of tumor development. These factors may influence
the level of estrogen and progestin in the body or augment the effect of these hormones on mammary tissue.
Estrogens and progestins stimulate growth and development of mammary tissue and may contribute to tumorigenesis through direct growth factor activity. Secondary
increases in growth hormone and insulin‐like growth
factor 1 may also contribute. In humans, estrogen and
progestin also increase DNA and chromosomal damage.
Early ovariohysterectomy is protective against mammary tumor development. Dogs spayed before their first
estrus have 0.5% lifetime risk. Dogs spayed before the second estrus have 8% risk and those spayed before the third
estrus 26% risk. The benefit of ovariohysterectomy beyond
the third heat appears slight, if any, though ovariohysterectomy once a mammary mass has been diagnosed may be
of some benefit. The age of first pregnancy and parity does
not appear to influence tumor development. Exposure to
exogenous progestins and estrogens increases the risk, and
has also been linked to tumor development at younger age.
Hormone exposure was confirmed or suspected in most
male dogs diagnosed with mammary tumors.
The entire mammary chain is exposed to the same
hormones and growth factors, which is known as field
effect carcinogenesis. As such, dogs are at risk for multiple mammary masses. Up to 66% of dogs have more than

one mass. There is histologic and chronologic evidence
that mammary masses may progress through benign, in
situ, and noninvasive stages before developing into invasive carcinoma. Estrogen and progesterone receptor levels appear to decrease as tumors become larger, less
differentiated, and more invasive.
Epidemiology
Mammary gland tumors are the most common tumors
in intact females, though the overall incidence depends
on the population in question. The lifetime risk of intact
female dogs has been reported to be as high as 26%. The
incidence in North America is lower than many other
regions due to the more common practice of early ovariohysterectomy. Evaluation of several European registries
showed that mammary tumors account for 50–70% of
tumors in intact female dogs. Approximately 1% of mammary tumors occur in males.
Signalment
Mammary masses occur most frequently in older female
dogs. The risk increases with age from 7 to 13 years, and
dogs with malignant masses tend to be older than those
with benign tumors. Increased risk is reported for ­poodles,
Chihuahuas, dachshunds, Yorkshire terriers, Maltese,
cocker spaniels, English springer spaniels, Brittany
spaniels, German shepherd dogs, German shorthair
pointers, English setters, and Doberman pinschers.
History and Clinical Signs
Most dogs with mammary tumors are otherwise
healthy. Dogs usually present for a palpable mass or a
mammary mass may be an incidental finding. Careful
palpation of the other glands, inguinal and axillary
