two caudal mammary glands are more commonly
affected.
Inflammatory mammary carcinomas account for
approximately 8% of mammary masses. Dogs are often
systemically ill, with painful, edematous mammary
glands. Dogs may also be inappetent, lethargic, and
febrile. Inflammatory mammary carcinomas may be misdiagnosed as mastitis, severe dermatitis or vasculitis.
Diagnosis
Evaluation of the mammary chain should be part of a
routine examination. The size, mobility, and appearance
may increase suspicion for malignancy. A minimum
database, including complete blood count, chemistry
profile, urinalysis, and thoracic radiographs, should be
completed. An abdominal ultrasound to assess visceral
lymph nodes is indicated and regional lymph nodes
should be aspirated when possible. The lymphatic drainage is unpredictable, but axillary, sternal, and inguinal
lymph nodes should be assessed.
Tumor stage has important prognostic and treatment
implications, and most clinicians use a modified five‐tier
World Health Organization (WHO) tumor, node, metastasis (TNM) staging scheme (Table 149.1). The original
WHO staging scheme has four stages. Tumor size has
been found to be prognostic, and so this delineates the
first three stages. The presence of lymph node metastases determines stage 4 disease regardless of tumor size,
and dogs with distant metastases have stage 5 disease.
Surgical resection and histopathology provide a
definitive diagnosis in most cases. Cytology can be performed if presurgical diagnosis is desired. Cytology has
been reported to be 67.5–93% accurate at differentiating benign from malignant masses, with sensitivity of
86–96% and 88–100% specificity for malignancy.
Cytologic diagnosis of malignancy also correlated well
with survival.

Forty to fifty percent of canine mammary masses are
benign. Both benign and malignant tumors may be simple or complex. Simple tumors are composed of only one
cell type whereas complex masses have both luminal and
myoepithelial components. In complex carcinomas, the
epithelial cells are neoplastic while the myoepithelium is
benign.
The most common benign masses include ductal ectasia, lobular and fibroepithelial hyperplasia, adenomatous
masses, and benign mixed tumors. Most malignant
tumors are carcinomas. Simple mammary carcinomas
are most often tubular, tubulopapillary, cystic, papillary,
cribriform or solid. Mucinous carcinoma, squamous cell
carcinoma, and malignant mixed tumors are less common. A histopathologic grading system for mammary
carcinomas exists, and has been found to be prognostic
in several studies. Criteria include the extent of tubule
formation, nuclear pleomorphism, and mitotic rate.
Mammary sarcomas are also reported, with extraskeletal
osteosarcoma being most common.
Therapy
Surgery is an integral part of therapy for mammary
tumors, with the exception of inflammatory carcinomas
and those with widespread metastases. In dogs, it is
unclear whether the extent of surgery is prognostic.
Most studies suggest that for a single mass, the outcome
is the same for mass resection and radical mastectomy as
long as excision is complete. However, given the prevalence of multiple tumors, unilateral radical mastectomy
has also been advocated. In a 2008 study, 58% of dogs
developed a second tumor which would have been prevented by unilateral mastectomy. However, in the same
study, had all dogs received unilateral mastectomies, 42%
would have had unnecessarily aggressive surgeries. If
multiple mammary masses are present, a regional, unilateral or staged bilateral mastectomy is indicated.
One study found that ovariohysterectomy at the time
of mass resection or within two years of developing
mammary carcinoma improved two‐year survival. This
may be because tumors in intact females retain some
hormone responsiveness. Hormone therapy with agents
like tamoxifen (estrogen receptor blocker) is not commonplace, in part because of the ease of sterilization and
also because of the significant risk of pyometra in intact
females. If the dog is to be spayed at the time of mass
removal, ovariohysterectomy should be performed first
to avoid tumor seeding.
For large, high‐grade, or metastatic tumors, surgery
alone is unlikely to be curative. However, the role of
chemotherapy for canine mammary carcinoma is
unclear. Adequately powered, randomized, controlled
trials are lacking. Chemotherapy is often recommended

VetBooks.ir

for masses larger than 3 cm in diameter, when aggressive
behavior is predicted histologically, or when metastasis
is present. It is also advised for mammary sarcomas.
In a small, nonrandomized clinical trial, adjuvant 5‐
fluorouracil and cyclophosphamide improved survival.
After two years, the median survival time of treated
dogs was not reached compared to six‐month median
survival for those treated with surgery only. A 2012
study evaluating carboplatin alone and in combination
with nonsteroidal antiinflammatory agents postoperatively also found significant benefit. A benefit for doxorubicin, docetaxol, and gemcitabine has not been shown.
Simon et al. (2006) showed a trend towards increased
local control and improved survival when doxorubicin
or docetaxol was administered postoperatively but the
results did not reach statistical significance. Larger,
randomized, controlled studies are needed to better
­
evaluate the role of chemotherapy and the most effective
agents.
Prognosis
The most significant prognostic factors are tumor size,
stage, and histologic grade. Several studies have found
that tumors less than 3 cm carry the best prognosis,
while others have shown that tumors up to 5 cm carry a
similar prognosis. The median survival time for dogs
with stage 1 and 2 disease exceeds two years in most
studies. One study found that tumor size in the absence
of lymph node metastasis was not prognostic. However,
86% of dogs with lymph node metastases had primary
tumors larger than 5 cm. Dogs with lymph node and distant metastases generally survive less than six months
when treated with surgery alone.
Inflammatory carcinomas and sarcomas carry a poor
prognosis. The reported survival time of dogs with
inflammatory carcinomas is 25–30 days. The prevalence
of metastases is extremely variable between studies, with
8–100% metastases reported at diagnosis. A recent study
found improved survival of 183 days when dogs with
inflammatory mammary carcinomas were treated with
piroxicam.

those spayed between 12 and 24 months have 11% reduction in risk. Ovariohysterectomy later in life has not been
found protective. Exposure to exogenous progestins is
also associated with increased risk. Female cats exposed
to exogenous hormones have 3.4 times the risk of unexposed cats. Over one‐third of affected male cats had a
known history of progestin exposure. Benign changes
are commonly associated with pregnancy, pseudopregnancy, and progestin administration.
Epidemiology
Mammary tumors are the third most common tumor
type in female cats, accounting for 12–25% of tumors in
female cats in North America. In Europe, the incidence
has been reported to be 25–40%. The three main risk
factors are hormone exposure, age, and breed, with
intact females having seven times the risk of spayed
female cats. Eighty to ninety-five percent of feline mammary masses are malignant.
Signalment
Mammary tumors most commonly affect intact females
and those spayed as adults. The risk of developing mammary tumors increases from 6 to 14 years of age, with
peak incidence at 10–12 years. Male cats account for
1–5% of malignant masses. Siamese cats are at increased
risk and also tend to be younger when diagnosed.
History and Clinical Signs
Most cats with mammary tumors present for a palpable
mass within the mammary chain and are otherwise
healthy. Large, adherent or ulcerated masses may be
painful. The caudal glands have been reported to be
affected more often although some studies have shown
equal occurrence. Multiple masses occur in up to 60% of
cats. Inflammatory mammary carcinomas are rare in
cats but present with systemic signs and edematous,
painful mammae as in the dog.

Benign masses do occur in cats, accounting for 10–20%
of masses. The most common benign diseases are fibroad­
enomas, mammary duct ectasia, and fibroadenomatous
hyperplasia. Fibroadenomatous hyperplasia usually
occurs in young females during pregnancy or pseudopregnancy but can be seen in male or altered cats due to
exogenous progestins.
Tubular, papillary, tubulopapillary, cribriform, and
solid carcinomas are the most common malignancies.
Sixty percent of mammary carcinomas are deemed moderately differentiated, 27.3% are poorly differentiated,
and only 12.7% are well differentiated. Feline mammary
sarcomas and inflammatory carcinomas have been rarely
reported. Metastatic disease occurs in 50–90% of cats,
with up to 83% showing lymph node or pulmonary
metastasis. Visceral metastasis and carcinomatosis also
occur.
Tumor stage has been found to be prognostic. The
most commonly used system is a modified WHO four‐
stage system (Table 149.2). The original staging system
was also four tier but criteria included whether a metastatic lymph node was fixed or mobile, which has not
been found prognostic.

is recommended. For multiple tumors involving both
mammary chains, staged bilateral radical mastectomies
should be performed. Unlike in dogs, the extent of surgery is prognostic, with cats undergoing radical mastectomies having longer disease‐free intervals. One study
found a trend towards increased survival, but a more
recent report did not show survival advantage. Most

The use of doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide in the

45–50% overall response rate. Two studies, which lacked
control groups, found no overall benefit to postoperative
doxorubicin therapy, but did report survival times for
cats with stage 3 tumors which were longer than historical controls. In these reports, cats with stage 3 tumors
survived a median of 448 and 460 days. McNeill et al.
(2009) did not find a benefit of adjuvant doxorubicin
chemotherapy over surgery alone. Within the population
of cats in the study, 47% had stage 1 tumors which are
expected to have long‐term survival with or without
chemotherapy. The authors comment that the study had
12% power to detect a difference between the groups.
Most clinicians advocate chemotherapy for cats with
tumors greater than 3 cm diameter, lymphatic invasion
or lymph node metastasis.
Prognosis
Median survival time is well correlated with tumor size
and stage. Reported survival times for cats with tumors
less than 2 cm range from 12 to 54 months. The median
survival times for cats with stage 2 disease range
between 9‐24 months. Cats with tumors larger than
3 cm or more advanced disease survive a median of 4–6
months when treated with surgery only. As noted above,
the addition of chemotherapy may improve the outcome for these cats, but clear benefit has not yet been
shown.
One study showed that tumor differentiation was also
prognostic, with 100% of cats with well‐differentiated
tumors being alive at one year, 57% with moderately differentiated tumors alive at one year, and no cats with
poorly differentiated tumors surviving to one year. As
most cats have moderately differentiated tumors, the
prognostic benefit of this information is limited. Age,
breed, percent necrosis, completeness of surgical excision, proliferative indices, and hormone receptor status
may also be prognostic.

Tumors of Bone and Joint
Stephanie L. Shaver, DVM, DACVS1, William T.N. Culp, VMD, DACVS1, and
Robert B. Rebhun, DVM, PhD, DACVIM (Oncology)2
1
2

School of Veterinary Medicine, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA, USA
Department of Surgical and Radiological Sciences, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Primary tumors of bone are most commonly diagnosed
in the appendicular skeleton, with osteosarcoma (OSA)
being the most common tumor type. Other neoplasms,
such as chondrosarcoma (CSA), fibrosarcoma (FSA),
hemangiosarcoma (HSA), and histiocytic sarcoma, are
less frequently identified. The metaphyseal region of
long bones is the typical location for appendicular OSA,
with the distal radius and proximal humerus being the
two most common sites. The proximal tibia and distal
femur may also be affected, with proximal femur, distal
tibia, distal humerus, and ulna being less common sites.
While many possible contributing factors have been
suggested, the precise etiology of OSA remains unknown.
Suspected risk factors include previous radiation therapy, fracture, and metal surgical implants. There is also
some evidence that the timing of spay/neuter may affect
the incidence of OSA, but a clear causal effect has not
been demonstrated.
Osteosarcoma is characterized by proliferation of
endosteal cells, which results in the tumor arising within
the medullary canal. This is responsible for the typical
radiographic appearance of bony lysis and periosteal
reaction. Two less common OSA variants, periosteal and
parosteal, exist. Periosteal OSA arises from cortical bone
but may invade the medullary canal; in contrast, parosteal
OSA is characterized by the development of tumor
external to the cortex, which does not invade into deeper
structures. While extremely rare, parosteal OSA likely
represents a less aggressive form of OSA.
Other neoplastic processes that can affect bone include
hematopoietic tumors (such as lymphoma, histiocytic
sarcoma, or multiple myeloma) and metastasis from a
solid tumor. Primary bone tumors such as osteosarcoma

­ etastatic
often metastasize to other bony sites; however, m
bony lesions secondary to other cancers are also common. Many carcinomas, particularly those arising from
the urogenital tract, often demonstrate a propensity for
bony metastasis. While not absolute, metastases are
commonly found in the diaphysis, whereas primary bone
tumors generally occupy the metaphyseal region.
Axial skeletal neoplasia may be caused by any of the
sarcoma types that affect the appendicular skeleton.
OSA remains the most common tumor in axial locations
as well, although it only accounts for about 25% of all
cases of axial skeletal neoplasia. The mandible and maxilla are the sites most often affected, but other bones of
the skull, the scapula, ribs, sternum, vertebrae, and pelvis
may also be affected. Multilobular osteochondrosarcoma
(MLO, also known as multilobular tumor of bone) typically affects the flat bones of the skull and is a slow‐growing, locally invasive tumor. The metastatic propensity of
MLO is largely dependent upon grade. In general, mortality from axial skeletal neoplasia occurs from local disease rather than metastasis, likely due to the challenging
nature of surgical resection in these areas. Mandibular
OSA appears to have a better prognosis than OSA in
appendicular or other axial locations. Improved prognosis may result from less aggressive biologic behavior
when compared with appendicular sites and from the
relative ease of complete surgical excision compared
with other axial sites.
Synovial cell sarcoma has been reported to be the most
common canine joint tumor; however, other reports also
describe a high incidence of histiocytic sarcoma affecting synovial surfaces. These tumors most commonly
affect large joints of the appendicular skeleton (e.g., stifle, elbow), and have biologic behavior similar to these
tumor types in other locations. Suspicion of a joint tumor

should be high for bony lesions where more than one
articular surface is involved.

­Epidemiology
Large‐ and giant‐breed dogs are most often affected with
appendicular OSA, and a genetic component to the disease has long been suspected based on observed breed
predilections. It should be noted that while small‐breed
dogs have a lower likelihood of developing OSA, they are
more likely to develop axial OSA than their large‐breed
counterparts.
Skeletal neoplasia is much less common in the cat,
where it is infrequently reported. OSA is the most common bone tumor in cats and, while locally invasive, carries a better prognosis than canine OSA due to the
overall lower incidence of metastasis and a protracted
course of disease in cats that do develop metastases. Like
dogs, appendicular OSA in cats occurs more frequently
than axial, but axial OSA is relatively more common
compared to the distribution in dogs.

­Signalment
Tumors of bone and joints typically affect dogs and cats
that are middle aged to older. A bimodal age distribution,
however, has been documented for canine OSA, with
two specific peaks at 1–2 years and 7–9 years of age.
Although the vast majority of dogs with OSA fall within
the older group, a young age should not preclude consideration of OSA as a diagnosis.
Large‐breed dogs are overrepresented, with breeds such
as the Great Dane, Rottweiler, golden retriever, German
shepherd, greyhound, Saint Bernard, Irish w
­ olfhound,
Scottish deerhound, borzoi, and Doberman pinscher
commonly diagnosed with bone tumors. No important
sex predilection between male and female dogs exists, but
neutered animals are potentially at greater risk.

­History and Clinical Signs
Dogs with appendicular bone or joint tumors typically
present for evaluation of lameness or swelling of a limb.
In many cases, the history may be that of a chronic, progressive lameness that has only been partially responsive
to analgesics. An animal may also present with an acute
onset of severe, nonweight‐bearing lameness, sometimes
due to pathologic fracture. It is not uncommon for owners to associate the acute onset with a nontraumatic
event such as running, jumping, etc. Axial lesions may go
longer without detection, but animals are often evalu-

ated for swelling or mass lesions. Site‐specific signs can
occur depending on the tumor location and systemic
signs such as lethargy or inappetence may occur from
paraneoplastic syndromes or simply result from pain
associated with the primary or metastatic tumors.

­Diagnosis
A complete physical examination should be performed
in all cases. Variable degrees of swelling, pain, and instability may be associated with the primary tumor. Each
patient should also be carefully assessed for any evidence
of metastasis, either to bone or to local lymph nodes.
Complete orthopedic and neurologic examinations
should be performed, particularly in cases of appendicular neoplasia where amputation may be considered as
the surgical treatment of choice. The presence of orthopedic or neurologic co‐morbidities does not preclude
amputation, but knowledge of these is essential for planning and owner education.
Routine laboratory evaluation by means of complete
blood count, chemistry panel, and urinalysis should be
performed. These tests serve to evaluate the patient’s
systemic health prior to anesthesia, surgery, and chemotherapy. In addition, elevated total alkaline phosphatase
(ALP) has been shown to be associated with a worse
prognosis in canine OSA.
The first step in attaining a bone tumor diagnosis is
orthogonal view radiographs of the affected limb or
region. OSA has a characteristic mixed osteolytic and
osteoproductive appearance, which when combined
with a metaphyseal location is highly suggestive of this
disease entity (Figure 150.1). As previously mentioned,
particular sites are more common for OSA, are often
described by the phrase “away from the elbow, towards
the knee,” with the thoracic limb being more commonly
affected. OSA does not generally cross an articular surface; this trait is more characteristic of a primary joint
tumor, or fungal or bacterial osteomyelitis. Metastatic
lesions are often diaphyseal and predominantly lytic,
although a spectrum of lytic versus productive disease is
possible with OSA. When radiographs demonstrate an
uncharacteristic lesion, other diagnostics, such as culture and biopsy, can be performed to obtain a definitive
diagnosis. Radiographs may also be evaluated for the
presence or absence of pathologic fracture.
Although classic radiographic findings may be sufficient to proceed with surgical treatment, many cases may
benefit from presurgical confirmation of neoplasia and/
or tumor type, particularly in patients that live or have a
travel history to fungal endemic areas. Ultrasound‐guided
fine needle aspiration and cytologic evaluation is a relatively noninvasive means of obtaining a diagnosis of

­neoplasia, although differentiation between types of cancer is often not possible with cytology alone. ALP ­staining
of cytologic samples may allow for more conclusive identification of OSA in some cases. When indicated or
desired, bone biopsy can be performed which typically
results in a specific tumor diagnosis in about 80% of cases.
Bone biopsy may be performed using an incisional
technique, Michele trephine, or Jamshidi needle.
Jamshidi needles yield a smaller biopsy but provide a diagnosis in the vast majority of cases. Bone biopsies should
be planned in order to minimize the size of the surgical
site and provide for appropriate tumor excision at the
time of definitive surgery. Samples should always be taken
from the center of the lesion, as a peripheral biopsy is
more likely to yield reactive bone rather than the true disease process. In addition to using the smallest sampling
tool thought likely to provide a diagnostic s­ample, it is
also recommended to avoid penetration of both cortices
to minimize the likelihood of pathologic fracture.

While micrometastatic disease is thought to be present in nearly all dogs diagnosed with appendicular OSA,
gross metastasis is only identified in about 10% of cases
at the time of initial diagnosis. Pulmonary and bony
metastases occur with approximately equal frequency at
the time of initial diagnosis, although metastasis to other
locations is possible.
Staging of patients is performed due to its relevance in
estimating survival time. Little distinction is made in
osteosarcoma regarding histologic grade due to the biologic aggressiveness of these tumors in nearly all cases;
however, the presence of gross metastasis (stage III disease) is associated with shorter survival times. Median
survival times (MST) in dogs with stage III appendicular
OSA are still highly variable, however, and are affected
by treatment provided. Grading of non‐OSA sarcomas is
generally thought to be associated with prognosis, with
grade III tumors much more likely to metastasize and
associated with a shorter survival time.
Staging in all cases should include three‐view thoracic
radiographs to evaluate for pulmonary metastasis.
Abdominal ultrasound may also be performed to check
for metastatic disease, particularly in cases with pelvic
limb neoplasia, lymphadenopathy, atypical presentation/
clinical findings, or in patients with histiocytic disease.
Similarly, lymph node aspirates should be performed
when lymphadenopathy is noted on physical examination or imaging studies or if the regional lymph node is
readily accessible.
Nuclear scintigraphy, performed with an intravenous
injection of technetium‐99m, allows for identification of
skeletal abnormalities with increased metabolic, particularly osteoblastic, activity. This diagnostic tool is highly
sensitive but lacks specificity; areas of increased uptake
may be due to neoplastic disease, infection, fracture, or
other orthopedic co‐morbidities. The input of an experienced radiologist, as well as follow‐up radiographs to
evaluate abnormal areas, can help to distinguish between
these differentials.
Computed tomography (CT) is being increasingly
used, both to evaluate for thoracic metastases and for
evaluation of the local tumor site. While traditional,
high‐quality radiography is able to detect pulmonary
metastases that are approximately 7–9 mm in size, CT
has a reported sensitivity for detection of lesions as small
as 1 mm. Despite this improved detection of disease, the
clinical relevance of smaller metastatic lesions with
regard to survival times is uncertain.
Assessment of the local tumor site in appendicular
OSA with CT is generally nonessential when the chosen
treatment is amputation. CT may help to evaluate the
extent of disease if alternative surgical treatments such
as limb‐sparing surgery are to be considered. In addition,
CT is often highly valuable for surgical planning in cases

1329

of proximal appendicular tumors or disease affecting the
axial skeleton. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is
generally less useful than CT for imaging bone, making
CT the imaging modality of choice in most cases. MRI
may be useful, however, in evaluating the local extent of
disease prior to limb‐sparing surgery, or to assess the
proximity of neoplasia to neurovascular structures.

­Therapy
Surgical margins around bone and joint tumors generally
fall into the categories of wide or radical excision. Wide
excision is defined as complete removal of disease with a
margin of normal tissue, and radical excision includes
the excision of a body part, such as limb amputation for
cases of appendicular neoplasia. Limb amputation followed by chemotherapy is the recommended treatment
for appendicular OSA, and amputation is often indicated
for CSA, FSA, HSA, and for excision of other appendicular tumors in which local excision with adequate margins
is not possible (Table 150.1). The decision to pursue limb
amputation is typically difficult for owners to make;
however, these dogs generally recover well from surgery
and owner satisfaction is quite high. Videos of amputee
dogs can sometimes be helpful to owners and are now
commonly posted for public viewing on numerous websites. Dogs that are obese or have concurrent musculoskeletal or neurologic disease may have a prolonged
recovery compared to the average patient and may
­benefit from physical rehabilitation after surgery.
Tumors of the thoracic limb are preferably treated by
forequarter amputation. Forequarter amputation including excision of the scapula is preferred due to the ease of
the surgical procedure, the likelihood of wide margins
around disease, and improved cosmetic appearance
when the scapula is removed, as muscle atrophy over this

bone can be unsightly. Tumors of the scapula may be
treated by partial or total scapulectomy with preservation of the limb; however, CT is recommended in these
cases to ensure adequate margins around the extent of
disease. Tumors of the ulna alone may be treated by
ulnectomy; CT is again recommended to evaluate local
disease for surgical planning.
Pelvic limb tumors are most commonly treated with
coxofemoral disarticulation; similarly, this surgical technique is generally preferred over a midshaft femoral
amputation due to ease of technique and wider surgical
margins. Tumors of the proximal femur may be treated
by en bloc excision of the acetabulum in addition to
amputation or hemipelvectomy. Pelvic tumors can also
be treated by partial or total hemipelvectomy. When performing hemipelvectomy, a detailed knowledge of
anatomy is important to avoid trauma to intrapelvic
­
structures such as the rectum and urethra. Preoperative
CT scan is indicated before hemipelvectomy, and if
incomplete or narrow surgical margins are likely, consultation with a radiation oncologist prior to surgery is
strongly recommended.
Recovery after amputation surgery is generally rapid,
with most dogs ambulating within a few days of surgery.
Perioperative analgesia is essential, and may be provided
with a wound soaker catheter or with systemically
administered medications. Recovery after hemipelvectomy surgery is similar to amputation. Complications of
these surgeries include seroma formation and, less commonly dehiscence, hemorrhage, and infection.
Limb‐sparing surgery is described for appendicular
bone tumors, but appropriate case selection and client
education are essential. Limb‐spare may be indicated for
cases in which the dog is unable to tolerate amputation
due to orthopedic or neurologic co‐morbidities, or when
owners have declined amputation. In general, limb‐­
sparing surgery is considered only for tumors of the

­distal radius. The presence of a pathologic fracture is
considered a relative contraindication for limb‐sparing,
as ­fracture may predispose to spread of tumor cells and
subsequent local recurrence. Significant complications
associated with limb‐sparing surgery include infection,
implant failure, and local recurrence. Infection rates
associated with limb‐sparing surgery are high, and have
been described as ranging between 30% and 70%. This
high rate of infection is likely due to a variety of factors
such as impaired vascular supply, minimal soft tissue
coverage, implants, and subsequent delivery of chemotherapeutics. Infection, however, has been associated
with a prolonged survival time compared to dogs that do
not experience infection; dogs with surgical site infection
have been shown to have median survival times approximately twice as long (an average of 250 days longer) as
dogs that did not develop postoperative infections.
Several different limb‐sparing options are available, but a
detailed explanation of the many techniques is beyond
the scope of this chapter.
Radiation therapy can also be used to treat local disease in canine OSA cases. Full course curative intent
radiation therapy is not routinely pursued due to the
cost, side‐effects to adjacent tissue, and lack of benefit
when compared with standard surgical treatment.
Developing techniques such as stereotactic radiosurgery
(SRS) and stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), in
which 1 to 5, high dose radiation treatments are delivered to the precise tumor location are showing promise.
SRS/SBRT have been shown to have comparable success
in some cases when compared to traditional surgical
treatment; however, they continue to have limited availability due to the need for specialized equipment and
highly trained personnel.
Palliative radiation therapy may also be pursued for
pain relief in cases where surgery is not possible or owners do not elect for aggressive therapy. Generally, palliative radiation therapy involves the delivery of several
large doses of radiation in 2–4 fractions. Decrease in
inflammation, slowing of osteolysis, and reduction in
tumor size are all benefits associated with palliative radiation therapy. Over 50% of patients respond to therapy,
with onset of pain relief in 1–2 weeks and improvement
lasting approximately 2–3 months on average.
While it is reported that only approximately 10% of
dogs will have documented metastasis at the time of
diagnosis, it should be noted that this number originates
from dogs presenting to referral hospitals. It is therefore
possible that the incidence in primary care veterinary
clinics could be higher since thoracic radiographs are
often performed at the time of diagnosis, and referrals
are probably less likely in dogs that have detectable
metastases. Even though 90% of dogs will have no
­detectable pulmonary metastasis, with rare exceptions,

appendicular OSA in the dog is assumed to be metastatic
at the time of diagnosis. The extremely high likelihood of
microscopic metastases is supported by studies evaluating survival of dogs undergoing amputation alone.
In dogs with OSA that receive amputation alone, the
one‐ and two‐year survival rates are only 11.5% and 2%
respectively. Systemic therapy to control the outgrowth
of micrometastasis is therefore recommended.
Many chemotherapy drugs and combination protocols
have been attempted, but a clear benefit of any one particular protocol has not been clearly documented; preferred protocols often vary by doctor or institution. In
general, chemotherapy with single‐agent carboplatin,
doxorubicin or alternating carboplatin and doxorubicin
seems currently most favored and generally results in
median survival times of 8–12 months. In the authors’
opinion, the literature does not provide convincing evidence that any protocol is superior to single‐agent therapy with carboplatin. Combined with the fact that
carboplatin is generally well tolerated and is not associated with cardiotoxicity, the authors routinely recommend single‐agent carboplatin. Additional prospective
studies are needed to determine whether either of these
protocols is superior and to determine the optimal number of doses. Cisplatin has shown significant efficacy and
is considered standard of care for human osteosarcoma,
but technical aspects and toxicity associated with administration coupled with the potential for renal toxicity
have made this protocol less often utilized in veterinary
patients. The administration of chemotherapy in the face
of gross metastasis is generally unrewarding, with
median survival times most often ranging from 30 to 90
days. Preliminary data support further studies to examine the potential of toceranib phosphate (Palladia™) to
slow disease progression but no definitive conclusions
can be made to date.
Multiple immunotherapy agents have shown some
efficacy either alone or in combination with chemotherapy. These include liposomal muramyl tripeptide phosphatidyl ethanolamine (LMTPPE) and various delivery
methods of interleukin (IL)‐2. However, these agents
are not commercially available and therefore are not
r­ outinely used.
Aminobisphosphonates (ABPs) are a group of synthetic analogs of organic pyrophosphate which possesses
multiple potential benefits for patients with bone tumors
or bony metastasis. Generally, this class of drugs is considered palliative in that they can induce apoptosis of
osteoclasts (inhibiting bone osteolysis), reduce pain,
improve quality of life, and may delay progression of
bony metastasis. In addition, in vitro studies have found
that this class also exhibits direct cytotoxic effects on
osteosarcoma cell lines. While oral ABP formulations are
available, this route of administration does not reach

1331

VetBooks.ir

1332

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

­levels believed to be required for the beneficial effects of
ABPs against neoplastic bony lesions. Pamidronate is the
most commonly used ABP in veterinary medicine as it is
the most reasonably priced. Infusions of pamidronate
were shown to be well tolerated in dogs and resulted in
increased tumor bone mineral density and pain reduction for four months in 28% of dogs with osteosarcoma.
When used in combination with palliative radiation
therapy, pamidronate also appeared to improve limb
function when compared with radiation therapy alone.
Another ABP, zoledronate, is much more expensive at
this time; zoledronate appears superior to pamidronate
in that 50% of dogs achieved pain alleviation for greater
than four months in one study.

­Prognosis
For dogs with appendicular osteosarcoma that are
treated with amputation alone, the MST is less than six
months. Amputation followed with chemotherapy significantly improves prognosis, with MST approximately
twice as long and between 25% and 62% of dogs alive at
one year. Longer survival times are associated with periosteal or parosteal OSA, small stature, and dogs developing surgical site infections after a limb‐sparing surgery.
Negative prognostic indicators include elevated serum
ALP, dogs developing OSA when they are less than
5 years old, metastatic disease (bone, lymph node or
lung), increased tumor necrosis, proximal humeral location, and larger tumor size. Amputation for cats with
appendicular osteosarcoma is often curative, although
metastasis can occur.
Chondrosarcoma has better survival times compared
to OSA, with histologic grade the most important prognostic factor. After amputation alone, dogs with grade I

CSA had a MST of six years, grade II MST approximately
half as long, and grade III CSA only associated with a
MST of 0.9 years. Metastatic rate was similarly dependent upon grade, with 0%, 31%, and 50% of grade I, II, and
III dogs developing pulmonary metastasis. Prognosis for
appendicular HSA is less favorable than other diseases,
due to the extremely high metastatic potential.
Variable prognoses have been described for axial OSA
based on location and type of treatment. Overall, small
dogs have a more favorable prognosis than large dogs,
irrespective of location. Mandibular OSA has a better
prognosis than other locations; when complete surgical
margins are achieved after surgical excision, a 70% one‐
year survival rate is reported. Negative prognostic indicators include incomplete surgical resection, larger dogs,
elevated ALP, and large tumors. Maxillary OSA has a
reported MST of approximately five months.
As with appendicular tumors, CSA of the axial skeleton
has a significantly better prognosis than OSA. Nasal CSA
has a low metastatic rate and reported MST of 210–580
days. Rib CSA treated with surgical excision has a MST of
1080 days. Grade, location, and completeness of surgical
excision have all been noted as possible prognostic indicators; however, only small case numbers have been evaluated. Similarly, MLO has moderate metastatic potential
but improved overall survival times when compared to
OSA. Mandibular location, low histologic grade, and
complete surgical excision were positive prognostic factors. MST after surgery ranges from 630 to 797 days, with
median time to metastasis between 420 and 542 days.
Prognosis associated with joint tumors is variable
depending on type of tumor and whether complete excision is possible. Synovial cell sarcomas treated with complete excision may have a MST of greater than two years
with surgery alone. Histiocytic disease typically exhibits
a much more aggressive clinical course.

Soft Tissue Sarcomas
Lauren Askin Quarterman, DVM, DACVR (Radiation Oncology)
PetCure Oncology, San Jose, California

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Soft tissue sarcomas (STS) are a group of tumors that
arise from mesenchymal tissues. Tumors within this
group tend to have different morphologic and histologic
features, but the biologic behavior is similar; therefore,
they are often treated as one. Several important biologic
features have been described:
ability to arise from any anatomic site
appear pseudoencapsulated but tend to infiltrate
through and along fascial planes
●● metastasize hematogenously in up to 20% cases, but
regional lymph node metastasis is unusual
●● local recurrence after conservative surgery is common
●● gross tumors generally have a poor response to chemotherapy and radiation therapy.
●●
●●

Not all lesions arising from the subcutaneous space are
malignant, and many are often benign or inflammatory.
Though histologic distinction is not clinically important in
the treatment of these tumors, the nomenclature is determined by the connective tissue (muscle, adipose, fascial,
fibrous, and neurovascular) from which they arise. Tumors
classified as STS include fibrosarcoma, peripheral nerve
sheath tumor, myxosarcoma, liposarcoma, undifferentiated sarcoma, and malignant fibrous histiocytoma. Soft
tissue tumors such as osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma,
hemangiosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, histiocytic sarcoma, nerve root/brachial plexus, oral sarcomas, and synovial cell sarcoma are not classified as STS as they have a
higher propensity for metastasis and/or local recurrence.

­Epidemiology
Soft tissue sarcomas comprise approximately 15% of all
skin and subcutaneous tumors in dogs and 7–9% in cats.

In dogs, sarcomas have been associated with radiation,
trauma, foreign bodies, implants, and the parasite
Spirocerca lupi. In cats, three different types of sarcomas
are seen: vaccine‐associated sarcomas (also referred to as
injection site sarcomas), viral‐induced sarcomas, and
nonviral nonvaccine sarcomas.
Vaccine‐associated sarcomas have been shown to be
linked to the administration of inactivated vaccines,
such as feline leukemia virus (FeLV) and rabies. The
development of sarcomas at sites of vaccine administration with FeLV or rabies is believed to be between 1/1000
to 1/10 000 cases. Some reports have shown an increased
risk with increasing number of vaccinations and with
repeated vaccination at the same site. The time to tumor
development at the site of vaccination has been reported
to be four weeks to 10 years but most commonly occurs
between two and 10 months post vaccination. The
majority of injection site sarcomas in cats arise from
vaccines, but it is important to keep in mind that there
have been reports of tumor development at the site of
lufenuron and microchip injections. It is hypothesized
that the formation of these tumors is related to inflammation created secondary to the injection. This is supported by the similar histologic appearance of injection
site sarcomas to tumors arising in the eyes of cats after
trauma.
Viral‐induced sarcomas are rare. Typically, these multicentric tumors are seen in young cats that are positive
for FeLV. FeLV can serve as a natural vector and transduce nonviral genetic elements from cat cellular DNA.
This can result in the formation of a recombinant virus,
termed feline sarcoma virus (FeSV), which exhibits
altered oncogenicity. FeSV has been isolated from naturally occurring fibrosarcomas of FeLV‐infected cats,
supporting the theory that FeSV can cause the transformation of cells and induce sarcoma formation in FeLV‐
positive cats.

­Signalment
Soft tissue sarcomas tend to occur in middle‐aged to
older dogs and cats. No specific breed or sex predilection
has been identified but medium and large‐breed dogs
seem to be overrepresented.

­History and Clinical Signs
Soft tissue sarcomas present as firm, fixed, often slow‐
growing masses most commonly affecting the trunk,
extremities, or oral cavity. Many times, they are initially
noted when they are small but go untreated as they are
assumed to be benign. The skin overlying these tumors
is often moveable. When tumors are small, they are
nonpainful but as they grow, they invade into the tissues which can result in the tumor becoming fixed or
ulcerated and infected. Clinical signs manifested from
the tumor are dependent on the site from which it
­originates; for example, tumors on a limb may result
in lameness.

­Diagnosis
A fine needle aspirate (FNA) is always warranted on
detection of any new mass or lesion. Cytology can be
beneficial in helping to rule out cysts or other tumor
types (mast cell tumors), but it is always important to
keep in mind that cytology is not sufficient for a definitive diagnosis of a STS. These tumors do not readily
exfoliate and can contain areas of inflammation and
necrosis. The presence of inflammatory cells and necrosis in the absence of neoplastic cells on cytology does not
rule out a STS. A study conducted on FNAs of 40 STSs
reported that only 62.5% of the cases yielded an accurate
diagnosis, while 15% were incorrectly diagnosed.
Biopsy and histopathology are needed for a definitive
diagnosis of a STS. There are two types of tumor biopsy
commonly employed: pretreatment and posttreatment
biopsy. Pretreatment biopsy is the preferred method and
includes needle core (Tru‐Cut), wedge or incisional, and
punch biopsy. All biopsies should be positioned so that
the biopsy tract can be included in the curative intent
treatment field. Posttreatment biopsy refers to an excisional biopsy, where the diagnosis is made after removal
of the gross tumor. Often, this method is attractive to pet
owners as it allows for treatment and diagnosis in one
step but unfortunately, posttreatment biopsies are rarely
curative. An excisional biopsy should only be performed
when it is possible to take a 2–3 cm margin around the
tumor and even then it may not be necessary as lesions
may prove to be benign.

Once a diagnosis of STS has been made, it is important
to determine the clinical stage or extent of disease.
Knowledge of the clinical stage will help determine the
appropriate treatment. Diagnostic tests that should be
performed prior to beginning definitive treatment
include three‐view thoracic radiographs, as the lungs are
the most common site of metastasis. Careful palpation of
regional lymph nodes with FNA or biopsy if accessible
and/or abnormal. Careful palpation of the mass is necessary to determine tumor size and fixation to surrounding
tissues. Advanced imaging with the use of computed
tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
can be helpful to evaluate the extent and invasiveness of
larger tumors, tumors in the head or neck, or tumors
within a body cavity.

­Therapy
Dogs
Surgery

Local tumor control accomplished with wide, surgical
excision is considered the treatment of choice, and
advances in reconstructive techniques have significantly
expanded surgical options for aggressive resection with
good functional and cosmetic outcomes.
The surgical approach is classified according to the
extent of the wound margins as intracapsular (when
the tumor is surgically penetrated); marginal (when the
tumor is excised just outside, or at, the pseudocapsule);
wide (when a portion of normal tissue is left around the
tumor); and radical (when an entire anatomic segment is
removed, for example, amputation). The minimum recommended margins for gross surgical resection are 3 cm
lateral to the tumor and one fascial plane deep. However,
if the tumor is attached to the muscle or fascial layer, the
entire layer may be compromised and should not be
considered a clean margin. Additionally, adipose and
connective tissue are not tumor barriers. Biopsy tracts
and any areas of fixation to surrounding tissue require
en bloc resection with the tumor, as these areas are considered contaminated.
Soft tissue sarcomas are typically surrounded by a pseudocapsule, which allows the tumor to be “shelled out” and
submitted for histologic evaluation. Unfortunately, this
type of marginal excision commonly results in tumor cells
extending to the edges of the resected tissue. Any surgical
procedure involving margins less than 3 cm and one
­fascial plane deep must be considered an incomplete
excision even if no macroscopic tumor is evident after
removal.
Histopathology of the tumor and surrounding tissue
following surgery is important as it provides surgical

VetBooks.ir

151 Soft Tissue Sarcomas

margins and tumor grade. Both are necessary in determining whether further treatment, including additional
surgery or radiation therapy, is necessary. Following
removal of the tumor, surgical margins should be clearly
marked on the specimen and completeness of excision
should be evaluated. The resected tumor should be
pinned out to the original dimensions to prevent shrinkage during formalin fixation. The following terminology
is commonly used when evaluating surgical margins and
considering additional treatment:
incomplete margins – neoplastic cells are continuous
with at least one surgical margin in any plane
●● narrow
margins – distance between surgically
created tissue edge and neoplastic cells is less
­
than 5 mm
●● adequate margins – distance between surgically
­created tissue edge and neoplastic cells is ≥ 5 mm and
<10 mm
●● ideal margins – distance between surgically created
tissue edge and neoplastic cells is at least ≥ 10 mm.
●●

Marginal and incomplete resection is associated with a
higher risk of local recurrence (26–60%). Further, dogs
with incomplete margins are 10.5 times more likely to
develop local recurrence than dogs with complete margins. Studies have also shown that the first surgery provides the best opportunity for local tumor control.
Subsequent surgeries increase morbidity, treatment
costs, and the risk of further local recurrences, while
decreasing survival time. If a second surgery is p
­ erformed
after inadequate resection, a margin of healthy tissue of
3 cm in all directions surrounding the scar is recommended, including the removal of normal‐appearing
subcutaneous fat and underlying fascia. In a study evaluating scar reexcisions, local recurrence was reported in
15% of dogs and residual tumor was identified in 22% of
the resected scars.
Prior to the routine availability of radiation treatment,
radical and often disfiguring surgery was the mainstay of
treatment and resulted in one‐year control rates of
70–80%. Although STS have historically been considered radiation resistant compared to other tumor types,
the multimodality approach of combining surgery with
radiation has been proven to help prevent local
recurrence.
Surgery and Radiation Therapy

The sequencing of radiation and surgery is based on
multiple factors and should be determined on an individual basis. There are several advantages and disadvantages to both preoperative and postoperative radiation
therapy. The rationale for administering postoperative
radiation therapy is that the radiation kills or prevents
the multiplication of any microscopic tumor cells left

behind. Some advantages of postoperative radiation
include the following:
wound complications are rare in tissues that are irradiated after the first inflammatory phase of wound
healing
●● removal of a larger tumor with necrotic regions or
infections may make the patient and patient’s family
more comfortable
●● postoperative treatment planning may be simpler than
preoperative planning in patients in which the size or
shape of a tumor creates difficulty in achieving a uniform dose distribution.
●●

Disadvantages of postoperative radiation include
increased radiation field size, damage to vasculature,
that may lead to local tissue hypoxia which decreases the
effectiveness of radiation, and potential delays if postsurgical wound complications occur. Postoperative radiation is generally started within 7–14 days after surgery.
The rationale behind preoperative radiation therapy is
to decrease the number of tumor cells, thus reducing
contamination of the surgical site. Advantages include a
smaller radiation field, reduction in the size of the tumor,
making surgical excision with wide margins less difficult,
and undisturbed tumor bed and blood supply, which
increases the effectiveness of radiation. Disadvantages
include the possibility of poor or delayed wound healing
in the irradiated field.
Radiation therapy is commonly used as an adjunct to
surgery. Radiation seems to have the greatest efficacy
when it is used to treat remaining microscopic disease
following surgical cytoreduction and is less effective
when used to treat bulky, gross disease. Marginal surgical resection combined with radiation therapy is an
attractive alternative to limb amputation for a STS on an
extremity. It can also be used following a planned marginal resection when wide surgical resection is not possible, such as with tumors of the head or neck. In these
cases, removal of all grossly visible tumor is advised.
Radiopaque clips are often placed during surgery to
mark the lateral, proximal, and distal extent of the tumor
to aid in radiation planning.
Several studies have evaluated radiation therapy for
incompletely excised soft tissue sarcomas in dogs. They
have shown that similar local control and survival rates
are attained with a better functional and cosmetic outcome by performing marginal surgical excisions plus
adjuvant radiotherapy compared to radical surgery
alone. A prospective study evaluated 48 dogs with soft
tissue sarcomas treated with surgery to decrease tumor
size to <3 cm. This was followed by conventionally fractionated, full course radiation therapy to a total dose of
63 Gy. The result was a five‐year ­survival rate of 76% and
a recurrence rate of 16%. The median time to recurrence

1335

VetBooks.ir

1336

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

was 23.3 months. Another study evaluating 35 dogs with
soft tissue sarcomas that were excised to microscopic
disease followed by daily radiation to a total dose of
42–57 Gy reported an overall median survival of 61.7
months.
Interestingly, a recent study evaluated intentional marginal excision of canine STS of the limb followed by a
coarsely fractionated radiation protocol consisting of
four, once weekly, 8–9 Gy ­fractions. Fifty‐six dogs were
included. The results compared favorably to studies
using more fractionated “definitive” protocols, as the
one‐, two‐, and three‐year disease‐free intervals were
82%, 74%, and 70%, respectively, with a local recurrence
rate of 18%. The main disadvantages of using coarsely
fractionated protocols are reduced efficacy and the
increased risk of late radiation toxicity, which may be significant and include bone necrosis and radiation‐induced
tumors at the site. In the study, the risk of developing late
radiation side‐effects was low when the fraction size did
not exceed 8 Gy.
Radiation Therapy

If surgical excision of a soft tissue sarcoma is impossible
because of tumor location or size, radiation therapy can
be applied; however, measurable and bulky tumors tend
to have a poor long‐term response to primary radiotherapy. Tumor control with conventional doses of radiation alone (40–48 Gy) are difficult to obtain because of
their low growth fraction, relatively long doubling time,
and tendency to develop hypoxic regions within the
tumor parenchyma. Reported one‐year control rates are
30% at 35 Gy (10 × 3.5 Gy), 35% at 40 Gy (10 × 4 Gy), 48%
at 45 Gy (10 × 4.5 Gy) and 67% at 50 Gy (10 × 5 Gy). At
two years, control rates vary from 12% at 40 Gy to 33%
at 50 Gy.
As a single modality, radiation has generally been considered palliative for STS with control defined as a slowly
regressing or stable tumor mass. The goal of palliative or
coarsely fractionated radiation therapy is to alleviate
pain, swelling, and inflammation associated with the
tumor, in the hope of improving quality of life. Typical
palliative protocols involve fewer fractions of larger radiation doses (4–10 Gy), often given on a weekly basis. The
delivery of a small fraction size once per week is unlikely
to lead to a durable response because tumor cells have a
significant amount of time to repair damage and proliferate between treatments. Therefore, larger doses of radiation are often delivered to optimize killing of tumor cells,
with the increased risk of late radiation toxicity accepted
as part of the treatment. Since palliative radiation therapy
is administered to improve quality of life, not to prolong
it, patients likely will not live long enough to experience
permanent late effects. A study evaluating nonresectable
STS treated with a palliative protocol (3 × 8 Gy) reported

stable disease in 87% of the tumors treated with a median
time to progression of 8.7 months.
As an alternative to once weekly fractionation, a retrospective study evaluated a palliative radiation protocol
consisting of 4 Gy fractions given over five consecutive
days. In this study, 10 soft tissue sarcomas were treated.
A measurable overall response rate of 80% was reported,
with tumor control achieved in 100% of patients and a
median progression‐free survival of 5.7 months. With
this protocol, the risk for late side‐effects is about half
that of the traditional 8 Gy × 4 fraction protocol.
Many advancements have been made in the field of
radiation oncology, and with these advancements and
improved technology, stereotactic radiation can now be
used to treat STSs. Stereotactic radiation consists of high
doses of radiation precisely targeted at the tumor with
rapid dose fall‐off outside the tumor to help spare normal tissues and limit side‐effects. Stereotactic protocols
generally consist of 1–3 fractions of radiation given on a
consecutive‐day basis. The goal of stereotactic radiation
is to deliver an ablative dose of radiation to the tumor
and achieve long‐term control of the disease. Currently,
there are no published veterinary studies on stereotactic
radiation and STS, but it is expected that this will be a
very viable treatment option for nonresectable STS.
Chemotherapy

Adjuvant chemotherapy at times is useful in the treatment of STS. It is best utilized when combined with radiation therapy and/or surgery. Chemotherapy alone does
not seem to be effective, with the exception of providing
palliation in some cases. Doxorubicin‐based protocols,
either alone or in combination with cyclophosphamide,
have shown the most promise with an overall response
rate of 23%.
Despite the fact that STS are slow to metastasize, the
metastatic rate for cutaneous STS is grade dependent
and varies from less than 15% (grade I and II) to 41%
(grade III). Due to the higher metastatic rate of grade III
soft tissue sarcomas, postoperative chemotherapy should
be considered as it may prevent or delay metastasis.
Single‐agent doxorubicin, mitoxantrone, or combination
protocols are most commonly used.
Metronomic chemotherapy (continuous administration of chemotherapy drugs at doses that are significantly
lower than conventional maximally tolerated dose therapy) has been evaluated in canine STS. A retrospective
study evaluated 85 dogs with incompletely resected
STSs. Thirty dogs received continuous cyclophosphamide (10 mg/m2) and standard‐dose piroxicam therapy
(0.3 mg/kg). Fifty-five control dogs did not receive additional therapy. When comparing these two groups,
treated dogs had a disease‐free interval of 13.7 months
which was significantly longer compared to 7.0 months

VetBooks.ir

151 Soft Tissue Sarcomas

for untreated dogs. Another study evaluated low‐dose
cyclophosphamide and its effects on T‐regulatory cells
and tumor angiogenesis in dogs with STS. This study
found that dogs receiving 15 mg/m2/day of cyclophosphamide had significant decreases in the number and
percent of T‐regulatory cells as well as microvessel density, further supporting that metronomic therapy may
provide antitumor effects.
Cats
Surgery and Radiation Therapy

Injection‐associated sarcomas are poorly encapsulated
tumors with extension and infiltration along fascial
planes. Surgically, 3 cm margins laterally and one fascial
plane deep to tumor have been utilized for the treatment
of vaccine‐associated sarcoma. However, this is not
­adequate considering the reported high rates of local
recurrence which range from 35% to 59%. In response to
this, surgical margins of >3 cm laterally and two fascial
planes deep to the tumor, along with partial scapulectomy, osteotomy of spinous processes or hemipelvectomy when indicated, are now recommended. Despite
attempting aggressive surgical margins, complete
resection is achieved in less than 50% of cats, and overall
one‐ and two‐year disease‐free intervals are only 35%
and 9%. A retrospective study evaluated radical excision
for treatment of 91 STSs. Radical excision was defined as
5 cm of tissue beyond the palpable edges of the tumor
and two fascial planes or bone deep to the tumor. With
this approach, surgery resulted in complete margins in
97% of cases and a local recurrence rate of 14%.
Due to the high rate of local recurrence following wide
surgical resection, full‐course radiation is considered
essential in the management of cats with vaccine‐associated sarcomas. The timing of the radiation therapy is
controversial, and there are pros and cons to preoperative versus postoperative approaches. The time to recurrence when the combination of surgery and radiation
therapy is used ranges from 13.5 months to 19.5 months.
In studies investigating preoperative radiation therapy,
complete resection significantly improved time to local
recurrence with a disease‐free interval for completely
excised tumors of 33 months versus 10 months for
incompletely excised tumors. Unfortunately, even with
combination therapy, recurrence rates still range from
40% to 45%.
Chemotherapy

The most common chemotherapy drugs used to treat
vaccine‐associated sarcomas are doxorubicin, carboplatin, and cyclophosphamide. Postoperative chemotherapy has been shown to have only a minimal effect on
survival in cats treated with curative‐intent surgery and

radiation therapy. Chemotherapy, however, may have
beneficial effects on local tumor control. The effect of
doxorubicin alone was evaluated in 12 nonresectable
vaccine‐associated sarcomas. An initial reduction of
>50% in tumor volume was seen in 50% of the animals.
Unfortunately, the response was not durable, and all cats
showed progressive disease. However, the median overall survival was significantly longer for cats that did
respond. More recently, tyrosine kinase inhibitors have
been shown to block the PDGF/PDGF receptor signaling
pathway in vaccine‐associated cell lines and to inhibit
vaccine‐associated growth in a murine model. These
drugs are currently being evaluated for treatment of
these tumors.

­Prognosis
Dogs
The overall prognosis for dogs with STS is good, but the
range of biologic behavior for these tumors can be broad.
The median survival time for dogs ranges from 3.9 years
following surgery alone to 6.2 years with surgery and
adjunctive radiation. Overall, up to 33% of dogs eventually die of tumor‐related causes.
Research has identified valuable prognostic information including histologic grade, mitotic index, and completeness of surgical margins. A complete histologic
margin predicts nonrecurrence and recurrence appears
to increase with grade. The metastatic rate for dogs with
grade I or grade II is less than 15% compared to 41% for
grade III STS. High mitotic index (>9 mitotic figures per
10 high‐power fields) is prognostic for recurrence,
metastais, and survival. Other factors, including markers
of cellular proliferation, tumor dimension, tumor location, histologic type, invasiveness, and cytogenetic profile, may be useful indicators of prognosis but presently
require further investigation.
Cats
The prognosis for vaccine‐associated sarcomas treated
with surgery alone, using traditional recommendations
of 3 cm margins and one fascial plane deep to the tumor
bed, is poor. Multimodal treatment (extensive surgery,
radiotherapy, chemotherapy) is recommended and the
use of sophisticated imaging techniques can improve
diagnosis and help in surgical planning. The combination of radiation therapy either pre‐ or postoperatively
has improved the disease‐free interval and overall survival time in cats with vaccine‐associated sarcomas.
Median survival time with combination therapy is
23 months compared to 19 months with surgery alone.

Vaccine‐associated sarcomas are graded from I (least)
to III (most aggressive) depending on mitotic index, differentiation, and necrosis. Approximately 15–24% of
vaccine‐associated sarcomas will metastasize to the
lungs or other sites, and evidence has suggested that a
higher grade is associated with an increased risk of

metastasis. In cats, it appears that completeness of excision is one of the most important prognostic factors.
Hence, it is very important that everything is done to
ensure the greatest possibility of obtaining complete
margins when recommending treatment for these
tumors in cats.

Hemangiosarcoma
Christine B. Oakley, DVM1 and John D. Chretin, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology) 2
1
2

VCA Specialists of the Valley, Los Angeles, CA, USA
TrueCare for Pets, Los Angeles, CA, USA

­Etiology and Pathophysiology
Etiology
Hemangiosarcoma (HSA) is a malignant cancer of
­vascular endothelial cells. Although ionizing radiation
has been associated with cutaneous HSA, there is no
clear etiology for the visceral and subcutaneous forms.
Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and other
growth factors such as basic fibroblast growth factor
(bFGF) and angiopoietin‐1 are found in above normal
levels in hemangiosarcoma. It is therefore hypothesized
that dysregulation of angiogenesis may play a key role.
Experimentally, it has been shown that overexpression of
VEGF can lead to malignant transformation of vascular
endothelial cells.
In humans, this disease is known as angiosarcoma and
has been related to arsenicals, vinyl chloride exposure,
and androgens as well as radiation exposure. These may
induce a mutation in the von Hippel–Lindau tumor
­suppressor gene leading to an increased synthesis of
hypoxia‐inducible factor‐1 (a transcription factor for
angiogenic proteins such as VEGF). Mutations in other
tumor suppressor genes such as p53 and PTEN have
also been found but studies are limited.
The etiology of dermal hemangiosarcoma differs from
visceral, myocardial, and other less common primary
forms. Dogs with repeated, prolonged exposure to direct
ionizing ultraviolet (UV) radiation have been documented
to have an increased risk. The predisposition for dogs to
develop dermal HSA regionally on the ventral abdomen
supports solar induction, as well as field cancerization
(a term used to describe the increased risk for regional
tumor development after exposure to carcinogens).

Pathophysiology
Location

Hemangiosarcoma as a primary tumor has been reported
to arise in the liver, kidney, bladder, prostate, perito­
neum, lung, right auricle, muscle, bone, oral c­ avity,
central nervous system (CNS) and integument, but can
arise from any vascular site in the body. In the dog, the
spleen is the most commonly affected organ (28–50%),
followed by the right atrium and auricle (3–50%) and
skin/subcutaneous tissue (13–14%). Multiple unrelated
primary tumors can occur as has been speculated in
dogs with concurrent splenic and myocardial forms.
Dermal hemangiosarcoma is a much less aggressive
disease than visceral hemangiosarcoma. It has been pro­
posed that there are two dermal forms: the solar‐induced
form, affecting thin‐coat predisposed breeds with a good
prognosis, and a nonsolar‐induced, more aggressive
form seen in nonventral locations in thicker coated, non­
predisposed breeds. Dermal hemangiosarcoma (both
solar and nonsolar) has a low metastatic rate. Common
sites of metastasis include lungs, oral or nasal tissue,
bone, heart, and CNS. The solar‐induced form histori­
cally carries the best prognosis. Hypodermal (subcuta­
neous) HSA is characterized as being aggressive with
higher local tumor invasion and a higher metastatic rate
than dermal forms.
Hemangiosarcoma is much less common in cats
than in dogs. In contrast to dogs, integumentary HSA
(subcutaneous and dermal) is more common than the
visceral or myocardial form. Seventy‐seven percent of
all reported feline cases arise from the integument.
The most common locations in decreasing order are
head/face, pinna, and ventral abdomen/inguinal region.

Metastasis

With few exceptions, hemangiosarcoma is a highly meta­
static malignancy. The multistep process involved in
metastasis is shared by all solid tumors and includes the
creation of new blood vessels (angiogenesis), mobility
and invasion into surrounding tissue, embolism into
­circulation, evasion of host immune defenses, lodging
into capillary beds, and extravasation into a new envi­
ronment. A detailed description of this cascade is beyond
the scope of this chapter.
Due to its intimate relationship with blood vessels,
HSA is readily able to mobilize and metastasize. The most
common route is via the vascular system but spread can
occur by tumor seeding onto the local organ parenchyma
and within body cavities after rupture.
Although the metastatic rate of hemangiosarcoma is
regarded as high, the rate can vary depending on site of
origin. The visceral and myocardial forms of HSA
are characterized by an extremely high metastatic rate
(80–90%) to local (liver, omentum, other intraabdominal
organs) as well as distant locations (lungs, CNS). Other
less common primary sites such as renal, retroperito­
neal, and lingual demonstrate metastatic rates of 75%,
88%, and 45% respectively. Primary integumentary forms
have a metastatic rate of 30% for dermal, 35–50% for
subcutaneous, and 75–90% for intramuscular locations.

­Epidemiology
Hemangiosarcoma accounts for 2–5% of cancers in the
dog, and between 0.5% and 2% in the cat. It is more com­
mon in the dog than in any other species, and has an
extremely high mortality. The dermal forms represents
<1% of all skin tumors in dogs and cats. Breeds such as
whippets, Italian greyhounds, greyhounds, English
pointers, Dalmations, and Staffordshire terriers are at
higher risk due to their thin coat and light complexion.
Lightly pigmented cats do not carry the same risk for
dermal HSA as dogs. However, they are prone to other
solar‐induced neoplasms such as squamous cell carci­
noma. For dermal forms, there are no other known risk
factors in the dog and cat. The strong breed association
with the visceral and myocardial forms suggests an
inherited predisposition for dogs. There is no known
predisposition for cats.

larger, middle‐aged to geriatric dogs such as golden
retrievers, Labrador retrievers, and German shepherds.
Dermal hemangiosarcoma is most common in older
dogs, median age 9 years. Dogs predisposed include
thin‐coated, lightly pigmented breeds. Hypodermal HSA
appears in 9–10‐year‐old dogs, with no sex or breed pre­
dilection. Primary renal and retroperitoneal hemangio­
sarcoma are extremely rare. The median age for both
forms is 10 years, with larger nonspecific breeds most
commonly affected. With the renal form, there appears
to be a predilection for males. Other primary sites
such as the tongue have no specific sex, breed or age
predilection.
Cat
The mean age for cats with HSA is 10 years. There is
no sex or breed predilection in this species.

­History and Clinical Signs
Dog
Visceral Nonmyocardial

Dogs with the visceral form of hemangiosarcoma can
present with a variety of symptoms, ranging from leth­
argy to acute death from hemorrhagic shock. The most
common presenting complaints are weakness, lethargy,
collapse, and gastrointestinal changes such as anorexia,
vomiting, and diarrhea.
Patients often present with pale mucous membranes,
delayed capillary refill time, tachycardia and/or arrhyth­
mias, poor pulse quality, and a palpable fluid wave in
the abdomen. If no rupture has occurred, findings
may be limited to a large cranial abdominal mass or
organomegaly.
Myocardial

Dogs with primary myocardial hemangiosarcoma
­present with symptoms of pericardial effusion such as
exercise intolerance, collapse, arrhythmias, and dyspnea.
They are at a higher risk for acute death due to the added
danger of tamponade. Physical exam findings may
include extreme weakness, tachycardia, muffled heart
sounds, and pulsus paradoxus.
Integument

­Signalment
Dog
Hemangiosarcoma can arise in any breed at any age.
The visceral and myocardial forms predominantly affect

Dogs with dermal HSA are often asymptomatic.
Symptoms of the hypodermal and intramuscular forms
vary greatly. Most patients present for lameness,
pain, bruising, swelling or a palpable mass that can
range from firm to soft and fluctuant. All forms of integ­
ument hemangiosarcoma can demonstrate ulceration.

VetBooks.ir

152 Hemangiosarcoma

Compared to dermal HSA which has a predisposition for
the ventral abdomen, subcutaneous and intramuscular
HSA have no predilection for location.
Uncommon Primary Locations

Unlike the above forms, renal hemangiosarcoma may
carry a more prolonged history of vague symptoms, with
a delay of 1–2 months between onset of clinical signs
and diagnosis. Some dogs will have hemoperitoneum.
The majority present with stage I disease (nonrupture,
localized). Presenting complaints include lethargy,
­anorexia, and abdominal pain. The left kidney is more
commonly affected.
Clinical signs of retroperitoneal HSA are similar to
patients with the renal form. However, time to diagnosis
is often shorter as acute hemorrhage is more common.
Dogs with HSA arising from the tongue may be asymp­
tomatic. Diagnosis often occurs as an incidental finding
identified during routine physical exam or dental proph­
ylaxis. One‐third of these dogs will have clinical signs
related to an oral mass, including bleeding from the
mouth, difficulty swallowing or difficulty eating. Lesions
on physical exam are small (<2 cm) and commonly
located on the ventral surface but can arise from the
­dorsal aspect as well. Up to one‐quarter of dogs can have
multiple lingual tumors.
Cat
Due to the most common location being the integument,
most symptoms include a red or bruised raised swelling
or mass. However, for visceral and myocardial forms,
similar symptoms as seen in the dog can be expected.

­Diagnosis
Complete blood count (CBC), serum biochemistry, uri­
nalysis (UA), abdominal ultrasound, echocardiogram,
three‐view thoracic radiographs, and coagulation testing
are recommended for most forms of HSA. With the
myocardial form or if an arrhythmia is present, an
­electrocardiogram (ECG) should also be pursued. The
exception to the above is with the dermal form. Because
of the lower metastatic rate, abdominal ultrasound,
echocardiogram and ECG may not be necessary.
The reader is cautioned to approach each patient on an
individual basis.
A high level of suspicion for HSA can be formulated
based on ultrasonography findings (70% of splenic
masses will be malignant and approximately 70% of those
will be HSA). Additionally, HSA often, but not always,
appears hypoechoic, cavitated, and nonhomogene­
ous. Nonetheless, caution must be exercised as other

­nonmalignant lesions such as hematoma or hemangioma
may have a similar appearance.
Effusions are typically serosanguinous to hemorrhagic
and samples characteristically lack clot formation.
Hematologic abnormalities may include anemia,
thrombocytopenia, schistocytes, acanthocytes, pro­
longed prothrombin time, prolonged activated partial
thromboplastin time, and increased fibrin degradation
products. Approximately 50% of all dogs with splenic
hemangiosarcoma meet disseminated intravascular
coagulation (DIC) criteria.
Dogs with myocardial hemangiosarcoma may demon­
strate a decreased amplitude of the QRS complex and
electrical alternans on ECG. A visible tumor can be
detected with echocardiography in 65–90% of cases.
With renal hemangiosarcoma, over half of patients
are anemic. Patients may present with hematuria,
­proteinuria, hypoproteinemia, and thrombocytopenia.
Ultrasonography often reveals a unilaterally, irregular,
enlarged kidney.
With all forms, cytologic or histologic analysis is
required for a definitive diagnosis. Ultrasound‐guided
fine needle aspiration for visceral forms can be attempted
but is associated with a significant risk of hemorrhage
and low sensitivity (38%). Therefore, most cases will
require surgical biopsy. If necessary, immunochemical
analysis for factor VIII‐related antigen (von Willebrand
factor), CD31, CD34, and vimentin can be performed.
In cats, full testing, including abdominal ultrasound,
three‐view thoracic radiographs, CBC, serum biochem­
istry and UA, is recommended regardless of primary
location. Echocardiography in cats may not be warranted
as cardiac HSA is extremely uncommon. The value of
this and other diagnostics should be determined on a
case‐by‐case basis.

­Staging System
Staging describes the severity of cancer based on its size,
local behavior, and presence of metastasis. This informa­
tion is utilized in treatment planning and in assessing
prognosis. Unfortunately, no standard staging system
has been established for the cat. For the dog, a modified
World Health Organization (WHO) tumor, node, metas­
tasis (TNM) system is commonly used (Table 152.1).
In this classification, there are three established stages.
For visceral HSA, stage I (T0 or T1, N0, M0) describes
a tumor <5 cm in diameter or microscopic with no
­evidence of nodal or distant metastasis and no evidence
of rupture. Stage II (T1 or T2, N0 or N1, M0) describes
no invasion into adjacent structures with or without
tumor capsule rupture, no measurable distant metastasis
with or without regional lymph node involvement.
