­Therapy
Surgery
Regardless of species and primary location, surgery
along with adjunctive doxorubicin‐based chemotherapy
(Table 152.2) is the treatment of choice. Notable
­exceptions include small dermal lesions (stage I) and
conjunctival forms; these presentations may not require
adjunctive chemotherapy as they carry a much lower risk
of metastasis.
Surgical mass removal is vital to minimize the risk
of fatal hemorrhage with splenic hemanigosarcoma.
Intraoperatively, arrhythmias are common, so continuous

Sterile
hemorrhagic
cystitis

ECG monitoring for a minimum of 24 hours postoper­
atively is recommended. Ventricular tachycardia,
sustained tachycardia (180 beats per minute) with
­
­paroxysmal runs of ventricular premature complexes
(VPCs) or patients that are symptomatic for ventricular
arrhythmias can be treated with lidocaine boluses or
­constant rate infusions. Most arrhythmias will resolve
within 24–48 hours.
Patients with splenic hemangiosarcoma commonly
have evidence of liver metastasis at the time of diagnosis.
However, all hepatic nodules identified at surgery should
not be assumed to be malignant as benign conditions
such as nodular hyperplasia are also commonly found
in the aged animal. It is necessary to perform a biopsy
of any suspicious lesion when removing an abdominal
mass.
Surgical excision of myocardial HSA is rarely per­
formed. Tumors in this location are a significant techni­
cal challenge and are seldom completely removed. For
most patients, laparoscopic or open thorax pericardiec­
tomy may be the only surgical option. Pericardiectomy
may provide palliation and short‐term survival gains as
it minimizes risk of pericardial tamponade. Owners
should be warned about sudden death from tamponade
if removal or pericardectomy is not pursued.

VetBooks.ir

152 Hemangiosarcoma

Complete surgical excision of dermal hemangiosar­
coma is strongly recommended. If the mass is small
and no evidence of subcutaneous invasion is found,
adjunctive chemotherapy may not be warranted as the
risk of metastasis for this form is low.
Unlike dermal tumors, where surgical excision alone
may be adequate, hypodermal and intramuscular tumors
require multimodal therapy. HSA in this location is
­associated with a high local recurrence and metastatic
rate. Therefore, wide surgical excision (3 cm minimum
margin) +/‐ adjunctive radiotherapy is recommended.
To address the risk of metastasis, systemic chemother­
apy (doxorubicin based) is always recommended.
In cats, complete histopathologic excision with wide
surgical margins is likewise recommended for all dermal
forms of hemangiosarcoma. As in dogs, subcutaneous
and other nondermal hemangiosarcoma forms have a
higher risk of metastasis. Hence adjunctive chemother­
apy should be considered.
Doxorubicin‐Based Chemotherapy
Doxorubicin is the most active chemotherapeutic for
hemangiosarcoma. It can be used alone or as part of a
multiple agent protocol (see Table 152.2). Regardless of
which is utilized, chemotherapy is regarded as well
tolerated by most animals. Gastrointestinal toxicity
­
(vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia) is often self‐limiting and is
seen in up to 20% of patients, but requires hospitaliza­
tion far less often. Like most chemotherapeutics, the
most common hematologic side‐effects are neutrope­
nia and thrombocytopenia, and, less likely, anemia.
Doxorubicin‐based protocols that incorporate dacar­
bazine result in a response rate of 47% but have more
significant hematologic and gastrointestinal side‐effects.
Oral temozolomide in place of dacarbazine has recently
been evaluated. The response rate was found to be
­similar but with less hematologic toxicity.
Doxorubicin, like all anthracyclines, is cardiotoxic. An
irreversible, dilated type cardiomyopathy can occur at
cumulative doses at or above 180–240 mg/m2. A more
cardioprotective anthracycline is epirubicin. Adverse
cardiac effects can be seen with its use but at doses
more than double that of doxorubicin. In one study, it
was shown to be equally effective as doxorubicin, but
more gastrointestinal side‐effects (vomiting, diarrhea)
occurred. Other formulations of doxorubicin such as
pegylated, liposome‐encapsulated (PL‐DOX) are availa­
ble. Encapsulation into liposomes leads to decreased
­cardiotoxicity and decreased drug uptake by phagocytes,
thereby prolonging exposure to the drug. Comparison
of response and survival time between pegylated
and nonpegylated forms has revealed no differences.
Of unique concern, PL‐DOX may induce palmar‐plantar

erythrodysesthesia (PPES), a painful desquamation
dermatitis. Adjunctive therapy with pyridoxine may
­
minimize symptoms and lessen risk.
Other notable toxicities of anthracyclines include
­anaphylactic type reactions during infusion and tis­
sue necrosis if extravasated. Proper administration
requires accurate intravenous catheter placement,
patient sedation when appropriate, and avoiding
bolus administration.
In the cat, adjunctive chemotherapy with a doxoru­
bicin‐based protocol is recommended following surgical
excision for all forms of HSA except small dermal lesions.
Single‐agent doxorubicin dosed at 25 mg/m2 every three
weeks, or a combination protocol with cyclophosphamide
and vincristine, should be considered.
Immunotherapy
Immunotherapy modifies a biologic response by enhanc­
ing a preexisting immune response, inducing an immune
response or suppressing an immune response. When
given in conjunction with chemotherapy, immunomod­
ulatory agents may enhance efficacy and improve
­prognosis. One such immunomodulatory agent is mura­
myl tripeptide‐phosphatidylethanolamine (L‐MTP‐PE),
a lipophilic derivative of muramyl dipeptide (MDP), a
molecule resembling the cell wall of bacteria. L‐MTP‐
PE stimulates cells of macrophage lineage to become
­tumoricidal. When a doxorubicin‐based protocol was
used in conjunction with L‐MTP‐PE (given twice weekly
for eight weeks), the median survival time was signifi­
cantly improved (277 days versus 143 days with chemo­
therapy alone). L‐MTP‐PE is not presently available in
the United States.
Antiangiogenic Therapy
Angiogenesis is a normal process involved in fetal devel­
opment, wound healing, and the female reproductive
cycle. In health, it is controlled by inhibitory regulators.
In the cancer patient, this process becomes abnormally
activated and unregulated and is involved in tumor
growth and metastasis.
Newer cancer treatment strategies focus on the
­inhibition of angiogenesis. Growth factors monitor and
activate endothelial cell growth and development. As
examples, VEGF and bFGF act directly on endothelial
cells; Transforming growth factor (TGF) and platelet‐
derived growth factor (PDGF) attract and activate
inflammatory cells and connective tissue, which thereby
promotes angiogenesis. Antiangiogenic agents are
directed towards inhibition of one or more growth
­factors or their receptors, thereby preventing further
angiogenesis, growth and metastasis of a tumor.

1343

VetBooks.ir

1344

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

Angiogenesis inhibitors are an attractive antineoplastic
treatment as they are not limited to cytotoxic therapy
and may be more acceptable and tolerable by both
the owner and the patient. Further, they do not induce
multidrug resistance as they do not target tumor cells
directly.
Metronomic Chemotherapy

Metronomic or continuous low‐dose oral chemotherapy
has been demonstrated to have antiangiogenic and
immune‐modulating effects. Its use has been shown to
improve survival in dogs undergoing splenectomy.
Cyclophosphamide, the most commonly prescribed, also
suppresses T‐regulatory cells, thereby improving host
antineoplastic immune function. In one study, cyclo­
phosphamide (12.5–25 mg/m2 PO) and etoposide
(50 mg/m2 PO) were administered daily on alternating
three‐week cycles with piroxicam (0.3 mg/kg/day PO).
Results revealed a median survival of 178 days, which
was significantly better than historical controls undergo­
ing surgery alone. Although low doses of chemotherapy
are used, owner compliance and care are required to
minimize risks for sterile hemorrhagic cystitis.
To date, very few metronomic protocols have been
evaluated in patients with hemangiosarcoma. Further
studies need to be done to determine efficacious drugs,
dosages, and timing.
Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors

Palladia™ (toceranib phosphate) is a receptor tyrosine
kinase inhibitor that affects the activities of multiple
receptors, including VEGF and PDGF‐alpha. Similar to
metronomic chemotherapy, it also has immunomodula­
tory effects against myeloid‐derived suppressor cells.
Masitinib mesylate (Masivet®), another receptor tyrosine
kinase inhibitor approved for use in dogs in Europe, was
shown to decrease T‐regulatory lymphocytes in the
bloodstream of dogs and was well tolerated when com­
bined with a metronomic dosage of cyclophosphamide.
However, neither Palladia nor Masivet has been shown
to lead to survival benefits for HSA. Imatinib mesylate
(Gleevec®), a human receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor,
has been shown to induce apoptosis in hemangiosar­
coma cell lines with a dose‐dependent killing effect
in vitro. It is associated with hepatotoxicity in the dog
and for most, is cost‐prohibitive.
Other Agents

Interferons are cytokines that have been used for antian­
giogenic therapy in humans; interferon‐alpha 2a inhibits
angiogenesis by suppressing bFGF and VEGF produc­
tion. Daily injections are required, making it less practi­
cal for the veterinary patient. Neutralizing antibodies

may also eventually be produced, making the use of esca­
lating doses necessary.
Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are another poten­
tial target for therapy. These enzymes degrade compo­
nents of the extracellular matrix, and play an important
role in wound healing and tissue remodeling. In the can­
cer patient, MMPs are involved in tumor invasion, prolif­
eration, and fostering a local environment to enhance
tumor growth. Minocycline is a synthetic agent that
inhibits MMPs. However, its use has not been shown to
significantly prolong survival in dogs with HSA when
combined with a doxorubicin‐containing protocol.
Complementary Treatment
Nutraceuticals or homeopathic remedies have been
explored as adjuncts to standard therapy for hemangio­
sarcoma in an effort to improve quality of life. Yun‐Zhi
PSP is the active ingredient in I’m‐Yunity (an extract of
Coriolus versicolor mushroom). The median time to
develop metastasis or progression of metastasis was
delayed in dogs receiving 100 mg/kg/day. Yunnan Baiyao
is a neutraceutical/homeopathic Chinese powder that
anecdotally has been shown to promote coagulation, and
help prevent intraabdominal and myocardial hemorrhage.
The definitive benefit of its use in dogs with hemangiosar­
coma has yet to be determined.

­Prognosis
Visceral and Myocardial Forms
The long‐term prognosis is grave for dogs with the vis­
ceral form of hemangiosarcoma. The median survival
time (MST) with surgery alone is approximately 72 days.
With adjunctive chemotherapy, the median s­ urvival time
is 6 months (one-year survival 6%). Stage has been shown
to be prognostic. Dogs with a stage III presentation have
an anticipated MST of three months in spite of standard
therapy. Death is typically due to resistant metastatic
­disease or hemorrhage.
The prognosis for dogs with myocardial HSA is like­
wise grave. Although survival may be similar to those
with the visceral form, a poorer outcome is more typical
(MST 4 months) as many do not undergo cytoreductive
surgery. In one study, the MST for dogs that had pericar­
dectomy alone was one month.
Both renal and lingual forms are exceptions. With
treatment, renal hemangiosarcoma has a MST of nine
months, with an approximately 30% one‐year survival.
Dogs with lingual hemangiosarcoma (grade I and II)
have an expected MST of 553 days. Local recurrence
following therapy for the lingual form is common.

VetBooks.ir

152 Hemangiosarcoma

Integument
Dermal hemangiosarcoma is associated with the best
prognosis. A MST of 2.5–3 years (one year 79%, two year
60% MST) can be anticipated. Prognostic factors include
breed, tumor location, presence of solar actinic changes,
and invasiveness. Predisposed breeds have a decreased
risk for ­developing metastasis, and have a longer survival
time (MST 1570 vs 593 days). Sun‐exposed locations
have a better prognosis and an increased overall survival
rate (1085 days vs 539 days for tumors of other loca­
tions). Additionally, dogs with solar changes on histology
such as solar elastosis, superficial dermal fibrosis, and
epidermal dysplasia have an increased overall survival
compared to those without solar changes (MST 1549 vs
545 days respectively). Of importance to note is that over
75% of dogs with dermal HSA will develop additional
tumors in the same region of skin over time (usually pre­
disposed breeds with the solar‐induced form on their
ventral abdomen).

The prognosis for dermal hemangiosarcoma is signifi­
cantly more guarded if invasion into the subcutis or mus­
cle has occurred. With surgery alone, MST is 172 days
for stage II and 307 days for stage III disease. One study
found the prognosis for dogs with stage II tumors was
improved with the addition of chemotherapy (MST 1189
days) but the prognosis for stage III tumors remained
similar (MST 273 days). Most dogs with stage III HSA
(intramuscular) will die of metastatic disease prior to
local recurrence.
Cat
In cats, similarl to dogs, location is a good predictor of
survival. Subcutaneous tumors had a longer MST than
visceral tumors, and dermal tumors had a longer MST
than subcutaneous tumors. Higher mitotic indices
(>3/10) were linked to shorter survival.

153
Melanoma
Philip J. Bergman, DVM, PhD, DACVIM (Oncology)
Katonah‐Bedford Veterinary Center, Bedford, Hills, NY, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology/
Epidemiology
Melanoma is a relatively common tumor of dogs, especially in those with significant levels of skin pigmentation. Melanomas in cats are relatively rare. The most
common location for canine melanoma is the haired
skin, where they grossly appear to be small brown to
black masses, but can also appear as large, flat, and/or
wrinkled masses. Primary melanomas also can occur in
the oral cavity, nailbed, footpad, eye, gastrointestinal
tract, or mucocutaneous junction. Ocular melanomas of
dogs and cats represent a distinct clinical syndrome and
will be discussed elsewhere. Metastatic sites for canine
malignant melanoma (CMM) can be varied, including
local draining lymph nodes, the lungs, liver, meninges,
adrenals, etc.
Melanoma arises from melanocytes, the cells which
generate pigment through the melanosome by a number
of melanosomal glycoproteins. In humans, cutaneous
melanoma can arise due to mutations induced by
repeated, intense exposure to ultraviolet light (for example, frequent tanning or working outdoors). Melanoma is
currently the most rapidly increasing incident human
cancer. Significant recent research into the etiology of
human melanoma suggests multiple causes which are
independent of the aforementioned UV‐associated
mutagenesis. Since most breeds of dogs have a hair coat,
which affords them protection from sunlight, UV‐associated melanoma is a less likely primary causative agent
in the dog. However, pigment cells divide every time
there is injury to the skin, or if there is constant
trauma (for example, areas where dogs scratch or lick).
Nevertheless, risk factors for canine melanoma are not
well established.

­Signalment
The most common oral malignancy in the dog is melanoma. Oral malignant melanoma is most commonly
diagnosed in Scottish terriers, golden retrievers, poodles, and dachshunds. Oral melanoma is primarily a disease of older dogs without gender predilection, but may
be seen in younger dogs. Additional oral tumor differentials include squamous cell carcinoma, fibrosarcoma,
epulides/odontogenic tumors, osteosarcoma, and others. Melanomas in the oral cavities of dogs are found in
the following locations in order of decreasing frequency:
gingiva, lips, tongue, and hard palate. Feline melanoma is
relatively rare, but appears to be malignant in most cases.

­Diagnosis/Pathology/Molecular
Biology
Melanomas can be difficult to diagnose pathologically in
some situations, especially anaplastic amelanotic melanomas which can masquerade as soft tissue sarcomas.
Numerous investigators have attempted to increase the
precision of identification of melanomas predominantly
through immunohistochemical (IHC) means. This may
be accomplished through the use of multiple IHC assays
on suspected melanoma tissue or through the use of an
IHC cocktail of antibodies. The use of PNL2 and tyrosinase, beyond the typical use of Melan A and S100,
appears to hold particular promise.
The molecular characterization of canine and feline
melanomas is not as well defined as it is in humans.
BRAF is a member of the MAPK signaling pathway,
which is commonly mutated in human cutaneous
­melanoma, but infrequently mutated in oral mucosal

melanoma. Interestingly, BRAF mutations are also
­
uncommon in canine oral malignant melanoma, suggesting that certain canine and/or feline malignancies
can have similar molecular signatures in addition to their
already well‐known clinical similarities in the context of
resistance to chemotherapy and/or radiation, prognosis,
and similar variable peculiar sites of metastatic propensity. A number of other investigators have reported a
variety of molecular abnormalities and/or associations in
canine and feline melanoma.

­Staging
The staging of dogs with melanoma is relatively straightforward. A minimum database should include a thorough history and physical exam, complete blood count
and platelet count, biochemical profile, urinalysis, three‐
view thoracic radiographs and local lymph node
­aspiration with cytology to determine whether lymphadenomegaly is present or not. Williams and Packer
reported that local nodes from dogs with oral melanoma
have ~70% metastasis when lymphadenomegaly was present, but more importantly, ~40% had metastasis when
no lymphadenomegaly was present. Abdominal ultrasound should be considered in cases with moderate to
high metastatic potential such as the oral cavity, feet or
mucosal surface of the lips, as melanoma may metastasize to the abdominal lymph nodes, liver, adrenal glands,
and other sites.
The use of sentinel lymph node mapping and lymphadenectomy is of diagnostic, prognostic and clinical
benefit in human melanoma. Relatively few investigations have been reported to date for sentinel lymph node
mapping and/or excision for dogs with malignancies and
this author strongly encourages additional investigation
in this area. Furthermore, the use of novel staging
modalities such as gallium citrate scintigraphy is also
encouraged.

­Therapy
Surgery
Surgery is the most effective local treatment modality for
melanoma. Incisional biopsy is an important part of the
diagnostic work‐up based on the clinical, therapeutic,
and prognostic heterogeneity of tumors on the differential diagnosis list. In cases for which cytology results
from draining lymph nodes are equivocal, lymph nodes
should be surgically excised and submitted for pathologic examination as this outcome holds prognostic and
therapeutic importance.

Cutaneous melanocytomas are often completely
excised with 1 cm lateral skin and one fascial plane deep
margins. In contrast, partial mandibulectomy and maxillectomy are typically required for complete removal of
oral melanomas arising from the gingiva or from other
oral mucosa in close proximity to bone. Imaging via
computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) can be helpful for delineation of tumor
extent/invasiveness and/or involvement of regional
lymph nodes. Melanomas in mucosal areas not adjacent
to bone such as tongue, lip or buccal mucosa may be
amenable to excision of the soft tissues only. Local recurrence rates vary from ~20% to 50% following mandibulectomy and maxillectomy, respectively. Quality of
life is typically very good to excellent and most dogs are
eating in the first day or two following mandibulectomy
or maxillectomy, with high owner satisfaction rates. The
combination of surgery and radiation plus adjuvant therapy should be considered in those patients with tumors
that are not amenable to clean margin resection.
Radiation Therapy
Radiation therapy can play an integral role in the treatment of a subset of canine and feline melanomas.
Radiation therapy is unfortunately ineffective at
­controlling distant metastasis and therefore should be
used for local tumor control when definitive local therapy via surgical removal is incomplete or not possible.
Melanoma has historically been believed to be a
relatively radioresistant tumor type. Therefore, most
­
radiation protocols used in dogs and cats have utilized
higher doses per fraction. Protocols with fewer treatments (“hypofractionated”) have less cost, reduced
­emotional and time commitment for owners, and fewer
anesthetic episodes with generally less severe acute side‐
effects when compared to full‐length normally fractionated protocols. A 2–3 cm ­margin around the tumor is
typical for most radiation plans with considerations for
irradiation of the local draining lymph node.
The overall response rate to radiation for canine OMM
is generally 80–90% with approximately 60% complete
response and 25% partial responses. Progression‐free
median survival times with radiation are typically 5–8
months with high recurrence rates. Median survival
times range from approximately five to 12 months. Dogs
with less advanced, incompletely resected oral melanoma (majority were stage I with some stage II) that were
treated with either carboplatin or cisplatin given once
weekly before radiation therapy had a median survival
time of approximately 12 months. The median survival
time for five cats with oral malignant melanoma treated
with radiation therapy and a variety of other adjuvant
therapies was only 146 days.

VetBooks.ir

153 Melanoma

Chemotherapy
Other modalities reported for local tumor control as
case reports and/or case series have included intralesional cisplatin implants, intralesional bleomycin with
electronic pulsing and many others, but widespread use
has not been reported to date.
In dogs with melanoma in anatomic sites predicted to
have a moderate to high metastatic rate, or dogs with
cutaneous melanoma with a high tumor score and/or
increased proliferation index through increased Ki‐67
expression, the use of systemic therapies is warranted due
to the high risk for metastasis. Rassnick and colleagues
reported an overall response rate of 28% using carboplatin
for dogs with malignant melanoma. Unfortunately, only
one dog had a minimally durable complete response (~150
days), and the rest were nondurable partial responses.
Similarly, Boria et al. reported an 18% response rate and
median survival time of 119 days with cisplatin and piroxicam in canine oral melanoma. Other reports using single‐agent dacarbazine, melphalan or doxorubicin suggest
poor or absent activity. More recently, and importantly,
three studies suggest that chemotherapy plays an insignificant role in the adjuvant treatment of canine melanoma, whereas one study suggests it may provide benefit.
While it can be argued that the studies performed to
date to evaluate the activity of chemotherapy in an adjuvant setting for canine melanoma have been suboptimal
for a variety of reasons, the extensive human literature
suggests that melanoma is an extremely chemotherapy‐
resistant tumor. It is clear that new approaches to the systemic treatment of this disease are desperately needed.
One potential therapeutic avenue which has not been
significantly reported to date in canine or feline melanoma is the use of COX‐2 inhibitors. A number of
authors have investigated the expression of COX‐2 in
canine melanoma and have found positive correlations
of COX‐2 expression to proliferation and survival.
Further studies investigating the clinical responsiveness
of canine melanoma to COX‐2 inhibitors (and potential
correlation to COX‐2 expression) are encouraged.
Immunotherapy
Immunotherapy represents one potential logical systemic
therapeutic strategy for melanoma. A variety of immunotherapeutic strategies for the treatment of human melanoma have been reported, with typically poor outcomes
due to a lack of breaking innate or acquired immune tolerance to the tumor. Immunotherapy targets and strategies to date in canine melanoma have used autologous
tumor cell vaccines (with or without transfection with
immunostimulatory cytokines and/or melanosomal
­differentiation antigens), allogeneic tumor cell vaccines

transfected with interleukin (IL)‐2 or granulocyte
­macrophage‐colony stimulating factor (GM‐CSF), liposomal‐encapsulated nonspecific immunostimulators (e.g.,
L‐MTP‐PE), topical imiquimod, intralesional Fas ligand
DNA, siRNA (small interfering) against the survivin and/
or Bcl‐2 genes, bacterial superantigen approaches with
GM‐CSF or IL‐2 as immune adjuvants, pegylated tumor
necrosis factor (TNF)‐alpha, suicide gene therapy, adenovector CD40 ligand and, lastly, canine dendritic cell vaccines loaded with melanosomal differentiation antigens.
Although these approaches have produced some clinical
antitumor responses, the methodologies for the generation of these products can be expensive, time consuming,
sometimes dependent on patient tumor samples being
established into cell lines, and fraught with the difficulties
of consistency, reproducibility, and other quality control
issues. Furthermore, we are just beginning to more fully
understand the native immune dysregulation potentially
induced by the malignancy through increased T‐regulatory (Treg) cells, which suppress antitumor responses.
The advent of DNA vaccination circumvents many of
the previously encountered hurdles in vaccine development. DNA is relatively inexpensive and simple to purify
in large quantities. The antigen of interest is cloned into a
bacterial expression plasmid with a constitutively active
promoter. The plasmid is introduced into the skin or
muscle with an intradermal or intramuscular injection.
Once in the skin or muscle, professional antigen‐presenting cells, particularly dendritic cells, are able to present
the transcribed and translated antigen in the proper context of major histocompatibility complex and co‐stimulatory molecules. Although DNA vaccines have induced
immune responses to viral proteins, vaccinating against
tissue specific self‐proteins on cancer cells is clearly a
more difficult problem. One way to induce immunity
against a tissue‐specific differentiation antigen on cancer
cells is to vaccinate with xenogeneic (­different species)
antigen or DNA that is homologous to the cancer antigen. As outlined in cartoon form in Figure 153.1, vaccina­ ifferentiation antigens
tion with DNA encoding cancer d
is ineffective when self‐DNA is used, but tumor immunity can be induced by DNA from another species.
Tyrosinase is a melanosomal glycoprotein, essential
in melanin synthesis and routinely found to be
­overexpressed in a wide variety of melanomas across
species. Immunization with xenogeneic human DNA
encoding tyrosinase family proteins induced antibodies
and cytotoxic T cells against syngeneic B16 melanoma
cells in C57BL/6 mice, but immunization with mouse
tyrosinase‐related DNA did not induce detectable
­
immunity. In particular, xenogeneic DNA vaccination
induced tumor protection from syngeneic melanoma
challenge and autoimmune hypopigmentation. Thus,
xenogeneic DNA vaccination could break tolerance

in 2009 (OnceptTM, Merial, Inc.).
We have also investigated the efficacy of local tumor
control and use of xenogeneic DNA vaccination in dogs
with digit malignant melanoma. These investigations
led to the development of a canine digit melanoma staging scheme and found an improvement in survival compared to historical outcomes with digit amputation
only. We also documented a decreased prognosis for
dogs with advanced stage disease and/or increased time
from digit amputation to the start of vaccination.
Phillips and co‐investigators have also recently reported
the use of Oncept in horses and determined the safety
and optimal use of the needle‐free delivery device into
the pectoral region in addition to documenting antigen‐
specific humoral responses after vaccination in all
horses.

Human Melanoma Immunotherapy
A similar approach has been used in human patients
with metastatic melanoma in the minimal residual disease setting. Although no clinical response data are
available since these patients did not have measurable
disease, several Phase I trials of xenogeneic DNA vaccines have been completed. Across studies of tyrosinase
and gp100 DNA immunization, approximately 40% of
patients develop quantifiable CD8+ T cell responses to
the target antigen.
Two exciting new approaches which appear to confer a
survival benefit in human metastatic melanoma are the
use of the anti‐CTLA‐4 antibody ipilimumab (YervoyTM,
Bristol‐Myers Squibb) and the selective BRAF inhibitors
vemurafenib (ZelborafTM, Genetech) and dabrafenib
(GSK2118436, GlaxoSmithKline), in patients who are
BRAF V600 mutation positive. As a small subset of dogs
with malignant melanoma have exon 11 KIT gene mutations, the more routine use of KIT testing by polymerase
chain reaction (PCR) of CMM and subsequent use of c‐
kit small molecule inhibitors (particularly in dogs with
advanced stage disease and/or lack of response to
Oncept) should be considered.
Canine malignant melanoma strongly appears to be a
more clinically faithful therapeutic model for human
melanoma when compared to more traditional mouse
systems, as both human and canine diseases are
­chemoresistant, radioresistant, share similar peculiar
metastatic phenotypes/site selectivity, and occur spontaneously in an outbred, immunocompetent scenario. It is
hoped that in the future, this same vaccine may also play
a role in the treatment of melanoma in other species
(e.g., horses, cats, humans, etc.) due to its xenogeneic
origins, and in melanoma prevention once the genetic
determinants of melanoma risk in dogs are further
defined.

­Prognosis
Melanomas in dogs have extremely diverse biologic
behaviors, depending on a large variety of factors. A
thorough understanding of these factors helps the clinician to delineate in advance the appropriate staging,
prognosis, and treatment options. The primary factors
which determine the biologic behavior of an oral melanoma in a dog are site, size, stage, and histologic
­parameters. Unfortunately, even with a comprehensive
understanding of all these factors, there are melanomas
which have an unreliable biologic behavior; hence the
need for additional research into this relatively common,
heterogeneous, but frequently extremely malignant

tumor. On divergent ends of the spectrum would be a
0.5 cm haired‐skin melanocytoma, which is highly likely
to be cured with simple surgical extirpation, in comparison to a 5 cm high‐grade malignant oral melanoma with
a poor to grave prognosis.
Similar to the development of a rational staging, prognostic and therapeutic plan for any tumor, two primary
questions must be answered: what is the local invasiveness of the tumor and what is the metastatic propensity?
The answers to these questions will ultimately determine
the prognosis and appropriate therapies.
Anatomic Site
The anatomic site of melanoma is highly, though not
completely, predictive of local invasiveness and metastatic propensity. Melanomas involving the haired skin
which are not in proximity to mucosal margins often
behave in a benign manner. Surgical extirpation through
a lumpectomy is often curative, but histopathologic
examination is imperative for delineation of margins as
well as a description of cytologic features. The use of
Ki67 IHC has been reported to more reliably predict
potential malignant behavior compared to classic histology for cutaneous melanoma.
Oral and/or mucosal melanoma has been considered
an extremely malignant tumor with a high degree of local
invasiveness and high metastatic propensity. This biologic behavior is similar to the typically grave prognosis
associated with human oral and/or mucosal melanoma.
Two recent studies have called the veterinary portion of
this dogma into question and suggest benign oral
­melanomas can occur more frequently than previously
published. Caution is necessary when assessing histopathologic descriptions suggesting a benign course for
oral melanoma as this author has seen approximately 25
dogs over the last 10 years presenting with florid systemic metastases with an original histopathologic report
suggesting an expectation for a benign clinical course
based on a high degree of differentiation. Similar to cutaneous melanoma, Ki67 appears to have prognostic
import in canine oral melanoma.
Anatomic sites of intermediate prognostic significance
between generally benign‐acting haired‐skin melanomas
compared to often malignant and metastatic oral/
mucosal melanomas in dogs include melanomas of the
digit and footpad. Dogs with melanoma of the digits
without lymph node or further metastasis treated with
digit amputation are reported to have median survival
times of ~12 months, with 42–57% alive at one year and
11‐13% alive at two years. Unfortunately, metastasis
from digit melanoma at presentation is reported to
be ~30–40%, and the aforementioned outcomes with

1351

VetBooks.ir

1352

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

­surgery alone suggest that subsequent distant metastasis
is common even when no metastasis is found at presentation or digit amputation. The prognosis for dogs with
melanoma of the footpad has not been thoroughly established; this author has found this anatomic site to be
anecdotally similar in metastatic propensity and prognosis to digit melanoma. Interestingly, human acral lentiginous melanoma (plantar surface of the foot, palms of the
hand and digit) has an increased propensity for metastasis, suggesting further similarities between human and
canine melanoma.
The most thorough review of prognostic factors in
canine melanocytic neoplasms was published by Smedley
et al. This review took a regimented, systematic approach
to analyze published reports to date in order to identify
those factors which appear to be repeatable and statistically defendable, while also identifying areas where additional work is necessary due to incomplete data.
Size and Stage
For dogs with oral melanoma, primary tumor size has
been found to be extremely prognostic. The WHO staging scheme for dogs with oral melanoma is based on size
and metastasis and is summarized in Box 153.1.
MacEwen and colleagues reported MST for dogs with
oral melanoma treated with surgery to be approximately
17–18, 5–6, and three months with stage I, II, and III disease, respectively. More recent reports suggest that stage
I oral melanoma treated with standardized therapies

including surgery, radiation and/or chemotherapy has a
MST of approximately 12–14 months, with most dogs
dying of distant metastatic disease, not local recurrence.
Other investigators have found dogs with stage I oral
melanoma to have median progression‐free survival
times of 19 months, similar to the original MacEwen
et al. report.

Nonmelanoma Skin Cancers
Barbara E. Kitchell, DVM, PhD, DACVIM (Oncology)
VCA Veterinary Care Animal Hospital and Referral Center, Albuquerque, NM, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
The skin is the largest organ in the body, and has a
­complex tissue structure made up of many cell types.
Any of these cell types could give rise to a tumor. Some
cells are more commonly affected by malignant transfor­
mation than others.
The skin is composed of layers, referred to as the epi­
dermis and dermis. The epidermis contains stratified
epithelium, while the dermis is largely composed of con­
nective tissue, including collagen, extracellular matrix,
fibrocytes, and fibroblasts. Within the dermis also reside
adnexal structures such as sebaceous or eccrine glands,
and the various cells that make up the hair follicles.
Below the dermis, subcutaneous tissues largely contain
adipocytes. Interspersed throughout the complex organ
we call skin are cells of the immune system, which
are present as either transient or permanent residents
(­lymphoid cells, macrophages, mast cells, Langerhans
dendritic cells). Panniculus skeletal muscle, neurons
and associated peripheral nerve sheath cells, vascular
epithelium and hemangiopericytes, and the specialized
neuroendocrine cells we know as melanocytes are all
important to normal skin structure.
Thus, the number of potential histopathologic diagno­
ses for tumors of the skin is quite expansive. Skin tumors
are generally classified as being of epithelial, mesenchymal,
melanotic, or round cell type. Mesenchymal, m
­ elanotic,
mast cell tumors, and cutaneous lymphoma will be dis­
cussed in other chapters.
The functions of this complex organ are also varied, and
include prevention of water and electrolyte loss, ther­
moregulation, respiration, and sensory perception. A crit­
ical skin function is to provide a physical barrier to
environmental insults, whether mechanical, chemical,
osmotic, thermal, or microbiologic. As the front line of
defense against environmental insults, the skin’s most

important defensive mechanism is its self‐renewal and
repair functions, which are dependent on the presence of
both lineage‐committed replicating cells and pluripotent
stem cells. These replicating cells are subject to mutation
as a consequence of repeated noxious environmental
exposures, which may ultimately result in carcinogenesis.

­Epidemiology
All cancers arise as a consequence of genetic predisposi­
tions and environmental exposures to carcinogens. The
skin is at particular risk for environmental injury. As a
tissue with cells that continuously replicate or that can be
recruited to replicate, mutagenic induction followed by
tumor cell promotion through repeated rounds of cell
replication result in skin tumors of various kinds. Thus,
cutaneous tumors are the most common type of neopla­
sia in both humans and dogs, although fortunately not all
skin tumors are malignant.
Genetic contributions to skin carcinogenesis are evi­
denced by human familial hereditary syndromes, as well
as by canine breed predispositions to specific tumor
types. The skin is the most prevalent location for tumors
in dogs, with an estimated 20–30% of these lesions being
malignant. It is estimated that 25% of tumors of cats arise
in the skin, and that 50–65% of these lesions are malig­
nant. Excluding the common basal cell tumor of cats,
which is generally benign, the incidence of malignancy in
feline cutaneous tumors is estimated to be 70–80%.
The estimated annual incidence of skin tumors in dogs
and cats is 90.4 and 34.7 per 100 000 animals at risk,
respectively, while for humans the annual incidence is
reportedly 5.2/100 000 people at risk. Nonmelanoma
cutaneous tumors are the most common malignant
­neoplasms affecting people in the United States, but
­fortunately are not the most fatal types of malignancy.

In dogs and cats, basal cell tumors (also called tricho­
blastomas), epitheliomas, sebaceous adenomas, epidermal
inclusion and other cysts, lipomas, and papillomas are
the most prevalent benign tumors noted. Mast cell tumor
is the most common malignant skin tumor in the dog,
and is discussed in Chapter 155.
Trichoblastomas, which are more commonly still
termed basal cell tumors, are the most common skin
tumors of cats; approximately 15–26% of all skin tumors
in cats are of this histology. Less than 10% of basal cell
tumors in cats are malignant in behavior. When malig­
nant, these lesions display a striking tendency toward
lymphatic metastasis, which can result in a “chain of
pearls” nodular progression up the draining lymphatics to
the local lymph node. In dogs, poodles and setters are pre­
disposed to basal cell lesions, which may be described by
their histologic subtypes of ribbon, medusoid, ­trabecular,
spindle, granular cell, and clear cell types. These lesions
are now believed to arise from the ­germinal cells of the
hair follicles, and are generally benign in behavior.
Dogs are commonly affected by benign tumors of glan­
dular origin in the skin, although this is a rare occurrence
in cats. Sebaceous hyperplasia, sebaceous adenoma, and
sebaceous epitheliomas are very common in dogs. These
lesions are most commonly benign and are rarely diag­
nosed as sebaceous gland carcinomas, which are gener­
ally locally aggressive and rarely metastatic. Benign
lesions are often seen in female dogs (especially hyper­
plasia), with peak incidence in dogs 7–13 years of
age. Miniature schnauzers, beagles, poodles, and cocker
spaniels are breeds at increased risk, as are Nordic
breeds, coonhounds, and terriers.
Apocrine gland adenomas and carcinomas arise from
sweat glands in both dogs and cats. These lesions are
rarely malignant but can be aggressive when transformed
to carcinomas. Feline apocrine gland carcinoma lesions
are seen primarily on the head, while benign lesions may
be present on the head, limbs or abdomen of older cats.
The front legs are the most common sites for canine
­apocrine gland carcinomas, with golden retrievers and
coonhounds being predisposed breeds. Lesions are
locally invasive with a predisposition to lymphatic
spreading. Apocrine gland adenocarcinomas of the
anal sac are ­discussed elsewhere.
Eccrine gland adenomas and carcinomas arise from
specialized sweat glands of the footpads in dogs and cats
and are exceedingly rare lesions.
Squamous cell carcinoma is common in both dogs and
cats. This tumor of the skin is frequently caused by chronic
ultraviolet light exposure in animals with white or fair
skin and scant hair or fur covering. As sunlight is most
damaging close to the equator and at high altitudes, these
geographic regions of the globe have the highest incidence
rates of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma in both

­people and animals. Lifestyle and behavior ­contribute to
sun exposure in all species of animals. Thus, white cats
living largely outdoors are particularly vulnerable to cuta­
neous squamous cell carcinoma in sun‐exposed areas of
their head, including ear tips, nasal planum, lower eyelids,
and the scantly furred preauricular area of the skin located
between the ears and eyes on the lateral forehead. Siamese
and other color‐point breeds of cats are protected from
cutaneous squamous cell formation by the pigment that is
present in the exact facial areas that put white cats at risk.
Similarly, dogs are most affected in areas of glabrous
(nonhaired) skin that receive excessive sunlight exposure.
This can occur when dogs “sunbathe” by lying on their
back or sides in full sun. Outdoor dogs with no pigment in
glabrous skin regions are most at risk. Thus, Dalmatians,
pointers, pit bulls, bull terriers, and other dogs with white
or pale skin on the ventral abdomen, prepuce, and medial
thighs may suffer actinic dermal injury that can ultimately
transition to squamous cell carcinoma. Dermal hemangi­
oma and hemangiosarcoma lesions may similarly arise in
areas of excessive ultraviolet light exposure.
In addition to physical carcinogenesis from ultraviolet
light exposure, there is also a viral etiopathogenesis
­associated with causation of cutaneous squamous cell
carcinoma. Papillomavirus infection in cats may cause
the feline equivalent of a human syndrome called Bowen
disease, which is a term used to identify multicentric
cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma in situ. This form of
squamous cell carcinoma occurs most frequently in
haired skin and has no predilection to arise in nonpig­
mented areas of the body. These lesions can be seen as
crusty, scabbed dermal lesions of the head, neck or trunk
of affected cats. Papillomavirus is also associated with
the development of feline fibropapillomas called feline
sarcoids. Interestingly, cats have been found to be sus­
ceptible to human papillomaviruses 5, 21, and 38, which
were discovered by polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
analysis of papilloma lesions in several cats.
Dogs also harbor papillomaviruses, which may be
involved in the causation of oral, footpad, and cutaneous
papillomas, and potentially even in squamous cell carci­
nomas. These lesions are particularly observed in dogs
that are immunocompromised.
Breed association is noted in dogs affected by tumors
of adnexal skin structures. Infundibular keratinizing
acanthomas are common benign tumors of dogs.
Synonyms for these tumors include intracutaneous
keratinizing epitheliomas, keratoacanthomas, and intra­
cutaneous cornifying epitheliomas. Breeds at risk for
these benign lesions include Norwegian elkhounds and
other Nordic breeds, German and Belgian shepherd
dogs, various terriers, and the Lhasa apso. These lesions
are benign and generally cured by local excision, although
they are frequently seen as multiple lesions.

VetBooks.ir

154 Nonmelanoma Skin Cancers

Trichoepitheliomas are tumors that demonstrate
­differentiation into elements of the hair follicle, and are
seen on the limbs, neck, and back of bassett hounds,
coonhounds, setters, and English springer spaniels.
These are rarely malignant, and are referred to as
malignant trichoepitheliomas or metrical carcinomas
­
in those rare cases.
Pilomatricomas are tumors of hair matrix cells, and are
also benign in general. Kerry blue, soft‐coated wheaten,
and Airedale terriers are the most affected, as are
­standard poodles, bichon frise, old English sheepdogs,
and bouviers des Flandres. These lesions may ulcerate
and ossify. While these lesions are rarely malignant, they
are reported to be highly metastatic when malignant
t­ ransformation occurs.
Neuroendocrine tumors of the skin are referred to as
Merkel cell tumors. They are thought to arise from
mechanoreceptors in the skin, and are also rare in dogs
and cats. While these tend to be highly malignant in
humans, they are more benign in dogs.
Ear canal tumors can be classed with skin tumors as
a continuous cutaneous organ. Most commonly seen
are ceruminous gland adenomas and carcinomas.
Ceruminous glands are modified apocrine glands local­
ized to the ear canal. Other tumors of the ear canal
include squamous cell carcinomas, basal cell carcino­
mas, mast cell tumors, histiocytomas, sebaceous gland
tumors, plasma cell tumors, melanomas, and various
sarcomas. Benign polyps arising in the ear canal are also
noted, particularly in young cats.

­Signalment
Most cutaneous tumors arise in aged animals, as it can
take a lifetime of exposure to environmental carcino­
gens, coupled with geriatric waning of immune surveil­
lance, to allow tumors to manifest. Occasionally skin
tumors will arise in younger animals, particularly in cats
affected by retroviruses or feline papillomavirus. There
is generally no sex predisposition in the development
of skin cancer. Many specific histologic types of skin
cancer, particularly those arising in adnexal structures,
are breed associated, as described in the section on
epidemiology.

­History and Clinical Signs
In most cases, the first sign of skin tumor development is
the presence of a mass. Masses may be indolent in their
growth pattern or may be rapidly progressive. Skin
tumors are generally nonpainful, unless infection or
inflammation occurs. Basal cell tumors tend to be slowly

growing or static in growth pattern, and may be alopecic,
ulcerated, and of blue‐black or pink color. Cysts and seba­
ceous adenoma lesions may rupture or become infected,
and thus may wax and wane in size. In many cases, own­
ers assume that squamous cell carcinoma on the nose of
a cat is a result of an infected fight wound. In these cases,
there is a wound that fails to heal properly, and is inter­
mittently scabbed or open and bleeding. Similarly, der­
mal hemangiosarcomas arise in areas of actinic injury,
with a clinical appearance of small red spots or “blood
blister” lesions that may bleed or become invasive.

­Diagnosis
Diagnosis of skin tumors is by cytology or biopsy.
Because these patients are often older, a minimum
database (complete blood count, serum chemistry
­
panel, and urinalysis) is helpful in anesthetic planning.
However, skin tumors are not typically associated with
paraneoplastic syndromes that could be detected on
bloodwork. Interestingly, humans affected by squamous
cell carcinoma may have hyperglobulinemia that is of
polyclonal nature and directed against specific cytokerat­
ins. Hyperglobulinemia may be noted in cats with sun­
light‐induced squamous cell carcinoma as well, although
it is clinically insignificant.
The method of biopsy is determined by size and
­location of the lesion. Small superficial lesions may be
best managed by excisional biopsy, which can be both
diagnostic and therapeutic. Larger lesions may require
incisional biopsy to allow for surgical or radiation treat­
ment planning. Advanced local imaging with computed
tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
may be helpful in determining the full extent of the lesion
to be addressed.
Carcinomas of the skin may merit clinical staging with
lymph node aspiration cytology or lymph node biopsy
and thoracic radiographs. Abdominal staging may be
considered in cases with malignant lesions on the cau­
dal portion of the body, where lymphatic spread to
intrapelvic or intraabdominal node sites may occur.
Lymphadenomegaly should be investigated with ­cytology
or biopsy. Pulmonary metastasis is rarely seen in dogs
with skin cancer, although squamous cell carcinoma
(SCC), malignant pilomatricomas, sebaceous gland car­
cinomas, apocrine gland carcinomas, and ­neuroendocrine
carcinomas have the potential to metastasize.
Ear canal tumors often cause pain, malodorous
­discharge, difficulty opening the mouth and neuro­
logic signs such as facial palsy and vestibular signs.
These signs may lead to delayed diagnosis of tumor, as
patients may undergo protracted periods of treatment of
suspected otitis before biopsy diagnosis is obtained.

Ear canal tumors often require advanced imaging
studies to determine operability and extent of surgery
necessary, or to plan for radiotherapy adjunctively
or as primary treatment of nonresectable, invasive
lesions.

­Therapy
Most skin tumors are best addressed by local surgical
excision. Benign lesions of the skin can be excised with
modest margins to affect a cure in most cases. Surgical
excision allows for accurate diagnosis, histologic grad­
ing, and surgical margin assessment, which can guide
further adjunctive therapy if necessary. However, surgery
can be disfiguring, particularly when the lesion arises on
the head and face. Squamous cell carcinoma of the ear
tips can be managed by pinna amputation in cats. Nasal
planum resection can also be curative in cats, although
surgery of SCC of the nasal planum in dogs is often
unsuccessful in controlling local disease. Surgery is
always the best primary modality for treatment of
any cancer, but owners may balk at the degree of disfig­
urement the dog or cat experiences with nasal planum
resection.
Serial resection of squamous cell carcinoma or
­hemangiosarcoma, while still small, dermal and arising
on glabrous skin, is recommended for dogs with field
carcinogenesis from sunlight exposure. Highly invasive
or large field lesions of the ventral abdomen, prepuce,
and medial thighs of such dogs may be less amenable to
surgical excision. In these cases, radiation therapy deliv­
ered to the local tumor site, or tumor site plus regional
nodes, may be curative. Radiation therapy for skin
tumors may involve traditional fractionated megavolt­
age irradiation with curative intent, or may be delivered
as palliative fractionated therapy. Superficial radiation,
such as delivered through topical plesiotherapy using a
strontium‐90 probe, is highly effective for small, nonin­
vasive lesions. Photodynamic therapy utilizing laser
light to activate photosensitizing agents is a common
treatment for human skin cancer patients, although
the technology is less readily available to veterinary
medicine.
Ear canal tumors generally require surgical excision,
which may entail vertical canal ablation in the case of
superficial benign tumors, but more likely requires a
more aggressive surgical approach with total ear canal
ablation and lateral bulla osteotomy. Extensive surgery
was associated with long median survivals in both dogs
and cats (>36 months and 50.3 months, respectively).
Mitotic rate was prognostic for a series of ear canal
tumors, with a mitotic index of 2 or less being more
favorable. Radiation therapy may be required for patients

with incompletely resected tumors of the ear canal,
regardless of histologic type of tumor.
Topical 5% fluorouracil cream may be applied to super­
ficial squamous or basal cell lesions in dogs, as is the
common practice in human dermatologic oncology. This
agent is applied topically twice daily by gloved finger or
cotton swab applicator for 3–6 weeks. Significant local
irritation and inflammation are seen as part of the thera­
peutic response. Dogs should be prevented access to the
treated site, as licking the topical cream can be harmful
to oral mucosa and may be toxic systemically. Critically,
fluorouracil should never be applied to cats, as even
­topical application can result in lethal neurotoxicity in
this species.
Topical immunotherapy for superficial squamous
cell carcinomas may be attempted. Imiquimod 5% cream
is a nonspecific active immunotherapeutic agent that
induces a strong macrophagic response when topically
applied. This immunostimulant causes inflamed, crusted
and scabbed lesions to arise in the treated area, which is
the basis of the therapeutic effect. Imiquimod is applied
topically to superficial lesions once daily, or in sensitive
cases three times weekly, for 3–6 weeks.
Intralesional therapy with chemotherapy in sesame oil
or purified bovine collagen matrix for depot delivery has
also been described in the literature. Agents such as
­carboplatin, cisplatin, bleomycin, and fluorouracil have
all been introduced intratumorally with sometimes
­striking results.
Systemic therapy with retinoic acid derivatives such as
13‐cis‐retinoic acid or isotretinoin has been attempted
as a cellular differentiation or cytotoxic strategy in
canine and feline skin tumors, particularly squamous
cell and infundibular keratinizing acanthoma (keratoa­
canthoma). Retinoid therapy has been reported in the
literature to have mixed success.
The use of COX‐2 inhibitors has shown modest effi­
cacy in treatment of squamous cell carcinomas of the
oral cavity, and thus may be helpful in cutaneous SCC
treatment as well. The COX‐2 inhibitor nonsteroidal
antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) have both antiangio­
genic and immunomodulatory effects, and are generally
helpful in pain control for veterinary patients. Similarly,
the newer class of agents called receptor tyrosine kinase
inhibitors (toceranib, masitinib, imatinib) are inhibitors
of cell signaling. These agents are promiscuous receptor
signaling blockers and may modulate tumor regression
through inhibition of vascular endothelial growth factor
(VEGF) and platelet‐derived growth factor (PDGF)
receptors, thus acting as antiangiogenic agents. The
therapeutic concept referred to as metronomic chemo­
therapy employs smaller daily or alternate‐day dosing of
NSAIDs, low‐dose cytotoxic agents such as cyclophos­
phamide, chlorambucil, or lomustine, often combined

VetBooks.ir

154 Nonmelanoma Skin Cancers

with receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors, to inhibit nor­
mal stromal cells that support neoplastic growth. Little
information is currently available about the use of daily,
low‐dose combination metronomic chemotherapy in
canine and feline skin or ear canal tumors.
Papilloma lesions may be addressed through the crea­
tion of an autologous vaccine. This approach is best used
in dogs with multicentric papillomas, as is sometimes
seen in dogs that have been heavily immunosuppressed
in the transplant or autoimmune disease setting, or in
dogs with immunosuppression from T‐zone lymphoma.
In this approach, 1–3 g of papilloma tissue are harvested
from the dog and macerated in a tissue grinder or mortar
and pestle along with 10 mL of sterile 0.9% saline. To this
mixture is added 1 mL of neutral buffered formalin,
which inactivates live virus as well as altering the struc­
ture of viral oncoproteins to facilitate immune recogni­
tion. The mixture is refrigerated for three days, and then
sieved through sterile cheesecloth or a large‐gauge filter
to remove residual particulate material. The resultant
autologous vaccine can be stored in the refrigerator in
1 mL sterile aliquots for future treatment. An immune
adjuvant such as Immunocidin® (Corynebacterium
­parvum derivative), squalene, or BCG is added before
injection into the residual papilloma lesions. This treat­
ment can be repeated at weekly intervals until lesion
regression is noted. There is no literature regarding use
of commercial papillomavirus‐preventive vaccines in the
therapeutic setting.
Systemic chemotherapy or local electrochemotherapy
has been attempted for aggressive or metastatic dermal
carcinomas. Relatively few agents have been used in this

setting, and results are generally anecdotal and not
well documented. Cisplatin, carboplatin, bleomycin,
actinomycin D, and mitoxantrone have all been used
sporadically, with modest response rates noted in the
literature. Local drug delivery enhanced by electro­
­
chemotherapy may increase the local efficacy of these
­cytotoxic agents.

­Prognosis
The prognosis for patients with localized tumors of the
skin, adnexal structures, or ear canals is generally highly
favorable. Many lesions are benign and early detection is
possible because of the superficial location of the tumors,
and ear canal tumors are frequently localized to within
the cartilaginous structures of the ear canal, which facili­
tates complete resection. Thus, most dogs and cats
affected by skin or ear canal tumors are cured by surgical
excision alone. Exceptions are noted in cases of malig­
nant skin neoplasia, particularly when metastasis to
nodes or distant sites is observed. Radiation therapy
can be helpful for large or nodally involved lesions,
as described earlier.
The most common aggressive skin tumors discussed
here are squamous cell carcinomas, which have median
survivals of 1–2 years with aggressive surgery and/or
radiation therapy in both dogs and cats. The exception to
this observed survival rate is in the case of nasal planum
squamous cell carcinomas in dogs, which are both locally
aggressive and metastatic to regional nodes, and have a
poorer overall outcome despite aggressive therapy.

Mast Cell Neoplasia
Zachary M. Wright, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology)
VCA Animal Diagnostic Clinic, Dallas, TX, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Mast cells are part of the normal canine, feline, and
human immune system. They primarily exist throughout
the skin, lungs, and intestinal tract but are rarely found
within peripheral blood.
Mast cells arise from pluripotent hematopoietic stem
cells of the bone marrow. Once mature, their cytoplasm
contains a large amount of metachromatic granules.
These granules contain a variety of substances including
histamine, serotonin, platelet activating factor, eosinophilic chemotactic factor, and heparin, among others.
In addition, mast cells produce a variety of cytokines that
include interleukin (IL)‐1, IL‐3, IL‐4, IL‐5, IL‐6, and
tumor necrosis factor (TNF)‐alpha.
The etiology for canine mast cell tumor development
is unknown partially because there is no clear human
model to provide key predictors.

­Canine Mast Cell Neoplasia
Epidemiology
Canine mast cell tumor (MCT) is the most common skin
tumor in dogs, representing upwards of 15–20% of all
skin tumors. They are one of the most common tumors
seen in practice.
Signalment
Mast cell tumor development has clear breed predispositions that include most brachycephalic breeds (boxer,
Boston terrier, and pug), Labrador and golden retrievers,
pit bull terriers, and shar‐peis. There is no reported sex
predilection and the mean age of diagnosis is 8.2 years.
Clinically, all breeds are capable of developing MCT.
While tumors are more often noted in middle‐aged to

older dogs, the author has seen numerous cases of MCT
in juveniles less than 1 year of age.
History and Clinical Signs
Most dogs with a MCT present with a single dermal lesion.
Twenty percent of all dogs, and specifically breeds that are
predisposed, may present with multiple tumors. The history may include a nonpainful mass that increases and
decreases in size. Physical manipulation of the tumor can
result in a rapid increase in size due to traumatic local
release of histamine (degranulation). Darier’s sign is the
dermatologic description of wheal formation, local erythema, and/or bruising secondary to manipulation of the
tumor. Most MCTs are clinically quiescent and are discovered on routine physical exam by the veterinarian or owner.
Mast cell tumors occur predominantly in the dermis
and are most commonly noted on the trunk and limbs.
A less commonly noted form, at mucocutaneous sites
(mouth, nasal planum, perirectal region), tends to have
a more aggressive clinical behavior (Figure 155.1).
Additionally, a lesser percentage of MCTs occur in the
subcutaneous tissue and many have a clinical appearance consistent with a lipoma.
Primary visceral mastocytosis is a very rare condition
in dogs. The disease has a predisposition for the intestinal
tract in older (>8 years) miniature‐breed dogs. Two independent studies have identified the Maltese breed as having a predisposition to the intestinal form. Clinical signs
are typical of most primary gastrointestinal pathology.
Diagnosis
Cytology of the lesion is diagnostic for a MCT. Because
of the clinical inefficiency and additional cost, premedication with an antihistamine prior to fine needle
aspiration of a simple dermal mass less than 5 cm in

staging of a MCT is dependent on physical exam findings.
Close attention should be paid to the regional draining
lymph nodes and organomegaly (hepatic and/or splenic).
Regional lymph nodes, regardless of size, should be
cytologically evaluated for metastasis. The determination of lymph node metastasis via cytology is very sensitive but has a low specificity due to the inability to
distinguish normal, responsive mast cells from malignant cells. Metastasis can be accurately confirmed
if mast cells are the predominant cell type. Additionally,
most pathologists will declare a node metastatic if
the mast cells are noted in clumps or sheets and/or have
marked cellular atypia. Biopsy or removal of the lymph
node is recommended if there is an increase in the numbers of well‐granulated mast cells but no other signs supportive of metastasis. Recent evidence supports that
dogs with no metastasis to regional nodes had a 0%
chance of distant metastasis.
Abdominal ultrasound is recommended for dogs
with a high‐grade MCT or proven lymph node metastasis. While a full abdominal ultrasound is encouraged,
focus should rest on the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes
(mesenteric, medial iliac, and sublumbar nodes). All
abnormal lesions of the liver and spleen should be
cytologically evaluated. Two independent studies confirmed that cytology of ultrasonographically normal

While historically pursued, bone marrow aspiration
for staging may no longer be indicated for a patient diagnosed with their first MCT or with no clinical evidence
of lymph node metastasis. For these dogs, the incidence
of bone marrow involvement is low (2.8%). This low
yield, combined with cost, invasiveness of the procedure,
and ability to prove distant metastasis on more routine
testing (abdominal ultrasound), suggests that bone marrow aspiration may not be necessary for every patient.
However, bone marrow metastasis/distant metastasis is
a significant prognostic indicator and dogs with a recurrent MCT or which develop subsequent MCTs may have
a higher incidence (18.7%).
Pulmonary metastasis is rare and sporadically reported
for MCT. Consequently, thoracic radiography is not considered part of routine staging but may be helpful in
assessing concomitant disease processes (cardiovascular,
respiratory, etc.).
The most important prognostic indicator is the grading scheme. Tumor grade is determined by histopathologic features. Incisional biopsy is rarely recommended
for a MCT due to the diagnostic capability of cytology
and the increased potential for wound dehiscence secondary to both histamine and heparin release from the
remaining tumor cells. If cytology is nondiagnostic, incisional biopsy should be minimal in size and in an area of
minimal inflammation or necrosis. The incisional site
should be easily excised in its entirety when the mass is
removed. Overall, excisional biopsy is superior for both
diagnostic and therapeutic purposes.

The Patnaik grading scheme is the most well known
and used in pathology reports. Tumors are divided into
three grades (I, II, and III). Grade I tumors have an indolent behavior with a metastatic potential of near 10%.
Grade III MCTs are exceptionally aggressive with a metastatic rate of 80%. Grade II MCTs are by far the most
common diagnosis. These tumors can behave similarly
to both grade I and III and have a metastatic potential
near 20%. Clinically, this grading scheme is very helpful
for grade I and III lesions, but less predictive for grade II
tumors.
As the vast majority of MCTs are in the grade II
­category, many clinicians struggle with interpretation
and prognosis. Consequently, a recent collaboration of
pathologists and oncologists proposed a new grading
scheme. Kiupel et al. offered a two‐tiered system composed of a low‐grade and high‐grade MCT. First, this
study found an improved interpathologist agreement
compared to the Patnaik scheme. Second, distinction
between the two grades is based on a scoring system that
evaluates mitotic index, karyomegaly, multinucleated
cells, and bizarre nuclei. It is imperative to always request
a microscopic description with mast cell histopathology
as these characteristics are evaluated by that grading
scheme. Low‐grade MCTs (the majority of previously
diagnosed grade I and IIs) have minimal metastatic
potential and a median survival time of greater than two
years. High‐grade MCTs have a median survival time of
less than four months due to the metastatic behavior of
these tumors. To further aid clinical decisions, many
diagnostic labs have started to report both grading systems in their histopathology reports.

Attempts have been made to link histologically determined cellular proliferation markers to MCT prognosis
and clinical behavior. Proliferating cell nuclear antigen
(PCNA), argyrophilic nucleolar organizing region‐
associated proteins (AgNORs), and the proliferation
protein Ki‐67 have all been evaluated with mixed
results. Mitotic index has been repeatedly shown to
have the most prognostic value and is required as part
of the initial histopathology report. Tumors with a
mitotic index of >5/10 hpf should be treated prognostically as high‐grade MCTs.
Evaluation of c‐kit mutation has prognostic utility but
only when closely linked to histopathologic grade. More
importantly, the presence of c‐kit overexpression or mutation indicates a tumor that is more likely to be responsive
to the new tyrosine kinase inhibitor class of drugs.
Therapy
The systemic toxicity of a MCT often requires treatment.
Histamine is the compound found in mast cell granules
that results in the most significant clinical changes.
Activation of histamine receptors (H1 and H2) can lead
to toxicity. Severe anaphylactic reactions are a result of
systemic H1 receptor activation and can be treated with
diphenhydramine and corticosteroids. In times of crisis,
intravenous use of steroids is recommended. As a vasoactive molecule, histamine may also lead to marked
hypotension which could require both colloidal and
crystalloid support. H2 is more responsible for stimulation of gastric acid. Excessive H2 activation can lead to
gastric ulceration and clinical side‐effects that include
anorexia, nausea, hematemesis, and melena. Routine H2
receptor antagonists such as famotidine and ranitidine
can be effective but proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole) appear to be more potent at reducing gastric acid
production and aiding healing of ulcers.
Currently, the author only recommends oral preventive diphenhydramine and famotidine (at routine dosing)
for patients with documented MCT metastasis or tumor
volumes greater than 5 cm in diameter.
Various components within mast cell granules are also
responsible for delays in wound healing. This phenomenon is most commonly appreciated during incisional
biopsy techniques. Wound failure is often noted within
the first 3–5 days postoperatively.
Heparin is also released from mast cell granules.
Coagulopathies are rare with MCTs as evidence suggests
there is less heparin in malignant MCTs than in normal
mast cells. Clinically, increased bleeding at the surgical
site of a MCT is the most common coagulopathy noted.
Surgical removal of all MCTs is considered standard of
care. Surgical removal of the lesion should include at
least 2 cm of healthy tissue lateral to the lesion and one

fascial plane deep to the tumor. Prior to pathology submission, it is recommended to mark margins with either
suture or ink. Histopathology reports should comment
on the surgical margins.
Many tumors are large or in too difficult of a location for
a reasonable expectation of complete removal. A short
trial (10–14 days) of antiinflammatory prednisone
(1 mg/kg/day) can often result in significant tumor reduction. A recent study found that 70% of all MCTs treated
with presurgical prednisone responded to therapy. The
median reduction in tumor diameter was 45% with a
median total tumor volume reduction of 80%. Tyrosine
kinase inhibitors are also used to reduce tumor volume for
surgery in situations where prednisone does not result in a
significant response. When surgically amendable, these
medications are not selected as the primary treatment
due to their possible toxicities and cost (Figure 155.4).
For low‐grade (both Kiupel grade I and the majority of
Patnaik grade II) MCTs with no evidence of metastasis,
complete surgical removal is considered curative and no
adjuvant therapy is indicated.
Often, clinicians must determine treatment plans
based on narrow tumor‐free margins of 1–5 mm. Tissue
specimens will constrict during processing. Adjuvant
treatment is indicated if surgery is incomplete and tumor
cells extend to the surgical margins. There are no clear
guidelines for “narrow” surgical margins (1–5 mm) and
each case should be evaluated uniquely. The author is
usually more aggressive in adjuvant treatment recommendations for tumors with ≤1 mm clean margins as
they have a higher potential to reoccur.
Numerous studies have suggested that there is a subset
population (20–70%) of cutaneous MCTs that do not
reoccur when tumor cells extend to the surgical margins.
Theories include the lack of tumor volume resulting in a
decrease in progrowth cancer signaling. The small tumor
volume may also be amenable to self immune defense.
Additionally, there is some belief that the peripheral
mast cells in a tumor are normal mast cells that respond
to chemotactic factors released by the tumor. When the
tumor is removed and the signals are interrupted, the
normal mast cells vacate the area.
Currently, there is no way to determine which low‐
grade MCT will reoccur. Thus, all incomplete excisions
should be treated the same. An additional surgery is the
ideal treatment and should be considered if there is
adequate local skin for wound closure. For incompletely
removed low‐grade tumors that cannot be excised,
radiation offers a 90% curative outcome. Radiation
­protocols usually entail a total of 45–55 Gy dispersed
evenly over 18–22 total fractions or treatments.
Although not evaluated in this adjuvant setting, hypofractionated radiation may also offer added benefit over
monitoring alone.

Either surgical removal or radiation of the draining
lymph nodes should be considered for cases where
regional node metastasis is confirmed (stage III).
There are a variety of chemotherapy treatment
options for a MCT. The European consensus statement on MCTs indicates that chemotherapy is used to
treat metastatic disease to either regional lymph nodes
or distantly; when radiation or surgery are not available
or possible; and as a neoadjuvant to reduce tumor burden prior to more traditional surgery or radiation. It is
important to understand that chemotherapy does not
offer the same curative results as radiation or surgery
and should not be used as a convenient alternative to
these modalities.
Prednisone has the longest history of use against
MCTs. It is unclear if the effects of prednisone are truly
cytotoxic or simply aid in reducing peritumoral edema
and inflammation secondary to histamine release. A
popular theory suggests that glucocorticoids block stem
cell factor release from regional epithelial cells and fibroblasts. Stem cell factor is a known activating protein of
the KIT pathway which is often mutated in MCTs.
Antiinflammatory dosing of prednisone at 1 mg/kg/day
is considered sufficient for MCTs. Immunosuppressive
doses have not been found to be more effective and only
increase the risk and severity of prednisone‐induced
side‐effects.
Traditional chemotherapy options include the vinca
alkaloids vinblastine and vinorelbine, the alkylating
agent lomustine, and a taxane, paclitaxel. Both lomustine
and vinblastine have an overall response rate of 40–50%.

of 65%. The micellar prepared paclitaxel has shown
promise against MCTs but is not yet commercially available. The current formulation of paclitaxel (suspended in

The tyrosine kinase receptor KIT is mutated and/or
overexpressed in up to 40% of MCTs. These tandem duplication mutations at the juxtamembrane coding region
result in the malignant behavior of cellular proliferation,
adhesion, migration, and maturation. Consequently, KIT
mutations have been found more commonly in higher
grade MCTs.
Recent advancements in MCT treatments have led to
the development of tyrosine kinase inhibitors. These
drugs block the effects of mutated KIT receptors
through competitive inhibition. Toceranib phosphate
(Palladia™, Zoetis) is the first FDA‐approved treatment
for canine MCTs. It is labeled for the treatment of
­recurrent or nonsurgical high‐grade mast cell tumors.
Additionally, masitinib (Kinavet®, AB Science) achieved
European regulatory approval under similar label guidelines but recently lost licensure by the FDA and is no
longer available for use in the United States.

The reported efficacy of Palladia is near 40%
(Figure 155.5). Palladia may be used for all grades of
MCT but is more effective against MCTs with the
known KIT mutation. The labeled dose of 3.25 mg/kg
every other day results in significant gastrointestinal
toxicity, myalgias, and neutropenia. Most clinical oncologists now prefer a lower dose of 2.5–2.75 mg/kg on a
Monday‐Wednesday‐Friday treatment schedule. Oral
famotidine and sucralfate may eliminate low‐grade nausea or anorexia. Diarrhea is routinely treated with standard doses of loperamide. Protracted or severe clinical
signs require a temporary discontinuation (drug holiday)
of the medication until clinical improvement. Routine
complete blood counts are recommended over the first
six weeks of therapy. Therafter, a complete blood count
chemistry panel and urinalysis are recommended
approximately once every six weeks for patients that
remain on tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Mild (grade I and
II) neutropenias are commonly noted and do not require
additional therapy or dosing alterations. However,
patients should be monitored for progression.
Idiosyncratic elevations in liver enzymes, hypertension
and protein‐losing nephropathies are also reported.
