Adjuvant therapy with vinblastine/lomustine or
Palladia for high‐grade MCT is recommended even if
the mass has been completely excised. Most adjuvant
treatment protocols strive for 3–6 months of therapy,
depending on tumor response and the patient’s tolerance. In the adjuvant setting, chemotherapy results in
median overall survival times of 11–16 months.
Prognosis
Multiple factors have prognostic value for canine
MCTs. A subset of tumors have a more aggressive
behavior based on their anatomic location. MCTs
of the inguinal region (groin, perivulvar, scrotal,
­p erianal) have historically been regarded as having
greater metastatic potential. Newer information has
revealed that survival is dependent on histologic
grade. However, dogs with MCTs in these locations,
specifically preputial and scrotal, have a decreased
disease‐free interval as both local recurrence and the
development of subsequent MCTs are common. The
biologic behavior of tumors in these areas is still
debated so it is reasonable to use caution and proceed
with routine MCT staging and more routine follow‐up
regardless of grade.
Mucocutaneous MCT (muzzle, vulva, sclera, etc.) and
oral locations (tongue, palate) have a greater metastatic
potential regardless of grade and should be aggressively
staged at the time of cytologic diagnosis.
Mast cell tumors are the third most common tumor of
the canine nailbed and have a more aggressive behavior
compared to a traditional cutaneous MCT. Finally, primary visceral mastocytosis should be considered a highly
aggressive neoplasm which is a terminal condition for
most dogs.
As previously stated, histopathologic grading offers
the most accurate prognosis. The majority of grade I
(Patnaik) or low‐grade (Kiupel) tumors are cured with
complete excision. Less than 10% of grade I MCTs are
reported to metastasize, with a median survival time of
greater than two years. Alternatively, over 80% of grade
III MCTs will metastasize and the median survival for
high‐grade MCT is less than four months.
Various proliferation markers may be used for additional prognostic information. Dogs with a Ki‐67 index
of <1.8 had a median survival time that was not reached
within the time frame of the study and suggested a curative outcome. Those with a Ki‐67 >1.8 had a median survival time of 9.7 months. While increases in both
AgNORs and PCNA repeatedly support more aggressive
tumors, they appear to only be prognostically valuable in
conjunction with tumor grade. When evaluated independently of grade, both indices are ineffective in determining prognosis.

­Feline Mast Cell Tumors
Epidemiology
Feline MCTs represent the second most common skin
tumor in the cat. A genetic correlation has been linked to
young Siamese cats. In addition, cats may develop both a
visceral form of MCT that primarily originates in the
spleen and a primary intestinal form.
Signalment
Cutaneous forms of feline MCTs are most commonly
found in cats 10 years of age, with no reported gender
predilection. Siamese less than 4 years of age are reported
to be predisposed to the less common histiocytic form of
cutaneous MCT. Visceral (both spleen and intestinal
involvement) forms more commonly occur in older cats.
History and Clinical Signs
The majority of cutaneous lesions occur on the head and
neck but can occur throughout the body. The most common presentation is a red, raised dermal lesion. As in the
canine form, MCTs can appear with many other cutaneous manifestations including ulcerations, plaques, etc.
(Figure 155.6).
Both abdominal forms of MCT result in a systemically ill
patient. Vomiting, lethargy, and weight loss are most commonly noted. Splenomegaly can be severe on abdominal
palpation while an intestinal mass is not always detected.
Diagnosis
Cytology is an appropriate diagnostic tool for both cutaneous and visceral lesions. Because of the incidence of

Figure 155.6 A clinically aggressive feline MCT. Note the change
in coloration and ulceration throughout the lesion as well as the
bruising at the base of the mass.

visceral mastocytosis associated with splenomegaly, the
author strongly suggests the use of systemic antihistamines prior to cytology of an enlarged spleen. It is equally
important to have corticosteroids readily available in
case the cytology procedure results in an acute anaphylactic reaction. It is not necessary to premedicate all
cats prior to cytology of an intestinal lesion. However,
evidence of mast cells on the cytology sample justifies
administration of antihistamines at that time.
An abdominal ultrasound is recommended for visceral
mastocytosis. Additionally, mastocytemia is often noted
on routine complete blood counts and can be isolated
within the buffy coat.
Due to the low risk of metastasis, routine presurgical
staging for skin tumors may not be indicated unless the
patient has a clinical presentation (rapidly growing
tumor) that supports a more aggressive phenotype.
However, visceral and intestinal MCT should undergo
complete staging with abdominal ultrasound, cytology
of the liver and spleen, thoracic radiographs, minimum
database bloodwork, buffy coat and potentially bone
marrow aspiration.
Therapy
Cutaneous lesions that are <1 cm in diameter can be
removed with routine excision. As their behavior is different from that of canine MCT, surgical margins of
2 cm are not indicated in cats. Routine “lumpectomy”
or excisional biopsy margins are appropriate. If a minimal surgery is attempted, it is important to allow room
for a second, wider surgery, should histopathology indicate a more aggressive lesion. For the clinically low‐
grade (dermal, <1 cm) tumors, local plesiotherapy with
strontium‐90 radiation probes offers the same curative
outcome and can be used in areas where routine
removal is unattainable.
Both intestinal and splenic (or true visceral) mastocytosis require abdominal exploratory surgery. Systemic
therapy with antihistamines and corticosteroids is
rarely effective at resolving clinical signs. Splenectomy
is the treatment of choice for cats with the splenic form.
Within reason, this procedure is still clinically applicable in the face of mild to moderate distant metastasis as
splenectomy results in significant reduction in tumor
burden and histamine release. However, splenectomy
itself can be a life‐threatening procedure due to the
massive histamine release caused during splenic manipulation. It is recommended to premedicate all cats with
appropriate dosing of diphenhydramine, famotidine,
and dexamethasone preoperatively. Additionally, the
spleen should be handled gently during vascular ligation and gently lifted out of the abdomen via a generous
abdominal incision.

The visceral form is rarely cured with splenectomy so
adjuvant treatment is recommended. Currently, there is
no one accepted standard chemotherapy protocol for
use in cats. Single‐agent lomustine has been evaluated
at a dose of 50–60 mg/m2 (author’s note: 10 mg/cat
is considered an acceptable lomustine dose) with a
reported overall response rate of 50%, with neutropenia
and thrombocytopenia the most common and significant toxicities. Due to the variation in clinical picture,
accurate survival times have not yet been determined.
Sixty‐seven percent of feline MCTs are noted to have a
c‐kit mutation. At the time of publication, there are no
published clinical data on the efficacy of tyrosine kinase
inhibitors against feline MCTs. Masitinib has been evaluated in cats in a Phase I trial. The results indicate the
drug is well tolerated at 12.5 mg/kg once a day with proteinuria noted as the most significant side‐effect. Based
on the tolerability of the medication and the proven c‐kit
mutation, use of tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy in
felines, in similar clinical situations as described in
canines, appears reasonable.
If possible, intestinal resection with 5–10 cm margins
should be considered for patients with the intestinal
form. Unlike the splenic form, the presence of metastasis
is much more clinically relevant as it will alter the prognosis significantly.
Prognosis
Neither the Patnaik nor Kiupel grading scheme is appropriate for feline cutaneous tumors. MCTs are labeled as
either the more common mastocytic form or the histiocytic form. The latter type is often found in juvenile
Siamese cats. The mastocytic form is then subtyped into
either compact or diffuse. Compact mastocytic (more
commonly referred to as well‐differentiated) MCT represents 50–90% of all cutaneous MCTs in cats. The
behavior of these lesions is benign and excisional biopsy
may be all that is required for the majority of patients.
The diffuse mastocytic form has a behavior similar to
canine MCT. Thus, additional wide surgical margins and
routine staging are indicated.
Splenectomy as a single treatment modality for the visceral form will result in a median survival time of 12–18
months. As previously stated, evidence of ­metastasis in
other organs (lungs, liver, etc.) does not eliminate splenectomy as a surgical option due to the significant reduction
in tumor burden and resulting improved clinical outcome.
However, in the face of severe multifocal disease, splenectomy alone should not be considered.
The primary intestinal form historically caried the
most guarded prognosis (4–6 weeks survival). However,
more recent studies indicate that the prognosis may be
far better (median survival time 531 days).

Apheresis in Companion Animals
Steven Suter, VMD, MS, PhD, DACVIM (Oncology)
Canine Bone Marrow Transplant Unit, NC State University College of Veterinary Medicine, Raleigh, NC, USA

Apheresis, which in Greek means “a taking away,” is an
extracorporeal therapy that has been an important part of
physician‐based medicine since the early 1970s. With the
development of sophisticated cell separator machines
and the commercial availability of human cytokines, centrifugal apheresis is an essential component in the treatment of a wide variety of human diseases, including
cancer. Fortunately, with the availability of used, human
cell s­eparator machines to veterinarians employed at
both academic institutions and high‐end specialty practices, centrifugal apheresis is beginning to be recognized
as a valuable tool in the treatment of a variety of canine
diseases. This review will discuss how cell separators
(also called apheresis machines) work, briefly d
­ iscuss
physician‐based applications of apheresis, and review the
current state of companion animal apheresis.

patients actually experience very little loss of blood

The most popular cell collectors for physician‐based
medicine are the COBE® Spectra and Spectra Optia®
apheresis systems manufactured by TerumoBCT (­formerly
CaridianBCT) and CS‐3000 Plus and AmicusTM apheresis
systems manufactured by Fresenius Kabi (formerly

size and portability, are the Haemonetics® MCS®+8150
Multicomponent Collection System (red blood cells and
plasma only) and the MCS®+9000 Mobile Platelet
Collection System.

­Cell Separator Machines

­Physician‐Based Applications
of Apheresis

All cell separator machines, regardless of the manufacturer, are designed to separate specific blood components, most often based on cell density centrifugation.
Therefore, an integral component of all machines is a
large‐scale centrifuge that is able to continuously separate blood into various fractions, including white blood
cells (WBCs), platelets, and serum using continuous
flow centrifugation (CFC). This means the blood can be
collected into the machine, centrifuged, and returned to
the patient simultaneously. The component of interest is
typically pumped into a separate collection bag while the
rest of the unused blood components are returned to the
patient. Therefore, patients undergoing apheresis typically have a catheter placed in each leg or a dual‐lumen
catheter placed in one leg that allows blood to enter into

The most widely used application of cell separator
machines in physician‐based medicine is the collection
of platelets (plateletpheresis) for use in cancer patients
receiving chemotherapy, radiation treatments, or bone
marrow transplants, as well as patients with aplastic
anemia and blood coagulation disorders. It takes
­
­approximately five whole units of blood to harvest
the amount of platelets that can obtained from one
90‐minute plateletpheresis. Therefore, one unit of platelets harvested using plateletpheresis can be used to treat
2–3 patients (www.redcrossblood.org/donating‐blood/
types‐donations/platelet‐donation). Plateletpheresis is
considered absolutely safe with the most common side‐
effect being a tingling sensation in the lips due to transient hypocalcemia that is treated with calcium‐containing
antacid tablets.

Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE), a form of plasmapheresis, is a procedure where the cell separator machine
separates and removes the patient’s plasma which is then
replaced with either donated plasma or a protein solution such as 5% human albumin. TPE is ­typically used to
remove disease‐causing antibodies that cause a variety of
immune‐mediated diseases, including Guillain–Barré
syndrome, chronic inflammatory ­
demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP), and myasthenia gravis. It can also be
used to treat thrombotic thrombocytopenia purpura
(TTP) patients in an effort to reduce the thickness of the
blood. TPE can also be used to remove large amounts of
medication if the need arises.
Low‐density lipoprotein (LDL) apheresis removes
LDL cholesterol from the blood of patients with hypercholesterolemia using two specific types of apheresis machines approved by the US Food and Drug
Administration (FDA). The Liposorber uses a filter covered with dextran that binds LDL cholesterol and
removes it from the circulation. Another machine, called
HELP, uses heparin to bind and remove LDL cholesterol.
Since hypercholesterolemia is usually caused by the
combination of mutations in a variety of genes (especially LDLRAP1) and lifestyle choices, treatment using
LDL apheresis is usually life‐long.
Photopheresis is a very specialized type of apheresis
where the harvested white blood cells are exposed to a
photoactive drug called methoxsalen which renders
them sensitive to ultraviolet (UV) light. The cells are
then exposed to UV light inside the machine and
returned to the patient. This procedure can improve the
symptoms of certain conditions such as graft versus host
disease (GVHD), cutaneous T cell lymphoma, or organ
transplant rejection, although it is currently not known
exactly how photophoresis works. The length and number of procedures needed to provide benefit are highly
variable.
Leukapheresis is used to remove extra white blood
cells from the blood in patients with diseases that can
cause very high white blood cell counts, including
acute lymphoblastic and acute myeloblastic leukemias.
Leukapheresis in these patients can significantly
decrease blood viscosity and also decrease the chance
of acute tumor lysis syndrome in patients starting
­induction chemotherapy.
Peripheral blood stem cell collections are used to
harvest monocytes from patients after some type of
­
blood cell mobilization, such as G‐CSF (Neupogen)
administration. A small percentage of the harvested
monocytes (~1–4%) are CD34+ progenitor cells that can
lead to complete hematologic reconstitution after some
type of myeloablative therapy (such as total body irradiation or high‐dose chemotherapy). This procedure is used

to collect CD34+ progenitor cells for their use in both
autologous and allogeneic bone marrow transplants
when treating patients with lymphoma, leukemia, and
multiple myeloma. The cells can also be used to treat
other conditions including myelodysplastic syndromes
and childhood neuroblastoma.

­Companion Animal Apheresis
Plasmapheresis (the separation of plasma from blood to
be used in primary and supportive disease management)
is the most commonly reported apheresis procedure in
the veterinary literature. In horses, plasmapheresis has
been explored using continuous‐flow cell separator
machines based on data showing that plasma harvested
from equine blood using fast erythrocyte sedimentation
contains a high number of erythrocytes that could cause
recipient sensitization and evidence that bacterial contamination can occur using an open collection system.
In two studies, Feige et al. found that automated
­plasmapheresis using a Blutz separator AS 104 (Fresenius,
Stans, Switzerland) was the method of choice when
­compared to whole‐blood collection followed by either
centrifugation or gravity sedimentation and that the
plasmapheresis procedure itself was very well tolerated
by the donor horses. To this author’s knowledge, the use
of TPE to treat equine patients with immune‐mediated
diseases has not been reported.
Canine plasmapheresis has also been reported
using both membrane filtration and continuous‐flow
centrifugation. Bartges et al. used discontinuous membrane filtration plasmapheresis (Therapore, Therapeutic
Apheresis Systems, Sarns/3M, Ann Arbor, MI) twice, in
conjunction with corticosteroids, to treat a dog with
acquired myasthenia gravis, which dropped the AchR
antibody titer by ~70%. Crump and Seshadri used
continuous membrane filtration (Prisma CRRT and
­
TPE Control Unit, Gambro Inc., Lakewood, CO) to
treat a dog with immune‐mediated hemolytic anemia.
In both reports, plasmapheresis was performed safely
minimal side‐effects and the dogs responded
with ­
clinically.
Canine TPE has also been reported, although the
majority of studies were performed in the 1980s. Matus
et al. used a cell separator (IBM 2997 cell separator, IBM
Corp., Princetown, NJ) to treat three dogs with an IgA
monoclonal gammopathy and secondary hyperviscosity. In all three dogs, one total plasma volume was
removed and replaced with lactated Ringer’s solution
(LRS) and all three dogs responded clinically within
24 hourrs of t­reatment. This same group also treated
one dog with systemic lupus erythematosus using a

VetBooks.ir

156 Apheresis in Companion Animals

combination of plasmapheresis and immunoabsorption.
Plasmapheresis was performed eight times over a period
of 45 days using the same cell separator and the harvested product was then passed over a column loaded
with Staphylococcus purified protein A/SSPA, which
binds canine IgG classes of antibodies. This dog also
responded well clinically. Based on this case report,
Matus et al. then treated five dogs with systemic lupus
and two dogs with immune‐mediated hemolytic anemia
using plasmapheresis alone, using the same IBM cell
separator. One total plasma volume was removed and
replaced with LRS and all dogs responded clinically
within 24 hourrs of the procedure.
Dogs have been undergoing leukapheresis in a research
setting since 1967, although the collection of large
amounts of cells needed for routine clinical use using
CFC was not possible until the cloning and large‐scale
production of recombinant hematopoietic cytokines in
the 1990s and the development of highly automated
computer‐controlled cell separators soon thereafter.
Although there is a large body of research literature
­utilizing dogs as a preclinical model to develop leukapheresis techniques to collect a sufficient number of
peripheral blood CD34+ cells to allow complete hematologic reconstitution following myeloablative therapy, the
use of leukapheresis in the veterinary clinical setting is
still in its infancy.
In 2006, Lupu et al. reported the use of a COBE Spectra
cell separator to harvest enough peripheral blood CD34+
progenitor cells (>5 × 106/kg) for use in an allogeneic
bone marrow transplant setting. Their choice of cell separator was based on the experience of the group at the
Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center which showed
that automated apheresis using a COBE Spectra machine
developed for humans could also be used in dogs. Our
group at North Carolina State University also found that
an adequate number of peripheral blood progenitor cells
could be safely harvested from dogs using a Fresenius
Kabi CS‐3000 Plus cell separator. We also showed that
the CD34+ component of the harvest product was adequate to achieve complete hematopoietic reconstitution
following lethal total body irradiation.
Finally, since all cell separator machines are designed
for adult humans and their use in small children and
dogs can be challenging, our group showed, similar to
human pediatric data, that apheresis using a COBE
Spectra cell separator can be safely performed in dogs
weighing <14 kg if appropriate machine priming techniques are utilized. The smallest dog on which our group
has performed apheresis on weighed 4.6 kg (unpublished
data). This combination of older and more recent data
clearly shows that canine leukapheresis is safe in a clinical setting and the procedure can harvest an adequate

amount of hematopoietic progenitor cells for use in the
canine bone marrow transplant setting.
Leukapheresis Followed by Bone Marrow
Transplantation
Early research, performed mainly at the Fred Hutchinson
Research Center, proved that canine peripheral blood
CD34+ progenitor cells harvested using human cell separators could lead to complete hematologic reconstitution following lethal myeloablative therapy. Further work
showed that dogs with lymphoma could be successfully
treated in both an autologous and allogeneic bone marrow transplant setting with long‐term survivals longer
than chemotherapy alone.
More recently, our group at North Carolina State
University used a combination of total body irradiation
and autologous peripheral blood CD34+ progenitor
cells, harvested using either a CS‐3000 Plus or COBE
Spectra cell separator, to treat dogs with high‐grade B
and T cell lymphoma. Five of 15 (33%) dogs with B cell
lymphoma transplanted while in remission for their
­disease remained alive >2 years (median overall survival
524 days), while two of 13 (15%) dogs with T cell lymphoma transplanted while in remission for their disease
remained alive >2 years (median overall survival 240
days). Importantly, when we transplanted dogs with B
cell lymphoma who were not in clinical remission, their
median disease‐free intervals were significantly shorter
than those who were in remission (52 days vs 456 days).
In dogs with T cell lymphoma, although a smaller percentage of dogs were alive >2 years compared with
the B cell lymphoma dogs, the median overall survival
from the time of diagnosis to death was 602 days (range
246–928 days), which is significantly longer than when
dogs are treated with chemotherapy alone.
Our group has also performed two allogeneic bone
marrow transplants using DLA‐matched donor peripheral blood CD34+ cells to treat one dog with B cell and
one dog with T cell lymphoma (unpublished data). Both
dogs underwent complete hematologic reconstitution
and achieved full donor engraftment within six weeks of
transplant. The dog with B cell lymphoma died of unexplained causes ~6 months post transplant, while the dog
with T cell lymphoma remains alive ~22 months post
transplant. We also treated a dog with acute large granular
lymphocytic leukemia using DLA‐matched donor peripheral blood CD34+ cells and this dog remains d
­ isease free
at ~30 months post transplant. Both autologous and allogeneic bone marrow transplantation as treatments of
canine lymphoproliferative disorders are currently offered
at North Carolina State University and three private
­practices in the United States (CA, WA, and OH).

Section 11 Oncologic Disease

Plateletpheresis
Although, as stated previously, one of the primary uses of
cell separator machines in physician‐based medicine is
plateletpheresis, canine plateletpheresis has been rarely
reported and remains an underutilized resource in the
clinical veterinary setting. Callan et al. used a Terumo
COBE Spectra machine to assess the safety and feasibility of plateletpheresis using 14 normal adult dogs. In all
cases, a high‐quality, leukoreduced (<1 × 106 WBCs)
platelet concentrate (mean total yield of 3.3 × 1011
­platelets) was collected in a mean procedure time of only
105 min. Since citrate‐induced hypocalcemia was noted
in some dogs, prophylactic IV Ca supplementation was
recommended. Appleman et al. then extended this work
by examining the effects of platelet in vitro function and
in vivo survival using two different methods of cryopreservation (6% DMSO or Thrombosol). Although
­cryopreserved platelets using either method were not
able to mimic fresh platelets in terms of in vivo platelet
recovery, the authors concluded that both cryopreserved

products could be considered for dogs with acute, life‐
threatening bleeding when fresh platelet products are
not available.

­Conclusion
Although cell separator machines are used daily in physician‐based medicine to treat a wide variety of diseases,
their use in veterinary‐based medicine remains largely
unexplored. Recent studies show that dogs can tolerate
apheresis using human cell separator machines and that
specific blood components can be harvested in a clinical
veterinary setting. Moreover, it is clear that animals with
a variety of diseases, including cancer, can achieve positive clinical outcomes when treated with cell separator
harvest products. As such, apheresis in veterinary medicine remains a largely untapped resource that should
expand in the future as more veterinarians become aware
of the technology and more machines become available
to our profession.

Approach to the Patient with Dermatologic Disease
Lisa V. Reiter, DVM, DACVD
McKeever Dermatology Clinics, Eden Prairie, and Inver Grove Heights, MN, USA

Skin and ear diseases are among the most common reasons why clients seek veterinary consultation. Not only
are diseases such as hypersensitivity disorders and skin
and otic infections very common, the skin is the most
accessible organ of the body, making it readily visible to
owners. Thus, owners can easily detect abnormalities in
the appearance, odor, and feel of the skin and haircoat,
as well as appreciate how the disease is impacting their
pet’s quality of life along with their own. Because dermatologic problems are usually multifactorial, chronic,
recurrent and noncurable, and often involve several dermatoses occurring simultaneously, owners and veterinarians alike can easily become overwhelmed.
It is the goal of this chapter to make the diagnosis and
management of dermatologic disease more rewarding by
guiding veterinarians toward a more methodical and
efficient approach to the dermatologic patient. This will
be accomplished by emphasizing the recognition of crucial lesions and their distribution, and assimilating these
findings and other physical exam abnormalities with the
history such that a comprehensive list of systematized
differential diagnoses will be formulated and the most
appropriate diagnostic tests selected. Finally, the chapter
will end with a discussion of the common diagnostic
tests utilized in the dermatologic patient, including indications, techniques, and interpretation.

­History
Despite its complexity, the skin has limited means by
which it “reacts” to indicate the presence of an underlying disease process, and because numerous skin diseases
will manifest clinically in a similar way, the patient history is vital. Not uncommonly, obtaining a thorough and
complete history will take longer than the examination
itself. This process can be expedited by having a history

form or questionnaire made available to the client to be
completed either in the reception area or, ideally, emailed
or mailed to the client prior to the consultation. There
are several examples of dermatologic history forms available from multiple textbooks (included in the Further
Reading section at the end of this chapter), online
through the Veterinary Information Network (www.vin.
com), and through various veterinary pharmaceutical
companies. These forms can be adapted and modified to
the clinician’s own preferences.
The previously completed dermatology history form
can be quickly reviewed with the client before or during
the consultation, which decreases the time needed to
extract a good history, and should begin with the client’s
primary complaint. Neglecting this can quickly result in
a dissatisfied, “unheard” client, especially when the
­veterinarian’s concerns do not immediately reflect the
primary concerns of the client. Addressing the chief
complaint will often result in an immediate list of differential diagnoses aimed at identifying the etiology of the
underlying disease process. During review of the dermatologic history form, additional questions can be asked
or posed in different ways to help extract pertinent information that pertains to specific problems. This is an art
and takes practice!
The patient’s signalment can further assist with formulating and ranking differential diagnoses, as there
are some skin diseases that are more likely to occur in
specific age ranges, sexes (including neuter status), and
in certain breeds. The age of onset of the dermatologic
disease can be particularly helpful in the very young
and very old patient. For instance, younger animals
are more commonly afflicted with diseases such as
demodicosis, otodectes, and dermatophytosis, as well
as ­congenital and hereditary diseases, whereas middle‐
aged to older animals are more commonly diagnosed
with autoimmune dermatoses, neoplastic conditions,

Clinical Small Animal Internal Medicine Volume II, First Edition. Edited by David S. Bruyette.
© 2020 John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Published 2020 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc.
Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/bruyette/clinical

VetBooks.ir

1376

Section 12 Skin and Ear Diseases

and endocrinopathies. However, most diseases manifest between approximately 1 year and 6–8 years of age
where no clear relationship between age and disease
exists. The breed of the patient may help with the development of an initial differential diagnosis list. There are
some breeds, including those with a specific coat color,
that seem to be predisposed to specific dermatologic
conditions. In addition, certain diseases are congenital
or have an identified heritable basis while others simply
occur more frequently in some breeds than in others
(Table 157.1).
Occasionally, sex predilections for various diseases
exist and can help in formulating and ranking the
differentials. For instance, females are anecdotally
­
reported to be more prone to systemic lupus erythematosus. Neuter status should also be taken into consideration. Estrus has been known to exacerbate pruritus
in females, and intact males are at increased risk for
male feminization syndrome.
The disease history can be further clarified by addressing some key questions including the date of onset (in
addition to the age of onset, discussed above), location
and appearance of the initial lesions, duration and progression of the disease. The approximate date of onset
may help to track seasonality or possibly create a timeline for assessment of a drug‐ or vaccine‐induced cutaneous reaction. Depending on geographic location,
disorders such as insect bite hypersensitivities and flea
allergy dermatitis tend to occur in the summer. In temperate climates, atopic dermatitis often begins as a seasonal disease, typically worsening in the spring, summer,
and/or fall. However, some patients with house dust
mite hypersensitivity may worsen in the winter in addition to having year‐round pruritus. Canine flank alopecia, also known as seasonal or cyclical flank alopecia,
tends to result in cyclical episodes of noninflammatory,
nonpruritic alopecia in the winter where a shorter photoperiod induces follicular arrest with resolution occurring in the spring.
Specifying the initial lesion location and pattern of distribution can be extremely helpful in developing a differential diagnosis list, as many diseases have distinct
areas of involvement. For instance, pemphigus foliaceus
affects the pinnae, dorsal aspect of the muzzle, and the
pawpads. Sarcoptic mange tends to affect the pinnal
margins, elbows, and tibiotarsal areas. The importance
of lesional distribution will be further discussed in the
physical exam (PE) section. Questions pertaining to disease duration and progression should include if and how
location, appearance, and distribution have changed,
whether the onset was acute or slow and insidious, and if
the disease is continuous or intermittent (seasonal or
nonseasonal). An acute onset of severe pruritus often
occurs with sarcoptic mange, and diseases such as

pemphigus foliaceus and contact dermatitis tend to
erupt rapidly. Cutaneous adverse food reaction may also
have a rapid onset, whereas endocrinopathies tend to
have a slow onset. A patient with seasonal pruritus would
not require a food elimination trial, as adverse food
­reactions cause year‐round signs.
One of the most important historical questions to
address is whether or not the disease was precipitated by
or associated with pruritus, as this information can rapidly help to generate and shorten the list of differentials.
If pruritus preceded the lesions, then allergic or parasitic
diseases are most likely. If lesions, such as alopecia, precede the pruritus, endocrinopathies, follicular dysplasias
and follicular demodicosis must be explored. If papules,
pustules, epidermal collarettes or crusts precede the
pruritus, the so‐called “rash that itches,” pursue bacterial, any nonpruritic dermatoses prone to developing
secondary bacterial infection such as endocrinopathies,
and sterile pustular diseases (e.g., pemphigus foliaceus).
Diseases that are typically or always pruritic include
atopic dermatitis, cutaneous adverse food reaction,
flea bite allergy, contact hypersensitivity, sarcoptic and
notoedric mange, and demodicosis caused by Demodex
gatoi in cats and Demodex cornei in dogs. Variably
­pruritic conditions include cheyletiellosis, demodicosis
caused by Demodex injai, Malassezia dermatitis, superficial pyoderma, feline dermatophytosis, autoimmune
diseases such as pemphigus foliaceus, and epitheliotropic lymphoma. Diseases that are nonpruritic include
endocrinopathies, follicular dysplasias, canine dermatophytosis, and demodicosis caused by Demodex canis and
Demodex cati. However, these conditions can be pruritic
if accompanied by secondary infection.
Identifying patterns of pruritus is also important for
identifying underlying disease triggers. A patient whose
pruritus always improves with a change in environment
likely has atopic or contact dermatitis. In a patient with
nonseasonal pruritus that also has seasonal “flares,”
adverse food reaction should be explored in addition to
atopic dermatitis. A patient that suddenly becomes pruritic after residing at a boarding kennel should be evaluated for sarcoptic mange.
Owners often do not recognize the various manifestations of pruritus, such as licking, biting, chewing, rubbing, rolling, and scooting, and the clinician needs to ask
about these variable signs. Therefore, evaluation of pruritus should not stop at asking if the patient “itches.”
Also, determining the level of pruritus is important in
the development of an adequate treatment plan and evaluating the patient’s response to treatment. Commonly,
owners are asked to rank their pet’s level of pruritus on a
scale of 0 to 10, with 0 representing no itch at all and 10
being so itchy that the pet cannot sleep at night (and
­neither can the poor owner!).

The presence of systemic signs and the pet’s general
health should be addressed, such as water intake, appetite, vomiting, diarrhea, frequency/number of bowel
movements, changes in urination, respiratory changes,
lethargy, and body condition changes. General information about the patient’s environment and geographic
location needs to be considered. Certain diseases are
endemic in various regions such as blastomycosis in the
Mississippi, Missouri and Ohio river valleys or coccidioidomycosis in the southwestern portion of the United
States. For the same reason, travel history should also be
obtained. It is pertinent to ask if other animals in the
home or the owners themselves are affected. If so, contagious and zoonotic diseases need to be considered.
Other medical problems, vaccine history, lists of previous and current treatments and medications, including
topical therapy, flea control products and frequency of
administration, need to be addressed, including the
responses to these therapies. Reviewing previous medical records can be particularly helpful regarding medication history, as often owners find it difficult to remember
all the previous medications, including the ones the
patient may be currently taking. Asking owners to bring
these medications to the initial consultation can also be
helpful in this regard. Any previous medical records
should be reviewed to help track episodes of recurrence
(is there a seasonality?) and progression of the skin disease, verify client observations, and identify past and
current medications, including dose and duration. The
response to various treatments can also be extremely
helpful in the identification of underlying disease processes. For example, a patient that presents on high doses
of glucocorticoids for suspected allergic dermatitis that
is still markedly pruritic needs to be evaluated for sarcoptic mange and/or undergo a treatment trial for this
disease if the mites cannot be found, as allergic patients
tend to be glucocorticoid responsive. When presented
with a patient that is on an appropriate dose and duration of antibiotic therapy for superficial pyoderma and is
not responding, a skin culture needs to be performed.
Finally, a complete dietary history including vitamins,
herbs, and other supplements should be taken. This will
be useful if a food elimination trial needs to be performed
as well as to assess if the diet is complete and balanced.
Poor diets can lead to keratinization disorders, poor
haircoat quality, and zinc‐responsive dermatosis.

­Physical Examination
The patient’s weight, rectal temperature, and pulse
should be obtained by the veterinary technician or assistant before or during review of the patient history. Every
patient examination should be approached in a systematic fashion to ensure a thorough PE. Avoid focusing

1381

VetBooks.ir

1382

Section 12 Skin and Ear Diseases

solely on the area(s) that the owner mentions or you may
miss hidden, subtle lesions that can offer important diagnostic clues pertaining to the underlying disease process.
A well‐lit room is essential and a hand‐held magnifying
lens may be useful for close examination of lesions. In
some instances, the hair may need to be clipped to
allow for proper visualization. Painful or “uncooperative” patients may require sedation.
Many dermatologists prefer to start with the nose and
head region and work caudally, including all accompanying mucosal and mucocutaneous surfaces. The interdigital spaces, claws, ungual folds, and pawpads must always
be evaluated with the patient either standing or in lateral
recumbency. Part the hair or roll the skin into individual
folds to separate the hair and allow for easier evaluation
of the cutaneous surface and follicular ostia while also
noting the haircoat quality, color, and luster. Throughout
the evaluation, look for evidence of pruritus, such as
excoriations and salivary staining, the latter of which
commonly manifests as a brownish‐red discoloration of
the haircoat. An otoscopic examination should be performed in all patients. Examination findings can be documented using topography maps available at www.vin.
com or in the texts listed in the Further Reading section.
These maps allow for quick illustration of lesion distribution and character during the initial consultation and subsequent rechecks which assist the clinician in making
comparisons regarding disease progression between
­
appointments. The patient should be auscultated, and
the lymph nodes and abdomen palpated. These aspects of
a general examination are important as they can reveal
an underlying systemic disease which may be giving rise
to the dermatologic changes. Also, findings on a general
PE may dictate or change the choice of drug therapy. For
instance, the discovery of a cardiac murmur in a feline
patient may prompt the clinician to be more cautious
with the administration of injectable glucocorticoids,
given that cats are at increased risk of developing congestive heart failure when receiving them, especially
methylprednisolone acetate.
During the course of the PE, the clinician must learn to
identify the major features of the skin lesions. This will
allow the disease to be placed in diagnostic categories
that facilitate diagnosis. Most important are the type of
lesions (primary or secondary) and lesion distribution
(body sites involved). Proper identification of lesions is
crucial, as they can be correlated with specific diseases.
Morphology of Lesions
Lesion morphology refers to the categorization of cutaneous lesions as primary, secondary, or either primary or
secondary. The ability to accurately identify these lesions
as well as having an understanding of their development

is critical in refining the list of differentials. Also, knowing how primary lesions typically evolve into secondary
lesions gives the clinician a better understanding of disease progression. A primary lesion develops spontaneously and is a reflection of the underlying disease process;
thus these lesions are the most important to identify.
Secondary lesions evolve from primary lesions or are
created by the patient scratching or external forces such
as trauma, medications, and infection of primary lesions.
Some lesions can be considered primary or secondary.
Table 157.2 provides a list and description of basic cutaneous lesion morphology. An accompanying figure is
provided for most of these lesions which elaborates on
their significance/pathomechanism and provides examples of differentials (Figures 157.1–157.18).

Distribution of Lesions
In addition to recognizing lesion morphology, the location
and distribution must be identified. Lesion distribution
refers to whether the lesions are localized, multifocal,
regionalized or generalized, bilaterally symmetric versus
asymmetric, and identifying the general regions of the
patient that are involved. Bilaterally symmetric lesions
tend to occur in endocrinopathies, immune‐mediated and
autoimmune diseases, and can also occur in allergic skin
diseases. Asymmetric lesions are often the result of infectious and parasitic disease processes. Certain diseases have
predilection sites for various areas of the body and familiarity with these regional characteristics is advantageous in
honing the list of differential diagnoses (Table 157.3).

and Techniques
After a list of differential diagnoses has been generated
based on a thorough history and PE, diagnostic tests can
be employed to further narrow the list of differentials

Screening Tests
Cytology

Cytology is a powerful tool, allowing one to quickly determine whether a lesion is sterile or if infectious organisms
and inflammation are present. It allows the clinician to presumptively diagnose a patient with autoimmune diseases,
such as pemphigus, when acantholytic cells are observed.
Neoplastic processes may also be identified, such as

Figure 157.10 Fissure – lesions may be caused by underlying
disease or injury when the skin is thick and then subjected to

dermatosis, chronic skin diseases, and keratinization disorders.
Photograph illustrates fissures on the metacarpal pawpad of a
dog with SND.

­cutaneous lymphoma and mast cell tumors. Cytology can
be performed in a number of ways depending on the area

Figure 157.11 Lichenification – results from chronic trauma, often

Figure 157.13 Scale – results from increased production of

Figure 157.14 Crust – forms when purulent exudate, serum,
blood, other dried exudates, or cells and/or scales adhere to the
skin surface. DDx – primary: SND, vitamin A‐responsive dermatitis,
zinc‐responsive dermatosis, primary idiopathic seborrhea.
Secondary: pyoderma, dermatophytosis, pemphigus, and lupus.
The coloration, thickness, and adherence of crusts can provide
insight as to the underlying disease process. Pyoderma can result
in brown‐dark red (indicating hemorrhage) or yellow‐green crusts.
Dark crusts indicate deeper tissue damage or hemorrhage as
occurs with traumatic wounds, furunculosis, and vasculitis.
Honey‐colored crusts usually indicate an infection but also occur
with some autoimmune diseases, particularly pemphigus
foliaceus. Thick, dry yellowish crusts are more common with
scabies and zinc‐responsive dermatosis. Tightly adhered crusts are
more common in zinc‐responsive dermatosis, SND, pemphigus,
and some cases of seborrhea. Photograph illustrates the typical
honey‐colored crusts associated with pemphigus foliaceus.

Impression Smear

Figure 157.16 Comedones – in general, these lesions may form as
a result of primary keratinization disorders or hyperkeratosis due
to endocrine abnormalities or inflammation. DDx – primary:
endocrinopathies, feline acne, some primary idiopathic
seborrheas, congenital hypotrichosis (e.g., Chinese crested dogs),

A routine impression smear is one of the most commonly employed dermatologic tests, and an excellent
technique to use when pustules, crusts, epidermal collarettes, and draining nodules are present and for moist
or greasy areas of the skin. When a pustule is present,
gently “open” the pustule by using a 25 gauge needle and
pass it in a parallel fashion through the tip of the pustule. Avoid directly “poking” or “sticking” the pustule, as
this will artefactually contaminate the specimen with
blood and blood‐associated leukocytes. When crusts

sample can be obtained by lifting the scales and crusts
from the perimeter and sampling the edge of the lesion
as described for crusts.
Once the lesion is prepared for an impression, a glass
slide should be gently pressed against the site, heat fixed
(either by using a lighter passed under the slide until a
light smoky black residue is observed or by using a slide
warmer for 20 seconds) or allowed to air‐dry, and stained
with a modified Wright’s stain (e.g., Diff‐Quik). Gram
stain or new methylene blue can also be used. When
using Diff‐Quik (which the author prefers), allow the
slide to sit in each reagent for approximately 20 seconds.
Rinse the slide gently with water after the third solution.
The slide should then be air‐ or blow‐dried.
The sample should first be evaluated under the microscope using low‐power magnification (×10) to peruse for
an infectious versus inflammatory versus neoplastic process. The author finds it easiest to look for acantholytic
cells and certain fungal organisms, such as blastomycosis,
under the low‐power objective, whereas immediate use of
the oil immersion objective (×100) may result in the missing of rare organisms or cells. The oil immersion objective
is then used (after a drop or two of immersion oil is placed
on the slide) to look for organisms and for closer observation and confirmation of inflammatory , neoplastic , and/
or acantholytic cells. Draining nodules can also be evaluated by directly pressing the slide to the draining contents
and staining as previously described.
Acetate Tape Preparation

This technique is helpful for sampling intertriginous
areas, nailfolds, interdigital areas, and dry, scaly, hyperplastic or lichenified skin surfaces. This is the author’s
preferred technique when Malassezia overcolonization
or infection is suspected. This test is performed by
pressing an approximately 2 cm piece of clear tape sticky
side down firmly against the skin several times. The tape
is then held at either end and immersed in the No. 3
Diff‐Quik stain for 15–20 seconds and then gently
rinsed with water to remove excess stain. The tape is

allowed to completely air‐dry or is blow‐dried. A strip of
immersion oil is placed on the slide and the tape is
placed sticky side down on the strip of oil. Another drop
of immersion oil is placed on top of the tape and microscopic evaluation is performed at ×10 and ×100 magnification. A cover slip is not needed.
Surface Skin Scrape

This technique is very useful when evaluating the skin
for bacteria and yeast and for sampling areas where an
impression smear may be difficult to obtain. However, it
is best reserved for sampling affected areas that are
greasy, otherwise the sample will not adhere well to the
scalpel blade. A No. 10 scalpel blade is used to gently
scrape just the surface of the affected area in the direction of the hair growth. It is not necessary to obtain capillary bleeding. Mineral oil is not utilized. The collected
material is smeared onto a glass slide and heat fixed,
stained, and microscopically evaluated according to the
guidelines indicated above for impression smears.
Cotton‐Tipped Applicator Smears

Cotton‐tipped applicators or swabs are useful for sampling moist lesions and intertriginous areas. The swab is
gently rubbed on the surface of the skin and the sample
is then rolled onto a glass slide. This technique can also
be utilized for hard‐to‐reach areas where the skin is dry,
except that the cotton swab is moistened with saline
prior to sampling in order to minimize cell damage during sample collection and preparation. Once the sample
is applied to the slide, it is heat fixed, stained, and evaluated as described above for impression smears.
Otic Cytology Otic cytology is also performed using
cotton‐tipped applicators. Samples are obtained from
each external ear canal using a separate cotton swab.
A standard system should be used for making slides
(i.e., the left ear sample is prepped next to the frosted
side of the glass slide and the right ear sample on
the other half of the slide). The slide is heat fixed and
stained as described above for impression smears. Begin

Fine Needle Aspirate

In general, surface‐dwelling mites such as Sarcoptes,
Notoedres, Cheyletiella, D. cornei, and D. gatoi are best
procured via superficial skin scrapes, whereas follicular
mites, including D. canis, D. cati, and D. injai, require
deep skin scrapes for diagnosis.
The superficial skin scrape is performed by applying
several drops of mineral oil onto the area to be scraped
or onto the chosen skin scraping tool. If necessary, the
overlying hair can be shortened with a No. 40 clipper
blade to facilitate the scraping procedure, but the clipper
blade should not touch the skin surface or any lesions, if
present. A No. 10 scalpel blade is used to scrape a large,
broad area approximately 10–15 times. Alternatively, a
skin scraping spatula (Jorgensen Laboratories, Loveland,
CO) can be used. Obtaining capillary bleeding is not
necessary, as it is more important to scrape broad, large
areas to increase the chances of procuring these difficult‐
to‐find surface‐dwelling mites. For scabies, preferred
sampling sites include the margins of the pinnae, elbows,
and tibiotarsal areas, as these are the most commonly
afflicted sites, even if one only identifies mild, subtle
lesions. Papules, if present, should also be scraped. The
material is then transferred to a glass slide and a cover
slip is applied. The sample is then evaluated microscopically with either ×4 (scanning objective) or ×10 magnification in a systematic fashion. The condenser should be
lowered to increase contrast and facilitate the finding of
mites. Look for all parasitic life stages. The observation
of just one egg is considered a positive finding; however,
a negative skin scrape does not rule out surface mites. In
these cases, when the aforementioned mites are suspected but cannot be confirmed with superficial skin
scrapings, a treatment trial may be needed to verify the
presence (or absence) of these mites (see Diagnostic
Treatment Trials below and see also Chapter 165).
Deep skin scrapes differ from the superficial version in
that the sample will be procured from a focal, localized
area, squeezing the skin prior to the scrape (and during
the scrape if possible) to facilitate extrusion of the mites
from the follicles. Several drops of mineral oil are applied
either directly to the sample area or to the No. 10 scalpel
blade or skin scraping spatula and the skin is scraped in
the direction of hair growth until capillary bleeding is
evident. Lesions that should be scraped include areas
where comedones, erythema, scaling, papules, and pustules are evident. The author finds that comedones are
especially important lesions to scrape when follicular
demodicosis is suspected. The collected material is then
transferred to a glass slide and a cover slip applied and
evaluated as described above. If properly performed with

Fine needle aspirates are best utilized for evaluation of
nodular to tumorous lesions. A 20–25 gauge needle
attached to a 6–12 cc syringe is used to aspirate the
lesion. It is important to release the pressure on the
syringe before the needle is withdrawn from the lesion.
Once the needle and syringe are removed from the
lesion, the needle is detached and the plunger of
the syringe is pulled back to draw air into the barrel. The
syringe is then reattached to the needle and the contents
are expressed onto a slide, gently smeared using a separate clean slide and allowed to air‐dry. Alternatively, the
fine needle capillary technique can be used. A 22–25
gauge needle is introduced into the lesion by holding
onto the hub. Several quick, back‐and‐forth movements
are then made in multiple directions within the lesion,
without completely withdrawing the needle, to ensure a
representative sample is obtained. The needle is then
withdrawn and attached to a syringe (6–12 cc) into which
air was already drawn. The plunger is then depressed to
expel the material within the needle onto a clean glass
slide, spread, and allowed to air‐dry.
Following the use of either technique, the slide is
then stained with Diff‐Quik. Other staining options
include gram stain or new methylene blue. Evaluation
for microorganisms, such as bacteria, yeast and deep
fungal species, and for the overall cell type (i.e., inflammatory or neoplastic) is performed by first evaluating
the specimen using the ×10 objective and finally with
the high‐power objective (×40). The oil immersion
objective can also be utilized to evaluate the sample in
greater detail.
Trichography (Hair Examination)

Trichography is used for a number of indications. It
can be used to detect the presence of parasitic or infectious organisms, such as Demodex and dermatophyte
arthrospores. Traumatic hair loss due to pruritic behaviors can be confirmed by the presence of hair shafts with
blunted tips. When hairs are predominantly found to be
in telogen (i.e., resting phase), this may be an indication
that an underlying endocrinopathy or follicular arrest
may be present. Finally, a presumptive diagnosis of various follicular dysplasias can be made when, for example,
marked melanin clumping is present within the hair
shafts. The author prefers to gently pluck the hairs using
the fingertips so as not to create iatrogenic trauma. The
hairs are then placed onto a slide with a drop of mineral
oil in an orderly array. A cover slip is placed atop the
sample and evaluation is initially performed using ×10

an appropriate number of deep skin scrapes along with
the sampling of appropriate lesions, a negative skin
scrape can rule out D. canis and D. cati. However, the
diagnosis of pododemodicosis may require biopsy and
certain breeds require biopsy to confirm a diagnosis,
particularly shar‐peis. The identification and treatment
of parasitic diseases will be discussed in Chapter 165.
Culture
Bacterial Culture

In this age of methicillin and multidrug resistance, bacterial culture and sensitivity has become a more routinely
implemented test in patients with superficial bacterial
folliculitis. While performing an aerobic bacterial culture
is never contraindicated, there are some instances which
make it a necessary test. These include the following:
poor response and the emergence of new lesions in
spite of appropriate antibiotic therapy
●● patients with chronic recurrent pyoderma, especially
those with a history of multiple courses of antimicrobial therapy
●● when rods or unusual organisms are present on cytology
●● in cases of deep pyoderma
●●

In cases of superficial bacterial folliculitis, pustules are
the ideal lesion to sample; however, epidermal collarettes
and crusts can also be sampled. The skin is not cleaned
prior to sampling. The pustule is gently lanced with
a sterile 25 gauge needle and a mini‐tip culturette is
touched to the purulent material, taking care to avoid
contact with the surrounding nonlesional skin. If crusts
are present, the culture should be obtained from underneath the crust. When epidermal collarettes are present,
the sample should be obtained from the leading edge
where the epithelium is lifted to avoid surface contaminants. The culturette is then placed back into the transport media device and refrigerated until sent overnight
to the laboratory. Mini‐tip culturettes are commercially
available through most microbiology laboratories.
Bacterial cultures of deep infection can vary somewhat
depending on the type of lesion being sampled. Fine needle aspiration can be performed to obtain specimens
from bullae and dermal or subcutaneous lesions with
pockets of fluid. Tissue cultures using sterile technique
are best when a nodule, tumor or cellulitis is present. It is
also ideal to obtain a tissue culture in the presence of
deep infection characterized by exudative draining
tracts, rather than merely swabbing any drainage, which
will often be contaminated with superficial organisms
while deeper organisms may be missed.
The surface should be aseptically prepared by gently
swabbing the area with 70% alcohol and can be followed
by a rinse with nonpreserved saline. Specimens are
obtained via punch biopsy from nonulcerated areas

(punch biopsy technique is described in detail below).
Local anesthesia is accomplished by infusing 1–2 mL of
2% lidocaine subcutaneously using a 25 gauge needle.
Care must be taken not to inject the lidocaine too superficially as it can inhibit microbial growth within the
­specimen. When in doubt, a ring block may be more
appropriate, especially if subcutaneous tissue is also
going to be submitted. Sterile instruments should be
used as well as gloves. The epidermis is then aseptically
removed with a No. 10 surgical scalpel and the remaining deep dermal tissue is used for culture. Removal of the
epidermis prevents overgrowth of the tissue culture by
surface bacteria that are not relevant to the deep infection. The dermal tissue is placed in a sterile red‐top tube
with just enough nonbacteriostatic sterile saline to keep
the sample moist, and refrigerated and shipped overnight to the laboratory. The tissue sample can be submitted for aerobic, anaerobic, and mycobacteria culture
purposes. The laboratory should be notified of the differential diagnoses, as culture media adjustments will be
made to facilitate the growth, isolation, and identification of the suspected organisms.
Fungal Culture
Fungal Culture for Deep Mycoses

When deep fungal
infection is suspected, samples are obtained using the
same principles as described above for bacterial cultures
of deep infection. Laboratories should be contacted in
advance of the differential diagnoses so that modification of culture techniques can be implemented in
advance, not only for diagnostic purposes but also
because of the human health risks associated with various fungal diseases. Laboratories should also be consulted regarding special requirements for tissue
submission. Depending on the suspected organism,
additional tests beyond culture may be required, such as
polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing.

Dermatophyte Culture In cases of suspected dermatophytosis, cultures (considered the gold standard for diagnosis) can be performed in hospital using dermatophyte
test medium (DTM) or, alternatively, samples may be submitted to a diagnostic laboratory. The clinician should
check with their laboratory regarding the preferred means
of sample submission. Dermatophyte test medium is most
useful because the red color indicator is a helpful diagnostic aid and it also contains inhibitors of bacterial and saprophytic contaminants (e.g., Sab‐Duets, Hardy
Diagnostics, Santa Maria, CA, USA). Sab‐Duets are also
popular in that they are double plated: one side contains
DTM and the other side contains plain Sabouraud dextrose agar. Dermatophyte test medium may decrease
development of conidia, and therefore it is best to perform
microscopic identification using the sample plated onto

1393

VetBooks.ir

1394

Section 12 Skin and Ear Diseases

Sabouraud dextrose agar. The most common dermatophytic agents include Microsporum canis, Microsporum
gypseum, and Trichophytan mentagrophytes.
When procuring samples for DTM, hairs should be
plucked from within the lesion close to the periphery. A
medical‐grade plug‐in long wave Wood’s lamp with
magnification can be helpful for identifying fluorescing
hairs that can be selected for culture in approximately
50% or more of cases caused by M. canis and rarely
with M. gypseum. The Burton Ultraviolet (Wood’s)
Exam Light (Philips Burton, Franklin Park, IL, USA) is
an excellent model as it provides magnification, and
replacement bulbs can be purchased. Medical‐grade
Wood’s lamps do not require a period to warm up, but
the room should be darkened and the evaluator allowed
to let their eyes adjust for 2–3 minutes. The lamp should
be held close to the skin (i.e., 4–10 cm). Infected hair
shafts will fluoresce a bright apple green. These are
often hiding under crusts, and thus it is important to lift
crusts and examine the hairs beneath. Fluorescing hairs
are then plucked for ­culture and can also be evaluated
by direct examination to confirm an infection (ectothrix
arthroconidia may be observed). Besides directly plucking hairs for culture purposes, the MacKenzie toothbrush technique can be used. Individually packaged
toothbrushes can be purchased readily online. This
method is especially helpful for sampling poorly circumscribed lesions and nonlesional patients when looking for asymptomatic carriers. A newly unwrapped
toothbrush is used to brush the lesions (or the entire
patient in asymptomatic animals), and the scales and
loose hairs caught in the bristles are gently embedded
onto the agar. A sterile needle or hemostat can also be
used to remove trapped hair and scale from the toothbrush for placement onto the culture medium.
After inoculation, the culture plate should be placed in
a sealable plastic baggie to prevent contamination and
dehydration, and put in an incubator. The incubation
temperature should be maintained at 75–80 °F and the
humidity should be approximately 30%. A digital aquarium thermometer can be used to monitor the temperature, and placing a pan of water in the incubator should
be enough to sustain adequate humidity. The plates
should be kept away from sunlight or fluorescent light.
Cultures should be examined daily and color change
(which occurs due to a change in the pH of the media)
and colony growth findings must be recorded. Pale, buff‐
colored to white colonies that simultaneously develop a
red ring of color around them as they grow are indicative
of dermatophytes. The colonies are typically cottony or
velvety and growth will often occur in 4–7 days. A contaminant is likely when there is colony growth and
no associated color change of the media or the color
change appears more than 10 days after colony growth.

Contaminants are also likely when there is a color change
but the colony is pigmented. Cultures should be incubated for three weeks before declaring them negative to
ensure that there is no late growth of a pathogen.
Cultures grossly suspicious for dermatophyte growth
should be evaluated microscopically. The sticky side of
clear acetate tape is gently brushed against the colony
growing on Sabouraud dextrose agar and placed over
several drops of lactophenol cotton blue stain on a glass
slide. The sample should sit for 5–10 minutes before
examination. This allows for proper absorption of the
stain by the spores and thus better visualization. The
sample is then ready to be evaluated with the ×10 and
×40 objectives. The macroconidia of M. canis are spindle‐shaped and have thick, spiny walls that have six or
more divisions with a knob at the terminal end. M. canis
does not produce as many macroconidia as M. gypseum,
which are thin‐walled and ellipsoid with rounded ends
having less than six divisions. Microscopic evaluation of
T. mentagrophytes will typically reveal large numbers of
spherical microconidia, rare cigar‐shaped macroconidia,
and spiral hyphae. The website https://drfungus.org/
contains helpful information regarding the macro‐ and
microscopic evaluation of dermatophytes.
Diagnostic Treatment Trials
Treatment trials are performed often in veterinary dermatology and are used to confirm a suspected diagnosis
where the response to therapy is either the only or the best
way to diagnose the possible underlying disease. Examples
of this include the improvement or elimination of clinical
signs with insecticidal therapy in presumptive cases of flea
bite hypersensitivity, sarcoptic mange, and D. gatoi infestation in cats. In other cases, confirmation of the underlying disease is made when a relapse is observed after
discontinuing the trial with subsequent resolution on
restarting the trial, as is the case when food elimination
trials are performed for diagnosing adverse food reactions. Another example of this concept is the use of glucocorticoids to support a diagnosis of allergic dermatitis
when other infectious and parasitic diseases have been
ruled out. Further discussion of specific treatment trials
can be found in the relevant chapters of this section.
Biopsy and Histopathology
There are several indications for performing skin biopsy
early on in the clinical work‐up. These include the presence of unusual lesions or lesions that evolve dramatically and/or severely, as in the case of a possible cutaneous
adverse drug reaction. Erosive to ulcerative draining dermatoses, especially those that are nodular, also should be
biopsied early on. At any point when there is concern of

VetBooks.ir

157 Approach to the Patient with Dermatologic Disease

a life‐threatening dermatosis, autoimmune or metabolic
disease, or the suspicion of n
­ eoplasia, biopsy should be
immediately undertaken. Finally, skin biopsies are particularly indicated when a specific condition is suspected
and the histopathology is recognized to be diagnostic of
that disease. Other less critical reasons for pursuing
biopsy include when other tests have not resulted in
identification of the condition and when treatment has
not resolved the problem. It is important to remember
that performing a skin biopsy is never useless. In the best
case scenario, it provides a definitive diagnosis, and in
the worst case it can rule out other dermatoses and narrow down the category of diseases to be considered.
Inform the owner that a precise diagnosis may not be
reached but in any case the information obtained will be
useful.
In order to maximize results, biopsies must be taken
that are representative of the entire disease process. This
entails the procurement of spontaneous, primary lesions
which generally occur earlier in the course of the disease,
along with secondary, more chronic lesions. Therefore,
in almost all cases, multiple biopsies should be taken in
order to capture the clinical spectrum and evolution of
the disease. It is prudent to select lesions that have not
been altered by scratching or infection. For depigmenting diseases (e.g., discoid lupus erythematosus), newly
depigmented areas are ideal sites for biopsy (e.g., the
slate gray areas of the nasal planum rather than the more
chronic white/pink or ulcerated areas). When ulcerated
areas need to be sampled, biopsy the advancing edge to
include some of the epidermis rather than the center of
the ulcer. For diseases characterized by alopecia, biopsies
should be obtained from the most chronic area of complete alopecia as well as from the junctional and normal
areas.
If possible, glucocorticoid therapy should be discontinued 2–3 weeks prior to biopsy. If a long‐acting injectable corticosteroid was administered to the patient, it is
best to postpone the biopsy for 6–8 weeks, when feasible. Generally, 3–5 biopsies are an acceptable average.
When possible, a 6 or 8 mm punch biopsy tool is used. A
3 or 4 mm instrument is used only for difficult‐to‐biopsy
areas (e.g., periocular region, pinnae, nasal planum or
footpad). In many cases, punch biopsies can be performed using local anesthesia with 2% lidocaine, with or
without sedation. However, when biopsying challenging
areas, general anesthesia may be best.
It is helpful to create a small dermatology surgery pack
so that all necessary instruments and materials are
readily available. Include a No. 10 scalpel blade and handle, straight and curved iris scissors, gauze, Mayo and
Metzenbaum scissors, needle and suture, an atraumatic
forceps such as a Debakey tissue forceps, and a needle
holder. Disposable biopsy punches and 10% formalin‐

filled vials are readily available in a number of sizes and
volumes, respectively.
The biopsy sites must remain perfectly intact and be
handled carefully. A scissors or clippers can be used if
necessary to gently shorten the overlying hair and
improve visualization of the area to be biopsied, taking
extreme care not to touch the skin surface or disturb the
lesion itself, including crusts. Preliminary scrubbing
should never be performed, except in the case of dermal
or subcutaneous nodules, where a light prep with 70%
alcohol should suffice. An indelible marker is used to circle the lesion and a local anesthetic, such as 2% lidocaine,
is injected subcutaneously using a 25 gauge needle and
fanning it under the area of the circle. The needle is
inserted at the periphery of the site to be biopsied so as
not to disturb the lesion itself. Typically 0.5–2.0 mL of
anesthetic per site should suffice. The maximum dose of
lidocaine that may be administered is 5 mg/kg in dogs
and 2.5 mg/kg in cats to avoid adverse effects, such as
cardiac arrhythmias. Wait at least five minutes prior to
biopsy to allow for optimal analgesic effect.
Center the lesion within the punch biopsy tool and
choose a size that minimizes the amount of normal skin
margin. However, for vesicles, bullae and pustules, which
are fragile and can easily rupture with biopsy, use the
largest punch possible or perform an excisional or wedge
biopsy. If the procurement of subcutaneous fat is essential to establishing an underlying diagnosis, it may also
be pertinent to use an excisional or wedge biopsy technique, and anesthetize the area using a ring block to minimize distortion of the subcutaneous tissue due to local
lidocaine infiltration. Rotate the punch biopsy tool in
one direction to minimize damaging shearing forces and
apply even, continuous pressure until an adequate depth
has been obtained to free the tissue down to the subcutaneous fat layer, which should be included in the specimen as it may be important for the accurate assessment
and diagnosis of many inflammatory processes. An edge
of the subcutaneous fat is gently grasped using an atraumatic tissue forceps to elevate the specimen. The epidermis or dermis should not be grasped, as this could result
in a crushing artifact and lead to a nondiagnostic sample.
The subcutaneous attachment is then cut. The author
prefers a straight or curved iris scissors in most cases.
The biopsy sample is then gently blotted to remove
excess artefactual blood from the surface.
The sample should be immediately placed in 10% formalin, with a minimum of 10 parts formalin to 1 part
tissue required for adequate fixation. Thin samples
should be placed, panniculus down, on a small piece of
tongue depressor before placement into the fixative to
prevent rolling of the specimen, which can make histopathologic evaluation more challenging. Affixed samples must be placed face down into the formalin jar. The

1395

VetBooks.ir

1396

Section 12 Skin and Ear Diseases

incision is then closed utilizing 1–2 simple interrupted
or cruciate sutures.
Provide a thorough history on your biopsy submission
form, as well as a description of the physical exam.
Preliminary diagnostic tests and their results should also
be included if applicable, along with a list of differential
diagnoses. Current and past therapy, including response,
may also be beneficial. Submission of digital photographs
can be very helpful and ideally a dermatohistopathologist should be utilized.
Tests of Noncutaneous Organs
When a dermatopathy is suspected to co‐exist with an
underlying systemic disease or endocrinopathy, a complete blood count, small animal chemistry profile, and
urinalysis may be indicated. These basic tests are also
advised to obtain baseline information prior to initiating

various treatments. Specific endocrine tests are available
for the evaluation of hypothyroidism, hypercortisolism,
and sex hormone abnormalities. Various imaging modalities may also be indicated such as radiography and ultrasound. Advanced imaging modalities, including magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography
(CT) scans, may also be needed in some cases. The indications and use of these various tests will be elaborated
upon in the relevant chapters of this section.

­Therapeutic Plan and Client Education
After thorough evaluation, the therapeutic plan most
beneficial to the patient can be formulated. Client education is one of the most important aspects of treating the
dermatologic patient adequately. Because many skin diseases are controllable but not curable, close communication is essential for a satisfactory long‐term result.

Principles of Therapy of Dermatologic Diseases
Sandra N. Koch, DVM, MS, DACVD
College of Veterinary Medicine, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA

This chapter gives a broad overview of a variety of
­dermatologic therapies and presents the most important
general principles that guide their use, including
­supporting concepts and most common indications. The
reader is referred to other chapters in this textbook or
reference therapeutic books for details regarding the
treatment of various dermatologic diseases using the
therapy modalities discussed here.

­Topical Therapy
Topical therapy is a useful and versatile treatment
modality widely used for skin and otic disorders.
Advantages of topical therapy include direct delivery to
the target tissue resulting in high drug concentration at
the treated site, replacement or reduction of the usage of
systemic ­therapy, avoidance of drug metabolism or gastrointestinal disturbances, lower cost compared to most
systemic medications and less probability of causing
microbial resistance as seen with systemic antibiotics.
On the other hand, topical therapy requires client education for proper use, and can be time‐consuming and
clients because of staining or greasy
unpleasant to ­
preparations.
There are many factors that need to be considered
when prescribing topical therapy such as the condition
of the skin and ears, the type of lesions present, the need
for residual activity, the presence of hair in the area, and
the body region and surface area to be treated. Other
­factors to consider include the active and inactive ingredients (i.e., vehicle) of the medication and administration
of adequate drug volume. The vehicle influences treatment effectiveness and may have therapeutic effects;
however, it may cause adverse effects such as irritant
dermatitis. The ability of the owners to follow instructions and frequency of use should also be considered.

Lastly, there are different formulations or delivery systems available that should be tailored to each patient’s
needs. These formulations include shampoos, rinses,
lotions, powders, creams, ointments, emulsions, sprays,
gels, mousses, spot‐on solutions, wipes, and ear cleaner
solutions. They may have similar active ingredients but
their vehicle, efficacy, irritant or cosmetic aspects, ease
of administration, and cost will be different according to
each formulation and method of application.
Common Formulations of Topical Agents
Shampoos

Medicated shampoos may be effective for cleansing and
hydrating the skin, soothing and reducing pruritus, and preventing or treating skin infections. Shampoos may be used
for localized or generalized skin disease and may vary in
their lathering effect. The type of shampoo and frequency of
use are decided on an individual basis according to the skin
disorder and ability of the client to bathe their pet. In most
shampoo formulations, the active ingredients have limited
residual effect; therefore it is generally recommended to
keep the shampoo in contact with the skin for 5–10 minutes
prior to rinsing. Shampoos are also frequently used as maintenance therapy, such as in allergic animals and those predisposed to skin infections. Different shampoos may be used
on an alternating basis or on different parts of the body.
Medicated shampoos are typically classified based on
their function, as emollient and moisturizing or hypoallergenic, antipruritic and/or anti–inflammatory, antiseborrheic (keratolytic and/or keratoplastic, and/or degreasing),
antibacterial and/or antifungal, and antiparasitic.
Rinses

Rinses are commonly used after shampoos and are available in different forms including those that need to be
rinsed off, leave‐on formulations that dry on the skin and

such as microemulsion sprays which can work well on
large body surfaces without the need for baths. The active
ingredients in rinses may vary but they often include
moisturizers, antiseborrheic agents, and antimicrobials.
