antimicrobial, and antiparasitic ingredients. Some animals may not allow their application. Alcohol‐containing
sprays, which are meant to quickly dry, may be irritating,
particularly in acute inflamed skin disorders.

Lotions

Mousses

Lotions are often used for their cooling, antipruritic,
antimicrobial, and drying effects, depending on their
inactive agents such as water, alcohol and propylene
­glycol, and their anti–inflammatory, antipruritic, and
­antimicrobial active ingredients. They are usually recommended for a determined period of time but may also
be used for maintenance.

Mousses are a new form of topical therapy in veterinary
medicine and provide an easy and pleasant way for pet
owners to deliver active ingredients to haired and nonhaired skin. The product must be applied directly to the
skin in order to be effective. Mousses may contain antipruritic, antimicrobial, and antiseborrheic agents.

Creams and Ointments

Spot‐on formulations include flea and tick preventatives,
fatty acids, ceramides and keratolytic or antiseborrheic
agents. These formulations are usually lipophilic with
large molecular weights which slow dermal absorption,
lower systemic bioavailability, and provide a large area of
distribution.

Creams and ointments lubricate the skin, facilitate hydration of the stratum corneum, help prevent water loss, and
form a protective covering increasing the p
­ enetration of
active ingredients. However, these formulations are contraindicated in exudative areas. They may contain water‐
washable bases such as polyethylene glycol or hydrophobic
oils such as mineral oil. The main disadvantages of these
products include their somewhat difficult application to
hairy skin, their occlusive properties which can potentially
lead to folliculitis, and they can be greasy and messy (ointments). Also, their use is ­limited to localized and small
areas such as the paws, elbows, and nose. They are also
often used in ears. Most commonly, these formulations
contain antimicrobials, anti–inflammatory, antipruritic,
keratolytic, and ultraviolet (UV) radiation‐blocking
agents. Creams are white and nongreasy and contain preservatives to protect against growth of bacteria and fungi.
Ointments are oil based or emulsions of oil and water
droplets that do not dissipate well when applied to the
skin. They are greasy and clear and do not require preservatives. Ointments are selected when increased absorption, hydration, and occlusion are required.
Gels

Gels do not have a sticky residue and are not messy, compared to creams and ointments. Most commonly, they
contain anti–inflammatory, antimicrobial, and keratolytic
agents in combination with other inactive agents such as
propylene glycol and carboxypolymethylene. They are
mostly used for localized treatment or small skin areas.
Sprays

Sprays can be very useful and convenient for the treatment of large body areas when frequent baths are not
possible and can also complement the use of medicated
shampoos. They may also facilitate treatment of difficult
areas such as perianal areas and the interdigital aspects
of paws. Sprays may contain emollients, moisturizers,

Spot‐On Solutions

Wipes

Medicated wipes are very useful for treatment of intertriginous areas such as the interdigital, perianal, perivulvar, facial, and tail skinfolds. They contain antimicrobials
or antiseptics and can be used for prevention and treatment of bacterial and yeast skin infections. Alcohol‐­
containing wipes may be irritating, particularly in acute
inflamed skin disorders.
Ear Cleaner Solutions

Ear cleaners can be used for the treatment of ear
­infections, on a maintenance regimen to help prevent
infections, and after bathing or swimming to keep the
ear canals dry. Ear cleaners are often used in conjunction
with topical antibiotics, antifungals, and/or glucocorticoids. The frequency of cleaning varies from once daily
to once weekly according to the needs of each patient. It
is important to demonstrate the cleaning technique to
pet owners to improve compliance and efficacy.
The choice of cleaner depends on the condition of the
ears. Ceruminolytic agents help remove dry waxy material by dissolving cerumen and include propylene glycol,
mineral and vegetable oils, essential oils, glycerine, and
xylene. Astringents work as drying agents, reducing
humidity and helping prevent maceration. They are indicated for moist ears and include isopropanol, boric acid,
benzoic acid, salicylic acid, acetic acid, and aluminum
acetate. Drying agents are typically used after debris or
exudate has been removed from the ear canals with a
ceruminolytic agent. Surfactants emulsify debris and are
good for removing tightly adhered debris and include
docusate, calcium sulphosuccinate, and sodium lauryl

purulent
­discharge and treat bacterial and fungal infections; they
include chlorhexidine, ethylenediaminetetraacetic ­acid‐

The appropriate use and indications for the various ear

­Systemic Therapy
Systemic therapy is commonly implemented to treat various dermatoses; however, it requires much knowledge
of the patient’s medical history, drug pharmacokinetics
and pharmacodynamics, potential side‐effects, toxicity
monitoring guidelines, and potential drug interactions.
The veterinarian needs to be familiar with the disease
being treated and be aware of all treatment options and
decide on the most appropriate therapeutic intervention
in order to achieve the best clinical efficacy with the least
possible toxicity.

­Categories and Indications of Topical
and Systemic Therapy
Some of the major categories used in veterinary dermatology include anti–inflammatory, antipruritic, immunosuppressive, antibacterial and antifungal agents, antiparasitics
and medications to treat hormonal disorders.
Anti–inflammatory Agents
Topical anti–inflammatory agents include glucocorticoids
and essential fatty acids. Topical glucocorticoids may be a
useful adjunct to systemic therapy in the treatment of both
allergic and autoimmune skin disease. They are often used
in pruritic and/or inflammatory skin and otic conditions.
Common topical glucocorticoids include betamethasone,
hydrocortisone, isoflupredone acetate, fluocinolone,
mometasone furoate monohydrate, and triamcinolone acetonide. These products are available in the form of ointments, creams, lotions, gels, wipes, shampoos, rinses, and
sprays. Many of the available products are otic preparations
containing antimicrobials that are also used extra‐label on
the skin. Topical essential fatty acids may be used as adjunctive therapy to treat inflammatory dermatoses including
atopic dermatitis and sebaceous adenitis, as well as keratinization disorders. They are available in formulations such as
spot‐on, sprays, shampoos, rinses, and mousses.
Systemic products with anti–inflammatory and/or
antipruritic and immunosuppressive effects include
­

glucocorticoids, cyclosporine, oclacitinib maleate,
­
­essential fatty acids, pentoxifylline, and a combination of
a tetracycline and niacinamide. Systemic glucocorticoid
therapy is somewhat arbitrarily divided into anti‐­
inflammatory and immunosuppressive, depending on
the dosage used to treat the disease.
There are many indications for the anti–inflammatory
effects of glucocorticoids including treatment of pruritic
dermatoses such as allergic skin diseases and otitis.
Indications for the immunosuppressive effects of glucocorticoids include many autoimmune skin disorders such
as the pemphigus complex and various sterile inflammatory dermatoses. Commonly used systemic gluco­
corticoids include methylprednisolone, prednisone or
prednisolone, dexamethasone, and triamcinolone acetonide. The glucocorticoid potency must be chosen based
on the disease being treated, its severity, and the patient’s
overall health. It has been shown that only 21% of orally
administered prednisone was present in the blood of
cats when compared to prednisolone, suggesting poor
prednisone absorption or inadequate conversion into
­
prednisolone in the liver. Therefore, prednisolone should
be used in cats instead of prednisone due to potential
lack of response to prednisone. Injectable glucocorticoids should be avoided for treatment of chronic skin and
ear diseases because this route of administration does
not offer any therapeutic benefits over oral administration and is associated with more severe hypothalamic‐
pituitary‐adrenal axis side‐effects.
Cyclosporine is a calcineurin inhibitor that is used as
an anti–inflammatory or immunosuppressive medication according to the condition being treated and the
dose used. It is labeled for the treatment of atopic dermatitis in dogs and cats. Other indications include perianal
fistulae in dogs, sebaceous adenitis, autoimmune diseases such as the pemphigus complex (particularly in
cats), and various sterile and inflammatory skin disorders. For most treated conditions, cyclosporine may take
4–6 weeks to be effective.
Oclacitinib maleate, a novel immunomodulatory drug,
is a selective Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor, preferentially
JAK‐1, labeled for the control of pruritus and inflammation associated with canine allergic skin diseases, including atopic dermatitis, in dogs at least 12 months of age. It
has a rapid mode of action in most patients, reducing
pruritus within 24 hours.
Essential fatty acids are nutritional supplements with
anti–inflammatory properties. They may be used concurrently with other medications to treat pruritic and/or
inflammatory dermatoses such as atopic dermatitis,
sebaceous adenitis, and symmetric onychodystrophy, as
well as keratinization disorders. They may also help
improve the skin barrier and hair coat quality and
­ameliorate dry and scaly skin. Omega‐3 formulations

1399

VetBooks.ir

1400

Section 12 Skin and Ear Diseases

(containing eicosapentaenoic acid [EPA] and docosahexaenoic acid [DHA]) are usually recommended for inflammatory conditions such as allergic skin diseases, while
omega‐6 or omega‐3/omega‐6 combination products
are typically recommended for keratinization disorders
or to improve the skin barrier. There is no current
­evidence of the ideal formulation, combination, dosage
or ratio of essential fatty acids and many different formulations are available. It may take 8–12 weeks for full
­clinical benefit to be seen.
Pentoxifylline is a methylxanthine derivative with
important anti–inflammatory and rheologic properties
which results in increased red blood cell pliability, an
especially important feature for the treatment of ischemic
dermatopathies such as vasculitis. It may be used as an
adjunctive or single agent for the treatment of various
dermatoses including vaccine‐induced dermatopathies,
canine familial dermatomyositis, symmetric onychodystrophy, cutaneous vasculitis, and various sterile inflammatory skin diseases. It may take 4–6 weeks for clinical
improvement to be seen.
Combinations of a tetracycline and niacinamide have
been used to treat a number of immune‐mediated
­diseases such as discoid lupus erythematosus, pemphigus foliaceus, symmetric onychodystrophy, and sterile
granulomatous diseases with variable response and a lag
period for efficacy of 4–6 weeks.
Antipruritic Agents
Topical antipruritic substances can provide temporary
relief and soothing effect for itching and also pain (e.g.,
lidocaine), and may be used for adjunctive treatment of
localized skin conditions including minor skin irritations, allergic or pruritic reactions, acute moist dermatitis, intertrigo, and acral lick dermatitis. These agents
include colloidal oatmeal, diphenhydramine hydrochloride (HCl), lidocaine, neutralized zinc and pramoxine HCl, and glucocorticoids (previously discussed).
Depending on the product, they are available as powders,
solutions, shampoos, lotions, conditioners, rinses, sprays,
gels, ointments, and creams.
Systemic antipruritic medications commonly used
include antihistamines and glucocorticoids (previously
discussed). Antihistamines are usually indicated for the
management of histamine‐mediated pruritic and allergic
skin diseases including urticaria and insect bite hypersensitivity. Despite the frequent use of antihistamines to
treat atopic dermatitis, currently there is no conclusive
evidence of the efficacy of type 1 antihistamines
for ­treatment of chronic and acute flares of canine atopic
dermatitis. The response to any selected antihistamine is generally individualized and unpredictable.
Commonly used antihistamines include amitriptyline

­ iphenhydramine, hydroxyzine HCl or pamoate,
HCl, d
chlorpheniramine maleate, and doxepin HCl. Their sedative effect can be beneficial when treating pruritic skin
disorders. Although the newer generation antihistamines such as fexofenadine HCl and cetirizine HCl present a more ­convenient once‐daily dosage, there is no
current evidence that these antihistamines have superior
efficacy compared to the older generation antihistamines. However, their less sedative effect may be a disadvantage for the treatment of pruritic skin disorders. A
novel anti-IL31 monoclonal antibody therapy, labeled
for the treatment of canine atopic dermatitis, is available
for subcutaneous administration, under veterinarian
supervision, with 4–8 weeks of efficacy duration.
Immunosuppressive Agents
Topical immunosuppressive agents include tacrolimus
and glucocorticoids (previously discussed). Tacrolimus is
a calcineurin inhibitor similar to ciclosporin; however, it is
available as an ointment and is 100% more potent. It may
be beneficial as adjunct therapy for allergic skin ­diseases,
discoid lupus erythematosus, pemphigus e­ rythematosus,
localized cutaneous vasculopathies, and perianal fistula.
Systemic immunosuppressive agents are commonly
used for the management of immune‐mediated skin
diseases including autoimmune diseases, such as the
­
pemphigus complex, cutaneous bullous diseases, and
various forms of cutaneous lupus erythematosus. These
medications include azathioprine, chlorambucil and
cyclophosphamide, in addition to glucocorticoids and
cyclosporine (previously discussed).
Azathioprine is a derivative of 6‐mercaptopurine and
is commonly used in conjunction with a glucocorticoid
for the first weeks or months as there is a lag period of up
to six weeks before its effect can be noted. The use of
azathioprine in cats is not recommended because cats
are very susceptible to bone marrow suppression when
treated with azathioprine.
Chlorambucil and cyclophosphamide are alkylating
agents that are more commonly used individually or in
conjunction with other drugs such as glucocorticoids.
Their lag period for efficacy is usually up to eight weeks.
Antibacterial Agents
Topical antibacterial agents are often used to treat localized bacterial skin infections such as those associated
with wounds, acne, perianal dermatitis, pododermatitis,
allergic skin diseases, acral lick dermatitis, and otitis
externa. They can also be a good adjunct to systemic
therapy in severe or generalized cases of bacterial skin
infection. These agents include acetic acid, boric acid,
bacitracin, benzoyl peroxide, clindamycin, gentamicin,

VetBooks.ir

158 Principles of Therapy of Dermatologic Diseases

neomycin, mupirocin, nitrofurazone, silver sulfadiazine,
nisin, and enzyme systems. Often, topical antibacterial
agents contain glucocorticoids and antifungals which
enhance their effect against other organisms and help
reduce inflammation and pruritus. Benzoyl peroxide
and clindamycin are often efficacious products for
acne cases. Mupirocin is particularly effective against
Staphylococcus infections, including methicillin‐resistant
bacteria. These products are usually available as creams,
ointments, gels, sprays, or wipes and some may also be
available in the form of shampoos, such as benzoyl peroxide, and ear solutions, such as acetic and boric acid.
Systemic antibiotics are usually indicated to treat
severe and generalized bacterial skin infections including superficial and deep pyodermas and wounds. The
use of systemic antibiotics in cases of otitis media
remains controversial; however, high doses of antibiotics
may be used in combination with topical therapy in
selective cases. The most common systemic antibiotics
used include amoxicillin‐clavulanic acid, cefovecin
sodium, cefpodoxime proxetil, cephalexin, clindamycin
HCl, potentiated sulfonamides, doxycycline HCl, chloramphenicol, ­enrofloxacin, and marbofloxacin. Ideally,
for recurrent or chronic infections, systemic antibiotic
selection should be based on bacterial culture and sensitivity. Broad‐spectrum antibiotics such as fluoroquinolones should be avoided empirically and as first‐choice
agents as they may select for bacterial resistance.
Ciprofloxacin has poor and variable oral bioavailability
in dogs and cats and should be avoided in these species.
Antifungal Agents
Topical antifungals are usually prescribed for localized
fungal infections, otitis externa associated with
Malassezia infections, or as concurrent therapy with
systemic medications for more generalized or severe
cases. The most commonly used topical antifungal
agents include clotrimazole, miconazole nitrate, nystatin, ketoconazole, posaconazole, terbinafine, and lime
sulfur. Some of these products may ­contain a combination of glucocorticoids and antibiotics which might be
beneficial when concurrent bacterial infection and
inflammation and/or pruritus are present. These agents
are usually available as creams, ointments, gels, solutions, shampoos, rinses, and wipes.
Systemic antifungals are usually indicated for extensive
or severe superficial, subcutaneous and systemic or deep
fungal infections including dermatophytosis, Malassezia
dermatitis, onychomycosis, candidiasis, sporotrichosis,
blastomycosis, cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, and
aspergillosis. Systemic antifungals may also be used in
severe otitis externa cases in conjunction with topical
therapy. The most commonly used systemic antifungal

agents include ketoconazole, itraconazole, fluconazole,
terbinafine, and amphotericin B.
Ketoconazole is most commonly used in cases of
Malassezia dermatitis and dermatophytosis in dogs. It
should not be used solely as a first choice for systemic
mycosis and should be avoided in cats due to its hepatotoxic effects.
Itraconazole is better tolerated in cats compared to
ketoconazole. Itraconazole is also commonly used in
­systemic infections and Malassezia dermatitis, but may
be cost‐prohibitive in large‐breed dogs.
Fluconazole can be used for Malassezia dermatitis,
but it is mostly useful in systemic infections when brain
or ocular penetration is needed.
Terbinafine has been reported to be effective in
Malassezia dermatitis and can also be used for dermatophytosis and systemic or deep mycoses.
Amphotericin B is mostly indicated for cases of systemic mycosis but potential nephrotoxicity is a limiting
factor to its use. Lipid‐based formulations are available
and are much less nephrotoxic than the traditional
(deoxycholate) form.
Antiparasitics
Antiparasitic products are used for prevention of fleas,
ticks and lice, and treatment of parasitic diseases such as
ear mites, demodicosis, sarcoptic mange, and cheyletiellosis. Most commonly used antiparasitic formulations
include collars, sprays, shampoos, dips, spot‐on solutions, otic solutions, and ointments.
Amitraz solution diluted and applied as a dip is labeled
for the treatment of canine demodicosis. Amitraz should
be avoided or used carefully in cats. Rotenone ointment
may also be used in localized forms of canine demodicosis.
Flea and tick preventatives are available in a variety of
combinations and include deltamethrin, imidacloprid, flumethrin, fipronil, (S)‐methoprene, dinotefuran, pyriproxyfen, permethrin, spinetoram, moxidectin, and indoxacarb.
An imidacloprid and moxidectin combination has also
been used successfully for the treatment of sarcoptic
mange, cheyletiellosis, and mild cases of demodicosis.
Products containing permethrin should not be used in
cats due to their sensitivity to this compound. Other pyrethroids should be used carefully and according to label
instructions, particularly in small kittens. Lime sulfur dip
is effective against canine and feline scabies (Notoedres),
feline surface demodicosis (Demodex gatoi), cheyletiellosis and lice, but it is ineffective against fleas. There are several effective products available for the treatment of ear
mites including products containing pyrethrin, ivermectin, milbemycin, selamectin, and thiabendazole.
Systemic antiparasitic agents include ivermectin,
doramectin, moxidectin, milbemycin oxime, selamectin,

Ivermectin, doramectin, moxidectin, and milbemycin oxime are macrocyclic lactones that have been

Selamectin is also a macrocyclic lactone and is labeled

of fleas, ticks and biting lice, and treatment of sarcoptic
mange in dogs and otoacariasis in dogs and cats. It has
also been used for the treatment of cheyletiellosis with
good results.
Nitenpyram is a neonicotinoid labeled for the control
and treatment of flea infestation in dogs and cats. Since
it is an adulticide, it should be combined with an insect
growth regulator.
Lufenuron is a benzoylurea compound that is used
as an insect growth regulator for flea control in dogs
and cats.
Spinosad stimulates the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor in insects with efficacy against adult fleas in dogs
and cats.
Isoxazolines work by selective inhibition of GABA- and
glutamate-gated chloride channels, leading to hyper-­
excitation and death of the flea or tick. They are indicated
for the treatment and prevention of adult fleas and tick
infestations. Additionally, they have been used successfully

extra-label for the treatment of parasitic diseases such as
demodicosis, sarcoptic mange, cheyletiellosis, and otodectes in dogs and cats.
Systemic Medications for the Treatment
of Hormonal Disorders
Systemic medications commonly used for the treatment
of hormonal disorders include mitotane, trilostane, melatonin, and levothyroxine sodium.
Mitotane is an adrenolytic agent that selectively
destroys the zonas fasciculata and reticularis of the adrenal cortex, while generally sparing the zona glomerulosa.
Mitotane is indicated for the treatment of pituitary‐
dependent hyperadrenocorticism in dogs and may also
be used in cases of adrenal‐dependent hyperadrenocorticism; however, the induction dose may be higher and the
duration longer compared to pituitary‐dependent cases.
Trilostane is an adrenal suppressant that reversibly
blocks 3‐beta‐hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, an enzyme
necessary for steroid synthesis in the adrenal cortex.
Trilostane is approved for the treatment of hyperadrenocorticism of pituitary or adrenal origin in dogs and may
also be beneficial for the treatment of hyperadrenocorticism in cats and alopecia X or hair cycle arrest in dogs.
Melatonin is a hormone synthesized in the pineal
gland used in dogs to treat alopecia X with anecdotal
success in 50% of cases. It may take 3–4 months for
­beneficial effects to be noticed.
Levothyroxine sodium is indicated for the treatment of
hypothyroidism in dogs and cats.

Atopic Dermatitis
Alison Diesel, DVM, DACVD
College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
In the dog, atopic dermatitis is defined as “a genetically
predisposed inflammatory and pruritic allergic skin disease with characteristic clinical features associated with
IgE antibodies most commonly directed against environmental allergens.” Although the exact pathogenesis of
disease development is incompletely understood, current theory supports a multifactorial involvement of
genetic predisposition, immunologic dysregulation, and
epidermal barrier dysfunction.
During sensitization, it is suspected that epidermal
barrier defects allow enhanced contact of allergens with
Langerhans cells in the epidermis. These cells capture
the allergens and migrate to regional lymph nodes, a­ cting
as antigen‐presenting cells. In the lymph nodes,
Langerhans cells interact with T lymphocytes, creating a
skewed distribution and formation of type 2 T helper
(Th2) cells. Upon repeated exposure to the allergen, the
sensitized Th2 cells produce a variety of inflammatory
cytokines which promote production of IgE and infiltration of inflammatory cells into the skin.
Increased levels of interleukin (IL)‐4, IL‐5, and IL‐13
are noted in dogs with atopic dermatitis, along with
­elevated levels of interferon (INF)‐gamma. Recent studies have also documented elevated levels of IL‐31 in dogs
with atopic dermatitis. This novel cytokine is also produced by Th2 cells and appears to be responsible for
much of the pruritus associated with clinical allergic skin
disease. In more chronic lesions, the response favors Th1
cytokine production which will contribute to perpetuation of the inflammatory process.
Historically, atopic dermatitis in dogs was believed to
be due primarily to immunologic dysregulation and
genetic predisposition (as evidenced by the current definition of the disease). However, more recent evidence
supports abnormalities in the epidermal barrier which

may also influence disease development. Abnormal
structure and composition of the stratum corneum intercellular lipid lamellae, altered ceramide content, and
abnormal expression of filaggrin (the epidermal filament‐­
associated protein responsible for binding keratin molecules) have been documented in many dogs with atopic
dermatitis. Subsequent to these structural abnormalities, increased transepidermal water loss is also noted.
The combination of these changes can increase inflammation and severity of disease. Whether these changes
are seen in all dogs with atopic dermatitis or only a
­percentage of patients is currently unknown. There is a
similar disease in dogs, termed “atopic‐like dermatitis,”
which manifests with identical history and clinical signs
(see below), but in which documentation of IgE involvement cannot be confirmed. Epidermal barrier dysfunction may be a more important contributing factor for
disease development in these patients.
In the cat, the etiology and pathogenesis are even less
well defined. Although many of the immunologic mechanisms appear to be similar to those seen in the dog,
there is a question of the true implication of IgE involvement with disease development. Additionally, epidermal
barrier function has not been evaluated in the cat as a
contributing factor. For these and other reasons, many
prefer to use the term “nonflea nonfood hypersensitivity
dermatitis” when discussing atopic dermatitis in cats.

­Epidemiology
Atopic dermatitis can present in dogs and cats worldwide, though geographic differences may play a role in
the development of disease (e.g., clinical signs may manifest earlier in life in animals in warm weather climates
where the level of allergen exposure is rather high), as
well as prevalence in that region. A few older studies have

reported variable prevalence of the disease, ranging from
less than 5% to greater than 25% of the canine ­population;
true prevalence of disease is uncertain. For the past few
years, atopic dermatitis (or “skin allergies”) has been consistently listed in the top 10 reasons for dogs and cats to
be presented to veterinarians in the United States.

­Signalment
Depending on literature cited, age of onset may range
from 4 months to 7 years, though the majority of dogs and
cats with atopic dermatitis will typically start to manifest
clinical disease between 6 months and 3 years of age.
There does not appear to be consensus on whether the
disease is more prevalent in females or males, or whether
sex predilection affects disease development. Although
any breed of dog may be diagnosed with atopic dermatitis,
breed predisposition has been reported due to the genetic
component of disease pathogenesis. More commonly
affected breeds include but are not limited to Boston terrier, boxer, Chinese shar‐pei, Dalmatian, English bulldog,
German shepherd, golden retriever, Labrador retriever,
pug, and West Highland white terrier dogs. Although
genetic involvement has also been noted in cats, no specific breed predispositions have been identified.

the inguinal region of a dog with atopic dermatitis.

­History and Clinical Signs
The hallmark of atopic dermatitis in both dogs and cats
is pruritus, which will often be reported as mild at first
but progresses to become more moderate to severe as
the disease advances. Depending on which specific allergens are involved and/or flare factors in the animal’s particular environment, pruritus may be present seasonally
or nonseasonally. This may also be affected by geographic location; in dogs and cats with historically mild
disease, the severity might increase if they move to a
warmer climate where allergen load is higher or different
from what they were exposed to historically. If concurrent allergic conjunctivitis or rhinitis is present, serous
ocular or nasal discharge, sneezing, or congestion,
respectively, may also be present with pruritic skin. In
cats, feline asthma may also be a concurrent finding.
In early stages of disease, pruritus may present sine
materia, or without concurrent lesions. More often,
though, dogs without secondary bacterial skin infection
or yeast overgrowth will present with fairly symmetric,
variably erythematous macules and patches (Figure 159.1)
or small papular lesions (Figure 159.2). Additionally,
signs of self‐trauma may be noted in the form of excoriations (often linear), hemorrhagic crusts, self‐induced
alopecia/barbered hair, hyperpigmentation, and lichenification (Figure 159.3).

Figure 159.2 Pinpoint, faint papules on the sternum of a dog with
mild atopic dermatitis.

Uncommonly, urticarial lesions (hives) may be seen in
dogs with atopic dermatitis. Salivary staining of the hair
is commonly noted, particularly in light‐colored
dogs, which also supports the presence of pruritus
(Figure 159.4).
On close physical examination, the clinician will often
find broken pieces of barbered hair stuck between the
gingival tissue and dental arcade, another “clue” that pruritus is present. When additional lesions are noted, such
as pustules, crusts, or epidermal collarettes, alternative
disease entities including parasites (Demodex) and

­infections (particularly superficial bacterial pyoderma
and dermatophytosis) need to be investigated.
The distribution pattern of lesions and pruritus is most
helpful when considering atopic dermatitis. Clinical disease in dogs most commonly affects ventral sparsely
haired areas including the abdomen, thorax, inguinal,
and axillary folds. Facial distribution including periocular skin and muzzle is also common. The dorsal and ventral interdigital webbing of the paws along with the lower
portion of the limbs is often concurrently pruritic; flexural surfaces of the elbows are included in this body
region. Otitis externa and perianal pruritus are often
reported by owners, and may manifest as head shaking

or scooting, respectively. In most cases, the dorsal aspect
of the dog is spared, unless concurrent flea allergy dermatitis is noted (caudal hind end distribution including
rump and tail head). In some dogs, a more widespread
distribution of lesions and pruritus is noted. This may be
seen more commonly in different breeds including
German shepherd, Chinese shar‐pei, and West Highland
white terrier dogs, which have shown phenotypic diversity compared to other dog breeds with more standard
distribution of lesions reflecting atopic dermatitis.
In cats, the distribution pattern and clinical lesions
tend to be less consistent. Cats will, however, generally
present with one or more cutaneous reaction patterns:
cervicofacial dermatitis (head, neck, pinnal pruritus)
(Figure 159.5), self‐induced noninflammatory alopecia
(Figure 159.6), miliary dermatitis (Figure 159.7) and/or
eosinophilic skin lesions (i.e., eosinophilic plaque)
(Figure 159.8), eosinophilic granuloma, and indolent
ulcer (Figure 153.9). None of these reaction patterns,
however, are pathognomonic for allergic skin disease in
the cat. Other causes of pruritus need to be investigated
prior to diagnosing atopic dermatitis. This is especially
true for eosinophilic lesions (particularly plaques and
indolent ulcers) as these are often manifestations of bacterial pyoderma in the cat.
In people, a phenomenon known as the “atopic march”
has been described where the disease starts with atopic
dermatitis or eczema and progresses to rhinitis and
asthma. Although the “atopic march” has not been

­Diagnosis
The diagnosis of atopic dermatitis is based on a consistent and fitting history, clinical signs, and exclusion of
all other pruritic dermatoses. There is no test which

VetBooks.ir

159 Atopic Dermatitis

definitively diagnoses atopic dermatitis (this is true for
dogs, cats, horses, and humans); rather, it is a diagnosis
of exclusion. This includes ruling out pruritus due to
the presence of parasites (fleas, lice, Sarcoptes,
Otodectes, Cheyletiella, Demodex), infections (staphylococcal pyoderma, Malassezia overgrowth, dermatophytosis), flea allergy dermatitis, and cutaneous adverse
reaction to food. As pruritus is an additive process,
meaning that several contributing factors/diseases can
result in the manifestation of pruritus in a given patient,
and multiple factors may be present at the same time
(e.g., atopic dermatitis with secondary superficial
­bacterial folliculitis), it is imperative to rule out confounding factors prior to arriving at a diagnosis of
atopic dermatitis. Additionally, every patient is slightly
different with regard to their “pruritic threshold.” Once
secondary problems or confounding pruritic dermatoses are identified and addressed, the clinician might
note that the patient’s baseline level of pruritus is much
less severe than what was initially thought.
Recently, a set of criteria has been proposed to aid in
the diagnosis of atopic dermatitis in dogs. Granted, the
parameters suggested may be seen along with other pruritic skin diseases but if the clinician takes the appropriate steps to rule out parasites and infections, the presence
of these criteria strongly supports a clinical diagnosis.
The presence of five of the criteria has a specificity of
79% and a sensitivity of 85% to differentiate dogs with
atopic dermatitis from those with other chronic and
­pruritic skin diseases. The presence of a sixth criterion
increases specificity to 89%, but sensitivity is decreased
to 58%. The criteria (referred to as Favrot’s criteria) are

lack of standardization protocols lead to a great deal of
variability between tests. Currently, comparison of tests
from different laboratories does not show appreciable
correlation.
Intradermal allergen testing is considered to be the
“gold standard” for documentation of IgE involvement in
atopic dermatitis in the dog. Intradermal injection of
various environmental allergens causes mast cell degranulation, extravasation of edema fluid, erythema, and formation of a wheal by IgE binding with sensitized
molecules (Figure 159.10). Intradermal testing in cats
tends to be more difficult and often frustrating; cats tend
to form less distinct wheals and more subtle positive
reactions when compared to dogs, although the test can
be beneficial in this species as well. This test is best performed by a board‐certified veterinary dermatologist; it
requires practice with regard to technique and interpretation, and cost of allergen upkeep may be prohibitive for
the general practitioner.
It is important to remember that a positive test result
must be viewed in light of the animal’s history and seasonality of disease. Additionally, these allergy tests can
be positive in approximately 50% of animals without a
clinical diagnosis of atopic dermatitis so it is imperative
that serum and intradermal allergen tests are not used to
diagnose disease. Rather, these tests become important
considerations if the owner wishes to pursue immunotherapy for their pet (see below). Their importance
stems from educated guidance on immunotherapy
formulation.

Once a clinical diagnosis of atopic dermatitis has been

With allergen serology tests, radioallergosorbent
(RAST), enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA),

identify the presence of allergen‐specific IgE in the
patient’s serum via colorimetric, fluorometric, or radiometric analysis. Various commercial laboratories utilize
different methodologies for detection of allergen‐­specific
IgE; specificity of the testing reagent (e.g., decreased
cross‐reactivity with IgG), allergen extracts used, and

Several factors can influence the results of allergen
testing, including time of year (particularly if seasonal
variation is noted), strength of allergens, and significant
inflammatory skin disease (either due to atopic dermatitis alone or other concurrent pruritic dermatosis).
Additionally, administration of antipruritic pharmacotherapy can dampen or mask “positive” test results. This
is especially true for intradermal allergen testing. A
recent review proposed optimal and minimal withdrawal
times of antipruritic drugs prior to allergen testing.
Based on a review of the current literature, antihistamines should be withdrawn for at least seven days, oral
and topical glucocorticoids (including otic preparations)
for at least 14 days, and a minimum of 28 days for longer‐
acting injectable glucocorticoids (although many dermatologists recommend at least 4–8 weeks withdrawal)
prior to intradermal allergen testing. There was insufficient evidence to make recommendations for medication withdrawal prior to serology allergen testing; these
tests may be less influenced by the presence of antipruritic pharmacotherapy but care must be taken with
regard to interpretation of results.

­Therapy
As with people and other domestic animal species, there
is no cure for atopic dermatitis in dogs or cats. However,
the disease can be fairly well managed with various therapeutic interventions. Therapy falls into two categories:
medical and allergen‐specific immunotherapy. Medical
therapies aim to primarily address the pruritus and
­discomfort associated with atopic dermatitis, whereas
allergen‐specific immunotherapy attempts to “retrain”
the immune system, shifting back towards a more “normal” Th1 response as opposed to Th2 dysregulation.
Medical Therapy
With regard to medical therapy for atopic dermatitis,
interventions span the spectrum from fairly conservative
to more aggressive. Options for conservative therapy
include implementation of environmental allergen
avoidance, bathing and other topical therapy, antihistamines, and essential fatty acid administration. More
potent, “aggressive” medical therapy includes administration of systemic glucocorticoids, ciclosporin, or oclacitinib. Additional/alternative therapies have also been
evaluated with variable success.
Avoidance

Avoidance of environmental allergens can be rather
difficult, particularly since many dogs and cats with
­

atopic dermatitis show reactions to allergens which cannot easily be avoided or eliminated. Pollens, for example,
are essentially impossible to eliminate. Owners will often
ask about changing the immediate environment to which
the dog or cat is exposed (e.g., removing problematic
trees or grasses from the property). However, the spread
of aeroallergens can have an approximately 100 mile
radius or more, depending on environmental conditions.
The statement “if it is not in your own yard, it might be in
your neighbor’s” holds a large amount of truth.
There is a large market as well for avoidance and reduction of house dust mite allergen (the most common environmental allergen implicated in atopic dermatitis in
dogs worldwide). Special air filters, pillow, and mattress
covers are designed to reduce the load of house dust mite
in the environment, and household cleaning products
have been designed to kill and thereby reduce house dust
mites in the home. These measures do not completely
eliminate allergens from the environment and therefore
are insufficient on their own to reduce severity of disease. Decreased exposure, however, may allow for a
reduced flare of atopic dermatitis and/or provide benefit
as an adjunct intervention with additional therapeutic
measures. Additional recommendations for improved
allergen avoidance include frequent washing of pet and
household bedding, maintained replacement of air filters
in the home, avoiding fresh cut grass (for pollen allergens), and frequent bathing.
Bathing and Other Topical Therapy

Along with mechanical removal of environmental allergens, bathing provides additional therapeutic benefit to
the atopic dog. Shampoos containing antipruritic ingredients such as colloidal oatmeal, pramoxine (topical
analgesic), antihistamine, or glucocorticoids are often
recommended as maintenance therapy for the allergic
dog; interestingly, however, studies have not documented
improvement with any specific ingredient over another.
A small study evaluated a lipid and complex sugar‐­
containing shampoo with and without the addition of
whirlpool bathing; bathing with the shampoo showed
evidence of clinical reduction of pruritus, which was
reduced further when a whirlpool was also used. Taken
together, the physical act of bathing may be the most
important factor for providing relief to the pruritic dog
as opposed to a specific ingredient or formulation. The
above ingredients, however, are benign and often owners
feel their pet experiences more beneficial results when a
particular product or ingredient is used.
Bathing is typically recommended once every 1–2
weeks long term. In the face of an allergic flare, more
­frequent bathing may be beneficial. In dogs where secondary bacterial or yeast skin infections are contributing
factors associated with atopic dermatitis, shampoos

VetBooks.ir

159 Atopic Dermatitis

containing antiseptic ingredients (e.g., chlorhexidine,
­
miconazole, ketoconazole, ethyl lactate) may be better
recommended for maintenance bathing.
Although bathing has historically been considered the
“gold standard” adjunct therapy for allergic dogs, newer
formulations of products are cropping up with increased
frequency. The addition of spray, mousse, and leave‐on
lotion formulations may increase client compliance due
to the decreased effort/time involved in application.
These products often are identical to or mimic their
shampoo counterparts with regard to active ingredients;
depending on the formulation, they may be used to
decrease frequency of bathing, or provide longer acting
beneficial response after the recommended bath. As
many cats are not overly fond of bathing, these alternative formulations may be of added benefit in this species
as part of the therapeutic regime.
Application of topical essential fatty acids, lipids, and
ceramides has been a newer area of investigation for
therapy of canine atopic dermatitis. These products aim
to improve the structure and/or function of the epidermal barrier by “normalizing” lipid and ceramide content
of the epidermis. Much of the information regarding
these therapies has been largely anecdotal; smaller studies indicate that benefits may take several weeks to be
apparent (upwards of 12 weeks to see maximal benefit).
In the mildly atopic patient, these formulations may be
sufficient solely (or with occasional additional conservative therapy) to control disease; however, they are likely
to be insufficient on their own to control a more severely
affected atopic dog. Their benefit in that case may be as
an adjunct therapy, allowing for reduction of more potent
therapeutic interventions. As it is still unclear whether
all or only some dogs with atopic dermatitis manifest
with epidermal barrier dysfunction as part of their clinical disease, the true benefit of these products is largely
uncertain.
Particularly when fairly localized pruritus is present in
the atopic patient, topical glucocorticoids may provide
beneficial results with minimal systemic absorption.
These may come in ocular or otic preparations, or in
topical lotions, creams, or sprays. The efficacy of various
products varies markedly with the potency of the steroid
used. Evidence exists in favor of utilization of a 0.0584%
hydrocortisone aceponate‐containing spray (Cortavance®
Virbac, Canada) or 0.025% budesonide‐containing leave‐
on lotion (Barazone®, Dermcare‐Vet, Australia) for management of atopic dermatitis in the dog; these products,
however, are not necessarily available worldwide (both
are currently unavailable in the USA). Depending on formulation and potency of steroid used, side‐effects can
include some systemic absorption, thinning and
decreased elasticity of the skin, phlebectasia, and milia
formation.

Similar to topical glucocorticoids, application of topical tacrolimus (Protopic® 0.03% or 0.1% ointment,
Astellas Pharma, Illinois, USA) may provide localized
control of pruritus in the atopic dog. This calcineurin
inhibitor acts similarly to ciclosporin; it more specifically
reduces T cell‐mediated inflammation without the side‐
effects of topical glucocorticoid therapy. It does, however, have a much slower onset and may not be beneficial
in the face of an acute pruritic flare.
Antihistamines

The benefit of antihistamines in atopic dermatitis is
markedly uncertain. As the manifestation of pruritus
involves many more inflammatory mediators other than
histamine, which may in fact only account for a very
small part of itch development in an atopic dog or cat,
antihistamine administration by itself may make a negligible difference in the management of the allergic patient.
According to a review of the evidence, their benefit has
not been convincing, particularly in the case of an acute
flare. That said, they may more importantly serve as an
adjunct therapeutic intervention, allowing for reduced
administration of more potent antipruritic therapy, in
particular systemic glucocorticoid administration.
Commonly used antihistamines in the dog include
cetirizine (0.5–1 mg/kg PO q24h), hydroxyzine (2 mg/kg
PO q12h), diphenhydramine (2.2 mg/kg PO q12h), amitriptyline (1–2 mg/kg PO q12h), chlorpheniramine
(0.4 mg/kg PO q8–12h), and loratidine (1 mg/kg PO
q12–24h). Additionally, some evidence exists to suggest
that fexofenadine (1–2 mg/kg PO q24h) may provide sufficient improvement in pruritus in atopic dogs. In cats,
additional options include clemastine (0.25–0.68 mg/kg
PO q12h) and cyproheptadine (2 mg/cat PO q12h). It is
important to remember that every allergic dog and cat is
a bit different; one antihistamine medication may be
more effective than another for reduction of pruritus.
Serial two‐week trials of antihistamine medications may
be necessary to arrive at an adequate therapeutic choice.
Essential Fatty Acids and Other Nutritional
Supplements

Similar to topical ceramide‐ and lipid‐containing products, systemic administration of essential fatty acids may
enhance epidermal barrier function by incorporating
more “normal” skin lipids into the epidermis. Although
the ideal ratio of omega‐3/6 essential fatty acids is
unknown, most dermatologists recommend dosing
based on eicosapentanoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). Supplementation of 180 mg/4.5 kg EPA
and 120 mg/4.5 kg DHA per day is favored for atopic dermatitis; the daily dose is calculated based on the concentration of EPA and DHA in a particular product.
Additional nutritional supplements such as choline,

1409

VetBooks.ir

1410

Section 12 Skin and Ear Diseases

­nicotinamide, histidine, and inositol have been shown to
possibly augment barrier function in healthy dogs by
increasing production of ceramide skin lipids; whether
they have beneficial results in dogs with atopic dermatitis, however, is uncertain. As with some of the other conservative medical therapies, their most important benefit
may be in the form of adjunct therapy for the disease,
thereby decreasing the need for additional medical
interventions.
Glucocorticoids

Glucocorticoids have historically been touted as a mainstay therapy for atopic dermatitis in dogs and cats. Their
efficacy in management of pruritus associated with the
disease is without question; in fact, excellent response to
glucocorticoid therapy can be a key factor in confirming
a clinical diagnosis of atopic dermatitis. Strong evidence
exists with regard to efficacy, particularly for controlling
nonlocalized pruritus associated with atopic dermatitis.
Particularly for the acute flare, short‐course oral glucocorticoid administration can be highly effective in managing the atopic patient. Recommended dosing for oral
glucocorticoids (prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone) is initiation of therapy at 0.5 mg/kg PO q12–
24h and then reducing to the lowest possible (ideally
alternate‐day) dosing which provides sufficient comfort.
In cats, it is imperative that either prednisolone or methylprednisolone be prescribed as most cats do not respond
as well to the prodrug (prednisone). Additionally, allergic
cats often require a higher initial dose (1–2 mg/kg PO
q24h) for clinical effect. The use of long‐acting injectable
glucocorticoids should be avoided for the management
of chronic inflammatory diseases such as atopic
­dermatitis, as they have a much stronger effect on the
hypothalamic‐pituitary‐adrenal axis. Moreover, their
antipruritic/­
antiinflammatory effect is not superior
compared to oral short‐acting glucocorticoids.
Although highly effective and cost‐effective (even for
large patients), the side‐effects of continued long‐term
glucocorticoid administration are concerning. Clinicians
are encouraged to consider and pursue alternative therapy for atopic dermatitis if glucocorticoid administration
is necessary for several months of the year to provide
benefit.
Ciclosporin

As with glucocorticoids, there is strong evidence to support ciclosporin administration for management of
atopic dermatitis in dogs and cats. This calcineurin
inhibitor more specifically targets T cell‐mediated
inflammation associated with atopic dermatitis. It is
important, however, to remember that the modified version of the drug (e.g., Atopica®, Elanco Animal Health,
Indiana, USA) must be administered for predicted

­efficacy. This microemulsion of the parent drug is more
predictably absorbed and metabolized in the dog and cat
compared to nonmodified formulations.
Dosing is initially recommended to be 5–7 mg/kg PO
q24h. Cats, particularly those with indolent ulcers, may
require a higher initial dose (7–10 mg/kg PO q24h) to
achieve initial beneficial results. When remission is
achieved, this dose or frequency of administration may
often be decreased while still achieving similar clinical
benefit on a long‐term basis. Although it is recommended to be given on an empty stomach, administration with food has not been proven to alter clinical
improvement. Additionally, drug level monitoring is
generally not indicated for the allergic patient; therapeutic drug levels do not typically correlate with clinical
improvement. Obtaining ciclosporin drug levels may,
however, be beneficial in a dog or cat with a clinical
­diagnosis of atopic dermatitis that is not responding
favorably to therapy.
Compared to glucocorticoids, ciclosporin is generally
better tolerated with fewer side‐effects, even long term.
This is not to say that side‐effects do not occur; it is recommended to monitor basic internal health (e.g., complete blood count, serum biochemistry, urinalysis and
urine culture and sensitivity) every 6–12 months long
term with continued ciclosporin administration. The
most commonly reported side‐effect is gastrointestinal
upset (e.g., vomiting, diarrhea, decreased appetite).
These side‐effects are typically self‐limiting and transient; gastrointestinal upset will typically resolve within
1–2 weeks of initiating therapy. Antinausea medication
(e.g., maropitant) may be necessary in the short term to
minimize undue patient discomfort.
Other less commonly reported side‐effects of ciclosporin include bacterial infections, bone marrow suppression, hirsutism and excessive shedding, gingival
hyperplasia, hepatitis, papillomatosis, and seizures.
Additionally, in cats, acute and fatal toxoplasmosis has
also been documented. It is recommended that cats
remain indoors and not be fed a raw diet, be completely
restricted with regard to scavenging and hunting, and
have serology documenting toxoplasma and feline leukemia virus/feline immunodeficiency virus (FeLV/FIV)
status prior to initiating therapy.
Ciclosporin levels in the blood may be influenced
by concurrent administration of other medications.
Ketoconazole and fluconazole, for example, can increase
the circulating ciclosporin levels via competitive binding
of the cytochrome P450 enzyme. Although this combination can be clinically useful (e.g., allowing for lowered
dose of ciclosporin required to achieve clinical results,
thereby decreasing the cost of therapy), it can also
increase the chance of side‐effects. Care must be taken
with other cytochrome P450‐associated medications

VetBooks.ir

159 Atopic Dermatitis

(e.g., metoclopramide, metronidazole) as concurrent
administration may increase side‐effects.
As opposed to glucocorticoids, which cause a rapid
reduction in pruritus, there is a lag associated with ciclosporin administration and clinical improvement.
Maximal benefit is typically noted within about 4–6
weeks. At that time, if the patient is sufficiently comfortable, the medication may be tapered.
Oclacitinib

Oclacitinib (Apoquel® Zoetis, New Jersey, USA) is a
novel Janus kinase inhibitor approved for dogs in the
USA and Europe to control the pruritus associated with
allergic dermatitis in general and, specifically, atopic
dermatitis. Oclacitinib rather specifically inhibits
­
­production of IL‐31 from T cells in the dog.
This targeted therapeutic is similar to other tyrosine
kinase molecules which have shown some benefits in the
treatment of atopic dermatitis (e.g., masitinib), but the
safety profile is markedly enhanced. In a recent study, side‐
effects were reduced compared to either glucocorticoids or
ciclosporin even when the medication was administered
long term. Vomiting and diarrhea were the most frequent
side‐effects reported but were typically transient and self‐
limiting and did not require additional therapy or withdrawal of medication. Minimal changes were noted on
bloodwork and urinalysis, with values remaining typically
within the normal range. Decrease in white blood cells was
noted in some patients, along with increased cholesterol
and lipase in others; however, n
­ either fell outside a normal
reference range. Efficacy for control of pruritus associated
with atopic dermatitis is considered excellent in most dogs.
Dosing is recommended at 0.4–0.6 mg/kg PO q12h for
the first two weeks, and then q24h long term. Increase in
pruritus is commonly noted as the frequency of administration is reduced to once daily; however, care should be
taken to not administer the dose twice daily longer than
the recommended two weeks because of increased risk
for concerning, long‐term side‐effects. The increase in
pruritus is likely because the drug has a rather short
serum half‐life and dividing the once‐a‐day dose to
twice‐a‐day administration may help control the pruritus flare in some patients. Oclacitinib has a very rapid
onset, often markedly decreasing pruritus within the
first one to two doses. It has not been extensively evaluated in cats with allergic skin disease and its use in this
species is not currently recommended.
Lokivetmab

Lokivetmab (Cytopoint, Zoetis)is the first anti-IL31 monoclonal antibody (mAB) licensed for the treatment of allergic
and atopic dermatitis in dogs. The injection is administered
subcutaneously at a minimum dose of 2 mg/kg under the
direction of the veterinarian. It can provide efficacy within

24 hours and can provide therapy for an average of 4–8
weeks, at which time it may be repeated. This therapy is
considered to be safe and is intended for both short- and
long-term use. Side effects are minimal; vomiting, diarrhea,
injection site discomfort, and lethargy are most commonly
reported and tend to be self-limiting in nature. It may be
used in dogs of any age, including those with concomitant
diseases. There are no drug-drug interactions reported
thereby adding to Cytopoint’s robust safety profile. As this
is a caninized mAB, it should only be administered in dogs.
Miscellaneous Therapies

Many additional therapeutic interventions have been
investigated for controlling pruritus associated with
atopic dermatitis in the dog. There is some evidence
to support administration of recombinant interferons
(either recombinant feline INF‐omega or recombinant
canine INF‐gamma); these injections have shown moderate efficacy and a good safety profile in several allergic
dogs. However, products are not necessarily available
worldwide. Other therapies such as azathioprine, various
cyclooxygenase/cyclooxygenase‐lipoxygenase
inhibitors, and pentoxifylline have been evaluated but have not
shown appreciable efficacy in atopic dogs.
Allergen‐Specific Immunotherapy
As opposed to addressing strictly the clinical signs associated with atopic dermatitis, allergen‐specific immunotherapy aims to address the underlying immunologic
dysregulation which is part of the disease pathogenesis.
Although the exact mechanism of action is uncertain,
successful therapy may lead to a more “normalized”
immunologic response to allergen exposure. This was
documented in one study where dogs that responded
favorably to therapy showed increases in less inflammatory cytokines (IL‐10) and regulatory T cells.
Allergen‐specific immunotherapy is a “cocktail” of
extracts of various environmental allergens based on the
results of allergen testing (see above). Although no well‐
controlled clinical studies have established an ideal treatment protocol, formulation, or administration schedule
for immunotherapy, benefits do appear to be noted in
some dogs and cats with atopic dermatitis. Efficacy,
however, does appear to be less when compared to other
options (e.g., glucocorticoids, ciclosporin, oclacitinib).
Based on anecdotal reports, approximately 50–75% of
dogs and cats with atopic dermatitis show beneficial
results with immunotherapy administration. As the therapy aims at changing the underlying immune response,
results may take several months to be apparent. Clinical
improvements may initially be seen within the first 3–6
months but maximal benefits may not be noted until
12–18 months. Most patients require the addition of

1411

VetBooks.ir

1412

Section 12 Skin and Ear Diseases

concurrent antipruritic pharmacotherapy during the
induction of immunotherapy.
Two formulations currently exist for immunotherapy:
subcutaneous injections and sublingual/oral drops.
Injections have been available much longer than the oral
formulation and so we have much more information
regarding their use. Although they are very safe, side‐
effects may include injection site pruritus, angioedema, or
anaphylaxis in a small percentage of patients. Anecdotally,
these effects may be more common in toy‐breed and very
small patients. They are generally well tolerated by cats.
Sublingual immunotherapy is a newer option; it is a needle‐free way to administer the formulated allergen “cocktail” which may improve client c­ ompliance. Although a set
protocol has yet to be developed, sublingual immunotherapy is typically administered more frequently (e.g., 1–3
times daily) compared to its injectable counterpart (e.g.,
q1–3 weeks long term). Although less information is
available for the sublingual formulation, trends appear to
follow what is seen for immunotherapy injections with
regard to time to improvement and percentage of animals
experiencing clinical benefit.
There are alternative options for immunotherapy
which have been developed more recently. Regional
immunotherapy and more generalized formulations
eliminate the need for allergen testing prior to formulation. How these less specific options compare to injectable or sublingual allergen‐specific immunotherapy has
yet to be determined.

­Prognosis
Although there is no cure for atopic dermatitis in the dog
or cat, the long‐term prognosis is considered to be good.
Most patients, however, require life‐long therapy for the
disease and, even with generally good control, flares may
periodically occur, necessitating additional therapeutic
intervention.

­Conclusion
Atopic dermatitis can be extremely frustrating to manage for the practitioner and owner alike. That being said,
thorough client education efforts can markedly enhance
compliance and, therefore, results long term. It is important to let clients know from the beginning that this
is a disease which can be managed but never cured.
Additionally, even with excellent control overall, flares
may periodically occur and the animal may still be considered more pruritic than a normal patient. Although
we strive for perfection, it is rarely achieved in a dog or
cat with atopic dermatitis. Goals for the patient should
be to improve their comfort (e.g., reduction of pruritus,
decreased frequency of secondary infections) by approximately 80–90% for approximately 80–90% of the time.
This may require a combination of therapeutic interventions including bathing/topical therapy along with
immunotherapy or various medications. Every patient
with atopic dermatitis is different; specific therapy needs
to be tailored to the individual based on both patient and
client feasibility. Having a client “onboard” with a multimodal approach to atopic dermatitis is imperative for
successful management.
Additionally, it is important to remember that rarely
does a therapy “stop working” for managing the disease.
For example, a dog has been doing fairly well on allergen‐specific immunotherapy injections for several
months/years and all of a sudden develops moderate to
severe pruritus. Prior to jumping to repeating allergen
testing/reformulating immunotherapy or abandoning
immunotherapy altogether for alternative medications,
secondary flare factors such as infections and parasites
(particularly fleas and Sarcoptes) should be investigated
and addressed appropriately. In endemic areas, all
patients should be treated year‐round with adulticide
flea prevention at least every 30 days to minimize the
chance of flea infestation leading to an increase in pruritus, thereby exacerbating atopic dermatitis.

Allergic Skin Diseases
Patrick Hensel, Dr. Med.Vet., DACVD
Tierdermatologie, Basel, Switzerland

This chapter includes common allergic skin diseases of
dogs and cats with the exception of atopic dermatitis and
cutaneous adverse food reactions, which are covered in
Chapters 159 and 161, respectively.

­Urticaria and Angioedema
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Immunologic and nonimmunologic mechanisms are
suspected to be involved in the pathogenesis of urticaria
and angioedema, causing degranulation of mast cells or
basophils which results in vascular dilation and recruitment of inflammatory cells. The inflammation remains
limited to the dermis in patients with urticaria, but it
extends to the subcutis with angioedema. While the
immunologic process is mediated by a predominantly
type I or III hypersensitivity reaction (e.g., allergies),
nonimmunologic causes (e.g., heat, cold, stress, chemicals) can also trigger mast cell degranulation (Table 160.1).
A hypersensitivity reaction to an offending substance
may not result in clinical signs at the first exposure, but
will more likely occur with repeated exposures. Repeated
exposures may also potentially result in more severe
reactions.
Epidemiology
Urticaria and angioedema are rare in cats and uncommon in dogs and have been associated with various
­triggering factors as described above.
Signalment
Urticaria and angioedema can occur at any age and affect
male and female animals equally. A specific breed
­predisposition has not been established.

History and Clinical Signs
Urticaria and angioedema typically have an acute onset
(minutes to a few hours). Urticaria is characterized by
erythematous wheals which are small (1–5 cm in diameter) and present in a multifocal to coalescing pattern
(Figure 160.1). They are transient and normally fade
within 24 hours but new lesions form as long as the animal remains exposed to the triggering factor. Angioedema
presents as a locally extensive and ill‐defined swelling of
the face and ventral neck due to edema in the deep
­dermis and subcutaneous tissue (Figure 160.2). In severe
cases, serum may leak through the skin. Very rarely and
only in severe cases, fever, lethargy, and anorexia may be
present. Pruritus may or may not accompany urticaria
and angioedema.
Diagnosis
The diagnosis is based on the patient’s history, clinical
presentation, behavior of the skin lesions, diascopy
(blanching) and, if necessary, histopathology. Identifying
any triggering factor should be a priority. For this reason,
a thorough patient history, including vaccination and any
drug exposure, should be recorded. Pyoderma and vasculitis are differential diagnoses consistent with urticaria,
but the lesions of those diseases will not blanch on
diascopy. Mast cell tumor, cutaneous lymphoma, and
­
amyloidosis should also be considered as differential diagnoses for urticarial lesions. Differential diagnoses consistent with angioedema are cutaneous lymphoma, juvenile
cellulitis, mast cell tumor, and infectious cellulitis.
Therapy
The triggering cause should be identified and eliminated
to evade symptomatic therapy and prevent recurrences;

mild cases, antihistamines are typically used as sole
therapy.
Prognosis
If the cause of the disease can be identified and exposure
eliminated, the prognosis is considered good.

­Allergic Contact Dermatitis
Etiology/Pathophysiology

Figure 160.1 Five‐year‐old male neutered mixed‐breed dog with
multifocal wheals on lateral trunk and hind legs.

Allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV hypersensitivity
reaction associated with a cell‐mediated allergic response
to haptens, which are small reactive lipid‐soluble molecules. Although an overlap between irritant and allergic
contact dermatitis has been reported in regard to
cytokine profile and inflammatory cell activation, allergen‐specific CD4+ T cells (CCR10+) and some
chemokines (e.g., IP‐10) seem to be expressed exclusively

VetBooks.ir

160 Allergic Skin Diseases

in allergic contact dermatitis, which may represent differences in regulatory mechanisms.
Epidemiology
A wide range of allergens, such as various plants (e.g.,
dandelion, Asian jasmine, cedar mulch), cement, plastic
toys and bowls, household cleaners, and topical drugs
(e.g., neomycin, propylene glycol), have the potential to
trigger contact hypersensitivity. An overlap of contact
hypersensitivity with atopic dermatitis (AD) may also
exist, since it is suspected that about 20% of dogs with
contact hypersensitivity also suffer from AD.
Signalment
Allergic contact dermatitis is considered to be a rare pruritic condition and has no age or gender predisposition.
However, some short‐haired breeds such as the boxer, pit
bull, dachshund, and Boston terrier appear to be affected
more frequently.
History and Clinical Signs
Skin lesions typically occur on sites which are sparsely
haired and directly exposed to allergens such as the ventral aspects of the neck, chest, abdomen, tail, digital
spaces, muzzle, concave aspects of the pinnae, and scrotum (Figure 160.3). Lesions may also develop in haired

areas if the sensitizer is in liquid, powder or aerosol form.
The skin lesions are characterized by macules, papules,
and erythema which may progress in chronic cases and
become lichenified, hyperpigmented, and alopecic.
Secondary bacterial and yeast infections are commonly
present. Excoriations may also occur due to the associated pruritus. As with other hypersensitivity reactions,
previous allergen exposure is necessary for the development of sensitization and resultant clinical signs.
Diagnosis
Allergic contact hypersensitivity is diagnosed based on the
patient’s history, physical examination findings, resolution
of clinical signs after elimination of the offending allergen,
provocation of skin lesions with reexposure, and patch
testing. The most common differential diagnoses associated with contact hypersensitivity are cutaneous adverse
food reaction, atopic dermatitis, scabies, pyoderma,
Malassezia dermatitis, and insect bite hypersensitivity.
Therapy
The primary goal should be to prevent further exposure
to the offending allergen. Symptomatic therapy with glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone/prednisolone at 0.5–1 mg/
kg PO daily) may be attempted where elimination is not
feasible; however, response to glucocorticoids occasionally fails. Pentoxifylline (10–30 mg/kg PO 2–3 times
daily) has shown some beneficial effect for long‐term
management and prophylaxis. Patients with a poor
response to glucocorticoids may benefit from treatment
with ciclosporin (5 mg/kg PO daily).
Prognosis
Prognosis is considered good if the allergen can be eliminated from the patient’s environment and good clinical
response can be achieved with immunomodulating drugs.

­Flea Allergy Dermatitis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Several allergens responsible for flea allergy dermatitis
(FAD) in dogs and cats have been identified in flea saliva.
So far, one major allergen, a protein called Ctef1 from the
cat flea Ctenocephalides felis, has been associated with
flea allergy in dogs.
Figure 160.3 Severe contact dermatitis to a plant fertilizer in a 5‐
year‐old golden retriever. Erythema, edema, serosanguinous to
purulent exudate, and brownish crusts were present on the
ventral abdomen and inner thighs. Source: Courtesy of Sheila
Torres.

Epidemiology
The prevalence of FAD varies greatly depending on the
climate and geographic location, but it is the most

1415

VetBooks.ir

1416

Section 12 Skin and Ear Diseases

common hypersensitivity in dogs and cats in flea‐
­
endemic areas. Fleas can be a perennial problem in subtropical and tropical climate zones, seasonal in more
temperate climate zones, and practically nonexistent in
arid, high elevation, or cold climates. Even if fleas are
considered to be absent from a particular area, there is a
possibility that animal movement or contact may bring
fleas into the area.
Signalment
Any dog and cat in a flea‐endemic area can become allergic to fleas but no breed or sex predilection has been
identified. Although FAD can develop at any age, dogs
predisposed to FAD will generally develop clinical signs
by 5 years of age.
History and Clinical Signs
The most typical clinical sign associated with fleas is
pruritus, but FAD must be differentiated from flea infestation. Clinical signs associated with flea infestation are
variable. The pruritus is generally intermittent and an
increased number of fleas is common.
The typical predilection sites for FAD in dogs are the
lumbosacral area, tail base, and caudomedial thighs, and
minimal flea burden is typical. In cats, skin lesions are
commonly found on the caudodorsal area, as in dogs, but
can also be present on the head and neck. Many dogs and
cats suffering from FAD may have concurrent atopic dermatitis and/or cutaneous adverse food reaction which
may complicate the clinical presentation and diagnosis.
The most common skin lesions seen in dogs with FAD
are erythematous papules and in more severe and
chronic cases, self‐induced alopecia, lichenification, and
seborrhea on the predilection sites (Figure 160.4).
In cats, skin lesions range from miliary dermatitis
(crusted papules) to excoriations to self‐induced alopecia. Cats also often show skin lesions consistent with
eosinophilic granuloma, especially indolent ulcers on the
upper lips which can be found in up to 60% of flea‐allergic cats (Figure 160.5).

Figure 160.4 Five‐year‐old female spayed mixed‐breed dog with
flea allergy dermatitis exhibiting alopecia, erythema, excoriations,
and seborrhea along the caudodorsal aspects of the trunk, tail,
and hindlegs.

Diagnosis
Any pruritic skin disease should be considered as a
potential differential diagnosis for FAD and mainly
includes other ectoparasitic disorders, microbial skin
infections, or other hypersensitivities. Diagnosis is based
on history, clinical signs, and response to therapy. The
presence of fleas is not an adequate indicator of FAD and
allergy skin testing with flea allergen can show false‐­
negative results. Nevertheless, flea combing should be
performed for direct identification of fleas or flea feces.

Figure 160.5 An indolent ulcer in a 4‐year‐old female spayed
domestic shorthair cat with flea allergy dermatitis.

VetBooks.ir

160 Allergic Skin Diseases

Therapy
The most effective treatment for animals with FAD is
avoiding exposure to fleas combined with aggressive flea
control. Veterinarians should be aware that none of the
current flea preventives have an effective repellent effect.
Since fleas in the pupal stage can survive up to 174 days
in the environment, it is not unusual for the response to
effective flea prevention to take a couple of months. For
this reason, it is strongly recommended to maintain regular application of flea products in endemic areas. Fast‐
acting systemic adulticides are recommended over
topically applied flea preventives because they reduce
the contact time between the flea and the animal, resulting in faster reduction of irritation and pruritus. Flea
preventives with a rapid adulticidal effect act through
activation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors or inhibition of gamma‐aminobutyric acid (GABA)‐gated chloride channels. Such products are available as oral tablets
and topical solutions, and contain either nitenpyram,
spinosad, or an isoxazoline (e.g., fluralaner, sarolaner,
afoxolaner, lotilaner). Cats are very sensitive to
permethrin so parasiticidals containing this product
­
should be avoided in this species.
Despite strict flea prevention and depending on the
severity of FAD, dogs and cats may develop episodes of

increased pruritus after exposure to a flea. For the symptomatic therapy of pruritus, antiinflammatory dosages of
oral glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone/prednisolone at
0.5–1 mg/kg PO daily) and/or topical therapy (e.g., hydrocortisone aceponate spray [Cortavance®,Virbac], available
only in Canada and Europe, or triamcinolone acetonide
topical spray [Genesis®, Virbac]) may provide sufficient
relief. In dogs, oclacitinib (Apoquel, Zoetis) can be
administered at a dose of 0.4-0.6 mg/kg PO BID for up to
2 weeks, then once daily thereafter to alleviate pruritus
associated with FAD. Lokivetmab (Cytopoint, Zoetis) is
now licensed for the treatment of allergic dermatitis in
dogs and, thus, could also be considered as an option for
treating pruritus. A minimum dose of 2 mg/kg is administered SC and can be repeated every 4 to 8 weeks as
needed. Other important measures include keeping the
affected animal indoors and treating all in‐contact pets.
Prognosis
Canine and feline FAD tends to worsen with age but with
strict flea control, control of other underlying hypersensitivities and other measures which may help to reduce
exposure to fleas, the disease can be well controlled.

Cutaneous Adverse Food Reactions
Ralf S. Mueller, Dr. Med.Vet., DACVD, FANZCVSc
Centre for Clinical Veterinary Medicine, Ludwig‐Maximilians‐University of Munich, Munich, Germany

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Cutaneous adverse food reactions include any skin reactions that are reproducible. Most commonly seen is pruritus, but recurrent pyoderma or edema have also been
reported. Food allergy is an immunologically mediated
reaction caused by food. Type I hypersensitivity mediated by food‐specific IgE antibodies is the most common
reaction, but delayed type II (T cell mediated) and type
III (where food‐specific antibodies and food antigens
form complexes) hypersensitivities may also occur.
In veterinary practice, the immunologic basis of food
reactions is rarely documented. Thus, technically, the commonly used term “food allergy” is inappropriate, because
adverse food reactions may also be nonimmunologically
induced (and are then called food intolerances). Food intolerance may be pharmacologic, such as those mediated by
pharmacologically active ingredients of the diet (e.g., histamine), toxic (caused by toxins in the food commonly produced by microorganisms in contaminated food stuffs), or
metabolic (ingredients in the food are metabolized in the
patient to a substance causing the reaction). If none of those
mechanisms can be identified, the reaction is idiosyncratic.
However, proving the exact pathogenesis in an individual patient in practice is very difficult. Serum IgE testing for food‐specific antibodies in normal dogs without
clinical problems is characterized by a high number of
false‐positive reactions and reliable tests for other types
of adverse food reactions are lacking. Thus, in most cases
the diagnosis of adverse food reaction is made by
response to an elimination diet and deterioration on
rechallenge, as described below.
In human medicine, food allergens are typically glycoproteins with molecular weights between 10 and 70 kDa
and some typical allergens come from nuts, shellfish,
milk, and eggs. In dogs, the most commonly identified
food antigens are beef, dairy products, chicken, soy, and

wheat – ingredients that are most commonly present in
commercial dog foods (Table 161.1). In the cat, beef,
dairy, fish, and chicken are the most common reported
offending antigens (see Table 161.1).
To what degree related proteins can cause clinical
problems via cross‐reactivity is not clear. One study evaluating individual rechallenges in dogs with adverse food
reactions could not demonstrate evidence of cross‐­
reactivity between, for example, beef and cow’s milk.
However, a case report of a dog with oral allergy syndrome described cross‐reactivity with tomato and cedar
pollen. A further in vitro study identified bovine IgG as a
major antigen in dogs and a potential source of cross‐
reactivity between beef, cow’s milk and potentially mutton (as there is a high homology between bovine and
ovine IgG), but whether this is clinically relevant has not
been demonstrated convincingly at this point.

­History and Clinical Signs
Adverse food reaction is characterized in most cases by a
pruritic and nonseasonal dermatitis. The face, feet, ventrum, and perianal area are often affected in the dog
(Figure 161.1). Otitis externa is common and may be the
only presenting sign in some dogs (Figure 161.2).
The skin may be erythematous; self‐trauma quickly
leads to alopecia and excoriation and in chronic cases
lichenification of affected skin (Figure 161.3).
Papules, pustules, and oily and scaly skin may be due to
common secondary infections with bacteria and/or yeast
organisms. Concurrent gastrointestinal signs are seen in
up to 25% of affected dogs. Beyond vomiting and diarrhea, gastrointestinal signs may include frequent defecation, borborygmi and flatulence, which may in some
dogs be the only noncutaneous clinical signs. Recurrent
bacterial infection and vasculitis were also reported in
