161 Cutaneous Adverse Food Reactions

­Diagnosis
Although serum testing for food allergen‐specific IgE is
offered in many countries, there is no evidence that this
test has any value in the diagnosis of adverse food
­reactions. In all previous publications, numerous false‐
positive and false‐negative reactions were detected, when
comparing test results with clinical rechallenges. In one
recent study, false‐negative reactions were less likely.
However, at this time there is unanimous agreement
amongst dermatologists worldwide that the only reliable
way to diagnose an adverse food reaction is an elimination diet with food stuffs previously not fed to the patient.
Choice of Elimination Diet
In dogs, one protein source and one carbohydrate source
not previously fed will be used exclusively; in cats, feeding only the protein source increases palatibility and
compliance. Thus, it is important to obtain a reliable and
detailed feeding history for the patient as well as the
ingredient lists of commercial foods fed in the past.
Ideally, the food should be home‐cooked to assure that
only the selected food stuffs are used. This is even more
important after evidence has been published that many
dog foods may include food sources not listed on the
label. However, convincing owners to cook for their pets
for several weeks may be more difficult nowadays than it
used to be half a century ago. In addition, home‐cooked
diets are rarely balanced, which typically does not lead to
clinical problems in adult dogs on a deficient diet for
only a short time such as a month or two. However, if
home‐cooked diets are fed for extended time periods or
if the patient is a young dog or cat still growing, care
must be taken to seek advice from a nutritionist and
­balance the diet to avoid nutritional deficiencies.
To what degree cross‐reactivities between related
allergens (for example, beef and mutton or cow’s milk)
are clinically relevant in the dog and cat is currently
unclear. One study showed in vitro evidence of reactivity
of most dog sera with specific IgE antibodies against
bovine IgG present in cow’s milk and lamb and beef
extract. Studies evaluating clinical cross‐reactivity are
rare and so far have not confirmed those findings. The
author prefers to use food sources removed as far as possible from the previously fed antigens; for example, animals fed predominantly meat such as beef, mutton or
pork will receive poultry proteins such as duck or goose
and pets on a predominantly chicken‐based food will be
recommended goat, buffalo or reindeer.
If owners cannot be convinced to cook for their pets,
commercial diets with selected protein and carbohydrate
sources are sold by many companies. Furthermore,
­hydrolyzed diets are also available. These diets contain
hydrolyzed proteins and their small sizes make

cross‐linking of IgE on the surface of inflammatory cells
less likely, and thus these diets can be considered truly
“hypoallergenic.” Hydrolyzed diets and selected protein
diets do not lead to remission in all animals with an adverse
food reaction and thus are the second best option for diagnosing the condition. The exact reason for this decreased
efficacy is not known at this time, but may relate to the
presence of a concurrent allergic condition, cross‐­
reactivities or adverse food reactions that are not immune
mediated in the first place. However, these diets are often
ideally suited for long‐term maintenance, once the diagnosis is made and patients have been shown to tolerate them.
If it is not possible for owners to feed a previously
unfed protein or carbohydrate source, either because
what is available is simply too costly (which may be relevant for owners of large dogs) or because dogs or cats
have been fed a wide variety of foods in the past, then it
is sensible to choose the food sources the animals have
seen the least or only in the more distant past, when clinical signs were not present. In one Dutch study of dogs
with an adverse food reaction being fed three commercial protein diets, no dog responded to all of the diets but
almost all dogs responded to at least one of them. Thus,
performing two or three commercial diet trials in dogs
with a suspected adverse food reaction may be useful.
Duration and Execution of the Diet
The ideal duration of an elimination diet is controversial.
In a study evaluating the duration until clinical remission
in 51 dogs with adverse food reaction, less than a quarter
of the dogs responded within the first three weeks, a
­further half after 4–6 weeks, 10 dogs after 7–8 weeks,
and three dogs after 9–10 weeks. However, although the
time to complete remission can be extended, most dogs
will start improving within the first 6–8 weeks and if a
patient shows no clinical improvement on an appropriate elimination diet within that time, the author considers adverse food reaction ruled out. One has to keep in
mind that the longer the trial duration, the higher the
likelihood for lack of owner compliance.
In most patients, a gradual switch from the original diet to
the elimination diet over a few days will help with compliance as well as gastrointestinal complications, particularly
in finicky dogs and in cats. In dogs, owners are the limiting
factor for most unsuccessful diet trials. However, cats often
prove more difficult and due to the threat of hepatic lipidosis after several days of refusing to accept the diet, particularly in obese cats, it is not uncommon to try a number of
feeding options before a suitable diet is identified.
The most important detail to relate to the owners is
the need for maximal compliance. Even small amounts of
food antigens fed infrequently can trigger pruritus and
thus mask improvement, so flavored medications or
treats such as rawhide, pig’s ears, and others must be

1421

VetBooks.ir

1422

Section 12 Skin and Ear Diseases

avoided during the time of the diet. In particular, dog
owners used to giving treats will often only be able to
complete a diet trial if suitable alternatives are agreed on
prior to starting the diet. For example, jerky of the meat
used for the elimination diet can be home‐made or
acquired in bigger pet stores as chews or treats. Dogs
with a high affinity for scavenging need to be kept on the
leash and cats with outdoor access are ideally kept
indoors. If those restraints are not possible for whatever
reason, then an elimination diet trial may still be
attempted but the limitation of these more relaxed elimination diets is that a lack of improvement does not rule
out adverse food reaction in that patient, although some
patients may still improve when the intake of the offending allergen is limited at least to some degree.
Interpretation of the Outcome
of an Elimination Diet
If a reevaluation after 6–8 weeks shows no improvement
on an appropriate elimination diet and a secondary
infection masking the improvement is not present, then
adverse food reaction is ruled out and the diet trial does
not need to be extended. If, however, there is some
improvement seen, then in some patients it may be
necessary to continue the trial for up to 12 weeks.
­
Improvement may be due to the elimination diet, concurrent treatments, seasonal changes or other factors, so
a rechallenge with the old diet is absolutely necessary for
the diagnosis (although some owners will need some
convincing) and leads to deterioration of clinical signs
within a few days. If after two weeks on the previous diet
there is no deterioration of clinical signs, adverse food
reaction is ruled out and improvement was due to other
factors. As soon as a deterioration is detected, the elimination diet is fed again and if clinical signs improve again
(typically much faster than at the initial introduction of
the elimination diet), the diagnosis is confirmed.
Subsequently, there are three choices for the client. The
easiest is to stay on the elimination diet long term. However,
ideally, one food source after another is i­ntroduced again
gradually for a few days to weeks, depending on the origi-

nal rechallenge. If a patient deteriorated after two days on
the old diet, then sequential rechallenges for four days
each should be sufficient. If the original rechallenge led to
deterioration after one week, then sequential rechallenges
should probably be performed for two weeks each. This
way, offending allergens can be identified and this knowledge permits greater flexibility in feeding, although it
requires more effort. And lastly, if a home‐cooked diet was
used for the diagnosis, a commercial diet can be tried
based on the feeding history of the patient.

­Therapy
Ideally, avoidance of the offending food antigens is the
best way to treat adverse food reactions in dogs and cats.
If home cooking is used for long‐term management, care
should be taken to create a well‐balanced diet and advice
from a veterinary nutritionist may be useful.
However, if avoidance is not possible or if flares due to
inadvertent ingestion of antigens are encountered, medical treatment with antiinflammatory drugs also used for
environmental atopic dermatitis may be attempted.
­
Glucocorticoids and ciclosporin are efficacious options
for dogs and cats suffering from cutaneous adverse food
reactions, although anecdotal evidence indicates that
higher doses are needed to achieve remission than with
atopic dermatitis due to environmental allergens.
Oclacitinib (Apoquel; Zoetis) and lokivetmab (Cytopoint;
Zoetis) are also licensed for the treatment of allergic dermatitis in dogs and thus are excellent, alternative options
for controlling pruritus in canine patients with cutaneous adverse food reaction.

­Prognosis
Once the diagnosis is established and offending allergens
are identified, the prognosis is excellent, although some
rare dogs and cats will develop a reaction against the new
food antigens with time and will have to undergo a
repeated change in their diet.

­Canine Familial Dermatomyositis
Dermatomyositis (DM) is a hereditary, ischemic dermatopathy and myopathy that occurs most commonly in
collies, Shetland sheepdogs, Beauceron shepherds,
Belgian tervurens, and Portuguese water dogs. Affected
dogs generally develop lesions when they are less than
6 months of age, and either sex can be affected.
Dermatomyositis is characterized by nonpruritic
­alopecia, erythema, scaling, and mild crusting of the face,
ears, distal limbs, digits, tail, and bony prominences
(Figure 162.1). Additionally, claws may slough and fragment and ulceration may be rarely present in the oral
cavity. Skin lesions may vary in severity depending on the
individual. The presence and degree of myositis also vary.
Clinical signs of myositis include regurgitation associated with megaesophagus, a high‐stepping stiff gait, and
atrophy of the masticatory muscles and distal limbs.
The diagnosis of DM is made through history, physical
examination, and skin biopsy. Punch biopsies should be
taken from the center of an alopecic area of skin. Crusted
lesions can also be biopsied. The skin should not be
scrubbed or clipped prior to procuring the biopsy. Care
should be taken to include only abnormal skin in the
biopsy. Histopathology will feature changes characteristic of ischemic dermatopathy.
Benign neglect may be an appropriate treatment
approach for minimally affected patients. Avoidance of
trauma to bony prominences and avoidance of prolonged
sun exposure may also be beneficial. Pentoxifylline,
prednisone, vitamin E, omega‐3 fatty acids, tetracycline
with niacinamide, and topical tacrolimus are therapies
that may be used either alone or in combination depending on patient response (Table 162.1).
Complications can include secondary pyoderma for
those dogs with more significant skin lesions and ­aspiration
pneumonia for those with megaesophagus. Amyloidosis

may rarely occur in chronically affected dogs. Minimally
affected dogs may experience spontaneous resolution of
skin lesions while other dogs may require lifelong therapy.

­Erythema Multiforme
Erythema multiforme (EM) is an inflammatory cutaneous reaction pattern of multifactorial etiology, and dogs
and cats of any age, breed or sex may be affected. It is
characterized by rarely pruritic, sometimes painful, erythematous macules or papules that coalesce and eventually form a clear center and acquire an annular to
arciform shape. Additional skin lesions may include
plaques, vesicles and bullae, ulcers, and urticaria. Classic
target lesions are present in only about one‐third of
cases. The axillae, groin, mucocutaneous junctions,
­pinnae, and footpads are most frequently affected. Oral
ulceration may be present in some cases. Erythema
multiforme can be classified into various categories
­
based upon severity; however, such classifications are
beyond the scope of this chapter.
The disease is diagnosed based on history, physical
examination, and skin biopsy findings. Punch biopsies
should be taken from the center of an erythematous area
of skin. The clinician should biopsy affected skin and avoid
ulcerated areas as ulcerated skin may yield a nondiagnostic sample. The skin should not be scrubbed or clipped
prior to procuring the biopsy. Care should be taken to
include only abnormal skin in the biopsy. Histopathology
reveals apoptosis of keratinocytes at ­various levels of the
epidermis combined with lymphocyte satellitosis.
Erythema multiforme has a variable appearance, and
therefore many potential clinical differentials. Some
­differential diagnoses include systemic lupus erythematosus, urticaria, superficial pyoderma, dermatophytosis,
demodicosis, bullous autoimmune disease, vasculitis

and necrotizing dermatoses, superficial necrolytic dermatitis, and zinc‐responsive dermatosis.
The identification and removal of the possible underlying cause are important in the management of EM;
however, some cases are idiopathic. Triggering causes
may include drugs, bacterial infections, Pneumocystis
pneumonia, parvovirus, food, neoplasia or possibly herpesvirus. Mildly affected individuals may experience
resolution of disease without additional therapy. Other
patients may need immunosuppressive therapy such as
glucocorticoids, azathioprine, ciclosporin, and/or intravenous immunoglobulin therapy (IVIG) (see Table 162.1).
Complications can include secondary pyoderma. The
prognosis depends on the severity of the lesions and
response to therapy.

­Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis
Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) is a severe vesiculobullous disorder affecting the skin and oral mucosa of
dogs and cats. Dogs and cats of any age, sex or breed can
be affected.
Toxic epidermal necrolysis is characterized by generalized erythematous or purpuric patches, and skin ulceration involving more than 30% of the body. Systemic signs
(pyrexia, lethargy, depression, and/or anorexia) typically
accompany the skin lesions.
Toxic epidermal necrolysis is often thought of as a
severe variation of EM although some clinicians consider the two as separate diseases. It is generally differentiated from EM based on the severity of skin lesions and
the percentage of the body that is affected.
The disease is diagnosed based on history, physical
examination, and skin biopsy findings. Punch biopsies

should be taken from an erythematous area of skin adjacent to an ulcer. The clinician should take care to avoid
sampling eroded or ulcerated skin. Ulcerated skin has
less diagnostic value. The skin should not be scrubbed or
clipped prior to procuring the biopsy. Care should be
taken to include only abnormal skin in the biopsy. The
histopathology reveals diffuse necrosis of the epidermis
with minimal dermal inflammation.
Clinical differential diagnoses include first‐degree
burn and toxic shock syndrome.
The identification and removal of a possible underlying cause are important in the management of TEN;
however, many cases are idiopathic. The most common
precipitating factor is drugs. Other less common triggers
include vaccination, neoplasia, infections, and pregnancy. Wound care and general supportive care are critical to attempt to prevent sepsis. The use of glucocorticoids
is controversial but ciclosporin and IVIG have been used
with beneficial results in some cases.
Complications can include severe pyoderma and
­sepsis. The prognosis is guarded.

­Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus
Discoid Lupus Erythematosus
Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) is a fairly common
photoaggravated or perhaps even photoinduced, depigmenting autoimmune skin disease. It affects middle‐
aged dogs, and collies, Shetland sheepdogs, German
shepherd dogs, and Siberian huskies are predisposed.
One case of generalized DLE has been reported in a
Chinese crested dog. DLE has rarely been reported
in cats. Sex and age predilections have not been
substantiated.
The disease is characterized by depigmentation and
loss of cobblestone architecture of the nasal planum
(Figure 162.2). Erosions and crusting may also develop.
While the nasal planum is most typically affected, lesions
may also be found extending proximal to the nasal
­planum, around the eyes, around the mouth, on the
­genitals and distal extremities. Oral ulceration may also
be present.
Diagnosis is based on history, physical examination,
exclusion of systemic involvement, and skin biopsy findings. The clinician should select a site of recent depigmentation for punch biopsy. Lesions with severe crusting,
ulceration or scarring should be avoided. The skin should
not be scrubbed or clipped prior to procuring the biopsy.
Care should be taken to include only abnormal skin in
the biopsy. Histopathology reveals lymphocytic interface
dermatitis. Direct immunofluorescence can further
­support the diagnosis.

Exfoliative cutaneous lupus erythematosus (ECLE) is an
autoimmune disease that affects German shorthaired
pointers. The disease occurs in puppies and young
adults. Sex predilection has not been noted.

Vesicular Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus

The disease is characterized by widespread scaling,
depigmentation, alopecia, ulceration and crusting on the
muzzle, pinnae, trunk, and limbs (Figure 162.3). Systemic
abnormalities such as lymphadenopathy, intermittent
pyrexia, joint pain, infertility, hyperglobulinemia, and
thrombocytopenia may also be present. Dogs often
assume a hunched stance.

Vesicular cutaneous lupus erythematosus (VCLE) is an
autoimmune blistering disease that primarily affects
middle‐aged to older, female Shetland sheepdogs and
collies. The disease generally occurs in the spring and
summer months, and sparsely haired areas of the skin
are most typically affected.
Vesicular cutaneous lupus erythematosus is characterized
by transient vesicles that develop into coalescing ulcers with
serpiginous borders (Figure 162.4). The abdomen, groin,
and axillae are most frequently affected, although lesions
may also occur on the mucocutaneous junctions.
Diagnosis is based on history, physical examination,
and skin biopsy findings. The skin should not be clipped
or cleaned prior to sampling with a punch biopsy.

­Autoimmune Subepidermal
Blistering Diseases
This group of diseases is autoimmune in nature and characterized by vesicle formation on various parts of the body. The
diagnosis is based on signalment, physical examination, histopathology, and response to therapy. Immunohistochemistry
or immunofluorescence is also sometimes required to
­differentiate among the blistering diseases.
Bulla or vesicles should be sampled via wedge biopsy
for diagnostic purposes. If only erosions and ulcers are
present, the clinician should obtain a wedge biopsy
encompassing both margins of an erosive lesion. It is
important to include epidermis in the sample. A biopsy
that includes only dermis (e.g., center of an erosion or
ulcer) will yield minimal diagnostic information. Samples
should be submitted to an experienced dermatohistopathologist to increase the chances of obtaining a definitive diagnosis. Response to therapy and lesion appearance
can also guide the diagnosis. Bullous pemphigoid and
mucous membrane pemphigoid are fairly glucocorticoid
responsive, while epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA)
is more glucocorticoid resistant.
The mucous membranes are predominantly affected
in mucous membrane pemphigoid. Areas of friction and
trauma (i.e., footpads) are predominantly affected in
EBA. Vesicular cutaneous lupus erythematosus (discussed above) features extensive abdominal erosions.
Bullous pemphigoid and EBA generally feature tense
vesicles, while the vesicles of vesicular cutaneous lupus
erythematosus are more flaccid.

Initial lesions develop on haired skin and include erythematous macules and patches that progress to turgid
vesicles. The lesions evolve to ulcers and crusts. Lesions
are not pruritic but can be painful. Pawpads are generally
spared and mucosa is less frequently affected than in
mucous membrane pemphigoid.
Diagnosis is based on the dermatohistopathologic
findings of skin biopsy and immunofluorescence or
immunohistochemistry. Refer to the subepidermal
­blistering diseases introduction for details about biopsy
technique and special testing. Histopathology reveals
subepidermal bullae.
Clinical differential diagnoses include EBA (although
EBA typically features footpad involvement), pemphigus
variants, VCLE, and mucous membrane pemphigoid.
The presence of nonmucosal involvement is m
­ ore
­suggestive of BP than mucous membrane pemphigoid.
Treatment involves topical glucocorticoids, oral glucocorticoids, tetracycline with niacinamide, and/or azathioprine (see Table 162.1). Complications include pyoderma.
Spontaneous remission has been reported although it
should be anticipated that life‐long therapy could be
necessary.
Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita
Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita is an autoimmune vesiculobullous disease that affects mostly young adult dogs.
Great Danes and male dogs are overrepresented.
Initial lesions include patchy erythema and vesicles of
the face, oral cavity, concave pinna, axilla, and groin
(Figure 162.5).
Vesicles may be hemorrhagic. Areas of friction tend to
have the most obvious lesions. The groin and axilla
develop erosions quickly. The oral mucosa and footpads
usually feature extensive sloughing. Affected individuals

Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is an autoimmune vesiculobullous disease that more often affects middle‐aged dogs.
Breed and sex predilections have not been identified.

may show systemic signs of illness. A localized variant of

Diagnosis is based on the dermatohistopathologic

Prognosis is guarded to poor because this disease does

Linear IgA Disease
Linear IgA disease (LAD) is a rare autoimmune disease
of dogs. There are no known breed, age or sex predilections. The disease is characterized by ulcerations of the
mucous membranes, mucocutaneous junctions, and
skin (particularly of the extremities, axillae, groin, and
pawpads). The initial lesions are vesicles, but their transient nature means they are rarely observed.
Diagnosis is based on the dermatohistopathologic
findings of skin or mucosal biopsy and immunofluorescence or immunohistochemistry. Refer to the subepidermal blistering diseases introduction for details about
biopsy technique and special testing. Histopathology
reveals subepidermal bullae with mild to moderate
inflammation. Clinical differential diagnoses include
bullous pemphigoid, mucous membrane pemphigoid,
EBA, VCLE, systemic lupus erythematosus, pemphigus
vulgaris, severe erythema multiforme, and bullous drug
eruptions.
Treatment has not been reported for this rare disease
in dogs; however, the same immunomodulatory/immunosuppressive drugs mentioned for the other autoimmune blistering diseases can be tried (see Table 162.1).
Prognosis is guarded due to the paucity of information
about this disease in dogs.
Mucous Membrane Pemphigoid
Mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP) is a rare autoimmune blistering disease of dogs and cats that affects the
mucous membranes and adjacent skin. Dogs are affected
in adulthood, with no recognized sex predilection.
German shepherd dogs may be predisposed.

Lesions are characterized by vesicles that progress to
form erosions, ulcers, and crusts. The oral cavity, nasal
planum, periocular region, genitalia, footpads, and concave pinnae can be affected. Hypopigmentation and
atrophic scarring may occur in some cases. The lesions
are nonpruritic, but may be painful. Lymphadenopathy
may be present.
Diagnosis is based on the dermatohistopathologic
findings of skin or mucosal biopsy and immunofluorescence or immunohistochemistry. Refer to the subepidermal blistering diseases introduction for details about
biopsy technique and special testing. Histopathology
reveals subepidermal bullae.
Clinical differential diagnoses include bullous pemphigoid, EBA, VCLE, pemphigus vulgaris, erythema multiforme, and bullous drug eruptions. The mucous
membranes are markedly affected in MMP. This characteristic can be useful in distinguishing MMP from other
blistering diseases.
Treatment involves immunosuppression. Lesions are
generally not severe, and tend to respond easily to therapy. Tetracycline and niacinamide should be considered
as initial treatment. Glucocorticoids and other immunosuppressants may be considered if the lesions are severe
or do not respond readily (see Table 162.1).
Prognosis is good to guarded. Complications include
secondary infections of the lesions.

­Pemphigus Complex
History, physical examination, impression smears, and
histopathology lead to the diagnosis of diseases
within the pemphigus complex. The hallmark of diseases in this category is acantholytic keratinocytes
(Figure 162.6) and these can be identified on cytology
and histology.
Trichophyton mentagrophytes and severe pyoderma
are the primary differentials for pemphigus because
acantholytic keratinocytes can occur in these conditions
as well.
A direct impression smear from under a moist crust or
the content of a pustule will reveal numerous nondegenerate neutrophils, acantholytic keratinocytes and sometimes eosinophils. Bacteria may be present if secondary
infections occur.
The punch biopsy technique is appropriate for d
­ iseases
in this category. The skin should not be shaved or cleaned
prior to obtaining the biopsy. Crusts should not be
removed because they contain acantholytic keratinocytes. With rare exceptions, skin devoid of epithelium
should not be biopsied because epithelium is required
for a histologic diagnosis. Moist, tightly adhered crusts,
pustules, vesicles or the epithelialized edge of an erosion

Pemphigus Foliaceus
Pemphigus foliaceus (PF) is a fairly common autoimmune disease that affects many species, including dogs
and cats. The disease affects middle‐aged to older animals. No sex predilection has been recognized.
Dogs may develop large pustules, erosions and crusts
on the face (particularly the periocular region and bridge
of the nose), concave aspect of the pinnae, pawpads, and/
or trunk (Figure 162.7). Pruritus may or may not be present. Pemphigus foliaceus in cats is characterized by
crusting on the pinnae, face, and/or nailfolds. Caseous
debris may also be present around the nails (Figure 162.8).
Pruritus is usually absent.
The reader is referred to the pemphigus introduction
above for details about biopsy technique and special testing. Histopathology reveals broad, subcorneal pustules
with acantholytic keratinocytes. Differential diagnoses
include superficial pyoderma, pustular dermatophytosis,
and drug reactions. Complications include fever, weight
loss, lethargy, and anorexia in pets that have widespread
lesions. Concurrent dermatophytosis and/or secondary
pyoderma may also be present.

erythema of the nailfold associated with pemphigus foliaceus.

Glucocorticoids are generally effective but often need
to be combined with azathioprine. Glucocorticoids can
also be combined with ciclosporin, chlorambucil, or tetracycline with niacinamide (see Table 162.1).
Topical flea and tick products that contain amitraz
have been associated with pemphigus‐like disease. The
first step in treatment should be to discontinue amitraz‐
containing flea/tick preventives. Immunosuppressive
therapy should then be started.

Prognosis is guarded for pets that do not respond to or

Prognosis is good for pets that respond easily to therapy

Pemphigus Erythematosus
Pemphigus erythematosus (PE) is an autoimmune
­disease with characteristics of pemphigus foliaceus and
DLE. Dogs and cats are affected; no breed or sex predilections have been identified.
It is characterized by lesions that are limited to the face
and pinnae. Specifically, the nasal planum and sometimes the concave aspect of the ears are affected with
pustules, erosions, crusts and sometimes depigmentation. Refer to the pemphigus introduction above for
details about biopsy technique and special testing.
Histopathology reveals acantholysis and interface dermatitis. Differential diagnoses include dermatophytosis
(Trichophyton mentagrophytes), DLE, and pemphigus
foliaceus. Complications include secondary infections of
lesional skin.
Treatment involves immunosuppression with one or a
combination of the following: tetracycline/niacinamide,
glucocorticoids, azathioprine, ciclosporin, and/or topical tacrolimus (see Table 162.1). Avoidance of intense
sun exposure may also be helpful. Prognosis is good.
Some cases may be more responsive to therapy than
others.
Pemphigus Vegetans
Pemphigus vegetans (PV) is an exceedingly rare autoimmune disease of dogs. Three cases are described in
the literature. The disease is characterized by wart‐like
projections on the pinnae, axillae, and sternum.
Additionally, pustules and vesicles may be present on
the abdomen and paws, and erosions may be present on
­ embranes. See the pemphigus introduction
mucous m
above for details about biopsy technique and special
testing. Histopathology in humans reveals suprabasilar
clefting.
Treatment is immunosuppression (see Table 162.1),
and prognosis is guarded due to the paucity of information regarding this disease in dogs.
Pemphigus Vulgaris
Pemphigus vulgaris is a rare autoimmune blistering
­disease of dogs and cats. This disease can occur at any
age and male dogs appear to be predisposed but there is
no breed predilection.
Characteristic lesions are dramatic and include flaccid
vesicles, erosions, and ulcers. Mucosal or mucocutaneous

lesions are generally observed first, followed by lesions
that may occur on the face and nose (see Figure 162.5).
Pressure points, pawpads, and intertriginous areas are
also usually affected. Refer to the pemphigus introduction above for details about biopsy technique and special
testing. In cases where mucosal erosions ­predominate, a
wedge biopsy encompassing both margins of the lesion
may be preferred over a punch biopsy. Histopathology
reveals suprabasilar clefting with a­ cantholytic keratinocytes and rounded basal cells.
Differential diagnoses include paraneoplastic pemphigus, mucous membrane pemphigoid, bullous pemphigoid, EBA, erythema multiforme, and epitheliotropic
cutaneous lymphoma. Complications include lethargy,
anorexia, weight loss, and secondary skin infections.
Treatment involves immunosuppression with glucocorticoids combined with azathioprine or chlorambucil
or tetracycline/niacinamide (see Table 162.1). Prognosis
is guarded as this disease may be refractory to therapy.

­Uveodermatologic Syndrome
Uveodermatologic syndrome or Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada‐
like syndrome is a rare disease of dogs. The pathomechanism is currently unknown but antibodies directed against
melanocytes and pigment‐associated proteins have been
identified, suggesting that autoimmunity plays a role.
There is evidence that genetics p
­ articipates in disease
development in akitas. Uveodermatologic syndrome
affects young to middle‐aged dogs, and there is no
apparent sex predilection. Akitas, Samoyeds, Siberian
huskies, Alaskan malamutes, and chow chows are
overrepresented, although numerous other breeds have
been affected.
The disease is characterized by acute onset of unilateral or bilateral uveitis and concurrent erythema, scaling
and depigmentation of the hair, lips, eyelids, nose and
occasionally the footpads, scrotum, anus, and hard
­palate. In most cases, the skin signs are mild with depigmentation being the main lesion. Pruritus may or may
not be present.
The diagnosis is based on history, physical (especially
ocular) examination, and skin biopsy findings. The
­clinician should biopsy an area of erythematous and
depigmented skin. Histopathology reveals lichenoid
granulomatous dermatitis with melanophages. Ocular
examination is necessary to diagnose uveitis.
Differential diagnoses include concurrent separate
ocular and skin diseases. Uveitis is often an indicator of
systemic disease and may be secondary to immune‐
mediated, infectious, neoplastic, toxic, metabolic,
­traumatic, or idiopathic processes. Other causes of hair
and mucocutaneous skin depigmentation include DLE,

VetBooks.ir

162 Autoimmune and Immune‐Mediated Skin Diseases

alopecia areata, vitiligo, pemphigus erythematosus, and
epitheliotropic cutaneous lymphoma.
Therapy should be directed towards preserving vision.
Skin lesions may respond while eye lesions continue to
progress. Frequent monitoring of the eyes is important.
Topical or intravitreal glucocorticoids, topical cycloplegics, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors should be insti-

tuted along with systemic glucocorticoids combined
with azathioprine or ciclosporin (see Table 162.1).
Complications may include secondary glaucoma,
­cataracts, and blindness. Prognosis is guarded, although
better when treatment is instituted early in the disease
course. Repigmentation of the skin and hair may or may
not occur.

Approach to Alopecia
Linda A. Frank, DVM, MS, DACVD
Department of Small Animal Clinical Sciences, College of Veterinary Medicine, University of Tennessee Institute of Agriculture, Knoxville, TN, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Alopecia or hypotrichosis are common reasons for
­presentation to a veterinarian. Alopecia implies complete
hair loss while hypotrichosis implies thinning of the hair
coat. The presentation of alopecia/hypotrichosis may be
localized or generalized and focal, patchy or diffuse,
depending on disease severity, duration, and the cause of
the hair loss. Alopecia may be traumatically induced, with
the patient scratching or licking the hair off, or due to hair
falling out or failing to regrow following normal shedding.
Trauma‐Induced Alopecia
Trauma‐induced alopecia is most often secondary to
pruritus. Common causes include allergies, ectoparasites, bacterial skin infections, and Malassezia dermatitis. Less common causes in older animals include
neoplastic diseases such as epitheliotropic lymphoma or
mast cell tumor and paraneoplastic syndromes.
Inflammation‐Induced Alopecia
Alopecia not associated with trauma may be due to an
inflammatory condition, such as pyoderma, follicular
demodicosis, dermatophytosis, or sebaceous adenitis
(Table 163.1).
Sebaceous adenitis is an immune‐mediated destruction of the sebaceous glands and is associated with scaling and alopecia. Breed predilections include the
standard poodle, Samoyed, akita, and vizsla. In short‐
coated dogs, these conditions present as a patchy or
“moth‐eaten” pattern of alopecia (Figure 163.1).
The lesions might not overtly appear inflammatory;
however, the multifocal pattern of the alopecia should
make you suspicious of an inflammatory cause. Hairs may
epilate easily from the periphery of these inflammatory

alopecic sites but not from other locations on the body.
While pruritus can be associated with these diseases and
may even be directed at the lesions, it is not the cause of
the alopecic spots.
Vasculitis from immune‐complex deposition secondary to infectious or immune‐mediated diseases may
cause multifocal alopecia due to local ischemia. Clinically,
the lesions may resemble dermatophytosis in that they
are circular and alopecic; however, they appear noninflammatory, lacking erythema and crusting with thin
rather than thickened skin, unless cutaneous necrosis
and ulceration occur (Figure 163.2).
A common example of focal ischemic alopecia is rabies
vaccination‐induced vasculitis. Vasculitis may also be
seen with drug reactions, tick‐borne diseases, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Dermatomyositis is an inherited (autosomal dominant with variable penetrance)
disorder that primarily affects collies and Shetland sheepdogs. Vasculitis and ischemic dermatitis are thought to be
part of the pathogenesis of the disease.
Autoimmune/immune‐mediated diseases such as alopecia areata or pseudopelade and neoplastic conditions such
as epitheliotropic lymphoma could result in areas of
inflammatory alopecia. Alopecia areata is an immune‐
mediated attack on the hair bulb while pseudopelade is an
immune‐mediated attack on the follicle wall, resulting in
focal to multifocal alopecia. Clinically, the areas of alopecia
may not show evidence of erythema, suggesting a noninflammatory mechanism; however, the pattern of alopecia
necessitates investigation into inflammatory differentials.
Paraneoplastic alopecia occurs in association with
internal neoplasia. This is a presumed inflammatory alopecia although the pathomechanism of the alopecia is
unknown. Paraneoplastic alopecia has been described in
cats in association with pancreatic and biliary carcinoma. The alopecia is acute and progressive with easy
epilation of hair and smooth thin skin.

Noninflammatory Alopecia
Alopecia may also occur as a consequence of abnormal
hair cycling or hair development. These are grouped
under noninflammatory causes of alopecia and include
endocrine diseases as well as congenital/hereditary and
idiopathic causes of alopecia. To understand these conditions, it is important to understand the hair cycle.
Briefly, the anagen phase of the hair cycle is when the
hair is actively growing. In most dogs and likely all cats,
this is a relatively short phase lasting at most a few
months until the hair reaches its maximum length. The
length of the anagen phase, and thus the length of hair, is
genetically determined and may be of different durations
for different regions of the body. From anagen, the hair
goes through a short catagen phase in which it reverts
into a nongrowing or telogen hair. The hair can remain in
telogen for a prolonged period of time before a new cycle

is started. For some breeds such as the malamute, this
may be a few years. The telogen hairs are well anchored
and do not epilate easily. Thus, the presence of telogen
hairs is not necessarily pathologic. Dogs that require frequent hair clipping, such as poodles, have a hair cycle
more similar to people in that they have a prolonged anagen phase with fewer hairs in telogen at any point in
time. These dogs are more likely to develop alopecia
from chemotherapeutic agents which inhibit actively
dividing cells. Shedding, or exogen, is separate from the
hair cycle and is independent of whether a new hair cycle
is starting.
Alopecia Associated with Abnormal Hair Growth

Abnormalities in hair growth occur during the anagen
phase of the hair cycle. There are only a few conditions
that fall into this category and they include follicular
dysplasias, congenital hypotrichosis, color dilution alopecia, and black hair follicular dysplasia. Follicular
dysplasias, where abnormal follicles fail to produce
healthy anagen hairs, are most often associated with
alopecic breeds (e.g., Chinese crested dog, Mexican hairless dog, and the Sphynx cat) in which the alopecia is a
breed characteristic. Congenital hypotrichosis is poorly
described in small animals. The hypotrichosis/alopecia occurs either at birth or within the first six months of
life and may be associated with other ectodermal
defects. Color dilution alopecia and black hair follicular
dysplasia are color‐restricted alopecias that begin

VetBooks.ir

163 Approach to Alopecia

gradually in the first three years of life (Figure 163.3).
The alopecia involves a defect in melanosome migration
and/or transfer, which occurs during the anagen phase of
the hair cycle.
Alopecia Associated with Hair Cycle Arrest

Alopecia associated with abnormal hair cycling typically
occurs because the hairs remain in telogen and a new
anagen cycle is not initiated. With time, the telogen hairs
are shed but are not replaced, resulting in a diffuse, often
symmetric alopecia. Areas of wear such as the neck,
pressure points, and tail may become alopecic first as
these hairs are removed by friction.
There are many conditions that appear to be associated with hair cycle abnormalities. These include

hypercortisolemia, hypothyroidism, hyperestrogenism,
­
alopecia X, patterned alopecia of various breeds, cyclic
flank alopecia, postclipping alopecia, and anagen/telogen defluxion. Some of these conditions are associated
with a temporary alopecia (postclipping alopecia, anagen/telogen defluxion), some may be seasonal (cyclic
flank alopecia), and others are likely permanent with
variable response to treatments (alopecia X, patterned
alopecia). The cutaneous changes associated with endocrine dermatoses may also occur with other hair cycle
abnormalities, including diffuse alopecia often sparing
the head and distal extremities, seborrhea, comedones,
hyperpigmentation, and cutaneous infections. In addition, many of the histologic characteristics associated
with endocrine dermatoses (telogen hairs, follicular keratosis, hyperkeratosis, excess trichilemmal keratinization [flame follicles], thin epidermis, and thin dermis)
may also be seen with other hair cycle abnormalities. It is
important to realize that, with a few exceptions, histopathology cannot differentiate endocrine diseases from
other causes of hair cycle arrest.
Specific Noninflammatory Alopecic Disorders
Alopecia X

Figure 163.3 Neck region of a 9‐year‐old female spayed gray and

Alopecia X is a hair cycle arrest that affects primarily
plush‐coated breeds but also toy and miniature poodles
(Table 163.2). It is presumed to be hereditary because of
the strong breed predilections although the specific
defects or mode of inheritance have yet to be determined. Dogs affected are usually young adults but alopecia X can affect any dog between 1 and 10 years of age.
There is no sex or neuter status preference with this condition. Clinically, dogs present with progressive symmetric alopecia that spares the head and distal extremities
(Figure 163.4).
The alopecia is often associated with hyperpigmentation of the skin. Because of the similarity of this condition with endocrine dermatoses, it is important to rule
those conditions out before a diagnosis of alopecia X can
be made. A unique feature of this disease is hair regrowth
at the site of biopsy or surgical trauma.

Patterned Alopecia

Patterned alopecia is a tardive hypotrichosis that often
starts at less than 1 year of age. Many syndromes have
been described that are breed restricted. These include
pinnal alopecia of dachshunds, ventral and caudal alopecia of dachshunds and Boston terriers (Figure 163.5),

Figure 163.5 Patterned alopecia in a young adult female spayed
Boston terrier with alopecia of the lateral thorax and ventrum.

Cyclic flank alopecia is a seasonal or cyclic truncal alopecia that usually occurs during or just after short daylength period. The alopecia affects the flanks, lateral
thorax, and sometimes caudodorsum and nose bridge
(Figure 163.6).
There are often bizarre patterns to the alopecia and the
skin may be intensely hyperpigmented. Less common presentations include hypotrichosis and hair pigment changes
without overt alopecia, also in strange patterns. The alopecia may not recur each year or in some cases may be permanent. Age of onset is 1.5–4.5 years. Breeds reported to be
affected by this condition include boxers, English and
French bulldogs, and Airedales (see Table 163.2).
Postclipping Hair Follicle Arrest

Postclipping alopecia or hair follicle arrest refers to failure of hair regrowth following close clipping, usually in
preparation for surgery (Figure 163.7).
It may occur more frequently in plush‐coated breeds
and there are two theories as to why this occurs. The first

Figure 163.6 Alopecia of the lateral thorax and flank in a male
castrated boxer with cyclic flank alopecia.

163 Approach to Alopecia

VetBooks.ir

­Signalment
The breed and age of onset should aid in the initial differential list (see Table 163.1). Congenital/hereditary alopecias are more likely to occur within the first few years
of life while endocrine dermatoses and neoplastic diseases occur in middle‐aged to older animals. Depending
on the trigger, immune‐mediated dermatoses can occur
within a wide age range and affect many breeds and their
crosses.

­History and Clinical Signs

Figure 163.7 Adult male castrated mastiff with postclipping
alopecia secondary to receiving an epidural injection.

is that the clipping/surgical preparation causes a hair
cycle arrest, possibly because of a temperature change
with vasoconstriction to the skin surface. The other theory applies primarily to the plush‐coated breeds. It is
thought that these dogs may have been clipped during a
time when their hair is in a prolonged telogen phase and
not able to initiate a new anagen cycle. It is also possible
that the clipping uncovered an endocrine or other noninflammatory alopecia condition. The hairs are not
cycling because of an underlying disease such as hypercortisolemia or alopecia X but alopecia has not yet
occurred. The clipping simply hastened the alopecia.
With postclipping hair follicle arrest, the hairs should
spontaneously resume normal cycling within 7–30
months, often following a strong stimulus for hair cycling
such as shortening day length.
Anagen/Telogen Defluxion

Anagen or telogen defluxion involves hair loss following
an illness. Telogen defluxion occurs more commonly in
small animals. The illness causes an abrupt cessation of
anagen, synchronizing all hairs in telogen. In 1–3 months
following the illness, large numbers of telogen hairs are
shed synchronously as a new anagen hair cycle begins.
Hairs epilate easily during this time. Anagen defluxion
occurs more commonly in large animals. The illness
causes a generalized disturbance of the anagen stage of
the hair cycle resulting in a sudden loss of coat. In contrast to telogen defluxion, hair loss occurs within two
days to one week following the illness. In both of these
conditions, hairs regrow normally.

When evaluating the dog or cat for alopecia, a thorough
history and physical examination are in order.
Determining the presence or absence of pruritus and the
distribution and pattern of hair loss will help determine
the ultimate cause of the alopecia.
Clinically, pruritus‐induced alopecias are characterized by broken hairs where the animal has been
scratching. Microscopic examination of the tips of the
hairs (trichogram) will show a blunted or fractured tip
instead of a tapered tip if the animal is inducing the
alopecia secondary to trauma. This technique is not
helpful if dogs are groomed and clipped regularly, as all
of their hairs will be blunted. Evidence of excoriations
supporting pruritus may also be observed in the alopecic areas.
Onset of Alopecia
If the onset of alopecia is rapid, infectious or paraneoplastic conditions need to be considered. Also, a recent
history of systemic illness could be the cause of a rapid
onset of alopecia.
Ease of Epilation
Easy epilation of hairs is more often associated with
inflammatory causes of alopecia such as pyoderma, dermatophytosis or demodicosis but can also be seen with
conditions that result in rapid progression of alopecia
such as anagen/telogen defluxion.
Distribution and Pattern of Alopecia
Distribution and pattern of the alopecia may be key to
identifying the underlying diagnosis or formulating your
differential diagnosis list but requires careful observation. If the alopecia is color restricted, likely this is color
dilution alopecia or black hair follicular dysplasia. If the

1437

VetBooks.ir

1438

alopecia is patchy throughout the coat, an inflammatory
cause is likely, whereas if the alopecia is diffuse and symmetric, a noninflammatory cause is more likely.

Minimum Dermatology Database
A minimum dermatology database consisting of skin
scrapings, fungal culture, and surface cytology should be
performed on all cases of alopecia. If infections are suspected by clinical presentation (patchy alopecia) or
detected by the dermatology database, then treatment

Trichogram
Trichogram involves the plucking of hairs and examination under the microscope. The tips of the hairs can
be examined to determine if the alopecia is traumatically induced (see above). The shafts of the hairs can
be examined to look for abnormal clumping of melanin and distortion of the hair shaft, suggestive of color
dilution alopecia. This method is not useful for black
hair follicular dysplasia, as the hair is too pigmented
to allow for this observation. The bulbs of the hairs
can be examined for evidence of a preponderance of
telogen hairs, which might suggest telogen defluxion
when coupled with ease of epilation and supportive
history.
Histopathology
Histopathology will help rule out many of the inflammatory causes of alopecia (e.g., folliculitis, sebaceous adenitis, vasculitis, alopecia areata, pseudopelade, neoplasia,
or paraneoplastic dermatitis) but, as stated before, it seldom allows differentiation of endocrine diseases from
other noninflammatory causes of alopecia such as alopecia X or patterned alopecias. It is helpful to first treat any
infections that are identified prior to performing a biopsy
as inflammation associated with the infection could
mask other causes of alopecia.
Endocrine Testing
If noninflammatory alopecia is first occurring in a
­middle‐aged dog, further investigation into a possible
endocrinopathy is warranted. This may include basic
bloodwork and urinalysis to screen for abnormalities
consistent with an endocrinopathy. However, even if all

laboratory parameters are within normal limits, endocrine testing may still be indicated.
Additional Diagnostic Tests
If an older dog or cat first develops alopecia, screening
for neoplasia becomes very important. Diagnostics in
this case may include basic bloodwork, urinalysis, histopathology, and imaging.

­Therapy
Treatment depends on the cause of the alopecia.
Table 163.3 lists treatment options for some of the
inflammation‐induced causes of alopecia.
For many of the noninflammatory causes of alopecia
associated with hair cycle arrest (alopecia X, patterned
alopecia, cyclic flank alopecia, and postclipping alopecia), melatonin therapy may result in hair regrowth. The
recommended dosage is 3 mg q12h for small dogs and
6–12 mg q12h for larger dogs. Side‐effects are minimal,
with the most common one being sedation. It is possible
that melatonin causes insulin resistance so it should be
used with caution in diabetic animals. Recently, medroxyprogesterone acetate injections were shown to be marginally effective for treating some Pomeranian dogs with
alopecia X.

­Prognosis
Alopecia in itself is seldom a life‐threatening condition
although, in some instances, it may be a cutaneous
marker for a systemic disease that could carry a guarded
to grave prognosis. Most alopecia caused by pruritus or
inflammation can be managed or treated once the underlying cause is identified. If follicular destruction occurs
secondary to severe inflammation or ischemia, alopecia
could be permanent. In addition, immune‐mediated
conditions such as alopecia areata and pseudopelade
may fail to respond to treatment.

163 Approach to Alopecia

Many congenital/hereditary alopecias have a guarded
prognosis for hair regrowth. Once the diagnosis has been
determined, it becomes of cosmetic concern only. While
some treatments may result in varying degrees of hair

regrowth for these individuals, the veterinarian and client must decide if the risks of the treatment are warranted for the disease.

This chapter will review the etiology, pathogenesis,
diagnosis, management, and prognosis of the most
common canine sterile papular and nodular dermatoses, including histiocytic disorders, sterile nodular
panniculitis, sterile granuloma/pyogranuloma syndrome,
and juvenile cellulitis.

­Canine Histiocytic Disorders
Canine histiocytic disorders include canine reactive histiocytosis (cutaneous and systemic) and histiocytic sarcoma complex (localized and disseminated histiocytic
sarcoma).
Canine Reactive Histiocytosis
Canine reactive histiocytosis includes systemic histiocytosis (SH) and cutaneous histiocytosis (CH). Both
forms are characterized by reactive proliferation of activated dermal dendritic cells. They affect mainly the
skin and subcutaneous tissue, but in the systemic form
other organ systems can be involved, including lymph
nodes, eyelids, sclera, nasal cavity, lungs, spleen, and
bone marrow.

Epidemiology

Age at the time of diagnosis ranges from 3 to 9 years and
males and females can both be affected, but one study
showed male predilection. Collies and Shetland sheepdogs may be predisposed.
Clinical Signs

Cutaneous histiocytosis is characterized by multiple
hairless, erythematous dermal to subcutaneous nodules
localized predominantly to the face, neck, nasal mucosa,
perineum, scrotum, and feet (Figures 164.1 and 164.2).
The lesions are not pruritic or painful, but larger lesions
may become ulcerated and cause discomfort. The lesions
wax and wane, with older lesions spontaneously regressing as new ones form. The disease is usually slowly progressive and, in some cases, may spontaneously resolve.
Diagnosis

The clinical differential diagnoses include other ­nodular
skin diseases such as neoplasia (e.g., multiple ­cutaneous
histiocytomas, mast cell tumors, cutaneous lymphoma),
infectious granulomas, sterile nodular panniculitis,

Therapy

Figure 164.1 Two‐year old Bernese mountain dog with

and planum nasale.

Immunosuppressive drugs have been used with mixed
results. Most cases respond completely or partially to
immunosuppressive therapy with glucocorticoids, but
require long‐term or intermittent therapy to induce
remission and prevent reoccurrence. Up to 50% of cases
respond to prednisone as sole therapy. Azathioprine,
ciclosporin, and leflunomide have also been shown to be
effective, and can be helpful in cases not responding to
glucocorticoid therapy. Tetracycline/niacinamide treatment has been found to be effective as maintenance therapy to avoid recurrence. Since tetracycline has been
unavailable in the US market, doxycycline or minocycline can be substituted for tetracycline.
Prognosis

Prognosis is guarded. Up to one‐third of patients have
reoccurrence of skin lesions and thus long‐term therapy
is required. Dogs with nasal involvement may be more
likely to have recurrence.
Systemic Histiocytosis

Systemic histiocytosis is considered a disseminated form
of cutaneous histiocytosis. In addition to the skin and
mucocutaneous junctions, lesions may be found in the
lungs, spleen, liver, lymph nodes, eyelids, sclera, and
bone marrow.
Figure 164.2 Close‐up of the lesions on the lips of the dog in
Figure 164.1. Note the multiple, crusted, erosive to ulcerative
nodules.

Histologically, the skin lesions are characterized by a
nodular to diffuse infiltrate that extends from middermis
to the subcutaneous tissue. The infiltrate is perivascular
and periadnexal. Early lesions have a linear or nodular
configuration, but it may become diffuse in chronic cases.
The infiltrate can invade the wall of blood vessels, causing
focal or multifocal areas of ischemic necrosis. Important
differential diagnoses for histopathology include sterile

Etiology/Pathophysiology

The etiology and pathogenesis of SH are currently
unknown. As for CH, since infectious agents have not
been identified and the disease responds to immunosuppressive therapy, immune‐dysregulatory mechanisms
are likely involved.
Signalment

Systemic histiocytosis was first recognized in Bernese
mountain dogs, but since then has been described in several other breeds. In one report including 26 dogs,
Bernese mountain dogs were overrepresented (11/26),

followed by Rottweilers (4/26), and golden and Labrador
retrievers (3/26). The age at the time of diagnosis varies
from 1 to 9 years. Males seem to be more frequently
affected in Bernese mountain dogs. No sex predisposition was observed in other breeds.

Ocular lesions may be more difficult to treat and often
require the use of ophthalmic ciclosporin preparations.
The use of high doses of glucocorticoids and cytotoxic
agents has shown poor response.

Clinical Signs

Prognosis

Systemic histiocytosis differs from CH in the extent of
lesions present and the multiorgan involvement. Lesions
affect the skin, with high prevalence for mucocutaneous
junctions; other organs commonly involved include the
nasal cavity, eyes, spleen, lymph nodes and testicular tissue. Bone marrow, liver, lungs, and gingiva can also be
affected. In a recent study, 2/26 dogs had hypercalcemia.
The clinical signs vary depending on the organs affected
and extension of the lesions. Anorexia, weight loss, conjunctivitis, and stertorous respiration are commonly
seen. The disease waxes and wanes and dogs are asymptomatic between clinical episodes. The clinical episodes
can increase in severity and respond less effectively to
therapy with chronicity.

The prognosis is guarded; the clinical course waxes and
wanes but it is usually prolonged. Most cases are euthanized due to relapse of clinical signs or poor response to
therapy.

Diagnosis

Clinical differential diagnoses include neoplasia, infectious and sterile granulomas, cutaneous histiocytosis,
and cutaneous sterile granuloma and pyogranuloma syndrome. The diagnosis is based on history, clinical signs,
cytology, histopathology, and ruling out infectious causes.
Cytologic findings are similar to CH, consisting mainly
of large numbers of histiocytes, with occasional bi‐ or
multinucleated giant cells. Histopathologic findings are
identical to those observed with CH, composed of multifocal nodular infiltrate affecting the deep dermis and
subcutaneous tissue. The cellular infiltrate consists
mainly of histiocytes, lymphocytes, and neutrophils. The
infiltrate is angiocentric and may invade the blood vessels, causing destruction of the vascular wall, thrombosis, and ischemic necrosis. Invasion of the blood vessel
wall has been observed more consistently in cases of SH.
The infiltrating histiocytes express CD1+, CD11c+,
MHC II+, CD4+, and Thy‐1+ (CD90), consistent with
activated dermal dendritic cells.
Therapy

The clinical signs wax and wane, and some dogs can
undergo long periods of remission, but most cases require
long‐term immunomodulatory therapy. The experimental use of thymosin, which modulates T lymphocyte
effector and regulatory function, has shown promising
results; however, further use of this treatment has not
been documented. Good response has been seen with
leflunomide and ciclosporin, both of which have an
inhibitory effect on T lymphocytes. The good response to
these drugs suggests an important role of T lymphocytes

Histiocytic Sarcoma Complex

Previously known as malignant histiocytosis, this complex includes localized and disseminated histiocytic sarcoma (HS). Histiocytic sarcoma is a highly aggressive
neoplasm. It may develop as a localized tumor or a
widely disseminated disease; animals with initially localized disease often develop metastasis. The disease is
characterized by infiltration of neoplastic proliferation
of cells of the histiocytic lineage, including dendritic
antigen‐presenting cells and macrophages. The presence of macrophages has been documented only in
cases of hemophagocytic HS, in which the histiocytes
are markedly erythrophagocytic. Histiocytic sarcoma is
highly breed specific, with Bernese mountain dogs,
Rottweilers, and flat‐coated and golden retrievers having a high prevalence. Immunohistochemistry plays an
important role in differentiating histiocytic tumors from
other neoplasias with similar histopathologic findings
such as lymphoma, poorly differentiated mast cell
tumors, and malignant fibrous histiocytoma.
Pathogenesis

Histiocytic sarcomas are characterized by localized
or disseminated infiltration of malignant histiocytes.
Expected immunohistochemical expression pattern
for HS in snap‐frozen tissue samples is CD1+, CD4‐,
CD11c+, CD11d‐, MHC II+, ICAM1+, Thy ‐1+/‐.
Hemophagocytic HS expresses MHC II, beta‐2 integrin,
and CD11d. The disease is familial in Bernese mountain
dogs in which an oligogenic mode of transmission has
been proposed.
Signalment

Histiocytic sarcoma affects mainly Bernese mountain
dogs, Rottweilers, flat‐coated and golden retrievers with
a median age at presentation of 8 years. The tumor has
been found to have a male predisposition in Bernese
mountain dogs and flat‐coated retrievers.
Clinical Signs

Localized HS is reported to be most common in the
bone, appendicular joints, and skin. Distant metastasis

to the lungs, lymph nodes, and abdominal viscera has
been reported in up to 91% of cases. Affected dogs are
usually presented for lameness or a soft tissue swelling.
In dogs with disseminated HS, the clinical signs are
vague and include anorexia, lethargy, and weight loss.
Pulmonary involvement is common and dogs may show
evidence of dyspnea at the time of initial presentation.
Neurologic abnormalities, including ataxia and paraparesis, are also common. Other organs often affected
include the liver and spleen. Although clinicopathologic
findings are nonspecific, anemia, thrombocytopenia,
and hypoalbuminemia were consistently reported in
cases of hemophagocytic HS. Diffuse splenomegaly
with ill‐defined masses was also consistently present in
these cases.

Diagnosis

­Sterile Nodular Panniculitis

The diagnosis is based on clinical signs, signalment, and
cytologic and histopathologic findings. The main clinical differential diagnoses are other neoplasias and systemic histiocytosis. Both localized and disseminated HS
have the potential for highly aggressive behavior so
complete staging to determine disease extent is recommended to determine possible treatments and prognosis. Cytologic finding include large round cells with
foamy cytoplasm and multinucleated giant cells admixed
with spindle‐shaped cells. Histopathologically, the tumors
are poorly demarcated and the neoplastic infiltrate consists of pleomorphic mononuclear cells and multinucleated
giant cells. Phagocytosis of neutrophils and erythrocytes is not uncommon. Marked anisokaryosis and
anisocytosis with high mitotic rate are also present. The
histopathologic findings and the use of immunohistochemical staining help differentiate these tumors from
other round cell tumors.
Recently, a screening program has been proposed for
early detection of disseminated HS in Bernese mountain
dogs. The program suggests screening of Bernese mountain dogs over 4 years of age every six months, including
diagnostic imaging and measurement of ferritin as a
blood‐borne marker of the disease.
Therapy

For cases of localized HS, improved outcome has been
reported with the use of localized therapy, including surgery and radiation therapy. Unfortunately, the rate of
metastasis is very high (up to 91%) so the use of adjuvant
systemic therapy may be beneficial. The disseminated
form of the disease usually has poor sensitivity to chemotherapy. Lomustine, doxorubicin, and vincristine have
been used with variable success. The use of bisphosphonates has been proposed to increase the effectiveness of
chemotherapy against HS cells. The use of a multiple
drug protocol including cyclophosphamide, vincristine,

Prognosis

In general, the prognosis is poor. Dogs with localized
HS receiving aggressive localized treatment and systemic chemotherapy may have a better prognosis with
a median survival time of 568 days. The median survival time for dogs with disseminated HS receiving
chemotherapy is 106 days. The presence of distant
metastasis or disseminated disease worsens the prognosis. Many dogs are euthanized at the time of diagnosis because of poor clinical condition and poor
prognosis.

Panniculitis refers to inflammation of the subcutaneous fat and it may be associated with a variety of conditions. Sterile nodular panniculitis (SNP) refers to
sterile inflammation of the subcutaneous fat tissue of
unknown origin. Clinical signs include single or multiple subcutaneous nodules, intermittent fever, and
anorexia.
Concurrent inflammation of the fat in other organs
can be seen in cases of SNP. Skin lesions can be solitary
or multiple and multiple lesions can be associated with
systemic signs including fever, lethargy, and anorexia.
Pathogenesis
Sterile nodular panniculitis has been documented in
association with systemic lupus erythematosus, pancreatitis and pancreatic tumors, rheumatoid arthritis, and
lymphoplasmacytic colitis. In people, a deficiency of
alpha‐1‐antitrypsin, a protease inhibitor, has been suggested to be a predisposing factor. In dogs, this association has not been made with certainty. In one dog with
panniculitis in which alpha‐1‐antitrypsin was found to
be low, a Bartonella infection was present, making it difficult to determine the cause. In one retrospective study,
37% (16/43) of the patients had prior surgery with lesions
developing at the surgery site.
Signalment
A large retrospective study did not identify any age,
breed or sex predilection; however, others suggest 3–5
years as the most common age of onset and dachshunds,
miniature poodles, and collies as the breeds at increased
risk for SNP. In two studies, the most affected dogs were
neutered, suggesting no gender predilection.

VetBooks.ir

164 Canine Sterile Papular and Nodular Skin Diseases

Clinical Signs
Clinically, SNP manifests as single or multiple subcutaneous nodules varying in size from a few millimeters
to several centimeters in diameter. Lesions can be of
normal skin color or be erythematous or bluish in
color. Initially, the nodules are firm but they may liquefy and become soft. Some lesions regress while others develop draining tracts and become ulcerated
(Figure 164.3).
Well‐delineated ulcers are characteristic. Draining
lesions discharge an oily, clear to yellowish brown material, which may also be hemorrhagic (Figure 164.4).
Nodules may heal with scarring and are more commonly found on the trunk but can occur anywhere.
Fever, lethargy, and anorexia are commonly seen in dogs
with multiple lesions; these signs occur simultaneously
or just before the beginning of nodule formation. Other

Figure 164.3 Multifocal areas of ulceration on the lateral thorax of
a Labrador retriever with sterile nodular panniculitis.

systemic signs reported include peripheral lymphadenopathy, joint effusion and pain, vomiting, and abdominal pain.
Diagnosis
Sterile nodular panniculitis must be differentiated from
other forms of panniculitis and other diseases with similar clinical presentation, including infectious diseases
such as bacterial, fungal or mycobacterial infection, sterile granuloma and pyogranuloma syndrome, foreign
bodies, injection site reaction, insect bite, drug reaction,
and neoplasia. Sterile nodular panniculitis is diagnosed
based on the patient’s history and clinical signs, exclusion of other causes of panniculitis, and cytologic and
histopathologic findings. It can be a cutaneous marker of
a concurrent disease process so a systematic diagnostic
approach is needed to help identify a possible etiologic
factor.
A complete history, physical examination, and minimum database including hemogram, chemistry profile
and urinalysis can serve as guides in deciding which
additional test(s) will be useful in the diagnosis. In a
recent study, neutrophilia, increased alkaline phosphatase (ALP), mild hypoglycemia, and hypoalbuminemia were present in over 50% of cases with systemic
involvement. Cytologic evaluation of aspirates from
intact lesions can vary in appearance from suppurative
to pyogranulomatous or granulomatous with fat droplets
or cells present and no microorganisms. Aspirates from
deep firm nodules may show spindle cells that resemble
neoplastic cells. The definitive diagnosis can be based
only on histopathologic findings. Wedge biopsies should
be performed to collect samples that include the epidermis, dermis, and subcutaneous tissue. The sample should
be collected aseptically if submitted for fungal, bacterial
(aerobic/anaerobic), and mycobacteria cultures. Bacterial
and fungal cultures of intact nodules yield no growth.
Special stains of biopsy samples can be used to help eliminate bacteria and fungi as causative agents. Some organisms are difficult to culture or identify with routine
methods, and molecular studies like polymerase chain
reaction (PCR) are necessary. This is particularly true for
mycobacteria and Leishmania.
Therapy

Figure 164.4 Oily, hemorrhagic discharge from an ulcerated
nodule in a Weimaraner with sterile nodular panniculitis.
Source: Courtesy of Dr Melanie Hnot.

Surgical excision of solitary masses can be curative. Dogs
with multiple lesions are treated with immunosuppressive drugs. In dogs, oral prednisone or prednisolone is
usually effective at 2 mg/kg/day for two weeks; then, the
patient should be reevaluated. If remission is achieved
within that time, the dose should be decreased by 25%
every seven days until the lowest effective dose is given

every 48 hours. Regression of the lesions may take 2–8
weeks. If remission has not been achieved after four
weeks of daily immunosuppressive doses of glucocorticoids, the case may require combination therapy with
other immunosuppressive drugs such as azathioprine or
ciclosporin. Topical and intralesional corticosteroids
have been effective in some cases, and may be the treatment of choice when systemic immunosuppressive therapy is contraindicated. In addition to immunosuppressive
treatment, vitamin E and potassium iodide have been
recommended, but their efficacy is unknown.
Prognosis
The prognosis is usually good, with most cases showing
a good response to treatment. Some cases may require
prolonged immunosuppressive therapy.

­Sterile Granuloma/Pyogranuloma
Syndrome
Sterile granuloma/pyogranuloma syndrome (SGPS) is an
uncommon disease presenting clinically with cutaneous
papules, nodules or plaques of unknown origin. The
lesions may be solitary or multiple, and localized or
generalized.
Pathogenesis
Sterile granuloma/pyogranuloma syndrome is an idiopathic canine skin disorder. The pathogenesis is
unknown, but the inflammatory nature of the infiltrate,
failure to demonstrate infectious agents, and the good to
excellent response to immunomodulating drugs support
it being an immune‐mediated disorder. However, it has
been hypothesized that SGPS may be related to an
immune response against persistent endogenous or
exogenous antigens, such as Leishmania spp. or
Mycobacterium spp. organisms or incomplete clearing of
associated antigens, causing a granulomatous/pyogranulomatous inflammatory reaction. The presence of
Leishmania spp. DNA has been documented in cases of
SGPS in Spain and Italy. The finding of antigenic fragments or organisms may become possible as we advance
our diagnostic techniques.

Clinical Signs
The clinical signs are characterized by firm, hair‐covered
to partially alopecic, erythematous papules, nodules, or
plaques. Lesions develop more commonly on the head
and distal extremities, and less commonly on the pinnae,
eyes, trunk, and abdomen. Lesions involving the tongue
and prepuce have been seen in individual dogs. In most
cases, the lesions are multiple and are not associated
with pain or pruritus. Occasionally, draining tracts and
ulceration can be observed, especially on lesions localized to the feet (Figure 164.5).
Lymphadenopathy was present in 31% of the cases in a
review including 29 dogs. Systemic signs associated with
this syndrome have not been reported. The condition
may resolve spontaneously or take a waxing and waning
course.
Diagnosis
Clinical differential diagnoses include bacterial and fungal infections, foreign bodies, SNP, cutaneous eosinophilic granulomas, and cutaneous neoplasms. Diagnosis
of SGPS is based on its clinical appearance, histopathologic findings, and failure to document the presence of
microorganisms. Wedge biopsies should be performed
to collect samples that include the epidermis, dermis,
and subcutaneous tissue. The samples should be collected aseptically if they are being submitted for cultures.
Histopathologically, SGPS is characterized by multifocal,
nodular to diffuse pyogranulomatous/granulomatous
dermal infiltrates. Special stains on biopsy samples are
negative. Aerobic and anaerobic bacterial cultures and
fungal culture from fresh tissue samples are also negative. Some organisms are difficult to culture or identify
with routine methods, and molecular studies such as

Signalment
Sterile granuloma/pyogranuloma syndrome can affect
dogs of any age and gender, but in a retrospective study
24/29 cases were male. It is seen more frequently in the
Great Dane, boxer, golden retriever, collie, dachshund,
English bulldog, and Weimaraner.

Figure 164.5 Partially alopecic, erythematous and ulcerated
nodule present in the interdigital space of digits 4 and 5 in a
dog with sterile granulomatous pyogranulomatous syndrome.
Source: Courtesy of Dr Wendy Lorch.

VetBooks.ir

PCR are necessary. This is particularly true for mycobacteria and Leishmania.
Therapy
Surgical excision can be curative for solitary nodules or
plaques. Systemic treatment is often needed for multiple lesions, including immunosuppressive doses of
glucocorticoids or other immunomodulating agents.
The use of tetracycline and niacinamide combination
was shown to be effective for long‐term management in
a case of SGPS. A trial with this combination is warranted before more potent immunosuppressive drugs
are used. Tetracycline/niacinamide is used at 250 mg
of each for dogs less than 10 kg, and 500 mg of each in
dogs more than 10 kg q8–12h. If tetracycline is unavailable, doxycycline at 5 mg/kg q12h can be used. If
shortage of doxycycline occurs, minocycline can be
substituted for doxycycline.
Prednisone or prednisolone can be used at 2.2–4.4 mg/
kg q24h PO until resolution of the skin lesions (usually
10–14 days), then the medication can be tapered to the
minimal effective dose (see treatment for sterile nodular
panniculitis). Most cases require long‐term alternate‐day
glucocorticoid therapy to avoid reoccurrence. Refractory
cases may require the addition of other immunomodulating agents like ciclosporin or azathioprine.
Prognosis
The prognosis is good. The condition may resolve spontaneously or take a waxing and waning course. Most cases
required prolonged use of immunomodulatory drugs.

­Juvenile Cellulitis
Canine juvenile cellulitis, also known as juvenile pyoderma, puppy strangles, or juvenile sterile granulomatous dermatitis and lymphadenitis, is an uncommon
lymphocutaneous disease. It is characterized by a sterile
granulomatous or pyogranulomatous dermatitis and
lymphadenitis and usually affects young puppies.
Pathogenesis
The cause of juvenile cellulitis is unknown. Cytologic
examination of aspirates of affected lymph nodes and
skin lesions does not reveal infectious agents, and culture results of intact lesions are always negative for bacterial and fungal growth. In addition, the condition
responds dramatically to treatment with glucocorticoids,
suggesting an immune dysfunction. There may be a
­heritable component as it has been documented more

frequently in certain breeds and within litters. Vaccine
reactions have been postulated as the cause of juvenile
cellulitis, but the role of vaccine or other viruses in the
disease development remains unclear. A nonviral infectious etiology has also been considered but attempts to
isolate bacteria and fungi have not been successful.
Signalment
Most cases are young puppies less than 4 months old,
with a few reported cases in older dogs. No sex predilection has been reported. Breeds that appear to be predisposed include golden retrievers, dachshunds, Gordon
setters, and Weimeraners. Other breeds reported include
the Labrador retriever, Siberian husky, miniature poodle, Chesapeake Bay retriever, Lhasa apso, and mixed‐
breed dogs.
Clinical Signs
Early clinical signs consist of edematous moist dermatitis affecting mainly the eyelids, lips, and muzzle. The
affected skin rapidly develops papules and pustules.
Lesions are characterized by severe edema, fistulation,
and drainage with copious purulent discharge and crust
formation. Purulent otitis externa and conjunctivitis are
also common; the pinnae are often severely swollen and
may develop ulcerative lesions. Affected skin is usually
painful. Submandibular and prescapular lymphadenopathy is commonly present. Concurrent neurologic signs
and orthopedic problems have been reported preceding
or associated with the signs of juvenile cellulitis. The
patient may be lethargic and depressed and older dogs
may present with more severe systemic signs and pyrexia.
Diagnosis
Clinical differential diagnoses include angioedema in
acute cases and as lesions progress; staphylococcal pyoderma, demodicosis, and adverse cutaneous drug reaction should also be considered. Other less likely
differential diagnoses include neoplasia (cutaneous lymphoma, mast cell tumor) or infectious causes such as
nocardiosis, actinomycosis, mycobacterial infections,
and subcutaneous opportunistic mycoses. Diagnosis is
often based on characteristic clinical presentation, but
can be confirmed by cytologic or histopathologic findings. Tests may include fine needle aspirates of lymph
nodes, impression smears or skin scraping, cytology or
skin biopsy. Cytology from fine needle aspirates of
affected lymph nodes reveals a sterile granulomatous or
pyogranulomatous inflammation. Histopathologic findings usually reveal granulomatous or pyogranulomatous
dermatitis which may extend into the panniculus.

1447

VetBooks.ir

1448

Section 12 Skin and Ear Diseases

Furunculosis and suppurative inflammation have also
been reported in advanced cases.
Therapy
Treatment consists of immunosuppressive doses of
glucocorticoids. Initial treatment should be aggressive, as scarring can be severe if the disease is not controlled quickly. Oral prednisone or prednisolone can
be given at 2 mg/kg/day until lesions resolve, usually
2–4 weeks, and then slowly tapered off completely
over the next few weeks. Some dogs may respond
­b etter to oral dexamethasone at 0.2 mg/kg/day (initial
dose). Antibiotics should be given if secondary bacterial

infections are present. Oral cephalexin can be given at
25–30 mg/kg q12h for the duration of the corticosteroid treatment. Ciclosporin has also been effective in
cases refractory to glucocorticoids. Griseofulvin was
used with good results in six puppies at the dose range
of 14.2–34 mg/kg q12h. All cases were completely
recovered within three weeks. The authors postulated
that griseofulvin could induce downregulatory signals
within the lesions.
Prognosis
The prognosis is good. Most cases respond well to treatment and relapses are uncommon.
