­Demodicosis
Canine Demodicosis
Etiology/Pathophysiology

Canine demodicosis is currently known to be caused by
three species of mites: Demodex canis, D. injai, and D. cornei. Demodex canis and D. injai are thought to be two separate species. However, D. cornei, a short‐bodied mite, is
believed to be a morphologic variant of D. canis. Demodex
canis and D. injai live within the hair follicles or sebaceous
glands, and D. cornei lives on the stratum corneum.
Recent studies using real‐time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) have validated the widely held belief that all
dogs, healthy and diseased, harbor D. canis mites in their
skin. Puppies are believed to acquire D. canis from their
mothers at birth. However, the mode of transmission of
D. injai and D. cornei is currently not known.
Demodex canis mites have a life cycle involving four
stages. They begin as fusiform eggs. These eggs develop
into six‐legged larvae, then eight‐legged nymphs,
­followed by the adults. The life cycle of D. cornei and
D. injai has not been investigated but it is likely to mirror
the life cycle of D. canis. Adult D. injai mites are much
longer than the D. canis species (Figure 165.1). Adult
D. cornei mites have a short tail (Figure 165.2).
Demodicosis caused by D. canis can occur in juvenile
(≤18 months) or adult dogs (>4 years). Older dogs that
develop demodicosis may have another disease process
leading to an immune dysfunction that allows the mites
to multiply and cause disease. Some examples include
hyperadrenocorticism, hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus, or malignant neoplasia. Immunosuppressive therapy
can also result in a proliferation of mites. This includes
topical and oral corticosteroids and oclacitinib maleate
(Apoquel® for dogs; Zoetis). Allergic dermatitis is often a
concurrent diagnosis. Often, no cause is identified for

the development of adult‐onset demodicosis. Demodex
injai has only been reported in adult dogs.
The reason for development of demodicosis in some
dogs versus others is not precisely known. We do know
that certain breeds develop disease more commonly than
others, suggesting the influence of genetics. Breeds more
commonly diagnosed with demodicosis caused by
D. canis include the shih tzu, West Highland white terrier,
English bulldog, and Boston terrier. In the author’s experience, pit bull terriers and Yorkshire terriers also seem
overrepresented. Demodicosis caused by D. injai has
been noted at greater frequency in terriers and shih tzus.
Other factors suggested to play a role include parasitism, inadequate nutrition, and stress. However, many
affected patients do not have these problems. Various ex
vivo studies have investigated the immune response of
dogs with juvenile‐onset generalized demodicosis caused
by D. canis, but a defect has yet to be identified.
Nevertheless, the current belief is that these dogs inherit
an immune dysfunction of variable severity linked to a
subset of T cells capable of recognizing specific mite
antigens and keeping the mites in small numbers. This
theory, however, needs to be validated. Overexpression
of the Toll‐like receptor 2 gene may result in the clinical
findings associated with demodicosis.
History and Clinical Signs

There are two types of infestations of Demodex mites:
localized and generalized. The localized variant consists
of one or more lesions usually on the face and forelegs.
These cases typically self‐resolve and affect puppies. An
infestation is considered generalized when large body
areas, several localized lesions, an entire body region, or
two or more paws are affected. This form primarily
begins at the puppy stage and may resolve, but typically
progresses without treatment as the puppy ages.

Demodex canis infestation can cause a variety of signs.
Lesions seen can include alopecia, erythema, scales, papules, and pustules. If hair follicles rupture (i.e., furunculosis), severe inflammation associated with tracts
draining serosanguineous to purulent exudate is noted
(Figure 165.3).
Lymphadenopathy and/or fever may occur in these
cases especially if large areas of the body are affected.
Follicular casts and comedones are very typical lesions.
Pruritus may or may not be present and is usually noted
when secondary infection or seborrhea occurs. Secondary
superficial or deep bacterial infection is often present in

Figure 165.3 Juvenile‐onset generalized demodicosis caused by
Demodex canis. Diffuse alopecia, erythema, and edema are noted.
Hemorrhagic crusts on the lateral aspect of the face correspond to
areas of furunculosis.

the generalized form of the disease and may aggravate
lesions, resulting in crusts, pustules, thickened skin,
and hyperpigmentation. Paws rarely are affected alone
and lesions can be similar to the ones described. Bullae

VetBooks.ir

165 Parasitic Skin Diseases

and fistulous tracts are also present on paws when furunculosis develops (Figure 165.4).
Demodex cornei mites have been found in demodicosis
caused by D. canis, suggesting that these mites are a morphologic variant of D. canis and not a separate species.
Demodex injai typically manifests with dorsal and
occasionally facial seborrhea oleosa (Figure 165.5). In
these areas, hypotrichosis is present. Pruritus may also
be noted.
Diagnosis

Diagnosis of D. canis infestation involves performing
multiple deep skin scrapings. As mites live in the hair
follicles and sebaceous glands, the lesional area is
squeezed before scraping in an attempt to extrude the
mites. The scraping should be deep enough that capillary
bleeding occurs. Multiple adult mites and/or immature
forms are diagnostic. Mites should be easy to find if skin
scrapings are performed adequately. If only a few mites
are found after multiple skin scrapings in an animal with

clinical signs suggestive of demodicosis, consider this
finding important. This scenario is typically encountered
in cases of juvenile, localized demodicosis.
Similar technique should be applied when D. injai
infestation is suspected; however, mites can be harder to
find because they are present in small numbers and often
in sebaceous glands, making their extrusion difficult.
Superficial scrapings should be adequate for D. cornei
but mites are typically not easy to find.
Trichoscopy may also reveal mites in severe cases of
demodicosis caused by D. canis. Various hairs are plucked
from affected areas, placed in mineral oil on a glass slide
and covered with a cover slip before microscopic evaluation. These may or may not be positive in affected dogs.
Acetate tape impressions of affected squeezed skin have
recently been shown to reveal mites in 100% of samples.
Mites can also be found on cytology of exudate collected
from draining tract lesions. Mites may also be identified
using a zinc sulfate centrifugal fecal flotation technique. It
is important to emphasize that sensitivity of these tests is
generally lower than that of deep skin scrapes adequately
performed. Biopsy may be needed in Chinese shar‐peis or
dogs with fibrotic lesions especially affecting the paws.
Mites can be found in the stratum corneum, hair follicles,
and on occasion the sebaceous glands. Inflammation
may present as an interface mural folliculitis, nodular
dermatitis, or a ­suppurative folliculitis and furunculosis.
Therapy

Figure 165.4 Feet of a dog with juvenile‐onset generalized
demodicosis caused by Demodex canis. Multiple tracts draining
serosanguineous exudate correspond to areas of furunculosis.

Figure 165.5 Excessive oil along the dorsum of a West Highland
white terrier with demodicosis caused by Demodex injai.

Affected dogs should be treated with appropriate systemic antibiotics, if indicated. Supportive care may be
needed in severe cases. Underlying disease processes
should be addressed. Localized cases are typically self‐
limiting and resolve without treatment in about 6–8
weeks. Generalized cases should be treated for one
month beyond two negative consecutive skin scrapings.
Skin scrapings are recommended monthly to assess
­progress. Numbers of live versus dead mites and their life
stages can help assess response to therapy.
The most effective treatments are amitraz, macrocyclic
lactones, and isoxazolines. The only treatment ­currently
licensed in the United States is amitraz. Labeled treatment is a 0.025% amitraz (Mitaban®; Zoetis) solution used
as a dip every 14 days. Variations of this therapy protocol,
such as weekly applications at 0.025%, 0.05%, 0.075% or
0.1%, can be considered for more difficult cases. Removal
of follicular debris, crusts, and hair that prevents penetration of the solution into the hair follicle is an important
part of this treatment regimen; therefore, medium to long
hair coats should be clipped and crusts removed prior to
dipping. This chemical is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor
as well as an alpha‐2‐adrenergic a­ gonist. Potential side‐
effects include lethargy, ataxia, vomiting and diarrhea,
polyuria and polydipsia, bradycardia, depression, and
hyperglycemia. The person ­providing treatment should

1451

VetBooks.ir

1452

Section 12 Skin and Ear Diseases

not directly contact the solution or inhale it. Application
in a well‐ventilated area is important.
Ivermectin is a therapy that is often very efficacious in
treating demodicosis. Herding breeds should be assessed
for a mutation of the ABCB1 (formerly MDR1) gene
which encodes for the cell membrane transporter
P‐­glycoprotein. This mutation can lead to severe toxicosis
with avermectins. Some of the breeds reported to be predisposed to this mutation include collies, border c­ ollies,
Shetland sheepdogs, Australian shepherds, Old English
sheepdogs, white Swiss shepherds, long‐haired whippets,
McNab, and silken windhound. This mutation is still
possible in any dog breed, but less likely. The genetic test
for the mutated gene can be done through Washington
State University College of Veterinary Medicine.
Possible side‐effects associated with ivermectin toxicosis include lethargy, vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia, mydriasis, and ataxia. In severe cases, seizures, coma, and death
can result. Side‐effects can also occur in dogs that carry a
normal ABCB1 gene and are often less severe and may
resolve by lowering the dosage. Due to possible side‐
effects, an incremental dose increase is strongly suggested.
The dosage range is 0.3–0.6 mg/kg once a day PO. The
author determines dosing by calculating the dose desired
in this range and starting at one‐third this dose. This is
given for one week, followed by two‐thirds the final dose
for one week, then ending at the final dose desired.
Other macrocyclic lactones that can be used are
­moxidectin and doramectin. Moxidectin is dosed at 0.2–
0.5 mg/kg/day PO. Again, gradual dosing is indicated.
Possible side‐effects include those listed for ivermectin.
Moxidectin is also available as a topical product in combination with imidacloprid (Advantage Multi® for dogs;
Bayer). This is an approved European treatment applied
weekly for demodicosis. It is labeled for monthly usage in
the United States but has shown better results when
applied every 1–2 weeks, primarily for juvenile‐onset cases
and mild forms of demodicosis. Doramectin can be given
at 0.6 mg/kg subcutaneously (SC) or PO once a week. The
SC administration has resulted in better outcomes.
Milbemycin oxime (Interceptor® for dogs; Elanco) is
another efficacious product. This can be used at 0.5 mg/
kg PO once daily increasing by 0.5 mg/kg every seven
days to a final dosage of 2.0 mg/kg/day. This medication
is generally well tolerated. Mild neurologic side‐effects
have been noted. Breeds that do not tolerate ivermectin,
including collies, may tolerate this medication but care is
recommended to ensure no adverse side‐effects ensue,
as neurologic effects are still possible. Ataxia has been
noted in dogs homozygous for the ABCB1 gene mutation at a dosage of 1.5 mg/kg/day PO.
The newest available therapies are in the isoxazoline
class. These drugs are not labeled for treatment of Demodex
sp. but have been found to be very efficacious. These
include lotilaner (Credelio® for dogs; Elanco) at 20 mg/kg

PO, and sarolaner (Simparica® for dogs; Zoetis) given at
2 mg/kg PO. These products are labeled for monthly usage
for flea and tick prevention and treatment. Fluralaner
(Bravecto® for dogs; Merck) given once at a minimum dosage of 25 mg/kg PO has also been found to be very efficacious at treating demodicosis. This product is labeled for
administration every 12 weeks for the prevention and
treatment of flea and tick infestations in dogs. Afoxolaner
(Nexgard®; Merial) given at the minimum dosage of 2.5 mg/
kg PO every 14 days for two months has been found to be
very effective. However, only one dose may result in deep
negative skin scrapings. It is labeled for monthly usage for
flea and tick control and can be used in dogs 8 weeks of age
and older, whereas fluralaner and sarolaner can only be
used in dogs at least 6 months of age. Lotilaner, like afoxolaner, may be used in dogs as young as 8 weeks of age.
These parasiticides act by blocking insect GABA‐ and glutamate‐gated chloride channels and are generally very safe
but should be used with ­caution in dogs with a history of
seizures. Possible side‐effects include vomiting and diarrhea. Sarolaner may cause tremors, unsteadiness, or seizures. Fluralaner may cause seizures in patients which do
not have a history of seizures, but is labeled as safe for use
in breeding, pregnant, and lactating dogs, and in those
with the ABCB1 gene mutation. Lotilaner may also cause
an increase in blood urea nitrogen. Afoxolaner should be
used with caution in dogs with a history of seizures.
Females or males that have been treated should be
neutered due to the potential for passing the predisposition to develop demodicosis to offspring. In addition,
females should be spayed because the stress of a heat
cycle or pregnancy could worsen the disease.
Prognosis

Overall, prognosis is good. Recurrence of disease can
occur, so following the treatment recommendation of
30 days past two consecutive negative skin scrapings can
help prevent recurrences. Life‐long therapy may be
needed in some cases. Long‐term glucocorticoids are
not recommended in patients with demodicosis or that
have had demodicosis. The author believes that any glucocorticoids or oclacitinib maleate (Apoquel; Zoetis)
should be used with great caution. A dog is not considered cured until one year after treatment is completed.
With the advent of isoxazolines as maintenance flea and
tick ­preventtives, the likelihood of recurrence or even
development of demodicosis will probably diminish.
Feline Demodicosis
Etiology/Pathophysiology

Three species of demodectic mites have been implicated
in feline demodicosis. These include D. cati, D. gatoi, and
an uncommon, unnamed, morphologically distinct
Demodex mite. Demodex cati spends its life cycle in the

VetBooks.ir

165 Parasitic Skin Diseases

hair follicles and sebaceous glands. This mite is slightly
narrower than D. canis. Demodex gatoi has a shortened
abdomen and spends its life cycle on the epidermal
­surface. The length of the unnamed mite is between
D. cati and D. gatoi.
Demodicosis due to D. cati is typically associated with
an underlying disease or immunosuppressive therapy.
Concurrent diseases that may be present include feline
immunodeficiency virus, feline leukemia virus, diabetes
mellitus, squamous cell carcinoma in situ or other ­neoplastic
disorders, toxoplasmosis, systemic lupus ­erythematosus,
and hyperadrenocorticism. It has been reported to be
more common in the Burmese and Siamese breeds.
Demodex gatoi, unlike D. cati, is not generally associated with an underlying disease. However, it has been
identified in scrapings along with D. cati in cats positive
for feline immunodeficiency virus. This mite is more
commonly located in certain geographic areas. In the
United States, it is more often found in the south,
­especially in the Gulf of Mexico area.
Little is currently known about the unnamed Demodex
mite. The published reports have found this mite in cats
diagnosed with other concurrent illnesses or had recently
­recovered from illness.
History and Clinical Signs

Demodex cati can cause either a localized or generalized
infestation, both of which are rare. Localized demodicosis is primarily located around areas on the head, including in the ears, causing a ceruminous otitis externa,
particularly in feline immunodeficiency virus‐positive
cats. Pruritus is variable but typically not present. Other
signs include alopecia, erythema, and the presence of
scales and crusts. Generalized cases often affect the head
but lesions are also found elsewhere on the body.
Presentation is similar to the localized form, but may
include hyperpigmentation.
Demodicosis caused by D. gatoi is more common than
the disease caused by D. cati. It is contagious between
cats and pruritic. Clinical signs are typically fitting with
the degree of pruritus. Traumatic alopecia often results
from the severe pruritus on the sides of the thorax,
abdomen, and the medial aspect of the legs. Other signs
include erythema, scale, excoriation, and hyperpigmentation. A common clinical presentation is self‐­induced,
clinically noninflammatory, symmetric alopecia
(Figure 165.6). Some cats can be asymptomatic carriers.
Diagnosis

Skin scrapings should be performed in cases where feline
demodicosis is suspected. Broad, superficial scrapings
are performed to detect D. gatoi (surface mite), whereas
deep skin scrapings must be done to diagnose D. cati (follicular). Demodex gatoi mites are typically more d
­ ifficult
to find due to their small size and low numbers as cats

Figure 165.6 Self‐induced, clinically noninflammatory, symmetric
alopecia on the dorsum and thighs of a cat with demodicosis
caused by Demodex gatoi.

ingest these mites during grooming. Therefore, scraping
areas where the cat cannot groom may increase the
chances of finding mites. Fecal flotation may be another
means of finding D. gatoi. Cellophane tape impressions
viewed under the microscope may help to reveal the
mites. A negative test does not rule out this infestation so
diagnosis in many cases may only be made based on history and response to a therapeutic trial. The unnamed
mite has been found via trichoscopy and skin scrapings.
Therapy

Underlying causes leading to the development of demodicosis caused by D. cati should be evaluated. This disease
when localized may resolve spontaneously if underlying
diseases have been controlled. Amitraz (Mitaban; Zoetis)
at concentrations of 0.0125–0.025% applied weekly may
help. Cats are sensitive to this product and it is not recommended in cats with diabetes. A generally safe option
is lime sulfur applied as a 2–4% solution every week.
Unfortunately, therapy may need to be continued long
term as relapses are possible. Other treatment options
include doramectin administered weekly at 0.6 mg/kg SC
and ivermectin at 0.2–0.3 mg/kg PO daily to every other
day. Cats should be monitored for side‐effects such as
neurotoxicity. The off-label use of the oral isoxazoline
fluralaner (Bravecto) for the treatment of demodicosis
has been reported in cats. A single oral dosage of 28 mg/kg
resolved D. cati in one case report. No side‐effects were
noted. Topical fluralaner, which is available for cats, may
cause vomiting and diarrhea, decreased appetite, or
lethargy. It may also cause alopecia or crusting. While a
single topical treatment has been shown to be efficacious
for the treatment of Otodectes cynotis in cats, there are

1453

VetBooks.ir

1454

Section 12 Skin and Ear Diseases

currently no studies evaluating it’s use in the treatment
of feline demodicosis. Independent of the parasiticidal
chosen, treatment should be continued for 30 days past
two consecutive negative skin scrapings performed 4–6
weeks apart.
Options for D. gatoi include the above treatment
protocols described for amitraz or lime sulfur dips.
­
Treatment ­typically is needed for 6–8 weeks. In‐contact
cats should be treated as well. Application of a moxidectin/imidacloprid (Advantage Multi for cats; BayerDVM)
spot‐on product every week to two weeks for up to three
months has been anecdotally reported to work well in
some cases. It has also been shown to be efficacious in
one case report, applied weekly for 10 doses. Also, ivermectin at 0.2–0.3 mg/kg PO every 24–48 hours may be
effective. The extra-label use of oral fluralaner (Bravecto)
at 26–34 mg/kg given once has recently been shown to
be another efficacious treatment option.
No specific treatment recommendations exist for the
unnamed mite, but concurrent daily ivermectin at
0.3 mg/kg PO and 8 oz/gal of diluted lime sulfur rinses
twice weekly for 6–8 weeks has been used. Also, SC ivermectin at 0.6 mg/kg daily for four weeks has been used.
For all types of feline demodicosis, isoxazolines may
prove to be efficacious. Also, topical fluralaner may be a
viable option as opposed to oral administration. More
studies are needed in this area.
Prognosis

The prognosis of feline demodicosis varies, especially in
cases of D. cati where underlying systemic disease is likely
present. Overall, prognosis varies from good to guarded.

Description of mite characteristics is important in differentiating canine scabies from the feline Sarcoptidae
mite, Notoedres cati. Sarcoptes scabei mites are ovoid
and small, with two anterior pairs of short legs with long
unjointed stalks and suckers. There are two pairs of
­rudimentary posterior legs that do not extend beyond
the body wall of the mite (Figure 165.7). The anus is
terminal.
Research suggests that young dogs of any breed and of
both sexes are more likely to become infested with the
mites, suggesting that age‐related immunity plays a role
in pathogenesis. Nutritional status and oxidative stress
also play a role in development of infestation. Specifically,
alterations in the oxidant and antioxidant balance and
greater apoptosis of peripheral leukocytes may contribute to a dog’s susceptibility to infestation.
History and Clinical Signs

Scabies causes an intense pruritus. It is important to
question if other pets or humans in the same household
are also pruritic as this is a valuable diagnostic clue.
However, some dogs can be asymptomatic carriers. As
previously mentioned, this mite typically affects specific
body regions but any body region can be affected.
Corticosteroids may be beneficial in some patients at the
beginning of therapy to reduce pruritus.
Early signs include papules and scales. Excoriations
may also be present. With chronicity, self‐induced alopecia, hyperpigmentation, hyperkeratosis or keratinous
crusts, and lichenification may develop. The crusts
may become thick and yellow (Figure 165.8). Peripheral
lymphadenopathy may be present. Some dogs only
­
develop erythema and excoriations.

­Scabies
Canine Scabies
Etiology/Pathophysiology

Sarcoptes scabei var. canis causes canine scabies, or
­sarcoptic mange. This is a highly contagious mite that is
transmitted between dogs as well as foxes and coyotes.
Fomites can also be a source of transmission. The female
burrows into the stratum corneum to lay eggs. The l­arvae
travel to the skin surface and develop into nymphs, which
may live on the skin surface or in the molting pocket that
may also be inhabited by larvae. The mites prefer areas
with less hair, so they are more commonly found on the
pinnae, elbows, hocks, and ventrum. They typically live
17–21 days. Depending on the humidity and temperature,
females and nymphs can survive 4–21 days away from the
host. These mites can cause disease at any time of year.
Other animals including cats, humans, and foxes can be
affected. Humans are usually only transiently affected.

Figure 165.8 Alopecia and thick yellowish crusts covering the ear
margin of a dog with scabies.

Cats that become infested with Sarcoptes scabei var.
canis can develop dermatitis of the face and pinnae.
Papules and crusts are present. Dermatitis of the paws as
well as claw abnormalities may develop. Some cats may
also develop crusting and scaling over the body. Pruritus
is a variable finding. Such infestations are uncommon
and rare cases have been noted in indoor cats not co‐
habiting with dogs.
Diagnosis

Infestations with this mite are often diagnosed based on
history, clinical signs, and response to therapy. Multiple
superficial skin scrapings are required for diagnosis.
Unfortunately, as few as 20% of skin scrapings may reveal
mites or eggs. Finding even one is diagnostic of canine
scabies. It is suggested to scrape the aforementioned
areas that are generally affected even in the absence of
lesions, as well as areas with papules and yellow crusts.
Large numbers of mites are typically found on scrapings
from cats infested with Sarcoptes scabei var. canis.
An additional supportive test is to demonstrate the
pinnal‐pedal reflex. This test entails scratching the
­pinnal edge with a resultant ipsilateral leg making a
scratching motion. Most dogs with scabies mites have
this reflex (sensitivity of 81.8%); however, it can be rarely
positive in other diseases (specificity of 93.8%).
Laboratory testing utilizing an enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) is available in certain countries.
This test has high specificity and sensitivity, but false‐
negative results are possible.
Therapy

Affected as well as in‐contact dogs should be treated.
Area treatments containing pyrethrins, permethrins or a
combination of these are available for use in the home
environment, keeping in mind that high concentrations

of permethrins (>0.1%) are toxic to cats. Discarding
­bedding is advised. In the United States, a licensed treatment is selamectin (Revolution® for dogs, Zoetis) applied
topically every 30 days for two doses; however, for better
results most dermatologists recommend administering it
every two weeks for 3–4 treatments. Lime sulfur dips at a
2–3% concentration every week for 4–6 weeks is another
option. Ivermectin at 0.2–0.4 mg/kg can be given PO
every seven days or SC every 14 days for 4–6 weeks.
Milbemycin given orally at 2 mg/kg every week for 4–6
treatments has been shown to be effective. An imidacloprid/moxidectin combination product (Advantage Multi)
is approved for the treatment of scabies in dogs and is
applied topically every 30 days for two doses. Amitraz
(Mitaban) solution at 0.025–0.03% applied over the whole
body every two weeks for three treatments or weekly for
4–6 treatments should be effective. Fipronil spray applied
to the entire body every two weeks for three applications
is another treatment option. Doramectin can be given at
0.2–0.6 mg/kg SC every seven days for 4–6 weeks.
Many of these patients have secondary infections
which should also be identified and addressed.
Isoxazolines have been shown to effectively treat scabies
as well. One dose of fluralaner (Bravecto) at a minimum
of 25 mg/kg orally or topically has been shown to eliminate scabies mites. Afoxolaner (Nexgard) given at a minimum dosage of 2.5 mg/kg PO for 1–2 monthly doses
should also eliminate these mites. Sarolaner (Simparica)
can also be used at approximately 2 mg/kg PO for two
monthly doses. There are no current publications relating to lotilaner (Credelio) and scabies mites, but the
author suspects it, too, would be efficacious at resolving
sarcoptic mange. Antiinflammatory doses of corticosteroids given for approximately one week may also help in
alleviating the pruritus caused by the mites.
The treatment protocols detailed under “Feline
­scabies” are also recommended for cats infested with
Sarcoptes scabei var. canis. However, three applications
of the moxidectin/imidacloprid (Advantage Multi)
­compound product applied every two weeks has been
shown to be more efficacious in five cats with sarcoptic
mange than weekly ivermectin at 0.2 mg/kg SC for four
weeks or selamectin (Revolution) administered every
two weeks for two treatments.
Prognosis

Most dogs with scabies are cured with treatment. Rare
cases have been noted to be refractory to ivermectin and
selamectin. The selamectin cases may have been related
to poor application on densely coated dogs. In some
cases, the author finds it beneficial to keep the patient on
monthly selamectin or an isoxazoline (unless it is fluralaner which is given every 3 months) when reinfestation is considered possible.

Feline Scabies
Etiology/Pathophysiology

Feline scabies or notoedric mange is caused by Notoedres
cati. This mite can also affect foxes, dogs, rabbits, and
humans. The lesions on humans are transient. It commonly affects other cats in multiple cat residences as it is
very contagious. This mite typically occurs epizootically
in endemic areas.
Notoedres cati follows the same life cycle as Sarcoptes
scabei var. canis. Morphologically, it is similar to the
canine scabies mite but is smaller, the unjointed stalk is
of medium length, more striations are present on the
body, and the anus is dorsally oriented.
History and Clinical Signs

Notoedres cati causes intense pruritus predominantly of
the facial region. The skin becomes thickened with folds
(Figure 165.9). Crusts are yellowish and tightly adherent.
Excoriations and partial alopecia may develop. Lesions
begin on pinnal edges and spread over the face and neck.
The paws and perineum may be affected and peripheral
lymphadenopathy may occur.
Diagnosis

Microscopy of superficial skin scrapings of affected cats
typically reveals several mites. Diagnosis is also achieved
by identifying the eggs or fecal pellets.
Therapy

sulfur dips for 4–8 weeks are beneficial. Treatment should
continue until negative skin scrapings and resolution of
lesions are obtained. Ivermectin at 0.2–0.3 mg/kg may be
given PO or SC every 1–2 weeks for 3–4 treatments.
Doramectin can also be given at a dose of 0.2–0.3 mg/kg
SC once. Selamectin (Revolution) applied topically once or
twice every 14–30 days is another option. The moxidectin/­
imidacloprid (Advantage Multi) topical product has been
shown to be effective after one application.

­Cheyletiellosis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Cheyletiella, also known as walking dandruff, is a mite
that generally results in a dermatitis of varying severity.
Cheyletiella parasitovorax, C. blakei, and C. yasguri are
the species of most concern in dogs and cats, with C. yasguri more likely to be found on dogs and C. blakei more
likely to be found on cats, although these species are not
entirely host specific. All species are contagious, and
humans in contact with animals carrying the mite can
become transiently affected.
These nonburrowing mites produce ova that attach to
the dog or cat hairs. They are large mites that live in the
keratin on the surface of the skin. They have four pairs of
legs with combs and their mouthparts have characteristic hooks (Figure 165.10).

Affected and in‐contact cats should be treated. Safety must
be considered in choosing treatments. Weekly 2–3% lime

Figure 165.9 Thick crusts on the convex aspect of the pinna of a
cat with chronic notoedric mange. Source: Courtesy of Dr Clarissa
Pimentel de Souza.

Figure 165.10 Cheyletiella yasguri mite; note the characteristic
hooks of the accessory mouthparts.

The mites complete their life cycle on the host but
mites and eggs attached to the hair shaft can contaminate the environment, creating a source for reinfestation.
The adult females can also live off the host for approximately 10 days.
History and Clinical Signs
This mite infestation may result in varying levels of pruritus and severity of clinical signs. Any breed may be
affected, but an increased incidence in cocker spaniels
and boxers has been anecdotally reported. The resultant
dermatitis manifests as dry scales along the dorsum
(Figure 165.11). This often worsens over time with hair
loss and an increase in pruritus. Cats can also develop
miliary dermatitis.
Diagnosis
To diagnose Cheyletiella, material is collected from
affected areas by acetate tape impressions, flea combings, or superficial skin scrapes. This material can be
directly examined by visual inspection (often utilizing a
magnifying glass) or using a microscope. If available,
evaluate material in a Petri dish in mineral oil utilizing a
dissecting microscope. Fecal examinations may also
reveal the mite as many pruritic animals will ingest the
offending parasite in the process of licking, biting or
chewing the affected areas. Two other means of garnering material for examination include a vacuum sample of
the affected area or performing a trichoscopy of affected
hairs. Some dermatologists find that scraping papules
(which are usually rare or absent) and microscopically

examining the sample with mineral oil increases the
chances of finding the mite. However, none of these
diagnostic tests is 100% sensitive so a treatment trial may
be necessary to confirm a presumptive diagnosis.
Therapy
Fortunately, cheyletiellosis typically responds well to
therapy. Options include weekly applications of lime
­sulfur or amitraz (Mitaban) dips, or pyrethrin shampoos
and sprays for 3–4 treatments. However, amitraz and
especially permethrins are not generally recommended
for cats due to drug sensitivities. Fipronil in the spray
form every two weeks for 3–4 treatments or topical concentrated solution every 30 days for three treatments are
other options. Selamectin (Revolution) can be applied
monthly or every two weeks for 4–6 weeks. Ivermectin at
0.2–0.3 mg/kg can be given PO weekly for 3–6 ­treatments
or by SC injection every 14 days for three treatments.
Doramectin is an option at 0.2–0.4 mg/kg SC every seven
days for 4–6 weeks. One other treatment is milbemycin
oxime (Interceptor) given at 2 mg/kg PO weekly for 3–4
doses. Because this is a highly contagious mite, all
­animals in the home should be treated.

­Lynxacarus radovsky
Etiology/Pathophysiology
This mite, otherwise known as the cat fur mite, is found
worldwide, typically in warm humid climates, such as in
Australia, Brazil, and Puerto Rico. In the United States, it
has been reported in Hawaii, Florida, and Texas. This
mite is specific to the cat, but has been found on a dog.
Cats acquire this mite through direct contact, but fomites
must also be considered.
History and Clinical Signs
Clinical signs include a dull, unkempt coat giving the hair
a “salt‐and‐pepper” appearance (Figure 165.12). Lesions
may include alopecia, papules, and crusting and are
typically present along the dorsum. Heavily infested cats
or those with a long‐term infestation can have exfoliative lesions. Pruritus is not typically present and when
noted, a search for fleas or other external parasites is
warranted.
Diagnosis

Figure 165.11 Cocker spaniel with cheyletiellosis showing
excessive scaling along the dorsum.

Diagnosis of L. radovsky infestation is accomplished by
identifying the mite with microscopy. Trichoscopy and
tape impressions are the ideal diagnostic methods. The

­Dermanyssus gallinae
Etiology/Pathophysiology
This mite primarily affects poultry but is contagious to
other animals including dogs, cats, and humans. It is a
vector of many significant diseases. Other names are the
poultry mite or red mite. These mites spend most of
their life span off the fowl host, residing in cracks, crevices, and nests within the poultry house. They feed at
night and once fed and engorged, they develop the red
coloration. Poultry mites are resilient and can survive up
to eight months away from fowl.
History and Clinical Signs

Figure 165.13 Lynxacarus radovsky mite. Source: Courtesy of
Dr Clarissa Pimentel de Souza.

Dogs and cats can be attacked by these mites when in
contact with poultry houses or from wild birds that enter
and nest in houses. This mite can cause severe pruritus
along with papules and crusts. Most cases present with
lesions on the limbs and dorsum.

Diagnosis
Finding the mite is best achieved by performing skin
scrapings. Mites may also be visualized microscopically
on samples collected with cellophane tape impressions.
Therapy
These mites generally respond well to almost all parasiticidal treatments. It is also recommended to treat the
­surrounding premises to prevent reinfestation.

­Pediculosis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Pediculosis refers to a dermatitis caused by lice. Two
types affect dogs, Anoplura, or sucking lice, and
Mallophaga, or chewing lice. Linognathus setosus is the
sucking louse of dogs and Trichodectes canis the chewing
louse. Cats are parasitized only with a chewing louse,
Felicola subrostratus. The eggs are deposited on the hairs
of the host. The lice typically stay on one host but can be
transmitted by close contact. They are species specific.
The chewing lice survive primarily on epidermal debris
and hair but some species also take blood. The canine
chewing louse may carry Dipylidium caninum, or tapeworms. Sucking lice solely feed on the blood of the host
and can result in severe anemia.
History and Clinical Signs
Pediculosis is relatively uncommon, but more likely to be
noted in young and uncared‐for animals. Chewing lice
on the dog typically affect the dorsum, head, and tail and
can cause severe pruritus. In the cat, the face, ears, and
back are most commonly affected. Lesions on the dog
typically consist of trauma‐induced alopecia, seborrhea,
and excoriations. Papules and crusts may also be present.
Cats can present with no clinical signs or have intense
pruritus. The coat may be matted with scale, crust, and
alopecia. Sucking lice are primarily present on the pinnae and dorsum, and can result in weakness from the
ensuing anemia. Pruritus with resultant excoriations and
alopecia may also occur.
Diagnosis
Lice can be distinguished based on the morphology of
the head and associated mouthparts. Sucking lice have
an elongated, narrow head, whereas chewing lice have a
broader head with mouthparts adapted for chewing.
They can sometimes be found with direct visualization

of the mite or the nit (egg). Microscopy can be utilized to
view acetate tape impressions of hair and scale.
Therapy
Treatment should target the affected animals as well as
those in contact. Clipping of matted hairs is recommended. Topical sprays and soaks such as lime sulfur can
be utilized twice two weeks apart. However, most insecticidal therapies are efficacious. These include but are not
limited to ivermectin at 0.2 mg/kg PO or SC twice two
weeks apart, selamectin (Revolution) every two weeks for
2–4 treatments, or spot‐on fipronil (Frontline®) or spray
every two weeks. One application of fipronil or selamectin may work as well for chewing lice. Doramectin can
also be used at 0.2–0.4 mg/kg SC weekly for 3–4 weeks.
Imidacloprid (Advantage) spot‐on alone for one application to treat chewing or sucking lice or the combination
with moxidectin (Advantage Multi) applied t­opically
once for chewing lice should be effective. Fluralaner
(Bravecto) given once PO has been shown to eliminate
Linognathus setosus. Appropriate supportive care may be
required for anemic animals. Premises should be treated
as lice can survive 1–2 days off the host.

­Trombiculosis
History and Clinical Signs
Trombiculosis is a dermatitis caused by chigger mites.
The larval forms can cause infestation of dogs and cats.
Eutrombicula alfreddugesi, a mite found in the southeast and south central United States, and Neotrombicula
autumnalis, a mite more commonly found in Europe, are
notably orange‐red in coloration (Figure 165.15). They
typically affect patients in late summer and fall. The
­larval forms attach to the skin.
Lesions often occur in body regions that contact the
ground. However, in cats they are most commonly noted
around the eyes, mouth, and base of the pinnae. The
­larvae pierce the skin and produce pruritic papules and
crusts. Scaling and alopecia may also be present. Some
animals are asymptomatic.
Walchia americana is a chigger mite that has been
reported in cats. It has been found in the southwestern
and eastern United States. These mites preferentially
affect the ventrum, dorsum, and ears but have been
noted on the medial legs and interdigital spaces. Reported
lesions include nodules, papules, and wheals with scales
and yellow exudate. Swollen paws and cracked claws
have been noted.
Straelensia cynotis has been noted on dogs in some
European countries. It too causes infestation primarily in

Treatment of Eutrombicula or Neotrombicula usually
consists of 1–2 applications of topical parasiticidal agents

secondary superficial pyoderma is present.
Treatment of Walchia americana consists of the same parasiticidal products used for the treatment of Eutrombicula
and Neotrombicula. Treatment of Straelensia cynotis has
been suggested with macrocyclic lactones or fipronil.

­Ticks
Ixodid (hard) ticks and argasid (soft) ticks both can affect
cats and dogs. The ixodid ticks, which have a chitinous
shield, can serve as vectors of rickettsial, protozoal, and
viral diseases. They may also cause a hypersensitivity
reaction from their bite, and can sometimes result in tick
paralysis. The types of ixodid ticks of importance will
not be elaborated on in this section.
Argasid ticks do not have the chitinous shield, or
s­ cutum. Otobius megnini can inhabit the ear canal in
dogs and cats. The larvae and nymphs of this tick can
lead to otitis externa. They can cause a severe irritation.
Treatment includes manual removal of the ticks. Oil‐
based ear treatments may smother the tick. Prevention is
key to help reinfestation. Many topical and oral parasiticidal treatments offer tick prevention.

Bacterial Pyodermas
Jennifer R. Schissler, DVM, MS, DACVD
College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Pyodermas are bacterial infections of the skin and commonly involve coagulase‐positive staphylococci. Indeed,
staphylococcal pyoderma is one of the most common
conditions treated in clinical practice. For this reason,
this chapter is focused exclusively on staphylococcal
pyodermas. Staphylococcal infection opportunistically
arises secondary to dermatologic or systemic diseases
that prompt cutaneous physical or immunologic function insults. These may include hypersensitivity, endocrine, conformational, and keratinization disorders, as
well as an immunocompromised status. Clinical presentations are diverse, and mimic a multitude of other
dermatopathies. In the current era of antimicrobial
­
resistance, optimal outcomes for staphylococcal pyoderma are achieved via correct diagnosis, rational treatment and follow‐up, and management of the inciting
cause(s).
Staphylococcus pseudintermedius, previously identified as Staphylococcus intermedius, is the most common
etiologic agent in canine pyoderma. Staphylococcus
aureus, Staphylococcus schleiferi subsp. coagulans, and
coagulase‐negative staphylococci such as Staphylococcus
schleiferi subsp. schleiferi are isolated at a lesser frequency on healthy or inflamed skin.
Staphylococcal pyoderma is less prevalent in cats
than dogs. Feline keratinocyte adhesion of S. aureus
and S. pseudintermedius is inferior compared to human
and dog keratinocytes, perhaps a reflection of inferior
host adaptation. S. pseudintermedius, S. schleiferi, and
S. aureus are most frequently isolated; S. aureus is isolated at a higher frequency than in dogs.

­Pyoderma Classifications
and Presentations
Pyodermas are often categorized based on the depth of
infection (surface, superficial or deep) and the site
involved, particularly when describing a pyoderma
that affects a specific body region (e.g., interdigital
pyoderma, nasal pyoderma). These categorizations are
useful, particularly the depth of infection because
it dictates the methods and duration of therapeutic
interventions.
Surface Pyodermas
Acute Moist Dermatitis

Acute moist dermatitis, also known as pyotraumatic dermatitis and commonly referred to as a “hot spot,” is characterized by the rapid development of a focal, erythematous,
erosive, and exudative lesion that develops due to intense
pruritus and self‐trauma (Figure 166.1).
Acute moist dermatitis is typically initiated by hypersensitivity disorders, including cutaneous adverse food
reaction, atopic dermatitis, and flea bite hypersensitivity,
or pruritogenic parasitic diseases such as pediculosis,
sarcoptic mange, and cheyletiellosis. Surface staphylococcal overgrowth is concurrently present in nearly all
cases of acute moist dermatitis. Cytology of exudate
obtained via surface impression smear reveals neutrophils and intracellular and extracellular cocci. Superficial
bacterial folliculitis lesions (see “Superficial bacterial folliculitis” section below) observed at the periphery of the
self‐trauma suggest a longer duration of staphylococcal
involvement and that the staphylococcal folliculitis itself

Figure 166.1 Acute moist dermatitis in a golden retriever dog
with atopic dermatitis and superficial staphylococcal folliculitis.

may be the inciting cause of the acute moist dermatitis.
This scenario is termed “pyotraumatic folliculitis.”
Patients may present on an emergency basis due to
rapid, severe progression. Lesions can be painful. Sedation
may be required prior to clipping of the coat for optimal
examination and initial topical treatment. A thorough
examination of the entire coat and obtaining a detailed
history are critical, as diagnosis and appropriate management of the underlying pruritic disease are very important, particularly in recurrent cases.
Initial treatment involves cleansing of the lesion
with an antimicrobial. A 2% aluminum acetate solution
(Domeboro® solution, Bayer) may be used as a topical
nonirritating drying and antimicrobial agent. At‐home
therapy involves daily application (1–3 times/day) of a
topical antimicrobial and/or drying agent; use of a topical anesthetic (e.g., pramoxine, lidocaine) or corticosteroid may be additionally beneficial. Limit daily topical
corticosteroid use to no more than one week to avoid
cutaneous side‐effects, such as demodicosis, comedones,
cutaneous atrophy, and ulceration.
Application of an Elizabethan collar or breathable
physical barrier is recommended in the first 3–7 days of
treatment to prevent self‐trauma. Oclacitinib (Apoquel®,
Zoetis), lokivetmab (Cytopoint®, Zoetis), or systemic
corticosteroid treatment is often required to provide
rapid relief of pruritus, and, for severe presentations,
may be required for several days before topical therapy
is attempted at home. Concurrent systemic antimicrobial therapy is required for pyotraumatic folliculitis
(see also “Treatment of pyodermas” section below).
The patient should be rechecked in 7–14 days to assess
response to antimicrobial and antiinflammatory
therapies.
Intertrigo

Increased warmth and humidity of the environment, friction, and the protected cutaneous microenvironments

of skinfolds are predisposing factors for staphylococcal
intertrigo. The aforementioned factors result in surface
maceration of the stratum corneum and bacterial overgrowth, predominantly with staphylococci. Concurrent
Malassezia overgrowth is common, and gram‐negative
bacteria may also contribute. It is largely a condition in
dogs, particularly in the context of hypersensitivity, and
is rare in cats. Intertrigo is typically pruritic. Locations
affected include abdominal, inguinal, vulvar, lip, tail, and
facial folds, with the latter two locations overrepresented
in English bulldogs and pugs. Moist erythematous skin,
purulent exudate, and in advanced cases ulcerative dermatitis are observed (Figures 166.2, 166.3, and 166.4).
Cytology of exudate obtained via surface impression
smear confirms the presence of cocci and may also
involve yeast and rods. Neutrophils are variably present.
Topical antimicrobial and drying agents are indicated.

and Malassezia nasal fold dermatitis with crusting staphylococcal
folliculitis in a pug with atopic dermatitis.

Figure 166.3 Dorsal interdigital moist erythema with Malassezia
and Staphylococcus overgrowth in a 5‐year‐old Rottweiler with
atopic dermatitis.

Superficial Bacterial Folliculitis

Figure 166.4 Severe, purulent tail fold intertrigo with mixed
bacterial overgrowth and crusting staphylococcal superficial
bacterial folliculitis in an English bulldog with atopic dermatitis.
Surgery was ultimately required for control of the dermatitis.

Superficial bacterial folliculitis is the most common
presentation of pyoderma and, as stated previously,
opportunistic S. pseudintermedius is the most common
etiologic agent. Infection of the hair follicle and epidermis produces characteristic follicular‐oriented papules,
pustules, and epidermal collarettes (Figure 166.5) progressing to crusts, “moth‐eaten” alopecia, and hyperpigmentation (Figures 166.6 and 166.7).
In short‐coated dogs, well‐demarcated areas of raised
hair resemble urticaria from afar. Papular crusting dermatitis (i.e., miliary dermatitis) is most frequently observed
in cats. Distribution is dependent on cause, and pruritus is
variable.
Differential diagnoses for folliculitis include, but are
not limited to, dermatophytosis, demodicosis, pemphigus foliaceus, and, in cats, hypersensitivity syndromes.
Systemic and topical treatment is indicated for patients

Surgical correction of redundant folds may be indicated
for severe, recalcitrant presentations.
Superficial Pyodermas
Impetigo

Impetigo, also referred to as “puppy pyoderma,” occurs
in puppies and juveniles less than 1 year old. It is typified
by subcorneal, often grossly large, pustules caused by
staphylococci, most commonly S. pseudintermedius. The
pustules do not necessarily involve the hair follicles and
are typically located in the axillary and inguinal areas.
The pustules progress to crusts and epidermal collarettes. Patients are not typically pruritic nor painful.
Cytology of pustules reveals degenerated neutrophils
and intracellular cocci.
Impetigo is often idiopathic in otherwise healthy puppies. It may also occur in immunocompromised patients
suffering from parasitic or infectious diseases, or suboptimal nutrition and housing conditions.
Impetigo is expected to self‐resolve in otherwise
healthy patients. Use of topical antimicrobial therapy
may hasten resolution and may be required for resolution in immunocompromised patients. Treatment
options include daily to alternate‐day shampoo treatment with a nondrying, antimicrobial shampoo including chlorhexidine or ethyl lactate. Alternatively, for focal
lesions, consider convenient antimicrobial wipes, sprays,
foams, and ointments/creams applied once or twice
daily. Continue topical therapies until lesion resolution.
For severe cases or cases that do not respond to topical
therapy, systemic antibiotics are indicated. Systemic
antimicrobial treatment should continue for one week
past resolution of lesions. Resolution of lesions is
expected to occur within 14 days.

Focal, mild presentations may resolve with daily topical

Diagnosis is achieved via cytology of exudate
obtained by rupture of a pustule or avulsion of crusts.
The presence of extracellular cocci or phagocytosed
cocci confirms the diagnosis. If cytology is negative,
culture and/or histopathology are required to make a
definitive diagnosis. Superficial pyoderma is commonplace, so it is rational to empirically treat cytology‐negative cases of folliculitis to assess for response,
particularly if demodicosis and dermatophytosis have
been ruled out.
Mucocutaneous Pyoderma

Mucocutaneous pyoderma, a crusting, erosive and depigmenting condition of the canine nasal planum and lip
margins, may be an inflammatory response to staphylococci, although the etiopathogenesis remains unknown
(Figure 166.8). It may occur alone or in the context of
cutaneous hypersensitivity.
Less commonly, lesions may involve the prepuce/
vulva, anus, or eyelids. Of note, the German shepherd
dog is overrepresented. Differentials for this condition
include discoid lupus erythematosus, pemphigus foliaceus, and epitheliotropic lymphoma. Mucocutaneous
pyoderma may occur secondary to these conditions, and
the histopathologic findings of mucocutaneous pyoderma are similar to that of discoid lupus erythematosus.
Thus, diagnosis of mucocutaneous pyoderma is typically
made via clinical response to antimicrobial therapy;
cytology of exudate may not confirm the presence of
cocci. Treatment involves antimicrobial systemic and
topical therapy. Empirical or culture‐based antimicrobial
for a minimum of three weeks prior to biopsy of the
aforementioned lesions is recommended to assess for

Figure 166.8 Mucocutaneous pyoderma with multifocal labial
and perioral depigmentation and erythema with multifocal
depigmentation and erosions of the nasal planum in a German
shepherd dog.

responsiveness and optimize likelihood of a diagnostic
biopsy reflective of the primary disease process.
Canine Chronic, Recurrent Pyoderma

Recurrent pyoderma is characterized by the chronic
reemergence of superficial bacterial folliculitis after successful treatment and confirmed clinical and cytologic
resolution. This syndrome is most commonly associated
with atopic dermatitis, cutaneous adverse food reaction
and hypothyroidism, and is typically pruritic when
lesions are present. Treatment of this syndrome includes
not only topical and/or systemic antimicrobial therapy to
treat active infection, but also identification and control
of the underlying dermatosis to prevent recurrence.
Patients with idiopathic recurrent pyoderma are
euthyroid, fail to respond to a proper elimination diet
trial, and have no other signs of atopic or cutaneous disease other than pyoderma typically associated with pruritus. Such patients may be managed via use of frequent
application of antimicrobial shampoos, wipes, or sprays
to limit chronic use of systemic antibiotics. The immune
response to staphylococci, perhaps a true hypersensitivity, may play a role in idiopathic recurrent pyoderma,
and in canine patients with atopic dermatitis. Indeed,

VetBooks.ir

166 Bacterial Pyodermas

subcutaneously injected commercial S. aureus phage
lysate antigens (Staphage Lysate®, Delmont Laboratories)
may be used as maintenance therapy to reduce or eliminate recurrence of pyoderma. This treatment is indicated
in patients with idiopathic or atopic recurrent pyoderma
cases failing to respond to topical maintenance therapy.
Deep Pyodermas
Generalized Deep Pyoderma

Generalized deep pyoderma arises due to furunculosis
(follicular rupture) and foreign body response directed
at the liberated hair shafts in the dermis. Lesions include
nodules, hemorrhagic bullae, ulcers, draining tracts and
crusts with variable pain and pruritus (Figures 166.9
and 166.10).
In cats, deep pyoderma most commonly presents in
the context of chin acne. In short‐coated breeds with

atopic dermatitis or cutaneous adverse food reaction,
cystic hemorrhagic, bullous lesions are often observed
on the chin and interdigital areas. Staphylococci represent the predominant organism but deep pyoderma
may also be accompanied by infection with Enterococcus,
Pseudomonas, and Proteus species as well as Escherichia
coli. Differentials include dimorphic and opportunistic
mycoses, pythiosis, lagenidiosis, neoplasia, foreign
body, sterile pyogranulomatous dermatitis, and other
bacterial etiologies, including species in the genera
Mycobacterium, Actinomyces, and Nocardia. Cytologic
presence of numerous extracellular cocci or phagocytosed cocci supports the diagnosis. Given the diverse
clinical differentials and requirement for prolonged
treatment, bacterial culture (aerobic and anaerobic)
and sensitivity, fungal culture, and histopathology are
recommended for definitive diagnosis and appropriate
treatment.
Canine Acne

Figure 166.9 Nonblanching, hemorrhagic, nodular, deep
staphylococcal pyoderma in a 5‐year‐old Rottweiler with
atopic dermatitis.

This disease is typified by deep folliculitis and furunculosis affecting the chin and perioral margin, and is a
focal form of deep pyoderma. Chin acne usually manifests in young dogs between 3 and 12 months of age
although it often persists throughout adulthood and
may be complicated by concurrent atopic dermatitis or
cutaneous adverse food reaction. Breeds with a short,
coarse hair coat are predisposed, including boxers,
English and French bulldogs, and Boston terriers.
Lesions consist of papules and nodules that often
become erosive and ulcerative with resultant draining
tract formation. Hemorrhagic bullae are also common
(Figure 166.11).
Demodicosis should be ruled out by performing deep
skin scrapes. Juvenile cellulitis is a differential diagnosis;
however, classic submandibular lymphadenopathy as well

as generalized muzzle, periocular, and pinnal involvement clinically differentiate it from chin acne in many
cases (see Chapter 164 for a more thorough discussion of
juvenile cellulitis). Chin acne is supported by the presence of cocci and a mixed population of inflammatory
cells on cytologic evaluation.
Treatment involves systemic antimicrobial therapy,
ideally based on aerobic culture and sensitivity testing
(see “Treatment of pyodermas” section below), with adjunct
topical antimicrobial therapy. Benzoyl peroxide gel, silver
sulfadiazine cream, clindamycin cream, and mupirocin
(reserved for resistant staphylococcal infections), are
often well tolerated when applied to the facial area.
Because furunculosis and subsequent deep pyoderma are
frequently present, treatment for a minimum of six weeks
may be required. Treatment should be continued for two
weeks past clinical and palpable resolution.
Interdigital Pyoderma

Interdigital pyoderma has a diversity of presentations and
therefore terms commonly used include canine pododermatitis, pedal folliculitis/furunculosis, and interdigital
“cysts.” Lesions may include interdigital erythema, salivary staining of hairs, papules, nodules, hemorrhagic bullae, and draining tracts. Clinical signs may include licking
and biting of the feet, and lameness. Staphylococci are
common bacterial etiologic agents of pododermatitis and
infection often occurs concurrently with Malassezia and
gram‐negative bacterial organisms. Interdigital pyoderma is a multifactorial disorder consisting of predisposing abnormal conformation, primary etiologies, and
secondary infections that perpetuate the dermatitis.
Abnormal weight bearing as a result of abnormal conformation, musculoskeletal disease, and/or obesity are
predisposing factors for the development of interdigital
pyoderma. In such cases, rather than generalized interdigital involvement, focal dorsal or ventral dermatitis is
often recurrent in one or several interdigital spaces.
Short‐coated dogs such as Labradors and English bulldogs appear to be predisposed.
Hypersensitivity, autoimmune, and inflammatory conditions are primary etiologies; secondary bacterial and
yeast surface overgrowth and/or bacterial folliculitis perpetuate the dermatitis. Occasionally, hypothyroidism
and hypercortisolism may result in interdigital bacterial
or yeast overgrowth.
A conformation‐related disorder involving ventrally
oriented cystic follicles, primarily on the forelimbs, has
been described. These dilated follicles may be grossly visible as comedones and milia. The cystic follicles rupture
in the dermis. The subsequent foreign body response
clinically manifests as dorsal interdigital nodules, hemorrhagic bullae, and edema (Figure 166.12). Draining tracts
and deep secondary bacterial infection frequently ensue.

Figure 166.12 Dorsal interdigital nodule with hemopurulent
exudate due to furunculosis and deep staphylococcal pyoderma
in a cairn terrier.

Treatment of this condition may include multiple carbon
dioxide (CO2) laser ablations of the ventral cystic lesions
in addition to antimicrobial therapy as described subsequently in this chapter (see “Treatment of pyodermas”).
Diagnosis involves obtaining a thorough history and
performing a physical examination to identify possible
primary causes. Deep skin scrapes or hair plucks for
demodicosis must be performed, as demodicosis may
demonstrate all the aforementioned clinical manifestations. In some cases of pododemodicosis, biopsy may be
required for diagnosis.
Perform multiple surface cytologic preparations of
erythematous interdigital spaces to confirm the presence
of bacterial organisms as well as Malassezia. Consider
aspiration of nodules and hemorrhagic bullae to assess
for secondary bacterial infection and other causes of
nodular dermatitis, including neoplasia. Consider the
possibility of a foreign body, particularly in the context of
a solitary nodular lesion with mixed inflammation.
Culture and sensitivity of tissue biopsies or aspirates of
nodular lesions should ideally be performed with confirmed or suspected bacterial involvement, as such
lesions indicate deep pyoderma and require prolonged
therapy. Avoid culture of draining tracts as they may not
be reflective of the relevant bacterial organisms within
the tissue.
Pedal pruritus (licking and biting of the feet) with generalized dorsal or ventral interdigital involvement persisting despite resolution of secondary infection is
suggestive of cutaneous adverse food reaction or atopic
dermatitis.
Topical antimicrobial therapy is ideal for secondary surface bacterial and yeast overgrowth. Chlorhexidine, benzoyl peroxide, or ethyl lactate‐based shampoos may be
used as a soak, particularly for painful feet, every 24–48
hours initially. Aluminum acetate solution (Domeboro)

VetBooks.ir

166 Bacterial Pyodermas

may be similarly used as a foot soak for drying and antimicrobial effects. Antimicrobial wipes and sprays may be
considered, but acid‐ and alcohol‐based products should
be avoided in erosive and ulcerative presentations (see
“Treatment of pyodermas” section for additional treatment recommendations).
Focal nodular staphylococcal or mixed bacterial lesions
may be treated with silver sulfadiazine cream, clindamycin ointment, or mupirocin ( reserved for resistant staphylococcal infections). Application of dimethyl sulfoxide
(DMSO) just before or after application of the topical
antimicrobial may improve its penetration and provide
additional antiinflammatory effects. Topical corticosteroid treatment (as the sole ingredient or a combination
product) may be helpful for additional antiinflammatory
benefits, particularly for hypersensitivity. Topical corticosteroids should be avoided in the presence of comedones and milia, as they may exacerbate these lesions.
Systemic antimicrobial therapy is indicated for nodules,
draining tracts or severe bacterial surface pyoderma (see
“Treatment of pyodermas” section). Deep pyoderma
(draining nodules, crusts, ulcerations) typically require a
minimum of six weeks of systemic antimicrobial therapy,
and should be continued four weeks beyond cytologic
and clinical resolution (including palpation).
Acral Lick Dermatitis

Although commonly encountered in canine practice, acral
lick dermatitis (ALD) is a challenging condition to manage
given its multifactorial genesis and chronic nature.
Optimal control is achieved via identification and control
of contributing factors. Acral lick dermatitis is characterized by repetitive licking, typically of the distal limbs.
Lesions, commonly known as lick granulomas, take the
form of erosive to ulcerative nodules or plaques with
purulent and/or hemorrhagic exudates (Figure 166.13).

Figure 166.13 Acral lick granuloma with erosive surface on the
carpus of a 9‐year‐old Labrador mix; deep staphylococcal
pyoderma and atopic dermatitis were contributing factors.

The most common primary factors are atopic dermatitis and cutaneous adverse food reaction, as well as
concurrent behavioral etiologies. Importantly, the
most common perpetuating factor is secondary deep
staphylococcal pyoderma. This must be treated to
reduce lesion size and severity. Common bacterial genera concurrently isolated from ALD lesions include
Pseudomonas and Enterobacter. Importantly, methicillin‐resistant and multidrug‐resistant staphylococcal
infections are common in ALD. Cultures obtained
from the surface of the lesions do not accurately represent the organisms within the lesion. Thus, tissue
biopsy for culture and sensitivity is indicated to select
antibiotic therapy, as treatment required is typically in
excess of eight weeks.

­Methicillin‐Resistant and Multidrug‐
Resistant Staphylococci
Antimicrobial resistance in veterinary medicine has
­rapidly evolved in recent years from a mere theoretical
possibility to an unwelcome reality. Of concern, methicillin‐resistant (MR) and multidrug‐resistant (MDR)
staphylococci pose a risk of difficult‐to‐treat nosocomial infections and, to a lesser extent, zoonotic infection. To best serve our community and patients in
the present era of antimicrobial resistance, critical
examination of infection control and antimicrobial
­prescribing practices as individuals and as a profession
is essential.
Methicillin‐resistant staphylococci possess the mecA
genetic element, encoding penicillin binding protein
2a (PBP2a). Beta‐lactam antibiotics cannot bind to
PBP2a, rendering them ineffective. The mecA gene is
present within staphylococcal chromosomal cassettes
(SCCs) that are also horizontally transferred amongst
Staphylococcus spp. Staphylococcal chromosomal cassettes may contain other antimicrobial resistance genes,
imparting multidrug resistance in nearly all strains of
MR staphylococci encountered in veterinary practice. Of
note, beta‐lactam antimicrobial use selects for survival
of MR staphylococci, but does not create, de novo, spontaneous resistance.
Cutaneous MR staphylococcal infection and colonization are a worldwide phenomenon, recognized in the
dog, cat, horse, cattle, and swine. In years past, MR
staphylococcus appeared to be very rare to absent in
the canine and feline population but a remarkable
increase in frequency of methicillin resistance in the
canine and feline population was noted early in the
21st century. The rapid rise of MR staphylococcal
infection in veterinary patients is thought to have

1467

VetBooks.ir

1468

Section 12 Skin and Ear Diseases

occurred via acquisition of the mecA gene from human
staphylococci and subsequent selection of resistant
strains via widespread use of beta‐lactam antimicrobials. Methicillin‐resistant canine and feline cutaneous
infections and colonization have been subsequently
reported worldwide, with MR S. pseudintermedius
most commonly seen. Prevalence varies by geographic
location.
Frequent antimicrobial treatment is a risk factor for
canine MR staphylococcal pyoderma and carriage of MR
staphylococci in healthy dogs and cats. Risk factors associated with MR S. aureus infection in the dog and cat
include frequent antimicrobial courses, frequent veterinary visits, multiple days of hospitalization, and the presence of surgical implants.
Recognition of Methicillin Resistance
Methicillin‐resistant and MDR staphylococcal pyoderma cases do not typically possess unique clinical
features. Rather, the first indication of resistance is
lack of response to empirical antimicrobial therapy.
Therefore, to ensure appropriate response, all patients
must be reexamined prior to conclusion of antimicrobial treatment. If resistance is suspected, perform a
cytologic evaluation to assess for the presence of cocci,
as well as bacterial culture and sensitivity. A sterile needle is used to rupture a pustule or lift the edge of an
epidermal collarette or crust to reveal exudate. The
sample is collected with a sterile swab. For cases of papular or nodular pyoderma, punch biopsies are recommended for culture.
Although “methicillin resistance” is the accepted term,
the more stable oxacillin is used as a surrogate in the
laboratory for methicillin susceptibility. Resistance to
oxacillin is a strong indicator of mecA acquisition and
resistance to all beta‐lactam antibiotics. Upon interpreting antibiograms, it is important to recognize that oxacillin‐resistant staphylococci may show in vitro sensitivity
to other beta‐lactams. Thus, interpretation of staphylococcal antibiograms should first involve noting oxacillin
susceptibility, rather than simply searching for reported
susceptible antimicrobials. If a bacterial strain is resistant to oxacillin, it should be considered resistant to all
beta‐lactam antibiotics.
Direct the laboratory to perform extended antimicrobial panels for suspected resistance. Additionally, species
identification of staphylococci is useful, as MR S. aureus
has a more significant zoonotic implication given that it
is host‐adapted to humans. Methicillin‐resistant, coagulase‐negative staphylococci, including S. schleiferi subsp.
schleiferi, are clinically significant and should not be
disregarded.

­Treatment of Pyodermas
Appropriate management of staphylococcal pyoderma is
an active area of investigation, which may result in future
changes in systemic antimicrobial dose and duration.
Systemic Therapy
Systemic antimicrobial therapy is indicated for regional,
generalized or severe superficial bacterial folliculitis,
mucocutaneous pyoderma, and forms of deep staphylococcal pyoderma. For milder presentations, expected
time of resolution with systemic therapy is 14–28 days.
Duration of therapy may be longer and treatment for one
week beyond clinical resolution is recommended. For
deep pyoderma, treatment may take 6–12 weeks to
achieve visual and palpable resolution. For severe presentations of deep pyoderma, consider continuation of
antimicrobial therapy four weeks beyond palpable resolution to prevent relapse. Importantly, all patients receiving antimicrobial therapy for staphylococcal pyoderma
must be periodically rechecked (every 2–4 weeks) prior
to conclusion of antimicrobial treatment to ensure
appropriate response.
Empirical and Culture‐Based Therapy

Rational antibiotic options for empirical treatment of
staphylococcal pyoderma include cephalexin (22–30 mg/
kg PO q12h), amoxicillin/clavulanate (13.75 mg/kg PO
q12h), cefpodoxime (5–10 mg/kg PO q24h), and cefovecin (8 mg/kg SC q14 days). Lincomycin (15–25 mg/kg
PO q12h) and clindamycin (5.5–10 mg/kg PO q12–24h)
are considered first‐line choices, but their conservation
is recommended as some MR and MDR staphylococcal
strains retain susceptibility to these antimicrobials. For
cases of resistant pyoderma, clindamycin should be used
with reservation if the laboratory has not tested for
inducible resistance (D‐test). This test should be
requested if erythromycin resistance is present. If this
test is not available and the bacterial strain is resistant to
erythromycin but susceptible to clindamycin, do not
prescribe the latter.
Culture and sensitivity‐based selection of a systemic
antimicrobial is indicated for patients that fail to clinically respond to empirical therapy, have evidence of deep
pyoderma, or have a chronic history of antimicrobial use
with unknown or lackluster response. Empirical treatment is not recommended in these cases as staphylococcal antimicrobial resistance patterns are unpredictable.
Dwindling rational systemic treatment options for MDR
staphylococcal pyoderma present a global practical challenge. A 2010 study examining 103 isolates of MRSP in
North America reported that nearly 90% of isolates were

VetBooks.ir

166 Bacterial Pyodermas

resistant to ciprofloxacin, clindamycin, erythromycin,
and trimethoprim sulfa (TMS); 69.9% were resistant to
tetracycline and gentamicin, and 57.3% were resistant to
chloramphenicol.
If resistant superficial bacterial folliculitis is present
with limited therapeutic options, consider daily topical
therapy prior to use of amikacin, rifampin, or chloramphenicol, as this may be sufficient to resolve the problem with minimal risk to the patient. Chloramphenicol
may be used with success in resistant cases, but vomiting and diarrhea can be frequent, and transient bone
marrow suppression is possible but apparently rare.
Reversible weakness (often seen in the hindlimbs) may
occur in dogs. Clients must also wear gloves to prevent
rare but fatal aplastic anemia of humans. At present,
resistance to rifampin is rare. Although it is often stated
that a secondary antimicrobial is required with use of
rifampin, successful treatment with monotherapy has
been documented with S. aureus and, therefore, this
long‐held concept may not apply to treatment of staphylococcal pyoderma. Hepatotoxicity can be life‐threatening and biochemistry values must be monitored every
seven days during administration. Given the potential
for renal failure, amikacin is reserved for patients with
severe, deep, resistant pyoderma with no other rational
systemic treatment options. When used, frequent urinalysis and monitoring for casts are recommended.
Although susceptibility to vancomycin, linezolid,
synercid (quinupristin/dalfopristin), and teicoplanin
may be provided in antibiograms, use of these antibiotics
is strongly discouraged. These are drugs of last resort
used for human MRSA patients with life‐threatening
infections and selection for further resistance must be
avoided.
Topical Therapy
Adjunct topical therapy is indicated in all forms of pyoderma and may be used as the sole treatment for surface
pyodermas such as acute moist dermatitis and intertrigo,
as well as with superficial pyodermas, including impetigo and superficial bacterial folliculitis. The use of topical therapy may shorten the duration of systemic therapy,
and thus reduce antibiotic selective pressures. The
choice of topical ingredient(s) and formulation is
dependent upon lesion location, distribution, type, and
compliance of the client and the animal.
Shampoo therapy is ideally performed 2–3 times
weekly as an adjunct for all forms of pyoderma. Active
ingredients include chlorhexidine 2–4%, benzoyl peroxide 2.5%, and ethyl lactate 10%. Benzoyl peroxide can
be drying and is best used for patients with greasy or
purulent dermatitis. A contact time of 5–10 minutes is

generally recommended. When instituted as a sole
therapy for superficial bacterial folliculitis, daily use is
recommended.
Wipes and sprays are convenient for frequent use,
and are a convenient sole therapy for intertrigo. These
preparations may include acids, such as acetic acid 2%
or boric acid 2%, and alcohols for antimicrobial and
drying effects. These drying ingredients are particularly helpful for intertrigo, but are painful if applied to
ulcerative lesions. Chlorhexidine (2–4%) is commonly
found in wipe and spray preparations, and nisin is
found in wipe preparations. Of note, chlorhexidine is
appropriate for both gram‐positive and gram‐negative
bacteria, whereas nisin is most appropriate for treatment of staphylococci alone. For sole therapy, apply
every 12–24 hours; for adjunct therapy, application
every 24–72 hours is appropriate.
Hypochlorous acid is available in a convenient, commercial spray formulation (Vetericyn VF®, Innovacyn). It
can be used solely once to twice daily for localized
superficial and deep pyoderma or as an adjunct to other
topical and systemic therapies for more generalized
conditions. Hypochlorous acid is the sodium salt of
­
sodium hypochlorite (household bleach). Dilute bleach
rinse solutions (0.005–0.01%) are used by human and
veterinary dermatologists, particularly for treatment of
allergy‐induced recurrent and resistant staphylococcal
pyoderma. The author uses a dilution of 2 tablespoons of
household bleach per gallon of water as a rinse. This
effective and affordable therapy can be used after bathing or applied directly to a focal area as frequently as
daily as a sole therapy or as infrequent as twice weekly as
an adjunct therapy. The patient is patted dry. Note that
this solution must be reconstituted daily. It is nonirritating, and there are some data to suggest it is antiinflammatory as well.
Creams, ointments, and gels are most appropriate
for focal presentations. Many commercial antibiotic
preparations (neomycin, polymyxin B, gentamicin) are
available combined with antifungal and corticosteroid
ingredients. Concurrent use of a topical corticosteroid
may obscure interpretation of antimicrobial response,
and chronic use may result in cutaneous atrophy and
ulceration. Creams and ointments containing an antimicrobial as the sole ingredient are therefore preferred.
Active ingredients include silver sulfadiazine, benzoyl
peroxide, fusidic acid, hydrogen peroxide, and mupirocin. Of note, mupirocin ointment should not be used
routinely, as mupirocin resistance has been documented, and it is used for decolonization of methicillin‐resistant S. aureus of humans. For sole therapy,
apply every 12–24 hours; for adjunct therapy, application every 48–72 hours is appropriate.

Staphylococcus aureus Phage Lysate Therapy
Subcutaneously injected commercial S. aureus phage
lysate antigens (Staphage Lysate) may be used as maintenance therapy to reduce or eliminate recurrence of pyoderma in canine patients with idiopathic recurrent
pyoderma or atopic dermatitis, and can be used in combination with maintenance topical therapy once active
pyoderma has been resolved.

Subcutaneous injection of 0.5 mL is administered
twice weekly for a trial period of 10–14 weeks. Topical
and/or systemic antimicrobial therapy is required at the
initiation of treatment if an active bacterial infection is
present. If beneficial, frequency may be tapered to the
least frequent administration required to increase the
interval between recurrences or prevent recurrences,
typically every 7–14 days.
