Otitis
Sue Paterson, MA, VetMB, DVD, DECVD, FRCVS
Veterinary Dermatologicals, Altrincham, Cheshire, UK

­Otitis Externa
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Otitis externa is inflammation of the external ear canal.
The microscopic structure of the external ear canal is
similar to that of the interfollicular epidermis of the skin.
It is a stratified cornified epithelium with adnexal organs
such as hair follicles and their associated sebaceous and
ceruminous glands. The epidermis lining the canal is
only a few layers thick and is punctuated by hair follicles.
Therefore, any disease that affects the skin can also affect
the external ear canals. Those diseases that cause otitis
externa are referred to as primary causes, the most
important of which are listed in Box 167.1.
It is crucially important that the primary cause is
­identified and managed adequately in all cases of otitis
externa. Failure to do so leads to recurrence of the
­problem and progression of the disease to produce a
chronically damaged ear. Primary disease initially causes
inflammation within the canal which leads to an increase
in epidermal turnover and hyperplasia of the canal wall
with narrowing of the lumen. As the disease process progresses, sebaceous glands become hyperplastic, often
with dilation of their ducts. This is followed more chronically by dramatic changes in the ceruminous glands and
ducts which become enormously enlarged, leading to
further loss of lumen diameter. Chronic change drives
the disease process once it has been established, causing
perpetuation of the otitis. Where this is not resolved,
effective therapy is difficult and disease perpetuation or
recurrence is inevitable. Where the disease process
becomes chronically irreversible, the lumen may be
completely obliterated and in some of these cases, ossification of the soft tissue may also take place. Once the
damage to the ear has become this extensive, medical
therapy is rarely effective. Progressive pathologic changes

lead to alterations in the microclimate within the
­external ear canal, causing an increase in temperature
and humidity, surface maceration, and an increase in
microbial colonization within the ear (Figure 167.1).
Infection is secondary to the inflammatory process
and although effective therapy is essential, if other ­factors
are not managed, recurrence is likely.
Signalment
Age

In young dogs, allergy, especially atopic dermatitis, is the
most common trigger of otitis. In cats, especially kittens,
Otodectes cynotis is more important, accounting for
about 80% of all cases of feline otitis externa. Otic
demodicosis is an uncommon cause of ear disease in
the dog and is very rare in the cat. Juvenile‐onset disease
is seen in animals less than 3 years of age. Adult‐onset
disease is seen in those older than 3 years.
Other examples of primary causes affecting young animals include primary idiopathic seborrhea and immune‐
mediated diseases such as juvenile cellulitis. In older
animals, systemic disease such as canine hypothyroidism
is important although hepatic, renal, and pancreatic
­diseases may also predispose animals to otic infection.
Rare primary causes for otitis externa that can occur in
animals of any age include keratinization disorders such
as sebaceous adenitis and autoimmune diseases such as
pemphigus foliaceus and discoid lupus erythematosus.
Breed

Primary disease triggered by atopic dermatitis is most
commonly seen in the West Highland white terrier,
Staffordshire bull terrier, Labrador retriever, German
shepherd dog, and boxer. Otitis due to cutaneous
adverse food ­reactions is most common in the Labrador

There are many breed characteristics that predispose

The key aims of history taking are to try to establish the
primary cause for the otitis and any predisposing, perpetuating or secondary factors that may be contributing
to the disease. Primary causes (see Box 167.1) should be
identified in all cases of otitis. Successful management of
these triggers is particularly important in chronic disease. Predisposing factors, which are listed in Box 167.2,
contribute to ear disease but do not cause it. Perpetuating
factors, listed in Box 167.3, and secondary factors which
are infections, listed in Table 167.1, are those that drive
the process once it has been established. They need to be
managed to ensure a complete resolution of disease is
achieved without danger of relapse.
In order to identify the primary causes and the other
contributory factors, a carefully taken history should
include all aspects of the dog’s general health and lifestyle. Dogs with atopic dermatitis usually demonstrate a
seasonal exacerbation of otitis, pollen‐allergic dogs being
worse in the spring and summer and house dust mite‐
allergic dogs being worse in the fall and winter. Allergic
dogs that swim commonly develop signs of “swimmer’s
ear.” Hypothyroid dogs may have more generalized
­systemic signs such as lethargy and a poor exercise tolerance. Where otitis has an acute onset and the disease
progresses rapidly to become severe, immune‐mediated

become worse after commencement of topical therapy.
Contact reactions may be to one of the active ingredients
in the topical product such as an antibiotic, antifungal
or glucocorticoid, or can be to the vehicle (e.g., propylene glycol).
Examination of each case should include a full physical
and dermatologic inspection before examining the pinnae and ear canal. A physical examination may reveal
signs, for example of bradycardia in a hypothyroid dog.
Accompanying signs of more generalized disease may
provide useful clues. Dogs with atopic dermatitis or
adverse food reaction may have pedal salivary staining
due to foot licking, or recurrent ventral pyoderma.
Dogs with endocrine disease may have seborrhea, a poor
hair coat or bilaterally symmetric alopecia which
­typically spares the face and distal extremities. Where
keratinization disorders cause otitis, lesions may be
more generalized (e.g., diffuse thinning of the coat with
prominent follicular casts on hairs in cases of sebaceous
adenitis). Dogs that shake their heads or traumatize their
pinnae without signs of otitis may be in the early stages
of allergy or may have disease that principally affects
the pinnae. These diseases include those caused by
ectoparasites such as Sarcoptes scabiei, Notoedres cati,
lice and the rabbit flea (Spilopsyllus cuniculi), and
immune‐mediated diseases such as vasculitis and
­dermatomyositis. The pinna is an excellent area to view
primary lesions, which tend to be better preserved at
this site due to the difficult accessibility. Pustular lesions
on the pinna may be seen with sterile autoimmune disease such as pemphigus foliaceus or, rarely, with pyoderma. Papular eruptions are most commonly seen with
ectoparasites, and ulcers with immune‐mediated disease
such as vasculitis.
Examination of the ear canal may be undertaken with
either a hand‐held or a video otoscope (Figure 167.2).
The latter obviously has the advantage of better
­illumination and magnification and allows for superior

Figure 167.2 Video otoscopic image of the external ear canal and
tympanic membrane of a dog.

visualization of the canal and tympanic membrane.
Assessment of the canal is important to decide which
predisposing and perpetuating factors are present.
Predisposing factors such as neoplasia, stenosis of the
canal, or the presence of a large amount of hair need to
be addressed as part of the overall management of the
otitis (Figure 167.3).
Identifying and treating perpetuating factors such as
chronic changes and otitis media are important to prevent relapse of the otitis. The degree of pathologic change
present helps the clinician decide if the otitis can be
treated medically or whether surgical intervention is
more appropriate. Assessment of the tympanic membrane can help in making a diagnosis of otitis media if
the structure is abnormal or ruptured.
Diagnosis
Predisposing and perpetuating factors, and to some
degree primary and secondary causes, can be recognized

Section 12 Skin and Ear Diseases

1474

Figure 167.3 Ceruminous gland adenomas in the ear of a dog
illustrating a predisposing factor of otitis externa.

by a history and clinical examination. Diagnostic investigations allow a more definitive identification of primary
and secondary factors. Where a history suggests a primary cause then appropriate diagnostic tests may include
food trials, in vitro or in vivo allergy tests, ectoparasite
assessment, endocrine function tests or skin biopsy.
Secondary infection can be identified by cytology of
­exudate and, where necessary, culture and susceptibility.
Samples should be collected, if possible, before cleaning
is performed using a shielded cotton swab (sample is
taken by inserting the swab down an alcohol‐cleaned otoscope cone) from the horizontal canal and rolled onto a
clean glass slide. Both unstained (to identify ectoparasites
such as Demodex spp. and Otodectes cynotis) and stained
(to identify inflammatory cells, bacteria, and yeast) samples should be examined. Samples to be stained should be
heat fixed before staining with a ­modified Wright’s stain
such as Diff‐Quik (Figures 167.4 and 167.5).
Cytologic findings and interpretation are shown in
Table 167.2. Cytology is often all that is needed to institute therapy in otitis externa. However, where rods are
found with cocci on cytology (Figure 167.6), where cocci
are identified but have failed to respond to rational
­therapy or where otitis media is suspected, culture and
susceptibility is advised as bacterial sensitivity patterns
may be unpredictable.
Therapy
Therapy can be divided into two parts; the first is the
selection of an appropriate cleaner and the second is
dealing with the pathologic process, which may be treating infection and/or reversing pathologic change within
the ear canal. Assessment of the otic discharge allows the
clinician to select the best cleaning product (Table 167.3).

Figure 167.4 Ear cytology stained with Diff‐Quik showing
Malassezia organisms and anucleated squamous epithelial cells.

Figure 167.5 Ear cytology stained with Diff‐Quik showing
degenerate neutrophils and phagocytosed cocci.

Where the discharge is thick and waxy (e.g., keratinization disorders, hypothyroidism and Malassezia infection) then the cleaner needs to be able to break up the
wax (i.e., ceruminolytic activity). Where an inflammatory infiltrate is present and the discharge is more purulent or mucopurulent (e.g., gram‐negative infection),
then an aqueous‐based flush is better.
Examples of agents with good ceruminolytic properties
include dioctyl sodium or calcium sulfosuccinate, carbamide peroxide, triethanolamine polypeptide oleate condensate, hexamethyltetracosane, and squalene. Propylene
glycol and mineral or vegetable oils are less potent ceruminolytics. Aqueous‐based flushing agents include ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid (EDTA)‐tris, 0.2% chlorhexidine,
and 2% acetic acid. Although the main function of an ear
cleaner is to clean, many contain components that have
antibacterial or antiyeast activity. Such actives include

EDTA‐tris, lactic acid, salicylic acid, isopropyl alcohol,

have antibacterial potentiating activity and will render bacteria more sensitive to topical antibiotic therapy with aminoglycosides or fluoroquinolones when the ear is presoaked

The cleaning solution should be used to flood the ear canal
and then gently massaged to dissolve debris before an
absorbent pad is used to remove excess material.
Antiparasitic agents are found in many different
ear preparations. Active ingredients with antiparasitic
actions include ivermectin (0.01%), pyrethrins (0.05–

0.15%), rotenone (0.12%), piperonyl butoxide (1.5%),
milbemycin oxime (0.1%), and thiabendazole (4%). All
products have activity against Otodectes cynotis. In addition, ivermectin and milbemycin applied topically would
be expected to have some activity against Demodex spp.
Products with generalized effects such as topical
selamectin and moxidectin may also be used to treat ear
mites. Finally, excellent results have been reported for
orally and topically administered, long-acting, systemic
parasiticides of the isoxazoline class for the treatment of
O. cynotis and demodicosis in dogs and cats.
Antibiotic therapy may initially be based on cytology.
However, where rods or mixed infection are seen on
cytology or where cocci are identified and the case has
not responded to previous therapy, culture and susceptibility should be performed. Antibiotics can be considered as first, second or third line for topical therapy of
otitis externa and indeed for otitis media (Table 167.4).
Glucocorticoids are useful in the therapy of otitis externa.
They reduce swelling, pruritus, inflammation, and glandular secretions. They can also help to open up the ear canal
to allow adequate penetration of topical drugs. They may
be given systemically or topically (Table 167.5).
The more potent topical steroids, such as mometasone
furoate and hydrocortisone aceponate, produce more
marked antiinflammatory effects than dexamethasone
or betamethasone, which are both more potent than
prednisolone.
Antiyeast drugs are rarely needed systemically. The
azole antifungals miconazole, clotrimazole, and posaconazole as well as nystatin are available in a range of licensed
veterinary ear drops in the United States and Europe.

­Otitis Media
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Otitis media is inflammation of the middle ear and
is often bacterial in origin. The organisms most commonly isolated are Staphylococcus pseudintermedius,
Pseudomonas spp., Escherichia coli, Proteus spp., and
Enterococcus faecalis. Occasionally, Malassezia pachydermatis may be involved. In most cases, infectious otitis
media is secondary, resulting from a descending infection as an extension of otitis externa, rather than an
ascending infection from the oropharynx or a result of
hematogenous infection. Other causes of otitis media
include primary secretory otitis media (PSOM) principally recognized in the Cavalier King Charles spaniel,
foreign bodies, nasopharyngeal polyps seen most commonly in cats and neoplasms such as squamous cell carcinomas and lymphoma.
Secondary otitis media is caused by the drainage of
exudate and infectious organisms into the tympanic
bulla from the external ear canal. This causes inflammation to the lining epithelium, the mucoperiosteum, which
forms a pseudostratified columnar epithelium containing increased numbers of secretory cells and glands. As a
result of ongoing inflammation, granulation tissue forms
within the bulla. With more chronic disease, this develops into dense connective tissue and, with time, bone
spicules may develop within this dense tissue.

Figure 167.7 Nasopharyngeal polyp in a cat.

Signalment
When otitis media occurs as an extension from otitis
externa, it most commonly affects middle‐aged or older
dogs. Occasionally, younger dogs may be affected. Breeds
that are predisposed to otitis externa will also be susceptible to developing otitis media. Nasopharyngeal polyps
can be seen in any age of cat, including very young
k­ ittens (Figure 167.7).
Primary secretory otitis media can be seen in young to
middle‐aged Cavalier King Charles spaniels.
History and Clinical Signs
Approximately 50–80% of all dogs with otitis externa of
more than six months duration will have otitis media.
Owners often report that dogs shake their heads and are
reluctant to open their mouths to, for example, carry a
ball, yawn, bark or eat hard food. This is generally due to
pain in the region of the temporomandibular joint. Owners
may complain that their dog’s hearing has deteriorated,
which may be due to conductive changes in hearing as a
result of fluid within the middle ear or cochlear damage if
infection has spread to the inner ear. Neurologic signs in
the form of ataxia or nystagmus are more suggestive of otitis interna than otitis media. Cranial nerve dysfunction
which can be seen with otitis media includes Horner syndrome, especially in cats, facial nerve paralysis and keratoconjunctivitis sicca which can occur due to damage to the
parasympathetic innervation of the lacrimal gland.
Diagnosis
The principal steps in diagnosis are otoscopy, myringotomy, and diagnostic imaging. Otoscopy is an insensitive modality for diagnosing otitis media. Where the

­tympanic membrane can be visualized and can be seen
to be ruptured or intact but abnormal, suggesting previous damage, then a diagnosis of otitis media is possible. If the tympanic membrane is ruptured, samples
may be taken from the middle ear. A clean otoscope
cone or videootoscope head should be inserted as far
into the horizontal canal as possible and a fine catheter
or microswab may be inserted through the tube or
working channel to “guard” it from discharge in the
external canal (Figure 167.8). Material can be gathered

onto the swab or suctioned up the catheter to sample
the middle ear.
If the tympanic membrane is intact but appears
abnormal, it is possible a previous defect in the tympanum has healed in the presence of ongoing otitis media.
In these cases, myringotomy should be performed to
take samples from the middle ear. Direct visual observation (ideally with a video otoscope) in a carefully
cleaned ear canal is important to avoid damage to sensitive structures. The myringotomy should be performed by an experienced clinician using a diode or
carbon dioxide (CO2) laser or manually using a sterile
rigid polypropylene catheter cut to an angle of 60°. A
small hole made in the pars tensa in the caudoventral
quadrant to avoid the pars flaccida and the manubrium
of the malleus (Figure 167.9) allows for collection of
material from the middle ear, which can be examined
cytologically and submitted for culture and sensitivity.
Cytology in otitis externa is useful but in otitis media,
the presence of mucus from the middle ear can make
identification of bacteria difficult. Where cytology
reveals signs of an inflammatory infiltrate and infectious organisms, a definitive diagnosis of otitis media
can be made. Where cytology is unremarkable, cultures are necessary and are probably best undertaken
in all cases.
Advanced imaging is useful in otitis media. Radiography
is only diagnostic in chronic disease. The open‐mouthed
view, which allows for comparison of both sides, and the
lateral oblique view provide the most information.
Changes on radiography that are consistent with otitis
media are increased density of the air‐filled bulla, thickening, lysis or irregularity of the tympanic bulla wall, or
formation of new bone. Computed tomography (CT) and
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are more ­sensitive
modalities, picking up subtle changes such as granulation
tissue or fluid or mucus within the middle ear.

Therapy of otitis media may be divided into several
stages:
flushing the bulla

VetBooks.ir

Flushing the bulla is the most important part of
treatment. This is best achieved in an anesthetized
animal, which should be intubated and the endotracheal cuff fully inflated to avoid the risk of inhalation
of any flush solution. An aqueous‐based flush helps
hydrate the mucous within the bulla and aid removal
by suction. Suitable flushes include water, sterile saline,
dilute chlorhexidine solution (<0.2%), and EDTA‐tris.
All have a high degree of middle ear safety.
Ceruminolytics are generally not necessary in otitis
media due to the nature of the discharge, and only
squalene has been shown to be safe in the dog. The
cat’s middle ear appears to be more sensitive to ototoxic effects and only water, sterile saline, and EDTA‐
tris are considered safe.
Once the ear has been cleaned, medication can be
administered. No medication is licensed for the therapy of otitis media so in each case, a careful assessment should be made of the risks of topical drugs
causing signs of ototoxicity versus the benefits in
resolving the infection. The safest antibiotics for infusion into the tympanic bulla are aqueous solutions of
fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, enrofloxacin, marbofloxacin) and aqueous gentamicin. Other aminoglycosides such as tobramycin and the semisynthetic
penicillin ticarcillin have been a­ ssociated with severe
hearing loss when used to treat otitis media. Antifungal
drugs that are considered safe are clotrimazole,
miconazole, nystatin, and tolnaftate, although the
author has seen temporary deafness caused by both
clotrimazole and miconazole that resolved when topical medication was withdrawn. Drugs that are infused
directly into the bulla are thought to stay trapped
within this structure for several days, providing high
local levels of the drug.
Therapy with glucocorticoids is important to reduce
the inflammation and exudation in middle ear disease
and to help reduce the formation of granulation tissue.
Many different protocols are available for therapy. The
author’s preference is to administer intravenous dexamethasone (2 mg/mL) at a dose of 0.1–0.2 mg/kg at the
time of the ear flush and then follow with antiinflammatory doses of prednisolone at 1–2 mg/kg daily PO for two
weeks. Alternative systemic glucocorticoids are listed in
Table 167.5. Aqueous dexamethasone, fluocinolone, and
a commercial product containing dimethyl sulfoxide
(DMSO) and fluocinolone (Synotic®, Fort Dodge Animal
Health) are recognized as having low ototoxic potential
and can be infused by catheter into the bulla after
flushing.
The use of systemic antibiotics in otitis media is a
subject of debate. The levels of systemic antibiotics

Follow‐up appointments are important in otitis media
and should be undertaken every 7–10 days. If necessary,
the dog should be readmitted to permit further flushing
of the tympanic bulla under anesthesia. Topical and systemic therapy may be adjusted on the basis of culture
and sensitivity results. Antiinflammatory therapy may
be reduced as the disease improves. The author will generally reduce prednisolone to an alternate‐day dosage
after two weeks and then taper, aiming to withdraw it
after a further two weeks. Therapy should be continued
until the ear appears clinically, cytologically, and culturally normal. Maintenance therapy should include regular ear cleaning and maintenance of any underlying
causes.

168
Cutaneous Manifestations of Systemic Disease
Kinga Gortel, DVM, MS, DACVD
Tri Lake Animal Hospital and Referral Centre, Lake Country, BC, Canada

The skin can manifest myriad changes associated with
systemic diseases. Some, such as the cutaneous manifestations of hyperadrenocorticism, are so well recognized
and characteristic that they provide obvious clues about
the underlying etiology. Others are more subtle or rare.
In addition to the diseases described in this chapter, the
skin can directly exhibit symptoms of bleeding disorders
(petechiae, ecchymoses, bruising), icterus, dehydration,
and cachexia. Changes in the skin can be a direct result
of a multisystemic disorder (e.g., vasculitis affecting multiple organs) or result from disease occurring in another
organ (e.g., superficial necrolytic dermatitis associated
with liver disease). The skin is an easier site to sample
compared to other organs, and skin biopsies (or in some
cases cytologic examination or cultures) can be essential
to facilitating the diagnosis of the underlying disease.
Although internal diseases are relatively uncommon as
a cause of skin disorders, their likelihood increases when
certain findings are present. Internal disease is more
likely in patients exhibiting unexpected changes in
weight, activity level, appetite, thirst, or urine production, and these signs should be investigated as part of the
history collection. Patients presenting with skin disease
for the first time at an advanced age without a readily
identifiable cause also warrant further work‐up for internal disease.

­Hormonal and Metabolic Disorders
Causing Cutaneous Manifestations
Canine and Feline Hypercortisolism
Hypercortisolism (i.e., Cushing disease, Cushing syndrome) is common in dogs and causes both nonspecific
and fairly distinct dermatologic changes. The signs are

similar whether endogenous or exogenous glucocorticoids are the cause. The most common but nonspecific
change occurs in the hair coat, with a lack of luster and
density, slower growth, and often a lightening of the
color. Hair is progressively lost, resulting in alopecia that
spares the head and distal extremities and predominantly
affects the trunk, typically in a symmetric pattern.
More specific signs include thinning skin and resultant
prominent blood vessels, as well as comedones, milia,
and calcinosis cutis. Easy bruising, seborrhea, slow
wound healing, and striae are also seen. Generalized
demodicosis can occur, and iatrogenic or spontaneous
hypercortisolism is an important consideration in adult‐
onset disease. Lesions of superficial bacterial pyoderma
are commonly seen in dogs with hypercortisolism.
Naturally occurring and iatrogenic hypercortisolism
are rare in cats. Cutaneous signs include alopecia and
thin skin. Skin fragility, described below, occurs in over
50% of cases, and may be more common in cats with adrenal neoplasia. A unique finding reported only in iatrogenic hypercortisolism is medial curling of the pinnae.
Calcinosis Cutis
Calcinosis cutis refers to the various forms of calcification of the skin. It most commonly occurs in association
with iatrogenic or spontaneous hypercortisolism in dogs.
It appears to be more common in large‐breed dogs. It is
more rarely seen with systemic fungal infections such as
blastomycosis, with diabetes mellitus, and with various
other diseases. Rarely, calcinosis cutis affecting multiple
footpads or the interdigital skin has been seen in dogs
and cats in association with chronic renal disease
(Figure 168.1). This site is not typically affected in dogs
with hypercortisolism, so renal failure should be considered in a patient with calcinosis affecting multiple feet.

Feline Skin Fragility Syndrome

Figure 168.2 Calcinosis cutis. Firm, coalescing erythematous
papules on the lateral thorax of a mature bulldog with iatrogenic
hypercortisolism.

Calcinosis cutis often starts as erythematous papules
that coalesce into very characteristically firm plaques
(Figure 168.2). The lesions can ulcerate and become
­pruritic. The axilla, groin, and dorsal trunk are commonly affected. The diagnosis is made on the basis of
characteristic clinical features and histopathology, and
investigation for the underlying cause is warranted in
all cases.
The treatment of calcinosis cutis relies on identification and removal of the underlying metabolic problem
and if this can be achieved, it is associated with a good
prognosis. Correction of hypercortisolism usually allows
calcinosis cutis to resolve within several months, but
some lesions can undergo osseous metaplasia and persist
indefinitely.

Feline acquired skin fragility syndrome is a rare condition characterized by extremely thin skin that tears and
bruises easily (Figure 168.3). It is associated with spontaneous or iatrogenic hypercortisolism and seems to be
more common with adrenal tumors. It can also result
from excessive levels of progestational compounds,
either administered therapeutically or secreted from
adrenal tumors. The syndrome has also been reported in
association with diabetes, cholangiohepatitis, hepatic
lipidosis, neoplasia (e.g., pancreatic and intestinal carcinoma), and other diseases.
Cats with acquired skin fragility syndrome may
­present for spontaneous skin tears following minimal
handling or trauma. They have extremely fragile, thin
skin that tears very easily during restraint. The skin is not
hyperextensible and bleeds minimally upon tearing.
The diagnosis is usually made by the very characteristic
clinical findings, although histopathology is confirmatory.
Affected cats have a poor prognosis.
Canine Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism is a common endocrine disorder of
dogs. Dermatologic changes occur in 60–80% of cases,
but can be subtle. Cutaneous signs of hypothyroidism
include progressive alopecia in areas of wear, including
the dorsal and distal tail (“rat tail” appearance), ventral
and lateral trunk, the upper limbs (typically caudal
thighs), and often the dorsal aspect of the muzzle. The
pattern of alopecia is somewhat different from the
­classic bilaterally symmetric alopecia sparing the head in
hypercortisolism. Some hypothyroid dogs maintain a

VetBooks.ir

168 Cutaneous Manifestations of Systemic Disease

normal hair coat. The loss of guard hairs, leaving behind
the finer undercoat, can lead to the appearance of a
“puppy coat.” The hair coat can also lighten due to longer
retention of hair and subsequent bleaching. Recurrent
pyoderma and otitis externa are common. Pruritus is not
a feature of hypothyroidism but can be seen if secondary
pyoderma, Malassezia dermatitis, or otitis externa are
present. Advanced cases can present with thick, puffy
skin (myxedema) due to accumulation of dermal glycosaminoglycans. This is a rare manifestation as most
hypothyroid dogs are diagnosed and treated before
­progressing to this stage.
The diagnosis of hypothyroidism relies on history,
examination findings, complete blood count and serum
biochemistry findings, thyroid hormone (total T4 and
free T4) and thyrotropin (TSH) measurements, and
occasionally skin biopsies. The total T4 is often assayed
in dogs with dermatologic disease. Because it is lowered
by multiple nonthyroidal factors (e.g., drugs and severe
nonthyroidal illness), it is easy to mistakenly diagnose
hypothyroidism using this measurement alone.
Confirmatory testing should be performed before
initiating treatment. Although a response to thyroid
­
­supplementation is sometimes used as a diagnostic tool,
treatment with thyroxine can result in temporary
improvement of many dermatologic conditions by stimulating hair growth. This can lead to false confirmation
of an incorrect diagnosis of hypothyroidism.
Treatment of hypothyroidism is usually very rewarding and most of the cutaneous abnormalities can be corrected. However, during the initial few weeks of therapy,
there can be increased scaling as well as profound hair
loss as telogen hairs are replaced due to a coordinated
initiation of the new hair cycle.
Sex Hormone Dermatoses
These uncommon dermatoses can be associated with
gonadal and adrenal disorders. They most often present
with truncal alopecia. Hyperestrogenism can occur in
intact male dogs with functional testicular tumors
(see section on Neoplastic and Paraneoplastic Disorders
Affecting the Skin at the end of this chapter), or in intact
female dogs with cystic ovaries or, more rarely, with
functional ovarian tumors.
Hyperandrogenism in male dogs is rare. It can be
idiopathic or associated with testicular neoplasia. In
­
the idiopathic form, young dogs exhibit hypersexual
behavior and sometimes aggression, as well as seborrhea
oleosa and truncal hair loss. Hyperandrogenism due
to testicular neoplasia results in hyperplasia of the
circumanal glands and the tail gland, which appear
­
­thickened and universally enlarged. Macular hyperpigmentation can also be seen. The diagnosis of these

conditions can be made with endocrine testing and
­
ultrasonography.
Superficial Necrolytic Dermatitis
Superficial necrolytic dermatitis, sometimes called hepatocutaneous syndrome, is most often seen in dogs with a
characteristic idiopathic hepatopathy. It can also be seen
with anticonvulsant medications and pancreatic tumors.
Superficial necrolytic dermatitis has been rarely reported
in cats. This condition is described in detail in
Chapter 169.
Xanthomas
Xanthomas are rare granulomatous skin lesions that
occur in association with an abnormality in lipid metabolism. Most have been associated with diabetes mellitus
or with the feeding of high‐fat foods. An underlying
hereditary defect of lipid metabolism has also been
reported. The lesions occur most commonly on the head
(particularly the preauricular area or ears), distal limbs,
and bony prominences, and consist of small white or
­yellow papules, nodules, or plaques. Histopathology is
needed to make the diagnosis.
The treatment of xanthomas relies on the correction of
the underlying metabolic problem and if this can be
accomplished, the prognosis is favorable. Xanthomas in
cats with idiopathic hypertriglyceridemia can undergo
regression with a low‐fat diet.
Amyloidosis
Amyloidosis refers to a diverse group of diseases featuring the extracellular deposition of protein fibrils with
characteristic staining properties (amyloid). In dogs and
cats, most cases of amyloidosis show systemic involvement, affecting the kidneys and less commonly other
organs. Skin lesions are seen in some patients.
Amyloidosis can also be limited to the skin. In this form,
dermal or subcutaneous nodules can be seen anywhere,
but most commonly on the ear. Purpuric macules have
also been reported. The diagnosis is made by histopathology. Solitary nodules can be excised but no effective
treatment is reported for more widespread lesions.
Other hormonal disorders that can sometimes cause
cutaneous manifestations include the most common
endocrine diseases of the cat. Diabetic cats sometimes
develop seborrheic skin disease, thin skin, and alopecia.
Hyperthyroid cats can exhibit an increased rate of claw
growth, excessive shedding and matting, alopecia due to
excessive grooming, and occasionally other changes.
Although pruritus is a well‐documented complication
of hepatobiliary disease in humans, it is not typically

1483

VetBooks.ir

1484

Section 12 Skin and Ear Diseases

recognized in companion animals. One case report
­
described pruritus in a puppy with a portosystemic shunt
whose pruritus resolved upon correction of the vascular
abnormality.

­Systemic Infectious Disease Causing
Cutaneous Manifestations
Feline Herpesviral Dermatitis
Feline herpesvirus‐1 (FHV‐1) can cause a characteristic
facial dermatitis in cats. The condition is most common
in adult cats, and not all cases exhibit the ocular or respiratory signs typical of this viral infection. There can be
a recent history of an upper respiratory tract infection in
the weeks preceding development of the lesions in some
cats. The lesions consist of inflamed and often ulcerated
areas near the nares. They most often affect the nasal
planum, dorsal aspect of the muzzle, and periocular skin
(Figures 168.4 and 168.5). The lesions do not appear pruritic even though eosinophils typically predominate. The
clinical appearance and eosinophilic inflammation can
lead to an inappropriate diagnosis of an eosinophilic
plaque or mosquito bite hypersensitivity, with inappropriate treatment using corticosteroids, which can lead to
marked worsening of the disease.
The diagnosis of feline herpesviral dermatitis is made
by the fairly striking clinical appearance of the facial
form, histopathology, and either immunohistochemistry
or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for FHV‐1
on biopsy samples. Viral inclusion bodies are difficult to
find on histopathology, so this condition should be considered in biopsies consistent with eosinophilic plaques
located on the face.

Figure 168.4 Feline herpesviral dermatitis and rhinitis in an adult
cat. Small crusts and a loss of the cobblestone architecture of the
nasal planum are seen.

Treatment of FHV‐1 infection with oral famciclovir is
effective for cutaneous, ocular, and respiratory symptoms. It can be more effective than other therapeutic
strategies. The drug appears to be well tolerated in cats
but there is some uncertainty about the dose and duration of treatment, with recent recommendations reflecting higher doses than had been used previously. In some
cats, the skin lesions can become recurrent or chronic.
Feline Leukemia Virus and Feline
Immunodeficiency Virus Infection
Feline leukemia virus (FeLV) usually causes skin lesions
by its immunosuppressive actions, although it can also
induce skin tumors. The cutaneous symptoms are quite
nonspecific. Affected cats are susceptible to a number of
secondary infections including recurrent abscesses, pyoderma, dermatophytosis, demodicosis, and paronychia.
Multiple cutaneous horns of the footpads are sometimes
seen in cats infected with FeLV. Giant cell dermatosis is a
histologically unique and rare manifestation causing
pruritus and crusting of the face and often other areas of
skin. Although feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV) is
more commonly associated with recurrent or chronic
oral disease, some cats also exhibit skin infections. The
signs of these two immunosuppressive viral diseases are
very similar. The diagnosis is made by serologic testing.
Canine Distemper
Canine distemper virus infection in dogs can be
manifested by a combination of respiratory, ocular,
­
­gastrointestinal, neurologic, and cutaneous signs that

Figure 168.5 Feline herpesviral dermatitis in an adult cat. Extensive
unilateral eosinophil‐rich ulceration is present on the face.

VetBooks.ir

168 Cutaneous Manifestations of Systemic Disease

appear simultaneously or sequentially. The classic but
uncommon cutaneous manifestation of canine distemper is “hard pad disease” – footpad and nasal hyperkeratosis. The footpads are thickened, fissured, and unusually
hard. The centers of the footpads can feel surprisingly
hard even when they appear minimally affected.
Widespread impetigo can also be seen in puppies.
The diagnosis is often made on the basis of clinical
signs in a dog with an inadequate vaccination history.
Histopathology and immunohistochemistry on affected
skin can also be useful to confirm the diagnosis.

The ideal diagnostic method for systemic or localized
mycoses is identification of the fungal organism by
cytologic and histopathologic examination of affected
tissues. Serology is useful as a noninvasive diagnostic
test for cryptococcosis and can also be used to monitor
response to therapy. A sensitive urine or serum antigen
test is currently available for the diagnosis of blastomycosis when organisms are not found on cytology
or ­histopathology. Sampling of the affected tissue for
a definitive mycotic rhinitis typically requires
rhinoscopy.

Systemic Mycoses

Leishmaniasis

Cutaneous lesions consisting of papules, nodules, ulcers,
abscesses, and draining tracts are seen in many systemic
mycoses. They are seen most commonly in blastomycosis (20–50% of cases) and feline cryptococcosis (40%),
and result from hematogenous spread of the fungus to
the skin. Sporotrichosis is generally transmitted by
­cutaneous inoculation of fungal spores, in most cases
resulting in cutaneous or cutaneous lymphatic signs.
However, cats with sporotrichosis have a high frequency
of upper respiratory and lung lesions, suggesting that the
inhalatory mode of infection also plays a role in this species, and the hematogenous route is important in the
cutaneous dissemination of the disease.
Nasal mycotic rhinitis in dogs (most commonly aspergillosis) is usually associated with profuse mucopurulent
nasal discharge and can cause crusting and ulceration of
the nasal planum (Figure 168.6). Depigmentation of the
nasal planum ventral to the nares is a characteristic
finding.

Leishmania organisms are protozoa of several species
that cause a spectrum of clinical disease in dogs and
other mammals, including cats. Leishmaniasis varies in
its clinical presentation from focal to generalized
­cutaneous disease to disseminated internal disease. The
severity varies from asymptomatic to fatal. Leishmania
protozoa are usually vector borne by sandflies, but vertical transmission and direct horizontal transmission are
likely important in certain populations of dogs.
Leishmaniasis has a worldwide distribution but is
endemic in parts of Europe (most commonly in the
Mediterranean basin) and South and Central America. It
was considered to be of minimal importance in North
America until the early 2000s, when Leishmania was
found in multiple foxhound kennels.
Leishmaniasis in dogs most frequently combines
­cutaneous and internal disease. The most common sign
is a nonpruritic exfoliative dermatitis with alopecia
that is generalized but most pronounced on the head
(Figure 168.7). A characteristic feature is adherent silvery‐white scale. Mucocutaneous ulcerations, alopecia,
and erythema can also be seen. Less commonly, nodular
skin disease is present.
The diagnosis of leishmaniasis can be made by cytology (from skin, lymph nodes, bone marrow aspirates),
histopathology, PCR testing of blood and other tissues,
and antibody serology testing.
Lagenidiosis

Figure 168.6 Mild nasal mycotic rhinitis in a mature dog with
nasal aspergillosis.

Lagenidiosis is a rare disease caused by a fungus‐like,
aquatic, “water mold” oomycete of the genus Lagenidia.
It occurs most often in dogs living in the southeastern
United States and has been reported in cats. The disease
is sometimes limited to the skin and local lymph nodes,
but often also causes lesions at distant sites, including the
great blood vessels, r­ espiratory tract, and mediastinum.
The systemic form is universally fatal. The diagnosis is
made by histopathology, which is similar to histopathology from tissues ­originating from dogs with pythiosis or

Figure 168.8 Zinc‐responsive dermatosis (syndrome I) in an adult

zygomycosis. More specific tests include serology for

The prognosis for dogs with systemic lagenidiosis is
grave. For dogs with only cutaneous lesions, aggressive
resection can be curative and amputation can be considered for those with distal limb lesions affecting one leg.
Radiography of the thorax and ultrasonography of the
abdomen is recommended prior to surgery because of
the frequency of systemic dissemination. Medical therapy with antifungal drugs is typically ineffective alone but
has been described as an adjunct to surgical resection.
Many other infectious diseases can present with
cutaneous manifestations. This list includes canine
­
herpesvirus infection, pseudorabies, feline infectious
­
peritonitis, feline calicivirus infection, toxoplasmosis,
neosporosis, brucellosis, pythiosis, entomophthoromycosis, and rickettsial and ehrlichial infections in dogs.

­Nutritional Disorders Causing
Cutaneous Manifestations
Zinc‐Responsive Dermatosis
Zinc‐responsive dermatosis is an uncommon skin disease in dogs. It includes syndromes caused by nutrient
deficiency, nutrient imbalances, and the inability
to absorb or utilize zinc. Absolute nutritional zinc

­deficiency is unlikely in a patient eating a well‐balanced
diet. Relative deficiencies can be seen in dogs when zinc
absorption is impaired by excessive amounts of other
nutrients.
Syndrome I zinc‐responsive dermatosis occurs in dogs
eating a well‐balanced diet and has been reported most
commonly in Siberian huskies and Alaskan malamutes.
A more severe form has been reported in a litter of
pharaoh hounds. Skin lesions usually begin in early
­
adulthood and consist of early erythema followed by
crusting, scaling, lichenification, and alopecia. The distribution is typically around the mouth, chin, eyes, and
ears (Figure 168.8). An inability to absorb zinc from
the gastrointestinal tract has been shown in some
malamutes.
Syndrome II zinc‐responsive dermatosis has been
reported predominantly in large‐breed puppies or young
adult dogs eating diets deficient in zinc or diets that
interfere with zinc absorption (e.g., excessively high in
calcium, other minerals and vitamins, or phytates). Dogs
with this syndrome have extensive crusting and fissuring
of the footpads and nasal planum, and generalized crusting plaques. Very similar but more severe clinical signs
have been seen in generic dog food dermatosis, which
was seen in North American in the 1980s but was
virtually eliminated with the reformulation of these
­
foods. In this syndrome, a deficiency of multiple nutrients is likely and more severe systemic signs are present.
The diagnosis of zinc‐responsive dermatoses is made
by clinical signs, dietary history, and histopathologic
findings.
The treatment of syndrome I zinc‐responsive dermatosis consists of oral zinc supplementation. Most cases
respond well within 4–6 weeks, but require ongoing

VetBooks.ir

168 Cutaneous Manifestations of Systemic Disease

treatment to maintain remission. Zinc methionine is a
commonly used veterinary preparation. The dose of elemental zinc is 2–3 mg/kg per day. The addition of low‐
dose corticosteroids has also been reported to benefit
patients not responding adequately to zinc supplementation. The intravenous administration of zinc sulfate has
been described in patients with a poor response. Young
dogs with syndrome II zinc‐responsive dermatosis show
a dramatic response to zinc and dietary correction, but
do not require lifelong supplementation.
Feline Pansteatitis
This rare condition has been reported in cats eating diets
high in polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) such as red
tuna, without adequate vitamin E consumption. PUFAs
increase oxidative stress through free radical production.
Affected cats show inflammation and necrosis of subcutaneous and intraabdominal fat resulting in firm, painful
nodules. They are often lethargic, anorexic, febrile, and
painful with movement and palpation.
The diagnosis is made by histopathology coupled with
a suggestive dietary history. Vitamin E supplementation
and a dietary change can be used, but the prognosis for
severe cases is poor.

­Immune‐Mediated Systemic Diseases
Causing Cutaneous Manifestations
Panniculitis
Panniculitis in dogs and cats can be due to myriad
etiologic factors, such as infectious agents, drug
­
reactions, and immune‐mediated diseases (systemic
­
lupus erythematosus, polyarthritis, or others). Patients
with panniculitis should be evaluated for pancreatic
­disease, as panniculitis has been associated with pancreatitis and pancreatic tumors. The reader is referred
to Chapter 164 for a more detailed discussion of
panniculitis.
Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)
This multisystem autoimmune disease shows highly variable signs affecting various organs. It is rare in dogs and
very rare in cats. Circulating autoantibodies directed
against a wide variety of tissue antigens are present. The
estimated frequency of skin lesions is 20–50% of affected
dogs and cats. The lesions can consist of mild alopecic
scarring, scaling, and crusting, to widespread ulcers
involving the skin and oral mucosa. Lesions of the nasal
­planum more typically seen with discoid lupus erythematosus may be present. Some patients exhibit lesions in

hairless areas exposed to light. In addition to skin d
­ isease,
other manifestations include polyarthritis, hematologic
changes, protein‐losing nephropathy, and other signs.
German shepherd dogs are predisposed to SLE.
The diagnosis of SLE can be difficult. Criteria for the
diagnosis of canine SLE include the presence of a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) titer as well as a number
of other clinical and laboratory findings. The reader is
referred to other sections within this book for a more
thorough discussion of these criteria. Skin biopsies can
be helpful but although the classic changes of SLE are
quite suggestive, the histopathologic findings in SLE are
variable. Direct immunofluorescence or immunohistochemistry can be used to demonstrate immunoglobulin
and complement at the dermoepidermal junction.
The prognosis for dogs with SLE is guarded, but some
patients can be controlled effectively for years. The
disease is highly variable in its severity, which can
­
also wax and wane. Corticosteroids are used most often,
frequently with the addition of steroid‐sparing agents.
Vascular Diseases
A variety of diseases affecting the cutaneous blood vessels can result in skin lesions. Vasculitis refers to vascular
diseases in which blood vessels appear to be the target of
an inflammatory response. Although many cases are idiopathic, vasculitis can be initiated by myriad factors
including drugs, rabies vaccination, infectious diseases,
and food allergy. Thus, the term vasculitis describes a
cutaneous reaction pattern rather than an etiologic
diagnosis.
Lesions are often found on the pinnal apex. The footpads are also commonly affected with central or m
­ arginal
ulcers. More widespread lesions can also be seen, consisting of purpura, erythematous plaques, hemorrhagic
bullae, and ulcers. The skin is often the only organ
affected but in some cases, other organs are concurrently
affected. For example, cutaneous and renal vasculopathy
of greyhounds is associated with renal disease.
Canine Uveodermatologic Syndrome
This rare syndrome consists of granulomatous uveitis
and concurrent depigmenting dermatitis. A genetic basis
is present, with akita dogs reported most frequently. The
uveitis is usually bilateral and acute in onset, with the
skin lesions occurring later in most cases. Depigmentation
is seen on the skin of the nasal planum, lips, eyelids, and
occasionally elsewhere. The diagnosis can be made tentatively based on the unique combination of clinical
signs, and definitely using skin biopsies.
Other systemic diseases with an immune‐mediated
etiology that cause cutaneous lesions include erythema

1487

VetBooks.ir

1488

Section 12 Skin and Ear Diseases

multiforme, toxic epidermal necrolysis, cryoglobulinemia
and cryofibrinogenemia, graft‐versus‐host disease, acute
eosinophilic dermatitis (Wells‐like syndrome), acute
­neutrophilic dermatitis (Sweet‐like syndrome), familial
canine dermatomyositis, and hypereosinophilic syndrome.

­Neurologic Disorders Causing
Cutaneous Manifestations
Canine Chiari‐Like Malformation
Canine Chiari‐like malformation has been reported
most frequently in young Cavalier King Charles spaniels.
It can be found in other breeds, and brachycephalic
small‐breed dogs are predisposed to the condition.
Chiari‐like malformation is a developmental abnormality leading to hypoplasia of the occipital bone and thus a
reduced volume of the caudal fossa, the part of the skull
that accommodates the cerebellum and brainstem. The
cerebellum variably herniates through the foramen magnum, crowding the spinal cord and altering the flow of
cerebral spinal fluid in that region with resultant syrinx
formation. It is easily mistaken for a dermatologic condition, as it often causes persistent unilateral or bilateral
scratching at the cervical and shoulder regions. A characteristic feature is that some dogs do not actually make
contact with the skin when exhibiting the scratching.
The presence of pruritus in this area, particularly if it is
unilateral and not accompanied by skin lesions, should
increase the suspicion of canine Chiari‐like malformation. Neck pain is a common feature and is found in most
affected dogs on physical examination.
The diagnosis can be made by the very characteristic
clinical signs in a predisposed breed, but definitive diagnosis requires magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The
reader is referred to the neurology section for a more
comprehensive discussion of Chiari‐like malformation.
Sensory Neuropathies
Both inherited and acquired sensory neuropathies can
result in cutaneous manifestations. A sensory neuropathy of English pointers, German short‐haired pointers,
English springer spaniels, and French spaniels results in
severe paw licking and chewing progressing to further
mutilation of the limbs and autoamputation. This condition has also been reported in one miniature pinscher.
Canine ganglioradiculitis is an inflammatory disease of
the cranial and spinal ganglia and nerve roots. Affected
dogs develop sensory deficits and mutilation/hyperesthesia. Cauda equina syndrome can cause lumbosacral
hyperesthesia, pruritus, and/or self‐inflicted lesions of
the hindlimb(s).

­Neoplastic and Paraneoplastic
Disorders Affecting the Skin
Male Feminizing Syndrome Secondary
to Testicular Neoplasia
Dermatologic manifestations of canine testicular tumors
are rarely encountered in parts of the world where neutering is common. Male feminization occurs most often
with Sertoli cell tumors, affecting 24–57% of dogs with
these tumors. Cryptorchid testes are at greatly increased
risk for development of neoplasia. The syndrome is
thought to be related to estrogen secretion from the
tumor, but other factors may play a role as elevated estrogen levels are not always found. Bilaterally symmetric
alopecia beginning in the perineal, inguinal, and flank
regions is most common in affected dogs. Seborrhea,
comedones, and hyperpigmentation of the skin, particularly in the inguinal and perianal areas, can also be seen
in more advanced cases. Gynecomastia, nipple enlargement, and a pendulous prepuce can be present. A characteristic clinical feature is linear preputial dermatosis: a
line of erythema with variable hyperpigmentation or
comedones extending from the opening of the prepuce
along its ventral aspect to the scrotum. Affected male
dogs may attract other male dogs.
The tumor may be palpable in the affected testicle,
and the nonneoplastic testicle can atrophy. However,
­testicular palpation is not universally abnormal and is
not possible in cryptorchid dogs. Affected dogs can also
exhibit myelosuppression. Approximately 20% of these
tumors are malignant and roughly 10% will metastasize
to the lungs and abdominal lymph nodes.
Although skin histopathology, estrogen levels
particularly estradiol‐17‐beta), ultrasonography and
(­
sometimes general bloodwork can be suggestive, the
­
constellation of characteristic clinical signs, histologic
confirmation of testicular neoplasia, and response to
castration are diagnostic for the syndrome.
Feline Paraneoplastic Exfoliative Dermatitis
Feline exfoliative dermatitis is a paraneoplastic syndrome seen in old and middle‐aged cats with thymomas.
Skin lesions usually precede systemic signs such as
­dyspnea and weight loss. Affected cats show generalized
erythema and severe scaling, often beginning on the
head and neck but progressing to widespread lesions.
The scales can become quite large, sometimes in excess
of 1 cm in diameter. Alopecia is a common finding. Some
patients also exhibit crusting, and brown keratosebaceous material can be present around the eyes and
mouth, in the ear canals, and in the interdigital spaces.
Pruritus is absent to mild unless secondary infections are

VetBooks.ir

168 Cutaneous Manifestations of Systemic Disease

present. Secondary Malassezia dermatitis and bacterial
overgrowth can occur.
The pathogenesis of the cutaneous syndrome is not
well understood, but is thought to be a cell‐mediated
immunologic reaction secondary to the underlying thymoma. A mediastinal mass can be detected in most
patients by radiography or ultrasonography and fine needle aspirates can be diagnostic. Surgical removal of the
thymoma induces regression of the skin lesions. Median
overall survival time after surgery in one small study was
1825 days, with a three‐year chance of ­survival of 74%.
Feline Paraneoplastic Alopecia
Feline paraneoplastic alopecia is a highly visually distinct, bilaterally symmetric progressive alopecia in which
the skin appears unusually thin and shiny (Figure 168.9).
The majority of affected patients are older cats with
pancreatic carcinoma, but the condition has also been
reported with biliary carcinoma. The pathogenesis of the
cutaneous lesions is poorly understood but is thought to
be induced by the cytokine milieu released by the tumor.
The alopecia typically begins on the ventral abdomen
and thorax, with progression to the head and medial
extremities. The hair epilates easily, revealing smooth,
shiny, glistening skin that is not fragile. Some affected
cats have scaly or fissured footpads that can be painful.
The condition is not always pruritic but affected cats
may groom excessively, especially if the skin disease is
complicated by secondary Malassezia dermatitis. The
onset is typically quite acute and rapidly progressive.
Affected cats are systemically ill and exhibit weight loss.
The clinical appearance is visually striking and distinctive. Histopathology confirms the diagnosis. Routine
hematology and serum biochemical profiles are typically

not helpful. Ultrasonography can be useful in finding the
underlying neoplasm, but often fails to reveal a mass.
Unfortunately, this disease carries a poor to grave prognosis as many tumors are not resectable and metastasis
is common.
Nodular Dermatofibrosis
Nodular dermatofibrosis is a syndrome of multiple cutaneous nodules of collagenous origin occurring in conjunction
with
renal
cystadenocarcinomas
or
cystadenomas in dogs. This syndrome most commonly
occurs in German shepherd dogs and their crosses, and
the renal disease is almost always bilateral. The disease is
typically diagnosed in middle age. In addition to the
renal tumors, intact females can develop uterine leiomyomas. In the German shepherd dog, an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance is suspected. Molecular studies
have suggested that nodular dermatofibrosis is not a
paraneoplastic syndrome but a genetic disease linked to
a mutation in the gene encoding folliculin. It is analogous
to Birt–Hogg–Dubé syndrome in humans. Rarely, nodular dermatofibrosis has been found in other breeds in the
absence of internal tumors.
Nodules are typically most numerous on the head and
limbs, including the feet, but can occur on other areas of
the skin, generally in a symmetric fashion. They are firm,
localized in the dermis or subcutaneous layer, mobile,
and covered by intact epidermis that can sometimes
ulcerate, causing lameness. The nodules range in size but
can be up to 5 cm in some cases. The disease has a protracted clinical course, with the appearance of renal failure or metastasis occurring months or more often years
from the time that the lesions are first noticed. The mean
time from first observation of nodular dermatofibrosis
to death is about 2.5 years.
The diagnosis of nodular dermatofibrosis is generally
made by histopathology of the skin masses combined with
abdominal ultrasonography. When skin biopsies are collected, the presence of multiple lesions and the suspicion
of this condition should be conveyed to the pathologist.
There are currently no reported effective treatment
options and because bilateral renal disease is virtually
always present, surgery is not an option. The cutaneous
nodules should be monitored and excised if they become
ulcerated or infected leading to patient discomfort or if
they disturb patient mobility due to their size or location.
It is important to relay the fairly slow progression of the
disease to owners of affected dogs.

primary lung tumors, particularly bronchial and bronchoalveolar adenocarcinoma. This syndrome warrants
mention because affected cats are most often presented
for their skin disease rather than for pulmonary disease.
Multiple digits on multiple feet are commonly involved.
The most commonly recognized clinical signs on presentation include swelling of the distal digits, ulceration
of the skin of the digit or nailfold, purulent discharge, as
well as constant extrusion, deviation, or loss of the nail.
The diagnosis is made by radiography of the digits,
which reveals osteolysis of the third phalanx, by thoracic
radiography, and by digital biopsy. Clinical signs and
radiography can provide a high index of suspicion for
“lung‐digit” syndrome. The prognosis for affected cats is
grave, with a median survival time of 67 days after presentation in one study.
Paraneoplastic Pemphigus
Paraneoplastic pemphigus is a very rare blistering disease involving the skin, mucocutaneous junctions, and
mucosal surfaces. It has been reported in two dogs, one

in association with thymic lymphoma and one with
splenic spindle cell sarcoma. Only one case has been
reported in a cat, in association with lymphocytic
thymoma. Autoantibodies develop as a result of the
­
neoplastic process which targets epithelial adhesion
­
molecules, mainly of the plakin family, leading to loss of
cellular cohesion.
Clinically, the disease is severe and very similar to
pemphigus vulgaris in which vesicobullous and erosive
to ulcerative lesions predominate in the skin and mucosal
surfaces. Histologically, it bears some of the same features of pemphigus vulgaris but also features of erythema
multiforme and the diagnosis is made on the basis of skin
biopsies and investigation for underlying neoplasia.
Other cancers are sometimes associated with skin
lesions. Superficial necrolytic dermatitis, although most
commonly associated with liver disease, has also been
found in dogs with pancreatic glucagonoma, in a cat with
a pancreatic tumor, and recently in a cat with primary
hepatic neuroendocrine carcinoma. One of the underlying causes for generalized adult‐onset demodicosis is
neoplasia, particularly indolent lymphoma.

Superficial Necrolytic Dermatitis
Mitchell D. Song, DVM, DACVD
VETMED Specialty Referral and 24‐Hour Emergency Care Veterinary Hospital, Phoenix, AZ, USA

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Superficial necrolytic dermatitis (SND), also known as
hepatocutaneous syndrome and metabolic epidermal
necrosis, is an uncommon, generally fatal, crusting and
scaling skin disease, which is similar to necrolytic migratory erythema in humans. It has been described in dogs,
cats, and black rhinoceroses. For the purposes of this
chapter, the remaining discussion will be confined to the
disease in dogs.
Superficial necrolytic dermatitis is an external manifestation of an internal disease, most commonly advanced
hepatopathy, but it has also been associated with glucagonoma, ingestion of mycotoxins or long‐term phenobarbital and phenytoin treatments. There is a recent case
report describing SND associated with an insulin‐ and
glucagon‐producing pancreatic carcinoma. Diabetes
mellitus can be a complication of this disease.
The exact etiopathogenesis of SND is currently unknown.
Several studies investigating the serum amino acid profile of
dogs with SND have found profound hypoaminoacidemia,
indicating that this may participate in the development of
skin lesions because amino acids are necessary to maintain
cellular integrity in the epidermis. In one study, glutamic
acid, phenylalanine, tryptophan, and ornithine were not significantly different but all other amino acids were 60% or less
than the mean reference values for normal dogs. In 72%
of the dogs studied, either glutamine or arginine was the
most diminished plasma amino acid. Deficiencies in
cutaneous essential fatty acids, zinc, and biotin have also
been suggested to play a role in skin lesion development.

­Signalment
Superficial necrolytic dermatitis is a disease of older
dogs, with an average age of 10 years. Currently, there are

not enough reported cases to enable accurate determination of breed or sex predilection, though one paper
reported a predilection towards Shih tzus.

­Clinical Signs
Skin lesions are mostly associated with those areas on the
body where trauma naturally occurs, including the footpads, muzzle, and mucocutaneous junctions (periocular,
perioral, anal and genital regions). It is not uncommon for
lesions to also develop on the elbows, hocks, and margins
of the pinnae. The development of cutaneous lesions is
often the reason for owners to seek veterinary advice. The
footpads typically become thickened, crusted, and fissured which often leads to pain and lameness (Figure 169.1).
The elbows, hocks, and prepuce may be alopecic, erosive
to ulcerated, erythematous, crusty, and scaly (Figure 169.2).
Secondary bacterial and fungal (often yeast) infections
occur frequently and aggravate the cutaneous lesions
associated with SND.
In cases where there is severe liver disease, dogs may
have jaundice of the sclera and/or mucous membranes.
In cases associated with diabetes, dogs may be polydipsic
and polyuric.
There are many laboratory abnormalities associated
with SND, which may vary according to the individual case and underlying disease. Those that have
been reported include mild to severe normocytic,
­normochromic, nonregenerative anemia, microcytosis,
hyperglycemia, glucosuria, and possibly ketonuria if the
patient has developed diabetes mellitus. Urine amino
acids including lysine, proline and 1-methylhistidine
are increased. Increases in liver enzymes, hypoalbuminemia, decreases in creatinine and phosphorus, and
increases in cholesterol and t­ riglycerides have also been
reported. It should be noted that there is no clinical

Abdominal ultrasound of dogs with hepatic disease
and SND reveals a liver with a slightly irregular s­ urface.
There are variable sized hyperechoic regions (strands)
present diffusely throughout the parenchyma. The strands
encompass round to oval hypoechoic areas. The result is a
“Swiss cheese” or “honeycomb” appearance to the liver.
Biopsies taken from the liver display a vacuolar hepatopathy with parenchymal collapse. Pancreatic tumors may be
visualized with ultrasound; however, if not visualized and
the liver ultrasound is normal, glucagon levels should be
assayed to rule out a glucagonoma.

­Diagnosis
Skin biopsies of early lesions display very characteristic
histologic changes. The epidermis has moderate to
severe parakeratotic hyperkeratosis and acanthosis.
There is both intercellular and intracellular edema with
keratinocyte vacuolation in the upper half of the epidermis, which results in significant epidermal pallor. There
is basilar epidermal hyperplasia. Because of the eosinophilic superficial keratin accumulation coupled with
central pallor and basilar hyperplasia which stains deep
blue, skin biopsies taken from early lesions display a
striking “red” (eosinophilic), “white” (central pallor), and
“blue” (basophilic basilar hyperplasia) pattern. Biopsy
tissues taken from chronic lesions often lose the central

Treatment for dogs with SND is usually short‐lived
and largely unrewarding. Most cases are fatal, with life
expectancy ranging from 1.7 to 6.4 months. One
reported case survived for 32 months before being
euthanized.
Treatment should initially be directed at stabilizing
dogs with diabetes. Surgical resection can be beneficial
in cases associated with glucagonomas but it is important to keep in mind that glucagonomas typically
metastasize rapidly, so the improvement post surgery
may be temporary. In one reported case, metastasis
precluded surgery, and the dog was treated with subcutaneous octreotide (2 μg/kg twice daily), a somatostatin analog that inhibits glucagon release. Skin
lesions and systemic signs improved within five days.
The dosage was increased to nearly 3 μg/kg twice daily
and all clinical signs improved further within 10 days.
Anorexia was the main side‐effect. The dose (1–3.4 μg/
kg) and frequency of administration (2–3 times daily)
of the octreotide injections were adjusted to maintain
disease control with minimal side‐effects. The dog was
later euthanized due to progressive metastatic disease.
In another case report, adipose tissue-derived mesenchymal stem cells were infused in addition to intravenous amino acids, 46 times over a 30 month period.
Survival time was increased to 32 months after
diagnosis.
Many dogs with liver disease have been treated with
amino acids, either intravenously or orally. Amino acid
solutions which have been used include Aminosyn® 10%
solution (Abbott Laboratories), Procalamine® (B. Braun
Medical Inc.) and Travasol® 8.5% amino acid injection
(Baxter Healthcare) though no particular product has

VetBooks.ir

169 Superficial Necrolytic Dermatitis

been especially more beneficial than any other. Because
of the hyperosmolarity of the solutions, they should be
administered via a central venous catheter over an
extended period of time (6–12h) and are repeated every
1–2 weeks until improvement is noted. The infusions are
then repeated as necessary to help control relapses.
Various doses have been suggested including 25 mL/kg
or 500 mL per dog. Some dermatologists advocate
administering the infusions three days in a row followed
by once‐ to twice‐weekly treatments thereafter and
repeating as signs relapse. Clinical improvement may be
noted within 5–10 days. If there is minimal to no
response after four or more infusions, the therapy is
unlikely to be of benefit to the patient. One dog was
reported to survive for 24 months but was also treated
with intravenous lipid infusions (Intralipid®, Baxter
Healthcare) at 1.4 g/kg every 6.5 weeks. In that dog, it
was proposed that the addition of the lipids was responsible for the extended survival time.

Oral supplementation with egg whites (cooked), zinc
(e.g., zinc methionine 2 mg/kg PO q24h), powdered
amino acid commercial supplements, and essential fatty
acids has been used and may be of some benefit though
all efficacy so far has been anecdotal.
Many dogs are treated with corticosteroids but this
practice should be discouraged. The beneficial effects and
improvement of clinical signs are short‐lived and the corticosteroid may increase the patient’s risk for developing
diabetes mellitus. Secondary bacterial and/or fungal
infections should be treated with appropriate antibiotics
or antimycotics.

­Prognosis
The prognosis is grave, with most dogs dying or being
euthanized within a few months after the beginning of
clinical signs.

Miscellaneous Skin Diseases
Lisa V. Reiter, DVM, DACVD1 and Sheila M.F. Torres, DVM, MS, PhD, DACVD2

­Sebaceous Adenitis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Sebaceous adenitis (SA), also referred to as granulomatous SA, is an uncommon dermatosis that occurs in dogs
and rarely in cats. The cause and pathogenesis of SA currently remain unknown, but several etiologic speculations exist, including an immune‐mediated disorder
targeting the sebaceous gland, a primary keratinization
disorder that obstructs the sebaceous gland duct leading
to inflammation and ultimately glandular destruction, a
developmental, genetically inherited defect resulting in
an inflammatory reaction directed against the sebaceous
gland and, lastly, aberrant lipid metabolism and/or storage that eventually leads to sebaceous gland destruction.
Despite our lack of understanding of the pathomechanism, the endresult is inflammation and obliteration of the
sebaceous glands, which normally produce and cover the
skin with a protective layer of sebum. Sebum is instrumental in maintaining epidermal moisture and hydration and
also has antimicrobial properties. Thus, a predisposition to
secondary bacterial and/or Malassezia overgrowth or
infection develops. Otitis may also occur. In addition, the
inflammation that targets the sebaceous glands ultimately
affects the hair follicles, which leads to abnormal changes
in the quality of the hair coat, and eventually hair loss.
A genetic predisposition to develop the disease is known
in some breeds. In standard poodles and akitas, the disease
is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. The mode of
inheritance in the Havanese is currently being investigated.
Signalment
Most commonly, SA tends to afflict young adult to
­middle‐aged dogs, but dogs of any age may be affected.

The disease appears to be slightly more common in
males. Sebaceous adenitis has been reported in over 50
breeds of dogs although specific breeds have been overrepresented including standard poodles, vizslas, akitas,
springer spaniels, German shepherd dogs and their cross‐
breeds, Samoyeds, and Havanese. Possible increased
­frequency exists in chow chows, dachshunds, beagles,
Lhasa apsos, miniature pinschers, and retrievers.
History and Clinical Signs
The cutaneous changes of SA generally include varying
degrees of alopecia, hyperkeratosis, and excessive scaling, with follicular casts (i.e., scales surround a single
hair or group of hairs) being a consistent feature.
However, the clinical presentation is somewhat dependent on hair coat type and breed. In general, short‐coated
breeds seem to differ clinically from long‐coated breeds.
In short‐coated breeds such as viszlas and dachshunds,
the disease is manifested by symmetric to asymmetric,
“moth‐eaten,” annular to coalescing and serpiginous to
rarely diffuse areas of alopecia with fine, white scaling
affecting the head, pinnae, neck, and trunk. Follicular
casts are subtle and hairs are easily epilated. Pruritus is
typically absent. In long‐coated breeds, such as the
standard poodle, the lesion distribution and lack of pruritus are similar to those of short‐coated breeds, but diffuse alopecia is more common and obvious follicular
casting is present. The hairs are often dull and brittle and
may lose their typical architecture (i.e., the classic curly
hair coat of the poodle becomes wavy or straight). The
hair may also become lighter or darker in color. Groups
of hairs surrounded by scales (i.e., follicular casts) are
easily epilated (Figure 170.1).
Commonly, the lesions initially affect the head, pinnae,
and neck and progress caudally to the dorsal and lateral

In cats, few case reports exist describing the clinical
