Initially, a tentative diagnosis of SA can be made based
upon the signalment, history, and physical examination
findings. Differential diagnoses include demodicosis,
dermatophytosis, superficial bacterial folliculitis, keratinization disorders such as primary idiopathic seborrhea,
ichthyosis, and vitamin A‐responsive dermatosis,
­follicular dysplasia, zinc‐responsive dermatosis, endocrinopathies, such as hypothyroidism, and hair cycle
arrest (i.e., alopecia X). Autoimmune/immune‐mediated
differentials to consider include alopecia areata and
pseudopelade. Surface cytology and deep skin scrapes
should be performed in every case to evaluate for superficial bacterial folliculitis and Malassezia dermatitis, and
to rule out demodicosis. A dermatophyte culture should
be performed if clinically applicable. If an underlying
endocrinopathy is suspected, appropriate screening
tests, such as a complete blood count (CBC), serum
chemistry profile, and urinalysis (UA), as well as thyroid
function testing should be performed.
Biopsy and histopathology are needed in order to confirm the diagnosis of sebaceous adenitis. Multiple punch
biopsies (3–5) should be procured from lesions of varying appearance and chronicity to improve confirmation
of the diagnosis. It is important to include very early

VetBooks.ir

170 Miscellaneous Skin Diseases

lesions in order to identify the inflammatory reaction
targeting the sebaceous glands. These lesions will likely
be missed if only chronic, alopecic lesions are sampled.
The histopathologic changes will vary depending upon
the stage of the lesion sampled and include granulomatous to pyogranulomatous dermal inflammation targeting the sebaceous glands, to complete absence of
sebaceous glands along with perifollicular fibrosis and
varying degrees of follicular keratosis.
Therapy
As the pathomechanism of SA appears to be due to a
combination of an immune‐mediated inflammatory disease and a keratinization disorder, treatments have been
aimed at controlling these two aspects and involve a
combination of systemic and topical therapies to reduce
further sebaceous gland inflammation and destruction,
prevent secondary skin and otic infections, remove
excessive scale, promote moisturization and protection
of the skin, and improve the quality of the hair coat.
In mild cases of SA, topical therapy along with high
doses of oral essential fatty acids (which can be used in all
cases as an adjunctive therapy) can be effective. The suggested dose of omega‐3 fatty acid supplementation is
180 mg eicosapentaenoic acid and 120 mg of docosahexanoic acid per 10 lb of body weight per day combined with
omega‐6 fatty acid supplementation. In general, topical
therapy involves an initial bath using a keratolytic and
keratoplastic shampoo, followed by an emollient rinse or
oil treatment, and concluded with a final bath aimed at
removing any residual oil and scale. In the interim, as
often as daily to as infrequently as once‐weekly treatments
consisting of sprays and rinses, spot‐on formulations,
conditioners, and mousses with emollient, humectant,
antimicrobial, and barrier repair functions are utilized.
Shampoos, such as those containing sulfur and salicylic acid, should be selected. These shampoos are commonly formulated with antimicrobials such as benzoyl
peroxide (Oxiderm + PS®, Ceva Animal Health, Lenexa,
KS, USA; DermaBenSs®, Dechra, Overland Park, KS,
USA) or chlorhexidine (MPA Seba‐Hex®, Vetoquinol,
Forth Worth, TX, USA). Products containing benzoyl
peroxide also act as excellent degreasers. The shampoo
should be lathered well and allowed contact with the skin
for 10 minutes while gently massaging followed by a
fresh, lukewarm water rinse.
A variety of oil‐based treatment regimens have been
suggested to further assist in loosening and removing
scales, follicular casts and crusts, and to replenish the
skin barrier. These include a 50:50 mixture of water and
baby oil or bath oil, such as Eucerin® skin calming dry
skin body wash (Beiersdorf AG, Hamburg, Germany) or
Alpha Keri® bath oil (Novartis Consumer Health,

Parsippany, NJ, USA), or a mixture of 50–75% propylene
glycol in water. The oil or propylene glycol mixture is
allowed a contact time of 1–2 hours. Once soaking is
complete, another bath is performed with the previous
shampoo. Alternatively, a liquid dish‐washing detergent
can be used such as Dawn dish soap (Proctor and Gamble,
Cincinnati, OH, USA), but may be too drying for some
dogs. Frequency will depend on the severity of the disease, but it tends to be more frequent (1–3 per week) in
the beginning and reduced as the patient improves (every
1–4 weeks). Between the bathing/oil treatment regimens, sprays such as DermAllay® oatmeal spray conditioner (Dechra) and Douxo® seborrhea micro‐emulsion
spray (Ceva) can be utilized for their moisturizing and
humectant properties. Mousse formulations, such as
Douxo seborrhea mousse (Ceva), provide another
­convenient means of restoring the skin barrier. When
maintenance antimicrobial therapy is needed, Douxo
chlorhexidine PS micro‐emulsion spray or chlorhexidine
climbazole mousse (Ceva) can be used once to twice
daily to twice weekly for maintenance. For more refractory cases, daily application of 50–75% propylene glycol
can be beneficial. Topical spot‐on treatments, such as
Dermoscent® Essential 6 spot‐on (Bayer, Shawnee
Mission, KS, USA) which contains omega‐3/omega‐6
fatty acids and essential oils, are easy to apply and can be
efficacious. Initially, it is applied as directed once weekly
for eight weeks and then decreased to once every two
weeks. Another alternative is Douxo seborrhea spot‐on
(Ceva) which contains phytosphingosine, a natural component of the epidermis that plays a key role in barrier
function. Oil soaks may eventually be replaced by these
products if an acceptable response is noted. Finally, extra
virgin olive oil and coconut oil have been anecdotally
reported to be effective moisturizers. These products are
inexpensive and also have mild antimicrobial properties.
In more severe cases of SA, systemic treatments
should be utilized in conjunction with topical therapy
and essential fatty acid supplementation. Among the
systemic treatments, vitamin A, synthetic retinoids, a
combination of a tetracycline antibiotic and niacinamide, and ciclosporin have been used for the management of SA with variable success. Retinoids have
antiproliferative, antiinflammatory, and immunomodulatory effects and generally require 4–8 weeks before
response is seen, although maximal response may not be
appreciated until 3–4 months of therapy are achieved.
Oral vitamin A (retinol) can be tried for milder cases of
SA and appears to be a safe and efficacious form of
adjunctive therapy for some dogs. Doses range from 400
to 1000 IU/kg PO daily. For more severe or refractory
cases, synthetic retinoids such as isotretinoin or acitretin (1 mg/kg PO q12–24h) should be considered for a
trial period of at least 4–8 weeks. If a positive response is

1497

VetBooks.ir

1498

Section 12 Skin and Ear Diseases

noted, the lowest effective dosage and frequency of
administration should be used as maintenance therapy
(i.e., 0.5–1.0 mg/kg PO q12–24h). These drugs are
expensive and can be difficult to obtain as they are
strictly regulated. Side‐effects include keratoconjunctivitis sicca (KCS), polyuria and polydipsia due to xerostomia, vomiting, and diarrhea. Laboratory abnormalities
can include elevation of liver enzymes, hypercholesterolemia, and hypertriglyceridemia.
All retinoids are potent teratogens. Monitoring should
include pretreatment measurement of tear production
via a Schirmer tear test (STT) and a serum biochemical
profile at minimum. The authors typically repeat the
STT and serum chemistry profile in 1–2 months and if
no abnormalities are noted, then once to twice a year.
The use of tetracycline, doxycycline or minocycline
and niacinamide may be beneficial for the treatment of
SA, especially in short‐coated breeds, given the antiinflammatory and immunomodulatory actions that can be
gained when these drugs are utilized in combination. It
generally requires 4–8 weeks before response to this
therapy is seen, although maximal effect may not be
appreciated until 3–4 months of therapy are achieved.
Side‐effects include vomiting, diarrhea, and decreased
appetite. Hepatotoxicity is also possible, albeit rare.
Tetracycline and niacinamide are dosed at 250 mg for
dogs <10 kg and 500 mg for dogs >10 kg q8h. When doxycycline is utilized in place of tetracycline, a dosage of
5–10 mg/kg PO q12h is suggested and minocycline can
be dosed at 5–12.5 mg/kg PO q12h. The dosage of niacinamide remains at 250 mg for dogs <10 kg and 500 mg for
dogs >10 kg q8h. If a positive response is noted, the
­lowest effective dosage and frequency of administration
should be used as maintenance therapy.
Ciclosporin is currently the preferred treatment for SA,
especially in severe cases or those that have not responded
acceptably to topical therapy and/or other systemic treatments. Ciclosporin is a calcineurin inhibitor with a number of immune‐modulatory functions. Perhaps most
important in the case of SA is its ability to impair T lymphocyte function. Ciclosporin has also been shown to
increase the numbers of sebaceous glands. Ciclosporin
(Atopica®, Elanco US, Greenfield, IN, USA) can be administered at an initial dosage of 5 mg/kg PO q24h.
Ciclosporin has an extended lag time of 4–6 weeks before
clinical response may be seen. If a positive response is
noted, the lowest effective dosage and frequency of
administration should be used as maintenance therapy.
Side‐effects include vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia, gingival hyperplasia, papillomatosis, secondary infections
including opportunistic urinary tract infections,
­hirsutism, and involuntary shaking. More serious side‐
effects include nephropathy, hepatopathy, bone marrow
suppression, and lymphoplasmacytoid dermatosis

although these effects appear to be extremely rare with
daily doses of approximately 5 mg/kg/day. The authors
typically recommend a baseline CBC, serum chemistry
profile, UA, and urine culture. These tests are repeated
every six months to yearly to monitor for possible
side‐effects.
In general, response to corticosteroids is poor. They
can be tried as a last resort if there has been no response
to other therapeutic options or in cases where those
options are cost prohibitive. A starting dosage of 1 mg/
kg/day PO can be used and gradually reduced to the lowest dosage and frequency possible. There may be a more
favorable response in cases where the histopathology
findings reveal severe inflammation.
It is important to recognize and treat secondary
­infections, as they can greatly contribute to the patient’s
morbidity. The reader is referred to Chapters 158, 166
and 167 in this section regarding the diagnosis and treatment of pyodermas, Malassezia dermatitis, and otitis.
Prognosis
The prognosis of SA ultimately depends upon the severity and chronicity of the disease and the degree and
recurrence of secondary infections. The response to
therapy is quite variable from one patient to the next.
The disease in the akita can be particularly refractory.
There is no cure for SA and it has a chronic, often
­progressive nature which requires lifelong therapy. In
and of itself, SA is not a lethal disease but a clinically and
cosmetically acceptable response is not always obtained
and/or may be too expensive or labor intensive for the
owner. For these reasons, euthanasia may ultimately be
chosen.

­Eosinophilic Dermatitis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Eosinophilic dermatitis, also known as eosinophilic dermatitis with edema and eosinophilic cellulitis, is an
uncommon syndrome that has been described in dogs
and has been compared to Wells syndrome in humans.
The disease is presumably multifactorial with myriad
possible triggers including allergic and parasitic diseases,
arthropod bites, immune‐mediated disease, stress, and
drugs, which culminates in an allergic hypersensitivity
and/or immune‐mediated reaction. In one study, more
than 50% of the dogs developed eosinophilic dermatitis
following treatment for vomiting and diarrhea. In a more
recent study that focused solely on the development
of eosinophilic dermatitis in dogs with signs of gastrointestinal disease, particularly vomiting, diarrhea and

VetBooks.ir

170 Miscellaneous Skin Diseases

­hematochezia, it was found that pancreatitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and adverse food reaction were the
most common triggers, although the cause of the gastrointestinal signs could not be documented for all dogs. In
some dogs, an adverse drug reaction was considered as a
possible trigger.
Signalment
Labrador retrievers and their crosses appear to be overrepresented, but the disease can occur in any breed. Age
and sex predilections have not been identified.
History and Clinical Signs
Eosinophilic dermatitis is a visually distinctive disease.
Lesions develop acutely and are characterized by arciform and serpiginous erythematous macules and plaques
with edema (Figure 170.4). The macules often have a
targetoid appearance although diffuse erythroderma may
be present. The ventral abdomen and thorax are commonly affected, as are the pinnae and face (Figure 170.5).
Edema may be generalized, affecting the face and limbs.
Often, patients are moderately to severely pruritic.
Lymphadenopathy may be present.
Diagnosis
The diagnosis of eosinophilic dermatitis is based upon
its distinct clinical presentation and disease course along
with biopsy and histopathology. Differential diagnoses
include erythema multiforme, vasculitis, and sterile neutrophilic dermatosis. Multiple biopsies should be procured early on from several different‐appearing lesions.
Edematous areas, if present, should also be sampled.
Histopathologic findings are variable and include mild to
severe perivascular to diffuse eosinophilic dermatitis
with varying amounts of edema, which is often protein

Figure 170.5 Diffuse erythroderma and edema present on the
ventral abdomen and pelvic limbs of a 3‐year‐old female spayed
dachshund.

rich in severe cases. Flame figures (degranulating eosinophils associated with collagen fibers) may be noted
along with variable degrees of vascular damage. CBC
and serum chemistry abnormalities are not common.
Occasionally, peripheral eosinophilia and basophilia
may be documented. In cases associated with gastrointestinal disease, hypoalbuminemia is a common finding.
Therapy
Appropriate drug withdrawal is paramount when a cutaneous adverse drug reaction is suspected. In addition,
patients respond favorably to antihistamines and/or corticosteroids. Diphenhydramine or hydroxyzine may be
administered at a dosage of 2 mg/kg PO q8–12h. In a
recent study, cetirizine was the most commonly prescribed antihistamine with doses of 0.6–1.1 mg/kg PO
q24h. Cetirizine has several antieosinophilic effects that
may make it particularly effective for treating eosinophilic dermatitis. Reported starting dosages of prednisone include a range of 0.6–2.8 mg/kg/day. In milder
forms of the disease, therapy may not be required with
lesional self‐resolution occurring within a few weeks.
Topical glucocorticoid therapy with hydrocortisone,
­betamethasone, or triamcinolone may also be considered. However, the treatment duration should not extend
beyond two weeks given the risk of localized cutaneous
atrophy and other complications that may occur from
prolonged topical steroid application.
Prognosis

Figure 170.4 Abdomen of an adult male castrated Labrador
retriever with serpiginous erythematous macules and edematous
plaques.

Eosinophilic dermatitis usually carries a favorable prognosis. Disease resolution tends to be swift, especially
when underlying triggers are identified and removed

(i.e., drugs). Typically, treatment duration varies from
one to four weeks, and only rarely will there be recurrences or a waxing and waning course.

­Sterile Neutrophilic Dermatosis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Sterile neutrophilic dermatosis is a rare disease which
closely resembles acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis
(Sweet syndrome) in humans. The few documented cases
in the veterinary literature all involve dogs. In people, the
disease is typified by pyrexia and a neutrophilic leukocytosis along with painful papular to nodular skin lesions
that consist predominantly of a diffuse infiltration of
mature neutrophils within the dermis on histopathology.
Extracutaneous sites of neutrophilic inflammation and
concurrent disease processes have also been identified in
humans, including respiratory and gastrointestinal tract
infections, inflammatory bowel disease, arthritis, and
neoplasia, although many cases are idiopathic. Disease
development has also been associated with various drugs.
In dogs, the clinicopathologic abnormalities mirror
those observed in humans. Concurrent neutrophilic
inflammation has been reported to affect the lungs,
heart, esophagus, and various joints. Adverse drug reactions appear to be an important cause of the disease in
dogs. Several case reports have been associated with the
administration of carprofen. Firocoxib has also been
implicated in an additional case report. The pathogenesis is not completely understood, but is thought to
involve an immune‐mediated process.
History and Clinical Signs
There are currently no known breed, gender, or age predilections given the paucity of reported cases. Similar to
the disease in humans, extracutaneous signs are commonly associated with the cutaneous manifestations, but
not obligatory. Pyrexia is a key feature, although it is not
always documented. Other reported clinical abnormalities include anorexia, lethargy, weakness, lameness, and
lymphadenomegaly. A mature neutrophilia may be present. Other laboratory abnormalities may be present and
are reflective of the various underlying disease processes.
Cutaneous lesions include the acute development of
erythematous macules and papules as well as pustules
and plaques. Ulcerations of the oral cavity and the body
have been reported. The ventral aspect of the abdomen,
axillae, and groin are preferentially involved, although
the lesions may occur anywhere. Edema may be present
and can extend ventrally to involve the legs. Pruritus is
usually absent.

Diagnosis
The diagnosis of sterile neutrophilic dermatosis is based
upon recognition of the sudden onset of systemic signs
that precede or occur simultaneously with the cutaneous
lesions in conjunction with the presence of a neutrophilic
findings.
leukocytosis and compatible histopathologic ­
Differential diagnoses include infectious dermatitides,
superficial pyoderma, pemphigus foliaceus, sterile pustular erythroderma of miniature schnauzers, eosinophilic dermatitis and edema, erythema multiforme, and
cutaneous adverse drug reactions. The diagnostic work‐
up should include skin cytology, CBC, serum chemistry
profile, and UA. Titers for tick‐borne diseases should
also be considered, depending upon geographic locale
and potential for exposure. Thoracic radiographs and
abdominal ultrasound are also indicated to evaluate for
underlying diseases. Multiple skin biopsies should be
procurred and tissue cultures submitted. Histopathologic
findings that are supportive of sterile neutrophilic dermatosis include dermal edema with a moderate to severe
perivascular to diffuse neutrophilic infiltrate.
Therapy
Treatment of this disease includes the discontinuation of
potentially offending drugs, along with supportive care
and immunosuppressive doses of corticosteroids. A positive response may be evident within 48 hours and remission has been documented to occur within a week in
some cases. In other cases, therapy may be slowly tapered
over the course of four weeks. In severe cases, intravenous or subcutaneous administration of dexamethasone
followed by a tapering course of prednisone may be
considered.
Prognosis
Sterile neutrophilic dermatosis has a fair to good prognosis depending upon the underlying etiology. It stands
to reason that in cases where the underlying disease is
severe and untreatable, the prognosis may be grave.

­Ichthyosis
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Canine ichthyosis is a rare hereditary cornification
­disorder recognized in various breeds such as Norfolk
terriers, Jack Russell terriers, golden retrievers, and
American bulldogs. The disease in dogs has been
­typically classified as either epidermolytic or nonepidermolytic based on histopathologic findings. With the
exception of Norfolk terriers and a Labrador cross, all

VetBooks.ir

170 Miscellaneous Skin Diseases

other breeds reported to date have had the nonepidermolytic form.
The disease is caused by the abnormal expression of
protein or lipid molecules that form the stratum corneum structure. Genetic studies have identified different
mutations of these molecules according to the breed
investigated as follows:
Norfolk terriers – a splice‐site mutation in keratin 10
(KRT10)
●● golden retrievers – a mutation in the PNPLA1 gene
that participates in lipid organization and metabolism
in the outer epidermis
●● American bulldogs– a mutation in the NIPAL‐4 gene
resulting in decreased expression of the protein icthyin
●● Jack Russell terriers – a loss‐of‐function mutation in
transglutaminase 1 (TGM1) which mediates calcium‐
dependent cross‐linking of proteins that form the
cornified envelope.
●●

A congenital ichthyosiform disease associated with keratoconjunctivitis sicca has been described in Cavalier
King Charles spaniels but a candidate gene has not been
identified to date.
More recently, a new variant of congenital ichthyosis
was described in 14 Great Dane puppies based on clinical, histopathologic, and transmission electron microscopy findings. Pedigree analysis of 13 of the 14 puppies
revealed that all dogs were related. The disease in these
puppies most resembles the congenital, autosomal recessive, nonepidermolytic, lamellar ichthyosis described in
the golden retriever. However, unique histologic differences were observed which have yet to be reported in
ichthyotic dogs. Of note, enlarged sebaceous glands that
were also composed of numerous degenerative sebocytes
containing an alcianophilic, lipid‐rich material within
the cytoplasm were documented. This same material was
also identified within dilated hair follicle lumina.
An autosomal recessive mode of inheritance has been
reported for all breeds where a pedigree analysis could
be performed thus far.

Golden Retriever

Affected dogs present with small to large, attached to
loose, white to gray scales localized primarily on the
neck, trunk, rump, and ventrum (Figure 170.6). A characteristic early sign is a dark, sandpaper‐like appearance
of the ventral glabrous skin (Figure 170.7). Pruritus is
typically not present but, may occur if secondary infections develop. Clinical signs may wax and wane with
periods of remission and exacerbation.
Norfolk Terrier

At birth, the disease is characterized by formation of
superficial bullae and erosions after mild mechanical

Figure 170.6 One‐year‐old golden retriever with ichthyosis.
Large, loose to adhered, white to gray scales localized to the
lateral trunk.

Signalment
As for most hereditary disorders, the clinical signs are
typically recognized early in life. The disease presents at
birth in Jack Russell terriers, Norfolk terriers, and
Cavalier King Charles spaniels. It is reported to ­manifest
before weaning in American bulldogs and has a variable
age of onset in golden retrievers (3 weeks to 3 years).
History and Clinical Signs
The disease phenotype can vary according to the breed and
this may be partially the result of different genetic mutations.

The ventral abdomen is covered with adhered gray scales, giving a
hyperpigmented appearance. The skin has a sandpaper‐like
texture when gently palpated.

Pruritus has not been described and footpads, claws,

Jack Russell Terrier

Affected dogs are born with thick, large, adherent, white
to dark scales in areas with sparse hair coat and loosely
adherent scales in other parts of the body. Footpads are

soft. Secondary bacterial and Malassezia infections may
be a complicating problem.

Great Dane

Clinically, Great Dane puppies present with generalized
fine, dry, white to yellow scaling along with a greasy,
leathery appearance to the axillary and inguinal regions.
Marked skin wrinkling is present on the head, muzzle
and distal limbs.
Other Breeds

Ichthyosis has been anecdotally reported in West

An epidermolytic form was described in a Labrador

American Bulldog

Shortly after birth, puppies present with a disheveled
hair coat and erythema associated with tightly adherent

groin) which acquires a wrinkled appearance. In adulthood, the hairless areas develop a reddish‐brown discoloration. Large, loosely adherent, white to tan scales are
present throughout the body (Figure 170.8). Foodpad
hyperkeratosis is a rare finding in adult dogs. Affected
dogs are very prone to developing Malassezia overgrowth which can be severe and result in pruritus

The clinical appearance of American bulldog ichthyosis is frequently misdiagnosed as atopic dermatitis which

its golden retriever predecessors.
Diagnosis
The diagnosis historically has been based on the characteristic history, clinical signs, and histopathologic findings. When performed, skin biopsies should be submitted
to a pathologist with experience in dermatology. A commercially available genetic test is now offered through
Optigen (www.optigen.com/) and is easily performed
using a venous blood sample and has become the authors’
primary means of confirming a diagnosis of ichthyosis in
breeds where testing is an option. Electron microscopy
and genetic studies are needed to characterize the
molecular abnormality and mode of transmission.
Therapy
The treatment goals should be to prevent/treat secondary
infections and reduce the excessive scaling, hyperkeratosis, and inflammation by restoring the stratum corneum
barrier. This may be achieved by various topical therapies
which should be tailored to the patient’s needs. Shampoos
with keratolytic and keratoplastic properties such as sulfur and salicylic acid, followed by a good moisturizer, can
be used 2–3 times weekly. Products containing lipids such
as phytosphingosine (Douxo seborrhea spot‐on or spray),
or fatty acids and essential oils (Dermoscent Essential 6
spot‐on) can be used after bathing. Combinations of oral
omega‐3 and omega‐6 fatty acids can be used as adjunctive therapy. Secondary infections should be treated
appropriately with topical and/or systemic antifungals or
antibiotics as required for each individual patient.

is still questionable but certain lesions have improved

cases remain idiopathic and some cats may be genetically
predisposed to develop this condition. Cats can have a
single lesion, multiples of the same type or a combination of different ones. Lesions may be refractory to treatment, resolve with or without treatment and not return,
or be recurrent.
Signalment
There is no breed, sex or age predilection but linear
granuloma lesions typically develop in cats less than
2 years of age.
History and Clinical Signs
Lesions associated with the complex include eosinophilic
granuloma, eosinophilic plaque, and indolent ulcer.
Eosinophilic Granuloma

This is the only true granulomatous lesion of the complex
and has various clinical presentations such as nodules,
papules or linear plaques. They can be single or multiple
and develop anywhere on the body, including the lips
(pouting lip), chin (fat chin), oral cavity, footpads, pinnae,
caudal aspect of thighs or other areas (Figure 170.11).

Prognosis
Clients have to understand that ichthyosis is a noncurable condition and the prognosis to achieve disease control is generally fair. Veterinarians should become familiar
with the different clinical presentations and breed‐related
disease severity and educate clients on what to expect.

­Eosinophilic Granuloma Complex
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Feline eosinophilic granuloma complex is a group of
lesions that affect the skin, mucocutaneous junctions,
and oral cavity. They can develop in cats with adverse

Lesions are often erythematous and those localized in
the oral cavity and footpads are more likely to erode or
ulcerate and have pale foci of necrosis. Pruritus is variable and circulating eosinophilia may be present.
Eosinophilic Plaque

Plaque lesions are typically multiple and coalescing,
eroded to ulcerated and more often localized to the ventral abdomen and medial thighs (Figure 170.12). Pruritus
is typically present and cats with eosinophilic plaques
often have an underlying allergic disease. Peripheral
­lymphadenopathy and circulating eosinophilia may be
present.
Indolent Ulcer

This is also known as eosinophilic ulcer or rodent ulcer.
It is characterized by a well‐demarcated ulcer which has
an elevated border and a center that is pinkish to yellowish. The lesion is typically localized to the upper lip and
can be very extensive and span the philtrum or be adjacent to the upper canine tooth (Figure 170.13). Pruritus
is not present.
Diagnosis
Typically, diagnosis is based on the history and clinical
appearance of the lesions. A biopsy will confirm the diagnosis and should be performed when lesions develop in
older cats to exclude neoplasia, are refractory to treatment or have an unusual presentation. Cytology is important to determine the presence of bacterial infection. The
presence of intracellular cocci indicates an infection but
extracellular rods suggest oral contamination. Eosinophils
may not be found on cytologic samples.

Figure 170.12 Five‐year‐old domestic longhair cat with
eosinophilic plaques. Coalescing erythematous plaques with an

Figure 170.13 One‐year‐old cat with an eosinophilic ulcer. This
cat also has eosinophilic granuloma lesions localized to the oral

Therapy
Identifying and controlling the underlying disease is an
important part of the treatment regimen as it may
­prevent recurrences. Most cases respond well to oral
glucocorticoid therapy such as prednisolone (2.2–4.0 mg/
kg), methylprednisolone (2.0–3.0 mg/kg), triamcinolone
(0.2–0.3 mg/kg) or dexamethasone (0.3–0.6 mg/kg), all
administered daily until remission and then every other
(prednisolone and methylprednisolone) or every third
day (triamcinolone and dexamethasone) as maintenance.
Injection of methylprednisolone acetate should only be
considered if the cat cannot receive oral therapy. The
recommended dose is 4.0–5.0 mg/kg subcutaneously
(SC) or intramuscularly (IM) given every 2–4 weeks until
remission. Cats are more prone to develop diabetes
mellitus with long‐acting, injectable glucocorticoids.
­
Ciclosporin at 5.0–7.5 mg/kg/day can be used in refractory cases or cases that cannot tolerate glucocorticoid
therapy. The lowest possible maintenance dosage should
be tried. Chlorambucil at 0.1–0.2 mg/kg/day until remission and then tapered to every other day can be used in
recalcitrant cases. A small number of cats have responded
to interferon‐alpha at 300–1000 units/day PO or SC for
30 days.

Radiotherapy, cryosurgery, surgical excision, and laser
therapy are options for single lesions refractory to medical therapy. Eosinophilic ulcers are most likely to benefit
from these treatment modalities but recurrences are
common.
Prognosis
Most lesions respond well to treatment but some are
quite refractory. In addition, recurrences are common
and a triggering cause for lesion development is often
not determined.

­Symmetric Lupoid Onychitis
(Symmetric Lupoid Onychodystrophy)
Etiology/Pathophysiology
The cause of symmetric lupoid onychitis (SLO) is
currently unknown but the predisposition of some
­
breeds to develop the disease suggests that genetics plays
a role. Moreover, the risk of developing SLO in the
Gordon setter has been associated with the dog leukocyte antigen (DLA) class II alleles.

Figure 170.14 Seven‐year‐old Labrador retriever with symmetric
lupoid onychitis. The claw of the fifth digit is showing onycholysis
(i.e., separation of the claw structure).

Signalment
Most dogs develop the disease between 2 and 6 years of
age but it can occur at any age. Gordon setters, English
setters, and German shepherd dogs appear to be predisposed but SLO has been recognized in various breeds.
There is no sex predilection.
History and Clinical Signs
Onychomadesis (sloughing of claws), onycholysis (separation of claw structure distally and progressing proximally), and paronychia (inflammation of claw folds),
causing the dog to lick the paws, along with lameness, are
typically the initial clinical presentation (Figure 170.14).
It may start in one or more claws of a single paw but
within weeks, it spreads to involve most, if not every,
claw of all four paws. Regrown nails are short, misshapen,
dry, and brittle (Figure 170.15). Secondary infection
associated with purulent exudate is common. The disease
only affects the paws.
Diagnosis
The diagnosis is generally based on the history and characteristic clinical presentation but a claw biopsy (onychectomy and submission of the entire third phalanx) may
be needed to rule out other causes of nail disorders and

Figure 170.15 Four‐year‐old mixed‐breed dog with symmetric
lupoid onychitis. Claws are misshapen, short, and brittle.

confirm the histopathologic changes expected with SLO.
Cytology of exudate is necessary to determine the presence of bacterial infection and culture and susceptibility
should be considered based on the cytologic findings
and the dog’s history of antibiotic therapy.
Therapy
No single treatment is universally effective in SLO. High
doses of omega‐6/omega‐3 essential fatty acids combined
with a tetracycline antibiotic (e.g., doxycycline at 5.0–
10.0 mg/kg q12h) and niacinamide (250 mg for dogs
<10 kg and 500 mg for dogs >10 kg q8h) are commonly
used as the initial therapy. Pentoxifylline at 15–20 mg/kg
q12h to q8h can be added to the treatment regimen. More

1505

VetBooks.ir

1506

Section 12 Skin and Ear Diseases

severe cases may require other immunomodulatory drugs
such as oral prednisolone (1.0–2.0 mg/kg/day), azathioprine (2.2 mg/kg/day) or ciclosporin (5 mg/kg/day).
Remission should be expected in two weeks with the
prednisolone and 4–6 weeks with the ciclosporin and azathioprine; therefore, taper the dose to avoid undesirable
side‐effects or discontinue treatment if no improvement.
Amputation of the third phalanx should be considered in
cases that are refractory to medical therapy.
An expected response to therapy translates to
cessation of onycholysis and onychomadesis and
­

­resolution of pain. In these cases, affected claws will
regrow but will have an abnormal structure. It may
take months before any significant improvement can
be noted.
Prognosis
Prognosis is poor for cure and fair for disease control.
Owners have to understand that claws will appear abnormal despite satisfactory improvement of the claw
disorder.

Matthew J. Allen, VetMB, PhD1 and Gert J. Breur, DVM, MS, PhD, DACVS2

­Skeletal Development and Growth
Skeletal Development
The first evidence of the developing axial and appendicular skeleton is seen during the embryonic period (day 19–35
after fertilization) when mesenchymal cells condense in
the areas of the future bones. The mesenchymal model
transforms into a cartilage model (the anlage), which then
enlarges and transforms into mature bone both pre‐ and
postnatally. The enlargement of the cartilaginous bones
occurs by formation of new cartilage in diaphyseal and epiphyseal growth centers and growth plates. The newly
formed cartilaginous bones transform into mature bone
via the processes of endochondral and intramembranous
ossification (see later). Joints cavities between the developing bones are formed by the processes of segmentation
and cavitation. The formation of the joint surfaces (see
later) and intraarticular structures follows thereafter.
Most of the longitudinal growth of long bones is contributed by the growth plates (approximately 75–80%)
and epiphyseal growth centers (approximately 20–25%),
with a minor contribution by the diaphyseal growth
center. In dogs, most bone length growth occurs when
the animal is between 12 and 26 weeks of age. This
period is characterized by the most rapid rate of bone
length growth and endochondral ossification, both in
epiphyseal growth centers and growth plates, that a dog
will experience during its entire lifetime. In addition,
growth and mineralization of many epiphyseal growth
centers commence and cease at predetermined times.
At the end of this period, cartilage only persists between
the epiphysis and the metaphysis (growth plate) and at
the articular surface covering the epiphyses. Growth
plate‐associated longitudinal growth continues thereafter at a much slower rate until the process stops

completely and the cartilaginous growth plates are
­
replaced by bone (growth plate fusion). Just as with the
epiphyses, the growth cessation and “fusion” of growth
plates occur at predetermined times (Table 171.1). The
rate of skeletal development and the final bone size vary
widely among canine and feline breeds.
Intramembranous and Endochondral Ossification
Bone is formed through two fundamentally distinct mechanisms: endochondral ossification (EO) and intramembranous ossification (IO). The key feature of EO is that it
involves the sequential resorption of hyaline cartilage that
is replaced with bone. Under physiologic conditions, EO
takes place in diaphyseal and epiphyseal growth centers,
growth plates and – at a very slow rate – at articular
surfaces. Endochondral ossification also occurs under
­
pathologic conditions and as a repair process. Examples are
secondary fracture healing, o
­ steophyte formation, synovial
osteochondromatosis, and heterotopic bone formation.
Intramembranous ossification occurs through condensation and differentiation of mesenchymal tissues,
without the requirement for an intermediate cartilage
form. During the embryonic period, it plays a role in the
development of flat bones (e.g., desmocranium). Later
during development, IO takes place in basic multicellular units (BMU or osteon) in Haversian canals, and on
endosteal, periosteal, and trabecular surfaces. It provides
an important mechanism for appositional bone growth
at the periosteal (outer) surface of bone, resulting in diaphyseal circumferential growth (i.e., widening) of bones
over time. Intramembranous ossification occurs under
pathologic conditions and/or as repair process seen, for
example, in panosteitis, hypertrophic osteoarthopathy,
and primary fracture healing.

Growth‐Plate Associated Growth
Growth plates facilitate bone length growth by the
formation of new cartilage. The volume increase of
­
­cartilage in a growth plate is a function of chondrocyte
proliferation, chondrocyte enlargement, and matrix
­formation. Because growth in width of a growth plate is
constrained, the newly formed cartilage pushes the epiphysis away from the metaphysis, thus elongating the

bone. At about the same time – albeit with a different
circadian rhythm – growth plate cartilage is converted
into bone at the junction of the growth plate and the
metaphysis via EO. Because the rate of bone length
growth and the rate of advancement of the EO mineralization from the metaphysis are approximately the same,
the thickness of a growth plate will not vary much from
day to day.

VetBooks.ir

171 Skeletal Development and Homeostasis

The growth plate is located between the epiphysis and
metaphysis, and may be divided into a resting zone, a
proliferative zone, a hypertrophic zone, and a mineralization zone.
Changes in the morphology of the chondrocytes and
the volume and composition of their surrounding matrix
in the different zones of the growth plate represent the
temporal alterations taking place through a chondrocyte’s life‐span. Chondrocytes in the resting zone are primarily stem cells, that divide at a slow rate, and daughter
cells. The daughter cells initially assume a flat morphology and divide, slowly enlarge, and synthesize a type 2
collagen and proteoglycan rich matrix; they are organized in so‐called clones, chondrons or columns. Cells in
this stage of the lifecycle are located in the proliferative
zone. Then, chondrocytes suddenly and rapidly increase
their cell volume by active swelling, while continuing the
synthesis of matrix. Chondrocytes in this stage of their
life cycle are spheroidal and relatively large and are
located in the hypertrophic zone. Shortly thereafter,
chondrocytes achieve their final size and shape and convert their surrounding matrix into one that is permissive
of mineralization. This cell type is located in the zone of
mineralization on the metaphyseal side of the growth
plate. Chondrocytes abutting the metaphyseal vasculature die abruptly, presumably via the process of apoptosis. The life‐span of chondrocytes varies and is mostly
dependent on the growth plate location, the animal’s age,
breed, and species.
The regulation of chondrocytic proliferation and
hypertrophy, the main determinants of bone length
growth, is complex and facilitated by various growth
factors, transcription factors, extracellular matrix proteins, and cell–matrix interactions. The traditional
understanding is that growth hormone while acting on
stem cells promotes the formation of insulin‐like growth
factor‐1 (IGF‐1)‐responsive daughter cells. Then,
through autocrine and paracrine systems, IGF‐1 stimulates clonal expansion of chondrocytes (dual effector
theory). The change from a proliferative chondrocyte
phenotype to a hypertrophic chondrocyte phenotype is
mainly controlled by a local feedback loop involving
parathyroid hormone‐related peptide (PTHrP), Indian
hedgehog (IHH), and transforming growth factor‐beta
(TGF‐beta). However, other regulators also may be
involved. More recently, transcription factors, extracellular matrix proteins, and cell–matrix interactions
functioning as regulators of chondrocytic proliferation
and differentiation have been identified. Research in
this area is largely driven by these regulators’ role in
the etiology and pathogenesis of skeletal dysplasias.
Discussion of these regulatory mechanisms and canine
and feline skeletal dysplasias is beyond the scope of
this chapter.

Essential to EO in the growth plate is the sequential
resorption of growth plate cartilage and its replacement
by metaphyseal bone. Chondrocytes with increased
membrane activity of alkaline phosphatase, in the zone
of mineralization, undergo their terminal differentiation.
They synthesize type X collagen and the surrounding
matrix now includes chondrocalcin, osteonectin, and
osteopontin. Chondrocytes juxtaposed to the metaphyseal vasculature (terminal hypertrophic chondrocytes)
die abruptly by apoptosis and their space is invaded and
taken over by metaphyseal blood vessels, a process facilitated by metalloproteinases (MMPs) and vascular
endothelial growth factor (VEGF) produced by hypertropic chondrocytes. Osteoprogenitor cells migrate via
the newly formed metaphyseal vessels, differentiate into
osteoblasts, and form woven bone on the calcified cartilage matrix of the longitudinal septa. The so‐called
­primary spongiosa thus formed consists of a lattice of
calcified cartilage and woven bone. The move from hyaline cartilage to bone is completed with the replacement
of primary spongiosa by secondary spongiosa, a lamellar
bone. The regulation of the conversion of cartilage to
woven bone is complex, but it appears that genetic,
nutritional, metabolic and mechanical factors all play a
role. Defects of growth plate EO are often seen with
­skeletal dysplasias and metabolic bone diseases.
Epiphysis‐Associated Growth
The epiphysis of developing bone consists of a mineralized center surrounded by hyaline cartilage. The cartilage on the end of immature bones, the articular‐epiphyseal
complex (AEC), consists of two functionally different
layers: a relatively thin outer layer and a relatively thick
inner part.
The outer layer is specialized immature articular cartilage, is avascular, and does not participate in epiphyseal
EO. Following maturation, the articular cartilage will
consist of a superficial zone, a transitional or middle
zone, a radial or deep zone and a zone of calcifying
­cartilage. Completion of the maturation process of the
articular surface is indicated by the presence of the tide
mark, a microscopically visible line(s) separating the
uncalcified radial zone from the zone of calcifying cartilage. The inner layer of the AEC is functionally similar to
the growth plate and is responsible for epiphyseal
enlargement by new cartilage formation and mineralization of the newly formed cartilage.
The cartilage on the metaphyseal side of the mineralized center of the epiphysis also consists of two layers.
Adjacent to the mineralized epiphysis is true epiphyseal
cartilage, while the cartilage on the metaphyseal side
represents growth plate cartilage. Morphologically, there
are two main differences between epiphyseal and growth

1511

VetBooks.ir

1512

Section 13 Diseases of Bone and Joint

plate cartilage. First, the chondroepiphysis is visually disorganized and does not have the ordered zonal and
columnar arrangement of the growth plate. Furthermore,
in contrast to the proliferative, hypertrophic and mineralization zones in the growth plate, the chondroepiphysis has a rich blood supply. Chondroepiphyseal blood
vessels originate from the perichondrium and are located
in so‐called cartilage canals. Under physiologic conditions, these cartilage canals play a role in the nourishment of epiphyseal chondrocytes, in the formation and
maintenance of the epiphyseal ossification center and in
providing mesenchymal stem cells. It has been suggested
that damage to cartilage canal vessels may result in osteochondrosis. Cartilage canal vessels are distinct from
vessels on the metaphyseal side of the growth plate.
Just as with growth plate‐associated growth, enlargement of the epiphysis‐associated growth is a function of
chondrocytic proliferation, chondrocytic enlargement,
matrix formation, and duration of chondrogenic activity
in the chondroepiphysis. Chondrocyte proliferation
mostly takes place on the epiphyseal periphery, whereas
EO occurs towards the center, where chondrocytes are
larger and surrounded by more matrix. Cartilage canals
regress through the process of chondrification as the
ossification front from the center of the epiphysis reaches
newly formed epiphyseal cartilage. Towards the end of
the growth period, blood vessels from the epiphyseal
bone marrow anastomose with cartilage canal vessels.
When epiphyseal growth and ossification are completed,
a thin layer of avascular articular cartilage and an avascular growth plate remain. The regulation of epiphyseal
enlargement and endochondral ossification is not well
understood and certainly not as well studied as the
regulation of the growth plate. However, most likely
­
there will be strong similarities with the regulation of the
growth plate.

­Bone Morphology
Composition of Bone
Bone is a composite material consisting of a fiber‐­
reinforced matrix (similar to reinforced concrete, or
Kevlar body armor). The fibers and the matrix in which
they are embedded are manufactured by bone‐forming
cells (osteoblasts) and are susceptible to breakdown by
bone‐resorbing cells (osteoclasts).
Bone Matrix

Bone is initially deposited as nonmineralized matrix
(osteoid), the major components of which are a proteoglycan‐rich ground substance with embedded fibers of
type 1 collagen. A number of important noncollagenous

proteins are also found in bone, including osteocalcin
(also known as bone Gla protein), osteopontin, and
­osteonectin. The importance of type 1 collagen is most
clearly evidenced by the profound clinical signs seen in
patients with congential defects in collagen 1 synthesis
(osteogenesis imperfecta, also known as “brittle bone
disease”). Abnormalities in either the quality or quantity
of type 1 collagen result in dramatic alterations in the
material and mechanical properties of bone by compromising the fiber reinforcement of osteoid. As a result, the
bone is embrittled and prone to fracture.
The next stage after formation of the osteoid is
­deposition of mineral, in the form of hydroxyapatite
(Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2). The process of matrix mineralization remains incompletely understood but is thought to
involve selective mineral deposition within matrix vesicles released by osteoblasts. Once they reach a certain
size, the needle‐like hydroxyapatite (HA) crystals are
released from the matrix vesicles into the extracellular
space, where they serve as templates for ongoing
­deposition of mineral within the collagen fibrils. The tissue‐nonspecific isoform of alkaline phosphatase is
believed to play a role in controlling the release of HA
crystals from the matrix vesicle, as well as in the progression of mineralization in the extracellular matrix.
Cells of Bone

Osteoblasts are the cells that synthesize new bone. They
are derived from mesenchymal precursor cells (variously
referred to as mesenchymal stem cells or marrow‐
derived stem cells) and exist either as flat resting cells or
as more metabolically active cuboidal cells. In both cases,
osteoblasts remain intimately attached the bone surface.
Over time, as additional osteoid is deposited and then
mineralized, osteoblasts become encased in bone, forming osteocytes. These cells are known to be critical determinants of cell–cell and matrix–cell signaling within
bone, playing an active role in transducing mechanical
stimuli (strain) into bone cell activity. Signaling is
­facilitated by the presence of long cellular extensions
(filopodia) on osteocytes; the filopodia run through
small channels (canaliculi) within the bone. The extended
surface area of the filopodia allows the osteocytes to
sense changes in the composition of the extracellular
fluid within the canaliculi, while their connectivity allows
for efficient signaling between cell bodies.
Osteoclasts are the cells that resorb bone. In contrast
with the mesenchymal origins of osteoblasts, osteoclasts
derive from hematopoietic cells via the recruitment,
activation, and fusion of mononuclear cell precursors.
Hallmarks of the osteoclast include a multinucleate cell
with a highly invaginated basal membrane (the so‐called
“ruffled border”) apposing the bone surface, expression
of the enzymes tartrate‐resistant acid phosphatase and

VetBooks.ir

171 Skeletal Development and Homeostasis

cathepsin K, and the formation of a “sealing zone”
through which cells attach to bone.
The process of osteoclastic bone resorption involves
local acidification by means of a vacuolar ATPase. Under
acid conditions, calcium and phosphorus are liberated
from the bone matrix. At the same time, cathepsin K
degrades the type 1 collagen, as well as other noncollagenous proteins within the bone matrix.
In cancellous bone, bone resorption occurs at the
bone surface; in cortical bone, osteoclasts may act
either directly on an exposed bone surface (e.g., on the
endosteum or periosteum) or within the interstitium of
bone, by resorbing bone within the longitudinally
­oriented Haversian canals, in a process known as intracortical remodeling.
Structure of Bone
The canine skeleton consists of approximately 319 bones
that can be classified as follows.
Long bones (e.g., femur, humerus)

Macrostructure of Bone

The shape of an individual bone is genetically determined but can be altered by changes in mechanical
­loading, blood supply, trauma, etc. For long bones, three
anatomically distinct regions are recognized.
Diaphysis – the shaft of the long bone, composed of
cortical bone surrounding the medullary cavity.
●● Epiphysis – the end of a long bone that is initially separated from the rest of the bone by the presence of a
growth plate (physis).
●● Metaphysis – the region between the epiphysis and the
diaphysis.
●●

Bone is present in one of two forms, cortical or cancellous. Cortical bone is very dense (it is also known as
compact bone) and is mainly found as an envelope for
the flat bones and in the diaphyseal regions of long
bones. Cancellous bone is less dense and exists as a
three‐dimensional network of interconnecting struts
(trabeculae), primarily within the metaphyseal and epiphyseal regions of the long bones, as well as in the irregular bones. Cancellous bone has a significantly higher
surface area (per unit volume) for cellular activity than
cortical bone and, as a result, is more metabolically
active. The regions of the skeleton in which there are
increased amounts of cancellous bone tend to be the
high turnover sites; in humans, these are the sites that

are most sensitive to hormonal change and most likely
to develop osteoporosis (proximal femur, spine, distal
radius).
Microstructure of Bone

Bone is organized as either lamellar bone or woven bone.
Woven bone is an immature form of bone and is only
seen in the skeletally mature animal at sites of fracture
healing, bone growth, and skeletal diseases such as neoplasia or panosteitis. When present in the adult skeleton,
it is rapidly remodeled into lamellar bone. Woven bone is
more cellular than lamellar bone and its collagen fibers
are aligned at random; as a result, woven bone is isotropic (i.e., mechanical properties do not depend on
specimen orientation).
Lamellar bone is found throughout the mature skeleton in both cortical and cancellous bone, irrespective of
whether the bone was formed by intramembranous or
endochondral ossification. The collagen fibers in lamellar bone are oriented in parallel with one another and, as
a result, lamellar bone displays anisotropy when tested
mechanically.
This means that the mechanical properties depend on
the direction of loading – similar to plywood, which is
easily cut in one plane (“with the grain”) but hard to cut
at right angles (“across the grain”).
Under polarized light microscopy, lamellar bone
appears to have a regular sheet‐like structure rather than
the irregular structure of woven bone. In cancellous
bone, the sheets of lamellar bone are oriented parallel to
the surface of individual trabeculae. In cortical bone,
lamellar bone is usually arranged in osteons, consisting
of a central vascular channel surrounded by multiple
concentric layers of lamellar bone; the osteons that comprise the osteonal complex are bounded externally by
circumferential lamellae and separated one from another
by interstitial lamellae.
The arrangement of bone within osteons provides the
cortical bone with strength and some limited flexibility
in bending and torsion.
Vascular Supply to Bone
In the long bone, there are three separate but related
c­ irculatory systems.
The nutrient artery enters the long bone through the
nutrient foramen in the diaphysis. Once within the
medullary canal, the nutrient artery divides into
ascending and descending medullary arteries that are
the primary blood supply to diaphyseal cortical bone.
Blood flow is centrifugal.
●● The metaphyseal vessels arise from geniculate arteries
that form the blood supply to periarticular tissues.
●●

1513

VetBooks.ir

1514

Section 13 Diseases of Bone and Joint

These vessels penetrate the cortex at the level of the
metaphysis. In addition, smaller proximal and distal
metaphyseal arteries derive from the ascending and
descending medullary arteries. The metaphyseal arteries are the primary blood supply to cancellous bone.
●● The periosteal capillaries supply the outer one‐third of
the cortex. These capillaries are derived from adjacent
soft tissues (muscles, fascia) that insert on the bone
(e.g., at the linea aspera on the femur). This blood
­supply is centripetal in nature.
There is considerable overlap and interplay between
the circulatory systems in bone, perhaps most evident
when bone is injured. If the medullary system is compromised, for example as a consequence of fracture or
intramedullary reaming, the periosteal blood supply will
increase in an attempt to revascularize the diaphysis.
External fixation devices and bone plates affect both the
endosteal supply and the periosteal supply. The design of
modern bone plates, with limited contact with the periosteal surface, represents an effort to try to reduce the
negative impact of plating on periosteal blood supply.
Preservation of an effective blood supply is a basic principle of surgery since it is a critical determinant of tissue
healing and subsequent function. Disturbances in blood
supply play a role in the pathophysiology of several
important orthopedic conditions, including ischemic
necrosis, osteomyelitis, delayed union, and nonunion of
fractures.

­Bone Physiology

structural support and bone turnover) and bone marrow
(important for hematopoiesis).
Bone remodeling, the process in which bone is first
removed and then replaced, is executed by the coupled
activities of bone‐resorbing osteoclasts and bone‐forming osteoblasts. Bone remodeling is temporally and spatially coupled, and proceeds through defined stages of
activation ⇒ resorption ⇒ formation. Bone remodeling
activity proceeds as a surface phenomenon on bone
­trabeculae within cancellous bone, or on the endosteal
or periosteal surfaces of cortical bone. However, cortical bone remodeling also occurs through osteonal
(Haversian) remodeling that is carried out by a complex
and unique structure, the basic multicellular unit (BMU),
that consists of a cutting cone of osteoclasts in front and
a closing cone of osteoblasts at the rear. The BMU moves
through bone over a period of several months, removing
damaged or unnecessary bone and replacing it as dictated by local mechanical and/or biologic stimuli. The
removal of damaged bone is critical to the replacement
of bone that has been microfractured, for example as a
result of chronic overload (as may be seen in elite human,
canine or equine athletes in training).
In the healthy adult animal, bone formation and
resorption (i.e., overall remodeling) are balanced.
However, imbalances in remodeling occur with aging.
The most important example of remodeling imbalance
is seen in postmenopausal osteoporosis in women,
in which loss of estrogen results in a relative increase in
bone resorption, reduced bone mass, and an increased
risk of “fragility” fracture.

Bone Modeling and Bone Remodeling

What Controls Bone Remodeling?

Bone remains a dynamic structure throughout life. This
is critical for both the maintenance of skeletal strength
and the continued role of bone as a mineral reservoir.
Mineral sequestered within the bone matrix can be
mobilized rapidly in response to calcitropic hormones
such as parathyroid hormone, vitamin D3, and calcitonin
that respond to, and modulate, circulating calcium
concentration.
Bone modeling is the process through which changes
in bone shape occur. In modeling, bone formation and
bone resorption can occur at different surfaces, resulting
in shape changes. For example, radial growth of a long
bone is achieved through new bone deposition at the
periosteal surface. If there was not concurrent removal
of bone from the endosteal surface, the net result would
be a bone with a very thick cortex and a very narrow
medullary canal. Removal of bone from the endosteum
leads to expansion of the medullary canal and preservation of a space for trabecular bone (important for both

The last 15 years have seen an explosion in what is known
about osteoclast biology, driven in large part by the quest
for greater understanding of disease states caused by
dysregulated osteoclast activity. The major clinical and
research emphasis has been on postmenopausal osteoporosis in women. Although the role of estrogen
­deficiency has long been recognized, we now know that
local paracrine factors play a critical role in driving the
excessive bone resorption that characterizes this disease.
At a cellular and molecular level, the control of bone
resorption depends on the availability of osteoclastic
precursor cells, local levels of macrophage colony‐stimulating factors (M‐CSF) and the activities of the receptor
activator of NF‐kappa B (RANK), its ligand (RANK
ligand, or RANKL) and its decoy receptor, osteoprotegerin (OPG). These interactions are illustrated in
