A number of drug therapies have now been developed
for modulating osteoclastic activity. The most widely
used antiresorptive agents are bisphosphonates such as
pamidronate, clodronate, alendronate, and zoledronate.
These compounds, which bind to mineral within the
bone matrix, are released when mineral is resorbed by
osteoclastic activity. Direct exposure of the osteoclast to
high levels of these drugs leads to osteoclast apoptosis
and a decrease in bone resorptive activity. Although
­initially introduced for osteoporosis, bisphosphonates
are now widely used in the management of patients with
other forms of pathologic bone resorption, including
hypercalcemia of malignancy (e.g., with anal sac adenocarcinoma), primary bone cancer (e.g., osteosarcoma,
feline oral squamous cell carcinoma) or secondary
bone metastases (e.g., from mammary or prostatic
carcinoma).
An alternative approach to controlling osteoclastic
activity involves targeting the RANK‐RANKL pathway
by administration of exogenous OPG or RANK‐Fc
­antibodies that serve as competitive antagonists for the
RANK receptor.
Decreases in normal bone resorptive activity are also
not without consequence. The most extreme example of
this can be seen in patients with osteopetrosis, a congenital disease in which there is failure of osteoclast formation or functionality. The classic clinical features of
bone fragility, osteoarthritis, and marrow failure can all
be explained by failures of osteoclastic resorption,
including an inability to remodel and expand the medullary canal (and an absence of space for hematopoiesis),
failure to remodel cortical and trabecular bone (leading
to increased bone mineral density) and failure to resorb

and replace damaged bone (leading to bone fragility
­secondary to bone fatigue failure).
Since net bone mass is sensitive to changes in both
­formation and resorption, attention has also been paid to
the role of anabolic factors that modulate skeletal activity. In the context of long bone growth, it has been shown
that growth hormone is capable of enhancing longitudinal bone growth in the immature skeleton. In the adult
animal, preclinical studies have confirmed the anabolic
potential of both exogenous parathyroid hormone (PTH)
and bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs). Intermittent
(daily) treatment with recombinant or synthetic forms of
human PTH is effective in enhancing overall bone mass
and accelerating bone repair after fracture. Bone morphogenetic proteins, including BMP‐2 and BMP‐7, have
been studied extensively in dogs and BMP‐2 is now available commercially as a potential treatment to accelerate
or enhance fracture healing.
Effects of Mechanical Loading on Bone
Julius Wolff (1836–1902) was a German surgeon who
first identified the relationship between mechanical
forces and bone structure. He likened the arrangement
of trabecular bone in the neck of the femur to the
arrangement of supports in a crane, with the trabeculae
being oriented to best resist the forces to which the
­femoral neck was being exposed. Although originally
published in German in 1892, Wolff ’s law can be summarized thus: “Bone changes its structure according to
the mechanical loads to which it is exposed.”
Once the adult skeleton has formed, it continues to
adapt to the prevailing mechanical environment. Graphic
evidence of the importance of mechanical loading
in driving the change in bone shape and bone mass
(bone modeling) comes from professional tennis players

1515

VetBooks.ir

1516

Section 13 Diseases of Bone and Joint

(who develop significant increases in bone mass in their
dominant forearm) or astronauts (who lose significant
bone mass after even a few weeks in the microgravity of
space). Practical examples of modeling in the context of
veterinary orthopedics include the remodeling of fracture callus, functional adaptation of the metacarpal,
metatarsal and central tarsal bones of racing greyhounds,
bone loss following limb disuse, the development of
stress fractures secondary to accelerated bone remodeling in racing thoroughbreds, and “stress shielding”
around orthopedic implants.

­Bone Pathophysiology
Bone Response to Injury
The basic biology of bone’s response to trauma has been
a subject of intense investigation over the years, particularly within the context of understanding what happens
after bone fractures. The fundamental response of bone
to trauma is similar to that seen in other tissues, and
includes cellular recruitment, differentiation, and formation of an appropriate replacement tissue. In the context
of normal bone healing after fracture, three overlapping
stages are recognized: the inflammatory stage, the repair
phase, and the remodeling phase.
Inflammatory Phase

Significant trauma, such as fracture, inevitably result in
disruptions to the medullary blood supply, leading to
extravasation of blood and the formation of a clot
between and around the ends of the fractured bone.
Damage to the periosteum also results in formation of
clot around the external surface of the bone. Although
mechanically incompetent, the clot acts as a rich source
of growth factors for angiogenesis and subsequent fracture healing. This last point is of critical significance
when contemplating surgery for a fracture – excessive
manipulation of the soft tissue clot results in loss of many
of the cells (and signaling molecules) that are ultimately
required for successful healing. An “open but do not
touch” approach allows the surgeon to assess the fracture
and to apply fixation methods that do not interfere with
(but instead harness) the body’s innate healing response.
This is the concept of biologic osteosynthesis.
Repair Phase

Macrophages that are brought in through the newly
forming capillary bed serve to remove tissue debris and
initiate the conversion of the clot into first granulation
tissue and then callus. Callus formation starts with the
deposition of collagen (initially types 1, 2, and 3) by
fibroblasts. At the same time, mesenchymal cells that

were brought into the area during the inflammatory
response differentiate into chondrocytes and deposit a
cartilage framework that is subsequently mineralized.
It should be noted that the progressive transition from
clot ⇒ granulation tissue ⇒ soft callus ⇒ hard callus
recapitulates the process of endochondral bone formation that occurs during normal bone formation.
Remodeling Phase

The final stage of fracture healing involves the gradual
incorporation of the relatively disorganized hard callus
into the skeleton. This is the longest phase of fracture
healing. Remodeling of the callus is governed by Wolff ’s
law and, ultimately, the process of bone remodeling
results in a structure that is best able to resist the
mechanical forces to which it is subjected.
Thermal Injury to Bone
Bone is damaged by temperatures exceeding 47 °C for
more than one minute. The most common scenarios for
thermal injury to bone occur during orthopedic surgery
and are related to the use of power tools to cut and shape
bone, or the bone cement that is used to secure total
joint replacement implants.
Power tools such as saws, drills, and reamers are used
every day in orthopedic surgery. In the operating room,
every effort is made to reduce the risk of thermal injury.
This involves the use of sharp drills or saw blades (old,
dull blades or drill bits will mill bone and generate heat);
low‐speed cutting and drilling whenever possible; short
rather than sustained bursts of drilling or sawing; and
copious saline lavage, which serves both to cool the tissue and to remove bone debris that can otherwise clog
up blades and drill flutes.
The standard bone cement used in orthopedic surgery
is acrylic cement based on polymethylmethacrylate (as
used in Plexiglas). Bone cement is used to secure joint
replacement implants into bone. Cement is typically
injected in a liquid state but then hardens through a
chemical process of polymerization that is exothermic.
Since bone cement is usually placed immediately adjacent to cortical or trabecular bone, there is potential for
heat injury to the constituent bone cells, as well as to the
vascular supply to the endosteum. Data from preclinical
animal models indicate that this thermal injury is typically reversible. However, care should be taken to use the
minimum volume of cement necessary and to ensure
protection of adjacent neurovascular structures.
Vascular Injury to Bone
Vascular trauma to bone may occur secondary to a
fracture or as an unwanted consequence of surgical
­

VetBooks.ir

171 Skeletal Development and Homeostasis

interventions. Traumatic disruptions during fracture
typically involve significant injury to the blood supply on
both endosteal and periosteal surfaces. Vascular injury
secondary to surgical procedures may affect the entire
bone (if, for example, a nutrient vessel is cut by accident)
or it may preferentially affect one region (for example,
damage to the outer surface of the bone or to the adjacent soft tissues has a greater effect of periosteal blood
supply, while introduction of an intramedullary pin or
bone cement into the medullary cavity will selectively
damage the endosteal blood supply). Application of a
plate to the surface of the bone also may damage the
­ eriosteal supply.
p
In most cases, regional changes in blood flow will
be able to restore effective vascularity to the bone.
For example, loss of periosteal blood supply results in an
increase in centrifugal blood flow through the cortex,
while endosteal damage results in increased centripetal
blood flow from the periosteal vascular network.
Periosteal Trauma
Periosteal trauma occurs either as a consequence of fracture, secondary to surgical manipulation of the bone, or
as a consequence of bone pathologies such as infection
or neoplasia. Data from preclinical animal models have
shown that traumatic loss of periosteum has the potential to result in overall bone loss and an increased risk of
fragility in the affected bone. At least two factors appear
to be involved in this response. First, loss of periosteal
bone‐forming cells will lead to a decreased ability to
make new bone at the periosteal surface. Second, loss of
the vascular supply to the periosteum results in transient
derangements in bone blood flow. In healthy animals,
the extent of periosteal trauma would have to be significant to cause a whole‐bone effect. However, if the bone is
otherwise compromised by disease, periosteal damage
may result in further bone loss and an increased risk of
catastrophic bone failure.
Reactive New Bone Formation
Reactive new bone is a relatively common radiographic
finding and a not uncommon confounding factor in bone
biopsies taken from sites of bone pathology. While the
underlying process of forming new bone represents a
biologically conserved and logical response to bone
trauma, the response is not specific to any one initiating
cause, making it extremely hard for radiologists or bone
pathologists to ascribe a specific underlying disease
entity as the cause of the new bone formation. Some
information may be gleaned from the location of the new
bone, with both endosteal and periosteal surfaces being
potential sources of reactive new bone formation.

At the periosteal surface, fracture, infection, and
­neoplasia are the most common causes of a reactive
­periosteal new bone formation (“periosteal response”).
The role of periosteal callus in fracture healing will be
discussed shortly. In the context of bone infection and
neoplasia, situations in which the periosteum can be
underrun by inflammatory or neoplastic infiltrates, the
typical response is for new bone formation. The mechanisms responsible for this are not well understood but
likely relate to the ability of periosteum to react to
increased local mechanical deformation by depositing
new bone. There are significant numbers of nociceptors
at the periosteal surface, and periosteal involvement in
neoplasia and infection tends to be extremely painful.
Radiographically, the observation of focal to local periosteal new bone is highly suggestive of aggressive bone
conditions such as neoplasia or osteomyelitis.
With neoplasia, disruption and lifting of the periosteum proceed too rapidly for the bone to mineralize in
the normal layered fashion, and the net result is that only
the edge of the lifted periosteum ossifies. Radiographically,
the mineralized flap of periosteum is described as
Codman’s triangle.
At the endosteal surface, reactive new bone formation
is seen predominantly in fracture healing and also as a
component of canine panosteitis, which will be discussed
later.
Pathologic Bone Resorption
Excessive and dysregulated activation of bone resorption
is a hallmark of several important developmental, inflammatory, infectious and neoplastic disorders in animals,
including periodontal disease, osteomyelitis, multiple
myeloma, and aseptic or septic loosening of total joint
replacement implants. A complete description of the
pathobiology of these conditions is outside the scope of
this short discussion, but it is important to note that the
fundamental biologic mechanisms through which bone
is removed are the same as are seen in normal (physiologic) bone remodeling. The major differences lie in the
nature of the inciting cause; for implant‐related bone
resorption (osteolysis), it is the inflammatory response
to metallic and polymeric debris liberated from the surfaces of the implant that stimulates the inflammatory
cascade. In metastatic tumors that target bone, proinflammatory cytokines released from the tumor appear
to modulate the osteoclastic response immediately
­adjacent to the tumor deposits.
Irrespective of the inciting cause, strategies for managing pathologic bone resorption focus on eliminating the
underlying inciting cause with appropriate medical therapy (antibiotics, chemotherapy) or surgical intervention
(to remove a loose or infected implant). The use of oral

1517

VetBooks.ir

1518

Section 13 Diseases of Bone and Joint

or injectable bisphosphonates also represents a logical
approach to suppressing ongoing bone loss in these
patients.
Bone Healing after Fracture
The goal of fracture fixation is to restore structure and
function to the skeleton. Fracture healing is influenced
by a wide array of factors, including the animal’s age,
location and type of fracture, stability of the fragments,
extent of soft tissue and vascular compromise, and presence or absence of necrotic and/or infected tissues.
Mechanical stability is known to be of paramount importance in determining the nature, time course, and efficiency of the fracture healing response. Under stable
conditions, the fracture will unite via direct (primary)
bone healing, in which new bone forms a direct bridge
across the fracture plane. Under unstable conditions, a
soft tissue callus first forms and it is this callus that is
then progressively mineralized in a process known as
indirect (secondary) fracture healing.
Role of Mechanical Factors in Fracture Healing

Fractures that are anatomically reconstructed and maintained under stable conditions through the use of internal fixation heal without significant callus. However,
even under conditions of ideal bone fragment alignment,
it is common to find microscopic discontinuities between
the ends of the fragments. The extent of the gap dictates
the nature of the reparative response that will predominate. In very small gaps, woven bone forms and continuity is restored between the ends of the bone. If the gap is
larger than ~1 mm, the gap will fill in with soft callus. As
long as the fracture site remains stable, the callus will
successfully mineralize and remodel. In fact, controlled
amounts of micromotion have been shown to accelerate
bone repair, a finding that has been used to great benefit
in distraction osteogenesis, a procedure in which controlled axial distraction of a small bone fragment is used
to stimulate and maintain new bone formation. Over
time, the regenerated bone formed in this way is capable
of filling in a significant defect in the original bone.
Distraction osteogenesis can be useful in the management of both large bone defects (e.g., secondary to
trauma or neoplasia) and the correction of angular limb
deformities.
In the presence of mechanical instability, either with
comminuted fractures or with fractures that are unstable
despite attempts at fixation, fracture healing is characterized by the formation of abundant callus that unites
the bone fragments. The biologic processes that underlie
the formation of callus have been described previously.
The mechanical properties of the callus similarly evolve
as the callus matures from a fibrous connective tissue,

through a cartilaginous intermediate and finally to bone.
The total area (volume) of the callus depends on (i) the
degree of displacement of the fragments and (ii) the
extent of mechanical instability at the site of fracture.
Once the mechanical properties of the callus are sufficient to minimize interfragmentary strain (2% is often
cited as the threshold for new bone formation), primary
bone repair can occur and the callus will be remodeled to
restore the medullary cavity and cortical profile. It should
be noted that the presence of external callus leads to a
rapid increase in the mechanical integrity of the bone, so
that bone that heals with abundant callus is able to withstand physiologic forces within a relatively short period
of time after fracture.
Other Factors that Influence Bone Healing
Certainly, any factor that compromises the ability of
­callus to form or to differentiate would be expected to
delay or prevent fracture healing. In addition to mechanical instability due to incomplete reduction or stabilization, other factors that can lead to delayed or nonunion
after fracture include vascular compromise, premature
or excessive weight bearing after surgery (hence the
importance of controlling activity levels after surgery),
infection, radiation therapy, systemic illness, or concurrent treatment with prolonged courses of drugs such as
corticosteroids. In humans, smoking is a critically important determinant of wound healing in general and a
major risk factor for complications following fracture
repair. The potential negative effects of nonsteroidal
antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) on bone healing have
been the subject of significant research efforts in humans
but data in animals are less clear, and there does not
appear to be any objective evidence that short‐term
treatment with NSAIDs has a significant effect on bone
healing after trauma or surgery.

­Complications with Fracture Healing –
Delayed Union, Malunion, and Nonunion
Although the majority of straightforward fractures will
go on to heal (unite) without complication, a subset of
patients will experience problems with healing. The primary causes of suboptimal fracture healing have been
described in the preceding sections, and include incomplete reduction of the fracture, uncontrolled or excessive
weight bearing, vascular compromise, infection, and
concurrent medical disease or therapy. Three general
categories of abnormal fracture healing have been
recognized: delayed union, malunion, and nonunion.
­
The diagnosis of disturbed fracture healing is made on

VetBooks.ir

171 Skeletal Development and Homeostasis

the basis of careful physical examination and radiographic findings.
Delayed union is probably the most challenging to
diagnose definitively since it represents healing that
occurs at a slower rate than would be expected for a
given fracture. As mentioned earlier, the rate and completeness of healing are sensitive to a range of variables,
and as a result there can be significant variations in how
fast a given fracture heals. Most delayed unions can be
managed conservatively, without the need for additional
surgical intervention.
Malunions are fractures that have gone on to clinical
union but with abnormalities in the alignment of the
fragments. In the middiaphysis, this may manifest as
rotational abnormalities or angulation between the
proximal and distal ends of the bone. At the articular
surface, healing without complete restoration of

the articular surface would be considered a malunion.
The consequences of malunion depend on both severity
and location; minor angular malalignment may be clinically asymptomatic, while discontinuities or irregularities in the articular surface can predispose to the
development of posttraumatic osteoarthritis.
Nonunion represents the most extreme disturbance in
normal fracture healing. The extent and nature of the
healing response can be quite variable, but nonunions can
broadly be classified into viable nonunions, in which the
tissues are still capable of biologic activity, and nonviable
nonunions that are devoid of biologic activity. The management of these fractures can be complex and lies outside the scope of this discussion, but often involves
aggressive surgical intervention. In select cases, there may
also be a role for local (e.g., BMP) or systemic (e.g., PTH)
anabolic drug therapies to boost new bone formation.

Metabolic Bone Diseases
Keren E. Dittmer, PhD, BVSc, DACVP
School of Veterinary Science, Massey University, Palmerston North, New Zealand

Metabolic bone diseases include osteoporosis, rickets
and osteomalacia, fibrous osteodystrophy (secondary
hyperparathyroidism), and scurvy (vitamin C deficiency).
Fibrous osteodystrophy is an important skeletal disease
of young dogs and cats. On the other hand, rickets and
osteomalacia are relatively rare. While osteoporosis is
the most common metabolic bone disease of humans, it
is seldom diagnosed in small animals, possibly due to the
lack of sensitive techniques to reliably diagnose the dis­
ease. Dogs and cats have the hepatic microsomal enzyme
L‐gulonolactone oxidase and can synthesize vitamin C
(ascorbic acid), therefore scurvy does not occur in these
species. The metabolic bone diseases covered in this
chapter include fibrous osteodystrophy, rickets and oste­
omalacia, with a brief discussion of osteoporosis.

­Calcium and Phosphorus Physiology
In order to truly understand the pathophysiology of
the metabolic bone diseases, good knowledge of nor­
mal calcium and phosphorus metabolism is required.
Therefore a brief description of calcium and phosphorus
homeostasis will be included here.
The hormones vitamin D, parathyroid hormone
(PTH), calcitonin, and fibroblast growth factor 23
(FGF23) are essential for controlling plasma calcium and
phosphorus concentrations. These hormones facilitate
calcium and phosphorus transportation in three main
organs: the kidney, intestine, and bone.
Calcium transport is predominantly under the control
of PTH and 1,25‐dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25(OH)2D3).
Parathyroid hormone is a small peptide secreted by the
parathyroid gland when the calcium‐sensing receptors
on chief cells detect low plasma calcium concentrations.
PTH binds to the PTH receptor 1 in renal tubules, result­
ing in activation of adenylate cyclase and phospholipase

C cell pathways, ultimately leading to opening of calcium
channels (such as transient receptor vanilloid potential 5,
TRPV5), and increased resorption of calcium from the
renal filtrate. Increased plasma phosphorus concentra­
tions may also lead to increased PTH secretion by an
unknown mechanism. Increased PTH leads to increased
breakdown of phosphate channels (Na+‐Pi ATPase
pump, NPT2), resulting in decreased resorption of
­phosphorus from the renal filtrate.
The actions of PTH on bone are dual and antagonistic.
Secretion of PTH in response to low plasma ionized cal­
cium leads to increased expression of receptor activator
of NF‐kB ligand (RANKL) by osteoblasts. When RANKL
binds to the RANK receptor on osteoclast precursors, it
leads to differentiation and maturation of these cells into
mature osteoclasts. At the same time, PTH leads to
decreased expression of osteoprotegerin (OPG/OCIF), a
decoy receptor that prevents binding of RANKL to
RANK. Increased production of osteoclasts ultimately
results in increased osteoclastic bone resorption and
release of calcium and phosphorus from bone matrix
into blood. The anabolic actions of PTH are used in the
treatment of osteoporosis in humans. Intermittent low‐
dose treatment with PTH analogs results in increased
differentiation and production of osteoblasts, and there­
fore increased bone formation.
Low plasma calcium concentration and PTH activate
the 1‐alpha‐hydroxylase enzyme in the kidney, resulting
in increased production of 1,25(OH)2D3. Active vitamin
D (1,25(OH)2D3) binds to the vitamin D receptor in the
nucleus of intestinal epithelial cells and renal tubular
­epithelial cells, leading to increased production of vita­
min D‐responsive proteins, such as calcium channels
(TRPV5, 6 and Na+/Ca2+ exchanger), phosphate chan­
nels (NPT2a, 2b, 2c), and calcium‐binding proteins
(­calbindin‐D9k and D28k). Increased production of these
proteins results in increased absorption of calcium and

Clinical Small Animal Internal Medicine Volume II, First Edition. Edited by David S. Bruyette.
© 2020 John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Published 2020 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc.
Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/bruyette/clinical

VetBooks.ir

1522

Section 13 Diseases of Bone and Joint

phosphorus from the renal tubules and intestinal tract.
Active vitamin D also has a negative feedback effect
on its own production. In the parathyroid gland,
1,25(OH)2D3 directly inhibits PTH production and
increases the sensitivity of the calcium‐sensing
­receptors to calcium, thereby acting to control PTH
secretion.
Like PTH, vitamin D may also have dual and antago­
nistic effects in bone. When plasma blood calcium
­concentrations decline, 1,25(OH)2D3 leads to increased
bone resorption by upregulating RANKL production
and inhibiting OPG production, likely in association
with PTH. In addition, 1,25(OH)2D3 upregulates inhibi­
tors of bone mineralization. However, 1,25(OH)2D3
can be produced locally in bone, by chondrocytes, osteo­
blasts, osteocytes and osteoclasts, where it leads to
increased bone formation and mineralization.
Calcitonin is the antagonistic hormone to vitamin D
and PTH and is released in response to increased plasma
ionized calcium concentrations. It inhibits osteoclast
motility and leads to retraction of osteoclasts from bone,
resulting in decreased bone resorption and therefore
decreased release of calcium and phosphorus into the
blood.
Traditionally, it was thought that the control of plasma
phosphorus concentrations was indirect, as a result of
the tighter control of calcium. However, a suite of com­
pounds, known as phosphatonins, are critically involved
in phosphorus control, the most important of which is
FGF23. Increased plasma phosphorus concentrations
and increased 1,25(OH)2D3 may both independently
increase FGF23 production by osteocytes in bone. The
main target organ for FGF23 action is the kidney. FGF23,
together with its co‐factor klotho, downregulates the
NPT2a and 2c phosphorus channels in the kidney, lead­
ing to decreased resorption of phosphorus from the
renal tubules. FGF23 also acts on the parathyroid gland
to decrease secretion of PTH. FGF23 in combination
with the decrease in PTH leads to inhibition of the renal
1‐alpha‐hydroxylase enzyme decreasing production of
active vitamin D. At the same time, there is activation
of the enzyme (24‐hydroxylase) that breaks down
active vitamin D, ultimately resulting in decreased
1,25(OH)2D3.

­Fibrous Osteodystrophy
Fibrous osteodystrophy (FOD) is a skeletal disease char­
acterized by the replacement of bone with a combination
of fibrous tissue and poorly mineralized woven bone.
While the focus of this section is on nutritional hyper­
parathyroidism, primary and renal hyperparathyroidism
may cause similar skeletal lesions.

Etiology/Pathophysiology
Fibrous osteodystrophy is the skeletal consequence of
hyperparathyroidism or a chronic increase in PTH.
There are four main causes of hyperparathyroidism.
Primary hyperparathyroidism – due to a functional
tumor of the parathyroid gland, resulting in autono­
mous secretion of PTH. The increased PTH leads to
hypercalcemia and mineralization of soft tissues, and
in long‐standing cases clinical FOD. This will be dis­
cussed in the endocrine section. A probable hereditary
primary hyperparathyroidism has been reported in a
litter of German shepherd puppies.
●● Renal hyperparathyroidism – due to chronic kidney
disease. While renal hyperparathyroidism is common
in animals with chronic kidney disease, clinical signs
due to skeletal changes are usually minimal in adult
animals. Nonetheless, recent studies have shown that
dogs and cats with chronic kidney disease have
decreased bone mineral density and increased bone
porosity. Young rapidly growing animals with familial
renal disease may develop severe skeletal lesions.
●● Nutritional hyperparathyroidism – due to a decreased
calcium to phosphorus ratio in the diet. This is a com­
mon condition of young rapidly growing cats and dogs
fed poorly balanced diets post weaning.
●● Pseudohyperparathyroidism
or hypercalcaemia of
malignancy – due to a tumor that produces calcitropic
hormones. Parathyroid hormone‐related peptide
(PTHrp) is the best characterized of these calcitropic
hormones and has the same effect as PTH. Tumors
that most commonly produce PTHrp are lymphoma
and apocrine gland adenocarcinoma of anal sac origin.
Occasionally, other carcinomas, malignant melanoma,
and other tumors may produce other factors that cause
hypercalcaemia, such as 1,25(OH)2D3, prostaglandins,
and various cytokines (TGF‐beta, IL‐1‐beta). Skeletal
changes are mild and difficult to detect; clinical signs
are the result of hypercalcemia.
●●

Signalment
Nutritional hyperparathyroidism is typically a disease of
rapidly growing young animals after weaning. A case of
nutritional hyperparathyroidism in an adult dog has
been reported; the Rottweiler was on a home‐made diet
due to the diagnosis a year previously of lymphocytic‐
plasmacytic enterocolitis and lymphangiectasia.
History and Clinical Signs
Nutritional FOD occurs when the diet contains excessive
phosphorus or deficient calcium. In actual practice,
most commonly it is due to a combination of decreased

VetBooks.ir

172 Metabolic Bone Diseases

calcium and increased phosphorus in the diet. The most
frequent cause of nutritional FOD is an all‐meat diet.
The ideal Ca:P ratio of a diet is 1:1. Meat and liver have
calcium to phosphorus ratios of 1:20 and 1:50 respec­
tively, and a diet based solely on these components can
lead to clinical signs of FOD within four weeks.
Animals with nutritional hyperparathyroidism most
commonly present with an ill‐defined lameness, disincli­
nation to move, and a failure to thrive. Some animals
may have angular limb deformities. In more severe cases,
pathologic fractures may occur with only mild trauma.
Resorption of alveolar bone in the mandible and maxilla
may lead to loosening of teeth. A few animals may
develop vertebral compression fractures, which in some
cases may lead to neurologic signs. While another term
for fibrous osteodystrophy is rubber jaw, this is usually
only seen in severe prolonged cases, and is more com­
mon in young animals with familial renal disease and
renal secondary hyperparathyroidism, rather than nutri­
tional hyperparathyroidism.
Diagnosis
Biochemistry

Animals with nutritional fibrous osteodystrophy have
low to low‐normal plasma total and ionized calcium
concentrations. The calcium deficiency in the diet
stimulates PTH release, which subsequently leads to
­
osteoclastic resorption of calcium from bone, thereby
maintaining plasma calcium concentration to the detri­
ment of bone mineral content. If the dietary deficiency of
calcium is severe or the amount of calcium released from
the bones is inadequate then the dog or cat will have
hypocalcemia.
The increased PTH concentration leads to increased
excretion of phosphorus from the kidney, and so results
in an increase in the fractional excretion of phosphorus.
Depending on the balance of dietary intake to renal
excretion, plasma phosphorus concentrations may be
low, normal or increased.
Serum alkaline phosphatase concentrations are
increased due to increased bone remodeling but, along
with the phosphorus concentration, need to be inter­
preted with caution as both may be increased in younger
animals due to growth.
Plasma intact PTH concentration will be increased but
there are a number of cautions to be considered when
interpreting plasma PTH concentrations. The first is
­collection of the sample. PTH is highly susceptible to
proteolysis, so serum or plasma should be separated
from red cells immediately (samples should be at room
temperature for less than two hours) and tested directly,
refrigerated for no more than 24 hours or stored frozen
at –20 °C. Samples should be shipped chilled/frozen.

Serum separator tubes should not be used as they lead
to decreased PTH concentrations. In addition, visible
hemolysis of the sample interferes with the assay.
Second, there are several different assays available for
measuring PTH, including radioimmunoassays (RIA/
ERMA) and enzyme immunoassays (EIA/ELISA). In
addition, assays are available for whole PTH (W‐PTH),
intact PTH, N‐terminal fragment of PTH, and C‐terminal
fragment of PTH. PTH undergoes proteolysis in the
liver, blood, and other organs, forming N‐terminal and
C‐terminal fragments. The N‐terminal PTH fragment
cannot bind to the PTH receptor and so does not elicit
the classic response to PTH; it is in fact thought to inhibit
PTH action. N‐terminal PTH fragments are increased in
chronic renal failure.
The W‐PTH assay is a third‐generation PTH assay
that is specific for whole 1‐84 PTH, while the I‐PTH is a
second‐generation assay that, in addition to measuring
1‐84 PTH, also measures large N‐terminal PTH frag­
ments. Human two‐site RIA/IRMAs for I‐PTH have
been validated in both cats and dogs, as has a combined
W‐PTH/I‐PTH assay. Human EIAs may not cross‐react
with canine or feline PTH. Canine‐specific I‐PTH ELISA
assays are also available. Reference ranges are assay spe­
cific and ideally should not be extrapolated from other
types/brands of assay.
The third important point is that ionized calcium, total
calcium, and phosphorus concentrations should be
measured on the same sample as PTH. These analytes
are essential for the interpretation of the plasma PTH
concentration.
Radiography

The predominant change seen on radiography is gener­
alized osteopenia of all bones. It may be most obvious in
those bones with a greater proportion of cancellous bone
which is more readily resorbed, such as the vertebrae.
The mandible may show a marked reduction in bone
density, particularly the alveolar bone around the teeth
(Figure 172.1). There may be evidence of pathologic frac­
tures (see Figure 172.1), such as compression fractures in
the vertebrae and infractions in the long bones. In more
severe cases, there may be complete fracture of the long
bones. The growth plates are normal in animals with
fibrous osteodystrophy, but there may be increased radi­
oopacity in the primary spongiosa directly beneath the
growth plate (see Figure 172.1). The cortices appear
thinner and more porous. The limbs may show angular
deformities, and lordosis of the spine can be present.
New technology such as dual‐energy X‐ray absorpti­
ometry (DEXA/DXA) and computed tomography (CT)
give a more accurate assessment of bone mineral density
than plain radiographs. Bone mineral density must be
decreased by more than 30% before it is detected on

­Rickets and Osteomalacia
Rickets is a disease of young animals and is due to a
­failure of mineralization of osteoid and cartilage at the
provisional zone of calcification in the growth plate.
Osteomalacia is essentially the same condition but in
adult animals. Since adult animals do not have growth
plates, in osteomalacia only new osteoid laid down
during the normal remodeling process is poorly
­
­mineralized. Both conditions are rare in dogs and cats.
Etiology/Pathophysiology
Figure 172.1 Radiograph from 12‐week‐old greyhound puppy
with fibrous osteodystrophy. (a) Tibia/fibula showing osteopenia,
with normal growth plate width, sclerosis of the metaphysis
beneath the physis, and a folding fracture. (b) Mandible showing
loss of alveolar bone surrounding the teeth. Source: Courtesy of
K.G. Thompson.

plain radiographs. DEXA and CT may be useful for
­monitoring the success of treatment. In one study, bone
mineral density, as measured by both DEXA and CT,
showed substantial improvement once the diet had
been corrected.
Therapy
Animals with nutritional FOD should be fed a commer­
cial balanced diet with the recommended 1:1 ratio of
Ca:P. Affected animals may also benefit from receiving
additional calcium, enough to raise the total Ca:P ratio of
the diet to 2:1. The additional calcium may be in lactate,
carbonate or gluconate forms and should be continued
for two months, after which time the animal can be
maintained on a commercial balanced diet. Animals
with microfractures or infractions may require pain
relief. An important component of treatment is confin­
ing affected animals for the first 3–4 weeks of treatment
in order to decrease the risk of further pathologic
fractures.
Prognosis
With correction of the diet, and provided catastrophic
fracture does not occur, the prognosis for a return to
normality is excellent. With time and the normal

Rickets and osteomalacia are due to either dietary vita­
min D deficiency or phosphorus deficiency. Phosphorus
deficiency is very rare in dogs and cats, and as described
in the FOD section, phosphorus excess is far more
common.
Dogs and cats are unusual in mammalian species in that
they do not appear to produce vitamin D in the skin under
the influence of ultraviolet light. In most animals, ultravio­
let B light results in the conversion of 7‐dehydrocholes­
terol, in keratinocytes and the dermis, to previtamin D3
which then undergoes thermal isomerization to vitamin
D3. However, cats and dogs have been shown to have only
10% of the 7‐dehydrocholesterol in their skin that rats do,
and cat skin contains a 7‐dehydrocholesterol‐delta7‐
reductase which breaks down 7‐dehydrocholesterol.
Therefore, irradiation of cat and dog skin with ultraviolet
light does not cause an increase in plasma vitamin D
­concentration. Cats and dogs are, for that reason, reliant
on their diet for their vitamin D requirements. However,
there are few reports of naturally occurring rickets in dogs
and cats in the literature, likely due to the widespread
feeding of commercial pet food. In addition, the most
common inappropriate diet fed to puppies and kittens is
meat and offal, which contain high levels of phosphorus
and adequate vitamin D.
Vitamin D deficiency leads to decreased absorption
of calcium and phosphorus from the intestine and
decreased reabsorption of calcium and phosphorus
from the kidney, leading to hypocalcemia and
hypophosphatemia. Animals that have rickets due to
vitamin D deficiency will often have concurrent FOD
due to hypocalcemia. Decreased plasma ionized cal­
cium concentration leads to increased PTH secretion
and therefore increased osteoclastic resorption of bone
and FOD.

VetBooks.ir

172 Metabolic Bone Diseases

In humans, rickets and osteomalacia are described in
patients with gastrointestinal malabsorption disorders,
due to failure to absorb fat‐soluble vitamins such as
­vitamin D, and reduced absorption of calcium. Rickets
has been described in a 17‐week‐old male border collie
with extrahepatic biliary atresia.
Aluminium toxicity from chronic antacid administra­
tion or long‐term total parenteral nutrition may also
cause rickets and osteomalacia in humans.
Osteomalacia may occur in combination with FOD in
dogs and cats with chronic kidney disase. Hyperphos­
phatemia results in increased plasma FGF23 concentra­
tions, leading to inhibition of the renal 1‐alpha‐hydroxylase
enzyme, causing decreased production of 1,25(OH)2D3.
This combination of osteomalacia and FOD is often
termed renal osteodystrophy. As mentioned earlier,
while bone changes do occur in adult animals with
chronic kidney disease, the changes seldom result in
clinical signs.
Vitamin D also has an important role in the immune
system, and has been associated with many different dis­
eases in both humans and animals. Low serum 25OHD
concentrations in dogs have been associated with
immune‐mediated disorders, various types of cancer,
acute pancreatitis, progression of leishmania, chronic
enteropathy, chronic valvular heart disease, and poor
outcome in congestive heart failure, while in cats, low
serum 25OHD has been associated with inflammatory
bowel disease, intestinal small cell lymphoma, and myco­
bacteriosis. However, care should be taken not to overin­
terpret the role of vitamin D in these diseases. Correlation
is not causation, and randomized clinical trials are
required to determine the significance of vitamin D in
the pathogenesis of different diseases and whether
changes in serum 25OHD are primary or occur second­
ary to the disease.
Signalment
Rickets occurs in young animals and cases of rickets in
the literature have been reported in 10–14‐week‐old pup­
pies and kittens. Nutritional rickets has been reported
most commonly in greyhound litters, presumably because
these animals are more likely to be fed unusual diets.
Rickets is extremely rare in cats, and naturally occur­
ring nutritional rickets has not been reported in the
­literature. However, rickets has been induced experi­
mentally in both cats and dogs fed vitamin D‐deficient
diets.
History and Clinical Signs
As with nutritional FOD, animals with rickets usually
have a history of an unusual postweaning ration. In two

of the reported cases of rickets in the literature, puppies
were fed a diet of milk and meat. Such a diet would likely
meet the calcium and phosphorus requirements for the
animals, but not vitamin D, as the vitamin D concentra­
tion of milk is low.
A case of rickets has occurred in a 10‐week‐old
Shetland sheepdog on a commercial renal failure diet.
Such diets are designed to be low in phosphorus and
­protein in order to alleviate some of the clinical and bio­
chemical changes associated with the disease. However,
the level of phosphorus in the diet fed to this young
dog was inadequate for a growing animal, leading to
phosphorus deficiency and rickets. Similarly, osteomala­
cia has been reported in an adult dog with food allergies
fed an unbalanced elimination ration.
Affected animals present with lameness, reluctance to
walk, and a failure to grow and gain weight. Animals may
have angular limb deformities, particularly affecting the
forelimbs. Rickets most commonly affects rapidly grow­
ing physes, such as the distal radius, proximal tibia, distal
femur, and proximal humerus. The metaphyses of long
bones, particularly the distal radius, may be swollen.
Animals may have swollen costochondral junctions,
known as the rachitic rosary. Affected animals may have
pathologic fractures, and delayed eruption of teeth and
enamel hypoplasia may also be seen. In animals with
severe hypocalcemia, seizures may be the presenting
clinical sign.
Osteomalacia is reported rarely in dogs, and this may
partly be due to the subtlety of the clinical signs. The
most common clinical sign of osteomalacia in humans is
bone pain, and in older dogs this may easily be mistaken
as reluctance to move due to chronic degenerative joint
disease and not investigated further.
Diagnosis
Biochemistry

Animals with rickets due to vitamin D deficiency will
have decreased or low normal serum calcium concentra­
tion, hypophosphatemia, increased serum alkaline
­phosphatase activity, and increased plasma PTH concen­
tration. Serum vitamin D concentrations depend on the
inciting cause of the rickets. In vitamin D deficiency
­rickets, usually both serum 25OHD and 1,25(OH)2D3
concentrations are decreased. However, confusingly in
some cases, the increase in PTH as a result of hypocalce­
mia leads to increased activity of the renal 1‐alpha‐
hydroxylase and normal to increased serum 1,25(OH)2D3
concentrations. Despite this, low serum 25OHD indi­
cates there is insufficient vitamin D being obtained
from the diet.
In phosphorus deficiency rickets, animals have severe
hypophosphatemia but serum calcium and 25OHD

1525

VetBooks.ir

1526

Section 13 Diseases of Bone and Joint

­concentrations are normal. Serum 1,25(OH)2D3 concen­
trations may be normal to increased.
Radiography

The key radiographic change seen in animals with rick­
ets is widening and increased lucency of the long bones
physes (Figure 172.2). A 10‐point radiographic scoring
method for rickets based on the severity of radiographic
changes in the wrists and knees, to produce a score indi­
cating the severity of nutritional rickets, has been devel­
oped for human patients. The key features of this scoring
system include widening of the growth plate, irregularity
of the physeal–metaphyseal interface, and concavity or
cupping of the metaphysis. Other radiographic changes
may include swollen costochondral junctions, infrac­
tions and other pathologic fractures, delayed appearance
of ossification centers, curving of long bones, metaphy­
seal sclerosis, and generalized osteopenia. Stress frac­
tures and decreased bone density are seen radiographically
in osteomalacia. In humans, the presence of Looser
zones is considered consistent with osteomalacia; these
are radiolucent areas surrounded by a zone of sclerosis in
the cortex.

Radiography can only give a qualitative indication of
bone mineral density (BMD). DEXA or quantitative CT
is required for a quantitative measurement of BMD.
These techniques are also more sensitive in detecting
mild to moderate decreases in BMD, and would be useful
for monitoring response to treatment.
Therapy
Animals with nutritional rickets should be placed on a
commercial balanced diet with the recommended 1:1
Ca:P ratio and adequate levels of vitamin D. This may be
supplemented with additional calcium, phosphorus, and
vitamin D as required. Care must be taken with vitamin
D administration, as vitamin D is toxic at high doses,
leading to widespread soft tissue mineralization, so regu­
lar monitoring of serum calcium and phosphorus con­
centrations is recommended. A recent study found that
treatment with 25OHD increased serum 25OHD faster
than cholecalciferol (vitamin D) treatment, although
sample numbers were small and a safe dosage was not
determined. Other vitamin D metabolite options
include dihydrotachysterol, calcitriol (1,25(OH)2D3), and
alfacalcidol.
Vitamin D2 or ergocalciferol may be used but large
doses are required initially, and its long half‐life means
that if an animal becomes hypercalcemic it takes up to
four weeks for the effects of ergocholecalciferol to wane.
Therefore, it is not considered an ideal treatment for
rickets in dogs and cats.
Dogs and cats with rickets will benefit from 3–4 weeks
of confinement in order to prevent further stress and
microfractures. Pain relief for those with microfractures
may be helpful.
Prognosis
The prognosis for dogs and cats with nutritional rickets
for return to normality is good, providing catastrophic
fracture does not occur and the predisposing reason
(such as malabsorption, total parenteral nutrition) is
removed. Once the poorly mineralized bone laid down
during the period of dietary deficiency is replaced
­during remodeling, the bones will return to normal
strength.

Inherited Rickets
Inherited forms of rickets resulting from inborn errors in
metabolism have been diagnosed in both cats and dogs.
There is confusion in the literature with regard to articles
on inherited rickets; a number of reported cases are
more consistent with a diagnosis of nutritional FOD
than inherited rickets. Care should be taken in making a

VetBooks.ir

172 Metabolic Bone Diseases

diagnosis of inherited rickets, and the diagnosis should
be confirmed with genetic testing.
There are three main groups of inherited rickets.
Vitamin D‐Dependent Rickets Type I

An autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in
the CYP27B1 (1‐alpha‐hydroxylase) gene that catalyzes
the conversion of 25OHD to 1,25(OH)2D3. Affected ani­
mals have clinical signs of rickets, hypocalcemia,
hypophosphatemia, very high serum 25OHD concentra­
tions, and low serum 1,25(OH)2D3 concentrations. One
unconfirmed case has been reported in a St Bernard dog,
and a number of cases reported in cats; however, only
two have reported causative mutations in the CYP27B1
gene. Long‐term treatment with 1,25(OH)2D3 (calcitriol)
is successful.
Hereditary Vitamin D‐Resistant Rickets (Vitamin
D‐Dependent Rickets Type II)

An autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in
the vitamin D receptor (VDR) gene. In order to produce
its calcemic effects, 1,25(OH)2D3 must bind to the VDR‐
retinoid X receptor which then binds to vitamin D
response elements in the promoter region of the vitamin
D‐responsive gene. Animals with mutations in the VDR
are severely hypocalcemic and hypophosphatemic and
have serum 1,25(OH)2D3 concentrations 5–20 times
greater than normal. Approximately 70–80% of human
cases also have partial to total alopecia that may be obvi­
ous at birth or develop over the first few months of life.
Confirmed cases have been diagnosed in a Pomeranian
dog (see Figure 172.2) and a cat. A small number of
human patients have been successfully treated with large
doses of 1,25(OH)2D3, but for most patients vitamin D
treatment is not successful. Long‐term intravenous cal­
cium infusion has been the most successful treatment
option for patients that did not respond to high doses of
1,25(OH)2D3.
Hypophosphatemic Rickets

This form may have X‐linked, autosomal dominant or
autosomal recessive inheritance. Mutations have been
found in the FGF23, dentin matrix protein 1 (DMP1),
and ectonucleotide pyrophosphatase/phosphodiesterase
1 (ENPP1) genes. Whichever gene is affected, the patho­
genesis behind the disease involves increased plasma
FGF23 concentration resulting in renal wasting of
­phosphate and severe hypophosphatemia, normal serum
calcium concentration, and low to low‐normal
serum 1,25(OH)2D3 concentration. This form of rickets
has not been described as yet in dogs or cats, but the
description of one case in a cat from the 1990s appears
clinically similar to an inherited phosphate wasting
disorder.

Tumor‐induced osteomalacia (TIO) is a disease with a
similar phenotype to inherited forms of hypophos­
phatemic rickets and occurs due to paraneoplastic pro­
duction of FGF23 by a tumor. TIO occurs in humans
with tumors known as phosphaturic mesenchymal
tumor, mixed connective tissue variant (PMT‐MCT),
which have many similarities to soft tissue sarcomas of
dogs. One study found that three of 49 soft tissue sarco­
mas from dogs had high relative expression of FGF23,
although no animals had clinical signs consistent with
osteomalacia.

­Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis is the result of an imbalance between bone
resorption and bone formation. In contrast to fibrous
osteodystrophy and rickets, the quality of the bone that
is formed is normal; there is just less of it. Although the
studies done on ovariectomized dogs have generally
been poorly controlled for diet, age and other variables,
it seems that unless dietary calcium is restricted,
­neutered dogs do not develop the postmenopausal oste­
oporosis that occurs in women. Potential causes of
­osteoporosis in dogs and cats include the following.
Senile osteoporosis – general decline in bone mineral
content with age, as osteoclastic resorption slowly
outstrips bone formation during normal bone
­
­remodeling. Generally, this decline is not clinically
significant.
●● Disuse osteoporosis – lack of weight bearing due to
immobilization or paralysis results in rapid loss of
BMD in the immobilized limb and increased BMD in
the contralateral limb. This effect is reversible once
weight bearing resumes, particularly in young animals.
●● Inflammatory bowel disease and malabsorption –
likely due to a combination of reduced absorption of
vitamin D and calcium, with increased inflammatory
cytokines such as IL‐6 leading to increased osteoclas­
tic bone resorption.
●● Corticosteroid‐induced – glucocorticoids decrease cal­
cium absorption from the intestinal tract, increase cal­
cium excretion from the kidney, decrease osteoblast
activity and increase bone resorption, all of which may
lead to osteoporosis. A study in beagles with hyper­
adrenocorticism found that bone trabecular volume was
decreased by 25% due to decreased bone formation.
●● Hyperthyroidism – increased thyroid hormone con­
centrations lead to increased osteoblastic bone
­formation and increased osteoclastic bone resorption;
however, the rate of bone resorption is greater
than bone formation, resulting in osteoporosis.
Pharmacologic doses of thyroxine administered to
●●

dogs led to increased bone remodeling. While markers
of bone formation (alkaline phosphatase and osteocal­

definitive data on the effect of thyrotoxicosis on bone

●● Drugs – in humans, ciclosporin and phenobarbital
have been associated with osteoporosis.

Osteoporosis is rarely diagnosed in cats and dogs, in part
possibly due to not considering it as a differential diag­
nosis for lameness or bone pain, and the insensitivity of
radiography for its diagnosis. The future use of improved
diagnostic testing such as DEXA and CT may reveal that
osteoporosis is more common in these ­species than is
currently thought.

Osteoarthritis in Small Animals
Steven A. Martinez, DVM, MS, DACVS, DACVSMR
Department of Veterinary Clinical Sciences, College of Veterinary Medicine, Washington State University, Pullman, WA, USA

Osteoarthritis (OA, syn. osteoarthrosis, degenerative
joint disease, DJD) is a syndrome that affects synovial or
diarthrodial joints and may manifest its presence by
causing pain in association with degeneration of articular cartilage (loss of extracellular cell matrix and chondrocytes, inflammatory response of synovium, and
critical changes in proteoglycan ratios within matrix and
synovial fluid) and changes in periarticular soft tissues.
Since typically a low‐grade inflammatory process is associated with the development and maintenance of the
degenerative process of articular cartilage, the underlying subchondral bone response (e.g., sclerosis), intra‐
and periarticular response (e.g., synovial hypertrophy,
periarticular fibrosis), the term osteoarthritis describes
the disease process of the diarthrodial joint better than
the older term degenerative joint disease. Typically, OA is
an insidiously progressive, degenerative condition that
targets high‐motion synovial joints. Osteoarthritis can
occur in two forms: primary and secondary, with secondary OA being the more common form presenting
clinically in veterinary medicine.

­Etiology/Pathophysiology
Primary OA is considered a “wear and tear” phenomenon of joint degeneration occurring in older patients.
Although primary OA may be more common in cats
than previously appreciated, it appears to be rare in dogs
compared to clinical presentations for secondary OA
issues. Causes of this form of OA in humans have been
linked to obesity, the hormone leptin, and the development of OA. The target or targeted effected tissues that
initiate the development of primary OA are unknown
but could involve the initial degeneration of the sub-

chondral bone resulting in secondary degeneration of
articular cartilage, primary degeneration of articular cartilage, the synovium, or another tissue or combination of
degeneration of tissues yet to be determined.
Secondary OA is due to an underlying or secondary
cause for the development of the disease. Joint instability,
direct joint trauma, infection, toxins, immune‐­mediated
disease, and developmental/congenital disease are some
of the known etiologies for the development of secondary OA and others may include infectious (e.g., septic
arthritis) or noninfectious (e.g., immune mediated,
trauma, developmental/congenital) environment development within the joint. The hyaline cartilage matrix
(type 2 collagen, proteoglycan molecules and chondrocytes) is directly damaged which results in chondrocyte
death. Synoviocytes are then stimulated to produce myriad cytokins and inflammatory mediators (e.g., interleukins, inducible encosinoids, nitrous oxide, tumor necrosis
factor‐alpha, etc.). These synoviocyte‐based products
then in turn stimulate surviving chondrocytes to produce many of the same cytokines and inflammatory
mediators which result in the production of chondrocyte‐based matrix metalloproteinases which catalytically
digest more cartilage matrix (increased aggrecans content of matrix and synovial fluid drawing more water into
matrix and synovium) and reduces the matrix’s ability to
biomechanically manage normal load and shear forces at
the cartilage surface (resulting in more matrix loss and
debris as well as fracturing of the supporting subchondral bone deep to the cartilage matrix). In addition, the
chondrocyte‐based cytokines and inflammatory mediators directly result in chondrocyte apoptosis. The cartilage matrix is now in a continuous metabolic state of
catabolism which will drive the progression of osteoarthritis in the affected joint (Figure 173.1).

Micro‐ and macroscopic changes within the synovial
joint may result in the clinical signs of lameness due to
joint pain (synovitis, microfractures of subchondral bone,
osteophytes, and joint effusion/distension) (Figure 173.2).

­Epidemiology
The radiographic incidence of OA in referral hospital‐
based cats is estimated at 26–82% depending on age
(older cats, greater incidence). In dogs, OA has been estimated to clinically affect 20% of the dog population in
the United States.
Figure 173.2 Photomicrograph of osteoarthritis. Osteoarthritis
cartilages: note the presence of fibrillation, fissuring, cloning
chondrocytes, loss of staining due to loss of proteoglycans in the
matrix, and fracture of subchondral bone. Source: Image courtesy
of Dr Steven Arnoczky.

­Signalment
Primary OA typically occurs in older males or female
cats with a higher incidence with older age. As previously

VetBooks.ir

173 Osteoarthritis in Small Animals

stated, primary OA appears to be relatively uncommon
in dogs but would also be hypothesized to occur in
older dogs.
Secondary OA can occur in any breed or sex of dog at
any age. Certain juvenile skeletal developmental diseases
(e.g., elbow dysplasia, hip dysplasia, osteochondritis
­dissecans. etc.) that result in secondary OA have the propensity to clinical affect dogs between the ages of 5 and
11 months. Skeletally mature dogs of either sex (>1 year
of age) may on occasion present with clinical signs of OA
due to juvenile skeletal developmental diseases. Many of
the juvenile skeletal developmental diseases that affect
joints are breed specific or may be breed nonspecific.
Osteoarthritis secondary to etiologies other than juvenile skeletal developmental diseases can occur with any
sex and any age of dogs. Cranial cruciate ligament rupture continues to be a common cause of OA in mature
dogs. With the exception of hip dysplasia, secondary OA
is usually recognized in cats of any sex, breed, or age
­following joint trauma such as articular fractures.

­History and Clinical Signs
The clinical history of most canine OA patients will
commonly be a noted lameness of the affected limb following activity. Typically, the lameness will worsen with
progressive activity. Hip dysplasia patients have a different gait history from other causes of OA which centers
on the appearance of stiffness to rise and then sudden
halting of activity (e.g., “sitting down”) rather than
increasing lameness. Owners may also note a classic
“bunny hopping” gait in a hip dysplasia patient when
running. With any form of OA, owners may also note
pain on flexion, extension, and/or with other manipulation of the affected joint.
The clinical history of most feline OA patients will
center on behavior/activity changes; more fractious or
more subdued with owner or other animal interactions
and less active than noted previously (sitting/crouching
for long periods of time).
The clinical signs associated with OA vary from patient
to patient and may range from subclinical to a severe
functional disability. The following clinical findings are
typical of patients with OA.
Gait Assessment
Reduced weight bearing of affected limb
Shorten stride length of contralateral normal limb
●● Audible clicking or “clunking” during gait
●● Pelvic swings enhanced to the contralateral side of the
affected pelvic limb
●● Head dorsiflexed on affected thoracic limb side
●● Narrowed pelvic limb stance

●●

Physical Exam Findings
Asymmetric or symmetric muscle atrophy
Asymmetric or symmetric joint thickening/joint effusion/heat

●● Decreased joint range of motion (flexion and/or
extension)
●● Crepitus during joint motion
●● Pain/discomfort on one or more aspects of joint

internal or external rotation)

­Diagnosis
Diagnostics are initially directed towards orthogonal
view radiographs of the affected joint and should include
the contralateral joint for comparative assessment.
Radiographic features indicative of OA include osteophytes, effusion, subchondral bone sclerosis with or
without lucencies or erosive patterns (Figure 173.3).
Other nonimaging modalities can be used for more
detailed joint evaluation, including computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance (MR) imaging . These
modalities may be beneficial if radiographic findings
are minimal or equivocal for radiographic features to
support a diagnosis of OA.
Arthrocentesis with synovial fluid cytology and fluid
analysis may be beneficial to confirm the diagnosis of OA or
to rule out other forms of joint disease, including immune‐
mediated arthropathies, septic arthritis, or neoplasia.
Typical secondary OA cytologic findings in dogs are 1000–
5000 nucleated cells/mm3, 88–100% mononuclear cells,
and 0–12% n
­ eutrophils. Viscosity may be normal to low.
If indicated (and rarely required beyond radiographic
diagnostics), minimally invasive diagnostics in dogs can
also be performed with arthroscopy. Direct macroscopic
visualization of the articular cartilage for evidence
of fibrillation, erosions, the presence of osteophytes,
and examination of the synovium for hypertrophy and
inflammation can provide a definitive diagnosis of OA
in a patient (Figure 173.4). Usually, arthroscopy can
­provide the etiology for the secondary OA as well (e.g.
ostochondritis dissecans (OCD), fragmented medial
coronoid disease, medical compartment disease of the
elbow, cranial cruciate ligament disease, etc.).

­Therapy
Management strategies for clinical OA patients are
focused on the fact that OA progression cannot be halted
or reversed. Fundamentally, no one treatment will be all‐
encompassing for all patients with OA. An individualized

Current treatment strategies used to treat OA patients
are multimodal medical management, surgery or, more
commonly, the integration of both treatment modalities.
A multimodal management “pyramid” with three
major components – weight control, exercise modification, and pharmaceuticals/nonpharmaceuticals – must
be considered when nonsurgically managing a patient

with OA (Figure 173.5). Exclusion of one or more of
these components from a treatment protocol will result
in an overall poorer clinical response from the patient.
Weight Control
Obesity is a major risk factor for the development of OA
in people and weight loss can reduce the symptomatic

VetBooks.ir

173 Osteoarthritis in Small Animals

Rx/N-Rx
Exercise
Modification

Weight Control

Figure 173.5 Multimodal approach to treating osteoarthritis.
Three basic components of the multimodal strategy for the

effects of OA. Recently, research shows the same is true
for other animals. A clinical study investigating the
effects of obesity in dogs with hip dysplasia concluded
that overweight dogs that achieved an 11–18% body
weight reduction were significantly less lame ­compared
to their preweight reduction lameness scores.
Weight control can be one of the most challenging
aspects of the medical management of OA in dogs for
several reasons.
A patient that is clinically inhibited by moving an OA
joint(s) will not be able to utilize consumed or stored
body energy efficiently and will instead increase body
stores of energy (fat) when given a constant caloric
intake.
●● Dogs with underlying endocrine disease (e.g., hyperadrenocorticism, hypothyroidism) will have the metabolic propensity to maintain body fat stores even in the
face of a reducing diet.
●● Dogs in a multipet household (e.g., other dogs and
cats) are more prone to consume greater volumes of
food than dogs in single‐pet households.
●● An inaccurate estimation of the animal’s ideal body
weight.
●● An inaccurate estimation of the animal’s energy
requirements.
●● The owner’s lack of willingness to be proactive in
­trying to reduce their pet’s body weight.
●●

Any one or a combination of the above factors will
­maintain the obese patient indefinitely.
Prior to starting a weight‐reducing program, a complete physical exam should be performed. The clinical
history (attempted weight reduction in the past with poor
results, lethargy, “heat seeking,” polyuria/polydipsia,
etc.) and physical exam findings (pendulous abdomen,
­symmetric alopecia, recurrent dermatopathy, etc.) may

warrant a complete minimum database (complete blood
count [CBC], serum chemistry profile, urinalysis [UA])
to rule out metabolic disease or endocrinopathies.
Weight reduction can be obtained in healthy patients
by four methods.
Reducing current caloric intakes, using reductions by
33–50% of the “normal” volume of the regular diet.
●● Calculating caloric content of regular diet and caloric
needs based on basal metabolic rates.
●● Using specially formulated commercial diets with
­recommended intake volumes per the manufacturer.
●● Pharmacologic management (e.g., dilotapide).
●●

Appropriate caloric restriction should result in the loss
of 1–2% of body weight per week.
All weight reduction/control programs must include
an exercise element to ensure constant weight loss and
eventual body weight maintenance. To encourage activity in the debilitated OA patient, regular pharmacologic
treatment may be required for a short period until the
patient becomes more ambulatory and physiologically
acclimated to the new level of physical activity.
Exercise and Activity Modification
Exercise is very important in people for maintaining
strength, stamina, and joint range of motion; there is also
less dependency on medication when OA patients are
allowed to exercise. It is assumed that the same is true in
other animals as well and this is supported by a study in
hamsters. Therefore, an important aspect in the management of OA in animals should be controlled exercise.
Depending on the animal’s activity history, it may be
necessary to modify a patient’s regular level and type of
activity.
It may seem intuitive that an OA animal should not be
allowed to have hard‐impact, prolonged exercise activity,
but controlled clinical studies have not been performed
to evaluate this recommendation. However, from clinical
experience, practitioners are used to hearing the usual
owner’s report of greater clinical signs in OA patients
after hard, prolonged activity. It is known from kinetic
and kinematic gait analysis that dogs with OA will modify
their gait to reduce the load of weight bearing and motion
of the affected joint. It is therefore safe to assume that
prolonged “overactivity” should result in greater modification of gait due to exacerbation of the discomfort associated with an OA joint. Some recommendations for the
duration of certain activities in dogs have been made but
recommendations for activity duration can also be based
on common sense and owner observations of their pet’s
apparent gait response/comfort level to an activity period.
Just as important as duration of activity is the type
of activity undertaken in the animal’s daily lifestyle.

1533

VetBooks.ir

1534

Section 13 Diseases of Bone and Joint

Low‐impact activities (e.g., walking, cycling) have positive effects on human OA patients. In veterinary medicine, low‐impact activities (walking, swimming) have
been traditionally favored over hard‐impact aerobic
activities (jumping, hard starting/running, vigorous
climbing/running on irregular terrain) which can overstress degenerative joints. High‐impact activities may
overstress OA joints and increase the inflammatory
­condition of OA. Low‐impact activities are thought to
reduce loads on an OA joint and result in less discomfort
for the patient in maintaining good muscle strength/
mass and joint function. Walking under controlled
­conditions (leash restraint) and/or swimming can be recommended to the owner with further instructions to
eventually attempt to have the patient increase the duration of these activities gradually so long as the animal
appears to remain comfortable in doing so. To strengthen
the active stabilizers (muscles and tendons) and to
improve the range of motion of joints in OA patients,
several physical rehabilitation modalities such as passive
and active range of motion exercises, message, deep
ultrasound heat applications, and laser therapy can be
administered by certified small animal physical rehabilitation technicians and specialists. In many OA cases, the
adjunct use of physical rehabilitation can help improve
patient comfort and function with very good to excellent
clinical results.
Pharmacologic/Nonpharmacologic OA Agents
The primary goal in the pharmacologic management of
OA is to relieve the patient of discomfort associated
with joint movement. Ideally, this would involve oral or
injectable agents with analgesic, antiinflammatory,
and potential chondromodulating properties (disease‐
modifying OA agents, DMOA). Such agents would ideally biochemically block the inducible cyclooxegenase‐2
(COX‐2) and lipoxygenase pathways. Several FDA‐
approved “COX‐selective” nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) have been developed for this
purpose (e.g., carprofen, meloxicam, firocoxib, etc.).
Robenaxocib is currently the only approved NSAID
for cats in the United States. Grapiprant, a newer class of
prostaglandin receptor antagonist; a non-COX pathway
inhibitor for the treatment of the clinical signs of OA,
has been developed with the intent to reduce the potential of adverse events of GI. renal, and liver disease seen
in the small percentages of patients administered select
and non-select COX-2 inhibitors. Grapiprant is specific
to the blockage of Prostaglandin E2 receptor 4 (EP4); a
primary mediator of OA-based pain and inflammation.
Although touted as a "non-NSAID" anti-inflammatory
and analgesic drug, OA patients administered grapiprant

can have the risk to develop adverse events that include
GI disease (emesis, diarrhea, and anorexia), and subclinical hyperalkaline phosphatemia and hypoproteinemia.
All COX‐selective (and nonselective) NSAIDs have
toxicity potential. Hepatic toxicosis due to NSAID
administration has been reported; however, all NSAIDs
have a toxicity potential especially if a patient has underlying hepatic or renal disease, or thrombocytopathy.
Several in vivo studies using chondrocyte cell cultures or
cartilage explants have reported a decrease in proteoglycan synthesis in those tissues incubated with selected
NSAIDs. It would appear to be a wiser clinical practice to
administer NSAIDs on a PRN basis, especially for the
patient that has only intermittent discomfort due to
osteoarthritis.
Disease‐modifying osteoarthritis agents have recently
been developed for the treatment of human and veterinary OA patients. These agents have become commonplace in the treatment of OA despite the lack of definitive
scientific studies confirming their efficacy. Most of these
products contain mixtures of glucosamine and chondroitin sulfate, which supposedly enhance cartilage health
by providing the necessary precursors to maintain and
repair cartilage. Glucosamine and chondroitin sulfate
reportedly have a positive effect on cartilage matrix by
enhancing proteoglycan production and inhibiting catabolic enzyme production or activity in OA joints. These
properties have contributed to the labeling of these
agents as “chondroprotective.” With the exception of one
product which is a true pharmaceutical by definition
(Adequan®, Luitpold Pharmaceuticals, FDA approved in
horses and dogs), these agents are marketed as oral nutritional supplements (“nutricueticals”) and not “drugs”
and as such, the FDA does not require the manufacturer
to provide efficacy data for their product. Bioavailability
of orally ingested forms of glucosamine and chondroitin
sulfate is 87% and 70% in humans and experimental animals, respectively. Limited investigations have been performed on the in vitro and in vivo activity of glucosamine
and chondroitin sulfate separately, but products containing both agents have become popular for treating OA
symptoms in humans and other animals. Synergism with
glucosamine and chondroitin sulfate has recently been
demonstrated histologically and with in vivo biochemical
analysis in a rabbit OA model.
Glucosamine and chondroitin sulfate are two regular
nutricuetical combinations used in many dietary supplenets for dogs and cats. Examples of these formulations are Cosequin® and Dasuquin® (similar to Cosequin®
but with the additions of with avocado/soybean
unsaponifiables and methylsulfonylmethane (MSM)
­
(Nutramax) and Glycoflex® (Vetri‐Science Laboratories).
Although clinically noted not to have predictable

VetBooks.ir

173 Osteoarthritis in Small Animals

­efficacy in all dogs, this combination of a precursor glycosaminoglycan and a glycosaminoglycan appears to
have a prophylactic effect on the development of OA in
dogs. Dogs undergoing a Pond‐Nuki model for the
development of OA with or without stifle stabilization
that were administered Cosequin for five months following surgery subjectively had less OA and less periarticular fibrosis than dogs not receiving Cosequin.
Chymopapain‐ induced acute carpal synovitis was
­significantly attenuated based on nuclear scintigraphy
and lameness evaluation when dogs were pretreated
with glucosamine and chondroitin sulfate (Cosequin).
Current research suggests that glucosamine and
chondroitin sulfate products may be prophylactically
­
beneficial in patients that are prone to develop OA (e.g.,
canine hip dysplasia [CHD], elbow dysplasia, OCD, cranial cruciate ligament injury, etc.) or patients that may
aggravate preexisting OA with activity. Further controlled clinical studies are still w
­ arranted to support
these statements.
Injectable forms of DMOA available include Adequan,
which is a polysulfated glycosaminoglycan (PSGAG)
product, and hyaluronic acid (HA), a nonsulfated GAG.
The US (Adequan) and European products (Arteparon®)
have been used in horses and dogs. Although conflicting
evidence exists that PSGAGs have a positive anabolic
effect on hyaline cartilage, studies have shown that
PSGAG may decrease hyaline cartilage catabolism. In one
study, immature dogs prone to hip dysplasia administered
Adequan developed better hip ­conformation than dogs
that were not treated with Adequan. A clinical study
investigating the use of PSGAG on hip dysplasia patients
found no significant difference in orthopedic scores
(lameness, range of motion, pain on manipulation of hip
joints) compared to PSGAG nontreated dogs. In a meniscectomy model in dogs, PSGAG provided partial protection to articular cartilage damage associated with the
meniscectomy. PSGAG has been reported to have chondroprotective properties in joints with a chemically
induced articular cartilage damage model versus no effect
on a physical articular cartilage damage model in horses.
Anecdotal reports have appeared indicating that there
may be a positive synergism between injectable PSGAG
and oral glucosamine and chondroitin sulfate when
administered concurrently to a patient.
Hyaluronic acid (sodium hyaluronate, HA) is a major
component of synovial fluid. HA acid is postulated to
enhance joint health by increasing the viscosity of the
joint fluid and reducing inflammation and scavenging
free radicals. A study using a Pond‐Nuki model for OA in
dogs followed by intraarticular injections of HA did not
modify OA and reduced overall proteoglycan concentrations in treated stifles.

Other products reported that have disease‐modifying,
anti‐OA potential include pentosan polysulfate, tetracyclines (doxycycline, minocycline, and modifications of
these molecules), methylsulfonylmethane (MSM), capsaicin, and fatty acid ratio manipulation (omega‐6:omega‐3).
S‐adenosyl‐L‐methionine (SAMe) has objectively not
been shown to have efficacy in dogs to resolve the clinical
signs of OA. Dietary management using omega‐3 fatty
acids has been reported to improve clinical scores and
ground reaction forces in approximately 25–82% of
patients. Metaanalysis evaluating the efficacy of various
nutritional‐based DMOAs concluded that only fatty acid
diet modifications appear to have the strongest evidence‐
based results to ameliorate the clinical signs of OA in dogs.
There are several commercially available OA diets that
incoroprate the use of omega-3 fatty acid in the dietary
formulations with other formulations adding antioxidants
such as Vitamin E, C, as well as glucosamine and chondrotin sulfate.
Adjuncts to pharmacologic, exercise/activity, and
weight control treatments that can also be considered
are the application of heat, cold, massage, hydrotherapy,
ultrasound/diathermy, and electrotherapy. Although
based on anecdotal observations only, these adjuncts
appear to help some patients. Laser, chiropractic, extracorporeal shockwave therapy (EST), and acupuncture
are professed to improve canine patients with the clinical
signs of OA. EST results reported can be variable with
regard to the joint evaluated and to date, acupuncture
has not been evaluated to be efficacious in dogs with OA
of the hip or elbow. Laser and chiropractic procedures
are anecdotally proclaimed to have efficacy in OA
patients or at best, may have only limited in vivo support
for efficacy. Unfortunately, placebo or negative controlled clinical studies are needed to test the supposition
that these and other developing modalities (e.g., radiation) have efficacy in veterinary OA patients.
Recently, the use of autogenic tissues such as adipose‐
derived mesenchymal stem cells and platelet‐rich plasma
or platelet‐enhanced plasma intraarticular injections has
been investigated as therapies to attenuate the clinical
signs of OA in dogs. Although early results appear promising for these therapies, additional controlled clinical
trials are needed to provide better evidence‐based proof
that they justify their high costs to the owner of an OA
patient.
Surgical management for the clinical signs of OA are
limited to arthroplasty (via arthroscopy or arthrotomy),
arthrodesis, total joint replacement for selected joints, or
limb amputation. Nonexcisional arthroplasties will typically require the integration of a multimodal medical
approach to provide better long‐term function for the
patient.
