­Prognosis
Dogs and cats can be significantly affected by OA; however, new concepts with a balanced multimodal management approach to treat the clinical signs of OA can result
in an acceptable quality of life for the majority of OA
patients, providing fair to excellent prognoses for lame‐
free function. Included in the formula for prognosis will
be the consideration of a specific joint affected by OA
(biomechanics, e.g., shoulder vs tarsus) and the degree of
disease present in that joint (e.g., cartilage erosions vs
minimal cartilage disease). Nonsurgical management
must be considered beyond conventional and nonconventional pharmacologic treatment to include a balance
created between exercise/activity and weight control
management. Failure to consider this multimodal
approach to OA treatment, especially in an individual-

ized medicine approach (i.e., not all dogs or cats will
respond the same with the same treatments), will usually
result in a poorer clinical response to therapy (surgical
and nonsurgical) and quality of life as perceived by the
owner of the OA patient.
Excellent progress continues in the development of
new pharmaceuticals and other agents to combat or even
reverse the degenerative processes of OA. In contrast,
research and development into exercise/activity management for the OA companion animal lag significantly
behind those of human medicine, but since the mid‐
1990s, it has become a major treatment focus in veterinary medicine. Nonetheless, large controlled clinical
trials are still needed for “evidence‐based” treatment
protocols (controlled clinical trials) that will allow us to
treat our OA patients beyond the individual clinician’s
clinical experience.

Developmental orthopedic diseases (DODs), a subset
of canine pediatric orthopedic diseases, are a group of
bone and joint diseases that initiate and develop during
postnatal skeletal growth, mostly during the first 26
weeks of life. During this period, joints attain their
adult morphology and bones assume their mature
length and shape. Pediatric orthopedic diseases are
aberrations of this ordered process (including endochondral ossification), described in more detail in
Chapter 172. Most DODs are caused by multifactorial
traits, with presumed or demonstrated genetic, nutritional, and environmental risk factors. Developmental
orthopedic diseases may affect bones or joints. In this
section, we will discuss hip dysplasia, osteochondrosis,
patella luxation, Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease, craniomandibular osteopathy, panosteitis, hypertrophic osteodystrophy, and slipped capital femoral epiphysis
(SCFE). Although all these diseases develop and usually
manifest during the period from birth to skeletal maturity, their long‐term clinical effects may be persistent
and profound.

­Developmental Orthopedic Diseases
Affecting Joints
Canine Hip Dysplasia
Etiology and Pathophysiology

Hip dysplasia literally means abnormal development of
the hip joint. The abnormal development appears to start
with laxity of the hip joint, with subsequent subluxation
and abnormal wear and tear of the joint. The joint capsule
becomes inflamed, the cartilaginous joint surface is

mechanically disrupted, and progressive osteoarthritis
(OA) ensues. The condition is usually bilateral.
At birth, the hip joints of puppies that will develop
canine hip dysplasia (CHD) are indistinguishable from
joints that will develop normally. After birth, laxity has
been associated with increased synovial fluid volume, as
well as swelling, damage, and excessive lengthening of
the ligament of the head of the femur. Dysplastic puppies
have a delayed onset and abnormal progression of mineralization of the head of the femur compared to nondysplastic puppies. Muscular development is also abnormal,
with predisposed breeds often having reduced pelvic
muscle mass, and atypical pectineal muscle fiber composition having been demonstrated in affected dogs.
In dysplastic animals with subluxated joints, greater
muscle forces are required to generate equivalent hip
motion compared to healthy animals. This, combined
with the smaller contact area of the incongruent opposing joint surfaces caused by the subluxation, results in
abnormal wear and tear of the articular surfaces with
subsequent synovitis and OA.
The etiology of laxity is not fully understood but
includes genetic, endocrine, and nutritional factors.
Canine hip dysplasia is mostly diagnosed in medium‐
and large‐breed dogs and strong breed predispositions
have been identified (Table 174.1). The condition is considered a polygenic trait with a heritability varying from
0.2–0.3 (based mostly on arthritic changes on the ventrodorsal extended hip joint radiographs) to 0.5–0.6
(mostly based on distraction index or dorsolateral subluxation index). Thus, somewhere between 20% and
60% of the phenotype of a patient affected with CHD
may be attributed by its genetic make‐up. Several
quantitative trait loci (QTLs; chromosomal regions

­containing a gene or group of genes influencing the phenotypic expression of a trait) for CHD and hip OA have
been identified on multiple canine chromosomes.
Several upgraded genes like COX‐2, MIG‐6/Gene 33,
DNCLl, LAMS, and ATF3 have been identified. Only
genetically predisposed animals exposed to certain specific environmental factors may develop clinical hip dysplasia, and dogs not predisposed but exposed to the
same environmental factors will not.
The hormones estrogen and relaxin have also been
implicated as etiologic factors of CHD. Both are present
in colostrum and may be absorbed from the puppy’s gastrointestinal tract. Estrogen is probably not a strong etiologic factor, as estrogen fluctuations during the estrus
cycle do not result in joint laxity changes. One of relaxin’s functions prepartum is to relax the ligaments of the
maternal pubic symphysis, and in dogs and humans it is
associated with joint laxity. However, the significance of
relaxin in the etiology of CHD is unclear.
Rapid growth and body weight have been associated
with the development of CHD. In recent studies, heavier
puppies developed hip OA requiring treatment at a much
younger age than lighter littermates. Similarly, ad libitum
feeding of Labrador retrievers accelerated the onset of hip
OA when compared to a control group fed a restricted diet.
High dietary concentrations of calcium and/or vitamin D3
have also been implicated, but not conclusively proven, as
etiologic factors. A high dietary anion gap and vitamin C
deficiency have also been proposed as causes of CHD, but
their clinical significance has not been demonstrated.
Epidemiology

Hip dysplasia is the most commonly diagnosed canine
orthopedic condition and in one North American epidemiologic study of canine appendicular musculoskeletal
disorders, it comprised 9.6–12.8% of all patients. In this
population, the incidence of CHD ranged from 21.1 to
28.1 per 1000 patients, but incidences as high as 50–70%
in some large breeds have been reported. Hip dysplasia
in cats is thought to be uncommon.
Signalment

Canine hip dysplasia is most commonly diagnosed in
medium‐ and large‐breed dogs (see Table 174.1). Male
and female dogs are equally affected. Patients younger
than 1 year of age are usually presented because of pain
and lameness caused by synovitis following hip laxity. As
a result of progressive joint capsule fibrosis, older, mature
patients usually have minimal laxity but suffer from subsequent hip OA.
History and Clinical Signs

Young patients with hip dysplasia (hip laxity) usually
present with uni‐ or bilateral lameness, bunny hopping,
difficulty rising, reluctance to walk, trot, jump, or climb

stairs, and exercise intolerance. Hips are often very painful in these animals. Older dogs mostly present with
similar signs but with a more chronic presentation due to
the slow progression of arthritic changes. Differentials
for these signs include panosteitis, iliopsoas myopathy,
bilateral cruciate disease, and lumbosacral disease.
Diagnosis

Affected hip joints have a decreased range of motion
and pain on extension and abduction, and may exhibit
crepitus on manipulation. There is often atrophy of the
large muscles round the thigh and hip joint. Hip laxity
may be clinically assessed using the Ortolani test. With
this test, the presumed lax hip joint is first manually
subluxated and then reduced. If the joint is lax, the subluxated hip will reduce with a palpable or audible clunk
or click. This evidence of reduction is regarded as a
positive Ortolani sign and is suggestive of hip laxity. In
the awake, unsedated patient, the Ortolani test can be
most easily performed with the dog in lateral recumbency, affected side up. The test may induce pain and
should be performed humanely. In the sedated patient,
the Ortolani maneuver also can be performed with the
patient in dorsal recumbency.
The diagnosis of CHD is confirmed using well‐positioned, ventrodorsal extended hip and lateral pelvic radiographs. The lateral pelvic view is mostly evaluated for
evidence of lumbosacral disease. The ventrodorsal hip‐
extended (VD) view is assessed for hip joint laxity, osteophytes, hip remodeling, and enthesophytes of the lesser
trochanter suggestive of iliopsoas muscle injury. This
view is also helpful in identifying transitional vertebrae,
for example sacralization of the last lumbar vertebra. Hip
laxity is suspected if on the VD view less than 50% of the
femoral head is within the acetabulum or if the cranial
half of the joint space is not uniformly wide and diverges
medially. Unfortunately, with this technique actual hip
laxity may be present in the absence of radiographic
signs. Thus this technique has limited sensitivity for the
detection of hip laxity as false‐negative results may be
obtained. Early nonspecific osteoarthritic signs can be
found around the femoral head (circumferential femoral
head osteophyte) and the femoral neck (caudolateral
curvilinear osteophyte = Morgan’s line). Osteophytes
may also be seen on the cranial and caudal acetabular
margins, and sclerosis of the craniodorsal acetabulum
may be noted. Later stages of the disease are characterized by varying degrees of remodeling of the femoral
head (flattening) and acetabulum (shallowing) and thickening of the femoral neck.
Radiography is also used as a screening tool to identify
dogs suffering from CHD and at risk for OA, to predict
progression of the disease, and to assist in identifying
suitable breeding animals. Several techniques are in use.
In the USA, the Orthopedic Foundation for Animals

1539

VetBooks.ir

1540

Section 13 Diseases of Bone and Joint

requires ventrodorsal hip‐extended views of the pelvis
for their examination. Their evaluation is mostly based
on evaluation of arthritic changes, and prediction of
future disease and suitability for breeding is based on
radiographs of dogs 2 years of age and older. Another US
registry for CHD, PennHIP, requires three views: a ventrodorsal hip‐extended view, a ventrodorsal hip view
with the limb in a neutral, weight‐bearing position with
the femoral heads pressed into the acetabula (compression view), and a ventrodorsal hip view with the limb in a
neutral, weight‐bearing position with the femoral heads
pulled out of the acetabulum (distraction view). The latter two views are used to determine joint laxity and the
“fit” of the femoral heads into the acetabula, respectively.
Crucial in the evaluation is the so‐called distraction
index (DI): a DI >0.3 is suggestive of laxity and an indicator of future disease. The DI can be used as a predictor of
CHD in dogs 16 weeks and older.
Prevention

The incidence of CHD may be reduced by selective
breeding based on the results of radiographic screening.
Restricted dietary intake and perhaps a diet with a low
calcium density may reduce the severity and/or slow
down the development of hip dysplasia and OA.
Treatment

Treatment may consist of conservative (nonsurgical) or
surgical management. The choice of treatment will
depend on the severity of clinical signs, the stage of the
disease, the patient’s age and the owner’s commitment
and expectations. The goal of nonsurgical management
in dogs younger than 1 year of age (predominantly hip
laxity) is to control the synovial pain and adjacent muscle spasm and increase muscle mass to stabilize the hip
joint. The treatment consists of NSAIDs, skeletal muscle relaxer, weight management, nutritional supplements (omega‐3 fatty acids, glucosamine/chondroitin
sulfate), exercise control (avoidance of intense/high‐
impact exercise, roughhousing and stairs; long walks
and swimming are beneficial), and physical therapy
(electrotherapy, joint manipulation and others). Most
young dogs respond well to conservative management
and the pain is well controlled although normal hip
function is not restored.
If a patient is refractory to conservative management,
has evidence of substantial hip dysplasia at young age or
is at risk to develop clinical hip dysplasia, surgical intervention may be required. Employed surgical interventions include juvenile pubic symphysiodesis (JPS), triple
pelvic osteotomy, intertrochanteric osteotomy, total hip
replacement, femoral head and neck ostectomy (FHNO),
and pectineal myectomy. Juvenile pubic symphysiodesis,
surgically induced premature closure of the pubic

­symphysis, is recommended for 10–20‐week‐old dogs with
palpable hip laxity and a distraction index of 0.3–0.5. The
goal of this procedure is to improve the dorsal acetabular
coverage of the femoral head by limiting mediolateral
length growth of the cranial pubic rami. In patients
between 6 and 11 months of age with no to minimal
osteoarthritic changes, a triple pelvic osteotomy (TPO)
may be recommended. With this procedure, the acetabular segment of a hemipelvis is rotated to increase the
acetabular coverage of the femoral head. Just as with the
JPS, this may retard the development of OA.
For patients over 1 year of age with moderate to severe
hip dysplasia, a total hip replacement (THR) may be considered. In the past decade, THR has to a large extent
replaced TPO. Pectineal myectomy is a procedure that
may provide pain relief for patients with hip dysplasia by
releasing the tension of the spasmodic muscles across
the inflamed synovium, although it will not alter the hip
joint congruity and the development of OA. Femoral
head and neck ostectomy is a salvage procedure that may
be employed if concerted medical management is unsuccessful and THR is not possible. Its outcome is most predictable in patients weighing less than 23 kg.
Dogs over 1 year of age (suffering from predominantly
secondary OA) may be treated as any other OA patient
with nonsurgical methods as above. If animals become
refractory to nonsurgical management, surgical treatment is indicated. The main surgical options are THR
and FHNO. Even though FHNO can benefit patient
of all body weights, it is most beneficial in patients
under 23 kg. In patients over 23 kg, THR is preferred.
Denervation of the synovium of the hip joint is a more
recently described surgical procedure for the treatment
of hip dysplasia. The goal of this procedure is palliative
and the procedure is not meant to change the course of
the disease. However, the pain relief is variable, and may
not be accompanied by improved limb function.
Prognosis

No treatment has been developed that can arrest or
revert the pathologic changes associated with hip dysplasia. However, conservative and surgical treatments
provide adequate pain relief and acceptable but not normal clinical function.
Osteochondrosis
Osteochondrosis (OC) is a disease of endochondral ossification (EOS), the normal process whereby epiphyseal
and growth plate cartilages expand (lengthen the bone)
and gradually transform into bone. It is a focal or multifocal disorder with an often bilaterally symmetric distribution, seen in young growing animals and humans.
The term most commonly refers to a disturbance of

endochondral ossification of epiphyseal growth centers,
resulting in articular cartilage disorders of the shoulder,
elbow, stifle or hock joints. Sometimes, disturbances of
endochondral ossification of growth plates of long and
cuboidal bones are also classified as OC. Generally
accepted and proposed manifestations of OC are listed
in Table 174.2.
In this section, we will first discuss the common etiology/pathophysiology and epidemiology of all OCs, followed by a description of signalment, history and clinical
signs, diagnosis, treatment and prognosis of OC of the
shoulder, elbow, stifle and hock joint, and the presumed
manifestation of growth plate OC, retained cartilaginous
core of the distal ulna.
Etiology and Pathophysiology

Osteochondrosis has a multifactorial etiology with several suggested risk factors playing a role: heredity, rapid
growth, dietary factors, and trauma.
Strong breed and bloodline predispositions for the different forms of OC strongly suggest a heritable etiologic
component. Reported heritability for these conditions
ranges from 10% to 45% and it is thought that most forms
of canine OC are inherited as a polygenic trait. In humans
and pigs, severity of OC lesions may be associated with
certain joint shapes and joint morphology also may be an
etiologic factor for canine OC.

Several nutritional factors have been implied in the etiology of OC. The relatively increased growth rate resulting from overnutrition (ad libitum feeding) presumably
predisposes the development of OC lesions by increasing muscle mass and body weight, resulting in biomechanical overload of structurally weak joint surfaces.
However, in a recent review, a direct role of rapid growth
from overnutrition in the etiology of osteochondrosis
was questioned. Another suggested nutritional predisposition is a diet high in calcium and/or vitamin D3. It is
evident that such diets cause a disturbance in endochondral ossification but there is no clear evidence that high
dietary calcium concentrations will cause or increase the
risk for OC in breeds other than Great Danes.
Both macro‐ and microtrauma have been implicated in
OC etiology. Microtrauma may presumably damage cartilage canal blood vessels at the chondroosseous junction
of the epiphysis, thus initiating OC. In dogs, exercise has
been suggested as a risk factor for osteochondrosis.
There are no studies demonstrating that in dogs macrotrauma will cause or initiate OC. However, studies in
pigs and humans suggest that macrotrauma may hasten
the conversion from an osteochondrosis manifesta to an
osteochondrosis dissecans lesion (see later).
A series of elegant, primarily histologic studies in
horses and pigs have suggested that the primary lesion of
OC is a focal necrosis of epiphyseal cartilage canals at

1541

VetBooks.ir

1542

Section 13 Diseases of Bone and Joint

the chondroosseous junction of the epiphysis, resulting
in areas of epiphyseal cartilage ischemia and chondronecrosis. Necrotic cartilage cannot undergo EOS. This
early lesion is called osteochondrosis latens. With progression of the epiphyseal mineralization, the area of
ischemic chondronecrosis may become located at the
cartilage–bone interface. This stage is called osteochondrosis manifesta and the resulting shape change of the
subchondral epiphyseal bone may be seen on radiographs. Several sequelae have been proposed. The chondronecrotic focus may heal, may develop into a bone
cyst, or may deform, resulting in an altered joint contour
and congruency. Commonly, fissures, clefts or cracks
may start at the necrotic cartilage lesion and propagate
along the osteochondral junction or tide mark. Fissures
may further propagate to the joint surface and form a
cartilage flap off the underlying subchondral bone,
resulting in synovitis, joint effusion, arthralgia, lameness, and OA. At this stage, OC is commonly known as
osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) or (more physiologically) osteochondrosis dissecans. This is the most well‐
known and described manifestation of OC. Cartilage
flaps may reattach, resorb, undergo dystrophic calcification or detach and form a so‐called joint mouse.
Epidemiology

In a large epidemiologic study of more than 400 000
canine patients, articular OC was diagnosed in approximately 3.7% of all dogs presented with an orthopedic
problem, translating into an incidence of 8.1 cases per
1000 patients. In dogs younger than 1 year of age, OC
was diagnosed in approximately 9% of the dogs presented with an orthopedic problem. Male dogs are more
commonly affected than female dogs and strong breed
predispositions for all forms of OC have been identified
(see Table 174.1). Feline OC is very uncommon.
Osteochondritis Dissecans of the Shoulder Joint
Osteochondritis dissecans of the shoulder joint is a common form of epiphyseal OC. The lesion is located on the
caudomedial humeral head.
Signalment

The disease is most commonly seen in large‐ and giant‐
breed dogs (see Table 174.1), and males are more commonly affected than females. Most dogs are presented
between 4 and 10 months of age.
History and Clinical Signs

Most dogs suffering from shoulder OCD develop clinical
signs between 4 and 8 months of age, but some dogs only
experience discomfort later in life. Most patients present
with an insidious unilateral lameness that worsens with

exercise and improves with rest. The condition is bilateral in 27–68% of cases but signs will predominate on
one side and can shift sides. Differentials include elbow
dysplasia, panosteitis, hypertrophic osteodystrophy
(HOD), injuries of the shoulder muscles, and cervical
nerve root pain. These conditions can occur concurrently with shoulder OCD.
Diagnosis

The presumptive clinical diagnosis is based on signalment, history, and pain on shoulder hyperflexion and/or
hyperextension. Crepitus and swelling of the shoulder
joint are usually not detected. The final diagnosis is
based on characteristic radiographic changes on the
mediolateral and craniocaudal view of the shoulder joint.
Most radiographic changes are seen on the mediolateral
projection and include flattening to saucer‐shaped and
radiolucent defects of the subchondral bone of caudal
humeral head. Occasionally, mineralizations representing dystrophic calcification of the cartilage flaps are evident either over the subchondral lesion if the flaps are
still attached, or removed from the lesion if they have
detached and become joint mice. These may appear anywhere in the joint, but most commonly are seen in the
caudoventral joint pouch or occasionally in the bicipital
tendon sheath. Because the disease is often bilateral,
both shoulders should be radiographed.
Treatment

Patients diagnosed with shoulder OC may be initially
treated with restricted activity, weight control, and
NSAIDs. If the patient is refractory to conservative management, the lameness has persisted for more than six
weeks, or the patient is older than 6 months of age, surgical treatment in the form of arthrotomy or arthroscopy is
indicated. The goal of the procedure is to remove the flap
and/or joint mouse, debride necrotic cartilage within the
defect, stimulate the formation of fibrocartilage, and
remove synovial fluid cytokines and wear debris through
joint lavage.
Prognosis

More than 90% of surgically treated patients return to
normal limb function. Long term, arthritic changes may
develop but these changes usually do not result in serious discomfort and lameness. Because shoulder OC is a
heritable trait, the owner should be advised that the
patient should not be used for breeding.
Elbow Dysplasia
Elbow dysplasia is an abnormal development of the
elbow joint due to fragmented medial coronoid process
(FMCP), OCD of the medial humeral condyle, elbow

VetBooks.ir

174 Developmental Orthopedic Diseases

incongruity, and/or ununited anconeal process (UAP).
These diseases have in common that they will cause varying degrees of OA. It is thought that FMCP, OCD of the
medial humeral condyle and UAP may be associated
with humeroradial and/or humeroulnar joint incongruity secondary to asynchronous growth of the radius and
ulna. It has been speculated that activity or exercise‐
induced microtrauma to a vulnerable medial coronoid
process or the growth plate of the anconeal process, due
to asynchronous growth of the radius and ulna, could
facilitate the initial chondronecrosis associated with
FCMP, OCD of the medial humeral condyle, and UAP
respectively. It also has been demonstrated that chondronecrosis is associated with a delay of endochondral
ossification of the medial coronoid process in animals
afflicted with FMCP. All three traits are thought to be
multifactorial. The reported heritability of FCMP ranges
from 0.18 to 0.31.
Signalment

Large‐ and giant‐breed dogs are most commonly affected
and unique breed predispositions for FMCP, OCD and
UAP have been identified (see Table 174.1). For all three
diseases, males are more often affected than females.
History and Clinical Signs

Dogs affected with elbow dysplasia are usually presented
for unilateral forelimb lameness. The lameness usually
starts insidiously, worsens with exercise, and improves
with rest. Clinical signs often develop between 4 and 8
months of age, but may be missed if the condition is
bilateral and the gait is symmetrically affected. Patients
also may present at later age, but then clinical signs are
usually due to secondary OA. Differentials are similar to
those of shoulder OC.
Diagnosis

The presumptive diagnosis of elbow dysplasia is based
on the patient’s signalment, history, clinical signs, and
orthopedic exam findings. Muscles of the affected limb
may be atrophied and affected joints may be swollen, initially due to joint effusion but later secondarily to capsular fibrosis. Hyperextension and/or hyperflexion of the
joint are painful and a decreased range of flexion and/or
extension may be present. Internal rotation of the antebrachium with the elbow joint in 90° of flexion may elicit
pain as the medial compartment is compressed (so‐
called Campbell maneuver). Crepitus may be noted during joint manipulation. The final diagnosis is based on
characteristic radiographic or computed tomography
(CT) findings. Recommended radiographic views
include a neutral and a flexed mediolateral view and a
craniocaudal view. Because the condition is often bilateral, both elbows should be radiographed.

Fragmented medial coronoid process and OCD of
the medial humeral condyle both are characterized by
secondary OA of the medial joint compartment as seen
on the craniocaudal view (osteophyte formation on the
medial coronoid process and the medial humeral condyle), but osteophytes also can be present on the anconeal process, caudodistal humerus, and the cranial
portion of the radial head (mediolateral view). Primary
changes of FMCP include fragmentation, blunting or
deformity of the medial coronoid process and sclerosis
of the subchondral bone of the trochlear notch (mediolateral view). Direct evidence of OCD includes flattening or a radiolucent concavity of the medial humeral
condyle (craniocaudal view). Radiography often results
in false‐negative interpretations for FMCP, OCD
and elbow incongruity and therefore oblique elbow
views have been suggested. However, CT is a much
better technique for visualization of FMCP and OCD
defects and elbow incongruity than orthogonal radiographic views. The diagnosis of UAP is made after 22
weeks (the normal time of growth plate fusion), on the
basis of a persistent lucent line or zone in the area
of the growth plate. This lesion is best seen on the
flexed mediolateral radiograph. Comparison radiographs of the opposite elbow may aid with establishing
the diagnosis.
Treatment

After an initial diagnosis of FMCP or OCD, the patient
may be treated conservatively with rest, weight control,
and NSAIDs. However, conservative management will
not arrest or retard progression of OA. Surgical intervention may be needed if conservative management does
not improve the clinical signs. The goal of the intervention is to remove loose fragments, debride the affected
coronoid process down to healthy subchondral bone,
stimulate the formation of fibrocartilage in areas with
eburnated cartilage, and remove synovial fluid cytokines
and wear particles. Recently, repair of OC defects of the
medial humeral condyle with osteochondral autografts
was reported. Patients with more advanced OA and
refractory to medical management may temporarily
benefit from surgical intervention to remove loose fragments, wear particles, and cytokines in the synovial fluid.
The elbow joint can be approached by open arthrotomy
or arthroscopy. Ulnar or humeral corrective osteotomies
may be indicated if significant elbow incongruity exists.
A total elbow replacement may be considered if a patient
with advanced OA has become unresponsive to conservative management.
Dogs with suspected UAP should be treated conservatively with rest, weight reduction, and NSAIDs
until the diagnosis can be confirmed when the patient
is older than 22 weeks of age. Once the diagnosis is

1543

VetBooks.ir

1544

Section 13 Diseases of Bone and Joint

made, surgical intervention should be considered.
Proposed procedures include excision of the ununited anconeal process, ulnar osteotomy, or a combination of ulnar osteotomy and lag screw fixation.
Excision controls a major trigger for secondary OA
but does not stop its progression. Ulnar osteotomy is
an effective treatment of lameness, and in dogs
younger than 7–8 months of age may lead to reattachment of the process. These procedures are not recommended for use in older dogs with UAP and
advanced OA; these patients should be treated for
their OA. If the patient becomes refractory to conservative management, a total elbow arthroplasty
may be considered.
Prognosis

The prognosis for FMCP and OCD depends on the
extent of articular cartilage damage, the state of joint
congruity and severity of the arthritic changes. In cases
with minimal cartilage damage and OA, the prognosis
may be good. If the articular cartilage damage is more
substantial, the prognosis is not as favorable and OA will
progress. In these cases, the condition can be particularly debilitating and hard to manage. The prognosis for
UAP following surgical treatment in young dogs is usually good if treated before secondary changes develop.
However, severe OA may develop, particularly if in combination with FMCP.
Osteochondritis Dissecans of the Stifle Joint
(Medial or Lateral Femoral Condyle)
Osteochondritis dissecans of the stifle joint is an uncommon form of epiphyseal OC. The lesion is located on the
weight‐bearing surface of the medial or lateral femoral
condyle.
Signalment

The disease is most commonly diagnosed in large‐ and
giant‐breed dogs (see Table 174.1). Males are more commonly affected than females.
History and Clinical Signs

abrupt stop of the cranial drawer motion will suggest that
the cranial cruciate ligament is intact. The final diagnosis
is based on characteristic radiographic changes on the
mediolateral and especially the craniocaudal view of the
stifle joint. Lesions are located on the medial or lateral
femoral condyle. Oblique views of the stifle may improve
visualization of the defect. Radiographic changes range
from subchondral bone flattening and subchondral
sclerosis to more severe radiolucent concave defects.
Effusion is always seen and secondary arthritic changes
are usually present.
Treatment

Patients may be treated initially with restricted activity,
weight control, and NSAIDs. If the patient does not
respond to conservative management, surgical treatment in the form of arthrotomy or arthroscopy is indicated. The purpose of the surgical intervention is to
remove the cartilage flap and debride the defect, stimulate the formation of fibrocartilage, and remove synovial
fluid cytokines and wear particles. The OC defect also
may be repaired with osteochondral autografts, or resurfaced with a single‐layer or bilayered implant. Dogs that
have developed severe secondary OA unresponsive to
conservative management may be treated with a total
knee replacement.
Prognosis

Treatment, including surgical treatment, does not
change the progression of secondary OA. Conservatively
managed dogs usually end up with an intermittent lameness. Surgical treatment usually improves the limb function but lameness may persist, especially after exercise.
There is no long‐term evidence yet that the currently
used osteochondral transplant techniques improve the
treatment outcome. The owner should be advised that
stifle OC most likely is a hereditary trait and that the
patient should not be used for breeding.
Osteochondritis Dissecans of the Hock Joint
(Medial or Lateral Trochlear Ridge of the Talus)

Dogs affected with stifle OCD become lame between 4
and 8 months of age, similar to other forms of joint OC.
Some dogs may develop lameness later in life. The lameness may range from mild to severe, and tends to worsen
with exercise.

Osteochondrosis of the hock joint is an uncommon epiphyseal OC. Lesions are localized on either the medial
(most common) or lateral trochlear ridge of the talus.
Most patients present between 4 and 10 months of age.

Diagnosis

Just as with the other articular OCs, this condition is
mostly seen in large‐ and giant‐breed dogs, and
Rottweilers, retrievers, and Great Danes are most predisposed (see Table 174.1). Male dogs are more commonly
affected than female dogs.

The presumptive clinical diagnosis is based on signalment, history, and pain on stifle hyperflexion and/or
hyperextension. Joint effusion and crepitus are usually
present. Mild cranial drawer also may be detected, but an

Signalment

VetBooks.ir

174 Developmental Orthopedic Diseases

History and Clinical Signs

Affected dogs usually present between 4 and 8 months of
age, but some dogs develop clinical signs later in life.
Affected dogs usually present with an insidious unilateral lameness that worsens with exercise and the patient
may be mildly exercise intolerant.
Diagnosis

The presumptive clinical diagnosis is based on signalment, age of presentation, history, and pain on hock
hyperflexion and/or hyperextension. A decreased range
of motion of the hock joint, as well as joint crepitus and
joint swelling/effusion, are often present. The final diagnosis is based on characteristic radiographic changes on
a neutral mediolateral and extended craniocaudal view
of the hock joint. Flexed mediolateral and craniocaudal
views facilitate visualization of the defect if not obvious
on the aforementioned views. With OC of the medial
ridge of the talus, flattening of the medial trochlear ridge
can be seen on both orthogonal views; widening of the
medial joint compartment (craniocaudal view) and periarticular mineralizations are also often present. OC of
the lateral trochlear ridge is characterized by subchondral fissures at the base of the lateral trochlear ridge. CT
may help to establish the diagnosis, particularly with lateral trochlear ridge OC.
Treatment

Patients suffering from hock OC may be initially treated
with restricted activity, weight control, and NSAIDs. If
the patient does not respond to conservative management, arthrotomy or arthroscopy is indicated. The goal
of the procedure is to remove the flap and/or joint mouse,
debride the defect and stimulate the formation of fibrocartilage, and remove synovial fluid cytokines and wear
particles.
Prognosis

Most dogs will have a fair to good quality of life despite
continued lameness. Conservative management usually
results in a continuous or intermittent lameness and progressive OA. Surgical management may improve limb
function, but progressive OA still may cause exercise‐
induced lameness. Affected dogs should not be used for
breeding as hock OC appears to be a heritable trait.
Retained Cartilaginous Core
Generically, retained cartilaginous core is caused by a
failure of endochondral ossification and can occur in any
metaphyseal growth plate. It is characterized by the projection of cones of unmineralized growth plate cartilage,
predominantly hypertrophic chondrocytes, into the
adjacent metaphyseal bone. The local thickening of the

growth plate may be caused by vascular events on the
epiphyseal or metaphyseal side of the growth plate.
Most cartilaginous cores will heal spontaneously and in
most growth plates will not have clinical consequences.
However, a retained cartilaginous core may have clinical
significance in the distal ulnar growth plate, a growth
plate with a rapid rate of length growth and with an adjacent paired radius. Here, they may be associated with a
reduced length growth of the ulna, leading to angular
limb deformities (radial bowing and valgus deformity)
and/or elbow incongruity, similar to cases with traumatic
closure of the distal ulna growth plate.
Signalment

The condition is most commonly seen in rapidly growing,
large‐ and giant‐breed dogs. Most patients are presented
between 4 and 10 months of age.
History and Clinical Signs

Patients are presented with angular limb deformity, radial
bowing, and/or valgus deformity that developed during
adolescence.
Diagnosis

The presumptive diagnosis is based on the patient’s signalment, history, clinical signs, and orthopedic exam
findings. Angular limb deformity, including radial bowing and/or valgus deformity, is often a prominent feature
and elbow incongruity (pain on hyperextension/hyperflexion) also may be present. The final diagnosis is based
on radiographic evidence of the presence of a cartilaginous core in the distal ulna (a long‐tapering radiolucent
triangle based on the physis) in combination with the
classic signs of angular deformity. Orthogonal radiographic views of the elbow joint, radius/ulna, and manus
are recommended to identify and assess the extent of the
deformities. If limb shortening is suspected, radiographs
of the humerus and comparative radiographs of the
opposite limb are useful.
Treatment

The choice of treatment is dependent on the age of the
dog, the remaining growth potential, and the severity of
the angular deformity. Treatment may consist of conservative management for patients with mild deformity and
limited remaining growth potential, or surgical intervention in patients with more substantial deformity and/or
bone shortening and more remaining growth potential.
Surgical techniques include ulnar ostectomy (for elbow
incongruity and mild deformity), static surgical deformity
correction (radial and ulnar osteotomy, followed by
deformity correction stabilized with an external fixator or
bone plate), and dynamic deformity correction (radial
and ulnar osteotomy, followed by deformity correction

1545

VetBooks.ir

1546

Section 13 Diseases of Bone and Joint

and bone lengthening with an adjustable external fixator). Surgical planning can be facilitated by 3D printed
(plastic) models of the deformity, based on a CT study of
the affected limb.
Prognosis

The prognosis for a normal limb function is good, particularly for patients with mild to moderate deformity. In
patients with significant limb shortening and elbow joint
incongruity, the prognosis may not be as favorable.
Patella Luxation
Etiology and Pathophysiology

Patella luxation (PL) may occur nontraumatically as a
consequence of quadriceps mechanism (quadriceps muscles, patella, and patellar tendon) malalignment with the
underlying bone and/or femoral trochlea articular surface secondary to the development of femoral and tibial
deformities during skeletal growth. Patella luxation also
may be acquired traumatically. The etiology of nontraumatic medial or lateral PL is not well understood. It has
been hypothesized that medial PL is initiated by a
decreased angle of inclination and a diminished angle of
anteversion of the proximal femur early in the postnatal
period. The resulting medial malalignment of the quadriceps mechanism produces eccentric forces across growth
plates and may cause bone deformities, such as coxa vara,
genu varum, distal femoral varus or external torsion,
proximal tibial varus or valgus, internal tibial torsion, and
medial rotation of the tibial tubercle. The malalignment
also may lead to rupture or weakening of periarticular
structures, thus facilitating PL. Malarticulation of the
patellofemoral joint may result in poor development and
shallowness of the trochlear groove, diminishing the normal retention of the patella.
It has been suggested that PL is a multifactorial polygenic disease. Strong breed predispositions have been
recognized (see Table 174.1). For instance, according to
the Orthopedic Foundation for Animals, 43% of examined Pomeranians had PL. A PL heritability of 0.17 was
reported and quantitative trait loci were identified on
chromosome 7 and 31 in a Dutch flat‐coated retriever
population. This moderate heritability suggests that
environmental factors play an important role in the
development of the disease.
Epidemiology

In general, small‐breed dogs are more likely to be affected
than large‐breed dogs. Medial PL is more common than
lateral PL in dogs of all sizes and lateral PL is more often
seen in large‐breed than in small‐breed dogs. Many
breeds have strong predispositions (see Table 174.1). In
small‐breed dogs, females appear to be more commonly

affected than males, while the opposite has been reported
for large‐breed dogs. Bilateral disease is common.
History and Clinical Signs

This condition is often asymptomatic, particularly in
small‐breed dogs, and may go unrecognized until incidentally discovered. Large‐breed dogs are rarely asymptomatic. Dogs suffering from PL may present with
lameness, intermittent skipping, a history of short acute
pain episodes, and/or exercise intolerance. Differential
diagnoses, particularly in small breeds, include cranial
cruciate disease, which often occurs concurrently, and
intervertebral disc disease.
Diagnosis

The diagnosis of medial or lateral PL is based on the
examiner’s ability to manually luxate the patella in medial
and/or lateral directions. Starting with the leg in full
extension, the patella is located and pushed in the medial
or lateral direction, while simultaneously slowly flexing
the hock and stifle joint and internally or externally
rotating the limb respectively. Simultaneously abducting
or adducting the limb may further encourage the patella
to luxate medially or laterally. This test is considered
positive (patella luxation) if during flexion of the stifle
joint the patella can be moved medial or lateral to the
medial or lateral femoral trochlear ridge. It should be
noted that with the stifle in full extension, the patella easily can be moved in medial and lateral direction; this
patellar mobility is normal and not indicative of patella
luxation.
The disease is classified according to the anatomic
relationship of the patella and trochlear groove during
the gait cycle. Patients with a grade I PL are usually
asymptomatic. Their patella is normally positioned in
the trochlear groove but the patella can be manually
luxated. Grade II is characterized by a normally positioned patella that may spontaneously luxate and relocate, which may cause acute pain and/or “skipping.”
The luxated patella may reduce spontaneously or can
be manually reduced. With a grade III PL, the patella
is found in a luxated position; the patella can be easily
reduced manually. In patients with a grade IV PL,
the patella is permanently luxated and cannot be
reduced. Bone angular deformities and trochlea maldevelopment become more severe with increasing
grade of PL.
The main purpose of radiography is to assess the severity of secondary osteoarthritic changes, determine the
location of the patella in the trochlear groove (lateral or
medially displaced or abnormally proximal or distal to the
normal central position, termed patella alta or patella
baja, respectively) and elucidate the degree of femoral
and tibial deformity. In cases of low‐grade PL and mild

VetBooks.ir

174 Developmental Orthopedic Diseases

skeletal abnormalities, mediolateral and caudocranial
views of the stifle will suffice. If more deformity is detected
during the orthopedic exam, additional orthogonal
(“alignment”) views of femur and tibia to characterize the
angular deformities are recommended. CT allows better
evaluation of the deformities and may be beneficial in
patients with severe deformities.
Treatment

Patients with grade I PL are asymptomatic and usually do
not require treatment. Grade II PL patients may require
treatment if the pain or skipping episodes increase in
duration or frequency. If clinical signs are mild, fewer
than 2–3 episodes per month, or if the owner is unable to
pursue surgical treatment, nonsurgical treatment is a
reasonable option. However, just as with grade I luxation, the patient should be reevaluated if the lameness
becomes more severe or frequent.
Surgical intervention is indicated for patients with
persistent lameness due to grade II, III or IV PL. The
purpose of the intervention is to realign the patella and
quadriceps complex over the trochlear groove and the
long axis of the femur, and to stabilize the patella in the
trochlear groove. In most patients with grade II or III
PL and mild femoral and tibial deformity, the alignment is obtained with a transposition of the tibial
tuberosity in the medial, lateral and/or distal direction.
The patella is stabilized in the trochlear groove with a
combination of trochleoplasty (deepening of the trochlear groove) and parapatellar soft tissue release and
imbrication techniques. Transposition is performed
after the apophyseal physis of the tibia has closed. In
patients with grade III or IV and more severe deformity, particularly large‐breed dogs, corrective distal femoral osteotomies may be needed to obtain adequate
alignment, in addition to the aforementioned techniques. In patients with grade III or IV PL and severe
osteoarthritic changes refractory to conservative management, a partial or total stifle replacement may be
indicated. The long‐term utility of partial stifle replacement (trochlea arthroplasty) in clinical patients has yet
to be described.
Prognosis

The prognosis for lateral and medial PL is similar and
mostly depends on the severity of the deformity. For
Grade II and III luxations, the prognosis for return of
function is good, while for most grade IV luxations the
prognosis is fair to good. However, for some patients
with chronic grade IV luxation with severe femoral
and tibial deformity, severe OA and/or severe muscle
atrophy and contracture, the prognosis is much more
guarded.

Legg–Calvé–Perthes Disease
Etiology and Pathophysiology

Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease (LCP) is an uncommon
cause of pelvic limb lameness in small‐breed dogs. The
lameness is associated with lysis, fragmentation, collapse, and deformity of the femoral head, including the
joint surface. These changes are the result of avascular
necrosis and structural weakening of the bone of femoral
head. Synonyms for LCP include osteochondritis coxae
juvenilis, osteochondrosis, coxa plana, aseptic necrosis
of the femoral head, and avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
The etiology of LCP is unknown but increased intracapsular pressure, abnormal anatomic conformation,
infarction of the femoral head, hormonal influences, and
heredity have been implicated as etiologic factors. Strong
breed predispositions exist (see Table 174.1) and it has
been suggested that LCP is a simple autosomal recessive
trait in West Highland white terriers and miniature poodles. In Manchester terriers, the trait is a simple autosomal recessive or multifactorial with high heritability.
Epidemiology

In one study, 277 of 33 633(0.82%) patients diagnosed with
an appendicular bone diseases were suffering from LCP.
Signalment

Predisposed breeds include terriers and toy‐breed dogs,
with affected dogs most commonly being presented
between 4 and 11 months of age. Males and females are
equally represented.
History and Clinical Signs

Patients present with unilateral or bilateral pelvic limb
discomfort, lameness, and muscle atrophy. Lameness
can be mild to nonweight bearing, although in minimally
affected cases the disease may be subclinical. Bilateral
involvement occurs in 12–16.5% of cases.
Diagnosis

Orthopedic exam findings may include muscle atrophy,
pain on hyperextension and manipulation of the hip
joint, and crepitus. An extended ventrodorsal and a
mediolateral view of the hip joint that include the proximal femurs are recommended. If positioning for this
view is causing discomfort, a flexed ventrodorsal (frogleg) view of the coxofemoral joint may be used. An additional advantage of this view is that it may help elucidate
the defect on radiographs. Early radiographic signs
sometimes include increased epiphyseal opacity but
more commonly, patients are presented with focal lytic
lesions of the femoral head. In later stages of the disease, collapse and flattening of the femoral head and

1547

VetBooks.ir

1548

Section 13 Diseases of Bone and Joint

remodeling of the acetabula, femoral neck lysis, and
possible associated compression fractures may be seen.
Computed tomography may be beneficial for the detection of small lesions in patients with early‐stage disease
where LCP is suspected but no radiographic evidence of
the disease is seen. Orthopedic examination will rule
out common differential diagnoses such as patellar luxation and cranial cruciate ligament rupture. Less common differential diagnoses include septic arthritis,
neoplasia, and osteomyelitis.
Treatment

Analgesics and rest result in lameness resolution in less
than 25% of cases. Surgical treatment with femoral head
and neck excision or total hip replacement is recommended if patients do not respond to conservative management. At the time of surgery, excised tissue should be
submitted for histopathology and bacterial culture to
rule out neoplasia and osteomyelitis.
Prognosis

Surgery resolves lameness and discomfort in 84–100% of
LCP cases. Persistent lameness may be due to the resultant change in biomechanics and reduced range of motion
associated with femoral head and neck excision.

Craniomandibular Osteopathy
Etiology and Pathophysiology

Craniomandibular osteopathy is characterized by unilateral or bilateral irregular symmetric osseous proliferation on mandibles and/or tympanic bullae, causing
difficulties opening the mouth. Temporal, frontal, maxillary, and long bones can also be affected. The disease can
be self‐limiting. Synonyms for craniomandibular osteopathy (CMO) include lion jaw, Scotty jaw, Westie jaw,
craniomandibular osteodystrophy, mandibular periostitis, and craniomandibular osteoarthropathy.
In affected mandibulae, lamellar bone is resorbed and
new bone originating from the periosteum invades the
adjacent connective tissue and muscle fibers. Bone
marrow is replaced by a highly vascular fibrous‐type
stroma and inflammatory cells (lymphocytes, neutrophils, and plasma cells) that surround the lesions. The
etiology of the disease is unknown but strong breed
predispositions suggest a hereditary etiology. The condition is autosomal recessive in West Highland white
terriers. A test to determine genetic predisposition for
the test is available.

Epidemiology

The disease has a reported incidence of 1.4 per 100 000
cases. The incidence of the disease is highest in the
southern and western regions of the United States.
Signalment

Dogs from many breeds, including large‐ and small‐
breed dogs, can be affected (see Table 174.1). Females
and males are equally represented. Patients younger than
6 months are at the highest risk for being affected by
CMO, while the probability for diagnosis decreases in
patients over 12 months of age.
History and Clinical Signs

Patients affected by CMO are most commonly presented
with complaints of not eating, difficulty eating or drinking or complete inability to open the mouth. Additional
clinical signs that have been reported include discomfort,
swelling of the mandibles, intermittent hyperthermia,
increased salivation, exophthalmia, and strabismus.
Diagnosis

Clinical signs include inability to partially or completely
open the patient’s mouth and swelling of the mandibles
and/or temporomandibular joint region. The final diagnosis is based on demonstration of osseous proliferation
on mandibles and/or tympanic bullae using ventrodorsal, lateral, and oblique radiographs of skull and mandibles. Computed tomography may be useful in identifying
small lesions in early stages of the disease and may also
allow the extent of the lesions to be more accurately
characterized. A complete blood count, serum chemistry, and urinalysis are recommended when systemic
signs are present. Fine needle aspirate/biopsy for histopathology and culture are recommended to rule out
other diseases, including osteomyelitis, neoplasia, and
metabolic bone diseases.
Treatment

There is no known medical or surgical cure for this condition. Treatment is primarily aimed at supportive care.
Feeding soft food, gruel food, or syringe‐fed food, and/or
placement of a feeding tube may be needed for as long as
the patient is unable to take in an adequate amount of
water and food. The level of treatment is based on the
severity of the condition and the patient’s ability to drink
and eat, so hydration and nutrition must be carefully and
frequently evaluated. Analgesics should be prescribed if
indicated. During febrile periods, patients may be treated
with antibiotics and steroids or NSAIDs. These treatments
are empirical and the benefits of these medications are
variable. Excision of osseous proliferations and/or rostral
hemimandibulectomy may be considered as salvage procedures for severe cases to permit improved alimentation.

VetBooks.ir

174 Developmental Orthopedic Diseases

Prognosis

The condition is often self‐limiting by 11–13 months of
age and until this time, supportive care is paramount.
There are no predictive factors to determine if the bony
proliferations will regress partially or completely. For
owners who are unable to provide adequate care, for the
rare severe case, and for cases with intractable discomfort, euthanasia is an option.
Panosteitis
Etiology and Pathophysiology

Panosteitis is a self‐limiting disease of the bone marrow
of fore‐ and hindlimb long bones. Synonyms for panosteitis include shifting leg lameness, enostosis, and eosinophilic panosteitis.
The earliest changes in affected long bones are seen
around the nutrient foramen. Vascular proliferation and
bone formation result in vascular congestion and increased
intraosseous pressure. In response to the increased intraosseous pressure, dogs develop lameness of the affected
limb and form bone in periosteum and medullary cavity.
Eventually, the affected bone marrow is replaced by
normal, healthy adipose bone marrow. The etiology of
panosteitis is unknown but strong breed predispositions
(see Table 174.1) suggest a genetic component.
Epidemiology

The reported incidence of panosteitis is 2.6 per 1000
patients. The disease incidence is higher in north central
and northeastern regions of the United States, especially
in the summer and fall.
Signalment

Panosteitis is primarily a disease of medium‐ and large‐
breed pure‐bred dogs. However, smaller dogs (either
mixed breed or pure bred) such as the American cocker
spaniel and the West Highland white terrier can also be
affected. Males are more frequently affected than females
(4:1), with patients most commonly affected between 5
and 12 months of age. However, patients have been diagnosed as young as 2 months and as old as 5 years. In a
study of 100 dogs, the median age of affected dogs was
12.4 months.
History and Clinical Signs

Panosteitis patients are often presented with a history of
lameness, often shifting between limbs (shifting lameness). Lameness ranges from mild to nonambulatory.
The occurrence can be acute in onset and may run a
waxing–waning course. There is a 4:1 ratio of lesions in
the forelimbs to hindlimbs, with 42%, 25%, 14%, 11%, and
8% occurrence in the ulna, radius, humerus, femur, and
tibia, respectively. The affected bones may be painful on

palpation. Systemic signs including fever, anorexia, lethargy, and weight loss may accompany the lameness. The
signs may regress and reoccur, but rarely continue past 2
years of age.
Diagnosis

Depending on the disease phase, radiographic findings
from orthogonal views of the affected bone(s) may vary
from completely normal to the classic blurring and inhomogeneity of the medullary cavity trabecular pattern.
The first stage, rarely seen, is characterized by a decrease
of the radiodensity of the medullary cavity near the
nutrient foramen. In the next stage, an increased medullary opacity with a granular pattern or loss of trabeculation, as well as periosteal bone formation, is seen. In a
later stage, changes in the medullary cavity become more
diffuse and homogeneous. After 4–6 weeks the lesions
regress and a coarse trabecular network develops. It
should be noted that radiographic signs are not correlated with patient discomfort or lameness.
Differential diagnoses include elbow dysplasia, OCD,
hip dysplasia, and HOD.
Treatment

There are no known medical or surgical cures for this
condition. Treatment consists primarily of analgesics
(NSAIDs) and rest.
Prognosis

The disease is self‐limiting, although recurrences are possible, reportedly even until the patient is 5 years of age.
Hypertrophic Osteodystrophy
Etiology and Pathophysiology

Hypertrophic osteodystrophy (HOD) is a disease of predominantly young, growing large‐breed dogs, characterized by metaphyseal swelling of affected bones and
lameness. Synonyms for HOD include infantile scurvy,
Moller Barlow disease, juvenile scurvy, osteodystrophy
II, skeletal scurvy, and metaphyseal osteopathy.
The etiology of HOD is unknown. Proposed theories
include overnutrition, vitamin C deficiency, infection,
vaccinations, and heritability. In more recent reports, the
etiologic roles of overnutrition and vitamin C deficiency
have been questioned.
Many large dog breeds are predisposed to HOD (see
Table 174.1) and therefore a genetic etiology has been
suggested. In a litter of affected Weimaraners, the heritability was estimated to be 0.68.
Several lines of evidence suggest an infectious etiology.
Specifically, many affected dogs have a history of, or
actually are suffering from, a systemic illness (for instance,
a respiratory infection). Active bacteremia (E. coli) in an

1549

VetBooks.ir

1550

Section 13 Diseases of Bone and Joint

affected dog has also been reported. Canine distemper
virus transcripts have been detected in the metaphysis of
dogs with HOD, but a direct relationship with canine distemper has not been demonstrated. More recently, it was
reported that clinical signs of HOD developed in six
Weimaraner puppies (five of the six were related), 10 days
after administration of a modified live vaccine of canine
distemper virus and canine adenovirus type 2. It was suggested that the HOD may have been facilitated by an
inherited immunodeficiency with low concentrations of
circulating immunoglobulins.
Epidemiology

Hypertrophic osteodystrophy is reported to occur in 2.8
per 100 000 cases. In one study, the incidence was highest in the northeastern regions of the United States, and
was highest in the fall and lowest in the winter.
Signalment

Several breeds are predisposed to HOD (see Table 174.1).
Males are more often affected than females (2.3:1) with
patients most commonly being presented between 2 and
6 months of age.
History and Clinical Signs

Hypertrophic osteodystrophy is a disease of young, rapidly growing dogs. The distal radius, ulna, and tibia are
the most commonly affected bones but the condition has
also been diagnosed in the humerus, mandible, ribs,
maxilla, femur, skull, vertebra, and scapula. Affected
patients have unilateral or bilateral swelling at the metaphyseal region(s) of affected bone(s). If the distal radius
and ulna are affected, an angular limb deformity may be
seen if a synostosis develops between radius and ulna.
Warmth and varying degrees of discomfort can be appreciated when palpating the swellings, with subsequent
lameness ensuing. The lameness may range from mild to
a complete inability to stand or walk. Additional systemic clinical signs may include anorexia, depression,
hyperthermia, and diarrhea.
Diagnosis

The hallmark radiographic finding is a metaphyseal radiolucent zone with adjacent sclerosis parallel and adjacent
to the growth plate. In a later stage, periosteal and
endosteal bone proliferation may be noted. Metaphyseal
enlargement and irregular widening of the growth plate
may be present in advanced disease stages. As the condition resolves, resolution of the radiolucent line and
remodeling of the periosteal reaction will occur. In
severely affected dogs with a secondary synostosis, an
angular limb deformity may develop. If a patient has systemic clinical signs, a complete blood count, serum
chemistry and urinalysis, as well as blood or synovial

fluid culture, may be indicated. Differential diagnoses
include septic polyarthritis, panosteitis, polyarthropathies, polyneuritis, polymyocytis, secondary nutritional
hyperparathyroidism, neosporosis, and toxoplasmosis.
In Newfoundlands, metaphyseal dysplasia also may be
considered.
Treatment

There are no known medical or surgical cures for this
condition. Treatment varies depending upon the severity
of the disease. In mildly affected dogs, a balanced diet (a
nutritional association has been reported) and NSAIDs
will be sufficient. In more severely affected dogs, more
supportive care may be needed, particularly if the patient
is reluctant to eat, hyperthermic, and/or unable to get
up. Antibiotics are indicated for patients with bacteremia. Severely affected Weimaraner puppies without bacteremia may respond better to steroids than to NSAIDs.
Prognosis

The prognosis is generally good to excellent for mild to
moderate cases. The disease is usually self‐limiting, typically within days to weeks, but can persist for months
with multiple recurrences possible. In severe cases, death
may occur. In cases with intractable disease and/or
refractory to treatment, euthanasia should be considered. All owners should be counseled on the potential for
secondary angular limb deformities.
Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
Etiology and Pathophysiology

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) is a nontraumatic, slowly progressive lateral slippage of the proximal
femoral metaphysis through the growth plate, resulting
in separation of the proximal femoral metaphysis from
the capital femoral epiphysis, causing pelvic limb lameness. The disease is most commonly seen in mature cats
but also has been reported in dogs. Synonyms include
spontaneous femoral capital physeal fracture, femoral
neck metaphyseal osteopathy, and femoral capital physeal dysplasia.
The etiology of the metaphyseal slippage is unknown.
Some have suggested that in cats, the slippage is the
result of weakening of the capital physis due to a multicentric dysplasia. Others proposed that SCFE in cats is
the result of early (juvenile) castration. The ensuing
delayed growth plate closure due to hypotestosteronism, together with obesity, exposes the physis to
increased/excessive/supraphysiologic cyclic shear forces
during the gait cycle, resulting in spontaneous slippage
and separation. The latter hypothesis is consistent with
the pathophysiology of SCFE in children and other animal species.

VetBooks.ir

174 Developmental Orthopedic Diseases

Epidemiology

The disease is uncommon, but an incidence has not been
reported.
Signalment

Cats are more commonly affected than dogs. Reported
feline cases are almost all neutered overweight males
presented when they were 4.5–42 months of age. In one
study of 13 cats, 23% were Siamese.
History and Clinical Signs

Clinical signs include uni‐ or bilateral lameness, decreased
ability to jump, weakness, and crepitus and pain during
palpation. Lameness can be acute in onset but is mostly
insidious and possibly intermittent. It was reported that
at initial presentation, 24–38% of cases were affected
bilaterally but not necessarily symmetrically.
Diagnosis

Radiographic lesions vary with the stage of the disease.
Early on in the disease, the capital growth plate is slightly

widened compared to the normal contralateral one and
slippage may be demonstrated on extended ventrodorsal
pelvic radiographs. In later stages, the proximal femoral
metaphysis may be craniodorsally displaced relative to
the epiphysis, with resorption and sclerosis of the femoral
neck. Ultrasound (slippage and periphyseal fluid accumulation) and/or computed tomography may be helpful
in early stages without obvious radiographic signs.
Treatment

The most common method of treatment is femoral
head and neck ostectomy because of progressive femoral neck resorption. Successful primary stabilization
with Kirschner wire and total hip replacement have
been reported.
Prognosis

The prognosis for patients treated with femoral head and
neck ostectomy is excellent, although limb function is
not normal. Unilateral cases can present with contralateral disease later in life.

Canine and Feline End of Life Care
Robin Downing, DVM, MS, DAAPM, DACVSMR
The Downing Center for Animal Pain Management, LLC, Windsor, CO, USA

The Buddhists say “Pain is inevitable; suffering is
optional.” Our obligation in veterinary medicine is to
recognize, relieve, and prevent pain and suffering in
the animals entrusted to our care. At no time is this
­obligation to advocate on behalf of beings who cannot
advocate for themselves more imperative than when an
animal approaches the end of its life.
Veterinary medicine and human medicine are intimately intertwined. Many of the life‐saving procedures
now used for human patients had their roots in animal
models. Likewise, most pharmaceuticals undergo animal
testing before they are brought to trials in human subjects. The flow of medical knowledge, information, technology, and techniques between human and veterinary
medicine is bidirectional. Advanced surgical techniques
(e.g., arthroscopy), advanced diagnostic technologies
(e.g., magnetic resonance imaging [MRI]), and critical
care interventions (e.g., mechanical ventilation) have
been embraced by veterinary medicine and have proved
to be game‐changers, allowing countless animals who
would otherwise have succumbed to their conditions or
been euthanized to be restored to life and health. It is a
logical extension of the search for better and broader
ways to practice veterinary medicine for veterinarians to
recognize the utility of evaluating human palliative medicine and hospice care for application to animal patients.
Companion animals have made a migration of Biblical
proportions from the backyard to the bedroom and from
the kennel to the couch. The evolving role of pets as
members of the family, coupled with advances in preventive and interventive medicine, has resulted in dramatically longer life expectancies among dogs and cats. One
consequence of longer lifespans in pets is the emergence
of age‐related diseases and physiologic breakdowns
that were once considered unusual. Examples include
multiple joint osteoarthritis, pulmonary hypertension,

systemic hypertension, advanced renal disease, and
­cancers of all types. When pets did not generally live as
long as they do now – when their cause of death was an
infectious disease or a violent event like being hit by a
car – neither veterinarians nor pet owners were faced
with the slow, incremental declines so often witnessed
now. Squiring companion animals into advanced old age
has opened the door to a new discipline of veterinary
palliative medicine and hospice care. Human palliative
and hospice medicine can provide veterinarians with a
template to follow when adapting and adopting these
principles and practices for veterinary application.
But a simple translation is not enough. In human end of
life care, the patient must, with rare exceptions, die on his
or her own. Exceptions at the time of this writing are found
in the states of Oregon, Washington, Montana, California,
New Jersey, and Vermont where physician‐assisted death
with ­dignity has been affirmed as legally available. Of note,
however, is that physician‐assisted death with dignity
remains ultimately the act of the patient, generally by
refusing food and water or by ingesting a lethal dose of
a barbiturate drug previously prescribed by a physician.
Only in a few jurisdictions worldwide, most notably the
Netherlands, can the physician take an active role in the
patient’s death by performing voluntary active euthanasia.
What that means for the majority of dying humans is that
they must die on their own.
The gift of euthanasia, translated from the Greek as
“good death,” remains, at least in the Americas, exclusively in the hands of veterinarians. The single most
important caution to the veterinary profession in
embracing wholesale the palliative medicine and hospice
care model provided by human medicine is to resist the
temptation to force animals to suffer to death rather than
providing compassionate, humane euthanasia. It is
equally important to resist the temptation to force heroic

interventions with little hope for success on animals
who are approaching their end of life. Finally, it is also a
veterinarian’s obligation to the pet, the pet owner, and
the precious human–animal bond not to force or rush
euthanasia on a patient whose care has shifted from that
of curative to palliative. Ours is a delicate balance to
negotiate.
In addition to drawing palliative care strategies from
the disciplines of pain management, physical rehabilitation, behavior medicine, and oncology, it is to the discipline of clinical bioethics that the veterinary profession
should turn for guidance when evaluating the application of interventive, palliative, or hospice techniques
in end of life care. The foundational principles of biomedical ethics – respect for autonomy, nonmaleficence,
beneficence, and justice – all have a role to play during
the decision making that occurs as an animal approaches
the end of its life. Before exploring the application of
the principles of biomedical ethics in end of life clinical
veterinary medicine, it is appropriate to consider the
development and evolution of veterinary palliative medicine and hospice care, as well as the many techniques
that can be used to sustain a life‐limited pet’s comfort
and quality of life until the time when humane euthanasia becomes the most reasonable choice.

­Veterinary Palliative Medicine
and Hospice Care
Veterinary palliative medicine and hospice care derive
their basic principles from human palliative and hospice
care, both directly and by analogy. Historically, hospices
were first places of refuge for travelers, often those on a
religious pilgrimage. In the 11th century, the focus
shifted to care of the incurably ill who either had no family or could not afford other care. Hospice providers were
typically members of various religious orders. In the 19th
century, the formal concept of caring for the dying
emerged, first in France in 1842. In the late 1800s and
early 1900s, several facilities that are still in existence
opened in England and Australia to attend to the dying.
Religious orders continued to provide care, as this
­preceded the phenomenon of “medicalizing” the dying
process. Hospice in the US began in earnest in the 19th
century, mirroring activities in the US and Australia. A
leap forward in the development of palliative care and
hospice occurred following the 1969 publication of Dr
Elisabeth Kübler‐Ross’ seminal work, On Death and
Dying. She and others created awareness about the lack
of adequate care for the dying, and sharpened the focus
on the important role palliative care and hospice can fill.

While the original hospices were places for the dying,
it is important to understand that hospice is a philosophy
of caring that “affirms the concept of palliative care as an
intensive program that enhances comfort and promotes
… quality of life … When cure is no longer possible, hospice recognizes that a peaceful and comfortable death is
an essential goal of health care…” This commitment to
quality of life and comfort care brought to the patient
lends itself well to the veterinary profession. Animal
patients can be seen and cared for in many settings,
including the clinic and the home. The emergence of
ambulatory companion animal veterinary practices
clearly demonstrates the response of the veterinary profession to the demand for veterinary care provided in the
comfort of the animal’s home. This paradigm of sophisticated in‐home care further reinforces the opportunity to
provide palliative and hospice care to pets who are
approaching the end of their lives.
The first formal discussion of hospice for animals
was presented at the Delta Society’s 10th Annual
Conference in Portland, Oregon by Drs Guy Hancock
and James Harris, and Ms Bonnie Mader. The presentation, “The hospice concept for animals,” was delivered at multiple regional, national, and international
conferences by Dr Hancock between 1995 and 2005.
Dr Eric Clough, a veterinarian in New Hampshire,
alongside his wife, June, a registered nurse with expertise in human hospice, were also pioneers in applying the concepts of animal ­hospice and palliative care.
In 2001, the American Veterinary Medical Association
approved the first “Veterinary Hospice Care Guidelines,”
an open‐access document available at www.avma.org.
In 2003, the Pet Hospice Volunteer Student Outreach
Program was launched by the Argus Institute at
the Colorado State University College of Veterinary
Medicine and Biomedical Sciences.
During the ensuing years, a clear focus on quality of
life during the end of life of companion animals has
emerged, leading to the establishment of the International
Association for Animal Hospice and Palliative Care
(www.iaahpc.org) as well as the provision of postgraduate continuing education on the subject for both veterinarians and veterinary technicians/nurses. Clearly, there
is a need for the veterinary profession to understand its
critical role in a pet’s end of life care. There truly is a
“space” between ceasing to pursue a cure and the time
when humane euthanasia is in the best interest of the
patient. It is also worth noting that while only recently
has the term “palliative care” entered the mainstream
veterinary vocabulary, veterinarians routinely provide
what qualifies as palliative care. Palliative medicine is
care that is not focused on a cure but rather on improving and maintaining good quality of life. Pets with many

VetBooks.ir

different conditions enjoy the benefits of this approach
long before they are at the end of life, including those
with diabetes mellitus, systemic hypertension, and
chronic kidney disease.
At the end of life, with the many sophisticated interventional options available, it is appropriate for veterinarians to exercise a more formal approach to the
necessary decision making that occurs. Veterinarians
must combine the following elements in order to help
the pet owner make ongoing care decisions that are in
the best interest of the pet approaching its death.
Regular evaluations of the animal’s quality of life in
dialogue with the pet owner.
●● Regular assessment of the human family’s quality of
life as they care for the pet.
●● Regular reevaluation of the therapeutic goals of care.
●● Application of the foundational principles of clinical
bioethics (respect for autonomy, nonmaleficence,
beneficence, and justice) to both the patient and the
human family during decision making to maximize
outcomes and to act in the best interest of all
parties.
●●

When considering any intervention as a pet approaches
the end of its life, it is important to ask the question, “Just
because we can, does that mean we should?”

­Evaluating and Maintaining Quality
of Life in End of Life Care
As soon as a life‐limiting disease is diagnosed, it is
appropriate to open a dialogue with the pet owner about
the anticipated arc of the disease process on the way
to the end of the pet’s life. Likewise, it is important to lay
the foundation for periodic ongoing evaluations of the
pet’s quality of life. Finally, it is important to consider
the effects of pet end of life care on the family’s quality
of life. Caring for a beloved animal family member at the
end of life can become overwhelming and fraught with
­emotional overload. The veterinarian’s obligation is to
advocate on behalf of a being who cannot advocate
for itself, and that obligation becomes even more
­critical when choreographing care at the end of life
(Figure 175.1).
Quality of life is an exquisitely subjective concept.
Quantifying a particular pet’s quality of life is equally
subjective. Each pet’s quality of life must be assessed on
a case‐by‐case basis as every animal is unique. Likewise,
every family situation must stand on its own merits in
order to assess both the financial and emotional
resources that are available for care of the pet approaching its death.

Figure 175.1 A comfort room lends itself well to end of life
consultations with pet owners. Source: Courtesy of Robin
Downing, DVM.

Dr Alice Villalobos has created a Quality of Life
Scale to use in dialogue with pet owners to offer a somewhat objective assessment of what is a very subjective
experience (Table 175.1). The scale considers seven
parameters, each scored 1–10 (10 is best). A score at or
above 5 in each category with an overall score of 35 or
greater generally suggests an acceptable quality of life.
While a particular score is important, the trend of scores
over time is a more accurate representation of how the
pet is doing. A single low score may illuminate a weakness in the palliative care plan, calling for a fine‐tuning of
care. On the other hand, a low score in even a single category may signal the time when humane euthanasia is in
the pet’s best interest. The seven parameters follow the
mnemonic HHHHHMM.
