Hurt
Adequate pain management is the cornerstone of end of
life care, and a key to sustaining an acceptable quality of
life. Dr Lloyd E Davis wrote in 1983:
[o]ne of the psychological curiosities of therapeutic decision making is the withholding of analgesic drugs because the clinician is not absolutely
certain that the animal is experiencing pain. Yet
the same individual will administer antibiotics
without documenting the presence of an infection. Pain and suffering constitute the only situation in which I believe that, if in doubt, one should
go ahead and treat.
Because pain is such a major factor in diminished quality
of life, excellent, aggressive, and comprehensive (e.g.,
multimodal) pain management plays a critical role in
applying palliative care and hospice principles to pets.
While humans have eschewed overt cruelty to animals
from Biblical times, it is only within the past several decades that human understanding of nonhuman pain and
suffering has expanded to include a more proactive
approach to recognizing and relieving that pain. Richard
D. Ryder, in his groundbreaking work Painism: A Modern

Morality, coined the term “panience” to describe the
principle that a moral code should be based on the capacity to feel pain. He went on to state that the terms “pain”
and “suffering” are interchangeable and “what matters
morally is the degree of pain and not who or what experiences it.” In Ryder’s worldview, pain is the common
enemy of all beings. Ryder’s work, alongside that of scientists like Marc Bekoff and Frank McMillan, lays the
foundation for applying clinical bioethical principles to
pet end of life and quality of life considerations. There
are several excellent resources for practitioners to access
in creating appropriate pain management plans for
patients approaching the end of life.
Appropriate pain management at the end of life is a
function of striking a balance between risks and benefits.
Regardless of the root of the palliative care patient’s pain,
the practitioner must always start with a careful pain palpation assessment to determine all the uncomfortable
areas on the body in order to create as comprehensive a
pain management strategy as possible. The ability to
breathe falls into this category, and trouble breathing
trumps all other concerns about quality of life. Because
animals cannot self‐report, measurement of oxygen saturation may be an important part of patient assessment
if breathing is compromised in any way.

One final consideration for managing pain at the end
of life is to use nonpharmacologic strategies. These
include modifying the pet’s environment and everyday
handling in order to maximize comfort (Figure 175.2).

Appetite stimulants as well as antinausea medications
may be indicated, at least in the short term. For an animal experiencing difficulty prehending, chewing, or

appropriate if other quality of life parameters remain
high. This is a minimally invasive technique requiring a
very short period of general anesthesia, and the contribution to overall quality of life can be significant.

Many techniques commonly employed in physical medicine lend themselves very well to relieving pain and
supporting comfort in veterinary palliative and hospice
care patients. Application of heat and cold, stretching,
joint mobilizations, massage, neuromodulatory acupuncture, photobiomodulation via therapeutic laser,
transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS),
neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES), as well as
some proprioceptive retraining and therapeutic exercise, can all contribute to pain relief in this population of
patients.
Hunger
Hunger can serve as an important barometer of a pet’s
quality of life. If the pet remains hungry and willing to
eat, it is reasonable to presume that it is still interested in
living. On the other hand, a decline in appetite is one
part of the natural process as the end of life approaches.
Nutritional support is important if hospice care is to
continue, and malnutrition and weight loss occur quickly
in an anorectic pet. Hand feeding or feeding a different
texture (canned versus dry kibble) may enhance appetite.

Hydration
Many animals approaching the end of life do not drink
enough to sustain metabolic functions. Dehydration not
only undermines quality of life, it hastens the decline of
all metabolic functions, particularly waste elimination by
the kidneys. Many animals readily accept the delivery of
subcutaneous (SC) fluids, and this is an easy technique
to teach pet owners (Figure 175.3). It is important to link
the delivery of SC fluids with something that the pet
enjoys, like tasty treats or gentle combing or brushing, in
order to minimize any objection the pet may have to
receiving fluids. If a pet receiving end of life care vigorously objects to receiving SC fluids in spite of all attempts
to make the procedure as comfortable as possible, it is
important to respect the animal’s expressed preference.
To force fluids on an uncooperative hospice patient
­compromises quality of life.
Hygiene
Good hygiene is an important component of good quality of life. As animals approach the end of their lives,
they may develop fecal and/or urinary incontinence,
which is the most likely hygiene issue these pet owners
will face. Preventing urine and fecal scalding is a priority

1559

VetBooks.ir

1560

Section 14 Social and Ethical Issues in Veterinary Medicine

in these patients. Keep hair trimmed short around the
genitals and anus to facilitate cleaning. It may be worth
considering a whole‐body trim to make day‐to‐day
grooming easier for both the pet and pet owner.
Reusable/washable diapers as well as diapers with
replaceable absorbent pads are available for animals
whose incontinence is intermittent or unpredictable.
Waterproof bedding covers facilitate clean‐up. Cats may
need to have one side of their litter pan cut away to make
entry easy. If the pet has any areas of devitalized tissue
that secrete serum and form crusts (e.g., a tumor that
cannot be removed), lemon juice in a 1:1 dilution with
water can be used to cleanse the area, and absorbent fabrics like cotton T‐shirts may be used to help manage
exudates. Waterless shampoos also work well to keep
immobilized pets clean.
Happiness
Happiness may be the most subjective of the quality of
life parameters to be measured during the pet’s end of
life time, but it is an important one. It is in this area in
particular that the veterinarian must listen very carefully
to the client’s report of how the pet is doing overall. The
pet’s mental state and psychosocial well‐being are critical components of quality of life. Dogs and cats communicate with their eyes, their facial expressions, and their
actions. These are social creatures, and their happiness
depends upon interaction with “their” humans. Animals
engage in many mutual care behaviors that can be mimicked by the human caregiver to contribute to happiness,
including stroking and sounds of contentment (e.g.,
purring while interacting with a cat patient).
Owners of animals receiving end of life care must be
instructed to think through the activities the pet has
enjoyed over its lifetime, and then to consider how those
activities and interactions may be modified to provide
joy to the pet. For instance, the author worked with a toy
poodle who had been felled by a stroke. She became paralyzed in the rear legs and profoundly paretic in the front
legs. Her greatest joy before her stroke was playing tug‐
of‐war with a cloth toy. She would bring the toy to one or
another family member and ask them to play. The family
simply modified this game by initiating play sessions
themselves. This dog obviously derived great joy from
these play sessions.
Many end of life pets will cheer up and greatly anticipate their interactions with their human family members. Feeding, grooming, play, simple stroking, and
strategic placement so that the pet may watch what the
family is doing are all simple strategies for enhancing
happiness. McMillan makes a strong case that animals
not only do experience happiness, but that their happiness contributes immeasurably to their quality of life. In
general, we can equate happiness with the will to live.

Figure 175.4 A cart can restore and maintain mobility. Source:
Courtesy of Robin Downing, DVM.

Mobility
As the inevitable decline toward approaching death proceeds, animals may lose their ability to move independently. How much of an impact this makes on the pet’s
quality of life and the family’s ability to continue end of
life care may depend on the size/weight of the patient as
well as the willingness of the pet to accept assistance.
There are many mobility assistance options available for
pets of all sizes, and simple environmental modification
may make a profound impact, allowing a pet to sustain
its own ability to get up and down and move around
(Figure 175.4). Providing nonskid floor surfaces, preventing unsupervised access to stairs, utilizing ramps for
entry and exit from vehicles, as well as slings, supportive
vests, and pet wheelchairs are all simple strategies for
sustaining mobility. The owners of immobilized end of
life pets must be instructed in the details of preventing
decubital ulcers. The size of the immobilized pet relative
to the size and strength of the pet owner must be considered when deciding whether to proceed with palliative
and hospice care versus opting for humane euthanasia.
More Good Days Than Bad
A single “bad day” in the end of life time of a pet is something to be expected, but more than a few bad days in a
row suggests that quality of life may be too compromised
to continue palliative and hospice care. If the pet is
“turned off” to life, is no longer responding to activities
in its immediate environment, or is withdrawing
from interactions with family members, then quality
of life is compromised. The overarching goal in a pet’s
end of life care is to maintain a healthy, two‐way, interactive human–animal bond (Figure 175.5). When the
HHHHHMM score drops below 35, it is likely that
the end is near. It is the obligation of the veterinarian

­The Four Foundational Principles
of Clinical Bioethics
In Principles of Biomedical Ethics, Tom L. Beauchamp
and James F. Childress describe four foundational principles that may serve as an analytical framework for the
formulation of rules guiding medical decision making.
Respect for autonomy (respecting and supporting
autonomous decisions).
●● Nonmaleficence (avoiding the causing of harm).
●● Beneficence (relieving, lessening, or preventing harm
and providing benefits, and balancing benefits against
risks and costs).
●● Justice (fairly distributing benefits, risks, and costs –
distribution of scarce resources).
●●

Figure 175.5 An end of life care patient quietly resting near family
activities. Source: Courtesy of Robin Downing DVM

coordinating end of life care to speak on behalf of the
dying pet when compassionate, humane euthanasia is in
the pet’s best interest. It is critical, when there are more
bad days than good, not to allow the beloved pet to suffer
to death.

­Pets Should Not Suffer to Death
Occasionally, the veterinary healthcare team will encounter a client whose personal or religious beliefs prohibit
the active ending of a life – any life. If this is the case, then
a deep discussion about the need to prevent an agonizing
death must be a part of the dialogue between the veterinarian and the owner. In a case like this, it is extremely
important to make available powerful pain medication
that can provide heavy sedation and relieve any suffering
that emerges as death approaches. The flipside of this is
the client who wishes to pursue treatments, interventions, and procedures that are futile in the face of the pet’s
life‐limiting disease. In both cases, it is essential to have a
back‐up plan in place to provide the gift of humane
euthanasia at any time of the day or night should the need
arise and should the family decide to pursue that option.
Applying the foundational principles of clinical biomedical ethics provides a useful framework and strategy
for assisting families to negotiate the emotional minefield that end of life care represents. This formal approach
to the decision making involved in end of life care serves
all parties – the pet owner, the veterinary health care
team, and, most importantly, the pet with a life‐limiting
condition who is receiving end of life care.

These four principles, by the authors’ assertion, do not
constitute a general ethical theory, but rather provide a
place to start in order to specify application to a particular patient or case. Application of these four principles of
clinical bioethics requires balancing among them to
decide what, ultimately, is in the best interest of the
patient. These principles have a role to play in clinical
veterinary medicine in general, but they should definitely
play a role leading up to and during a pet’s end of life care
in order to maximize outcomes and quality of life for the
pets and the families who love them.
A conventional application of the four pillars of clinical
bioethics in the context of veterinary end of life care is to
the interactions with the pet owner as the surrogate decision maker. It is, after all, the pet owner who ultimately
makes all the caregiving decisions and who must carry
out all the caregiving activities for the pet approaching
the end of its life. Considering each of the four principles
as described by Beauchamp and Childress, we begin with
respect for autonomy.
Acting autonomously, according to Beauchamp and
Childress, involves three steps.
1) Intentionality (to make and follow a plan).
2) Understanding the consequences of decisions that
will be made.
3) Freedom from control or undue influence in the decision making process.
Respect for the autonomy of the pet owner during a pet’s
end of life care is fairly straightforward and hinges on the
veterinarian providing the owner with enough information in an understandable form that he or she may act as
autonomously as possible at each step of the decision‐
making algorithm as the pet’s dying progresses. While,
legally, the pet is property and can be subjected to nearly
any decision the pet owner might make, aside from gross
negligence or abuse, it is acknowledged that the human–
animal bond helps to define us as humans. James Serpell

1561

VetBooks.ir

1562

Section 14 Social and Ethical Issues in Veterinary Medicine

states that it is “hard to escape the conclusion that the
child‐like qualities of many animals can evoke in people
a strong desire to nurture and provide parental care and
protection.” The pet owner must make end of life decisions analogous to those made by parents on behalf of
children. The information that must be provided to the
owner of a dying pet in order for him or her to make
autonomous decisions on behalf of that animal includes
the expected arc of progression of the co‐morbidities the
pet possesses as well as the expected cause of death, costs
associated with various techniques and/or procedures
that may be recommended, statistics for expected outcomes of any interventions, a balanced presentation of
the pros and cons of any treatment or interventional
options, as well as guidance when humane euthanasia is
the better choice for the pet.
The principles of nonmaleficence and beneficence as
applied to the owner of the pet approaching death are
closely allied and related. According to Beauchamp and
Childress, nonmaleficence “obligates us to abstain from
causing harm to others” and beneficence “potentially
demand(s) more than the principle of nonmaleficence”
because it obligates us to “take positive steps to help
others, not merely refrain from harmful acts.”
­
Nonmaleficence and beneficence in this situation
demand full revelation of the facts, costs, and potential
consequences of pursuing any particular treatment or
care option during the pet’s end of life care. The positive
obligations of beneficence in veterinary palliative care
and hospice include active and ongoing patient and ­client
support by the veterinary healthcare team, a clear outline of the pet‐specific care required, and contingency
planning for unexpected or unplanned events.
Finally, applying the principle of justice to the owner
whose pet has entered end of life care involves full disclosure of the costs and details about the anticipated care
to each pet owner equally. Each pet owner and family is
unique and must be able to conduct a fair appraisal of the
investment (monetary and emotional) that they must
make. It is not appropriate for the veterinarian to cherry‐
pick the information that is provided to the client based
on his or her impression of what the client can and cannot afford or accomplish. Justice suggests that it is the
veterinarian’s obligation to the client to guide the decision making based on what is medically in the dying pet’s
best interest.

­Bioethical Principles and The Life‐
Limited Pet
Turning our attention to the pet entering end of life care,
it is not only appropriate but necessary to consider how
at least three of the four foundational principles – respect

for autonomy, nonmaleficence, and beneficence – apply,
despite the fact that animals cannot participate in the
caregiving decisions made on their behalf. This reflects a
novel application of clinical bioethical principles in clinical veterinary medicine, and acknowledges that animals
can and do express preferences, which can guide caregiving decisions.
In order to apply the principles of clinical bioethics to
animals, we must first consider them as moral agents and
thus appropriate targets of such an application. This
involves issues of consciousness and a need to respect
the preferences they express. Darwin himself recognized
that animals possess the fundamentals of consciousness.
His reasoning was that “if animals show emotion through
behavioral expression, then the behavioral expression of
emotion in man must share a similar neurobiological
evolution with other animals capable of expressing similar emotions.” As cited earlier, Richard D. Ryder laid the
foundation for considering animals as moral agents in
his work Painism: A Modern Morality. An updated narrative on the need for humans to recognize the moral
agency and emotional richness of animals is presented in
the provocative volume Wild Justice: The Moral Lives of
Animals by Marc Bekoff and Jessica Pierce. They argue
compellingly, based on robust behavioral science, that
“differences between species are differences of degrees
rather than differences in kind.” They go on to state that
in “including some animals within the sphere of morality,
we force a reconsideration of what have been assigned to
be the essential ingredients of morality – reflective judgment, agency, and conscience.” This and other contemporary work opens the door to applying the principles of
clinical bioethics in a serious way to the pets themselves
who are entering end of life care.
Animals do express preferences, if only the human is
willing to listen. When applying the principles of clinical
bioethics to animals receiving end of life care, we accept
the limitations presented by beings who do not possess
decisional capacity as we strive to achieve optimal outcomes for them, ultimately leading to a peaceful and pain‐
free death. The animal receiving end of life care must
be considered carefully. The pet’s personality, willingness
to be handled, willingness to take medication – basically,
the pet’s willingness to participate in its own care – must
weigh in the balance. In applying respect for this
pet’s autonomy, we must evaluate these preferences, as
expressed by the pet, before embarking on a complex path
of end of life medical management. To force medication
or painful wound care on an animal whose response is
either anxiety or aggression clearly violates the autonomy
the pet can express, independent of its inability to actively
choose specific end of life care. McMillan would argue
that forced medication or other forced procedures,
performed without the animal’s c­ooperation, present
­

VetBooks.ir

175 Canine and Feline End of Life Care

a sufficiently aversive stimulus to activate a powerful
­sympathoadrenal response that can precipitate negative
gastrointestinal and cardiovascular changes.
Nonmaleficence and beneficence are intertwined when
applied to the pet receiving end of life care. Nonmaleficence
is the requirement to avoid harm, and this principle is in
play when considering a procedure or other interventive
technique for an end of life patient. On balance, the
benefit must clearly outweigh any potential harm to
­
the patient. Beneficence means acting in the patient’s
best interest. At each decision‐making step, it must be
considered that the patient may be best served by
the compassionate application of humane euthanasia.
Nonmaleficence and beneficence are tightly aligned with
the pet’s willingness to participate in its own care. Without
that willingness, the animal itself is expressing its preferences and we have an obligation to heed the message if we
are unable to change the circumstances of care to improve
quality of life. While animals cannot anticipate or fear
their own death, they certainly can and do anticipate and
fear pain, and unrelenting pain is a deal‐breaker for the
continued imposition of care on a dying pet.
McMillan might argue that one barometer of our ability to monitor and measure our success in applying the
principles of respect for autonomy, nonmaleficence, and
beneficence is the animal’s ability to experience and
express happiness. As elusive a concept as happiness is,
ongoing active engagement with the environment and
human family members, the ability to exert some level of
control over activities, and modification of activities that
had previously brought enjoyment (e.g., tug‐of‐war
games) appear to contribute to an animal’s happiness
(Figure 175.6). This provides a slightly richer context for
consideration of quality of life issues.

­End of Life Care and The Human–
Animal Bond
End of life discussions are among the most difficult for
both the pet owner and the veterinary healthcare team,
yet they are among the most important. Taking a systematic approach to the practicalities of end of life care
allows the veterinarian to exhibit and express compassion while at the same time providing the client and family with a longer view of the arc of care that will be
required as the pet’s condition deteriorates.
The veterinarian should start with an initial consultation to assess the client’s goals, beliefs, concerns, and
financial resources/constraints. It is important to discuss
all of the pet’s co‐morbidities to ensure that all relevant
issues are addressed to maximize comfort and function.
Schedule regular quality of life evaluations and pain reassessments. The trend over time of the quality of life

Figure 175.6 A healthy human–animal bond is a two‐way
relationship. Source: Courtesy of Robin Downing, DVM.

scores is generally more important than individual
scores. Provide regular ongoing guidance to the client
about comfortable bedding for the pet, safe surroundings, medications, feeding, wound management when
necessary, assistive devices, physical medicine techniques to enhance comfort and function, and environmental enrichment. Construct a preparedness plan for
the inevitable decline in the pet’s health status, including
an advanced directive (e.g., “Do not attempt resuscitation” – DNAR) and options for euthanasia at any time of
the day or night. Plan for unexpected escalations of pain
or discomfort, providing the client with specific steps to
take. Plan for in‐home euthanasia if that is preferable to
the client and available in the community. Plan ahead for
preferred body handling when the animal dies. Be ready
to refer the client and family for grief support services if
that becomes necessary.
Planning ahead for the anticipated and inevitable
events that occur at the end of life supports the human–
animal bond and helps to prevent the client from being
overwhelmed with decisions once the animal’s death day
arrives.

­Conclusion
Veterinary medicine has long prided itself on its commitment to scrutinize advances in human medicine and
to evaluate the possible application of those advances to

1563

VetBooks.ir

1564

Section 14 Social and Ethical Issues in Veterinary Medicine

animal patients. In fact, many of the medical and surgical
techniques now utilized in human medicine were first
developed in animal models. There exists now a paradigm in human and veterinary medicine that recognizes
the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration in
order to foster synergistic attention to enhance the care
of animals, humans, and the environment. This is the
One Health Initiative –www.onehealthinitiative.com/).
The mission statement of the One Health Initiative recognizes “that human health (including mental health via
the human‐animal bond phenomenon), animal health,
and ecosystem health are inextricably linked” seeking to
“promote, improve, and defend the health and well‐being
of all species by enhancing cooperation and collaboration between physicians, veterinarians, [and]other scientific and environmental professionals.” With such a
commitment to cross‐pollination between medical disciplines, it is logical to consider ways in which palliative
and end of life care options for animals may be expanded.
In pursuing such expansion, however, it is critical also
to expand the ethical framework within which palliative
and end of life care decisions are made on behalf of pets
who are either experiencing life‐limiting disease or
actively dying. In addition to applying human medical
principles and practices in end of life care for pets,
including aggressive pain management and other palliative care techniques, it is appropriate for veterinary
healthcare teams to understand and apply the foundational clinical bioethical principles and practices as well.
The pet owner is in an analogous situation to the parent
of a dying child when making decisions on behalf of
the pet. The pet clearly does not possess decisional
capacity – that is, the animal cannot weigh the evidence
and decide for itself, among the care options, which one

is in its best interest. It is up to the pet owner – the “pet
parent” – to listen to the explanation provided by the
veterinarian and veterinary healthcare team, to weigh
the options to try to determine the risk to benefit ratio,
and then to decide on behalf of the pet what treatment or
procedure will be performed or withheld.
This huge responsibility to act in the best interest of
the pet must be borne by both the owner and the veterinarian coordinating care. In no other context of
­veterinary care is this shared obligation greater than at
the end of life. The veterinarian possesses knowledge
about the procedures and probabilities for various
­outcomes that the owner simply cannot know in the
same way. The late physician Edmund Pellegrino, MD,
acknowledged to be the father of modern medical ethics,
would affirm by analogy that every time a veterinarian
sees a patient and client and asks, “What is wrong?” she
is committing herself to having the competence to help
that animal patient as well as the judgment “to use that
competence in the best interests of the patient.”
In the end of life time for animal patients, it is especially important for veterinarians to find guidance in the
bioethical principles of respect for autonomy, nonmaleficence, and beneficence as applied to their patients
in determining what actions – or withholding of
actions – are in the best interest of that animal at that
time, in dialogue with the pet’s human family. It is important not to reach for euthanasia too early, but equally
important not to withhold it when that action reflects
the best interest of the animal. Reaching a decision about
what will best serve the animal patient at the end of life
may, in fact, demand answering the question mentioned
earlier in this chapter: “Just because we can, does that
mean we should?”

Role of Immunization
Melissa Kennedy, DVM, PhD, DACVM
Department of Biomedical and Diagnostic Sciences, College of Veterinary Medicine, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN, USA

The immune system is a complex network of interacting
cells and molecules. Manipulation of the immune
response is an attractive prospect, and has been achieved
in part through immunization. Immunization is the process of exposing an animal to whole or parts of microbes
in order to stimulate an acquired response. Immunization
takes many forms, and continues to advance as a field of
research. This chapter focuses on several aspects of
immunization in veterinary medicine.
Before one can understand immunization, one must
understand the nature of the acquired or adaptive immune
response. Acquired immunity is that which is developed
after an animal is born and is restricted primarily to the T
and B lymphocytes. This is to distinguish it from innate
immunity with which an animal is born. This latter form
of immunity is nonspecific in nature and involves many
cell types and molecules such as cytokines and complement. Acquired immunity is distinct in that it has a high
degree of specificity and diversity of antigen recognition,
as well as memory. It is this latter trait that is exploited by
immunization – the ability to establish an immunologic
memory of an encountered foreign antigen.
The major cells involved in the specific immune
response, and the only ones that manifest these properties of adaptive immunity, are the lymphocytes. Different
lymphocyte lineages are distinguished by cell surface
markers and perform different functions in the immune
response. The B lymphocytes, the producers of antibodies, or the humoral response, are critical for defense
against extracellular pathogens. The cytotoxic T lymphocytes, which force altered and invaded cells to
undergo apoptosis, are critical for defense against intracellular pathogens. The overseers of the entire response,
T helper lymphocytes, direct and modulate the response
using cell surface molecule expression and cytokine
production and secretion. It is important to understand
how various lymphocyte lineages recognize antigens in

order to design or select the most appropriate antigen
delivery method.
B lymphocytes are able to detect free and soluble antigens, while T lymphocytes are only able to recognize
antigens presented to them “on the pedestal” of the major
histocompatibility complex (MHC) structures. For the
latter to occur, the foreign antigen must be processed
within a cell and displayed on the MHC for T lymphocyte
recognition. MHC structures are classified as class I or
class II. The former are expressed on all nucleated cells
and express only antigens that are produced within that
cell. The cytotoxic T lymphocytes recognize antigens
presented in MHC I. MHC class II are expressed on antigen‐presenting cells (APCs), such as macrophages, dendritic cells, and B lymphocytes. The antigen displayed by
these structures is produced outside of and taken up
by the APCs via endocytosis or phagocytosis. The antigen is then processed and inserted in MHC II for presentation to T helper lymphocytes. Understanding how
lymphocytes differ in this antigen recognition process is
critical to designing and selecting efficacious vaccines.
B lymphocytes bear immunoglobulins on their surface
for antigen recognition. As mentioned above, these antigens are extracellular, such as free‐living bacteria and
parasites and the extracellular form of viruses and other
intracellular parasites. In response to antigen recognition and assistance from T helper lymphocytes, naive B
lymphocytes will proliferate and differentiate into plasma
cells, which secrete antibody and are relatively short‐
lived, or memory cells, which are long‐lived cells that are
more easily activated and respond more quickly and with
higher magnitude and antibody affinity than naive B
lymphocytes. Producing a significant population of the
latter is the goal of most vaccines. Antibodies, the effector mechanism of B lymphocytes, will opsonize, neutralize, clump for easy removal of, or activate complement to
destroy the infecting agent.

Clinical Small Animal Internal Medicine Volume II, First Edition. Edited by David S. Bruyette.
© 2020 John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Published 2020 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc.
Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/bruyette/clinical

VetBooks.ir

1568

Section 15 Preventive Care

T helper lymphocytes use the T cell receptor to recognize antigens displayed in MHC II by APCs. These antigens originate outside of and are “ingested” and processed
by the APCs. Thus, as with B lymphocytes, the antigen is
extracellular. In response to antigen recognition, the T
helper lymphocytes begin to proliferate and differentiate
into cytokine‐producing cells. These cytokines, such as
interleukin 2, enhance or modulate the immune response.
In addition, depending on signals received by the T
helper from the APC, the former will direct the immune
response in the most appropriate direction – the humoral
response for extracellular pathogens or cell‐mediated
immunity for intracellular pathogens. Thus, the T helper
lymphocyte is critical to an effective immune response,
whether humoral or cell mediated. T helper memory
cells develop, as with B lymphocytes, into long‐lived,
easily activated cells, and their production is a critical
goal of vaccination.
Cytotoxic T lymphocytes detect antigens presented to
them in MHC I using T cell receptors on their surface.
The antigen displayed in MHC I, as described above, is
produced within a cell and displayed on the surface. The
presence of foreign peptide from an intracellular invader
in MHC I results in induction of apoptosis in the infected
cell by the cytotoxic T lymphocyte. This type of response
is critical for elimination of an intracellular pathogen, as
it is inaccessible to most other defense mechanisms.
Thus, for protective immunity against most intracellular
pathogens, activation of cytotoxic T lymphocytes must
occur; to do this, the vaccinal agent must be replicating
in order to produce a peptide for display in MHC I. As
with T helper and B lymphocytes, this process leads to
proliferation and differentiation of the cytotoxic T lymphocyte into effector and memory cells.
It goes without saying that there are many other components to an effective immune response, including
granulocytes, natural killer cells, cytokines such as interferon, and inflammatory mediators. But the goal of vaccination remains lymphocyte stimulation and memory
cell production. How this is accomplished depends not
only on the antigen presented but how it is delivered.
Induction of adequate protection depends on appropriate vaccine selection and immunization protocols. As
stated by Shams (2005), “an ideal vaccine should be inexpensive, stable, adaptable to mass administration, and
confer a strong and long‐lasting immunity with no or
minimal adverse side effects in the vaccinated animal.”

­Antigen Delivery Systems
Vaccines can be divided into two basic groups depending
upon whether or not there is transcription/replication of
the agent after inoculation, referred to as infectious or

noninfectious, respectively. There are an increasing variety of strategies to produce vaccines in both categories,
and each has its advantages and disadvantages.
Noninfectious Vaccines
These vaccines may contain inactivated whole organisms or pieces (subunits) of the organism. Killed vaccines
contain whole organisms that have been altered or inactivated to destroy their ability to replicate. These vaccines are generally inexpensive to produce. Subunit
vaccines contain purified immunogenic and protective
antigens, often microbial proteins. These proteins may
be purified from the whole organism or may be generated using molecular technology (recombinantly produced). Conjugation to carrier proteins may be required
for the antigen to stimulate an effective response; this is
expensive and currently laborious. Peptide vaccines contain immunogenic epitopes that have been generated
synthetically. Conjugation to carriers is required for
effective immunogenicity of peptide vaccines.
In all cases, the vaccine is nonreplicating; thus, no
amplification of the antigenic mass occurs after inoculation. In addition, because no transcription/translation/
replication is occurring, MHC I presentation of microbial antigens, in general, does not occur. Thus, these vaccines stimulate primarily humoral immunity. They may
require multiple inoculations to be effective, but this is
not always the case. Most noninfectious vaccines also
require an adjuvant to enhance the immune response.
These substances nonspecifically increase the immune
response, often by unknown mechanisms. Concern
exists, particularly for feline vaccines, about the potential
for adverse effects due to adjuvants.
Still, noninfectious vaccines have several advantages.
Because they contain killed/inactivated organism or only
a portion of the infecting agent, there is no chance for
reversion to virulence. In general, they are safe for pregnant animals as well as for animals that may be immunocompromised or have an underlying disease. In addition,
noninfectious vaccines are stable in field conditions and
are usually inexpensive to produce.
Infectious Vaccines
Infectious vaccines contain metabolically active agents
that undergo transcription and translation at a minimum
and often the entire replication cycle of the inoculated
organism. For infectious whole organisms, the agent is
attenuated in some way such that it is no longer virulent
while retaining its antigenicity. Examples of infectious
vaccines include whole organism live vaccines, recombinant vectors, and DNA vaccines. Because infectious
vaccines undergo transcription and translation after
­

VetBooks.ir

176 Role of Immunization

inoculation, presentation of an antigen in MHC I will
occur, thus enabling stimulation of cytotoxic T lymphocytes. Meanwhile, the extracellular form of the agent will
be detected by B lymphocytes as well as APCs, which
will process it for presentation and activation of T helper
lymphocytes. Thus, both cell‐mediated and humoral
arms of the immune response are activated.
Modified Live Vaccines
Modified live vaccines contain organisms altered to
remove their disease‐causing ability. Attenuation may be
accomplished by acquisition of multiple genetic mutations. Alternatively, virulence genes may be removed
using recombinant technology. The attenuation process
must remove the virulence without altering the immunogenicity of the organism. In addition, the attenuated
organism must be genetically stable.
Recombinant Vector Vaccines
These are a variation on the theme of modified live vaccines in which one or more genes encoding immunogenic microbial proteins are engineered into a harmless
bacterial or viral carrier. Examples of this technology are
the canarypox virus vectored vaccines containing genes
of rabies virus or feline leukemia virus. The recombinant
vector expresses the cloned gene as well as its own genes
during transcription and translation. This technology is
useful for pathogens that would otherwise be too unsafe
to administer as a live vaccine. DNA vaccines use purified DNA containing microbial genes of immunologic
importance. They are taken up by cells after inoculation,
and the cloned genes are expressed within the cell and
presented in MHC.
Generally, for infectious vaccines, a lower antigen mass
is required, and no adjuvant is needed to achieve a protective response. There are drawbacks to infectious vaccines. Attenuated organisms can potentially revert to a
virulent state, though this is very uncommon. For recombinant vectors and DNA vaccines, reversion to virulence
is not possible. Infectious vaccines may be less stable in
field conditions than noninfectious vaccines. Finally,
infectious vaccines are not generally recommended for
pregnant or immunocompromised animals.
Vaccine programs may vary with each patient and client. Core vaccines, those recommended to be given routinely to all dogs and cats, are outlined in the guidelines
published by various organizations, including the AAFP,
AAHA, AVMA, and WSAVA (see list at end of chapter).
Additional vaccines are available for a number of pathogens, including feline immunodeficiency virus and
Chlamydia for cats, and Leptospira, Lyme, and canine
influenza for dogs. Administration of these vaccines

varies with epidemiology of the organism and risk of
exposure to the animal. Also severity of disease, cost
and efficacy of the vaccine, and potential for adverse
reactions should be considered.
Vaccine administration for the majority of vaccines
is parenteral, with subcutaneous being the route of
choice for most vaccines. When multiple vaccines are
given at the same visit, it is recommended that administration be done at different sites so that local adverse
reactions can be documented for the specific vaccine
that induced them.

­Vaccine Failures
Vaccine failures do arise and have several potential causes.
The most common reason in puppy‐ and kittenhood is
interference from maternal antibodies. For the majority of
puppies and kittens, the amount of maternal immunity
present at any point in time is unknown. Thus, vaccination generally begins at the earliest point when most will
begin losing protection from maternal antibodies and
continues through the latest point at which the majority of
animals do not have significant levels of interfering antibodies. The booster vaccine given during this period is
actually a misnomer, as multiple vaccines are given not to
boost preexisting immunity but to insure that the animal
responds to at least one vaccine in the series. Because we
do not know at what time point this occurs for each animal vaccinated, and it is not feasible to measure antibodies
multiple times throughout this period, we give multiple
vaccines with the intention that one of the series will work.
For example, some puppies may have immunity that has
waned by 6–7 weeks of age; these pups will respond to the
vaccine given at 8–9 weeks of age. In reality, this would be
the only vaccine necessary (for live vaccines) if we knew
for certain that maternal immunity had waned and the
pup had responded to the vaccine. The vaccines that follow at 12 and 16 weeks will in fact be neutralized by the
antibodies induced from vaccination. If maternal immunity does not wane until 13–14 weeks of age, only the 16‐
week vaccine will induce full protection. Because we do
not know the individual status at multiple time points for
each animal and against multiple pathogens, we start at
the early end of the susceptibility window and continue
through the late end of this window.
Other causes of vaccine failure that are host related
include immunosuppressive disorders and occurrence of a
genetic nonresponder. The former should likely not be vaccinated with live vaccines until the disorder is corrected.
For the latter, vaccinating with a different strain of the
agent may be able to overcome the nonresponsiveness.
Vaccine factors also play a role in vaccine failures. Vaccine
design, strain variation, and route of administration

1569

VetBooks.ir

1570

Section 15 Preventive Care

may all factor in to the level of protection induced. Human
error is also a concern, including improper storage, preparation, and administration.
Duration of immunity is likely much longer than current revaccination recommendations. Studies have shown
duration of immunity of years, and in many cases it is
likely lifelong, especially following infectious vaccines.
Detectable antibody levels to administered vaccines have
been found as long as 14 years after vaccination for canine
distemper virus and canine parvovirus in dogs. Challenge
studies in dogs vaccinated for canine distemper and canine
parvovirus have shown protection as long as nine years
post vaccination. Similar results have been reported in
cats. Current guidelines recommend revaccinating every
three years, but some are electing not to boost senior animals that have a strong vaccination history.
How young is too young? Generally, most live vaccines
cannot safely be administered to neonatal animals, as they
may cause disease in the neonate. Noninfectious vaccines
can be used as can intranasal live vaccines. However, in
the very young, the response may be less than adequate
due to immaturity of the immune system and interference from maternal antibodies. The exception to this

interference is the intranasal vaccines which can be used
in high‐risk settings where the history of the neonate may
not be known.
How old is too old? This is a difficult question to
answer, and varies with each animal. Health status of the
animal, previous vaccination history, and exposure of the
animal to infection all must be considered when vaccinating senior animals. Rabies requires adherence to local
vaccination policies.

­Conclusion
Vaccination remains an important tool in preventive veterinary medicine. Against the common pathogens affecting dogs and cats, their use has led to decline in disease
prevalence. Canine rabies, for example, has been eradicated from the USA, though rabies from wildlife still
occurs in dogs and cats. There are many choices among
current vaccines, and selection of vaccines is an important action for any practitioner. The practitioner must
remain vigilant as new strains of pathogens emerge and
new vaccines appear on the market.

Behavior Triage for Internists and the General Practitioner
Karen Lynn C. Sueda, DVM, DACVB
VCA West Los Angeles Animal Hospital, Los Angeles, CA, USA

All veterinarians are behaviorists to some degree,
whether they care for the mind or the body. Because we
treat nonverbal species, our patients cannot tell us
what hurts or how they feel. We rely upon behavioral
observations – either our clients’ or ours – to determine
if a pet is ill and to evaluate its response to treatment.
Just as physical illness may produce behavioral changes,
mental illness may also generate somatic signs. For example, anxiety may trigger compulsive behaviors such as psychogenic polydipsia or a proinflammatory response as in
feline urologic syndrome. It is important that ­veterinarians
recognize this mind–body interaction and be able to
address the behavioral component when necessary.
The objectives of this chapter are to help veterinarians
recognize the interplay between internal and behavioral
medicine and to provide an algorithm and recommendations for triaging behavior cases. Diagnosis and treatment of specific behavioral problems are beyond the
scope of this chapter. Recommended clinical small
­animal behavioral medicine texts which discuss the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of canine and feline
behavior problems are listed at the end of the chapter.

­Behavioral Presentations
The relationship between internal and behavioral medicine is more complex than one may assume at first
glance. In addition to physical illnesses triggering behavioral problems and vice versa, medical treatments may
also affect a pet’s behavior. Likewise, a pet’s misbehavior
may hinder the veterinarian’s ability or the client’s willingness to run diagnostic tests or implement treatment
plans. Examples of ways in which the diagnosis and
treatment of physical ailments may be influenced by
the pet’s behavior are listed below.

Physical Illness Causing a Behavioral Problem
While treating a pet for a physical problem, veterinarians
may learn from the client that the pet has started to misbehave. For example, a polyuric cat may have urinated
outside the litter box or a dog with pancreatitis may have
begun growling when his owner picks him up. Although
the behavior problem should resolve once the underlying
physical cause has been addressed, the client may
become frustrated with their pet’s behavior during the
treatment process. As such, veterinarians should query
clients regarding behavioral changes at each appointment and be able to provide short‐term treatment
­recommendations to alleviate them.
Ruling Out Physical Causes for a Behavior Problem

Clients may bring their pet to you to determine whether
there is a physical explanation for their pet’s behavior.
When a behavioral change is the first or only clinical sign
that the client observes, it is often unclear whether or
not a physical ailment is to blame. Physical causes for
behavioral problems should always be ruled out before
assuming the issue is purely psychological in nature. At
minimum, a complete physical exam, baseline bloodwork (i.e., complete blood count [CBC], chemistry panel,
total thyroid level), urinalysis and any other indicated
diagnostics tests (e.g., fecal exam for a pet defecating in
the house; radiographs or other imaging if pain is elicited
on physical exam) should be performed.
The likelihood of finding a physical cause for a behavior
problem varies widely and depends in part on the clinical
signs and history. For example, the odds of diagnosing a
physical cause for a cat’s sudden onset of house soiling are
much higher than finding a medical reason for a dog’s
eight‐year history of aggressive behavior toward strangers.
Of course, physical illness, if diagnosed, must be
addressed. However, if no such cause is determined or if

Clinical Small Animal Internal Medicine Volume II, First Edition. Edited by David S. Bruyette.

Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/bruyette/clinical

VetBooks.ir

1572

Section 15 Preventive Care

the behavior persists despite medical treatment, veterinarians should be prepared to offer behavioral treatment
recommendations.
Behavioral Problem Causing a Physical Illness
A pet may present with a physical illness that was caused,
either directly or indirectly, by a behavioral problem.
The link between the pet’s mental and physical ailments
may be straightforward. Examples include toxicity or
vomiting due to pica, polyuria secondary to psychogenic
polydipsia, and hair loss caused by psychogenic alopecia.
Because a psychological diagnosis for a behavior problem depends on excluding potential physical causes, it is
extremely important to discuss the necessity of diagnostic testing with clients.
In other cases, the connection between the physical
clinical signs and behavioral problem is less o
­ bvious. For
example, a cat presenting for rodenticide toxicity may be
hunting outdoors because he housesoils and is no longer
allowed inside. A dog with unexplained weight loss may
be suffering from separation anxiety, his weight loss
occurring because he does not eat and constantly paces
when home alone for 10 hours. In such cases, the client
may be unaware that their pet’s behavior plays a role in
their physical ailment. The veterinarian should look
beyond the presenting complaint to explore potential
psychological or behavioral issues that may be contributing to the disease. If the underlying behavioral cause is
not determined and addressed, it is very likely that the
pet will present for the same issue on subsequent
occasions.
Medical Treatment Causing a Behavioral
Problem
Unfortunately, medical treatment may cause undesirable behavior in some cases. Patients may have idiosyncratic reactions to certain medications. For example,
acepromazine may trigger aggressive behavior in some
patients, while opioids and metoclopramide may elicit
various behavioral changes, including agitation, in
others. Steroid‐induced polyphagia may result in
­
counter‐surfing, trash‐raiding or resource‐guarding
­
behavior. Similarly, frequent veterinary visits, physical
handling, restraint and manipulation, and constant
medication administration may trigger anxiety, depression or aggressive behavior in pets that do not understand that the veterinary staff and their owners are
trying to help them. In these situations – especially
if the treatment cannot be discontinued or altered –
veterinarians must provide behavioral recommendations to alleviate these behaviors or risk poor compliance
with their treatment plan.

Preexisting Behavior Problem Hindering
Medical Diagnostics and/or Treatment
Clients and veterinary staff may simply be unable to perform diagnostic tests or treatments because of the pet’s
behavior and temperament. The most common scenario
is the client who is unable to give oral medication to his
or her cat because the cat becomes aggressive when
restrained and is too finicky to consume medication hidden in food. Clients may find it impossible to administer
insulin injections to their diabetic dog that bites. A client
living in a busy household may not be able to conduct a
food trial if her dog knocks down her two‐year‐old son to
steal cookies out of his hand. Similarly, veterinarians and
staff may not be able to provide the best care to a patient
that is fractious or difficult to work with. Clients may
also hesitate to bring their pet to the hospital if the pet
does not travel well (e.g., hides from the carrier; is agitated or anxious during car rides) or is fearful or aggressive at the clinic. If the veterinarian or client is unable to
implement the ideal diagnostic or treatment plan because
of behavioral reasons, discuss other treatment options or
behavioral management solutions that may entail environmental changes, behavior modification and training
and/or referral to a behavior practitioner.
Client Declines Diagnostics or Treatment
Because of a Preexisting Behavioral Problem
The most insidious way in which behavior affects the veterinary practice occurs when the human–animal bond
has been broken due to a pet’s problematic behavior.
Clients may elect to not pursue diagnostic or treatment
options because their pet’s poor behavior factors into their
­decision. In the client’s mind, it may be difficult to justify
spending money to treat a pet that bites, destroys their
house, runs away or is a nuisance. Because clients rarely
admit to this aspect of their decision‐making process, it is
especially important that veterinarians screen for behavioral problems at each visit, as part of a general “systems
check.” Behavioral problems can be caught early and dealt
with before the human–animal bond has been affected.

­Behavioral Triage
Once a behavior problem has been identified, obtaining
complete medical and behavioral histories and conducting a physical exam and ancillary diagnostic tests will
allow the veterinarian to determine whether the behavior is normal or aberrant/abnormal and whether it is
physical or psychological in origin. The veterinarian may
then recommend an appropriate course of treatment,
which may include referral to an appropriate behavioral

Figure 177.1 Behavioral triage algorithm.

professional depending on the type and severity of the
issue. The algorithm in Figure 177.1 may help veterinarians triage behavioral issues they encounter.
1) Determine if the behavior is normal or abnormal.
–– Normal. These are behaviors you would expect
from another animal of similar species, breed, age,
lifestyle, experience, etc. These behavior problems
arise because normal expression of canine or feline
behavior is often incompatible with human rules.
Labeled “nuisance” or “unruly” behaviors, these
problems are often due to inadequate or inappropriate training or a lack of appropriate outlets for
the expression of species‐typical behavior. Anxiety
and aggression are not present. An underlying
medical cause is not present.
Problems stemming from normal behaviors are
extremely common and remain a frequent cause of
relinquishment and euthanasia. It is important to
identify these issues early and provide owners with
treatment resources. Client handouts outlining treatment protocols are available in veterinary behavior
textbooks and from veterinary, shelter, and training
websites. Depending on the particular behavior,
appropriate use of training aids such as head halters,
body harnesses, puzzle toys, etc. may also provide
clients with a “quick fix.” Because the problem does

not have an underlying physical or psychological
cause, referral to a qualified trainer or other behavior
professional is an appropriate measure.
–– Aberrant/Abnormal. An animal of similar species,
breed, age, lifestyle, experience, etc. would not be
expected to exhibit these behaviors. This category
includes but is not limited to anxiety and aggression.
Anxiety and aggression are normal behaviors when
expressed in rational contexts and with appropriate
intensity (e.g. cat hisses when a painful limb is manipulated). They are included in this category because
anxiety and aggression may be clinical signs of an
underlying physical and/or psychological disorder.
2) If the behavior is aberrant/abnormal, determine if the
primary cause is physical, psychological or a combination of both.
–– Physical. If the primary cause of the behavior problem is determined to be physical, diagnose and treat
the underlying physical cause of the behavior and
continue medical management until both the
­physical and behavioral clinical signs have resolved.
If the behavioral signs do not resolve or new
behavior problems arise, reassess your original
diagnosis and medical management and follow
Step 1 accordingly. Consider the possibility that the
original behavior problem had both physical and

1573

VetBooks.ir

1574

Section 15 Preventive Care

psychological causes and that medical treatment
only addressed the former. For example, a cat that
continues to urinate outside the litter box
despite elimination of its cystic calculi may have
concurrent feline urologic syndrome (physical
cause), litter box aversion due to inadequate cleaning by the client (normal behavior) or a learned litter box aversion because urination in the box had
been associated with pain (psychological cause).
–– Both physical and psychological. Diagnose and
treat the physical component. Assess whether the
behavioral clinical signs are normal or abnormal
and follow Step 1 accordingly. For example, a dog
that is aggressive when he is lifted into the car
may be painful due to osteoarthritis (physical
cause) but also fearful of car travel (psychological
cause). Similarly, an elderly cat that vocalizes at
night might have hyperthyroidism (physical
cause) but has also been reinforced by his owners
because they fed him when he cried (normal,
learned behavior).
–– Psychological. A primarily psychological etiology is
diagnosed once physical causes have been ruled out
or addressed. Unlike problems due to normal
behaviors, “abnormal” behavioral problems typically stem from an underlying emotional (e.g., fear
or anxiety) or neurochemical pathology rather than
a lack of training or opportunities to express species‐typical behavior. Simply reinforcing commands in these situations is unlikely to alter the
animal’s underlying emotional response to a situation they find threatening. These cases should be
referred to a behavior professional both adept at
interpreting canine or feline body language and
behavior and who understands the clinical applications of learning theory.
3) If you prefer not to manage the behavioral aspects of
the case yourself, determine the type of behavior
professional to refer to based on the presence or
absence of aggressive behavior, the severity of the
behavior problem, and whether the behavior itself is
common or atypical.
–– Human‐directed aggression. Ideally, cases involving
human‐directed aggression should be referred to a
veterinary behaviorist or a veterinarian experienced in treating aggression cases. Aggression
cases often require extensive and protracted care,
including an honest discussion with the owners
regarding risk assessment, development of a
­treatment plan tailored to the owner and pet and
ongoing communication – potentially for months
to years – to assess and monitor the response to
treatment. Because clients frequently inquire about
the role medication might play in treating their

pets’ aggression, referral to a veterinarian with
expertise in using and ability to prescribe behavior‐
modifying medications is best. Additionally, cases
involving human‐directed aggression may be at risk
of future legal involvement. Documented referral
to a veterinary specialist or another veterinarian
who establishes their own veterinarian–client–
patient relationship may be preferable to referring
to a nonveterinarian in these cases. If a veterinary
behaviorist or veterinarian with behavior experience is not locally available, consider a veterinarian‐to‐veterinary specialist consultation via phone
to discuss treatment and/or referral to another
behaviorist.
–– Common problems (mild). A common behavior
problem is one that, while abnormal, occurs frequently in that species. When they are mild in
severity, common behavior problems typically do
not require behavior‐modifying medication and
may be addressed through consistent behavior
modification and environmental changes. Although
it is always appropriate to refer to a veterinary
behaviorist, these cases suitable for referral to a
well‐qualified trainer or nonveterinary behaviorist.
–– Common problems (moderate to severe) or atypical problems. This category includes any behavior that is moderate to severe in intensity,
frequency or duration, atypical for that species or
signalment, or for which a typical trigger or pattern cannot be discerned (e.g., behaviors that are
idiopathic or occur “out of the blue”). These are
cases in which medication and extensive, long‐
term behavior modification may be necessary.
These cases should be referred to a veterinary
behaviorist or veterinarian experienced with
behavior cases.

­Referrals
Clients have become increasingly educated regarding
animal behavior and are seeking the advice of veterinarians when their pets misbehave rather than resorting to
relinquishment or euthanasia. Whether or not to refer
depends entirely on the individual veterinarian’s comfort
level and experience (Figure 177.2). “Normal” behavior
problems or mild forms of common behavior problems
may easily be addressed by the veterinarian “in house.”
Guidance on how to diagnose and treat canine and feline
behavior problems is available in various texts (see the
Further Reading list at the end of the chapter). If the veterinarian does not feel comfortable treating behavior
problems or lacks the time or interest to do so, many
referral options exist.

Veterinary Referrals
Veterinary Behaviorists

Board‐certified veterinary behaviorists (Diplomates
of the American College of Veterinary Behaviorists
[ACVB]) are veterinarians who have completed a residency training program, published behavioral
research and passed a qualifying exam covering medicine, ethology, pharmacology, and clinical behavior
of domestic and nondomestic species. As specialists,
they have a breadth of clinical experience and
advanced knowledge of behavioral treatment options.
Referral to a veterinary behaviorist is always appropriate and may be preferable in certain situations
(Box 177.1).
If a board‐certified veterinary behaviorist does not
practice within a reasonable distance of your clinic, consider a veterinarian‐to‐veterinary specialist consult via
phone or email to discuss the case or refer to a nonboarded veterinarian with behavioral experience in your
local area.

Nonboarded Veterinarian with Behavioral Experience

These are veterinarians who are not board certified but
are experienced with behavior cases. This category
includes, but is not limited to:
current veterinary behavior residents or residency‐
trained veterinarians. These are veterinarians currently
in their university or private practice residency programs or who have completed their residency but have
not yet passed their board‐administered examination
●● nonresidency‐trained
veterinarians with extensive
behavior education and experience. There are many
excellent veterinarians who have devoted their careers
to the study and practice of veterinary behavior but
have not completed a formal residency. They may have
behavior‐only private practices or see behavior cases
as part of their general practice.
●●

The American Veterinary Society of Animal Behavior
(AVSAB) is an organization consisting of veterinarians
and research professionals whose mission is to promote

Individual veterinarians’ background training, experience level, and continuing education vary widely.
Before referring to a nonboarded veterinarian, ask for

directly to ­discuss the case.
Nonveterinary Referrals
Certified Applied Animal Behaviorists (CAAB)

Most CAABs are not veterinarians but have a Master’s
or PhD degree in behavioral science, multiple scientific
publications, hands‐on experience with animals and
have met coursework and experience requirements for
certification as set forth by the Animal Behavior Society.
Their scientific background makes CAABs knowledgeable about learning theory, ethology, and animal behavior. However, the amount of clinical or practical
experience working with animals may vary by individual. Inquire as to their level of hands‐on experience with
clinical cases prior to referral.
Because most CAABs are not veterinarians, their
insight into the interaction between physical and

behavioral illness may be limited. It is therefore important that the referring veterinarian and CAAB work in
partnership so physical issues are not overlooked.
CAABs cannot prescribe medication and must refer
cases back to a veterinarian for a prescription. It is the
prescribing veterinarian’s duty to ensure that the medication prescribed is appropriate for the patient and
behavior being addressed. If the prescribing veterinarian is not familiar with psychopharmaceutical medications, it is appropriate to ask the CAAB for supporting
documentation (in the form of journal articles, book
references, etc.). The prescribing veterinarian must
also obtain informed consent from the client, including
discussing potential physical and behavioral adverse
effects and conducting appropriate tests to ensure the
health of the patient prior to starting medication.
Trainers and Animal Behaviorists

Many skilled, professional trainers and nonveterinary/
non‐CAAB animal behaviorists are available to help veterinarians, clients, and patients. These individuals may
provide a range of services that veterinary and CAAB
behaviorists do not, including private, in‐home training,
group classes, board and train, etc. Additionally, trainers
are often able to work with clients and their pets on a
more frequent and regular basis than a veterinary or
CAAB behaviorist could. This is extremely helpful especially for clients who require extensive, hands‐on training or encouragement to consistently comply with a
treatment plan.
As a group, trainers and nonveterinary/non‐CAAB
behaviorists are a valuable resource. However, it is
important to remember that individuals vary widely in
regard to their knowledge, experience, training techniques, and ethics. This spectrum exists because there is
no agency or governing body that oversees or regulates
the qualifications of these professions. Anyone may label
themselves a trainer or animal behaviorist regardless of
their background. Animal behavior and training certifications can be obtained through various programs, some
of which are more rigorous and require more education
and experience than others. Training philosophies, such
as the use of positive reinforcement versus punishment‐
based training techniques, also differ from school to
school.
Always research the individual before recommending
any trainer or animal behaviorist, veterinary or nonveterinary. Both the ACVB and AVSAB have published
guidelines for selecting and working with trainers on
their websites. These recommendations should be
applied to any behaviorist, veterinary or nonveterinary,
you may refer a client to. Because experience, training
methods, and skillsets of trainers and behaviorists vary

VetBooks.ir

177 Behavior Triage for Internists and the General Practitioner

widely, it is advisable to create different referral lists
depending on the needs of the clients and patients. For
example, some individuals may be highly accomplished
trainers (able to teach basic obedience, agility, nosework,
etc.) but do not have the background or education to
treat behavior problems. Other behaviorists may feel
comfortable treating “normal,” training‐related behavior
problems but not “aberrant/abnormal” cases such as
aggression or anxiety disorders. Some behaviorists specialize only in a ­particular species.
Summary
A team effort is required to successfully treat behavior
problems. Every member of the team – referring veterinarian, behaviorist, and client – should feel comfortable
working with each other for the pet’s benefit. Ask your
clients for feedback regarding their experience with the
behaviorist or trainer they worked with so you know
whom to refer to in the future. No matter to whom you
refer, referrals reflect on you and your practice.

­Safety and Avoidance: Short‐Term
Recommendations
Unless they have an interest in behavioral medicine, the
veterinarian should not feel obligated to provide a comprehensive behavioral treatment plan to the client.
However, the veterinarian should provide short‐term,
interim recommendations geared toward keeping the pet
and people safe and to prevent the pet’s behavior from
worsening until referral to a qualified individual occurs.
Treat physical conditions that affect the pet’s behavior.
Encourage clients to treat any medical problem that
may contribute to the behavioral disorder.
●● Avoid situations that cause the undesirable behavior to
occur. Avoiding situations that cause anxiety or aggression may be necessary to prevent the pet from becoming self‐injurious or harming other animals or people.
Avoidance also prevents the pet from developing a
progressively stronger averse response to the situation
due to repeated exposure (sensitization). Rather than
simply instructing clients not to let their dog or cat
become anxious or aggressive, provide specific avoidance recommendations tailored to the pet and behavior problem. Relevant guidelines may be found in
behavior textbooks.
●● Recognize early signs of fear, anxiety, and aggression.
Pets often exhibit subtle signs of discomfort before
their anxiety or aggression intensifies. Teach clients to
recognize physical cues such as pinned ears, crouched
●●

body posture and tucked or lashing tails as well as
behavioral signs including refusing treats, not following commands and displacement behaviors like yawning, lip licking, and grooming. Handouts on canine
and feline body language (available in behavior
­textbooks) may be sent home with clients to aid identification. To reduce the frequency and severity of
subsequent undesirable behaviors, clients should
remove their pet from the situation as soon as they
recognize the initial signs of impending aggression
or anxiety.
●● Do not use punishment or confrontational training
techniques as these may exacerbate fear, anxiety, and
aggression. Warn clients that physical corrections – such as hitting, swatting, kicking, forcibly holding the pet down (“alpha rolling”), choke or prong
collar use, scruffing, etc. – foster negative associations
with the client and create anxiety and mistrust. If
incorrectly used, punishment‐based techniques may
physically harm the pet and worsen their behavior. For
additional information on the hazards of punishment‐
based training, see the AVSAB Position Statement on
the use of punishment for behavior modification in
animals available on the AVSAB website.
●● Reward the pet for desirable behaviors. Encourage clients to reward their pet when it behaves appropriately
(positive reinforcement). Recommend that clients
think proactively rather than reactively by identifying
desirable behaviors, creating situations that allow their
pet to behave in an appropriate manner and rewarding
it when it does so. For example, rather than punishing
a dog for jumping on them, the client may preemptively instruct the dog to sit before he jumps up, and
then reward him with attention while he is seated.
Encourage clients to formally train their pets. Training
provides clients and their pets with a common language
in which to communicate. Dogs and cats can be taught
simple commands such as “sit,” “down,” “stay,” and “come”
which are used to facilitate behavior modification techniques such as desensitization and counterconditioning
to specific triggers. When positive reinforcement training techniques are used, the pet enjoys interacting with
the client and its anxiety decreases because interactions
are consistent, predictable, and rewarding.

­Managing Client Expectations
Many clients have unrealistic goals such as wanting
their pet “to be friendly with every person and animal”
or “to never to be anxious or aggressive again.”
Alternatively, clients may not realize that their dog or

1577

VetBooks.ir

1578

Section 15 Preventive Care

cat’s behavior puts the pet, people or other animals at
serious risk of injury. A frank discussion regarding risk
assessment and realistic prognosis may be necessary
before the client invests time, money, and emotional
effort in treating their pet’s behavior.
An in‐depth discussion of risk assessment is beyond
the scope of this chapter but is addressed in several
behavioral texts (see Further Reading).
Prognosis depends on the individual case but is usually guarded since most behavior problems cannot
be “cured.” Abnormal behavior problems not due to
­physical illness are caused by emotional and/or neurochemical disease states that cannot be fully eliminated.
The goal of treatment is remission – management of the
behavior and reduction in symptom severity and frequency such that the pet and client have an improved
quality of life.
In most situations, consulting with a behavior professional and compliance with a behavior modification plan
will improve the pet’s behavior. The veterinarian or behavior professional should establish reasonable short‐term
and long‐term goals for the pet. Ongoing communication

between the behavior professional and client along with
periodic recheck appointments are essential to ensure
that the treatment plan is successful or, if not, to adjust the
recommendations accordingly.

­Conclusion
The goals of both behavioral and internal medicine are
the same: establish a diagnosis and alleviate clinical
signs of the disease. When behavioral issues complicate
physical illness or vice versa, diagnosis and treatment
will not be successful without identifying and addressing both. Once a behavioral cause has been established,
veterinarians must be prepared to triage these cases and
provide the clients with short‐term recommendations
and referral to the appropriate behavior professional.
This multidisciplinary approach addresses both the
physical and behavioral components of the disease process and provides the best prognosis for successful resolution of ­clinical signs, thus improving the quality of life
for the pet and client.
